notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away: time to start hardening off your seedlings. Put them outside for a couple of hours today in a sheltered, partly shaded spot, then bring them back in. Add more time and more direct sun each day over the next week. This gradual process helps the plant adjust to outdoor wind, temperature swings, and stronger sun before it goes out for good.
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away. Begin putting your plants outside for a few hours each day; start sheltered, increase exposure gradually. This week of adjustment makes a real difference to how they settle in after transplanting.

notifications.title_beginner: Last frost has passed: time to transplant
notifications.body_beginner: Your beefsteak tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deeper than they sit in the pot: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. New roots will form all along the buried stem, which gives the plant a larger, stronger root system and makes it more drought-tolerant through the season.
notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost has passed: time to transplant
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deep: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Roots will form all along the buried stem and give you a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant.

notifications.title_beginner: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body_beginner: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a fertilizer higher in potassium now (look for 'tomato fertilizer' or something labeled for fruiting). Give the flowering stems a gentle shake each morning to help pollen release and improve fruit set. Each flower is a potential tomato.
notifications.title_seasoned: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body_seasoned: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a high-potassium feed now, and give the flowering stems a gentle shake in the morning to help pollination. Each flower is a potential tomato.

notifications.title_beginner: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_beginner: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Beefsteak tomatoes are ready when fully colored and give just slightly to a gentle squeeze. Pick ripe ones regularly; the more you harvest, the more the plant produces.
notifications.title_seasoned: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_seasoned: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Pick when fully colored and slightly soft to the touch. The more you pick, the more the plant produces; stay on top of it.

notifications.title_beginner: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks: finish strong
notifications.body_beginner: Your season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips at the top of each stem now; this stops the plant from putting energy into new growth and sends it all into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest everything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a cool windowsill.
notifications.title_seasoned: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks: finish strong
notifications.body_seasoned: Your growing season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips now so the plant puts all its remaining energy into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest anything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a windowsill.

notifications.body_beginner: You haven't logged anything in a couple of weeks. How's the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Checking in regularly helps you catch problems before they get serious.
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a couple of weeks. How is the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Regular check-ins help you catch problems early.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost tonight: cover your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Freezing temperatures are forecast tonight. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one hard freeze can kill the plant. Cover them with an old bedsheet, a bucket, or frost cloth before dark, and uncover in the morning once temperatures are back above freezing. Container plants can be moved inside.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning: protect your tomatoes tonight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Temperatures are dropping close to freezing tonight. Cover plants with fleece or old bedsheets, or bring containers inside. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one cold night can end your season early.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Very hot days ahead: help your tomatoes through
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Several very hot days are forecast. Above about 95°F, tomato flowers tend to drop without setting fruit; this is heat stress, not a disease. Water deeply in the early morning so the soil stays moist through the day, and add a layer of mulch around the base to hold that moisture. Shade cloth draped over the plant during the hottest part of the afternoon can help if you have it.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress warning for your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Several very hot days ahead. Tomato flowers can drop when temperatures stay above 95°F. Water deeply in the early morning, add mulch around the base to retain moisture, and consider shade cloth during the hottest part of the day.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: It's been dry: water your tomatoes deeply
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Dry conditions have been building. Uneven watering right now can cause blossom end rot (dark patches on the fruit bottom) and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base of the plant; aim for 1 to 2 inches this week. A thick layer of mulch around the stem helps hold moisture between watering sessions.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: It has been dry. Inconsistent watering at this stage causes blossom end rot and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base; aim for 1-2 inches this week. Mulching around the stem helps hold moisture.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: High humidity: check your tomato leaves
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Humid weather creates ideal conditions for fungal diseases like early and late blight. Take a few minutes to check the lower leaves for brown spots, yellow patches, or anything unusual. If you spot affected leaves, remove them right away and don't put them in your compost. Keeping the plant staked and open for airflow is your best prevention.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions are ideal for early and late blight. Check lower leaves for dark spots with yellow halos. Remove any affected leaves immediately and do not compost them. Good airflow around the plant is your best defense.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain coming: harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A lot of rain in a short period can cause ripe tomatoes to split; beefsteaks are especially prone to cracking because of their size. Pick anything that looks close to ready before the rain arrives. After the rain, check the lower leaves; soil splashed up by heavy rain can spread disease spores onto the plant.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain: harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A lot of rain in a short time can split ripe fruit. Pick anything that is nearly ready before it cracks, and check for soil splash on lower leaves which can spread disease.

germination.text_beginner: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. If you have a heat mat, use it; if not, the top of a refrigerator or any spot that stays consistently around 75°F works well. Most beefsteak tomato seeds sprout within 5 to 7 days with steady warmth.
germination.text_seasoned: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. A heat mat, the top of your refrigerator, or anywhere consistently warm works well. Most tomato seeds germinate in 5-7 days at 75°F.

germination.text_beginner: Cover your seed tray with a plastic dome or cling wrap until the first sprout appears, then remove it right away. The dome traps humidity to keep the seed surface moist during germination; but once the shoot emerges, that same warm, still air is the ideal environment for damping off, a fungal problem that collapses the seedling stem at the soil line and kills it overnight with no recovery.
germination.text_seasoned: Cover your tray with a humidity dome or cling film until the first sprout appears. Remove it immediately when you see growth; leaving it on causes damping off.

seedling.text_beginner: If your seedlings are tall and thin and look weak, they need more light, not less water. Move the tray right next to your brightest window, or set up a grow light to shine on them for 14 to 16 hours each day. Pale color is a sign of the same problem.
seedling.text_seasoned: Leggy, stretched seedlings almost always mean not enough light, not overwatering. Get them as close to a bright window as possible, or use a grow light 14-16 hours a day.

seedling.text_beginner: Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. You can bury the stem deeper than it was sitting; tomatoes form roots all along any buried stem tissue, so a deeper pot-up now means a stronger root system later.
seedling.text_seasoned: Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so you can bury them deeper than they were; it builds a stronger plant.

established.text_beginner: Harden off properly: a week of outdoor time before transplanting, starting with just a couple of hours in a sheltered spot. Plants that skip this step often struggle for two to three weeks after transplanting, which eats into the long season beefsteak tomatoes need.
established.text_seasoned: Harden off properly: a week of outdoor time before transplanting, starting with just a couple of hours in a sheltered spot. Plants that skip this step sulk for weeks after transplanting.

established.text_beginner: Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots, and a larger root system means a more drought-tolerant, productive plant.
established.text_seasoned: Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot. Bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots.

flowering.text_beginner: Give the flowering stems a gentle shake each morning to help pollen transfer and improve fruit set. It sounds fussy, but it genuinely makes a difference, especially in a sheltered spot without much natural breeze. Each flower is a potential tomato.
flowering.text_seasoned: A gentle shake of the flowering stem in the morning helps pollen transfer and improves fruit set. It sounds fussy but it genuinely makes a difference, especially in a sheltered spot without much breeze.

flowering.text_beginner: Stop high-nitrogen fertilizing the moment flowers appear. Nitrogen drives leafy growth; what you want now is potassium. Switch to a tomato-specific feed or any formula with a higher third number; that third number on the fertilizer bag is the potassium.
flowering.text_seasoned: Stop high-nitrogen feeding the moment flowers appear. Nitrogen pushes leafy growth. What you want now is potassium: switch to a tomato-specific or high-K feed.

harvest.text_beginner: Pick every ripe tomato every time you visit the plant. The more you harvest, the more the plant produces. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine is the most common reason production slows mid-season; the plant has less reason to keep setting new fruit.
harvest.text_seasoned: Pick every ripe tomato you can find, every time you check the plant. The more you harvest, the more the plant produces. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine is the most common reason production slows mid-season.

harvest.text_beginner: Taste as you go. Beefsteak tomatoes peak at slightly different moments depending on the variety and the weather; some are best when just fully colored, others benefit from another day or two. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.
harvest.text_seasoned: Taste as you go. Different varieties peak at different moments; some are best just before fully ripe, others need a few more days. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.

end_of_season.text_beginner: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips at the top of each stem. This stops the plant from putting energy into new growth and channels everything into ripening the fruit already on the vine.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips. The plant will stop trying to set new fruit and put everything into ripening what is already there.

end_of_season.text_beginner: Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool and dark, not the refrigerator, which damages the texture and kills the flavor.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool and dark, not the refrigerator, which kills flavor.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 10-20 lbs over the season; fewer fruit than cherry or roma types, but each fruit is large (8-16 oz for most varieties; heirloom types may reach 2+ lbs). Yield is heavily variety- and zone-dependent: in short-season zones (3-5), total yield is constrained by season length, not productivity. In zones 7-9, a well-managed indeterminate plant at peak often exceeds 20 lbs.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Expect roughly 10 to 20 pounds of tomatoes per plant over the season. You get fewer tomatoes than cherry or roma types, but each one is big (about 8 to 16 ounces, and some heirlooms top 2 pounds). In short-season cold areas the total is smaller simply because the season is shorter, while in warmer zones a well-tended plant can top 20 pounds.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: A healthy indeterminate beefsteak at peak produces 1-3 large fruits per week per plant. Production follows a seasonal arc: slow start as the plant builds its vine structure, then a peak window of 4-8 weeks in mid-season, tapering as autumn cool-down slows ripening. The arc is distinct from cherry, which produces more continuously and maintains higher counts. Beefsteak fruit set is most reliable when nighttime temperatures stay between 55-75°F; below 55°F, pollen viability drops; above 75°F, pollen becomes sterile.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: At its peak, a healthy plant gives you 1 to 3 big tomatoes a week. Plants start slow while they grow their vines, hit a busy stretch of about 4 to 8 weeks in midsummer, then taper off as fall cools down. Fruit sets best when nights stay between about 55 and 75°F; colder or hotter nights than that and the flowers often fail to set fruit.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Your first beefsteak season will probably feel slow. The plant spends the first half of summer building its root system and vine structure before it really starts setting fruit. Getting 3 to 5 large tomatoes in your first season is a real success; don't measure yourself against experienced gardeners who know every trick. Focus on two things: get a strong cage or stake in place early (before you think you need it), and keep the watering consistent when the plant starts flowering.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: First-season beefsteaks frequently disappoint on yield, not because of mistakes, but because the plant architecture is building for the first half of the season. Getting 3-5 large fruit in a first season is a genuine success. Focus on getting the support structure right early and on consistent watering at fruit set; those two factors drive the difference between a partial and a full-season harvest.
factors_seasoned: hours of direct sunlight
consistent watering
feeding schedule
staking and airflow

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You'll see the leaves turn black or dark brown and go limp, sometimes overnight after a single cold night. Tomatoes are tropical plants with no cold tolerance at all. Even without a hard freeze, temperatures below 50°F cause what's called chilling injury: the plant's cells start to break down, and young transplants are especially vulnerable because they haven't yet built up a protective waxy coating on their leaves. A plant hit hard by frost usually won't recover. For next time: both your nighttime air temperature AND your soil temperature need to be reliably above 60°F before you transplant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until nighttime temperatures are reliably above 50°F AND your soil is above 60°F before transplanting; check soil temperature 2 to 3 inches deep with an inexpensive probe thermometer. In Zones 3 to 5 this often means waiting until late May or early June regardless of what the calendar says.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are tropical plants and suffer the moment temperatures drop near freezing. Even a brief cold night can blacken leaves and kill young plants. If it happened at transplant, the plant was likely moved out too early; soil temperature matters as much as air temperature.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until both night temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. A cheap soil thermometer removes the guesswork.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Beefsteak tomatoes can run into a few common problems. Blight is a leaf disease that starts on the lower leaves first and spreads fastest in wet, humid weather. Blossom end rot shows up as a dark, sunken patch on the bottom of the fruit; it looks like a nutrient problem, but it's almost always caused by uneven watering (dry for a stretch, then suddenly soaked). Adding extra calcium won't fix it. Consistent moisture will.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water at the base of the plant, not from overhead, and stake the plant for good airflow. Leaves that dry quickly after rain are much harder for blight to infect. Move your tomatoes to a different bed each year; blight spores can survive in the soil over winter. For blossom end rot: mulch heavily and water deeply and consistently rather than in small frequent amounts.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are susceptible to blight, blossom end rot, and several common pests. Blight spreads fast in wet, humid conditions and usually starts at the lower leaves. Blossom end rot is caused by calcium deficiency triggered by irregular watering, not a nutrient problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently at the base, not overhead. Remove any affected leaves immediately. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year and stake plants to improve airflow.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Overwatered tomatoes show yellowing leaves starting at the bottom of the plant, and roots that can't get oxygen; waterlogged soil suffocates them. Inconsistent watering is actually more damaging than steady overwatering: if the soil dries out and then you flood it, the sudden change in moisture causes the fruit skin to expand faster than the inside, and the tomatoes crack. Blossom end rot (dark patches on the fruit bottom) can follow the same pattern.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water deeply two or three times a week rather than a small amount every day. Deep watering encourages roots to grow down into the soil rather than staying shallow near the surface. A thick layer of mulch around the base of the plant evens out moisture and dramatically reduces the wet-dry swings that cause cracking.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Overwatered tomatoes show yellowing lower leaves, cracked fruit, and roots that cannot get oxygen. Inconsistent watering, dry then suddenly wet, causes fruit splitting and blossom end rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply twice a week rather than a little every day. Mulching around the base dramatically improves moisture consistency.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Drought stress during flowering causes blossom drop; the flowers fall off before fruit can set, and those potential tomatoes are gone for good. During fruiting, inconsistent moisture (dry spells followed by heavy watering) causes blossom end rot and cracked skin. Beefsteak tomatoes are large-fruited and especially water-hungry; they need steady moisture throughout the whole season.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Beefsteak tomatoes need about 1 to 2 inches of water per week. Mulch heavily around the base to hold moisture in the soil between waterings. Always water at the base of the plant, not the leaves; wet leaves in the evening invite disease.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering causes blossom drop; no flowers, no fruit. During fruiting, inconsistent moisture causes blossom end rot and cracked skin.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes need 1-2 inches of water per week. Mulch heavily to retain moisture, and water at the base never the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Tomatoes need at least 6 to 8 hours of direct sun each day to produce fruit well. In a shady spot the plant will grow, sometimes quite lushly, but will set little or no fruit, and will be much more prone to fungal disease because the leaves stay damp instead of drying out. Beefsteak types in particular need full sun to develop their large, dense fruit properly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Tomatoes are one of the most sun-hungry vegetables in the garden. If your current spot is getting less than 6 hours of direct sun, move the tomatoes to your sunniest bed next season and plant something more shade-tolerant, like lettuce or spinach, in the shadier spot.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes need a minimum of 6-8 hours of direct sun to produce well. In shade they grow leafy but set little or no fruit, and are much more prone to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes are one of the most sun-hungry vegetables. If your current spot is marginal, prioritize this bed for tomatoes next season and move something more shade-tolerant elsewhere.

succession_policy.tip_beginner: You only need to plant beefsteak tomatoes once; the same plant will keep producing fruit all summer until frost kills it. No need to replant partway through the season. If you live in a very warm climate (think Southern California, Phoenix, or South Florida, Zone 9 or warmer,), you can start a second planting in late summer for a fall and winter harvest.
succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Not a true succession crop; one indeterminate plant produces all season until frost. A second planting started mid-season in most zones would be killed by frost before its 75-100 day maturity window closes. In zones 9-11 a late-summer planting (July-August) is viable as a separate fall crop, not a succession.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Beefsteak is an indeterminate crop that continues setting new flower clusters until frost. A single plant produces continuously through the season, making succession planting unnecessary and impractical, since a second planting started weeks later would simply be frost-killed before reaching its long (75-100 day) maturity window in most zones. In zones 9-11 where a fall planting is common, that is a separate season, not a succession.

crops.description_beginner: Beefsteak tomatoes are the big slicing tomatoes you see at farmers markets, the kind that fill an entire slice of bread. They take longer to ripen than cherry or roma types (most varieties need 75 to 100 days from transplant), so they need the full growing season. These are indeterminate plants, meaning they keep growing and setting new fruit until frost kills them, so they need a strong cage or stake from the start; plan for a plant that reaches 5 to 6 feet tall. They're more demanding than cherry tomatoes, but if you get the watering and support right, the payoff is big, meaty slices all summer. Good first choices include Celebrity (disease-resistant, widely adapted) and Early Girl (shorter maturity, better for short-season zones).
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick when the fruit is fully colored all the way up to the shoulders; a tomato that's red-sided but still greenish at the top isn't done yet. Give it a gentle squeeze; it should have a little give without feeling mushy. The skin will look slightly less shiny than when it was still ripening. Large beefsteak fruit (bigger than a baseball) takes a few extra days compared to smaller types; give it time. If you're not sure, check again the next day; slightly under-ripe picked tomatoes will continue to ripen on the counter.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: It is possible to start tomatoes from seeds indoors about six to eight weeks before you'll want to move them outside. (MSU)
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Beefsteak (larger-fruited, slower-maturing) varieties require the 8-week end of this range to reach transplant size.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Many gardeners plant transplants the last week or two of May, after danger of frost has passed and air and soil temperatures warm. (MSU)
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start your warm season crops indoors for transplanting in mid-June, once the threat of frost has passed. Transplant outdoors after all danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed. Don't be in a rush to transplant these tropical species. (UMaine, northern Maine Z3-4; UMN; NDSU)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Most traditional tomato varieties take 70 to 85 days from the time plants are placed in the ground to the time fruits are ready to harvest; beefsteak varieties sit at the upper end of this range (80-85 days). (UMN Extension; MSU Extension)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Pick all the fruit and bring it indoors before the first frost at the end of summer. (UMN)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative policy: harvest_end = first_frost - 5 days to buffer against frost-risk week and to ensure notifications arrive before plants are killed.

northern_tier.plantings_provenance: Zone-promoted and re-verified from cold zones 3-7 (m16_beefsteak_step3_5_region_shells, 2026-06-07). Supersedes the Phase A verbatim lift.

3.notes: Very challenging in Zone 3: 80+ day maturity leaves little margin. Choose Fast varieties like Jet Star. Use season extenders.
3.zone_notes: Zone 3 is marginal for large beefsteak varieties (80-100 day maturity). Choose a faster 75-day variety (Celebrity, Early Girl) or consider cherry tomatoes for more reliable harvest. Start 8 weeks before last frost.

4.notes: Start 8 weeks early. Choose varieties under 85 days. Heavy mulching and black plastic help.
4.zone_notes: Start indoors 8 weeks early. Beefsteaks push the limits of Zone 4, so choose carefully.

5.notes: Plant after last frost. Stake heavily, as beefsteaks get large and heavy. Consistent watering prevents blossom end rot.
5.zone_notes: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost.

6.notes: Excellent zone for beefsteaks. Long season allows full flavor development. Remove suckers to focus energy on fruit.
6.zone_notes: Beefsteaks need 80+ days, so plant by mid-May at latest for harvest before first frost.

7.notes: Heat stress above 95°F can cause blossom drop. Shade cloth and deep watering help through July to August peak.
7.zone_notes: Plant by late May. Too late to do a second planting, so focus on one great crop.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold northern states (zones 3 through 7) you grow beefsteak tomatoes once a year, as a single summer crop. What limits the season here is frost on both ends, not summer heat. Because big beefsteak tomatoes are slow to ripen (about 75 to 90 days after transplanting), start the seeds indoors well before your last frost, then set the plants out a week or two after that last frost, once nights stay warm and the soil has warmed up. That single planting gives you one long harvest until the first fall frost ends it. There is no summer break the way hotter regions have, because northern summers usually are not hot enough to stop the plants from setting fruit. Unlike cherry tomatoes, beefsteaks take too long to fit in a second crop, so plan on one well-timed planting and choose faster varieties. In the coldest zones, start seed early indoors, pick quick-maturing varieties, and warm the soil with black plastic mulch or season-extending covers so the fruit ripens before frost returns.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 through 7) grows beefsteak tomatoes as a single frost-bracketed summer crop: the limiting factor on both ends is frost, not heat. Because large-fruited beefsteak types are slow (about 75 to 90 days from transplant), the season is started indoors well ahead of the last frost, transplants go out a week or two after that last spring frost once nights hold above the low 50s°F and soil warms past about 60°F, and that one planting then produces a single continuous harvest until plants are cut short by the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat exclusion here: northern summers rarely sustain the high day and night temperatures that stop fruit set, so the only gaps are the winter cold pauses and the season between them is uninterrupted. Unlike cherry types, beefsteak's longer days-to-maturity leaves no room for a second crop even at the warm end of the band, so the whole region runs on one well-timed planting; the short-season north strongly favors the faster large-fruited varieties and starting seed indoors. The coldest zones (3 and 4) depend on early indoor starts, fast-maturing varieties, and season extension (black plastic mulch, Wall-O-Waters) to ripen fruit before frost. Frost dates shift sharply across the band, so confirm your local last and first frost. (University of Minnesota Extension; North Dakota State University Extension; Michigan State University Extension; University of Maine Cooperative Extension)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the southern high desert (around Las Cruces, New Mexico) you can grow beefsteak tomatoes in spring and again in fall, with a hot-summer gap. Plant the spring crop in late March or early April so it makes fruit before the July heat. You can try a fall crop planted in mid-July, but big beefsteak tomatoes set fruit poorly in the July and August heat and are slow to ripen, so the fall crop is a bit of a gamble before the November frost. Pick fast-maturing, heat-tolerant varieties.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The southern high desert (Las Cruces, Mesilla Valley; Chihuahuan high desert, zone 8) runs two beefsteak windows split by peak summer heat. Set the spring crop out in late March to early April, after the local last frost (about March 19), so it sets fruit before July. A fall crop can be transplanted in mid-July per the Dona Ana County Master Gardener chart, but for large-fruited beefsteak this is marginal: fruit set is poor once day temperatures exceed 95 °F through July and August, and a 75-90 day plant only just matures before the November frost (about November 12). Favor fast-maturing, heat-tolerant cultivars for the fall attempt. The fall window and two-window structure rest on the single Las Cruces Master Gardener chart, a regional source; the spring dates are anchored to the high-desert frost data with NOAA cross-check. (NMSU Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardener Las Cruces planting chart)

harvest_end.label: primary

11.calendar_basis: Beefsteak tomato can be planted YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free) and no documented summer no-sow exclusion: CTAHR HGV-5 states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing adapted varieties, and names no seasonal fruit-set gap. UNLIKE cherry (which CTAHR treats as cleanly heat resistant), CTAHR's Field Tomato Production Guidelines specifically warn that large-fruited varieties set fruit poorly under Hawaii's warm lowland nights (optimum fruit set 60-70 deg-F). This is a fruit-set-QUALITY caveat, disclosed in the seasoned region_note, not an absolute no-sow month, so the year-round structure holds (guardrail: heat_pause is read from the source per region, never defaulted; HGV-5 documents no exclusion month). Hawaii's dominant challenge is disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant locally bred cultivars (Kewalo, Anahu, Healani, N-series) and cultural practice. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason; year_round:true makes the all-active calendar machine-readable. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii's tropical lowlands you can plant beefsteak tomatoes any month of the year; there is no cold winter and no planting season to wait for. The catch is that big beefsteak tomatoes do not set fruit well in the warm tropical nights, so they do best at cooler elevations and in the cooler parts of the year, and you will have the most luck with heat-tolerant or locally bred varieties. The bigger day-to-day challenges are disease, bugs, and heavy rain.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical zone 11 grows beefsteak year-round: CTAHR gives a year-round planting capability for most of the islands contingent on adapted varieties, with no winter cold pause and no documented summer no-sow exclusion. The important caveat for beefsteak specifically is fruit-set quality, not timing: CTAHR's field production guidance notes that large-fruited varieties are sensitive to high night temperatures and set fruit poorly in the warm lowland (optimum set 60-70 °F), unlike heat-resistant cherry types. Favor cooler-elevation siting, the cooler part of the year, and heat-tolerant or locally bred wilt-resistant cultivars (Kewalo, Anahu, Healani, the N-series). The dominant production challenges here are disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant varieties and cultural practice rather than a seasonal stop. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, beefsteak tomato is a two-season crop. Plant Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest, then plant again Sep 15 - Oct 15 for a fall crop. Skip the hottest stretch of summer: the flowers drop in the worst heat before they can set fruit, so there is nothing to gain by planting through it. It rarely if ever frosts here, so both the spring and fall windows run on Valley heat, not on a frost date.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Beefsteak tomato in the RGV runs on the Valley's two-crop calendar: set out Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest running Apr 30 - Jun 18, then set out again Sep 15 - Oct 15 for a fall harvest running Nov 29 - Dec 15. Sustained Valley summer heat causes blossom drop: the flowers abort before they can set fruit, so production stops even though the plants stay alive (TAMU AgriLife notes high heat drops tomato blossoms). Frost is essentially absent here, so both plantings are timed against heat, not cold. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 8 weeks before set-out; OSU's Oregon planting table (EM9027) gives tomatoes 8 weeks indoors before transplanting.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out after the last frost and once the soil has warmed; OSU's table gives the Willamette Valley a May window and the immediate coast a wider May-June window (EM9027), corroborated by WSU's tomato seeding spec (EM057E Table 4, 70-85F soil temp).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Matures in about 75 to 90 days from transplant. Cool marine summers routinely stretch a large-fruited beefsteak toward the long end of this range, so treat 90 days as the realistic planning figure, not the 75-day best case.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest winds down at the first fall frost; pick remaining fruit (green, if needed) a few days ahead of the average date to ripen indoors.

8.zone_notes: The Willamette Valley and Puget lowlands are the warmer of the two PNW zones for this stretch crop; OSU's table gives a single May set-out window here. Even so, treat the 90-day upper end of the maturity range as the realistic planning figure, not the 75-day best case, and lean on an early-maturing beefsteak variety.

9.zone_notes: The immediate coast runs cooler and cloudier than the valley even though OSU's own table gives it a wider May-June set-out window; this is the more marginal of the two zones for a big, slow slicer. Lean toward the early end of the window, pick the fastest-maturing beefsteak variety available, and give it the single warmest site in the garden.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Beefsteak is a stretch crop in the maritime Pacific Northwest: our cool, marine-tempered summers do not always deliver enough sustained warmth to fully ripen a big, slow slicer before fall weather sets in. Start seed indoors about 8 weeks before setting plants out in May (a bit later on the immediate coast), and choose an early, fast-maturing beefsteak type rather than a full 90-day heirloom-style slicer. Give it the single warmest, most sheltered, sunniest spot in the garden; a cloche or wall-o-water at transplant time helps bank extra heat early on. Some years you will get a full crop of big, ripe tomatoes; in a cooler summer, expect smaller fruit, a later harvest, or green tomatoes that need to finish ripening indoors ahead of the first fall frost.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Beefsteak is genuinely marginal in the maritime Pacific Northwest, the region's defining warm-season weak point. Set transplants out after the last frost once the soil is reliably warm, in May in the Willamette Valley or across OSU's wider May-June coastal window; but treat the published 75-to-90-day maturity range as optimistic here. Cool marine summers routinely stretch it, so plan around the long end and choose an early or fast-maturing beefsteak-type variety over a full 90-day heirloom-scale slicer. Site the crop in the single warmest, most reflective, most sheltered microsite available, and consider a cloche or wall-o-water at transplant to bank early heat. Harvest runs into fall behind the region's mild first frost, but a cool year can leave the latest fruit unripened; pick green fruit ahead of frost to finish indoors rather than lose it. (OSU EM9027; WSU EM057E)

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 8 weeks before spring set-out (Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331).

Set transplants out a few weeks after your last frost, harvest through mid July, then plant again for a fall crop of big slicers.

Spring transplants go out about a week after the last frost (zone 8: mid April; zone 7: late April) for a harvest running into mid to late July. nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Give beefsteak the fuller head start it wants where possible, but Southern Nevada's UNR calendar keeps indoor starts to early February, about six weeks before the mid-March set-out (UNR Extension SP-99-11's range runs six to eight weeks; kept to the six-week end so January stays a dormant month).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out in mid-March, once frost danger has passed, per UNR's practical Southern Nevada last-frost date of March 15 and the UNLV Master Gardener chart's March tomato window; large-fruited beefsteak, being slower than cherry or grape types, should aim for the early part of the window to bank as much growing time as possible before the heat wall.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins ripening about 82 days after the mid-March transplant, the slowest of the Shape A tomatoes here, so first fruit does not arrive until Jun.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop finishes by late June as daytime highs climb past 90°F and fruit set stops; UNR does not recommend a fall replanting in Southern Nevada, so a late transplant leaves little room to spare before the heat wall.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Las Vegas Valley summers routinely run past 100°F from June into September, and large-fruited beefsteak tomato fruit set fails above about 90°F day / 55°F night, so the spring crop is harvested before the heat and no fall crop is set (University of Nevada, Reno Extension SP-99-11 and Fact Sheet FS-02-61).

nevada.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley you grow beefsteak tomatoes as a single spring crop, not two like the Arizona low desert. Start seed indoors in early February, set transplants out in mid-March once frost is past, and expect the big slicing fruit from mid-June through the end of the month. Once daytime highs pass 90°F in summer the plants stop setting fruit, so there is a long summer break, and unlike Phoenix a fall crop is not recommended here because frost returns by late November. Beefsteak's 82-day fruit set is the slowest of the tomato types here, so in the cooler zone 8 pockets the harvest window can run as short as the last few days of June: get transplants in as early in the window as you safely can.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) runs beefsteak tomato on one spring cycle, per University of Nevada, Reno Extension. Seed goes in indoors in early February; transplants set out in mid-March, after the valley's practical last frost (SP-99-11 gives March 15, later at the cooler zone 8 edge, earlier at Laughlin in zone 10). At an 82-day days-to-maturity, fruit does not ripen until mid-June, and daytime highs past 90°F shut fruit set down from July into September, so the zone 8 window narrows to roughly the last week of June. UNR explicitly does not recommend a fall or second tomato planting for Southern Nevada, unlike the Phoenix low desert's fall reflush; frost returns around November 25 in zone 9. This is the tightest margin of any Shape A crop in the roster here, so an early transplant and an early-maturing beefsteak cultivar both matter more in Southern Nevada than in a longer desert season.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: In St. George's Dixie you grow beefsteak tomatoes as a single spring crop. Start seed indoors in late February (beefsteak wants the fuller eight-week head start), set transplants out around April 1 once frost is past, and expect big slicing tomatoes from late June. Because beefsteak is the slowest tomato of the bunch, the picking window is short before daytime highs pass 95°F and the plants stop setting fruit for the summer. A fall crop is not recommended here since frost returns by about November 1, so make the most of the spring window with your biggest, healthiest transplants.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs beefsteak tomato on one spring cycle, per USU Extension. Seed goes in indoors in late February, the full eight-week lead beefsteak needs; transplants set out about April 1, the St. George Group D (Very Tender) date, just after the March 30 average last frost. At an 82-day days-to-maturity, the first slicers do not arrive until late June, leaving only about a week of harvest before daytime highs past 95°F shut fruit set down from July into September. USU does not recommend a fall or second tomato planting for the St. George area; frost returns around November 1. Given how tight the window runs, this is one to start on time and baby along rather than delay.

crops.description_seasoned: Indeterminate, large-fruited tomatoes grown for slicing. The beefsteak label covers three biologically close sub-types: true beefsteak-shape varieties (Big Boy, Mortgage Lifter), oblate globe slicers commonly marketed as beefsteak (Celebrity), and large heirloom slicers (Brandywine), with uniform cultivation requirements across all. Indeterminate growth means the plant continues extending and setting fruit until frost kills it; this also means it requires strong caging or staking from the start. Large fruit mass places sustained calcium and water demand on the plant, which is the main reason blossom-end rot and cracking are more common in beefsteaks than in cherry or paste types. Requires a long frost-free window: most varieties need 75-100 days from transplant to first ripe fruit, making them marginal in short-season zones (3-4) without season-extension measures. In zones 9-11, the challenge reverses: summer heat above 90°F causes blossom drop, and fall planting is the standard workaround.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when the fruit has reached full variety color all the way to the shoulders, yields to gentle pressure without feeling mushy, and the skin has transitioned from a hard glossy sheen to a softer, slightly matte surface. Skin sheen loss signals the completion of cell-wall softening as lycopene (or variety-appropriate anthocyanins for dark varieties) accumulates and pectin in the outer cell layers begins breaking down. The abscission zone at the stem attachment weakens as the fruit ripens; slight twist resistance is still present at peak eating quality; zero resistance means overripe. Shoulders turning color last: a fruit that is red-sided but green-shouldered is underripe. For large beefsteak fruit (12-16 oz), allow a few extra days compared to cherry or slicer types; mass slows the ripening front.

pet_safe.note: Ripe tomatoes are fine, but the leaves, stems, and unripe fruit are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Roma Tomato

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Roma tomatoes want soil that drains well and is rich in organic matter. If water pools on your bed after rain, or the soil stays soggy for more than a day, drainage is a problem: soggy roots rot even in otherwise good soil. The easiest fix is to work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, which improves drainage and fertility at once. Tomatoes are heavy feeders, so starting with rich soil means less fertilizing later. Because romas are especially prone to blossom-end rot, soil that holds moisture evenly, helped by that compost and a layer of mulch, matters even more here than for most vegetables.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Roma tomatoes perform best in well-drained loam or sandy loam with high organic matter. Drainage is non-negotiable: waterlogged roots invite Pythium root rot and nutrient lockout even in fertile soil. Working 2 to 3 inches of compost in before planting addresses texture and fertility together. Organic matter also buffers soil moisture, which is more important for paste types than for most tomatoes because steady moisture is the primary defense against the blossom-end rot romas are prone to. Tomatoes are heavy feeders, and organically rich soil reduces the mid-season fertilizer burden.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures acidity on a scale from 1 to 14, where 7 is neutral. Roma tomatoes do best between about 6.2 and 6.8, slightly acidic, where the nutrients they need are most available. Calcium availability matters a lot for roma in particular, because these plants are prone to blossom-end rot, which is a calcium delivery problem. Soils in the interior West (Arizona, Nevada, Utah, Colorado) often run alkaline, above 7, which can lock up nutrients even when you fertilize, so growers there often add sulfur before planting. Eastern and Midwestern soils are frequently in the right range already, but a $10 soil test from your local extension office tells you for certain.
ph.note_seasoned: Roma tomatoes prefer a soil pH of about 6.2 to 6.8. pH governs the solubility of phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium, the three nutrients tomatoes consume in the largest quantities, and calcium availability is especially relevant for a paste type prone to blossom-end rot. Below 5.5, manganese and aluminum reach phytotoxic levels and impaired calcium uptake raises blossom-end rot risk. Above 7.0, iron and manganese deficiencies drive interveinal chlorosis on younger leaves. In the alkaline soils common across the interior West, growers routinely acidify before planting. Eastern soils often sit naturally in the preferred band; Pacific Northwest soils vary widely by parent material.

fertilizer.timing: starter at transplanting, then side-dress about 3 to 4 weeks later
fertilizer.example_product: Miracle-Gro Tomato Plant Food
fertilizer.notes_beginner: When you see the first flowers opening, switch fertilizers. Use a balanced or all-purpose fertilizer early in the season, then switch to a tomato-specific or high-potassium fertilizer once flowers appear. Too much nitrogen (the first number on the package) after flowering pushes the plant to grow more leaves instead of fruit.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time for your tomatoes' first side-dressing, about 3 to 4 weeks after planting out, then again every 3 to 4 weeks. Once flowers appear, switch to a tomato or high-potassium fertilizer to keep the fruit coming.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Look for three numbers on the fertilizer bag: those are the NPK ratio (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium). A soil test is the surest guide, and it is what both extension services behind this guide recommend first. Without one, a low-nitrogen balanced formula such as 5-10-10 is a sensible default. Go easy on the first number: too much nitrogen gives you a big leafy plant that is slow to set fruit. Skip the high-phosphorus bags sold as bloom boosters unless a soil test actually calls for phosphorus, because many soils already hold plenty.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Switch from balanced to high-potassium feed at flowering. Too much nitrogen produces leafy plants with little fruit.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: First side-dress is due, about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, then every 3 to 4 weeks through harvest. Switch to the high-potassium formula at flowering.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Soil test governs. Absent one, a low-nitrogen balanced formula such as 5-10-10. UMN advises a low- or no-phosphorus feed unless a test specifically calls for phosphorus, and warns that excess nitrogen produces bushy, leafy plants slow to bear fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About 1 pound of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet side-dressed three to four weeks after transplanting, repeated every 3 to 4 weeks through harvest; if no soil test, work in about 1.5 pounds of a complete fertilizer per 100 square feet before planting. The crop's high-potassium hint above governs the formula; this is the rate.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A common rate is about 1 to 2 tablespoons of fertilizer scratched into the soil around each plant, 6 to 8 inches out from the stem, starting about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting and then every 3 to 4 weeks. Always water it in, and keep the granules off the stem and leaves.

companions.note_beginner: Most tomato companion advice is garden tradition rather than tested fact. The clearest exception is marigolds, which can cut down on root pests, but only when planted thickly as a cover crop a couple of months ahead, not scattered among the tomatoes. In practice: keep fennel away, keep tomatoes away from their relatives like potatoes and eggplant if disease has been a problem for you, and try nasturtiums as a trap for aphids if aphids gave you trouble in past seasons.
companions.note_seasoned: Roma tomato companions are dominated by traditional lore with selective extension backing. The marigold/nematode connection is the best-documented pairing in this crop's companion set, effective as a dense pre-season cover crop, not as scattered concurrent interplanting. For most growers, the practical guidance is straightforward: avoid fennel, keep tomatoes away from other Solanaceae family members (potatoes, eggplant) if disease pressure is a concern in your region, and consider nasturtiums as an aphid trap crop if aphid pressure was a problem in past seasons.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Basil
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Long-established pairing; flavor-improvement claims are traditional. Basil's aromatic compounds may deter some pest insects, though not extension-documented for this specific pair, but widely practiced and low risk.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Flavor-improvement and pest-deterrence claims are classic companion-planting tradition. Not documented in peer-reviewed research or T1 extension literature for this specific pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A long-standing pairing. Many gardeners say basil improves tomato flavor and may keep some pests away. There is no hard proof for this exact pair, but it is widely done and harmless.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigolds
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: French marigolds suppress root-knot nematodes, most effectively as a dense cover crop planted 2+ months before tomatoes, not as concurrent interplanting. Extension-documented mechanism.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension and UF/IFAS ENY-056 document alpha-terthienyl release suppressing root-knot nematodes. Extension consensus: dense cover crop 2+ months pre-season is effective; scattered concurrent interplanting has minimal effect. Whitefly deterrence claims are traditional and not extension-supported.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: French marigolds can reduce root-knot pests in the soil, but only when planted thickly as a cover crop a couple of months before the tomatoes, not as a few plants tucked in alongside them.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Parsley
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Flowering umbellifers attract predatory wasps and beneficial insects; mechanism is documented in biological control literature though the specific parsley-tomato pairing is not directly extension-tested.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Umbellifers attracting parasitic wasps and beneficial insects is a documented biological control mechanism (UC IPM, Cornell). The specific parsley-tomato pairing benefit is inferential: the mechanism is real but pairing-specific evidence is thin.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: When parsley is left to flower, the blooms draw in helpful insects that prey on garden pests. The effect is well established in general, though this exact parsley and tomato pairing has not been tested directly.

good_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots' deep taproot partitions the root zone differently from tomato's fibrous roots, theoretically reducing below-ground competition. This is a plausible root-zone partitioning inference, not an extension-tested pairing.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning between taprooted and fibrous-rooted crops is a real ecology concept. The specific carrot-tomato pairing benefit is a plausible inference that has not been directly studied in extension research.

good_seasoned.name: Borage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Borage flowers attract pollinators over an extended bloom period; may also repel tomato hornworm (traditional claim). Pollinator attraction is biologically plausible; hornworm repellence is tradition.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Borage as pollinator attractor is plausible and consistent with floral-resource literature. The hornworm-repellence claim is traditional companion-planting lore without T1 extension backing.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Nasturtiums function as a trap crop for aphids: aphids preferentially colonize nasturtiums, drawing them away from tomatoes. UC IPM documents trap-crop use of nasturtiums in vegetable gardens.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap-crop principle is documented in IPM literature. UC IPM references nasturtiums as aphid attractors. The specific nasturtium-tomato trap-crop pairing is referenced in extension-adjacent IPM guidance; strongest evidence is for brassica pests, but aphid trap-crop mechanism applies broadly.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is broadly allelopathic and suppresses growth of many neighboring plants. Extension literature documents fennel as a poor companion for most vegetables; the specific tomato interaction is traditional but consistent with fennel's known allelopathic properties.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel's allelopathic properties are real and documented, but the specific 'stunts tomatoes' claim is traditional rather than directly extension-tested for this pair.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Fennel releases substances that stunt the growth of many plants around it, so it is a poor neighbor for most vegetables. The trouble with tomatoes is traditional advice, but it fits fennel's known habit of holding back its neighbors.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both brassicas and tomatoes are heavy feeders; close interplanting creates real competition for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Not a toxic pairing, but productivity of both crops is reduced under competition.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for macronutrients between heavy feeders is a real agronomic concept. The specific brassica-tomato pair is traditional; the underlying competition mechanism is mechanistically sound.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage-family plants and tomatoes are both hungry feeders, so planting them close together makes them compete for the same nutrients. It is not harmful, but both crops produce less.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both crops host the tomato fruit worm / corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea, same species). Planting together creates a concentrated host reservoir that amplifies pest pressure on both crops.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: H. zea (tomato fruit worm = corn earworm) is documented on both tomato and corn in UC IPM and Cornell IPM literature. Shared-host concentration is a well-established IPM principle. Planting these crops together in a home garden concentrates the pest population.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn and tomatoes are fed on by the same caterpillar pest. Growing them side by side gives that pest more to feed on and builds up the pressure on both crops.

bad_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both are Solanaceae and share primary diseases (late blight, Phytophthora infestans; early blight, Alternaria solani) and several pests. Planting together creates a continuous host bridge that sustains inoculum across the season and into following years. Crop rotation separating Solanaceae is the standard extension recommendation for disease management.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Extension literature (UMN, Cornell, Clemson HGIC) documents shared disease and pest pressure within Solanaceae and recommends rotation to break disease cycles. The specific tomato-potato pairing as a disease-management risk is extension-backed.

bad_seasoned.name: Eggplant
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Same family (Solanaceae), shares Colorado potato beetle pressure and early blight. Interplanting concentrates beetle and disease pressure; separating Solanaceae crops, even within a season, reduces crossover pest load.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Colorado potato beetle and early blight are documented shared pests/pathogens across Solanaceae in extension IPM literature. The specific eggplant-tomato bad-companion claim follows from the well-documented within-family pest/disease sharing principle.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or black insects on the growing tips and the undersides of leaves, often so small they look like dots. The leaves may start to curl or feel sticky. You might see ants walking up the stems, as they farm aphids for the sweet liquid the aphids produce.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the colonies directly with a strong jet of water from a hose. For persistent infestations, apply insecticidal soap or neem oil spray, making sure to coat the leaf undersides where the aphids cluster.
pests.prevention_beginner: Plant marigolds or nasturtiums near your tomatoes, as both attract beneficial insects that eat aphids. Avoid over-fertilizing with high-nitrogen fertilizer, which produces the soft new growth aphids prefer.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny soft-bodied insects that cluster on stems and the undersides of leaves. Their numbers can build up very fast in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on high-nitrogen fertilizer. Heavy feeding pushes out the soft new shoots aphids like best, so a leaner-fed plant gives them less to build up on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen drives the flush of soft growth colonies multiply on; moderating the feed removes the resource that lets populations explode in warm weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the clusters off with a strong jet of water from the hose, aiming at the growing tips and the undersides of the leaves where they gather. Spray early in the day so the leaves can dry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A hard water jet dislodges colonies from tips and leaf undersides as a first physical knock-back before reaching for any spray; do it early enough in the day that foliage dries quickly.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Let the aphids' natural enemies work for you. Plant marigolds or nasturtiums nearby, since both draw in beneficial insects, the helpful bugs such as ladybugs that eat aphids.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserve the resident natural enemies before spraying anything: interplanted marigolds and nasturtiums attract aphid predators, and avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides keeps them alive to do the work.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For an infestation you have actually found, you can buy and release ladybugs or lacewings onto the affected plants. Release onto aphids that are present, not ahead of time.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Purchased ladybug or lacewing releases go onto a located, active colony once conservation is already in place; results are more conditional than what the resident predators give you for free.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For colonies that keep coming back, spray insecticidal soap right onto them, coating the undersides of the leaves where they cluster; it works only where it wets the insects. Avoid spraying above 90°F or on a drought-stressed plant, which can burn the leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is a contact material for infestations you can coat directly. Target the colonies on the leaf undersides and spare clean foliage, since it also kills soft-bodied beneficials it wets; skip it above 90°F or on water-stressed plants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil is the other spray option for persistent colonies; coat the leaf undersides where they cluster. Do not spray in heat above 90°F, and keep it off anything in flower so bees are not exposed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Neem is a low-residue option that spares beneficials once dry; direct coverage of the colonies on the undersides is what does the work. Observe the 90°F ceiling, avoid drought-stressed plants, and keep it off open bloom while bees forage.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_beginner: Large sections of leaves or whole stems stripped overnight. Look for fat green caterpillars (up to 4 inches long) that blend almost perfectly into the stems, but they are easier to spot by looking for the black droppings on the leaves below.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Hand-pick and drop in soapy water, it sounds simple but it works well. If you spot any with small white oval capsules stuck to their backs, leave those ones; parasitic wasps have laid eggs on them and the wasps will do the work for you.
pests.prevention_beginner: Till or turn your soil in autumn to destroy overwintering pupae. Planting dill or fennel nearby attracts the predatory wasps that prey on hornworms.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.cause_beginner: Large green caterpillars, the larvae of a moth, that feed on leaves and stems. They show up mostly in mid to late summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick, they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them, as parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

control_ladder.note_beginner: After the season ends, till or turn the soil in that bed. Hornworms spend the winter as pupae, the resting stage buried in the soil, and turning the bed destroys them before next year.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Autumn tillage of the finished bed breaks up overwintering pupae, cutting next season's emergence; weigh it against no-dig practice where pressure is light and handpicking is keeping up.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them into soapy water. It sounds too simple, but it works well. They blend into the stems, so look for the black droppings on the leaves below and trace upward to find them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hand removal is effective despite the camouflage; scout by the frass on lower leaves rather than by the larvae themselves, and pull them into soapy water on a regular walk-through.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Tiny parasitic wasps, helpful wasps that lay their eggs on hornworms, will do much of the work if you let them. If you find a hornworm with small white oval capsules stuck to its back, leave that one alone; the wasps are already finishing it off. Planting dill or fennel nearby helps draw the wasps in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserve the parasitoids: a larva carrying white cocoons is already parasitized and doomed, so leave it in place as a wasp nursery, and interplant dill to attract the adults. Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that would remove them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If picking is not keeping up, spray Bt, short for Bacillus thuringiensis, a bacteria-based spray that targets caterpillars. Spray while the caterpillars are still young, and reapply after rain. It acts on caterpillars as a group, so keep it off any plants you grow for butterflies.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Bt kurstaki controls larvae best while they are small; reapply after rain or a flush of new growth. It is caterpillar-wide, taking swallowtails and monarchs along with the pests, so confine it to the affected crop.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny round holes scattered across the leaves, especially on young plants and seedlings. If you approach the plant quickly you'll see tiny shiny black beetles jumping off the leaves: that's the flea beetle.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover seedlings with floating row cover until plants are a few inches tall and growing strongly. Diatomaceous earth dusted on and around the leaves can help; reapply after rain.
pests.prevention_beginner: Transplanting larger, more established plants rather than direct-sowing reduces flea beetle damage, since seedlings are most vulnerable.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.cause_beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas when disturbed and chew tiny holes in leaves. They are most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover young transplants with a floating row cover, a light fabric blanket that lets sun and rain through but keeps the beetles off, until the plants are a few inches tall and growing strongly. Seedlings take the worst damage, so protection matters most early.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover excludes the beetles through the vulnerable seedling stage, which is where the shot-hole feeding concentrates; established plants are far less at risk. Do not lay it over a bed that carried the same family last year, or emerging soil pests can be trapped underneath with the crop.

pests.name: Whiteflies
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny white moth-like insects that fly up in a little cloud when you brush the plant, clustered on the undersides of the leaves. Leaves may yellow, and a sticky coating (honeydew) can develop, sometimes followed by black sooty mold. Whiteflies are worst in warm regions and on greenhouse or container plants.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every 5 to 7 days because the eggs keep hatching. Yellow sticky traps catch the adults, and a strong jet of water knocks many off. Remove heavily infested lower leaves.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check new transplants before you buy them, since whiteflies often arrive on nursery plants. Reflective (silver) mulch confuses them, and keeping plants healthy without over-feeding nitrogen reduces the soft growth they prefer.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clouds of tiny white insects on leaf undersides that flush up when disturbed. Yellowing leaves, honeydew, and sooty mold in heavy infestations. Most severe in warm regions, greenhouses, and on container plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several species (greenhouse whitefly, silverleaf/sweetpotato whitefly). Populations build rapidly in warm weather, and some species transmit plant viruses.
pests.cause_beginner: Small white flying insects that suck sap from the leaves. They multiply fast in warm weather and can spread plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Insecticidal soap or neem oil on leaf undersides, repeated every 5 to 7 days to catch newly hatched nymphs. Yellow sticky traps for adults. Conserve natural enemies (Encarsia wasps, ladybugs). Remove heavily infested foliage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect transplants before introducing them. Reflective mulch deters colonization. Avoid excess nitrogen. Monitor leaf undersides early in warm weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the plants healthy without over-feeding nitrogen. Heavy feeding produces the soft growth whiteflies prefer, so a moderate feed gives them less to work with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen; the soft flush it drives is what colonizing whiteflies build on, and populations climb fastest in warm weather. Monitor the leaf undersides early in the warm season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay a reflective (silver) mulch under the plants while they are still small. The shiny surface confuses incoming whiteflies looking for a place to land.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch deters colonization by disorienting incoming adults; lay it at planting while the crop is small, before a population is established.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Snap off the lower leaves that are heavily infested and get them out of the garden. Each leaf removed takes part of the population with it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing the most heavily infested foliage lowers the resident population and the honeydew load that would otherwise feed sooty mold.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A strong jet of water from the hose knocks many of them off the leaf undersides. Spray early in the day so the foliage dries quickly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A hard water jet dislodges a good share of the population from the undersides as a first knock-back; keep it early in the day so leaves dry.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hang yellow sticky traps near the plants to catch the flying adults, the little cloud that rises when you brush the foliage. The traps do not reach the young stages on the leaves, so pair them with the other steps.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Yellow traps pull down the adult flight and double as a monitoring tool; the nymphs on the leaf undersides are untouched, so traps supplement coverage sprays rather than replace them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Whiteflies have natural enemies, including ladybugs and tiny wasps that attack them. Protect these helpers by avoiding broad sprays that kill everything, and they will help hold the numbers down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserve Encarsia wasps, ladybugs, and the rest of the natural-enemy complex; avoid broad-spectrum materials, which kill the beneficials along with the pests.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spray insecticidal soap onto the undersides of the leaves where the whiteflies sit, and repeat every 5 to 7 days, because the eggs keep hatching after each spray. Avoid spraying above 90°F or on drought-stressed plants, which can burn the leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap works by contact on the nymphs, so underside coverage and a 5 to 7 day repeat cycle to catch new hatch are both essential. Mind the 90°F limit, and spray only where pests are, since it kills soft-bodied beneficials it wets.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil is the other spray choice; coat the leaf undersides and repeat every 5 to 7 days for the same reason, the eggs keep hatching. Do not spray above 90°F, and keep it off open flowers so bees are not exposed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Neem on the undersides, repeated on the same 5 to 7 day cycle, is a low-residue alternative that spares beneficials once dry; observe the 90°F ceiling and the bee precaution around anything in flower.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark brown spots on the lower leaves, often with rings inside them like a target pattern. The leaves around the spots turn yellow, then the whole leaf dies and drops. The pattern starts at the bottom of the plant and moves upward.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and throw away (do not compost) any affected leaves as soon as you spot them. Mulch the soil around the base of the plant to stop rain from splashing soil and fungal spores up onto the lower leaves.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rotate your tomatoes, avoiding the same spot for at least 3 years. Water at the base of the plant rather than from overhead, and stake the plant to keep the foliage off the ground.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that causes dark spots on the lower, older leaves first. It spreads in warm, wet weather, so keep the leaves as dry as you can.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move your tomatoes to a different spot each year, and do not bring them back to the same bed for at least 3 years. The fungus carries over where tomatoes grew before.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes out of the old ground for 3 to 4 years to starve the carryover inoculum; with a splash-driven disease, distance in time is the foundation the other steps build on.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the base of the plant instead of over the top. This fungus spreads in warm, wet weather, so keeping the leaves as dry as you can slows it down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soil-level irrigation keeps foliage dry and cuts the splash that lifts soil and spores onto the lower leaves, which is where infection starts before it moves up the plant.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay mulch over the soil around the plant. Rain splashing bare soil is how the fungus reaches the lower leaves, and mulch blocks the splash.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mulch over the soil intercepts the splash that lifts carryover spores onto the lower canopy, complementing base watering by handling the rain you cannot redirect.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give each plant room, and stake it so the leaves are up off the ground and air can move through. Foliage that dries quickly gets less disease.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spacing for airflow plus staking keeps the canopy drier and the lowest leaves off the soil, working against the warm, wet conditions the fungus favors.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The moment you spot the dark target-patterned spots, pull those leaves off and throw them in the trash, not the compost. Removing them early slows the disease's climb up the plant.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rogue out affected leaves immediately and destroy rather than compost them; the disease ladders upward from the lowest leaves, so early removal buys time.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If it keeps spreading, a copper-based fungicide can protect the remaining leaves, but it works as prevention, not a cure, so it has to go on early. Follow the label rate, and keep spray and runoff away from ponds and drains, since copper is very harmful to fish and other water life.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper is a protectant, applied preventively at or before first symptoms rather than into an infected canopy. Respect the label rate to avoid leaf injury, limit repeat use over the years since copper accumulates at the soil surface, and keep it out of waterways.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
