7.zone_notes: Two crops possible: start first batch indoors in March, second batch indoors in late May for transplanting in July, as roma tomatoes ripen in about 70 to 80 days from transplant, still before first frost in these zones.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold northern states (zones 3 through 7) you grow roma tomatoes once a year, as a single summer crop. What limits the season here is frost on both ends, not summer heat: you plant after the last spring frost, pick all summer, and the plants are finished when the first fall frost arrives. There is no summer break the way hotter regions have, because northern summers usually are not hot enough to stop the plants from setting fruit. Wait to set out transplants until a week or two after your last frost, when nights stay warm and the soil has warmed up. Roma tomatoes ripen fast (about 55 to 65 days after transplanting), so they finish in time even where summers are short. In the coldest zones, pick quick varieties and warm the soil with black plastic mulch or season-extending covers; in the milder zones 6 and 7 you have time to plant a second batch in early summer for a fall crop.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 through 7) grows roma tomatoes as a single frost-bracketed summer crop: the limiting factor on both ends is frost, not heat. Transplants go out a week or two after the last spring frost, once nights stay above the low 50s°F and soil warms past about 60°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through summer until plants are cut short by the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat exclusion here: unlike the Southeast or the desert valleys, northern summers rarely sustain the high day and night temperatures that stop fruit set, so the winter gaps are frost pauses and the season is uninterrupted between them. Roma types (55 to 65 days from transplant) are well suited to short seasons and ripen before first frost even in zone 3. The cold end (zones 3 and 4) leans on fast-maturing varieties and season extension (black plastic mulch, Wall-O-Waters), while the warm end (zones 6 and 7) has room for a second transplanting in early-to-mid summer for a fall harvest. Frost dates shift sharply across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (University of Minnesota Extension; North Dakota State University Extension; Michigan State University Extension; University of Maine Cooperative Extension)

(UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: high day and especially night temperatures push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Roma is a standard paste type and is no more heat tolerant than other large-fruited tomatoes, so this pause spans the full summer heat window for it. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf area you can grow roma tomatoes twice a year, once in spring and again in fall, with a summer break in between when it gets too hot for the plants to set fruit. Roma tomatoes are about as heat sensitive as other large tomatoes, so their summer break lasts the full hot season. Plant your spring crop early enough to pick before the worst heat, then plant again in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf region runs two roma tomato seasons, spring and fall, split by a summer heat window when high day and night temperatures cause blossom drop and fruit set fails. Roma is a standard paste type and is no more heat tolerant than other large-fruited tomatoes, so its summer heat pause spans the full hot season, as for other large tomatoes. Time the spring crop to ripen before peak heat; set the fall crop out in mid-to-late summer to produce into the cooler autumn. The warmer zone 9 end of the region plants the spring crop earlier and the fall crop later than the zone 8 interior. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's interior valleys you plant roma tomatoes once, in spring (April or May), and then pick them all the way through summer and into fall until the first frost. You do not plant a second fall crop the way gardeners do in hotter, more humid places, because here roma tomatoes handle the summer heat well and just keep producing from that one planting. Wait to plant until the soil has warmed up, usually late April, even though the last frost is earlier.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: The interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and similar) grow roma tomatoes as a single long season rather than the spring-and-fall split used in the humid Southeast. Transplants go out in April and May, after the mediterranean-climate last frost and once soil warms past about 65°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through the hot summer into fall up to first frost. Roma is a standard paste type without special heat tolerance, so fruit set slows in peak valley heat; there is still no separate fall crop, just a midsummer lull in set. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC ANR)

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roma tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after a May transplant (about 70 to 80 days to maturity, mid near 75), bringing the first North Coast fruit in around July. Cool coastal summers can slow ripening relative to inland, so first pickings may run a little later in the foggier locations. (UC Master Gardener Program; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: North & North Coast: May
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: From the single May planting the North Coast produces one warm-season harvest that carries through summer and tapers in October as the coast cools and days shorten. The season is bounded on the back end by falling temperatures and light rather than by a hard frost: coastal first frost comes late, but roma production winds down once the warm-season window closes. Microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm locally. (UC Master Gardener Program; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's North Coast (the foggy coast from about Monterey north, including Marin), you plant roma tomatoes once, in May, and then pick them through summer into early fall. Here the thing holding tomatoes back is a lack of heat, not frost: the coast stays cool and foggy, and nights can drop below 55°F even in summer, so the plants need the warmer late-spring weather before they will really grow. Wait until May to set out transplants, give them the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have, and choose varieties that do well in cool summers. There is no second fall planting here, because the warm season is short.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The North Coast (Monterey County north, including the cool marine-influenced counties such as Marin) grows roma tomatoes as a single short warm season set by heat availability rather than frost. Transplants go out in May, later than the interior valleys, because coastal summers are cool and nights can sit below 55°F in any month. A single planting then carries one harvest through summer and tapers in October as the coast cools and days shorten, ahead of the late coastal first frost. This is the cool-limited case: the limiting factor is insufficient summer heat, not a midsummer heat exclusion, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Cool-summer-adapted varieties and the warmest, most sheltered sites do best, and microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives North & North Coast tomatoes as May (transplant), a single month with no semicolon and no fall window (contrast the table's genuine two-window crops such as snap beans 'July; May-June'). UC Marin Master Gardeners ('Tomato time!') independently confirms an early-May transplant and the cool-limit mechanism (Marin nights below 55F in any month; tomatoes need warmth). San Mateo/San Francisco MG and Monterey Bay MG corroborate cool coastal summers and a May start. Two independent T1 sources confirm single-window and the absence of a second window.
plantings_provenance.cool_limited_exception: ca_north_coast is the documented cool-limited exception to the warm-region heat-primary anchoring rule. The warm season is SHORT because summer never gets hot enough (marine layer, sub-55F nights), NOT because of a midsummer heat exclusion. No heat_pause is authored: there is no summer pause, the season is bounded by lack of heat at both shoulders. Contrast ca_desert / ca_interior summer behavior.
plantings_provenance.harvest_end_basis: Back-end boundary is production/temperature-limited (coast cools and days shorten in fall), not a hard frost cutoff. Coastal zone 9b/10a first frost is late (Nov-Dec or later), but roma production winds down in October as the warm-season window closes. harvest_end set to end of October; calendar fall months read 'wait' rather than 'cold_pause' because the season closes on heat/light, not frost. Table 13.2's own disclaimer (microclimate varies sharply) is surfaced in region_notes.
plantings_provenance.no_heat_pause_reason: Cool-limited region: the limiting factor is insufficient heat, so there is no summer heat exclusion to encode. Roma heat-resistance (relevant where a summer heat pause exists, e.g. se_gulf month 7) does not apply here.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: start plants indoors 6-8 weeks prior to the date you want to plant the garden
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start roma tomato seed indoors about six weeks before the spring transplant, placing seeding in late February into March. The South Coast warm season opens earlier than the North Coast because the marine climate is milder, so transplants can go out from April. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: tomatoes ... South Coast: April - July 15
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set roma tomato transplants out on the South Coast across a long window from April through about mid-July, the widest planting window of the California regions. The mild marine climate (San Diego and the Los Angeles basin coast) has no midsummer heat exclusion, so there is no summer planting pause: gardeners plant once in this window for a single long season rather than a spring-and-fall split. Plant when the soil has warmed and nights stay mild. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County)

harvest_start.label: primary

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roma tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after the spring transplant (about 70 to 80 days to maturity, mid near 75), bringing the first South Coast fruit in around early summer; the mild marine coast can then carry harvest through summer and fall, in the frost-free immediate coast as far as the end of the year. (UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County; UC Master Gardener Program)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Summer vegetables are warm season plants that span from March-August, depending on where you live
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: On the mild South Coast a single planting carries one long harvest through summer and fall. In the frost-free immediate coast (zone 10) fruit can be picked through the end of the year; slightly cooler inland-edge sites (zone 9) taper a little earlier in late fall. The season is bounded by cooling and the late or absent coastal frost, not by summer heat. Roma sets fruit through the mild warm season. (UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County; UC Master Gardener Program)

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's South Coast (the mild coast of San Diego and the Los Angeles basin), you plant roma tomatoes once, anytime from April through about mid-July, and then pick them through summer and fall. Right on the frost-free coast you can often harvest all the way to the end of the year. The weather here is gentle, so there is no summer break in planting the way hotter inland and southeastern areas have, and there is no separate fall crop, just one long season from a single planting. Plant when the soil has warmed and give the plants full sun.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The South Coast (San Luis Obispo County south, including the San Diego and Los Angeles basin coast) grows roma tomatoes as a single long warm season. Transplants go out across a wide April through mid-July window, the longest planting window of the California regions, into a mild marine climate with no midsummer heat exclusion. A single planting then carries one continuous harvest: on the frost-free immediate coast (zone 10) fruit can be picked through the end of the year, while slightly cooler inland-edge sites (zone 9) taper a little earlier in late fall. The season is bounded by fall cooling and the late or absent coastal frost rather than by summer heat, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Roma sets fruit through the mild coastal warm season; coastal microclimate varies, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives South Coast tomatoes as 'April - July 15' -- a single long continuous plant-out window with no semicolon (not a two-window split). UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County (growing guide / Vegetable Resources) independently confirm the long single season: tomatoes harvest 'from early summer through the end of the year in coastal areas', summer transplants go in during the March-April frame as soil warms, and the mild marine coast has no midsummer heat exclusion. The 'two-season' framing seen in some secondary sources is the OPTION to plant a later batch within this long window, not a forced spring-pause-fall split. Two T1 sources agree on single continuous window.

start_indoors.source_quote: start plants indoors 6-8 weeks prior to the date you want to plant the garden
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the main desert crop, start roma tomato seed indoors in fall (about October into November) for the winter transplant. The desert calendar is inverted: the main planting goes out in the mild winter months, not spring, to beat the lethal summer heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: tomatoes ... Desert Valleys: Dec-March
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the main roma tomato crop out in the desert valleys across the mild winter window, December through mid-March, so plants flower and set fruit before the summer heat arrives. This is the inverse of cold-climate timing: in Imperial and Coachella the winter is the growing season and the summer is the exclusion. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The main desert crop begins ripening roughly two months after the winter transplant (about 70 to 80 days to maturity, mid near 75), bringing spring fruit from around February into June before the heat shuts production down. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The main spring harvest runs into June and then ends as summer heat halts fruit set. A separate fall crop (see second planting) reopens the season after the heat breaks. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

start_indoors.label: fall
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall desert crop, start seed in mid-to-late summer (July into August) so transplants are ready to go out in September once the worst heat passes. The fall window is set by the break in the summer heat exclusion, not by the Time-of-Planting table (which lists only the Dec-March main desert window for tomatoes). (Mechanism: UC Statewide IPM Program; main-window table: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

plant_out.label: fall
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall desert crop out in September, once the summer heat exclusion breaks, for harvest through the mild late fall and winter. The September timing is taken from the end of the summer fruit-set-failure window rather than from the Time-of-Planting table, which lists only the Dec-March main desert window for tomatoes. (Mechanism: UC Statewide IPM Program; main-window table: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

harvest_start.label: fall
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening around November and produces through the mild desert winter into January. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

harvest_end.label: fall
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall harvest carries through the mild desert winter, ending around January as the next winter-spring main crop begins. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: The desert summer is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the Imperial and Coachella Valleys, June through August daytime highs run well past 95°F and often above 110°F, and tomato flowers fail to set fruit once temperatures stay above about 95°F (high heat reduces viable pollen). This desert pause is climatic-absolute and wide: peak desert summer heat stops fruit set for roma as for any large-fruited tomato. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella), the calendar is flipped: you grow roma tomatoes in the cool months and take the summer off, because summer here is too hot for tomatoes to make fruit. Plant your main crop in winter, from December through mid-March, so the plants can grow and set fruit before the heat. From about June through August it is too hot (often over 110°F), and tomato flowers will not set, so there is a summer break. Then plant a second crop in September for tomatoes through the mild late fall and winter. Even heat-loving roma tomatoes cannot handle the peak desert summer, so the summer break is not optional here.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella) grow roma tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar built around a hard summer heat exclusion. The main crop is transplanted in the mild winter window, December through mid-March, and harvested from spring into June; then June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs past 95°F and often above 110°F, which collapses viable pollen), so planting pauses. A second, fall crop is set out in September as the heat breaks and produces through the mild desert winter into January. This summer pause is climatic-absolute: desert peak heat stops fruit set for roma as for any large-fruited tomato. Confirm local frost and heat timing, which vary across the desert. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives Desert Valleys tomatoes as 'Dec-March' -- the mild-winter MAIN plant window (inverted calendar). UC Statewide IPM Program and UC ANR home-garden guidance anchor the summer heat-exclusion mechanism (desert summer daytime highs past 95-110F; fruit set fails above ~95F as viable pollen collapses). The two-window structure (winter-spring main + September fall crop bracketing a lethal summer) is the canonical desert pattern; UC Riverside County MG (Coachella low desert, read-not-cited, not catalogued) and University of Arizona Extension 'Growing Tomatoes' (low-desert two-season, read-not-cited, AZ source) independently corroborate. Two-window with structured summer heat_pause.
plantings_provenance.heat_inversion_note: Inverted calendar: winter is the growing season, summer is the exclusion. Main plant window Dec-Mar (mild winter), summer heat_pause Jun-Aug, fall replant Sep. This is the heat-inverted mirror of the cool-limited ca_north_coast and the mild ca_south_coast.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_present: Jun-Aug (months 6,7,8). Climatic-absolute exclusion: Imperial/Coachella peak summer (>95-110F) stops fruit set. Mechanism anchored to UC IPM / UC ANR 8159 (>95F collapses viable pollen).
plantings_provenance.cherry_pause_not_narrowed: CONTRAST se_gulf (gs_exemplar_finding_001): there, extra heat tolerance narrowed the pause to a single month (month 7). HERE the desert pause is NOT narrowed by roma resistance -- peak desert summer heat is so extreme that even heat-tolerant roma types cannot set fruit. The Jun-Aug pause is the real lethal span regardless of roma resistance. This is a per-region roma judgment, not a universal narrowing.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: start the seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before transplanting
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start roma tomato seed indoors about six weeks before the spring transplant date. For a mid-to-late-March beginner transplant in Las Cruces (zone 8) that places seeding in early-to-mid February. The Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces chart starts seed earlier, in mid-January, to feed the experienced-grower early-March transplant. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Plant these after all danger of frost
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set roma tomato transplants out in spring once frost danger has passed. For Las Cruces and the Mesilla Valley (zone 8, Chihuahuan high desert) the average last frost is around March 19, so a beginner-safe transplant date is mid-to-late March. The Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces chart shows an earlier, early-March transplant (seed started indoors in mid-January); that earlier date reflects experienced-grower practice setting plants out right at or just before the frost-free point, often with frost protection. For a first season, waiting until after the last frost is the more reliable choice. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: 55 to 70 days
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roma tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after transplanting. With a mid-to-late-March transplant the spring crop in Las Cruces begins coming in from about mid-to-late May, well ahead of the peak midsummer heat that suppresses fruit set. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: do not set fruit well ... when daytime temperatures exceed 95
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop winds down as peak midsummer heat sets in and daytime temperatures above about 95 degrees F push fruit set toward failure. Roma, a standard paste type, is no more heat tolerant than other large-fruited tomatoes and stops setting fruit as midsummer heat arrives. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: start the seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before transplanting
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed indoors about six weeks before the midsummer transplant date, roughly early-to-mid June. For the fall window choose an early-maturing paste variety, since roma needs about 70 to 80 days to mature. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Tomatoes ... start ... transplant
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out after the peak of midsummer heat, in mid-to-late July, so plants establish as temperatures begin to ease and produce into the cooler fall. The local Las Cruces planting chart shows this second tomato transplant window; it is timed to follow the brief midsummer fruit-set pause. (Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart; NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: 55 to 70 days
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about two months after the midsummer transplant, bringing first roma tomatoes in roughly late September into October. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: harvest ... before frost
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop produces into the cooler autumn and is harvested up to the first fall frost, which in Las Cruces (zone 8 high desert) arrives around mid-November. Roma types, heat resistant and quick to mature, make the most of the shorter fall window. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the warm arid Southwest, daytime temperatures above about 95°F at the peak of midsummer push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail (NMSU Circular 457 gives 95°F day and 55°F night as the set thresholds). Roma types are heat resistant and the arid climate's cool nights aid recovery, so this pause is brief, roughly the single hottest month, and shorter for roma than for large-fruited tomatoes. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: Where you live gets very hot in midsummer, so roma tomatoes grow best in two rounds. Plant the first round in mid to late March, after the last frost, and you will start picking tomatoes in mid to late May. When it gets hottest, around July, the plants stop setting new tomatoes for a few weeks because the flowers cannot set in the heat. Plant a second round in mid to late July for a fall crop that keeps going into November, until the first frost. Roma tomatoes handle heat well and your cool nights help, so they bounce back faster than big tomatoes.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid Southwest, including Las Cruces and the Mesilla Valley in zone 8, gives roma tomatoes two planting windows around the peak of summer heat. Set the first crop out in mid to late March, once frost danger has passed (the average last frost is around March 19), for a harvest that begins in mid to late May, well before the most intense heat arrives. Through the hottest stretch of midsummer, daytime temperatures above about 95°F suppress fruit set, so production lulls for roughly the single hottest month, around July. Set a second crop out in mid to late July, transplanting through the heat so plants establish and then set as temperatures ease, for a fall harvest that runs into early November until the first frost. Roma varieties handle the heat better than large slicing tomatoes and the cool desert nights help them keep setting, so the summer lull is shorter for them. A note on sourcing: the spring window follows NMSU statewide guidance and Las Cruces frost data, while the second, midsummer planting comes from the Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces planting chart, a single regional Master Gardener source that we have not been able to corroborate independently. The Dona Ana chart also shows an earlier, early-March transplant for the spring crop, which reflects experienced-grower practice setting out right at the frost-free point; a mid-to-late-March transplant is the more reliable first-season choice.

plantings_provenance.structure_basis: Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart shows two distinct tomato transplant windows (Path A chart read 2026-06-07: 1st transplant early March, 2nd transplant mid-July) separated by a midsummer set-failure window; NMSU Circular 457 fruit-set thresholds (>95F day) plus Mesilla Valley high-desert summer climate independently support a midsummer set-failure pause at month 7. Spring dates frost-anchored (arid_highland); fall dates single-source (MG chart, uncorroborated, disclosed).
plantings_provenance.spring_date_basis: Spring transplant timed to the zone-8 arid_highland last frost (Mar 19; Chihuahuan high desert, BSk; confirmed against NOAA 30% last-32F for Las Cruces = Mar 20). Beginner-safe plant-out mid-to-late March. The Dona Ana County MG chart's earlier early-March transplant (seed mid-Jan) is the seasoned/source anchor, reflecting experienced-grower practice at/just before frost-free. Beginner-safety divergence (hybrid ruling, same pattern as low_desert_az). CORRECTS the prior desert-analogy May transplant.
plantings_provenance.fall_window_basis: Fall transplant window (mid-to-late July; start indoors mid-June) taken from the Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces chart (Path A chart read, 2026-06-07: tomato row shows 1st planting start mid-Jan -> transplant early March; 2nd planting start mid-June -> transplant mid-July). SINGLE-SOURCE, not independently corroborated; disclosed in region_notes_seasoned. Harvest re-derived to arid_highland first frost (Nov 12).
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_basis: Roma-narrowed to month 7 only (set-failure dip, not a plant/harvest exclusion). The chart transplants the fall crop IN mid-July, so July is not a do-not-plant month; it is the peak fruit-set-failure window (CR457: >95F day stops set). Calendar token at month 7 = heat_pause, mirroring the shipped se_gulf zone-8 roma cell (same biology: fall transplant into peak-heat July, plant action carried by second_planting{} on its own track). heat_pause.months=[7] kept coherent with calendar[Jul]=heat_pause for release_verify. Mesilla Valley zone 8 is hot but arid with strong nighttime recovery (nights into the 60s), unlike the zone-9 low deserts where the pause is climatic-absolute and not narrowed. Beefsteak re-derives independently and will likely hold a wider pause.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: start seeds indoors or in a greenhouse in January, six weeks before the last frost
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the spring crop, start roma tomato seed indoors in late fall to early winter so transplants are ready by February. The Arizona low desert runs an inverted, race-the-heat calendar: the spring crop must be in the ground early to set fruit before summer. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: start in mid-March in Southern Arizona as soon as frost damage has ended
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the spring roma tomato crop out in the low desert in February, right after the last frost, so plants flower and set fruit before the summer heat wall. In Phoenix and the Maricopa low desert that heat wall hits hard by late May, so early planting is essential. Choose short-season roma or plum types (45 to 80 days). (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: Choose short-season varieties (less than 70 days)
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop begins ripening about two months after the February transplant, bringing fruit in April and May before the heat shuts production down. Short-season roma types make the narrow spring window. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Poor fruit development during the heat of summer in southern Arizona (July - August) is expected
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring harvest ends in late May to June as summer heat halts fruit set. A separate fall crop (see second planting) reopens the season in September after the heat passes. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

start_indoors.label: fall
start_indoors.source_quote: Start new seeds for September planting in June
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed in June (or take cuttings from straggly spring plants in August) so transplants are ready for a September planting. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

plant_out.label: fall
plant_out.source_quote: Gardeners will get a second chance for healthy tomatoes in September, when summer heat has passed
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out in September as the summer heat passes. Without the hard deadline the spring crop faces, fall plants have time to grow and produce well into the mild low-desert winter. Many low-desert gardeners consider fall their better tomato season. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_start.label: fall
harvest_start.source_quote: hit peak production in October and November
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop reaches peak production in October and November, when low-desert weather is mild. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_end.label: fall
harvest_end.source_quote: fall plants can grow and produce well into December in the low desert
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall harvest runs into December in the low desert before winter frost ends the season. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: The low-desert summer is a hard heat exclusion. In the Phoenix and Maricopa low desert, poor fruit development is expected through the peak of summer (July and August), because daytime temperatures above 90°F reduce the number of viable pollen grains and stop fruit set. The main spring crop runs from a mid-March transplant through late June, then the July-August peak halts set; planting resumes in September once the heat passes. As in the California desert, this pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by extra heat tolerance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

As in the California desert, this pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by extra heat tolerance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Yuma, and similar), the calendar is flipped and you get two short tomato seasons around a too-hot summer. Plant your spring crop early, in February right after the last frost, and pick fruit in April and May before the heat. From about June through August it is too hot (over 90°F) for tomatoes to set fruit, so there is a summer break. Then plant a second crop in September for tomatoes through fall and into December, which many desert gardeners think is the better season. Pick fast-maturing roma types (45 to 80 days) so they finish before the heat. Even heat-loving roma tomatoes cannot set fruit in peak desert summer.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Maricopa, Yuma) grows roma tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar around a hard summer heat exclusion. The spring crop is transplanted early, in February right after the last frost, and must set fruit before the heat wall arrives by late May; it harvests April into June. June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs above 90°F collapse viable pollen), so planting pauses. A fall crop is set out in September once the heat passes and produces through the mild desert fall into December, often the more productive of the two seasons. Short-season roma and plum types (45 to 80 days) are essential to make the narrow spring window. As in the California desert, the summer pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by extra heat tolerance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

Maricopa County planting calendar az1005 and the AZ1615 Yuma guide corroborate the spring (Feb) / fall (Sep) two-season structure. Spring transplant Feb (race the late-May heat wall); fall plant Sep. Two-window with structured summer heat_pause.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula the roma tomato season is the cool, dry half of the year, so seed is started in late summer for fall transplanting. UF/IFAS South Florida starts tomato seed in August for the fall garden; counting back about six weeks from the September-October transplant window places indoor sowing in August. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Easy crops that can be grown now include beans, broccoli, carrots, collards, lettuce, green onions, peppers, radishes, spinach, and tomatoes
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set roma tomato transplants out across the long cool-season window. The South Florida calendar opens the fall tomato transplant in September-October and keeps planting open through February, the last month to plant tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Frost is rare on the peninsula, so this is one continuous cross-year window rather than separate spring and fall crops. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roma tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after transplant (about 70 to 80 days to maturity). With fall transplanting from September into the fall, the peninsula's cool-season harvest begins in November and carries through the mild winter and spring. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Peninsular roma tomato production runs through the mild winter and spring and winds down as peak-summer heat arrives. Larger-fruited tomatoes stop earlier and are grown as a cool-season crop only; roma types, being heat resistant, hold a productive tail into early summer before the July-August pause. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula the summer gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; roma types are heat resistant, so the exclusion is narrowed to the two peak months for them, and a few varieties keep setting through it. UF/IFAS South Florida lists roma tomatoes among the crops that can still be planted in June, and reopens tomato planting with August seed-starting for the fall garden. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: On the Florida peninsula (roughly Orlando south to Miami and the Keys), roma tomatoes are a cool-weather crop. Frost is rare here, so you plant in the fall, from about September through February, and pick through the mild winter and spring. The hard part is summer, not winter. In July and August it gets too hot, over about 78°F at night, for tomatoes to set fruit, so plants take a break then. Big slicing tomatoes only grow in the cool season here, but roma types handle the heat better, so they hold on a little into early summer and a few keep going. Pick fast-maturing roma varieties and start your seeds indoors in August for fall planting.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11, south of about Orlando) grows roma tomatoes on a single long cool-season window rather than the spring-and-fall pattern of cooler regions. Because frost is rare, the planting window runs continuously from the fall transplant in September and October through February, the last month UF/IFAS lists for planting tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Production carries through the mild winter and spring. The limiting season is summer: in July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) cause blossom drop and fruit-set failure. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; roma types are heat resistant, so the exclusion narrows to those two peak months for them and a few varieties keep setting through it. Start seed indoors in August for fall transplanting, and choose fast-maturing roma types. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UF/IFAS divides Florida into North, Central, and South planting regions; the Florida peninsula (zones 10-11) is South Florida, served by one calendar (ENH1191/EP452 South Florida Gardening Calendar) plus VH021's statewide guide. Oct 2024) opens the fall tomato transplant in September-October ('tomatoes' listed in the October planting list) and closes the cool-season planting in February ('last month to plant ... tomatoes for a late spring harvest'); August is tomato seed-start for the fall garden. start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: In Hawaii (tropical, zone 11) roma tomato has no frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window: CTAHR states tomato can be "grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing varieties adapted" to the local area. Seed is started indoors in any month and transplanted about 3 to 5 weeks after sowing (CTAHR HGV-5); the plant-level baseline of six weeks indoors is the cooler-mainland figure. The year-round window rests on cultivar choice -- the locally bred, nematode- and disease-resistant UH cultivars (the determinate 'Anahu', 'Healani', 'Kewalo' and the indeterminate hybrids in the N-series) plus roma types -- rather than on hitting a particular season. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set roma tomato transplants out in any month of the year. CTAHR's home-garden tomato guidance gives a year-round planting capability for most of Hawaii contingent on adapted varieties, with no spring/fall bracketing and no summer exclusion stated; the limiting factors named are disease, insect, and rain pressure, not a season boundary. Keeping plants caged or staked and off the ground, and irrigating the soil rather than the foliage (in the morning when overhead water is used), are the management levers. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roma tomatoes begin ripening about two months after transplant. CTAHR gives most tomato varieties 60 to 80 days to mature; roma types sit at the fast end, and the crop-level roma figure is roughly 70 to 80 days (about 62 mid). Because planting is year-round and the UH-bred hybrids are indeterminate -- producing continuously while healthy -- harvest is effectively continuous across the year from successive and overlapping plantings. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: There is no season-ending harvest boundary in tropical zone 11: roma tomato is planted and harvested continuously through the year. Production does not close at a frost or at a sustained-heat date; it is refreshed by successive plantings, which also helps stay ahead of the disease and pest pressure CTAHR flags as the real constraint in Hawaii. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

11.zone_notes: Hawaii tropical (USDA zone 11; frost-free, frost_free_days 365). No frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for roma tomato: CTAHR gives tomato a year-round planting capability for most of Hawaii, contingent on adapted varieties. The limiting factors are disease (tomato spotted wilt and tobacco mosaic viruses, and warm-wet leaf spots and blights), insect pests (whitefly, leafminer, fruit fly, thrips), and fruit cracking in heavy rain, managed with resistant locally-bred UH cultivars, staking or caging to keep fruit off the ground, morning soil-only irrigation, and successive plantings, rather than by pausing a season. Roma types and the compact determinates (for example 'Healani') also do well in 3 to 5 gallon containers here.
11.calendar_basis: Roma tomato is grown YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free, frost_free_days 365) and no summer no-sow exclusion: CTAHR HGV-5 states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing varieties adapted to the area, and names no seasonal fruit-set gap. This is the per-region source finding: the roma summer heat_pause documented for the Florida peninsula and the deserts does not universalize to Hawaii's oceanic lowland (guardrail: heat_pause is read from the source per region, never defaulted). Hawaii's challenge is disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant locally-bred cultivars and cultural practice, not a production stop. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field); year_round:true makes the all-active calendar's intent machine-readable. hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, roma tomatoes grow year-round, so you can start a few plants in any month rather than waiting for a season. There is no frost here, so the calendar is open all year. The hard part is not heat but pests and disease, which thrive in the warm, humid weather, plus heavy rain that can crack the fruit. Give yourself the best odds: pick varieties bred for Hawaii or tough roma types, keep plants up off the ground on a cage or stake, water the soil rather than the leaves (in the morning if you use a sprinkler), and start a fresh planting every few months so you always have healthy young plants coming on. Roma types and a few compact varieties also do well in 3 to 5 gallon pots.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical calendar is aseasonal for roma tomato: plant and harvest year-round, with no frost anchor and no summer heat pause. University of Hawaii CTAHR states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in the state by choosing locally adapted varieties, and names no seasonal fruit-set exclusion. This is the per-region finding, not a default: the roma summer heat_pause documented for the Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11) and for the low and high deserts does not carry to Hawaii's oceanic lowland, whose nights do not sustain the fruit-set-stopping highs of peninsular summer. The binding constraints here are disease and pests: tomato spotted wilt virus (thrips-vectored) and tobacco mosaic virus, plus warm-wet fungal and bacterial leaf spots and blights, whitefly, leafminer, and fruit fly, along with fruit cracking in heavy rain. CTAHR's primary lever is genetic: the locally bred, root-knot-nematode- and disease-tolerant UH cultivars, the determinate open-pollinated 'Anahu', 'Healani', and 'Kewalo' and the indeterminate N-series hybrids that fruit continuously while healthy; roma types and compact determinates such as 'Healani' suit 3 to 5 gallon containers. Cultural practice carries the rest: stake or cage to keep fruit off the ground, irrigate the soil (not the foliage; morning if overhead), and refresh with successive plantings. Most varieties mature in 60 to 80 days, roma types at the fast end. Windows verified against University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5 (Home Garden Tomato), with the 1943 bulletin B-91 (Home Gardening in Hawaii) as historical corroboration only.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Roma's whole strategy, one concentrated batch of paste tomatoes for sauce or canning, is a harder sell in the maritime Pacific Northwest's cool summer than in a hotter climate, because that flush needs sustained warmth to size and ripen all at once. Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before setting plants out in May, choose an early-maturing paste variety rather than a full 80-day type, and give it the warmest, sunniest spot you have. A cloche or wall-o-water at transplant time helps it get going. In a warm summer you will get a good concentrated harvest for canning; in a cool one, the flush can arrive late and only partly ripen, so plan to pick some fruit green near the first fall frost and finish it indoors.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Roma's determinate, one-flush habit is a genuine stretch in the maritime Pacific Northwest: the concentrated fruit set needs sustained summer warmth to size and ripen together, and this region's cool, marine-tempered summer does not reliably supply it. Set transplants out after the last frost once the soil has warmed, in May in the valley or across OSU's wider May-June coastal window, but plan around the long end of the 70-to-80-day maturity range, and favor an early-maturing paste variety over a full 80-day type. Reserve the warmest, most sheltered microsite for it; a cloche or wall-o-water at transplant helps bank early heat. The flush can run late into fall behind the region's mild first frost, and in a cool year may only partially ripen; pick remaining fruit green ahead of frost rather than lose the batch. crops.description_seasoned: Roma tomatoes, also called paste or plum tomatoes, are the workhorse of the sauce and canning garden. Unlike the cherry class, roma is determinate: the plant grows to a compact, bushy size, sets most of its fruit in a few heavy clusters, and ripens that crop over a concentrated two to four week window rather than trickling out fruit all season. That concentrated set is the whole point, giving you a batch large enough to cook down into sauce, paste, or canned tomatoes in one or two sessions. The fruit is egg to plum shaped, meaty and dense, with thick walls, few seeds, and little juice, which is exactly what you want for cooking because there is less water to boil off. A determinate plant stays short enough to hold up in a sturdy cage rather than a tall stake, and it needs little to no pruning: clear the suckers below the first flower cluster and otherwise leave the plant full. The disorder roma growers fight most is blossom-end rot, a dark sunken patch on the bottom of the fruit driven by uneven calcium delivery when soil moisture swings; steady watering and mulch are the fix, not calcium sprays. In warm zones (9 to 11) a second planting extends the canning season; in short-season zones (3 to 5) choose an early paste variety so the concentrated set finishes before first frost.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when the fruit is fully and uniformly red and firm to the touch. Paste tomatoes are typically harvested a touch firmer than slicing types because they are destined for cooking, where dense, meaty flesh holds up. Full color indicates complete lycopene synthesis and peak flavor. The fruit should detach with a gentle twist. Because a determinate roma ripens much of its crop together, it is fine to let the fruit color up and pick in one or two large harvests for a canning batch. Harvest in the morning when cooler.

pet_safe.note: Ripe tomatoes are fine, but the leaves, stems, and unripe fruit are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Bell Pepper

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Bell pepper wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter, and a soil that warms early and holds steady moisture. As a warm-season crop it sulks in cold, wet ground, so a sandy loam that warms quickly in spring suits it better than a heavy, slow-warming clay. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, and on heavy or cool soils many growers lay black plastic or fabric mulch to raise soil temperature and set transplants into warmer ground. Even soil moisture in a freely draining bed is the target, because the wide swings between dry and soaked that a poorly drained soil produces are the direct cause of the calcium-starved blossom-end rot bell peppers are prone to.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Bell peppers like rich, well-drained soil that warms up in the sun, since they are warm-season plants that dislike cold, soggy ground. Mix in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch laid down before planting warms the soil and gives peppers the head start they want. Aim for soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, because uneven watering is what causes the dark, sunken blossom-end rot on the bottom of the fruit.

ph.note_seasoned: Bell pepper grows best at a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, with Clemson placing the sweet spot near 6.0 to 6.5 and Minnesota noting peppers do well up to about 7.0. In that band the nutrients peppers need, including the calcium that guards against blossom-end rot, stay most available. Peppers tolerate a somewhat wider range, roughly 5.5 to 7.5, but uptake of iron, manganese, and other micronutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline, showing as yellowing between the veins of the youngest leaves. Alkaline soils common across the interior West often need sulfur worked in ahead of planting; most Eastern and Midwestern soils sit naturally near the target. A soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant.
ph.note_beginner: Bell peppers like slightly acidic soil, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where peppers take up nutrients best, including the calcium that prevents blossom-end rot. If your soil runs alkaline, common in the dry interior West, you may need to add sulfur before planting. An inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress after fruit set
fertilizer.type: Balanced at planting, then calcium nitrate at fruit set
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress about three to four weeks after transplanting and again once fruit sets
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 at planting, then calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) as a side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Bell pepper is a moderate feeder that rewards restraint with nitrogen. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10, or 2 to 3 pounds of it per 100 square feet, into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate about three to four weeks after transplanting and again as the first fruits set. Hold nitrogen back early and never overdo it: too much drives a big, bushy, dark-green plant that flowers late and sets little fruit. The calcium nitrate side-dress does double duty, feeding the plant while supplying the calcium that, paired with even watering, heads off blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Bell peppers like steady but modest feeding, and going heavy on nitrogen backfires. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the soil before planting. Then, a few weeks after planting and again once the first peppers set, feed with a nitrogen fertilizer like calcium nitrate. Do not overdo it: too much nitrogen gives you a large leafy plant with few peppers. Calcium nitrate also supplies calcium, which, along with even watering, helps prevent blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your bell pepper is setting its first fruit, a good time to side-dress with a calcium nitrate source to feed the plant and supply calcium against blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your bell pepper is setting fruit. Feed it now with a nitrogen fertilizer such as calcium nitrate to keep it producing and to help prevent blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked in at planting, then a calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) side-dress three to four weeks after transplanting and again at fruit set. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which gives leaf at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 5-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed such as calcium nitrate once the plant is growing well and setting fruit. Do not overdo the nitrogen or you get all leaves and few peppers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common rate is 2 to 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before transplanting. For the side-dress, Clemson suggests about 5 pounds of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 1000 square feet or 300 feet of row, applied three to four weeks after transplanting and repeated three to four weeks later, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix 2 to 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet (or a few inches of compost) into the soil before planting. Then, a few weeks after planting and again at fruit set, scratch a small amount of calcium nitrate into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in.

companions.note_seasoned: Most pepper companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The aromatic-herb and flower companions (basil, marigold, nasturtium, alliums) are grown to deter or trap the aphids and thrips that trouble peppers and to draw beneficial insects, a plausible, habitat-based effect rather than an isolated one. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep peppers away from their Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which share the full pepper pest and disease complex.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful pepper companions are strong-smelling herbs and flowers like basil, marigold, and nasturtium, which can help deter or lure away aphids and other pests. The one rule that really matters is to keep peppers away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which are all close relatives and share the same pests and soil diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Basil
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Basil is a classic pepper neighbor. Its strong scent is thought to help confuse soft-bodied pests like aphids and thrips, and it tucks neatly between young pepper plants. A pleasant, low-risk companion.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional interplanting with peppers; the aromatic foliage is thought to deter aphids and thrips and to draw pollinators and beneficial insects. The effect is habitat-based and traditional rather than trial-isolated for pepper.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Basil is a long-standing companion for peppers; aromatic-herb pest confusion is plausible and habitat-based, not trial-isolated for pepper.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigold
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Marigolds are a classic companion flower for peppers, grown to help keep pests down. Mostly tradition, but cheerful and low-risk.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A long-standing companion tradition near peppers; French marigold grown as a cover crop has documented nematode-suppressive effects, though the interplanted marigold-pepper pest benefit is traditional rather than trial-isolated.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: French marigold has documented nematode suppression as a cover crop; the interplanted marigold-pepper effect is traditional, not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are often planted near peppers to lure aphids away from the crop. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planted as a trap and deterrent for aphids, drawing them off the peppers. Trap cropping is a documented principle, though the specific nasturtium-pepper effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap cropping and aphid attraction by nasturtium is documented in principle; the nasturtium-pepper pairing is not trial-isolated.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep peppers away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant. They are all close relatives that share the same soil diseases and pests, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share pepper's pest and disease complex, including bacterial leaf spot, the mosaic viruses, Phytophthora blight, anthracnose, and aphids. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 year cycle.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant are all Solanaceae and share pepper's pest and disease complex; grouping them concentrates that pressure. A sound epidemiology and rotation principle, not a trial-tested adjacency.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from peppers and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong T1 mechanism for a pepper-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel is a widely cautioned anti-companion said to inhibit many vegetables; the pepper-fennel antagonism is garden lore without a strong T1 mechanism.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, most often green peach aphid, cluster on growing tips and the undersides of leaves, curling and yellowing the foliage, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit the mosaic viruses that mottle and distort pepper leaves, which is their most serious effect on the crop.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft green insects gather on new growth and the undersides of leaves, making them curl and yellow, often with a sticky film and black mold. They can also spread plant viruses to peppers.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species, predominantly green peach aphid, that suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces. As virus carriers they matter out of proportion to the feeding damage they do.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that multiply quickly in warm weather, especially on soft, over-fertilized growth. They also carry viruses from plant to plant.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants and slows virus spread.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work. A silver reflective mulch under young plants helps keep aphids off.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ease up on nitrogen fertilizer. Aphids multiply fastest on the soft, lush growth that heavy feeding pushes out, so a moderately fed pepper gives them less to build on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen drives the succulent growth aphids favor; restrained feeding slows colony buildup on growing tips and leaf undersides before any other step is needed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay a silver reflective mulch, a shiny sheet spread on the soil, under young peppers. It helps keep aphids from landing, and since aphids carry plant viruses, it slows virus spread too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch deters colonizing aphids from young plants, and because virus transmission is their most serious effect on peppers, cutting early landings slows virus spread as well as feeding injury.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the aphids off with a strong jet of water from the hose, aiming at the undersides of the leaves where they gather. Go back every few days while they keep returning.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water jet dislodges colonies from tips and leaf undersides; populations rebuild quickly in warm weather, so repeat at a few days' interval.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps all eat aphids and usually bring them under control on their own. Welcome these helpers, and avoid spraying broadly so you do not wipe them out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserved ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually bring aphids under control; supporting natural enemies rather than spraying broadly keeps that pressure working for you.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the colonies keep growing, spray insecticidal soap onto the undersides of the leaves where the aphids sit, and repeat every few days. It only works where it actually touches them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap demands thorough coverage of leaf undersides, since it acts only on contact; repeat every few days to catch the colonies that rebuild.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil made for plants, is the other option at this step. Like soap, it has to coat the aphids, so wet the undersides of the leaves well and repeat every few days.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil is the alternative contact material at this rung, carrying the same coverage demand on leaf undersides and the same need for repeat passes.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny shot-hole punctures riddle the leaves, a scatter of small round holes that is the classic flea-beetle signature. Damage is worst on seedlings and young transplants, whose small leaf area a heavy infestation can shred; established peppers tolerate considerable feeding. Brush a plant and the small dark beetles spring away like fleas.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The leaves are peppered with lots of tiny round holes, as if hit by birdshot. It hits young plants hardest. Touch the plant and you will see tiny dark beetles jump away.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several flea beetle species that feed on pepper foliage, overwintering as adults in debris and emerging to attack the earliest, most vulnerable plants in spring. Young transplants are far more at risk than large, established plants.
pests.cause_beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas and chew tiny holes in the leaves. They are most active in spring and target young plants early in the season.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover until they are large and vigorous, removing it at flowering so pollinators can reach the blooms. Set out stout, well-hardened transplants so plants can outgrow the damage, and treat heavy early infestations with spinosad or kaolin clay.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are big and strong, then take it off when they flower. Setting out larger transplants helps them outgrow the damage. For heavy attacks, an organic spray such as spinosad helps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, delay setting plants out until soil and air are warm so they grow away fast, and clean up crop debris and weeds that harbor overwintering adults.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants early with row cover, set out larger transplants into warm soil so they grow quickly, and clear away weeds and old plant debris where the beetles hide over winter.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear away weeds and old plant debris at the end of the season. The adult beetles spend the winter hiding in that litter and come out in spring aimed at your youngest plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Adults overwinter in crop debris and weedy cover; clearing both lowers the spring emergence that falls hardest on the earliest, most vulnerable transplants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover young plants with a floating row cover, a light fabric that lets in sun and water while keeping beetles out, from transplanting until they are big and sturdy. Take it off when they flower so pollinators can reach the blooms.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover from transplanting excludes beetles through the window when leaf area is smallest; remove at flowering for pollinator access, by which point established plants tolerate considerable feeding.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For a heavy attack on young plants, coat the leaves with kaolin clay, a fine white mineral powder you mix with water and spray on. The film helps deter the beetles from feeding.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Kaolin's particle film is a tool for heavy early infestations on small transplants; established peppers shrug off the shot-holing and rarely need treatment.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a heavy early attack is shredding young plants, spinosad, an organic spray derived from a soil bacterium, helps. Bigger established plants can usually outgrow the damage without it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reserve spinosad for heavy early infestations on transplants whose small leaf area is at risk; mature plants tolerate the feeding, so routine application is not warranted.

pests.name: Pepper maggot
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fruit that colors up early and unevenly, sometimes with a soft, rotting spot and a pinhole scar on the skin, and a white, legless maggot tunneling in the flesh inside. Cut the pepper open and the winding feeding channels and the maggot give it away. It is a regional pest, most troublesome in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Some peppers turn red too early and rot from the inside, and cutting one open reveals a small white maggot tunneling through the flesh. It is mainly a problem in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larva of the pepper maggot fly, which lays eggs in developing fruit through mid to late summer, leaving a tiny egg-puncture scar. The maggot feeds inside, and infested fruit ripens prematurely and often rots.
pests.cause_beginner: A fly that lays its eggs in young peppers in summer; the maggot that hatches feeds inside the fruit, causing early ripening and rot. It is worst where the pest is established locally.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for an infested fruit, so control targets the egg-laying flies: remove and destroy affected peppers promptly to break the cycle, and where pressure is high time labeled sprays to the egg-laying period. A yellow sticky trap helps confirm when the flies are active.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot save an infested pepper, so pick off and destroy any that ripen early or show a pinhole scar to stop the next generation. Removing wild host weeds like horsenettle nearby helps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Remove nearby wild solanaceous weeds such as horsenettle that host the fly, rotate peppers away from last year's bed, clean up and destroy infested fruit, and in problem areas protect fruit with a labeled spray timed to the flight or with row cover before fruit set.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear away wild nightshade weeds nearby, move peppers to a new spot each year, and destroy any infested fruit. In areas where it is a known problem, a floating row cover put on before fruit forms keeps the flies out.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear out wild weeds in the nightshade family growing near the garden, especially horsenettle. They host the fly that starts this problem.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Wild solanaceous weeds such as horsenettle host the pepper maggot fly; removing them from around the planting takes away the reservoir it works from.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant your peppers in a different spot from last year so the flies do not pick up right where they left off.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotating peppers away from last year's bed puts distance between the crop and the population carried over from the previous planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off and destroy any pepper that turns red too early or shows a tiny pinhole scar on its skin. You cannot save a fruit once the maggot is inside, but removing it stops the next generation.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no rescue for infested fruit, so prompt removal and destruction of prematurely coloring or scarred peppers is what breaks the cycle; culls left in place finish rearing the next generation.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where this pest is a known local problem, put a floating row cover, a light fabric barrier, over the plants before fruit starts to form so the flies cannot reach the peppers.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: In problem areas, cover before fruit set to exclude the egg-laying flies; once eggs are in the fruit, nothing applied later reaches the maggot.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hang a yellow sticky trap, a bright card coated in glue, near the plants. It helps confirm when the flies are active so your other steps are timed right.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A yellow sticky trap serves as a flight monitor, helping confirm when adults are active so exclusion and any treatment can be timed to the egg-laying period.

pests.name: Tomato and tobacco hornworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large sections of leaf, and sometimes whole shoots, are stripped down to the veins, with dark pellet droppings on the leaves below. The culprits are big green tomato or tobacco hornworms, up to four inches long, that blend into the stems and are easiest to find by their frass.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Whole leaves vanish, leaving just the veins, with dark droppings on the leaves below. The cause is a large green caterpillar that hides against the stems, easier to spot by its droppings than by sight.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tomato and tobacco hornworms, the larvae of large sphinx moths, which feed on solanaceous foliage including pepper from midsummer on. A few caterpillars can do conspicuous damage given their size, and they will chew into fruit as well as leaves.
pests.cause_beginner: Big green caterpillars, the young of large moths, that feed on pepper leaves and fruit mostly in mid to late summer. Even a few can strip a lot of foliage.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick the caterpillars, which is effective in a home garden, and apply Bacillus thuringiensis to younger larvae where numbers are high. Leave any hornworm studded with white parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the wasps will kill it and breed more.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them in soapy water. If you find one covered in small white capsules, leave it, those are parasitic wasps that will do the work for you. An organic Bt spray works on the smaller caterpillars.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till the soil in fall to destroy overwintering pupae, scout for frass and stripped leaves from midsummer, and encourage the parasitic wasps and other natural enemies that keep hornworms in check.
pests.prevention_beginner: Turn the soil at the end of the season to destroy the pupae, watch for droppings and missing leaves from midsummer, and welcome the helpful wasps that attack hornworms.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Turn the soil over in fall once the plants come out. The caterpillars pass the winter underground as pupae, the resting stage between caterpillar and moth, and tilling destroys them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Fall tillage destroys overwintering pupae in the bed, trimming the local carryover before the next summer's moths emerge.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the big caterpillars off by hand and drop them into soapy water. They blend into the stems, so look for the dark droppings, called frass, on the leaves below and search just above that spot.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Handpicking is effective at home-garden scale; frass on lower leaves locates larvae far more reliably than scanning the stems they match.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If you find a hornworm covered in small white capsules, leave it right where it is. Those are the cocoons of parasitic wasps that will kill it and go on to attack other hornworms.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Leave any larva studded with parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the emerging wasps kill it and breed more; encouraging these natural enemies is part of what keeps hornworm numbers in check.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When there are more caterpillars than you can pick, Bt, short for Bacillus thuringiensis, is an organic spray that works on the smaller, younger ones.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Apply Bt where numbers run high, aimed at younger larvae; it is the material for small caterpillars, with handpicking covering the full-grown ones.

pests.name: Pepper weevil
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Buds and small fruit drop from the plant, and cut-open fruit is black and frass-filled inside, its core rotted where a grub has fed. The dark, long-snouted adult weevil, about an eighth of an inch, feeds on buds and leaves. It is a serious pest of the warm South and, once established, is very hard to shake.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Flower buds and little peppers drop off the plant, and peppers that hold on are black and rotten inside. A tiny dark, long-nosed beetle is the cause. It is mainly a problem in the warm South.
pests.cause_seasoned: Anthonomus eugenii, a small weevil whose larvae develop inside pepper buds and fruit. Adults feed on foliage and lay eggs in buds and young fruit, causing them to drop; multiple overlapping generations build fast in warm climates, and the pest overwinters on volunteer peppers and nightshade weeds.
pests.cause_beginner: A small weevil whose grubs develop inside pepper buds and fruit, causing them to drop and rot. It builds up quickly in warm weather and survives on leftover pepper plants and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no home-garden cure for infested fruit, so sanitation is central: pick up and destroy all dropped buds and fruit promptly to break the breeding cycle, remove volunteer peppers and nightshade weeds, and end the season by pulling and destroying spent plants. Where established, labeled sprays are timed to the adults.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot save infested peppers, so gather and destroy every dropped bud and fruit to stop the next generation, and pull up old pepper plants and nearby nightshade weeds at season's end. Keeping the area clean is the main defense.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean transplants (the weevil moves on infested plants), remove volunteer peppers and solanaceous weeds that harbor it, destroy dropped fruit through the season, and rotate away from last year's pepper ground.
pests.prevention_beginner: Buy healthy transplants, keep the garden free of leftover pepper plants and nightshade weeds, clean up dropped buds and fruit, and do not plant peppers in the same spot as last year.
