growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves reach 3 to 6 inches at about 37 to 50 days (baby leaf earlier); harvest outer leaves cut-and-come-again or cut the whole rosette above the crown for regrowth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Crop frequently in the cool morning, taking outer leaves or whole-plant cuts; pick faster as days lengthen and warm to beat the bolt.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you harvesting, and is the plant still flat (not bolting)?

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The center of the plant stretches up and starts to form a flower stalk, and the leaves turn bitter and arrow-shaped. This happens as the days get long and warm.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Harvest everything usable right away, because the leaves only get more bitter. Then pull the plant and use the space for something else.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your spinach starting to bolt (stretch up)?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The rosette elongates into a flowering stalk as days pass about 13 to 14 hours and warm; leaf flavor turns bitter and texture coarsens.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Strip the remaining usable leaves immediately, then pull the plant; an overwintered crop bolts in spring, so clear it before the stalk elongates.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Has it bolted, and have you cleared the bed?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your spinach should have 3 to 4 true leaves now. Thin to 3 to 4 inches apart for full plants and eat the thinnings as baby spinach.
notifications.body_beginner: Your spinach seedlings should be big enough to thin. Space them about 3 to 4 inches apart and eat the little ones you pull.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your spinach leaves should be 3 to 6 inches and tender. Crop the outer leaves or cut the whole rosette above the crown, and pick in the cool morning.
notifications.body_beginner: Your spinach leaves should be big enough to pick. Take the outer leaves or cut the whole plant about an inch above the soil so it can regrow.

notifications.title_beginner: Warm, long days ahead: pick your spinach
notifications.body_seasoned: Days are lengthening and warming, which triggers bolting in spinach. Harvest the spring crop promptly and clear bolting plants, since the leaves turn bitter once the stalk forms.
notifications.body_beginner: The days are getting long and warm, which makes spinach flower and turn bitter. Pick your spring spinach now while it is still good.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your spinach
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above about 75 to 80°F, especially with long days, pushes spinach to bolt and turns the leaves bitter. Keep moisture even, harvest promptly in the cool morning, and treat summer as off-season; in hot regions spinach is a fall-through-spring crop.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot weather makes spinach flower early and turn bitter. Water evenly, pick everything usable in the cool morning, and remember spinach is really a cool-season, fall-to-spring crop.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Spinach is very cold-hardy and tolerates frost; mature plants survive into the low 20s°F and overwinter under snow or row cover. For most freezes simply keep harvesting; in the coldest zones a low tunnel or row cover carries the crop through winter for an early-spring picking.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Spinach handles frost and even hard freezes well, so you usually do not need to do anything. In very cold areas, a row cover or low tunnel helps it survive winter and start up again in early spring.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 0.5 inch deep into a moist, uncrusted seedbed; spinach germinates from about 40°F and reliably at 60 to 70°F, but poorly above 75 to 85°F.
germination.text_beginner: Plant seeds about half an inch deep in damp soil. Spinach sprouts even in cold soil, so you can sow it very early.

germination.text_seasoned: For the fall crop, pre-sprout or water the furrow to cool it, or wait for soil to drop below 75°F, since warm soil is the main cause of poor late-summer stands.
germination.text_beginner: If you sow in late summer for fall, wait until the soil cools down, because spinach seeds will not come up well in hot soil.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to 3 to 4 inches at the 3-to-4-true-leaf stage and eat the thinnings; crowding stunts plants and speeds bolting.
seedling.text_beginner: Thin seedlings to about 3 to 4 inches apart once they have a few real leaves, and eat the ones you pull.

seedling.text_seasoned: Set floating row cover at sowing to exclude leafminer flies and flea beetles, the two main seedling pests.
seedling.text_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover to keep leafminer flies and flea beetles off.

established.text_seasoned: Hold even moisture at roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week and side-dress nitrogen once; drought and heat both trigger bolt.
established.text_beginner: Water steadily and give one feeding of nitrogen so the plants grow fast and tender and do not bolt early.

established.text_seasoned: Scout leaf undersides for aphids and the first leafminer mines; pick and destroy mined leaves before larvae drop to pupate.
established.text_beginner: Check under the leaves for aphids and pick off any leaves with pale tunnels (leafminer) before the bugs spread.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest at 3 to 6 inch leaf size, either outer leaves cut-and-come-again or the whole rosette cut about an inch above the crown for regrowth; pick in the cool morning.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick spinach when the leaves are 3 to 6 inches. Take outer leaves, or cut the whole plant an inch above the soil and let it regrow.

harvest.text_seasoned: As days lengthen and warm, harvest faster and watch for the central stalk; once it elongates, the leaves turn bitter, so clear the crop.
harvest.text_beginner: When the weather warms and the plant starts to stretch up, pick everything quickly, because the leaves turn bitter once it flowers.

bolting.text_seasoned: Spinach bolts mainly on long days (over about 13 to 14 hours), sped by heat and drought; there is no reversing it, so harvest and replace the planting.
bolting.text_beginner: Once spinach starts to flower it will not stop, so pick what you can and pull the plant. It bolts when days get long and warm.

bolting.text_seasoned: Favor the fall and overwintering crop, which grows under shortening days and rarely bolts; clear overwintered plants in spring before the stalk forms.
bolting.text_beginner: Fall is the best time to grow spinach because the short days keep it from bolting. Spinach that lives through winter will bolt in spring, so pick it before that.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single spinach plant yields a modest rosette of leaves, roughly 0.25 pound, over a few weeks; the crop is grown in quantity rather than per plant. Utah State cites about 4 to 6 pounds per 10-foot row.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each spinach plant gives a small bunch of leaves, so it is grown in rows or patches rather than one big plant. A short row of plants gives several pickings before they bolt.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Production peaks in the cool weeks of fall and early spring; a spring crop produces hard for a few weeks and then ends abruptly at bolt, while the fall crop holds longer under shortening days and, with cover, into winter.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Spinach produces the most in the cool weather of fall and early spring. A spring crop gives a few good weeks and then bolts, but a fall crop lasts longer and can carry into winter under a cover.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The key to total yield is timing and frequent picking: get the crop in early enough to mature before the bolt-triggering long days, harvest often once leaves size up, and lean on the fall and overwintering crops for the longest harvest. New growers usually sow too late in spring and lose the crop to bolt.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The trick with spinach is timing. Plant early in spring or in late summer for fall, and pick often once the leaves are big enough. Most beginners plant too late in spring and the plants flower before giving much, so try fall, which is easier.
factors_seasoned: Timing: a crop that matures before the long, warm days of late spring yields well; one sown too late bolts before producing. Fall and overwintering crops yield longest.
Variety: slow-bolting (long-standing) and disease-resistant types extend the productive window.
Even moisture and nitrogen: steady water and one nitrogen feed keep leaves tender and delay bolt; stress cuts yield and quality.
Spacing and airflow: thinning to 3 to 4 inches prevents crowding and the downy mildew that crowded, wet plantings invite.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing spinach planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by soil temperature, day length, and frost dates instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting (flower stalk and bitter leaves)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Long, warm days of late spring, or an overwintered plant flowering in spring.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your spinach shot up a central stalk and the leaves turned bitter and arrow-shaped. Spinach bolts (runs to flower) when the days get long and warm, which tells it to make seed, and once it bolts the leaves are no good. People often blame themselves, but it is the plant's normal response to day length. Next time, sow as early as you can in spring, choose slow-bolting varieties, and lean on a fall crop, which grows under short days and rarely bolts.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Sow very early in spring, use slow-bolting varieties, and grow a fall crop for the easiest, longest harvest.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The rosette elongated into a seed stalk and leaf quality collapsed. Bolting is driven mainly by lengthening days (over about 13 to 14 hours), accelerated by heat and drought; an overwintered crop bolts as spring warms. Growers most often sow too late in spring. Next time sow at first workable soil, use long-standing cultivars, hold even moisture, and favor the fall and overwintering window.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Long-day photoperiod, accelerated by heat and drought, or spring bolt of an overwintered plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow at first workable soil, choose long-standing cultivars, keep moisture even, and lean on fall and overwintering crops.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tunnels and tan blisters in the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Spinach leafminer, whose maggots tunnel inside the leaves.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You found pale winding tunnels that widened into tan blisters on the leaves, with no good way to wash them off. That is the spinach leafminer, a fly whose maggots eat inside the leaf. Because you eat the leaves, the damage ruins them. Next time, cover the plants with a row cover from the day you sow so the flies cannot lay eggs, pull weeds like lambsquarters that host them, and pick off mined leaves early.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use a row cover from sowing, pull host weeds, and remove mined leaves before the maggots spread.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Leaves showed serpentine mines opening into translucent blotches, the signature of the spinach leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami), which has three to four generations and overwinters as soil pupae. Sprays reach larvae inside the leaf poorly. Next time exclude the adult flies with row cover from sowing, control goosefoot weeds, rotate away from spinach, beets, and chard, and remove mined leaves before pupation.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Spinach leafminer larvae mining the leaves, with soil-overwintering pupae and multiple generations.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Row-cover from sowing, control host weeds, rotate the goosefoot crops, and strip mined leaves before larvae drop.

failure_diagnostics.label: Yellow patches with gray mold underneath
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Downy mildew (blue mold), the main spinach disease, in cool, damp, crowded conditions.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your spinach got pale yellow patches on top with fuzzy gray-purple mold underneath, and the leaves yellowed and collapsed. That is downy mildew, which thrives in the same cool, wet weather spinach likes, especially when plants are crowded and stay wet. Next time, grow resistant varieties, thin the plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and rotate where you plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow resistant varieties, thin for airflow, water at the base, and rotate your spinach bed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Chlorotic upper-surface lesions with grayish-purple sporulation beneath indicate downy mildew (Peronospora effusa), the most important spinach disease, favored by cool temperatures and long leaf wetness, with races that defeat resistance. Next time choose the broadest available race resistance, widen spacing, switch to drip, and lengthen the rotation.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Peronospora effusa under cool, wet, humid, crowded conditions.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use broadly race-resistant cultivars, widen spacing for airflow, irrigate by drip, and rotate away from spinach.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor or patchy germination
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Soil too warm, old seed, or crusted soil.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your spinach came up thin and patchy, or barely at all. Spinach seed will not sprout well in warm soil (above about 75 to 85°F), loses its vigor quickly with age, and can be blocked by a hard soil crust. Next time, sow in cool soil (early spring or once late-summer soil cools), use fresh seed each year, and keep the surface moist so it does not crust.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Sow in cool soil, use fresh seed, and keep the surface moist so it does not crust over.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stand was thin and uneven. Spinach germination is inhibited above roughly 75 to 85°F, the seed is short-lived and drops in vigor within a year or two, and a crust blocks the weak shoots. Next time sow into cool soil (or pre-sprout for late-summer sowings), buy fresh seed yearly, and keep the seedbed moist and uncrusted.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Warm soil inhibiting germination, low-vigor or old seed, or a soil crust.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into cool soil (pre-sprout in late summer), use fresh seed yearly, and keep the bed moist to prevent crusting.

3.zone_notes: The coldest zone: a short spring crop sown at snowmelt is cut in June before the long days of midsummer bolt it, then the bed sits out the high-summer heat and long days; the dependable crop is a late-summer sowing harvested through fall. Overwintering is possible only under heavy mulch or a low tunnel.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat-and-daylength exclusion (July): spinach grows best below about 75°F and bolts to seed and turns bitter once long summer days and heat arrive, with seed germinating poorly above 75 to 85°F. Midsummer here is too warm, so the calendar pauses and the crop resumes as a fall sowing. (Clemson HGIC; USU Extension)

4.zone_notes: A short spring crop is harvested in June before the lengthening days bolt it; the main crop is sown in August for a fall harvest that runs through the frosts spinach shrugs off. Overwintering works under a row cover in milder spots.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat-and-daylength exclusion (July): spinach grows best below about 75°F and bolts to seed and turns bitter once long summer days and heat arrive, with seed germinating poorly above 75 to 85°F. Midsummer here is too warm, so the calendar pauses and the crop resumes as a fall sowing. (Clemson HGIC; USU Extension)

5.zone_notes: Sow as soon as the soil is workable in late March for a spring crop cut in May and June, before midsummer long days bolt it; sow again in August for the main fall crop. Under a low tunnel an overwintered sowing gives the earliest spring picking.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat-and-daylength exclusion (July): spinach grows best below about 75°F and bolts to seed and turns bitter once long summer days and heat arrive, with seed germinating poorly above 75 to 85°F. Midsummer here is too warm, so the calendar pauses and the crop resumes as a fall sowing. (Clemson HGIC; USU Extension)

6.zone_notes: A short early-spring sowing is harvested in April and May; the summer is too long-dayed and warm, so the bed rests; the main fall sowing is harvested October into November. Fall-sown spinach reliably overwinters under cover here for the earliest spring harvest.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat-and-daylength exclusion (June through August): spinach grows best below about 75°F and bolts to seed and turns bitter once long summer days and heat arrive, with seed germinating poorly above 75 to 85°F. Midsummer here is too warm, so the calendar pauses and the crop resumes as a fall sowing. (Clemson HGIC; USU Extension)

7.zone_notes: Overwintering is the headline crop: spinach sown September into November sizes up, holds through a mild winter, and gives a heavy late-winter and early-spring harvest under a row cover. Summer is left out for heat and long-day bolting; an early-spring sowing is also possible for a quick April cut.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat-and-daylength exclusion (May through August): spinach grows best below about 75°F and bolts to seed and turns bitter once long summer days and heat arrive, with seed germinating poorly above 75 to 85°F. Midsummer here is too warm, so the calendar pauses and the crop resumes as a fall sowing. (Clemson HGIC; USU Extension)

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold regions, grow spinach in spring and especially in fall. Sow as soon as the soil can be worked in spring for a quick crop before summer, then sow again in late summer for fall. In the milder cold zones, a fall sowing covered with a row cover lives through winter and gives you the earliest spring spinach.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier spinach is a spring-and-fall crop bracketing a summer it cannot grow through: the region's rapidly lengthening days (to 15 or 16 hours by mid-June) bolt even slow-standing varieties, so the spring window is short and the summer is left out. Fall, grown under shortening days, is the main and most reliable season, and from zone 6 southward a fall sowing overwinters under a row cover or low tunnel for the earliest spring harvest. There is no summer heat_pause object here: the exclusion is a long-day bolt and end-of-cool-season effect, not the thermal exclusion the hot regions carry.

8.zone_notes: Spinach is a fall, winter, and early-spring crop on the Gulf coastal plain. Sow in February for a spring harvest and again from September for the long winter harvest; the hot, humid summer is left out, when spinach bolts and germination fails.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. Spinach is a cool-season crop that grows best when temperatures stay below about 75°F, and its seed germinates poorly above 75 to 85°F. Through the hot months of the inland coastal plain it bolts almost at once under long days and high heat, the leaves turn bitter, and new sowings fail to establish, so spinach is grown here as a fall-through-spring crop and the summer is left out of the planting calendar.

9.zone_notes: Warm coastal zone 9: the productive window is the cool fall through spring, with a long winter harvest, and only a brief early-spring sowing. The hot season stretches May through August, when spinach bolts and will not germinate.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. Spinach is a cool-season crop that grows best when temperatures stay below about 75°F, and its seed germinates poorly above 75 to 85°F. Through the hot months of the lower coastal plain it bolts almost at once under long days and high heat, the leaves turn bitter, and new sowings fail to establish, so spinach is grown here as a fall-through-spring crop and the summer is left out of the planting calendar.

10.zone_notes: Warm coastal zone 9: the productive window is the cool fall through spring, with a long winter harvest, and only a brief early-spring sowing. The hot season stretches May through August, when spinach bolts and will not germinate.

Spinach is a cool-season crop that grows best when temperatures stay below about 75°F, and its seed germinates poorly above 75 to 85°F. Through the hot months of the lower coastal plain it bolts almost at once under long days and high heat, the leaves turn bitter, and new sowings fail to establish, so spinach is grown here as a fall-through-spring crop and the summer is left out of the planting calendar.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Along the Gulf and the coastal plain, grow spinach in the cool months, fall through spring, not in summer. Plant in late summer and early fall for a long winter harvest, and again in February for spring. Summer is too hot, the seeds will not sprout and the plants bolt.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: On the Gulf and southeastern coastal plain spinach is a cool-season crop grown fall through spring, with the long, mild winter as the main harvest and a short February sowing for spring. The hot, humid summer is a true heat exclusion: above roughly 75 to 85°F spinach will not germinate and bolts at once, so summer is left out of the calendar in both zones.

8.zone_notes: In the interior valleys spinach is grown fall through spring. Sow in February for spring and from September for the long winter harvest; the hot, dry summer is excluded.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. Spinach is a cool-season crop that grows best when temperatures stay below about 75°F, and its seed germinates poorly above 75 to 85°F. Through the hot months of the dry interior valleys it bolts almost at once under long days and high heat, the leaves turn bitter, and new sowings fail to establish, so spinach is grown here as a fall-through-spring crop and the summer is left out of the planting calendar.

9.zone_notes: The warmer interior zone 9 has a longer hot season, June into September, so the fall sowing waits until October; the cool fall, winter, and early spring carry the crop.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. Spinach is a cool-season crop that grows best when temperatures stay below about 75°F, and its seed germinates poorly above 75 to 85°F. Through the hot months of the hot interior valleys it bolts almost at once under long days and high heat, the leaves turn bitter, and new sowings fail to establish, so spinach is grown here as a fall-through-spring crop and the summer is left out of the planting calendar.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot inland valleys, grow spinach in the cool seasons. Plant in early spring and again in fall for a long winter harvest, and skip the hot summer, when spinach bolts and the seed will not sprout.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's interior valleys grow spinach fall through spring, with the mild winter as the main season and a short late-winter sowing for spring. The hot, dry summer is a heat exclusion: spinach germinates poorly above 75 to 85°F and bolts in the heat and long days, so summer is left out and the warmer zone 9 has the longer pause.

nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) grows spinach on two direct-sown cycles, per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart. Spring sowing runs roughly mid-February to the end of March, with harvest beginning about 45 days later. University of Nevada, Reno Extension's home-vegetable guidance (Fact Sheet FS-02-61) notes plants generally stop growing well once daytime highs run past 90°F, and spinach bolts and turns bitter fast in that heat, so the chart splits into a real spring cycle and a distinct late-summer fall cycle, the fall being the longer and more reliable of the two. The fall sowing (about mid-August to mid-September) goes in as the heat breaks and carries past the valley's first fall frost, since spinach is cold tolerant. Zone 8's cooler pockets reach frost sooner, tightening the fall finish; zone 10 at Laughlin has the most room to spare.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spinach is very cold tolerant and keeps producing into the cool weeks that follow St. George's November 1 average first frost, per Utah State University Extension's Washington County frost and elevation notes.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation notes put St. George over 100°F in June, July, and August; the spring spinach crop finishes before the documented fall window opens, leaving May, Jun as bare ground between the two cycles.

8.zone_notes: The fall stand's Nov 17 finish runs about two and a half weeks past St. George's Nov 1 average first frost; that extension rests on spinach's own strong cold tolerance (general cold-hardiness), not a USU-dated fall-harvest line specific to spinach.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: In St. George's Dixie, sow spinach direct in mid-February for a spring crop cut by mid-April, before it bolts to seed in rising heat. The bed then sits idle through May and June, since St. George routinely tops 100°F in June. Sow again from July 1 to August 15 for a fall and early-winter crop; spinach is very cold tolerant, so you can keep cutting leaves well past the first frost around November 1.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) grows spinach on two direct-sown cycles, per Utah State University Extension's suggested vegetable planting dates for Utah. The spring sowing runs February 15 to March 1, the Group A (Hardy) date for St. George, with leaves ready in about 45 days and the crop cut by mid-April before it bolts. USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation notes put St. George over 100°F in June, July, and August, and USU's Group E "Special Plants for Fall Harvest" table does not open the fall spinach window until July 1, so May and June together form a genuine two-month bare-ground pause, the longest of this family's fall-paired crops. Spinach is very cold tolerant, so the fall stand, sown July 1 to August 15, keeps producing well past the November 1 average first frost.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Spinach matures fast and bolts hard, so sow small batches every 1 to 2 weeks through the cool windows rather than all at once: across spring until days lengthen and warm, and again from late summer through fall, which is the longer, more reliable run. In hot regions skip summer entirely and succession-sow through the cool fall, winter, and spring.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant a little spinach every week or two instead of all at once, so you get a steady supply before it bolts. Do this in early spring and again in late summer for fall. In hot areas, skip summer and keep sowing through the cool months.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Spinach is ready when the leaves are 3 to 6 inches long, dark green, and tender, usually 37 to 50 days from sowing (baby leaf sooner). Harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again, or cut the whole rosette about an inch above the crown and let it regrow; pick in the cool morning and crop faster as days lengthen, since the leaves turn bitter once the plant bolts.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Spinach is ready to pick when the leaves are about 3 to 6 inches long and tender, around 37 to 50 days after planting. Take the outer leaves a few at a time, or cut the whole plant an inch above the soil so it grows back. Pick in the cool morning, and harvest it all before it starts to flower (bolt), because the leaves get bitter then.
crops.description_seasoned: Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a fast, very cold-hardy leafy annual in the goosefoot family, grown for its tender, nutrient-dense leaves in the cool halves of the year. It is one of the hardiest garden vegetables, surviving hard frost into the low 20s°F and overwintering under snow or a row cover for the earliest spring harvest, yet it is also one of the quickest to bolt: lengthening days past about 13 to 14 hours, sped by heat and drought, send it to seed and turn the leaves bitter. That combination makes fall the main season nearly everywhere, with a short early-spring window and, in hot regions, a fall-through-spring winter crop. Spinach comes in three leaf types, smooth (flat), semi-savoy, and savoy (heavily crinkled), and is sensitive to acidic soil, preferring a near-neutral, fertile, evenly moist bed.
crops.description_beginner: Spinach is a fast-growing, very cold-hardy leafy green grown in the cool parts of the year. It handles frost better than almost any other vegetable and can even live through winter under a cover to give you the first greens of spring. But it does not like heat and long summer days, which make it bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter quickly. That is why spinach grows best in fall and early spring, and why in hot places it is a winter crop. It comes in smooth-leaf types that are easy to wash and crinkly savoy types that are extra hardy, and it likes rich, moist soil that is not too acidic.

crops.name: Carrot

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Carrots want deep, loose soil with no rocks or hard clumps, the looser the better. This matters more for carrots than for most vegetables: a carrot growing down into heavy clay or packed soil will come out short, forked, or twisted instead of long and straight. Loosen the soil at least 8 inches down before you plant, and mix in some compost. Go easy on fertilizer that is high in nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much makes big leafy tops but small roots. If your soil is heavy clay, a raised bed or a deep container filled with loose mix is the easiest fix.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Carrots need deep, loose, friable soil free of stones, clods, and debris, ideally a light sandy loam or loam worked to at least 8 inches deep (deeper for long Imperator types). The texture matters more for carrots than for almost any other vegetable: roots grown in heavy clay or compacted ground grow poorly and come out forked, stunted, or misshapen. Work in well-rotted compost or manure before planting, but go easy on nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy top growth at the expense of root development and can cause forking and splitting. Moderate organic matter improves both moisture retention and friability; the goal is an open, stone-free root channel, not a rich heavy bed.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Carrots like it right around 6.0 to 6.8, slightly acidic. They are not very fussy about it, so do not stress over pH if your roots are coming out fine, getting the soil loose and stone-free matters more. If you want to know your number for certain, a cheap soil test from your local extension office will tell you, and let you know whether to add anything before planting.
ph.note_seasoned: Carrots grow best in neutral to slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.8, with extension sources placing the optimum band between about 5.8 and 6.8. Below 5.5, phosphorus, calcium, and molybdenum availability drops; above 7.5, micronutrients including boron, manganese, and iron become less available. pH is rarely the first thing that limits a home carrot crop (soil texture and even moisture matter more), but a $10 to $15 soil test from your local extension office removes the guesswork and tells you whether lime or sulfur is warranted before sowing.

fertilizer.timing: Work compost into the bed before sowing; optional single light side-dressing once tops are established.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: In decent garden soil amended with compost, carrots often need no supplemental feeding at all. If growth is weak, a single light side-dressing of a low-nitrogen fertilizer once the tops are established is enough. Avoid fresh manure and high-nitrogen lawn-type feeds entirely, since they cause the forking and excessive top growth carrots are prone to.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: If your soil has compost mixed in, carrots usually need no extra feeding. If they look weak and pale, you can give one light feeding of a low-nitrogen fertilizer after the leafy tops fill in. Never use fresh manure or high-nitrogen lawn fertilizer, because that is exactly what causes forked roots and too many leaves.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Carrots are light feeders, and excess nitrogen is the classic mistake: it grows lush tops and forked, hairy roots at the expense of a clean taproot. Favor a low-nitrogen blend with adequate phosphorus and potassium to support root development, such as a 5-10-10. Most of the feeding is done by working modest, well-finished compost into the bed before sowing.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Carrots do not want much of the first one: too much nitrogen makes big leafy tops but forked, hairy roots. Pick a fertilizer that is low in the first number with more of the other two, like a 5-10-10, and mostly just mix compost into the soil before planting.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Carrots are light feeders. Work 1 to 2 pounds of a low-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 per 100 feet of row into the bed before sowing (UC IPM), then, only if the tops pale, side-dress nitrogen lightly once plants are 3 to 4 inches tall, on the order of 0.1 to 0.5 pound of actual nitrogen per 100 feet of row. Excess nitrogen produces forked, hairy roots and lush tops, so err low.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Carrots do not need much feeding. Mix a little low-nitrogen vegetable fertilizer into the bed before you plant, following the label rate. Only feed again, lightly, if the tops look pale and growth stalls. Going heavy on fertilizer, especially nitrogen, gives you leafy tops and forked, hairy roots instead of clean ones.

companions.note_beginner: Carrots are easygoing about neighbors. The most reliable trick is sowing a few fast radishes in the carrot row to mark it and save space. Onions and chives are a popular choice to help fend off the carrot fly, though they do not always work. The main plants to keep away are carrot's close relatives, dill, parsnip, and fennel, since they share the same pests. Do not trust every companion-planting chart online; many of their claims have not held up when tested.
companions.note_seasoned: Carrots fit easily into mixed beds. The best-supported pairing is the radish row-marker trick, which extension research presents as a genuine space-saver. Allium pairings (onion, chives) for carrot rust fly are popular and mechanistically plausible but not firmly proven, useful, not guaranteed. The clearest avoids are carrot's own family, dill, parsnip, and fennel, which share its pests and diseases. Treat most other companion-chart claims with skepticism: university reviews find many are not backed by evidence.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Radishes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Radishes sprout in just a few days, while carrots can take 2 to 3 weeks. Sow a few radishes in the same row and they show you where the carrot row is; pull and eat them before they crowd the carrots. This is a proven space-saving trick from university gardening guides.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: UMN Extension names radish-and-carrot as the canonical space-saving interplant (a soil-use and succession benefit, not a pest mechanism). The space/timing rationale is mechanistically sound and extension-endorsed; the broader pest-deterrence folklore is not. Labeled traditional/medium: the practice is well-founded and widely taught, but its real value is the agronomic timing trick rather than a measured pest effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Radishes earn their spot mostly through timing, not chemistry. They germinate in days while carrots can take two to three weeks, so a light scatter of radish seed down the carrot row marks the line, lets you cultivate and weed before the carrots are even up, and is pulled out well before the carrots need the room. The pest-deterrence claims are thinner, so treat the benefit as row-marking and space-sharing rather than protection.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions, chives, leeks, and garlic have a strong smell that many gardeners use to help hide carrots from the carrot fly, a pest whose larvae tunnel into the roots. It is a popular pairing, though the evidence for it is mixed rather than ironclad.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: The carrot/onion intercrop is one of the few companion claims with direct intercropping trial support: the scent-masking mechanism against carrot rust fly (Psila/Chamaepsila rosae) is well documented and classic mixed-cropping studies report substantial fly-damage reductions at small scale. research_backed is earned by the mechanism + trial literature. confidence is medium, not high, for two reasons: (1) a 2022 organic-ag intercropping paper notes the small-scale benefit is difficult to replicate at larger scale, and (2) I could not open a single measured carrot-fly-reduction figure to a directly-verified T1 source in this session (ResearchGate 429), so I am declining to treat a specific percentage as confirmed. Density and arrangement materially affect whether the effect shows up.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: This is the carrot pairing with the most real evidence behind it. Onions, leeks, chives, and garlic give off sulfur volatiles that mask the carrot's scent and make it harder for the carrot rust fly to find the row and lay eggs; classic intercropping trials have measured meaningful reductions in fly damage where the two are grown together. Two practical catches: you need enough allium density relative to carrots for the masking to matter (roughly one allium per two carrots, in alternating rows), and the strongest results come from small mixed plantings rather than large blocks. Alliums are shallow-rooted and slow, so they share the bed without crowding the carrot's taproot.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other leafy greens
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce and other shallow-rooted greens grow near the surface and finish fast, while carrots reach deeper, so they share a bed without fighting for the same space. A handy way to fit more into a small garden.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Rests on the same agronomic logic UMN endorses for radish/carrot and for early-short-season-crop interplanting generally: complementary root depths, canopy shading, weed suppression, efficient succession. The benefit is real and extension-aligned in principle but is a space/soil-use rationale, not a measured carrot-specific pest or yield effect, so traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce and carrots work as a classic interplant on root structure and timing. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick, carrots are deep-rooted and slow, so they pull from different parts of the soil profile and the lettuce canopy shades the surface, holding moisture and suppressing weeds while the carrots establish. Harvest the lettuce as the carrots fill in. This is a space-and-soil benefit rather than a pest one, and it is one of the more reliable interplants for that reason.

good_seasoned.name: Radishes
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Radishes germinate in days while carrots take 2 to 3 weeks, so radishes sown in the same row mark the slow carrot row and are pulled before they compete. UMN Extension presents radish-and-carrot interplanting as a research-backed space-saving pairing.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: UMN Extension's research-reviewed companion-planting guide names radishes and carrots as a documented space-saving example.

good_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums (chives, leeks, garlic)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are widely recommended by extension master-gardener channels to mask carrots from the carrot rust fly, with onions reciprocally protected from thrips. UMN's research review does not list the carrot-onion pairing among insect relationships it considers proven, so this is a plausible, commonly cited pairing rather than a research-verified one.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking against carrot rust fly is mechanistically plausible and repeated across extension master-gardener outreach, but UMN's research-backed list does not include it; treat as likely, not proven.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other shallow-rooted greens
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shallow-rooted, fast greens occupy the surface layer while carrots develop their deeper taproot, an example of the different-root-depth interplanting extension guides describe for efficient use of bed space. General space-efficiency principle rather than a carrot-specific tested pairing.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Extension companion guidance endorses pairing shallow- and deep-rooted crops for space and soil use; the specific lettuce-carrot benefit is a reasonable application of that principle, not a directly studied pairing.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Dill
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Dill is a cousin of the carrot and shares the same pests. Once it flowers it can draw in the carrot fly and may slow nearby plants, so keep it in another part of the garden.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Two folk rationales travel together: (1) dill and carrot are both Apiaceae, so they share pests (carrot rust fly) and can cross-pollinate if both flower (a real concern only for seed-savers, since carrot is biennial and usually harvested before bolting), and (2) flowering dill is reputed to release compounds that stunt carrot root development. The cross-pollination/shared-pest reasoning is botanically sound; the growth-inhibition claim is folk-level and unmeasured. Near-universal caution, no extension contradiction, mechanism partly sound -> traditional/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill and carrot are both in the carrot family, so they share pests like the carrot rust fly, and if both are left to flower they can cross-pollinate, which matters if you are saving carrot seed. There is also an old claim that flowering dill stunts carrot roots; that part is folk wisdom rather than measured, but the shared-pest and cross-pollination reasons are real, so it is worth keeping them apart in a seed-saving bed.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Parsnips
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Parsnips are close carrot relatives and get the same pests and diseases. Growing them right next to carrots lets those problems build up, so give them separate spots.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Parsnip is also Apiaceae, so the caution is shared-pest and shared-disease (carrot rust fly, leafhopper, common root diseases) plus competition between two long-season root crops for the same phosphorus and soil space. This is sound rotation/diversity logic rather than a measured antagonism, and it is consistently repeated without dispute -> traditional/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Parsnips are close carrot relatives, so the two share the same pests and diseases, including carrot rust fly and common root rots, and clustering them concentrates that pressure. They are also both long-season root crops drawing on the same phosphorus and the same below-ground space for months. Spread them out and rotate where each goes rather than running them side by side.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Fennel is another carrot relative that many gardeners find does not play well with neighbors. Plant it well away from your carrots.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Same call as beefsteak-tomato's Fennel entry (precedent set 2026-06-25). The fennel-as-bad-companion rule is near-universal folk consensus, not contested. A real allelopathic mechanism underlies it (fennel essential oil / anethole, alpha-pinene, fenchone suppress seed germination and seedling growth in multiple in-vitro bioassays), but every such study targets weed species, not carrot at garden spacing. For carrot specifically there is the added Apiaceae shared-pest overlap. Dominant traditional rule, mechanism-backed, never directly measured on carrot -> traditional/medium. Not disputed (no active expert contradiction).

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is a poor neighbor for most of the garden, carrots included. It is reputed to release compounds from its roots that hold back nearby plants, and while the lab work behind that is on weeds rather than carrots, it is a near-universal caution worth heeding. Fennel and carrot also share carrot-family pests. The simple handling is to give fennel its own bed or a large container, away from the carrot rows.

bad_seasoned.name: Dill
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill is in the same family as carrots (Apiaceae) and shares its pest spectrum; once it flowers it can cross-attract the carrot rust fly and is reported to suppress nearby growth. As a fellow umbellifer it can also cross with carrot if both are allowed to set seed. Commonly cited avoid, mechanistically grounded in shared-family pests rather than a controlled extension trial.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared Apiaceae pest pressure and flowering-dill allelopathy are mechanistically plausible and widely repeated, but not established in a T1 extension carrot trial. Labeled likely.

bad_seasoned.name: Parsnips
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Parsnips are close carrot relatives (Apiaceae) and share key pests and diseases, including carrot rust fly, carrot weevil, and leaf blights. Planting the two together sustains a shared pest and disease bridge, the same reason extension sources advise rotating among related root crops.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared-family pest and disease overlap between carrots and parsnips is documented at the family level; the specific co-planting risk is a sound inference from that overlap rather than a directly studied pairing.

bad_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is another Apiaceae relative with the same pest spectrum and a reputation for releasing compounds that inhibit many neighboring plants. Traditional companion-planting lore treats fennel as antagonistic to most garden crops; for carrots the concern is shared pests plus allelopathy.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel's broad antagonism is long-standing companion-planting tradition with limited controlled support; shared-family pest overlap is the plausible mechanism. Labeled traditional.

pests.name: Carrot rust fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: There are usually no aboveground symptoms until damage is advanced, when foliage may look rusty, wilted, or stunted. The real signs are in the root: the larvae, small stiff white maggots, mine surface tunnels through the lower portion of the taproot, and the tunnels fill with a rusty-brown mush. Damaged roots are scarred, off-flavored, and prone to secondary rot in storage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Aboveground you often see nothing until it is bad, when the leaves may look rusty, wilted, or stunted. The damage is underground: small stiff white maggots tunnel just under the surface of the lower part of the root, leaving winding tunnels filled with rusty-brown mush. Affected carrots are scarred, taste off, and tend to rot in storage.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the carrot rust fly (Psila rosae), a small fly whose females are drawn to the scent of carrot foliage and lay eggs near the crown; the hatching maggots burrow into the roots. It also attacks parsnip, celery, parsley, and other carrot-family plants. The fly is a weak flier with localized populations and is most damaging in cool, humid, maritime regions, far less so in hot-summer areas.
pests.cause_beginner: The maggots (young larvae) of the carrot rust fly, a small fly. The female is drawn to the smell of carrot leaves and lays her eggs near the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow into the roots. It also goes after parsnip, celery, and parsley. It is mainly a problem in cool, damp, coastal areas and much less common where summers are hot.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no home rescue for roots already mined; trim damaged portions before use. Limit further damage by harvesting promptly rather than leaving roots in the ground, removing and not composting infested roots, and clearing nearby wild or volunteer carrots that sustain the population.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot fix roots that are already tunneled, just cut away the damaged parts before eating. To limit more damage, harvest on time instead of leaving carrots in the ground, throw away (do not compost) badly infested roots, and clear out any wild or leftover carrots nearby that keep the flies going.
pests.prevention_seasoned: The most reliable home defense is a floating row cover or fine mesh set over the bed at sowing and sealed at the edges, since the low-flying females cannot reach the crowns to lay. Rotate carrots well away from last year's bed, time sowings to miss the main egg-laying flights (in cold areas an early-summer sowing; in mild areas, in late winter or in late summer), harvest in blocks, and do not overwinter roots in the ground where the fly is active.
pests.prevention_beginner: The best home defense is a row cover, a light fabric or fine mesh laid over the bed right after sowing and tucked in at the edges, because the low-flying female cannot get to the plants to lay eggs. Also move carrots well away from last year's spot, time planting to dodge the main egg-laying periods (in cold areas sow in early summer; in mild areas, in late winter or in late summer), harvest a block at a time, and do not leave carrots in the ground over winter where this fly is active.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant carrots well away from where they grew last year. This fly is a weak flier that tends to stay in one small area, so simply moving the bed can leave much of the local population behind.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate well away from the previous season's carrot ground. Psila rosae is a weak flier with localized populations, so distance from last year's bed is a meaningful lever rather than a token move, and it compounds with sanitation of overwintered roots.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Time your sowing to dodge the periods when the female flies are out laying eggs. In cold areas that means sowing in early summer; in mild areas, in late winter or in late summer. The right window depends on your region, so treat these as starting points.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Schedule sowings to miss the main egg-laying flights: an early-summer sowing in cold regions, late winter or late summer in mild ones. Pressure is concentrated in cool, humid, maritime areas and much lighter where summers are hot, so weight this step by your local flight pattern rather than a carried-over calendar date.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear out wild carrots and any leftover or self-sown carrots growing nearby. Those plants feed the flies between your plantings and keep the local population going.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Remove wild and volunteer carrots around the garden; they sustain the localized fly population between crop plantings, and clearing them denies the flights a reservoir your rotation cannot touch.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Harvest on time instead of leaving carrots sitting in the ground, and where this fly is active, do not leave roots in the soil over winter. Pulling a whole block at once, rather than a few here and there, gives the maggots less to live on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Harvest promptly and in blocks rather than holding mature roots in the ground, and do not overwinter roots in soil where the fly is active. Roots left in place extend the feeding window and carry the population into the next season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When you find tunneled carrots, trim off the damaged parts before eating the rest, and throw badly infested roots in the trash rather than the compost so they cannot keep feeding the next generation.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no rescue for roots already mined; trim damaged portions at the kitchen and dispose of heavily infested roots outside the compost so larvae do not complete development on your culls.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The most dependable defense at home is a row cover, a light fabric or fine mesh laid over the bed right at sowing with the edges tucked in tight. The female fly flies low and is blocked from reaching the base of the plants to lay her eggs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A row cover or fine mesh set at sowing and sealed at the edges is the most reliable home defense: the low-flying females are excluded from the crowns where they lay. Pair it with rotation, since covering ground that carried carrots last year risks confining any overwintered flies with the crop.

pests.name: Root-knot nematode
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The diagnostic sign is galling: firm, beadlike knots on the feeder and lateral roots, distinct from the fine, soft secondary roots of aster yellows. The taproot forks, twists, and grows malformed, often with several prongs, because the nematodes enter the root tip and disrupt it. Aboveground, plants in affected patches are stunted and yellowish and pull from the soil easily. Galls from northern root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne hapla) are small; other Meloidogyne species make larger, more conspicuous galls.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The giveaway is little firm bumps or knots on the small side roots, called galls, which is different from the soft, fine hairy roots of aster yellows. The main root forks and twists into a deformed, often many-pronged carrot, because the tiny worms enter the root tip and disrupt it. Aboveground, plants in bad spots are stunted and yellowish and pull up easily. Northern root-knot nematode makes small knots; some other kinds make bigger, more obvious ones.
pests.cause_seasoned: Microscopic soil roundworms in the genus Meloidogyne (the root-knot nematodes), including the northern species M. hapla and warm-climate species such as M. incognita and M. javanica. They are most active and damaging in warm, sandy soils and largely inactive in cool soil, which is why cool-season and winter carrots often escape. Carrots are among the more susceptible garden crops, and the nematodes persist in soil and feed on many hosts.
pests.cause_beginner: Microscopic worms in the soil called root-knot nematodes (in the genus Meloidogyne). They are most active and most damaging in warm, sandy soil and go quiet in cool soil, which is why carrots grown in cool weather or winter often come through fine. Carrots are one of the crops they hit hardest, and they live in the soil and feed on many different plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no home cure once a crop is infested; pull and dispose of affected carrots rather than composting them. Manage for future seasons: where infestation is known, grow carrots in the cool part of the year when nematodes are inactive, rotate to non-host or less-susceptible crops, and build soil organic matter, which supports the natural enemies that suppress nematodes.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home cure once the soil is infested, so pull up and throw away affected carrots instead of composting them. Plan around it next time: grow carrots in the cool season when the worms are inactive, rotate to other crops, and add organic matter to the soil, which helps the natural enemies that keep nematodes down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: In warm, sandy soils prone to nematodes, time carrot sowings so the roots develop in cool soil, below roughly 55 to 64°F depending on the species, since the nematodes do not invade roots in cool soil. Rotate away from beds with a history of root-knot, avoid following known host crops, build soil organic matter, and where pressure is severe consider raised beds with clean soil.
pests.prevention_beginner: If your soil is warm and sandy and prone to nematodes, plant carrots so they grow in cool soil (below about 55 to 64°F), since the worms do not attack roots when the soil is cool. Keep carrots out of beds that have had root-knot problems, do not plant them right after other crops the worms love, add organic matter, and in bad cases use a raised bed filled with clean soil.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no home cure once the soil has these tiny worms, so pull up affected carrots and throw them in the trash, not the compost. Getting galled roots out of the garden keeps you from spreading the problem around.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: No home treatment rescues an infested crop; rogue out galled carrots and dispose of them outside the compost. This limits what you return to the bed, though the nematodes themselves persist in the soil.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep carrots out of beds where knotted, deformed roots have shown up before, and do not plant them right after crops these worms feed on heavily. Rotating to other crops helps, though it is not a complete fix, since the worms can live on many different plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate away from beds with a root-knot history and avoid following known host crops. Carrots are among the more susceptible garden crops, and because Meloidogyne persists in soil and feeds on a wide host range, rotation suppresses rather than eliminates pressure.

diseases.name: Leaf blight (Alternaria and Cercospora)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown to black, irregularly shaped spots with yellow halos appear first on the older, lower leaflet margins and tips; this is Alternaria dauci. Tan to gray circular spots with darker margins, showing on younger leaves and earlier in the season, point to the closely related Cercospora carotae. As the spots multiply they run together and the foliage takes on a scorched, blighted look, and large lesions can girdle and kill the petioles. The two fungi are difficult to tell apart and are managed identically. The roots are not infected directly but size up poorly when the canopy is badly damaged. A third, bacterial blight (Xanthomonas campestris pv. carotae), looks similar, with water-soaked, varnished lesions that track down the veins.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: You will see spots on the leaves. Alternaria blight makes dark brown to black ragged spots with a yellow edge, starting on the older, lower leaves. Cercospora blight makes tan or gray round spots and can show up on younger leaves too. As the spots spread and join together, the leaves look burned and can die back. The two are hard to tell apart, and you treat them the same way. The carrots underground are not infected directly, but if the leaves get badly damaged the roots stay small.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Two fungi, Alternaria dauci and Cercospora carotae, that are seedborne and also survive on infected crop debris and on wild carrot. They spread in splashing water and need leaf wetness to infect, so prolonged wet foliage from rain, dew, or overhead watering drives the disease, especially in warm, humid weather.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungi that travel on the seed and survive on old carrot debris and on wild carrots nearby. They spread in splashing water and need wet leaves to take hold, so long spells of wet foliage from rain, dew, or overhead watering bring them on, especially in warm, humid weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for tissue already infected; management slows the spread. Remove and destroy badly infected leaves, thin to proper spacing to improve airflow, and water at the base in the morning so foliage dries quickly. In a wet season, a copper-based fungicide labeled for vegetables can suppress spread if started early, but cultural control is the mainstay for a home crop.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure leaves that are already infected, only slow it down. Pick off and throw away (do not compost) the worst leaves, thin crowded plants so air can move through, and water at the soil in the morning so the leaves dry fast. In a very wet year a copper fungicide labeled for vegetables can help if you start early, but keeping the leaves dry and the plants uncrowded does most of the work.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean or treated seed, rotate carrots and other carrot-family crops out of the bed for at least two years, and clear crop debris and volunteer or wild carrots that harbor the fungi. Avoid overhead watering, space and thin for airflow, and choose tolerant varieties where blight recurs.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use fresh, clean seed, and do not grow carrots (or relatives like parsley and dill) in the same spot two years in a row. Clear away old carrot tops and any wild carrots nearby, since the fungi live on them. Water at the base instead of overhead, give plants room so the leaves dry, and pick a blight-tolerant variety if it keeps coming back.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If leaf blight keeps coming back in your garden, pick a blight-tolerant variety at seed-buying time rather than fighting it on a susceptible one every year.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Where Alternaria or Cercospora blight recurs, choose tolerant varieties at ordering time; tolerance lowers the load the cultural steps have to carry through a wet season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with fresh, clean seed. These fungi can travel on the seed itself, so the packet you buy is your first line of defense.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Both pathogens are seedborne, so start from clean or treated seed; infected seed puts the disease in the row before any in-season practice can act.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not grow carrots, or relatives like parsley and dill, in the same spot two years running. Keeping the family out of the bed for at least two years starves the fungi waiting in the soil and old debris.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate carrots and other carrot-family crops out of the bed for at least two years; the fungi carry over on infected debris, and a same-family replant hands them their host back.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear away wild carrots and any self-sown carrots near the garden. The blight fungi live on them between your plantings, so those weeds can reinfect a clean bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Remove wild and volunteer carrots around the planting; they harbor Alternaria dauci and Cercospora carotae between crops and undercut rotation if left standing at the bed edges.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Thin crowded rows and give plants room so air can move through and the leaves dry quickly after rain or dew. These fungi need wet leaves to take hold, so faster drying works directly against them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Thin to proper spacing so the canopy dries fast; infection requires prolonged leaf wetness, and a crowded planting in warm, humid weather supplies exactly that.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil instead of over the leaves, and do it in the morning so any splashed foliage dries fast. The spots spread in splashing water, so keeping the tops dry slows them down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Irrigate at the base in the morning rather than overhead; the fungi spread in splashing water and need leaf wetness to infect, so removing the one wetness period you control matters, especially in warm, humid spells.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off the worst-spotted leaves and throw them away, not in the compost, and clear out old carrot tops after harvest. Leaves already infected cannot be cured, so removing them protects the rest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy badly blighted leaves during the season and clear crop debris afterward, since both fungi overwinter on what is left behind.

control_ladder.note_beginner: In a very wet year, a copper fungicide labeled for vegetables can help slow the spread if you start early, before the spots are everywhere. It backs up the other steps rather than replacing them; keeping leaves dry and plants uncrowded does most of the work. Follow the label rate, and keep spray and runoff away from ponds and drains since copper is harmful to fish and other water life.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: In a wet season a copper product labeled for vegetables can suppress spread if begun early; it does not cure established lesions, and cultural control remains the mainstay for a home planting. Mind the label rate to avoid foliage injury, limit repeat use over the years since copper accumulates in the surface soil, and keep spray and runoff out of waterways.

diseases.name: Aster yellows
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Infected carrots push up yellowed, then reddish-purple, twisted new foliage that clusters into a weak, bunchy top, while the taproot turns pale and tapered and grows a dense mat of fine hairy secondary roots. The root tastes bitter and is inedible. Affected plants usually appear scattered singly through a planting rather than spreading plant to plant, and there is no cure once a plant is infected.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: An infected carrot grows strangely: the new leaves turn yellow, then reddish-purple, twist, and bunch into a weak clump, and the root underneath comes out pale and tapered with a thick fuzz of fine hairy roots. The carrot tastes bitter and is not good to eat. You will usually see just a scattered plant here and there, not a spreading patch, and there is no way to cure a plant once it has it.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A phytoplasma, a bacterium-like organism that lives in the plant's food-conducting tissue, spread by the aster leafhopper. The insect picks the pathogen up from infected weeds or crops, often arriving on migrating leafhoppers, and injects it while feeding. Many weeds, including wild carrot, dandelion, and thistle, serve as reservoirs.
diseases.cause_beginner: It is caused by a phytoplasma (a bacterium-like organism) that lives inside the plant. A small insect called the aster leafhopper carries the phytoplasma from infected weeds or plants and passes it on when it feeds on your carrots. Weeds like wild carrot, dandelion, and thistle can hold it and pass it along.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No treatment cures an infected plant. Pull and destroy symptomatic plants promptly so they cannot serve as a source for leafhoppers to spread it further, and do not compost them.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no way to cure a plant that already has it. As soon as you spot one, pull it up and throw it away, not in the compost, so leafhoppers cannot pick it up from that plant and carry it to your other carrots.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Control broadleaf weeds in and around the garden that host the phytoplasma and the leafhopper, especially wild carrot and dandelion. Row covers exclude the leafhopper from a planting, and prompt removal of any infected plant limits a local reservoir. Risk is highest where migrating aster leafhoppers are abundant, which varies by region and year.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep weeds down in and around the garden, especially wild carrot and dandelion, since they shelter both the germ and the insect that spreads it. A row cover, a light fabric laid over the plants, keeps the leafhopper off, and pulling any sick plant right away keeps it from spreading. How common this is depends on your area and the year.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no cure for a plant that already has it. Pull any carrot with the twisted, yellow-to-purple bunchy top as soon as you spot it and throw it in the trash, not the compost, so leafhoppers cannot pick the disease up from that plant and carry it to the rest of your row.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: No treatment recovers an infected plant. Rogue out symptomatic carrots promptly and destroy them rather than composting; each one left standing is a reservoir the aster leafhopper can acquire the phytoplasma from and spread onward.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A row cover, a light fabric laid over the planting, keeps the aster leafhopper, the insect that carries this disease, off your carrots in the first place. How much this matters varies by region and by year, since it depends on how many leafhoppers arrive.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover excludes the aster leafhopper from the planting, which intercepts transmission rather than the pathogen itself. Risk tracks the abundance of migrating leafhoppers, which varies by region and year, so weight this step by your local pressure.

diseases.name: Cavity spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sunken, elliptical lesions a few millimeters long on the taproot surface, sometimes darkening or cracking. There are no aboveground symptoms, so it is found at harvest. It is a quality and storage problem rather than a plant-killer, and it tends to show up in larger in-ground plantings on wet, heavy, poorly drained soil rather than in a well-drained raised bed.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small sunken oval pits, usually only a few millimeters long, on the surface of the carrot root, sometimes turning dark or cracking. The leaves look fine, so you usually notice it only when you pull and wash the carrots. It does not kill the plant; it just blemishes the roots. It mostly turns up in larger in-ground rows on wet, heavy, poorly drained soil, so a well-drained raised bed is low risk.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Pythium species, chiefly Pythium violae and Pythium sulcatum, that infect the developing root. The disease is favored by prolonged wet soil, acidic conditions, and poor drainage, and older roots left in the ground longer are more susceptible. The pathogens persist in soil as resting spores and have a wide host range, so rotation alone does not eliminate them.
diseases.cause_beginner: Tiny soil organisms called Pythium, which are fungus-like water molds (mainly Pythium violae and Pythium sulcatum), that infect the growing root. They thrive where soil stays too wet, drains poorly, or is too acidic, and carrots left in the ground a long time are more likely to get it. They survive in soil for years and attack many plants, so simply rotating crops does not get rid of them.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue treatment once roots are infected. Management is preventive and cultural: improve drainage, avoid overwatering, and harvest promptly rather than holding mature roots in wet ground.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no spray that fixes roots once they are infected. The fix is in how you grow them: improve drainage, do not overwater, and harvest on time instead of leaving mature carrots sitting in wet soil.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Grow carrots in loose, well-drained soil, raise beds where drainage is poor, avoid overwatering, and keep soil pH in the recommended slightly acidic to neutral range rather than letting it run low. Harvest at maturity, since the longer roots stay in infested wet soil the worse it gets, and choose tolerant varieties where there is a history of the disease.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in loose, well-drained soil, and use a raised bed if your ground stays soggy. Do not overwater, keep the soil pH in the right range (around 6.0 to 6.8, not too acidic), and harvest carrots when they are ready instead of leaving them in wet ground, since the longer they sit the worse it gets.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If your carrots have come up with these sunken pits before, pick a tolerant variety at seed-buying time. It is a soil problem that rotation alone does not clear, so variety choice is one of the few levers you set in advance.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Where cavity spot has a history in the bed, choose tolerant varieties; the Pythium species persist in soil as resting spores with a wide host range, so rotation alone does not eliminate them and tolerance is a lever worth setting at ordering time.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Grow carrots in loose soil that drains well, and use a raised bed if your ground stays soggy. Go easy on watering too. The organisms behind these pits thrive where soil sits wet, so a well-drained bed is low risk to begin with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Plant into loose, well-drained ground, raise beds where drainage is poor, and avoid overwatering; the causal Pythium species are favored by prolonged wet soil and poor drainage, which is why the problem concentrates in wet in-ground rows rather than well-drained raised beds.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull carrots when they are ready instead of leaving them sitting in wet ground. The longer mature roots stay in infested wet soil, the worse the pitting gets.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Harvest at maturity rather than holding roots in the ground; older roots left longer in infested wet soil are more susceptible, so lifting on time caps the exposure.

diseases.name: Damping-off
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Seeds fail to emerge, or young seedlings topple and die soon after emergence, typically with a dark, water-soaked, shriveled spot at the stem base right at the soil line. Losses often appear as bare patches in the row. Because carrot germination is slow, often 2 to 3 weeks, the seedbed is held moist for a long time, which is exactly the condition the pathogens exploit; the same Pythium can also leave young roots stubby and branched if it kills the root tip early.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that never come up, or tiny seedlings that flop over and die soon after sprouting, usually with a dark, pinched, water-soaked spot on the stem right at the soil line. You often see it as bare gaps in the row. Because carrot seed is slow and the bed is kept damp for 2 to 3 weeks, conditions favor it; the same organism can also leave young roots stubby and forked if it kills the root tip early.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne pathogens, chiefly Pythium species along with Rhizoctonia and others, that attack germinating seed and young seedlings. They are favored by cool, wet, poorly drained soil and by overwatering, and they spread in soil water. Old or weak seed and a crusted, slow-draining seedbed increase losses.
diseases.cause_beginner: Soil organisms (mostly Pythium, a fungus-like water mold, plus a few others) that attack sprouting seeds and baby seedlings. They thrive in cool, wet, poorly drained soil and when you overwater, and they move in soil water. Old or weak seed and a hard, soggy seedbed make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Affected seedlings cannot be saved. If damping-off appears, stop watering and let the surface dry somewhat to slow the pathogens, and clear out collapsed seedlings. The real lever is prevention, since there is no effective home cure once it takes hold.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Seedlings that have collapsed will not recover. If it shows up, stop watering for a bit and let the soil surface dry out some to slow it down, and clear away the fallen seedlings. Mostly, though, this one is about prevention, because there is no good home cure once it starts.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow into warm-enough, well-drained soil rather than cold, wet ground, and keep the seedbed evenly moist without keeping it saturated, maintaining moisture at seed depth rather than soaking the surface. Use fresh seed, avoid sowing too deep, improve drainage or use raised beds on heavy soil, and do not overwater during the long germination window.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Wait to sow until the soil is warm enough and not cold and soggy, and keep the seedbed evenly damp without letting it stay soaking wet. Use fresh seed, do not plant too deep, improve drainage or use a raised bed if your soil is heavy, and resist the urge to overwater during the long wait for the seeds to come up.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the seed its best start: sow fresh seed, not too deep, and wait until the soil is warm enough rather than cold and soggy. Carrot seed can take 2 to 3 weeks to come up, so keep the bed evenly damp at seed depth without soaking it, and resist the urge to water more during the long wait.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sow fresh seed at proper depth into warm-enough, well-drained soil, and hold the seedbed evenly moist at seed depth rather than saturated. Carrot's 2 to 3 week germination keeps the bed damp for exactly the stretch Pythium and Rhizoctonia exploit, so restrained watering through that window is the core of prevention.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If your soil is heavy or crusts over and stays soggy, improve the drainage or sow into a raised bed. These organisms move in soil water, so a bed that sheds extra water gives seedlings a fair chance.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: On heavy or slow-draining ground, improve drainage or use raised beds; the pathogens spread in soil water and are favored by cool, wet, poorly drained conditions, and a crusted, slow-draining seedbed raises losses.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Seedlings that have flopped over will not recover, so clear the fallen ones away. If damping-off shows up, also hold off on watering for a bit and let the soil surface dry out some to slow it down; there is no good home cure once it starts.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Collapsed seedlings cannot be saved; clear them out, and pause irrigation so the surface dries somewhat to slow the pathogens. Prevention is the real lever, since there is no effective home cure once damping-off takes hold.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, and it matters most in the first few weeks. From sowing until the seedlings are up, often 2 to 3 weeks, the surface must never dry out or crust, so light daily watering may be needed in warm or windy weather. Once established, carrots want steady moisture rather than a wet-dry swing: aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings that draw the roots downward.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, and pay closest attention in the first few weeks. From planting until the sprouts appear (which can take 2 to 3 weeks), the surface must stay moist and never dry into a hard crust, so you may need to water lightly every day in warm or windy weather. After that, give about 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings so the roots grow down.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week including rainfall once established, adjusted up in heat or sandy soil and down in cool or clay soil. The seedbed needs only enough to stay evenly moist near the surface during germination, not soaking.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, including rain, once the plants are growing. Give more in hot weather or sandy soil and less in cool weather or heavy soil. While the seeds are sprouting, just keep the top of the soil damp, not soggy.
