growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow only once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth; there is no advantage to planting early, and every advantage to waiting. Sow about 1 inch deep into a moist, well-drained bed and avoid soaking the soil, which suffocates the germinating seed and feeds root rot fungi.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Wait to plant until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F. There is no reward for planting early with beans, only rotted seed. Plant about 1 inch deep in moist, well-drained soil, and do not keep the bed soggy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your beans emerged? Note the date to track days to maturity from a real sowing rather than the seed packet.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your beans come up yet? Write down the date you first saw them break the soil.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The cotyledons open and the first true leaves appear: a pair of single leaflets, followed by the bean's characteristic three-part (trifoliate) leaves. Growth is quick once the plant is up and the weather is warm. Young seedlings are the stage most vulnerable to bean leaf beetle feeding, which can thin a stand.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The two seed leaves open, then the real leaves appear, first a single pair, then the three-leaflet leaves that beans are known for. Once they are up and the weather is warm, they grow fast. This young stage is when beetles can do the most damage to the little plants.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free; young beans compete poorly with weeds. Cultivate shallowly, since bean roots run close to the surface and are easily damaged. There is no thinning to do: bush beans are sown at their final spacing and are not thinned.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and pull weeds early, because small beans do not compete well with them. Weed and hoe shallowly, since bean roots are close to the surface. You do not need to thin bush beans, they are planted where they will grow.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is your bean stand looking? Note any gaps or beetle damage on the young leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young bean plants look? Note any chewed leaves or bare patches in the row.

growth_stages.name: Leafy growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady leafy growth as the bush fills out to its full height of about two feet and builds the canopy that will support flowering. The plant is fixing much of its own nitrogen now through root nodules, so vigorous but not lush, overfed growth is the goal. Overly dark, leafy plants with little branching signal excess nitrogen and forecast a poor pod set.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows leafier and fills out to its full size, usually about two feet tall, building up before it flowers. Beans make much of their own food (nitrogen) at this stage. You want healthy green growth, not huge dark leafy plants, which often mean too much fertilizer and fewer beans later.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold steady, even moisture and resist the urge to feed. Beans need little nitrogen, and adding more now pushes leafy growth at the expense of flowers and pods. A single light side-dressing before bloom is plenty, and only on poor or sandy soil.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady and do not add fertilizer now. Beans need very little, and extra fertilizer gives you big leafy plants but fewer beans. One light feeding right before they flower is all they need, and only in poor soil.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your bean plants filling in? Note their height and how bushy they look.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How big are your bean plants getting? Note how tall and full they look.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white, pink, or purple flowers open across the bush. Bush beans flower over a concentrated window, so most of the crop is set here within a week or two. This is the moisture-critical stage: water stress now aborts blossoms, and sustained heat above about 90°F causes blossom drop, especially in varieties like Blue Lake 274. Pod set resumes once the weather cools.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small white, pink, or purple flowers open all over the plant. Bush beans flower in a short burst, so most of your crop is decided in a week or two. This is the most important time for water. If the plants dry out or the weather stays above about 90°F, the flowers drop without making beans. They start setting beans again once it cools off.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom; this is where water stress directly cuts yield. Avoid overhead watering, which spreads disease onto the now-dense canopy. In a heat wave, water deeply the day before and consider temporary afternoon shade, but mostly the plant will recover and reflower when temperatures ease.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants are flowering, because dry soil now means fewer beans. Water the soil, not the leaves, to avoid spreading disease. If a heat wave hits, water deeply the day before, but mostly just wait it out, the plants will flower again when it cools.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your beans flowering? Note the date bloom started and any blossom drop in heat.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your beans flowering yet? Note when the flowers opened and whether any dropped in hot weather.

growth_stages.name: Pod set and fill
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tiny pods appear where flowers were and lengthen quickly, plumping as the seeds inside begin to fill. This and flowering are the two moisture-critical stages; drought here produces small, stringy, misshapen pods. Pods can go from pickable to overmature in a few days, so the window is short.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Little pods form where the flowers were and grow quickly, getting plumper as the beans fill inside. Along with flowering, this is when steady water matters most: dry soil now makes small, tough, crooked pods. Pods can go from just right to too old in only a few days.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain even moisture near field capacity right through pod fill; this is the payoff stage for steady watering. Begin checking pods daily as they size up, since the pickable window is brief and the first pods reach harvest size quickly.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist all through this stage, it is what all the steady watering was for. Start checking the pods every day as they grow, because they are ready for only a short time before they get too old.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are pods forming and filling? Note the date you first saw pods and how fast they are sizing up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are pods forming? Note when you first saw them and how quickly they are growing.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly when bent, picked before the enlarging seeds bulge the pod wall. Most bush varieties reach this around 50 to 60 days. Because bush beans crop over a concentrated two-to-three-week window, the plants come on heavily and then taper; regular picking every couple of days keeps them producing and catches pods at peak tenderness.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Firm, crisp pods that break with a clean snap, picked before you can see the seeds bulging through the pod. Most bush beans are ready around 50 to 60 days. They produce a big batch over two to three weeks, so pick every couple of days to keep them coming and to catch the beans while they are tender.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick in the early morning for best quality, breaking pods off above the cap so the brittle stems are not torn. Harvest every two to three days; leaving mature pods on the plant signals it to stop flowering and ends the crop early. Do not pick when foliage is wet, which spreads bacterial blight.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick in the morning for the best beans, snapping the pod off above its little cap so you do not tear the stem. Pick every two or three days, because leaving old pods on the plant tells it to stop making more. Do not pick when the leaves are wet, since that spreads disease.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you made your first picking? Log the harvest date and how the pods sized up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your first beans? Note the date and how they turned out.

notifications.body_seasoned: Direct-sow bush beans after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth. Sow about 1 inch deep into a moist, well-drained bed; there is no advantage to planting earlier.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant bush beans right in the garden after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F. Plant about 1 inch deep in moist, well-drained soil. There is no benefit to planting earlier.

notifications.title_seasoned: Sow your next short row of beans
notifications.title_beginner: Plant your next row of beans
notifications.body_seasoned: Bush beans crop over a concentrated two-to-three-week window, then taper. Sow a fresh short row now, about two weeks after your last sowing, to keep fresh beans coming. Stop about two months before your first fall frost.
notifications.body_beginner: Bush beans give a big crop over two to three weeks, then slow down. Plant a new short row now, about two weeks after the last one, to keep beans coming. Stop planting about two months before your first fall frost.

notifications.title_beginner: Start checking your beans every day
notifications.body_seasoned: Most bush beans are ready around 50 to 60 days. Begin checking daily and pick firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly, before the seeds bulge. Harvest every two to three days to keep the plants producing.
notifications.body_beginner: Most bush beans are ready around 50 to 60 days. Start checking every day and pick firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly, before the seeds bulge through. Pick every two or three days to keep more beans coming.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost expected, protect or harvest beans
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost is coming, cover or pick your beans
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Beans are frost-tender and a light frost will kill them. If frost is forecast, harvest any pickable pods and cover plants with row cover or sheets overnight. In fall, a hard frost ends the crop, so pick everything usable first.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Beans are killed by even a light frost. If frost is forecast, pick any beans that are ready and cover the plants with row cover or sheets overnight. In fall, a hard frost ends the crop, so pick everything you can use first.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather can make flowers drop
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above about 90°F during bloom causes beans to drop blossoms instead of setting pods, especially varieties like Blue Lake 274. Keep moisture steady and water deeply ahead of the heat; the plant will resume setting pods once it cools.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: When it stays above about 90°F while beans are flowering, they drop their flowers instead of making beans, especially varieties like Blue Lake 274. Keep the water steady and water deeply before the heat. The plants will start setting beans again once it cools.

germination.text_seasoned: Bean seed rots in cold, wet ground. Wait until the soil is at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing, since early planting only invites poor stands, seed rot, and seedcorn maggot. There is no head start to be had: beans sown into warm soil quickly overtake those sown into cold soil.
germination.text_beginner: Bean seeds rot in cold, wet soil. Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, because planting early just leads to rotted seed and missing plants. Beans planted into warm soil catch up fast, so there is nothing to gain by rushing.
germination.author: plant

germination.text_seasoned: Sow beans where they will grow rather than starting them indoors. Beans resent root disturbance and germinate fast in place, so transplanting offers no advantage and sets plants back. Sow about 1 inch deep into a moist, well-drained bed.
germination.text_beginner: Plant bean seeds right in the garden instead of starting them inside. Beans do not like having their roots disturbed and sprout quickly anyway, so there is no benefit to transplanting. Plant about 1 inch deep in moist, well-drained soil.
germination.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Weed early and cultivate shallowly. Young beans compete poorly with weeds, but their roots run close to the surface, so deep hoeing does more harm than the weeds. Hand-pull and scuffle-hoe lightly near the row, especially in the first six weeks.
seedling.text_beginner: Pull weeds early, but weed shallowly. Young beans do not compete well with weeds, yet their roots are near the surface, so digging deep hurts the plant more than the weeds do. Pull by hand and hoe lightly near the row, especially in the first six weeks.
seedling.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Hold off on nitrogen. As legumes, beans fix much of their own through root nodules, and extra nitrogen now drives leafy growth at the expense of flowers and pods. At most, a single light side-dressing just before bloom, and only on poor or sandy soil.
vegetative.text_beginner: Do not add nitrogen fertilizer now. Beans make much of their own from the air through their roots, and extra fertilizer just gives you big leafy plants with fewer beans. At most, feed once lightly right before they flower, and only if your soil is poor.
vegetative.author: plant

flowering.text_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom. Flowering and pod set are the moisture-critical stages, and water stress now aborts blossoms and directly cuts the crop. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead, to keep the dense canopy dry and limit disease.
flowering.text_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants flower. Flowering and pod-forming are the times beans most need water, and letting them dry out now makes the flowers drop and the crop shrink. Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves, to keep disease down.
flowering.author: plant

flowering.text_seasoned: Expect blossom drop in sustained heat above about 90°F, especially in varieties like Blue Lake 274. The plant aborts flowers when it is too hot to set pods, then resumes once the weather cools. Water deeply ahead of a heat wave, but mostly let the plant recover and reflower.
flowering.text_beginner: When it stays hotter than about 90°F, beans drop their flowers, especially varieties like Blue Lake 274. The plant gives up on flowers when it is too hot to make beans, then starts again once it cools. Water deeply before a heat wave, but mostly just wait, the plants will flower again.
flowering.author: plant

pod_set_fill.text_seasoned: Do not let the bed dry out as pods size up. Drought during pod fill produces small, stringy, misshapen pods, while steady moisture near field capacity gives plump, well-formed ones. This is the payoff stage for all the even watering that came before.
pod_set_fill.text_beginner: Do not let the soil dry out while the pods are growing. Dry soil now makes small, tough, crooked beans, while steady moisture gives you plump, well-shaped ones. This is what all that careful watering was building toward.
pod_set_fill.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick every two to three days, before the seeds bulge the pod. Bush beans crop heavily over a short window, and leaving mature pods on the plant signals it to stop flowering, ending the crop early. Frequent picking keeps the plant producing and catches pods at peak tenderness.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick every two or three days, before the seeds swell the pods. Bush beans give a big crop over a short time, and leaving old pods on the plant tells it to quit making more. Picking often keeps the beans coming and catches them while they are tender.
harvest.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick in the early morning for best quality, but only once the dew has dried. Handling wet bean plants spreads bacterial blight through the planting, so wait for the foliage to dry before working down the rows.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick in the morning for the best beans, but wait until the dew has dried off the plants. Touching wet bean plants spreads disease through your patch, so let the leaves dry before you start picking.
harvest.author: plant

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Bush beans yield modestly per plant, which is why they are grown in short rows or blocks rather than singly. A 10-foot row of bush beans typically returns about 5 to 10 pounds of pods over its concentrated cropping window.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each bush bean plant gives only a modest amount, which is why they are grown in short rows or patches rather than one at a time. A 10-foot row usually gives about 5 to 10 pounds of beans over its main picking weeks.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Bush beans crop heavily over a concentrated two-to-three-week window, then taper. Most of a row's yield comes in that burst, which is why succession sowing every couple of weeks is the way to keep a steady supply rather than facing one large glut.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Bush beans give most of their crop in a short two-to-three-week burst, then slow down. That is why planting a new short row every couple of weeks keeps beans coming steadily instead of arriving all at once.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Bush beans are among the most dependable first-year crops: they germinate quickly, ask little, and produce a real harvest in about 50 to 60 days. A first-year grower can reasonably expect a solid pick from even a short row, with steady moisture through flowering and pod fill being the main lever on yield.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Bush beans are one of the most reliable crops for a first-year garden. They come up fast, need little fuss, and give a real harvest in about 50 to 60 days. Even a short row should give you a good pick, and the main thing that affects how much you get is keeping the water steady while they flower and form pods.
factors_seasoned: Steady moisture through flowering and pod fill (the moisture-critical stages; drought here aborts blossoms and shrinks pods)
Temperature during bloom (sustained heat above about 90°F causes blossom drop and cuts the set)
Stand density (bush beans crop best at full spacing; thin or gappy stands reduce total yield)
Regular picking (leaving mature pods on the plant signals it to stop flowering and ends the crop early)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No university extension or peer-reviewed source supports timing bush bean planting by moon phase. No recommendation is made here: sow beans by soil temperature, which should be at least about 60°F, and by your frost-free date, not by the lunar cycle.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers dropped without setting pods
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Flowers fell off without making beans
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant flowered but the blossoms dropped instead of setting pods, because sustained heat above about 90°F interferes with pollination and the plant aborts flowers it cannot fill. Some varieties, such as Blue Lake 274, are especially prone. Water stress during bloom has the same effect. It is a weather problem, not a disease, and the plant usually resumes setting pods once temperatures cool.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant flowered, but the flowers fell off without making beans, because steady heat above about 90°F stops the flowers from being pollinated and the plant drops them. Some varieties, like Blue Lake 274, are hit harder. Letting the plants dry out while flowering does the same thing. It is a weather problem, not a disease, and the plant usually starts setting beans again once it cools off.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time plantings so bloom misses the hottest part of summer, sowing early enough to crop before peak heat or as a late-summer succession for a fall crop. Keep moisture steady and ample through flowering, water deeply ahead of a heat wave, and choose more heat-tolerant varieties where summers are reliably hot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plan your planting so the flowering time skips the hottest part of summer, either early enough to finish before peak heat or as a late-summer planting for a fall crop. Keep the water steady while they flower, water deeply before a heat wave, and pick more heat-tolerant varieties if your summers are very hot.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds rotted or came up poorly
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Seeds rotted or did not come up
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The seeds were sown into soil that was too cold and wet, so they sat without germinating and rotted, or came up as a thin, patchy stand. Bean seed does not germinate well below about 60°F, and a slow, cold start invites soilborne root rot fungi and seedcorn maggot, both of which attack the lingering seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The seeds went into soil that was too cold and wet, so they sat there instead of sprouting and rotted, or came up thin and patchy. Bean seeds do not sprout well below about 60°F, and a slow, cold start lets soil fungi and a seed-eating maggot get to the seed while it waits.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing; there is no benefit to planting early. Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than low, wet spots, plant about 1 inch deep, and do not keep the bed soggy after sowing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, since there is no reward for planting beans early. Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of low, wet spots, plant about 1 inch deep, and do not keep the bed soggy after planting.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Big leafy plants but few beans
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Big leafy plants but hardly any beans
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plants grew large and dark and leafy but set few pods, because they were given too much nitrogen. As legumes, beans fix much of their own nitrogen, and extra fertilizer over-stimulates leaf growth, delays flowering, and reduces pod set.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plants grew big, dark, and leafy but made very few beans, because they got too much nitrogen. Beans make much of their own nitrogen from the air, so extra fertilizer just pushes leafy growth, delays flowering, and gives you fewer beans.
failure_diagnostics.cause: too much nitrogen
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Skip the nitrogen feeding. Work in only a little balanced fertilizer or compost before planting, and at most one light side-dressing just before bloom, and only on poor or sandy soil. Let the plant's own nitrogen fixation carry the crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Skip the extra fertilizer. Mix in just a little balanced fertilizer or compost before planting, and at most one light feeding right before they flower, and only if your soil is poor. Let the beans make their own nitrogen.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pods small, tough, or stringy
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Beans came out small, tough, or stringy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The pods came out small, fibrous, or misshapen, usually from drought stress during and after flowering, which is the moisture-critical window, or from leaving pods on the plant past their tender stage, when the enlarging seeds make the pod woody. Both are easy to prevent.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The beans came out small, tough, or crooked, usually because the plants dried out while flowering and filling pods, which is the time they most need water, or because the pods were left on too long, until the swelling seeds made them woody. Both are easy to fix.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample from first flower through pod fill, and pick every two to three days, harvesting pods while they are still firm, crisp, and before the seeds bulge. Frequent picking also keeps the plant producing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the water steady from the first flowers through pod-filling, and pick every two or three days while the pods are still firm and crisp, before you can see the seeds bulging. Picking often also keeps more beans coming.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Bush beans crop heavily over a short two-to-three-week window, then taper. Sow a fresh short row every two weeks from the last spring frost until about two months before your first fall frost, and you will keep fresh beans coming all season instead of facing one big glut.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: A row of bush beans gives you a lot of beans all at once, then slows down. To keep beans coming, plant a new short row every couple of weeks through the summer. Stop planting about two months before your first fall frost so the last batch has time to finish.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In colder areas you grow green beans in one long stretch. Wait until after your last spring frost, when the soil has warmed, then plant a new short row every couple of weeks. Stop planting around mid to late July so the last beans have time to ripen before the first fall frost. Frost kills bean plants, so the season ends when the cold arrives.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold zones, bush beans run as one continuous season. Sow once the soil holds above 60°F and the last spring frost has passed, then sow a fresh short row every two weeks. Stop sowing in mid to late July, even where the calendar looks open longer: a late sowing meets cool, short fall days during pod fill and rarely finishes a full crop before the first fall frost kills the plants. The earliest sowings begin yielding in roughly 50 days, and harvest carries through until frost.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: snap beans set during deep-summer heat abort their blossoms before pods form. Blossom drop becomes a problem once daytime highs run above about 90 degrees F, made worse by warm nights (night temperatures above the high 60s suppress pollen viability), and the plants resume setting pods as temperatures cool. (UGA Cooperative Extension C963; UF/IFAS VH021)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Here you get two bean seasons, one in spring and one for fall, with a summer break in between. Plant in spring after the last frost. Then stop during the hottest part of summer, when it is too hot for beans to form pods. Plant again in mid summer for a fall harvest. Each planting takes about 50 to 60 days to give you beans.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf run two bean seasons split by summer heat. Sow in spring after frost, then again in mid summer for a fall crop. The gap is real: through the hottest weeks blossoms drop and pods fail to set, so there is no point sowing into peak heat. Middle Georgia anchors the spring sowing to roughly mid March and the fall sowing to early July; the deeper South shifts spring earlier and fall later. Each sowing reaches a pickable crop in about 50 to 60 days.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In the valleys you plant green beans twice: once in spring and once in late summer, with a break when it is hottest. Plant in April and May. Then stop in the heat of summer, because beans will not set pods when it is too hot. Plant again in July for a fall crop. Water steadily and pick often so the plants keep making beans.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: The interior valleys carry a spring crop and a late summer crop with a midsummer break. Sow in April and May, then pause through the peak of summer heat, when daytime highs stall pod set and the spring planting winds down. Resume sowing in July for a fall crop as the worst heat eases. Spring sowings yield from late May into June; the fall sowings carry harvest into October. Direct sow into warm soil after frost and pick every couple of days to keep plants productive.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the desert you grow green beans in cooler weather: a winter to spring crop and a fall crop, with a long summer break. Plant from mid January through March. Then stop for the hot months, because beans cannot make pods in extreme heat. Plant again in August once it starts to cool. Spring beans finish by late May, and the August planting gives a fall harvest.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The desert valleys carry a winter to spring crop and a fall crop, with a long, hard summer break. Sow from mid January through March, then stop entirely through the hottest months, when extreme heat ends pod set and the spring crop finishes. Resume sowing in August as the heat begins to ease. Spring sowings yield from spring into late May; the August sowing carries harvest into fall. The summer gap is not optional here, it is when nothing sets.

In central Florida you plant a spring crop and a fall crop, with a break in the hot, wet summer: plant from late winter through April, then again in August. fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: Peninsular Florida inverts the calendar. Each sowing reaches a crop in about 50 to 60 days; the right window depends on how far south the garden sits.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: West of the Cascades, bush beans are a solid summer crop. Wait until the soil has warmed after the last spring frost, then sow a new short row every two to three weeks so you always have young beans coming. On the immediate coast, keep sowings to May and June since the cooler, foggier summer there favors an earlier stop; inland in the Willamette Valley and Puget lowlands you can keep sowing into July. Beans are frost-tender, so the whole planting keeps producing right up until the first fall frost ends it.

Sow a fresh short row every two to three weeks through the window for a steady, non-succession-dependent supply; the earliest sowings begin yielding in about 50 to 60 days. Because this crop is frost-tender, harvest simply continues until the first fall frost kills the plants, so there is no need to plan a stop date beyond the sowing cutoff itself.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, direct-sow bush beans outdoors in spring once the last frost has passed, from about Mar 10 through Apr 20, for a harvest before the worst heat hits. Once daytime highs push past 90°F in summer, blossoms drop and pods fail to set, so the plants take a long break. Sow again from about Jul 15 to Aug 10 for a fall crop that ripens as the weather cools, picked before the first frost.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) grows bush beans on two direct-sown cycles, per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart. Spring sowing runs roughly Mar 10 to Apr 20, with harvest beginning about 55 days later; the crop is picked before summer's real heat wall. Once daytime highs run past 90°F, blossoms drop and pods fail to set, so the chart calls for a real gap through the hottest weeks rather than a continuous summer run. The chart's late-summer window (about Jul 15 to Aug 10) restarts the crop as the heat breaks, timed to finish picking a few days ahead of the valley's first fall frost. Zone 8's cooler pockets compress both ends: a later spring set-out and an earlier fall sowing to beat that zone's earlier frost; zone 10 at Laughlin runs the opposite, earlier spring and a later fall sowing, with its later frost.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: In St. George's Dixie, direct-sow bush beans outdoors around March 15, about two weeks before the average last frost, since USU Extension lists this as the local planting date for a quick, compact bush bean. Expect to start picking around May 9, and keep harvesting through June. Once daytime highs push past 95°F in July, plants stop producing for the summer, and there is no fall replanting here, so the season is over once the June harvest ends. Bush beans crop over a few weeks rather than all at once; pick pods young and often to keep plants productive through late June.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs bush beans on one spring cycle only, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah. Direct-sow around March 15, the Group C (Tender) date for St. George, about two weeks ahead of the March 30 average last frost; the table's explicit local date runs earlier than a generic frost-relative rule would. Harvest begins about 55 days later, around May 9, and continues into late June. Once St. George's daytime highs push past 95°F and the county's own frost-and-elevation data show summer highs routinely reaching 100°F in June through August, blossoms drop and pods fail to set. USU documents fall planting for cool-season crops in the St. George area but gives no fall or summer-replant window for bush beans, so there is no second cycle here; frost returns around November 1, well after the plants have already stopped producing for the year.

crops.description_seasoned: Bush snap beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are a fast, frost-tender warm-season legume grown for their tender immature pods. Compact and self-supporting, they crop heavily over a concentrated two-to-three-week window, which makes succession sowing the key to a steady supply. Direct-sown into warm soil after the last frost, they fix their own nitrogen, ask little of the gardener, and reach a pickable crop in about 50 to 60 days.
crops.description_beginner: Bush beans are one of the easiest vegetables to grow and a great first crop. They are small, tidy plants that do not need staking, and they go from seed to harvest in about two months. You plant the seeds straight in the garden after the last frost, keep them watered, and start picking. Because a patch produces a big batch all at once, planting a new short row every couple of weeks keeps fresh beans on the table all summer.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when pods are firm, crisp, and snap cleanly, before the enlarging seeds bulge the pod. Harvesting every couple of days keeps plants producing and catches pods at peak tenderness.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Beans are ready when the pods are firm and crisp and break with a clean snap, before you can see the seeds bulging inside. Pick every few days to keep more beans coming.

crops.name: Sugar Snap Peas

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Snap peas like loose, fertile soil that drains well, with some compost mixed in. The main thing they care about is good drainage, because peas planted in cold, soggy soil tend to rot before they sprout. If water sits on your bed for a long time after rain, work in compost or plant on a raised bed first.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Sugar snap peas do best in a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam with compost worked in before sowing. The critical trait is drainage: pea seed sown into cold, wet, poorly drained ground rots before it germinates, and the soilborne root rots that follow are the main early-season risk. Steady, even moisture without waterlogging carries the crop through flowering and pod fill, the stage that decides whether the pods plump up. Peas are legumes and fix much of their own nitrogen, so the bed needs fertility and tilth more than heavy feeding.

ph.note_beginner: Snap peas grow best in soil from about 6.0 to 7.0, which is slightly acidic to neutral. They do poorly in strongly acidic soil below 6.0, so if a soil test reads low, mix in some lime before planting. Most garden beds are already in a good range.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0. Clemson targets 6.0 to 6.5 for peas, and growth is inhibited on acid soils at pH 6.0 and below, so lime an acid plot the season before sowing. Peas tolerate up to roughly 7.5, and a soil test is the reliable way to confirm both pH and fertility before the season starts.

fertilizer.type: balanced pre-plant, little to no nitrogen
fertilizer.timing: work a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the bed before sowing
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 pre-plant
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Sugar snap peas are light feeders. As legumes they fix much of their own nitrogen through root nodules, so heavy nitrogen drives leafy vine growth at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the bed before sowing; that is usually all peas need. An inoculant of the right Rhizobium bacteria is optional and can help nodulation where peas have not been grown before. Avoid high-nitrogen feeds, which delay flowering and cut pod set.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Peas make much of their own food from the air, so they barely need fertilizer. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant and that is enough. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy vines but fewer pods. If you like, you can coat the seed with a pea inoculant powder, which helps the roots make nitrogen, but it is optional.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced 5-10-10 worked in before sowing if no soil test is available; skip extra nitrogen, which peas supply themselves.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 mixed into the bed before planting is plenty.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet worked in before sowing, per Clemson, when no soil test is available.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet, mixed into the bed before planting.

companions.note_beginner: Snap peas get along with most cool-season vegetables. They grow happily beside carrots, radishes, and lettuce, and because they leave nitrogen in the soil, they are a good crop to grow before a leafy green. The pairing to avoid is planting peas right next to onions or garlic.
companions.note_seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, sugar snap peas leave the soil richer for what follows and sit comfortably among the other cool-season crops grown in the same early-spring and fall windows: carrots, radishes, and lettuce are classic bed-mates. The long-standing caution is to keep peas away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress legumes through the same root-bacteria interference seen with beans.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrot
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A classic cool-season neighbor that shares snap peas' early-spring and fall timing; the carrots root deep while the peas climb, so they use the bed without crowding.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Carrots and peas are a long-standing cool-season companion pairing; the benefit is shared timing, complementary root-vs-vine habit, and the peas' nitrogen lightly helping the carrots. Traditional/medium: well grounded in shared conditions, not a measured pest effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots and peas grow in the same cool windows and use the bed in complementary ways: the carrot works the soil deep while the pea climbs above it, and the peas' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the carrot. The pairing is traditional and compatibility-based rather than a measured pest defense, so expect easy cohabitation more than active protection.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Radish
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Radishes sprout fast and mark the pea rows while the slower peas come up, then are pulled long before the peas need the space.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Radish-as-quick-marker interplanted with a slower crop is a standard, low-risk home-garden practice; both are cool-season and the radish is harvested before competition matters. Traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Radishes germinate in days and mark the rows while the peas emerge, and they finish and come out weeks before the vines size up, so they never compete. Both are cool-season crops sown at the same time, which makes them a tidy, low-risk interplant rather than a measured protective pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce shares snap peas' cool-season timing and stays low, tucking in along the base of the pea row or trellis.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Lettuce and peas share cool-season conditions and occupy different layers (low leafy crop under the climbing vine); a sound shared-conditions compatibility, by close analogy to other cool-season interplants. Likely rather than research_backed (no pea-specific lettuce trial located).

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce slots in below a pea trellis or alongside a bush row, sharing the same cool-season window and water needs while occupying a different layer of the bed. As the peas leaf out they offer the lettuce a little light afternoon shade that delays bolting. It is a compatibility pairing on sound shared-conditions grounds rather than a measured protective one.

good_seasoned.name: Carrot
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional cool-season pairing: carrots and peas share early-spring and fall timing and use the bed in complementary ways, the carrot rooting deep while the pea climbs.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing cool-season companion pairing (shared timing, root-vs-vine complementarity, light N benefit); not experimentally quantified.

good_seasoned.name: Radish
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sown with the peas, fast radishes mark the rows and are pulled well before the vines need the space; both are cool-season crops with the same timing.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Standard quick-marker interplant; radish finishes before competition matters. Traditional/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from peas, which are said to grow poorly near them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: The same allium-versus-legume mechanism reported for beans: allium sulfur compounds are held to disrupt the Rhizobium bacteria peas depend on to fix nitrogen, stunting the vines. Mechanistic/medium: a sound, repeatedly cited mechanism, not a controlled pea-yield trial opened this session.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Onions next to peas is the better-grounded of the 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds that are widely held to interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria on pea roots, the bacteria the plant relies on to fix nitrogen, so pea growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. The useful corollary is that peas grown before an allium crop leave the soil better for it.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for peas.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Garlic is an allium with the same antibacterial sulfur chemistry as onion; same Rhizobium-disruption mechanism. Mechanistic/medium for the same reasons.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Garlic acts on peas the way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds held to disrupt the nitrogen-fixing bacteria on pea roots, slowing the vines. Treat garlic and peas as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the pea-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

bad_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are the classic traditional caution near peas and other legumes; the pairing is widely advised against, attributed to allium compounds interfering with the pea's nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing allium-versus-legume garden caution; mechanism plausible but not experimentally established here.

bad_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: As with onion, garlic is traditionally kept apart from peas.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium caution, traditional.

pests.name: Pea aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of soft, pinhead-sized green aphids clustered on the growing tips, flower stalks, and leaf undersides. Heavy feeding curls and yellows the new growth, stunts the vines, and can drop blossoms; a sticky honeydew and sooty mold may follow. Most important, pea aphids transmit the virus diseases of peas, including pea enation mosaic, so even modest numbers matter.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of small, soft green insects packed onto the growing tips, flower stems, and undersides of the leaves. They curl and yellow the new growth and stunt the plants, and they leave a sticky residue. The bigger problem is that pea aphids spread virus diseases from plant to plant, so they are worth catching early.
pests.cause_seasoned: The pea aphid (Acyrthosiphon pisum), a large green aphid that builds up fast in the cool, mild weather of spring and fall, exactly the seasons peas grow. It reproduces rapidly, so colonies form before natural enemies catch up.
pests.cause_beginner: The pea aphid, a large green aphid that multiplies quickly in the cool weather of spring and fall when peas are growing. It builds up fast, before helpful insects like ladybugs catch up.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water, or treat with insecticidal soap, which controls aphids on contact; begin as soon as colonies are found, while numbers are low. Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually bring populations down on their own. Because the real risk is virus transmission, act early rather than waiting for visible damage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast the colonies off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap, which works on contact. Start as soon as you see them, while there are only a few. Ladybugs and other helpful insects usually finish the job. Since aphids spread viruses, it is worth dealing with them early.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Lay reflective mulch, which disorients aphids and reduces both feeding and virus spread, and control nearby weeds and clover that harbor them. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor, and choose virus-resistant snap varieties such as Cascadia or Sugar Sprint where pea viruses are a known problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Lay down reflective mulch, which confuses aphids and cuts the viruses they spread, and pull nearby weeds that shelter them. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is exactly what aphids like. Where pea viruses are common, plant a resistant variety like Cascadia or Sugar Sprint.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where pea viruses turn up in your area, start at the seed rack. Cascadia and Sugar Sprint are snap varieties that resist those viruses. The resistance is to the virus rather than to the aphid itself, so you may still see the insects.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cascadia and Sugar Sprint carry virus resistance, worth choosing where pea viruses are a known local problem. It addresses the transmission outcome, not the aphid population, so pair it with the steps below.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay reflective mulch, a silvery plastic or foil sheet, on the soil while the plants are still small. It confuses aphids looking for somewhere to land and cuts down the viruses they carry in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch disorients incoming aphids, reducing both feeding and the virus spread that is the real risk here. Lay it early, while the canopy is still open enough for the soil to show.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull the weeds and clover near the bed. Aphids shelter and build up in them before moving across onto your peas.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Nearby weeds and clover act as a reservoir. Clearing them before sowing and holding the row edges clean through the season cuts the source population that colonizes the crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. Too much nitrogen pushes soft, lush new growth, which is the growth aphids prefer.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen produces the succulent tissue pea aphid favors. Feeding restraint makes the crop a poorer host rather than treating an infestation after it forms.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the colonies off with a strong jet of water from the hose. Do this as soon as you spot them, while there are only a few clusters on the tips.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water spray dislodges colonies from growing tips, flower stalks and leaf undersides. Most useful while numbers are low, which is also when the virus risk is easiest to blunt.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the helpful insects a chance to work. Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which lay their eggs inside aphids, usually bring the numbers down on their own.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Lady beetles, lacewings and parasitoid wasps generally catch up with pea aphid without intervention. The lag is widest in cool spring and fall weather, when the aphid reproduces faster than they build.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the colonies keep building, insecticidal soap kills the aphids it touches directly, so wet the growing tips and the undersides of leaves where they cluster. Start while numbers are still low.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is contact-only, so coverage of tips and leaf undersides governs the result. Begin at the first colonies rather than waiting for curling or yellowing, since transmission runs ahead of visible damage.

pests.name: Pea weevil
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small notches chewed from the leaf margins of young plants in spring, and adults feeding on the blossoms. The real damage is hidden: larvae bore into the developing seeds inside the pods and feed there, leaving tiny round exit holes in the dried peas. Because snap peas are eaten pod and all, weevil-infested pods are especially unwelcome. Saved seed with holes is the giveaway, and the pea weevil feeds only on peas (Pisum).
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little notches chewed out of the leaf edges of young plants, and beetles on the flowers in spring. The hidden damage is worse: the grubs tunnel into the peas forming inside the pods, leaving tiny round holes in the dried seeds. Since you eat snap peas pod and all, infested pods are especially unwelcome. Holes in saved seed are the tell, and the pea weevil eats only peas.
pests.cause_seasoned: The pea weevil (Bruchus pisorum), a small brownish beetle whose host range is peas alone. Adults overwinter in debris and trash, move into the crop at bloom to lay eggs on young pods, and the larvae develop inside the seeds. There is one generation a year.
pests.cause_beginner: The pea weevil, a small brown beetle that feeds only on peas. The adults spend the winter in garden trash, move in when the peas flower to lay eggs on the young pods, and the grubs grow up inside the seeds. There is one generation each year.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Monitor for adults during bloom, when egg-laying begins. In a home patch, handpicking and floating row cover over the crop at flowering reduce egg-laying. At season's end, inspect dried peas for the small round exit holes before storing seed; freezing saved seed for several days kills any larvae inside.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Watch for the beetles while the peas are flowering, which is when they lay eggs. Picking them off and covering the plants with a light row cover at flowering both help. At the end of the season, check dried peas for tiny round holes before you save seed, and freezing saved seed for a few days kills any grubs inside.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clean up and destroy pea debris after harvest to remove overwintering shelter, and rotate peas away from last year's bed. Do not save or replant seed showing exit holes. Where the weevil is established, an early sowing that finishes pod fill before peak adult activity escapes the worst.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear away and destroy the old pea plants after harvest so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter, and move your peas to a new spot each year. Do not save seed that has holes in it. Planting early so the pods finish before the beetles get busy also helps.

control_ladder.note_beginner: After harvest, pull the spent pea plants and destroy them instead of leaving them in the bed. The adult beetles spend the winter in that trash.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Destroying pea residue after harvest strips the overwintering shelter adults use. With a single generation a year, removing that refuge acts directly on next spring's pressure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sow next year's peas in a different part of the garden, away from the bed that just carried them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotating off last year's pea ground puts distance between emerging adults and the new crop. Host range is peas alone, so a bed of anything else offers them nothing.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where this beetle is established, sowing early helps. If the pods finish filling before the adults are at their busiest, the crop can slip past the worst of it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: An early sowing that completes pod fill ahead of peak adult activity escapes the heaviest egg-laying. Adults move in at bloom, so bloom through pod fill is the stretch that has to be missed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Watch the plants while they are flowering, which is when the beetles arrive to lay eggs, and pick off the ones you find on the blossoms.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Scout blossoms through bloom, the egg-laying window, and remove adults by hand. Practical at home-patch scale, and it cuts the eggs placed on young pods.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put a light row cover over the planting once the peas start to flower. It keeps the beetles off the young pods so they have nowhere to lay.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover applied at flowering excludes adults through the egg-laying window, the narrow period that decides how many larvae end up developing inside the seeds.

pests.name: Armyworms and cutworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Cutworms sever young seedlings at or just below the soil line overnight, leaving toppled plants and thinned rows in spring. Armyworms are smooth caterpillars that chew foliage and can move through a planting in numbers, skeletonizing leaves and nicking pods. Both feed mostly at night and hide in the soil or debris by day.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Cutworms cut off young pea seedlings right at the soil line overnight, so you find plants toppled over and gaps in the row. Armyworms are smooth caterpillars that chew the leaves and sometimes the pods, and they can show up in numbers. Both feed at night and hide during the day.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several night-feeding caterpillars, including cutworms (the larvae of various moths) and beet or western yellowstriped armyworms. They overwinter or move in from weedy ground and grassy cover, and seedlings are the most vulnerable stage.
pests.cause_beginner: Several kinds of night-feeding caterpillars: cutworms and armyworms, the young of different moths. They come in from weedy or grassy areas, and young seedlings are the most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick caterpillars in the evening or early morning, and check the soil around toppled seedlings for the curled cutworm. A cardboard or foil collar around a seedling stops cutworms; Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) controls young armyworms on the foliage. A floating row cover keeps egg-laying moths off the planting.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the caterpillars off in the evening or early morning, and dig a little around fallen seedlings to find the curled-up cutworm. A collar of cardboard or foil around a seedling blocks cutworms, and a Bt spray controls young armyworms on the leaves. A light row cover keeps the moths from laying eggs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clear weeds and grassy cover before sowing to remove egg-laying sites, and turn the bed a couple of weeks ahead of planting to expose and dry out resident larvae. Keep row edges weed-free through the season, and protect emerging seedlings, the vulnerable stage, with a row cover where these caterpillars are a known problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear weeds and tall grass before planting so the moths have fewer places to lay eggs, and turn the soil a couple of weeks before sowing to expose the grubs. Keep the edges of the bed weeded, and cover young seedlings with a row cover if these caterpillars are a problem where you are.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear the weeds and tall grass around the bed before you sow. That cover is where the moths lay, so taking it away means fewer caterpillars to deal with later.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Weedy and grassy cover supplies the egg-laying sites. Clearing it before sowing and keeping the row edges clean all season shrinks the pool that moves into the planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Turn the soil in the bed a couple of weeks before you plant. It brings the caterpillars already living there up to the surface, where they dry out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Working the bed roughly two weeks ahead of sowing exposes resident larvae and dries them out before emergence, which is the stage that suffers most.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go out in the evening or first thing in the morning and pick the caterpillars off. When you find a toppled seedling, scratch around in the soil right beside it and you will usually turn up the cutworm, curled tight.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Both groups feed at night and shelter in soil or debris by day, so scout at dusk or first light. A toppled seedling marks the spot, with the cutworm curled in the soil alongside it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ring each young seedling with a collar of cardboard or foil pushed a little way into the soil. It blocks cutworms from reaching the stem.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A cardboard or foil collar set at the soil line physically blocks cutworms during establishment. Worth the labor only over the seedling stage they target.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover the young seedlings with a light row cover. It keeps the egg-laying moths off the planting, and it is worth doing if these caterpillars show up most years where you garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover over emerging seedlings denies the moths a place to lay and protects the vulnerable stage. Reserve it for beds with a local history of this problem.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For armyworms already chewing the leaves, Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis, a bacterium that affects caterpillars) is the spray. It works on young ones, so treat while they are small.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Bt covers the foliage-feeding armyworm half of this pair and is most effective on young larvae. The cutworm half is addressed by the collar rung above rather than by a foliar application.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine silvery or whitish scarring and flecking on leaves and pods, with tiny dark specks of excrement, as the slender insects rasp the surface and feed on the released sap. Heavy feeding distorts new growth and can scar pods cosmetically. Thrips also vector some plant viruses.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Fine silvery streaks and pale flecks on the leaves and pods, with tiny dark specks, where the slender insects scrape the surface and feed. Bad infestations twist the new growth and leave scars on the pods. Thrips can also spread some viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several thrips species, slender insects a fraction the size of an aphid that build up in warm, dry stretches late in the pea season. They rasp the plant surface and feed on the sap that wells up.
pests.cause_beginner: Thrips, slender insects much smaller than an aphid that build up in warm, dry weather toward the end of the pea season. They scrape the surface of the plant and feed on the sap.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Peas usually outgrow light thrips feeding without treatment. Where numbers climb, a strong spray of water and insecticidal soap reduce them, and natural enemies such as minute pirate bugs and lacewings help. Keep plants unstressed and well watered, since drought-stressed peas are more prone.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Peas usually shrug off a little thrips damage. If they build up, a strong spray of water and insecticidal soap knock them back, and helpful insects pitch in. Keep the plants watered and unstressed, since dried-out peas are more likely to be hit.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Control weeds that harbor thrips, lay reflective mulch to disorient them and reduce virus spread, and keep moisture even so plants are not drought-stressed. Most home pea crops finish before thrips become a real problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pull nearby weeds that shelter thrips, lay reflective mulch to confuse them, and keep the soil evenly moist so the plants are not stressed. Most home pea crops are done before thrips become a real problem.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull the weeds near the bed, since thrips shelter in them and move across into the peas from there.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Weedy hosts around the planting carry thrips populations. Clearing them and keeping the edges clean limits what moves in during the warm, dry stretch late in the pea season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Reflective mulch, a silvery sheet laid on the soil, confuses them on the way in and helps with the viruses they can carry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch disorients incoming thrips and reduces virus spread. Laid early, while the canopy is still open enough for the soil to show.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Peas usually shrug off light thrips damage, so often you need do nothing at all. If numbers climb, a strong jet of water from the hose knocks them back.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Light feeding is generally outgrown untreated. Where numbers climb, a forceful water spray reduces them, and most home pea crops finish before pressure peaks.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Helpful insects such as minute pirate bugs and lacewings feed on thrips and often keep them in check for you.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Minute pirate bugs and lacewings contribute real suppression. Conserving them is the better trade on a low-severity problem the crop usually outruns.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If they keep building, insecticidal soap reduces them on contact, so wet the leaves and pods where you can see the silvery scarring.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap works only where it lands, so coverage governs the result. Hold it for the uncommon case where feeding is distorting new growth or scarring pods, and keep the crop watered, since drought-stressed vines are more prone.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white to grayish powdery coating that starts as small spots on the upper leaf surfaces and spreads to cover leaves, stems, and pods. Affected leaves yellow and dry, vines lose vigor, and pods are spotted and off-flavored, which matters more for a snap pea eaten pod and all. It is the classic late-season pea disease, arriving as the spring crop runs into warmer, drier weather.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white to gray powdery dust that starts as spots on top of the leaves and spreads over the leaves, stems, and pods. The leaves yellow and dry out, the vines weaken, and the pods get spotted, which matters more when you eat the whole pod. It is the classic late-season pea problem, showing up as the weather warms and dries toward the end of the spring crop.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Erysiphe pisi, favored by warm days, cool nights, and dry foliage, the conditions that arrive late in the pea season. Spores spread on the wind, and the disease moves fast once established, which is why early control and resistant varieties matter most.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Erysiphe pisi) that thrives in warm days, cool nights, and dry leaves, which is exactly the weather at the end of the pea season. It spreads on the wind and moves fast once it starts, so catching it early and planting resistant varieties matter most.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Powdery mildew is best managed at the very first signs; once it covers the leaves and yellowing sets in, control is difficult. Remove the worst-affected leaves and improve airflow. Sulfur or a labeled biofungicide, begun early and repeated per the label, suppresses it. On a spring crop that is nearly done, harvesting promptly and pulling the planting is often the practical choice.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Powdery mildew is easiest to handle the moment you first see it; once it covers the leaves, it is hard to stop. Pick off the worst leaves and open up the planting for airflow. A sulfur spray started early and repeated per the label helps. If the spring crop is nearly finished, the simplest move is to pick what is ready and pull the plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, the single most effective step: Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint all carry powdery mildew resistance. Sow early so the crop finishes pod fill before the late-season mildew weather, give plants room and a trellis for airflow, and avoid working among wet vines.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant a resistant variety, which is the best defense: Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint resist powdery mildew. Plant early so the crop finishes before the mildew weather arrives, give the plants room and a trellis so air moves through them, and stay out of the patch when the vines are wet.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here. A resistant variety is the best defense against this one, and the snap peas give you choices: Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint each resist powdery mildew.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resistance is the highest-leverage step against a disease that moves fast once established and is difficult to arrest late. Three snap cultivars offer it: Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sow as early as the ground can be worked so the crop finishes before the mildew weather arrives, which is this crop's guidance along with the resistant variety this ladder starts with. Mildew tends to build late, so an early sowing simply finishes ahead of it; this method's cautions carry the cold-soil trade that comes with the early date.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: An early sowing lets the crop finish pod fill before the late-season mildew weather, which is this crop's guidance, and it works because the pressure is seasonal: mildew builds late, and spring sowings mostly finish ahead of it. It sits beside the resistant varieties at the front of the ladder, a when beside their what. The early edge has its own cost in cold, wet soil, and this method's cautions carry it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the plants room and put up a trellis so air moves through the vines instead of sitting still inside a tangle.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spacing and a trellis hold the canopy open through the season. This is a planting-time decision and the cheapest one on the ladder.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off the worst-hit leaves as soon as you notice the powdery patches. Catching it at the first spots is what makes the difference, because once it has spread across the leaves it is hard to turn around.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Pulling the most heavily coated leaves early removes inoculum and opens the canopy at the same time. The value is concentrated at first signs, since control gets difficult once coverage and yellowing set in.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A biofungicide, a spray based on helpful microbes, can hold it back if you start at the first spots and repeat as the label directs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A labeled biofungicide suppresses rather than cures. Begin at first signs and repeat on the label interval, since no curative role is on offer once the leaves are coated.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sulfur is the standard organic spray for powdery mildew. Start it at the first signs and repeat as the label says. If the spring crop is nearly finished anyway, picking what is ready and pulling the plants is often the simpler move.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sulfur suppresses powdery mildew when begun early and repeated per label. On a spring crop close to done, harvesting out and pulling the planting is frequently the more practical call than starting a spray program.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A yellowing of the lower leaves that progresses up the plant, with downward curling, stunting, and wilting; a cut through the lower stem shows a reddish or orange discoloration of the water-conducting tissue. Plants often die before pod fill. Symptoms appear in patches and worsen as the soil warms.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The lower leaves turn yellow and the yellowing creeps up the plant, which becomes stunted, curls, and wilts. If you cut the lower stem, the tissue inside is stained reddish or orange. Affected plants often die before making a crop. It shows up in patches and gets worse as the soil warms.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. pisi, which enters through the roots, plugs the vascular system, and persists in the soil for years. Several races exist. Warm soil favors it, and once a bed is infested the fungus cannot be eradicated, so resistant varieties and rotation are the management.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that lives in the soil and enters through the roots, clogging the plant's plumbing. It survives in the soil for years and likes warm soil. Once it is in a bed you cannot get rid of it, so the answer is resistant varieties and moving your peas around.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected plants; remove and destroy them to limit buildup. Management is preventive: the disease is handled through resistant varieties and rotation, not treatment.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant is infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) the affected plants. You manage this one by preventing it, with resistant varieties and rotation, not by spraying.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant Fusarium-resistant varieties, which are widely available among snap peas: Sugar Snap and Cascadia both carry wilt resistance. Rotate peas on a three-to-four-year cycle away from infested ground, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil between beds.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant a wilt-resistant snap variety such as Sugar Snap or Cascadia. Move your peas to a new spot on a three-to-four-year cycle, improve drainage, and avoid carrying infected soil from bed to bed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This is the main answer. Sugar Snap and Cascadia are snap varieties that carry wilt resistance, and resistant snap peas are easy to find.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resistant snap peas are not hard to source, Sugar Snap and Cascadia among them. Several races of the fungus exist, and with no curative option and a soil population that lingers for years, variety choice still carries the program.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Shift the crop to fresh ground and let three to four years pass before peas come back, so they are not dropped straight into infested soil.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A three to four year rotation off infested ground is the second lever. The fungus persists in soil for years, so rotation manages exposure rather than clearing the bed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Work on the drainage where you grow peas. Better-drained ground is part of the standard advice for keeping this one down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Improve drainage before peas return to the bed, and treat it as a companion to the rotation above rather than a substitute for it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull affected plants and throw them out rather than composting them. Nothing will cure a plant once it is infected, so removal is about keeping the fungus from building up. Try not to carry soil from an infested bed onto a clean one.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Infected plants are not recoverable, and removing and destroying them limits further buildup. Avoiding the transfer of infested soil between beds keeps clean ground clean.

diseases.name: Root rots and damping-off
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Seed that rots before emerging, and seedlings that damp off, collapsing at a water-soaked, pinched stem base. On older plants the root rot complex stunts the vines, yellows and kills the lower leaves, and rots the roots and lower stem brown. Damage is worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil that slows germination and keeps seedlings vulnerable.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that rot before they come up, and seedlings that flop over at a pinched, water-soaked spot near the soil. On bigger plants the roots rot, the vines stunt, and the lower leaves yellow and die. It is worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil that makes the seed sit too long before sprouting.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A complex of soilborne fungi and water molds, chiefly Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Fusarium solani, and Aphanomyces euteiches. Cold, saturated soil and root injury at planting set the stage; Aphanomyces in particular builds up in beds cropped to peas too often and severe infections kill plants outright.
diseases.cause_beginner: A group of soil fungi and water molds (including Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Aphanomyces) that attack seeds, roots, and seedlings. Cold, soggy soil and damaged roots at planting let them in, and they build up where peas are grown too often in the same spot.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for rotted seed or collapsed seedlings; replant into warmer, better-drained conditions once the soil has dried. Removing affected plants and improving drainage limits further loss, but prevention is the real lever since the organisms are already in the soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no saving seed or seedlings that have rotted; replant once the soil is warmer and drains better. Pulling affected plants and improving drainage help, but the main thing is preventing it, since these organisms live in the soil.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than cold, low, wet spots, and do not sow peas into waterlogged soil. Avoid root injury at planting, rotate peas on a three-to-four-year cycle to keep Aphanomyces down, and clear crop debris after harvest. Some varieties offer partial root-rot tolerance.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of cold, wet, low spots, and never sow peas into soggy ground. Avoid damaging the roots when planting, move your peas around the garden on a three-to-four-year cycle, and clear away the old plants after harvest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sow into ground that drains well, or build a raised bed. A cold, low, wet corner of the garden is the hardest place to bring peas up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Site and drainage set the outcome here. Free-draining or raised ground shortens the spell in which cold, saturated soil holds ungerminated seed and slow seedlings exposed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Wait for the soil to warm and drain before you sow, and keep seed out of soggy ground. Be gentle with the roots as you plant. If a sowing has already rotted, sow again once the soil has dried and warmed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soil warmth and moisture at sowing govern this one: hold off on waterlogged ground, avoid root injury at planting, and replant a failed stand only once conditions have improved, since rotted seed and collapsed seedlings offer nothing to rescue.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the bed a break. Plant peas somewhere else and let three to four years go by before they return, since growing them in one spot too often lets these organisms build up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A three to four year rotation is aimed particularly at Aphanomyces, which accumulates in beds cropped to peas too frequently and kills plants outright where infection is severe.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull any plants that have already rotted, and clear the old pea vines out of the bed after harvest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing affected plants in season and stripping crop debris after harvest limits further loss. The organisms are resident in the soil, so this supports prevention rather than standing in for it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Some pea varieties offer partial tolerance to root rot, worth asking about if this keeps happening in your garden. Treat it as extra help rather than a fix.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Partial root-rot tolerance exists in some varieties. It is a margin on top of drainage, sowing conditions and rotation, not a control in its own right.

diseases.name: Ascochyta blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown to purplish-black spots and streaks on leaves, stems, and pods, often with darker margins; a blackening at the base of the stem (foot rot) in one form, and sunken lesions on the pods that can carry the fungus into the seed. It develops in cool, wet spring and fall weather and is carried on infected seed and debris.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Brown to purple-black spots and streaks on the leaves, stems, and pods, sometimes with a blackened stem base. Sunken spots on the pods can carry the disease into the seed. It shows up in cool, wet spring and fall weather and rides in on infected seed and old plant debris.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A complex of related fungi (the Ascochyta blight complex). The fungi survive on infected seed and on pea debris in the soil, and cool, wet conditions with splashing water drive infection and spread.
diseases.cause_beginner: A group of related fungi that survive on infected seed and on old pea plants left in the soil. Cool, wet weather and splashing water spread them. Once they are on the seed, they travel with it to the next planting.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected plants and all debris to limit spread. Cultural control is the mainstay for a home crop, since the disease is seed- and debris-borne.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure tissue that is already infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) affected plants and all the old debris to slow it down. For a home garden, prevention does most of the work, since the disease travels on seed and old plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Remove all pea debris after harvest and rotate peas off the ground for a minimum of three to four years before returning. Avoid overhead watering and working among wet vines, which splash and carry the fungus.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Clear away all the old pea plants after harvest, and do not grow peas in that spot for at least three to four years.
