failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time, water more evenly so the soil is never bone dry or soggy, keep feeding through flowering, and give a little shade or shelter if a heat wave hits while it is blooming.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Healthy tree, plenty of leaves, but little or no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree looks great but makes no fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most often the tree is simply too young, since a grafted lemon does not crop meaningfully until about its third year. Excess nitrogen also pushes leafy growth at the expense of fruit, and severe pruning removes flowering wood. Lemons need no pollinator, so a missing partner is not the cause.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually the tree is just too young, because a grafted lemon does not really fruit until around year three. Too much fertilizer can also make it grow leaves instead of fruit, and hard pruning cuts off the flowering wood. It does not need a second tree, so that is not the issue.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Give a young tree time, ease off high-nitrogen feeding in favor of a balanced citrus fertilizer, and prune only lightly so you keep flowering wood.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Be patient with a young tree, do not over-fertilize, and prune only a little so you do not remove the parts that would have flowered.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaves, twigs, or fruit damaged after a cold snap
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Cold weather hurt the tree
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Standard lemons are among the most frost-tender citrus, with leaf and fruit injury when temperatures fall into the high 20s F and possible death of young wood in a hard freeze. Damage is worse on unprotected young trees and in exposed sites without a warm microclimate.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Lemons are the citrus most easily hurt by cold. Temperatures in the high 20s F damage leaves and fruit, and a hard freeze can kill a young tree. An unprotected young tree in an open spot is most at risk.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site the tree in the warmest microclimate available, protect every cold night with covers, trunk wraps, or a soil bank over the graft, and in marginal zones grow in a container that can move indoors. Wait until new spring growth to assess and prune freeze damage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Put the tree in the warmest spot you have, cover or wrap it on cold nights, and in a borderline-cold area keep it in a pot you can bring inside. Wait for spring growth before cutting off cold-damaged wood, so you can see what survived.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Gumming on the lower trunk with a declining canopy
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Sticky gum on the trunk and a sad-looking tree
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: This is the signature of Phytophthora foot or root rot, driven by poor drainage, a buried graft union, mulch against the trunk, or overwatering. The giveaway is foliage that yellows and wilts but does not recover after watering, separating it from drought stress.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Gum oozing low on the trunk plus a thinning, yellowing tree usually means root rot from soggy soil, a buried graft union, or mulch piled on the trunk. A clue: the leaves do not perk up even after you water.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Correct drainage, pull soil and mulch back to expose the crown and graft union, scrape active cankers back to healthy bark and let them dry, and stop overwatering. Replant high on a mound if drainage cannot be fixed in place.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Fix the drainage, clear soil and mulch away from the base so the trunk can dry, and water less. If the spot stays soggy, replant the tree higher on a mound.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Yellow leaves with green veins, mostly on new growth
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Yellow leaves but the veins stay green
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: This interveinal pattern is micronutrient chlorosis, typically iron or zinc, common where soil is alkaline or calcareous and the nutrients are chemically locked up. It is a soil-availability disorder rather than a deficiency of the nutrient in the ground, and overwatering worsens uptake.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Yellow between the veins with green veins means the tree cannot get enough iron or zinc, which happens a lot in alkaline soil. The nutrients are there, the tree just cannot absorb them, and soggy soil makes it worse.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron, zinc, and manganese, or a chelated iron and zinc product (EDDHA iron holds up best on high-pH soil), and improve drainage. Foliar micronutrient sprays give a faster short-term green-up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Feed a citrus fertilizer with iron and zinc, or a chelated iron and zinc product made for alkaline soil, and improve drainage. A spray on the leaves greens it up faster for a while.

lemon carried frost_tolerance_f = 28 and a "high-20s F" prose claim while hardiness_notes_seasoned credited "Clemson HGIC, Texas A&M AgriLife, UF/IFAS". Of those three, ONLY UF/IFAS publishes lemon cold figures: HS1153/HS402 "Lemon Growing in the Florida Home Landscape" (cited by this crop as uf_ifas_hs1153) gives defoliation at 22-24F, severe wood damage at 20F, flowers and young fruit killed at 29F, and mature fruit damaged at 28F to 31F. Clemson's cold-tolerance page publishes satsuma and kumquat at 15F and no lemon number; TAMU's citrus fact sheet publishes satsuma 18F plus freeze-protection operating points (sprinkler 28F calm / 30F windy) and no lemon number. So the mis-credit is TWO of three, not three of three. RESOLVED by minting uc_anr_8100 (UC ANR 8100), which publishes the damage ONSET for tender citrus at 29F sustained 30 minutes or longer and whose Table 1 rates lemon Citrus limon H, and by moving frost_tolerance_f 28 -> 29 to match that onset. HISTORY WORTH KEEPING: an earlier pass reported this number appeared in 0 of the 17 readable documents lemon cites and nearly filed that as an absence. The zero was the instrument -- the scan required a temperature to be "lemon-adjacent", and in HS402 the nearest "lemon" is 333 characters from the figures because on a crop monograph the crop is the section subject and the passage's own subject noun is "trees". Any proximity window under ~333 chars returns a confident zero. tools/cited_claim_scan.py is the regression. STILL OWED, deliberately not done here because this promote moved no consumer prose: the hardiness_notes_seasoned credit parenthetical still reads "(Sources: Clemson HGIC, Texas A&M AgriLife, UF/IFAS.)" and should name UC ANR 8100 and UF/IFAS HS402 for the number. [CORRECTION 2026-08-06: the credit parenthetical quoted above as STILL OWED has now been corrected, in the follow-on promote that produced this record. It reads "(Sources: cold-damage temperatures UC ANR 8100 and UF/IFAS HS1153; cold-hardiness ranking and freeze protection Clemson HGIC and Texas A&M AgriLife.)". The change is PER-CLAIM, not a swap: Clemson HGIC and Texas A&M AgriLife are removed from the TEMPERATURE, which neither publishes, and kept for the cold-hardiness ranking and the freeze-protection guidance that they do (TAMU excludes lemon from its cold-hardy list and carries the container-culture and sprinkler operating points; Clemson publishes the 15F hardiest-citrus figure). Bare "UF/IFAS" was made specific to HS1153, because this crop cites both HS1153 and HS132 and it is HS1153 that publishes lemon figures. Nothing else in the string moved: the claim text before the parenthetical is byte-identical to 6b2dcb8e, including the leaves-and-fruit stage wording that an earlier draft wrongly proposed rewriting.]

That was scoped to the two pages we cite and was wrong about the host: UC IPM publishes a freezing-and-frost-damage-to-citrus page we did NOT cite, verified live at HTTP 200, which states that "Eureka lemon and grapefruit are among the most cold-sensitive scions, whereas mandarin, Meyer lemon, and sweet orange are more cold hardy". Both cells are SUITABILITY cells (survives_no_fruit at z8, marginal at z9) and a sensitivity RANKING is exactly the right support for a suitability enum, so both are repointed. The ucanr_ext arm of these same two cells stays bare; that is hunt #3 and it is still open.

The TAMU citrus fact sheet (aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/fruit-nut/fact-sheets/citrus/) refers in prose to a "Table 1" of variety characteristics which may carry a cold-hardiness column, but that table is NOT present in the cached text layer of the page. It is the one thing that could still change the answer on hunts #26 and #27, whose zone cells are repointed at this document in this promote on the strength of its cold-hardy-types list (which excludes lemon) rather than on any table.

Six T1 citrus cold documents were read for a lemon-applicable damage temperature, and they do not agree. Recorded so the next reader does not re-hunt this. UC ANR 8100 publishes 29F as the damage ONSET for tender citrus, qualified "for 30 minutes or longer", under a "Trees" heading kept separate from its "Fruits" section, and it discriminates by sensitivity class: its Table 1 rates lemon Citrus limon H. LSU AgCenter publishes about 26F for leaf or wood damage, but as ONE category-level figure for "all other citrus" -- everything except satsumas and kumquats, which lumps M-rated grapefruit and orange in with H-rated lemon and lime. 8100 wins on SCOPE, not on being the warmer number: it is the more specific instrument for a crop its own table rates H. CRITICALLY, 8100 frames a damage CURVE and not a cliff ("Greater damage occurs with colder temperatures, a longer duration of cold, or higher relative humidity"), so a colder figure further along that curve is NOT a contradiction: UF/IFAS HS402 gives lemon-specific DEFOLIATION at 22-24F and severe wood damage at 20F, which are severity ENDPOINTS, never competing onsets. Fruit is a separate axis again: HS402 gives mature fruit damage at 28-31F and 8100 Table 2 gives buds and blossoms 27.0F and tree-ripe lemons 26.0-30.5F. Documents that publish NO lemon-applicable damage temperature at all: Clemson cold-tolerance (satsuma and kumquat 15F only), TAMU citrus fact sheet (satsuma 18F and freeze-protection operating points), UF/IFAS HS132 (cold annotations for calamondin, kumquat and Key lime, and none for lemon), UC IPM freeze page (a ranking, zero temperatures). Twelve of lemon's 29 cited URLs are uncached and remain UNDETERMINED rather than silent. [AMENDMENT 2026-08-06: a SEVENTH document, never cited by lemon, publishes a figure for exactly this crop. UCCE Placer/Nevada 31-018C (Fake, 2020), "Growing Citrus in the Sierra Nevada Foothills", gives a cultivar-named ladder ending "grapefruit (26F) > true lemons (Eureka, Lisbon) (28F) > lime (30F)". It names Eureka and Lisbon, the cultivars this parent entry covers, and its 28 matches the value this dataset carried before ae15df4 moved it to 29 -- and its lime 30 matches our lime exactly, two rungs on a seven-rung ladder, which is a strong inference that this ladder or its lineage is where our citrus numbers came from uncited. Trevor RULED KEEP 29 on 2026-08-06: UC ANR 8100 is a numbered, peer-reviewed publication giving a duration-qualified damage ONSET (29F sustained 30 minutes or longer) and is the warmer safety edge, whereas 31-018C self-describes its numbers as "guidelines to assist in selecting appropriate species" -- a selection guideline, not an onset threshold. Tier plus claim-type decides it; 31-018C's greater cultivar specificity does not override. CAUTION: 31-018C is NOT INDEPENDENT of the Meyer 22F figure this crop already cites (Fake & Norton, 134971.pdf) -- same author, same ladder, ONE lineage, the reprint trap in a new costume. AND THIS FINDING'S OWN FRAMING OF 26F IS NOW UNDERSTATED: it presents LSU AgCenter's 26F as a lone category-level figure, but UC MG Sacramento GN 127 independently publishes "Lemons and grapefruit 26F" for leaf and branch damage. TWO institutions publish 26F, not one. The ruling to keep 29 still holds -- 29 remains the only duration-qualified onset figure and the safety edge -- but the record must be honest about what sits on the other side.]

MODELED DECLARATION, scoped to the documents read. No UC document read for campaign D publishes a lemon-specific harvest window for California's Central Valley, so ca_interior harvest_start and harvest_end remain modeled rather than sourced. Enumerated per absence-findings-are-document-scoped: UC MG Sacramento GN 127 (Central Valley) gives GENUS-LEVEL harvest only, "most citrus varieties ripen from late fall through winter", and its recommended home-garden varieties are navel and Valencia oranges, Satsuma mandarin, Meyer lemon and Bearss lime -- no true lemon; UCCE Kern KC9382 (San Joaquin) is a cultural and troubleshooting guide and publishes none; UC IPM's citrus timing chart is explicitly Central Valley but its Harvest row is GENERIC CITRUS; UCCE Merced's only citrus resource is UCCE Placer/Nevada #15C, the Fake lineage already covered. WHY THE GENUS-LEVEL STATEMENTS ARE NOT USED even though the form is admissible: F5 accepts LSU's category-level "about 26F for all other citrus", so a "most varieties" claim is admissible in FORM -- but lemon is the documented EXCEPTION to genus-level citrus harvest patterns, described as ever-bearing or year-round by four independent sources, so applying a most-varieties window to the crop repeatedly named as the exception is the wrong instrument. PARTIAL EXPLANATION, stated as partial: Sacramento's variety list suggests UC does not publish a Central Valley true-lemon harvest window because it does not really recommend true lemon there for home gardens. EVIDENCE AGAINST THAT, recorded rather than omitted: the Crop Profile for Citrus in California (2003) states Lisbon lemons are better adapted to the Desert, Interior and San Joaquin Valley regions with fruit harvested over a nine-month period. Both can be true -- the Crop Profile is commercial and Sacramento is home-garden. The Crop Profile is a LEAD, NOT A SOURCE: it gives a duration with no anchor, so citing it for harvest_start or harvest_end would credit a document for a claim it does not make, and its authorship is a stakeholder panel rather than extension-authored or peer-reviewed despite the UC host. Tier undecided; not admitted. WHAT "MODELED" DOES AND DOES NOT CLAIM HERE. It is a PROVENANCE statement -- this value came from the model rather than from a document -- and it is NOT a statement that the value is correct. An unqualified declaration would read as modeled-and-therefore-fine. ca_interior's harvest span is 95 days, which sits inside the suspect group flagged by PLA-151 (evergreen_fruit_tree harvest arms model an ever-bearing habit through a bloom-anchored offset built for determinate fruit): all 478 tree harvest arms anchor on bloom_start, which is correct for a determinate deciduous fruit and the wrong instrument for an evergreen ever-bearing one, doubly so here because lemon's bloom is itself modeled. So this cell may be both UNSOURCED and TOO NARROW, and those are separate defects with separate fixes.

MODELED DECLARATION. lemon's bloom arm stays modeled in EVERY region, including the Central Valley where a chart does exist. No T1 publishes a lemon bloom window for ca_north_coast, ca_south_coast, ca_desert or low_desert_az at all. For ca_interior a chart exists and is deliberately NOT used as lemon's bloom: UC IPM's citrus timing chart (UC ANR Pub 3441), re-derived from raw HTML 2026-08-06 rather than from a rendered image, gives a Bloom period of March plus the first half of April and is explicitly scoped to California's Central Valley -- but it is a COMMERCIAL Pest Management Guideline covering citrus generally, and Central Valley commercial citrus is dominated by navels and mandarins. It is citable for the main bloom of Central Valley CITRUS GENERALLY and must not be written as lemon's bloom. THE DEEPER REASON and the ruling behind this declaration: lemon may not have a discrete bloom window at all. Four independent sources describe it as ever-bearing -- Mauk & Shea (Improved Meyer "bears year round"), UC MG Santa Clara (Eureka "some fruit year-round"), UC Marin MG ("lemons and limes are considered ever-bearing"), UCCE SLO (flowers and fruit in spring, summer and fall) -- so filling a single Mar to mid-Apr window would assert a discrete bloom for the crop repeatedly named as the exception, the same error as reading lemon off UC IPM's generic Harvest row or off Lazaneo's hardiness ranking. Three UC counties PLACE the spring bloom without publishing it, by timing work around it: Sacramento fertilizes "in March before bloom", Santa Clara "February or March before bloom", SLO notes maximum stored food "late February/early March just before spring bloom". Placing is not publishing.

USER-FACING CONTENT FINDING, not citation hygiene. Documents were FOUND for the low_desert_az, ca_desert and ca_south_coast harvest arms and were deliberately NOT cited, because no citation is admissible for these arms as they are currently structured. The documents publish ABSOLUTE CALENDAR WINDOWS; the cells compute from bloom_start plus an offset; and bloom is itself MODELED (see lemon_bloom_modeled_every_region). So the displayed value is produced by the model, not by any document. Repointing would credit a document for a value it did not produce, which is the defect F1 exists to record. Converting the documents' absolute windows into bloom-anchored offsets would be worse: it pushes a sourced window through an unsourced anchor and then cites the document for the composite. THE CONSEQUENCE, SCOPED HONESTLY AFTER THE SOURCE-TRUTH SAMPLE. There are TWO reader-facing harvest surfaces and they disagree with each other. The zone-level harvest STRING is separately authored and is broadly consistent with the sources, several cells carrying an explicit year-round caveat: ca_south_coast reads "Nov - Mar (and scattered year-round; heaviest late winter to spring)" against Mauk & Shea's "bears year round on the coast", and low_desert_az reads "Nov - Mar (Eureka bears year-round)". The OFFSET-COMPUTED arms are the narrower surface: low_desert_az computes about 60 days where UA AZ1001 marks Eureka and Lisbon across fourteen half-month cells, August through February inclusive. Both surfaces render -- harvest_start and harvest_end drive plant-astro's SuccessionCard, TodayCommunityCard and PlantingCalendarCard, while the zone string renders elsewhere. AN EARLIER DRAFT OF THIS FINDING SAID a first-season grower is shown a harvest season roughly five months too short. THE SOURCE-TRUTH SAMPLE REFUTED THAT before it shipped: the reader also sees the harvest string and its year-round caveat, so the alarming version was not established. What IS established is narrower and still worth fixing: the two surfaces disagree, the offset-derived one is narrower than every source read, and low_desert_az's string omits August through October entirely -- three months AZ1001 marks for both cultivars. INTERNAL CORROBORATION NEEDING NO DOCUMENT: lime shares all nine of lemon's regions and is described by the same sources as the same ever-bearing habit, yet lime is modeled at a 180-day span in eight of them while lemon runs 60 to 125. AZ1001 is reachable at https://extension.arizona.edu/sites/extension.arizona.edu/files/pubs/az1001.pdf ; the /publication/low-desert-citrus-varieties path 403s in both plain and browser user-agent modes while the host root returns 200, so the block is path-specific rather than a bot policy. NOT YET RESOLVED: whether this is lemon-specific or an evergreen_fruit_tree modelling issue is under separate diagnosis.

ADJUDICATING DECLARATION for lemon's bare regional anchor ids, filed to CLOSE the decisions rather than to describe them. NAMES the ids and DECLARES the anchor, which is the distinction that matters: the findings filed in the section-7 promote named `ucanr_ext` and `uariz_ext` only to DECLINE them ("the ucanr_ext arm stays bare; that is hunt #3 and it is still open"), which satisfies a vocabulary scan and closes nothing. DECLARED HERE, for `ucanr_ext` on ca_interior, ca_north_coast, ca_south_coast and ca_desert, for `uariz_ext` on low_desert_az, ca_desert and warm_arid, and for `clemson_hgic` on warm_arid (hunt #31, whose plantings container and plant_out arm have no sibling citrus document at all): on the arms that still cite them bare -- `plantings`, `bloom`, `harvest_start`, `harvest_end`, `resolved_by_zone` and low_desert_az `plant_out` -- these ids are INSTITUTION-ROOT PORTALS standing for the UC ANR and University of Arizona Cooperative Extension programmes, and the windows they anchor are MODELED, not lifted from a chart. The campaign D document read was exhaustive and is recorded across this crop's findings: no T1 publishes a lemon bloom window for any region (see lemon_bloom_modeled_every_region); no UC document publishes a lemon harvest window for the Central Valley (see lemon_ca_interior_harvest_modeled_no_uc_window); and UA AZ1001, which does publish a low-desert harvest window, is inadmissible for arms computed from a modeled bloom anchor (see lemon_harvest_arms_uncitable_as_structured_and_may_render_too_narrow). PLANT_OUT IS THE EXCEPTION AND IS NOW SOURCED: four CA plant_out arms are repointed in this promote onto the UC documents that publish the frost-anchored planting rule (UCCE Kern KC9382, UC Marin MG, Lazaneo/San Diego, Mauk & Shea/Riverside). low_desert_az plant_out stays declared because AZ1001 publishes no planting date.

THE LIMITATION THIS CAMPAIGN CLOSES ON, recorded so no future reader mistakes the completion signal for the state of the data. `campaign_d_reprice` answers "are the DECISIONS adjudicated", not "are the CITATIONS fixed", and on lemon and lime those two diverge by 51. MECHANISM, measured not inferred: `bare_host_scan` sets is_sole=False when a cell cites ANY non-bare source, and the re-price filters on it. So a bare citation is invisible to the count whenever a PATHED CO-SOURCE sits on the same cell, whatever its source id. Adding a pathed document alongside a bare one therefore REMOVES the bare citation from the metric without fixing it. Rootstocks used include rough lemon (C. jambhiri), 'Cleopatra mandarin' (C. reticulata), Volkamer lemon (C. volkameriana), sour orange (C. aurantium) and macrophylla (C. macrophylla) (Tucker and Wardowski 1976). Trees on rough lemon rootstocks are extremely vigorous and susceptible to foot rot (phytophthora). [...] Trees on macrophylla are also very vigorous and susceptible to tristeza [...] Lemons on Cleopatra mandarin are slower to come into bearing and fruit size appears smaller.   ||   (pruning target, not mature size) Trees should be maintained at 7 to 10 ft (2.1–3.1 m) high and 10 to 15 ft (3.1–4.6 m) wide.". northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: You cannot grow a lemon tree in the ground here. The winters are too cold. If you want one, grow it in a pot you can bring inside before the first frost and keep in a sunny window all winter.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Lemons are not a landscape crop in the northern tier. The only practical approach is a container-grown tree (Improved Meyer is the hardiest option) kept outdoors in the warm months and moved into a bright, frost-free space for winter; in the ground, an unprotected lemon does not survive the cold.
northern_tier.cold_basis_seasoned: Across the northern tier (zones 3-7) winter lows run from about 10°F down to -40°F, far below the high-20s°F at which lemon leaves and fruit are damaged and the hard freeze that kills an unprotected tree to the ground. A true lemon cannot live outdoors here through winter; it is grown, if at all, as a container plant moved into protection before frost.
northern_tier.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here are far too cold for a lemon tree outdoors. Cold in the high 20s°F already hurts a lemon, and these zones go much colder than that. You would grow one only in a pot that comes indoors for winter.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Lemons can grow here but the winter is the hard part. In the warmer parts (zone 9) you can get fruit in mild years if you cover the tree on freeze nights. In the colder parts (zone 8) the tree may live but the cold usually takes the fruit.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the SE and Gulf, lemon is a frost-managed crop. In zone 9 a sheltered, well-sited tree fruits in milder years but needs covering on freeze nights; in zone 8 the tree may survive under protection but freezes take the crop. Site against a south wall, away from low cold-air pockets, and be ready to cover or to move a container tree indoors.
se_gulf.cold_basis_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf band runs from zone-8 lows near 10-20°F to zone-9 lows of 20-30°F. Lemons and limes are the most cold-tender citrus, and Gulf winters almost always bring one or more freezes; the upper-8 zones lose the crop to those freezes even when a protected tree survives, while zone 9 can fruit in milder years with frost defense.
se_gulf.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here usually bring at least one freeze. Lemons are the citrus most easily hurt by cold, so the colder zone-8 areas keep the tree alive at best, and zone 9 can fruit in milder winters if you protect it.

ca_interior.cold_basis_seasoned: The California interior (Central Valley and inland valleys) runs zone-8 lows near 15-20°F up to zone-9 lows of 20-30°F. ca_interior.cold_basis_beginner: Inland California gets cold, clear winter nights when frost settles in low areas. In the colder zone-8 parts a lemon survives but loses its fruit; in zone 9 you can get fruit most years if you protect the tree on the coldest nights.

ca_north_coast.cold_basis_beginner: The ocean keeps winters mild along the cool north coast, so hard frosts are rare. Lemons do well here because, unlike sweet oranges, they do not need a hot summer to make good fruit.

10.suitability_note_beginner: Lemons fruit reliably in the Arizona low desert (zone 9), mostly November to March. Just shade young trunks in summer and cover the tree on the rare cold night. Grow Eureka or Lisbon, since Meyer is not sold here.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is an occasional risk. Clear-night lows can reach the high-20s°F where lemon fruit and growth are damaged; cover young trees on hard-freeze nights. Protecting the trunk from intense summer sun is the bigger seasonal task.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: Lemons grow easily in the Arizona low desert, with fruit mostly from November to March. The heat and sun are what to manage, not the cold. Water deeply and shade young trunks. Note: Meyer lemons are not sold in Arizona, so grow Eureka or Lisbon.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: Lemons are a low-desert staple in Arizona, harvested roughly November through March; Eureka in particular fruits throughout the year. Manage summer sun and heat (whitewash or shade young trunks, irrigate deeply) more than winter cold, and cover young trees on the occasional hard-freeze night. Meyer is unavailable in-state; choose Eureka or Lisbon.
low_desert_az.cold_basis_seasoned: The Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Tucson basins) is hot with mostly frost-free winters; lows generally hold in the high-20s to high-30s°F, with occasional clear-night radiative dips toward the high-20s°F lemon-damage point. Note that Meyer is not available in Arizona (citrus tristeza virus history), so true lemons (Eureka, Lisbon) are the standard.
low_desert_az.cold_basis_beginner: The Arizona low desert is hot and rarely freezes hard, though a clear cold night can occasionally nip a lemon. Meyer lemons are not sold in Arizona, so people grow Eureka or Lisbon.

10.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Peninsular zone 10 fruits reliably and near year-round; frost is rare and the humid heat produces large, juicy fruit. Disease pressure (canker, greening), not cold, is the limiting factor.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Lemons fruit reliably in zone 10 Florida, nearly all year, with big juicy fruit. Watch for citrus diseases rather than frost.
10.harvest: Sep - Mar (and scattered year-round in the humid climate)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the concern in peninsular zone 10. Only an unusual hard freeze near the high-20s°F would threaten fruit; routine protection is unnecessary, and disease management dominates instead.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Peninsular zone 11 is frost-free and fruits reliably year-round, with large, juicy, high-acid fruit in the near-tropical climate. Cold is a non-issue; disease and wet-season fungal pressure are the management focus.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Lemons fruit reliably and year-round in zone 11 Florida. There is no frost worry here, just citrus diseases to watch.
11.harvest: Sep - Mar (and scattered year-round in the humid climate)
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a factor in zone 11. Lows do not approach the high-20s°F damage point; no cold protection is needed.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: Lemons fruit reliably in peninsular Florida, nearly year-round, and the fruit gets big and juicy. Plant in full sun with good airflow. The main things to watch here are citrus diseases, not frost.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula lemon fruits reliably and near year-round; UF/IFAS notes the more tropical climate gives larger, juicier, higher-acid fruit. Site in full sun with good air movement so flowers dry quickly. The real challenges are disease management (canker, greening) and wet-season fungal issues, addressed in care guidance rather than frost defense.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_seasoned: The Florida peninsula (central-south) is largely frost-free, with winter lows generally in the mid-30s to high-40s°F, rarely reaching the high-20s°F lemon-damage point south of the central ridge. The humid, near-tropical climate yields large, juicy fruit; the dominant constraints are disease (citrus canker, citrus greening) rather than cold.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_beginner: Peninsular Florida rarely gets a damaging frost. Winters stay mild, and the humid climate makes big, juicy lemons. The harder problems here are citrus diseases, not cold.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In lowland tropical Hawaii lemon fruits reliably and continuously; there is no cold constraint, so the calendar is effectively year-round bloom and harvest. As in other humid climates, site for good air movement and full sun to limit fungal issues, addressed in care guidance.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_seasoned: Lowland tropical Hawaii has no winter to speak of; lows hold around 45-55°F or warmer, never approaching the high-20s°F lemon-damage point. There is no frost limit on lemon here; bloom and harvest run year-round in the even, warm climate.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_beginner: Hawaii has no frost in the lowlands. Lemons grow and fruit all year because it stays warm.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

9.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Lemon is one of the more cold-tender common citrus, slightly hardier than lime but far more tender than grapefruit, orange, or mandarin, and only marginal on much of the Gulf Coast. The Rio Grande Valley's near-total absence of hard freezes lets it fruit reliably here, though a hard-freeze year can still damage fruit or set the tree back before grapefruit or orange feel it. Multiple bloom flushes keep fruit setting through much of the year, with the main crop ripening fall into winter (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension).
9.suitability_note_beginner: Lemon does well in the Valley, even though it is one of the more cold-sensitive citrus, a bit hardier than lime but noticeably more tender than grapefruit, orange, or mandarin. Winters here are mild enough that it fruits reliably, though a hard freeze can still set it back more than it would the other citrus here. The tree can flower and set fruit in more than one flush through the year.
9.harvest: Oct - Feb (main crop; scattered fruit can ripen nearly year-round from repeat bloom flushes)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a practical concern in the Valley, but it matters more for lemon than for grapefruit, orange, or mandarin: lemon is one of the more cold-tender common citrus, second only to lime. On the rare hard freeze, cover the tree or move a container lemon under cover for the night.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: Lemon fruits reliably in the Rio Grande Valley. Unlike on the Gulf Coast, where lemon is often just a marginal, freeze-risk crop, the Valley's mild winters let it produce well. It is one of the more cold-sensitive citrus though, so cover the tree or bring a container plant in on the rare hard-freeze night. It flowers more than once a year, so you may see fruit at different stages, with the main harvest from fall into winter.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Lemon is one of the more cold-tender common citrus, slightly hardier than lime but far more tender than grapefruit, orange, or mandarin, and it is only marginal in colder parts of the Gulf South. The Rio Grande Valley's near-total absence of hard freezes lets it fruit reliably, though an occasional hard-freeze year can still damage fruit or set the tree back before grapefruit or orange feel it. Repeat bloom flushes through spring keep fruit setting across much of the year, with the main crop ripening October into February. Heat is ample and never a limiting factor for lemon.
rgv.cold_basis_seasoned: Lemon is one of the more cold-tender common citrus, slightly hardier than lime but far more tender than grapefruit, orange, or mandarin: fruit and foliage damage in the high 20s°F, a threshold that Gulf Coast winters cross most years. The Rio Grande Valley rarely reaches that threshold, which is exactly why it fruits reliably here where it does not elsewhere in Texas. The winter-low band used here, roughly 24 to 34°F, is a synthesis anchored to the closest analog frost-free citrus regions, the milder Gulf Coast and the Arizona low desert, not a single verbatim figure from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension; that source is the basis for the bloom and harvest windows above.
rgv.cold_basis_beginner: Lemon is hurt by cold more easily than most citrus, second only to lime, but Valley winters are mild enough that this rarely matters. On the rare hard freeze, cover the tree or bring a container lemon indoors for the night.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 west of the Cascades is too cold for an in-ground lemon. Lemon fruit and leaves are damaged once temperatures fall into the high 20s°F, and this zone's coldest nights drop well below that, into the teens or lower, so an unprotected tree does not make it through a typical winter, let alone one of the region's periodic harder freezes. Grow it as a container tree brought under cover for the coldest nights instead.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for a lemon tree planted outside. Grow it in a pot you can bring under cover on the coldest nights.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: WSU's own western-Washington fruit guidance notes that even a typically mild maritime winter brings a periodic harder frost some years; that is well within reach of zone 8's colder nights, and lemon is hurt at a far milder temperature than the hardy tree fruit this region is known for.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9's milder coastal and protected pockets sit closer to lemon's cold edge, and a container-grown tree (Improved Meyer is the hardier choice) can survive there long-term if it is moved under cover, or into a garage or bright room, whenever a hard freeze threatens. Even so, an occasional deeper freeze can still damage or kill an unprotected tree, so there is no dependable in-ground crop, only a protected container planting.
9.suitability_note_beginner: A bit milder here, so a potted lemon (an Improved Meyer is the toughest option) can survive for years if you bring it under cover on the coldest nights. It still is not safe to leave outside unprotected all winter.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 9's typical winter low sits nearer lemon's damage point than zone 8's, but the region's occasional harder freeze can still reach cold enough to hurt or kill an unprotected tree, so container culture with winter protection is still the honest recommendation.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Lemon does not work as an in-ground tree here. Winters in the maritime Pacific Northwest are usually mild, but an occasional hard freeze gets cold enough to hurt or kill one. Grow it in a container (an Improved Meyer is the toughest choice) that you can bring under cover on the coldest nights; in the milder zone 9 pockets that can keep a tree alive for years, though it still will not give you a dependable outdoor crop.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Lemon is not a landscape tree in the maritime Pacific Northwest. The region's winters run mild in most years, close to what a hardened lemon can tolerate at its edge, but the occasional harder freeze, a known feature of the climate even in an otherwise mild winter, reaches well below lemon's high-20s°F damage point. Zone 8's colder interior lowlands make in-ground culture a non-starter; the milder zone 9 coastal and protected pockets can support a long-lived container specimen (Improved Meyer for its extra cold tolerance) moved under cover for the worst nights, but not a dependable in-ground crop.
pnw.cold_basis_seasoned: Zone 8's colder nights (roughly 10 to 20°F) are far past the high-20s°F point where lemon fruit and leaves are damaged; zone 9's milder band (roughly 20 to 30°F) sits closer to that edge, but the region's documented periodic harder freeze, on top of an otherwise mild winter, still reaches cold enough to threaten an unprotected tree in either zone (WSU).
pnw.cold_basis_beginner: Even our milder zone 9 winters get cold enough some years to hurt an unprotected lemon tree, and zone 8 is colder still. A pot you can move under cover is the safe way to grow one here.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 7's Piedmont winters bring hard freezes well below the high-20s°F point where true lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is damaged, and even below the low-to-mid 20s°F threshold of the hardier Improved Meyer hybrid. There is no in-ground establishment window this far inland; grow it as a container tree brought fully indoors for winter.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for a lemon tree outside, even the hardier Meyer type. Grow one in a pot you bring fully indoors for winter.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard freeze every winter in the Piedmont is well past even Improved Meyer's cold tolerance, let alone true lemon's.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone sits close to the edge for the hardiest lemon option: Improved Meyer, a lemon x mandarin hybrid, tolerates cold into the low-to-mid 20s°F and is documented surviving the milder half of zone 8 with protection. A container Meyer brought under cover, or fully indoors, on hard-freeze nights can persist here for years, but this zone's colder pockets and periodic harder freezes still reach past that threshold, so there is no dependable in-ground or even reliably fruiting container crop, only a protected specimen that may bloom in milder winters. True lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is more tender still and does not belong outdoors here at all.
8.suitability_note_beginner: This is about as good as lemon gets here: Improved Meyer, the cold-hardy lemon type, can survive in the milder Tidewater pockets of this zone for years if you bring it under cover, or fully indoors, on the coldest nights. It still is not a plant you leave outside all winter, and do not expect a reliable crop of fruit. Regular lemon types are too tender to try here at all.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Improved Meyer's own documented cold limit, the low-to-mid 20s°F, sits right at this zone's milder Tidewater edge; the zone's colder pockets and any harder freeze still exceed it, so container culture with real winter protection is the honest baseline, not a dependable outdoor planting.

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Lemon does not work as an in-ground tree anywhere in the Mid-Atlantic. In the colder Piedmont even the hardiest lemon type cannot survive winter outdoors. In the milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone, a potted Improved Meyer lemon, brought under cover or fully indoors on the coldest nights, can live for years, but do not count on a real harvest of fruit.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: Lemon is not a landscape tree anywhere in this belt. The Piedmont's winters are too cold for even the hardiest lemon selection. In the milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone, Improved Meyer, a naturally more cold-tolerant lemon x mandarin hybrid, is documented surviving with protection at the mild edge of zone 8, so a container tree brought under cover, or fully indoors, for the coldest nights can be a long-lived planting there. Even so, this zone's colder pockets and its own periodic harder freeze still reach past Meyer's cold limit, so there is no dependable outdoor crop, only a protected specimen. True lemon types (Eureka, Lisbon) are more cold-tender still and are not a realistic choice outdoors in either zone.
mid_atlantic.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 10 to 20°F in the milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone to 0 to 10°F in the cooler Piedmont. True lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is damaged in the high 20s°F and does not belong outdoors in either zone; Improved Meyer, a hardier lemon x mandarin hybrid, tolerates cold into the low-to-mid 20s°F and is documented surviving the milder half of zone 8 with protection, the one real cold-edge option this belt supports (Clemson HGIC; Texas A&M AgriLife).
mid_atlantic.cold_basis_beginner: Regular lemon is too tender for either part of this region. The hardier Meyer type can survive winter in the milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone if you protect it on cold nights, but even that needs help, and the Piedmont is too cold for it too.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8's cooler, higher pockets bring winter lows well below the high-20s°F point where true lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is damaged, and even below the low-to-mid 20s°F tolerance of the hardier Improved Meyer hybrid. There is no in-ground establishment window this far into the region's cold edge; grow it as a container tree brought fully indoors for winter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for a lemon tree outside, even the hardier Meyer type. Grow one in a pot you bring fully indoors for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard freeze most winters in this zone reaches well past even Improved Meyer's cold tolerance, let alone true lemon's.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley floor sits close to the edge for the hardiest lemon option: Improved Meyer, a lemon x mandarin hybrid, tolerates cold into the low-to-mid 20s°F, near this zone's colder nights. The Las Vegas Valley floor, at about 2,000 feet, runs colder in winter than the lower Phoenix desert (near 1,100 feet), so lemon does not fruit reliably here the way it can in Arizona. A container Meyer brought fully under cover on hard-freeze nights can persist for years, but this stays a protected specimen, not a dependable in-ground or fruiting tree; true lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is more tender still and does not belong outdoors here at all.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The best lemon can do in the Las Vegas Valley is survive in a pot: Improved Meyer, the cold-hardy lemon type, can live for years if you bring it under cover on the coldest nights, but do not expect a real harvest. Regular lemon types are too tender to try here at all.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The valley's frost season (last freeze around Feb 28, first around Nov 25, NWS Las Vegas normals) brackets a winter whose harder nights reach past even Improved Meyer's low-to-mid 20s°F cold limit in most years.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Laughlin/Colorado River corner is the region's mildest pocket, and Improved Meyer's ordinary winter lows here mostly clear its low-to-mid 20s°F cold limit. This is still a single small area with no dedicated local citrus field data, and a periodic harder freeze can reach past that limit, so a protected container Meyer, not an in-ground tree, is the honest call; true lemon remains too tender to try even here.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Laughlin gives lemon its best shot in this region, with the hardy Meyer type, but keep it in a container you can protect rather than planting in the ground. Regular lemon is still too tender to try even in this warmer corner.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Even the region's mildest corner sees an occasional harder freeze that can reach Improved Meyer's low-to-mid 20s°F cold limit; a movable container is the safer bet.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Regular lemon does not work outdoors anywhere in this region. The hardier Meyer type can survive in a container, brought under cover on cold nights, in the Las Vegas Valley and does a little better at the milder Laughlin corner, but do not count on a real harvest in either spot. The cooler high pockets of the region are too cold even for Meyer.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: Lemon is not a landscape tree anywhere in the Nevada high desert. The region's cooler zone-8 pockets rule out even the hardiest selection. In the Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) and the milder Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10), Improved Meyer, a naturally more cold-tolerant lemon x mandarin hybrid, sits close to its own low-to-mid 20s°F cold limit, so a container tree brought fully under cover for the coldest nights can be a long-lived planting, but not a fruiting one. The Las Vegas Valley floor, at about 2,000 feet, runs colder in winter than the lower Phoenix desert (near 1,100 feet), the reason lemon is judged more cold-limited here than in Arizona's low desert. True lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is more cold-tender still and is not a realistic choice outdoors anywhere in this region.
nevada.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 30 to 40°F in the mild Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10) to 20 to 30°F in the Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) to 10 to 20°F in the region's cooler, higher pockets (zone 8). True lemon is damaged in the high 20s°F and does not belong outdoors anywhere here; Improved Meyer, the hardier lemon x mandarin hybrid, tolerates cold into the low-to-mid 20s°F, the one real cold-edge option in the valley and Laughlin. The Las Vegas Valley floor, at about 2,000 feet, runs colder in winter than the lower Phoenix desert (near 1,100 feet).
nevada.cold_basis_beginner: Regular lemon is too tender for this region. The hardier Meyer type can survive winter in a container in the Las Vegas Valley or the milder Laughlin corner if you protect it on cold nights, but even that needs help, and the cooler high pockets of the region are too cold for it too.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost data) are well past true lemon's high-20s°F damage point and still edge past Meyer lemon's own low-to-mid 20s°F cold tolerance, so there is no dependable in-ground planting here, and citrus is absent from USU's Washington County Fruits recommendation for this elevation. A container Meyer lemon, brought under cover on hard-freeze nights, can be kept alive for years and may set some fruit in an unusually mild winter; true lemon is too tender to attempt outdoors here at all.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Regular lemon is too tender for St. George's winters, which drop to ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F. The hardier Meyer lemon, bred for cold-marginal climates, does a bit better and can survive for years in a container you bring under cover on freezing nights, but do not expect a reliable harvest even from it.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter cold (last frost near March 30, first frost near November 1, USU Extension Washington County) reaches well past true lemon's high-20s°F damage point and edges past even Meyer lemon's low-to-mid 20s°F tolerance, so hard-freeze nights are a real risk for an unprotected tree most winters.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Regular lemon does not work outdoors in St. George; winters here, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, are too much for it. The hardier Meyer lemon, bred for cold-marginal gardens, can survive for years in a container brought under cover on freezing nights, and may give you fruit in an unusually mild winter, but do not count on a dependable harvest.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's zone 8b winters run roughly 15 to 20°F on an ordinary cold night, and USU's Washington County Fruits page, which names the fruits recommended at this elevation, includes no citrus at all. True lemon is damaged in the high 20s°F and is not a realistic outdoor choice here. Meyer lemon, a lemon by mandarin hybrid bred for marginal climates, tolerates cold into the low-to-mid 20s°F, closer to St. George's winter low but still not clearing it reliably. The honest call is a protected container Meyer, brought under cover on hard-freeze nights, that can live for years and occasionally set fruit in a mild winter.
utah_dixie.cold_basis_seasoned: St. George sits in USDA zone 8b, with ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost and elevation data). True lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is damaged in the high 20s°F, well above that band; the hardier Meyer lemon, a lemon by mandarin hybrid bred for cold-marginal climates, tolerates cold into the low-to-mid 20s°F, still short of St. George's ordinary winter low. USU's Washington County Fruits page, which lists the fruits recommended at this elevation, names no citrus at all.
utah_dixie.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here bring ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F. Regular lemon is too tender for that outright; even the hardier Meyer lemon, bred for cold-marginal gardens, cannot reliably take it either. Grow Meyer lemon in a container you bring under cover on the coldest nights, and skip regular lemon outdoors altogether.

crops.description_seasoned: Lemon (Citrus limon) is an evergreen subtropical tree prized for its tart, aromatic fruit and near-continuous productivity in mild climates. It is among the most cold-sensitive common citrus but also one of the most rewarding and forgiving to grow where adapted, thriving in full sun and sharply drained soil. Cold-climate growers keep it in containers and move it to shelter for winter, and fruit conveniently holds on the tree for weeks to months, spreading the harvest.
crops.description_beginner: The lemon is an evergreen tree that grows in warm climates and gives tart, fragrant fruit for much of the year. It is one of the more cold-sensitive citrus, but it is also one of the most rewarding to grow, loving full sun and well-drained soil. In cold areas people grow it in a pot and bring it indoors for winter, and a handy bonus is that ripe lemons keep on the tree for weeks, so you can pick them as you need them.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest by color, size, and feel: lemons can be picked from green-mature through full yellow, are usually heavy for their size with a slight give when ripe, and the surest test is taste, since color alone can mislead. Clip or twist fruit free without tearing the rind. Because mature fruit holds well on the tree, the harvest window is forgiving and fruit can be left and picked as needed.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick lemons when they have reached good size and turned from green toward yellow; ripe fruit feels heavy and gives slightly when gently squeezed. The best test is to taste one, because color can fool you. Twist or snip the fruit off without tearing the skin. The nice thing is you can leave ripe lemons on the tree and pick them as you go.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Unlike most citrus, which flower and set almost entirely on the spring growth flush, lemons (and limes) flower and set fruit nearly year-round across several flushes, with the heaviest bloom in spring and a secondary peak common in fall. Flowering and fruiting often occur on the tree at the same time. Because the fruit takes many months to mature, the bloom-to-harvest span is long, often crossing the year boundary, which is why a lemon can carry ripe fruit, green fruit, and flowers together. (Sources: Texas A&M AgriLife, UC ANR.)
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Lemons bloom heaviest in spring but flower on and off much of the year, so you will often see flowers and fruit on the tree at the same time. Each lemon takes several months to ripen.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Standard lemons (Eureka, Lisbon) are among the most frost-tender of all citrus: leaves and fruit are damaged when temperatures fall into the high 20s F, and a hard freeze can kill an unprotected young tree to the ground. In the landscape they survive reliably in zones 9-10 and crop dependably from about zone 9b through 11; at the zone 8b edge they need a warm microclimate and active freeze protection (cover, soil bank on the graft, or a container moved indoors). Cold hardiness is driven more by scion choice than rootstock, and exposure to gradually cooling fall weather hardens a tree off so a mature lemon tolerates more cold than a young one. Improved Meyer is meaningfully hardier than true lemons (down to the low-to-mid 20s) and is the better choice at the cold edge. (Sources: cold-damage temperatures UC ANR 8100 and UF/IFAS HS1153; cold-hardiness ranking and freeze protection Clemson HGIC and Texas A&M AgriLife.)
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Lemons are the citrus most easily hurt by frost. Cold in the high 20s damages them. Plan on growing one outdoors year-round only in a mild, nearly frost-free spot (roughly zones 9b-11). In a colder place, grow it in a pot you can move indoors when frost is coming, or choose an Improved Meyer, which takes a bit more cold.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Lemons are subtropical evergreens with essentially no winter chilling requirement (about 0 chill hours). They never go fully dormant, so bloom is triggered by warmth and the day-to-night temperature swing rather than by accumulated winter cold. Chill hours, the limiter for deciduous fruit like peaches and apples, are not what governs where a lemon fruits; frost is. (Sources: UF/IFAS, UC ANR.)
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Lemons do not need a cold winter to fruit. What they cannot handle is freezing. That is the thing to plan around.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Lemon flowers are fragrant and attractive to honey bees and other pollinators, but because the tree is self-fruitful and partly parthenocarpic, pollinator presence improves set rather than being required. The main practical case where it matters is a tree kept permanently indoors, away from insects, which may need hand pollination. (Sources: UC ANR.)
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Bees like lemon flowers and help fruit set, but you do not need to do anything. The tree sets fruit on its own outdoors.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Lemons need deep, well-drained soil above all else: they will not tolerate a saturated root zone, and poor internal drainage invites Phytophthora foot rot. Plant on a raised mound or bed on heavy clay. Set the tree so the graft union sits well above grade; never dig a watering depression that holds water against the trunk. Keep organic mulch at least a foot from the trunk to reduce foot-rot risk. (Sources: Texas A&M AgriLife, UF/IFAS.)
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick a spot where water never sits after rain. On heavy clay, plant on a low mound so the roots stay drained. Keep the knobby graft on the trunk above the soil line, and keep mulch a hand's width back from the trunk.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Lemons are self-fruitful: a single tree sets a full crop without a second variety nearby. Flowers are insect-pollinated (mostly bees), and many lemons are partly parthenocarpic, setting some seedless fruit without pollination at all. Only about 1-2% of blooms need to set to make a heavy crop. A tree brought indoors away from pollinators may set lighter, so hand-moving pollen with a small brush can help in that case. (Sources: UC ANR, University of Arkansas / UADA, UF/IFAS.)
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one lemon tree. It pollinates itself, so it will fruit on its own. Bees just help it along.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: Citrus needs little pruning. Do any shaping or thinning in spring after the main harvest, never a hard dormant-season cut (the tree is never dormant). Remove dead, crossing, or frost-damaged wood, and always strip shoots arising below the graft union, which come from the rootstock and never bear good fruit. Lemons are vigorous and resent repeated heavy pruning, which lowers production.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Lemons barely need pruning. In spring after you have picked the fruit, snip out any dead or crossing branches and pull off shoots growing from below the graft (the knobby bend low on the trunk). Do not cut it back hard.

crops.establishment_note: A grafted lemon usually sets a few fruit in its second year and begins a real crop in about its third year, building toward full production over the following years. Seed-grown trees take much longer (commonly 3-7 years) and are not recommended. (Sources: Texas A&M AgriLife, UF/IFAS.)
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Rootstocks are usually not a choice at retail garden centers, because trees come grafted onto industry-standard rootstocks. UF/IFAS matches lemon rootstocks to the soil: Swingle citrumelo on acid to neutral sandy soils, and rough lemon or macrophylla on high-pH, calcareous soils. Lemons are susceptible to severe tristeza strains whatever the rootstock, and to less-severe strains on macrophylla and rough lemon. Tristeza can kill citrus trees quickly, especially on sour orange rootstock. Buying a certified disease-free tree reduces the chance of bringing home an infected one. In colder areas, trifoliate orange adds cold hardiness, but it does poorly in saline or highly alkaline soil.

rootstock_options.name: sour orange (Citrus aurantium)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Retail citrus usually comes already grafted, so ask which rootstock your tree is on. Buy a certified disease-free tree.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Sour orange is one of the rootstocks UF/IFAS lists for lemons. It is the most common rootstock in Texas and adapts to most soils that citrus is grown in. UF/IFAS rates it good in saline, high-pH and clay soils. It resists Phytophthora foot rot. Tristeza virus can kill citrus trees quickly on sour orange rootstock. Lemons are susceptible to severe tristeza strains whatever the rootstock. Texas A&M recommends it for the lower Texas coast and most of southern Texas.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Sour orange is a long-established rootstock that handles most soils and resists foot rot. Its weak spot is tristeza, a virus spread by aphids that can kill trees on sour orange quickly.

rootstock_options.name: trifoliate orange (Citrus trifoliata)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: In a colder area with soil that is not salty or alkaline, ask whether the tree is on trifoliate orange.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Trifoliate orange is more cold-hardy than sour orange and makes a smaller tree. UC Cooperative Extension calls it semi-dwarfing. It is immune to Phytophthora foot rot. It is not well adapted to saline or highly alkaline soils. Texas A&M prefers it for colder areas where the soil suits it.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Trifoliate orange handles cold better than sour orange and keeps the tree somewhat smaller. It does not get foot rot, but it struggles in salty or very alkaline soil.

rootstock_options.name: Swingle citrumelo
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: On sandy soil that is acid to neutral, ask whether the tree is on Swingle citrumelo.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Swingle is a citrumelo, a cross of Duncan grapefruit and trifoliate orange. UF/IFAS says lemons on acid to neutral sandy soils do well on it. UC Riverside found it well adapted in some cases to Lisbon-type lemons. It resists Phytophthora foot rot and citrus nematode, and it tolerates tristeza virus. Its cold hardiness is good. It is not adapted to heavy clay or calcareous soils.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Swingle is a common rootstock for lemons on sandy soil that is not alkaline. It resists foot rot and holds up against tristeza virus and cold. It does poorly in heavy clay or alkaline soil.

rootstock_options.name: Rough lemon / macrophylla (alemow)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: If your soil is alkaline, ask whether the tree is on rough lemon or macrophylla.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: UF/IFAS recommends rough lemon or macrophylla (alemow) for lemons in high-pH, calcareous soils. Trees on either rootstock are very vigorous. Rough lemon is susceptible to Phytophthora foot rot. Lemons on these rootstocks are susceptible to less-severe tristeza strains as well as severe ones. Because macrophylla is susceptible to tristeza, UF/IFAS says removing rootstock sprouts is important. UC rates both as highly sensitive to frost.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: These are vigorous rootstocks for alkaline soil. They are more prone to tristeza virus, rough lemon is prone to foot rot, and both are very sensitive to frost. Pull off any shoots that sprout from below the graft.

pet_safe.note: The fruit is fine, but the peel, leaves, and citrus oils can upset the stomach of cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about building a tree, not picking lemons. Set the plant so the graft union, the knobby joint low on the trunk where your lemon variety was joined to its roots, stands two to three inches clear of the finished soil, and keep mulch pulled back from the trunk: a union that sits damp is the classic way citrus gets foot rot. Water it in well, then wait for new growth before the first feeding, because fertilizer given to roots that have not started working just washes past them. Pinch off every flower and any fruit that sets this year. One or two early lemons are not worth the slower, weaker tree you trade for them. Feed little and often through the season rather than one heavy dose, since young citrus roots are shallow and burn easily.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Prioritize root and canopy development over fruit in the planting year. Set the graft union two to three inches proud of the finished grade on a mound and keep mulch off the trunk; a buried or mulch-packed union is the standard entry point for Phytophthora foot rot and gummosis, and a settling mound can swallow a union that looked correct on planting day. Irrigate in thoroughly to collapse air pockets, then withhold fertilizer until active flush, since feeding an inactive root system leaches nitrogen past it and raises salt load. Strip all first-year bloom and set. Little-and-often citrus feeding through the growing season suits a shallow, salt-sensitive young root system far better than a single heavy application. Scout tender flush for Asian citrus psyllid while the tree is still small enough to inspect properly.
crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: A grafted lemon usually sets its first few fruit in the second year, and it is genuinely a few: treat this as a taste rather than a crop. Keep the soil moisture even right through flowering, because a dry spell during bloom is what makes a young tree drop its blossoms and its small fruit. Do not prune hard now. Lemons flower on recent growth, so cutting the tree back at bloom removes the very wood carrying this year's lemons; save shaping for after harvest. As the fruit sizes, water deeply and on a steady rhythm rather than swinging between bone-dry and soaked, since that swing is what splits rinds.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: Expect a token second-year set on a grafted tree, sized to sample rather than to crop. Moisture stability through bloom is the controlling variable: drought stress during flowering drives blossom and young-fruit abscission, and lemon is self-fruitful so there is no pollinator to protect, only the flowers the tree already carries. Defer structural pruning past harvest; lemon flowers on recent growth, so heavy cuts at bloom remove the current crop's bearing wood. Through fruit development, irrigate deeply on a consistent interval: the pulp swells faster than the rind can stretch, so wet-dry oscillation is what produces rind split and drop. On high-pH or sandy ground, watch new leaves for interveinal yellowing and correct with a citrus feed carrying iron, zinc and manganese, which a general fertilizer will not.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From about the third year the tree carries a real crop, and lemon has a habit worth knowing: judge ripeness by feel and taste, not by color. A lemon can be fully juicy while still greenish, and waiting for a deep yellow often means picking past its best. Lift a fruit that feels heavy for its size, taste one, and let that set your standard for the tree. Then use the tree as your storage. Ripe lemons hold on the branch for weeks and even months with little loss, so pick as you need them rather than stripping the tree and scrambling to use the crop. Keep pruning light: deadwood, crossing limbs, and any shoots coming from below the graft union, which are rootstock and will never bear a lemon.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from roughly year three. Harvest on weight and flavor rather than rind color: lemon reaches eating quality while still green-tinged in many climates, and color-led picking runs late. The tree is also the store. Fruit holds on the branch for weeks to months with minimal quality loss, so harvest incrementally against demand instead of stripping and then racing the crop. Maintenance pruning stays minimal: deadwood, crossing limbs, and rootstock suckers below the graft union, which carry rootstock genetics and will never bear your variety, yet will take the canopy if left. In borderline-cold zones a mature tree still needs frost protection: citrus injury escalates from leaf and fruit loss into wood kill as temperature drops and the cold holds, so cover or add heat before a hard night, not after.

crops.name: Blueberry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Sandy loam high in organic matter, with sharp drainage. Blueberry roots are fine, fibrous, and shallow, and they lack the root hairs most plants use to take up water and nutrients, so they depend on loose, moist, acidic, well-aerated soil.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Blueberries do best in sandy soil rich in organic matter that drains quickly. Their roots are thin, delicate, and shallow, and they take up water and nutrients less easily than most plants, so they need soil that stays loose, moist, acidic, and full of air.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Heavier loams can work if you blend in generous peat moss or aged pine bark to open them up and add organic matter. On marginal sites, planting on a raised mound or ridge keeps the shallow roots out of standing water.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Heavier loam soils can work if you mix in plenty of peat moss or aged pine bark to loosen them up and add organic matter. On tricky sites, planting on a raised mound keeps the shallow roots up out of any standing water.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Heavy, wet clay is the worst case: it holds water around the shallow roots and invites root rot, and it resists the acidification blueberries need. If clay is all you have, a raised bed of acidic mix or a large container is a more reliable path.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Heavy, wet clay is the hardest soil for blueberries. It holds water around their shallow roots and can cause root rot, and it fights the acidity blueberries need. If clay is all you have, growing them in a raised bed filled with acidic soil mix, or in a large container, is a more reliable choice.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Blueberries want loose, acidic soil that drains well and is rich in organic matter. Their roots are shallow and delicate, so heavy clay or soggy ground is a problem. Mixing in peat moss or aged pine bark before planting helps a lot.

ph.note_seasoned: This is the make-or-break detail. Blueberries need a soil pH of roughly 4.5 to 5.5, far more acidic than most garden plants. Test your soil first. If the pH is above that range, lower it with elemental sulfur or by working in peat moss, and do it several months before planting, because sulfur takes time to act. Above about pH 5.5 the plant cannot take up iron and the leaves yellow between the veins.
ph.note_beginner: Blueberries are fussy about one thing above all: they need very acidic soil, around pH 4.5 to 5.5. Most garden soil is not acidic enough. Get a cheap soil test before you plant. If your soil reads higher, mix in peat moss and add garden sulfur a few months ahead of planting to bring the acidity down. Get this right and the rest is easy.

fertilizer.timing: split: at budbreak in spring and again about six weeks later
fertilizer.example_product: ammonium sulfate or an acid-forming fertilizer blended for azaleas and rhododendrons
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Blueberries take up nitrogen in the ammonium form rather than nitrate, so feed with an acid-forming fertilizer such as ammonium sulfate or a blend made for azaleas and rhododendrons. Avoid nitrate fertilizers and anything containing lime, which raise pH and can injure the plant. Young bushes need very little; increase the amount gradually as the plant grows. Split the season's feeding between budbreak and about six weeks later.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed blueberries with a fertilizer made for azaleas, rhododendrons, or blueberries. These are acid-forming, which is exactly what blueberries want. Skip ordinary garden fertilizer and never add lime. Go light, especially on young plants, and feed in spring when the buds start to swell.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: An acid-forming complete fertilizer; ammonium-form nitrogen, not nitrate.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use an azalea or rhododendron food (an acid fertilizer).
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Light for young bushes, increasing gradually with age; follow the product label and a soil test.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A small amount in spring, following the package directions for blueberries or azaleas.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Rhododendron
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Rhododendrons and azaleas love the same acidic soil as blueberries, so they make easy, good-looking neighbors in the same bed.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned per worksheet. Same extension-documented shared-acid-soil basis as the good_seasoned Rhododendron entry (OSU). extension_backed/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Rhododendron is a natural blueberry companion because the two are close relatives in the heath family and want the same ground: strongly acidic (about pH 4.5 to 5.5), rich in organic matter, moist but well-drained. That shared chemistry is the real benefit, you can build and maintain one acidic bed and both thrive, where most plants would struggle in soil that acidic. They bloom around the same time to share pollinators, and the rhododendron's foliage shades blueberry's shallow, heat-sensitive roots. Match it to blueberry on sun and keep larger rhododendrons from casting the berries into shade.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Azalea
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Azaleas thrive in the same acidic, well-drained soil blueberries need, so they fit naturally alongside them.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned per worksheet. Same extension-documented shared-acid-soil basis as the good_seasoned Azalea entry (OSU). extension_backed/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Azalea works with blueberry for the same reason rhododendron does, they are heath-family cousins that demand the same acidic, organically rich, moisture-retentive soil blueberry needs, so one well-built acid bed serves both. Azalea tolerates a little more shade than blueberry and brings a heavy spring bloom that draws pollinators during the berry's flowering window. It is a slightly smaller-scale choice than rhododendron where space is tighter. Keep both in at least four hours of sun and avoid letting the azalea overshade the fruit.

good_seasoned.name: Rhododendron
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: An Ericaceous relative that shares the blueberry's acidic, well-drained, high-organic-matter soil requirement, making it a compatible bed companion that thrives under the same culture.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared-culture compatibility (same Ericaceae family, same acid-soil regime) is mechanistically sound; not a tested pairing yield benefit, so labeled likely rather than research_backed.

good_seasoned.name: Azalea
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Another acid-loving Ericaceous shrub with the same soil and drainage needs as blueberry; a natural companion in an acidified bed rather than a productivity booster.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Compatibility is by shared acid-soil culture within the same plant family; mechanistically grounded but not a pair-tested benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Pine
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Pines pair unusually well with blueberries: they shed acidifying needles and do not crowd the root zone the way hardwoods do. UF/IFAS notes the two are compatible neighbors, whereas bushes set near hardwood roots fruit poorly.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: UF/IFAS Blueberry Gardener's Guide explicitly states blueberries and pines are compatible whereas plants near hardwood roots produce few fruit; an extension-stated siting compatibility.

companions.note_seasoned: Blueberry is not a heavy-companion crop; the main siting rule is what to keep it away from. Plant it clear of hardwood tree roots, which compete heavily and sharply reduce fruiting (pines are the exception and are compatible). Its best neighbors are other acid-loving Ericaceous plants such as azaleas and rhododendrons that share the same acidified bed, more for shared culture and aesthetics than any tested yield gain. Do not crowd the shallow root zone.
companions.note_beginner: Blueberries do not need companion plants to do well. The one thing that matters is keeping them away from large shade trees, whose roots crowd them out and cut down on fruit (pine trees are fine). If you want neighbors, other acid-loving plants like azaleas and rhododendrons share the same soil and look good together.

pests.name: Birds
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripening and ripe berries stripped from the bush, often the entire crop in a few days as fruit colors up. Pecked and partly eaten berries left behind.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Birds eating your berries, often clearing the bush right as the fruit ripens.
pests.cause_seasoned: Birds (robins, cedar waxwings, and others) are drawn to ripening blueberries and are widely rated the number-one blueberry pest by growers.
pests.cause_beginner: Birds love ripe blueberries and are the biggest blueberry pest there is.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Netting is the most effective control. Drape bird netting (about 1/2 to 3/4 inch mesh) over the bush or a frame before berries begin to color, and secure it at the base so birds cannot get underneath.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover the bush with bird netting before the berries turn blue, and tuck it in at the bottom so birds cannot sneak in. Netting works far better than scare devices.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Install netting pre-ripening every season. Scare tactics (reflective tape, decoys) help only briefly as birds habituate; physical exclusion is the reliable answer.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put netting up every year before the fruit ripens. Shiny tape and fake owls stop working once birds get used to them, so netting is the dependable fix.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Reflective tape and fake owls cost little to try and can push birds off the bush for a while. Birds get used to them, so move the devices around and swap types, and treat this as a stopgap rather than the thing that saves your crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Visual scares buy a short reprieve before habituation sets in, so reposition and rotate rather than leaving one arrangement standing. Growers widely rate birds the top blueberry pest, and deterrents on their own do not hold that pressure; hang them alongside exclusion, not in place of it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This is the step that holds. Drape bird netting, roughly 1/2 to 3/4 inch mesh, over the bush or over a frame before the berries start to turn blue, and tuck the edges in at the base so birds cannot get underneath. Put it up again every season.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Netting at about 1/2 to 3/4 inch mesh, carried on the bush or a frame with the skirt secured at ground level, is the exclusion that works; an unprotected bush can be stripped within days of color break, and pecked, half-eaten fruit is left behind. Install pre-ripening every year rather than after the first losses.

pests.name: Spotted-wing drosophila (SWD)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small white maggots inside ripe berries; fruit softens, collapses, and leaks when squeezed. A tiny vinegar-fly-like adult, the male with a dark spot near each wingtip. Damage often unseen until fruit is opened.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny maggots inside ripe berries, with fruit going soft and mushy. The adult is a small fly with a spot on the wing.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spotted-wing drosophila (Drosophila suzukii), an invasive vinegar fly whose females cut into healthy ripe fruit to lay eggs, unlike common fruit flies that only use rotting fruit.
pests.cause_beginner: A small invasive fruit fly that lays eggs in good, ripe berries (not just rotten ones), and the maggots feed inside.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Harvest frequently and completely (every one to three days) so ripe fruit is not left on the bush, and remove and destroy any fallen or overripe berries (bag them, do not compost). Fine exclusion netting (less than 1 mm mesh) over fruiting plants reduces egg-laying. Monitor with apple-cider-vinegar traps.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick ripe berries often and clean up any fallen or overripe ones (seal them in a bag, do not compost). Very fine netting keeps the flies off. You can monitor with a cup of apple cider vinegar as a trap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Choose early-ripening cultivars to dodge peak fly pressure, keep the planting clean of dropped fruit, and harvest on a tight schedule. Combine monitoring with exclusion before berries ripen.
pests.prevention_beginner: Grow early varieties when you can, keep the ground clear of fallen berries, and pick often. Fine netting before ripening is the best prevention.
