northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Northern highbush is the classic blueberry for cold-winter gardens, and it is the right choice here. It drops its leaves each fall and needs a real winter to fruit well, which your area gives it. Plant young bushes in early spring in very acidic soil, and you will pick berries from about midsummer into early fall. Always plant two or more different varieties near each other so they pollinate and you get a bigger crop.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Up here the blueberry to grow is northern highbush, a fully deciduous shrub that wants the long, cold winter your zones deliver (commonly 800 to 1000 or more chill hours). Set 2 to 3-year-old plants in early spring, give them strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5), and expect ripening from roughly July into early September, latest in the coldest zones. Plant at least two cultivars for better fruit set, and lean on the hardiest varieties and a slope with good air drainage in zones 3 and 4.

8.type_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is gated in by your moderate chill (about 350 to 650 hours) and long, hot summers. It is native to the region, the most heat-tolerant type, and blooms late enough to dodge most spring freezes; northern highbush gets too little chill here and resents the summer heat.
8.type_note_beginner: Rabbiteye is the type that loves the warm Southeast. Your winters are not cold enough for northern types, but they are just cold enough for rabbiteye, which also handles the summer heat and flowers late enough to usually avoid frost damage.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye blooms later than southern highbush and usually escapes spring freezes, but a warm late-winter spell can push bloom early, and a hard freeze on open flowers can cut the crop sharply. Later-blooming cultivars are the safer bet.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is a permanent evergreen shrub in the Gulf South, planted once and productive for decades; it holds its leaves through the mild winter and stays in leaf year round. The year runs from a late, frost-dodging bloom to harvest from roughly late May into July, then a quieter care period of light shaping and feeding. Rabbiteye needs a second, different rabbiteye nearby to cross-pollinate and set a crop.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your rabbiteye blueberry is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for many years, and here it stays green all year. It flowers late enough to usually miss spring frosts, ripens berries from late spring into summer, then moves into a calmer stretch of light tidying and feeding. One key point: it must have a second, different rabbiteye variety planted nearby so the two can pollinate each other and make fruit.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, rabbiteye blueberries are the easy, dependable choice. 9.type_note_seasoned: Blueberry is the least-suited berry crop in the Rio Grande Valley, and growers should not expect reliable fruit. Two separate problems stack here: Texas A&M AgriLife's statewide crop guidance records 0 acres of commercial blueberry production in the Lower Valley and notes rabbiteye, Texas's usual recommendation for most of the state, is grown in acid soils, while Valley soils run alkaline; and the Valley's near-zero winter chill falls short even of rabbiteye's minimum, let alone standard highbush types. The only remotely viable option is the lowest-chill southern highbush selections, grown in containers filled with an amended acidic mix, and even that is a genuine stretch, not a dependable crop.
9.type_note_beginner: Blueberry is the hardest berry to grow well in the Rio Grande Valley, and you should not expect a reliable harvest. Two things work against it: Valley soil is alkaline, and blueberries need acid soil, and Valley winters do not get cold enough even for the low-chill types normally recommended for Texas. Your best (still uncertain) shot is a very-low-chill southern highbush variety grown in a container filled with acidic potting mix, not planted in the ground.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a factor for blueberry in the Valley; the limiting factors are insufficient winter chill and alkaline native soil, so bloom and fruiting are erratic even with a well-chosen container planting.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Valley, blueberry is a niche, uncertain crop grown almost always in a container with an amended acidic mix, since native soils are alkaline and unsuited to this plant regardless of chill. Only the very lowest-chill southern highbush cultivars have any real chance, and even they may bloom and fruit erratically given how little chill the Valley banks most winters. Treat any harvest as a bonus, not an expectation, and plant more than one cultivar for better pollination.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Valley, grow blueberry only in a container with a special acidic potting mix, since the ground here is too alkaline for it. Pick the lowest-chill southern highbush variety you can find, and know that even then, fruiting may be hit or miss because Valley winters rarely get cold enough. Plant more than one variety.

Northern highbush is the recommended_type in both zones, matching WSU's own framing of northern highbush as the common Washington type and the ample WSU Skagit-station-sourced winter chill (968 to 1,950 hours z8, 700 to 1,500 hours z9, region_chill_delivered.pnw) against this crop's 1,000 hour requirement. Plant/bloom/harvest windows sourced to WSU Skagit County Extension, 'Growing Blueberries: Start With the Right Soil' (Ranten 2025, citing WSU NWREC small-fruit horticulturist Lisa Wasko DeVetter): plant January-March (dormant), net against birds mid-June through harvest completion in August, prune in winter or early spring. Bloom month (April) is a reasoned placement (the source states pre-bloom dormant pruning and dormant planting windows but no explicit bloom date; April is the standard maritime-PNW Vaccinium bloom window and clears both zones' last frost with margin). Both zones share one window; the source is a general western-WA guide, not zone-differentiated. resolution_method is frost_anchored_resolved per the pnw cell contract's frost-anchored invariant (not berries_woody_precompute, which other regions use); resolved_from carries the real NOAA-normal frost dates per zone.

8.type_note_seasoned: Northern highbush is the blueberry to plant here. West of the Cascades, winters bank about 968 to 1,950 hours (average around 1,468) of winter chill, WSU Skagit County Extension station data, comfortably clearing this crop's roughly 1,000 hour chill requirement. The other real requirement is soil: native soils west of the Cascades are rarely acidic enough on their own, so start right by testing and amending to pH 4.5 to 5.5, or grow in containers or raised beds with an acidic mix (WSU).
8.type_note_beginner: Plant northern highbush blueberries here. Our winters are plenty cold for this type. Net the bushes against birds from mid-June through the end of harvest, and prune in the dormant season, winter into early spring, just before growth resumes. Plant at least two cultivars near each other for the best fruit set.

7.type_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is NC State's own top pick for most soils below 2,500 feet elevation, and that covers the Piedmont: it names Premier among its recommended rabbiteye cultivars for this belt. Highbush (Duke, Jersey) is a real alternative on the higher-organic soils some Piedmont gardens have; both are already on this crop's canonical variety list. Rabbiteye's real winter here, unlike the mild Deep South, means it drops its leaves and rests fully dormant rather than holding foliage nearly year round.
7.type_note_beginner: Rabbiteye is the type NC State recommends for most soils in this area, including Premier. Highbush (Duke, Jersey) also works if your soil is especially rich. Here in the Piedmont's real winter, rabbiteye loses its leaves and rests like a typical fruit bush, unlike in the much milder Deep South.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye blooms later than highbush and usually escapes spring freezes here; a warm late-winter spell can occasionally push bloom early in a mild year.
7.grown_as_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is a permanent deciduous shrub in the Piedmont's real winter, planted once and productive for decades. It rests dormant and leafless through winter, then blooms in spring, sets fruit, and ripens across early summer. After leaf drop, prune late in the dormant season, just before bud break. It needs a second, different rabbiteye variety nearby to cross pollinate and set a crop; NC's own abundant winter chill (typically over 1,000 hours) is never the limiting factor here.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: Your rabbiteye blueberry is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for many years. Here it loses its leaves and rests over winter like a typical fruit bush. 8.type_note_beginner: Rabbiteye, including Premier, is NC State's top recommendation for most soils here. 8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is a permanent deciduous shrub on the Coastal Plain too; the region's real winter, milder than the Piedmont's but still a genuine cold season, means it drops its leaves and rests dormant each year rather than holding foliage. Plant a second, different rabbiteye variety nearby so the two can pollinate each other.

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: The Mid-Atlantic is real blueberry country. Rabbiteye, including the variety Premier, is NC State's top pick for most soils here, though highbush types like Duke and Jersey are also great on richer Coastal Plain soils. Unlike the Deep South, our real winter means the bush loses its leaves and rests each year. Plant in early spring, expect flowers in late winter to spring, and pick berries from June into midsummer. mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: The Piedmont and Coastal Plain are genuine rabbiteye and highbush blueberry country: NC State names rabbiteye, including Premier, as the best choice for most soils below 2,500 feet, with highbush (Duke, Jersey) and southern highbush called out specifically for the Coastal Plain's higher-organic soils. mid_south.plantings_provenance: Region fill (Task 7, Claude Code lane, 2026-07-20). recommended_type CORRECTED 2026-07-30: z7 northern_highbush, z8 rabbiteye. The original fill set rabbiteye in BOTH zones from the 2026-07-20 sourcing note, whose 'below 2,500 feet' steer is NC State's claim about the NORTH CAROLINA PIEDMONT, carried across when this region was built from the mid_atlantic template and relabeled as a University of Arkansas steer; no Arkansas document supports it for the uplands. THREE University of Arkansas documents place the types the other way: FSA6104 ('the northern highbush type is better adapted to the northern part of the state'), FSA6130 (headers 'Northern Highbush (Northern and Central Ark.)' vs 'Rabbiteye (Central and Southern Ark.)'), and the Arkansas Berries page ('northern highbush blueberries are grown in the northern counties, and rabbiteyes are grown in more central and southern areas'). z7 is the Ozark upland/northern belt and takes northern highbush; z8 is central Arkansas, where rabbiteye is correct and stays. Both types are already canonical varieties. leaf_habit is deciduous in both zones (not evergreen): unlike se_gulf's near-frost-free z8-10, the Mid-South has a real winter in both z7 and z8, so rabbiteye drops its leaves and rests dormant here, a genuinely new deciduous+rabbiteye combination per the cell contract section 5.3. Windows frost-reconciled against the real the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension/the University of Arkansas frost dates; calendar[] DERIVED by derive_deciduous_berry_woody_calendar (A16).

7.type_note_seasoned: Northern highbush is the type the University of Arkansas recommends for the northern part of the state, and that covers the Ozark uplands: Duke and Bluecrop are the dependable defaults, both named by the University of Arkansas as long adapted in Arkansas. The belt's winter chill, roughly 1,000 to 1,300 hours, comfortably meets their 800 to 1,000 hour requirement. Rabbiteye belongs to central and southern Arkansas rather than these uplands: it is the less cold hardy type, and its low chill requirement, about 350 to 600 hours, lets a warm late-winter spell push it into bloom ahead of a killing freeze. Northern highbush drops its leaves and rests fully dormant through the belt's real winter.
7.type_note_beginner: Northern highbush, such as Duke or Bluecrop, is the type the University of Arkansas recommends for this part of the state. Your winters are cold enough to give these bushes the chilling they need, and they bloom late enough to dodge most spring freezes. Rabbiteye is the type for central and southern Arkansas: up here it is more likely to be hurt by winter cold, or tricked into blooming early by a warm spell and then caught by a freeze. Your bush will lose its leaves and rest each winter.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Northern highbush will not break bud until it has taken its full chilling, so it blooms late here and usually escapes spring freezes; Duke is specifically noted for blooming relatively late. A warm late-winter spell moves it far less than it moves the low-chill southern types.
7.grown_as_note_seasoned: Northern highbush is a permanent deciduous shrub in the Ozark uplands' real winter, planted once and productive for decades. It rests dormant and leafless through winter, then blooms in spring, sets fruit, and ripens across early summer. After leaf drop, prune late in the dormant season, just before bud break. Plant at least two different northern highbush cultivars with overlapping bloom: this type is self fertile, but the University of Arkansas notes that two or more cultivars improve fruit size and number. The belt's winter chill, roughly 1,000 to 1,300 hours, comfortably covers this type's 800 to 1,000 hour requirement.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: Your rabbiteye blueberry is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for many years. Here it loses its leaves and rests over winter like a typical fruit bush. It flowers in spring and ripens berries by early summer. Plant a second, different rabbiteye variety nearby so the two can pollinate each other and make fruit.

8.type_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is the University of Arkansas's top pick for most soils, and that holds across the lowland South, with Premier, Powderblue, and Tifblue among the dependable cultivars. On the lowland South's more acidic, well-drained soils, low-chill southern highbush (Emerald, Jewel) is a strong second choice and can ripen a bit earlier than rabbiteye. Both types are already on this crop's canonical variety list; rabbiteye remains the broader, more soil-forgiving default across the belt, while the University of Arkansas also lists northern highbush as adapted to central Arkansas, so it is a workable second choice toward the belt's cooler, upland edge.
8.type_note_beginner: Rabbiteye, such as Premier or Tifblue, is the University of Arkansas's top recommendation for most soils here. If your soil is especially acidic and well drained, low-chill southern highbush like Emerald or Jewel is also a strong choice and can ripen a bit earlier. Either way, this belt's real winter means the bush loses its leaves and rests each year.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye blooms early here and can occasionally meet a late-winter freeze in a mild year; later-blooming cultivars are the safer bet.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is a permanent deciduous shrub on the lowland South too; the region's real winter, milder than the Ozark uplands' but still a genuine cold season, means it drops its leaves and rests dormant each year rather than holding foliage. It blooms early, in March, and ripens from June into mid-July. Prune late in the dormant season, just before bud break, and plant a second, different rabbiteye variety nearby for cross pollination. Abundant regional chill (roughly 900 to 1,300 hours a year, far more than rabbiteye needs) is never the limiting factor.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your rabbiteye blueberry on the lowland South is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for years. It loses its leaves and rests over winter, flowers early in spring, and ripens berries from June into mid-July. Plant a second, different rabbiteye variety nearby so the two can pollinate each other.

mid_south.region_notes_beginner: The Mid-South is real blueberry country. Rabbiteye, such as Premier and Powderblue, is the type the University of Arkansas recommends for most home gardens here. Low-chill southern highbush like Emerald or Jewel is a good second option where the soil is naturally acidic and well drained. Unlike the Deep South, our real winter means the bush loses its leaves and rests each year. Plant in early spring, expect flowers in late winter to spring, and pick berries from June into midsummer. Always plant two different rabbiteye varieties together so they can pollinate each other.
mid_south.region_notes_seasoned: The Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands are genuine blueberry country. The University of Arkansas recommends rabbiteye (Premier, Powderblue, Brightwell, Tifblue) as the best all-around choice for most soils across the belt, with low-chill southern highbush (Emerald, Jewel) a strong option where the soil is naturally acidic and well drained. Northern highbush struggles in the region's summer heat and is not the pick here. Unlike se_gulf's mild winter, this belt's real winter in both zones means rabbiteye is grown here as a fully deciduous shrub, dropping its leaves and resting dormant rather than holding foliage year round. Chill is never the limiting factor: the belt banks roughly 900 to 1,300 hours a year against rabbiteye's roughly 350 to 600 hour requirement. Plant at least two different rabbiteye cultivars for cross pollination, and prune in the dormant season just before bud break.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)
nevada.plantings_provenance: Nevada high desert region (roadmap item 10), Task 8 Perennials, 2026-07-21. Structural donor = this crop's own low_desert_az z9 (bloom Jan-Feb / harvest Apr-May, evergreen, southern_highbush, container-only-on-alkaline-soil framing) for the Las Vegas Valley floor and Laughlin corner, and warm_arid z8 (bloom Mar / harvest May-Jun, deciduous) for the cooler zone 8 pockets; z10 rides zone 9's evergreen shape with the warmer zone 10 frost anchor per the shard method note. JUDGMENT CALL (no direct Nevada blueberry source exists): leaf_habit is deciduous at z8 and evergreen at z9/z10, mirroring which AZ donor each zone number matches (warm_arid z8 vs low_desert_az z9/z10) -- z8's cooler, higher pockets plausibly bank enough real winter chill for true dormancy, while the Las Vegas Valley floor and the hot Laughlin/Colorado River corner stay mild enough that this guide keeps the low_desert_az evergreen, container-culture framing there. The container-only, acidified-soil constraint (the crop's actual binding limit here per the task) is stated uniformly across all three zones regardless of leaf_habit, since Mojave soil alkalinity is a region-wide trait, not an elevation-dependent one. No Nevada-specific blueberry source exists, so sources are the general Southern Nevada seasonal/heat-ceiling framework (unr_fs0261) plus the NWS frost anchor (nws_vef); never carries the AZ donors' uarizona_ext/tamu_agrilife sources forward. calendar[] DERIVED by berry_woody_calendar.

9.type_note_seasoned: Blueberry is very marginal in the Las Vegas Valley low desert, and the limiting factor is not chill but soil: blueberries need acidic soil around pH 4.5 to 5.5, and the Mojave's native soil is strongly alkaline, hostile ground for this plant. Grow only the lowest-chill southern highbush selections, only in large containers filled with an amended acidic mix (peat or pine bark), acidify the irrigation water, and give afternoon shade through the summer heat. Even then, treat any harvest as a bonus, not a dependable crop.
9.type_note_beginner: Blueberry is a very hard sell in the Las Vegas Valley. The real problem is the soil: it is too alkaline (not acidic enough) for blueberries, which need acidic soil to thrive. Grow a low-chill variety in a large container filled with a special acidic potting mix, never in the ground, water it with acidified water, and give it shade in summer. Expect this to be a fussy experiment, not a sure harvest.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the limiting factor for blueberry in the low desert; alkaline soil, extreme summer heat, and marginal winter chill are the binding constraints, so an early harvest before the worst heat matters more than frost protection.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Las Vegas Valley low desert, blueberry is a container-only crop, since the native soil is too alkaline for in-ground planting; grown in pots, it stays mild enough through the winter that this guide treats it as evergreen here, keeping its leaves year round. The year runs from a winter bloom to an early harvest, April into May, then a care period of light shaping, feeding, and acidified watering. Shield it from extreme heat.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, blueberries have to be grown in large containers because the ground soil is too alkaline. Grown that way, it is a long-lived bush that stays green year round in this mild-winter zone. It flowers in winter and ripens berries in spring, around April to May, then settles into a calmer stretch of light care and careful watering. Protect it from the harshest heat.

8.type_note_seasoned: Blueberry is still very marginal in the cooler zone 8 pockets: the alkaline Mojave soil is just as hostile here as on the valley floor, so blueberry still needs a large container filled with an amended acidic mix and acidified irrigation water regardless of elevation. The extra winter chill at this elevation lets the plant go properly dormant and supports a wider range of southern highbush selections, but soil, not cold, remains the binding constraint. Expect a genuine experiment, not a dependable harvest.

crops.description_seasoned: Blueberries are long-lived, acid-loving woody shrubs that reward patience: a well-sited bush can produce for decades. Success turns on three things most growers underestimate: matching the type to your winter chill, getting the soil acidic enough, and planting more than one cultivar for cross-pollination.
crops.description_beginner: Blueberries are bushes, not annual plants, and a healthy one can fruit for decades. They are easy to grow once you nail two things: very acidic soil and the right type for your climate. Plant at least two different varieties so they pollinate each other, and you are set for years.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Ripe berries turn fully blue and develop a dusty bloom, and they detach with a light roll of the thumb. Color comes a few days before full sweetness, so wait until they part easily from the cluster. Pick every 5 to 10 days through the ripening window; rabbiteye flavor improves with a slightly longer interval.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A blueberry is ready when it is completely blue and falls off into your hand with a gentle roll of the thumb. Berries turn blue a few days before they are truly sweet, so give them a little longer, then taste one. Pick over the bush every several days as more ripen.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Blueberries bloom in spring, with the exact timing set by type, cultivar chill, and region. Low-chill southern highbush flowers earliest, which is why late frost is its main risk; rabbiteye flowers later, dodging more spring freezes. Each flower cluster opens over a one-to-two-week window.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Blueberries flower in spring. Earlier-blooming types can get caught by late frosts, while later-blooming ones usually escape them. The white or pink bell-shaped flowers open over a week or two before the berries begin to form.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Cold-hardiness depends on the type. Northern highbush handles deep cold (cold-hardy cultivars and half-high types reach the coldest zones); southern highbush and rabbiteye are less cold-tolerant and are matched to mild-winter regions. A plant that survives a winter is not the same as one that fruits reliably through it, so the region recommendation targets dependable fruiting, not bare survival.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: How much cold a blueberry can take depends on its type. The northern types are very cold-hardy; the southern types are not and belong in milder climates. Surviving the winter and actually producing berries are two different things, so follow the type the app recommends for where you live.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Chill hours are the hours of winter temperature below 45°F a blueberry needs to break dormancy and bloom normally. The requirement varies sharply by type: northern highbush wants roughly 800 to 1000 hours, rabbiteye about 350 to 650, and southern highbush as little as 150 to 600. Too little chill for the type gives weak, erratic bloom and little fruit; the figure is the single best predictor of whether a given cultivar will crop where you live.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Blueberries need a stretch of cold winter weather before they will flower and fruit, measured in chill hours (time below 45°F). Each type needs a different amount: northern highbush needs a lot of cold, southern highbush very little, rabbiteye somewhere in between. This is why choosing the type that matches your climate matters so much.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Plant at least two different cultivars of the same type with overlapping bloom. Rabbiteye is self-incompatible and needs a second rabbiteye to set a crop at all. Highbush, both northern and southern, is partially self-fertile but yields noticeably larger, earlier, more abundant fruit with a cross-pollinating partner. Cross types do not pollinate each other reliably, so pair rabbiteye with rabbiteye and highbush with highbush.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Plant two or more different blueberry varieties of the same type so they can pollinate each other. Some types, like rabbiteye, will barely fruit without a partner. Others fruit a little on their own but do far better with a second variety nearby. Just make sure both plants are the same type, since types do not cross well.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Focus the first year or two on root and shoot growth, not fruit. Pick off the flower buds so the bush builds structure; this sacrifices an early handful of berries for far better long-term yields. Keep the soil evenly moist through the establishment season and mulch heavily to protect the shallow roots.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: In the first year or two, pinch off the flowers so the plant puts its energy into growing strong instead of making a few berries. It feels wrong, but it pays off with much bigger harvests later. Water steadily and keep a thick mulch around the base while the plant settles in.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Test the soil the season before planting. If pH is above 5.5, work in elemental sulfur at the soil-test rate several months ahead, since sulfur needs time to acidify. Blend generous peat moss or aged pine bark into the planting zone for acidity, organic matter, and drainage. Where native soil is unsuitable or alkaline, a raised bed of acidic mix or a large container is the more reliable route.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Prepare the soil before you plant. Do a soil test, and if it is not acidic enough, mix in garden sulfur a few months ahead following the test's directions. Work plenty of peat moss or pine bark into the spot where the plant will go. If your soil just will not get acidic, grow your blueberry in a pot of acidic mix instead.
crops.planting_method_notes_seasoned: Set the plant at the depth it grew in the nursery, in acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark. On heavy or wet ground, plant on a raised mound or ridge at least 6 inches high to keep the shallow roots out of standing water. Space plants by type: about 4 to 5 feet apart for highbush, 5 to 6 feet for the larger rabbiteye.
crops.planting_method_notes_beginner: Dig a hole and set the plant so it sits at the same depth it was in its pot, then backfill with soil mixed with peat moss or pine bark. If your ground stays wet, plant on a raised mound instead. Give each bush room: about 4 to 5 feet between highbush plants, a bit more for the bigger rabbiteye types.

pollination.notes_seasoned: See pollinator_notes for the full guidance. In short, blueberry uses a simple model: plant two or more different cultivars of the same type with overlapping bloom. There is no apple-style specific pollinizer pairing to chart; any two compatible cultivars of the same type cross-pollinate. Rabbiteye requires a second rabbiteye to set a crop; highbush is partially self-fertile but yields far better with a partner.
pollination.notes_beginner: See the pollination notes above for details. The short version: plant at least two different kinds of blueberry of the same type so they can pollinate each other. You do not need to match specific varieties, just grow two that bloom at the same time.

crops.establishment_note: Pick off the flower buds the first year or two after planting so the bush spends its energy building roots and wood instead of fruit. It pays off in far better yields once the plant is established.
crops.cane_management_seasoned: Not applicable in the cane-fruit sense. Blueberry is a crown-forming bush, not a cane fruit like raspberry or blackberry. Its pruning is old-wood renewal: once the bush is established, remove the oldest, least productive stems at ground level each dormant season to keep a balance of young and mature wood. This rides the dormant-season prune beat in the care calendar rather than a cane-by-cane training structure.
crops.cane_management_beginner: Not applicable the way it is for raspberries. Blueberries grow as a bush, not on canes you tie up. Once the plant is a few years old, cut out the oldest, woodiest stems at the base each winter to make room for fresh growth. That is the whole job.
crops.type_selection_seasoned: Which type you grow is decided by your winter chill, not preference. Northern highbush (about 800 to 1000 chill hours) is the cold-climate type, deciduous and truly cold-hardy. Southern highbush (roughly 150 to 600 hours) and rabbiteye (about 350 to 650 hours) are the warm-climate types for mild winters; in the warmest zones they hold their leaves year-round. Plant a high-chill type where winters are too mild and it never breaks dormancy properly, so it barely fruits; plant a low-chill type where winters are cold and it blooms too early and loses the crop to frost. Match the chill, and pick the type the page recommends for your region.
crops.type_selection_beginner: There are different kinds of blueberry, and the right one depends on how cold your winters get, not which you like best. In cold-winter areas, grow northern highbush. In mild-winter areas, grow southern highbush or rabbiteye. The plant tag usually says which type it is. If you plant the wrong one for your climate, it may grow fine but produce almost no berries. The app will point you to the type that fits your region.
crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: Blueberry asks for patience twice over. Keep picking the flower buds off through the second year: it feels wasteful, but the energy goes into roots and wood instead, and an established bush can then fruit for decades. The other job this year is watching the leaves. Pale yellow new leaves with green veins mean the soil is not acid enough for the plant to take up iron, and that is the single most common way a blueberry fails. Test and acidify the soil, and use a chelated-iron spray to buy time while the sulfur works. Feed at bud break with an acid fertilizer and again about six weeks later, keeping it light, and never use lime.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: Continue bud removal through year two; redirecting that energy into root and shoot development is what builds a bush capable of decades of production, and the deferral is short against that lifespan. Nutrition is the crop's defining constraint and the usual cause of failure: interveinal chlorosis on new foliage indicates high-pH iron unavailability rather than an iron shortage in the soil, so the correction is pH, with chelated foliar iron as a holding measure while elemental sulfur acts. Feed at bud break with an ammonium-form acid fertilizer and again roughly six weeks later at light rates, avoiding lime and nitrate nitrogen, both of which raise pH and injure the plant. Blueberry roots are shallow and fibrous, so moisture must be steady rather than heavy.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From the third year the bush carries a full crop over a window of roughly two months, so you pick it every few days rather than all at once. Take only fully blue berries that come away with a gentle roll of the thumb; any red still showing at the stem end means underripe, and it will not sweeten off the bush. Pick in the cool of the morning once the dew has dried, and refrigerate promptly. Get netting up before the berries start to color, because birds are the number one blueberry pest and will clear a ripening bush in days, and secure it at the base so they cannot get underneath. Pruning is simple: each winter take out one to three of the oldest, woodiest stems at the base so the bush keeps renewing itself.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from year three across a roughly two-month window, harvested on a several- day cycle. Index maturity on complete blue color and clean abscission under a thumb roll; residual red at the calyx indicates immaturity, and the crop is non-climacteric so it will not improve after picking. Harvest after dew burn-off in the cool morning and cool promptly, since field heat shortens shelf life and surface moisture drives bruising and decay. Bird exclusion netting goes up ahead of color break and is secured at ground level. Renewal pruning is the whole structural task: remove one to three of the oldest canes at the base each dormant season alongside weak and crowded wood. Pair it with sanitation, raking and removing mummified fruit and burying residual inoculum under fresh mulch against mummy berry.

crops.name: Heirloom Tomato

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes do best in loose, well-draining soil rich in organic matter: think compost-improved garden beds rather than hard clay. Good drainage matters even more for heirlooms than for hybrids, because most heirlooms have no built-in resistance to the soilborne wilt diseases that thrive in wet, compacted soil. Work in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If water pools after rain and takes more than an hour to soak in, improve the bed or use a raised bed filled with a topsoil-and-compost mix before planting.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Heirloom tomatoes perform best in well-drained loam or sandy loam with high organic matter. Because heirlooms generally lack the VFN resistance bred into hybrids, drainage is doubly important: waterlogged, compacted soil favors Fusarium and Verticillium wilt and Pythium root rot, to which heirlooms are fully susceptible. The indeterminate, heavily fruiting habit also places sustained calcium and phosphorus demand on the soil, and large-fruited types strain calcium uptake, which is why blossom-end rot tracks moisture consistency. Working in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting builds structure and fertility and moderates the calcium-availability swings that drive blossom-end rot in big heirloom fruit.

ph.note_beginner: Heirlooms want slightly acidic soil: a pH between 6.0 and 6.8. Outside that range, nutrients the plant needs get locked up in the soil even if they're there. Blossom-end rot (the dark sunken spot on the bottom of the fruit) is often triggered by pH problems limiting how much calcium the plant can absorb. If you've never tested your soil, an inexpensive test kit from a garden center is worth doing before your first season. Many extension offices also offer low-cost testing.
ph.note_seasoned: Tomatoes are particularly sensitive to pH because it governs the solubility of phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium, three nutrients they consume in large quantities. At pH below 5.5, manganese and aluminum become increasingly available at phytotoxic levels; blossom-end rot risk rises as calcium uptake is impaired. Above 7.0, iron and manganese deficiencies drive interveinal chlorosis on younger leaves. In the alkaline soils common across the interior West and alkaline-irrigation regions, growers routinely need to acidify before planting. Eastern soils often run naturally in the preferred range; Pacific Northwest soils vary widely by parent material.

fertilizer.timing: starter at transplanting, then side-dress about 3 to 4 weeks later
fertilizer.example_product: Miracle-Gro Tomato Plant Food
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes are heavy feeders and need regular fertilizing throughout the season. Start with a balanced fertilizer at transplant time, then switch to a fertilizer higher in potassium once flowers appear: look for 'tomato fertilizer' or a formula where the third number on the bag (potassium) is the largest. Feed every two weeks through the fruiting period.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time for your tomatoes' first side-dressing, about 3 to 4 weeks after planting out, then again every 3 to 4 weeks. Once flowers appear, switch to a tomato or high-potassium fertilizer to keep the fruit coming.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Look for three numbers on the fertilizer bag: those are the NPK ratio (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium). A soil test is the surest guide, and it is what both extension services behind this guide recommend first. Without one, a low-nitrogen balanced formula such as 5-10-10 is a sensible default. Go easy on the first number: too much nitrogen gives you a big leafy plant that is slow to set fruit. Skip the high-phosphorus bags sold as bloom boosters unless a soil test actually calls for phosphorus, because many soils already hold plenty.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Heavy feeder. Start with balanced feed at transplant, switch to high-potassium once flowering begins.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: First side-dress is due, about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, then every 3 to 4 weeks through harvest. Switch to the high-potassium formula at flowering.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Soil test governs. Absent one, a low-nitrogen balanced formula such as 5-10-10. UMN advises a low- or no-phosphorus feed unless a test specifically calls for phosphorus, and warns that excess nitrogen produces bushy, leafy plants slow to bear fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About 1 pound of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet side-dressed three to four weeks after transplanting, repeated every 3 to 4 weeks through harvest; absent a soil test, incorporate about 1.5 pounds of a complete fertilizer per 100 square feet before planting. Use the high-potassium formula from the hint above at this rate.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A common rate is about 1 to 2 tablespoons of fertilizer worked into the soil around each plant, 6 to 8 inches from the stem, beginning about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting and repeating every 3 to 4 weeks. Water it in each time and keep it off the stem and leaves. A big heirloom plant is a heavier feeder than a cherry type.

companions.note_beginner: The most reliable companion for heirloom tomatoes is marigolds: plant them around the edges of the bed, not between the tomatoes, since heirloom plants get large and will shade out anything too close. Nasturtiums at the bed perimeter draw aphids away from your tomatoes (aphids prefer the nasturtiums). Keep heirlooms away from fennel, which stunts many neighboring plants, and away from potatoes and eggplant, which share the same diseases and pests. Basil is a popular choice to plant nearby and does well in the same sun and water conditions.
companions.note_seasoned: Heirloom tomato companions follow the same species-level lore as other tomatoes, with two heirloom-specific nuances. First, heirloom's large plant footprint (24-36 inch spacing, 6-foot cages) shades out many traditional companion candidates; prioritize companions that tolerate partial shade or position them at the drip-line edge rather than between plants. Second, the marigold/nematode connection is the best-documented pairing in this crop's companion set, effective as a dense pre-season cover crop, not as scattered concurrent interplanting. For most growers the practical guidance is: avoid fennel, avoid planting near potatoes or eggplant if disease pressure has been a problem, and consider nasturtiums as an aphid trap crop at the bed perimeter where they won't be shaded.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Basil
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Long-established pairing; flavor-improvement claims are traditional. Basil's aromatic compounds may deter some pest insects, though not extension-documented for this specific pair, but widely practiced and low risk.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Flavor-improvement claims are classic companion-planting tradition. Not documented in peer-reviewed research or extension literature.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Basil is a classic tomato partner. Gardeners have grown the two together for generations, and basil's strong scent may put off some pest insects. It is not a proven effect for this exact pair, but it is harmless and worth trying.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigolds
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: French marigolds suppress root-knot nematodes, most effectively as a dense cover crop planted 2+ months before tomatoes, not as concurrent interplanting. Extension-documented mechanism.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: French marigolds help fight root-knot nematodes (tiny soil worms that attack roots). They work best when grown as a thick patch a couple of months before you plant tomatoes, rather than just tucked in alongside them at the same time.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Nasturtiums function as a trap crop for aphids, since aphids preferentially colonize nasturtiums, drawing them away from tomatoes. UC IPM documents trap-crop use of nasturtiums in vegetable gardens. Particularly useful for heirloom plants, which are large and difficult to spray thoroughly once fully grown.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap-crop principle is documented in IPM literature. UC IPM references nasturtiums as aphid attractors. The specific nasturtium-tomato trap-crop pairing is referenced in extension-adjacent IPM guidance; strongest evidence is for brassica pests, but aphid trap-crop mechanism applies broadly.

good_seasoned.name: Borage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Borage flowers attract pollinators over an extended bloom period, coinciding with heirloom's long indeterminate fruiting season. Heirloom's larger flowers benefit from robust pollinator activity during the extended set window. Hornworm repellence is a traditional claim without T1 backing.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Borage as pollinator attractor is plausible and consistent with floral-resource literature. The hornworm-repellence claim is traditional companion-planting lore without T1 extension backing.

good_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots' deep taproot partitions the root zone differently from heirloom's fibrous roots, theoretically reducing below-ground competition. This is a plausible root-zone partitioning inference, not an extension-tested pairing. Note: give carrots adequate distance from heirloom's cage footprint (24-36 inch spacing), or they will be shaded out.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning between taprooted and fibrous-rooted crops is a real ecology concept. The specific carrot-tomato pairing benefit is a plausible inference that has not been directly studied in extension research.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is broadly allelopathic and suppresses growth of many neighboring plants. Extension literature documents fennel as a poor companion for most vegetables; the specific tomato interaction is traditional but consistent with fennel's known allelopathic properties.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Fennel gives off natural chemicals that stunt the growth of many plants around it, so it is a poor neighbor for most vegetables, including tomatoes. It is best kept in its own spot away from the garden beds.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both brassicas and tomatoes are heavy feeders; close interplanting creates real competition for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Not a toxic pairing, but productivity of both crops is reduced under competition.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Both brassicas and tomatoes are heavy feeders; close interplanting creates real competition for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Not a toxic pairing, but productivity of both crops is reduced under competition.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage-family plants (like broccoli, kale, and cabbage) and tomatoes are both hungry feeders, so planting them close together makes them fight over nutrients in the soil. It will not poison either one, but both end up less productive.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both crops host the tomato fruit worm / corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea, same species). Planting together creates a concentrated host reservoir that amplifies pest pressure on both crops.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Both crops host the tomato fruit worm / corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea, same species). UC IPM and Cornell document H. zea as a shared host pest across Solanaceae and Poaceae. Planting together creates a concentrated host reservoir that amplifies pest pressure on both crops.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn and tomatoes are attacked by the very same caterpillar (the tomato fruitworm, also called the corn earworm). Planting them side by side gives that pest two favorite foods in one place and makes the problem worse for both crops.

bad_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both are Solanaceae and share primary diseases (late blight, Phytophthora infestans; early blight, Alternaria solani) and several pests. Planting together creates a continuous host bridge that sustains inoculum across the season and into following years. Crop rotation separating Solanaceae is the standard extension recommendation for disease management.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Extension literature (UMN, Cornell, Clemson HGIC) documents shared disease and pest pressure within Solanaceae and recommends rotation to break disease cycles.

bad_seasoned.name: Eggplant
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Same family (Solanaceae), shares Colorado potato beetle pressure and early blight. Interplanting concentrates beetle and disease pressure; separating Solanaceae crops, even within a season, reduces crossover pest load.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Colorado potato beetle and early blight are documented shared pests/pathogens across Solanaceae in extension IPM literature.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or black insects on the growing tips and the undersides of leaves, often so small they look like dots. Leaves may start to curl or feel sticky. You might notice ants walking up the stems; ants actually farm aphids for the sweet liquid they produce, so ants are a good early warning sign.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the clusters directly with a strong jet of water from a hose; this dislodges most of them. For a persistent infestation, apply insecticidal soap or neem oil spray, making sure to coat the leaf undersides where the aphids cluster.
pests.prevention_beginner: Plant marigolds or nasturtiums near your tomatoes; both attract beneficial insects that feed on aphids. Avoid over-fertilizing with high-nitrogen fertilizer, which produces the soft, fast-growing shoots that aphids prefer.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species (most often green peach and potato aphids) colonize tomatoes. They reproduce asexually and explosively in warm weather, so a few founders become dense colonies on tender new growth within days. Soft, nitrogen-flush growth from over-fertilizing is especially attractive, which is why feeding history drives outbreak severity as much as weather.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are tiny soft-bodied insects that breed very fast in warm weather, so a few quickly turn into crowds on the soft new growth at the tips. Too much fertilizer makes that soft growth they love, so going easy on feeding helps keep them down.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on high-nitrogen fertilizer. It pushes out the soft, fast new growth that aphids settle on first, so a lighter feeding hand gives them less to work with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Nitrogen-flush growth is the preferred feeding substrate, which is why feeding history drives outbreak severity about as much as weather does. Moderate the nitrogen and there is less tender tip growth to support rapid colony buildup.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hit the clusters with a strong jet from the hose, aiming up under the leaves where they hide. This dislodges most of them and it is the first thing to reach for.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A directed jet knocks the colony off mechanically, which suits an insect that reproduces asexually and rebuilds within days. Repeat as fresh tip growth is recolonized, and work the leaf undersides.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings and small parasitic wasps feed on aphids and will usually bring an outbreak down on their own. Planting marigolds or nasturtiums near your tomatoes draws them in and gives them a reason to stay, and skipping broad sprays keeps them working.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserving resident natural enemies is the higher-return move: interplanted marigold and nasturtium recruit them without a purchase, and avoiding broad-spectrum material is what keeps them in the planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: You can also buy ladybugs or lacewings and release them onto active clusters. Treat it as a top-up rather than the plan: they need aphids already there or they move on, and in an open garden they are free to leave.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Released predators supplement the resident population rather than replacing it. UC IPM notes the best results come from creating favorable conditions for naturally occurring predators, and that released predators starve or migrate elsewhere if prey is not available when they arrive, so time a release to a located infestation.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For an infestation that keeps coming back, spray insecticidal soap, a soap-based spray that acts on soft-bodied insects it touches. Coat the undersides of the leaves, since that is where the aphids sit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Coverage decides the outcome: target leaf undersides and growing tips where the colonies concentrate, and expect to re-treat as populations rebuild in warm weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil, pressed from the seeds of the neem tree, is the other spray option for stubborn clusters. Like the soap, it has to reach the aphids, so wet the leaf undersides thoroughly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Interchangeable with soap where colonies rebuild after washing. Direct the application onto the colonies themselves, leaf undersides and growing tips, rather than over the top of the canopy.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_beginner: Large sections of leaves or whole stems stripped very quickly, sometimes overnight. Look for fat green caterpillars up to 4 inches long that blend almost perfectly into the stems and leaves. The easiest way to find them is to look for the dark green or black droppings they leave on leaves below.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Hand-pick and drop them in a bucket of soapy water; it's simple but effective. If you find any with small white oval capsules stuck to their backs, leave those alone; parasitic wasps have already laid eggs on them and the wasps will take care of the rest.
pests.prevention_beginner: Turn or till the soil in autumn to expose and kill overwintering pupae. Planting dill or fennel nearby attracts predatory wasps that prey on hornworms.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the five-spotted hawk moth (Manduca quinquemaculata). Adult moths lay eggs on tomato foliage from early summer; the caterpillars feed and grow through mid-to-late summer, reaching up to about four inches and defoliating fast because a single large larva eats a great deal. They pupate in the soil over winter, so the prior season's population carries forward in an unworked bed.
pests.cause_beginner: These are the caterpillars of a large moth. The moth lays eggs on the leaves in early summer, and the caterpillars grow big (up to about four inches) through mid and late summer, eating a lot of leaves fast. They spend the winter in the soil, so a bed left undug can carry them into next year.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick; they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them; parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Turn or till the soil in your tomato bed in autumn. The caterpillars spend the winter in the soil as pupae, a resting stage, and digging brings them up, which cuts how many carry over into next year.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Larvae pupate in soil and overwinter there, so an unworked bed carries the prior season's population forward. Autumn tillage exposes the pupae and lowers local carryover.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick them off by hand and drop them into a bucket of soapy water. They blend into the stems, so look for the dark droppings on the leaves below and search upward from there. If a caterpillar has small white capsules stuck on its back, leave it in place: parasitic wasps have laid eggs on it and are already at work.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Handpicking is the workhorse. A single large larva strips a great deal of foliage, so pulling a few off by hand goes further than it would with a small pest. Frass on lower leaves is the locating cue. Leave larvae bearing white cocoons so the wasp brood completes.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant dill, fennel, or basil near your tomatoes. They attract predatory wasps that prey on hornworms, and those wasps are the reason some caterpillars end up carrying white capsules.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Dill, fennel, and basil interplantings support the predatory wasps that attack hornworms. The white cocoons on a larva's back are that biological control already running, so preserving parasitized larvae feeds the next wasp generation.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Bt, short for Bacillus thuringiensis, is a naturally occurring bacterium sold as a spray that acts on caterpillars which eat treated leaves. It is worth considering when there are more hornworms than you want to pick off one by one.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Bt is the material option where handpicking cannot keep pace. It acts through feeding, so coverage on the foliage the larvae are actively working is what determines the result.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves, making them look like they've been peppered with a hole punch, most noticeable on seedlings and young plants. The beetles themselves are tiny, shiny, and black; they jump when disturbed, which is how they got their name.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover fabric to keep beetles off young plants. Sprinkle diatomaceous earth (a fine powder made from fossilized algae) around the base and on the leaves; it damages soft-bodied insects on contact. Neem oil spray also works.
pests.prevention_beginner: Wait to transplant until plants are large and well-established; flea beetles cause the most damage to small seedlings. Larger, established plants can usually tolerate some feeding without major harm.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several flea beetle species. They overwinter as adults and emerge in spring, so pressure is heaviest early, on seedlings and freshly set transplants whose small leaf area makes the shot-hole feeding proportionally damaging. Established plants with ample foliage tolerate the same beetle numbers easily, which is why the timing of the attack matters more than its size.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are tiny black beetles that jump when you disturb them and chew small round holes in leaves. They come out in spring and hit young seedlings hardest, because small plants do not have many leaves to spare. Bigger, established plants shrug off the same chewing.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Drape row cover fabric, a light woven sheet, over seedlings and young plants. It is a physical barrier that keeps the beetles off during the stretch when small plants suffer most.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Exclusion during the early window is the main play. Overwintered adults emerge in spring and hit small transplants, whose limited leaf area makes shot-hole feeding proportionally damaging; the timing of the attack matters more than its size.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil, pressed from the seeds of the neem tree, is a spray option if the peppering gets heavy on small plants. Cover the leaves where you see fresh holes.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The material fallback where exclusion was not in place early. Reserve it for the seedling stage, since well-established plants with ample foliage usually tolerate the same feeding without major harm.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_beginner: A fine stippling or scattering of tiny yellow or white dots across the upper surface of leaves, making them look dull and washed out. In heavier infestations you may see fine webbing on the undersides of leaves. Spider mites are barely visible to the naked eye; hold a white sheet of paper under a leaf and tap; if you see tiny dots moving, that's them. Worst in hot, dry weather.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the plant, especially the leaf undersides, with a strong jet of water repeatedly over several days to knock off mites and disrupt their colonies. Follow up with neem oil or insecticidal soap applied to the undersides of leaves.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather; water-stressed plants are far more vulnerable. Avoid dusty, dry conditions around the garden if possible.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Twospotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae) and relatives. They thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions and complete a generation in under a week in summer heat, so populations explode late in the season. Drought-stressed plants are far more vulnerable, which makes consistent watering and dust suppression the primary cultural controls rather than an afterthought.
pests.cause_beginner: Spider mites are tiny mites (so small they look like moving dust) that love hot, dry, dusty weather and multiply incredibly fast, so they tend to flare up late in summer. Plants that are short on water suffer the most, so keeping plants watered and dust down is the best defense.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep plants well watered through hot weather. Mites hit water-stressed plants hardest, so steady moisture is your strongest everyday defense. Keeping dust down around the bed helps too, since dry, dusty conditions suit them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Drought stress raises susceptibility sharply and the mites favor hot, dry, dusty conditions, so consistent irrigation plus dust suppression are the primary cultural controls here rather than an afterthought.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spray the plant with a strong jet of water, especially under the leaves, and repeat over several days. That knocks mites off and breaks up their colonies.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Repeated jetting dislodges mites and disrupts colony structure and webbing. Repetition is what makes it work against a pest that completes a generation in under a week in summer heat.

control_ladder.note_beginner: You can buy and release predatory mites, which are mites that hunt spider mites, so a living control is working on the plants for you. Release them onto an infestation you have actually found: with no spider mites to eat, they starve or move on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Released predatory mites put a control into the canopy itself, which is useful late in the season when spider mite populations are compounding fastest. UC IPM names the western predatory mite and Phytoseiulus as the commercially available species and puts a working ratio at about one predator per ten spider mites, while noting that the best results still come from favoring the predators already present.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Insecticidal soap, a soap-based spray that acts on the pests it touches, is a good follow-up after the water blasts. Aim it at the leaf undersides where the mites and webbing are.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Follow-up to the water treatment. Leaf-underside coverage is the whole game, and the short summer generation time sets the reapplication interval.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil, pressed from the seeds of the neem tree, is the other follow-up spray. Same rule as the soap: it has to reach the undersides of the leaves to do anything.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Interchangeable with soap as the post-jetting follow-up. Direct it at the leaf undersides where the colonies and webbing sit.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark brown spots with a target-ring pattern (concentric rings, like a bullseye) appear on the lowest leaves first. Those leaves yellow and drop, and the disease works its way up the plant over the season.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove affected leaves as soon as you see them and bag them for the trash, not the compost. A copper-based fungicide slows the spread. Mulch around the base to stop soil splash, which is how the fungal spores travel from the ground up onto the leaves.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Move your tomatoes to a new spot each year, because the spores persist in the soil. Water at the base, never overhead. Stake or cage plants so leaves stay off the ground with good airflow. Heirlooms lack the blight resistance some hybrids carry, so these habits matter more.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first; affected leaves yellow and drop, and the disease spreads upward through the plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Alternaria solani. It overwinters on infected debris and in the soil, then splashes up onto the lowest leaves in warm, wet weather, so infection starts low and climbs. Repeated tomato plantings build soil inoculum. Most heirlooms lack the partial early-blight tolerance bred into some modern hybrids, so unmanaged heirlooms tend to defoliate faster; rotation and mulch to block soil splash are the core preventions.
diseases.cause_beginner: Early blight is a fungus that lives in old plant debris and soil and splashes up onto the lowest leaves in warm, wet weather, which is why it starts at the bottom and climbs. Planting tomatoes in the same spot builds it up. Heirlooms are not bred to resist it, so moving the planting and mulching the soil are the main defenses.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes every 3 to 4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow and prune to open the canopy. Stake to keep foliage off the ground.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move your tomatoes to a new spot each year. The spores build up in soil where tomatoes keep going in, so shifting the planting keeps that buildup from working against you.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes out of a bed on a 3 to 4 year cycle. Repeated plantings build soil inoculum, and the fungus carries over on infected debris and in the soil between seasons.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay mulch over the soil around the base of each plant. Rain splashing off bare soil is how the fungus travels from the ground onto the lowest leaves, and a mulch layer gets in the way of that.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mulch interrupts the splash pathway that carries overwintered inoculum from soil onto the lowest foliage, which is why infection starts low and climbs. Core prevention here, not a finishing touch.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the top of it. Overhead watering drives soil up onto the lowest leaves, which is exactly the route the spores take.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soil-level irrigation removes an operator-generated splash event; paired with mulch it closes the main route from soil inoculum to lower foliage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stake or cage your plants and give them room, so the leaves stay off the ground and air moves through. Pruning out the densest growth helps as well.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Staking lifts foliage clear of the soil surface, while spacing and canopy pruning keep air moving. Heirlooms mostly lack the partial early-blight tolerance bred into some modern hybrids, so this canopy work carries more of the load.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off the spotted lower leaves as soon as you notice them, since getting them off the plant early slows how fast the disease climbs. Bag what you pull and put it in the trash rather than the compost pile, and clear old tomato debris out of the bed too, since the fungus rides out the winter on it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: In-season removal of symptomatic lower leaves takes out sporulating tissue and slows the upward progression, so act on the first bullseye lesions rather than waiting for the lower canopy to yellow and shed. The pathogen overwinters on infected debris, so offsite disposal of both the removed foliage and the end-of-season residue lowers what is available to splash up the following spring. Composting symptomatic tissue keeps it in circulation.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A copper-based spray can slow how fast the disease moves up the plant. It does its best work applied before the disease takes hold, so treat it as protection rather than a rescue once spots are everywhere.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper is a preventive application, most useful through warm, wet spells when splash infection is active. It slows spread rather than clearing established lesions.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Water-soaked patches that turn brown and expand fast on leaves and stems; this disease moves very quickly and can destroy a plant in a matter of days. In humid weather you may see white fuzzy growth on the leaf undersides. It is the most serious tomato disease in the garden.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and immediately bag and bin all affected plant material; do not compost any of it. A copper-based fungicide can help as a preventive in wet spells. If a plant is badly affected, pull it entirely so it cannot spread to neighbors.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Good airflow is your best defense: stake and space plants so air moves through. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter. Because heirlooms rarely carry late-blight resistance, choose a resistant variety only if this disease has hit your area before, and watch closely in cool, wet weather.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems; white fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The oomycete Phytophthora infestans, the pathogen behind the Irish potato famine. Its spores travel on wind and rain over long distances and infect leaves, stems, and fruit directly, spreading explosively in cool, wet weather. Because the inoculum arrives airborne, rotation helps little; resistant varieties and immediate removal of infected plants matter most, and heirlooms almost never carry the late-blight resistance genes bred into a few modern hybrids.
diseases.cause_beginner: Late blight is a fast, destructive disease whose spores blow in on wind and rain rather than starting from the soil. In cool, wet weather it can kill a plant in a few days. Because it arrives through the air, the best protection is pulling out any infected plant right away; heirlooms are not bred to resist it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately; do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter. Choose a resistant variety where late blight recurs, since heirlooms rarely carry resistance.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Airflow is your best defense here. Stake your plants and space them so air moves freely through the leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excellent airflow is the leading cultural control. Stake and space generously to keep the canopy open, which matters because this pathogen spreads explosively once cool, wet weather sets in.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull off and bin affected leaves and stems the moment you spot them, and if a plant is badly hit, take the whole plant out so it cannot spread to its neighbors. Clear every bit of tomato debris out of the garden before winter, and send affected material to the trash rather than the compost pile.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Immediate removal of infected tissue, and roguing whole plants that are badly affected, is the highest-value in-season action against a pathogen that can take a plant down in days. Tomato debris left in the garden over winter is the local carryover to close: bag and bin infected material, since composting it returns the tissue to the bed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Heirlooms rarely carry late-blight resistance. If this disease has hit your area before, it is worth growing a resistant variety and watching all your plants closely through cool, wet weather.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resistance matters more here than rotation, since the inoculum arrives airborne over long distances. A few modern hybrids carry late-blight resistance genes and heirlooms rarely do, so reserve the variety swap for areas with a recurrence history.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A copper-based fungicide can help as protection during wet spells. Apply it ahead of trouble rather than expecting it to save a plant that is already collapsing.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper is preventive here. Time applications to wet weather windows and pair them with removal, since this disease outruns a curative approach.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small circular spots with a dark brown border and a pale gray or tan center, appearing first on the lower leaves, sometimes with a faint yellow ring. Over time the spotted leaves yellow and drop.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and discard affected leaves right away; do not compost them. Apply a copper-based fungicide. Keep the plant staked and prune very dense growth so air moves through.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rotate your tomatoes to a new spot each year. Water only at the base, never overhead. Mulch around the base to prevent soil splash. Heirlooms are not bred to resist leaf-spot diseases, so airflow and sanitation carry the load.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular spots with dark borders and pale gray centers, starting on lower leaves; spots may carry yellow halos.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Septoria lycopersici, one of the most common tomato leaf diseases. Like early blight it carries over on debris and infected soil and spreads by water splash onto lower foliage in warm, wet, humid weather, defoliating from the bottom up. Heirlooms carry no bred resistance, so the same moisture-management and sanitation practices, rather than a single spray, are the fix.
diseases.cause_beginner: Septoria leaf spot is a very common tomato fungus. Like early blight it overwinters in old debris and soil and splashes onto the lower leaves in warm, humid weather, working up the plant. The same habits that slow early blight, moving the planting, watering low, and mulching, keep it in check.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper fungicide. Ensure good air circulation through spacing and pruning.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Mulch around plants. Open the canopy for airflow.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Shift your tomatoes to a new spot each year. This fungus overwinters in old debris and soil, so a fresh bed starts you with less of it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotation reduces the carryover this pathogen holds in debris and infested soil, the same lever that works on early blight.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Mulch the soil around the base of your plants. The spores travel in water splashing off bare soil onto the lowest leaves, and mulch blocks that route.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mulch interrupts the splash route from infested soil to lower foliage, which is how the bottom-up defoliation gets started.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the base of the plant instead of overhead, so you are not splashing soil onto the lower leaves yourself.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soil-level irrigation removes an operator-generated splash event during the warm, humid weather when this fungus spreads fastest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep plants staked and prune out very dense growth so air moves through the canopy. Heirlooms are not bred to resist leaf-spot diseases, so airflow does a lot of the work here.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spacing and canopy pruning are load-bearing on heirlooms, which carry no bred leaf-spot resistance. Open canopies plus sanitation stand in for the genetics.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Strip off the spotted lower leaves as soon as you find them. The sooner they are off the plant, the slower the spots climb. Send what you remove to the trash rather than the compost pile, and clear old tomato debris out of the bed, since the fungus carries over on it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt removal of symptomatic lower leaves reduces the sporulating tissue driving defoliation from the bottom up; pair it with canopy opening rather than treating it as the alternative. Carryover lives on debris and in infested soil, so offsite disposal of removed foliage and end-of-season debris keeps that reservoir from rebuilding.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A copper-based fungicide is an option once you are keeping up with leaf removal and airflow. It supports those habits rather than replacing them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper is a supporting material. Moisture management and sanitation, rather than a single spray, are what hold this back on a host with no bred resistance.

diseases.name: Fusarium and Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant wilts on hot afternoons and recovers at night at first, then whole branches yellow and wilt for good, often on just one side of the plant or one side of a leaf. Cut a wilted stem lengthwise near the base and you may see brown streaking inside. There is no cure once a plant is infected.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no spray that cures a wilted plant; remove and bag badly affected plants so they do not seed the soil further. Focus on protecting the rest: keep plants watered evenly and avoid wounding the roots. Next year, plant into a fresh bed and choose resistant varieties if you can.
diseases.prevention_beginner: This is the big one for heirlooms: most heirlooms have little or no resistance to these two soil fungi, while many hybrids are bred to resist them (look for V and F on a hybrid's tag). Rotate tomatoes out of a bed for several years, keep soil well drained, and if wilt has struck before, grow heirlooms in containers of fresh mix or graft them onto resistant rootstock.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Non-uniform yellowing and wilting, frequently on one side of the plant or one half of a compound leaf; early on the plant wilts in the heat of the day and recovers overnight, then collapses. Vascular browning is visible in a split lower stem.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Two soilborne fungi, Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici and Verticillium dahliae, which invade through the roots and plug the water-conducting vascular tissue. Both survive in soil as resting structures for many years (Fusarium favors warm soils, Verticillium cooler ones).
