This is the defining heirloom vulnerability: most heirlooms lack the V and F resistance genes bred into modern hybrids (the VFN codes), so they are fully susceptible where the pathogens are established. Cherokee Purple is a notable heirloom exception with some tolerance.
diseases.cause_beginner: These are two soil fungi that get in through the roots and clog the plant's water pipes, so it wilts and dies. They live in the soil for years. Modern hybrids are often bred to resist them (the V and F on the tag), but heirlooms usually are not, which is why heirlooms are more likely to wilt.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No curative treatment exists; rogue out and destroy infected plants. Manage by prevention: long rotation, good drainage, resistant rootstock for grafting, or container culture in fresh medium.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Long rotation (4 to 6 years out of the bed). Maintain drainage and avoid root injury. Where wilt is established, use resistant (VF) rootstock for grafting or grow heirlooms in containers of pathogen-free mix; heirlooms carry no bred resistance.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep tomatoes out of an affected bed for several years. Both fungi survive in soil for a long time, so a one-year break does not clear them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Long rotation, on the order of 4 to 6 years out of the bed, because both pathogens persist as resting structures in soil for many years. Fusarium favors warm soils and Verticillium cooler ones, so an infested bed stays risky across a range of seasons.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For heirlooms this is the control that matters most. Most heirlooms have little or no resistance to these two soil fungi, while many hybrids are bred to resist them; look for V and F on a hybrid's tag. Cherokee Purple is one heirloom reported to have some tolerance.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The V and F of the VFN codes mark exactly the bred resistance heirlooms lack, leaving them fully susceptible where these pathogens are established. Cherokee Purple is a noted heirloom exception with some tolerance.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where wilt has struck before, an heirloom can be grafted onto resistant rootstock, meaning the root system of a resistant plant supporting the heirloom top. That lets you keep growing the variety you want on ground a rotation cannot clear.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: On infested ground, grafting onto resistant rootstock keeps the heirloom fruit on a root system that holds up. It is the option that matters here because both pathogens persist as resting structures in soil for many years, so rotation alone does not free a bed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the bed well drained. Good drainage is one of the few site conditions that works in your favor here, so improve or avoid ground that stays soggy.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Drainage is a standing site condition to maintain, sitting alongside long rotation as prevention, since no curative material exists once the vascular tissue is colonized.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Once a plant has wilted for good, no spray will bring it back. Pull it, bag it, and get it out of the garden so it does not add more fungus to the soil.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rogue out and destroy symptomatic plants. The purpose is limiting further soil loading rather than rescue, since the fungi plug the water-conducting tissue and no curative treatment exists.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A dark, sunken, leathery patch on the bottom (the blossom end) of the tomato, opposite the stem. It hits the first fruits of the season most and is not contagious.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Mulch around the plant and water deeply and consistently; blossom end rot comes from uneven moisture, not a nutrient shortage, so steady watering is the real fix. Remove affected fruit so the plant can put energy into the next ones.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The single most important prevention is consistent watering. Avoid disturbing the roots at the base of the plant, and do not over-fertilize with high-nitrogen fertilizer. Large heirloom fruit is especially prone, so keep moisture even once fruit sets.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the blossom end of the fruit; affects the first fruits most and is not contagious.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Not an infection but a calcium-delivery failure in the developing fruit. Calcium moves with water, so when soil moisture swings between wet and dry (or roots are damaged), the fast-growing blossom end is starved of calcium and its cells break down. It tracks watering consistency, not soil calcium levels, and large-fruited heirlooms show it more severely than small types.
diseases.cause_beginner: Blossom end rot is not a bug or an infection. It happens when the fruit cannot get enough calcium, almost always because watering swung from wet to dry and back. Calcium travels with water, so steady, even watering, not adding calcium, is what prevents it. Even calcium-rich soil gets it when watering is uneven.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Steady watering is the fix. This is not an infection and it is not a shortage of calcium in your soil: the fruit misses out on calcium when watering swings from wet to dry and back, because calcium travels with water. Water deeply on a regular rhythm once fruit sets, mulch around the plant to smooth out the swings, and try not to disturb the roots at the base. Adding calcium is not the answer.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: This tracks watering consistency, not soil calcium levels. Calcium moves with water, so moisture swings or root damage starve the fast-growing blossom end and its cells break down. Deep, regular irrigation, mulch to buffer the soil, and no root disturbance at the base are the control. Large-fruited heirlooms show it more severely, and the first fruits of the season take the worst of it, so hold the rhythm tightest early.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spread a layer of mulch over the soil around the plant. It slows how quickly the ground dries between waterings, so the soil holds a steadier moisture level instead of drying hard and then soaking again, which is the pattern that starves the fruit end.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mulch functions here as a moisture buffer on the root zone, damping the swings between irrigations so calcium keeps moving into the developing fruit. It supports the watering rhythm rather than substituting for it, and it earns the most on large-fruited heirlooms carrying the season's first set.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on heavy nitrogen feeding, ammonium-based fertilizers included, while fruit is setting. The problem here is calcium reaching the fruit, and pushing a lot of nitrogen at the plant works against that rather than helping.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hold the nitrogen back through fruit set, ammonium sources included, since a heavy feed pulls against the calcium delivery this disorder actually tracks. Skipping the sidedress is the move, not offsetting it with a calcium product, because soil calcium levels are not the limiting factor.

diseases.name: Fruit cracking
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Splits in the skin of ripening fruit, either rings around the stem end (concentric) or lines running down the sides (radial). Cracks often appear after a heavy rain that follows a dry spell.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cracks cannot be undone, so pick cracked fruit promptly and use it quickly before it rots or attracts insects. The real work is prevention through even watering. Fruit that is close to ripe can be picked just before a big rain to beat the cracking.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep soil moisture as even as you can: water deeply and regularly during dry spells, and mulch to buffer the swings. Many heirlooms have thin skins and crack easily, so pick ripe fruit right away, especially before heavy rain.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Radial (vertical, down the sides) or concentric (rings at the stem end) splits in the skin of ripening fruit, typically after rapid water uptake such as heavy rain following a dry period.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Cracking occurs when rapid changes in soil moisture make the fruit interior expand faster than the skin can grow. Radial cracking is the more serious form and worsens in hot, humid weather. Variety matters: many heirlooms are thin-skinned and large-fruited and split more readily than crack-resistant hybrids, so heirlooms are among the more crack-prone tomatoes.
diseases.cause_beginner: Cracking happens when the inside of the fruit swells faster than the skin can stretch, usually after a big drink of water following a dry stretch. Thin-skinned heirlooms split more easily than tougher-skinned hybrids.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No treatment reverses a crack; harvest promptly to avoid secondary rot and insect entry. Manage by keeping moisture even.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Maintain even soil moisture through deep, regular watering during drought and mulch to buffer fluctuations. Harvest near-ripe fruit ahead of heavy rain; heirlooms are more crack-prone, so pick promptly.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Even soil moisture is the whole defense. Water deeply and regularly through dry spells and mulch to soften the swings, so the inside of the fruit is not suddenly swelling faster than the skin can stretch. A crack cannot be undone, so pick cracked fruit promptly and use it quickly; if heavy rain is coming, pick the nearly ripe fruit first.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cracking follows rapid water uptake, typically heavy rain onto a dried-out bed, when the interior expands faster than the skin can grow. Deep, regular irrigation during drought plus mulch to buffer the fluctuation is the control; harvesting near-ripe fruit ahead of a forecast soaking takes the vulnerable fruit out of the event. Radial cracking is the more serious form and worsens in hot, humid weather, and thin-skinned, large-fruited heirlooms split more readily than crack-resistant hybrids.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay mulch over the soil around the plant. It keeps the ground from drying out hard between waterings, so a heavy rain lands on soil that is already damp and the fruit gets a gentler change rather than a sudden one.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The buffer earns its place going into a dry stretch: mulched soil holds moisture more evenly, so a soaking does not translate into the fast uptake that outpaces skin growth. Run it with the deep watering rhythm, since thin-skinned, large-fruited heirlooms have less margin in that event.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 2-3 days in peak summer heat; weekly or less when temperatures are moderate. The correct interval is driven by soil moisture at 2-3 inch depth, not a fixed schedule, as evapotranspiration rates in a heirloom at full canopy can pull 1+ inch per week in hot weather.
watering.frequency_beginner: In the hottest part of summer, water about every 2 to 3 days; when it is cooler, once a week or less is plenty. Rather than following a strict schedule, check the soil a few inches down and water when it is starting to dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: 1-2 inches per week, delivered to depth. Heirloom roots extend 18-24 inches in good soil; shallow frequent watering keeps roots near the surface where they are more vulnerable to heat and drought stress. Deep, infrequent watering drives root development downward.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches of water a week, and water deeply so it soaks well down. Heirloom roots go quite deep, and deep watering pulls them down where they handle heat and dry spells better; quick shallow sprinkles keep roots near the surface where they dry out fast.
watering.method_seasoned: At soil level: drip, soaker hose, or hand-water at the base. Overhead irrigation wets foliage and creates the leaf-surface moisture that Septoria leaf spot and early blight require for spore germination. Morning is preferred over evening: any foliage wetted accidentally dries before nightfall, narrowing the infection window.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant, not over the top, using a drip line, soaker hose, or just the hose at the soil. Wet leaves invite leaf-spot diseases, so keeping the foliage dry helps. Watering in the morning is best, so any leaves that do get splashed dry off before night.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Yellow leaves on the lower part of the plant, especially if the soil stays wet for days at a time. Cracked fruit is another sign: the plant drinks unevenly when soil stays wet, then surges when it dries out, which splits the skin. If the soil feels wet to your finger 2 inches down and the plant still looks unhappy, too much water is the likely cause, not too little.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Leaves wilting in the morning and not recovering overnight; afternoon wilt on a hot day is normal and not a reliable indicator, but wilt that's still there at sunrise means the plant is stressed. Flowers dropping off before making fruit is the other big warning sign; water stress at flower time cuts your harvest. Dry, cracked soil that pulls away from the container or bed edge confirms the problem.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellow lower leaves (nitrogen displaced from anaerobic root zone), cracked fruit (surge uptake after dry spell), and persistently soggy soil. In waterlogged soil, roots shift from aerobic respiration to fermentation, which impairs calcium and potassium uptake and accelerates the blossom-end rot cycle even when soil calcium is adequate.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in morning that does not fully recover overnight, blossom drop, dry cracked soil. Flower abscission is triggered by water stress at the abscission zone at the base of each pedicel; once flowers drop, that fruit set opportunity is gone for the season. Prolonged drought stress followed by heavy watering also causes fruit cracking and blossom-end rot via the same calcium-uptake disruption as overwatering.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep the starting mix evenly moist
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep the starting mix evenly moist until sprouts emerge; a dome or cover holds surface moisture between gentle waterings.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the tray damp until the seeds sprout. A clear lid keeps the surface from drying out between waterings.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep cells evenly moist, never soggy
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Grow seedlings on with even, moderate moisture, letting the surface approach dryness between waterings; standing wetness in the cells is the damping-off risk.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the seedlings lightly damp. Let the top of the mix start to dry before each watering so the stems stay healthy.

schedule_by_stage.rate: 1 to 2 inches per week, delivered to depth
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Read the soil rather than a schedule: a full heirloom canopy can pull more than an inch a week in heat, so check 2 to 3 inches down and soak deeply when drying, every 2 to 3 days in peak summer, weekly or less when moderate. Roots run 18 to 24 inches; water to depth at the base.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Check the soil a few inches down instead of watering on a fixed schedule. Soak deeply at the base when it starts to dry: every 2 to 3 days in hot weather, weekly or less when cool.

schedule_by_stage.rate: 1 to 2 inches per week, kept even
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: From flowering through fruit set, water stress costs fruit directly: drought-stressed flowers abscise and are gone for the season. Hold moisture even as the first fruit begin the long heirloom sizing run.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep moisture steady once flowers show. A dry spell now makes flowers fall off, and every lost flower is a lost tomato.

schedule_by_stage.rate: 1 to 2 inches per week, as steady as possible
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Large heirloom fruit are among the most crack-prone and blossom-end-rot-prone of the tomatoes when moisture swings during their long sizing weeks. Mulch, keep 1 to 2 inches a week steady, and avoid drought followed by a flood.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Heirlooms have big, tender fruit that split and get dark bottoms if dry soil suddenly gets drenched. Water steadily and deeply while the fruit size up and ripen.

schedule_by_stage.rate: little needed as the plant winds down
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: As nights fall below 50°F and fruit set stops, cut irrigation back; late soggy soil does the declining plant no favors.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: When the nights get cold, the plant slows way down and needs little water. An occasional drink is enough while the last fruit finish.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Keep water off the foliage: overhead irrigation creates the leaf-surface wetness Septoria leaf spot and early blight need to infect. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so foliage dries before nightfall. Mulch to steady soil moisture, which also limits the blossom-end rot that large-fruited types are especially prone to.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil and not the leaves. Wet leaves invite leaf-spot diseases, so if you do use a sprinkler, water in the morning. A layer of mulch keeps the soil evenly moist, which matters even more for big heirloom fruit that crack and rot on the bottom when watering is erratic.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The moisture-critical window runs from transplant establishment through flowering, fruit set, and the long fruit-sizing period that large-fruited heirlooms demand. Inconsistent moisture during fruit development is the direct cause of blossom-end rot and cracking, which show up more severely on big fruit than on small-fruited types.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The time to be most careful about even watering is from flowering through the weeks the big fruit are sizing up. Large heirloom tomatoes are the most prone to cracking and to dark sunken spots on the bottom when the soil dries out and then gets flooded, so keep moisture steady once fruit has set.

start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Hardening off means gradually introducing your seedlings to outdoor conditions before transplanting. Start about a week before your planned transplant date: put the plants outside for a couple of hours in a sheltered, partly shaded spot, then bring them back in. Add more time and more direct sun each day. This helps the plant build up its waxy leaf coating and adjust to outdoor wind and temperature swings. Plants that skip this step often struggle for two to three weeks after transplanting.
start_method.notes_beginner: Start seeds 8 weeks before your last frost date; heirloom tomatoes need a long season, so starting on time is important. Plant two seeds per cell about a quarter inch deep in seed-starting mix, somewhere warm (a heat mat helps a lot). At transplant time, bury the stem deeper than it sat in the pot: right up to the lowest set of leaves. New roots will form along the buried stem and give the plant a stronger, more drought-tolerant foundation.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 8 weeks before last frost; heirlooms need a long season. Harden off carefully. Bury stem deep at transplant.

container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Minimum 18-inch depth. Wide containers (15+ inches diameter) preferred to accommodate the root spread of large indeterminate plants. Standard 20-gallon nursery containers work for compact varieties; full-size indeterminates will struggle even in 20+ gallon containers without aggressive pruning.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a pot at least 18 inches deep, and a wide one (15 inches across or more) so the big roots have room. A 20-gallon pot works for smaller varieties, but full-size heirloom plants will struggle even in a 20-gallon pot unless you prune them back hard.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Empty any standing water from the saucer within an hour of watering. Heirloom's high water demand means containers are often watered daily in heat, but roots left sitting in pooled water lose oxygen and begin to rot, so the saucer must catch overflow without becoming a reservoir.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Pour out any water that collects in the saucer within an hour of watering. In hot weather you may water a pot every day, but the roots should never sit in standing water or they start to rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a potting mix made for containers (look for bags labeled 'potting mix' or 'container mix', not garden soil or topsoil, which gets too dense in pots and doesn't drain well).
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in about 20-25% perlite (those small white volcanic pellets sometimes pre-mixed into potting soil) to keep the mix from compacting around the roots as the season progresses. Heirloom plants get heavy and their roots fill the container fast, so good drainage matters. Stir in a slow-release granular fertilizer at planting following the label rate, then add liquid fertilizer every 1-2 weeks once flowers appear.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: container_potting_mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Incorporate 20-25% perlite by volume to compensate for compaction under a heavy plant. Add slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting; supplement with liquid balanced fertilizer every 1-2 weeks once flowering begins. Heirloom's heavy fruit load makes nutrient buffering especially important in containers.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Container heirlooms dry out much faster than in-ground plants. In hot weather, check the soil every day and water when the top 2 inches feel dry; daily watering is normal during summer heat. Don't let the container dry out completely between waterings; uneven moisture is the main cause of blossom-end rot in containers. Large 20-gallon containers hold moisture better than smaller ones, but even these need checking frequently during heat waves.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container soil runs out of nutrients faster than garden beds. Once the first flowers open, feed with a liquid tomato fertilizer every 1 to 2 weeks through the rest of the season. If the bottom of the fruit develops a dark sunken spot (blossom-end rot), it's almost always a calcium and watering issue, not a fertilizer deficiency; keep moisture consistent rather than adding more fertilizer.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes are a tough fit for containers; they're not well-suited to pot growing. The plants get very large, the roots need a lot of space, and you need a sturdy cage that's hard to anchor in a pot. If you want to try, use at least a 15-gallon container (20 gallons is better) and look for compact varieties like Stupice or Stupice, which stay smaller than standard indeterminate heirlooms. A raised bed is a much better option if you have any outdoor space at all.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Heirloom tomatoes are generally not well-suited to container growing. Indeterminate varieties develop extensive root systems that are cramped even in 20-gallon containers, and the large fruit load requires very robust staking that is difficult to anchor in a pot. If container growing is necessary, use compact or determinate heirloom-type varieties (Stupice, Bloody Butcher) in 15-20 gallon containers with heavy-duty caging. Raised beds are strongly preferred for full-size indeterminate varieties.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry significantly faster than in-ground soil; daily watering is common during summer heat for a large plant drawing heavily on a limited root volume. Check moisture 2 inches below the surface daily. Consistent moisture is critical; irregular watering drives blossom-end rot, which is more severe in containers than in-ground. Large containers (20+ gallons) provide some buffer but heirloom's demand typically exceeds that buffer in peak heat.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container medium has limited nutrient buffering capacity, and heirloom's fruit load is higher than most tomato types. Supplement with liquid balanced fertilizer every 1-2 weeks once flowering begins, or apply slow-release granular at planting plus a liquid mid-season boost. Calcium deficiency (blossom-end rot) is common in containers; consider a calcium supplement if symptoms appear.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container helps a heirloom hold the steady moisture that prevents blossom-end rot, but match the pot to the plant: these are large, thirsty vines that need a big reservoir and a big soil volume, so undersized self-watering pots run dry fast in heat. Keep the reservoir filled in peak summer, let the mix draw down between fills rather than sitting saturated, and top-water occasionally to flush accumulated salts.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot can work for a heirloom tomato and keeps the water steady, which helps prevent rot on the bottom of the fruit. Use the largest one you can, because these are big, thirsty plants. Keep the reservoir full in hot weather, and now and then water from the top to rinse out built-up minerals.

recommended: Brandywine (large pink slicer)
Cherokee Purple (dusky red-purple)
Mortgage Lifter (large pink, mild)
Black Krim (dark, rich flavor)
Green Zebra (green-striped, tangy)
Hillbilly (large bicolor)
San Marzano (paste)
Amish Paste (paste)
varieties.note_beginner: Heirlooms are open-pollinated, so you can save seed from your best fruit and grow the same variety again next year. Good starting choices: Brandywine and Mortgage Lifter for classic big pink slicers, Cherokee Purple and Black Krim for deep, rich flavor, Green Zebra for something tangy and different, and San Marzano or Amish Paste for sauce. If disease has been a problem in your garden, Cherokee Purple tends to hold up a little better than most heirlooms. Brandywine is delicious but slower and a bit fussier, so it makes a great second-season variety once you have the basics down.
varieties.note_seasoned: Heirlooms are open-pollinated cultivars, so seed saved from a healthy fruit grows true to type; that is what lets named heirlooms persist across generations. The class spans the full range of the species: large pink slicers (Brandywine, Mortgage Lifter, Hillbilly), dark or dusky varieties (Cherokee Purple, Black Krim), green-when-ripe types (Green Zebra), and open-pollinated paste tomatoes (San Marzano, Amish Paste). Days to maturity vary widely, roughly 70 to 90 days, with the big pink slicers at the long end. Because almost all heirlooms lack the VFN (Verticillium, Fusarium, nematode) resistance bred into hybrids, expect more disease pressure and lean on rotation, sanitation, and airflow; Cherokee Purple is a notable heirloom with some wilt tolerance.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, and potatoes. All four are nightshades and share the same soilborne diseases, chiefly early blight and the Fusarium and Verticillium wilts, whose spores persist in the soil for several years. Following one nightshade with another lets that inoculum build, so heirloom does best on a bed that has been out of the family for about three years.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant heirloom where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, or potatoes grew recently. They are all in the same family and share the same soil diseases (mainly early blight and the wilt diseases), which build up in the soil over several years. Give the bed about three years off from this family before planting tomatoes there again.
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, legumes, corn, root vegetables
rotation.note_beginner: Don't plant tomatoes in the same bed two years in a row. Move them to a fresh spot every year if you can, and wait at least 3 years before coming back to the same location. The same rule applies to peppers, eggplant, and potatoes; they're all in the same family and share the same soil diseases, so rotating one without rotating the others doesn't help much. If you've had plants wilt and die even with good watering, look for disease-resistant varieties: a 'V' or 'F' on the seed packet means the variety is bred to resist the most common soilborne wilts.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate nightshades to a fresh bed every 3 years. Fusarium oxysporum and Verticillium dahliae, the two primary soilborne wilts in tomatoes, persist as chlamydospores in soil for 4-6 years and infect through root wounds. Rotation delays pathogen buildup but does not eliminate it; in beds with confirmed wilt history, resistant varieties (coded VF or VFN on seed packets) are the stronger intervention.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Up to 1 week at room temperature, stem-scar side down. Ethylene continues to drive sugar development after harvest; room temperature keeps ethylene-sensitive receptors active, allowing flavor to continue developing. The stem scar is the primary permeability site for moisture loss; resting it downward reduces desiccation.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Keep tomatoes on the counter for up to a week, stem-scar side down. They actually keep getting sweeter and tastier at room temperature, and resting them scar-side down helps them lose less moisture.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Avoid refrigeration for any tomato intended for fresh eating. Below 50-55°F, chilling injury disrupts membrane integrity in mesocarp cells; the damage is irreversible and converts firm flesh to mealy, waterlogged texture. Flavor compounds (volatile esters and aldehydes) are also suppressed by cold and do not recover when the fruit warms. Even a few hours below the threshold causes detectable texture loss in large heirloom fruit.
storage.fridge_beginner: Do not refrigerate tomatoes you plan to eat fresh. Cold below about 50 to 55°F permanently damages them, turning the flesh mealy and watery and dulling the flavor for good, even after they warm back up. Just a few hours in the fridge can leave a big heirloom slice noticeably worse.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Core and slice before freezing; freeze on parchment-lined trays until firm, then bag. Cell walls rupture at freezing temperatures; thawed heirloom will be soft and collapsed. This makes frozen heirloom unsuitable for fresh eating but fully functional for sauces, soups, and roasting where texture is cooked out anyway. Large heirloom slices freeze well and are convenient for winter sauce use.
storage.freezer_beginner: To freeze, core and slice the tomatoes, freeze the slices on a parchment-lined tray until firm, then bag them up. Freezing makes them soft, so they are not good for fresh eating, but they are perfect for sauces, soups, and roasting where they get cooked down anyway.
storage.notes_beginner: Keep tomatoes on the counter, never in the refrigerator. Cold temperatures break down the texture permanently and kill the flavor; even a few hours in the fridge makes a noticeable difference in a large heirloom. Store stem-scar side down to slow moisture loss. If a big fruit is starting to soften unevenly, use the softest sections first. Over-ripe heirlooms that are too soft to eat fresh make excellent sauce; don't throw them away.
storage.notes_seasoned: Never refrigerate a heirloom you intend to eat fresh; cold breaks down cell structure and kills flavor compounds irreversibly. Room-temperature storage extends eating quality. If the fruit is very large and beginning to soften unevenly, prioritize the softest sections first and use firmer sections later. Over-ripe large heirlooms are still excellent for sauce.

det_indet.detail_beginner: Indeterminate means the plant keeps growing and producing all season until frost; it will not stop at a set height. Most heirloom tomatoes are indeterminate and can reach 6 feet or more, so they need a strong cage or stakes put in at planting time. Unlike determinate types that ripen one big batch and stop, an indeterminate heirloom keeps setting new fruit as long as you keep picking and the weather holds.
det_indet.detail_seasoned: Most heirloom tomatoes are indeterminate: the vine keeps growing and setting fruit until frost and can reach 6 to 8 feet, so it needs sturdy staking or caging and continuous support. Prune to one or two main stems for larger fruit and better airflow, which also helps limit the foliar diseases heirlooms are prone to. A few heirlooms are compact or semi-determinate (the open-pollinated Stupice runs early and bushy; paste types like Amish Paste are often semi-determinate), but the classic large slicers (Brandywine, Cherokee Purple, Mortgage Lifter) are strongly indeterminate.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale curved shoot pushing upward through the soil. The shoot will straighten and the first two small leaves will unfold at the top.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Tomato seeds need warm soil to sprout: around 75 to 85°F is ideal. A heat mat under the seed tray is the easiest way to get there; without one, try the top of your refrigerator or any consistently warm spot. Cover the tray with a clear plastic lid or cling wrap until the first sprout appears, then take it off right away.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale shoot pushing upward through the soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil temperature in the 70-85°F range. A heat mat makes a real difference for staying in the optimal zone. Cover with a humidity dome until sprouts appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you seen any sprouts yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any little sprouts poking up yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Two small flat leaves open first; those are the seed leaves. Then the first true leaves emerge between them; they'll have the distinctive jagged edges and tomato-leaf smell.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Take off the plastic cover the moment you see the first green sprouts; leaving it on after emergence creates the warm, still, humid conditions that cause damping off, a fungal problem that collapses seedling stems at the soil line and kills them fast. Move the tray as close to your brightest light as possible. If seedlings grow tall and floppy instead of short and stocky, they need more light, not more water; that stretched-out look (called etiolation) means the seedling is reaching toward brighter light.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Two seed leaves open flat, then the first true leaves emerging between them; they will look distinctly tomato-shaped.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove the humidity dome the moment sprouts appear; trapped moisture after emergence drives damping off (Pythium/Rhizoctonia fungal complex attacking the hypocotyl). Get seedlings as close to your brightest light source as possible. Leggy, etiolated growth is caused by light deficiency, not overwatering; the seedling is elongating its internode lengths to search for brighter light.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings looking?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young seedlings look so far?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A strong, thick stem, 3 to 4 sets of true leaves, and a deep green color. The plant looks sturdy and compact rather than tall and floppy.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Start hardening off about a week before you plan to transplant: put the plant outside for a couple of hours in a sheltered spot, then bring it back in. Add more time and more direct sun each day. This gradual process thickens the plant's waxy leaf coating and helps it adjust to outdoor wind and temperature swings; plants that skip it tend to struggle for weeks after transplanting. When you plant, bury the stem deeper than it sits in the pot, right up to the lowest set of leaves; new roots will form all along the buried stem.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong stem, 3-4 sets of true leaves, deep green color. Ready to pot up or transplant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin hardening off 7-10 days before transplant date: short outdoor exposures starting in a sheltered spot, progressively longer and less sheltered. Hardening triggers thicker cuticular wax deposition and stomatal adaptation to outdoor vapor pressure deficit; plants that skip this step show photoinhibition and sulk for 2-3 weeks post-transplant. Plant deep: bury the stem right up to the lowest leaves. Adventitious roots form all along buried stem tissue, building a substantially larger root system than transplanting at pot depth alone would produce.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are they outside yet, or still hardening off?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your plants outside in the garden yet, or still getting used to outdoor air?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small yellow flowers appearing in clusters. Each flower is a potential tomato.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Switch from a general fertilizer to one higher in potassium once flowers appear: look for 'tomato fertilizer' or a formula like 5-10-10. Too much nitrogen at this stage (the first number on the fertilizer bag) pushes the plant into producing more leaves instead of fruit. Give the flowering stems a gentle shake each morning to help pollen release and improve fruit set; heirloom flowers are self-pollinating, but a little movement makes a real difference, especially in calm weather.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small yellow flowers in clusters. Each flower is a potential fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Switch from a balanced feed to a high-potassium fertilizer when flowers appear. Nitrogen drives vegetative (leaf) growth via chlorophyll and cell division pathways; excess nitrogen at flower set pushes resources back into the canopy rather than into fruit development. Potassium supports sugar loading, cell turgor, and the hydraulic pressure that drives fruit fill. Gently tap or shake the flowering stems in the morning to assist pollination; heirloom flowers are self-fertile but buzz pollination (vibration dislodging pollen from anthers) substantially improves fruit set, especially in still air.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Flowers open yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have any flowers opened up yet?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fully colored fruit that gives slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin may start to lose its shine when perfectly ripe.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick every ripe tomato at each visit to the plant. Harvesting regularly signals the plant to keep producing; leaving ripe fruit on the vine slows that process down. Heirloom tomatoes keep producing until frost on a healthy plant, so staying on top of harvesting is the single biggest thing you can do to keep production going.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fully colored fruit that gives slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin may start to lose its sheen when perfectly ripe.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every ripe tomato at each visit; the plant is an indeterminate sink that routes photosynthate toward existing fruit. Ripe fruit remaining on the vine is an energy sink that competes with new fruit development and reduces total yield. Harvest also removes the ethylene-producing ripe fruit that can accelerate ripening of nearby fruit faster than you want.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First tomatoes picked? Log your harvest.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Picked your first tomatoes? Add them to your log.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant slows down: fewer new flowers, yellowing on the lower leaves, and nights cooling consistently below 50°F.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When nights are reliably below 50°F, pinch out all the growing tips at the top of each stem. This stops the plant from putting energy into new growth and directs what's left into ripening the fruit already on the vine. Heirloom tomatoes won't fully color below 50°F, so bring any threatened green tomatoes inside and let them ripen at room temperature, never in the refrigerator, which ruins the flavor.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, yellowing lower leaves, nights cooling below 50°F.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: When nights drop regularly below 50°F, pinch out all growing tips (apical meristems). Removing the apical meristem ends auxin-driven vegetative extension and concentrates the remaining photosynthate into ripening existing fruit. Heirloom fruit needs temperatures above 50°F to complete lycopene synthesis; fruit that stays on the vine below this threshold will not fully color. Bring threatened green tomatoes inside to ripen at room temperature; chilling injury below 50°F is irreversible.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How was your season? Worth logging what worked.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How did the season go? It helps to jot down what worked and what did not.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to start your heirloom tomatoes indoors
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, the right window to get heirloom tomato seeds started. Fill small trays or cells with seed-starting mix, plant one or two seeds per cell about a quarter inch deep, and put them somewhere warm (70 to 80°F is ideal). Cover with a plastic dome or cling wrap until you see sprouts, then remove it right away. Heirloom tomatoes need a long season, so starting on time really matters.
notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start your tomatoes indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, the perfect window to get tomato seeds into trays. Find somewhere warm (70-80°F), keep the soil consistently moist, and cover with a dome until you see sprouts. This is where your season begins.

notifications.title_beginner: Start introducing your tomatoes to the outdoors
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away: time to start hardening off your seedlings. Put them outside for a couple of hours today in a sheltered, partly shaded spot, then bring them back in. Add more time and more direct sun each day over the next week. This gradual process helps the plant adjust to outdoor wind, temperature swings, and stronger sun before it goes out for good.
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away. Begin putting your plants outside for a few hours each day; start sheltered, increase exposure gradually. This week of adjustment makes a real difference to how they settle in after transplanting.

notifications.title_beginner: Last frost has passed: time to transplant
notifications.body_beginner: Your heirloom tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deeper than they sit in the pot: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. New roots will form all along the buried stem, which gives the plant a larger, stronger root system and makes it more drought-tolerant through the season.
notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost has passed: time to transplant
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deep: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Roots will form all along the buried stem and give you a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant.

notifications.title_beginner: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body_beginner: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a fertilizer higher in potassium now (look for 'tomato fertilizer' or something labeled for fruiting). Give the flowering stems a gentle shake each morning to help pollen release and improve fruit set. Each flower is a potential tomato.
notifications.title_seasoned: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body_seasoned: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a high-potassium feed now, and give the flowering stems a gentle shake in the morning to help pollination. Each flower is a potential tomato.

notifications.title_beginner: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_beginner: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Heirloom tomatoes are ready when fully colored and give just slightly to a gentle squeeze. Pick ripe ones regularly; the more you harvest, the more the plant produces.
notifications.title_seasoned: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_seasoned: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Pick when fully colored and slightly soft to the touch. The more you pick, the more the plant produces; stay on top of it.

notifications.title_beginner: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks: finish strong
notifications.body_beginner: Your season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips at the top of each stem now; this stops the plant from putting energy into new growth and sends it all into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest everything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a cool windowsill.
notifications.title_seasoned: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks: finish strong
notifications.body_seasoned: Your growing season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips now so the plant puts all its remaining energy into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest anything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a windowsill.

notifications.body_beginner: You haven't logged anything in a couple of weeks. How's the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Checking in regularly helps you catch problems before they get serious.
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a couple of weeks. How is the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Regular check-ins help you catch problems early.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost tonight: cover your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Freezing temperatures are forecast tonight. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one hard freeze can kill the plant. Cover them with an old bedsheet, a bucket, or frost cloth before dark, and uncover in the morning once temperatures are back above freezing. Container plants can be moved inside.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning: protect your tomatoes tonight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Temperatures are dropping close to freezing tonight. Cover plants with fleece or old bedsheets, or bring containers inside. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one cold night can end your season early.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Very hot days ahead: help your tomatoes through
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Several very hot days are forecast. Above about 95°F, tomato flowers tend to drop without setting fruit; this is heat stress, not a disease. Water deeply in the early morning so the soil stays moist through the day, and add a layer of mulch around the base to hold that moisture. Shade cloth draped over the plant during the hottest part of the afternoon can help if you have it.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress warning for your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Several very hot days ahead. Tomato flowers can drop when temperatures stay above 95°F. Water deeply in the early morning, add mulch around the base to retain moisture, and consider shade cloth during the hottest part of the day.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: It's been dry: water your tomatoes deeply
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Dry conditions have been building. Uneven watering right now can cause blossom end rot (dark patches on the fruit bottom) and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base of the plant; aim for 1 to 2 inches this week. A thick layer of mulch around the stem helps hold moisture between watering sessions.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: It has been dry. Inconsistent watering at this stage causes blossom end rot and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base; aim for 1-2 inches this week. Mulching around the stem helps hold moisture.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: High humidity: check your tomato leaves
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Humid weather creates ideal conditions for fungal diseases like early and late blight. Take a few minutes to check the lower leaves for brown spots, yellow patches, or anything unusual. If you spot affected leaves, remove them right away and don't put them in your compost. Keeping the plant staked and open for airflow is your best prevention.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions are ideal for early and late blight. Check lower leaves for dark spots with yellow halos. Remove any affected leaves immediately and do not compost them. Good airflow around the plant is your best defense.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain coming: harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A lot of rain in a short period can cause ripe tomatoes to split; heirlooms are especially prone to cracking because of their size. Pick anything that looks close to ready before the rain arrives. After the rain, check the lower leaves; soil splashed up by heavy rain can spread disease spores onto the plant.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain: harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A lot of rain in a short time can split ripe fruit. Pick anything that is nearly ready before it cracks, and check for soil splash on lower leaves which can spread disease.

germination.text_beginner: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. If you have a heat mat, use it; if not, the top of a refrigerator or any spot that stays consistently around 75°F works well. Most heirloom tomato seeds sprout within 5 to 7 days with steady warmth.
germination.text_seasoned: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. A heat mat, the top of your refrigerator, or anywhere consistently warm works well. Most tomato seeds germinate in 5-7 days at 75°F.

germination.text_beginner: Cover your seed tray with a plastic dome or cling wrap until the first sprout appears, then remove it right away. The dome traps humidity to keep the seed surface moist during germination; but once the shoot emerges, that same warm, still air is the ideal environment for damping off, a fungal problem that collapses the seedling stem at the soil line and kills it overnight with no recovery.
germination.text_seasoned: Cover your tray with a humidity dome or cling film until the first sprout appears. Remove it immediately when you see growth; leaving it on causes damping off.

seedling.text_beginner: If your seedlings are tall and thin and look weak, they need more light, not less water. Move the tray right next to your brightest window, or set up a grow light to shine on them for 14 to 16 hours each day. Pale color is a sign of the same problem.
seedling.text_seasoned: Leggy, stretched seedlings almost always mean not enough light, not overwatering. Get them as close to a bright window as possible, or use a grow light 14-16 hours a day.

seedling.text_beginner: Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. You can bury the stem deeper than it was sitting; tomatoes form roots all along any buried stem tissue, so a deeper pot-up now means a stronger root system later.
seedling.text_seasoned: Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so you can bury them deeper than they were; it builds a stronger plant.

established.text_beginner: Harden off properly: a week of outdoor time before transplanting, starting with just a couple of hours in a sheltered spot. Plants that skip this step often struggle for two to three weeks after transplanting, which eats into the long season heirloom tomatoes need.
established.text_seasoned: Harden off properly: a week of outdoor time before transplanting, starting with just a couple of hours in a sheltered spot. Plants that skip this step sulk for weeks after transplanting.

established.text_beginner: Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots, and a larger root system means a more drought-tolerant, productive plant.
established.text_seasoned: Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot. Bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots.

flowering.text_beginner: Give the flowering stems a gentle shake each morning to help pollen transfer and improve fruit set. It sounds fussy, but it genuinely makes a difference, especially in a sheltered spot without much natural breeze. Each flower is a potential tomato.
flowering.text_seasoned: A gentle shake of the flowering stem in the morning helps pollen transfer and improves fruit set. It sounds fussy but it genuinely makes a difference, especially in a sheltered spot without much breeze.

flowering.text_beginner: Stop high-nitrogen fertilizing the moment flowers appear. Nitrogen drives leafy growth; what you want now is potassium. Switch to a tomato-specific feed or any formula with a higher third number; that third number on the fertilizer bag is the potassium.
flowering.text_seasoned: Stop high-nitrogen feeding the moment flowers appear. Nitrogen pushes leafy growth. What you want now is potassium: switch to a tomato-specific or high-K feed.

harvest.text_beginner: Pick every ripe tomato every time you visit the plant. The more you harvest, the more the plant produces. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine is the most common reason production slows mid-season; the plant has less reason to keep setting new fruit.
harvest.text_seasoned: Pick every ripe tomato you can find, every time you check the plant. The more you harvest, the more the plant produces. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine is the most common reason production slows mid-season.

harvest.text_beginner: Taste as you go. Heirloom tomatoes peak at slightly different moments depending on the variety and the weather; some are best when just fully colored, others benefit from another day or two. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.
harvest.text_seasoned: Taste as you go. Different varieties peak at different moments; some are best just before fully ripe, others need a few more days. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.

end_of_season.text_beginner: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips at the top of each stem. This stops the plant from putting energy into new growth and channels everything into ripening the fruit already on the vine.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips. The plant will stop trying to set new fruit and put everything into ripening what is already there.

end_of_season.text_beginner: Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool and dark, not the refrigerator, which damages the texture and kills the flavor.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool and dark, not the refrigerator, which kills flavor.

end_of_season.text_beginner: Because heirlooms are open-pollinated, you can save seed from your best fruit and grow the same variety again next year. Scoop the seeds and pulp from a fully ripe tomato into a jar with a little water, let it ferment 3 to 4 days until a film forms on top, then rinse the seeds clean, dry them on a plate or screen somewhere warm and airy, and store them cool and dark. Seed saved from a hybrid will not come back true, but heirloom seed will.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: Heirlooms are open-pollinated, so seed saved from a healthy, ripe fruit grows true to type. Ferment the seed and gel in water for 3 to 4 days to break down the gel coat and suppress seedborne pathogens, then rinse, dry, and store cool and dark. Save from your best plants; hybrid seed segregates and will not reproduce the parent.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Highly variety-dependent: an indeterminate heirloom typically yields 8 to 20 lbs over the season, but fruit size ranges enormously, from 2 to 4 oz Green Zebra and paste types to 1 to 2 lb Brandywine and Hillbilly slicers, so per-fruit counts vary widely. In short-season zones (3 to 5) total yield is limited by season length; in zones 7 to 9 a well-managed vine often exceeds 20 lbs. Heirlooms frequently yield somewhat less than disease-resistant hybrids because foliar and wilt disease shortens the productive window, which is the main yield tradeoff for the flavor.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Expect roughly 8 to 20 pounds of tomatoes per plant over the season, though it depends a lot on the variety: a big Brandywine plant makes fewer, huge fruit, while a paste or Green Zebra plant makes many smaller ones. Heirlooms often yield a bit less than modern hybrids because they catch disease more easily, but most gardeners grow them for the flavor rather than the weight.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: A healthy indeterminate heirloom at peak produces a steady flow of fruit for roughly 4 to 8 weeks in mid-season, then tapers as fall cools and, for many heirlooms, as foliar disease advances. Weekly counts depend on fruit size: a few large slicers, or many small paste and salad types. Fruit set is most reliable when night temperatures stay between about 55 and 75°F; below 55°F pollen viability drops, and above about 70 to 75°F pollen becomes non-viable and flowers drop.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: At its peak a healthy plant produces steadily for about 4 to 8 weeks in midsummer, then slows as fall arrives. Big-fruited heirlooms give you a few large tomatoes a week; smaller paste or salad types give you many. Fruit sets best when nights stay between about 55 and 75°F; much colder or hotter than that and the flowers often drop without setting.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Your first heirloom season will probably feel slow. The plant spends the first half of summer building its root system and vine structure before it really starts setting fruit. Getting 3 to 5 large tomatoes in your first season is a real success; don't measure yourself against experienced gardeners who know every trick. Focus on two things: get a strong cage or stake in place early (before you think you need it), and keep the watering consistent when the plant starts flowering.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: First-season heirlooms frequently disappoint on yield, not because of mistakes, but because the plant architecture is building for the first half of the season. Getting 3-5 large fruit in a first season is a genuine success. Focus on getting the support structure right early and on consistent watering at fruit set; those two factors drive the difference between a partial and a full-season harvest.

consistent watering
feeding schedule
staking and airflow

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You'll see the leaves turn black or dark brown and go limp, sometimes overnight after a single cold night. Tomatoes are tropical plants with no cold tolerance at all. Even without a hard freeze, temperatures below 50°F cause what's called chilling injury: the plant's cells start to break down, and young transplants are especially vulnerable because they haven't yet built up a protective waxy coating on their leaves. A plant hit hard by frost usually won't recover. For next time: both your nighttime air temperature AND your soil temperature need to be reliably above 60°F before you transplant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until nighttime temperatures are reliably above 50°F AND your soil is above 60°F before transplanting; check soil temperature 2 to 3 inches deep with an inexpensive probe thermometer. In Zones 3 to 5 this often means waiting until late May or early June regardless of what the calendar says.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are tropical plants and suffer the moment temperatures drop near freezing. Even a brief cold night can blacken leaves and kill young plants. If it happened at transplant, the plant was likely moved out too early; soil temperature matters as much as air temperature.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until both night temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. A cheap soil thermometer removes the guesswork.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes can run into a few common problems. Blight is a leaf disease that starts on the lower leaves first and spreads fastest in wet, humid weather. Blossom end rot shows up as a dark, sunken patch on the bottom of the fruit; it looks like a nutrient problem, but it's almost always caused by uneven watering (dry for a stretch, then suddenly soaked). Adding extra calcium won't fix it. Consistent moisture will.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water at the base of the plant, not from overhead, and stake the plant for good airflow. Leaves that dry quickly after rain are much harder for blight to infect. Move your tomatoes to a different bed each year; blight spores can survive in the soil over winter. For blossom end rot: mulch heavily and water deeply and consistently rather than in small frequent amounts.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are susceptible to blight, blossom end rot, and several common pests. Blight spreads fast in wet, humid conditions and usually starts at the lower leaves. Blossom end rot is caused by calcium deficiency triggered by irregular watering, not a nutrient problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently at the base, not overhead. Remove any affected leaves immediately. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year and stake plants to improve airflow.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Overwatered tomatoes show yellowing leaves starting at the bottom of the plant, and roots that can't get oxygen; waterlogged soil suffocates them. Inconsistent watering is actually more damaging than steady overwatering: if the soil dries out and then you flood it, the sudden change in moisture causes the fruit skin to expand faster than the inside, and the tomatoes crack. Blossom end rot (dark patches on the fruit bottom) can follow the same pattern.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water deeply two or three times a week rather than a small amount every day. Deep watering encourages roots to grow down into the soil rather than staying shallow near the surface. A thick layer of mulch around the base of the plant evens out moisture and dramatically reduces the wet-dry swings that cause cracking.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Overwatered tomatoes show yellowing lower leaves, cracked fruit, and roots that cannot get oxygen. Inconsistent watering, dry then suddenly wet, causes fruit splitting and blossom end rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply twice a week rather than a little every day. Mulching around the base dramatically improves moisture consistency.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Drought stress during flowering causes blossom drop; the flowers fall off before fruit can set, and those potential tomatoes are gone for good. During fruiting, inconsistent moisture (dry spells followed by heavy watering) causes blossom end rot and cracked skin. Heirloom tomatoes are large-fruited and especially water-hungry; they need steady moisture throughout the whole season.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes need about 1 to 2 inches of water per week. Mulch heavily around the base to hold moisture in the soil between waterings. Always water at the base of the plant, not the leaves; wet leaves in the evening invite disease.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering causes blossom drop; no flowers, no fruit. During fruiting, inconsistent moisture causes blossom end rot and cracked skin.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes need 1-2 inches of water per week. Mulch heavily to retain moisture, and water at the base never the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Tomatoes need at least 6 to 8 hours of direct sun each day to produce fruit well. In a shady spot the plant will grow, sometimes quite lushly, but will set little or no fruit, and will be much more prone to fungal disease because the leaves stay damp instead of drying out. Heirloom types in particular need full sun to develop their large, dense fruit properly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Tomatoes are one of the most sun-hungry vegetables in the garden. If your current spot is getting less than 6 hours of direct sun, move the tomatoes to your sunniest bed next season and plant something more shade-tolerant, like lettuce or spinach, in the shadier spot.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes need a minimum of 6-8 hours of direct sun to produce well. In shade they grow leafy but set little or no fruit, and are much more prone to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes are one of the most sun-hungry vegetables. If your current spot is marginal, prioritize this bed for tomatoes next season and move something more shade-tolerant elsewhere.

succession_policy.tip_beginner: You only need to plant heirloom tomatoes once; the same plant will keep producing fruit all summer until frost kills it. No need to replant partway through the season. If you live in a very warm climate (think Southern California, Phoenix, or South Florida, Zone 9 or warmer,), you can start a second planting in late summer for a fall and winter harvest.
succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Not a true succession crop; one indeterminate plant produces all season until frost. A second planting started mid-season in most zones would be killed by frost before its 75-100 day maturity window closes. In zones 9-11 a late-summer planting (July-August) is viable as a separate fall crop, not a succession.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Heirloom is an indeterminate crop that continues setting new flower clusters until frost. A single plant produces continuously through the season, making succession planting unnecessary and impractical, since a second planting started weeks later would simply be frost-killed before reaching its long (75-100 day) maturity window in most zones. In zones 9-11 where a fall planting is common, that is a separate season, not a succession.

crops.description_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes are open-pollinated varieties, which means you can save their seed and grow the same tomato again next year (hybrid tomatoes do not do this; their saved seed comes up as a mix). They come in an amazing range of colors, shapes, and sizes: deep purple-brown Cherokee Purple and Black Krim, green-striped Green Zebra, huge pink Brandywine and Mortgage Lifter slicers, and slender paste types like San Marzano. Most heirlooms are indeterminate, meaning the plant keeps growing and setting new fruit until frost, so it needs a strong cage or stake from the start; plan for a plant 5 to 6 feet tall or more. The main catch is that heirlooms usually do not have the built-in disease resistance that modern hybrids are bred for, so they are more likely to run into wilt diseases, leaf blights, and cracked fruit. You keep ahead of that with good spacing and airflow, watering at the base, moving your tomatoes to a fresh spot each year, and steady, even watering. The flavor is why people grow them: many gardeners think heirlooms are the best-tasting tomatoes there are.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: The tricky part with heirlooms is that many of them are not red when ripe. Cherokee Purple and Black Krim ripen to a dusky purple-brown and keep green shoulders, Green Zebra stays green with a yellow blush, and Brandywine turns deep pink. Learn what your variety looks like ripe, then pick when it has full color, gives a little to a gentle squeeze without being mushy, and the skin looks slightly less shiny than before. Big heirlooms take a few extra days than small ones. Heirlooms split easily, so pick them as soon as they are ripe, especially right after rain.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Heirloom (larger-fruited, slower-maturing) varieties require the 8-week end of this range to reach transplant size.

plant_out.label: primary

Transplant outdoors after all danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed. Don't be in a rush to transplant these tropical species. (UMaine, northern Maine Z3-4; UMN; NDSU)

3.notes: Very challenging in Zone 3: 80+ day maturity leaves little margin. Choose Fast varieties like Stupice. Use season extenders.
3.zone_notes: Zone 3 is marginal for large heirloom varieties (80-100 day maturity). Choose a faster 75-day variety (Stupice, Bloody Butcher) or consider cherry tomatoes for more reliable harvest. Start 8 weeks before last frost.

4.notes: Start 8 weeks early. Choose varieties under 85 days. Heavy mulching and black plastic help.
4.zone_notes: Start indoors 8 weeks early. Heirlooms push the limits of Zone 4, so choose carefully.

5.notes: Plant after last frost. Stake heavily, as heirlooms get large and heavy. Consistent watering prevents blossom end rot.
5.zone_notes: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost.

6.notes: Excellent zone for heirlooms. Long season allows full flavor development. Remove suckers to focus energy on fruit.
6.zone_notes: Heirlooms need 80+ days, so plant by mid-May at latest for harvest before first frost.

7.notes: Heat stress above 95°F can cause blossom drop. Shade cloth and deep watering help through July to August peak.
7.zone_notes: Plant by late May. Too late to do a second planting, so focus on one great crop.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold northern states (zones 3 through 7) you grow heirloom tomatoes once a year, as a single summer crop. What limits the season here is frost on both ends, not summer heat. Because big heirloom tomatoes are slow to ripen (about 75 to 90 days after transplanting), start the seeds indoors well before your last frost, then set the plants out a week or two after that last frost, once nights stay warm and the soil has warmed up. That single planting gives you one long harvest until the first fall frost ends it. There is no summer break the way hotter regions have, because northern summers usually are not hot enough to stop the plants from setting fruit. Unlike cherry tomatoes, heirlooms take too long to fit in a second crop, so plan on one well-timed planting and choose faster varieties. In the coldest zones, start seed early indoors, pick quick-maturing varieties, and warm the soil with black plastic mulch or season-extending covers so the fruit ripens before frost returns.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 through 7) grows heirloom tomatoes as a single frost-bracketed summer crop: the limiting factor on both ends is frost, not heat. Because large-fruited heirloom types are slow (about 75 to 90 days from transplant), the season is started indoors well ahead of the last frost, transplants go out a week or two after that last spring frost once nights hold above the low 50s°F and soil warms past about 60°F, and that one planting then produces a single continuous harvest until plants are cut short by the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat exclusion here: northern summers rarely sustain the high day and night temperatures that stop fruit set, so the only gaps are the winter cold pauses and the season between them is uninterrupted. Unlike cherry types, heirloom's longer days-to-maturity leaves no room for a second crop even at the warm end of the band, so the whole region runs on one well-timed planting; the short-season north strongly favors the faster large-fruited varieties and starting seed indoors. The coldest zones (3 and 4) depend on early indoor starts, fast-maturing varieties, and season extension (black plastic mulch, Wall-O-Waters) to ripen fruit before frost. Frost dates shift sharply across the band, so confirm your local last and first frost. (University of Minnesota Extension; North Dakota State University Extension; Michigan State University Extension; University of Maine Cooperative Extension)

In the Southeast and Gulf region that is roughly mid-February for the Georgia interior (zone 8) and two to three weeks earlier toward the warmer Gulf-coastal zone 9 end. plant_out.label: primary

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set heirloom transplants out in spring once frost danger passes. UGA gives late March into the first half of April for middle Georgia (zone 8); the warmer zone 9 end runs two to three weeks earlier. Heirloom is large-fruited and slower to mature than cherry types, so time it to set fruit before peak summer heat arrives. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Heirloom begins ripening roughly three months after transplanting (about 75 to 90 days to maturity, longer than cherry types). The spring crop comes in from late June, just as the summer heat begins to shut fruit set down. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop ends as summer heat sets in. Large-fruited tomatoes are more sensitive to high day and night temperatures than cherry types, so blossom drop and fruit-set failure begin earlier for heirloom, by about June. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: tomatoes will take 6 weeks
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed indoors about six weeks before the late-summer transplant date, roughly mid-to-late spring across the region. Because heirloom needs 75 to 90 days to mature, start early enough that the fall transplant can go out as soon as the summer heat-pause lifts. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Plant the following vegetables no later than July 20 ... tomatoes
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out as the worst summer heat eases so plants establish and produce into the cooler fall. UGA gives a fall tomato deadline of about July 20 for middle Georgia (zone 8) so the crop matures before frost; large-fruited heirloom, being slower than cherry, should hit the early end of the fall window. The warmer zone 9 end runs about two weeks later, into early August. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about three months after the late-summer transplant, bringing heirloom tomatoes in from roughly October across the region. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Harvest mature green peppers and tomatoes before frost gets them
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop produces into the cooler autumn and is harvested up to first frost. Large-fruited heirloom has a shorter productive fall tail here than quick-maturing cherry types. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer fruit set fails from heat, not frost: like all tomatoes, heirloom flowers abort and drop once daytime highs pass the upper 80s to 90s°F and nights stay above about 70°F, when pollen turns non-viable. Large-fruited heirlooms are as heat-sensitive as any large tomato, so Jun through Aug is a set-failure window rather than a growing gap. (Penn State Extension, Heat Stress and Tomatoes; University of Missouri IPM, Understanding Tomato Fruit Set)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf area you can grow heirloom tomatoes twice a year, once in spring and again in fall, with a summer break in between when it gets too hot for the plants to set fruit. Big heirloom tomatoes handle the heat less well than small cherry tomatoes, so their summer break is longer, running through most of the summer. Plant your spring crop early enough to pick before the heat, then plant again in late summer once the worst heat passes for a fall crop.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf region runs two heirloom seasons, spring and fall, split by a summer heat window when high day and night temperatures cause blossom drop and fruit set fails. Large-fruited heirloom is more heat-sensitive than cherry types, so its summer pause is wider, spanning roughly June through August rather than a single midsummer month. Heirloom also needs 75 to 90 days to mature, longer than cherry, so time the spring crop to set fruit before peak heat and set the fall crop out promptly once the heat eases (UGA gives a July 20 fall deadline for middle Georgia so the crop beats frost). The warmer zone 9 end plants the spring crop earlier and the fall crop later than the zone 8 interior. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UGA Cooperative Extension C943 gives two major planting periods (spring March-May, fall mid-July-September) with an explicit fall tomato deadline (no later than July 20 for middle Georgia), corroborated by UF/IFAS VH021 (North FL tomato Late Mar-Apr + Aug). Two-window is the source grammar, not analogy.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_basis: WIDER than cherry (Jun-Aug vs single Jul). Large-fruited tomatoes are not heat-set-bred and abort flowers at lower thresholds (UF/IFAS VH021: 'Cherry types are heat resistant' -- large-fruited not; Alabama Coop Ext and U.Missouri IPM: day >85 / night >72 deg-F abort). SE/Gulf high summer breaches this June through August.
