ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's interior valleys you plant heirloom tomatoes once, in spring (April into May), and the same plant produces all summer into fall. You do not need a second planting. Big heirloom tomatoes may slow down and set fewer fruit during the hottest weeks of summer, then pick back up as the nights cool in late summer and fall.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin) grow heirloom as a single long warm season: set transplants out April into May and harvest from midsummer into fall up to first frost. UC ANR lists one April-May tomato window with no separate fall planting, so this is one continuous crop, not a spring-and-fall split. Large-fruited heirloom sets fewer fruit through the peak-heat weeks of the valley summer (it is more heat-sensitive than cherry types), with set resuming as nights cool; the plant stays in the ground through the dip. Cages suit the valley heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

Large-fruited heirloom needs warm days to ripen and can be slow in the coolest coastal pockets, so choose a variety matched to your season length and give it the warmest, most sheltered exposure. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's low desert (Imperial and Coachella valleys) you grow heirloom tomatoes in the cool months, not the summer. Plant the main crop from December through March so it makes fruit before the extreme heat, and plant a second crop in early fall (around September) once the worst heat breaks. Summer (June through August) is simply too hot for any tomato to set fruit, so the plants rest then.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: California's desert valleys (Imperial, Coachella) grow heirloom on an inverted, two-window calendar driven by extreme summer heat. The main crop is set out across the cool season, December through March, to mature and set fruit before summer; a second fall crop goes out in early fall (about September) as the heat breaks and produces into the mild winter. June through August is a climatic-absolute fruit-set exclusion: complete blossom drop for every tomato type, not narrowed for heirloom, which is at least as heat-sensitive as cherry. plant_out.source_quote: 2nd planting ... transplant mid-July
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall heirloom crop out in mid-July to early August (the Las Cruces chart transplants the fall tomato crop in mid-July). For large-fruited heirloom this fall crop is marginal in this short-autumn high desert: a 75-90 day plant set in mid-July only just matures before the November frost, and fruit set through the hot July-August transplant period is poor. (Dona Ana County Master Gardener Las Cruces planting chart; NMSU Circular 457)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about three months after the mid-July transplant, bringing fruit in from roughly mid-October. (NMSU Circular 457)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop is harvested up to the high-desert first frost (about November 12); the productive tail is short for slow-maturing heirloom. (NMSU Circular 457)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Peak summer heat is a fruit-set exclusion, not a frost gap: like all tomatoes, heirloom flowers drop and fail to set once daytime highs pass the upper 80s to 90s°F and nights stay above about 70°F, when pollen turns non-viable. In this high-desert band July is the hottest set-failure month, though arid nights recover enough that the shoulders of summer still set. Large-fruited heirlooms are as heat-sensitive as any large tomato. (Penn State Extension, Heat Stress and Tomatoes; University of Missouri IPM, Understanding Tomato Fruit Set)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the southern high desert (around Las Cruces, New Mexico) you can grow heirloom tomatoes in spring and again in fall, with a hot-summer gap. Plant the spring crop in late March or early April so it makes fruit before the July heat. You can try a fall crop planted in mid-July, but big heirloom tomatoes set fruit poorly in the July and August heat and are slow to ripen, so the fall crop is a bit of a gamble before the November frost. Pick fast-maturing, heat-tolerant varieties.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The southern high desert (Las Cruces, Mesilla Valley; Chihuahuan high desert, zone 8) runs two heirloom windows split by peak summer heat. Set the spring crop out in late March to early April, after the local last frost (about March 19), so it sets fruit before July. A fall crop can be transplanted in mid-July per the Dona Ana County Master Gardener chart, but for large-fruited heirloom this is marginal: fruit set is poor once day temperatures exceed 95 °F through July and August, and a 75-90 day plant only just matures before the November frost (about November 12). Favor fast-maturing, heat-tolerant cultivars for the fall attempt. The fall window and two-window structure rest on the single Las Cruces Master Gardener chart, a regional source; the spring dates are anchored to the high-desert frost data with NOAA cross-check. (NMSU Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardener Las Cruces planting chart)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: Dona Ana County MG Las Cruces chart (Path A, carried from cherry 5e read 2026-06-07): 1st planting start mid-Jan -> transplant early March; 2nd planting start mid-June -> transplant mid-July. NMSU CR457 confirms southern NM gets both spring + fall windows. Chart is the window-count authority; frost data is the date authority.
plantings_provenance.frost_basis: zone-8 arid_highland NOAA variant (BSk): last_spring Mar 19, first_fall Nov 12, 236 frost-free days. Las Cruces/Mesilla is Chihuahuan high desert, not generic humid-subtropical z8. Same basis as cherry's warm_arid.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop produces into the mild desert winter, limited by occasional light frost rather than heat. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005)

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In Arizona's low desert (around Phoenix) you grow heirloom tomatoes in the cooler months, not the summer. Plant the spring crop in late winter (finish by about early March) so it makes fruit before the brutal heat, then plant a fall crop in September once the worst heat breaks. June through August is too hot for any tomato to set fruit, so the plants rest then. Choose fast-maturing varieties.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: Arizona's low desert (Maricopa County, around Phoenix) grows heirloom on a two-window calendar bracketing the extreme summer. Set the spring crop out in late winter, finishing by about early March, so a slow 75-90 day heirloom sets and matures before the June heat wall; plant the fall crop in September as the heat breaks, for a late-fall and winter harvest. June through August is a complete fruit-set exclusion for all tomatoes, and large-fruited heirloom fails earlier than cherry, so the pause runs the full June-August. AZ1005 marks no tomato transplant through that span. Favor quick-maturing cultivars. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005)

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: On the Florida peninsula you grow heirloom tomatoes in the cool months, not the summer, which is the opposite of most of the country. Plant from early fall (September) through mid-winter (February) and harvest from late fall into spring. The hot, humid summer (about June through September) is too much for big tomatoes to set fruit, so that is the off-season here.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula grows heirloom on an inverted, near-continuous winter calendar: set transplants out from about September through mid-February and harvest from late fall into spring. The hot, humid peninsula summer, June through September, is a fruit-set exclusion for large-fruited heirloom; high day and night temperatures with high humidity drive blossom drop, and large-fruited types are not heat resistant the way cherry types are, so the pause is wider here. Set fruit fails by late spring as the heat returns. Confirm local timing: south Florida (zone 11) plants and harvests on a slightly earlier, longer inverted calendar than the zone 10 central peninsula. (UF/IFAS VH021)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UF/IFAS VH021 gives central FL tomato as Jan-Feb + Aug-Sept and south FL as Aug-Feb (inverted winter-growing season). Near-continuous cool-season planting with a deep-summer pause. Single band on an inverted calendar (no spring/fall split -- the whole cool season is one window).

start_indoors.source_quote: transplanted 3-5 weeks after sowing
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start heirloom seed and transplant three to five weeks after sowing, in any month. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set heirloom transplants out in any month of the year. CTAHR gives year-round tomato planting for most of Hawaii contingent on choosing adapted varieties, with no spring/fall bracketing and no summer no-sow exclusion. Note that large-fruited heirloom sets fruit poorly under Hawaii's warm lowland nights, so cooler-elevation siting, cooler-season timing, and heat-tolerant or locally bred cultivars give the best results. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: Most varieties mature in 60-80 days
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Heirloom begins ripening about two and a half to three months after transplanting (CTAHR gives 60-80 days for most varieties; large-fruited heirloom runs to the longer end). (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest is continuous through the year on healthy indeterminate plants; there is no seasonal production stop, only the steady disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure of the tropical lowland. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

11.calendar_basis: Heirloom tomato can be planted YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free) and no documented summer no-sow exclusion: CTAHR HGV-5 states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing adapted varieties, and names no seasonal fruit-set gap. UNLIKE cherry (which CTAHR treats as cleanly heat resistant), CTAHR's Field Tomato Production Guidelines specifically warn that large-fruited varieties set fruit poorly under Hawaii's warm lowland nights (optimum fruit set 60-70 deg-F). This is a fruit-set-QUALITY caveat, disclosed in the seasoned region_note, not an absolute no-sow month, so the year-round structure holds (guardrail: heat_pause is read from the source per region, never defaulted; HGV-5 documents no exclusion month). Hawaii's dominant challenge is disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant locally bred cultivars (Kewalo, Anahu, Healani, N-series) and cultural practice. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason; year_round:true makes the all-active calendar machine-readable. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii's tropical lowlands you can plant heirloom tomatoes any month of the year; there is no cold winter and no planting season to wait for. The catch is that big heirloom tomatoes do not set fruit well in the warm tropical nights, so they do best at cooler elevations and in the cooler parts of the year, and you will have the most luck with heat-tolerant or locally bred varieties. The bigger day-to-day challenges are disease, bugs, and heavy rain.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical zone 11 grows heirloom year-round: CTAHR gives a year-round planting capability for most of the islands contingent on adapted varieties, with no winter cold pause and no documented summer no-sow exclusion. The important caveat for heirloom specifically is fruit-set quality, not timing: CTAHR's field production guidance notes that large-fruited varieties are sensitive to high night temperatures and set fruit poorly in the warm lowland (optimum set 60-70 °F), unlike heat-resistant cherry types. Favor cooler-elevation siting, the cooler part of the year, and heat-tolerant or locally bred wilt-resistant cultivars (Kewalo, Anahu, Healani, the N-series). The dominant production challenges here are disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant varieties and cultural practice rather than a seasonal stop. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)

The no-pause structure is the source finding; the size-specific set caveat is the honest heirloom-vs-cherry difference.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start heirloom tomato seed indoors about 8 weeks before transplanting, timed to the Feb 14 - Mar 20 Rio Grande Valley set-out window (TAMU AgriLife RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Heirloom tomato transplants go out Feb 14 - Mar 20 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide, corroborated by the Bilingual LRGV planting table's 70 to 90 day maturity figure for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest spring harvest at about 70 days from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest spring harvest at about 90 days from the latest set-out date.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start the fall round indoors about 8 weeks before the Sep 15 - Oct 15 set-out window.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall heirloom tomato transplants go out Sep 15 - Oct 15 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide / Bilingual LRGV fall window for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest fall harvest at about 70 days from the earliest fall set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest fall harvest, extending into the mild Valley winter tail before spring returns.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Sustained Valley summer heat causes blossom drop: the flowers abort before they can set fruit, so production stops even though the plants stay alive (TAMU AgriLife notes high heat drops tomato blossoms). (Jul, Aug sit outside both plant windows.)

Sustained Valley summer heat causes blossom drop: the flowers abort before they can set fruit, so production stops even though the plants stay alive (TAMU AgriLife notes high heat drops tomato blossoms). (Jul, Aug sit outside both plant windows.)

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, heirloom tomato is a two-season crop. Plant Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest, then plant again Sep 15 - Oct 15 for a fall crop. Skip the hottest stretch of summer: the flowers drop in the worst heat before they can set fruit, so there is nothing to gain by planting through it. It rarely if ever frosts here, so both the spring and fall windows run on Valley heat, not on a frost date.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Heirloom tomato in the RGV runs on the Valley's two-crop calendar: set out Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest running Apr 25 - Jun 18, then set out again Sep 15 - Oct 15 for a fall harvest running Nov 24 - Dec 15. Sustained Valley summer heat causes blossom drop: the flowers abort before they can set fruit, so production stops even though the plants stay alive (TAMU AgriLife notes high heat drops tomato blossoms). Frost is essentially absent here, so both plantings are timed against heat, not cold. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 8 weeks before set-out; OSU's Oregon planting table (EM9027) gives tomatoes 8 weeks indoors before transplanting.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out after the last frost and once the soil has warmed; OSU's table gives the Willamette Valley a May window and the immediate coast a wider May-June window (EM9027), corroborated by WSU's tomato seeding spec (EM057E Table 4, 70-85F soil temp).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Matures in about 70 to 90 days from transplant. Classic large-fruited heirlooms (Brandywine, Cherokee Purple, Mortgage Lifter) sit at the long end of this range in a cool marine summer; an early-maturing heirloom (Stupice, Oregon Spring) is a more realistic bet.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest winds down at the first fall frost; pick remaining fruit (green, if needed) a few days ahead of the average date to ripen indoors.

8.zone_notes: The valley is the warmer PNW zone and the more forgiving of the two for heirlooms, though still a stretch; treat the 90-day upper end of the maturity window as the honest planning figure and favor an early-maturing heirloom variety.

9.zone_notes: The cooler, marine-influenced coast is the more marginal zone here despite OSU's own wider May-June set-out window; lean toward the earliest transplants, the fastest-maturing heirloom variety you can find, and the single warmest site available.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Classic large-fruited heirlooms are a genuine stretch in the maritime Pacific Northwest: many popular varieties want more sustained summer warmth than our cool, marine-influenced summers reliably deliver. Start seed indoors about 8 weeks before setting plants out in May, choose an earlier-maturing heirloom over a full 90-day classic slicer, and give it the warmest, sunniest, most sheltered spot you have. A cloche or wall-o-water at planting time helps the young plant bank heat early. Expect variable results: a warm summer can ripen a full crop of big heirlooms, while a cool one may leave you picking smaller or green fruit to finish ripening indoors before the first fall frost.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Heirloom tomatoes sit at the marginal end of what the maritime Pacific Northwest's cool summer can reliably ripen. Set transplants out after the last frost once the soil has warmed, in May in the valley or across OSU's wider May-June coastal window, but plan around the long end of the 70-to-90-day maturity range rather than the short end; a cool marine summer routinely slows large-fruited heirloom types. Favor an early-maturing heirloom variety over a full-season classic slicer, and reserve the single warmest, most sheltered microsite for it; a cloche or wall-o-water at transplant helps bank early heat. Harvest can run into fall behind the mild first frost, but in a cool year expect to pick unripened fruit ahead of frost to finish indoors rather than lose the crop outright. (OSU EM9027; WSU EM057E)

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 8 weeks before spring set-out (Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out about a week after the last frost, once soil has warmed (VCE 426-331 Table 4, the belt's zone 7/8 tomato rows).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins ripening about 80 days after transplanting (VCE 426-331).

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop's harvest winds down as the hot, humid Piedmont and Coastal Plain midsummer sets in and fruit set stalls (VCE 426-331).

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed indoors roughly 8 weeks ahead of the VCE-documented fall set-out window (VCE 426-331 Table 4).

plant_out.source_quote: Zone 8a/8b Fall: July 1-Aug 10 | Zone 7a Fall: June 20-Aug 1
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out on VCE 426-331 Table 4's explicit documented fall tomato window for this belt (zone 8: July 1 to August 10; zone 7: June 20 to August 1).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about 80 days after the late-summer transplant (VCE 426-331).

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop is harvested up to just ahead of the belt's real first frost, which kills tomato vines outright (VCE 426-331 frost-date table).

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Large-fruited heirloom tomatoes are more heat-sensitive than cherry or grape types: fruit set weakens across a wider stretch of Piedmont and Coastal Plain summer heat. Virginia Cooperative Extension's documented fall transplant window for tomatoes in this belt restarts the crop for a real fall harvest. (VCE 426-331)

crops.description_seasoned: Open-pollinated, mostly indeterminate tomatoes grown for flavor and diversity. The defining trait of an heirloom is that it is open-pollinated: it breeds true from saved seed, so a Brandywine grown from last year's seed comes back as Brandywine, unlike an F1 hybrid whose saved seed segregates into a mix of the parent traits. Heirlooms span an enormous range of size, color, and shape, from the dusky Cherokee Purple and Black Krim, to the green-when-ripe Green Zebra, to two-pound pink Brandywine and Hillbilly slicers, to open-pollinated paste types like San Marzano and Amish Paste. Most classic heirlooms are indeterminate: the vine keeps extending and setting fruit until frost, so it needs strong staking or caging and benefits from pruning to one or two main stems. Days to maturity vary widely by variety, roughly 70 to 90 days from transplant. The main tradeoff is disease: heirlooms generally lack the Verticillium, Fusarium, and nematode resistance (the VFN codes) bred into modern hybrids, so they are more prone to the soilborne wilts, to early and late blight and Septoria leaf spot, and to fruit cracking, and they reward attentive rotation, sanitation, and even watering. Like all tomatoes they need a long frost-free window and set fruit poorly once day temperatures pass the upper 80s°F or nights stay above about 70°F.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: The ripeness cue depends on the variety's ripe color, which for heirlooms is often not red: Cherokee Purple and Black Krim ripen to a dusky brick-purple with shoulders that stay green, Green Zebra ripens green with a yellow blush and softens rather than reddens, and pink types like Brandywine deepen to rose. Across types, pick when the fruit has reached its full variety color, yields to gentle pressure without feeling mushy, and the skin shifts from a hard glossy sheen to a softer, slightly matte surface. Learn each variety's ripe look rather than waiting for red. Large heirloom slicers (12 oz and up) take a few extra days than small types; mass slows the ripening front. Heirlooms crack readily, so pick promptly when ripe, especially after rain.

pet_safe.note: Ripe tomatoes are fine, but the leaves, stems, and unripe fruit are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Grape Tomato

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Grape tomatoes want soil that drains well and is rich in organic matter. If water sits on top of your bed after rain or stays soggy for more than a day, drainage is a problem, soggy roots will rot even if the soil is otherwise good. The easiest fix for most soils is to work in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting, which improves both drainage and fertility at once. Tomatoes are heavy feeders, so starting with rich soil means less fertilizing mid-season.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Grape tomatoes perform best in well-drained loam or sandy loam with high organic matter content. Adequate drainage is non-negotiable, waterlogged roots invite both Pythium root rot and nutrient lockout even in otherwise fertile soil. Working in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting addresses both texture and fertility in one amendment. Tomatoes are heavy feeders, and organically rich soil reduces the mid-season fertilizer burden considerably.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH is a measure of acidity on a scale from 1 to 14, where 7 is neutral. Grape tomatoes do best at a soil pH of 6.2 to 6.8, the slightly acidic range where the nutrients they need are most available. Soils in the interior West (Arizona, Nevada, Utah, Colorado) often run alkaline (above 7), which can lock up nutrients even when you fertilize; growers there often add sulfur before planting. Eastern and Midwestern soils are frequently already in range, but an inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you for sure.
ph.note_seasoned: Grape tomatoes, like all tomatoes, are sensitive to pH because it governs the solubility of phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium, the three nutrients they draw down most heavily. The target band is 6.2 to 6.8. Below about 5.5, manganese and aluminum climb toward phytotoxic levels and calcium uptake falters, raising blossom-end rot risk; above 7.0, iron and manganese deficiencies drive interveinal chlorosis on younger leaves. In the alkaline soils common across the interior West and alkaline-irrigation districts, growers routinely acidify before planting. Eastern soils often sit naturally in range; Pacific Northwest soils vary widely by parent material.

fertilizer.timing: starter at transplanting, then side-dress about 3 to 4 weeks later
fertilizer.example_product: Miracle-Gro Tomato Plant Food
fertilizer.notes_beginner: When you see the first flowers opening, switch fertilizers. Use a balanced or all-purpose fertilizer early in the season, then switch to a tomato-specific or high-potassium fertilizer once flowers appear. Too much nitrogen (the first number on the package) after flowering pushes the plant to grow more leaves instead of fruit.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time for your tomatoes' first side-dressing, about 3 to 4 weeks after planting out, then again every 3 to 4 weeks. Once flowers appear, switch to a tomato or high-potassium fertilizer to keep the fruit coming.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Look for three numbers on the fertilizer bag: those are the NPK ratio (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium). A soil test is the surest guide, and it is what both extension services behind this guide recommend first. Without one, a low-nitrogen balanced formula such as 5-10-10 is a sensible default. Go easy on the first number: too much nitrogen gives you a big leafy plant that is slow to set fruit. Skip the high-phosphorus bags sold as bloom boosters unless a soil test actually calls for phosphorus, because many soils already hold plenty.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Switch from balanced to high-potassium feed at flowering. Too much nitrogen produces leafy plants with little fruit.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: First side-dress is due, about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, then every 3 to 4 weeks through harvest. Switch to the high-potassium formula at flowering.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Soil test governs. Absent one, a low-nitrogen balanced formula such as 5-10-10. UMN advises a low- or no-phosphorus feed unless a test specifically calls for phosphorus, and warns that excess nitrogen produces bushy, leafy plants slow to bear fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About 1 pound of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet side-dressed three to four weeks after transplanting, repeated every 3 to 4 weeks through harvest; if no soil test, work in about 1.5 pounds of a complete fertilizer per 100 square feet before planting. The crop's high-potassium hint above governs the formula; this is the rate.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A common rate is about 1 to 2 tablespoons of fertilizer scratched into the soil around each plant, 6 to 8 inches out from the stem, starting about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting and then every 3 to 4 weeks. Always water it in, and keep the granules off the stem and leaves.

companions.note_beginner: Most tomato companion advice is garden tradition rather than tested fact. The clearest exception is marigolds, which can cut down on root pests, but only when planted thickly as a cover crop a couple of months ahead, not scattered among the tomatoes. In practice: keep fennel away, keep tomatoes away from their relatives like potatoes and eggplant if disease has been a problem for you, and try nasturtiums as a trap for aphids if aphids gave you trouble in past seasons.
companions.note_seasoned: Grape tomato companions are dominated by traditional lore with selective extension backing. The marigold/nematode connection is the best-documented pairing in this crop's companion set, effective as a dense pre-season cover crop, not as scattered concurrent interplanting. For most growers, the practical guidance is straightforward: avoid fennel, keep tomatoes away from other Solanaceae family members (potatoes, eggplant) if disease pressure is a concern in your region, and consider nasturtiums as an aphid trap crop if aphid pressure was a problem in past seasons.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Basil
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Long-established pairing; flavor-improvement claims are traditional. Basil's aromatic compounds may deter some pest insects, though not extension-documented for this specific pair, but widely practiced and low risk.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Flavor-improvement and pest-deterrence claims are classic companion-planting tradition. Not documented in peer-reviewed research or T1 extension literature for this specific pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A long-standing pairing. Many gardeners say basil improves tomato flavor and may keep some pests away. There is no hard proof for this exact pair, but it is widely done and harmless.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigolds
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: French marigolds suppress root-knot nematodes, most effectively as a dense cover crop planted 2+ months before tomatoes, not as concurrent interplanting. Extension-documented mechanism.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension and UF/IFAS ENY-056 document alpha-terthienyl release suppressing root-knot nematodes. Extension consensus: dense cover crop 2+ months pre-season is effective; scattered concurrent interplanting has minimal effect. Whitefly deterrence claims are traditional and not extension-supported.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: French marigolds can reduce root-knot pests in the soil, but only when planted thickly as a cover crop a couple of months before the tomatoes, not as a few plants tucked in alongside them.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Parsley
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Flowering umbellifers attract predatory wasps and beneficial insects; mechanism is documented in biological control literature though the specific parsley-tomato pairing is not directly extension-tested.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Umbellifers attracting parasitic wasps and beneficial insects is a documented biological control mechanism (UC IPM, Cornell). The specific parsley-tomato pairing benefit is inferential: the mechanism is real but pairing-specific evidence is thin.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: When parsley is left to flower, the blooms draw in helpful insects that prey on garden pests. The effect is well established in general, though this exact parsley and tomato pairing has not been tested directly.

good_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots' deep taproot partitions the root zone differently from tomato's fibrous roots, theoretically reducing below-ground competition. This is a plausible root-zone partitioning inference, not an extension-tested pairing.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning between taprooted and fibrous-rooted crops is a real ecology concept. The specific carrot-tomato pairing benefit is a plausible inference that has not been directly studied in extension research.

good_seasoned.name: Borage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Borage flowers attract pollinators over an extended bloom period; may also repel tomato hornworm (traditional claim). Pollinator attraction is biologically plausible; hornworm repellence is tradition.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Borage as pollinator attractor is plausible and consistent with floral-resource literature. The hornworm-repellence claim is traditional companion-planting lore without T1 extension backing.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Nasturtiums function as a trap crop for aphids: aphids preferentially colonize nasturtiums, drawing them away from tomatoes. UC IPM documents trap-crop use of nasturtiums in vegetable gardens.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap-crop principle is documented in IPM literature. UC IPM references nasturtiums as aphid attractors. The specific nasturtium-tomato trap-crop pairing is referenced in extension-adjacent IPM guidance; strongest evidence is for brassica pests, but aphid trap-crop mechanism applies broadly.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is broadly allelopathic and suppresses growth of many neighboring plants. Extension literature documents fennel as a poor companion for most vegetables; the specific tomato interaction is traditional but consistent with fennel's known allelopathic properties.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel's allelopathic properties are real and documented, but the specific 'stunts tomatoes' claim is traditional rather than directly extension-tested for this pair.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Fennel releases substances that stunt the growth of many plants around it, so it is a poor neighbor for most vegetables. The trouble with tomatoes is traditional advice, but it fits fennel's known habit of holding back its neighbors.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both brassicas and tomatoes are heavy feeders; close interplanting creates real competition for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Not a toxic pairing, but productivity of both crops is reduced under competition.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for macronutrients between heavy feeders is a real agronomic concept. The specific brassica-tomato pair is traditional; the underlying competition mechanism is mechanistically sound.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage-family plants and tomatoes are both hungry feeders, so planting them close together makes them compete for the same nutrients. It is not harmful, but both crops produce less.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both crops host the tomato fruit worm / corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea, same species). Planting together creates a concentrated host reservoir that amplifies pest pressure on both crops.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: H. zea (tomato fruit worm = corn earworm) is documented on both tomato and corn in UC IPM and Cornell IPM literature. Shared-host concentration is a well-established IPM principle. Planting these crops together in a home garden concentrates the pest population.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn and tomatoes are fed on by the same caterpillar pest. Growing them side by side gives that pest more to feed on and builds up the pressure on both crops.

bad_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both are Solanaceae and share primary diseases (late blight, Phytophthora infestans; early blight, Alternaria solani) and several pests. Planting together creates a continuous host bridge that sustains inoculum across the season and into following years. Crop rotation separating Solanaceae is the standard extension recommendation for disease management.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Extension literature (UMN, Cornell, Clemson HGIC) documents shared disease and pest pressure within Solanaceae and recommends rotation to break disease cycles. The specific tomato-potato pairing as a disease-management risk is extension-backed.

bad_seasoned.name: Eggplant
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Same family (Solanaceae), shares Colorado potato beetle pressure and early blight. Interplanting concentrates beetle and disease pressure; separating Solanaceae crops, even within a season, reduces crossover pest load.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Colorado potato beetle and early blight are documented shared pests/pathogens across Solanaceae in extension IPM literature. The specific eggplant-tomato bad-companion claim follows from the well-documented within-family pest/disease sharing principle.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or black insects on the growing tips and the undersides of leaves, often so small they look like dots. The leaves may start to curl or feel sticky. You might see ants walking up the stems, as they farm aphids for the sweet liquid the aphids produce.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the colonies directly with a strong jet of water from a hose. For persistent infestations, apply insecticidal soap or neem oil spray, making sure to coat the leaf undersides where the aphids cluster.
pests.prevention_beginner: Plant marigolds or nasturtiums near your tomatoes, as both attract beneficial insects that eat aphids. Avoid over-fertilizing with high-nitrogen fertilizer, which produces the soft new growth aphids prefer.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny soft-bodied insects that cluster on stems and the undersides of leaves. Their numbers can build up very fast in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on high-nitrogen fertilizer. Heavy feeding pushes out the soft new shoots that aphids prefer, so a leaner plant gives them less to build up on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Restrained nitrogen keeps the plant from flushing the soft, sappy growth aphid colonies multiply on; excess feeding invites the problem before it arrives.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the clusters off with a strong jet of water from the hose, aiming right at the colonies on the growing tips and the undersides of leaves. Spray early in the day so the leaves dry quickly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water jet directed into the colonies dislodges them from tips and leaf undersides; the first physical knock-back to try before reaching for any spray.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Let the aphids' natural enemies work for you. Planting marigolds or nasturtiums near your tomatoes draws in the helpful insects that eat aphids.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserve the resident predator complex: interplant marigolds and nasturtiums to draw in aphid-eating beneficials, and avoid broad-spectrum sprays that would remove them along with the pest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For colonies that keep building, you can buy and release ladybugs or lacewings, insects that eat aphids, directly onto the infested plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Releasing purchased ladybugs or lacewings supplements the predators already present; aim the release at colonies you have actually found rather than releasing ahead of the pest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the colonies persist, spray insecticidal soap directly onto them, wetting the undersides of the leaves where they gather, since it works only where it touches. Wear gloves and eye protection when mixing and spraying.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: For persistent infestations, insecticidal soap applied directly to the colonies with thorough underside coverage; a contact material that spares beneficials it does not wet. Avoid applying above 90°F or on water-stressed plants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil spray is another option for a stubborn infestation. Coat the leaf undersides where the aphids cluster, keep it off anything in flower, and skip it in heat above 90°F.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Neem oil applied to the colonies is the low-residue alternative to soap; cover leaf undersides thoroughly, do not let it drift onto anything in flower, and avoid drought-stressed plants and temperatures above 90°F.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_beginner: Large sections of leaves or whole stems stripped overnight. Look for fat green caterpillars (up to 4 inches long) that blend almost perfectly into the stems, but they are easier to spot by looking for the black droppings on the leaves below.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Hand-pick and drop in soapy water, it sounds simple but it works well. If you spot any with small white oval capsules stuck to their backs, leave those ones; parasitic wasps have laid eggs on them and the wasps will do the work for you.
pests.prevention_beginner: Till or turn your soil in autumn to destroy overwintering pupae. Planting dill or fennel nearby attracts the predatory wasps that prey on hornworms.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.cause_beginner: Large green caterpillars, the larvae of a moth, that feed on leaves and stems. They show up mostly in mid to late summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick, they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them, as parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

control_ladder.note_beginner: After harvest, till or turn over the soil in the bed. Hornworms spend the winter as pupae, the resting stage buried in the soil, and turning the bed in autumn destroys them before next season.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Autumn tillage of the finished bed destroys overwintering pupae in the soil, cutting next year's moth emergence at the source; weigh it against soil-structure costs where pressure is light and handpicking keeps up.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them into soapy water; it sounds too simple but it works well. They blend into the stems, so find them by the black droppings on the leaves below. If one carries small white capsules on its back, leave it be: a helpful wasp has laid eggs on it and will do the rest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Handpicking is effective despite the camouflage; scout by the black frass on lower foliage. Spare any larva carrying the white cocoons of parasitic wasps, since those parasitoids are already providing the control.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Invite the hornworm's enemies in. Planting dill or fennel near your tomatoes attracts the wasps that prey on hornworms, so the garden starts policing itself.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserve parasitoid pressure by interplanting dill, fennel, or basil to draw in the predatory wasps that attack hornworms; the more of that pressure you keep, the less often a spray is needed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If picking cannot keep up, spray Bt, short for Bacillus thuringiensis, a bacteria-based spray that acts on caterpillars. Apply it while the caterpillars are still young, reapply after rain, and keep it off any plants you grow for butterflies, since it affects their caterpillars too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) is the biological escalation for hornworm larvae; apply to young caterpillars and reapply after rain or new growth. It acts on lepidopteran larvae as a group, so keep it off butterfly host plants.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny round holes scattered across the leaves, especially on young plants and seedlings. If you approach the plant quickly you'll see tiny shiny black beetles jumping off the leaves: that's the flea beetle.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover seedlings with floating row cover until plants are a few inches tall and growing strongly. Diatomaceous earth dusted on and around the leaves can help; reapply after rain.
pests.prevention_beginner: Transplanting larger, more established plants rather than direct-sowing reduces flea beetle damage, since seedlings are most vulnerable.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.cause_beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas when disturbed and chew tiny holes in leaves. They are most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover young plants with floating row cover, the light spun fabric that lets light and water through, and keep it on until they are a few inches tall and growing strongly. Seedlings take the worst damage, so shielding that stage matters most.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover over seedlings excludes the beetles through the vulnerable establishment window; damage matters far less once plants are large and established. Avoid covering ground that carried a same-family crop last year, or emerging soil pests can be trapped under it.

pests.name: Whiteflies
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clouds of tiny white, moth-like insects that fly up when you brush the plant, with the immature stages sitting still on the undersides of leaves. Leaves may yellow, and a sticky honeydew coating can develop, sometimes followed by black sooty mold. Whiteflies are worst in warm regions and on greenhouse or container plants.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil directly onto the leaf undersides where the young whiteflies feed, and repeat every few days since eggs keep hatching. Yellow sticky traps help you monitor and knock back the adults. Remove and bag heavily infested lower leaves.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check new transplants before buying, since whiteflies often arrive on nursery plants. Keep weeds down around the garden, and use reflective (silver) mulch, which confuses the adults and reduces landings.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny white, moth-like adults that flush from the canopy when disturbed; flat, scale-like nymphs on leaf undersides. Feeding causes yellowing and honeydew, with sooty mold following. Whiteflies also vector viruses (including tomato yellow leaf curl), making them more than a nuisance in warm regions.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several species, chiefly greenhouse and silverleaf (Bemisia) whiteflies. Populations build fastest in sustained warmth, so pressure is highest in southern regions, greenhouses, and on container plants.
pests.cause_beginner: Small white flying insects whose young feed on the undersides of leaves. They multiply fast in warm weather and are most common in southern gardens, greenhouses, and on potted plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Target leaf undersides with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on a repeat schedule to catch successive hatches; deploy yellow sticky traps; conserve natural enemies (Encarsia parasitoids, lacewings). Remove and destroy heavily colonized lower foliage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect and quarantine incoming transplants, the usual introduction route. Control weedy alternate hosts, use reflective mulch to suppress adult landing, and avoid excess nitrogen that fuels the soft growth whiteflies favor.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay reflective silver mulch under the plants. The shiny surface confuses the adult whiteflies as they fly in, so fewer of them land and settle on your tomatoes.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch laid at planting suppresses adult landing; it is a preventive set-up step, most useful while the crop is still small.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the ground around your tomatoes weeded. Weeds can act as a home base where whiteflies build up before moving onto your plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Control weedy alternate hosts around the planting and keep the edges clean; resident weeds sustain whitefly populations that reinvade the crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not overdo nitrogen fertilizer. Heavy feeding produces the soft, lush growth that whiteflies favor.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Restrained nitrogen keeps the plant from pushing the soft growth whiteflies favor; a preventive feeding habit rather than a response.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull off lower leaves that are heavily coated with whiteflies and their young, and bag them for the trash rather than dropping them in the garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Remove and destroy heavily colonized lower foliage to take out the scale-like nymphs wholesale; bag it out of the garden rather than composting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hang yellow sticky traps near the plants. The adults are drawn to the color and stick to the cards, which shows you how bad the problem is and thins out the flying adults.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Yellow sticky cards serve double duty, tracking the population trend while removing a share of the winged adults; a monitoring aid to time the other steps as much as a control.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Protect the helpful insects that hunt whiteflies, such as lacewings and tiny parasitic wasps. Mostly that means not reaching for harsh sprays that would wipe them out along with the pest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserve Encarsia parasitoids and lacewings, the resident enemies suppressing the nymphs; avoid broad-spectrum insecticides, which kill the beneficials as well as the pests.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spray insecticidal soap onto the undersides of the leaves, where the young whiteflies feed, and repeat every few days, because eggs keep hatching after each spray. Wear gloves and eye protection when mixing and spraying.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap on a repeat schedule targeted at leaf undersides catches the successive hatches a single pass misses; it is a contact material, so coverage of the nymphs is the whole game. Avoid applying above 90°F or to water-stressed plants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil works much the same way: spray the leaf undersides and repeat every few days, since it works only where it coats. Do not spray in heat above 90°F or on plants that are dry and stressed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Horticultural oil is the alternative contact material for the underside nymphs, on the same repeat schedule and with the same coverage demand, applied in mild weather; keep it off anything in flower and separate it from any sulfur spray by at least 30 days in the growing season, checking the oil label since some specify longer.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark brown spots on the lower leaves, often with rings inside them like a target pattern. The leaves around the spots turn yellow, then the whole leaf dies and drops. The pattern starts at the bottom of the plant and moves upward.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and throw away (do not compost) any affected leaves as soon as you spot them. Mulch the soil around the base of the plant to stop rain from splashing soil and fungal spores up onto the lower leaves.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rotate your tomatoes, avoiding the same spot for at least 3 years. Water at the base of the plant rather than from overhead, and stake the plant to keep the foliage off the ground.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that causes dark spots on the lower, older leaves first. It spreads in warm, wet weather, so keep the leaves as dry as you can.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move your tomatoes to a different spot each year, and keep them out of any bed they have grown in for at least 3 years. The fungus carries over where tomatoes grew before.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate on a 3 to 4 year cycle away from ground that has carried tomatoes; rotation denies the resident Alternaria the host it needs to renew itself.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water the soil at the base of the plant instead of sprinkling from above. The disease moves in water splashed onto the leaves, so keeping the foliage dry slows it down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Base watering keeps foliage dry and avoids the splash that carries spores from soil onto the lower leaves, the entry point the disease works upward from.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover the soil around the plant with mulch. It stops rain from splashing soil, and the fungus riding in it, up onto the lower leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soil-covering mulch breaks the rain-splash route that moves spores from the soil onto the lowest leaves, which is where this disease gets its start.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give each plant room, and stake it so the leaves are held up off the soil. Moving air dries the foliage faster, and the disease favors warm, wet leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spacing for airflow and staking the foliage clear of the ground both shorten leaf wetness, the condition this warm-wet-favored fungus needs, and lift the lower canopy away from soil contact.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The moment you spot the dark, target-patterned spots, pull those leaves off and put them in the trash, not the compost. Every spotted leaf you remove is a source of spread taken away.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rogue out symptomatic leaves as soon as they appear and destroy rather than compost them; prompt removal cuts the inoculum feeding the bottom-to-top spread.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the disease keeps advancing, a copper-based fungicide can protect the leaves that are still healthy. It works as prevention, so start before spots are everywhere. Follow the label rate, and keep the spray out of ponds and streams, since copper is very harmful to fish.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper applied preventively protects clean foliage; timing is before or at first sign, not after the canopy is spotted. Copper accumulates at the soil surface with repeat use, and the acute-hazard band varies by compound, from Low for copper octanoate to the DANGER band for copper hydroxide, so read the active ingredient.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, sunken, leathery patches on the bottom of the fruit, the end where the flower was attached. It usually appears on the first fruits of the season. It is not contagious and doesn't spread between plants.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: The fix is consistent watering, not calcium supplements. Mulch around the base to help the soil hold moisture evenly, and water on a regular schedule rather than in big irregular bursts. Remove affected fruit; they won't recover.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Water consistently and deeply, as the most common trigger is irregular watering during fruit development. Avoid disturbing the roots by cultivating too close to the plant, and don't over-fertilize with nitrogen, which pushes the plant to grow faster than it can absorb calcium.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage, not a pest or disease.
diseases.cause_beginner: A dark, sunken patch on the bottom of the fruit. It is not a pest or a disease: the fruit cannot get enough calcium, usually because watering has been uneven. Water steadily to prevent it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water deeply and on a steady, regular schedule rather than in big bursts with dry spells between. Uneven watering is the most common trigger, because the fruit cannot take up enough calcium when soil moisture swings. Calcium sprays are not the fix; steady water is.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Consistent deep irrigation is the primary control: the disorder is a calcium-delivery failure in the sizing fruit driven by moisture swings, not a pathogen, so evenness of supply does the work no amendment can.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spread mulch around the base of the plant. It keeps the soil moisture from swinging between soaked and dry, which is exactly the swing that brings on the rot.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mulch buffers soil moisture between waterings, smoothing the wet-dry cycling behind the calcium shortfall; lay it at planting on a crop with a history of the disorder.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Take off any fruit that shows the dark sunken patch; it will not recover. The disorder does not spread from fruit to fruit, so think of this as housekeeping that lets the plant put its energy into the fruits still coming.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cull affected fruit as you find it; the lesion is permanent, the disorder is not contagious, and removal redirects resources to later, less-affected fruit.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small circular spots on the leaves, with tan or pale gray centers with dark brown borders, often with a faint yellow halo around the outside. They start on the lower leaves and move upward. Not as aggressive as early blight but disfiguring.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide if the problem is spreading. Improve airflow by staking or caging so leaves aren't touching each other.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Water at the soil level rather than overhead. Mulch to prevent soil splash. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular spots with dark borders and pale gray centers, starting on lower leaves. Spots may have yellow halos.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Septoria lycopersici fungus. One of the most common tomato diseases.
diseases.cause_beginner: A common fungus that makes many small, round spots on the leaves. It spreads in wet conditions, so water at the soil and keep the leaves dry.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper fungicide. Ensure good air circulation.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Mulch around plants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant your tomatoes in a different bed each year. Moving the crop keeps it off ground that carried the fungus.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Annual rotation to fresh ground separates the crop from carried-over inoculum; the standard base layer for splash-driven tomato leaf spots.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil, not over the top of the plant. This fungus spreads in wet conditions, so the drier you keep the leaves, the slower it moves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soil-level irrigation denies the wet-leaf conditions the fungus spreads under and avoids splashing it up the plant; the spots begin on lower leaves and work upward.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Mulch the ground under the plant so soil cannot splash onto the leaves when it rains. The fungus travels in that splash.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mulch interrupts splash dispersal from soil to lower canopy; the leaf spots start where splash lands, so covering the soil narrows the fungus's entrance.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stake or cage the plant so the leaves are not piled against each other. Open, airy foliage dries quickly, and dry leaves give the spots little to work with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Staking or caging opens the canopy so foliage dries fast; leaf-on-leaf contact holds the moisture that keeps new infections cycling.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off spotted leaves as soon as you see them and get them out of the garden. Each leaf you remove takes some of the disease with it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Immediate removal of symptomatic foliage lowers the inoculum load driving the lower-to-upper progression; take leaves at the first spots.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If new spots keep appearing despite the steps above, a copper-based fungicide can slow the spread. Follow the label rate, and keep it away from ponds, streams, and drains, since copper is very harmful to fish and other water life.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper is the escalation when spread outpaces sanitation; it is preventive in action, so cover clean foliage early. Mind cumulative soil loading with repeat use, and note the acute-hazard band varies by copper compound, from Low for copper octanoate to the DANGER band for copper hydroxide.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Large, irregularly shaped brown patches that look water-soaked and spread fast, days not weeks. In humid weather you may see white fuzzy growth on the undersides of affected leaves. This one is serious; it can kill a healthy plant in a week.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy all affected plant material immediately, bag it and throw it in the trash, do not compost it. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively if you see it starting in your area and conditions are wet.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Choose disease-resistant varieties whenever possible. Stake for good airflow. Never leave tomato plant debris in the garden over winter, clear it all out at season's end.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fast-moving disease that can collapse a plant within days in cool, wet weather. Remove and throw away affected plants right away so it does not spread.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately, do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When you buy seed or transplants, pick varieties described as resistant to late blight whenever you can. With a disease that can kill a healthy plant in a week, the variety you choose in spring is a real defense.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cultivar resistance is the front line against a pathogen that can take a planting down in days; select for late blight resistance at seed-buying time where it is available.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stake your plants and keep the foliage open so air moves through and the leaves dry quickly. The disease takes off when plants stay wet.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Staking and an open canopy shorten the leaf wetness this cool-wet-weather pathogen depends on; airflow is a set-up condition, not a rescue.

control_ladder.note_beginner: At the first sign, remove every affected leaf or plant, bag it, and put it in the trash. Do not compost it. At season's end, clear all tomato debris out of the garden rather than leaving any over winter.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Immediate rogueing of infected material, bagged and trashed rather than composted, is the containment move for a pathogen this fast; close the season by clearing tomato debris so nothing carries over winter.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If late blight is showing up in your area and the weather is wet, a copper-based fungicide applied before your plants are infected can protect them. It is a preventive spray, so waiting until brown patches appear is too late to start. Follow the label rate and keep it away from ponds and streams.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper deployed preventively, on area reports plus wet conditions, is the one spray option in scope; it protects tissue rather than rescuing it. Watch cumulative soil copper across seasons and read the active ingredient, since acute hazard runs from Low for copper octanoate to the DANGER band for copper hydroxide.

diseases.name: Fusarium and Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Whole plants that wilt and yellow even when the soil is moist, often starting on one side or on the lower leaves and creeping upward. The plant may perk up at night early on, then decline for good. If you cut the main stem near the base, you will see brown streaking inside. There is no spray that cures it.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant is infected, so remove and bag affected plants, and do not compost them, to limit spread. The real answer is prevention for next season: choose resistant varieties and rotate where you plant.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant resistant varieties; look for the letters V, F, or FN after the name on the tag, which mean the variety resists Verticillium and Fusarium wilt. Rotate tomatoes and their relatives (peppers, eggplant, potatoes) to a different bed for at least 3 years, since these fungi live in the soil.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Progressive wilting and yellowing, often unilateral (one side of a leaf, one branch, or one side of the plant) and advancing upward from the base. Vascular browning is visible in a cut stem. Fusarium (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici) favors warm soils; Verticillium (Verticillium dahliae) tolerates cooler soils; both plug the water-conducting xylem, so symptoms resemble drought despite adequate moisture.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne fungi that persist in soil and debris for years and enter through the roots. Once established they cannot be cured in the home garden.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungi that live in the soil and clog the plant's water pipes from the inside. They cannot be cured once a plant is infected, so prevention is everything.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No curative treatment exists for the home gardener; rogue and destroy symptomatic plants to reduce inoculum. Management is genetic and cultural: resistant cultivars and rotation.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant cultivars (V, F, FF, or FFF designations for Verticillium and the Fusarium races; many grape hybrids carry VFN resistance). Rotate out of Solanaceae for at least 3 years, sanitize tools and stakes, and remove infected debris. Grafting onto resistant rootstock is an option where the disease is established.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Buy resistant varieties. On the tag or seed packet, look for the letters V, F, or FN after the name; they mean the variety resists Verticillium and Fusarium wilt. Since there is no cure once a plant is infected, this choice is your strongest move.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Genetic resistance is the primary control: choose cultivars carrying V, F, FF, or FFF designations for Verticillium and the Fusarium races. Many grape hybrids carry VFN resistance.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where these wilts are already in your soil, another option is a grafted plant: the variety you want to eat growing on roots from a resistant type, so the plant meets the soil with roots the fungus struggles to enter.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Grafting a susceptible cultivar onto resistant rootstock is an option where the disease is established in a bed; you keep the fruiting variety while swapping out the root system these soilborne fungi enter through.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move tomatoes and their relatives, peppers, eggplant, and potatoes, to a different bed and keep them out of the old one for at least 3 years. These fungi live in the soil, so the bed itself needs the break.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Keep the bed out of Solanaceae for a minimum of 3 years; the pathogens persist in soil and debris for years and enter through the roots of any susceptible family member planted back too soon.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no spray that cures an infected plant, so once one is clearly sick, pull it, bag it, and put it in the trash rather than the compost. That limits how far the fungus spreads through your garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rogue and destroy symptomatic plants to reduce soil inoculum, remove infected debris, and sanitize tools and stakes that have worked contaminated ground; none of it cures, all of it lowers carryover.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 2-3 days during hot weather, once a week when temperatures are cool. The difference is driven by evapotranspiration rate: at air temperatures above 80-85°F, plants lose water through leaves several times faster than at 60°F, so the soil dries proportionally faster. Container-grown plants dry out faster still and may need daily checking in peak summer heat.
watering.frequency_beginner: Every 2 to 3 days in hot weather, and about once a week when it is cool. Plants drink and lose much more water when it is hot, so the soil dries out faster. Plants in containers dry out even quicker and may need checking every day in peak summer heat.
watering.amount_seasoned: 1-2 inches of water per week total from rain plus irrigation. The goal is to wet the soil to 8-12 inches depth, deep enough to reach the main root mass and encourage roots to grow downward rather than staying near the surface. Light, shallow watering trains roots upward, making the plant more sensitive to heat and drought stress.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 to 2 inches of water a week, counting rain and watering together. Water deeply enough to soak the soil down about 8 to 12 inches, where the main roots are. Deep watering pulls the roots downward, which makes the plant tougher in heat and dry spells; frequent shallow watering keeps the roots near the surface, where they dry out fast.
watering.method_seasoned: At soil level: soaker hose, drip line, or a hose placed at the base. Wet foliage is the primary route of entry for Septoria leaf spot, early blight, and late blight: fungal spores on the soil surface travel upward in splash water, and wet leaf surfaces give spores the moisture film they need to germinate and penetrate. Morning watering, if overhead watering is unavoidable, allows foliage to dry before evening, the most disease-permissive period.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the soil, not over the top of the plant: use a soaker hose, a drip line, or just hold the hose at the base. Wet leaves are how most tomato leaf diseases get started, so keeping the leaves dry is one of the best things you can do. If you do have to water from above, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off before evening.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: The clearest signs are yellow lower leaves and soil that stays soggy. Yellow leaves near the bottom mean the roots are waterlogged and cannot get air. Grape tomatoes resist cracking much better than cherry tomatoes because of their thicker skin, so you will see far less split fruit, but a sudden heavy watering after a dry stretch can still split even a tough-skinned grape. Aim for steady, even moisture.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting during the day that bounces back overnight is the clearest sign your plant is thirsty: if it perks up after the sun goes down, water is the issue. If flowers drop before forming fruit, the plant may be under water stress: when it can't sustain fruit development, it sheds the flower at the stem (called abscission). Note that extreme heat above 90°F does the same thing, so blossom drop can happen even when you're watering regularly during a heat wave.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellow lower leaves and persistently soggy soil are the main signs of overwatering. Yellowing lower leaves indicate roots sitting in oxygen-depleted, waterlogged soil. Grape tomatoes crack far less than cherry types thanks to their thicker skin, so fruit cracking is a less reliable overwatering flag here; when a grape tomato does split, it is usually after a heavy soak following a dry spell. As with all tomatoes, the underlying issue is inconsistency, not just total volume.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting leaves that recover overnight, blossom drop, dry cracked soil. Overnight recovery distinguishes water stress from heat stress or disease: if leaves perk up after the temperature drops, moisture is the limiting factor. Blossom drop under drought stress occurs because the plant triggers an abscission layer at the flower stem when it cannot sustain fruit development; high temperatures (above 90°F day / below 55°F night) cause the same response, so both stressors can operate simultaneously.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep the starting mix evenly moist
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Even moisture in the tray until emergence; bottom-water or mist so the fine surface never dries mid-germination.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the tray gently damp until sprouts show. Watering from below keeps the surface even without washing the seeds around.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep cells evenly moist, never soggy
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Steady, moderate moisture under lights. Let the surface approach dryness between waterings; saturated mix is what rots young seedlings.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the mix damp but never soggy. If the top stays shiny-wet all the time, you are watering too often.

schedule_by_stage.rate: 1 to 2 inches per week, soaked 8 to 12 inches deep
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Water deeply at the base: 1 to 2 inches a week soaking 8 to 12 inches down, every 2 to 3 days in hot weather and weekly when cool. Drip or soaker keeps foliage dry; morning is the fallback if overhead is unavoidable.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water at the soil, not over the leaves: a deep drink every 2 to 3 days in heat, about weekly when cool, 1 to 2 inches a week in total. Deep watering builds tough, deep roots.

schedule_by_stage.rate: 1 to 2 inches per week, kept even
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Hold moisture even from flowering through fruit set and sizing. Drought triggers blossom drop, and wide dry-wet swings can still bring on blossom-end rot even in small-fruited types.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water evenly and do not let the soil dry right out now. Dry spells make flowers fall off, and big swings can give the fruit dark sunken bottoms.

schedule_by_stage.rate: 1 to 2 inches per week, kept even
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Grape tomatoes' thick skins resist the cracking that plagues cherry types, so an occasional lapse is forgiving; keep the steady 1 to 2 inches a week anyway for yield and quality through the long picking run.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep up steady watering while you pick. Grape tomatoes rarely crack thanks to their thicker skins, but even moisture keeps the plant producing well.

schedule_by_stage.rate: little needed as the plant winds down
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Water demand drops sharply once cool nights end fruit set. Taper irrigation and let the final clusters ripen out.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: As the weather cools and the plant slows, water only now and then while the last fruit colors up.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering wherever practical: wetting the foliage is the main entry route for Septoria leaf spot and the blights. If overhead is unavoidable, water in the morning so leaves dry before the disease-permissive evening hours. Mulch to buffer soil moisture and to block soil-borne spores from splashing up onto lower leaves.
watering.method_note_beginner: Try to keep the leaves dry: water the soil, not the plant. If you must use a sprinkler, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off by evening. A layer of mulch helps keep the soil evenly moist and stops disease from splashing up off the ground.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Even moisture matters most from transplant establishment through flowering, fruit set, and fruit sizing. Wide swings between dry and saturated soil during fruit development drive blossom-end rot; grape tomatoes' thick skin makes them much less prone to the skin cracking that plagues cherry types, but consistency still protects yield and quality.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time for even watering is once flowers and fruit have set and the tomatoes are sizing up. Letting the soil go bone-dry and then soaking it can still cause blossom-end rot (dark, sunken spots on the fruit bottom). Grape tomatoes crack much less than cherry tomatoes, but steady moisture is still the goal.

start_method.hardening_off_beginner: These plants were raised indoors and have never felt wind, direct sun, or cool nights. Hardening off means introducing them to outdoor life slowly over 7 to 10 days, starting with a few hours outside in a sheltered spot the first day, then more time and more sun each day. Skip this step and the plants will sulk for weeks after transplanting, or the leaves will scorch on the first sunny day. It is not optional for tomatoes.
start_method.notes_beginner: Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost date (look yours up if you don't know it, as it varies by 6 to 8 weeks across zones). When you transplant, dig a deeper hole than the pot and bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves, as new roots form all along the buried stem and make for a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant from the start.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost. Harden off over 7-10 days before transplanting. Transplant deep: bury stem up to lowest leaves to encourage roots.

container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Deep preferred over wide; minimum 12-inch depth for adequate root development. Standard round 5- to 10-gallon nursery containers work well.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: A deep pot matters more than a wide one. Aim for at least 12 inches deep so the roots have room. A standard round 5 to 10 gallon pot works well.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Elevate container off saucer or remove standing water within an hour; saucers are useful for heat retention but roots should not sit in pooled water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of standing water. Lift the pot off the saucer, or empty the saucer within an hour of watering. A saucer is fine for keeping the pot warm, but the roots should never sit in pooled water.
