soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of potting mix made for containers. Do not use soil dug from the garden, which packs down too tightly and drains poorly in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: If your potting mix feels heavy or dense, mix in about 20% perlite, a lightweight volcanic material that keeps the mix from compacting around roots. Stir in a slow-release granular fertilizer at planting, following the label rate.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: container_potting_mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Incorporate 20-25% perlite by volume if the mix feels dense; add slow-release balanced fertilizer (e.g., 10-10-10 granular) at planting per label rate.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds, so in summer heat you may need to water every day. Stick your finger two inches into the soil; if it feels dry there, water thoroughly. Keeping moisture steady matters: letting the soil swing from bone-dry to soaked is the most common cause of blossom end rot (dark, sunken patches on the fruit bottom) in container tomatoes.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Potting mix can't hold onto nutrients the way garden soil does, so container tomatoes need regular feeding. Once your plant starts flowering, apply a balanced liquid fertilizer every one to two weeks. Alternatively, mix slow-release granules into the soil at planting and add one liquid feed mid-season. Don't skip this, as container plants run out of food faster than in-ground ones.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Grape tomatoes grow well in large pots, but they are vigorous indeterminate plants, so go big: a 10-gallon pot is the practical minimum, with 5 gallons only for a single plant kept well watered. Add a sturdy cage or stake at planting, because these vines get tall. There are very few dwarf grape varieties, so unlike compact cherry tomatoes, do not expect a tidy patio plant. In hot weather, container plants dry out fast and may need water every day.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: A productive container crop, but treat it as a full-size indeterminate: use 10-gallon containers where possible (5-gallon minimum for one plant) and cage or stake at planting. Compact or hanging-basket grape cultivars are scarce, so plan for a tall plant. Water daily in heat; steady moisture limits blossom-end rot.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry significantly faster than in-ground soil, so daily watering is often required during summer heat. Check moisture 2 inches below the surface daily. Consistent moisture is critical; irregular watering is a primary driver of blossom-end rot in containers.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container medium has limited nutrient buffering capacity. Supplement with liquid balanced fertilizer every 1-2 weeks once flowering begins, or apply slow-release granular at planting plus a liquid mid-season boost. Containers are less forgiving of nutrient deficits than in-ground beds.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits grape tomatoes well, since the wicking reservoir smooths out the moisture swings that drive cracking and blossom-end rot in a heavy summer feeder. Keep the reservoir topped up in peak heat, but let the mix draw down rather than staying saturated, and water from the top occasionally to flush salts that concentrate with constant sub-irrigation.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot works well for grape tomatoes because it keeps the water steady, which helps prevent cracked fruit. Keep the bottom reservoir filled during hot weather, and every so often water from the top too, which rinses out built-up minerals.

recommended: Santa (F1, classic red grape, heavy clustered yields)
Juliet (F1, elongated mini-Roma grape, very crack-resistant, AAS winner)
Sweet Hearts (F1, deep red, super-sweet, best-selling grape)
Five Star Grape (F1, firm and meaty, sweet, high-yielding)
Smarty (grape, about 70 days, indeterminate)
Red Grape (classic red grape type)
varieties.note_beginner: Grape tomatoes are small and oblong, sweeter and thicker-skinned than they look. If you are not sure which to try, Santa and Juliet are the two most common and both are reliable and crack-resistant. Sweet Hearts is the go-to if you want the sweetest fruit. All of these need a tall cage or stake because the plants keep growing all season.
varieties.note_seasoned: Grape tomatoes are small, oblong, thick-skinned types grown for sweetness, crack resistance, and shelf life. Santa and Juliet are the most widely grown; Juliet is often called a mini-Roma for its elongated shape and is prized for cracking resistance and long storage. Sweet Hearts is a top-selling super-sweet red, and Five Star Grape is noted for firm, meaty, low-juice flesh. Nearly all are indeterminate and need staking.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant grape tomatoes where you grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, or potatoes last year. These plants are all in the same family and share the same soil diseases, which can build up and carry over to the next crop.
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, legumes, corn, root vegetables
rotation.note_beginner: Move your tomatoes to a different part of the garden each year, and don't come back to the same spot for at least 3 years. Soil diseases, including the wilts and blights that affect tomatoes, can survive in the soil or on old plant debris for multiple seasons. Rotation is the main tool home gardeners have to keep these in check. The same rule applies to peppers, eggplant, and potatoes: they share the same diseases, so avoid planting any of them where tomatoes grew recently.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate nightshades to a fresh bed every 3 years minimum. Soilborne pathogens, particularly Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici), Verticillium wilt, and early blight (Alternaria solani), can persist in soil or on plant debris for multiple seasons. Fusarium and Verticillium are soil-systemic and resistant to most home-garden interventions once established; the primary management tool for the home gardener is rotation combined with resistant varieties. Avoid planting tomatoes after any Solanaceae crop (peppers, eggplant, potatoes), as these share the same pathogen suite.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: 2 to 3 weeks at room temperature (65 to 70°F), noticeably longer than round cherry tomatoes because the thicker skin and firmer, less watery flesh resist softening and moisture loss. Ripe fruit continues producing small amounts of ethylene, which sustains flavor. Holding fruit stem-side down slows moisture loss through the stem scar, the most permeable point on the surface.
storage.room_temp_beginner: About 2 to 3 weeks at room temperature, longer than most cherry tomatoes keep. The thicker skin is what gives grape tomatoes their long shelf life. Set them out of direct sun, stem-side down, and they hold their texture and flavor well on the counter.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Avoid refrigerating ripe fruit. Below 50 to 55°F, cell membranes lose selective permeability and the flesh turns mealy while flavor mutes; the damage is irreversible. Grape tomatoes' firmer flesh withstands a brief chill marginally better than a thin-skinned cherry, but the flavor cost is the same, so refrigerate only to rescue fruit from waste and use within a few days.
storage.fridge_beginner: Try not to refrigerate ripe grape tomatoes. The cold makes the texture mealy and dulls the flavor, and it cannot be undone. They already keep well on the counter, so there is rarely a need. If some would otherwise go to waste, refrigerate and use them within a few days.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze whole for cooking, not for eating fresh. Freezing ruptures cell walls, so thawed fruit is soft, but the skins slip off easily, which suits sauces and cooked dishes. The meaty, low-juice flesh of grape types holds up particularly well in cooked applications. Blanching first is optional and extends storage quality.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze whole grape tomatoes to cook with later, but they will be soft once thawed, so do not plan to eat them fresh. The skins slip right off after thawing, which is handy for sauces, and their meaty flesh cooks down nicely.
storage.notes_beginner: Keep them on the counter out of direct sun. Grape tomatoes are firmer than cherry tomatoes, so they bruise less if a few pile up, but a single layer in a wide bowl still keeps them longest.
storage.notes_seasoned: Store at room temperature out of direct sun, stem-side down. Direct sun accelerates softening. Grape tomatoes are firm enough to hold a few layers deep in a bowl without bruising as readily as soft cherries, though a single wide layer still gives the longest hold.

det_indet.detail_beginner: Indeterminate means the plant keeps growing and producing fruit all season, rather than ripening everything at once and stopping. Nearly all grape tomatoes, including Santa, Juliet, and Sweet Hearts, grow this way, which is why one plant is so productive. Because they keep climbing, they need a tall, sturdy cage or stake. Unlike cherry tomatoes, there are very few compact or hanging-basket grape varieties, so give them a big support.
det_indet.detail_seasoned: Grape tomatoes are almost always indeterminate: they grow, flower, and fruit in long clusters all season until frost, so they need sturdy staking or caging. Popular grape hybrids such as Santa, Juliet, and Sweet Hearts are all indeterminate. Truly compact or determinate grape types are uncommon, so plan on a tall support.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Tomato seeds need warm soil to sprout, about as warm as a sunny windowsill, or 75°F if you have a soil thermometer. A heating mat under your seed tray is the easiest way to get there. Cover the tray with a clear plastic lid until the first green shoots appear, then take it off.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale curved shoot pushing up through the soil. The shoot will straighten and the first two small leaves will unfold at the top.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you seen any sprouts yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale shoot pushing upward through the soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil temperature in the 70-85°F range. A heat mat makes a real difference for staying in the optimal zone. Cover with a humidity dome until sprouts appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you seen any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: The moment you see the first green sprouts, take off the plastic lid covering your seed tray, as leaving it on causes a fungal problem called damping off that kills seedlings. Move the tray as close to your brightest light as you can get it. If seedlings grow tall and floppy instead of short and stocky, they need more light, not more water; that stretched-out look is called etiolation (reaching for the light), and a weak stem won't fully recover.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Two small flat leaves (the seed leaves) open first, then the first true leaves emerge between them, which will have the distinctive serrated edges and smell of tomato leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How are your seedlings looking?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Two seed leaves open flat, then the first true leaves emerging between them, which will look distinctly tomato-shaped.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove the humidity dome the moment the first sprouts appear, as waiting causes damping off. Move seedlings as close to your brightest light source as possible. Tomato seedlings require 14-16 hours of light equivalent to bright natural light to grow compact and stocky; at less than that, they etiolate (stretch toward the light) producing a weak, thin stem that never fully recovers. Leggy seedlings are almost always a light deficiency, not a watering problem.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings looking?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Before you move seedlings outside, you need to harden them off, meaning giving them short outdoor stints first (start with an hour or two in a sheltered spot), adding more time and sun each day over 7-10 days. Indoor-grown seedlings aren't used to wind, direct sun, or temperature swings; skipping this step shocks the plant and sets it back. When you plant, go deep: bury the stem all the way up to the lowest set of leaves. Tomatoes grow roots from buried stem, so a deeper planting gives you a bigger, more drought-tolerant root system.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The stem is thicker, the plant has 3 or 4 sets of true leaves, and the color is deep green throughout. If you squeeze the stem gently it holds its shape rather than feeling floppy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are they outside yet, or still hardening off?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong stem, 3-4 sets of true leaves, deep green color. Ready to pot up or transplant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin hardening off 7-10 days before transplant: start with 1-2 hours outdoors in a sheltered spot, extending time and sun exposure each day. Indoor seedlings have thinner cuticles and underdeveloped stomatal regulation, so gradual exposure allows the plant to upregulate protective responses before full outdoor conditions. Plant deep: bury the stem up to the lowest set of leaves. Tomatoes develop adventitious roots from buried stem tissue, so a deeper planting produces a larger, more drought-resistant root system than a shallow one.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are they outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When the first yellow flowers appear, change to a tomato fertilizer (those usually have more potassium, which the plant needs for fruit). Each morning, give the flowering stems a gentle shake or tap. This helps the flowers make fruit, and it really does work, especially indoors or in places without much wind.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small bright yellow flowers appearing in clusters, each one star-shaped with petals swept back. Each flower is a potential tomato.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Flowers open yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small yellow flowers in clusters. Each flower is a potential fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Switch from a balanced fertilizer to a high-potassium, low-nitrogen formulation. Nitrogen drives vegetative growth, which is counterproductive once flowering begins. Potassium governs sugar transport into fruit and is the limiting nutrient for fruit quality and weight at this stage. Gently tap or shake the flowering stems each morning, as tomatoes are self-fertile but require vibration to release pollen efficiently from the anther cone. In still, sheltered environments, this manual step measurably improves fruit set.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Flowers open yet?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick ripe tomatoes every day or two during peak summer. Ripe fruit left on the vine releases a ripening gas (ethylene) that hurries along the fruit around it, which sounds useful, but in an indeterminate plant that keeps flowering all season, leaving ripe tomatoes hanging too long also pulls the plant's energy away from new flowers and young fruit. Regular picking keeps production moving.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fruit is fully colored (red, orange, or yellow depending on variety) and gives slightly when you press it gently. Very ripe fruit may start to look a little less shiny than it did.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: First tomatoes picked? Log your harvest.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fully colored fruit that gives slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin may start to lose its sheen when perfectly ripe.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick regularly, every 1-2 days at peak production. Ripe tomatoes on the vine produce ethylene gas, which accelerates ripening of neighboring fruit and, in indeterminate varieties, can slow the initiation of new flower clusters. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine also creates a physical energy sink: the plant continues investing carbohydrates in already-ripe fruit rather than channeling resources to new flowers and developing fruit.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First tomatoes picked? Log your harvest.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When nighttime temperatures stay below 50°F regularly, pinch off all the growing tips, the fuzzy little shoots at the ends of each stem. New flowers won't set fruit in that cold anyway (pollen stops working below about 55°F at night), and removing the tips redirects the plant's remaining energy into the tomatoes already on the vine. Bring green tomatoes inside before any frost, as they'll keep ripening on a countertop at around 60-65°F. Don't refrigerate them: cold below 50°F damages the tomato's texture and flavor permanently (this is called chilling injury).
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant is producing fewer new flowers, lower leaves are yellowing, and nights are regularly feeling cold. The plant is winding down.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How was your season? Worth logging what worked.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, yellowing lower leaves, nights cooling below 50°F.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips to halt new vegetative growth. Below 55°F, pollen viability declines sharply and new fruit is unlikely to set regardless of how many flowers open. Removing growing tips eliminates the hormone source (auxin from the apical meristem) that pulls resources toward new stem growth, redirecting carbohydrates into the fruit already present on the vine. Bring green tomatoes inside before frost, as they will continue ripening at 60-65°F and store far better than refrigerated tomatoes, which suffer irreversible chilling injury below 50°F.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How was your season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to start your tomato seeds indoors
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, now is the right window to start tomato seeds. Fill small trays or cells with seed-starting mix, plant one or two seeds per cell about a quarter inch deep, and put them somewhere warm (70 to 80°F is ideal). Cover with a plastic dome or cling wrap until you see sprouts, then remove it right away. This is where your season begins.
notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start your tomatoes indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, the perfect window to get tomato seeds into trays. Find somewhere warm (70-80°F), keep the soil consistently moist, and cover with a dome until you see sprouts. This is where your season begins.

notifications.title_beginner: Start introducing your tomatoes to the outdoors
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away, time to start hardening off your seedlings. Put them outside for a couple of hours in a sheltered, partly shaded spot today, then bring them back in. Add more time and more direct sun each day over the next week or two. This gradual transition helps them adapt to wind, sun, and temperature swings before they go out for good.
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away. Begin putting your plants outside for a few hours each day, starting sheltered and increasing exposure gradually. This week of adjustment makes a real difference to how they settle in after transplanting.

notifications.title_beginner: Frost has passed, your tomatoes are ready to go out
notifications.body_beginner: Now is the time to transplant. Dig a hole deeper than the pot and bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves, as roots form all along the buried stem and make for a stronger plant. Water well, and if the weather is still cool, wait for nighttime temps to be consistently above 50°F before planting out.
notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost has passed, time to transplant
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deep: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Roots will form all along the buried stem and give you a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant.

notifications.title_beginner: Flowers are coming, switch your fertilizer now
notifications.body_beginner: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a tomato fertilizer or a high-potassium fertilizer now (look for a bag with the third number largest, like 5-10-10). Gently shaking the flower stems in the morning helps pollen move between flowers. Each flower is a potential tomato.
notifications.title_seasoned: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body_seasoned: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a high-potassium feed now, and give the flowering stems a gentle shake in the morning to help pollination. Each flower is a potential tomato.

notifications.title_beginner: Your first tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_beginner: Based on when you planted, ripe or almost-ripe fruit should be appearing now. Pick when the tomato is fully colored and gives slightly when you press it gently. The more you pick, the more the plant produces, so check the plant every day or two once fruit starts coming in.
notifications.title_seasoned: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_seasoned: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Pick when fully colored and slightly soft to the touch. The more you pick, the more the plant produces, so stay on top of it.

notifications.title_beginner: Frost coming in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks, time to finish strong
notifications.body_beginner: Your growing season is nearly over. Pinch out the growing tips at the top of each stem now so the plant puts its remaining energy into ripening the fruit already there rather than growing new stems. Harvest everything you can, and bring in any green tomatoes, as they will ripen on a windowsill indoors over the next few weeks.
notifications.title_seasoned: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks, finish strong
notifications.body_seasoned: Your growing season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips now so the plant puts all its remaining energy into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest anything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a windowsill.

notifications.body_beginner: You haven't logged anything in a couple of weeks. How does the plant look? Any fruit coming in, any spots on the leaves, or anything that looks off? Catching problems early makes a big difference, and a quick look around the plant takes two minutes.
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a couple of weeks. How is the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Regular check-ins help you catch problems early.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost tonight, cover your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Freezing temperatures are forecast tonight. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one hard freeze can kill the plant. Cover them with an old bedsheet, a bucket, or frost cloth before dark, and uncover in the morning once temperatures are back above freezing. Container plants can be moved inside.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning, protect your tomatoes tonight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Temperatures are dropping close to freezing tonight. Cover plants with fleece or old bedsheets, or bring containers inside. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one cold night can end your season early.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Very hot days ahead, help your tomatoes through
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Several very hot days are forecast. Above about 95°F, tomato flowers tend to drop without setting fruit, not a disease, just heat stress. Water deeply in the early morning so the soil stays moist through the day, and add a layer of mulch around the base to hold that moisture. If you have shade cloth, draping it over the plant in the hottest part of the afternoon can help.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress warning for your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Several very hot days ahead. Tomato flowers can drop when temperatures stay above 95°F. Water deeply in the early morning, add mulch around the base to retain moisture, and consider shade cloth during the hottest part of the day.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: It's been dry, water your tomatoes deeply
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Dry conditions have been building. Uneven watering right now can cause blossom end rot (dark patches on the fruit bottom) and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base of the plant, aiming for 1 to 2 inches this week. A thick layer of mulch around the stem helps hold whatever moisture the soil has between watering sessions.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: It has been dry. Inconsistent watering at this stage causes blossom end rot and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base, aiming for 1-2 inches this week. Mulching around the stem helps hold moisture.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: High humidity, check your tomato leaves
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Humid weather creates ideal conditions for fungal diseases like early and late blight. Take a few minutes to check the lower leaves for brown spots, yellow patches, or anything unusual. If you spot affected leaves, remove them right away and don't put them in your compost. Keeping the plant staked and open for airflow is your best prevention.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions are ideal for early and late blight. Check lower leaves for dark spots with yellow halos. Remove any affected leaves immediately and do not compost them. Good airflow around the plant is your best defense.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain coming, harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A lot of rain in a short period can cause ripe tomatoes to split. Pick anything that looks close to ready before the rain arrives. After the rain, check the lower leaves, as soil splash from heavy rain can spread disease spores up onto the leaves.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain, harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A lot of rain in a short time can split ripe fruit. Pick anything that is nearly ready before it cracks, and check for soil splash on lower leaves which can spread disease.

germination.text_beginner: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. If you have a heat mat, use it; if not, the top of a refrigerator or any spot that stays around 75°F works well. Most grape tomato seeds sprout in 5 to 7 days with steady warmth.
germination.text_seasoned: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. A heat mat, the top of your refrigerator, or anywhere consistently warm works well. Most tomato seeds germinate in 5-7 days at 75°F.

germination.text_beginner: Cover your seed tray with a plastic dome or cling wrap until the first sprout appears, then remove it immediately. The dome traps humidity to keep the seed surface moist during germination, but once the shoot emerges, that same warm, still air is the ideal environment for damping off, a fungal problem that collapses the stem at the soil line and kills the seedling overnight with no recovery. Remove the dome at first sprout and give the seedlings fresh air; slightly drier conditions at the soil surface prevent it.
germination.text_seasoned: Cover your tray with a humidity dome or cling film until the first sprout appears, then remove it immediately. The dome holds humidity to prevent the seed surface from drying out during germination, but once the shoot emerges the same warm, still, humid air becomes the ideal environment for Pythium and Rhizoctonia, the soilborne fungi that cause damping off. Damping off collapses the stem at soil level; there is no recovery. Fresh air and slightly drier conditions at the soil surface after emergence are the primary prevention.

seedling.text_beginner: If your seedlings are tall and thin and look weak, they need more light, not less water. Move them right next to a bright window (but pull them back a few inches at night if the window gets cold), or set up a grow light to shine on them for 14-16 hours each day. Pale color is a sign of the same problem.
seedling.text_seasoned: Leggy, stretched seedlings almost always mean not enough light, not overwatering. Get them as close to a bright window as possible, or use a grow light 14-16 hours a day.

seedling.text_beginner: Once you have two sets of true leaves, move the seedling into its own small pot or 3-inch cell. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so plant it a little deeper than it was sitting, as the buried stem becomes more roots.
seedling.text_seasoned: Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so you can bury them deeper than they were, which builds a stronger plant.

established.text_beginner: Hardening off takes 7 to 10 days and is worth every day of it. The seedlings have been raised in still indoor air with no wind or direct sun, and their leaves aren't built for outdoor conditions yet. Start with 1 to 2 hours outside in a sheltered, partly shaded spot, then add more time and more sun each day. Plants that are hardened off gradually settle in within a week of transplanting; plants that skip it can take 3 weeks to recover.
established.text_seasoned: Harden off over 7-10 days, a gradual introduction to outdoor conditions rather than an abrupt move. Indoors, seedlings have thin cuticles, less concentrated chlorophyll, and stomata that have never experienced wind. Sudden outdoor exposure causes sunscald, wilting, and cold stress even on mild days. Start with 1-2 hours in a sheltered, partly shaded spot, adding time and sun exposure each day. Plants that skip hardening off sulk for 2-3 weeks after transplanting while they adapt.

established.text_beginner: Plant your tomatoes deeper than the pot they came in. Dig a hole deep enough to bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves, as every bit of buried stem grows roots, and more roots means a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant from day one.
established.text_seasoned: Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot. Bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots.

flowering.text_beginner: Give the flowering stems a gentle shake or tap in the morning to help with pollination. Tomato flowers release pollen when they vibrate, and bees do this naturally, but in sheltered gardens or when bee activity is low, giving the stems a quick shake does the same job. Without it, some flowers drop before setting fruit.
flowering.text_seasoned: A gentle shake or tap of the flowering stem in the morning helps pollen transfer. Tomato flowers are self-fertile, but pollen is released most efficiently by vibration: bumblebees accomplish this naturally through buzz pollination, where wing-beat frequency resonates the anthers and dislodges pollen. In sheltered gardens, polytunnels, or indoor growing environments without significant wind or bee activity, the plant depends on incidental vibration for pollination. Shaking the stem in the morning (when pollen is freshly released) is the practical substitute. Under-pollinated flowers drop without setting fruit.

flowering.text_beginner: Once flowers open, stop any high-nitrogen fertilizer and switch to a tomato fertilizer or one with a high third number (potassium). Nitrogen is what makes plants grow leaves, exactly right early on but exactly wrong once flowering starts. Potassium is what the plant needs to build good fruit.
flowering.text_seasoned: Stop high-nitrogen feeding when flowers appear and switch to a high-potassium, low-nitrogen feed. Nitrogen drives vegetative growth by stimulating cell division and chlorophyll synthesis, exactly what you want early in the season and exactly what you don't want once flowering starts; potassium plays a different role: it regulates stomatal opening, drives sugar transport from leaves into developing fruit, and is critical for cell wall formation in the fruit itself. A tomato-specific or high-K fertilizer (look for an NPK ratio with a high last number, such as 5-10-10 or 4-12-8) used from first flowering onward translates directly into heavier, better-flavored fruit.

harvest.text_beginner: Pick regularly, every day or two once fruit is coming in. Leaving ripe tomatoes on the vine slows the plant's production of new fruit, especially with indeterminate varieties like most grape tomatoes.
harvest.text_seasoned: Pick regularly, as ripe fruit left on the vine slows new fruit production, especially in indeterminate varieties.

harvest.text_beginner: Try a few tomatoes at different stages to find what your palate likes. Some varieties are sweetest just at peak color; others improve with a few more days. Your own taste is the best harvest guide you have.
harvest.text_seasoned: Taste as you go. Different varieties peak at different moments: some are best just before fully ripe, others need a few more days. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.

end_of_season.text_beginner: When nights drop regularly below 50°F, pinch out the growing tips, the very top of each stem. Below 55°F, tomatoes stop setting new fruit reliably. By removing the growing tips, you redirect the plant's energy into ripening the fruit already on the vine rather than trying to grow new stems that won't produce before frost.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: When nights drop regularly below 50°F, pinch out all the growing tips. Below 55°F, pollen viability drops sharply and fruit set becomes unlikely even if flowers are still opening. At 50°F and below, the plant is physiologically in decline for new fruit production. Pinching the growing tips, the terminal bud at the top of each stem, removes the hormone sink that draws resources toward new vegetative growth, redirecting carbohydrates toward the fruit already on the vine. A plant with 10-15 near-ripe tomatoes will finish them faster once it has stopped trying to grow new stems.

end_of_season.text_beginner: Green tomatoes brought in before frost will ripen indoors. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool (60 to 65°F) and dark, not the refrigerator. Refrigerator temperatures cause chilling injury, which produces the mealy, flavorless texture that makes people think they dislike tomatoes. Room temperature speeds ripening but hurts flavor; 60 to 65°F is the right balance.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool (60-65°F) and dark, not the refrigerator. Refrigerator temperatures (below 50°F) cause chilling injury: cell membranes in the fruit lose their selective permeability, releasing enzymes that break down cell walls, producing the mealy texture and muted flavor characteristic of cold-stored tomatoes. The damage is irreversible once it occurs. Ripening indoors at 60-65°F is slower than at room temperature but preserves flavor better than hurrying at 70°F+.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 4 to 8 lbs per plant over the season, with vigorous indeterminate grape hybrids often at the upper end. Fruit is borne in long, heavy clusters, so a productive plant can be strikingly loaded. Production continues until frost.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: About 4 to 8 pounds of fruit per plant over the season, often at the higher end for these vigorous plants. Grape tomatoes set fruit in long, heavy clusters, so a single healthy plant produces a lot, and the vines keep going until frost.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: At peak, a healthy plant yields a generous bowlful every 2 to 3 days, with whole clusters ripening in sequence. Production accelerates from first harvest, peaks in the hottest weeks, then slows as temperatures drop and days shorten. Because the fruit holds well on the vine and cracks little, a missed picking day costs less than it would with cherries.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: At its peak, a healthy plant gives you a generous bowlful every 2 to 3 days, with clusters ripening a few fruit at a time. It builds up after the first tomatoes, peaks in the hottest weeks, then slows as the season cools. Because grape tomatoes crack so little, missing a picking day is far less costly than with cherry tomatoes.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Your first year, expect to land somewhere in the lower part of the range while you learn what your specific spot needs. The four things that make the biggest difference are sun (at least 6 hours of direct sun daily), consistent watering, good soil, and catching pest or disease problems early. If you're picking enough tomatoes to fill a salad bowl every week or two, that is a real first-season success.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: First-season plants often yield at the low end of the range as growers learn site-specific conditions. Soil organic matter, sun hours, consistent watering, and timely disease response each contribute materially to where within the 4-8 lb range a plant lands. Getting enough tomatoes to fill a salad bowl regularly is a genuine first-season success.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You'll see the leaves turn black or dark brown and go limp, sometimes overnight after a cold night. Tomatoes have no cold tolerance at all. Even without a hard freeze, temperatures below 50°F cause what's called chilling injury: the plant's cells start to break down, and young transplants are especially vulnerable because they haven't built up a protective waxy coating yet. It's tempting to think the plant just needs time to recover, but if it was hit by frost, it usually won't come back. For next time: wait until both your nighttime lows and your soil temperature are reliably above 60°F before transplanting.
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until nighttime temperatures are reliably above 50°F AND your soil is above 60°F before transplanting, checking soil temperature 2 to 3 inches deep with an inexpensive probe thermometer. In Zones 3 to 5 this often means waiting until late May or early June no matter what the calendar says.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are warm-season crops with tropical origin and have no cold tolerance mechanism, unlike brassicas or root vegetables, they cannot harden or acclimate to cold. Chilling injury begins below 50°F and cell damage accelerates near freezing; a single frost event at the transplant stage usually kills the plant outright because young transplants have not yet developed the protective waxy cuticle layer that provides some buffer in established plants. Soil temperature is as important as air temperature: roots in cold soil (below 60°F) cannot take up water or nutrients efficiently even when air temperatures are acceptable, which causes transplant shock that looks like cold damage but persists for weeks after the weather improves.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until both nighttime air temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. Check soil temperature with a probe thermometer 2-3 inches deep in the actual planting bed, as a south-facing raised bed can be 10°F warmer than a shaded in-ground bed on the same day. In zones 3-5, this means waiting until late May or even early June, regardless of calendar date.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Tomato plants can run into a few common problems. Blight is a leaf disease that shows up first on the bottom leaves and spreads fastest in wet, humid weather. Blossom end rot is the black or brown sunken spot on the bottom of the tomato, it looks like a nutrient problem, but it's almost always caused by uneven watering (dry one day, soaked the next). Adding calcium won't fix it. Steady moisture will.
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water at the base of the plant (not from overhead) and stake the plant for good airflow, as leaves that dry quickly after rain are far harder for blight to infect. Move your tomatoes to a different bed each year; blight spores can persist in the soil and on old plant material. For blossom end rot: mulch heavily and water deeply and consistently rather than in small, frequent amounts.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Two of the most common problems, blight and blossom end rot, are frequently misdiagnosed and mistreated. Blight (early or late) is a fungal or oomycete disease that enters through wet leaf surfaces; spores splash up from soil and spread rapidly in warm, humid conditions, progressing from lower leaves upward. Removing affected leaves immediately slows but does not stop spread once established. Blossom end rot presents as a sunken, dark patch on the blossom end of developing fruit. Despite appearances, it is not a fungal disease and adding calcium to the soil rarely fixes it. The actual mechanism is calcium transport failure: calcium moves into developing fruit through the water stream in the xylem, and when watering is inconsistent, especially dry periods followed by heavy irrigation, the transpiration-driven flow to the blossom end is interrupted, and those cells die. Steady moisture at the root zone is the only reliable fix.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water at the base, never overhead, to eliminate the splash route that delivers blight spores to leaves. Stake and prune for airflow, as leaves that dry quickly after rain or dew are far less vulnerable. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year; blight spores persist in soil and on plant debris, and a fresh location breaks the inoculum cycle. For blossom end rot: mulch heavily to buffer moisture swings, and water deeply and consistently rather than shallowly and frequently.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Yellow lower leaves and wilting even when the soil is wet are the signs of overwatering. Soggy soil pushes out the air roots need, so the roots suffocate and the plant wilts even though there is plenty of water. People often respond by watering more, which makes it worse. Cracked fruit is a related problem, but here is some good news: grape tomatoes have thick skins and crack far less than cherry tomatoes, so cracking is much less of a worry. When it does happen, it follows a heavy watering after a dry stretch. The fix either way is consistency: steady moisture rather than dry spells followed by big soakings.
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water deeply and less often rather than a little every day. Deep watering encourages roots to grow down where the soil stays more stable; roots near the surface are the first to suffocate or dry out. A 2 to 3 inch layer of mulch around the base dramatically reduces moisture swings between waterings.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Waterlogged soil drives out the oxygen roots need for respiration, so roots in anaerobic conditions die back and the plant cannot take up water or nutrients even as the soil stays wet. Yellowing lower leaves come first, then a general wilt that paradoxically mimics drought. Fruit cracking is a related but distinct problem: grape tomatoes resist it far better than cherry types because their thicker, less elastic skin tolerates the rapid cell expansion that splits a thin cherry skin. When a grape does crack, it is typically after a sudden surge of water on a fruit whose skin has stopped stretching. Both problems trace to inconsistency rather than sheer volume; a plant on a steady 1 to 2 inches per week rarely shows either.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply and less frequently rather than a small amount every day. Deep watering (wetting the soil to 8-10 inches) encourages roots to grow down where soil moisture is more stable; shallow watering concentrates roots at the surface where they are most vulnerable to both drought and saturation. Mulching 2-3 inches around the base dramatically reduces moisture swings between waterings, which is the single most effective intervention against both fruit cracking and blossom end rot.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Flowers dropping before they form fruit and dark sunken patches on the bottom of tomatoes are the two big signs of insufficient or uneven watering. When water gets cut off during flowering, the plant sheds its flowers to conserve resources, physically cutting them loose at the stem. The dark patch on the fruit's base is called blossom end rot; it looks like a nutrient problem but it's almost always caused by uneven soil moisture, not a lack of calcium in your soil. People often add calcium supplements, but that won't fix it; steady, consistent watering will. Note that heat above 90°F causes the same flower-drop, so both can happen at the same time.
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Not enough water
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Aim for 1 to 2 inches of water per week, delivered consistently. Mulch around the base with straw or shredded leaves to slow the soil from drying out. In hot climates (Zones 8 to 11), a drip line on a timer is the most reliable way to keep moisture steady without thinking about it every day.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Water stress during flowering triggers an abscission response: the plant activates an enzyme-driven separation layer at the base of each flower stem, dropping the flower before fruit can form. The same response is triggered by extreme heat (above 90°F daytime, below 55°F nighttime), which means during a heat wave, blossom drop can occur even if the soil seems adequately moist. During fruit development, inconsistent soil moisture is the primary cause of blossom end rot: calcium is transported to developing fruit through the transpiration stream, and interrupted water flow to the blossom end kills those cells. The external result is a sunken, darkened patch on the fruit's base.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Aim for 1-2 inches of water per week delivered consistently. Mulch heavily around the base to buffer the soil against rapid drying, as a 2-3 inch layer of straw or shredded leaves can halve moisture loss on a hot day. In zones 8-11, where summer heat makes consistent moisture especially difficult, a drip system on a timer is the most reliable tool. Water at the base of the plant, never the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: If your plant grows tall and leafy but produces very little fruit, or pale, flavorless tomatoes, sun is probably the problem. Tomatoes need at least 6 hours of direct sun per day; below that, the plant puts its energy into growing stems and leaves instead of fruit. What fruit does form tends to be bland because sugar development depends on sunlight. A secondary sign: shaded plants tend to stay wet longer and get more disease, because leaves don't dry out well in low light. If your spot gets 4-5 hours, you'll get some fruit, but manage expectations: fewer tomatoes, smaller, and less sweet than a full-sun plant.
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Tomatoes need at least 6 hours of direct sun per day, and this is not negotiable. If your current spot is borderline, walk your garden at different times of day and look for a spot a few feet over that gets more morning sun before something shades it. Compact grape tomato varieties like dwarf or patio types tolerate slightly less sun than full-size plants.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are among the most light-demanding vegetables: photosynthesis is the energy source for both vegetative growth and fruit sugar development, and fruit quality is directly proportional to the plant's photosynthetic output. Below 6 hours of direct sun, the plant redirects what energy it has toward survival, stem elongation and leaf area, rather than reproduction. Fruit set drops sharply, and what fruit does form is typically thin-skinned, pale, and bland. A secondary effect is increased disease: shaded plants stay wetter longer after rain or irrigation, and poor airflow through dense, etiolated growth creates the humid microclimate that blight and leaf mold need to establish.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes are not negotiable on sun requirements. Below 6 hours of direct sun, expect significantly reduced yields and higher disease pressure regardless of everything else done correctly. If the current spot is marginal (6-7 hours), it is worth mapping sun across the garden before committing the bed again, as a spot that gets shade from a fence or tree in the afternoon may have 2-3 more hours of morning sun available just a few feet away. Dwarf or patio-type grape tomatoes tolerate slightly less sun than full-size plants.

crops.description_beginner: A small, sweet tomato shaped like an oblong grape, and an easy, heavy producer for a first garden. Grape tomatoes grow like cherry tomatoes and taste similarly sweet, but they have a thicker skin and meatier, less juicy flesh. That thicker skin is the reason gardeners love them: the fruit cracks far less than thin-skinned cherry tomatoes, and it keeps much longer after picking, often a week or more on the counter. The plants are indeterminate, which means they keep growing and setting fruit in long clusters from early summer until frost instead of ripening everything at once. One plant gives you a lot of tomatoes over 10 to 14 weeks. Modern varieties like Santa, Juliet, and Sweet Hearts also have built-in disease resistance. If you are in a cold zone (3 to 5), pick a faster variety, around 65 days, and warm the soil before planting. If you are in a warm zone (9 to 11), you can plant again in late summer for a second, cool-season crop.

succession_policy.tip_beginner: One planting gives you tomatoes all summer until frost kills the plant, no need to replant mid-season. If you're in a warm climate like Zone 9 or warmer (think Southern California, Phoenix, or South Florida), you can start a second planting in late summer for a fall and winter harvest.
succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Not a true succession crop, one planting produces all season. In Zone 9+ you can start a second batch in late summer for a winter harvest.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Produces continuously from one planting all season. In Zone 9+ a second late-summer sowing can extend into winter.

crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick when the tomato is fully and evenly colored, usually deep red, and firm with just a little give when you squeeze it gently. Grape tomatoes are more forgiving than cherry tomatoes about exactly when you pick: the thicker skin means they crack much less if you leave them on the vine an extra day or two to sweeten up. A ripe one twists off easily; if you have to tug, give it another day. The fruit grows in long clusters, and they do not all ripen at the same time, so pick the ripe ones and come back for the rest in a few days. Try to harvest in the morning when it is cooler, since fruit held in hot sun goes soft faster.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start tomatoes from seeds indoors, five to six weeks before planting outside. In most of Minnesota, this is mid-April. Grape and cherry tomatoes mature faster than larger-fruited types; 6-week indoor start is appropriate. (UMN)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Many gardeners plant transplants the last week or two of May, after danger of frost has passed and air and soil temperatures warm. (MSU)
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start your warm season crops indoors for transplanting in mid-June, once the threat of frost has passed. Transplant outdoors after all danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed. Don't be in a rush to transplant these tropical species. (UMaine, northern Maine Z3-4; UMN; NDSU)

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Grape tomato varieties typically mature 65-75 days from transplant. (UGA Vegetable Garden Calendar; Clemson HGIC; MSU Extension)

harvest_end.label: primary

harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative policy: harvest_end = first_frost - 5 days to buffer against frost-risk week and to ensure notifications arrive before plants are killed.

Grape types (65-75 days from transplant) finish a fall crop before the first frost in these zones. (Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331; Clemson HGIC)

plant_out.label: primary

VCE gives a zone-6 fall tomato transplant window of June 10-July 10; Clemson sets a fall tomato transplant deadline of about July 25 for the warmer zone-7 end. Back-timed from each zone's first-frost date. (Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331; Clemson HGIC)

harvest_start.label: primary

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest runs until the first fall frost cuts the plants short, late October in zone 6 and mid-November in zone 7. (Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331)

4.notes: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost. Wall-O-Waters can extend your season by 2-3 weeks.
4.zone_notes: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost. Choose fast-maturing varieties for best yield.

5.notes: Plant after soil hits 60°F. Mulch to retain moisture and prevent soil splash on lower leaves.
5.zone_notes: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost. Protect transplants if late frost threatens.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold northern states (zones 3 through 7) you grow grape tomatoes once a year, as a single summer crop. What limits the season here is frost on both ends, not summer heat: you plant after the last spring frost, pick all summer, and the plants are finished when the first fall frost arrives. There is no summer break the way hotter regions have, because northern summers usually are not hot enough to stop the plants from setting fruit. Wait to set out transplants until a week or two after your last frost, when nights stay warm and the soil has warmed up. Grape tomatoes ripen fast (about 65 to 75 days after transplanting), so they finish in time even where summers are short. In the coldest zones, pick quick varieties and warm the soil with black plastic mulch or season-extending covers; in the milder zones 6 and 7 you have time to plant a second batch in early summer for a fall crop.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 through 7) grows grape tomatoes as a single frost-bracketed summer crop: the limiting factor on both ends is frost, not heat. Transplants go out a week or two after the last spring frost, once nights stay above the low 50s°F and soil warms past about 60°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through summer until plants are cut short by the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat exclusion here: unlike the Southeast or the desert valleys, northern summers rarely sustain the high day and night temperatures that stop fruit set, so the winter gaps are frost pauses and the season is uninterrupted between them. Grape types (65 to 75 days from transplant) are well suited to short seasons and ripen before first frost even in zone 3. The cold end (zones 3 and 4) leans on fast-maturing varieties and season extension (black plastic mulch, Wall-O-Waters), while the warm end (zones 6 and 7) has room for a second transplanting in early-to-mid summer for a fall harvest. Frost dates shift sharply across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (University of Minnesota Extension; North Dakota State University Extension; Michigan State University Extension; University of Maine Cooperative Extension)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: high day and especially night temperatures push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Grape types are heat resistant, so this pause is shorter for them than for large-fruited tomatoes, and a few varieties keep setting through it. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf area you can grow grape tomatoes twice a year, once in spring and again in fall, with a summer break in between when it gets too hot for the plants to set fruit. Grape tomatoes take the heat better than big tomatoes, so their summer break is shorter. Plant your spring crop early enough to pick before the worst heat, then plant again in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf region runs two grape tomato seasons, spring and fall, split by a summer heat window when high day and night temperatures cause blossom drop and fruit set fails. Grape types handle this better than large-fruited tomatoes: they are heat resistant and quick to mature, so the summer pause is shorter for them and a few varieties keep setting through it. Time the spring crop to ripen before peak heat; set the fall crop out in mid-to-late summer to produce into the cooler autumn. The warmer zone 9 end of the region plants the spring crop earlier and the fall crop later than the zone 8 interior. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

start_indoors.source_quote: start plants indoors 6-8 weeks prior to the date you want to plant the garden
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start grape tomato seed indoors about six weeks before the spring transplant date. In the interior valleys that places seeding in late February into March. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC ANR)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: tomatoes ... Interior Valleys: April-May
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set grape tomato transplants out in the interior valleys in April and May, after the last frost and once the soil has warmed. Although the mediterranean-climate last frost passes in late January to mid February, tomatoes wait for warm soil: plant transplants when soil is about 65 degrees F and nights stay above 50 degrees F, which in the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys is typically late April. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC ANR)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: Interior Valleys: April-May
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Grape tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after transplanting (about 55 to 70 days to maturity, mid near 62), bringing the first interior-valley fruit in around late June into July. (UC Master Gardener Program)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Interior Valleys: April-May
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: From a single spring planting the interior valleys produce one long harvest tail, carrying grape tomatoes through the hot summer and into fall up to first frost. Grape types are heat resistant and keep setting through the peak summer heat better than large-fruited tomatoes, so the valley grows one continuous season rather than splitting into spring and fall crops. (UC Master Gardener Program; UC ANR)

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's interior valleys you plant grape tomatoes once, in spring (April or May), and then pick them all the way through summer and into fall until the first frost. You do not plant a second fall crop the way gardeners do in hotter, more humid places, because here grape tomatoes handle the summer heat well and just keep producing from that one planting. Wait to plant until the soil has warmed up, usually late April, even though the last frost is earlier.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: The interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and similar) grow grape tomatoes as a single long season rather than the spring-and-fall split used in the humid Southeast. Transplants go out in April and May, after the mediterranean-climate last frost and once soil warms past about 65°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through the hot summer into fall up to first frost. Grape types are heat resistant and keep setting fruit through the peak valley heat better than large-fruited tomatoes, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop here. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC ANR)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives interior-valley tomatoes as April-May (spring transplant) with no documented fall window; Sacramento County MG monthly tips corroborate a single late-April soil-temperature-gated planting. UC Davis Plant Sciences (read for confidence, not cited: catalog admission deferred to Claude Code lane) independently frames Central Valley tomato as a single spring planting with one long harvest tail. Sources agree on single-season. No second_planting band and no heat_pause authored: grape is heat resistant and the canonical extension framing is one continuous warm season, not a spring/summer-pause/fall split. Contrast se_gulf (UGA C943 gives an explicit fall tomato deadline, hence two-window).

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: start plants indoors 6-8 weeks prior to the date you want to plant the garden
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start grape tomato seed indoors about six weeks before the May transplant date, placing seeding in the second half of March. On the cool North Coast the indoor head start matters more than inland: nights stay cool and the outdoor window does not open until the soil and air warm in May. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: tomatoes ... North & North Coast: May
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set grape tomato transplants out along the North Coast in May, once the marine-influenced spring has warmed enough for the plants to grow. The limiting factor here is heat, not frost: the last frost passes earlier, but tomatoes wait for warmth because coastal nights can sit below 55 degrees F in any month and cool summers slow growth. In Marin and similar coastal counties early May is usually warm enough to transplant. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: North & North Coast: May
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Grape tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after a May transplant (about 55 to 70 days to maturity, mid near 62), bringing the first North Coast fruit in around July. Cool coastal summers can slow ripening relative to inland, so first pickings may run a little later in the foggier locations. (UC Master Gardener Program; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: North & North Coast: May
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: From the single May planting the North Coast produces one warm-season harvest that carries through summer and tapers in October as the coast cools and days shorten. The season is bounded on the back end by falling temperatures and light rather than by a hard frost: coastal first frost comes late, but grape production winds down once the warm-season window closes. Microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm locally. (UC Master Gardener Program; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's North Coast (the foggy coast from about Monterey north, including Marin), you plant grape tomatoes once, in May, and then pick them through summer into early fall. Here the thing holding tomatoes back is a lack of heat, not frost: the coast stays cool and foggy, and nights can drop below 55°F even in summer, so the plants need the warmer late-spring weather before they will really grow. Wait until May to set out transplants, give them the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have, and choose varieties that do well in cool summers. There is no second fall planting here, because the warm season is short.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The North Coast (Monterey County north, including the cool marine-influenced counties such as Marin) grows grape tomatoes as a single short warm season set by heat availability rather than frost. Transplants go out in May, later than the interior valleys, because coastal summers are cool and nights can sit below 55°F in any month. A single planting then carries one harvest through summer and tapers in October as the coast cools and days shorten, ahead of the late coastal first frost. This is the cool-limited case: the limiting factor is insufficient summer heat, not a midsummer heat exclusion, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Cool-summer-adapted varieties and the warmest, most sheltered sites do best, and microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives North & North Coast tomatoes as May (transplant), a single month with no semicolon and no fall window (contrast the table's genuine two-window crops such as snap beans 'July; May-June'). UC Marin Master Gardeners ('Tomato time!') independently confirms an early-May transplant and the cool-limit mechanism (Marin nights below 55F in any month; tomatoes need warmth). San Mateo/San Francisco MG and Monterey Bay MG corroborate cool coastal summers and a May start. Two independent T1 sources confirm single-window and the absence of a second window.
plantings_provenance.cool_limited_exception: ca_north_coast is the documented cool-limited exception to the warm-region heat-primary anchoring rule. The warm season is SHORT because summer never gets hot enough (marine layer, sub-55F nights), NOT because of a midsummer heat exclusion. No heat_pause is authored: there is no summer pause, the season is bounded by lack of heat at both shoulders. Contrast ca_desert / ca_interior summer behavior.
plantings_provenance.harvest_end_basis: Back-end boundary is production/temperature-limited (coast cools and days shorten in fall), not a hard frost cutoff. Coastal zone 9b/10a first frost is late (Nov-Dec or later), but grape production winds down in October as the warm-season window closes. harvest_end set to end of October; calendar fall months read 'wait' rather than 'cold_pause' because the season closes on heat/light, not frost. Table 13.2's own disclaimer (microclimate varies sharply) is surfaced in region_notes.
plantings_provenance.no_heat_pause_reason: Cool-limited region: the limiting factor is insufficient heat, so there is no summer heat exclusion to encode. Grape heat-resistance (relevant where a summer heat pause exists, e.g. se_gulf month 7) does not apply here.
plantings_provenance.second_planting_absence: z9 + z10 single-season; no sourced fall window. Table 13.2 lists a single May tomato window for North Coast; no second-planting band authored. Explanation carried in region_notes per the calendar-UI surfacing decision (2026-06-05).

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: tomatoes ... South Coast: April - July 15
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set grape tomato transplants out on the South Coast across a long window from April through about mid-July, the widest planting window of the California regions. The mild marine climate (San Diego and the Los Angeles basin coast) has no midsummer heat exclusion, so there is no summer planting pause: gardeners plant once in this window for a single long season rather than a spring-and-fall split. Plant when the soil has warmed and nights stay mild. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: Summer vegetables are warm season plants that span from March-August, depending on where you live ... Tomatoes typically need a range of 65 degrees F (nighttime) to 90 degrees F to produce and set fruit
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Grape tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after the spring transplant (about 55 to 70 days to maturity, mid near 62), bringing the first South Coast fruit in around early summer; the mild marine coast can then carry harvest through summer and fall, in the frost-free immediate coast as far as the end of the year. (UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County; UC Master Gardener Program)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Summer vegetables are warm season plants that span from March-August, depending on where you live
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: On the mild South Coast a single planting carries one long harvest through summer and fall. In the frost-free immediate coast (zone 10) fruit can be picked through the end of the year; slightly cooler inland-edge sites (zone 9) taper a little earlier in late fall. The season is bounded by cooling and the late or absent coastal frost, not by summer heat. Grape types are heat resistant and keep setting through the warm season. (UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County; UC Master Gardener Program)

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's South Coast (the mild coast of San Diego and the Los Angeles basin), you plant grape tomatoes once, anytime from April through about mid-July, and then pick them through summer and fall. Right on the frost-free coast you can often harvest all the way to the end of the year. The weather here is gentle, so there is no summer break in planting the way hotter inland and southeastern areas have, and there is no separate fall crop, just one long season from a single planting. Plant when the soil has warmed and give the plants full sun.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The South Coast (San Luis Obispo County south, including the San Diego and Los Angeles basin coast) grows grape tomatoes as a single long warm season. Transplants go out across a wide April through mid-July window, the longest planting window of the California regions, into a mild marine climate with no midsummer heat exclusion. A single planting then carries one continuous harvest: on the frost-free immediate coast (zone 10) fruit can be picked through the end of the year, while slightly cooler inland-edge sites (zone 9) taper a little earlier in late fall. The season is bounded by fall cooling and the late or absent coastal frost rather than by summer heat, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Grape types are heat resistant and set well through the warm season; coastal microclimate varies, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives South Coast tomatoes as 'April - July 15' -- a single long continuous plant-out window with no semicolon (not a two-window split). UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County (growing guide / Vegetable Resources) independently confirm the long single season: tomatoes harvest 'from early summer through the end of the year in coastal areas', summer transplants go in during the March-April frame as soil warms, and the mild marine coast has no midsummer heat exclusion. The 'two-season' framing seen in some secondary sources is the OPTION to plant a later batch within this long window, not a forced spring-pause-fall split. Two T1 sources agree on single continuous window.
plantings_provenance.no_heat_pause_reason: Mild marine South Coast has no midsummer heat exclusion (unlike ca_desert / low_desert_az / se_gulf). No heat_pause authored. Grape heat-resistance further supports continuous warm-season set.

start_indoors.source_quote: start plants indoors 6-8 weeks prior to the date you want to plant the garden
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the main desert crop, start grape tomato seed indoors in fall (about October into November) for the winter transplant. The desert calendar is inverted: the main planting goes out in the mild winter months, not spring, to beat the lethal summer heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: tomatoes ... Desert Valleys: Dec-March
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the main grape tomato crop out in the desert valleys across the mild winter window, December through mid-March, so plants flower and set fruit before the summer heat arrives. This is the inverse of cold-climate timing: in Imperial and Coachella the winter is the growing season and the summer is the exclusion. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The main desert crop begins ripening roughly two months after the winter transplant (about 55 to 70 days to maturity, mid near 62), bringing spring fruit from around February into June before the heat shuts production down. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The main spring harvest runs into June and then ends as summer heat halts fruit set. A separate fall crop (see second planting) reopens the season after the heat breaks. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

start_indoors.label: fall
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall desert crop, start seed in mid-to-late summer (July into August) so transplants are ready to go out in September once the worst heat passes. The fall window is set by the break in the summer heat exclusion, not by the Time-of-Planting table (which lists only the Dec-March main desert window for tomatoes). (Mechanism: UC Statewide IPM Program; main-window table: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

plant_out.label: fall
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall desert crop out in September, once the summer heat exclusion breaks, for harvest through the mild late fall and winter. The September timing is taken from the end of the summer fruit-set-failure window rather than from the Time-of-Planting table, which lists only the Dec-March main desert window for tomatoes. (Mechanism: UC Statewide IPM Program; main-window table: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

harvest_start.label: fall
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening around November and produces through the mild desert winter into January. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

harvest_end.label: fall
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall harvest carries through the mild desert winter, ending around January as the next winter-spring main crop begins. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: The desert summer is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the Imperial and Coachella Valleys, June through August daytime highs run well past 95°F and often above 110°F, and tomato flowers fail to set fruit once temperatures stay above about 95°F (high heat reduces viable pollen). Unlike the milder southeastern summer, this desert pause is climatic-absolute: it is wide and is not narrowed by grape's heat resistance, because even heat-tolerant grape types cannot set fruit in extreme desert summer heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)
