ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella), the calendar is flipped: you grow grape tomatoes in the cool months and take the summer off, because summer here is too hot for tomatoes to make fruit. Plant your main crop in winter, from December through mid-March, so the plants can grow and set fruit before the heat. From about June through August it is too hot (often over 110°F), and tomato flowers will not set, so there is a summer break. Then plant a second crop in September for tomatoes through the mild late fall and winter. Even heat-loving grape tomatoes cannot handle the peak desert summer, so the summer break is not optional here.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella) grow grape tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar built around a hard summer heat exclusion. The main crop is transplanted in the mild winter window, December through mid-March, and harvested from spring into June; then June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs past 95°F and often above 110°F, which collapses viable pollen), so planting pauses. A second, fall crop is set out in September as the heat breaks and produces through the mild desert winter into January. This summer pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by grape's heat resistance: unlike the milder southeastern Gulf summer, desert peak heat stops fruit set even for heat-tolerant grape types. Confirm local frost and heat timing, which vary across the desert. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives Desert Valleys tomatoes as 'Dec-March' -- the mild-winter MAIN plant window (inverted calendar). UC Statewide IPM Program and UC ANR home-garden guidance anchor the summer heat-exclusion mechanism (desert summer daytime highs past 95-110F; fruit set fails above ~95F as viable pollen collapses). The two-window structure (winter-spring main + September fall crop bracketing a lethal summer) is the canonical desert pattern; UC Riverside County MG (Coachella low desert, read-not-cited, not catalogued) and University of Arizona Extension 'Growing Tomatoes' (low-desert two-season, read-not-cited, AZ source) independently corroborate. Two-window with structured summer heat_pause.
plantings_provenance.heat_inversion_note: Inverted calendar: winter is the growing season, summer is the exclusion. Main plant window Dec-Mar (mild winter), summer heat_pause Jun-Aug, fall replant Sep. This is the heat-inverted mirror of the cool-limited ca_north_coast and the mild ca_south_coast.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_present: Jun-Aug (months 6,7,8). Climatic-absolute exclusion: Imperial/Coachella peak summer (>95-110F) stops fruit set. Mechanism anchored to UC IPM / UC ANR 8159 (>95F collapses viable pollen).
plantings_provenance.grape_pause_not_narrowed: CONTRAST se_gulf (gs_exemplar_finding_001): there, grape's heat resistance narrowed the pause to a single month (month 7). HERE the desert pause is NOT narrowed by grape resistance -- peak desert summer heat is so extreme that even heat-tolerant grape types cannot set fruit. The Jun-Aug pause is the real lethal span regardless of grape resistance. This is a per-region grape judgment, not a universal narrowing.
plantings_provenance.second_planting_present: z9 + z10 both two-season. Discrete fall crop: start_indoors Jul15-Aug15, plant_out Sep, harvest_start Nov, harvest_end Jan. Structured as a discrete second_planting (NOT succession). Mild desert winter lets the fall crop run into January.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: start the seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before transplanting
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start grape tomato seed indoors about six weeks before the spring transplant date. For a mid-to-late-March beginner transplant in Las Cruces (zone 8) that places seeding in early-to-mid February. The Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces chart starts seed earlier, in mid-January, to feed the experienced-grower early-March transplant. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Plant these after all danger of frost
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set grape tomato transplants out in spring once frost danger has passed. For Las Cruces and the Mesilla Valley (zone 8, Chihuahuan high desert) the average last frost is around March 19, so a beginner-safe transplant date is mid-to-late March. The Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces chart shows an earlier, early-March transplant (seed started indoors in mid-January); that earlier date reflects experienced-grower practice setting plants out right at or just before the frost-free point, often with frost protection. For a first season, waiting until after the last frost is the more reliable choice. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: 55 to 70 days
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Grape tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after transplanting. With a mid-to-late-March transplant the spring crop in Las Cruces begins coming in from about mid-to-late May, well ahead of the peak midsummer heat that suppresses fruit set. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: do not set fruit well ... when daytime temperatures exceed 95
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop winds down as peak midsummer heat sets in and daytime temperatures above about 95 degrees F push fruit set toward failure. Grape types, being heat resistant and quick to set in the cooler arid mornings and evenings, hold a little longer into early summer than large-fruited tomatoes before the brief midsummer pause. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: start the seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before transplanting
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed indoors about six weeks before the midsummer transplant date, roughly early-to-mid June. Grape and cherry varieties suit the fall window well because of their shorter days to maturity. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Tomatoes ... start ... transplant
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out after the peak of midsummer heat, in mid-to-late July, so plants establish as temperatures begin to ease and produce into the cooler fall. The local Las Cruces planting chart shows this second tomato transplant window; it is timed to follow the brief midsummer fruit-set pause. (Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart; NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: 55 to 70 days
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about two months after the midsummer transplant, bringing first grape tomatoes in roughly late September into October. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: harvest ... before frost
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop produces into the cooler autumn and is harvested up to the first fall frost, which in Las Cruces (zone 8 high desert) arrives around mid-November. Grape types, heat resistant and quick to mature, make the most of the shorter fall window. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the warm arid Southwest, daytime temperatures above about 95°F at the peak of midsummer push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail (NMSU Circular 457 gives 95°F day and 55°F night as the set thresholds). Grape types are heat resistant and the arid climate's cool nights aid recovery, so this pause is brief, roughly the single hottest month, and shorter for grape than for large-fruited tomatoes. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: Where you live gets very hot in midsummer, so grape tomatoes grow best in two rounds. Plant the first round in mid to late March, after the last frost, and you will start picking tomatoes in mid to late May. When it gets hottest, around July, the plants stop setting new tomatoes for a few weeks because the flowers cannot set in the heat. Plant a second round in mid to late July for a fall crop that keeps going into November, until the first frost. Grape tomatoes handle heat well and your cool nights help, so they bounce back faster than big tomatoes.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid Southwest, including Las Cruces and the Mesilla Valley in zone 8, gives grape tomatoes two planting windows around the peak of summer heat. Set the first crop out in mid to late March, once frost danger has passed (the average last frost is around March 19), for a harvest that begins in mid to late May, well before the most intense heat arrives. Through the hottest stretch of midsummer, daytime temperatures above about 95°F suppress fruit set, so production lulls for roughly the single hottest month, around July. Set a second crop out in mid to late July, transplanting through the heat so plants establish and then set as temperatures ease, for a fall harvest that runs into early November until the first frost. Grape varieties handle the heat better than large slicing tomatoes and the cool desert nights help them keep setting, so the summer lull is shorter for them. A note on sourcing: the spring window follows NMSU statewide guidance and Las Cruces frost data, while the second, midsummer planting comes from the Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces planting chart, a single regional Master Gardener source that we have not been able to corroborate independently. The Dona Ana chart also shows an earlier, early-March transplant for the spring crop, which reflects experienced-grower practice setting out right at the frost-free point; a mid-to-late-March transplant is the more reliable first-season choice.

plantings_provenance.structure_basis: Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart shows two distinct tomato transplant windows (Path A chart read 2026-06-07: 1st transplant early March, 2nd transplant mid-July) separated by a midsummer set-failure window; NMSU Circular 457 fruit-set thresholds (>95F day) plus Mesilla Valley high-desert summer climate independently support a midsummer set-failure pause at month 7. Spring dates frost-anchored (arid_highland); fall dates single-source (MG chart, uncorroborated, disclosed).
plantings_provenance.spring_date_basis: Spring transplant timed to the zone-8 arid_highland last frost (Mar 19; Chihuahuan high desert, BSk; confirmed against NOAA 30% last-32F for Las Cruces = Mar 20). Beginner-safe plant-out mid-to-late March. The Dona Ana County MG chart's earlier early-March transplant (seed mid-Jan) is the seasoned/source anchor, reflecting experienced-grower practice at/just before frost-free. Beginner-safety divergence (hybrid ruling, same pattern as low_desert_az). CORRECTS the prior desert-analogy May transplant.
plantings_provenance.fall_window_basis: Fall transplant window (mid-to-late July; start indoors mid-June) taken from the Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces chart (Path A chart read, 2026-06-07: tomato row shows 1st planting start mid-Jan -> transplant early March; 2nd planting start mid-June -> transplant mid-July). SINGLE-SOURCE, not independently corroborated; disclosed in region_notes_seasoned. Harvest re-derived to arid_highland first frost (Nov 12).
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_basis: Grape-narrowed to month 7 only (set-failure dip, not a plant/harvest exclusion). The chart transplants the fall crop IN mid-July, so July is not a do-not-plant month; it is the peak fruit-set-failure window (CR457: >95F day stops set). Calendar token at month 7 = heat_pause, mirroring the shipped se_gulf zone-8 grape cell (same biology: fall transplant into peak-heat July, plant action carried by second_planting{} on its own track). heat_pause.months=[7] kept coherent with calendar[Jul]=heat_pause for release_verify. Mesilla Valley zone 8 is hot but arid with strong nighttime recovery (nights into the 60s), unlike the zone-9 low deserts where the pause is climatic-absolute and not narrowed. Beefsteak re-derives independently and will likely hold a wider pause.
plantings_provenance.frost_basis: zone_frost_data zone-8 arid_highland variant (Southwest High Desert, Koppen BSk): last_spring Mar 19, first_fall Nov 12, 236 frost-free days. Selected over the generic zone-8 anchor (Feb 15 / Dec 1) because Las Cruces / Mesilla Valley is Chihuahuan high desert (BSk). Cross-checked against NOAA 1991-2020 30%-probability last-32F for Las Cruces (Mar 20) and first-32F (Nov 7-13 band). The prior cell's May transplant and Oct harvest_end were artifacts of the wrong (desert-analogy) anchor.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: start seeds indoors or in a greenhouse in January, six weeks before the last frost
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the spring crop, start grape tomato seed indoors in late fall to early winter so transplants are ready by February. The Arizona low desert runs an inverted, race-the-heat calendar: the spring crop must be in the ground early to set fruit before summer. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: start in mid-March in Southern Arizona as soon as frost damage has ended
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the spring grape tomato crop out in the low desert in February, right after the last frost, so plants flower and set fruit before the summer heat wall. In Phoenix and the Maricopa low desert that heat wall hits hard by late May, so early planting is essential. Choose short-season grape or plum types (60 to 80 days). (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: Choose short-season varieties (less than 70 days)
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop begins ripening about two months after the February transplant, bringing fruit in April and May before the heat shuts production down. Short-season grape types make the narrow spring window. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Poor fruit development during the heat of summer in southern Arizona (July - August) is expected
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring harvest ends in late May to June as summer heat halts fruit set. A separate fall crop (see second planting) reopens the season in September after the heat passes. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

start_indoors.label: fall
start_indoors.source_quote: Start new seeds for September planting in June
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed in June (or take cuttings from straggly spring plants in August) so transplants are ready for a September planting. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

plant_out.label: fall
plant_out.source_quote: Gardeners will get a second chance for healthy tomatoes in September, when summer heat has passed
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out in September as the summer heat passes. Without the hard deadline the spring crop faces, fall plants have time to grow and produce well into the mild low-desert winter. Many low-desert gardeners consider fall their better tomato season. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_start.label: fall
harvest_start.source_quote: hit peak production in October and November
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop reaches peak production in October and November, when low-desert weather is mild. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_end.label: fall
harvest_end.source_quote: fall plants can grow and produce well into December in the low desert
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall harvest runs into December in the low desert before winter frost ends the season. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: The low-desert summer is a hard heat exclusion. In the Phoenix and Maricopa low desert, poor fruit development is expected through the peak of summer (July and August), because daytime temperatures above 90°F reduce the number of viable pollen grains and stop fruit set. The main spring crop runs from a mid-March transplant through late June, then the July-August peak halts set; planting resumes in September once the heat passes. As in the California desert, this pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by grape's heat resistance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

The low-desert summer is a hard heat exclusion. In the Phoenix and Maricopa low desert, poor fruit development is expected through the peak of summer (July and August), because daytime temperatures above 90°F reduce the number of viable pollen grains and stop fruit set. The main spring crop runs from a mid-March transplant through late June, then the July-August peak halts set; planting resumes in September once the heat passes. As in the California desert, this pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by grape's heat resistance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Yuma, and similar), the calendar is flipped and you get two short tomato seasons around a too-hot summer. Plant your spring crop early, in February right after the last frost, and pick fruit in April and May before the heat. From about June through August it is too hot (over 90°F) for tomatoes to set fruit, so there is a summer break. Then plant a second crop in September for tomatoes through fall and into December, which many desert gardeners think is the better season. Pick fast-maturing grape types (60 to 80 days) so they finish before the heat. Even heat-loving grape tomatoes cannot set fruit in peak desert summer.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Maricopa, Yuma) grows grape tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar around a hard summer heat exclusion. The spring crop is transplanted early, in February right after the last frost, and must set fruit before the heat wall arrives by late May; it harvests April into June. June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs above 90°F collapse viable pollen), so planting pauses. A fall crop is set out in September once the heat passes and produces through the mild desert fall into December, often the more productive of the two seasons. Short-season grape and plum types (60 to 80 days) are essential to make the narrow spring window. As in the California desert, the summer pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by grape's heat resistance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078 'Growing Tomatoes' (peer-reviewed, Feb 2024) states the low desert allows two short growing seasons; poor fruit development in the heat of summer (July-August); a second chance in September when summer heat has passed; fall plants produce into December. Maricopa County planting calendar az1005 and the AZ1615 Yuma guide corroborate the spring (Feb) / fall (Sep) two-season structure. Spring transplant Feb (race the late-May heat wall); fall plant Sep. Two-window with structured summer heat_pause.
plantings_provenance.heat_inversion_note: Inverted two-window calendar like ca_desert, but with AZ-specific dates: spring window opens LATER (February transplant, racing the late-May Phoenix heat wall) than the CA desert's Dec-March winter window; fall replant September into December. Zone 9 only.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_present: Jun-Aug (months 6,7,8). az2078: poor fruit development July-August; >90F reduces viable pollen and stops fruit set.
plantings_provenance.grape_pause_not_narrowed: Same judgment as ca_desert: the desert summer pause is NOT narrowed by grape's heat resistance (contrast se_gulf month-7 single-month narrowing). Peak low-desert summer heat stops fruit set even for heat-tolerant grape types.
plantings_provenance.second_planting_present: Zone 9 two-season. Discrete fall crop: start_indoors Jun, plant_out Sep, harvest_start late Oct, harvest_end mid-Dec. az2078 notes fall is often the better season (no hard heat deadline). Discrete second_planting, not succession.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: Start seeds of eggplant, okra, peppers, pumpkin, squashes, and tomatoes for the fall garden
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula the grape tomato season is the cool, dry half of the year, so seed is started in late summer for fall transplanting. UF/IFAS South Florida starts tomato seed in August for the fall garden; counting back about six weeks from the September-October transplant window places indoor sowing in August. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Easy crops that can be grown now include beans, broccoli, carrots, collards, lettuce, green onions, peppers, radishes, spinach, and tomatoes
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set grape tomato transplants out across the long cool-season window. The South Florida calendar opens the fall tomato transplant in September-October and keeps planting open through February, the last month to plant tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Frost is rare on the peninsula, so this is one continuous cross-year window rather than separate spring and fall crops. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Grape tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after transplant (about 55 to 70 days to maturity). With fall transplanting from September into the fall, the peninsula's cool-season harvest begins in November and carries through the mild winter and spring. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Peninsular grape tomato production runs through the mild winter and spring and winds down as peak-summer heat arrives. Larger-fruited tomatoes stop earlier and are grown as a cool-season crop only; grape types, being heat resistant, hold a productive tail into early summer before the July-August pause. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula the summer gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; grape types are heat resistant, so the exclusion is narrowed to the two peak months for them, and a few varieties keep setting through it. UF/IFAS South Florida lists grape tomatoes among the crops that can still be planted in June, and reopens tomato planting with August seed-starting for the fall garden. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

On the Florida peninsula the summer gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; grape types are heat resistant, so the exclusion is narrowed to the two peak months for them, and a few varieties keep setting through it. UF/IFAS South Florida lists grape tomatoes among the crops that can still be planted in June, and reopens tomato planting with August seed-starting for the fall garden. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: On the Florida peninsula (roughly Orlando south to Miami and the Keys), grape tomatoes are a cool-weather crop. Frost is rare here, so you plant in the fall, from about September through February, and pick through the mild winter and spring. The hard part is summer, not winter. In July and August it gets too hot, over about 78°F at night, for tomatoes to set fruit, so plants take a break then. Big slicing tomatoes only grow in the cool season here, but grape types handle the heat better, so they hold on a little into early summer and a few keep going. Pick fast-maturing grape varieties and start your seeds indoors in August for fall planting.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11, south of about Orlando) grows grape tomatoes on a single long cool-season window rather than the spring-and-fall pattern of cooler regions. Because frost is rare, the planting window runs continuously from the fall transplant in September and October through February, the last month UF/IFAS lists for planting tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Production carries through the mild winter and spring. The limiting season is summer: in July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) cause blossom drop and fruit-set failure. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; grape types are heat resistant, so the exclusion narrows to those two peak months for them and a few varieties keep setting through it. Start seed indoors in August for fall transplanting, and choose fast-maturing grape types. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UF/IFAS divides Florida into North, Central, and South planting regions; the Florida peninsula (zones 10-11) is South Florida, served by one calendar (ENH1191/EP452 South Florida Gardening Calendar) plus VH021's statewide guide. EP452 (rev. Oct 2024) opens the fall tomato transplant in September-October ('tomatoes' listed in the October planting list) and closes the cool-season planting in February ('last month to plant ... tomatoes for a late spring harvest'); August is tomato seed-start for the fall garden. Frost is rare in South Florida (VH021). This is ONE continuous cross-year cool-season window, NOT the desert two-window shape and NOT two discrete crops -> no second_planting band.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_present: Jul-Aug (months 7,8). Grape-narrowed: the UF/IFAS Broward South Florida planting guide lists grape tomatoes among June-plantable crops (with okra, southern peas, tropical vegetables) while restricting 'tomatoes (larger fruit varieties)' to Sep-Mar; legacy zone-11 note: new fruit set fails above ~78°F nighttime. Peak fruit-set-failure months are July-August.
plantings_provenance.grape_pause_narrowed: Yes -- same direction as se_gulf (grape's heat resistance narrows the summer pause), NOT the absolute desert pause. Distinct from se_gulf in that the peninsula has NO frost gap and NO spring crop: it is a single cool-season window with a two-month peak-summer exclusion, not two crops bracketing a one-month pause. Larger-fruited beefsteak will re-derive (wider; likely cool-season-only with a longer exclusion).
plantings_provenance.zone_split_decision: z10 and z11 carry IDENTICAL resolutions. VH021/EP452 do not separate zone 10 from zone 11 -- both are 'South Florida.' The legacy zones{} 10-vs-11 difference was a USCRN climate-data artifact and is NOT carried forward as verified (per Trevor 2026-06-06, source-decides).

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: In Hawaii (tropical, zone 11) grape tomato has no frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window: CTAHR states tomato can be "grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing varieties adapted" to the local area. Seed is started indoors in any month and transplanted about 3 to 5 weeks after sowing (CTAHR HGV-5); the plant-level baseline of six weeks indoors is the cooler-mainland figure. The year-round window rests on cultivar choice -- the locally bred, nematode- and disease-resistant UH cultivars (the determinate 'Anahu', 'Healani', 'Kewalo' and the indeterminate hybrids in the N-series) plus grape types -- rather than on hitting a particular season. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)
start_indoors.from_year_round_note: Anchor from:'year_round'. Frost-independent: zone 11 has no last_frost/first_frost to offset against (frost_free_days 365). Resolver keys 'skip frost resolution, use authored windows as-is' off this named anchor; resolved_by_zone[11].year_round:true is derivable (region anchor = year_round <=> resolved-cell flag set). Mirrors lettuce hawaii_tropical (m15_na3g), adapted from direct_sow to the transplant (start_indoors + plant_out) shape because tomato is transplanted.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set grape tomato transplants out in any month of the year. CTAHR's home-garden tomato guidance gives a year-round planting capability for most of Hawaii contingent on adapted varieties, with no spring/fall bracketing and no summer exclusion stated; the limiting factors named are disease, insect, and rain pressure, not a season boundary. Keeping plants caged or staked and off the ground, and irrigating the soil rather than the foliage (in the morning when overhead water is used), are the management levers. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)
plant_out.from_year_round_note: Region-constant plant_out uses a distinct from:'year_round' anchor (not a frost anchor overloaded with window_days:365), so the resolver keys 'use authored windows as-is' off a named anchor and resolved_by_zone[11].year_round:true is derivable. Verifier asserts: region plant_out anchor == 'year_round' <=> resolved-cell year_round flag set.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Grape tomatoes begin ripening about two months after transplant. CTAHR gives most tomato varieties 60 to 80 days to mature; grape types sit at the fast end, and the crop-level grape figure is roughly 55 to 70 days (about 62 mid). Because planting is year-round and the UH-bred hybrids are indeterminate -- producing continuously while healthy -- harvest is effectively continuous across the year from successive and overlapping plantings. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: There is no season-ending harvest boundary in tropical zone 11: grape tomato is planted and harvested continuously through the year. Production does not close at a frost or at a sustained-heat date; it is refreshed by successive plantings, which also helps stay ahead of the disease and pest pressure CTAHR flags as the real constraint in Hawaii. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Year-round cell: harvest_end mirrors the continuous window (from:'year_round', 365) rather than a frost or heat boundary, because the season does not close. The all-active calendar carries no season_over state by construction.

11.zone_notes: Hawaii tropical (USDA zone 11; frost-free, frost_free_days 365). No frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for grape tomato: CTAHR gives tomato a year-round planting capability for most of Hawaii, contingent on adapted varieties. The limiting factors are disease (tomato spotted wilt and tobacco mosaic viruses, and warm-wet leaf spots and blights), insect pests (whitefly, leafminer, fruit fly, thrips), and fruit cracking in heavy rain, managed with resistant locally-bred UH cultivars, staking or caging to keep fruit off the ground, morning soil-only irrigation, and successive plantings, rather than by pausing a season. Grape types and the compact determinates (for example 'Healani') also do well in 3 to 5 gallon containers here.
11.calendar_basis: Grape tomato is grown YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free, frost_free_days 365) and no summer no-sow exclusion: CTAHR HGV-5 states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing varieties adapted to the area, and names no seasonal fruit-set gap. This is the per-region source finding: the grape summer heat_pause documented for the Florida peninsula and the deserts does not universalize to Hawaii's oceanic lowland (guardrail: heat_pause is read from the source per region, never defaulted). Hawaii's challenge is disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant locally-bred cultivars and cultural practice, not a production stop. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field); year_round:true makes the all-active calendar's intent machine-readable. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

12.zone_notes: Hawaii tropical (USDA zone 11; frost-free, frost_free_days 365). No frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for grape tomato: CTAHR gives tomato a year-round planting capability for most of Hawaii, contingent on adapted varieties. The limiting factors are disease (tomato spotted wilt and tobacco mosaic viruses, and warm-wet leaf spots and blights), insect pests (whitefly, leafminer, fruit fly, thrips), and fruit cracking in heavy rain, managed with resistant locally-bred UH cultivars, staking or caging to keep fruit off the ground, morning soil-only irrigation, and successive plantings, rather than by pausing a season. Grape types and the compact determinates (for example 'Healani') also do well in 3 to 5 gallon containers here.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, grape tomatoes grow year-round, so you can start a few plants in any month rather than waiting for a season. There is no frost here, so the calendar is open all year. The hard part is not heat but pests and disease, which thrive in the warm, humid weather, plus heavy rain that can crack the fruit. Give yourself the best odds: pick varieties bred for Hawaii or tough grape types, keep plants up off the ground on a cage or stake, water the soil rather than the leaves (in the morning if you use a sprinkler), and start a fresh planting every few months so you always have healthy young plants coming on. Grape types and a few compact varieties also do well in 3 to 5 gallon pots.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical calendar is aseasonal for grape tomato: plant and harvest year-round, with no frost anchor and no summer heat pause. University of Hawaii CTAHR states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in the state by choosing locally adapted varieties, and names no seasonal fruit-set exclusion. This is the per-region finding, not a default: the grape summer heat_pause documented for the Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11) and for the low and high deserts does not carry to Hawaii's oceanic lowland, whose nights do not sustain the fruit-set-stopping highs of peninsular summer. The binding constraints here are disease and pests: tomato spotted wilt virus (thrips-vectored) and tobacco mosaic virus, plus warm-wet fungal and bacterial leaf spots and blights, whitefly, leafminer, and fruit fly, along with fruit cracking in heavy rain. CTAHR's primary lever is genetic: the locally bred, root-knot-nematode- and disease-tolerant UH cultivars, the determinate open-pollinated 'Anahu', 'Healani', and 'Kewalo' and the indeterminate N-series hybrids that fruit continuously while healthy; grape types and compact determinates such as 'Healani' suit 3 to 5 gallon containers. Cultural practice carries the rest: stake or cage to keep fruit off the ground, irrigate the soil (not the foliage; morning if overhead), and refresh with successive plantings. Most varieties mature in 60 to 80 days, grape types at the fast end. Windows verified against University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5 (Home Garden Tomato), with the 1943 bulletin B-91 (Home Gardening in Hawaii) as historical corroboration only.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start grape tomato seed indoors about 6 weeks before transplanting, timed to the Feb 14 - Mar 20 Rio Grande Valley set-out window (TAMU AgriLife RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Grape tomato transplants go out Feb 14 - Mar 20 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide, corroborated by the Bilingual LRGV planting table's 65 to 75 day maturity figure for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest spring harvest at about 65 days from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest spring harvest at about 75 days from the latest set-out date.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start the fall round indoors about 6 weeks before the Sep 15 - Oct 15 set-out window.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall grape tomato transplants go out Sep 15 - Oct 15 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide / Bilingual LRGV fall window for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest fall harvest at about 65 days from the earliest fall set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest fall harvest, extending into the mild Valley winter tail before spring returns.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Sustained Valley summer heat causes blossom drop: the flowers abort before they can set fruit, so production stops even though the plants stay alive (TAMU AgriLife notes high heat drops tomato blossoms). (Jul, Aug sit outside both plant windows.)

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, grape tomato is a two-season crop. Plant Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest, then plant again Sep 15 - Oct 15 for a fall crop. Skip the hottest stretch of summer: the flowers drop in the worst heat before they can set fruit, so there is nothing to gain by planting through it. It rarely if ever frosts here, so both the spring and fall windows run on Valley heat, not on a frost date.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Grape tomato in the RGV runs on the Valley's two-crop calendar: set out Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest running Apr 20 - Jun 3, then set out again Sep 15 - Oct 15 for a fall harvest running Nov 19 - Dec 15. Sustained Valley summer heat causes blossom drop: the flowers abort before they can set fruit, so production stops even though the plants stay alive (TAMU AgriLife notes high heat drops tomato blossoms). Frost is essentially absent here, so both plantings are timed against heat, not cold. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before set-out; OSU's Oregon planting table (EM9027) gives tomatoes 6 weeks indoors before transplanting.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out after the last frost and once the soil has warmed; OSU's table gives the Willamette Valley a May window and the immediate coast a wider May-June window (EM9027), corroborated by WSU's tomato seeding spec (EM057E Table 4, 70-85F soil temp).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Matures in about 65 to 75 days from transplant. Small fruit size lets grape tomatoes size and ripen reliably within a cool marine summer, so the lower end of this range is a realistic planning figure here.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest winds down at the first fall frost; pick remaining fruit (green, if needed) a few days ahead of the average date to ripen indoors.

8.zone_notes: The valley's summer ripens grape tomatoes with room to spare; no early-variety caution is needed.

9.zone_notes: Even on the cooler coast, grape tomatoes ripen dependably given OSU's own wider May-June set-out window; this is one of the two reliable tomato types for the maritime PNW.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Grape tomatoes ripen reliably in the maritime Pacific Northwest's cool summer, right alongside cherry tomatoes as the region's most dependable tomato choice. Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before setting plants out in May, and expect a steady harvest of small, oblong fruit from midsummer into fall. A warm, sunny site still helps yield, but this is not a marginal crop here; you do not need to hunt for a special early variety the way you would for a big slicer.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Grape tomatoes are one of the maritime Pacific Northwest's more dependable tomato choices: their small fruit size lets the crop size and ripen well within this region's cool, marine-tempered summer, unlike larger-fruited types. Set transplants out after the last frost once the soil has warmed, in May in the valley or across OSU's wider May-June coastal window, with fruit maturing in about 65 to 75 days. Harvest carries into fall until the region's mild first frost. A warm, sheltered site still helps, but ripening reliability is not the concern here that it is for beefsteak, heirloom, or roma. (OSU EM9027; WSU EM057E)

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before spring set-out (Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out about a week after the last frost, once soil has warmed (VCE 426-331 Table 4, the belt's zone 7/8 tomato rows).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins ripening about 70 days after transplanting (VCE 426-331).

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop's harvest winds down as the hot, humid Piedmont and Coastal Plain midsummer sets in and fruit set stalls (VCE 426-331).

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed indoors roughly 6 weeks ahead of the VCE-documented fall set-out window (VCE 426-331 Table 4).

plant_out.source_quote: Zone 8a/8b Fall: July 1-Aug 10 | Zone 7a Fall: June 20-Aug 1
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out on VCE 426-331 Table 4's explicit documented fall tomato window for this belt (zone 8: July 1 to August 10; zone 7: June 20 to August 1).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about 70 days after the late-summer transplant (VCE 426-331).

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop is harvested up to just ahead of the belt's real first frost, which kills tomato vines outright (VCE 426-331 frost-date table).

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer fruit set can fail across the Piedmont and Coastal Plain's hottest, most humid weeks, but grape tomatoes are heat resistant and keep setting fruit further into summer than large-fruited tomatoes. Virginia Cooperative Extension's own documented fall transplant window for tomatoes in this belt picks up as the spring crop winds down, carrying a second harvest into fall. (VCE 426-331)

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Grape tomatoes do well on two crops a year in the Piedmont and Coastal Plain: spring and fall, with only a short break between them for the worst summer heat. Like cherry tomatoes, grape types keep setting fruit later into summer than big slicers. Set transplants out about a week after your last frost, then plant a second round in July for fruit into fall.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: Grape tomatoes follow the belt's standard two-cycle tomato calendar (Virginia Cooperative Extension Pub. 426-331): spring transplants about a week after the last frost (zone 8: mid April; zone 7: late April) for a harvest through late June into early July. Grape types are heat resistant like cherry tomatoes, so fruit set holds up later into summer than large-fruited types before VCE's documented fall window (zone 8: July 1 to August 10; zone 7: June 20 to August 1) restarts the crop for fall.

mid_south.region_label: Mid-South: Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before spring set-out (University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension planting-date tables).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out about a week after the last frost, once soil has warmed (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's spring planting-date table carries tomato as a March through May set-out for central Arkansas).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins ripening about 70 days after transplanting (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension).

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop's harvest winds down as the hot, humid Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands midsummer sets in and fruit set stalls (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension).

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed indoors about six weeks ahead of the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's fall set-out window (fall vegetable planting-date table).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: The University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's fall vegetable table gives fall tomatoes a tight early-July transplant window; this belt sets the fall crop out Jul 1 to Jul 15 in zone 8, shifted about a week earlier in the cooler zone 7 uplands (Jun 24 to Jul 8).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about 70 days after the midsummer transplant (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension).

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop's season is closed out by the belt's first fall frost, which kills tomato vines outright (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension frost-date table).

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer fruit set can fail across the Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands' hottest, most humid weeks, but grape tomatoes are heat resistant and keep setting fruit further into summer than large-fruited tomatoes. The University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's tight early-July fall transplant window for tomatoes picks up as the spring crop winds down, carrying a second harvest into early October. (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension)

mid_south.region_notes_beginner: Grape tomatoes do well on two crops a year in the Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands: spring and fall, with only a short break between them for the worst summer heat. Like cherry tomatoes, grape types keep setting fruit later into summer than big slicers. Set transplants out about a week after your last frost, then plant a second round in the tight early-July fall window for fruit from early September into October.
mid_south.region_notes_seasoned: Grape tomatoes follow the belt's standard two-cycle tomato calendar (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension planting-date tables): spring transplants go out about a week after the last frost (zone 8 Apr 10 to May 1, zone 7 Apr 17 to May 8) for a harvest through late June into early July. Grape types are heat resistant like cherry tomatoes, so fruit set holds up later into summer than large-fruited types before the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's tight fall window (zone 8 Jul 1 to Jul 15, zone 7 Jun 24 to Jul 8, seed sown indoors about six weeks ahead) restarts the crop; the fall harvest runs from early September into early October.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start grape tomato seed indoors about six weeks before the mid-March set-out, so transplants are ready as the last frost passes (UNR Extension SP-99-11 gives a six to eight week head start; kept to six weeks so January stays a dormant month).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out in mid-March, once frost danger has passed, per UNR's practical Southern Nevada last-frost date of March 15 and the UNLV Master Gardener chart's March tomato window; grape tomato's smaller, fast-setting fruit clusters make it one of the quicker Shape A crops to bring in before the heat wall.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins ripening about 70 days after the mid-March transplant (grape tomato's smaller fruit sets faster than a slicing type), bringing the first fruit in by late May.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop finishes by late June as daytime highs climb past 90°F and fruit set stops; UNR does not recommend a fall replanting in Southern Nevada.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Las Vegas Valley summers routinely run past 100°F from June into September, and tomato fruit set fails above about 90°F day / 55°F night, so the spring crop is harvested before the heat and no fall crop is set (University of Nevada, Reno Extension SP-99-11 and Fact Sheet FS-02-61).

nevada.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley you grow grape tomatoes as a single spring crop, not two like the Arizona low desert. Start seed indoors in early February, set transplants out in mid-March once frost is past, and pick the small, fast-setting fruit from late May through June. Once daytime highs pass 90°F in summer the plants stop setting fruit, so there is a long summer break, and unlike Phoenix a fall crop is not recommended here because frost returns by late November. Grape tomato's quick, 70-day fruit set makes it one of the easier Shape A picks for the tight spring window.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) runs grape tomato on one spring cycle, per University of Nevada, Reno Extension. Seed goes in indoors in early February; transplants set out in mid-March, after the valley's practical last frost (SP-99-11 gives March 15, later at the cooler zone 8 edge, earlier at Laughlin in zone 10). At a 70-day days-to-maturity, fruit ripens from late May into June, then daytime highs past 90°F shut fruit set down from July into September. UNR explicitly does not recommend a fall or second tomato planting for Southern Nevada, unlike the Phoenix low desert's fall reflush; frost returns around November 25 in zone 9. Grape tomato's quicker fruit set gives it a wider harvest window before the heat wall than the large-fruited slicing types.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start grape tomato seed indoors in late February, about six weeks before the April 1 set-out, so transplants are ready once frost passes (USU Extension lists St. George as a Group D crop planted about April 1).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out about April 1, once frost danger has passed, per USU Extension's St. George Group D (Very Tender) planting date.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins ripening about 70 days after the April 1 transplant, bringing the first sweet, bite-size fruit by mid-June.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop keeps producing heavily through the rest of June before daytime highs climb past 95°F in July and fruit set stops; USU does not recommend a fall tomato planting in the St. George area.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: St. George summers routinely reach 100°F in June, July, and August, and tomato fruit set fails above about 95°F day or below 50°F night, so the spring crop is harvested through June and no fall crop is set (USU Extension: How to Grow Tomatoes in Your Garden; Washington County Elevations and frost dates).

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: In St. George's Dixie you grow grape tomatoes as a single spring crop. Start seed indoors in late February, set transplants out around April 1 once frost is past, and pick sweet, bite-size fruit from mid-June through the end of the month. Grape tomato is one of the quicker crops in this group, so it gives you a good three weeks of picking before daytime highs pass 95°F in summer and the plants stop setting fruit. A fall crop is not recommended here since frost returns by about November 1.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs grape tomato on one spring cycle, per USU Extension. Seed goes in indoors in late February; transplants set out about April 1, the St. George Group D (Very Tender) date, just after the March 30 average last frost. At a 70-day days-to-maturity, the fastest of this crop family here, fruit ripens from mid-June and keeps coming through the rest of the month before daytime highs past 95°F shut fruit set down from July into September. USU does not recommend a fall or second tomato planting for the St. George area; frost returns around November 1. Grape tomato's short days-to-maturity makes it one of the more forgiving picks for this compressed spring window.

crops.description_seasoned: Grape tomatoes are small, oblong, grape-shaped fruit on vigorous indeterminate plants, and they are one of the most rewarding small tomatoes for a first-season grower. Like cherry tomatoes they are sweet and produce continuously from first flowering until frost, but the fruit is a different animal: the skin is noticeably thicker and the flesh is meatier and less watery. That gives grape types two practical advantages over round cherries. First, they crack far less, both on the vine after rain and in the bowl, because the tougher skin resists the sudden swelling that splits a thin-skinned cherry. Second, they hold much longer after picking, often a week or more at room temperature. The plants are almost always indeterminate and set fruit in long, heavy clusters over a 10 to 14 week season, so a single plant is highly productive. Most modern hybrids (Santa, Juliet, Sweet Hearts, Five Star Grape) also carry disease tolerance. In warm climates (zones 9 to 11), a second late-summer planting can extend harvest into winter; in the coldest zones (3 to 5), choose the faster grape hybrids, around 65 days, and warm the soil before transplanting.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when the fruit is fully and evenly colored, usually deep red, and firm with just a slight give. Grape tomatoes hold their quality on the vine longer than round cherries because the thicker skin resists cracking, so an extra day or two of hang time to deepen color and sugar is lower risk here than with a thin-skinned cherry. Full color indicates that lycopene synthesis and sugar accumulation are complete. Ripe fruit detaches with a gentle twist; if it resists, the abscission zone has not fully formed, so give it another day. The fruit is borne in long clusters, and the individual grapes within a cluster ripen in sequence rather than all at once, so plan to pick a cluster over several visits. Harvest in the morning when temperatures are cooler, as fruit held at 90°F and above deteriorates faster.

pet_safe.note: Ripe tomatoes are fine, but the leaves, stems, and unripe fruit are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Banana Pepper

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Banana pepper wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter, and a soil that warms early and holds steady moisture. As a warm-season pepper it sulks in cold, wet ground, so a sandy loam that warms quickly in spring suits it better than a heavy, slow-warming clay. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, and on heavy or cool soils many growers lay black plastic or fabric mulch to raise soil temperature and set transplants into warmer ground. Even soil moisture in a freely draining bed is the target, because the wide swings between dry and soaked that a poorly drained soil produces are the direct cause of the calcium-starved blossom-end rot peppers are prone to.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Banana peppers like rich, well-drained soil that warms up in the sun, since they are warm-season plants that dislike cold, soggy ground. Mix in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch laid down before planting warms the soil and gives peppers the head start they want. Aim for soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, because uneven watering is what causes the dark, sunken blossom-end rot on the bottom of the fruit.

ph.note_seasoned: Banana pepper grows best at a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, with Georgia and Clemson both placing the target near 6.0 to 6.5. In that band the nutrients peppers need, including the calcium that guards against blossom-end rot, stay most available. Peppers tolerate a somewhat wider range, roughly 5.5 to 7.5, but uptake of iron, manganese, and other micronutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline, showing as yellowing between the veins of the youngest leaves. Alkaline soils common across the interior West often need sulfur worked in ahead of planting; most Eastern and Midwestern soils sit naturally near the target. A soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant.
ph.note_beginner: Banana peppers like slightly acidic soil, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where peppers take up nutrients best, including the calcium that prevents blossom-end rot. If your soil runs alkaline, common in the dry interior West, you may need to add sulfur before planting. An inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress after fruit set
fertilizer.type: Balanced at planting, then calcium nitrate at fruit set
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress about three to four weeks after transplanting and again once fruit sets
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 at planting, then calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) as a side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Banana pepper is a moderate feeder that rewards restraint with nitrogen. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 or 13-13-13, about 2 pounds per 100 square feet, into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate about three to four weeks after transplanting and again as the first fruits set. Hold nitrogen back early and never overdo it: too much drives a big, bushy, dark-green plant that flowers late and sets little fruit. The calcium nitrate side-dress does double duty, feeding the plant while supplying the calcium that, paired with even watering, heads off blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Banana peppers like steady but modest feeding, and going heavy on nitrogen backfires. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the soil before planting. Then, a few weeks after planting and again once the first peppers set, feed with a nitrogen fertilizer like calcium nitrate. Do not overdo it: too much nitrogen gives you a large leafy plant with few peppers. Calcium nitrate also supplies calcium, which, along with even watering, helps prevent blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your banana pepper is setting its first fruit, a good time to side-dress with a calcium nitrate source to feed the plant and supply calcium against blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your banana pepper is setting fruit. Feed it now with a nitrogen fertilizer such as calcium nitrate to keep it producing and to help prevent blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) side-dress three to four weeks after transplanting and again at fruit set. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which gives leaf at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed such as calcium nitrate once the plant is growing well and setting fruit. Do not overdo the nitrogen or you get all leaves and few peppers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common rate is about 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before transplanting. For the side-dress, Clemson suggests about 5 pounds of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 1000 square feet, or roughly half a pound per 100 square feet, applied three to four weeks after transplanting and repeated three to four weeks later, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix about 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet (or a few inches of compost) into the soil before planting. Then, a few weeks after planting and again at fruit set, scratch a small amount of calcium nitrate into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in.

companions.note_seasoned: Most pepper companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The aromatic-herb and flower companions (basil, marigold, nasturtium, alliums) are grown to deter or trap the aphids and thrips that trouble peppers and to draw beneficial insects, a plausible, habitat-based effect rather than an isolated one. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep banana peppers away from their Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which share the full pepper pest and disease complex.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful pepper companions are strong-smelling herbs and flowers like basil, marigold, and nasturtium, which can help deter or lure away aphids and other pests. The one rule that really matters is to keep banana peppers away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which are all close relatives and share the same pests and soil diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Basil
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Basil is a classic pepper neighbor. Its strong scent is thought to help confuse soft-bodied pests like aphids and thrips, and it tucks neatly between young pepper plants. A pleasant, low-risk companion.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional interplanting with peppers; the aromatic foliage is thought to deter aphids and thrips and to draw pollinators and beneficial insects. The effect is habitat-based and traditional rather than trial-isolated for pepper.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Basil is a long-standing companion for peppers; aromatic-herb pest confusion is plausible and habitat-based, not trial-isolated for pepper.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigold
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Marigolds are a classic companion flower for peppers, grown to help keep pests down. Mostly tradition, but cheerful and low-risk.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A long-standing companion tradition near peppers; French marigold grown as a cover crop has documented nematode-suppressive effects, though the interplanted marigold-pepper pest benefit is traditional rather than trial-isolated.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: French marigold has documented nematode suppression as a cover crop; the interplanted marigold-pepper effect is traditional, not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are often planted near peppers to lure aphids away from the crop. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planted as a trap and deterrent for aphids, drawing them off the peppers. Trap cropping is a documented principle, though the specific nasturtium-pepper effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap cropping and aphid attraction by nasturtium is documented in principle; the nasturtium-pepper pairing is not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions, garlic, and chives have a strong smell that gardeners traditionally use to confuse pests around peppers, and they take up little room. A low-risk, space-saving neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Pungent alliums are a traditional interplant said to mask the crop and deter soft-bodied pests; the effect is habitat-based and traditional rather than trial-isolated for pepper.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep peppers away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant. They are all close relatives that share the same soil diseases and pests, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share pepper's pest and disease complex, including bacterial leaf spot, the mosaic viruses, Phytophthora blight, anthracnose, and aphids. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 year cycle.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant are all Solanaceae and share pepper's pest and disease complex; grouping them concentrates that pressure. A sound epidemiology and rotation principle, not a trial-tested adjacency.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from peppers and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong T1 mechanism for a pepper-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel is a widely cautioned anti-companion said to inhibit many vegetables; the pepper-fennel antagonism is garden lore without a strong T1 mechanism.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, most often green peach aphid, cluster on growing tips and the undersides of leaves, curling and yellowing the foliage, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit the mosaic viruses that mottle and distort pepper leaves, which is their most serious effect on the crop.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft green insects gather on new growth and the undersides of leaves, making them curl and yellow, often with a sticky film and black mold. They can also spread plant viruses to peppers.
pests.cause_seasoned: Green peach aphid and related species suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces. As virus carriers they matter out of proportion to the feeding damage they do, with colonies often establishing by early summer.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that multiply quickly in warm weather, especially on soft, over-fertilized growth. They also carry viruses from plant to plant.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants and slows virus spread.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work. A silver reflective mulch under young plants helps keep aphids off.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ease up on nitrogen fertilizer. Aphids multiply fastest on the soft, lush growth that heavy feeding pushes out, so a moderately fed pepper gives them less to build on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen drives the succulent growth aphids favor; restrained feeding slows colony buildup on growing tips and leaf undersides before any other step is needed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay a silver reflective mulch, a shiny sheet spread on the soil, under young peppers. It helps keep aphids from landing, and since aphids carry plant viruses, it slows virus spread too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch deters colonizing aphids from young plants, and because virus transmission is their most serious effect on peppers, cutting early landings slows virus spread as well as feeding injury.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the aphids off with a strong jet of water from the hose, aiming at the undersides of the leaves where they gather. Go back every few days while they keep returning.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water jet dislodges colonies from tips and leaf undersides; populations rebuild quickly in warm weather, so repeat at a few days' interval.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps all eat aphids and usually bring them under control on their own. Welcome these helpers, and avoid spraying broadly so you do not wipe them out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserved ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually bring aphids under control; supporting natural enemies rather than spraying broadly keeps that pressure working for you.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the colonies keep growing, spray insecticidal soap onto the undersides of the leaves where the aphids sit, and repeat every few days. It only works where it actually touches them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap demands thorough coverage of leaf undersides, since it acts only on contact; repeat every few days to catch the colonies that rebuild.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil made for plants, is the other option at this step. Like soap, it has to coat the aphids, so wet the undersides of the leaves well and repeat every few days.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil is the alternative contact material at this rung, carrying the same coverage demand on leaf undersides and the same need for repeat passes.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny shot-hole punctures riddle the leaves, a scatter of small round holes that is the classic flea-beetle signature. Damage is worst on seedlings and young transplants, whose small leaf area a heavy infestation can shred; established peppers tolerate considerable feeding. Brush a plant and the small dark beetles spring away like fleas.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The leaves are peppered with lots of tiny round holes, as if hit by birdshot. It hits young plants hardest. Touch the plant and you will see tiny dark beetles jump away.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several flea beetle species (potato, tobacco, and palestriped) feed on pepper foliage, overwintering as adults in debris and emerging to attack the earliest, most vulnerable plants in spring. Young transplants are far more at risk than large, established plants.
pests.cause_beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas and chew tiny holes in the leaves. They are most active in spring and target young plants early in the season.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover until they are large and vigorous, removing it at flowering so pollinators can reach the blooms. Set out stout, well-hardened transplants so plants can outgrow the damage, and treat heavy early infestations with spinosad or kaolin clay.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are big and strong, then take it off when they flower. Setting out larger transplants helps them outgrow the damage. For heavy attacks, an organic spray such as spinosad helps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, delay setting plants out until soil and air are warm so they grow away fast, and clean up crop debris and weeds that harbor overwintering adults.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants early with row cover, set out larger transplants into warm soil so they grow quickly, and clear away weeds and old plant debris where the beetles hide over winter.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear away weeds and old plant debris at the end of the season. The adult beetles spend the winter hiding in that litter and come out in spring aimed at your youngest plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Adults overwinter in crop debris and weedy cover; clearing both lowers the spring emergence that falls hardest on the earliest, most vulnerable transplants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover young plants with a floating row cover, a light fabric that lets in sun and water while keeping beetles out, from transplanting until they are big and sturdy. Take it off when they flower so pollinators can reach the blooms.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover from transplanting excludes beetles through the window when leaf area is smallest; remove at flowering for pollinator access, by which point established plants tolerate considerable feeding.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For a heavy attack on young plants, coat the leaves with kaolin clay, a fine white mineral powder you mix with water and spray on. The film helps deter the beetles from feeding.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Kaolin's particle film is a tool for heavy early infestations on small transplants; established peppers shrug off the shot-holing and rarely need treatment.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a heavy early attack is shredding young plants, spinosad, an organic spray derived from a soil bacterium, helps. Bigger established plants can usually outgrow the damage without it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reserve spinosad for heavy early infestations on transplants whose small leaf area is at risk; mature plants tolerate the feeding, so routine application is not warranted.

pests.name: European corn borer and corn earworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small entry holes near the stem-end cap of the fruit, often with crumbly frass, and a caterpillar tunneling inside that leads to premature ripening and rot. The borer also tunnels stems, which can wilt or break, while the corn earworm chews holes in the fruit. Both are common pepper pests in the corn-growing Midwest, South, and East, with damage building into late summer.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little holes near the top of the pepper, sometimes with sawdust-like droppings, and a caterpillar tunneling inside that makes the fruit rot. It is common where field corn is grown.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the European corn borer moth and the corn earworm moth, which lay eggs on peppers and corn in summer; the caterpillars bore into fruit through the cap and, for the borer, into stems. Two or more generations a season are common, with the heaviest pressure by late summer.
pests.cause_beginner: Caterpillars, the young of moths, that bore into peppers near the cap and into the stems, causing rot and breakage. They have more than one generation each summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Scout for eggs and early larvae and apply Bacillus thuringiensis or spinosad to young caterpillars before they bore into the fruit, since once inside they are protected. Remove and destroy infested fruit, and clean up crop and nearby corn debris at season's end.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Catch it early: an organic Bt or spinosad spray works on the young caterpillars before they tunnel in, but does nothing once they are inside a pepper. Pick off and destroy any bored fruit.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Destroy crop debris and nearby cornstalks where the borer overwinters, scout from midsummer when moths are flying, and time treatment to newly hatched larvae. Choosing an earlier variety can dodge the worst of the flight in some areas.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up old pepper and corn stalks at the end of the season, watch for the caterpillars from midsummer, and treat while they are small. Cleaning up where they overwinter is the biggest help.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clean up old pepper plants and nearby cornstalks at the end of the season, since the borer spends winter in that debris; removing it is the biggest help. During the season, pick off and destroy any pepper with a bored hole.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The borer overwinters in crop debris and nearby cornstalks, so destroying both at season's end removes its carryover; through the season, remove and destroy bored fruit, which cannot be salvaged once tunneled.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Watch for the caterpillars from midsummer and spray Bt, short for Bacillus thuringiensis, an organic caterpillar spray, while they are still small and outside the fruit. Once one tunnels into a pepper, no spray reaches it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Time Bt to newly hatched larvae before they bore in, scouting from midsummer when the moths fly; once inside fruit or stem the caterpillar is protected from any application.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spinosad, another organic spray, works the same way: only on the young caterpillars before they tunnel inside. Catch them early or not at all.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad shares Bt's timing constraint, effective on young surface-feeding larvae and useless after entry, so it is an alternative for the same early window rather than a rescue for bored fruit.

pests.name: Pepper maggot
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fruit that colors up early and unevenly, sometimes with a soft, rotting spot and a pinhole scar on the skin, and a white, legless maggot tunneling in the flesh inside. Cut the pepper open and the winding feeding channels and the maggot give it away. It is a regional pest, spread from New Jersey through much of the eastern half of the country, and most troublesome in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Some peppers turn red too early and rot from the inside, and cutting one open reveals a small white maggot tunneling through the flesh. It is mainly a problem in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larva of the pepper maggot fly, which lays eggs in developing fruit through mid to late summer, leaving a tiny egg-puncture scar. There is one generation a year and it overwinters as a pupa in the soil; the maggot feeds inside and infested fruit ripens prematurely and often rots.
pests.cause_beginner: A fly that lays its eggs in young peppers in summer; the maggot that hatches feeds inside the fruit, causing early ripening and rot. It is worst where the pest is established locally.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for an infested fruit, so control targets the egg-laying flies: remove and destroy affected peppers promptly to break the cycle, and where pressure is high time labeled sprays to the egg-laying period. A yellow sticky trap helps confirm when the flies are active.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot save an infested pepper, so pick off and destroy any that ripen early or show a pinhole scar to stop the next generation. Removing wild host weeds like horsenettle nearby helps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Remove nearby wild solanaceous weeds such as horsenettle that host the fly, rotate peppers away from last year's bed, clean up and destroy infested fruit, and in problem areas protect fruit with a labeled spray timed to the flight or with row cover before fruit set.
