succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Banana pepper is not a succession crop. One planting produces continuously through the whole warm season, so you set plants out once rather than at intervals. In most zones a later sowing would be caught by frost before its long warm season could finish. Only in the warmest, frost-free or near-frost-free zones, and across the hot South and the deserts where the crop splits around midsummer heat, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season rather than a true succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant banana peppers once for the season. A single planting keeps producing all through the warm months, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. In most places a later planting would not have time to fruit before frost. Only in very warm, nearly frost-free areas, or the hot South and desert, can you fit a spring and a fall planting, and that is really two separate seasons.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Banana pepper is a single long-season crop that bears continuously from one planting through the warm months, so interval succession sowing does not apply; a second sowing in most zones would not mature before frost. The hot South, the deserts, and frost-free zones support a separate spring and fall planting split around midsummer heat, which is a distinct season rather than a succession.

crops.description_seasoned: Banana pepper is a warm-season fruiting vegetable (Capsicum annuum) in the nightshade family, a close relative of tomato and eggplant grown for its long, tapered, waxy fruit that ripens from pale yellow through orange to red. The common name covers two very different peppers that look nearly identical on the plant: the SWEET banana types (Sweet Banana, Sweet Hungarian) are mild and low-heat, among the mildest peppers grown, while the HOT Hungarian wax types (Hungarian Hot Wax) carry real heat that climbs as the fruit ripens, so it pays to know which you planted. Like most peppers the fruit can be picked at two stages: at its pale-yellow stage, or left on the plant to color up and sweeten (or, in the hot types, grow hotter). Banana peppers are prolific setters, self-fertile and largely self-pollinating so a single plant fruits, and a touch more tolerant of cool conditions than the big blocky bells, though still warm-loving and grown from transplants set into warm soil. They are only moderate feeders, easily pushed to leaf by excess nitrogen. Two disorders define the crop's troubles: blossom-end rot, a dark sunken patch on the fruit caused by uneven watering interfering with calcium delivery, and sunscald on fruit exposed by thin foliage. Fruit set itself fails in extreme heat, when daytime highs past about 90°F and warm nights drop the blossoms, so across the hot South and the deserts the crop splits into a spring and a fall planting around a midsummer pause. The pest and disease complex, aphids (and the mosaic viruses they carry), flea beetles, pepper maggot, corn borers, hornworms, and the pepper weevil, plus bacterial leaf spot, Phytophthora blight, and anthracnose, is held off by even moisture, warm well-drained soil, and rotation away from its nightshade relatives.
crops.description_beginner: Banana pepper is a warm-season vegetable in the same family as tomatoes and eggplant, grown for its long, tapered fruit that ripens from pale yellow to orange and red. The name covers two kinds that look almost the same: sweet banana peppers are mild, and hot Hungarian wax peppers are spicy and get hotter as they ripen, so it helps to know which you planted. Like most peppers you can pick them at two stages: yellow, or left on the plant to color up and sweeten (or, for the hot ones, get hotter). Banana peppers are heavy producers, they pollinate themselves so one plant will fruit, and they take cool weather a little better than big bell peppers, though they still love warmth and are grown from transplants set into warm soil. They are only light feeders, so going heavy on fertilizer gives you a big leafy plant with few peppers. The two things to watch are blossom-end rot, a dark sunken spot on the bottom of the fruit caused by uneven watering, and sunscald, a pale burned patch on peppers left exposed to strong sun. In very hot weather the flowers drop and the plant stops setting fruit for a while, so in hot climates peppers are grown in spring and fall with a summer break. The main things to get right are warmth, steady and even watering with mulch, modest fertilizer, full sun, and rotating peppers away from where tomatoes, potatoes, or eggplant grew.

Warm-season Solanaceae: spring transplant into warm soil, then a continuous summer-to-frost harvest in cooler regions. Banana pepper, like all peppers, sets fruit poorly in extreme heat (blossom drop when daytime highs pass about 90°F with warm nights), so across the hot South and the deserts the crop splits into a spring and a fall planting around a backed midsummer heat_pause, while the northern and coastal regions carry a single continuous crop.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In cold zones banana pepper is a single summer crop. Start transplants indoors about 8 weeks early, then set them out only once nights hold above 50 to 55°F and the soil is warm, a week or two after your last frost. Harvest at the pale-yellow stage from midsummer, or let some fruit color up, until the first frost ends the plant. Banana and Hungarian wax types take cool conditions a bit better than the big bells and set fruit reliably here, which makes them a good pepper for a short northern season; even so, in the coldest zones (3 and 4) use black mulch and row cover and keep watering even to head off blossom-end rot.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold areas banana pepper is a one-crop-a-summer plant. Start seeds indoors about 8 weeks early, and plant out only when nights stay above 50 to 55°F and the soil is warm. Pick peppers yellow from midsummer, or let some turn color, until frost. Banana peppers handle cool weather a little better than big bell peppers, so they are a good choice for a short season; in the very coldest zones, warm the soil with black plastic.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Banana pepper, like all peppers, drops its blossoms and sets little fruit through the hot, humid heart of a Gulf, Florida, or desert summer, when daytime highs above about 90°F combine with warm nights above the mid-70s°F. Peppers here are grown as a spring crop and a fall crop, with midsummer paused for poor fruit set, a lull compounded in the humid South by heavy disease and pest pressure. The pause reflects heat-driven blossom drop, not cold, and is grounded in pepper-specific heat thresholds rather than a tomato source. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional pattern.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Along the Gulf and coastal plain banana pepper is grown as two crops, spring and fall, around a hot midsummer pause. Set transplants out after the last frost for a late-spring-into-June harvest, then plant again in early September for a fall crop that runs to first frost. Through July and August the heat drops blossoms and set stalls, and disease and pest pressure peak, so peppers coast rather than set. Water evenly and mulch against blossom-end rot, and rotate away from other nightshades to limit the heavy regional disease load.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: On the Gulf coast, grow banana peppers in spring and again in fall, with a summer break. Plant after the last frost for early-summer peppers, then plant again in early September for a fall crop. In the hottest part of summer the flowers drop and the plant takes a rest. Water evenly and mulch to prevent blossom-end rot.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's hot interior valleys banana pepper is a long single crop. Set transplants out in mid-spring once the soil warms, and harvest from midsummer to first frost. Peak summer heat can briefly stall fruit set, but banana peppers carry through the season better than a spring-and-fall split demands here. Full sun, even moisture, and mulch head off blossom-end rot in the dry heat.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot valleys, plant banana peppers in mid-spring after the soil warms and harvest from midsummer until frost. Very hot spells may pause fruit set for a bit. Water evenly and mulch to prevent blossom-end rot in the dry heat.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The cool, foggy north coast is a stretch for peppers, but banana and Hungarian wax types set fruit in cooler weather better than the big blocky bells, so they are the smart pepper choice here. Set plants out once the soil warms in late spring, choose the warmest, most sheltered spot you have, and expect a modest but real harvest from late summer into fall. Yields lag the hot interior; the cool-tolerant banana types simply do better in the fog than most peppers would.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: The cool, foggy north coast is hard on peppers, but banana peppers handle cool weather better than most, so they are a good pick. Plant in late spring in your warmest, most sheltered spot, and expect a modest harvest from late summer into fall.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The mild south coast gives banana pepper a long, gentle season. Set transplants out from mid-spring, and harvest from early or midsummer well into fall, since frost is late and light. The moderate coastal heat rarely forces a true midsummer pause, so one continuous planting carries the season. Keep moisture even and mulch against blossom-end rot.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: The mild south coast is a great place for banana peppers. Plant from mid-spring and harvest from summer into fall. The weather is rarely hot enough to stop fruit set for long, so one planting carries the whole season. Water evenly and mulch to prevent blossom-end rot.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the low California deserts banana pepper is a cool-season-shoulder crop grown around a brutal summer. Set transplants out in late winter for a spring harvest, take the plant through a paused, blossom-dropping midsummer, then plant again in early September for a fall-into-early-winter crop. The searing July and August heat stops fruit set entirely, so time the two windows to the mild shoulders. Even moisture and mulch are essential against blossom-end rot in the dry heat.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California desert, grow banana peppers in the mild parts of the year around a brutal summer. Plant in late winter for a spring crop, then again in early September for a fall crop. In July and August it is too hot for peppers to set fruit. Water evenly and mulch to prevent blossom-end rot.

The most intense heat can briefly stall fruit set, but banana peppers generally carry a single long season here. The dry, sunny climate suits peppers well; keep moisture even and mulch, since the fast dry-down of arid soil is a classic trigger for blossom-end rot.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In southern New Mexico and West Texas, plant banana peppers in mid-spring after frost and harvest from midsummer to fall. The hottest spells may pause fruit set briefly. The dry, sunny weather suits peppers, but water evenly and mulch, because soil that dries out fast causes blossom-end rot.

Banana pepper, like all peppers, sets fruit poorly in extreme heat (blossom drop when daytime highs pass about 90°F with warm nights), so across the hot South and the deserts the crop splits into a spring and a fall planting around a backed midsummer heat_pause, while the northern and coastal regions carry a single continuous crop.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Banana pepper, like all peppers, drops its blossoms and sets little fruit through the hot, humid heart of a Gulf, Florida, or desert summer, when daytime highs above about 90°F combine with warm nights above the mid-70s°F. Peppers here are grown as a spring crop and a fall crop, with midsummer paused for poor fruit set, a lull compounded in the humid South by heavy disease and pest pressure. The pause reflects heat-driven blossom drop, not cold, and is grounded in pepper-specific heat thresholds rather than a tomato source. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional pattern.

low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In Arizona's low desert banana pepper is grown around the summer, not through it. Set transplants out in late winter for a spring harvest, pause through a fruit-dropping midsummer, then plant again in early September for a fall-into-early-winter crop. July and August are simply too hot for peppers to set fruit. Even moisture and mulch are essential against blossom-end rot in the desert heat.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula banana pepper is a cool-season crop grown in the mild months and rested through the hot, wet summer. Set transplants out from winter into early spring for a spring harvest, then plant again in early September for a fall-through-winter crop. July and August bring heat-driven blossom drop plus heavy disease and pest pressure, so peppers pause. Plant on raised, well-drained ground against Phytophthora, water at the base, and rotate away from other nightshades.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, grow banana peppers in the cooler months. Plant from winter into early spring for a spring crop, then again in early September for a fall-and-winter crop. Skip the hot, wet middle of summer, when the flowers drop and disease is worst. Plant on raised beds so water drains, and water at the soil.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii and the frost-free tropics banana pepper can be grown nearly year-round, with the most reliable fruit set in the cooler, drier stretches. Warm, muggy midsummer nights can slow set and raise disease pressure, so many growers favor plantings that fruit in the milder months. Choose well-drained ground against Phytophthora, water at the base, and rotate away from other nightshades. The exact windows are a broad frost-free default rather than a variety-specific local calendar.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start banana pepper seed indoors about 3 weeks before transplanting, timed to the Feb 14 - Mar 20 Rio Grande Valley set-out window (TAMU AgriLife RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Banana pepper transplants go out Feb 14 - Mar 20 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide, corroborated by the Bilingual LRGV planting table's 90 to 100 day maturity figure for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest spring harvest at about 90 days from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest spring harvest at about 100 days from the latest set-out date.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start the fall round indoors about 3 weeks before the Jul 15 - Aug 15 set-out window.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall banana pepper transplants go out Jul 15 - Aug 15 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide / Bilingual LRGV fall window for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest fall harvest at about 90 days from the earliest fall set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest fall harvest, extending into the mild Valley winter tail before spring returns.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, banana pepper is a two-season crop. Plant Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest, then plant again Jul 15 - Aug 15 for a fall crop. Skip the hottest weeks of summer: the plant just does not perform well in the worst of the heat, so most Valley gardeners skip it. It rarely if ever frosts here, so both the spring and fall windows run on Valley heat, not on a frost date.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Banana pepper in the RGV runs on the Valley's two-crop calendar: set out Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest running May 15 - Jun 28, then set out again Jul 15 - Aug 15 for a fall harvest running Oct 13 - Nov 23. TAMU AgriLife's Valley planting guidance simply leaves that stretch off the calendar for this crop, rather than asserting a specific heat-failure mechanism. Frost is essentially absent here, so both plantings are timed against heat, not cold. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley
pnw.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh banana pepper pnw windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (70 to 85 days from transplant) plus the region's frost anchors (NOAA Sea-Tac z8, NOAA Astoria z9) and OSU Extension EM9027's regional vegetable planting table (Region 2/valley = z8 'May-June'; Region 1/coast = z9 'May' only), corroborated by WSU EM057E; per-zone dates are not independently verified against a banana-pepper-specific pnw trial calendar. OSU's table does not differentiate among pepper types, so the same planting window is shared across this batch's five peppers; banana pepper's own existing region cells elsewhere in this dataset already note it sets fruit more reliably than big bell types in cool conditions, a fact carried forward honestly here. No heat_pause: the shortfall in this climate is summer heat, not an excess of it.

9.zone_notes: OSU's Region 1 (coast) planting window for peppers is a single month, May, narrower than the valley's May-June; banana pepper sets fruit more reliably than big bell types in the coast's cooler conditions, but the shorter effective summer still caps the harvest.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: West of the Cascades, banana pepper is one of the easier peppers to grow. It sets fruit more reliably than big bell peppers in a cool summer, which makes it a good choice for this mild marine climate. Start seeds indoors in late winter, and set plants out in mid-May once the soil is warm. Pick pods pale yellow-green from midsummer, or let some turn orange-red, until the season winds down. A warm, sunny spot and black plastic mulch still help, especially close to the coast.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Banana pepper is one of the more forgiving warm-season crops for the maritime Pacific Northwest: it sets fruit more reliably than the big-fruited bell types in a cool, cloud-prone summer (OSU EM9027 / WSU EM057E), though it is still a warm-season crop asking more heat than this region's default. Start transplants indoors about 10 weeks ahead and set out in May, once nights have warmed; the Willamette Valley (z8) carries a longer, more dependable harvest than the cooler, foggier immediate coast (z9). Pick continuously from midsummer at the pale yellow-green stage, or let some pods color up where the site is warm enough; black plastic mulch and a sheltered, sunny spot widen the margin, particularly near the coast.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 8 weeks before the last frost, consistent with the crop's own weeks_indoors (8); VCE 426-331 lists a single Peppers (T) spring transplant window per zone, not a per-variety split.

plant_out.source_quote: Peppers (T): Zone 8a Apr 10-Aug 10 | Zone 7a Apr 20-Jul 20
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out a few days to about a week after the last frost, once the soil has warmed, matching VCE 426-331 Table 4's Peppers (T) spring start date for each zone.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: First fruit is ready roughly 77 days after transplanting, this crop's own days_to_maturity_mid (from_transplant).

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest runs until just ahead of the belt's first frost; peppers have no frost tolerance and are killed outright by the first freeze.

mid_atlantic.plantings_provenance: VCE 426-331 Table 4 lists a single 'Peppers (T)' row (spring z8 Apr 10-Aug 10, z7 Apr 20-Jul 20; fall not recommended) shared by all pepper types. Authored as one spring-set planting per zone: plant_out matches VCE's transplant start, start_indoors offsets 8 weeks (this crop's weeks_indoors) before it, and harvest_start offsets 77 days (days_to_maturity_mid, from_transplant) after plant_out. harvest_end sits 2 days ahead of the zone's first frost (peppers carry no frost tolerance). This crop shares bell pepper's 90°F heat_threshold_f (heat_effect poor_fruit_set); the belt's real midsummer heat, backed by NC State Extension's general Piedmont/Coastal Plain summer characterization, is modeled as a heat_pause (z8 Jul-Aug, z7 Aug only, shorter in the cooler zone), carving a two-flush harvest from the one planting, the same 'reflush' shape already used for jalapeno/cayenne/habanero in this dataset's warm_arid and ca_desert cells, adapted here to Mid-Atlantic sourcing and dates. mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Set out banana pepper transplants a few days after your last spring frost. This mild, sweet pepper grows and bears through early summer, then, like bell pepper, pauses in the hottest stretch of July and August before picking back up as nights cool in September, all from the one spring planting. Extension guides for this region do not list a separate fall planting for peppers.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: Banana pepper follows bell pepper's pattern in the Piedmont and Coastal Plain: a single spring transplant, not a spring-and-fall pair, per VCE 426-331's Peppers (T) window (Apr 10 to Aug 10 zone 8, Apr 20 to Jul 20 zone 7; fall "not recommended"). No frost tolerance; the first freeze ends the season.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start banana pepper seed indoors about six weeks before the mid-March set-out, so transplants are ready as the last frost passes (UNR Extension SP-99-11 gives a six to eight week head start for warm-season transplants; kept to six weeks so January stays a dormant month).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set banana pepper transplants out in mid-March, once frost danger has passed, per UNR's practical Southern Nevada last-frost date of March 15 and the UNLV Master Gardener chart's spring pepper and eggplant window.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: First fruit is ready roughly 77 days after the mid-March transplant, this crop's own days_to_maturity_mid, bringing the mild pickling pods in by early June.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop finishes by the end of June as daytime highs climb past 90°F and blossoms drop; UNR does not recommend a fall pepper planting for Southern Nevada.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Banana pepper drops its blossoms and stops setting fruit once days push past about 90°F with warm nights, this crop's own heat_threshold_f; Las Vegas Valley summers routinely run past 100°F from June into September, so the spring crop is picked out before the heat and no fall crop is set (University of Nevada, Reno Extension SP-99-11 and Fact Sheet FS-02-61).

nevada.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley you grow banana pepper as a single spring crop. Start seed indoors in early February, set transplants out in mid-March once frost is past, and pick the mild, tangy pods from early June through the end of the month. Once daytime highs pass 90°F in summer the plants stop setting fruit, and there is no fall replanting here the way there might be in a milder climate, because Southern Nevada's desert heat and University of Nevada guidance both rule it out. Pick pods pale yellow-green for the classic pickling stage before the heat wall shuts things down.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) runs banana pepper on one spring cycle, per University of Nevada, Reno Extension. Seed goes in indoors in early February; transplants set out in mid-March, after the valley's practical last frost (SP-99-11 gives March 15, later at the cooler zone 8 edge, earlier at Laughlin in zone 10). At this crop's 77-day days_to_maturity_mid, first fruit is ready in early June and picking continues to the end of the month, when daytime highs past 90°F stall blossom set (this crop's own heat_threshold_f). UNR's seasonal framework (FS-02-61) and its no-fall-Solanaceae guidance (SP-99-11) both argue against a second planting here, so the cooler, later-transplanted zone 8 gets the shortest of the three windows.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start banana pepper seed indoors in late February, about six weeks before the April 1 set-out, so transplants are ready once frost passes (USU Extension lists St. George as a Group D crop planted about April 1).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out about April 1, once frost danger has passed, per USU Extension's St. George Group D (Very Tender) planting date.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins ripening about 77 days after the April 1 transplant, bringing the first mild, tapered peppers in mid to late June.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop runs less than two weeks before daytime highs climb past 90°F and blossoms drop; USU does not carry a fall pepper planting for the St. George area.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Banana pepper drops its blossoms and stops setting fruit once days push past about 90°F, this crop's own heat threshold; St. George summers routinely reach 100°F in June, July, and August, well past that ceiling, so the spring crop is picked out before the heat and no fall crop is set (USU Extension: How to Grow Tomatoes in Your Garden, extended to the wider Solanaceae group; Washington County Elevations and frost dates).

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: In St. George's Dixie you grow banana peppers as a single spring crop. Start seed indoors in late February, set transplants out around April 1 once frost is past, and pick the mild, tapered fruit from mid to late June, either pale yellow for pickling or left to ripen further if the season allows. Once daytime highs pass 90°F in summer the plants stop setting new fruit, so there is a long summer break, and a fall crop is not recommended here since frost returns by about November 1.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs banana pepper on one spring cycle, per USU Extension. Seed goes in indoors in late February; transplants set out about April 1, the St. George Group D (Very Tender) date, just after the March 30 average last frost. At a 77-day days-to-maturity, fruit sizes up from mid to late June, leaving under two weeks before daytime highs past banana pepper's own 90°F fruit-set ceiling shut things down from July into September. USU does not recommend a fall or second pepper planting for the St. George area; frost returns around November 1.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-1 cert (2026-07-05): source-truth review (CC agent, WebFetch) -> CERTIFY_CLEAN, no fixes. Every load-bearing number resolves to a cited T1 page: sweet-vs-hot framing internally consistent with NO fabricated SHU (UGA C1005 places sweet banana among the mildest peppers 'at the bottom of the Index'; UMN classifies sweet banana as a sweet type and hot banana / Hungarian wax as a hot type); DTM 70-85 from transplant (UGA/Clemson/UMD); pH 6.0-6.5; fert 10-10-10 + calcium-nitrate side-dress; blossom-drop physiology pepper-sourced (UMN/UMD/Iowa State). Disease<->pest anchoring is CORRECT and the jalapeno insect-page mis-scope defect is ABSENT: all pests cite the NCSU insect page, all diseases cite the NCSU disease pages + the anthracnose page. Scoville kept qualitative (uf_ifas_gs carried in sources_summary but not used as a numeric consumer anchor).

open_findings.summary: The heat framing is T1-backed qualitatively (UGA C1005 places sweet banana among the mildest peppers at the bottom of the heat index; UMN classifies the sweet banana as a sweet type and the hot Hungarian/hot banana as a hot type; Clemson/UMD/Iowa list banana under sweet peppers), and the UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions Scoville page frames the scale with comparators (bell 0, jalapeno 2,000-8,000, cayenne 25,000-50,000, habanero 100,000-350,000). No T1 page read this session states a specific Scoville value for sweet banana (commonly ~0-500 SHU) or Hungarian wax (commonly ~1,000-15,000 SHU); the prose therefore states the heat comparatively (mild / near the bottom of the scale for sweet banana; distinctly hot, jalapeno-and-up for Hungarian hot wax) WITHOUT attributing a numeric SHU to a source that does not state it. Pin exact SHU to a T1 table at the biology review if one is available.

Per-zone resolved_by_zone planting/harvest windows are MODELED from days-to-maturity (70 to 85 from transplant) plus the shared crop-invariant frost anchors plus representative extension planting dates, paralleling the certified bell-pepper warm-season pattern. Individual per-zone dates are not each source-verified against a live regional banana-pepper planting calendar.

Banana pepper carries a backed midsummer heat_pause (months [7,8]) with a spring/fall split in the hot South (se_gulf z8/z9, fl_peninsula z10/z11) and the deserts (ca_desert z9/z10, low_desert_az z9), mirroring the certified bell-pepper footprint. The thermal basis is pepper blossom drop in extreme heat (day highs past ~90F with warm nights), sourced to pepper pages (UMN, UMD) rather than a tomato source; the exact pause months and split-window dates are modeled from the regional pattern, not a live per-region banana-pepper calendar.

days_to_maturity is [70,85] FROM TRANSPLANT (UGA C1005 and Clemson both give 70 to 85 days after transplanting for peppers; UMD gives sweet/hot types 70-85 from transplant; banana-pepper seed-trade norms run ~65-72 to the yellow stage, ~80 to red). Green/yellow-stage fruit is nearer 70; fully colored runs ~85. From SEED add the ~8 week indoor start. Confirm at the biology review.

Variety days_to_maturity values (Sweet Banana 70, Banana Supreme 65, Sweet Hungarian 70, Hungarian Hot Wax 65, Inferno 65) are modeled from widely published breeder/seed-catalog norms, not pinned to a per-variety T1 extension page. Sweet Banana and Banana Supreme are named by UGA C1005 and Clemson; Sweet Hungarian, Hungarian Hot Wax, and Inferno are standard banana/wax types (UMN classifies the hot banana / Hungarian wax as a hot type). The sweet-vs-hot split is well established; re-anchor individual figures at the biology review.

Several regional planting-window cells anchor to institution-level extension portals (ucanr_ext time-planting, uga_c963, nmsu_ext, tamu_agrilife, uariz_ext_az1005, ufifas_ext, uf_ifas_vh021, uhawaii_ctahr) rather than a banana-pepper-specific regional planting-date page read this session. The core agronomy is verified against UGA C1005/Clemson/UMD/UMN/Iowa State/NCSU/UC IPM; the regional portals back the MODELED windows, mirroring the certified bell-pepper sourcing.

hawaii_tropical z11 window is a broad frost-free default; the catalogued CTAHR sources are scanned/image PDFs not parseable by WebFetch this session (same case as the bell-pepper/eggplant hawaii open findings). No fabricated source.

ph.preferred_range is [6.0, 6.8]; both banana-pepper-specific T1 pages (UGA C1005 and Clemson) give the target as 6.0 to 6.5, and UMN notes peppers do well up toward 7.0, so 6.0-6.8 brackets them; tolerated_range [5.5, 7.5]. The first prose range (6.0 to 6.8) matches the structured preferred_range for A34 consistency. Confirm at the biology review.

This is a widely reported banana/wax trait but is not pinned to a single T1 comparative statement read this session; the frost-anchored windows themselves stay conservative. Confirm the cool-tolerance framing at the biology review.

crops.name: Cayenne Pepper

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Cayenne wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam that warms early in spring, since like all peppers it is a warm-season crop that sulks in cold, wet ground. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting to feed a long season and improve moisture holding. On heavy or slow-warming soil, a raised bed or a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch lifts the soil temperature and gives transplants the warm start they need. Above all the soil must drain freely: saturated ground stalls the roots, invites the Phytophthora blight and root rots peppers are prone to, and the uneven moisture it causes drives blossom-end rot on the developing pods. Steady moisture in freely draining soil is the target.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Cayenne likes rich, well-drained soil that warms up nicely in the sun, because peppers are warm-season plants that dislike cold, soggy ground. Mix 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a raised bed or a sheet of black plastic mulch warms it up and helps peppers get going. The most important thing is drainage: soggy soil stalls the plant, causes root and fruit rots, and the uneven watering that comes with it leads to blossom-end rot on the pods.

ph.note_seasoned: Cayenne grows best at a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, the range where the nutrients peppers need stay most available; Penn State reports best yields in the 6.0 to 6.8 band, and Clemson and UGA center a slightly tighter 6.0 to 6.5. It tolerates a little either side of this, but as the soil turns strongly acidic or above about 7.0 the uptake of several nutrients tightens and growth suffers. Most Eastern and Midwestern garden soils sit naturally near the target; alkaline soils common across the interior West often need sulfur worked in before planting. A simple soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant.
ph.note_beginner: Cayenne likes soil that is slightly acidic, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where peppers take up nutrients best. If your soil runs alkaline, common in the dry interior West, you may need to add sulfur before planting. An inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress after fruit set
fertilizer.type: Balanced at planting, then a light nitrogen side-dress at fruit set
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods set
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 at planting, then calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) as a light side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Cayenne is a moderate feeder rather than a heavy one, and the timing matters more than the amount. Work a complete fertilizer such as 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet, or a few inches of compost, into the bed before transplanting. Then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods have set. The cardinal rule is to go easy on nitrogen: too much gives a big, bushy, leafy plant with plenty of foliage but few blooms and little fruit, the single most common pepper-feeding mistake. Pair modest feeding with steady moisture, since even watering, not extra fertilizer, is what fills clean pods and heads off blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Cayenne does not need heavy feeding, and the timing matters more than the amount. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10, or a few inches of compost, into the soil before you plant. Then feed lightly with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods set. The big rule: go easy on nitrogen. Too much gives you a large, leafy plant with lots of leaves but hardly any peppers. Steady watering matters more than extra fertilizer for a good crop.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your cayenne has set its first pods, a good time for a light nitrogen side-dress to keep it producing. Go easy: too much nitrogen gives leaves, not peppers.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your cayenne is setting its first peppers. Give it a light nitrogen feed to keep it going, but do not overdo it or you will get all leaves.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a light nitrogen side-dress (for example calcium nitrate, 15.5-0-0) 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again at fruit set. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which gives foliage at the expense of pods.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a light nitrogen feed once pods set. Do not overdo the nitrogen, or you get all leaves and few peppers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common rate is 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before transplanting, then a light side-dress of about 0.5 pound of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 100 square feet 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods set, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in. Skip further nitrogen if the plants are lush and leafy but not fruiting.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet, or a few inches of compost, into the soil before planting. Then, 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once pods set, scratch a little nitrogen fertilizer into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in. If the plant is big and leafy but not fruiting, hold off on more nitrogen.

companions.note_seasoned: Most cayenne companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The useful ones share the warm, sunny, evenly watered culture peppers want and help deflect their pests: basil and a border of nasturtium or marigold are the classic aphid and flea-beetle deflectors, alliums such as onions and chives are traditional pungent deterrents, and low root or leaf crops like carrots and lettuce use different space without sharing pepper problems. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep cayenne away from its Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which share its aphid-vectored viruses, flea beetle, bacterial spot, and the soilborne Phytophthora and verticillium.
companions.note_beginner: Most cayenne companions are more tradition than proven science, but the sensible ones share the warm, sunny, well-watered conditions peppers like and help with pests. Basil, and a ring of nasturtiums or marigolds, can lure aphids and flea beetles away, onions and chives are traditional pest deterrents, and low crops like carrots and lettuce fit around peppers without competing. The one rule that really matters is to keep cayenne away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which are close relatives that share the same pests and soil diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Basil
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Basil is a classic partner for peppers, thought to keep aphids and other pests away, and it likes the same warm, sunny, well-watered spot. A pleasant, low-risk companion.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional pepper companion said to repel aphids and thrips, and a good match because it wants the same warm, sunny, evenly watered conditions cayenne does. The pest effect is folklore rather than trial-isolated, but the shared culture makes it a natural, low-risk neighbor.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep cayenne away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant. They are all close relatives that share the same pests, viruses, and soil diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share cayenne's pest and disease complex: aphids and the mosaic and other viruses they vector, the flea beetle, bacterial leaf spot, and the soilborne Phytophthora blight and verticillium wilt. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 to 4 year cycle.

provenance.reason: Tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant are all Solanaceae and share cayenne's pest and disease complex (aphids and the viruses they vector, flea beetle, Phytophthora blight, bacterial spot, verticillium). Grouping them concentrates that pressure and defeats rotation. A sound epidemiology and rotation principle, not a trial-tested adjacency.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often green peach aphid, cluster on growing tips and leaf undersides, discoloring and mottling the foliage, curling and puckering leaves, and coating them in sticky honeydew on which sooty mold grows. Their most serious harm is indirect: aphids transmit the mosaic and other viruses that mottle, distort, and stunt pepper plants, so an aphid problem is also a virus risk.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft green or black insects gather on new growth and the undersides of leaves, making them curl, mottle, and yellow, often with a sticky film and black mold. Worse, aphids spread plant viruses, so they are a bigger threat than their feeding alone suggests.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species, predominantly green peach aphid, that suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather and build up fast on soft, over-fertilized growth. As they probe plant to plant they carry mosaic viruses into the crop, which is why aphid control and virus control go together on peppers.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that multiply quickly in warm weather, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. As they move around they spread viruses, so keeping their numbers down protects against disease too.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control, and remove badly virus-infected plants, which cannot be cured.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them. Pull out any plant that is clearly stunted and mottled by virus, since it will not recover.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips regularly, use reflective mulch to deter aphids from young plants, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Controlling aphids early is the main defense against the viruses they carry.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves often, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything. Keeping aphids down early is the best way to avoid the viruses they spread.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on nitrogen fertilizer. The soft, lush growth that heavy feeding pushes out is exactly what aphids multiply on fastest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen drives the succulent growth aphids favor, so restrained feeding slows colony buildup on growing tips and leaf undersides before any intervention is needed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay reflective mulch, a silvery sheeting, around young plants. It puts off arriving aphids, and keeping them away early matters because they spread viruses as well as feed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants, and since early arrivals are also the virus introductions, deterrence at this stage is the front end of the defense against the mosaic viruses they carry.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull out any plant that is clearly stunted and mottled by virus. It will not recover, and aphids feeding on it can carry the virus to your healthy peppers.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Badly virus-infected plants cannot be cured; removing them takes away the reservoir aphids probe and move on from, which is why aphid control and virus control go together on peppers.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the colonies off with a strong jet of water from the hose, aiming at the undersides of the leaves where they gather. Go back every few days.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A hard jet of water strips the colonies off growing tips and leaf undersides; go back over the planting every few days, since warm weather lets survivors rebuild quickly.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, and the tiny wasps that parasitize aphids usually hold them down without any help from you. Welcome them, and avoid spraying everything, which harms the helpers too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually bring aphids under control on pepper; conserving them by not spraying broadly does more than routine treatment would.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If numbers keep climbing, spray insecticidal soap and be thorough on the undersides of the leaves, since it only works where it lands. Repeat every few days.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is contact material, so thorough coverage of the leaf undersides governs the result; repeat every few days to catch survivors and newly emerged nymphs.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil, is the other choice at this step. It also works only where it touches, so coat the leaf undersides well and repeat every few days.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil carries the same thorough-coverage and repeat-interval demands as soap; either material serves once the softer steps have not held the colonies down.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny beetles chew small, round, shot-hole pits and holes through the leaves, and large numbers of these punctures can stunt or kill seedlings and young transplants, whose small leaf area is quickly overwhelmed. Established plants tolerate considerable feeding. Brush a plant and the small dark beetles spring away like fleas.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The leaves are peppered with lots of tiny round holes, as if hit by birdshot. It hits young plants hardest and can stunt or kill seedlings, while big plants shrug it off. Touch the plant and you will see tiny dark beetles jump away.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several flea beetle species that overwinter as adults in debris and emerge to attack the earliest, most vulnerable plants in spring. Large populations concentrate on small transplants, so the damage is an early-season, seedling-stage problem more than a threat to mature peppers.
pests.cause_beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas and chew tiny holes in the leaves. They are most active in spring and hit young plants hardest, so they are mainly a seedling problem.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover until they are large and vigorous, removing it at flowering. Set out stout, well-hardened transplants rather than tiny seedlings so plants outgrow the damage, and treat heavy early infestations with spinosad or kaolin clay. Mature plants rarely need treatment.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are big and strong, then take it off when they flower. Setting out larger transplants helps them outgrow the damage. For heavy attacks on seedlings, an organic spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating helps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, delay setting plants out until the soil and air are warm so they grow away fast, and clean up crop debris and weeds that harbor overwintering adults. A nasturtium or other trap planting at the bed edge can draw beetles off the crop.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants early with row cover, set out larger transplants into warm soil so they grow quickly, and clear away weeds and old plant debris where the beetles hide over winter. A border of nasturtiums can lure them away.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear away weeds and old crop debris, since that is where the beetles hide over winter before coming out in spring to attack your youngest plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Adults overwinter in debris and weedy cover; removing both lowers the spring emergence that concentrates on the earliest, most vulnerable transplants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A border of nasturtiums at the edge of the bed can lure the beetles away from your peppers. Treat it as a sacrifice planting, not part of the crop, and follow this method's cautions on tending and removing it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The crop guidance names a nasturtium or other trap planting at the bed edge to draw beetles off the crop. It works by preference, not by removal, so its value rests on the tending and destruction obligations in this method's cautions; a loaded patch left standing concentrates beetles beside the crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover, a thin fabric that lets light and water through while keeping beetles off, until they are big and strong. Take it off when they flower.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover from transplanting excludes adults through the seedling window, when a small leaf area is quickly overwhelmed; remove at flowering. Established plants tolerate considerable feeding without it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For a heavy attack on seedlings, coat the leaves with kaolin clay, a fine white mineral powder mixed with water and sprayed on. The film helps put the beetles off feeding.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A kaolin particle film helps against heavy early infestations on seedlings and young transplants; mature plants rarely need treatment, so this is a transplant-stage tool.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spinosad, an organic spray derived from a soil bacterium, is for a heavy attack that threatens to stunt or kill seedlings. Bigger plants shrug the holes off and rarely need it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reserve spinosad for heavy early infestations at the seedling stage; established plants tolerate the shot-holing, so treatment past that window is rarely warranted.

pests.name: Pepper maggot
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Adult flies puncture young pods to lay eggs, and the cream-colored larvae tunnel and feed inside the fruit for about 18 days; maggot-damaged peppers often color up (turn red) prematurely and begin to rot from within, with the larva hidden inside. Thin-walled, slender types such as cayenne are noted to suffer far less than thick-walled bell and pimento peppers, so cayenne is a relatively low-susceptibility host.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A fly lays eggs in young pods, and the maggots feed hidden inside the fruit. An infested pepper often turns red too early and starts to rot from the inside, with the grub tucked away where you cannot see it. Slim, thin-walled peppers like cayenne are much less bothered than fat-walled bell peppers.
pests.cause_seasoned: The pepper maggot, the larva of a small fly that lays eggs in developing pods in mid to late summer. It is most damaging on thick-walled peppers; cayenne and other slender, thin-walled, hot types are documented as far less affected, though not immune where the fly is active.
pests.cause_beginner: The maggot of a small fly that lays its eggs in young peppers in summer. It mostly attacks thick-walled peppers, so slim cayenne is much less at risk, though not completely safe where the fly is around.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for an infested pod: remove and destroy affected fruit promptly, and drop fallen and culled peppers into the trash rather than the compost so larvae do not complete development in the garden. Where the fly is a known local problem, a well-timed labeled insecticide at first fly activity is the reliable control, but on cayenne the low susceptibility usually makes sanitation enough.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot save an infested pepper, so pick off and throw away any that rot or color up early, and put fallen fruit in the trash, not the compost. Cayenne is rarely hit hard, so cleaning up damaged fruit is usually all a home garden needs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Grow the thin-walled hot types (cayenne among them) that the maggot largely avoids, clean up dropped and cull fruit through the season, and rotate away from where peppers grew. In areas with a known pepper-maggot history, cover plants or time a labeled spray to first adult activity.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cayenne's slim, thin walls already make it a poor target, so the main thing is to clean up any dropped or damaged peppers during the season and move peppers to a new spot each year. Where the fly is a known local pest, covering plants helps.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Growing cayenne already does most of the work. This fly goes for thick-walled peppers like bells, and slim, thin-walled types like cayenne are much less bothered, though not immune where the fly is around.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Host preference runs to thick-walled bell and pimento types; cayenne and the other slender, thin-walled hot peppers are documented as far less affected, so the variety choice itself carries most of the control, though it is not immunity where the fly is active.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move your peppers to a new spot each year instead of planting back where they grew before.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotating away from where peppers grew adds distance from local carryover, complementing the sanitation that removes the fruit larvae develop in.

control_ladder.note_beginner: You cannot save a pepper once the maggot is inside, so pick off any that rot or turn red too early, and put fallen and damaged fruit in the trash, not the compost. On cayenne this cleanup is usually all a home garden needs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no rescue for an infested pod; prompt removal of affected fruit, with drops and culls trashed rather than composted so larvae cannot complete development in the garden, is usually sufficient on a low-susceptibility host like cayenne.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where the pepper maggot is a known local pest, covering the plants helps keep the fly from reaching the young pods.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: In areas with a pepper-maggot history, covering plants blocks the adult fly from puncturing young pods to lay eggs; once eggs are laid the larva feeds hidden inside the fruit, out of reach.

pests.name: Pepper weevil
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Adults feed on foliage, buds, and tender pods, but the larvae do the real harm: infested buds and blossoms yellow and drop, pods may drop prematurely or grow misshapen, and the inside of an affected pod turns dark and fills with frass. It is chiefly a problem in the warm South (Florida, the Gulf, the Southwest) where the weevil can persist; it cannot overwinter in colder regions.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A small weevil whose grubs feed inside the buds and pods. Affected buds and flowers turn yellow and drop, pods may fall early or come out misshapen, and inside an infested pepper looks dark and full of grub droppings. It is mostly a warm-South problem and does not survive cold winters.
pests.cause_seasoned: The pepper weevil, a small snout beetle whose larvae develop inside buds and pods. It is a serious pepper pest in Florida, the Gulf Coast, and the warm Southwest, moving in on infested transplants or from nearby solanaceous weeds and abandoned pepper plantings; in cold-winter regions it does not establish.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny weevil whose grubs grow up inside pepper buds and pods. It is a warm-climate pest, common in Florida and the Gulf, and often arrives on infested plants. It cannot survive cold winters, so northern gardens rarely see it.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no home-garden cure for an infested pod. Pick up and destroy dropped buds and pods promptly (in the trash, not the compost) to break the cycle, remove volunteer peppers and solanaceous weeds that harbor the weevil, and in endemic areas a labeled insecticide program is often needed for a clean crop. Start with clean, locally grown transplants.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot save an infested pepper, so gather up and throw away any dropped buds and pods (in the trash, not the compost) to slow it down, and pull nearby weedy nightshades. In warm areas where it is common, you may need a labeled spray, and always start with healthy, locally grown plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Buy transplants grown where the pepper weevil is not established rather than importing the problem, clean up dropped fruit and nightshade weeds through the season, and remove and destroy spent plantings promptly so the weevil has nowhere to carry over. Rotation and garden sanitation are the backbone of control.
pests.prevention_beginner: Start with healthy transplants grown in your area, not shipped in from warm regions where the weevil lives, clean up dropped peppers during the season, pull weedy nightshades, and clear out old plants at season's end. Keeping the garden clean is the main defense.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cleanup is the main defense. Gather dropped buds and pods promptly and put them in the trash, not the compost, and clear out the spent plants as soon as harvest ends so the weevil has nowhere to carry over.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt destruction of dropped buds and pods breaks the cycle, since the grubs finish developing inside them, and clearing spent plantings as soon as harvest ends denies the weevil a carryover home; sanitation is stated as the backbone of control.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull the weedy nightshades growing near the peppers, and get rid of volunteer pepper plants, the strays that come up on their own. The weevil survives on both between crops.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Volunteer peppers and solanaceous weeds harbor the weevil between pepper crops; clearing them removes the bridge it carries over on.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give peppers a new spot rather than replanting where they grew last year.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotation pairs with sanitation as the backbone of control, moving the crop away from ground and surroundings where the weevil carried over.

pests.name: Tomato and tobacco hornworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large sections of leaf, and sometimes whole shoots or the surface of a pod, are stripped or gouged overnight, with dark pellet droppings on the leaves below. The culprits are big green tomato or tobacco hornworms, up to three or four inches long, that blend into the stems and are easiest to find by their frass. Peppers are a secondary host, so damage is usually less than on tomato, but a few caterpillars can defoliate a plant fast.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Whole leaves vanish overnight, leaving just the veins, sometimes with gouged pods, and dark droppings on the leaves below. The cause is a large green caterpillar that hides against the stems, easier to spot by its droppings than by sight. Peppers are a side dish for it compared with tomato, but even a few can strip a plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tomato and tobacco hornworms, the larvae of large sphinx moths, which feed on solanaceous foliage including pepper from midsummer on. Given their size, even a few caterpillars can do conspicuous damage, though peppers are less preferred than tomato.
pests.cause_beginner: Big green caterpillars, the young of large moths, that feed on pepper and tomato leaves mostly in mid to late summer. Even a few can strip a lot of foliage, though they prefer tomatoes.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick the caterpillars, which is effective in a home garden, and apply Bacillus thuringiensis to younger larvae where numbers are high. Leave any hornworm studded with white parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the wasps will kill it and breed more.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them in soapy water. If you find one covered in small white capsules, leave it, those are parasitic wasps that will do the work for you. An organic Bt spray works on the smaller caterpillars.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till the soil in fall to destroy overwintering pupae, scout for frass and stripped leaves from midsummer, and encourage the parasitic wasps and other natural enemies that keep hornworms in check.
pests.prevention_beginner: Turn the soil at the end of the season to destroy the pupae, watch for droppings and missing leaves from midsummer, and welcome the helpful wasps that attack hornworms.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Turn the soil over in fall once the plants come out. The caterpillars pass the winter underground as pupae, the resting stage between caterpillar and moth, and tilling destroys them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Fall tillage destroys overwintering pupae in the bed, trimming the local carryover before the next summer's moths emerge.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the big caterpillars off by hand and drop them into soapy water. They blend into the stems, so look for the dark droppings, called frass, on the leaves below and search just above that spot.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Handpicking is effective at home-garden scale; frass on lower leaves locates larvae far more reliably than scanning the stems they match.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If you find a hornworm covered in small white capsules, leave it right where it is. Those are the cocoons of parasitic wasps that will kill it and go on to attack other hornworms.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Leave any larva studded with parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the emerging wasps kill it and breed more; encouraging these natural enemies is part of what keeps hornworm numbers in check.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When there are more caterpillars than you can pick, Bt, short for Bacillus thuringiensis, is an organic spray that works on the smaller, younger ones.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Apply Bt where numbers run high, aimed at younger larvae; it is the material for small caterpillars, with handpicking covering the full-grown ones.

pests.name: Cutworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Young transplants are found cut off cleanly at or just above the soil line, felled overnight, with the severed plant lying nearby. Climbing cutworms may also feed on leaves and fruit higher up. The damage strikes right after transplanting, when the loss of a stem at the base kills the whole young plant.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A young pepper plant is found toppled, cut right through at the soil line, as if snipped. It happens overnight, soon after planting. Sometimes the same caterpillars climb up and chew leaves and fruit too.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cutworms, the soil-dwelling larvae of several moths, that shelter in the soil by day and sever young stems at night. They are worst on newly set transplants in spring, especially in beds recently turned from sod or weeds.
pests.cause_beginner: Fat caterpillars that hide in the soil during the day and chew through young stems at night. They are worst on new transplants in spring, especially in ground that was recently grass or weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set a collar (a cardboard tube, tin can, or cup with the bottom removed) around each transplant, pushed an inch into the soil, to block cutworms. Check for and hand-pick the curled gray caterpillars in the soil around a felled plant at dusk, and keep beds clear of the weeds and debris they shelter in.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Put a collar around each young plant, such as a cardboard tube or a cup with the bottom cut out, pushed a little into the soil, so cutworms cannot reach the stem. If a plant is cut down, dig in the soil nearby to find and remove the curled caterpillar.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Ring transplants with collars at planting, clear the bed of weeds and old plant debris a couple of weeks ahead, and lightly cultivate the soil before planting to expose and disrupt overwintering larvae. Beds newly broken from lawn are highest-risk.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put a protective collar around each plant when you set it out, clear weeds and debris from the bed ahead of time, and turn the soil before planting to expose the caterpillars. Beds that were recently lawn are the riskiest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear weeds and old plant debris out of the bed a couple of weeks before planting. Cutworms shelter in that cover, and beds fresh out of lawn are the riskiest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Stripping weeds and debris ahead of transplanting removes the daytime shelter cutworms work from; ground newly broken from sod or weeds carries the highest pressure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put a collar around each transplant, a cardboard tube, a tin can, or a cup with the bottom cut out, pushed about an inch into the soil so the caterpillars cannot reach the stem.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A collar seated an inch into the soil around each transplant blocks stem access through establishment, the window in which a severed base is fatal to the whole transplant.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a plant is found cut down, dig gently in the soil around it at dusk. The curled gray caterpillar hides nearby and can be picked out and destroyed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Search the soil around a felled plant at dusk for the curled gray larva; hand removal at the site of fresh damage is the direct follow-up when a collar was missing or breached.

diseases.name: Bacterial leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, water-soaked spots on the leaves enlarge and turn dark brown with a yellow halo, and heavily spotted leaves yellow and drop prematurely; the resulting defoliation exposes the pods to sunscald. On the fruit, small raised blisters develop into dark brown, scabby, cracked lesions. It is one of the most damaging pepper diseases in warm, wet weather.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small wet-looking spots on the leaves turn brown with a yellow ring, and badly spotted leaves drop off, which lets the sun scald the exposed peppers. The fruit can develop dark, raised, scabby spots. It is worst in warm, rainy weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Xanthomonas bacteria that are seed- and debris-borne and spread in splashing water and on hands and tools, thriving in warm, humid, rainy conditions. Once established in wet weather it moves fast, so clean seed, resistant varieties, and dry foliage are the keys to control.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterial disease carried on seed and in old plant debris that spreads in splashing water and on wet hands and tools. It loves warm, wet weather. Starting with clean seed and keeping leaves dry are the main defenses.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove badly affected leaves and plants and avoid working among wet plants. Copper-based sprays can slow spread as a protectant in wet spells but do not cure the disease. Focus on limiting splash and moisture.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so remove the worst-affected leaves and plants and stay out of the patch when it is wet. A copper spray can slow it down in rainy spells but will not cure it. Keeping the leaves dry matters most.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with certified disease-free or resistant seed and transplants, rotate peppers out of the bed for several years, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, avoid handling wet plants, and remove crop debris at season's end.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean, resistant seed and healthy transplants, do not plant peppers in the same spot for several years, water at the soil instead of over the leaves, mulch, and clean up old plants at the end of the season. Do not work among the plants while they are wet.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with certified disease-free seed and healthy transplants. The bacteria can ride in on the seed itself, so a clean start keeps the disease out of the garden in the first place.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogen is seed-borne, so certified clean seed and disease-free transplants close the primary introduction route; with no cure once plants are infected, control is built up front.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Choose a resistant variety where you can find one. With no cure available, what you plant matters as much as how you tend it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resistant varieties sit alongside clean seed and dry foliage as the stated keys to control for a disease that moves fast once established in warm, wet weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not plant peppers in the same spot year after year. Give that bed several years' break so the bacteria in old debris die out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotating peppers out of the bed for several years lets the debris-borne inoculum decline before the crop returns.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Remove the worst-spotted leaves and any badly affected plant, since they cannot be cured, and clear out all the old pepper plants at the end of the season.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing badly affected leaves and plants lowers inoculum rather than rescuing them, and end-of-season debris removal takes out the overwintering reservoir; heavy defoliation also exposes pods to sunscald, so the losses compound if it stays.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves. The bacteria travel in splashing water, so leaves that stay dry are much harder for them to reach.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soil-directed watering removes the overhead splash that spreads the bacteria; keeping foliage dry is central, since warm, wet conditions are what let this disease move fast.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spread mulch under the plants so rain cannot splash soil and old debris up onto the leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mulch intercepts splash off soil and residue, limiting one of the short-range routes the bacteria use to reach clean foliage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Space the plants so air moves between them and the leaves dry quickly after rain. This disease is at its worst in warm, wet weather.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spacing for airflow shortens leaf-wetness periods, working directly against the warm, humid, rainy conditions the disease thrives in.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stay out of the pepper patch while the plants are wet. The bacteria spread on wet hands and tools as readily as in rain splash.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogen moves on hands and tools among wet plants, so timing work for dry foliage removes a transmission route that no irrigation choice controls.

control_ladder.note_beginner: In a rainy spell, a copper spray can slow the disease down, but it will not cure it. Keep leaning on dry leaves and cleanup as the real defense.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper acts as a protectant that can slow spread through wet spells; it is not curative, so it supplements rather than replaces the splash- and moisture-limiting steps.

diseases.name: Mosaic and other viruses
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves become mottled light and dark green, distorted, sometimes crinkled or narrowed, and the plant stunts; fruit may be mottled, distorted, or ripen unevenly. Several viruses cause this picture (tobacco and cucumber mosaic, pepper mottle, potato virus Y, and others), often spread by aphids, and there is no cure. Tobacco mosaic can also be carried on hands after handling tobacco.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The leaves turn a patchy light-and-dark green, get distorted or crinkled, and the plant is stunted, with mottled or oddly ripening peppers. Several viruses cause this, usually spread by aphids, and none can be cured. Tobacco products can carry one of these viruses to peppers on your hands.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A complex of viruses (tobacco mosaic, cucumber mosaic, pepper mottle, potato virus Y, and others) transmitted chiefly by aphids probing plant to plant, and in the case of tobacco mosaic by contaminated hands and tools. Because there is no cure, control is entirely about prevention: manage aphids and remove infected plants.
diseases.cause_beginner: A group of viruses spread mainly by aphids, and one of them by tobacco on your hands. There is no cure, so the whole game is prevention: keep aphids down and pull out infected plants before they spread it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no treatment; promptly remove and destroy infected plants to limit spread to healthy ones. Control the aphids that vector the viruses, and wash hands after any tobacco use before touching peppers. Do not compost infected plants.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure. Pull out and destroy infected plants so they do not spread it to the rest. Keep aphids under control, and wash your hands after handling tobacco before touching your peppers. Do not compost sick plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties where available, start with clean transplants, control aphids early with the measures above, use reflective mulch to repel them from young plants, remove infected plants at first sign, keep weeds that host viruses down, and avoid tobacco contact with the crop.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Look for resistant varieties, start with healthy plants, keep aphids down, remove infected plants right away, control weeds, and do not handle peppers right after using tobacco. Prevention is the only tool with viruses.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Look for virus-resistant varieties where they are available. An infected plant cannot be cured, so resistance is the strongest tool you have.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resistant cultivars, where available, lead the program for a virus complex with no curative option; everything after planting is damage limitation.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with healthy transplants so you do not bring the problem home with the plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Clean transplants avoid introducing infection at planting; with no cure, control is entirely preventive.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay reflective mulch, a silvery sheet, around young plants. It repels the aphids that carry most of these viruses from plant to plant.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch repels aphids from young plants; since aphids are the chief vectors, deterring them early is virus prevention directly, alongside the rest of the aphid program.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull out and destroy any mottled, stunted plant at the first sign, and do not compost it. Keep the weeds down around the bed, and if you use tobacco, wash your hands before touching the plants, since one of these viruses can travel on your hands.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rogue infected plants promptly to remove the source aphids spread from, and do not compost them. Keep down the weeds that host these viruses, and wash hands after tobacco use before handling the crop, since tobacco mosaic also moves on contaminated hands and tools.

diseases.name: Phytophthora blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, water-soaked lesions develop on the crown and stem at or near the soil line, turn brown, and girdle the stem, so the whole plant wilts and dies suddenly, often after heavy rain or in a poorly drained spot. The disease can also cause dark leaf lesions and a firm fruit rot with white, cottony mold. It persists in soil for years and spreads fast in warm, wet, saturated conditions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, wet-looking patches form on the stem near the soil, girdle it, and the whole plant wilts and dies quickly, often after heavy rain or in a soggy spot. It can also rot the fruit with white fuzzy growth. It lives in the soil for years and spreads fast in warm, wet ground.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora capsici, a water mold that thrives in saturated soil and spreads in splashing and running water. It survives in soil and debris and moves rapidly in warm, wet weather, especially on heavy or poorly drained ground and in low spots that stay wet, which is why drainage is the central control.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that lives in wet soil and spreads in splashing and running water, attacking plants in warm, soggy conditions. It moves fast once it starts, so good drainage is the main way to keep it out.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no home-garden cure once plants collapse; remove and destroy affected plants and fruit promptly and improve drainage immediately. Because the pathogen persists in soil, control is preventive and drainage-based rather than curative.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home cure once plants collapse. Pull and destroy affected plants and fruit, and fix the drainage right away. Prevention is really the only tool.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on raised, well-drained beds, avoid low spots that stay wet, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, do not overwater, rotate away from peppers and other solanaceous and cucurbit crops on a long cycle, and keep pods up off saturated soil.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant on raised beds or mounds so water drains away, avoid soggy low spots, water at the soil, do not overwater, and rotate away from peppers, tomatoes, and squash. Good drainage is the whole game with this one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant on raised beds or mounds so water drains away, and avoid low spots that stay soggy after rain. This disease lives in wet soil, so drainage is the main defense.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Raised, well-drained beds and avoidance of low spots that stay wet deny this water mold the saturated soil it thrives in; the pathogen persists in soil for years, so control is preventive and drainage-based rather than curative.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil instead of over the leaves, and do not overwater. Soggy ground is what invites this disease in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soil-directed, restrained irrigation limits both the saturation the pathogen needs and the splashing water that spreads it; volume is as much a control point as placement.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Mulch under the plants to cut down on splash, since the disease spreads in splashing and running water.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mulch limits splash off infested soil, one of the routes by which the pathogen moves through a planting in warm, wet weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move peppers away from ground that grew peppers, tomatoes, or squash, and give it a long break, since the disease survives in the soil for years.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate away from solanaceous and cucurbit hosts on a long cycle; multi-year persistence in soil and debris makes a short gap ineffective.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When a plant wilts and collapses, pull it and any rotted fruit out promptly and destroy them, then fix the drainage right away.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt removal and destruction of collapsed plants and rotted fruit limits what splashing and running water can carry onward; there is no home-garden cure once plants go down.

diseases.name: Anthracnose (ripe fruit rot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, sunken, circular lesions appear on the pods, often in concentric rings, and develop moist masses of salmon-to-pink spores in the center. It typically shows up as the fruit ripens (a ripe-fruit rot), and because infection can be latent, cayenne left to color fully red for drying is especially exposed in warm, wet seasons. It also spots leaves and stems.
