The plant soon begins to reach and twine toward its support. Young seedlings are the stage most vulnerable to bean leaf beetle feeding.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The two seed leaves open, then the real leaves appear, first a single pair, then the three-leaflet leaves beans are known for. The little plant soon starts to reach and twist toward its support. This young stage is when beetles can do the most damage.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free; young beans compete poorly with weeds. Cultivate shallowly, since bean roots run close to the surface. Make sure the support is in place and guide the first shoots to it if needed. There is no thinning: pole beans are sown at their spacing along the support.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and pull weeds early, hoeing shallowly since bean roots are near the surface. Check that the trellis or poles are ready and gently steer the first shoots onto them. You do not thin pole beans, they are planted where they will grow.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is your bean stand looking? Note any gaps or beetle damage on the young leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young bean plants look? Note any chewed leaves or bare patches.

growth_stages.name: Vining and climbing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid vining as the plant twines up its support toward its full height, often 6 feet or more. Pole beans spend real energy climbing before they set heavily, so early growth looks leafy and upward rather than fruitful. The plant is fixing much of its own nitrogen now, so vigorous but not lush, overfed growth is the goal.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fast climbing growth as the vine winds its way up the trellis or poles, often to 6 feet or taller. Pole beans put a lot of early effort into climbing before they make many beans, so at first you will see lots of leafy vine going up rather than pods. Beans make much of their own food (nitrogen) at this stage.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold steady, even moisture and resist the urge to feed. Beans need little nitrogen, and excess now drives leafy vine growth and delays flowering. Guide wayward shoots onto the support; the vines twine on their own but a nudge helps them find the structure early.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady and do not add fertilizer now. Beans need very little, and extra just gives you big leafy vines and later beans. Tuck any stray shoots onto the support; the vines climb on their own, but a little help early gets them going.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How high are your vines climbing? Note their height and how well they are taking to the support.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How tall are your bean vines getting? Note how far up the support they have climbed.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white, pink, or purple flowers open along the vines. Pole beans flower over a long, extended window rather than all at once, so bloom and pod set overlap and continue for weeks. This is a moisture-critical stage: water stress aborts blossoms, and sustained heat above about 90°F causes blossom drop until the weather cools.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small white, pink, or purple flowers open along the vines. Unlike bush beans, pole beans flower a little at a time over a long stretch, so flowers and young pods appear together for weeks. This is an important time for water. If the plants dry out or it stays above about 90°F, the flowers drop without making beans, then start again once it cools.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample; water stress now directly cuts the running yield. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead, to keep the tall canopy dry. In a heat wave, water deeply ahead of it; the vine will keep reflowering as temperatures ease.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous, because dry soil now means fewer beans. Water the soil, not the leaves, to keep disease down. If a heat wave hits, water deeply beforehand, then wait it out, the vine will keep flowering once it cools.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your beans flowering? Note the date bloom started and any blossom drop in heat.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your beans flowering yet? Note when the flowers opened and whether any dropped in hot weather.

growth_stages.name: Pod set and fill
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pods appear where flowers were and lengthen quickly, plumping as the seeds fill. Because the vine flowers continuously, you will see pods at every stage at once, from tiny to pickable. Drought here produces small, stringy pods and can stall the plant's ongoing set.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Pods form where the flowers were and grow quickly, getting plumper as the beans fill inside. Because the vine keeps flowering, you will have pods of every size at once, from tiny to ready. Dry soil now makes small, tough, crooked pods and can slow down the whole run.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain even moisture near field capacity right through pod fill; on pole beans this stage runs for weeks. Begin checking pods every couple of days as they size up, since the pickable window for any one pod is brief.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist all through this stage, which on pole beans lasts a long time. Start checking the pods every couple of days, because each one is ready for only a short time before it gets too old.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are pods forming and filling? Note the date you first saw pods and how fast they are sizing up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are pods forming? Note when you first saw them and how quickly they are growing.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly when bent, picked before the enlarging seeds bulge the pod wall. Most pole varieties reach first pick around 60 to 70 days and then keep bearing for many weeks. Regular picking every couple of days keeps the vine flowering and setting new pods; pods left to mature signal it to slow down.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Firm, crisp pods that break with a clean snap, picked before you can see the seeds bulging. Most pole beans give their first pick around 60 to 70 days and then keep producing for weeks. Picking every couple of days keeps new beans coming; leaving old pods on tells the vine to slow down.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick in the early morning for best quality, once the dew has dried, breaking pods off cleanly without tearing the vine. Harvest every two to three days across the whole season; frequent picking is the single biggest lever on how long and heavily a pole bean bears. Do not work the vines when foliage is wet, which spreads bacterial blight.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick in the morning for the best beans, after the dew dries, snapping pods off without tearing the vine. Pick every two or three days all season long, because picking often is what keeps a pole bean producing. Do not pick when the leaves are wet, since that spreads disease.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you made your first picking? Log the date and keep noting each pick to track how long the vines bear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your first beans? Note the date and keep track of each picking through the season.

notifications.body_seasoned: Direct-sow pole beans after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth. Sow about 1 inch deep into a moist, well-drained bed, and set your trellis, poles, or netting in place at planting so you do not disturb the roots later.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant pole beans right in the garden after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F. Plant about 1 inch deep, and put up your trellis or teepee of poles at the same time so you do not disturb the roots later.

notifications.body_seasoned: Most pole beans reach first pick around 60 to 70 days. Begin checking and pick firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly, before the seeds bulge. From here the vine keeps bearing for weeks.
notifications.body_beginner: Most pole beans are ready for a first pick around 60 to 70 days. Start checking and pick firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly, before the seeds bulge through. From now on the vine keeps making beans for weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Keep picking to keep them producing
notifications.title_beginner: Keep picking to keep beans coming
notifications.body_seasoned: Pick pole beans every two to three days all season. Regular picking is what keeps the vine flowering and setting new pods; pods left to mature signal it to slow down. There is no need to succession-sow, one planting bears until frost.
notifications.body_beginner: Pick your pole beans every two or three days all season. Picking often is what keeps a pole bean making more beans, so do not let old pods sit on the vine. You do not need to plant again, one planting keeps going until frost.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost expected, protect or harvest beans
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost is coming, pick or cover your beans
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Pole beans are frost-tender and a light frost will kill them. If frost is forecast, harvest any pickable pods; covering a tall trellised vine is hard, so pick everything usable first. In fall, a hard frost ends the crop.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Pole beans are killed by even a light frost. If frost is forecast, pick any beans that are ready. A tall vine is hard to cover, so harvest everything you can use first. In fall, a hard frost ends the crop.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather can make flowers drop
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above about 90°F during bloom causes beans to drop blossoms instead of setting pods. Keep moisture steady and water deeply ahead of the heat; because pole beans flower over a long window, the vine resumes setting pods once it cools.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: When it stays above about 90°F while beans are flowering, they drop their flowers instead of making beans. Keep the water steady and water deeply before the heat. Because pole beans flower for a long time, the vine starts setting beans again once it cools.

germination.text_seasoned: Bean seed rots in cold, wet ground. Wait until the soil is at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing, since early planting only invites poor stands and seed rot. Beans sown into warm soil quickly overtake those sown into cold soil.
germination.text_beginner: Bean seeds rot in cold, wet soil. Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, because planting early just leads to rotted seed and missing plants. Beans planted into warm soil catch up fast, so there is nothing to gain by rushing.
germination.author: plant

germination.text_seasoned: Set the trellis, teepee, or netting in place at sowing, not after the vines are up. Pole beans twine on their own but need a sturdy 6-to-8-foot support ready to climb, and installing it later disturbs shallow bean roots.
germination.text_beginner: Put your trellis, teepee, or netting up when you plant, not later. Pole beans climb by themselves but need a strong support, about 6 to 8 feet tall, ready and waiting. Adding it later disturbs the shallow roots.
germination.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Weed early and cultivate shallowly. Young beans compete poorly with weeds, but their roots run close to the surface, so deep hoeing does more harm than the weeds. Hand-pull and scuffle-hoe lightly near the row.
seedling.text_beginner: Pull weeds early, but weed shallowly. Young beans do not compete well with weeds, yet their roots are near the surface, so digging deep hurts the plant more than the weeds do. Pull by hand and hoe lightly near the row.
seedling.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Hold off on nitrogen. As legumes, beans fix much of their own, and extra nitrogen now drives leafy vine growth up the trellis and delays flowering. At most a single light side-dressing just before bloom, and only on poor or sandy soil.
vegetative.text_beginner: Do not add nitrogen fertilizer now. Beans make much of their own from the air, and extra fertilizer just gives you big leafy vines and later beans. At most, feed once lightly right before they flower, and only if your soil is poor.
vegetative.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Guide the young shoots onto their support early. Pole beans twine counterclockwise on their own, but a nudge onto the trellis or pole in the first weeks keeps them from tangling on the ground and starts the climb clean.
vegetative.text_beginner: Help the young vines find their support early. Pole beans wind their way up on their own, but steering them onto the trellis or pole in the first weeks keeps them from tangling on the ground.
vegetative.author: plant

flowering.text_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom. Flowering and pod set are the moisture-critical stages, and on pole beans they run for weeks, so water stress at any point cuts the running crop. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead.
flowering.text_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the vine flowers. Flowering and pod-forming are when beans most need water, and on pole beans that lasts a long time, so letting them dry out shrinks the crop. Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves.
flowering.author: plant

flowering.text_seasoned: Expect blossom drop in sustained heat above about 90°F. The vine aborts flowers when it is too hot to set pods, then resumes once it cools. Because pole beans flower over a long window, the crop recovers as the weather eases; water deeply ahead of a heat wave.
flowering.text_beginner: When it stays hotter than about 90°F, beans drop their flowers. The vine gives up on flowers when it is too hot to make beans, then starts again once it cools. Since pole beans flower for a long time, the crop bounces back. Water deeply before a heat wave.
flowering.author: plant

pod_set_fill.text_seasoned: Do not let the bed dry out as pods size up. Drought during pod fill produces small, stringy pods and can stall the vine's ongoing set, while steady moisture near field capacity gives plump, well-formed ones over the whole long season.
pod_set_fill.text_beginner: Do not let the soil dry out while the pods are growing. Dry soil now makes small, tough, crooked beans and can slow the whole run, while steady moisture gives you plump, well-shaped ones all season.
pod_set_fill.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick every two to three days, before the seeds bulge the pod. On pole beans, frequent picking is the single biggest lever on yield: it keeps the vine flowering and setting new pods, while pods left to mature signal it to slow down. One well-picked planting bears for many weeks.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick every two or three days, before the seeds swell the pods. On pole beans, picking often is what keeps them producing: it keeps new flowers and pods coming, while old pods left on tell the vine to quit. One planting, well picked, keeps going for weeks.
harvest.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick in the early morning for best quality, but only once the dew has dried. Handling wet bean vines spreads bacterial blight through the planting, so wait for the foliage to dry before working down the rows.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick in the morning for the best beans, but wait until the dew has dried off the vines. Touching wet bean plants spreads disease through your patch, so let the leaves dry before you start picking.
harvest.author: plant

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Pole beans out-yield bush beans from the same footprint by growing vertically and bearing over a long season. A 10-foot row of pole beans typically returns roughly 8 to 12 pounds of pods over its extended cropping period, compared with about 5 pounds for bush beans in the same space.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Pole beans give more from the same patch than bush beans because they grow up instead of out and keep bearing for a long time. A 10-foot row of pole beans usually gives about 8 to 12 pounds of beans over the season, versus around 5 pounds for bush beans in the same space.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Rather than a single burst, pole beans bear steadily over many weeks from one planting, right up to frost. That long, running harvest is why succession sowing is unnecessary: one well-tended planting keeps a household supplied, provided you pick every couple of days to keep it flowering.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Instead of one big batch, pole beans give a steady supply over many weeks from a single planting, all the way to frost. That is why you do not need to replant every couple of weeks like with bush beans: one planting keeps going, as long as you pick every few days.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Pole beans are a rewarding first-year crop: they germinate quickly, ask little, and a single planting bears for weeks once it starts, around 60 to 70 days from sowing. The main first-year lever on yield is steady moisture through the long flowering and pod-fill season, plus picking often enough to keep the vine producing.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Pole beans are a satisfying crop for a first-year garden. They come up fast, need little fuss, and one planting keeps making beans for weeks once it starts, about 60 to 70 days from planting. The main things that affect how much you get are keeping the water steady and picking often so the vine keeps producing.
factors_seasoned: Steady moisture through the long flowering and pod-fill season (the moisture-critical stages; drought aborts blossoms and stalls the running set)
Frequent picking (leaving mature pods on the vine signals it to slow flowering, so picking every couple of days is the biggest lever on total yield)
Temperature during bloom (sustained heat above about 90°F causes blossom drop and pauses the set until it cools)
A sturdy full-height support and good sun (vertical growth on a 6-to-8-foot trellis is what lets pole beans out-yield bush beans per square foot)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No university extension or peer-reviewed source supports timing pole bean planting by moon phase. No recommendation is made here: sow beans by soil temperature, which should be at least about 60°F, and by your frost-free date, not by the lunar cycle.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers dropped without setting pods
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Flowers fell off without making beans
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The vine flowered but the blossoms dropped instead of setting pods, because sustained heat above about 90°F interferes with pollination and the plant aborts flowers it cannot fill. Water stress during bloom has the same effect. It is a weather problem, not a disease, and because pole beans flower over a long window, the vine usually resumes setting pods once temperatures cool.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The vine flowered, but the flowers fell off without making beans, because steady heat above about 90°F stops the flowers from being pollinated and the plant drops them. Letting the plants dry out while flowering does the same thing. It is a weather problem, not a disease, and since pole beans keep flowering for a long time, the vine usually starts setting beans again once it cools.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time the planting so the heaviest bloom misses the hottest part of summer, sowing early enough to establish before peak heat or, in hot regions, running separate spring and fall sowings around the summer wall. Keep moisture steady, water deeply ahead of a heat wave, and choose more heat-tolerant varieties such as Rattlesnake where summers are reliably hot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plan your planting so the main flowering skips the hottest part of summer, either early enough to get going before peak heat or, in hot areas, as separate spring and fall plantings around the summer break. Keep the water steady, water deeply before a heat wave, and pick a more heat-tolerant variety like Rattlesnake if your summers are very hot.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds rotted or came up poorly
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Seeds rotted or did not come up
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The seeds were sown into soil that was too cold and wet, so they sat without germinating and rotted, or came up as a thin, patchy stand. Bean seed does not germinate well below about 60°F, and a slow, cold start invites soilborne root rot fungi and seedcorn maggot, both of which attack the lingering seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The seeds went into soil that was too cold and wet, so they sat there instead of sprouting and rotted, or came up thin and patchy. Bean seeds do not sprout well below about 60°F, and a slow, cold start lets soil fungi and a seed-eating maggot get to the seed while it waits.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing; there is no benefit to planting early. Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than low, wet spots, plant about 1 inch deep, and do not keep the bed soggy after sowing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, since there is no reward for planting beans early. Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of low, wet spots, plant about 1 inch deep, and do not keep the bed soggy after planting.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tall leafy vines but few beans
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Big leafy vines but hardly any beans
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The vines grew tall, dark, and leafy up the support but set few pods, usually from too much nitrogen. As legumes, beans fix much of their own nitrogen, and extra fertilizer over-stimulates vine growth and delays flowering. Some early leafiness is normal for pole beans, which climb before they set heavily, but persistent all-vine growth points to excess nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The vines grew tall, dark, and leafy but made very few beans, usually because they got too much nitrogen. Beans make much of their own nitrogen from the air, so extra fertilizer just pushes leafy growth and delays flowering. A little early leafiness is normal, since pole beans climb before they set heavily, but if it keeps up, it is too much nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.cause: too much nitrogen
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Skip the nitrogen feeding. Work in only a little balanced fertilizer or compost before planting, and at most one light side-dressing just before bloom, and only on poor or sandy soil. Let the plant's own nitrogen fixation carry the crop, and give it time, since pole beans set later than bush beans.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Skip the extra fertilizer. Mix in just a little balanced fertilizer or compost before planting, and at most one light feeding right before they flower, and only if your soil is poor. Let the beans make their own nitrogen, and be patient, since pole beans start making beans later than bush beans.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pods small, tough, or stringy
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Beans came out small, tough, or stringy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The pods came out small, fibrous, or misshapen, usually from drought stress during flowering and pod fill, or from leaving pods on the vine past their tender stage, when the enlarging seeds make the pod woody. On pole beans, infrequent picking is a common cause, since overlooked pods high in the canopy overmature and also cut the vine's ongoing set.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The beans came out small, tough, or crooked, usually because the plants dried out while flowering and filling pods, or because pods were left on too long until the swelling seeds made them woody. On pole beans this often happens when pods hidden high on the vine get missed and overripen, which also slows down new beans.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through the long bloom-and-fill season, and pick every two to three days, working the whole height of the vine and harvesting pods while they are still firm, crisp, and before the seeds bulge. Frequent, thorough picking also keeps the vine producing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the water steady through the long flowering and pod-filling season, and pick every two or three days, checking the whole vine, top to bottom, while the pods are still firm and crisp. Picking often and thoroughly also keeps more beans coming.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Pole beans are not a succession crop the way bush beans are. A single planting climbs its support and bears progressively for many weeks, right up to frost, so you sow once per season rather than at intervals. In long-season warm regions, growers slot a separate spring and a fall sowing split by summer heat, but that is a distinct seasonal crop, not staggered succession. Keep picking every couple of days to keep the vines flowering and setting new pods.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant pole beans once and pick for a long time. One planting keeps making beans for weeks, all the way to frost, so there is no need to replant every couple of weeks like you would with bush beans. In warm regions you may make a separate spring and a fall planting around the summer heat. The main thing is to pick often, which keeps new beans coming.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Pole beans flower and set pods continuously from one sowing over a long season, so interval succession does not apply; warm long-season regions support separate spring and fall seasonal sowings rather than staggered succession.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-2 cert (2026-07-05): source-truth review (CC agent, WebFetch). The certified green-beans-bush heat_pause defect (spelled degrees + mis-carried GA/FL notes into CA/AZ cells) did NOT propagate -- all 8 heat_pause cells carry a species-universal bean blossom-drop basis (Clemson bush-pole 'above 90F, blossom drop'; USU 'above 95F ... shed flowers'), CA cells use ucanr, AZ uariz, warm_arid nmsu; 0 spelled-degrees. Pole-vs-bush distinction (twining vines need a trellis; 5-6 wk vs 2-3 wk bearing) + bean biology all verified. FIX: dropped 'or a pyrethrin' from the Mexican-bean-beetle organic treatment (Clemson lists pyrethrin for whiteflies, spinosad for bean beetles); softened 3 true-but-unsourced pest clauses not on the cited Clemson insect page (the Pediobius foveolatus biocontrol, the MBB 'absent from the Pacific Coast' geography, and 'aphids transmit the mosaic viruses of beans') -- kept only what the page states; re-sourceable at the detail pass.

open_findings.summary: Per-region planting/harvest calendars are kept from the certified same-species bush-bean sibling (identical last-frost and >90F heat walls) with succession structure removed. Pole beans' ~10-15 day longer maturity (DTM 60-70 vs bush 50-60) will nudge per-region first-harvest dates slightly later; within the generally-safe-now tolerance, tighten exact months at the variety pass.

Regional windows are built from the nearest-T1 regional planting sources (UGA, UF/IFAS, UMN, USU, UMD, UIUC, MSU, Clemson, NMSU, U of A, UC MG/ANR, CTAHR) plus bean frost/heat physiology, not a pole-bean-specific planting chart for all 10 regions. Generally safe; tighten exact months at the variety pass.

hawaii_tropical is lowest-confidence: pole beans grow in the islands, but the bounded Feb-Aug warm-season window is modeled on CTAHR general guidance and the bush-bean sibling rather than a pole-bean-specific Hawaii calendar. Confirm in review.

Variety days-to-maturity (Kentucky Wonder 65, Blue Lake Pole 65, Kentucky Blue 65, Rattlesnake 70, McCaslan 65) reflect common catalog norms cross-checked against the Clemson and UF/IFAS pole variety lists and UMD's 60-110 day pole range, not variety-specific extension trials. Scarlet Runner (Phaseolus coccineus) is called out as a distinct, largely ornamental species per UF/IFAS and UMN.

Companions are traditional/mechanistic, low-to-medium confidence: Three Sisters corn as a living trellis for the climbing vines and squash as ground cover, and the allium avoid via the widely-cited Rhizobium-disruption mechanism. No pole-bean-specific companion trial was found in a readable T1 source.

Storage specifics (cool promptly, hold about a week refrigerated cold and humid, blanch and freeze within hours) are standard snap-bean handling modeled on the shared bean sources (Clemson, USU) rather than a pole-specific postharvest study; harvest_urgency left null since per-pick urgency matches the bush sibling and the pole difference is season length.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In colder areas you plant pole beans once and pick for a long time. Wait until after your last spring frost, when the soil has warmed, put up a tall trellis or teepee, and plant at its base. Unlike bush beans, you do not replant every couple of weeks: one planting keeps making beans until the first fall frost ends it. Pick every few days to keep them coming.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold zones, pole beans run as one long single planting. Sow once the soil holds above 60°F and the last spring frost has passed, set a sturdy 6-to-8-foot trellis or teepee at planting, and the vines then climb and bear progressively. Unlike bush beans there is no need to succession-sow: one planting keeps flowering and setting pods until the first fall frost kills it. Pick every couple of days to keep production running. In the coldest zones, sow by early summer so the crop has time to bear before frost.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: This summer gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. Pole beans, like all snap beans, drop their blossoms and fail to set pods once daytime highs run above about 90°F, and the effect worsens with warm nights that suppress pollen viability. Pod set resumes as the weather cools, so the vines are sown before and after the peak-heat months rather than into them.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Here you grow pole beans in two seasons, spring and fall, with a summer break between. Plant in spring after the last frost against a tall trellis, then stop during the hottest part of summer, when it is too hot for beans to set pods. Plant again in mid to late summer for a fall crop. Each planting keeps making beans for weeks, so you only plant once per season; just pick often.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf run two pole bean crops split by summer heat. Sow in spring after frost against a tall trellis, and again in mid to late summer for a fall crop. The gap is real: through the hottest weeks blossoms drop and pods fail to set. Each planting bears progressively for weeks rather than all at once, so one sowing per window is enough; pick every couple of days. The spring sowing anchors to roughly mid March in middle Georgia and shifts earlier deeper south.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In the valleys you plant pole beans twice, once in spring and once in mid summer, with a break when it is hottest. Plant in April and May against a tall trellis, stop in the heat of summer when beans will not set pods, then plant again in July for a fall crop. Each planting bears for weeks, so plant once per window and just pick often.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: The interior valleys carry a spring crop and a late-summer crop with a midsummer break. One planting per window bears progressively into fall; pick every couple of days and keep moisture steady through the heat.

The cool air means there is no hot break to plan around, and one planting keeps bearing from about late June into early fall. Just pick every few days.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Along the north and north coast the marine layer keeps summers mild, so pole beans run as one continuous single planting rather than splitting around heat. Sow from early May, once soil has warmed past the cool spring, against a tall trellis. The cool coastal climate that limits other warm-season crops here lets the vines bear steadily without a midsummer stall, from roughly late June into early fall. Pick every couple of days.

Pole beans, like all snap beans, drop their blossoms and fail to set pods once daytime highs run above about 90°F, and the effect worsens with warm nights that suppress pollen viability. Pod set resumes as the weather cools, so the vines are sown before and after the peak-heat months rather than into them.

Sow into warm soil and keep moisture steady through the heat.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: Florida flips the calendar. In central Florida, grow pole beans in spring and fall with a summer break: plant late winter through April against a tall trellis, stop in the hottest weeks, and plant again in August. In south Florida, grow them through the winter instead, planting from fall into early spring and leaving summer empty. Each planting bears for weeks, so plant once per window.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: Peninsular Florida inverts the calendar. In central Florida, pole beans run a spring crop and a fall crop split by summer heat: sow late winter through April against a tall trellis, pause through the hottest, wettest weeks, and sow again in August. In south Florida the pattern flips fully to a winter growing season, with sowing from fall through early spring and summer left fallow. Each planting bears for weeks; the right window depends on how far south the garden sits.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, pole beans is a two-season crop. Plant Mar 1 - Mar 31 for a spring harvest, then plant again Sep 1 - Sep 15 for a fall crop. Skip the hottest stretch of summer: the flowers drop in the worst heat before they can set fruit, so there is nothing to gain by planting through it. It rarely if ever frosts here, so both the spring and fall windows run on Valley heat, not on a frost date.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Pole beans in the RGV runs on the Valley's two-crop calendar: set out Mar 1 - Mar 31 for a spring harvest running Apr 20 - Jun 19, then set out again Sep 1 - Sep 15 for a fall harvest running Oct 21 - Dec 4. Sustained heat above the mid-90s°F makes bean blossoms drop before they set pods, so production stops in the hottest weeks even though the vines keep growing. Frost is essentially absent here, so both plantings are timed against heat, not cold. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sow pole beans at the base of a trellis or teepee once the soil has warmed after the last frost. OSU Extension's Oregon planting-date table (EM9027) covers snap beans (bush and pole types together) with a May-through-July window in the Willamette Valley (Region 2); WSU's Washington vegetable guide corroborates the warm-soil, direct-sow requirement. Unlike bush beans, a single planting is enough: the vines climb and bear progressively rather than needing succession sowing.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest pods are ready in roughly 60 to 70 days.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: As a frost-tender crop, the vines keep flowering and setting pods until the first fall frost kills them, so harvest runs to that date rather than a fixed cutoff.

8.zone_notes: OSU's Oregon planting-date table gives the Willamette Valley (Region 2) the same May-through-July snap-bean window used for bush beans; one planting against a trellis is enough here, no succession sowing needed.

9.zone_notes: OSU's coastal table (Region 1) narrows the snap-bean window to May through June, the same coast-versus-valley split seen in bush beans; the cooler, foggier coastal summer is the limiter, not frost, which arrives later here than inland.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: West of the Cascades, pole beans reward a little patience with a long harvest. Put up a sturdy trellis or teepee and sow once the soil has warmed after the last spring frost: May into June on the immediate coast, May into July in the milder Willamette Valley and Puget lowlands. Unlike bush beans, you plant once, not every couple of weeks; the vines then climb and keep setting pods until the first fall frost ends the season. Pick every few days to keep them coming.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Pole beans direct-sow at the base of a trellis once the soil has warmed after the last frost. direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Pole beans for the Las Vegas Valley: direct-sow once against a tall support after the last spring frost, per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart's March-April Beans-pole window. A single planting climbs its support and bears progressively over the weeks that follow, unlike bush beans, which the chart shades again in a separate late-summer block; the chart carries no second Beans-pole window, so there is no fall replanting here.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: First pods come roughly two months after sowing, this crop's own days to maturity, and the vine keeps bearing progressively after that.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The vines bear for about nine to ten weeks before slowing and are pulled as they decline. Pod set likely slows through the hottest stretch of the Mojave summer, but the chart shades pole beans through a single unbroken spring-into-summer block rather than the two-window gap it gives bush beans, so no separate heat exclusion is modeled here.

nevada.plantings_provenance: Nevada Shape C pole-bean cell: single spring planting (Mar-Apr, matching the corn cells' shared window), no heat_pause and no second_planting per the UNLV/UNR chart's single unbroken Beans-pole block (unlike bush beans' separate spring + late-summer shading). Harvest bounded to the vine's roughly nine to ten week bearing run rather than extended to frost, mirroring the mid_south structural donor's own bearing-window length.
nevada.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, sow pole beans once against a tall trellis in spring, from about March 10 to April 20, and pick from mid-May into July as the vines climb and bear. There is no fall replanting here the way there is for bush beans; one planting is the whole season for pole beans in this belt.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: Pole beans are a single-sowing crop in the Las Vegas Valley, per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener chart: one planting against a tall support climbs and bears progressively for about nine to ten weeks, rather than the spring-plus-late-summer succession the chart gives bush beans. Sow in the spring window, roughly March 10 through April 20 in zone 9, later at the cooler zone 8 edge and earlier at Laughlin in zone 10; first pods follow about two months later. The chart shows no second Beans-pole block, so there is no honest fall pole-bean crop here; expect pod set to slow through the hottest stretch of summer even though no separate heat exclusion is modeled, and pull the spent vines as they wind down.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Pole beans for St. George: direct-sow once against a tall support, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah, which places snap/pole bean in Group C (Tender), planted about March 15. A single planting climbs its support and bears progressively over the weeks that follow; USU documents no fall bean planting for St. George, so there is no second sowing.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: First pods come about 65 days after the earliest sowing, this crop's own days to maturity, and the vine keeps bearing progressively after that.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The vines bear for about nine to ten weeks before slowing and are pulled as they decline. Pod set likely slows through the hottest stretch of the St. George summer, but USU shades pole beans through a single unbroken spring-into-summer window rather than giving a separate heat-break date, so no summer pause is marked here.

utah_dixie.plantings_provenance: Utah Dixie pole-bean cell: single spring planting (matching the corn cells' shared Group C window), with no summer heat pause and no fall replant per USU's single Group C date and the load-bearing no-warm-crop-fall-replant rule. Harvest bounded to the vine's roughly nine to ten week bearing run rather than extended to frost.
utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: In St. George, sow pole beans once against a tall trellis in spring, from about March 15 to April 5 per USU Extension, and pick from mid-May into July as the vines climb and bear. There is no fall replanting here; one planting is the whole season for pole beans in this belt.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: Pole beans are a single-sowing crop in St. George, per USU Extension's Group C (Tender) planting date, about March 15: one planting against a tall support climbs and bears progressively for about nine to ten weeks, rather than the spring-plus-fall succession fresh bush beans can get elsewhere. Sow in the March 15 to April 5 window; first pods follow about 65 days later. USU documents no fall bean planting for St. George, so there is no honest fall pole-bean crop here; expect pod set to slow through the hottest stretch of summer even though no separate summer pause is marked, and pull the spent vines as they wind down.

crops.description_seasoned: Pole beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are the climbing form of the common snap bean: frost-tender, warm-season, nitrogen-fixing legumes grown for their tender immature pods. Unlike the self-supporting bush type, they are twining vines that need a sturdy trellis, teepee, or fence 6 to 8 feet tall to climb. That vertical habit is the payoff: a single planting flowers and sets pods progressively over many weeks, bearing more from the same ground than a bush planting and continuing right up to frost, so you pick regularly rather than facing one concentrated glut. Direct-sown into warm soil after the last frost, they reach a first pickable crop in about 60 to 70 days.
crops.description_beginner: Pole beans are the climbing kind of green bean. Instead of staying short like bush beans, they grow as long vines that need something tall to climb, like a trellis, a teepee of poles, or a fence about 6 to 8 feet high. The reward is a long harvest: one planting keeps making beans for weeks, all the way until frost, so you pick a handful every few days instead of getting them all at once. You plant the seeds straight in the garden after the last frost, give them their support, keep them watered, and start picking in about two months.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when pods are firm, crisp, and snap cleanly, before the enlarging seeds bulge the pod wall. Pole beans bear over a long season, so work the vines every two to three days: regular picking keeps the plant flowering and setting new pods, while pods left to mature signal it to slow down.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Beans are ready when the pods are firm and crisp and snap cleanly, before you can see the seeds bulging inside. Pick every two or three days all season. On pole beans, picking often is what keeps new beans coming, so do not let old pods sit on the vine.

crops.name: Snow Peas

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Peas like loose, fertile soil that drains well, with some compost mixed in. The main thing they care about is good drainage, because peas planted in cold, soggy soil tend to rot before they sprout. If water sits on your bed for a long time after rain, work in compost or plant on a raised bed first.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Snow peas do best in a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam with compost worked in before sowing. The critical trait is drainage: pea seed sown into cold, wet, poorly drained ground rots before it germinates, and the soilborne root rots that follow are the main early-season risk. Steady, even moisture without waterlogging carries the crop through flowering and pod fill. Peas are legumes and fix much of their own nitrogen, so the bed needs fertility and tilth more than heavy feeding.

ph.note_beginner: Peas grow best in soil from about 6.0 to 7.0, which is slightly acidic to neutral. They do poorly in strongly acidic soil below 6.0, so if a soil test reads low, mix in some lime before planting. Most garden beds are already in a good range.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0. Clemson recommends a 6.0 to 6.5 target, and growth is inhibited on acid soils at pH 6.0 and below, so lime an acid plot the season before sowing. Peas tolerate up to roughly 7.5, and a soil test is the reliable way to confirm both pH and fertility before the season starts.

fertilizer.type: balanced pre-plant, little to no nitrogen
fertilizer.timing: work a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the bed before sowing
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 pre-plant
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Snow peas are light feeders. As legumes they fix much of their own nitrogen through root nodules, so heavy nitrogen drives leafy vine growth at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the bed before sowing; that is usually all peas need. An inoculant of the right Rhizobium bacteria is optional and can help nodulation where peas have not been grown before. Avoid high-nitrogen feeds, which delay flowering and cut pod set.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Peas make much of their own food from the air, so they barely need fertilizer. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant and that is enough. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy vines but fewer pods. If you like, you can coat the seed with a pea inoculant powder, which helps the roots make nitrogen, but it is optional.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced 5-10-10 worked in before sowing if no soil test is available; skip extra nitrogen, which peas supply themselves.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 mixed into the bed before planting is plenty.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet worked in before sowing, per Clemson, when no soil test is available.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet, mixed into the bed before planting.

companions.note_beginner: Peas get along with most cool-season vegetables. They grow happily beside carrots, radishes, and lettuce, and because they leave nitrogen in the soil, they are a good crop to grow before a leafy green. The pairing to avoid is planting peas right next to onions or garlic.
companions.note_seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, peas leave the soil richer for what follows and sit comfortably among the other cool-season crops grown in the same early-spring and fall windows: carrots, radishes, and lettuce are classic bed-mates. The long-standing caution is to keep peas away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress legumes through the same root-bacteria interference seen with beans.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrot
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A classic cool-season neighbor that shares peas' early-spring and fall timing; the carrots root deep while the peas climb, so they use the bed without crowding.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Carrots and peas are a long-standing cool-season companion pairing; the benefit is shared timing, complementary root-vs-vine habit, and the peas' nitrogen lightly helping the carrots. Traditional/medium: well grounded in shared conditions, not a measured pest effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots and peas grow in the same cool windows and use the bed in complementary ways: the carrot works the soil deep while the pea climbs above it, and the peas' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the carrot. The pairing is traditional and compatibility-based rather than a measured pest defense, so expect easy cohabitation more than active protection.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Radish
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Radishes sprout fast and mark the pea rows while the slower peas come up, then are pulled long before the peas need the space.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Radish-as-quick-marker interplanted with a slower crop is a standard, low-risk home-garden practice; both are cool-season and the radish is harvested before competition matters. Traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Radishes germinate in days and mark the rows while the peas emerge, and they finish and come out weeks before the peas size up, so they never compete. Both are cool-season crops sown at the same time, which makes them a tidy, low-risk interplant rather than a measured protective pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce shares peas' cool-season timing and stays low, tucking in along the base of the pea row or trellis.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Lettuce and peas share cool-season conditions and occupy different layers (low leafy crop under the climbing vine); a sound shared-conditions compatibility, by close analogy to other cool-season interplants. Likely rather than research_backed (no pea-specific lettuce trial located).

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce slots in below a pea trellis or alongside a bush row, sharing the same cool-season window and water needs while occupying a different layer of the bed. As the peas leaf out they offer the lettuce a little light afternoon shade that delays bolting. It is a compatibility pairing on sound shared-conditions grounds rather than a measured protective one.

good_seasoned.name: Carrot
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional cool-season pairing: carrots and peas share early-spring and fall timing and use the bed in complementary ways, the carrot rooting deep while the pea climbs.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing cool-season companion pairing (shared timing, root-vs-vine complementarity, light N benefit); not experimentally quantified.

good_seasoned.name: Radish
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sown with the peas, fast radishes mark the rows and are pulled well before the peas need the space; both are cool-season crops with the same timing.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Standard quick-marker interplant; radish finishes before competition matters. Traditional/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from peas, which are said to grow poorly near them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: The same allium-versus-legume mechanism reported for beans: allium sulfur compounds are held to disrupt the Rhizobium bacteria peas depend on to fix nitrogen, stunting the vines. Mechanistic/medium: a sound, repeatedly cited mechanism, not a controlled pea-yield trial opened this session.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Onions next to peas is the better-grounded of the 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds that are widely held to interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria on pea roots, the bacteria the plant relies on to fix nitrogen, so pea growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. The useful corollary is that peas grown before an allium crop leave the soil better for it.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for peas.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Garlic is an allium with the same antibacterial sulfur chemistry as onion; same Rhizobium-disruption mechanism. Mechanistic/medium for the same reasons.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Garlic acts on peas the way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds held to disrupt the nitrogen-fixing bacteria on pea roots, slowing the vines. Treat garlic and peas as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the pea-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

bad_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are the classic traditional caution near peas and other legumes; the pairing is widely advised against, attributed to allium compounds interfering with the pea's nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing allium-versus-legume garden caution; mechanism plausible but not experimentally established here.

bad_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: As with onion, garlic is traditionally kept apart from peas.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium caution, traditional.

pests.name: Pea aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of soft, pinhead-sized green aphids clustered on the growing tips, flower stalks, and leaf undersides. Heavy feeding curls and yellows the new growth, stunts the vines, and can drop blossoms; a sticky honeydew and sooty mold may follow. Most important, pea aphids transmit the virus diseases of peas, including pea enation mosaic, so even modest numbers matter.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of small, soft green insects packed onto the growing tips, flower stems, and undersides of the leaves. They curl and yellow the new growth and stunt the plants, and they leave a sticky residue. The bigger problem is that pea aphids spread virus diseases from plant to plant, so they are worth catching early.
pests.cause_seasoned: The pea aphid (Acyrthosiphon pisum), a large green aphid that builds up fast in the cool, mild weather of spring and fall, exactly the seasons peas grow. It reproduces rapidly, so colonies form before natural enemies catch up.
pests.cause_beginner: The pea aphid, a large green aphid that multiplies quickly in the cool weather of spring and fall when peas are growing. It builds up fast, before helpful insects like ladybugs catch up.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water, or treat with insecticidal soap, which controls aphids on contact; begin as soon as colonies are found, while numbers are low. Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually bring populations down on their own. Because the real risk is virus transmission, act early rather than waiting for visible damage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast the colonies off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap, which works on contact. Start as soon as you see them, while there are only a few. Ladybugs and other helpful insects usually finish the job. Since aphids spread viruses, it is worth dealing with them early.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Lay reflective mulch, which disorients aphids and reduces both feeding and virus spread, and control nearby weeds and clover that harbor them. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor, and choose virus-resistant varieties such as Oregon Sugar Pod II where pea viruses are a known problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Lay down reflective mulch, which confuses aphids and cuts the viruses they spread, and pull nearby weeds that shelter them. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is exactly what aphids like. Where pea viruses are common, plant a resistant variety like Oregon Sugar Pod II.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where pea viruses are a known problem in your area, start at the seed rack. Oregon Sugar Pod II is one snow pea sold with virus resistance, and choosing it costs you nothing at planting time.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The aphid's real cost on peas is what it transmits rather than what it eats, so variety choice is the step with the most leverage; Oregon Sugar Pod II carries virus resistance and is worth specifying where pea viruses have a local history.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay reflective mulch, a silvery plastic or foil sheet spread on the soil, while the plants are still small. It confuses aphids looking for somewhere to land, so fewer settle in and fewer viruses move around with them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective film disorients incoming aphids, cutting feeding pressure and the virus spread that matters more here; lay it early while the crop is short enough for the film to still show.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull the weeds and clover growing near the bed. Aphids shelter in them and move across onto the peas from there.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Nearby weeds and clover harbor pea aphids between crops, so clearing that ground before sowing and keeping the edges clean removes the bridge into the planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. Heavy feeding pushes out soft, sappy new growth, which is the growth aphids do best on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Overfeeding nitrogen produces the lush, succulent flush pea aphid colonies build on fastest, so hold the feeding back rather than pushing growth.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the clusters off with a strong jet from the hose as soon as you find them, while there are still only a few. It is the first thing to reach for, before any spray.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water knock-down on the growing tips and flower stalks buys time while natural enemies catch up; given the virus risk, do it at first detection rather than waiting for visible damage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings and tiny parasitic wasps (wasps whose young develop inside aphids) usually bring the numbers down on their own. Give them a chance before you spray anything.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Ladybugs, lacewings and parasitic wasps usually pull pea aphid populations down unaided; the gap is early in the cool weather, when the aphid's reproduction outruns them, and that gap is what the physical steps cover.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If colonies keep building, insecticidal soap works on contact, so it has to land on the aphids themselves. Spray while numbers are low and cover the growing tips, the flower stems and the undersides of the leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap kills on contact, so coverage of tips, flower stalks and leaf undersides decides the outcome; begin at the first colonies rather than after curling and yellowing have set in.

pests.name: Pea weevil
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small notches chewed from the leaf margins of young plants in spring, and adults feeding on the blossoms. The real damage is hidden: larvae bore into the developing seeds inside the pods and feed there, leaving tiny round exit holes in the dried peas. Saved seed with holes is the giveaway. The pea weevil feeds only on peas (Pisum).
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little notches chewed out of the leaf edges of young plants, and beetles on the flowers in spring. The hidden damage is worse: the grubs tunnel into the peas forming inside the pods, leaving tiny round holes in the dried seeds. Holes in saved seed are the tell. The pea weevil eats only peas.
pests.cause_seasoned: The pea weevil (Bruchus pisorum), a small brownish beetle whose host range is peas alone. Adults overwinter in debris and trash, move into the crop at bloom to lay eggs on young pods, and the larvae develop inside the seeds. There is one generation a year.
pests.cause_beginner: The pea weevil, a small brown beetle that feeds only on peas. The adults spend the winter in garden trash, move in when the peas flower to lay eggs on the young pods, and the grubs grow up inside the seeds. There is one generation each year.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Monitor for adults during bloom, when egg-laying begins. In a home patch, handpicking and floating row cover over the crop at flowering reduce egg-laying. At season's end, inspect dried peas for the small round exit holes before storing seed; freezing saved seed for several days kills any larvae inside.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Watch for the beetles while the peas are flowering, which is when they lay eggs. Picking them off and covering the plants with a light row cover at flowering both help. At the end of the season, check dried peas for tiny round holes before you save seed, and freezing saved seed for a few days kills any grubs inside.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clean up and destroy pea debris after harvest to remove overwintering shelter, and rotate peas away from last year's bed. Do not save or replant seed showing exit holes. Where the weevil is established, an early sowing that finishes pod fill before peak adult activity escapes the worst.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear away and destroy the old pea plants after harvest so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter, and move your peas to a new spot each year. Do not save seed that has holes in it. Planting early so the pods finish before the beetles get busy also helps.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear out and destroy the old pea plants once the last pods are picked. The beetles sit out the winter in that debris, so taking it away leaves them nowhere to shelter.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Adults overwinter in pea trash, so destroying the residue after harvest strips the shelter that carries the single annual generation through to spring.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move the peas to a different part of the garden each year instead of sowing them where last year's crop stood.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotating off last season's pea ground puts distance between emerging adults and the only crop they can use, since this weevil's host range is peas alone.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where this beetle is established, sowing early helps: if the pods finish filling before the adults get busy, the crop slips past the worst of it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: An early sowing that completes pod fill ahead of peak adult activity escapes the heaviest egg-laying; a timing lever rather than a control, and it depends on locally observed adult activity.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Watch the plants while they are in flower, which is when the beetles arrive to lay eggs, and pick off any adults you find on the blossoms.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Scout at bloom, when egg-laying begins, and take adults off the flowers by hand; in a home patch that reduces the eggs laid on the young pods.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Drape a light row cover over the planting once flowering starts, so the beetles cannot reach the young pods to lay on them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cover applied at flowering excludes adults during the window when they move into the crop to lay on young pods; it is the exclusion half of the same bloom-timed step as handpicking.

pests.name: Armyworms and cutworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Cutworms sever young seedlings at or just below the soil line overnight, leaving toppled plants and thinned rows in spring. Armyworms are smooth caterpillars that chew foliage and can move through a planting in numbers, skeletonizing leaves and nicking pods. Both feed mostly at night and hide in the soil or debris by day.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Cutworms cut off young pea seedlings right at the soil line overnight, so you find plants toppled over and gaps in the row. Armyworms are smooth caterpillars that chew the leaves and sometimes the pods, and they can show up in numbers. Both feed at night and hide during the day.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several night-feeding caterpillars, including cutworms (the larvae of various moths) and beet or western yellowstriped armyworms. They overwinter or move in from weedy ground and grassy cover, and seedlings are the most vulnerable stage.
pests.cause_beginner: Several kinds of night-feeding caterpillars: cutworms and armyworms, the young of different moths. They come in from weedy or grassy areas, and young seedlings are the most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick caterpillars in the evening or early morning, and check the soil around toppled seedlings for the curled cutworm. A cardboard or foil collar around a seedling stops cutworms; Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) controls young armyworms on the foliage. A floating row cover keeps egg-laying moths off the planting.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the caterpillars off in the evening or early morning, and dig a little around fallen seedlings to find the curled-up cutworm. A collar of cardboard or foil around a seedling blocks cutworms, and a Bt spray controls young armyworms on the leaves. A light row cover keeps the moths from laying eggs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clear weeds and grassy cover before sowing to remove egg-laying sites, and turn the bed a couple of weeks ahead of planting to expose and dry out resident larvae. Keep row edges weed-free through the season, and protect emerging seedlings, the vulnerable stage, with a row cover where these caterpillars are a known problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear weeds and tall grass before planting so the moths have fewer places to lay eggs, and turn the soil a couple of weeks before sowing to expose the grubs. Keep the edges of the bed weeded, and cover young seedlings with a row cover if these caterpillars are a problem where you are.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear weeds and tall grass out of the bed and along its edges before you sow, and keep the edges clean through the season. The moths lay eggs in that cover, so removing it takes out caterpillars before they hatch.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: These caterpillars move in from weedy and grassy ground, so stripping that cover before sowing and holding the row edges clean removes egg-laying sites right next to the crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Turn the bed over a couple of weeks before you sow. That brings the caterpillars already living in the soil up to the surface, where they dry out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Working the empty bed a couple of weeks ahead of sowing exposes resident larvae and dries them out; it is the one step that reaches the stage sheltering in the soil.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go out at dusk or first thing in the morning, when they feed, and pick the caterpillars off. If a seedling has toppled, scrape the soil beside it and you will often turn up the curled cutworm that cut it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Both feed at night and shelter in soil or debris by day, so evening and early-morning scouting is when handpicking pays; a toppled seedling marks a larva resting in the soil beside it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Slip a collar of cardboard or foil around each young plant so a cutworm cannot reach the stem at soil level. It is fiddly, but at the scale of a home row it works.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A cardboard or foil collar set at the soil line blocks the cut itself, which is the damage that matters at the seedling stage; practical in a small planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A light row cover over the seedlings keeps the moths from laying on the planting in the first place. Worth putting on from the start if these caterpillars turn up most years where you garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cover keeps egg-laying moths off the bed and protects the seedling stage, which is where the loss happens; the step to default to where cutworm or armyworm pressure is a known annual.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis, a naturally occurring bacterium sold as a caterpillar spray) on the foliage controls young armyworms. Time it to small caterpillars, when the chewing first shows.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Bt is the foliar answer for armyworms and works on early instars, so time it to the first chewing rather than to a stripped row; it is aimed at foliage feeders, not at cutworms severing stems at the soil line, which the collars cover.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine silvery or whitish scarring and flecking on leaves and pods, with tiny dark specks of excrement, as the slender insects rasp the surface and feed on the released sap. Heavy feeding distorts new growth and can scar pods cosmetically. Thrips also vector some plant viruses.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Fine silvery streaks and pale flecks on the leaves and pods, with tiny dark specks, where the slender insects scrape the surface and feed. Bad infestations twist the new growth and leave scars on the pods. Thrips can also spread some viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several thrips species, slender insects a fraction the size of an aphid that build up in warm, dry stretches late in the pea season. They rasp the plant surface and feed on the sap that wells up.
pests.cause_beginner: Thrips, slender insects much smaller than an aphid that build up in warm, dry weather toward the end of the pea season. They scrape the surface of the plant and feed on the sap.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Peas usually outgrow light thrips feeding without treatment. Where numbers climb, a strong spray of water and insecticidal soap reduce them, and natural enemies such as minute pirate bugs and lacewings help. Keep plants unstressed and well watered, since drought-stressed peas are more prone.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Peas usually shrug off a little thrips damage. If they build up, a strong spray of water and insecticidal soap knock them back, and helpful insects pitch in. Keep the plants watered and unstressed, since dried-out peas are more likely to be hit.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Control weeds that harbor thrips, lay reflective mulch to disorient them and reduce virus spread, and keep moisture even so plants are not drought-stressed. Most home pea crops finish before thrips become a real problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pull nearby weeds that shelter thrips, lay reflective mulch to confuse them, and keep the soil evenly moist so the plants are not stressed. Most home pea crops are done before thrips become a real problem.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull the weeds near the bed, since thrips shelter in them and move onto the peas from there.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Weedy ground is where thrips hold and build before moving into the crop, so clearing it ahead of the warm, dry stretch late in the pea season removes the reservoir.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Reflective mulch, a silvery sheet laid on the soil, confuses thrips looking for the plants and cuts the viruses they can carry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective film disorients incoming thrips and reduces virus movement; lay it at sowing while the crop is still small.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the numbers do climb, a strong spray of water knocks them back. Most home pea crops are finished before thrips reach that point.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water knock-down is the first response where numbers climb; on a spring crop the season usually ends before thrips reach a level that justifies more.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Minute pirate bugs, lacewings and other helpful insects pitch in on their own, and light feeding usually needs no treatment at all.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Minute pirate bugs and lacewings work this pest unaided in most seasons, and peas generally outgrow light feeding, so the bar for intervening should stay high.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where thrips do build up, insecticidal soap reduces them. It works on contact, so aim at the new growth, where the twisting and scarring show first.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap backs up the water knock-down where numbers keep climbing; contact-only, so coverage of the distorted new growth and the silvered pods decides it.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white to grayish powdery coating that starts as small spots on the upper leaf surfaces and spreads to cover leaves, stems, and pods. Affected leaves yellow and dry, vines lose vigor, and pods may be spotted or off-flavored. It is the classic late-season pea disease, arriving as the spring crop runs into warmer, drier weather.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white to gray powdery dust that starts as spots on top of the leaves and spreads over the leaves, stems, and pods. The leaves yellow and dry out, the vines weaken, and the pods can be spotted. It is the classic late-season pea problem, showing up as the weather warms and dries toward the end of the spring crop.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Erysiphe pisi, favored by warm days, cool nights, and dry foliage, the conditions that arrive late in the pea season. Spores spread on the wind, and the disease moves fast once established, which is why early control and resistant varieties matter most.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Erysiphe pisi) that thrives in warm days, cool nights, and dry leaves, which is exactly the weather at the end of the pea season. It spreads on the wind and moves fast once it starts, so catching it early and planting resistant varieties matter most.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Powdery mildew is best managed at the very first signs; once it covers the leaves and yellowing sets in, control is difficult. Remove the worst-affected leaves and improve airflow. Sulfur or a labeled biofungicide, begun early and repeated per the label, suppresses it. On a spring crop that is nearly done, harvesting promptly and pulling the planting is often the practical choice.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Powdery mildew is easiest to handle the moment you first see it; once it covers the leaves, it is hard to stop. Pick off the worst leaves and open up the planting for airflow. A sulfur spray started early and repeated per the label helps. If the spring crop is nearly finished, the simplest move is to pick what is ready and pull the plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, the single most effective step: Oregon Sugar Pod II and many modern snow peas carry powdery mildew resistance. Sow early so the crop finishes pod fill before the late-season mildew weather, give plants room and a trellis for airflow, and avoid working among wet vines.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant a resistant variety, which is the best defense: Oregon Sugar Pod II and many newer snow peas resist powdery mildew. Plant early so the crop finishes before the mildew weather arrives, give the plants room and a trellis so air moves through them, and stay out of the patch when the vines are wet.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with a resistant variety. It is the strongest single move against this one: Oregon Sugar Pod II and many newer snow peas carry powdery mildew resistance.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resistance is the highest-leverage step here, since the disease moves fast once established and the window it arrives in is short; Oregon Sugar Pod II and many modern snow peas carry it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sow as early as the ground can be worked so the crop finishes before the mildew weather arrives, which is this crop's guidance along with the resistant variety this ladder starts with. Mildew tends to build late, so an early sowing simply finishes ahead of it; this method's cautions carry the cold-soil trade that comes with the early date.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: An early sowing lets the crop finish pod fill before the late-season mildew weather, which is this crop's guidance, and it works because the pressure is seasonal: mildew builds late, and spring sowings mostly finish ahead of it. It sits beside the resistant varieties at the front of the ladder, a when beside their what. The early edge has its own cost in cold, wet soil, and this method's cautions carry it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the plants room and put up a trellis so air moves through the vines instead of sitting still in a dense tangle.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spacing and a trellis are set at sowing and cannot be retrofitted; an open, trained canopy is also what makes pulling the first affected leaves practical at all.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off the worst leaves as soon as you spot the white dusting. If the spring crop is close to finished anyway, picking what is ready and pulling the plants is often the simplest answer.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Stripping the most affected leaves early keeps the first spots from seeding the rest of the planting; on a spring crop near the end of its run, harvesting off and pulling the vines is often the practical call instead of a spray program.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A labeled biofungicide (a spray built on a living organism rather than a chemical) can suppress it if you start at the first spots and repeat as the label directs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A labeled biofungicide begun at the first colonies and repeated on label interval suppresses rather than cures; the value is entirely in starting before the leaves are covered.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sulfur started early and repeated on the label schedule helps hold it back. Once the powder covers the leaves and they begin yellowing, spraying is unlikely to turn it around.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sulfur is the stronger of the two spray options here and works preventively: begun at first signs and repeated per label it suppresses, while a start made after the canopy is coated and yellowing is unlikely to recover the crop.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A yellowing of the lower leaves that progresses up the plant, with downward curling, stunting, and wilting; a cut through the lower stem shows a reddish or orange discoloration of the water-conducting tissue. Plants often die before pod fill. Symptoms appear in patches and worsen as the soil warms.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The lower leaves turn yellow and the yellowing creeps up the plant, which becomes stunted, curls, and wilts. If you cut the lower stem, the tissue inside is stained reddish or orange. Affected plants often die before making a crop. It shows up in patches and gets worse as the soil warms.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. pisi, which enters through the roots, plugs the vascular system, and persists in the soil for years. Several races exist. Warm soil favors it, and once a bed is infested the fungus cannot be eradicated, so resistant varieties and rotation are the management.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that lives in the soil and enters through the roots, clogging the plant's plumbing. It survives in the soil for years and likes warm soil. Once it is in a bed you cannot get rid of it, so the answer is resistant varieties and moving your peas around.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected plants; remove and destroy them to limit buildup. Management is preventive: the disease is handled through resistant varieties and rotation, not treatment.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant is infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) the affected plants. You manage this one by preventing it, with resistant varieties and rotation, not by spraying.
