notifications.title_seasoned: Heat incoming: watch your greens for bolting
notifications.title_beginner: Heat incoming, watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body_seasoned: Hot weather pushes leafy greens to bolt, sending up a flower stalk and turning the leaves bitter. Harvest everything you can now, before the heat sets in. Steady watering and a bit of afternoon shade buy a little time, and a fresh sowing in late summer will give you a tender fall crop once temperatures ease.
notifications.body_beginner: Hot weather pushes leafy greens to bolt, sending up a flower stalk and turning the leaves bitter. Harvest everything you can now, before the heat sets in. Steady watering and a bit of afternoon shade buy a little time, and a fresh sowing in late summer will give you a tender fall crop once it cools down.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.title_beginner: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body_seasoned: About eight weeks before your first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outdoes spring: the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter leaves, and many greens, kale especially, actually taste better after a light frost.
notifications.body_beginner: About eight weeks before your first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often beats spring: the cooling weather means slower bolting and sweeter leaves, and many greens, kale especially, actually taste better after a light frost.

notifications.body_seasoned: Leafy greens move fast in warm weather and can bolt before you notice. A quick look every few days helps you catch leaves at their best and spot a flower stalk early, while there is still time to harvest before the flavor turns.
notifications.body_beginner: Leafy greens grow fast in warm weather and can bolt before you notice. A quick look every few days helps you catch the leaves at their best and spot a flower stalk early, while there is still time to harvest before the flavor turns.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert: harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heat alert, harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat is the enemy of leafy greens. They bolt quickly and the flavor turns bitter fast, so harvest as much as you can before the hot spell arrives. Shade cloth over the bed can buy you roughly another week in marginal temperatures by keeping the plants a few degrees cooler.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Heat is hard on leafy greens. They bolt quickly and the flavor turns bitter fast, so harvest as much as you can before the hot spell arrives. A piece of shade cloth over the bed can buy you roughly another week in borderline temperatures by keeping the plants a few degrees cooler.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Unexpected frost, protect young greens
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Most leafy greens take a light frost in stride once they are established, and some even sweeten with it, but young seedlings are vulnerable. If a frost is forecast and your plants are still small, cover them with fleece or row cover tonight and uncover them in the morning.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Most leafy greens handle a light frost just fine once they are established, and some even get sweeter from it, but young seedlings are vulnerable. If frost is forecast and your plants are still small, cover them with fleece or row cover tonight and uncover them in the morning.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity: watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.title_beginner: High humidity, watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid, still conditions are what downy mildew needs to take hold on leafy greens. Make sure air can move between the plants, water at soil level early in the day rather than in the evening, and keep picking so the planting stays open and dries faster after rain or dew.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Humid, still conditions are just what downy mildew needs to take hold on leafy greens. Make sure air can move between the plants, water at the soil early in the day rather than in the evening, and keep picking so the planting stays open and dries faster after rain or dew.

germination.text_beginner: Lettuce and other leafy greens sprout easily in cool, moist soil. The catch is heat: once the soil gets above about 80°F, the seeds mostly stop sprouting, which is why seed sown in the heat of summer often just fails. Sow a little more thickly than the spacing on the packet, then thin the seedlings out to that spacing once they are up.
germination.text_seasoned: Leafy greens are some of the easiest crops to germinate in cool, moist soil, but germination drops off sharply once soil climbs above roughly 80°F, which is why midsummer sowings so often fail. Sow a little more thickly than your final spacing and thin to the recommended distance.

germination.text_beginner: The little seedlings you pull out when thinning are completely edible. Rinse them and toss them into a salad as microgreens. With leafy greens, thinning and harvesting are the same job.
germination.text_seasoned: The thinnings from leafy greens are completely edible; use them as microgreens in salads. Thinning is harvesting.

seedling.text_beginner: Thinning your seedlings out to the spacing on the packet feels wasteful, but do it anyway. Plants packed too close together get poor air movement and grow small, lower-quality leaves.
seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to the recommended spacing even though it feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens get less airflow and produce smaller, lower-quality leaves.

seedling.text_beginner: A thin layer of mulch (straw, shredded leaves, or compost) around your seedlings keeps the soil moist and holds weeds down. Both matter a lot for leafy greens, which need steady moisture to grow well.
seedling.text_seasoned: A light mulch around seedlings keeps moisture in and suppresses weeds, both important for leafy greens which need consistent moisture.

established.text_beginner: Start picking the outer leaves as soon as they are big enough to use. This is how leafy greens are meant to be harvested: take the outer leaves and the center keeps pushing out new growth, so one plant feeds you for weeks.
established.text_seasoned: Start harvesting outer leaves as soon as they reach a useful size; this is how leafy greens work. The center keeps producing new growth as you remove the outer leaves.

established.text_beginner: Try to water on a steady schedule rather than letting the soil dry out and then soaking it. When the weather turns hot, that on-and-off watering makes lettuce and spinach bolt sooner. Bolting is when the plant shoots up a flower stalk and the leaves turn bitter. Steady moisture buys you more harvest time as it heats up.
established.text_seasoned: Water consistently. Under heat stress, irregular watering pushes lettuce and spinach to bolt sooner, so steady moisture buys time as temperatures climb.

harvest.text_beginner: Pick your greens in the morning, when the leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Get them into the fridge right away in a slightly damp bag so they stay fresh.
harvest.text_seasoned: Always harvest in the morning when leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Refrigerate immediately in a damp bag.

harvest.text_beginner: When you harvest a cut-and-come-again crop (one you cut from again and again rather than pulling up), leave at least half the plant standing. Taking too much at once sets it back and slows the next flush of leaves.
harvest.text_seasoned: Leave at least half the plant intact when harvesting cut-and-come-again crops. Taking too much at once sets the plant back.

bolting.text_beginner: When you spot a flower stalk shooting up from the center, the plant is bolting, which means it is going to seed. Harvest the whole thing right away. The leaves are still safe to eat, but they get more bitter every day from here.
bolting.text_seasoned: Once you see a flower stalk, harvest everything immediately. The leaves are still edible but will become more bitter every day.

bolting.text_beginner: A bolted plant (one that has shot up a flower stalk and gone to seed) is not a failure on your part, it is just the plant finishing its natural life cycle. A fall planting often does better than a spring one, because the weather is cooling down instead of heating up.
bolting.text_seasoned: Bolted leafy greens are not a failure: it is the plant completing its lifecycle. A fall sowing often outperforms spring because the weather is cooling rather than warming.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single leaf-lettuce plant keeps producing as long as it stays in active vegetative growth, which in practice means until rising heat pushes it toward bolting. Picked as cut-and-come-again, one plant yields repeated cuttings over several weeks rather than a single harvest, but the productive window is bounded by temperature, not a fixed calendar: once sustained days above about 75°F trigger the seedstalk, the leaves turn bitter and the plant is finished. In cool spring and fall stretches that window runs longer; through summer heat it closes fast.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A single leaf-lettuce plant keeps producing as long as it is still growing leaves, which in practice means until heat pushes it to send up a flower stalk (bolt). Picked a few outer leaves at a time, one plant gives you repeated harvests over several weeks rather than all at once. But the limit is temperature, not the calendar: once you get steady days above about 75°F, the plant starts to bolt, the leaves turn bitter, and it is finished. In cool spring and fall weather that window lasts longer, and in summer heat it closes fast.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: There are two harvest rhythms, and they run on different clocks. Picking individual outer leaves off a standing plant can be done every few days as new leaves size up, taking the oldest first. Cutting the whole plant back to about an inch above the crown, the full cut-and-come-again method, gives a larger single harvest but then needs roughly 2 to 4 weeks of regrowth before the next cutting, and a plant will usually give two such cuttings, sometimes a third. For a steady supply, succession sowing matters more than pushing any one plant.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: There are two ways to harvest, and they work on different timelines. You can pick individual outer leaves off a standing plant every few days as new ones size up, always taking the oldest first. Or you can cut the whole plant back to about an inch above the base, which gives a bigger single harvest but then needs about 2 to 4 weeks to grow back before the next cut. A plant will usually give two such cuttings, sometimes a third. For a steady supply, sowing a new small batch every couple of weeks matters more than pushing any one plant.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce is one of the fastest and most forgiving crops for a first season. You can be cutting baby leaves in roughly a month from sowing, while a full-sized plant takes longer, about 40 to 80 days depending on the type, with loose-leaf varieties the quickest and heading types the slowest. Because you do not have to wait for a head to form, the early baby-leaf harvest is what makes it feel so quick.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Irregular watering is one of the biggest bolting triggers in lettuce and spinach. A dry spell followed by heat stresses the plant and pushes it to flower and set seed in a hurry, cutting the leafy harvest short.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture steady. A light mulch around leafy greens holds soil moisture and evens out the swings that trigger bolting. Water in the morning so the leaves dry through the day, which also helps keep mildew down.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Heat and long days drive most leafy greens to bolt, and it is the single most common reason they disappoint. The plant is not dying; it is doing exactly what it is built to do once the season turns. Once it bolts, the leaves go bitter and inedible fast.
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Bolted too quickly
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: For leafy greens, a fall sowing almost always beats spring: the cooling weather gives you longer-lasting, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth and steady watering can stretch the spring crop by a couple of weeks, but timing the sowing to the cool shoulders of the season is what really works.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Bolted too quickly
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Heat and long days drive most leafy greens to bolt, and it is the single most common reason they disappoint. The plant is not dying; it is doing exactly what it is built to do once the season turns. Once it bolts, the leaves go bitter and inedible fast.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For leafy greens, the fall sowing almost always beats spring: cooling temperatures give you longer-lasting, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth and steady watering can stretch the spring crop by a couple of weeks, but timing the sowing to the cool shoulders of the season is what really works.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Succession sow at roughly 2-week intervals through the cool-season window for your climate. Where summers are cold-limited, that means spring through early summer plus a late-summer fall sowing; where summers are hot, it means fall through spring with a summer heat pause. Lettuce bolts and turns bitter above about 75°F, so anchor your sowings to the cool side of the season and stop before sustained heat. Sow just enough for 1-2 weeks of salads per batch rather than a full bed at once.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Sow a short row every couple of weeks instead of one big planting, so you always have fresh lettuce coming in. In cold-winter areas, start in spring once the soil warms and keep going into early summer, then sow again in late summer for a fall crop. In hot-summer areas, do the reverse: grow through fall, winter, and spring, and skip the heat of summer. Either way, lettuce turns bitter and goes to seed (bolts) once it is too hot, so pause your sowings whenever the hottest stretch arrives.
succession_policy.count_note_seasoned: Season total is not a fixed cap; it is the per-zone sum of spring-arm and fall-arm sowings at the 2-week cadence, bounded by the bolt-driven spring close, the summer-heat limit on when fall sowing can begin, and baby-leaf harvest before/through light frost. Cold zones 3-7 range roughly 7-10 sowings/season. The prior single value (6) carried no T1 basis and undercounted the spring arm; superseded by methodology v1.5 Clause C (per-arm count != season cap).

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool season crops such as spinach, leaf lettuce, peas, onions, and root crops can germinate at minimum soil temperatures of 35-40 degrees F. harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Harvest extends to approximately first_frost + 5 days for hardy greens; first_frost - 5 days for tender greens like lettuce.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring succession arm: sow looseleaf lettuce every 2 weeks from when soil reaches 40 degrees F through the bolt-driven close of the spring window. Leafy greens germinate at 35-40 degrees F minimum and mature in 40-60 days, so sequential plantings give consistent production; the arm ends as rising heat (above ~75 degrees F) triggers bolting and bitterness. (USU Extension; UMN Extension; University of Maryland Extension)
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Spring arm capped at the fall-arm start so spring and fall sowings do not overlap in the coldest zones. Latest spring sow otherwise bounded by spring-harvest close minus 30-day baby-leaf maturity (Clause B).

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall succession arm: sow fast-maturing looseleaf lettuce every 2 weeks starting about 3 months before the first fall frost, harvesting baby leaves as temperatures cool. Lettuce is semi-hardy and tolerates light frost, so the latest sowing leaves roughly 30 days to baby-leaf size near the first frost rather than a full head well before it. In the coldest zones, where three months before the first frost still falls in peak summer heat, the fall start is clamped to roughly July 1 (a heat floor) rather than the full first frost minus 90 days, because soil above about 80 degrees F causes germination failure. (UMN Extension; University of Maryland Extension; USU Extension)
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Fall arm start = heat-floored first_frost offset (methodology v1.5 Clause A). Latest sow = first_frost - 30d (baby-leaf; light-frost-tolerant, no extra hard margin). Per-arm count derived per zone (Clause C); not the season cap.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Midsummer heat gap (July): sustained temperatures above roughly 75°F drive lettuce to bolt and turn bitter, and warm soil inhibits germination, so the spring succession ends and no new sowing occurs until the crop resumes as a fall planting. Not a frost gap but a summer heat exclusion; the warm edge of this cold region carries both a midsummer heat gap and a winter cold pause. (University of Minnesota Extension; Virginia Cooperative Extension)

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), lettuce is a spring-and-fall crop built around frost, not heat. Start sowing in spring as soon as the soil warms to about 40°F, usually a few weeks before your last frost, and sow a short row every couple of weeks for a steady supply. Plant again in mid to late summer for a fall crop. Skip the hottest part of summer, when lettuce bolts (sends up a flower stalk) and turns bitter. For the most reliable results your first season, aim for the spring window from when the soil is workable into early summer, and a fall sowing in July or August depending on your zone, leaving roughly a month before your first frost so young leaves size up while it is still mild. Lettuce takes light frost in stride, so a fall crop can keep going right up to the first hard freeze.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Region calendar is frost-governed and spring-centric, the standard (non-inverted) lettuce pattern the warm regions invert against. Two succession arms bracket the summer: a spring arm sown from the soil-40°F crossing (a few weeks ahead of last frost) through the bolt-driven close as sustained heat above about 75°F sets in, and a fall arm whose start is heat-floored to roughly July 1 in the coldest zones rather than a flat first-frost-minus-90, since the unclamped offset would fall in peak summer heat and cause germination failure (soil thermoinhibition above about 80°F). The fall arm targets fast-maturing looseleaf at the 30-day baby-leaf end, harvested through light frost rather than to a full head, so the latest viable sow sits about 30 days ahead of first frost with no extra hard margin. Per-arm sowing counts are derived per zone (not a fixed season cap) and range roughly 7 to 10 across zones 3 through 7. Frost is the governing constraint at both ends; summer heat is the interior limit. Spring-sow timing is anchored to MSU (cool-season germination minimum 35 to 40°F) and UMN (direct sow as soil reaches 40°F, 2 to 4 weeks before last frost); the fall arm and heat floor to UMN midsummer-planting guidance and USU (fall lettuce 50 to 75 days before maturity, light frost tolerated to 32°F), with NDSU corroboration for the coldest-zone fall window. In the milder cold zones (6 and 7), a cold frame or row cover extends the harvest several weeks past the outdoor season, with slow winter growth that holds the standing crop rather than expanding it; this is season extension under protection, not part of the default outdoor calendar (VCE and UMN give cold frames and row cover a two-to-four-week spring and fall extension).

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the Southeast and Gulf region, fall through spring is the primary lettuce season; summer is excluded by heat. Sow after sustained summer heat subsides in late summer to early fall. UGA gives leaf-lettuce fall planting as approximately September 1 to October 1 for middle Georgia, shifting later toward the warmer (zone 9) Gulf-coastal end of the region. (UGA Cooperative Extension B577; UGA Cooperative Extension C963) In Florida and the Gulf states, lettuce production runs from late September into spring. (UF/IFAS)

uscrn_validation.zone_coverage_note: soil at 5cm is already at or above 35F when the year opens in 88% of watched years here, so this sowing date is not gated by soil temperature

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: The region's second window is late winter into early spring, before returning heat triggers bolting. UGA gives leaf-lettuce spring planting as approximately January 15 to March 1 for middle Georgia, running earlier at the warmer Gulf-coastal end. The window closes as sustained daytime temperatures climb toward bolting; harvest before then. (UGA Cooperative Extension B577; UGA Cooperative Extension C963)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall and winter leaf lettuce in the region matures more slowly than spring plantings because cooler temperatures and shorter days slow growth; first cuttings run roughly 60 days from sowing for the fall window. UGA lists 60 to 85 days to maturity for lettuce, with leaf types at the faster end. (UGA Cooperative Extension B577; UGA Cooperative Extension C963)

harvest_start.label: secondary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring-window leaf lettuce begins harvest sooner than the fall window as warming lengthens growth; leaf types reach cut-and-come-again size at the fast end of the maturity range. (UGA Cooperative Extension B577; University of Maryland Extension) Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UMN Extension)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The region's harvest closes when returning spring heat triggers bolting, which turns leaves bitter and pushes a seed stalk. Harvest before sustained warm daytime temperatures. Lettuce tolerates light frost but not prolonged heat. (UMN Extension; UGA Cooperative Extension)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf region, lettuce is a fall-through-spring crop, the reverse of the North. Plant after summer heat eases (around September), grow it through the mild winter, and plant again in late winter for a spring crop. Skip high summer, when lettuce turns bitter and bolts. Winter is the best, most reliable season here.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Region calendar is heat-inverted: two cool-season windows (fall sowing from late summer once heat subsides; late-winter sowing before spring heat returns) bracketing a summer heat pause. Peak production is winter (UF/IFAS: highest production January-February). Frost is a secondary modifier at the cooler zone-8 interior end, where hard freezes can damage an exposed crop; lettuce tolerates light frost. Zone-9 Gulf-coastal end runs the windows earlier in spring and later in fall. Windows verified against UGA B577/C963 (leaf lettuce: spring Jan 15-Mar 1, fall Sep 1-Oct 1, middle-Georgia baseline) with UF/IFAS corroboration for the Gulf-coastal end.

(UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2) Sacramento County Master Gardeners note lettuce germinates poorly in warm summer soil because heat can cause seed dormancy, and bolts under high-temperature stress. ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In the California interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and nearby), lettuce grows in two stretches: a quick late-summer planting in August as the worst heat starts to ease, and a long main season from November through March over the mild winter. Skip the heart of summer (roughly May through July), when it is too hot, lettuce won't germinate well, and plants bolt and turn bitter. Harvest the winter crop before spring heat returns.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Interior-valley calendar is heat-inverted with two windows (Table 13.2: August, then November through March). The August window is a short late-summer sowing as peak heat eases; the November-March window is the long mild-winter main season, closing as spring heat returns and drives bolting. Summer (roughly May through July) is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: lettuce germinates poorly in warm summer soil and bolts under high-temperature stress (Sacramento County trials bolted in weeks of 106-107°F). Frost is a minor secondary factor at the cooler zone-8 end. Windows verified against UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2, with UC Master Gardeners of Sacramento County corroboration for interior-valley heat behavior.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the California north coast (Monterey County north), summer is actually lettuce's best season, the opposite of hot inland areas. The cool, foggy summers let you grow lettuce from late winter all the way through summer. Plant from February through August. The cold, wet winter, not summer heat, is what ends the season here.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: North-coast calendar is cool-limited and summer-inclusive (Table 13.2: February through August), the inverse of the heat-inverted interior and desert. The cool maritime summer is the active growing season, so there is no summer heat pause; the season is bounded instead by the cold, wet winter. Spring sowing begins once soil is workable and warming; the crop runs through summer and closes as winter sets in. In the mildest coastal microclimates, lettuce can be grown nearly year-round with careful variety selection (UC Marin Master Gardeners), but that is a microclimate refinement, not the regional window. Windows verified against UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2, with UC Marin Master Gardeners corroboration for the maritime cool-season pattern.
ca_north_coast.microclimate_note_seasoned: UC Marin Master Gardeners note that lettuce, generally a cool-season annual, can be grown throughout the year in Marin with advance planning and judicious plant selection. (UC Marin Master Gardeners)

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: South-coast calendar is summer-excluded and winter-dominant (Table 13.2: August through April), a single long mild-season window. Plant from September through December, grow it through the mild winter, and skip summer entirely, when desert heat is far too high for lettuce. Once spring warms up and days get longer, plants bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter, so harvest before the heat arrives.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: Desert calendar is heat-inverted with a single fall-through-winter window (Table 13.2: September through December sowing). The crop finishes ahead of the spring heat ramp, when lengthening days and rising temperatures drive bolting. Frost is not the limiting factor here. direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the warm arid Southwest (southern New Mexico, West Texas), fall is a primary lettuce season: sow once cresting summer heat subsides in late summer to early fall. Texas A&M AgriLife gives leaf-lettuce fall planting for Texas Region III (USDA zone 8) as approximately September 1. The El Paso County planting calendar places leaf lettuce in the fall garden as the heat breaks. (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension EHT-056; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension El Paso County)

direct_sow.label: secondary

NMSU notes lettuce germinates best near 65-70F and bolts when temperatures climb above about 70F with long days; the El Paso County calendar plants leaf lettuce as one of the very earliest spring crops. Sow as soon as the soil is workable and harvest before sustained spring heat. (New Mexico State University Extension Circular 457; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension El Paso County)

(New Mexico State University Extension Circular 457-B)

harvest_start.label: secondary

harvest_end.label: primary

8.zone_notes: Arid USDA zone 8 (e.g. Las Cruces NM, El Paso TX): frost-free roughly April through early November. Lettuce runs a spring window (late winter into early spring) and a fall window (late summer into fall), with a hard summer heat pause between them. Light frost is tolerated at the cool winter shoulders; intense summer heat, not frost, governs the season.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: in the arid Southwest, soil and air above the bolting/germination threshold cause germination failure and bolting in lettuce through the May-August heat. NMSU: lettuce bolts above about 70°F with long days and germination is inhibited above about 79°F. (New Mexico State University Extension; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the warm arid Southwest, lettuce grows in the cooler shoulders of the year, not the summer. Plant a spring crop in late winter to early spring, and a fall crop in late summer once the worst heat breaks. Skip planting through the summer heat, about May through August, when lettuce bolts (sends up a flower stalk) and turns bitter. If you are squeezing in a last spring sowing, get it in by early May; for fall, wait until the heat eases, usually around late August. Light frost in winter is fine; summer heat is the real limit here.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: Region calendar is heat-inverted with two cool-season windows bracketing a summer heat pause: a spring window (sow as soil becomes workable in late winter/early spring, harvest before the spring heat ramp triggers bolting) and a fall window (sow once cresting summer heat subsides in late summer, into fall). The governing constraint is heat, not frost. Texas A&M AgriLife gives leaf lettuce for Texas Region III (USDA zone 8) a fall planting near September 1; the El Paso County calendar runs leaf lettuce as a very-early spring crop and again in fall. NMSU gives leaf lettuce about 46 days to harvest, optimal germination near 65-70°F, and bolting above about 70°F with long days. Frost is a secondary modifier at the cool winter shoulders (arid zone 8 is frost-free roughly April through early November); light frost is tolerated. The summer heat pause (May-August) is a hard exclusion. Windows verified against Texas A&M AgriLife EHT-056 and the El Paso County planting calendar, with NMSU Circular 457/457-B for maturity and bolting biology.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the Arizona low desert (Maricopa County ~9b, Yuma), lettuce is a fall-through-winter crop on a single long window; summer is excluded entirely by extreme heat. Sow once summer heat subsides in early-to-mid fall and the soil cools, then continue sowing through the mild winter into late winter. University of Arizona guidance places leaf-lettuce planting across the cool season, and the Yuma calendar gives a September-through-February cool season for lettuce and other non-fruiting greens. Plant after about September 15 once nights and soil cool; avoid sowing while soil is at or above 85 degrees F. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005; AZ1615)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall and winter leaf lettuce in the low desert matures over roughly 45 to 65 days; cooler winter temperatures and shorter days slow growth relative to warm-season conditions. University of Arizona gives leaf lettuce about 30 to 90 days to harvest depending on variety and season. Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach usable size. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The low-desert lettuce season closes as the spring heat ramp returns; lettuce bolts and turns bitter as days lengthen and temperatures climb. University of Arizona notes germination is inhibited at high temperatures (thermoinhibition, roughly 77 to 95 degrees F) and the warm season from March onward suits fruiting crops rather than lettuce. Harvest before sustained spring heat; do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1099; AZ1615)

9.zone_notes: Arizona low desert (USDA zone 9b; Maricopa County/Phoenix, Yuma). Frost is occasional and light; lettuce tolerates the rare light frost but not sustained heat. Last spring frost averages around February 15, but winter is mild growing weather for lettuce rather than a pause. The limiting factor is summer heat, not frost: triple-digit highs return in May and persist through August.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: May through August is excluded by extreme low-desert heat: soil and air well above the lettuce thermoinhibition range cause germination failure and bolting. In metro Phoenix the first 100°F day averages early May, and June through August average highs of about 104 to 106°F, far above the 77 to 95°F range that inhibits lettuce germination (University of Arizona AZ1099). April (average high about 85°F) is the spring bolting-close for an established crop rather than a no-sow month, and September is the soil-gated fall sow-resume, so the hard no-activity gap is May through August. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1099; AZ1615)

In metro Phoenix the first 100°F day averages early May, and June through August average highs of about 104 to 106°F, far above the 77 to 95°F range that inhibits lettuce germination (University of Arizona AZ1099). April (average high about 85°F) is the spring bolting-close for an established crop rather than a no-sow month, and September is the soil-gated fall sow-resume, so the hard no-activity gap is May through August. low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Yuma), lettuce is a winter crop. Plant from about mid-September, once nights cool and the soil is no longer hot, and keep sowing through the mild winter into February. Grow it through the winter and skip summer entirely, when desert heat is far too high for lettuce. As spring warms up and the days get longer, plants bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter, so harvest before the real heat arrives, usually by April. A rare light winter frost is fine; summer heat is the real limit here.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: Low-desert calendar is heat-inverted with a single long fall-through-winter window (sow from about mid-September, once soil drops below the high-temperature germination block, continuing through the mild winter into late February). Summer (May through August) is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. University of Arizona gives a September-through-February cool season for lettuce in the low desert; the Yuma calendar names lettuce as a primary cool-season crop over that span, and Maricopa County guidance runs leaf lettuce across the cool months with a summer break. Germination is inhibited at high soil temperatures (thermoinhibition, roughly 77 to 95°F), which is why the fall sowing waits for the soil to cool rather than for a frost date. The crop finishes ahead of the spring heat ramp, when lengthening days and rising temperatures drive bolting; in metro Phoenix the first 100°F day averages early May. Frost is a minor, occasional modifier at the winter shoulders, not the season boundary. Windows verified against University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005 (Maricopa County), AZ1615 (Yuma), and AZ1099 (lettuce germination physiology).

bolting.text_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, lettuce is a winter crop, so grow it from about mid-September through February and skip summer entirely. As spring warms and the days lengthen, plants bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter fast. When you spot a flower stalk, harvest the whole plant right away, and do not try to carry a crop into the desert summer.
bolting.text_seasoned: Low-desert lettuce finishes ahead of the spring heat ramp; expect bolting as days lengthen and highs climb past the mid-80s toward the first 100°F days of early May. Harvest the whole plant at the first flower stalk. Do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In peninsular Florida (central and south), leaf lettuce is a cool-season crop grown on a single continuous window from fall through late winter. UF/IFAS gives the peninsular planting window as September through February for both central and south Florida. (UF/IFAS VH021, Table 1) Sowing begins once the worst summer heat eases in September and continues through February; the regional calendars list lettuce among the crops to plant from October onward, with February the last month to sow for a late-spring harvest in the deep south. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1191; UF/IFAS Central Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1189)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce reaches harvest roughly 60 days after sowing under peninsular Florida's cool-season conditions; UF/IFAS lists lettuce at 60-80 days to harvest. (UF/IFAS VH021, Table 1) Fall and early-winter sowings mature into the winter production peak.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Peninsular harvest closes in spring as sustained heat returns and triggers bolting, which turns leaves bitter. The last February sowings finish by roughly April; lettuce is absent from the regional plant calendars from March onward as warm-season crops take over. Harvest before sustained daytime heat. (UF/IFAS VH021, Table 1; UF/IFAS Central Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1189)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

10.zone_notes: Central Florida (USDA 10 portion, between State Roads 40 and 70). Frost and light freezes are likely in January and February; protect an exposed crop when a freeze is forecast. Lettuce tolerates light frost but not sustained heat.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: peninsular Florida summers run above the bolting threshold, causing germination failure and bolting in lettuce. Lettuce is absent from the central Florida plant calendar from March onward as warm-season crops take over; beds are commonly solarized through summer for fall planting. The sowing window closes in February and the last sowings finish harvest by roughly April, so the no-activity gap is May through August. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS Central Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1189)

11.zone_notes: South Florida (USDA 11, below State Road 70). Frost and freezes are rare; the limiting factor is summer heat, not cold. February is the last month to sow for a late-spring harvest. Lettuce tolerates light frost but not sustained heat.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: south Florida summers run above the bolting threshold, ending cool-season production. Lettuce is absent from the south Florida plant calendar from March onward as tropical and heat-tolerant crops take over; beds are commonly solarized through summer for fall planting. The sowing window closes in February and the last sowings finish harvest by roughly April, so the no-activity gap is May through August. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1191)

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, lettuce is a cool-season crop, the opposite of up north. Plant from fall through late winter (about September into February), grow it through the mild winter, and skip the summer, when lettuce turns bitter and goes to seed. Winter is your reliable lettuce season here. For the easiest results, aim for the heart of the season, roughly November through January, when temperatures are most consistently cool, rather than the warm edges in early fall or the spring heat ramp.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: Region calendar is heat-inverted and single-window: one continuous cool-season sowing window (September through February per UF/IFAS VH021 Table 1, central and south Florida) bracketed by a summer heat exclusion, not split into two windows the way the more northern Southeast/Gulf zones are. Peak production is winter. The limiting factor is heat-driven bolting, not frost. The two peninsular zones differ mainly in frost exposure: central Florida (zone 10) sees likely January-February freezes that can damage an exposed crop (cover when a freeze is forecast), while south Florida (zone 11) rarely freezes and is heat-limited at both ends. Windows verified against UF/IFAS VH021 (Table 1) with the central (ENH1189) and south (ENH1191) Florida gardening calendars confirming the March warm-crop flip and the September reopening.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In Hawaii (tropical, zone 11), leaf lettuce is sown year-round; there is no frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for the leaf type. University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation and states that leafy and semi-head types can be grown year-round at low elevations, especially under overhead sprinkler irrigation, and that lettuce is grown year-round in most home and community gardens. Heading types are the seasonal exception (cooler months at low elevation, or high elevation) and are not the leaf-lettuce case here. Sow in any month; the heat of summer is managed with a heat-tolerant cultivar and afternoon shade rather than by skipping a season. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164; HGV-2)
direct_sow.from_year_round_note: Anchor from:'year_round' (Decision 3, NA-3g). Frost-independent: zone 11 has no last_frost/first_frost to offset against (zone_frost_data: frost_free_days 365). The resolver keys its 'skip frost resolution, use authored windows as-is' path off this named anchor; resolved_by_zone[11].year_round:true is derivable from it (region anchor = year_round <=> resolved-cell flag set).

uscrn_validation.zone_coverage_note: soil at 5cm is already at or above 35F when the year opens in 88% of watched years here, so this sowing date is not gated by soil temperature

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce in Hawaii reaches cut size in roughly 50 to 60 days from a direct-seeded sowing; CTAHR gives about 50 to 60 days to harvest for direct-seeded Manoa lettuce, the standard low-elevation leaf type, and a few days earlier from transplants. Harvest single leaves or the whole young head as soon as it reaches usable size; harvesting earlier also sidesteps tip-burn and bolting in warm weather. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: There is no season-ending harvest boundary in tropical zone 11: leaf lettuce is sown and harvested continuously through the year. Successive sowings keep a supply coming rather than the crop closing at a frost or a sustained-heat date. In the hottest, longest-day stretch, growth quality dips (tip-burn, faster bolting) but production does not stop; it is managed with cultivar choice and shade. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164; HGV-2)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Year-round cell: harvest_end mirrors the continuous window (from:'year_round', 365) rather than a frost or bolt boundary, because the season does not close. The all-active calendar carries no season_over state by construction.

11.zone_notes: Hawaii tropical (USDA zone 11; frost-free, frost_free_days 365). No frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for leaf lettuce. The limiting factor is summer heat quality, not a season boundary: in the hottest months leaf lettuce is grown with a heat-tolerant cultivar (Manoa, Anuenue) and afternoon shade, or moved to higher elevation, rather than paused. Heavy rain can bruise the soft leaves and is the other warm-month management concern.
11.calendar_basis: Leaf lettuce is grown YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free) and no summer no-sow exclusion: University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation, and states leafy/semi-head types grow year-round at low elevations and in most home gardens. The summer heat brings a quality dip (tip-burn, faster bolting), managed with a heat-tolerant cultivar and afternoon shade or higher elevation, not a production stop. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field); the year_round:true flag makes the all-active calendar's intent machine-readable. hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, leaf lettuce grows year-round, so you can plant a little any month of the year. Pick a heat-tolerant variety such as Manoa or Anuenue, which were bred here to handle the warmth and are slow to bolt. In the hottest, sunniest months, give plants some afternoon shade and keep them well watered, and protect the soft leaves from pounding rain. Lettuce can still bolt (send up a flower stalk and turn bitter) in a hot spell, so harvest leaves young and often. True head lettuce only does well up at higher, cooler elevations; down near the coast, stick with leaf and semi-head types.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical calendar is aseasonal for leaf lettuce: sow and harvest year-round, with no frost anchor and no summer heat pause. University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation and notes that leafy and semi-head types grow year-round at low elevations, especially under overhead sprinklers, while heading types are the seasonal, higher-elevation exception. The locally bred 'UH Manoa' (a Green Mignonette selection) and 'Anuenue' are the low-elevation standards; CTAHR describes Manoa as heat-tolerant, slow to bolt, and tip-burn resistant, grown year-round. The hot, long-day months bring a quality dip rather than a production gap: expect faster bolting and more tip-burn, managed with cultivar choice, roughly 40 percent afternoon shade at hot low-elevation sites (per CTAHR shade trials), and a move to higher elevation for head types. Germination falls off above about 81°F, so warm-season sowings benefit from primed seed or a cooler germination spot. Keep soil moisture steady; protect soft-leaved types from heavy rain. Windows verified against University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164 (Lettuce Production Guidelines for Hawaii), HGV-2 (Lettuce for the Home Garden), and B-91 (Home Gardening in Hawaii).

bolting.text_beginner: In Hawaii you grow lettuce year-round, so you do not skip a season; instead you manage the heat. Use a heat-tolerant variety like Manoa or Anuenue, give plants afternoon shade in the hottest, brightest months, and keep them watered. They will still bolt (send up a flower stalk and turn bitter) faster in a warm spell, so harvest leaves young and pick the whole plant once you see a stalk. Up at cooler, higher elevations, bolting is slower and you have more leeway.
bolting.text_seasoned: Hawaii is aseasonal for leaf lettuce: manage bolting with cultivar and microclimate rather than a seasonal pause. Grow heat-tolerant types (UH Manoa, Anuenue), add roughly 40 percent afternoon shade at hot low-elevation sites, and harvest young; bolting and tip-burn accelerate with heat and long days. Harvest the whole plant at the first flower stalk. Higher elevations extend the bolt-free window; head types are reliable only up there.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce set out Sep 1 - Feb 14 in the Rio Grande Valley, per Bilingual LRGV planting table (Vegetable Crops of the Lower Rio Grande Valley). Direct-sown September through mid-February (Bilingual LRGV table); 40 to 60 days to harvest supports rolling succession sowings rather than a single planting.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest harvest at about 40 days, from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest harvest at about 60 days, from the latest set-out date, before RGV's spring heat closes the window.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, grow leaf lettuce in the cool season, not summer. Plant Sep 1 through Feb 14 and harvest from Oct 11 into spring; it rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold. Leaf lettuce is a succession crop here: sow it every few weeks from September clear through mid-February and you will have cut-and-come-again greens all winter. Skip planting leaf lettuce from spring through summer: the Valley heat keeps it from growing well here.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Leaf lettuce in the RGV runs on the winter-garden calendar: direct-sow Sep 1 through Feb 14, with harvest running Oct 11 through Apr 15. Direct-sown September through mid-February (Bilingual LRGV table); 40 to 60 days to harvest supports rolling succession sowings rather than a single planting. Frost is essentially absent here, so timing is heat-bounded rather than cold-bounded. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: the TAMU AgriLife sources describe a single Valley-wide planting calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: OSU's Oregon planting table (EM9027) recommends starting leaf lettuce transplants about 5 weeks before setting them out; the Willamette Valley's own window runs from April into August.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set out (or direct sow) leaf lettuce from April into August in the Willamette Valley, staggering plantings every couple of weeks for a steady supply; the immediate coast's own OSU window opens earlier, from February.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce cuts in as little as 30 to 45 days; the mild maritime summer keeps it productive without bolting the way a hot inland summer would.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The last sowings finish up as the season's cool, wet fall weather settles in; leaf lettuce tolerates a light frost.

8.notes: Succession sow every 2 weeks for a continuous supply of baby leaves; cut single leaves as soon as they reach usable size.
8.zone_notes: OSU's Willamette Valley table opens leaf lettuce sowing in April, a full two months later than the immediate coast's February start; the valley's own spring soil warms more slowly than the coast's maritime-buffered ground despite a similar last-frost date.

9.notes: Succession sow every 2 weeks for a continuous supply of baby leaves; cut single leaves as soon as they reach usable size.
9.zone_notes: OSU's coastal table gives leaf lettuce the widest window in the region, February clear through August, exploiting the immediate coast's exceptionally mild, marine-buffered winter and spring soil.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: West of the Cascades, leaf lettuce grows through a long, cool season. In the Willamette Valley, start seeds indoors in late winter and sow or set out plants from April into August, a new short row every couple of weeks, for a steady supply into fall. Right on the coast, the window opens even earlier, in February, since winters there are especially mild. Summer is simply the growing season here; there is no need to dodge the heat the way hot-summer gardeners do.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Leaf lettuce runs on a long, continuous succession-sown window across the maritime Pacific Northwest, per OSU's Oregon planting table. In the Willamette Valley, start transplants indoors in late winter and sow or set out from April into August; on the immediate coast, OSU's own window opens two months earlier, from February, thanks to the coast's exceptionally mild, marine-buffered winter and spring soil. Sow every 2 weeks through either window for a continuous harvest; the region's cool, mild summer keeps lettuce sweet and slow to bolt rather than forcing a heat-driven pause the way hot-summer regions require.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set out the spring crop per Virginia Cooperative Extension's zone 8 Lettuce, baby salad table (Mar 10 to May 1); zone 7 runs about two to three weeks later.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring harvest begins as the crop reaches maturity, before the belt's hot, humid summer sets in.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: End of the spring harvest window, before summer heat stalls quality.

plant_out.source_quote: Lettuce, baby salad zone 8 fall: Sep 1-Oct 20
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set out the fall crop per Virginia Cooperative Extension's zone 8 Lettuce, baby salad table (Sep 1 to Oct 20), the belt's real second cycle; zone 7 runs the window earlier and shorter.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop matures as nights cool, often the belt's better crop of the two.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall harvest continues into the cool season; this crop tolerates the belt's light frosts well.

7.notes: Succession sow every 2 weeks for a steady supply; cut single leaves as soon as they reach usable size.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, direct-sow leaf lettuce in late winter through spring, from about mid-February to the end of March, for a spring harvest. Once daytime highs push past 90°F, lettuce bolts and turns bitter, so stop sowing and let the ground rest. nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) grows leaf lettuce on two direct-sown cycles, per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart. Spring sowing runs roughly mid-February to the end of March, with harvest beginning about 38 days later. University of Nevada, Reno Extension's home-vegetable guidance (Fact Sheet FS-02-61) notes plants generally stop growing well once daytime highs run past 90°F, and lettuce bolts and turns bitter fast in that heat, so the chart splits into a real spring cycle and a distinct late-summer fall cycle. The fall sowing (about mid-August to mid-September) goes in as the heat breaks and carries past the valley's first fall frost, since leaf lettuce tolerates a light frost. Zone 8's cooler pockets reach frost sooner, tightening the fall finish; zone 10 at Laughlin has the most room to spare.

crops.description_seasoned: One of the fastest, most forgiving crops in the garden, and a strong first-season choice. Sow it directly where it will grow and harvest the outer leaves as cut-and-come-again, taking the oldest first while the center keeps producing. Lettuce is a cool-season crop: it bolts and turns bitter once sustained heat arrives, so the productive window is the cool shoulders of the year. Succession sow small batches every couple of weeks through spring, then again in fall, to keep tender leaves coming rather than harvesting one bed all at once.
crops.description_beginner: One of the fastest and most forgiving crops you can grow, and a great pick for a first garden. Sow the seed right where the plants will grow, then harvest the outer leaves a few at a time, taking the oldest first while the center keeps making new ones. Lettuce is a cool-season crop, which means it grows best in the mild parts of the year: once steady heat arrives it turns bitter and sends up a flower stalk (this is called bolting). To keep tender leaves coming, sow a small batch every couple of weeks in spring, then again in fall, instead of planting one big bed all at once.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick the outer leaves whenever they reach usable size, taking the oldest from several plants and leaving the crown to keep growing, or cut the whole plant back to about an inch above the crown for a single larger harvest that regrows. Harvest in the cool of the morning, when leaves are crisp and full of water. The limiting factor is heat: once the central stem begins to elongate (bolting), the plant shifts to flowering, and the leaves turn bitter and tough, so take your fullest harvests before sustained warm weather sets in.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick the outer leaves whenever they are big enough to use, taking the oldest ones from several plants and leaving the center to keep growing. Or cut the whole plant back to about an inch above the base for one larger harvest that will grow back. Harvest in the cool of the morning, when the leaves are crisp and full of water. Heat is the limiting factor: once a stalk starts to rise from the center (this is bolting, the plant shifting to making flowers), the leaves turn bitter and tough, so take your biggest harvests before steady warm weather arrives.

crops.name: Swiss Chard

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Swiss chard likes loose, fertile, well-drained soil with plenty of compost worked in. Unlike its cousin the beet, chard is grown for its leaves and stalks rather than a round root, so it is not as fussy about deep, stone-free soil, but a loose bed that does not crust still gives the best start. The seed is slow to come up, so keep the top of the soil moist and crumbly so the seedlings can push through. Mix in compost, aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, and chard is happy in most garden soils that drain well.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Chard does best in a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. As a leaf-and-stalk crop rather than a root crop, it is less demanding of stone-free depth than beet or carrot, but a loose, non-crusting seedbed still matters because the multigerm seedball is slow to germinate and the seedlings cannot break a hard surface crust. Work in well-finished compost to feed the long cut-and-come-again harvest. Chard tolerates a slightly acidic to neutral pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 and, like its relative the beet, handles mildly alkaline soil better than most greens; it is notably more acid-tolerant than spinach, growing well down to about pH 6.0.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Swiss chard does best from about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral, and it is more forgiving of soil type than many greens. It handles a touch of alkalinity better than spinach and is happy in most garden soils. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number and whether you need to add lime.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral. The University of Minnesota notes chard tolerates soil somewhat more acidic than spinach, as low as about pH 6.0, and Clemson cites a 6.0 to 6.5 range; like the beet it is the same species as, chard also handles mildly alkaline soil (to about 7.5) better than most leafy greens. Acidity well below 6.0 is the main risk, where germination and micronutrient uptake suffer. A standard soil test removes the guesswork before sowing.

fertilizer.frequency: at planting, then side-dress through the long harvest
fertilizer.timing: work compost and a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing, then side-dress with nitrogen about 4 weeks after the seedlings are up and again every 4 to 6 weeks through the cutting season
fertilizer.example_product: 21-0-0, calcium nitrate, or blood meal over a balanced base
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Chard is a leafy crop that runs on nitrogen, and because it is cut over a long season it benefits from periodic feeding rather than a single dose. Work compost and a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing, then side-dress with nitrogen about 4 weeks after emergence and again every 4 to 6 weeks while you keep cutting. Utah State suggests about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row. Steady nitrogen and even moisture keep the leaves large, tender, and dark; repeated harvesting pulls a lot out of the plant, so do not let it run hungry.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Swiss chard grows lots of leaves and likes nitrogen to keep making them. Mix some compost and a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed it with a nitrogen fertilizer about a month after the seedlings come up, and again every 4 to 6 weeks while you are picking. Because you cut from the same plant for months, a steady supply of food keeps the leaves big and tender.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your chard with nitrogen.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to give your chard a feeding.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: High nitrogen for sustained leafy growth, e.g. a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 ft of row or calcium nitrate, side-dressed every 4 to 6 weeks over a balanced base worked in at sowing. Phosphorus and potassium per a soil-test baseline.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer, repeated every 4 to 6 weeks while you harvest, over a balanced fertilizer mixed in at planting.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row per side-dressing, repeated every 4 to 6 weeks through the cutting season.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, feeding every 4 to 6 weeks while you pick.

companions.note_beginner: Swiss chard is an easygoing neighbor that shares a bed nicely with many crops. It grows well next to beans, the cabbage family (broccoli, cabbage, kale), onions and other alliums, and low herbs. The main plants to keep apart from chard are its close relatives beets and spinach, which share the same leafminer pest, so do not crowd them together. As always, do not trust every companion chart online, since many of their claims have never been tested.
companions.note_seasoned: Chard fits easily into mixed beds and its companion list mirrors the beet's, since they are the same species. West Virginia University's companion guide lists beans, the cabbage family, and onions among the good neighbors for the chard and beet group, all reasonable on space-and-timing grounds. The one well-grounded caution is to separate chard from its goosefoot-family relatives beets and spinach, which share the leafminer and several leaf diseases, a rotation and pest principle more than a tested adjacency effect. Treat the rest as sensible defaults: as the University of Minnesota stresses, most companion claims are tradition rather than tested science, so use them as a starting point and watch your own results.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Bush beans and chard make easy bedfellows, and the beans add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy chard can use. Keep tall pole beans out of the way, though, since they shade the low chard.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: WVU's companion guide lists beans among the good companions for the beet and chard group; the legume-nitrogen and complementary-habit rationale is sound and extension-listed, but it is a space-and-soil benefit rather than a measured chard-specific effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beans interplant well with chard on structure and soil: bush beans share the bed without crowding the chard rosette and fix a little nitrogen the leafy crop draws on. WVU lists beans among the good companions for the beet and chard group. A space-and-soil benefit rather than a pest one; keep climbing pole beans away, as they shade the low, sun-loving chard.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cabbage family (broccoli, cabbage, kale)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Chard and the cabbage-family crops both like the same cool-to-mild weather and do not compete much, with the low chard sitting under the taller brassicas. A productive way to fill a bed.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: WVU lists the cabbage family among the good companions for the beet and chard group; the pairing rests on shared season and complementary canopy structure rather than a tested interaction.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Chard and brassicas share a long cool-to-mild season and a complementary structure, the low chard rosette under the taller cabbage-family canopy, so they coexist without much competition. WVU lists the cabbage family among the good companions for the beet and chard group. A sensible structural pairing rather than a measured effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions, leeks, and garlic grow tall and narrow with shallow roots, so they tuck between chard plants without crowding them, and their strong smell is widely used to help keep some leaf-eating pests away.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Alliums are widely recommended as companions for the beet and chard group for efficient space use and scent-based pest masking. The space benefit is sound; the pest deterrence is mechanistically plausible but not established in a chard-specific trial, so likely rather than research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a classic interplant for the beet and chard group: shallow-rooted and upright, they share the bed without competing, and their sulfur volatiles are widely credited with masking the crop from some leaf-feeding pests. The space benefit is solid; the pest deterrence is plausible but not proven for chard specifically.

good_seasoned.name: Beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Bush beans share the bed without crowding the chard and fix a little nitrogen for the leafy crop; WVU lists beans among the good companions for the beet and chard group. A space-and-soil benefit, not a tested effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: WVU Extension lists beans as a companion for the beet and chard group; legume-nitrogen and complementary-habit rationale rather than a measured chard-specific effect.

good_seasoned.name: Cabbage family (broccoli, cabbage, kale)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shared cool-season timing and a layered canopy let the low chard grow under the taller brassicas; WVU lists the cabbage family among the good companions for the beet and chard group.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: WVU Extension lists the cabbage family as a companion for the beet and chard group; rests on shared season and structure rather than a tested interaction.

good_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Upright, shallow-rooted alliums share the bed without crowding the chard, and their scent is commonly credited with masking the crop from leaf pests; a popular but not chard-trial-proven pairing.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Allium space-use and scent-masking are widely recommended for the beet and chard group and mechanistically plausible, but not established in a chard-specific trial; labeled likely.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Beets and spinach
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep chard away from beets and spinach. They are close relatives in the same plant family and share the same leafminer pest and some leaf diseases, so planting them together helps those problems build up.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Chard, beet, and spinach are all goosefoot-family (Amaranthaceae) hosts of the beet and spinach leafminer and share leaf diseases such as Cercospora and downy mildew; clustering them concentrates the shared pest and pathogen load. A sound epidemiological and rotation mechanism rather than a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Chard, beet, and spinach all belong to the goosefoot family and are the favored hosts of the beet and spinach leafminer, whose maggots blister and ruin the leaves; they also share Cercospora leaf spot and downy mildew. Planting them side by side or in succession concentrates the leafminer and disease pressure and feeds the soil-overwintering pupae. Separate them in space and rotate so goosefoot crops do not follow one another.

bad_seasoned.name: Beets and spinach
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Chard, beets, and spinach are goosefoot-family relatives and the shared hosts of the leafminer plus Cercospora and downy mildew, so grouping them concentrates the pest and disease load. Separate them and rotate the goosefoot crops apart.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared leafminer host range and shared leaf diseases are extension-documented across the goosefoot family; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound agronomic principle, not a formally pair-tested effect.

pests.name: Leafminer (beet and spinach leafminer)
pests.symptoms_beginner: You will see pale, winding tunnels in the leaves that widen into large tan blisters or blotches, with the green skin of the leaf intact above and below. Hold a leaf to the light and you can see the tiny maggot working inside. Since you eat chard leaves, this ruins the damaged parts.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs on the underside of the leaves, and the maggots that hatch tunnel inside, eating between the top and bottom layers. Chard, beets, and spinach are its favorites, which is why it helps not to plant them together.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once a maggot is inside a leaf, sprays do not reach it well, so pick off and destroy mined leaves as soon as you see them, before the maggots drop to the soil. Crushing the maggot inside the leaf works too. Keep the plant healthy and it will outgrow light damage.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover the plants with a light row cover right after sowing so the flies cannot lay eggs, pull nearby weeds like lambsquarters that host the pest, and move chard away from where you grew chard, beets, or spinach last year.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Slender, winding mines enlarge into translucent tan blotches; because the crop is the leaf, even light feeding downgrades it, and heavily mined chard is unusable. The pale legless maggots are visible inside the leaf against the light.
pests.cause_seasoned: The beet and spinach leafminer (Pegomya species) overwinters as pupae in the soil; females lay rows of white eggs on leaf undersides, and the maggots tunnel between the leaf surfaces. There are several overlapping generations a season on chard, beets, spinach, and goosefoot weeds, the reason these relatives are rotated and spaced apart.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Insecticides reach larvae inside the leaf poorly, so rely on cultural control: pick and destroy mined leaves before larvae drop to pupate, and crush maggots in the leaf. Vigorous, evenly watered plants outgrow light damage, and naturally occurring parasitic wasps usually keep numbers in check.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude the egg-laying flies with floating row cover from sowing, control goosefoot weeds (lambsquarters, chickweed) that host the pest, rotate away from where chard, beets, or spinach grew, and remove the first mined leaves promptly to break the cycle.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give chard a different bed than the one that held chard, beets, or spinach last season. The flies spend the winter in the soil under those crops, so a fresh spot starts you off with fewer of them nearby.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Pupae overwinter in the soil beneath the previous host crop, so siting chard away from last year's chard, beet, or spinach separates the emerging adults from the planting. Keeping these relatives apart in the garden rather than side by side works on the same logic.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull the weeds around the bed, particularly lambsquarters and chickweed, which feed the same pest. Clearing spent chard, beet, and spinach leaves helps too, since they give the flies somewhere to keep going.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Goosefoot weeds such as lambsquarters and chickweed carry the leafminer between plantings, so weeding the bed and its margins narrows the host bridge that the several overlapping generations depend on across a season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put a light row cover over the bed as soon as the seed is in the ground, and leave it on while the plants are young. If the flies cannot reach the leaves, they cannot start the tunnels.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Exclusion has to be in place from sowing, ahead of the first egg-laying flight. Females deposit rows of white eggs on leaf undersides, so any open edge or gap in the cover gives them the access they need.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The moment you spot a tunneled leaf, take it off the plant and get rid of it, or pinch the leaf and squash the maggot inside. Do it before the maggots drop out to the soil, where they turn into the next round of flies.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing mined leaves ahead of larval drop is the main lever, because the larva sits protected between the leaf surfaces where insecticides reach it poorly. Crushing in place is the alternative when you would rather not strip leaf area off a young plant.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Tiny wild wasps that attack the maggots are usually already working in the garden, and they often hold the numbers down on their own. Go easy on sprays that kill a wide range of insects so those helpers stay in the bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Naturally occurring parasitic wasps generally keep leafminer numbers in check, which is a large part of why this pest is handled culturally. An insecticide application tends to cost more in parasitoids than it takes out of larvae shielded inside the leaf.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or black insects collect on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, leaving leaves curled, yellowed, and sticky. They can hide down in the crinkled leaves and along the stalks, and they can spread plant viruses.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck sap from the plant. They breed quickly, especially on soft growth from too much nitrogen, and fly in from weeds and other plants.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, which often does the trick, or use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on the undersides of the leaves. Ladybugs and other helpers usually take care of the rest. Do not over-feed with nitrogen.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings by not spraying broadly, go easy on nitrogen, keep weeds down, and check the new growth and leaf undersides now and then so you catch them early.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of soft-bodied aphids on leaf undersides, new growth, and along the petioles distort and yellow the foliage; honeydew and sooty mold downgrade the crop, and the crinkled leaves of savoyed types shelter colonies. Aphids also transmit virus diseases.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on chard sap; populations build fastest in mild weather and on the soft, lush growth that excess nitrogen produces, with winged forms moving in from weeds and other crops.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A strong water jet dislodges colonies and is often enough; where needed, insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on leaf undersides is effective. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, and avoid pushing growth with nitrogen.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout new growth and petioles early, avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and control nearby weed hosts. Row cover used against the leafminer also excludes aphids.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ease off high-nitrogen feeding. A lot of nitrogen pushes out soft, sappy new leaves, and that is the growth aphids multiply on fastest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen produces the lush, soft tissue on which colonies build most quickly, so feeding for steady growth rather than a flush leaves the crop less favorable to them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the weeds down around the planting. Winged aphids fly in from weeds and other plants nearby, so fewer of those close by means fewer arrivals landing on your chard.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Weedy margins act as a reservoir for the winged forms that colonize the crop, so clearing them lowers the immigration pressure that scouting otherwise has to catch on the new growth.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The same light row cover you would put up against leafminers keeps aphids off as well, so if it is already over the young plants you are covered for both.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover deployed for the leafminer also excludes colonizing aphid flights, so one exclusion decision on this crop returns against two pests.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A hard jet from the hose knocks the clusters off, and that is often enough on its own. Aim up underneath the leaves and down into the crinkles and along the stalks, where they hide.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A strong water jet dislodges colonies from leaf undersides and petioles and is frequently sufficient by itself. Savoyed types need the jet worked into the crinkling, which shelters colonies from a straight-on spray.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, and small wasps eat aphids and usually clean up what is left after a water blast. They stay around if you skip broad sprays, so give them a few days to work before doing anything else.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserving ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps generally handles the residual population. Broad-spectrum applications cost more in natural enemies than they return against a pest that rebuilds quickly from winged immigrants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If colonies keep rebuilding, spray insecticidal soap and wet the undersides of the leaves, since that is where the aphids sit. It only affects what it actually lands on, so coverage is the whole job.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is a contact material, so results track coverage of undersides and petioles rather than dose, and it needs repeating as new colonies appear on fresh growth.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil is the other option and works the same way, by coating the aphids where the spray lands, so again get it well up under the leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Horticultural oil fills the same contact niche as soap on leaf undersides; the limiting factor is placement into sheltered colonies, not choice of the two materials.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes peppering the leaves of young plants, like buckshot, made by small dark beetles that hop away like fleas when you come near. On big plants it is mostly a looks problem, but on tiny seedlings heavy damage can stunt or kill them.
pests.cause_beginner: Small jumping beetles called flea beetles chew the holes. They spend winter in garden debris and come out in spring, hitting tender young plants hardest in warm, dry weather. They feed on chard, beets, and spinach.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Keep seedlings well watered and growing fast and they will usually outgrow the damage. If beetles are swarming young plants, dust the leaves with kaolin clay or use a vegetable-labeled product, and clear out weeds nearby. Grown chard rarely needs anything.
pests.prevention_beginner: A row cover over the seedbed during the early weeks is the best protection, keeping the beetles off while the plants are small. Clean up old plant debris where the beetles spend winter.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes and pits riddle the leaves, heaviest on young seedlings, giving the foliage a sandblasted look; the small dark beetles jump when disturbed. Damage is mostly cosmetic on established plants but can stunt or kill seedlings at high pressure and it disfigures leaves grown for greens.
