hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, chard grows well in the cooler months and at cooler elevations can grow year-round. It takes the warmth better than spinach, but the hot, humid lowland summer is still too much, so plant from fall through winter at low elevation.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In tropical Hawaii chard is a cool-season or upland crop that handles the warmth better than spinach: at low elevation it grows from fall through spring and is excluded in the hot, humid summer, while cooler highlands extend it year-round. The window is modeled on CTAHR cool-season and elevation guidance (the relevant CTAHR bulletin is an older scanned publication that did not parse cleanly).

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Swiss chard set out Sep 1 - Feb 14 in the Rio Grande Valley, per Bilingual LRGV planting table (Vegetable Crops of the Lower Rio Grande Valley). Direct-sown September through mid-February (Bilingual LRGV table); about 50 days to first harvest, then a long cut-and-come-again picking season through the cool months.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest harvest at about 50 days, from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest harvest at about 50 days, from the latest set-out date, before RGV's spring heat closes the window.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, grow swiss chard in the cool season, not summer. Plant Sep 1 through Feb 14 and harvest from Oct 21 into spring; it rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold. Swiss chard is one of the most forgiving winter greens here: sow direct any time from September through mid-February and keep cutting outer leaves for months. Skip planting swiss chard from spring through summer: the Valley heat keeps it from growing well here.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Swiss chard in the RGV runs on the winter-garden calendar: direct-sow Sep 1 through Feb 14, with harvest running Oct 21 through Apr 5. Direct-sown September through mid-February (Bilingual LRGV table); about 50 days to first harvest, then a long cut-and-come-again picking season through the cool months. Frost is essentially absent here, so timing is heat-bounded rather than cold-bounded. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: the TAMU AgriLife sources describe a single Valley-wide planting calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: OSU's Oregon planting table (EM9027) marks chard as not suitable for indoor starting; it is direct sown. The Willamette Valley's own window runs from April into July; the immediate coast's window is different again, February into May.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Chard matures in about 50 to 60 days to first cutting, then keeps producing cut-and-come-again from the same crown for months.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Chard tolerates a light frost easily and continues cropping well past the season's first frost in this mild maritime climate.

8.notes: One planting is cut leaf by leaf and regrows from the same crown for months; a second sowing is unnecessary and rarely done. Cut outer leaves and leave the center to keep producing.
8.zone_notes: OSU's Willamette Valley table gives chard a single April-to-July direct-sow window; once established, a spring planting keeps cropping right through fall and well into December, since chard tolerates the region's typically light frosts easily.

9.notes: One planting is cut leaf by leaf and regrows from the same crown for months. On the immediate coast a single spring sowing can crop nearly all year.
9.zone_notes: OSU's coastal table is a genuinely different window from the valley: February into May, not April into July. Once established, this coastal planting keeps producing through the mild winter with barely a pause, close to a year-round stand, since the coast's extreme winter lows run milder than the valley's.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Chard here is one long-season planting, not a spring-and-fall pair. In the Willamette Valley, direct sow from April into July, and once it is established you can cut outer leaves for months, right through fall and into December in most years. Right on the coast, sow earlier, February into May, and a single planting can keep producing almost all year, with only a brief pause. No need to resow for a second crop; just keep cutting the outer leaves.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Chard runs as a single long-season direct-sown crop across the maritime Pacific Northwest rather than the spring-and-fall pattern used by faster greens. OSU's Willamette Valley table gives an April-to-July sowing window; a spring planting then crops cut-and-come-again well into December, tolerating the region's typically light frosts easily. succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Swiss chard is a cut-and-come-again crop, not a succession crop. A single planting is cut leaf by leaf and regrows from the same crown for months (a full season, or most of the year in mild climates), so staggered sowings are unnecessary; you harvest continuously from one stand rather than from a series of plantings. A spring and a separate late-summer or fall sowing are the most anyone typically makes, and even those overlap in production. The successioned analog is a quick leafy green like lettuce or arugula, a separate crop.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Swiss chard is ready to start cutting when the outer leaves reach a usable size, roughly 8 to 12 inches long (or smaller for tender baby leaves), usually about 50 to 60 days from sowing. Harvest cut-and-come-again: snap or cut the outer leaves an inch or two above the crown and leave the central growing point, and the plant keeps generating new leaves for months. Crop regularly to keep new growth tender, and cook the colorful stalks as a separate vegetable, giving them a head start over the quicker leaves.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Swiss chard is ready to pick when the outer leaves are about 8 to 12 inches long (or smaller for baby leaves), around 50 to 60 days after planting. Cut or snap off the outer leaves and leave the middle of the plant to keep growing, and it will produce for months from the same plant. Pick a few leaves from each plant regularly, and save the bright stalks to cook on their own, since they take a little longer than the leaves.
crops.description_seasoned: Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris) is a leafy member of the goosefoot family grown for its large, tender leaves and its broad, often vividly colored edible stalks. It is the same species as the beet, selected for leaf and stem rather than root, and it shares the beet's pests, diseases, and multigerm seedball. Its defining trait is an unusual tolerance of both heat and cold: unlike lettuce and spinach, chard does not bolt in summer heat or long days (as a biennial it flowers only after a winter), so a single spring planting crops straight through the summer and well into fall, and in mild zones it overwinters for a harvest that spans much of the year. Harvested cut-and-come-again, the outer leaves picked while the crown keeps producing, one chard plant yields for months. The colorful-stemmed types such as Bright Lights are as ornamental as they are useful, and the stalks cook as a vegetable in their own right.
crops.description_beginner: Swiss chard is a leafy green grown for both its big, tender leaves and its colorful, edible stalks, which come in white, gold, pink, orange, and red. It is actually the same plant species as the beet, just grown for the leaves and stems instead of a root. What makes chard special is that it handles both heat and cold better than most greens: it does not flower and turn bitter in summer the way lettuce and spinach do, so one spring planting keeps producing right through summer and fall, and in mild-winter areas it lives nearly all year. You harvest it cut-and-come-again, picking the outer leaves while the center keeps growing, so a few plants feed you for months. The rainbow-stemmed kinds are pretty enough for a flower bed, and you can cook the bright stalks like a vegetable on their own.
