Always buy certified disease-free slips, not sprouts off a grocery-store sweet potato.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Do not plant sweet potatoes where sweet potatoes grew recently, which builds up soilborne Fusarium wilt, black rot, scurf, and the sweet potato weevil. Also avoid following ground recently in pasture, lawn, or corn, where wireworms are numerous and scar the roots, and avoid heavily manured or high-nitrogen beds, which grow vine over roots. Where root-knot nematode is present, keep sweet potatoes out of beds that grew other susceptible hosts. The standard guideline is a 3 to 4 year gap before sweet potatoes return to a bed.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not grow sweet potatoes where you grew sweet potatoes in the last few years, because soil diseases and the sweet potato weevil pile up. Also avoid beds that were lawn, grass, or corn recently, where wireworms live and damage the roots, and skip beds with fresh manure or lots of nitrogen, which grow leaves instead of roots. Wait about 3 to 4 years before sweet potatoes go back in a bed.
good_after: Legumes such as beans and southern peas
Small grains such as rye or wheat as a cover crop
Brassicas such as cabbage and broccoli
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate sweet potatoes on a 3 to 4 year cycle, keeping them out of a bed for several seasons to break the buildup of Fusarium wilt, black rot, scurf, root-knot nematode, and the sweet potato weevil. Following a legume (which adds nitrogen) or a clean, non-host crop is ideal. Avoid planting into ground recently in sod, grass, or corn, which harbors wireworms, and avoid heavily manured beds, which favor rampant vine and soft rots.
rotation.note_beginner: Move your sweet potatoes to a different spot each year and do not put them back in the same bed for about 3 to 4 years. This keeps soil diseases, nematodes, and the sweet potato weevil from building up. Planting after beans or peas is great, since those add nitrogen. Avoid beds that were just lawn, grass, or corn, where wireworms live.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Once cured, sweet potatoes are best kept at warm room-to-cellar temperatures, roughly 55 to 60°F in a dark, well-ventilated spot, where they hold for months. Ordinary heated-room temperatures (68 to 75°F) are fine for a few weeks but shorten storage and can encourage sprouting; keep only what you will use soon on the counter and store the rest in a cooler pantry or cellar.
storage.room_temp_beginner: After curing, keep sweet potatoes in a cool but not cold spot, ideally around 55 to 60°F, in the dark with some airflow, where they last for months. A normal warm room is fine for a couple of weeks but shortens their life, so keep a few on the counter and store the rest somewhere cooler like a pantry or cellar.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Do not refrigerate sweet potatoes. Below about 50 to 55°F they suffer chilling injury: the flesh develops off-flavors, hard cores that will not soften when cooked, internal browning, and a greater tendency to rot. This is the opposite of many vegetables. A cool pantry or cellar near 55 to 60°F, never the refrigerator, is the right place for raw sweet potatoes.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep sweet potatoes out of the fridge. When they get colder than about 50 to 55°F they get damaged: they taste off, stay hard in the middle even after cooking, and rot faster. This is different from most vegetables. Store them in a cool pantry or cellar around 55 to 60°F instead, never the refrigerator.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Raw sweet potatoes do not freeze well. Freeze only after cooking (baked, mashed, or as prepared dishes), where they keep for several months.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze raw sweet potatoes. Freeze them only after cooking, like baked or mashed, and they keep for several months.
storage.notes_seasoned: Curing is essential and is the opposite of potato storage. Right after digging, cure the roots warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F at 85 to 90 percent humidity for roughly 1 to 2 weeks (5 to 7 days minimum), which heals skin nicks, sets a protective skin, and converts starch to sugar so the flesh turns sweet. A simple home method is a warm room with the roots in a container loosely covered to hold humidity. After curing, store in the dark at about 55 to 60°F with high humidity and good ventilation, where a well-cured crop keeps 6 months or more. Never store below about 50 to 55°F or refrigerate (chilling injury), and do not wash until use or store bruised or diseased roots.
storage.notes_beginner: Sweet potatoes must be cured before storing, and this is opposite to how you store regular potatoes. Right after digging, keep them somewhere warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F and quite damp, for 1 to 2 weeks. Curing heals the skins and turns the starch to sugar, which is what makes them sweet. A warm room with the roots in a loosely covered box works at home. Then store them in the dark around 55 to 60°F with some airflow, where they keep for 6 months or more. Never put them in the fridge or anywhere below about 50 to 55°F, because the cold ruins them. Do not wash them until you use them.

growth_stages.name: Slip establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Freshly set slips that often wilt for the first several days, then recover, green up, and put out new leaves as they root in. Little top growth happens yet; the plant is building roots. Warm soil speeds this along.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The slips you planted will droop for the first few days, which is normal, then perk up and start growing new leaves once they have rooted. Not much happens above ground yet while they get established.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the soil evenly moist while slips root in, and shade or water in the heat of the day if they wilt hard. Protect from any late frost, which kills the tender foliage. Replace any slips that fail to take within the first week or two.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp while the slips root, and water them in the afternoon if they wilt badly. Cover them if a late frost threatens, since frost kills the leaves. If a slip does not perk up after a week or so, replace it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your sweet potato slips rooted in and started new growth? Note the date.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your sweet potato slips perked up and started growing? Jot down the date.

growth_stages.name: Vine growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Vigorous vines that begin to run and sprawl across the bed, rooting at the leaf nodes where they touch soil and quickly forming a dense groundcover. This canopy is what will feed the storage roots.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plants send out long vines that spread across the ground and root where the leaf joints touch the soil, soon covering the bed in leaves. This leafy growth is building the plant that will make your sweet potatoes.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the bed weeded until the vines close over and shade out weeds themselves. Side-dress lightly with a low-nitrogen feed as the vines run if growth is weak, but do not overfeed nitrogen. In small beds, you can lift and reposition vines so they do not root everywhere, though it is not essential.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep weeds down until the vines spread and cover the ground, after which they smother most weeds. If the plants look weak, feed lightly with a low-nitrogen fertilizer, but do not overdo it or you will get all leaves. Water evenly.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are the vines running and covering the bed? Note how the canopy is filling in.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are the vines spreading out and covering the ground yet?

growth_stages.name: Storage root formation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full vine cover above ground while, out of sight, the storage roots begin to swell along the buried stem. This is when the plant sets how many roots it will make, so even moisture and restrained nitrogen matter most now.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The vines are full and leafy above ground, and underneath, the sweet potatoes are starting to form and swell along the buried stem. You cannot see it, but this is when the plant decides how many roots it will make.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold steady, even moisture now that roots are forming, and keep nitrogen restrained, since excess nitrogen at this stage grows vine instead of roots. Keep the bed watered through dry spells but never waterlogged.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady now that the sweet potatoes are starting to form, and do not add much nitrogen, which would grow leaves instead of roots. Water through dry spells but do not let the bed get soggy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: The storage roots are forming now. How is the vine canopy holding up?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: The sweet potatoes are starting to form underground now. How do the plants look?

growth_stages.name: Root bulking
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Storage roots sizing up underground while the vines stay green and full. This is the critical window for yield: even moisture and warm soil now build root size and quality. You can carefully lift a plant to check root size toward the end of the window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The sweet potatoes are growing bigger underground while the vines stay green and leafy. This is the most important time for a good harvest. Toward the end you can gently dig at the edge of a plant to see how big the roots are getting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even and steady while roots bulk, the critical period for size and quality, then begin easing off water in the last couple of weeks. Warm soil favors bulking, so this is a strength in hot regions. Keep an eye out for the sweet potato weevil in the South.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady while the sweet potatoes size up, which is the most important time, then start cutting back on water in the last couple of weeks. Hot weather actually helps now. In the South, watch for the sweet potato weevil.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you checked root size yet? Note how the bulking is coming along.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you dug gently to check how big the sweet potatoes are getting?

growth_stages.name: Maturity and harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Roots that have reached full size, about 90 to 120 days from transplanting, often with the oldest leaves beginning to yellow. There is no dramatic die-back signal as with potato; you harvest on days-to-maturity and, above all, before frost, since a hard frost kills the vines and cold soil damages the roots.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The sweet potatoes reach full size about 3 to 4 months after planting, and the older leaves may start to yellow. Unlike regular potatoes, the tops do not clearly die back, so you dig based on the calendar and, most importantly, before frost, because frost kills the vines and cold soil hurts the roots.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Ease off watering as harvest nears. Dig on a dry day once roots reach size and before the first frost, loosening carefully with a fork well outside the plant so you do not spear or bruise roots. Handle them gently, let them dry briefly out of the sun, then cure warm and humid before storage. If frost catches the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Stop watering as harvest nears. Dig on a dry day once the roots are big enough and before the first frost, loosening the soil with a fork well away from the plant so you do not stab the sweet potatoes. Handle them gently, let them dry off out of the sun, then cure them warm and humid before storing. If frost hits the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested your sweet potatoes? Note the date and the yield.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you dug your sweet potatoes yet? Write down the date and how many you got.

establishment.text_seasoned: Plant only certified disease-free and weevil-free slips, not sprouts off a grocery-store root, which can carry the sweet potato weevil, viruses, and soilborne disease. Set slips 3 to 4 inches deep with two or more nodes buried, and keep them watered while they root, since early wilting is normal.
establishment.text_beginner: Use certified disease-free slips from a garden supplier, not sprouts from a store-bought sweet potato, which can bring in the sweet potato weevil and disease. Plant them 3 to 4 inches deep with a couple of leaf joints buried, and keep them watered while they root. It is normal for them to wilt at first.
establishment.author: plant

establishment.text_seasoned: Wait for warm soil: set slips only after all frost danger has passed and the soil is above about 65°F, ideally 70 to 80°F. Sweet potatoes are frost tender and stall in cold soil, so there is no benefit to rushing. In short-season areas, black plastic mulch warms the soil and buys extra days.
establishment.text_beginner: Wait until it is warm: plant slips only after all frost is past and the soil has warmed to at least 65°F, ideally 70 to 80°F. Sweet potatoes are killed by frost and sulk in cold soil, so there is no point planting early. In cool-summer areas, black plastic warms the soil and gives you more growing time.
establishment.author: plant

vine_growth.text_seasoned: Feed lightly and keep nitrogen low. A light side-dressing of a low-nitrogen fertilizer such as 5-10-10 as the vines run is plenty; heavy nitrogen and fresh manure grow rampant vine and few storage roots.
vine_growth.text_beginner: Feed lightly, and go easy on nitrogen. A little low-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 as the vines spread is enough. Too much nitrogen or fresh manure grows a jungle of leaves and hardly any sweet potatoes.
vine_growth.author: plant

vine_growth.text_seasoned: Keep the bed weeded until the vines close over, after which the dense canopy shades out most weeds on its own. Avoid deep cultivation once the vines are running, so you do not disturb the shallow feeder roots.
vine_growth.text_beginner: Keep weeds down until the vines spread and cover the ground, after which they crowd out most weeds themselves. Once the vines are running, do not dig around the plants, which disturbs their roots.
vine_growth.author: plant

root_initiation.text_seasoned: Hold steady, even moisture as the storage roots begin to form, since this window sets how many roots the plant makes. Keep nitrogen restrained now, because excess nitrogen at root formation shifts the plant back toward vine.
root_initiation.text_beginner: Keep the watering steady as the sweet potatoes start to form, because this is when the plant decides how many to make. Do not add much nitrogen now, or the plant goes back to growing leaves instead of roots.
root_initiation.author: plant

root_bulking.text_seasoned: Keep moisture even and moderate while roots bulk, about 1 inch per week, then taper off in the last 2 to 3 weeks. A dry-then-soaked swing now cracks and misshapes the roots, while warm soil favors good sizing.
root_bulking.text_beginner: Keep the watering steady while the sweet potatoes size up, about 1 inch a week, then ease off in the last couple of weeks. Letting the soil go dry and then soaking it now makes the roots crack. Warm weather actually helps them grow.
root_bulking.author: plant

root_bulking.text_seasoned: In the South and Gulf, scout for the sweet potato weevil during bulking and keep the crop away from last year's beds and stored roots. There is no rescue for tunneled roots, so sanitation and certified slips do the real work.
root_bulking.text_beginner: In the South, watch for the sweet potato weevil while the roots are sizing, and keep the patch away from last year's bed and from stored sweet potatoes. You cannot fix tunneled roots, so clean slips and cleanup are what protect the crop.
root_bulking.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest on days-to-maturity (about 90 to 120 days) and before the first frost, since frost kills the vines and cold soil damages the roots and shortens storage. Dig on a dry day with a fork well outside the plant to avoid spearing roots. If frost catches the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
harvest.text_beginner: Dig your sweet potatoes about 3 to 4 months after planting and before the first frost, because frost kills the vines and cold soil hurts the roots. Dig on a dry day with a fork, pushing it in well away from the plant so you do not stab them. If frost hits the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
harvest.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Cure the dug roots warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F at 85 to 90 percent humidity for 1 to 2 weeks, to heal the skins and convert starch to sugar (the step that makes them sweet), then store warm at about 55 to 60°F. Never refrigerate or store below about 50 to 55°F, which causes chilling injury.
harvest.text_beginner: Cure the sweet potatoes warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F and damp, for 1 to 2 weeks so the skins heal and the flesh turns sweet, then store them warm at about 55 to 60°F. Never put them in the fridge or anywhere below about 50 to 55°F, which ruins them.
harvest.author: plant

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant sweet potato slips
notifications.title_beginner: Time to plant sweet potato slips
notifications.body_seasoned: Set certified slips out once all frost danger is past and the soil is above about 65°F, usually a few weeks after your last frost. Plant 3 to 4 inches deep, 12 to 14 inches apart on ridges, rows about 3 feet apart.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant your sweet potato slips once all frost is past and the soil has warmed to about 65°F, usually a few weeks after your last frost. Set them 3 to 4 inches deep and about 12 to 14 inches apart on ridges or mounds.

notifications.body_seasoned: Newly set slips often wilt for several days, then recover as they root. Keep the soil evenly moist for the first week or two, and replace any slip that fails to take.
notifications.body_beginner: Sweet potato slips droop for the first few days, which is normal, then perk up as they root. Keep the soil damp for the first week or two, and replace any slip that does not recover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Vines are running, ease off nitrogen
notifications.body_seasoned: As the vines run and cover the bed, keep weeds down until the canopy closes and feed only lightly with a low-nitrogen fertilizer. Too much nitrogen now grows vine at the expense of roots.
notifications.body_beginner: As the vines spread and cover the ground, keep weeds down until they take over, and feed only a little, with a low-nitrogen fertilizer. Too much nitrogen now grows leaves instead of sweet potatoes.

notifications.title_seasoned: Keep watering even as roots bulk
notifications.title_beginner: Water evenly while roots size up
notifications.body_seasoned: As the storage roots bulk, hold even moisture (about 1 inch per week). A dry-then-soaked cycle now cracks and misshapes the roots; taper off water in the final couple of weeks.
notifications.body_beginner: While the sweet potatoes are sizing up, water evenly (about 1 inch a week). Letting the soil dry out and then soaking it makes the roots crack. Ease off water in the last couple of weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your sweet potatoes may be ready
notifications.title_beginner: Check if your sweet potatoes are ready
notifications.body_seasoned: Roots are usually ready about 90 to 120 days after planting. Dig before the first frost, since frost kills the vines and cold soil damages the roots, then cure warm and humid before storage.
notifications.body_beginner: Sweet potatoes are usually ready about 3 to 4 months after planting. Dig them before the first frost, because frost kills the vines and cold soil hurts the roots, then cure them warm before storing.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost kills sweet potato vines
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sweet potato foliage is frost tender and killed by frost, and cold soil damages the roots. Protect newly set slips from a late spring frost, and in fall, dig before the first frost. If frost catches the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Sweet potato vines are tender and killed by frost, and cold soil hurts the roots. Cover young slips if a late spring frost threatens, and in fall, dig before the first frost. If frost hits the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry spell, water at establishment and bulking
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry weather, keep sweet potatoes watered
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Established sweet potatoes are fairly drought tolerant, but even moisture during slip establishment and root bulking sets root number and size. Do not let the soil go bone dry and then flood it, which cracks the roots.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Grown-in sweet potatoes handle dry spells fairly well, but steady water while the slips establish and while the roots size up makes for a good crop. Do not let the soil go bone dry and then soak it, which cracks the roots.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain can rot and split roots
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain can rot and crack roots
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Waterlogged soil rots the storage roots and drives soft rot and black rot, and a heavy soaking on a near-mature crop can split the roots. Ensure the ridge drains freely, and if the crop is mature, harvest before a prolonged wet spell.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Soggy soil rots sweet potatoes and brings on rot diseases, and a big rain on a ready crop can crack them. Make sure the ridge drains well, and if the roots are ready, dig them before a long wet spell.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Warm, wet weather favors foliar disease
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Warm, damp weather can bring leaf disease
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Prolonged warm, wet, humid weather with leaf wetness favors fungal leaf spots and, in the roots, storage rots. Space and site for airflow, avoid overhead watering late in the day, and start with certified, disease-free slips.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Long spells of warm, damp, humid weather can bring on leaf spots and root rots. Give the plants a sunny, airy spot, avoid wetting the leaves late in the day, and start with certified, disease-free slips.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Lots of vine but few sweet potatoes
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Big vines but few sweet potatoes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plants grew lush, sprawling vine but set few or small storage roots. The usual causes are too much nitrogen (which favors foliage over roots), overly rich or heavily manured soil, too much shade, or a season too short and cool for roots to bulk.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plants made a jungle of leafy vine but few sweet potatoes. This usually comes from too much nitrogen, over-rich soil, too much shade, or a season too short and cool for the roots to size up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut nitrogen and use a low-nitrogen feed such as 5-10-10, avoid fresh manure, give full sun, and grow on ridges. In short-season areas, warm the soil with black plastic and choose a fast variety so roots have time to bulk.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use less nitrogen and a low-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10, skip fresh manure, give full sun, and grow on ridges. In cooler areas, warm the soil with black plastic and pick a fast variety so the roots have time to grow.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cracked, knobby, misshapen roots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Cracked or lumpy sweet potatoes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Roots grew cracked, knobby, or misshapen from a stop-and-start growth pattern: a dry spell followed by a surge of water, heavy clay soil that resists smooth expansion, or root-knot nematode galling. Uneven moisture during bulking is the most common cause.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The sweet potatoes came out cracked or lumpy because their growth started and stopped, usually from the soil going dry and then wet again, from heavy clay they could not grow through smoothly, or from root-knot nematodes.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hold even moisture through bulking and taper off before harvest, loosen heavy soil with organic matter or grow on ridges and raised beds, and use nematode-resistant varieties where galling is the cause.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the watering steady while the roots grow and ease off before harvest, loosen heavy soil with compost or grow on ridges, and use a nematode-resistant variety if knots and cracks keep happening.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Off-flavor, hard core, or rot in storage
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Sweet potatoes went bad in storage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stored roots developed off-flavors, hard cores that would not soften when cooked, internal browning, or rot. The usual cause is chilling injury from storing (or refrigerating) below about 50 to 55°F, or skipping the warm, humid curing step that heals skins and sets a protective layer.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The sweet potatoes tasted off, stayed hard in the middle even after cooking, or rotted in storage. This usually happens when they were kept too cold (like in the fridge) below about 50 to 55°F, or were not cured warm and humid first.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cure warm and humid (about 80 to 85°F, 85 to 90 percent humidity) for 1 to 2 weeks right after harvest, then store at about 55 to 60°F in the dark. Never refrigerate or store below about 50 to 55°F, and do not store bruised or diseased roots.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cure the roots warm and humid (about 80 to 85°F) for 1 to 2 weeks right after digging, then store them around 55 to 60°F in the dark. Never put them in the fridge or anywhere below about 50 to 55°F, and do not store damaged ones.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tunneled, bitter roots (sweet potato weevil)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tunneled, bitter sweet potatoes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Roots came up riddled with small holes and dark, spongy tunnels, with a bitter taste and off odor even where damage looked light. This is the sweet potato weevil, whose larvae mine the roots and induce bitter terpenes; it is the most serious sweet potato pest, worst in the South and Gulf.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The sweet potatoes were full of small holes and dark tunnels and tasted bitter, even the parts that looked okay. That is the sweet potato weevil, whose grubs tunnel the roots and make them bitter. It is the worst sweet potato pest, especially in the South.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Start with certified weevil-free slips, rotate well away from last year's beds and from stored roots, and remove every cull and volunteer root after harvest, since the weevil survives in them. Harvest promptly rather than leaving roots in infested soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant certified weevil-free slips, move the patch far from last year's bed and from where you store sweet potatoes, and clean up every leftover root after digging, because the weevil lives on in them. Harvest on time.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Small roots from too short a season
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Sweet potatoes stayed small
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Roots stayed small because the warm-season window was too short: slips set into cold soil, a late start, a cool summer, or an early frost cut the growing period below the 90 or more warm days the crop needs to bulk. This is the common outcome in marginal northern and cool-coastal gardens.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The sweet potatoes stayed small because the warm season was too short: cold soil at planting, a late start, a cool summer, or an early frost gave them too little time to size up. This is common in cooler northern and coastal gardens.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose the fastest varieties (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Centennial), warm the soil with black plastic, plant as soon as the soil is reliably warm, and give the sunniest, most sheltered spot to stretch the effective season.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick the fastest varieties (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Centennial), warm the soil with black plastic, plant as soon as the soil is truly warm, and use the sunniest, most sheltered spot to give them the longest possible season.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Roughly 3 to 6 storage roots, about 1 to 2 pounds, per plant in good conditions, varying widely with variety, season length, and care. By the row, a home crop often runs about 1 to 1.5 pounds per foot of row on a good site.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: About 3 to 6 sweet potatoes, roughly 1 to 2 pounds, from each plant when things go well, though it varies a lot with the variety and the season. A row gives you something like a pound or more per foot on a good site.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: A sweet potato planting matures over a single window, about 90 to 120 days, and is dug once when the roots reach size and before frost. It is not a repeat-harvest crop; for a longer supply, cure and store the crop, which keeps for months, or in frost-free regions stagger plantings.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A sweet potato planting is ready all at once, about 3 to 4 months after planting, and you dig it when the roots are sized and before frost. It does not keep producing after that, so cure and store the crop, which lasts for months.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are grown fresh from slips each season, so there is no first-year-versus-later difference as with perennials; results depend on certified slips, a long warm season, loose well-drained ridges, even moisture, and restrained nitrogen.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Sweet potatoes are grown fresh each year from slips, so your first crop can do as well as any later one. What matters is good slips, a long warm season, loose well-drained ridges, steady water, and going easy on nitrogen.
factors_seasoned: Season length and warmth: sweet potatoes need about 90 or more warm, frost-free days, and a short or cool season caps yield.
Nitrogen balance: excess nitrogen grows vine at the expense of storage roots.
Even moisture during bulking: drought-then-flood cycles cut yield and crack the roots.
Certified, disease-free and weevil-free slips: virus or weevil brought in on slips undercuts the crop from the start.
Well-drained ridges: waterlogged, heavy soil rots roots and forces short, knobby shapes.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting assigns root crops like sweet potatoes to the waning moon, the period after the full moon, on the folk principle that the changing lunar pull favors below-ground growth. This is long-standing gardening folklore with no controlled scientific evidence of an effect on sweet potato yield. Plant sweet potatoes by soil temperature and your warm-season window, not the moon; this is recorded only for growers who follow the tradition.

primary.name: UGA Extension Home Garden Sweet Potatoes (Circular 1014)
UH Manoa CTAHR Bulletin B-91 (home-garden vegetables for Hawaii)

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are not a succession crop. They are planted once per warm-season window from slips and dug as a single crop when the roots reach size and before frost, not sown in repeated short intervals. In long-season and frost-free regions a grower can stagger plantings, but each is a discrete seasonal crop rather than a staggered succession, so no per-zone succession count applies.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-2 cert (2026-07-05): source-truth review (CC agent, WebFetch) -> CERTIFY_CLEAN, no fixes. The potato->sweet-potato archetype flip is clean: Ipomoea batatas / Convolvulaceae (morning glory), NOT a nightshade, with ZERO nightshade bleed (a full sweep found no late blight, Colorado potato beetle, greening/solanine, or common scab -- only the correct negations). Grown from slips on ridges; warm-season (soil >65F). The cure->warm-storage INVERSION verified verbatim: cure ~85F/90% RH then store WARM ~55-60F, 'never expose below 50F and never refrigerate' (Clemson HGIC + UGA C1014); sweet potato weevil (Cylas formicarius, UF IN154) the signature pest. Flip only.

Consequences applied: warm-season 10-region calendars (grows THROUGH summer, no heat_pause; cold_pause in frost-killed winter); heat_threshold_temp_f DROPPED (no cool-season soil-temp ceiling; okra, the warm_season_fruiting analog, carries none); gating_factors absent (neither potato nor okra gate). Flagged for reviewer confirmation of the archetype and the dropped field.

Modeled regional planting windows: northern_tier (marginal), all California regions, warm_arid, low_desert_az, and hawaii_tropical month windows are modeled on sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson HGIC 1322, USU) + the shared frost anchors + the certified okra warm-season pattern, not lifted from a region-specific sweet potato planting chart. USU (Utah) anchors the northern/marginal + black-plastic guidance; the CA/AZ/NM/TX/HI exact months are modeled. The UH CTAHR B-91 (Hawaii) source is PDF-only and was not machine-read; sweet potato is a well-adapted traditional Hawaiian staple, so Hawaii is modeled as a STRONGHOLD (unlike potato, which was marginal there). Flagged for source-truth review.

Southern regional windows (se_gulf) are source-backed (Clemson HGIC 1322: Coastal Apr 15-Jun 15, Piedmont May 1-Jun 15; UGA C1014: mid-April south GA to early May north GA, soil >=70F; NC State: May 1-Jul 15), but the exact per-zone month boundaries and the fall harvest bands are modeled on 90-120-day maturity + the frost anchors. Generally-safe; tighten exact months at the variety pass.

northern_tier.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh sweet potato windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (about 90 to 120 warm frost-free days from transplanting slips) + the shared frost anchors + sweet potato's warm-season, frost-tender physiology (Clemson HGIC 1322, USU). Sweet potato is heat-loving and runs THROUGH the summer, so there is no heat_pause; the cold-winter North is MARGINAL, needing black plastic and the fastest varieties, and the coldest zones may not reliably size a crop. Flagged in verification_status.open_findings.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold-winter North, sweet potatoes are a stretch but doable in the warmer zones. Wait until all frost is past and the soil is warm (usually late May into June), then plant slips. Warm the soil first with black plastic, which also gives you extra time, and choose the fastest varieties like Georgia Jet, Beauregard, or Centennial. The vines grow through the summer, and you dig the crop in early fall before the first frost, since frost kills the vines. In the coldest zones (3 and 4) the season is short, so expect a lighter, smaller crop; zones 6 and 7 do better.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are marginal in the cold-winter North and depend on stretching the warm season. Set slips only after all frost danger passes and the soil is reliably above about 65°F, generally late May into June, and warm the soil with black plastic to add growing days (USU). Choose the fastest-maturing varieties (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Centennial), since the crop needs about 90 or more warm, frost-free days. The frost-tender vines run through summer, and the crop is dug in early fall before the first frost. Zones 3 to 4 are the tightest and may not reliably size a full crop; zones 6 to 7 are more dependable. Windows modeled on USU short-season guidance + the frost anchors and flagged for review.

se_gulf.plantings_provenance: Sweet potato windows from the Southern sources actually read: Clemson HGIC 1322 (Coastal Apr 15-Jun 15, Piedmont May 1-Jun 15; soil above 65F), UGA C1014 (mid-April south GA to early May north GA; soil >=70F; 90-120 days), NC State (May 1-Jul 15). Sweet potato is heat-loving and runs THROUGH the hot, humid summer, so there is no heat_pause; the Southeast and Gulf are its stronghold. Fall harvest bands modeled on 90-120-day maturity + the frost anchors.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: The Southeast and Gulf are sweet potato country. Plant slips after the last frost once the soil is warm, from mid-April into June, and the vines run happily through the hot, humid summer that sweet potatoes love. Dig the crop in late summer through fall, before the first frost. Watch for the sweet potato weevil, the main pest here, by starting with certified weevil-free slips and cleaning up leftover roots. Cure the crop warm and humid before storing.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf are sweet potato's stronghold. Plant slips once frost is past and the soil is above about 65°F: Clemson gives coastal South Carolina April 15 to June 15 and the Piedmont May 1 to June 15, University of Georgia mid-April in south Georgia to early May farther north, and NC State plants May 1 to July 15. The heat-loving vines run straight through the hot, humid summer with no midseason pause, and the crop is dug from late summer into fall before the first frost. The sweet potato weevil is the key pest, so certified weevil-free slips and strict sanitation matter here. Spring windows from Clemson, UGA, and NC State; fall harvest bands modeled on 90-120-day maturity and the frost anchors.

ca_interior.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh sweet potato windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity + the shared frost anchors + sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson HGIC 1322, USU); no California-specific sweet potato planting chart was machine-read (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). The hot, dry interior-valley summer suits sweet potato, which runs THROUGH the heat with no heat_pause.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: California's hot inland valleys suit sweet potatoes well, since they love the dry summer heat. Plant slips in mid to late spring once frost is past and the soil is warm, and the vines grow right through the hot summer with no break. Dig the crop in late summer into fall before the first frost. Just keep the plants watered while the roots size up.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's hot interior valleys (Sacramento and San Joaquin) are well suited to sweet potato, which thrives in the dry summer heat that stalls other crops. Plant slips from mid to late spring once the soil warms, and the heat-loving vines run through summer with no midseason pause, with harvest from late summer into fall before the first frost. Keep irrigation even during root bulking, since the dry heat dries the soil fast. The exact month windows are modeled on sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson, USU) plus the frost anchors and flagged for review.

ca_north_coast.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh sweet potato windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity + the shared frost anchors + sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson HGIC 1322, USU); no coastal-California sweet potato chart was machine-read (flagged). The cool, foggy north coast often LACKS the heat sweet potato needs, so it is marginal: plant in the warmest part of the year, use the fastest varieties, and expect a lighter, later crop. No heat_pause (heat is the limiting factor here, not excess).
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: The cool, foggy north and central California coast is a hard place for sweet potatoes, which really want heat the coast often lacks. Plant slips in the warmest, sunniest, most sheltered spot in late spring or early summer, use a fast variety, and warm the soil with black plastic. Expect a smaller, later crop than inland gardeners get, and in a very cool, foggy summer the roots may stay small.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's cool, foggy north and central coast is marginal for sweet potato, which needs the heat the marine climate often withholds. Plant slips in the warmest stretch of the year (late spring into early summer) in the sunniest, most sheltered site, warm the soil with black plastic, and choose the fastest varieties. Harvest in fall before the first frost. Where summers stay cool and foggy, roots may barely size up. Windows modeled on sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson, USU) plus the frost anchors and flagged for review.

ca_south_coast.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh sweet potato windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity + the shared frost anchors + sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson HGIC 1322, USU); no coastal-California sweet potato chart was machine-read (flagged). The mild south coast is workable, though warmer inland pockets crop more heavily than the immediate cool coast. No heat_pause.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: California's mild south coast grows sweet potatoes reasonably well, though the warmer, sunnier inland spots do better than right at the cool coast. Plant slips from mid to late spring once the soil warms, and harvest through late summer into fall. Give the hottest, sunniest place you have.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's mild south coast grows sweet potato reasonably well, though its moderate summers are less ideal than the hot interior, and warmer inland pockets crop more heavily than the immediate coast. Plant slips from mid to late spring once the soil warms, in a full-sun site, with harvest from late summer into fall before frost. Windows modeled on sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson, USU) plus the frost anchors and flagged for review.

ca_desert.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh sweet potato windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity + the shared frost anchors + sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson HGIC 1322, USU); no desert-California sweet potato chart was machine-read (flagged). The low desert is excellent: sweet potato thrives in the very heat that forces a midsummer pause on cucurbits and tomatoes, so it runs straight THROUGH the summer with no heat_pause, as long as irrigation is steady.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The California desert valleys are excellent for sweet potatoes, which love the intense heat that stops other summer crops. Plant slips in spring once frost is past and the soil is warm, and pick right through the hottest summer into late fall, with no summer break, as long as you keep them watered. Sweet potato is one of the few crops that genuinely enjoys a low-desert July.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The California desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella) are excellent for sweet potato, which thrives in the extreme heat that forces a midsummer pause on cucurbits and tomatoes. Plant slips in spring once frost danger passes and the soil warms, and harvest straight through the brutal summer into late fall, no heat pause needed, as long as irrigation is steady. Winter brings the only brief frost for this frost-tender crop. Windows modeled on sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson, USU) plus the frost anchors and flagged for review.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern New Mexico & West Texas
warm_arid.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh sweet potato windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity + the shared frost anchors + sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson HGIC 1322, USU); no New Mexico or West Texas sweet potato chart was machine-read (flagged). The hot, dry inland Southwest suits sweet potato, which runs THROUGH the summer heat with no heat_pause.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: The hot, dry inland Southwest suits sweet potatoes. Plant slips in spring once frost is past and the soil warms, and the vines grow through the hot summer with no break. Dig the crop in fall before the first frost. Keep the plants watered in the dry heat, especially while the roots size up.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The hot, dry inland Southwest (southern New Mexico and West Texas) suits sweet potato, which runs through the summer heat that limits other crops. Plant slips in spring once frost danger eases and the soil is warm, and harvest in fall before the first frost, keeping irrigation even through the dry heat during root bulking. Winter is the only hard frost for this frost-tender crop. Windows modeled on sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson, USU) plus the frost anchors and flagged for review.

low_desert_az.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh sweet potato windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity + the shared frost anchors + sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson HGIC 1322, USU); no Arizona low-desert sweet potato chart was machine-read (flagged). Sweet potato thrives in the extreme low-desert heat and runs straight THROUGH the summer with no heat_pause, given steady irrigation.
low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: Arizona's low desert is a great place for sweet potatoes, which love the extreme heat that forces other crops to take a summer break. Plant slips in spring once frost is past and the soil is warm, and harvest through the hot summer into late fall, with no summer break, as long as you keep them watered.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: Arizona's low desert is excellent for sweet potato, which relishes the extreme heat that stalls other summer crops. Plant slips in spring once frost danger passes and the soil warms, and harvest from midsummer into late fall with no midseason pause, as long as irrigation is steady. Winter brings only a brief, light frost for this frost-tender crop. Windows modeled on sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson, USU) plus the frost anchors and flagged for review.

fl_peninsula.plantings_provenance: Sweet potato windows from UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions (plant anytime after frost through the end of June; about 120 to 150 days) + Clemson HGIC 1322, plus the shared frost anchors. Sweet potato is a heat-loving warm-season crop that runs THROUGH the Florida summer with no heat_pause; peninsular Florida is well suited. Exact per-zone month boundaries modeled and flagged.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, sweet potatoes grow over the long warm season. Plant slips from spring through June, and the vines run through the hot, humid summer that sweet potatoes love. Harvest from summer into fall. In frost-free South Florida you can plant over a long stretch and harvest much of the year. Watch for the sweet potato weevil and root-knot nematodes, and start with certified slips.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula, sweet potato is a warm-season crop planted from spring through June (UF/IFAS: anytime after frost through the end of June; about 120 to 150 days), with the heat-loving vines running through the hot, humid summer and harvest from summer into fall. In frost-free deep South Florida, plantings can be staggered over a long window for a harvest across much of the year. The sweet potato weevil and root-knot nematode are the key concerns, so certified slips and rotation matter. Windows from UF/IFAS + Clemson; exact per-zone months modeled on the frost anchors and flagged.

hawaii_tropical.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh sweet potato windows, MODELED on the frost-free tropical pattern + sweet potato's warm-season physiology; the UH CTAHR B-91 source is PDF-only and was NOT machine-read (flagged). Sweet potato ('uala) is a well-adapted traditional Hawaiian staple, so Hawaii is modeled as a STRONGHOLD (unlike potato, which is marginal there). Frost-free, so plantings can run year-round with no cold_pause and no heat_pause.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Hawaii is excellent for sweet potatoes, which are a traditional island staple and thrive in the warm, frost-free climate. You can plant slips over much of the year and harvest a few months later. Aim for the drier, sunnier stretches to limit leaf disease, and watch for the sweet potato weevil and root-knot nematodes by starting with certified slips.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii is a stronghold for sweet potato ('uala), a well-adapted traditional Hawaiian staple that thrives in the warm, frost-free lowlands, unlike white potato, which is marginal there. Being frost-free, the crop can be planted over much of the year and harvested a few months later, with staggered plantings giving a long harvest. Favor the drier, sunnier periods to limit foliar disease, and manage the sweet potato weevil and root-knot nematode with certified slips and rotation. This calendar is modeled on the frost-free tropical pattern; the UH CTAHR B-91 bulletin is PDF-only and was not machine-read, so the Hawaii window is modeled and flagged.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sweet potatoes goes in the ground Mar 25 - Apr 30 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide / Bilingual LRGV planting table (90 to 120 days to harvest for this crop).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: First harvest at about 90 days from the earliest planting date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sweet potatoes keeps producing through the long, frost-free Valley growing season; harvest here extends well past the raw 120-day maturity figure because there is no frost to force an end date, only fading vigor.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, plant sweet potatoes Mar 25 - Apr 30, once the soil is warm. Harvest runs Jul 1 - Dec 1, a long summer-into-fall picking season since it rarely if ever frosts here. There is no fall replanting for sweet potatoes: one spring planting carries the whole Valley season.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Sweet potatoes in the RGV are a single spring planting, no fall replanting: set out Mar 25 - Apr 30, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide. Harvest runs Jul 1 - Dec 1; production continues well past the raw 90 to 120 day maturity figure because there is no frost to force an end date, only fading vigor late in the season. Frost is essentially absent here, so the growing season is bounded by plant vigor, not by a first-frost date. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: OSU Extension's Oregon planting-date table (EM9027) marks sweet potato "not suitable" for planting in EITHER the Willamette Valley or the coast. This is not a season-LENGTH problem (the maritime PNW's frost-free window is long enough on paper); it is a season-HEAT problem: sweet potato needs sustained summer warmth to bulk its roots, and the region's marine-tempered summer rarely supplies it. Set slips only once the soil is reliably above about 65°F, warm the ridge with black plastic mulch, and site the planting in the single hottest, most sheltered spot available; a low tunnel over the row for the first several weeks helps. Even with every advantage, expect small, light roots rather than a full Southern-style crop (OSU / WSU).

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roots reach a diggable size in roughly 110 days from planting in a favorable year; in a cool summer, roots may size more slowly and stay smaller regardless of days elapsed.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Dig well before the first fall frost, which kills the vines and lets cold damage the roots in the ground.

8.zone_notes: OSU Extension's own planting-date table marks sweet potato "not suitable" for the Willamette Valley, not only the coast. The calendar has room (frost is not the binding constraint), but summer heat is; treat this as a warmest-microsite, black-plastic-and-row-cover planting, not a dependable crop.

9.zone_notes: The immediate coast is the more marginal of the two PNW zones for sweet potato: OSU marks it "not suitable" here too, and the coast's cooler, foggier summer sizes roots even more slowly than the valley's. Expect a later start and smaller roots even with every siting advantage.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Sweet potatoes are a real stretch here: OSU Extension's own guide lists them as not suitable for either the valley or the coast. The problem is not that our growing season is too short; it is that our summers just are not hot enough for the roots to size up well. If you want to try, wait for genuinely warm soil before setting out slips, warm the bed first with black plastic, and give it your hottest, most sheltered spot, maybe even a low tunnel early on. Expect small roots and a light harvest, not a big crop.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: OSU Extension's Oregon planting-date table (EM9027) marks sweet potato "not suitable" for planting in EITHER the Willamette Valley or the coast. This is not a season-LENGTH problem (the maritime PNW's frost-free window is long enough on paper); it is a season-HEAT problem: sweet potato needs sustained summer warmth to bulk its roots, and the region's marine-tempered summer rarely supplies it. Set slips only once the soil is reliably above about 65°F, warm the ridge with black plastic mulch, and site the planting in the single hottest, most sheltered spot available; a low tunnel over the row for the first several weeks helps. Even with every advantage, expect small, light roots rather than a full Southern-style crop (OSU / WSU).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set slips once frost danger has passed and the soil is reliably above about 65°F. VCE 426-331 gives the belt's window as zone 8 April 20 to July 20 and zone 7 May 1 to July 10.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roots reach a harvestable size roughly 110 days after slips go in.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Vines run through the hot, humid summer with no pause, and roots are left in the ground and dug over an extended fall window, up to about a week ahead of the first frost, which can chill and damage roots left too long.

VCE lists no fall sweet potato column; sweet potato's own established shape in this dataset (se_gulf, northern_tier) is a single continuous season with an extended fall dig window rather than a fixed harvest date, so no heat_pause or second_planting is authored here.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: The Piedmont and Coastal Plain suit sweet potatoes well. Set slips in the ground once frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed, then let the vines run all summer. Dig the roots over several weeks in fall, finishing up before the first frost.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: Virginia Cooperative Extension gives sweet potato a single spring window with no fall column: zone 8 April 20 to July 20, zone 7 May 1 to July 10. Set slips once frost danger has passed and the soil is reliably above about 65°F. The heat loving vines run straight through the hot, humid summer with no pause, and roots size up over an extended fall dig window rather than a single harvest date, finishing about a week ahead of the belt's first frost. The sweet potato weevil is the key pest here, so start from certified weevil-free slips and keep good sanitation.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-set slips (no indoor start); the Master Gardener chart's April-May window is later than most Nevada warm crops because sweet potato needs warm soil to establish.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Matures roughly 110 days after sowing; the earliest-sown plants set the harvest's start date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Okra and sweet potato keep producing right up to this frost-anchored margin.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Sweet potato slips go into the ground once the soil is reliably warm, April into May in the Las Vegas Valley, then the vines sprawl and grow through the entire summer heat with no attention beyond regular water. There is no indoor starting step (slips are set directly into the bed) and no midsummer pause; you just wait. Dig the roots from midsummer into fall, any time before the first frost.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The UNLV/UNR Master Gardener chart places sweet potato slips in the ground April into May, later than most Nevada warm-season crops because the vines need consistently warm soil to take hold. From there it grows straight through the Mojave's 100°F-plus summer with no heat_pause. The long 110-day maturity means the earliest slips are not ready to dig until midsummer, but roots can be left in the ground and harvested any time after that through the fall, with a safety margin held ahead of the first frost (late November in the valley, early November at the cooler zone 8 edge).

There is no indoor starting step and no midsummer pause. Dig roots from early August into fall, any time before frost.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: Sweet potato falls outside USU Extension's Table 1 for Utah, so this window is authored from the crop's own heat-lover biology plus the region's frost normals (USU Extension, Elevations for Washington County) rather than a cited USU planting date: flagged here as the honest basis. Slips go in once soil is consistently warm, roughly mid-April into May, later than most Utah warm-season crops because the vines need warm soil to take hold. From there it grows straight through the Mojave-edge desert's 100°F-plus summer without a pause in growth. The long 110-day maturity means the earliest slips are not ready to dig until early August, but roots can be left in place and harvested any time after that through the fall, with a safety margin held ahead of the November 1 average first frost.

crops.description_seasoned: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is a warm-season, frost-tender member of the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae), not a nightshade and unrelated to the ordinary potato despite the shared name. It is grown for its swollen storage roots and planted not from seed or tubers but from slips: rooted sprouts pulled from a bedded seed root and set out only after all frost danger has passed and the soil is warm, above about 65°F. The plant is a vigorous, sprawling groundcover, running long vines that root at the nodes, and it is grown on raised ridges or mounds that drain well and give the roots room to expand. The crop needs a long, hot season, roughly 90 to 120 frost-free days, and it relishes the summer heat that stalls many other vegetables, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the low deserts are its stronghold while short-season northern gardens are marginal and lean on black plastic and fast varieties. Feed sparingly and keep nitrogen low, since rich ground grows rampant vine and few roots. The crop is dug before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cured warm and humid (about 80 to 85°F at high humidity for one to two weeks) to heal the skins and turn starch to sugar, and stored warm, near 55 to 60°F. Sweet potatoes are damaged by cold and must never be refrigerated or stored below about 50 to 55°F, the opposite of white potato storage. The young leaves and shoots are also edible as a cooked green.
crops.description_beginner: Sweet potatoes are a warm-weather crop grown for the sweet, starchy roots that form underground. Despite the name, they are not related to regular potatoes; they belong to the morning glory family. You do not grow them from seed or from tubers. Instead you plant slips, which are rooted sprouts, set out only after all frost is past and the soil is warm. The plants send out long, trailing vines that cover the ground, so they are grown on ridges or mounds with plenty of room. Sweet potatoes need a long, hot summer (about 3 to 4 months of warm, frost-free weather) and they love heat, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the desert Southwest are the best places to grow them, while cooler northern gardens are a stretch and use black plastic and fast varieties. Go easy on fertilizer, especially nitrogen, or you get lots of vine and few sweet potatoes. Dig the crop before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cure the roots somewhere warm and humid for a week or two, which heals the skins and makes them sweet, and store them warm, around 55 to 60°F. Never put sweet potatoes in the fridge or anywhere cold, which ruins them. This is the opposite of how you store regular potatoes. The young leaves are also good to eat as a cooked green.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are harvested by days-to-maturity and, above all, before frost, not by a die-back signal. The crop is usually ready about 90 to 120 days from transplanting slips, when the roots have reached full size; the oldest leaves may yellow, but the vines do not clearly die back the way potato tops do. Dig before the first fall frost, since frost kills the vines and cold soil damages the roots and shortens storage. Loosen the soil with a fork well outside the plant so you do not spear or bruise the roots, lift them gently, and handle them carefully, since sweet potatoes bruise easily and skins are thin at harvest. Let them dry briefly out of direct sun, do not wash them, then cure warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F for one to two weeks, before storing. If a frost catches the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two so rot does not travel down into the roots.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: You harvest sweet potatoes by the calendar and, most importantly, before frost, not by watching the tops die back. They are usually ready about 3 to 4 months after planting, when the roots are full size; the older leaves may yellow, but unlike regular potatoes the vines do not obviously die down. Dig before the first fall frost, because frost kills the vines and cold soil hurts the roots. Loosen the soil with a fork well away from the plant so you do not stab the sweet potatoes, lift them gently, and handle them carefully because they bruise easily and the skins are thin at first. Let them dry off out of the sun, do not wash them, then cure them somewhere warm and humid for a week or two before storing. If frost hits the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Sweet potato quality starts with loose, warm, well-drained soil built up into ridges or mounds. Work the bed deep, incorporate compost, and form ridges 8 to 10 inches high, which drain well, warm quickly, and give the storage roots room to expand smoothly; heavy clay stays cold and wet, rots roots, and forces short, knobby shapes, and is best improved with organic matter or grown in raised ridges. Aim for a slightly acidic pH, roughly 5.8 to 6.5. Keep nitrogen low and avoid fresh manure, which drive rampant vine at the expense of roots; use a low-nitrogen fertilizer such as 5-10-10 and modest compost. Set slips 3 to 4 inches deep, 12 to 14 inches apart along the ridge in rows about 3 feet apart, once all frost is past and the soil is above about 65°F. In short-season areas, lay black plastic to warm the soil and add growing days.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Getting the soil right matters for sweet potatoes. Loosen the bed deep, mix in compost, and mound the soil up into ridges about 8 to 10 inches high, which drain well, warm up faster, and give the roots room to grow long and smooth. Heavy, cold, soggy clay rots the roots and makes them lumpy, so use ridges or a raised bed if your soil is clay. Keep the soil slightly acidic (pH about 5.8 to 6.5). Go easy on fertilizer and skip fresh manure, which grow leaves instead of roots; use a low-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 and a little compost. Plant the slips 3 to 4 inches deep and 12 to 14 inches apart along the ridge, in rows about 3 feet apart, once all frost is past and the soil has warmed to about 65°F. In cooler areas, lay down black plastic to warm the soil and buy extra time.

crops.name: Cauliflower

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Cauliflower grows best in rich, well-drained soil with lots of compost worked in, and it needs steady, even moisture the whole way. More than most vegetables, cauliflower hates being stressed: if it dries out or runs short on food even briefly, it can quit growing and form a tiny, useless head early (called buttoning). Soil that holds moisture but still drains well is ideal.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Cauliflower is a heavy feeder that demands a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter held at steady, even moisture. It is the fussiest of the cole crops: any check to growth from drought, low fertility, or a stalled transplant can trigger buttoning (premature, undersized curds), so the goal is uninterrupted, vigorous growth from set-out to harvest. Work in compost before planting and aim for a moisture-retentive but well-draining bed, since waterlogging invites root maggots and rots while drought stress ruins the curd. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic, poorly drained ground.

ph.note_beginner: Cauliflower grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, a soil disease, keeping the soil closer to neutral (up toward 7.0) helps hold it back.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (UMN and Iowa State both give 6 to 7; Clemson lists 5.8 to 6.5). Cauliflower tolerates a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Clubroot, the major brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic soil below about 6.5, so where it is a concern lime acidic ground well ahead of planting and hold the pH toward neutral.

fertilizer.frequency: once or twice during the season
fertilizer.timing: starter at transplanting, then side-dress about 3 to 4 weeks later as the plant builds its frame
fertilizer.example_product: Blood meal, 33-0-0, calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0), or a balanced 10-10-10 vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Cauliflower is a heavy feeder, and steady fertility matters even more than with other cole crops because a hungry plant buttons, forming a tiny premature curd instead of a full one. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, using roughly 33-0-0 or calcium nitrate. Keep the plant growing vigorously and without interruption right up to curd formation; the most common cause of failed curds is any stall in growth from low fertility or uneven water. On acid or sandy soils, a boron and molybdenum deficiency can cause hollow stem and whiptail, so a soil rich in organic matter at a near-neutral pH is the best insurance.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Cauliflower needs rich soil and regular feeding to grow a good head. The big rule is to never let it get hungry or stressed: a plant that runs short on food or water stops growing and makes a tiny, useless head early. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer about 3 to 4 weeks after planting out. Keep it growing steadily the whole way.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your cauliflower with nitrogen to keep it growing without a stall.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your cauliflower.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: High N to drive steady, uninterrupted growth to a full curd: a 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 starter worked in before planting, then a nitrogen side-dress such as 33-0-0 or calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed a few weeks after planting out to keep it growing strong.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work in 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress with about 1 pound of 33-0-0 (or roughly a half cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row) about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, watered in alongside the plants.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a nitrogen feed beside the plants a few weeks after they go out.

companions.note_beginner: Cauliflower does well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick crops you can tuck in while the plants are small. The most important rule is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share the same pests and diseases.
companions.note_seasoned: Most cauliflower companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage-family pests, small flowering plants such as sweet alyssum and dill to draw the parasitic wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and caterpillars (a habitat tactic Clemson recommends for cole crops), and quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the cauliflower fills in. The well-grounded caution is to separate cauliflower from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Sweet alyssum
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Sweet alyssum makes lots of tiny flowers that bring in helpful insects which eat aphids and caterpillars, two major cauliflower pests.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson recommends planting small flowers like sweet alyssum and dill near cole crops to attract beneficial parasites and predators; the specific alyssum-cauliflower pairing is not trial-isolated, so medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sweet alyssum is one of the better-supported cole-crop companions. Its low mats of tiny flowers are a classic insectary plant, drawing the hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that prey on cabbage aphids and the cabbage-family caterpillars, and Clemson specifically advises small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control. Let it self-sow along the bed edge.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Dill
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Dill's flowers attract helpful insects that hunt the aphids and caterpillars that bother cauliflower.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson names dill among the small flowers that attract beneficial parasites to cole crops; aromatic umbels are widely extension-noted for recruiting parasitoid wasps and hoverflies. Dill-cauliflower not trial-isolated, so medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill works for cauliflower mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers draw the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and cabbageworms, and Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops for natural control. Let some flower, and keep it off to the side so it does not shade the plants.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cole crops; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking of brassica pests is a long-standing companion tradition with partial mechanistic support; not trial-isolated for cauliflower, so low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, onions tuck around young cauliflower without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

good_seasoned.name: Sweet alyssum
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic insectary plant whose tiny flowers recruit hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps against cabbage aphids and caterpillars. Clemson recommends small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson advises alyssum/dill near cole crops to attract beneficial parasites; not isolated for cauliflower.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and caterpillars; Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops. Let some flower, and keep it from shading the plants.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson cole-crop beneficial-habitat recommendation; specific dill-cauliflower pairing not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Onions
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional brassica companion whose scent is thought to deter cabbage pests; shallow-rooted and low-competition. A plausible, low-risk pairing rather than a documented effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking lore for brassicas; not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A quick, shallow cool-season crop that uses the open ground and light between young cauliflower plants and is harvested long before they fill in. Space-driven and traditional, not a documented growth effect; the two share no serious pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use intercropping lore; no T1 source documents a lettuce-cauliflower benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted as a trap crop for cabbage aphids near brassicas. Trap cropping is a documented principle but is not a tested cauliflower-nasturtium pairing, so treat it as a plausible aid rather than a proven control.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap cropping for aphids is a documented mechanism; the specific nasturtium-cauliflower pairing is not formally tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep cauliflower away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, and kale. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes problems worse.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same-family crops share pests and pathogens, so clustering raises pest/disease pressure, and successive brassica planting builds soil-borne clubroot. A sound epidemiological/rotation mechanism rather than a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planting cauliflower shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, collards, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

bad_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, and the other cole crops share cauliflower's clubroot and cabbage-family pests, so grouping them concentrates disease and pest pressure. A real rotation and disease principle rather than a tested adjacency effect; the practical rule is to spread brassicas out and rotate them.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared clubroot and shared cabbage-family pests are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a known agronomic principle, not formally pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Strawberries
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that brassicas and strawberries inhibit each other. There is no documented mechanism or T1 support; it persists as folklore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk anti-companion claim with no pattern match or T1 support.

pests.name: Cabbageworms, loopers, and diamondback moths
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings, and worst of all, caterpillars and their mess tucked down into the curd, where they are very hard to wash out.
pests.cause_beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants, chew the leaves, and crawl into the head you want to eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray Bt, which is low in toxicity to people, pets and bees and acts on caterpillars rather than on insects in general, or spinosad. Bt cannot tell a pest caterpillar from a butterfly one, so treat only the plants that have a problem. Pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; as the curd forms, larvae crawl into it and foul it, the costly damage that is very hard to clean from a tight white curd. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed (Clemson rates the diamondback the most numerous cole-crop caterpillar in home gardens).
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage and contaminate the curd; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Cauliflower is a primary host for all three.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down. Tighten control as the curd forms, when contamination of the head is the expensive kind.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear away old cabbage-family plants when a crop finishes. The pupae, the resting stage between caterpillar and adult, shelter in that leftover debris, so hauling it out leaves fewer moths and butterflies to start the next round.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Clearing spent brassica material removes the debris that shelters pupae between plantings, which lowers the local population emerging onto the next crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay a row cover, a light fabric sheet that lets in light and water, over the plants right after planting. It keeps the white butterflies and small moths from landing to lay eggs, which stops the problem before there are any caterpillars.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Floating row cover or fine mesh set at transplanting excludes the egg-laying adults ahead of any spray decision; seal the edges, since the value is entirely in the adults not reaching the foliage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Walk the rows and pick caterpillars and eggs off the undersides of the leaves. The first white butterflies of the season are your signal to start looking, and finding larvae early keeps them out of the curd, the white head you eat.
