growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: From seed, the first thin, grassy blades pushing up. Chive seed is slow and can take 2 to 3 weeks, up to 4 to 6 in cool soil, and emergence is uneven. A division or nursery clump skips this stage entirely.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: If you sowed seed, the first thin little green blades. Chive seed is slow, often a couple of weeks or more, so be patient. A bought or divided clump skips this step.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the surface evenly moist through the long germination and do not let it crust or dry. If you want a faster start, set out a division or nursery clump instead of sowing seed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp but not soggy until the seedlings appear, which can take a few weeks. For a quicker start, plant a small pot or a split clump instead of seed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Any sprouts yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Establishment (first year)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A young clump filling out with several upright blades. In the first year it is building the root and bulblet reserves it needs to overwinter and return.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A small clump of grassy leaves getting fuller. In its first year the plant is putting energy into its roots so it comes back next spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest sparingly the first year and keep moisture steady so the clump can bank strength for winter; a light feeding helps a weak plant. Thin or space seedlings to about 6 to 12 inches.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Go easy on cutting the first year and keep the soil moist so the plant gets strong for winter. Space plants about 6 to 12 inches apart.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is the clump filling in?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How is it filling in?

growth_stages.name: Harvest (cut-and-come-again)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full clumps 6 inches or more tall that you cut from repeatedly: shear the outer blades to about 1 to 2 inches and the clump regrows for months, spring through fall in cold regions and through the cool season where summers are hot.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Full clumps about 6 inches tall you can keep cutting from. Snip the leaves to about 1 to 2 inches above the soil and they grow back again and again.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut blades near the base, leaving some green so the clump keeps feeding itself, and never shear it fully bare. Regular cutting keeps tender new growth coming; shear the whole clump hard after flowering to renew it.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the leaves to about 1 to 2 inches, leaving some green behind, and they grow back. Cutting often keeps them tender. After the flowers fade, cut the whole clump back to freshen it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Harvesting regularly?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Harvesting regularly?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Round pink to pale purple flower globes rising above the leaves in late spring to early summer (white in late summer for garlic chives). The blooms are edible, but foliage near the scapes coarsens.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Round pink-purple flowers on stalks above the leaves in late spring or early summer. They are pretty and edible, but the leaves near them get tougher.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Enjoy or harvest some flowers just as they open, then shear the clump to about 1 to 2 inches to remove spent scapes before they seed and to force a fresh flush of tender leaves. Deadhead to prevent prolific self-seeding.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick a few flowers to eat, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches. This stops it from seeding everywhere and brings back fresh, tender leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Flowering yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any flowers yet?

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy and spring return
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: In cold regions the foliage yellows and dies back to the ground with hard frost, and the clump rests dormant over winter, pushing up fresh blades as one of the first herbs of spring. In mild regions it may stay semi-evergreen.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In cold areas the leaves die back and the plant rests over winter, then greens up again very early in spring. In mild areas it may stay green most of the year.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let the clump die back naturally; tidy old remains in late winter and mulch in the coldest zones. Do nothing to force it; it returns on its own. Divide overgrown clumps in early spring as growth resumes.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Leave the plant alone as it dies back; clean up the old leaves in late winter. It will come back on its own in spring. Split crowded clumps in early spring.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Died back or greening up?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Resting or coming back up?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your chive clump is establishing. Harvest only lightly this first year and keep moisture steady so it banks strength to overwinter and return.
notifications.body_beginner: Your chives are young. Cut only a little this first year so the plant gets strong for winter.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your chives are full enough to cut. Shear the outer blades to about 1 to 2 inches, leave some green, and the clump keeps regrowing all season.
notifications.body_beginner: Your chives are big enough to snip. Cut the leaves to about 1 to 2 inches and leave some green, and they grow back.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your chives are sending up pink-purple flowers. Enjoy some, then shear the clump to about 1 to 2 inches to prevent self-seeding and force fresh tender leaves.
notifications.body_beginner: Your chives have flowers. Eat a few, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches so it does not seed everywhere and grows back tender.

notifications.body_seasoned: In cold regions your chives will die back with frost and rest over winter. Tidy the old remains in late winter; they return on their own in spring.
notifications.body_beginner: Your chives will die back for winter and come back on their own in spring. Just clean up the old leaves in late winter.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat can stall your chives
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather and your chives
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Chives are cool-preferring and, unlike heat-tolerant herbs, can slow, scorch, and go semi-dormant in extreme sustained heat. Keep moisture even, mulch the roots, give afternoon shade in the hottest regions, and shear a scorched clump to the base to regrow when it cools. In the low desert and subtropical summer, chives simply rest until the weather eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Chives like cool weather and can wilt or rest in very hot spells. Water evenly, mulch, give them afternoon shade where summers are brutal, and cut a scorched clump back so it regrows when it cools. In the hottest places they just rest until cooler weather returns.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Chives are extremely frost-hardy (roughly zone 3) and a hard freeze simply pushes them into their normal winter dormancy; no protection is needed. The foliage dies back and the clump returns on its own in spring. A late-fall pot can be mulched or moved to keep cutting a little longer.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Chives are very hardy, so a hard freeze just sends them into their normal winter rest and you do not need to do anything. The leaves die back and the plant comes back in spring on its own.

germination.text_seasoned: Chive seed is slow, germinating over about 2 to 3 weeks (4 to 6 in cool soil) and unevenly. Sow shallowly, keep the surface from drying or crusting, and be patient, or skip the wait entirely by planting a division or nursery clump.
germination.text_beginner: Chive seeds are slow, often taking a couple of weeks or more. Sow them shallowly, keep the soil moist, and do not give up too soon. For a fast start, plant a small pot or a split clump instead.

establishment.text_seasoned: Do not over-harvest first-year chives: taking too many leaves weakens a young clump and hurts its ability to overwinter. Cut lightly, keep moisture steady, and space plants about 6 to 12 inches so the clumps have room to widen.
establishment.text_beginner: Go easy cutting chives the first year, since taking too much weakens the young plant before winter. Keep the soil moist and space plants about 6 to 12 inches apart.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest chives by shearing blades near the base, down to about 1 to 2 inches, taking some from each clump rather than shearing it bare; leaving green keeps the plant feeding itself. Cutting low, not just tipping, keeps leaves tender and pushes fresh bulblets and regrowth.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut chives down to about 1 to 2 inches above the soil, not just the tips, and leave some green behind. This keeps the leaves tender and the plant grows right back for more cutting.

flowering.text_seasoned: When chives bloom, harvest a few flowers to eat, then shear the whole clump to about 1 to 2 inches to remove the scapes before they set seed and to force a fresh flush of tender leaves. Deadheading also prevents prolific self-seeding, which is heaviest in garlic chives.
flowering.text_beginner: When chives flower, eat a few blooms, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches. That stops the seeds from spreading everywhere and brings back fresh, tender leaves.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Chives are a hardy perennial: let the foliage die back on its own in fall, remove old remains in late winter, and mulch in the coldest zones. The clump returns each spring for years. Lift and divide an overgrown or hollow-centered clump in early spring to keep it vigorous.
dormancy.text_beginner: Chives come back every year. Let the leaves die back in fall, clean them up in late winter, and the plant returns in spring. Every few years, dig up a big or thinning clump in early spring and split it to keep it healthy.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single established chive clump yields fresh leaves for years, cut repeatedly through each season; one clump supplies a kitchen, and it multiplies into many as you divide it. Yield builds as the clump widens, so a two- or three-year-old plant gives far more than a first-year one.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One chive clump gives you leaves for years and only gets bigger, so a plant or two is plenty for a kitchen. You can split a big clump into several new ones for free.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Production peaks in the cool of spring and again in fall. In cold regions chives run through the northern summer; in hot regions they slow or rest in peak heat and rebound as it cools. Cutting the clump back after flowering renews a flush of tender leaves.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Chives are most productive in cool spring and fall weather. In cold areas they keep going through summer; in hot areas they slow down in the worst heat and pick back up when it cools.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Chives are a rewarding, low-effort perennial, but the first year is about establishment: harvest sparingly so the young clump banks strength to overwinter, and expect the big yields from year two on. The main beginner mistakes are over-cutting a new clump, shearing only the tips instead of cutting low, and letting the flowers seed a lawn of volunteers.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: In its first year, go easy on cutting chives so the plant gets strong for winter; the big harvests come in later years. Cut low, not just the tips, and snip off flowers before they seed so you do not get seedlings everywhere.
factors_seasoned: Age and division: a clump yields more as it widens, and dividing every 2 to 3 years keeps it vigorous and prevents a dead, hollow center.
Harvest method: shearing low (to 1 to 2 inches), not tipping, keeps leaves tender and pushes fresh regrowth and bulblets.
Cool weather and even moisture: chives crop hardest in the cool of spring and fall and with steady water; extreme heat slows them.
Post-bloom shearing: cutting the whole clump back after flowering renews a flush of tender leaves and prevents self-seeding.
Type: common chives for onion flavor and fine leaves; garlic chives for garlic flavor and greater heat and drought tolerance.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing chive planting or harvest by moon phase. Establish plants by soil temperature and frost dates, and simply cut the leaves as you need them.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor or very slow germination from seed
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Chive seed is naturally slow, and cold or dry soil makes it worse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your chive seed came up thin, very late, or not at all. Chive seed is slow by nature, often 2 to 3 weeks or more, and does poorly in cold, dry soil. Next time, keep the surface moist, use fresh seed, and wait longer, or just start with a division or a nursery pot, which is much faster.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the surface moist, use fresh seed, be patient, or plant a division instead of seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stand was thin, delayed, or failed. Chive germination is intrinsically slow (2 to 3 weeks, up to 4 to 6 in cool soil) and is inhibited by cold, dry, or crusted soil. Next time sow into warm, evenly moist soil, keep the surface from crusting, use fresh viable seed, and allow the full window, or bypass seed with a division or nursery clump.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Slow seed nature plus cold, dry, or crusted soil inhibiting the long germination.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into warm moist soil, keep the surface from crusting, use fresh seed and the full window, or establish from divisions.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tough, hollow leaves and flower stalks in early summer
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The clump is flowering, which is normal for a perennial; the leaves near the flowers turn tough.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your chives sent up flower stalks and the leaves got tough and hollow. That is normal: chives flower in late spring or early summer. Next time, enjoy some flowers, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches to bring back fresh, tender leaves and to stop it from seeding everywhere.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Shear the whole clump back to 1 to 2 inches after it flowers to renew tender leaves.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The clump bolted into flower scapes and the surrounding foliage coarsened and turned hollow. This is the normal late-spring to early-summer bloom of a perennial allium, not a heat or care failure. Next time harvest some flowers, then shear the clump hard (to 1 to 2 inches) to remove scapes before seed set and force a fresh flush of tender leaves.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Normal perennial flowering; foliage near the scapes coarsens as the plant blooms.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Shear the whole clump to 1 to 2 inches after bloom to renew tender leaves and prevent self-seeding.

failure_diagnostics.label: Silvery streaks, orange spots, or leaf mines
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: One of the onion-family pests or diseases: thrips (silvery streaks), rust (orange spots), or leafminer (pale mines).
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your chive leaves showed silvery streaks, orange spots, or wavy pale tunnels. Those are onion-family troubles: thrips, rust, or allium leafminer. Chives usually shrug them off. Next time, shear a marked-up clump to the base to regrow clean, give plants airflow and even water, and use row cover in spring and fall against the leafminer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Shear the clump to regrow clean, space plants for airflow, and use row cover against the leafminer.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Silvery stippling (onion thrips), bright orange pustules (rust), or white oviposition dots and mines (allium leafminer) marked the foliage. Chives are usually trouble-free, so these are occasional. Next time reset the clump by shearing to the base, open crowded stands by dividing, water at the soil line, moderate nitrogen (rust), and row-cover through the leafminer's spring and fall flights.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Occasional allium pests and diseases: onion thrips, allium rust, or allium leafminer, favored by stress, crowding, or their seasonal flights.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Shear to reset the clump, divide for airflow, water low, moderate nitrogen, and row-cover against the leafminer.

failure_diagnostics.label: Clump thinning or dying out in the center
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The clump has grown too crowded and needs dividing, which perennials need every few years.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your chive clump got crowded and the middle went thin or died out, with weaker growth. That is a sign it is overdue for dividing. Next spring, dig up the whole clump, pull or cut it into several smaller pieces (each with a handful of little bulbs), and replant them with fresh spacing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Dig and divide the clump in early spring every 2 to 3 years to keep it vigorous.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The clump crowded itself, vigor fell, and the center thinned or died out, a classic sign an established perennial chive is overdue for division. Next spring lift the clump and split it into divisions of at least several bulblets each, discarding a dead center, and replant at 6 to 12 inch spacing in refreshed soil.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Overcrowding: chives should be divided every 2 to 3 years, or the clump loses vigor and dies out in the middle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Lift and divide every 2 to 3 years in early spring, discarding the dead center and replanting vigorous divisions.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Chives, pets, and the kitchen
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Are chives safe for pets and cooking
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Important safety note: chives are in the onion (allium) family, and all alliums are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses. They contain organosulfur compounds (N-propyl disulfide) that damage red blood cells and can cause hemolytic anemia, with cats the most sensitive, and raw, cooked, and dried parts are all toxic. Chives are safe for people in normal culinary amounts, but unlike a pet-safe herb such as rosemary, keep the plant and its trimmings away from pets. NC State lists Allium schoenoprasum as a problem for cats, dogs, and horses.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Chives are in the onion family, which is toxic to cats and dogs (and horses), even though it is perfectly fine for people to eat. Keep the plants and any trimmings away from pets.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Grow chives where pets do not graze, and dispose of clippings where cats and dogs cannot reach them; if a pet eats a significant amount, contact a veterinarian.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep chives and their clippings away from cats and dogs, and call a vet if your pet eats a lot.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Chives are a perennial planted once, not a succession crop. A single clump returns every year and is cut repeatedly, so there is nothing to stagger by re-sowing; you increase supply by dividing an established clump, not by successive plantings. The clump should be lifted and divided every 2 to 3 years to keep it vigorous.

Chives carry a summer heat_pause where a cool-preferring perennial genuinely struggles: se_gulf, ca_interior, ca_desert, low_desert_az, fl_peninsula (and a brief Jul-Aug pause in warm_arid). They run straight through summer (NO heat_pause) in the northern tier and on the mild CA north/south coasts, and near year-round on the coasts and Hawaii. Each heat_pause cell carries a backed object (months + chives-specific basis_seasoned + sources with URLs), anchored to UF/IFAS (chives as a cool-season herb needing afternoon shade) + UMN; the exact pause months per region are modeled from the regional summer heat pattern, not a chives-specific regional chart. Chives is LESS heat-tolerant than parsley, so its heat_pause set is broader than parsley's.

The directly-read chives pages (Wisconsin, UMN, MSU) state chives have FEW pest/disease problems. The pest/disease entries are therefore the ALLIUM family set modeled onto chives and framed honestly as occasional: onion thrips and onion maggot (UMN onion page), allium leafminer (UMd explicitly names chive A. schoenoprasum as a host), aphids (minor; chives repel them); downy mildew, rust, white rot (Sclerotium cepivorum), and botrytis (allium disease overviews; UVM, uncatalogued, corroborated chives as a host for several). Rust and white rot are anchored to the UMN garlic page + USU; downy mildew/botrytis to the UMN onion page + USU. Flagged for the source-truth sample. [CORRECTION 2026-09-03: the source-truth sample ran and the APHIDS entry has been REMOVED. No US extension publication treats aphids as a chives pest; USU's Chives in the Garden, NC State's plant toolbox and PlantVillage each enumerate chives' problems and omit it, the cited Wisconsin page states chives have no significant insect or disease problems, and UC IPM's onion and garlic guidelines carry no aphid page at all, so the entry failed both the crop-level and the allium-class test the rest of this set rests on. This is not a claim that aphids never occur on chives: onion aphid (Neotoxoptera formosana) is a real Allium specialist. The aphid-repelling companion claim is unaffected and remains recorded under companions, hedged as tradition. The remaining seven entries stand.]

hawaii_tropical is the lowest-confidence cell: common chives is cool-preferring and marginal in tropical lowland heat, reliable mainly at elevation or as a cool-season/container plant. Modeled as a near-year-round grower with NO heat_pause, cited generally to UH CTAHR rather than a chives-specific Hawaii calendar. Confirm in review. Garlic chives would tolerate the heat better.

Companions are TRADITIONAL/low-to-medium except the beans-and-peas avoid. The chives-under-roses (aphids/black spot), chives-around-apple (scab), and chives-with-carrots/tomatoes pairings are relayed by MSU citing Penn State as tradition with a plausible allium-volatile mechanism, not measured trials. The one extension-backed, high-confidence call is the allium-legume antagonism (alliums inhibit beans and peas). No chives-specific companion trial found in a readable T1 source.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up North (zones 3 through 7), chives are one of the hardiest, easiest herbs you can grow. Plant a clump once in spring after hard frost, or start slow seed indoors, and it returns on its own every year: it dies back over winter, then greens up as one of the very first herbs of spring. One planting gives leaves right through the mild northern summer and into fall. Cut low, leave some green, and split the clump every few years.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), chives are a frost-hardy perennial, reliable to roughly zone 3. Establish a clump in spring after hard-frost danger, from a division or an indoor-started seedling, and it overwinters dormant and regrows early each spring. A single planting produces through the whole mild northern summer, since chives are cool-tolerant and not heat-stressed here, and holds into fall until hard frost. Shear low to keep leaves tender, shear the clump after flowering, and divide every 2 to 3 years.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Chives are a cool-preferring perennial that grows best in mild weather; in this region's extreme summer heat the plants slow, the foliage scorches, and many clumps go semi-dormant, so the planting and cutting calendar pauses through the hottest months and picks back up as the weather cools. Clumps already in the ground are best carried with afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water. The exact pause months here are modeled from the region's summer heat pattern and chives' cool-season preference, not a chives-specific regional chart.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 and 9), chives are a cool-season perennial herb. Plant a clump in fall and it grows through the mild winter and spring, then slows or rests in the worst of the hot, humid summer before rebounding as it cools. Give it afternoon shade and steady water in the heat, cut low, and it returns year after year.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 and 9), chives run as a cool-season perennial, productive fall through spring and overwintering easily in the mild winter. High summer heat and humidity push a cool-preferring plant into a semi-dormant slump, so the leaf calendar pauses through the hottest weeks (roughly June through August in zone 8, into September in the hotter zone 9) and resumes as it cools. Establish in fall, carry summer clumps with afternoon shade and mulch, and divide every 2 to 3 years.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Chives are a cold-hardy allium that grows nearly year round in frost-free climates, mirroring the Jan-Feb establishment window on chives's own hawaii_tropical cell. Chives are not in either TAMU RGV vegetable table, so this is a CONSERVATIVE placement built from its thermal class (a hardy, clump-forming perennial allium) plus the general Valley frost-free season model.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: First harvest a few weeks after establishment; established clumps are cut nearly year round.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Chives are cold-hardy and tolerate the Valley's mild winter well, so harvest continues most of the year.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Chives are a cool-preferring perennial that grows best in mild weather. The Rio Grande Valley's summer runs hotter and drier than the Florida peninsula's, so this cell adopts chives's own fl_peninsula heat_pause precedent (rather than mirroring the no-pause hawaii_tropical shape used elsewhere in this cell) as the more climate-analogous, more conservative choice for a hot-summer subtropical climate. In the Valley's extreme summer heat the plants slow, the foliage scorches, and many clumps go semi-dormant, so the cutting calendar pauses through the hottest months and picks back up as the weather cools. Clumps already in the ground are best carried with afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water. The exact pause months are modeled from chives's own fl_peninsula evidence and the Valley's summer heat pattern, not a chives-specific Valley chart.

Establish new plants in January and February and harvest through the cooler months; the clumps slow down and rest during the peak summer heat, then pick up again as it cools. Chives are not in either TAMU RGV vegetable table, so this is a conservative placement built from chives's own known behavior in other frost-free regions of this dataset, not a stated RGV date.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Chives are not covered in either TAMU AgriLife RGV vegetable planting table; this cell is CONSERVATIVE, mirroring the near-year-round shape of chives's own hawaii_tropical cell (a Jan-Feb establishment window, harvest March through December). Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10, since chives's cold hardiness and the Valley's essentially frost-free climate do not differentiate between them. Unlike hawaii_tropical, this cell adopts a summer heat_pause (May through September) from chives's own fl_peninsula cell rather than Hawaii's no-pause shape: the Rio Grande Valley's summer runs hotter and drier than the Florida peninsula's, so Florida's own precedent (chives semi-dormant in peak heat) is the more climate-analogous, more conservative choice for this cool-preferring perennial.

crops.description_seasoned: Chives (Allium schoenoprasum) are a hardy, clump-forming perennial in the onion family (Amaryllidaceae), grown for their slender, hollow, grass-like leaves and their edible pink to pale purple pom-pom flowers. Unlike the annual and biennial kitchen herbs, chives are planted once and come back on their own year after year: the clump dies back to the ground over winter, rests dormant, and pushes up fresh green blades as one of the very first herbs of spring. They are among the hardiest herbs grown, reliable to roughly USDA zone 3, and among the easiest, with a mild onion flavor and few real pests. Give them full sun to light shade, average to rich well-drained soil, and steady moisture, though an established clump tolerates short dry spells. The clumps slowly widen from year to year and are best lifted and divided every 2 to 3 years to keep them vigorous. Chives are cool-preferring: in cold regions they run right through the northern summer, while in the hot South and desert they are a cool-season herb that slows or rests in the worst summer heat and revives as it cools. A close relative, garlic chives (Allium tuberosum), is a distinct species with flat leaves, a mild garlic flavor, and white late-summer flowers.
crops.description_beginner: Chives are one of the easiest and hardiest herbs you can grow. They are a perennial in the onion family, so you plant them once and they come back every year on their own. The plant dies back over winter, then sends up fresh, thin, grassy green leaves very early in spring, and it carries pretty pink-purple flowers in early summer that you can eat too. Chives like full sun to a little shade, decent soil, and regular water, but they forgive a lot. The clump gets bigger each year, so dig it up and split it every few years. They have a mild oniony taste and hardly any pests. There is also a relative called garlic chives, with flat leaves and a mild garlic flavor.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Start cutting chives once an established clump is 6 inches or more tall, which from seed is roughly 60 to 90 days but from a division or nursery clump can be just a few weeks. Harvest by shearing the outer leaves down to about 1 to 2 inches above the soil with scissors, taking some blades from each clump rather than shearing it bare; the leaves regrow and you can cut the same plant again and again through the season. Leave enough green so the plant keeps feeding itself, and in the first year cut sparingly so the young clump can build strength to overwinter. Pick in the cool morning, and use the leaves fresh for the best flavor. The pink-purple flowers are edible too and are best picked just as they open.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: You can start cutting chives once the clump is about 6 inches tall. From seed that takes a couple of months, but a bought or divided plant is ready much sooner. Snip the leaves down to about 1 to 2 inches above the soil, taking some from each clump, and they grow right back so you can keep cutting all season. Always leave some green behind so the plant stays healthy, and go easy the first year. Cut in the cool morning and use the leaves fresh. The flowers are edible too.

pet_safe.note: An allium: toxic to cats, dogs, and horses, and it can damage their red blood cells.

crops.name: Mint

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Mint likes rich, moist soil and, unlike most kitchen herbs, it loves damp ground. Give it soil with some compost worked in and keep it evenly moist; it will even grow in part shade and in a low, wet spot where other herbs sulk. What it does not like is dry, sandy ground that dries out fast. Because mint spreads so fast underground, most gardeners plant it in a pot or a buried barrier so it cannot take over the bed.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Mint grows in most soils but does best in rich, moist to even damp ground high in organic matter, the opposite of the sharp-drained, lean sites the Mediterranean herbs want. Clemson notes mints prefer rich, moist or even damp soil in part shade, and NC State lists it as unsuited to dry soils, tolerating clay, loam, or sand and both occasionally wet and occasionally dry conditions. Utah State recommends rich, moist, slightly acidic soil with no more than about 1 inch of well-composted organic matter per 100 square feet; do not overfeed, since rich soil and heavy nitrogen make the growth floppy and dilute the flavor. Keep the bed evenly moist but not permanently saturated, and remember mint runs by rhizomes and stolons, so grow it in a sunken bottomless container or a lined bed to keep it in bounds.

ph.note_beginner: Mint grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0, and it is not fussy. Most garden soil is fine; a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral. Utah State describes mint as preferring slightly acidic soil, NC State lists it as tolerant across roughly 6.0 to 8.0, and the University of Minnesota's general herb guidance is a well-drained soil near 6.0 to 7.5, so mint is forgiving and rarely needs any pH adjustment beyond a soil-test baseline.

fertilizer.timing: a light feeding in early spring as growth resumes, with a second light feeding midseason only if the patch looks pale
fertilizer.example_product: 16-16-16 or a balanced all-purpose fertilizer, or a topdressing of compost
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Mint is a light feeder and is easily overfed. Utah State suggests about one teaspoon of a balanced 16-16-16 fertilizer per plant in early spring as growth resumes; a compost-rich bed often needs no more than a light topdressing. Go easy, because rich soil and heavy nitrogen push soft, floppy stems and thin the essential oils that carry mint's flavor and aroma, a point Wisconsin Horticulture makes for mints grown in lean ground. In a container, where frequent watering leaches nutrients, a dilute liquid feed every few weeks through the growing season keeps the leaves green.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Mint does not need much feeding, and too much makes it flop and lose flavor. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the soil in spring, then leave it alone. If you grow it in a pot, feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every few weeks, since watering washes nutrients out.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to give your mint a light spring feeding as it regrows.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to give your mint a light feeding.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A light, balanced feed is all mint wants: about a teaspoon of 16-16-16 per plant in early spring, or a compost topdressing. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which makes the stems floppy and waters down the flavor.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 16-16-16, just a light feeding in spring. Do not overdo it; too much makes mint floppy and bland.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About one teaspoon of 16-16-16 per plant in early spring (Utah State); a compost-rich or container bed often needs only a light topdressing or a dilute liquid feed every 3 to 4 weeks.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A teaspoon of balanced fertilizer per plant in spring, or a thin layer of compost; in a pot, a diluted liquid feed every few weeks.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the growing tips and the undersides of the leaves. Where they feed, the foliage curls, yellows, or stops growing, and the leaves can turn sticky with honeydew.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer, and they can spread plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Knock them off with a strong jet of water first, aiming up into the leaf undersides, and repeat every few days. If they keep coming back, insecticidal soap or a horticultural oil will work, but only where you can wet the undersides, and not on a plant that is dry at the roots or on a very hot day.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check new growth often.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies build on the growing tips and leaf undersides, which is where Utah State puts mint's aphids; several species are involved rather than one, and soft, overfed growth carries the heaviest numbers. UC IPM's Pest Notes supplies the reason to catch them early: aphids can carry viruses from plant to plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on mint; they reproduce rapidly and favor the lush growth that excess nitrogen and rich soil produce.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Break the colonies up with a water jet before reaching for anything else, then treat with soap or a horticultural oil only if numbers hold, taking the undersides with a high volume of water and repeating. UC IPM's line is not to use these materials on a drought-stressed plant or when it is very hot. Lady beetles, lacewings, syrphid larvae and small parasitic wasps do most of the work if broad-spectrum insecticides stay off the patch.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout the tips early, avoid overfeeding, and conserve natural enemies; because you eat the leaves, lean toward a strong water spray before anything else.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go light on feeding. A rich feed makes the plant throw out soft, juicy shoots, and those are the ones that end up covered in aphids. Mint does not need much anyway: you are picking it all season, and that is what keeps it in new leaf.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Aphid reproduction tracks the flush, and UC IPM's rule is never to use more nitrogen than necessary. On mint the fertilizer is the part to hold back, because cutting the plant already keeps fresh growth coming without any help.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hit the plant with a forceful jet of water and knock the aphids off, working up underneath the leaves where the clusters sit. Look again in a few days and repeat if they are back.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Lean on plain water before anything sprayed on a crop you cut and eat fresh; it is the one control both Utah State and UC IPM give for aphids in the same breath. UC IPM's monitoring interval is at least twice a week while plants are growing rapidly, which is what makes an early knock-back possible.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lady beetles, lacewings, hoverfly larvae and small parasitic wasps will usually take an aphid run down for you. Broad bug sprays kill them along with the aphids, so leaving the patch alone is often the fastest route.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM names those four groups as mint-scale aphid natural enemies and tells you to avoid broad-spectrum insecticides toxic to them. Conservation costs nothing and it is the reason a light infestation is usually worth watching for a week before it is worth treating.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the aphids hold on after repeated hosing, insecticidal soap will take them out, but it only kills what it lands on. Wet the undersides of the leaves, not just the tops, and expect to go again.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Utah State names insecticidal soap for mint directly. Apply it in a high volume of water and cover the undersides, and respect UC IPM's two exclusions: not on a drought-stressed plant, and not when it is very hot.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A horticultural oil is the other choice at this level, put on the same way: thorough wetting, undersides included, and never on a plant that is dry at the roots or during a hot spell.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's application language for oils is a 1 to 2 percent solution in a high volume of water, targeting leaf undersides as well as tops. Like soap it kills only on contact, so a missed underside is a surviving colony, and the drought and heat exclusions are the same.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_beginner: A fine stippling or speckling on the leaves, sometimes with faint webbing on the undersides, worst in hot, dry weather. Leaves look dull, sandy, or bronzed.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny sap-sucking mites, not true insects, that explode in hot, dry, dusty conditions and are easy to miss until the leaves are speckled.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock the mites off, and keep the plant well watered, since drought stress is what lets them build. If they persist, insecticidal soap will work, but not on a plant that is dry at the roots and not above 90°F.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep mint evenly moist and mulched, since drought stress invites mites, and rinse dusty foliage in hot spells.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Twospotted and related spider mites, which UC IPM lists for mint, stipple the foliage with pale flecks and spin fine webbing on the undersides; they flare in hot, dry, dusty conditions and on drought-stressed plants, which is why mint's moisture love is also its best mite defense.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spider mites feeding with piercing mouthparts; populations build fastest in heat and drought and on dusty, water-stressed plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hose the undersides forcefully and repeat daily while it is hot, hold steady soil moisture, and treat with insecticidal soap only where you can coat the undersides, since these materials kill on contact and nothing else. Conserve whatever is already hunting them: UC IPM's Pest Notes names predatory mites, minute pirate bugs, bigeyed bugs and lacewing larvae, and its peppermint guidelines name a predatory mite released on mint itself, Neoseiulus fallacis. It also reports that spider mites frequently become a problem after an insecticide has been applied.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Do not let mint dry out or get dusty, mulch to hold moisture, and scout the undersides in hot weather when mites move fastest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep mint evenly moist and mulched. Mites build up fastest on a plant that has been allowed to dry out, so steady water is the main defense on this crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM puts water-stressed plants in the highly susceptible class and has mite numbers climbing through June into September. The bad mite years on mint are the ones where a pot or a bed edge went dry and hot more than once.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Wash the undersides of the leaves with a strong spray of water. Done regularly, and in hot weather even daily, this alone often holds mites down, and it keeps the foliage from getting dusty.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's finding is that regular forceful spraying often reduces mite numbers adequately, with a water spray or mist to leaf undersides at least once a day in a hot spell. Confirm the mites before starting: a hand lens is needed to tell mites and their eggs and webbing from stippling something else left.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Predatory mites can be bought and released onto an infestation. UC IPM names one for mint specifically, Neoseiulus fallacis, and a release makes more sense on a big patch than on a few plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The published release figures are commercial, quoted per acre and triggered off a sampled leaf count, so the numbers do not scale to a garden bed; what transfers is that a mint-specific predatory mite exists and is sold. Conserve what is already present first, because UC IPM also reports that mite outbreaks frequently follow an insecticide application.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Insecticidal soap will knock mites back, but only where the spray actually reaches them, so coat the leaf undersides and expect to repeat. Do not use it on a plant that is dry at the roots, and not when the temperature is above 90°F.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap kills mites on contact and nothing else, so coverage decides the outcome and repeat applications are normal. The 90°F ceiling and the water-stress exclusion are UC IPM's, and they bite hard here, because mite weather and spray-injury weather are the same weather.

pests.name: Cutworms
pests.symptoms_beginner: Young shoots and newly set plants are found cut through at or just below the soil line, with the severed top lying beside the stump.
pests.cause_beginner: Cutworms are caterpillars that live in the soil and feed at or just below ground level, chewing straight through the stems of young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Ring each newly set plant with a collar at the base: a rim cut from a plastic pot, or a can with both ends out, sunk about an inch into the ground. If a shoot goes down anyway, turn the top inch of soil beside the stump and remove the caterpillar you find there.
pests.prevention_beginner: Protect new plants at planting time rather than after the first one goes down, since the damage happens overnight and cannot be undone.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Utah State lists cutworms among mint's insect pests: the larvae feed at or below ground level and sever the stems of seedlings and young plants, so the damage reads as a clean cut at the base rather than as chewed foliage. The loss is per plant and it lands during establishment.
pests.cause_seasoned: Soil-dwelling caterpillars feeding at or below the soil surface. No cited document gives a species for mint, and Utah State names none, so this stays at the group level. The feeding position is what decides the control: a stem cut underground is not reachable by anything applied to the foliage.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Utah State's control for mint is a collar or a trap on individual plants, so the work is per plant and belongs to the planting-out window rather than to the season. Searching the soil at the point of fresh damage is the follow-up where a collar was missed. Utah State's other listed option is a registered insecticide; this record stops at the barrier, because the pest is a soil-level chewer on a crop that is cut and eaten fresh.
pests.prevention_seasoned: The window is establishment. Collars go on as plants are set out and come off once each plant has several stems, because after that a running mint patch has more growing points than a soil-level chewer can reach.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Set a barrier around each new plant when you put it in: a rim cut from a plastic pot, or a can with both ends out, sunk about an inch into the ground so nothing can reach the stem from the soil.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: This is Utah State's own control for cutworms on mint, protecting the individual plant, and it earns its keep only through establishment, while one severed stem is the entire plant. The barriers come off once a plant has spread and has stems to spare.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A felled shoot marks the spot. Sift the top inch or two of soil beside it and you will usually turn up the caterpillar, which can be lifted out by hand.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Utah State places the larvae at or below ground level, which tells you where to search: fresh damage is a located target, and turning soil there is far more productive than any general hunt across the bed.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: The leaves come up peppered with small holes. The beetles making them are tiny, black and glossy, and they are easy to miss because they leave the plant as you lean in.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small leaf-chewing beetles that show up in spring and feed on the new leaves, leaving them full of little holes.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover new plantings in spring with a floating row cover, a light fabric that lets in sun and rain but keeps the beetles off. That is the practical control; there is nothing to wash or pick off once the holes have been chewed.
pests.prevention_beginner: Get the cover on early in spring, when the new growth is coming and the beetles are on the move.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Utah State lists flea beetles among mint's insect pests and describes small, shiny black beetles chewing tiny holes in the leaves. Its control for them is a row cover in spring, which places the pressure on new growth early in the season rather than on a stand in full run.
pests.cause_seasoned: Flea beetles as a group rather than one named species: Utah State's mint listing gives no binomial and no admitted document ties a particular flea beetle to garden mint. The pressure is a spring one, which is why the published control is exclusion at that time of year rather than a treatment applied to damage.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Utah State offers two controls for mint, a spring row cover or a registered insecticide. The cover is the one that belongs on a crop cut and eaten fresh, and it has to go on before the beetles arrive rather than after the first holes appear, because the feeding damage does not heal.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclusion is timed against the spring flush. Utah State's instruction is to cover plants in spring, which makes this a planting-season job rather than a response to damage, and there is no preventive step published for it later in the year.

control_ladder.note_beginner: In spring, before the beetles turn up, spread a light row cover fabric over the mint and weight the edges down. Water and light reach the plants through it; the beetles do not. Take it off once the patch is growing hard.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Utah State's stated control for flea beetles on mint is to cover plants in spring with row covers, so the timing is the whole of it: on before the beetles move, off when the stand is in full growth. Nothing applied afterwards repairs a chewed leaf, so the cover has to go on ahead of the damage and never in response to it.

pests.name: Mint root borer
pests.symptoms_beginner: A patch that thins and weakens with nothing obviously wrong above ground. Lift a piece and the underground runners are tunneled and hollowed where a small caterpillar has fed inside them.
pests.cause_beginner: The mint root borer is a moth caterpillar that feeds inside mint's underground runners. There is one generation a year, and the adults are flying in early summer.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no spray for a caterpillar sitting inside a runner. What works is turning the bed over in late fall or early spring, while the larvae are just under the soil surface, and starting a fresh planting on ground that has not grown mint.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check the runners when you divide the patch in fall, and reset a declining patch into ground that has not carried mint.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The damage is below ground and shows as decline in a stand rather than as a mark on a leaf. UC IPM's account is that the larvae feed on leaves for two to four days, then drop to the soil surface and burrow into a rhizome, and the feeding that matters happens inside it. Its own sampling window is September through October, which is when lifting a runner and looking will actually find them.
pests.cause_seasoned: Fumibotys fumalis, the mint root borer. UC IPM puts adult emergence between early and mid-June with peak flight from mid to late July, one generation a year; the larvae leave the rhizomes in October and overwinter in the soil an inch or so below the surface, then pupate in spring. Every step that works against it is keyed to that calendar.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: UC IPM's timing is explicit: tillage works in late fall or spring, when the borer is overwintering, or before adults emerge in June. Rotation to a non-host is the other published option. Parasitic nematodes are used against it as well, released through the irrigation, which at home is a watered-in soil drench; the published release rate is per acre and is not a garden figure.
pests.prevention_seasoned: UC IPM samples for larvae from September through October, which is also when a home patch is lifted and divided, so the check costs nothing extra. Its treatment threshold is a commercial one and is not the point at this scale; finding larvae at all is reason enough to use one of the two tillage windows UC IPM names, late fall or before adults emerge in June.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Turn the bed over in late fall, or in spring before June. That is when the caterpillars are sitting in the soil just under the surface instead of inside the runners, and digging through reaches them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's window is exact: tillage is effective in late fall or spring while the borer is overwintering, or before adults emerge in June. The larvae leave the rhizomes in October and sit an inch or so down, so a fall dig follows them out of the runner and into reach, and a spring dig catches them before they pupate.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where a patch has been going downhill, move the mint to fresh ground and put something else in the old bed for a season or two.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM lists rotation to a non-host as an option, which at garden scale means resetting divisions into ground with no mint history rather than replanting the same corner. With one generation a year and mint as the host, a bed given a season without mint gives the next generation nothing to go back into.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Beneficial nematodes, sold as a soil drench, are used against this pest. Water them into moist, warm soil where the larvae are, rather than spraying anything on the leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM releases parasitic nematodes through the irrigation system against mint root borer. The published rate is a per-acre commercial figure and does not translate, so follow the pack for dose; what carries over is the delivery, a watered-in drench onto soil holding larvae, and the timing, the fall stretch after the larvae have left the rhizomes.

diseases.name: Mint rust
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small orange to rust-brown powdery spots on the undersides of the leaves and on the stems and leaf stalks. Badly affected leaves curl, turn yellow then brown, and fall. Pick the affected growth off and get rid of it as soon as you see it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rust fungus that spreads on airborne spores and needs the leaves to stay wet. It lives through the winter on last year's stubble and fallen leaves, and it can also ride in on the cuttings or runners you plant with, so a patch left standing reinfects itself each spring.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pull off and bin the rusted growth as soon as it shows, before the dark overwintering spots form on it. Thin a crowded patch so air moves through, water at the soil rather than over the top, and clear the stubble and fallen leaves off the bed in fall. Where it comes back every year, start again from cuttings taken off clean, rust-free plants.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants for good airflow, avoid wetting the foliage, keep the patch from getting congested, and start new plantings from clean stock.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Mint rust is Puccinia menthae, named by both RHS and WSU; NC State lists rust as one of spearmint's two main diseases without naming the fungus. Golden to cinnamon-brown pustules build on the stems and leaf undersides through the season, and a heavy infection defoliates the patch and reduces the essential oil in what is left. The stage worth learning is the early spring one: systemic infections throw up twisted, distorted shoots whose stems break easily, carrying pale blister-like pustules on the stems and leaf stalks, and those few plants are what seeds the rest of the year.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Puccinia menthae. Wet, cloudy weather and long spells of leaf wetness from rain, dew or sprinklers drive it, and under those conditions WSU has it recycling every 8 to 10 days. It carries over as dark overwintering pustules on stubble and fallen foliage, and on the runners and cuttings used for propagation, with resting spores in the soil as well; escaped mint growing nearby is a second reservoir the bed itself does not control.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rogue the twisted, distorted shoots out in early spring, before they throw spores across the rest of the patch, and keep taking infected leaves off through the season ahead of the dark resting stage. Open the stand up by dividing, move the water to the soil line or at least to the morning, and take the stubble and fallen foliage off the bed in fall, which is where the fungus is sitting when the season ends. Renew from inspected, rust-free cuttings: WSU's instruction is to monitor cuttings closely and discard infected ones rather than plant through the problem.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Airflow, dry foliage, and uncongested spacing are the defenses; propagate only from rust-free plants and reset a chronically infected patch elsewhere.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Take the rusted leaves off as you see them, and in fall clear the old stems and fallen foliage right off the bed. That debris is where the fungus spends the winter, and leaving it is what starts next spring.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: WSU puts the overwintering stage on mint stubble and foliage, where the pustules go dark chocolate brown in late summer and fall and become the following spring's inoculum. RHS supplies the in-season deadline: take affected growth out before the black resting spores form and reach the soil.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Thin or divide a crowded patch so air moves through it and the leaves dry off faster after rain or dew.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: WSU has the disease recycling every 8 to 10 days whenever moisture sits on the foliage, so the lever is the number of hours a day the canopy stays wet. Utah State treats thinning and dividing as maintenance a spreading mint patch needs anyway, which makes this the cheapest thing you can do about rust: it costs an afternoon you were going to spend on the patch regardless.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water in the morning, and get it down at the roots rather than over the top. What feeds rust is foliage that stays damp all night, so the aim is to have the leaves dry by evening.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Utah State's rust row gives both halves: use drip irrigation, or apply overhead water before mid-day, and avoid wet leaves overnight. Dew and rain still wet the canopy, so watering this way shortens the wet hours rather than removing them, which is enough to cut the number of cycles in a season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Mint escapes. If there are patches of wild or run-away mint near the bed, cut them back, because rust comes across from them in spring.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: WSU names escaped and non-cultivated mint as a spring source of infection, which matters more on this crop than on most: the plant runs out of a bed and keeps going, and an untended stand along a fence or a ditch is a reservoir that no amount of tidying inside the bed will reach.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start new plants from cuttings taken off clean, healthy mint. Rust travels on the cuttings and runners you plant with, so a new bed can begin infected.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: WSU traces outbreaks to systemic infections and pustules on the rhizomes and stem cuttings used in propagation, and its instruction is to inspect source material, monitor cuttings closely and discard infected ones promptly. Propagation is the one point in the cycle where the disease can be kept out of a new bed entirely.

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves yellow from the edges inward, curl up and die, starting low on the plant, and whole shoots wilt and die back. There is no spray that cures it; an affected plant is pulled out.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil-borne fungus that gets into the plant's water-carrying tissue and blocks it. There is no cure for a plant once it is infected, and the fungus stays in the ground for years after the plant is gone. UC IPM puts a number on the cost: a stand that might have run five years or longer can be cut back to as little as two to four.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for an infected plant, so pull it out. Start the new planting from clean cuttings in a bed with no history of the disease. Go easy on the fertilizer as well: Utah State names over-feeding as something to avoid here. And once wilt has been in a bed, do not follow the mint with potatoes or strawberries, which build the same fungus up.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant clean stock in ground with no history of the disease. Where wilt has already shown up, that ground needs a long break: UC IPM's figure is at least five years in crops that do not feed the fungus, and it says not to follow with mint, potatoes or strawberry. Corn, onions, garlic and cereals are on its acceptable list.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Utah State lists verticillium wilt for mint and describes leaf yellowing that starts at the margin, with the leaves curling and dying; UC IPM's peppermint guidelines carry it through to wilting and plant death. The fungus is Verticillium dahliae, and the reason this is a siting problem rather than a spraying one is that it survives between crops and through winter as microsclerotia, pinhead-sized hardened bodies in the soil. Neither document offers any chemical control.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Verticillium dahliae, a soilborne fungus that invades the vascular system. It survives between crops as microsclerotia, and UC IPM's figure for infested ground is a minimum of five years in crops that do not build it up, with mint, potatoes and strawberry named as the ones not to rotate to.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rogue out affected plants and manage by prevention: propagate disease-free cuttings, establish new patches in clean ground away from prior verticillium hosts, and rotate the mint bed on a multi-year cycle where the disease appears.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean stock: UC IPM's standard for commercial plantings is rootstock certified free of Verticillium dahliae, and the home equivalent is taking divisions from a patch that has never wilted. Avoid working through or cultivating an infected patch, since that spreads the microsclerotia, and clean the soil off tools and boots on the way out. Note which way the rotation warning runs: UC IPM is telling you what not to plant after mint in infested ground, and it adds that strains specialized on other crops such as potatoes usually do not attack mint, so old potato ground is not the hazard for mint that a general verticillium warning would imply.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Dig out a wilting plant, roots and all, and get it off the bed. Knock the soil off your tools and boots before you walk to another bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's field sanitation is cleaning equipment, vehicles and shoes, and the shoe clause scales straight down to a garden: the fungus travels as microsclerotia in soil, so soil on a spade is the vector. Minimizing cultivation in an affected bed matters for the same reason, since digging through spreads them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not push the patch with fertilizer. Utah State lists over-feeding as one of the things to avoid where verticillium wilt has shown up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: This is Utah State's third named control for the disease on mint, alongside rotation and removal, and it is the only one that costs nothing and changes nothing about the bed. Feed for steady growth rather than for a flush.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Once wilt has been in a bed, keep mint out of it for at least five years, and keep potatoes and strawberries out too. Corn, onions, garlic and cereals are fine to grow there in the meantime.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's minimum is five years in crops that do not build the fungus up, and it names both sides: do not rotate to mint, potatoes or strawberry; acceptable are grass hays, corn, sudangrass, alfalfa, cereals, onions and garlic. At garden scale that constraint is the real cost, because five years is longer than most beds go without a susceptible crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start a new patch from cuttings or divisions off plants that have never wilted, not from a piece of the bed that is going down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The commercial standard is rootstock certified free of Verticillium dahliae. No certification scheme exists for a garden division, so the working equivalent is provenance: propagate from a stand with no wilt history, and never carry divisions out of an affected bed into clean ground.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white to gray powdery coating on the leaves, stems and leaf stalks. It starts as small round patches, up to about half an inch across, that spread and run together until they cover the plant. In a bad case the leaves yellow and fall.
diseases.cause_beginner: A powdery mildew fungus. Unlike most leaf diseases it does not need wet leaves to get going; what it wants is crowding, shade and soft growth.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut out the worst-covered stems and thin the patch so light and air get in. Do not try to fix this one by keeping the leaves dry, because it is not a wet-leaf disease. If it turns up every year, sulfur applied early, before the coating appears, is the treatment that works; once it is established it is hard to shift.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give the patch room and light, and go easy on the nitrogen. Crowding, shade and soft, over-fed growth are what this disease needs; whether the leaves are wet or dry makes far less difference.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White to gray mycelium and spores on leaves, stems and petioles, appearing as discrete round colonies up to half an inch across that gray with age, run together and can spread over the whole plant; severe infections yellow the leaves and drop them. Susceptibility is not uniform across the mints: WSU has Scotch spearmint severely damaged, with peppermint and native spearmint usually not seriously affected.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A powdery mildew of the mint family, and not a settled single species: WSU notes the name commonly applied to it has been split into more than twenty, with several powdery mildews attacking Lamiaceae in the Pacific Northwest, so this record does not hard-name the fungus. The drivers it does publish are young, succulent growth from heavy nitrogen and irrigation, and humid, shady conditions, which is why greenhouse mint gets it worst. It overwinters on infected mint plants, on stubble, and on wild hosts of the mint family.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Timing decides this one: WSU's point is that once powdery mildew is established it is very hard to control, and its sulfur program starts when plants are 4 to 6 inches tall rather than at first symptom. Sulfur carries two limits, and on a culinary herb the harvest one bites hardest: not within 30 days of cutting, because sulfide from it taints the oil that carries mint's flavor, and not at all if temperatures will exceed 90°F within three days. Leaf wetness is not the lever here and treating it as one wastes the effort: mint under overhead sprinklers is generally not a powdery mildew problem, and it is when that irrigation stops for a few days that the disease runs, on the humidity trapped in the canopy.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Site and feeding do the work here. WSU has the disease most severe on young succulent plants produced by heavy nitrogen and irrigation, and severe on greenhouse mint because of humid, shady conditions, so an open, sunlit stand fed modestly is the prevention. Clearing infected plants and stubble in fall matters too, since that, together with wild mint-family hosts, is where it is thought to overwinter.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Thin the patch and give it light. Powdery mildew builds where growth is packed and shaded, and mint fills in until the middle of a stand is both.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Crowding and shade are the levers on this disease, and leaf wetness is not one of them. WSU has it severe on greenhouse mint because of humid, shady conditions, so opening the stand and siting it in sun takes away both drivers at once. Mint is one of the few crops this dataset is happy to put in part shade, which is exactly why the siting decision carries weight here.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Feed lightly. The soft, fast growth that a heavy dose of nitrogen produces is what this fungus takes hold on first.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: WSU's driver is explicit: the disease is most severe on young, succulent plants such as those resulting from heavy nitrogen fertilization and irrigation. On a herb you cut repeatedly there is a standing temptation to push regrowth with fertilizer, and that flush is what the mildew colonizes.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull out badly coated plants, and clear the old growth off the bed at the end of the season along with any wild mint growing beside it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: WSU's overwintering account is infected mint plants, stubble and wild hosts of the mint family, so clearing up in fall is preventive for next year rather than curative for this one. Rust and anthracnose on the same crop want the identical fall clear-out, which is the argument for doing it once and doing it thoroughly.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sulfur works on powdery mildew, but only if you get in before the coating appears, and on a herb there is a catch: WSU says not to apply it within 30 days of harvest. If you are cutting mint every week or two, that makes sulfur an early-season option and not something to reach for once you are picking. Do not spray it either if the temperature is heading above 90°F in the next three days.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: WSU starts sulfur when plants are 4 to 6 inches tall, a calendar trigger rather than a symptom one, and warns that once the disease is established it is very hard to control. Two limits govern it. No application within 30 days of harvest, because sulfide from sulfur taints the essential oil that carries mint's flavor, and none if temperatures will exceed 90°F within three days. Together those put the only usable window early, well before a patch is in regular cutting, which on most home plantings means this material stays in the shed.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small water-soaked spots on the leaves and on the stems. A badly hit patch looks spotted and ragged rather than dusted or coated.
diseases.cause_beginner: A leaf-spotting fungus that gets going in a crowded, damp patch and keeps spreading while the foliage stays wet. No spray is offered for it on mint: Utah State's fix is to take the diseased plants out, cut the patch to the ground in fall, and move the planting to fresh ground.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Take out the spotted plants. Water at the soil so the leaves stay dry, thin the patch to let sun and air in, and cut the whole planting to the ground in fall and clear the debris away.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give the patch sun and space, water at the soil line, and start a new bed in fresh ground if the spotting comes back year after year.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Utah State's description for mint is small water-soaked spots on the leaves and stems. NC State's spearmint page lists leaf spot as one of the crop's two main diseases without naming an organism, so this record describes anthracnose on mint from Utah State alone; no admitted document gives it a binomial.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A leaf and stem spotting fungus. No admitted document names the organism on mint, so this record does not name it either. Utah State's general disease line for the crop is the mechanism it publishes: appropriate watering and enough sunlight prevent most of it, drip irrigation is named as the way to keep the foliage dry, and thinning or dividing a thickening patch is part of keeping mint healthy.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Utah State's control is three parts: rotate the planting area, remove diseased plants, and prune healthy plants to the ground in fall. The fall cut is the one that does the work, and it is a fall sanitation step rather than the mid-season shear the old record described. No spray is offered for this disease on mint by any source read for it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Utah State's preamble is the prevention: most of mint's diseases can be minimized by appropriate watering and enough sunlight, with drip irrigation named as the way to keep the foliage dry and thinning or dividing treated as maintenance a spreading patch needs anyway. Rotating the planting area is the fourth part, and it is the one that takes planning rather than an afternoon.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull the diseased plants out, and in fall cut the healthy growth right down to the ground and rake the debris off the bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Two of Utah State's three named controls for anthracnose on mint are here: remove diseased plants, and prune healthy plants to the ground in fall. Note where it places the cut, in fall and after the season, not as a mid-season shear to force clean regrowth; on a perennial that regrows from the crown the fall version costs nothing.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Thin or divide the patch so it is not a solid mat. Sun into the middle of the stand and air moving through it is what Utah State's general advice for mint comes down to.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Utah State frames thinning and dividing as maintenance mint needs anyway and pairs proper sunlight with appropriate watering as the way most of the crop's diseases are minimized or eliminated. A mint bed left to itself becomes exactly the dense, shaded, slow-drying interior this fungus wants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put the water on the soil, not on the leaves. Drip or a soaker hose is the easiest way to manage that on a bed of mint.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Utah State calls out drip irrigation by name as the way to provide regular water and keep foliage dry. Unlike powdery mildew on the same plant, this is a disease where the dry-foliage instruction is the correct one, which is precisely why the two are separate records now.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where the spotting comes back year after year, move the mint to fresh ground rather than replanting the same bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotating the planting area is the first of Utah State's three anthracnose controls. On a perennial it is a division-and-reset decision rather than an annual one, and it pairs naturally with the fall cut-down, which is when the patch is easiest to lift.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Roughly 1 to 2 inches of water per week, kept even; mint is a moisture lover that must not dry out, and Utah State advises 1 to 2 inches per week while cautioning against overwatering, which invites disease.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water often enough to keep the soil evenly moist, about 1 to 2 inches a week. Mint likes damp soil, so do not let it dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 to 2 inches per week, more in heat and in containers, which dry fast; the goal is steady, even moisture rather than a soak-and-dry cycle. Mulch helps hold it.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches a week, more when it is hot or in a pot. Keep the soil damp but not swampy.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks mint rust, powdery mildew, and leaf spot on a crop eaten fresh, which Utah State reinforces with its drip-irrigation and no-overnight-wet-leaves advice.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent the leaf diseases mint is prone to.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and root or crown rot in ground that stays waterlogged, plus more rust and mildew where the foliage stays wet; mint tolerates damp soil but not standing water.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant can rot at the base if the soil stays soggy, and wet leaves bring on leaf diseases.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, dull or bronzed leaves, and a spike in spider mites; sustained drought stress checks growth and, in hot dry regions, scorches the foliage, since mint has little drought tolerance.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting, dull leaves and more spider mites when the soil dries out. Mint does not handle drought well, so keep it watered.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 to 2 inches per week, kept even
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Steady moisture matters most while a new division or cutting roots in; mint is a moisture lover and must not dry out as it establishes. Water at the soil line and mulch to hold even moisture.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while a new mint plant gets rooted. Mint loves damp soil, so do not let it dry out now.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 to 2 inches per week, even and generous
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Mint is the rare kitchen herb that thrives in damp ground and part shade, the opposite of rosemary or thyme: give an even, generous 1 to 2 inches a week (USU's figure), more in heat or in fast-drying containers, aiming for steady moisture rather than a soak-and-dry cycle. The one caution is disease, so water the soil, not the leaves, against mint rust, powdery mildew, and leaf spot.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Mint likes damp soil, unlike most herbs. Keep it evenly and generously watered, about 1 to 2 inches a week and more in heat or in a pot, but never swampy. Water the soil, not the leaves, to avoid the diseases mint gets.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 to 2 inches per week, even and generous
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep the same even, generous moisture through the cutting season; mint has little drought tolerance, and a dry spell checks growth, dulls or bronzes the leaves, and can bring on spider mites.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep mint evenly and generously watered while you cut it. If it dries out the leaves go dull and bronzed and spider mites move in, so keep the soil damp.

schedule_by_stage.rate: little needed while dormant
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Cut back watering as the patch dies back for winter; a dormant patch needs little, and constantly waterlogged winter ground invites root and crown rot.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water little while mint is dormant over winter. Soggy winter ground can rot the roots, so ease right off.

schedule_by_stage.rate: resume about 1 to 2 inches per week
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: As shoots push up in spring, resume even, generous watering to drive the tender new growth; an established patch is tougher but still resents drought.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: As new shoots come up in spring, start watering evenly again to push tender new growth.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Even, generous moisture is the whole trick with mint: it is the rare kitchen herb that thrives in damp ground and part shade, so treat it the opposite of rosemary or thyme. The one caution is disease, so water the soil, not the leaves.
