succession_policy.tip_seasoned: N/A. Rosemary is a perennial planted once, not a crop sown in succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: N/A. You plant rosemary once; you do not resow it through the season.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Rosemary is a woody evergreen perennial harvested continuously from a single long-lived plant, so succession sowing does not apply.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-3 REDO cert (2026-07-06, clean post-incident review, Trevor-ruled). woody_ornamental re-stamp verified (hardiness z7-10 verbatim MSU; NCSU 8a-10b disclosed; Arp/Hill-Hardy cultivars named on Clemson); root/crown rot correctly Phytophthora-only (UC IPM, Pythium already dropped); overwatering-is-the-#1-killer verbatim (UWI). FIXES: R1 dropped the dangling 'that prey on aphids and caterpillars' clause from the cabbage/beans companion provenance (bees/butterflies are pollinators, not predators; Clemson supports only pollinator draw); R2 dropped ncsu_ext from the cut_back tip (NCSU says severe pruning encourages dense growth and does NOT support 'no resprout from bare old wood'; claim stands on UWI 'avoid cutting into woody parts'); R3 softened the uncited 'listed as non-toxic to cats/dogs/horses' to general culinary-herb safety framing (no toxicity source in the cited .edu set). [CORRECTION 2026-09-04: "root/crown rot correctly Phytophthora-only" is no longer supported. The PNW Plant Disease Handbook's rosemary root-rot page, unreadable at the time of the 2026-07-06 cert and retrieved during PLA-8 batch 25, names Pythium, Berkeleyomyces sp. (formerly Thielaviopsis basicola) and Rhizoctonia and no Phytophthora, so Pythium was dropped on a reading that document does not carry. The taxon is treated as UNRESOLVED: rosemary's rot is pinned to the problem-class umbrella `crown-and-root-rot` and its consumer prose names no genus. CAVEAT, and it bounds this correction: that page was reached through a text proxy plus a corroborating search snippet, which is two consistent retrievals and NOT a first-party read. Enough to retract an over-claim; NOT enough to assert those three genera, and nothing does. -- see docs/2026-09-04-pla8-batch25-herbs-handoff.md §7.]

open_findings.summary: Regional planting and bloom windows are MODELED (frost-resolved off the reused per-zone climate dates plus rosemary bloom phenology), not read from a rosemary-specific per-region extension planting chart, which does not exist for most of the 10 regions. Windows are generally-safe; tighten exact months at the variety-delta pass.

Cold-zone (northern_tier z3-6) grown_as=annual cells carry a MODELED first-summer bloom window; no T1 source gives a calendar-month first-year bloom for a container/replant rosemary set out after spring frost, and many rosemary plants bloom little in their first cold-zone season. Bloom timing there is a frost-resolved derivation; harvest of leaves (the real use) is continuous through the warm season.

Humid z10/z11 (fl_peninsula, hawaii_tropical) modeled as perennial-marginal: rosemary is genuinely grown there but is prone to root/crown rot and powdery mildew in humidity and needs excellent drainage or raised beds; UF/IFAS supports year-round Florida culture with freeze protection in colder areas. The reliably-perennial in-ground case in deep-humid lowland is under-sourced. Community-correction invited.

Judgment calls / modeled scalars: hardiness_zone_min=7 (species/most cultivars are z8 per NCSU/WI, hardy Hill Hardy z7, Arp z6; 7 chosen as the hardy-cultivar-inclusive reliable floor, driving the grown_as flip); hardiness_zone_max=10 (NCSU 10b); spacing 24-36 in (PSU 2 ft plus large upright sizes); productive_lifespan 10-15 yr and pH preferred 6.0-7.0 modeled from clustered guidance (NCSU lists acid <6.0 as an outlier); germination_temp 70F nominal (rosemary is propagated by cutting/transplant, not seed). Storage fridge/freezer methods are standard kitchen practice; only the drying claim is T1-cited. [CORRECTION 2026-10-02: spacing_inches is 24 in since PLA-10 promote 1 (24-36 in was 2 ft plus a modeled allowance for large upright plants); no row figure is authored, row_spacing_reason not_authored -- see PLA-10 promote 1, d021116.]

Companions are TRADITIONAL/low-to-medium: fellow Mediterranean herbs (sage, thyme, oregano, lavender) on shared-conditions co-cultivation grounds; the cabbage/beans pest-repel pairing is folk tradition with a real beneficial-insect draw (Clemson) but an unproven repellent claim and a soil-moisture mismatch. No rosemary-specific companion trial in a read T1 source.

mid_atlantic z7 credits NC State with rosemary's "zone 7 to 8" hardy floor, but NC State's Plant Toolbox gives Salvia rosmarinus as 8a-10b, read from raw bytes 2026-07-31. The NUMBER is sound and is not in question: 7 is our own hardy-cultivar-inclusive floor per rosemary_pilot_finding_004 ("Hill Hardy z7, Arp z6", with the species itself noted as z8 per NCSU), and it matches rosemary.hardiness_zone_min = 7. It is the CREDIT that overstates, since NC State does not publish 7. Same defect shape as the mid_south UAEX credits removed 2026-07-31, but in a different region and so out of that hunt's scope. Needs its own ruling: either drop the NC State credit as mid_south's was dropped, or restate the sentence as our own cultivar-inclusive judgment.

plantings.label: establishment
plantings.synthesis_note_seasoned: Region-constant arms span the zone range. Rosemary is set out as a nursery transplant or rooted cutting, in the coldest zones only after the last spring frost and in mild zones in fall or late winter to spring. Bloom is frost/phenology-resolved (small blue flowers, late winter into spring in mild climates, later in cooler zones), not read from a planting-date table; the per-zone display windows are computed per zone. Where rosemary is not hardy, the coldest zones are grown as annual / bring-in container plants (MSU, UMN).
plantings.synthesis_note_beginner: These cover the whole region. Plant rosemary after your last spring frost in cold areas, or in fall to spring in mild areas. It flowers in late winter or spring in warm zones and later where it is cooler, and in the coldest zones you grow it for the season or in a pot you bring indoors.

3.grown_as_note_seasoned: Annual or container. Zone 3 is colder than rosemary's reliable hardiness (about zone 7 to 8), so it is grown as a single-season plant or, better, kept in a container moved to a bright, cool, protected spot for winter and set back out after frost. Hardy cultivars such as Arp can overwinter in a very sheltered, sharply drained zone 6 microclimate, but this is not the reliable default.
3.grown_as_note_beginner: Rosemary usually will not survive a zone 3 winter in the ground. Either grow it for one season or, better, keep it in a pot you move somewhere bright and protected for the cold months, then set it back out in spring. The tough cultivar Arp can sometimes make it through in a sheltered spot.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Too cold to overwinter reliably in the ground here, so grow rosemary as an annual or in a container moved indoors for winter. Set plants out only after the last spring frost; the season ends at the first hard freeze.
3.synthesis_note_seasoned: grown_as=annual (cold flip): rosemary is reliably hardy only to about zone 7 to 8, so in zone 3 it does not overwinter in the ground and is grown as a single-season plant or a bring-in container plant (MSU, UMN, PSU). plant_out is frost-resolved from the last spring frost (May 15); the season ends at the first hard freeze (Sep 15). The bloom window is a MODELED first-summer derivation (a mature container plant set out in spring can flower in summer); no T1 source gives a first-year cold-zone bloom month, so this is the weakest-sourced part of the cell. Leaf harvest, the real use, runs continuously through the warm season. Flagged as a blocks_launch:false open finding; community correction invited.

7.grown_as_note_seasoned: Perennial. Zone 7 is within rosemary's hardy range, so it grows as an evergreen perennial in the ground. Give it full sun and sharply drained, lean soil, water deeply but infrequently, and shape it lightly after bloom. Overwatering, not cold, is the main risk here.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: Rosemary lives outdoors year-round in zone 7. Give it full sun and fast-draining soil, water deeply but rarely, and trim to shape after it flowers. The main danger here is too much water, not cold.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Marginal for in-ground winter survival; choose a hardy cultivar with sharp drainage and a sheltered site, and protect it in the coldest snaps. Overwatering remains the bigger risk.

7.synthesis_note_beginner: Rosemary lives outdoors year-round in zone 7 of northern tier. It flowers around apr - jun and you can snip leaves through much of the year. Give it full sun and fast-draining soil, water deeply but rarely, and shape it after it flowers.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier, rosemary is at the cold edge of its range. In zone 7 it can live in the ground as an evergreen perennial if you choose a hardy cultivar (Arp or Hill Hardy), give it sharply drained soil and a sheltered, sunny spot, and protect it in the hardest freezes. In zones 3 through 6 it will not reliably survive winter outdoors, so grow it as a single-season plant or, better, keep it in a container you move to a bright, cool, protected spot for winter and set back out after frost. In every zone, overwatering and wet soil, not cold alone, are the main day-to-day risk.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the northern part of the country, rosemary is right at its cold limit. In zone 7 a tough type like Arp or Hill Hardy can live outdoors year-round with good drainage and a sheltered spot. In colder zones (3 to 6), it will not survive winter outside, so grow it for one season or keep it in a pot you bring inside for the winter. Everywhere, the biggest everyday danger is too much water, not cold.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: In the Southeast and Gulf South, rosemary grows as an evergreen perennial and blooms mainly from late winter into spring, but the region's heat and humidity make root and crown rot and powdery mildew the real threats. Plant it in full sun on sharply drained ground, ideally a raised bed or mound, water deeply but infrequently, and give it room for airflow. Fall or late-winter planting lets roots establish before summer. It is genuinely grown here, but treat drainage as the make-or-break factor.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, rosemary lives outdoors year-round and flowers in late winter and spring, but the heat and humidity can rot it, so drainage is everything. Plant it in full sun on a raised bed with fast-draining soil, do not overwater, and give it room for air to move around it. Plant in fall or late winter so it settles in before summer.

crops.description_seasoned: Rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis) is a woody evergreen Mediterranean subshrub in the mint family, grown mainly for its aromatic, needle-like culinary leaves and secondarily for its small blue flowers. It comes in upright forms that reach several feet and low trailing forms that spill over walls. Unlike hardier culinary perennials such as sage and thyme, rosemary is relatively cold tender: it is reliably perennial only in mild zones (roughly zone 7 or 8 and warmer, with the hardy cultivar Arp pushing into zone 6), and in colder regions it is grown as an annual or overwintered indoors in a pot. It wants full sun, lean sharply drained soil, and little water; overwatering and wet, poorly drained soil, not cold alone, are its most common killers.
crops.description_beginner: Rosemary is an evergreen shrubby herb with fragrant, needle-like leaves and small blue flowers. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it loves sun and hates wet feet. You grow it mostly for the leaves, which you can snip year round in mild climates. It is less cold hardy than sage or thyme: it lives outdoors year after year only in warmer areas (about zone 7 or 8 and up), and in cold-winter places most people grow it in a pot and bring it inside for the winter. Give it full sun, fast-draining soil, and go easy on the water, since too much water is the fastest way to kill it.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Rosemary is grown for its leaves, and in mild climates you can snip fresh sprigs almost year round. For the strongest flavor and oil, harvest sprigs from the soft green growth in the morning, just before or as the plant begins to flower. Cut individual stems above a leafy node to encourage bushy regrowth, and do not remove more than about 20 percent of the plant at any one time. For drying, cut sprigs before or at flowering, then hang them in small bundles in a warm, airy place and strip the leaves once dry.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: You grow rosemary for the leaves, and in mild areas you can snip sprigs almost any time of year. For the best flavor, cut sprigs from the soft green growth in the morning, especially just before it flowers. Snip stems just above a leafy joint so the plant grows back bushy, and take no more than about a fifth of the plant at once. To dry it, cut sprigs before or during flowering, hang small bunches somewhere warm and airy, and strip the leaves off once they are dry.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Rosemary is relatively cold tender for a woody herb. The species and most cultivars are reliably perennial only in about zones 8 to 10, and hardy selections such as Hill Hardy push into zone 7 while Arp is the hardiest, surviving into zone 6 with good drainage and a sheltered spot. Below that, in roughly zone 6 and colder, rosemary is grown as an annual or, better, kept in a container and moved to a bright, cool, protected place for winter. This is the opposite of hardier culinary perennials like sage and thyme, which overwinter outdoors much farther north.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Rosemary is less cold hardy than most herbs. It lives outdoors year after year mainly in warmer areas (about zones 8 to 10), and a few tough types like Hill Hardy and Arp can handle zone 7 or even zone 6 with shelter and good drainage. In colder places, grow rosemary in a pot and bring it inside for the winter, since it will not survive a hard freeze in the ground the way sage or thyme can.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the first year, focus on root establishment: water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper toward deep, infrequent watering. Shape the young plant with light tip pinching to build a bushy framework, and harvest only lightly. A seed-grown plant takes about three years to reach full size, which is why rosemary is almost always started from a cutting or a nursery plant.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about getting the roots going. Water fairly regularly until the plant is established, then cut back. Pinch the tips to help it grow bushy, and harvest only a little the first season. Rosemary is slow from seed, so most people start with a small plant or a cutting.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Choose the sunniest, best-draining spot you have. Rosemary wants lean, gritty, sharply drained ground, so work in coarse sand or grit on heavy soil rather than piling on rich compost. On clay or in humid regions, plant on a mound or raised bed so water drains away from the crown.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick the sunniest spot with the best drainage. If your soil is heavy, mix in coarse sand or grit so water runs through fast, and skip the rich compost. On clay or in a humid, rainy area, plant rosemary on a little mound or raised bed.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Rosemary has small blue flowers (sometimes pink or white). In warm areas it usually flowers in late winter and spring; in colder places it blooms later, in spring or summer. The flowers are a nice bonus for pollinators, but you grow rosemary mostly for the leaves.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Rosemary blooms with small blue, and occasionally pink or white, flowers. In mild-winter climates it flowers mainly from late winter into spring, roughly January through April, and may rebloom; in colder regions it flowers later, in spring into summer. Bloom is a secondary feature, since rosemary is grown chiefly for its leaves, but the flowers are a strong draw for bees and other pollinators.

dormancy_window.note_seasoned: Rosemary is evergreen, but in zones with real winter cold its growth stops for the season. In hardy zones, hold off on watering and feeding and leave any shaping for spring. Where rosemary is not hardy, bring container plants to a bright, cool, protected indoor spot before the first hard freeze; it is a hard freeze or persistently wet soil, not the mere presence of cold, that usually kills it.
dormancy_window.note_beginner: Rosemary keeps its leaves through winter, but in cold areas it stops growing. In mild zones, just stop watering and feeding and save trimming for spring. In cold zones, bring potted rosemary inside to a bright, cool spot before hard frost, since a hard freeze or soggy soil is what kills it.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Rosemary is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer partner; it is grown for its leaves, not fruit, so no cross-pollination planning is required. Its flowers are highly attractive to bees and other pollinators.
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one rosemary plant, and it does not need a partner plant. Bees love the flowers, but that is a bonus for your garden, not something the plant needs.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: Shape rosemary and control its size after the main bloom, or in spring, by cutting into soft green growth only. Rosemary does not reliably resprout from bare, leafless wood, so never cut hard into the old woody base. Regular light harvesting doubles as pruning and keeps the plant bushy; avoid a hard cut heading into a hard freeze.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Trim rosemary to shape it after it flowers, or in spring, cutting only into the green leafy growth. It usually will not grow back from bare woody stems, so never cut into the old wood. Snipping sprigs as you cook keeps it bushy, but do not cut it back hard right before winter.

pet_safe.note: A culinary herb the ASPCA lists as non-toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Oregano

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: light, sandy, gritty, or loamy soil with sharp drainage
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Oregano likes light, sandy or loamy soil that drains fast.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: average loam or shallow rocky soil that drains freely
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Average loam or shallow rocky soil is fine, as long as it drains well.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: heavy or wet clay that stays soggy around the roots
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Heavy or wet clay is a problem because it stays soggy around the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Lean, well-drained soil in full sun. Oregano is a Mediterranean herb that does best in poor, dry ground; it dislikes wet, poorly drained soil, where root and stem rot set in and the flavor turns weak. On heavy clay, plant in a raised bed or mound for drainage rather than feeding the soil.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Oregano likes poor, dry, well-draining soil and full sun. That sounds backward, but it comes from the dry Mediterranean hills, so rich, damp soil actually makes it weak, rot-prone, and bland. If your soil is heavy clay, plant oregano in a raised bed or mound so water drains away fast, and skip the compost.

ph.note_seasoned: Oregano prefers a near-neutral to slightly alkaline soil, roughly pH 6.5 to 7.5, and tolerates ground from about 6.0 up to 8.0. It is intolerant of acidic soil, so on sour ground a light addition of garden lime helps. As with most herbs, sharp drainage matters more than hitting an exact pH.
ph.note_beginner: Oregano likes soil that is neutral to a little bit chalky, about pH 6.5 to 7.5, and copes anywhere from 6.0 to 8.0. It does not do well in acidic soil, so if your soil is sour, a small amount of garden lime nudges it where oregano wants it.

crops.tip_seasoned: Treat oregano lean and dry: full sun, well-drained soil, infrequent water, and almost no feeding. Overwatering and rich soil are the top killers and the surest way to dull the flavor. Pinch it back for bushy growth, harvest often, and pinch or cut off the flower buds to keep the leaves at their most pungent. Oregano spreads by creeping stems and self-sown seed, so contain it in a pot or with edging and deadhead before it seeds.
crops.tip_beginner: The trick with oregano is to not fuss over it. Give it the sunniest, best-draining spot you have, water it only when the soil dries out, and do not feed it much. Pinch the tips to keep it bushy, snip it often, and pinch off the flower buds to keep the leaves tasting their best. Oregano spreads fast by creeping roots and dropped seed, so grow it in a pot or use edging, and cut the flowers before they set seed.

fertilizer.timing: At planting, or a light annual feed
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Oregano has low fertility needs and is easy to over-feed. A little compost worked in at planting, or at most one balanced feeding a year, is plenty; lean soil gives the best flavor. Over-fertilizing pushes soft, leafy growth at the expense of the concentrated oils that make oregano pungent, and rich soil dulls the taste.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Oregano barely needs feeding, and too much fertilizer works against it. A little compost mixed in when you plant, or a single light feeding once a year, is enough. Feed it heavily and you get lots of soft leaves with weaker flavor.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: N/A. Oregano is not fed by N-P-K targets; the goal is lean soil and minimal feed, so no fertilizer analysis applies. At most, one annual application of a balanced general-purpose fertilizer.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: N/A. There is no fertilizer number to hit here, since the aim is to feed oregano as little as possible.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: At most a little compost at planting, or one balanced feeding per year.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little compost at planting, and usually nothing after that.

companions.note_seasoned: Oregano pairs naturally with other sun-loving, low-water Mediterranean herbs that share its lean, well-drained conditions, such as thyme, rosemary, sage, and lavender; group these together so one dry, waterwise bed suits them all, and their flowers draw bees and butterflies. Oregano is also a traditional companion in the vegetable garden, where growers have long planted it near cabbage-family crops in the belief its aroma helps deter cabbage pests. Keep it away from thirsty, rich-soil plants whose watering would rot it, and remember it spreads, so give it its own edge or container rather than crowding slower neighbors.
companions.note_beginner: Plant oregano next to other plants that also like full sun and dry soil, such as thyme, rosemary, sage, and lavender. Many gardeners also tuck it near cabbage and its relatives, believing the scent helps keep pests away. Keep oregano away from plants that need a lot of water, because that wet soil will rot it. Remember that oregano spreads, so give it room at the edge of a bed or grow it in a pot.

good_seasoned.name: Thyme
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low, spreading Mediterranean herb with the same full-sun, lean-soil, low-water needs, so it shares a dry bed with oregano without forcing the wet conditions that rot it.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Thyme and oregano are both drought-tolerant Mediterranean sub-shrubs wanting full sun and sharp drainage, so co-cultivating them lets one waterwise bed serve both. traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility, not a measured pest or yield effect.

good_seasoned.name: Rosemary
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A woody Mediterranean herb that thrives on the same lean, dry, sunny conditions, making it an easy dry-border companion for oregano.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Rosemary shares oregano's full-sun, well-drained, low-water requirements, so the pairing is sound co-cultivation in one dry bed. traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility.

good_seasoned.name: Sage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Another woody Mediterranean herb with matching lean-soil and low-water needs; it and oregano make a natural, drought-tolerant herb grouping.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Garden sage wants the same full sun, sharp drainage, and lean water as oregano, so co-cultivation is straightforward. traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility.

good_seasoned.name: Lavender
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A woody Mediterranean sub-shrub that wants the identical lean, dry, sharply drained conditions as oregano and draws the same pollinators; the two are classic dry-garden partners.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Lavender and oregano are both Mediterranean sub-shrubs demanding full sun, sharp drainage, and low water, and both are strong pollinator draws, so they co-cultivate well in a dry bed. traditional/medium: shared-conditions plus pollinator benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Cabbage and other brassicas
good_seasoned.timing: plant nearby in the vegetable bed
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional companion pairing: growers have long set aromatic oregano near cabbage-family crops in the belief its scent helps discourage cabbage pests. Framed as tradition, not a measured effect, and the soil-moisture needs differ, so site oregano at the dry edge of the bed.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic herbs including oregano are a long-standing folk companion for the cabbage family, said to deter cabbage moths and worms. This is grower tradition rather than a documented trial, and brassicas want richer, moister soil than oregano, so the cultural match is loose; flagged at low confidence.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Thyme
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Likes the same sunny, dry spot as oregano.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same shared-conditions co-cultivation basis as the good_seasoned Thyme entry. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Thyme is a natural oregano partner because it asks for the same things: full sun, lean soil, and not much water. Grow them together and you can run one dry, waterwise bed rather than a watering compromise, which is what keeps both from rotting at the roots. They also look at home together as a low, fragrant herb patch.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Rosemary
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Another sun-and-dry-soil herb that grows happily beside oregano.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Rosemary. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Rosemary wants the same dry, sunny, well-drained conditions as oregano, so the two share a bed with no fuss. Keeping them together means you water the whole group sparingly, which is exactly what oregano needs to stay healthy and full-flavored.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Sage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Shares oregano's love of sun and dry soil.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Sage. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sage is a tough Mediterranean herb that likes the same lean, dry, sunny spot as oregano, so the two make an easy, drought-tolerant pairing. Group them and you can keep the watering light for both, which is the key to good flavor and healthy roots.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lavender
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Loves the same dry, sunny conditions and brings in pollinators.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Lavender. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lavender and oregano are classic dry-garden partners: both come from the Mediterranean and want full sun, sharp drainage, and very little water, so one lean bed suits them both. Both also draw bees and butterflies when they flower. Plant them together in free-draining ground and resist the urge to pamper either.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cabbage and other brassicas
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A traditional pairing; many gardeners plant oregano near cabbage to help keep pests off.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same traditional folk-companion basis and soil-moisture caveat as the good_seasoned brassicas entry. traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Setting fragrant oregano near the cabbage family is an old companion-planting habit, the idea being that its strong scent helps confuse or deter cabbage moths and worms. Treat this as grower tradition rather than proven fact. One honest caveat: cabbages want richer, moister soil than oregano's lean, dry ideal, so plant oregano at the dry edge of the bed rather than in the heart of it.

bad_seasoned.name: Basil and other thirsty herbs
bad_seasoned.timing: keep in a separate, wetter bed
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Basil and similar moisture-loving herbs want steady water and richer soil, the opposite of oregano's lean, dry, sharply drained ideal. Grown together, the watering that keeps basil happy keeps oregano's roots too wet and invites rot, so give them separate conditions.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Basil is a tender annual needing consistent moisture and fertile soil, while oregano demands lean, dry, sharply drained conditions; the watering regimes are incompatible and the wetter one drives oregano toward root rot. mechanistic/medium: a clear cultural-conflict rationale, not a documented trial.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on the tender new growth of young plants. Mature oregano's aroma tends to repel them, so this is usually a minor, early-season problem that fades as the plant fills out.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small soft bugs grouped on the new growth of young plants. Grown oregano's scent tends to keep them away, so this is normally minor and eases off as the plant matures.
pests.cause_seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find oregano, mainly at the seedling stage, before the plant is mature enough for its own aroma to put them off. Oregano is relatively pest-resistant, and a heavy nitrogen feed is the surest way to change that, since the soft growth it pushes is what aphid numbers track.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that sometimes turn up, mostly on young plants that are not yet big enough for their own scent to put the insects off. Oregano has few pest problems, though feeding it heavily with a high-nitrogen fertilizer makes aphids more likely, because it pushes out soft new growth.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock them off with a strong stream of water, and where a colony sits on a few shoot tips, prune those out and dispose of them. Insecticidal soap is the next step if numbers keep climbing, and since it has no residual, coverage is what makes it work.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water. If they are clustered on a few shoot tips, pinch those off and put them in the trash. Insecticidal soap works when there are a lot of them, but only where the spray lands on the insect.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Feed lightly: a heavy nitrogen dose pushes out the soft growth aphid numbers build on. Check the new growth of seedlings and young plants at least twice a week while they are growing fast, which is when a colony is both easiest to find and cheapest to deal with, and leave the ladybugs and lacewings that turn up to finish the job.
pests.prevention_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer, since rich feeding gives aphids the soft new growth they multiply on. Look young plants over a couple of times a week while they are growing fast, and let the ladybugs and lacewings that show up do their work.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. Oregano does not need rich feeding, and the soft, sappy shoots that a heavy dose of nitrogen pushes out are exactly what aphids breed on. Feeding lightly, or not at all, gives them much less to work with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Aphid reproduction tracks the soluble nitrogen in new growth, so a heavy feed raises the ceiling on a colony rather than simply feeding one that was coming anyway. Feed in small portions rather than in one push, and judge the effect by how fast a colony builds, not by whether one turns up at all.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When the aphids are packed onto two or three shoot tips, pinch those tips off and put them in the trash. On a plant the size of an oregano that can be the whole treatment.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's own line is that where populations are localized on a few curled leaves or new shoots, pruning those out and disposing of them may be the best control. It works here because oregano's aphids concentrate on young growth, so the infested tissue is a small, identifiable fraction of the plant rather than something spread through the canopy.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock them off with a hard jet from the hose, aiming under the leaves and into the shoot tips. Most of the aphids that land on the ground never make it back. Do it in the morning so the plant dries through the day.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Expect to repeat it every few days while numbers are climbing; one pass thins a colony rather than ending it. The catch on this crop is that oregano's aphids concentrate on seedlings and young plants, and a stream forceful enough to dislodge a colony will flatten a seedling, so hold the hose back until the plant has some substance to it and pinch out the infested tips instead until then.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings and tiny wasps eat aphids, and on a plant this small they usually find the colony before you would have. Give a light infestation a week or two and watch it before reaching for anything.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conservation costs nothing and is why most oregano aphid flare-ups end on their own. The real cost sits on the other side: a broad-spectrum insecticide takes the predators out along with the aphids, and the colony that rebuilds afterward has nothing left holding it down. Ants working the plant do the same job from the other direction, driving predators off a colony they are farming for honeydew.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a young plant is being overwhelmed, insecticidal soap works, but only where the spray actually lands on an insect. Cover the undersides of the leaves and plan on repeating it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap leaves no residual, so this is a coverage problem rather than a dose problem and anything the spray misses is the population that rebuilds. Keep it off a plant that is already dry and stressed, and off any plant when the temperature is near 90°F, since that is when the foliage burns. It also kills the soft-bodied predators it wets, so spray the colony rather than the planting.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellowing on the leaves with faint webbing on the stems, most likely in hot weather and on plants sitting where dust settles or where the rootball has been left dry. Oregano is relatively pest-resistant, so this is usually minor.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves that look faded and finely speckled all over rather than spotted in patches, with a little webbing between the stems in bad cases. Look for it in hot spells, on plants coated in path dust or left to dry right out. It is rarely serious on oregano.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tiny sap-feeding mites that build up in hot, dusty conditions and on plants under water stress. They are usually found first at the margins of a garden and beside dusty paths and roadways, which is where the practical lever sits.
pests.cause_beginner: Very small sap-sucking mites that build up in hot weather, especially where dust settles on the leaves or where a plant has been left dry. They usually show up first at the edge of a garden or beside a dusty path.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Check that the mites are still present before treating: the stippling stays on the leaf after they have gone, and plants often recover on their own. If they are there, rinse the plant with a forceful spray of water, which often reduces numbers adequately by itself, and fall back on insecticidal soap or horticultural oil only if that is not holding.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: First make sure the mites are still there, since the speckling stays on the leaf long after they leave and plants often recover by themselves. If they are, rinse the plant hard with water, getting under the leaves, and use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil only if that is not enough.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Do not let a container plant bake bone-dry through a heat wave, since water-stressed plants are the ones that flare. Damp down dusty paths and bare ground beside the bed at regular intervals, and keep broad-spectrum insecticides off the planting, since they touch off mite outbreaks by clearing out the predators.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not let a potted plant dry out completely in a heat wave. Wet down dusty paths and bare ground near the plants now and then, and avoid all-purpose bug sprays, which kill the mites' natural enemies and make outbreaks worse.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Mites build up fastest on a plant that has been left dry and stressed. Oregano likes it on the dry side, but a pot baking through a heat wave is a different thing, so water it before it starts to wilt.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The distinction worth holding on a drought-adapted herb is between soil that drains fast and a rootball that has actually run out. The first is how oregano should be grown; the second is what tips a mite population into a flare, because water-stressed plants are highly susceptible. Containers reach that point first, since they hold days of water where a bed holds weeks.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rinse the plant hard with the hose, getting the water under the leaves where the mites actually sit, and repeat every few days in hot weather. On a garden plant this alone often settles it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's finding for gardens and small plants is that regular, forceful water spraying often reduces mite numbers adequately on its own, which puts this ahead of any product rather than beside one. It also works on the second half of the problem: mites are first found on plants next to dusty roadways and at garden margins, so wetting the paths and bare ground nearby at regular intervals belongs in the same habit.

control_ladder.note_beginner: You can buy predatory mites, but be honest about the scale. They are meant for a large planting, and on a few oregano plants most of them will simply leave. The predators already in your garden do more.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM scopes purchase and release to large plantings and orchards, and released predators starve or move on when prey is not already there, so on a herb bed this is a top-up rather than a plan. If you do release, the working guideline is roughly one predator per ten spider mites, and it closes off sulfur afterward, which harms predatory mites that are not sulfur-resistant.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Before you spray anything, make sure the mites are still there. The speckling stays on the leaf long after they have gone. If they are, insecticidal soap kills what it touches, so cover the undersides of the leaves and plan on repeating it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The published instruction is to be sure mites are present before treating, because they are often gone by the time the damage is noticed and plants recover on their own once they leave. Stippling is a record of the past, not a reading of the present, so confirm with a hand lens first. Then treat for coverage: there is no residual, and whatever the spray misses is the population that comes back.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Light horticultural oil smothers mites the same way and can be the better choice on a heavier infestation. Do not use it on a dry, stressed plant or when it is above 90°F.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap and oil are the two selective materials UC IPM names for mites, and the reason to stop at them is that broad-spectrum insecticides do the opposite: they set off mite outbreaks by clearing out the predators that were holding numbers down. Keep oil and sulfur at least 30 days apart in the growing season, since the combination injures foliage, and check the oil label, since some specify longer.

diseases.name: Root and stem rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Gradual wilting, yellowing and dieback that does not recover with watering, with the roots underneath turning brown to black or decaying away. Oregano is drought-tolerant and generally resistant to disease, but it will not survive ground that stays wet.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant slowly wilts, yellows and dies back even though the soil is wet, and the roots underneath are brown or black and rotted away. Oregano copes with drought and with most diseases, but it will not survive soggy ground.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne rot organisms that take hold in saturated, poorly drained soil and destroy the roots. NC State lists oregano among the herbaceous perennials susceptible to Phytophthora and names prolonged watering, poor drainage and standing water as what favors the disease. Wet ground over winter is the hardest case, because the plant is drawing almost no water down while the soil holds what it gets.
diseases.cause_beginner: Rot organisms in the soil that take hold when the ground stays soggy and drains badly, and destroy the roots. Wet ground over winter is the worst of it, because the plant is taking up hardly any water while the soil holds everything it gets.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: A rotted oregano does not recover, so the only live decisions are how fast it comes out and what happens to the ground it stood in. NC State records both halves of the bad news: the pathogen survives in soil from season to season and cannot be eradicated from an infested bed without extreme measures, and there is a lack of OMRI-approved products that manage it effectively. On ground that has already taken one plant, the answer RHS gives for oregano is to stop fighting the bed and grow it in a raised bed or a container instead, where you set the drainage yourself. Sanitize the tools and the pot first, or you carry the problem into the new mix.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: An oregano whose roots have rotted cannot be saved. Lift it, bin it, and wash anything that touched it. No spray fixes this, and the disease stays behind in that soil, so instead of replanting in the same place, put the next one in a pot or a raised bed where you control the drainage.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in sharply drained soil and keep plants on the dry side; on heavy or damp ground use a raised bed or a container, where drainage is better. Space plants with their mature size in mind, and where a plant has already rotted, put the next one somewhere else, because the pathogen survives in that soil from season to season.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in fast-draining soil, keep it on the dry side, and never let oregano sit in soggy ground. On heavy clay, plant on a raised bed or grow it in a pot instead. If a plant does rot, do not put the next one in the same spot, because the disease stays in that soil.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This is the whole game. Oregano will take drought and will not take wet feet, so plant it where water drains away fast, and on heavy ground put it on a raised bed or grow it in a pot. Water it, then let it dry out before watering again.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Drainage is the control here, not a preference: the rot organisms need free water in the soil pores to move and infect, so a bed that is still saturated hours after a soaking is the disease condition itself. NC State groups prolonged watering, poor drainage and standing water together as what favors it, and RHS puts the same weight on winter, when the plant is drawing almost nothing down and the ground holds everything it gets.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Look at what you are bringing home. Slide a new plant out of its pot and check that the roots are pale and firm rather than brown, black and mushy, so you are not carrying the rot into a clean bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: These pathogens arrive with the plant more often than they arrive on their own, and a bed that has been infested stays infested, so the inspection at purchase buys more than anything available afterward. The same care applies to a division handed over the fence, which comes with a rootball and its own soil.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Once the roots have gone there is no bringing the plant back, so pull it out and get rid of it. Wash the pot and the tools before they touch anything else.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no rescue at the crown, so the only in-season decisions are how quickly the plant comes out and what the tools and containers touch next. Sanitizing both sits on NC State's cultural list, and it matters most on the way out: a pot that grew a rotted plant is the shortest route to the next one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not put another oregano into the spot where one rotted. The disease stays in that soil, so give the new plant fresh ground or a pot of new mix.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: This is the fact that changes the advice from remove the plant to do not replant here: NC State records that the pathogen survives in soil from season to season, and that once a bed is infested it cannot be eradicated without extreme measures. UC IPM's oregano guidance says the same thing in one line, to avoid areas that have had previous disease problems. Treat the ground as spent for susceptible plants rather than treating the plant that died.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a bed has already killed a plant or two and you want it back, you can cook it: wet the bare soil, cover it with clear plastic, and leave it through the hottest four to six weeks of summer. It costs you the bed for a season, and it lowers what is living down there rather than clearing it out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Solarization is on NC State's list, and the same document's line that the pathogen cannot be eradicated without extreme measures is the honest expectation to hold: this reduces the load, it does not sterilize the ground. It also needs a genuinely hot, clear stretch to drive lethal temperatures into the top foot, so it is worth attempting only where summer reliably delivers that. Nothing waits behind it either: NC State records a lack of OMRI-approved products that effectively manage Phytophthora diseases, so the soil is where the whole of this disease gets dealt with and there is no spray to fall back on.

diseases.name: Mint rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular spots with dusty orange to brown pustules on the leaves and stems, sometimes followed by darker pustules later in the season. Pale, distorted shoots in spring can be the same disease showing before any pustules do, and it will spread through a planting if it is left alone.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small round spots and dusty orange or brown powder on the leaves and stems, sometimes turning darker later in the season. Shoots that come up pale and twisted in spring can be the same disease. Left alone, it spreads through the planting.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The same fungal disease gardeners meet on mint, which is where the name comes from; it runs on marjoram and savory as well. Every opening it gets comes down to how long the foliage stays wet, so a damp, crowded, poorly ventilated planting and water thrown over the top of the plant are what it needs.
diseases.cause_beginner: This is the same rust that turns up on mint, which is how it got its name. It gets in while the leaves are wet, so crowded plants sitting in still, damp air are the ones that catch it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected plants promptly, before the dark resting spores form, and take out a heavily infected plant rather than trying to prune the disease off it. Bag what you remove instead of shaking it out over the bed, and put it in the trash rather than the compost heap.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pull out badly infected plants rather than trying to cut the disease off them, and do it before the spots turn black. Carry what you remove out in a bag and put it in the trash, not on the compost heap.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants so the foliage dries quickly after rain and dew, and water at the soil rather than over the top. Take divisions and cuttings only from plants that showed no rust this season, and clear the old growth away at the end of the year.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room so the leaves dry off quickly after rain, and water the soil rather than the leaves. When you divide a plant or take cuttings, use one that has stayed clean all season, and clear away the old growth in fall.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give each plant room and an open spot where the sun and a bit of breeze reach it, so the leaves dry off soon after rain or dew. Rust needs the leaf to stay wet to get in, so the faster it dries the fewer chances it gets.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: What you are really setting with spacing and site is how many hours the foliage stays wet. A crowded mat holds moisture well into the morning after an open plant has dried, and that difference is what decides whether a spore landing overnight gets the window it needs. This is a layout decision, so it is made once, at planting, and is hard to undo afterward without taking a knife to an established clump.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water the soil at the foot of the plant instead of sprinkling over the top, and water in the morning where you can. Wet leaves are exactly what rust needs, and a sprinkler hands it that for free.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Overhead water does two jobs for the fungus at once: it keeps the leaf wet long enough for a spore to germinate, and it splashes spores from a marked leaf onto a clean one. Rain and dew are outside your control, which is why this sits alongside spacing rather than replacing it. What is inside your control is not adding hours of leaf wetness to a plant that is already carrying the disease.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Oregano gets passed around as divisions and cuttings, and rust can travel with them. Take pieces only from a plant that has stayed clean all season, and look a new plant over before it joins the bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: On mint, where this disease is best documented, outbreaks are usually traced to infection already inside the rhizomes and stem cuttings used for propagation rather than to spores arriving on the wind, and the published response is to inspect source material and discard anything infected. The oregano side of that has not been documented to the same depth, so treat clean stock as the prudent move rather than a proven mechanism, and simply do not propagate from a plant that showed rust this year.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the rusty leaves off as soon as you see them and put them in the trash, not on the compost heap. If a plant is covered in pustules, take the whole plant out: that is the step that protects the rest of the bed. Clear the old growth away at the end of the season.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removal, not spot pruning, is what the control literature calls for. RHS's instruction is to remove affected plants promptly, before the black resting spores form, and cutting the marked leaves off a badly infected plant leaves the fungus in tissue that has not spotted yet. Carry what you remove out in a bag rather than shaking it over the bed, since rust spores move easily on air currents.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A dry white bloom on the leaf surface, heaviest inside a crowded clump where the air sits still and dense enough there to whiten whole shoots. It grows on the surface rather than rotting the leaf, so what it costs is vigor and appearance; on oregano it stays a minor problem next to root rot.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery film on the leaves, worst where plants are packed together and the air does not move. It spoils how the plant looks and slows it down, but it will not kill it, and it is a much smaller problem than root rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A leaf fungus that gets going on crowded plants where the air does not move and humidity builds inside the canopy. The band that favors it is moderate rather than extreme, roughly 60°F to 80°F, and shade favors it too, so the plant at risk is the one tucked into a shaded, still corner rather than the one out in the summer heat. Unlike most leaf diseases, it does not need water sitting on the leaf in order to infect.
diseases.cause_beginner: A leaf fungus that takes hold on crowded plants where the air sits still and humidity builds up among the leaves. It likes mild weather, around 60°F to 80°F, and shade, so a plant squeezed into a shady corner is the one to watch. It is not caused by wet leaves, which is what makes it different from most leaf diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Open the planting up: thin a crowded clump and cut back the growth that is shading its middle, which is the step that changes the conditions. If it keeps returning on a plant you are picking from, a sulfur spray or dust used as a protectant is the standard organic option, applied to label and kept off the plant in heat.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Thin out crowded growth and cut back anything shading the center of the plant, so air can move through it. If the mildew keeps coming back on a plant you are harvesting, a sulfur spray or dust is the usual organic option; follow the label, and do not use it in hot weather.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for air circulation, at 10 to 12 inches apart or wider, and give them an open, sunny position. Thin an established clump rather than letting it close over, which is where the still, humid air that favors this disease collects.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give each plant room, 10 to 12 inches apart or more, in an open sunny spot so air can move through the leaves. Thin a clump that has grown dense rather than leaving it packed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give plants room and an open, sunny spot. Air moving through the planting is the thing that reliably keeps powdery mildew down on oregano, because a crowded clump holds still, humid air right where the leaves are.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UF/IFAS recommends spacing plants 10 to 12 inches apart to improve air circulation and prevent the extra humidity that attracts pests and diseases. To prevent powdery mildew, UF/IFAS pairs good air circulation with avoiding overhead watering. Oregano generally resists disease but can occasionally get powdery mildew or root rot, especially in humid conditions.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If mildew keeps coming back on a plant you actually want to pick from, sulfur spray or dust is the standard organic option. It works by stopping new infection rather than clearing what is there, so it goes on early, and you follow the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UF/IFAS names sulfur or copper for oregano, and sulfur is the one with established powdery mildew activity, so it is the one worth buying. It is a protectant: it stops spores landing on treated tissue from establishing and does nothing to the colonies already on the leaf, which makes it worth reaching for only on a plant with a history of the disease, applied before the season turns. Keep it off the plant near or above 90°F and at least 30 days away from any oil spray in the growing season, check the oil label since some specify longer, and observe the label's interval before harvest.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep and infrequent. Water new plants until they are established, then let the soil dry between waterings; mature oregano needs little water and is quite drought-tolerant. Container plants dry faster and need checking, but should still dry out between drinks.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply but not often. Water a new plant until it settles in, then let the soil dry out before watering again. An established oregano needs very little water. Pots dry faster, so check them, but still let them dry between waterings.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to settle new plants while establishing; once mature, only occasional deep watering in prolonged dry spells. Keep plants on the dry side to avoid root and stem rot.
watering.amount_beginner: A regular soak for a new plant, then much less once it is established.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base and let the soil dry between waterings. Avoid wetting the foliage, which invites rust and rot in humid conditions.
watering.method_beginner: Pour water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves, and let it dry out before watering again. Wet leaves and a soggy base are what make oregano rot.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing leaves, wilting or dieback of whole shoots, and a plant that fails despite watering signal too-wet roots and likely root or stem rot, not drought. Flavor also weakens in soft, over-watered growth.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If leaves yellow and shoots wilt or die back even though you are watering, the problem is almost always too much water, not too little. Soggy roots rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Established oregano rarely shows true drought stress; light wilting in extreme heat that recovers overnight is normal and not a reason to increase watering.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Oregano almost never gets too little water once established. A little droop on a very hot afternoon that bounces back by morning is fine.

schedule_by_stage.rate: a regular soak to settle new plants
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: The first season is the only time regular watering matters: water new oregano until it is established, then let the soil dry between waterings. Water at the base and keep the foliage dry against rust and rot in humid conditions.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water a new oregano regularly until it settles in, then let the soil dry out before watering again. Water at the base to keep the leaves dry.

schedule_by_stage.rate: occasional deep watering in dry spells
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Mature oregano needs little water and is quite drought-tolerant: only occasional deep watering in prolonged dry spells, letting the soil dry between drinks. The most common way to kill it is overwatering, and its flavor also weakens in soft, over-watered growth, so keep it on the dry side. Container plants dry faster and need checking, but should still dry out between waterings.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Mature oregano needs very little water. Give it an occasional deep drink only in a long dry spell, and let the soil dry between waterings. Too much water not only rots it but also weakens the flavor. Pots dry faster, so check them, but still let them dry out between waterings.

schedule_by_stage.rate: little to none while dormant
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through dormancy oregano wants very little water; keep it on the dry side and do not let the crown sit in wet winter soil.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: In winter oregano needs almost no water. Keep it on the dry side and never let it sit in soggy soil.

watering.method_note_seasoned: The most common way to kill oregano is overwatering. When in doubt, water less.
watering.method_note_beginner: Remember: more oregano dies from too much water than too little.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The first season after planting is the only time regular watering matters; taper off sharply once the plant is established.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water fairly regularly the first year while it gets established, then back off a lot.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Nursery transplants are already hardened; set them out after the last spring frost. Divisions and rooted cuttings should be hardened gradually before planting out.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you buy a plant from a nursery, you can put it straight in the ground after your last spring frost. There is no seed-starting step you must do.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Oregano is most reliably started from a nursery transplant, a division of an established clump, or a softwood cutting; all can be done in spring. It also grows readily from seed (germinating in about four days in warm soil), but the tiny seed needs light to germinate so should not be covered, and seed-grown plants vary in flavor and do not come true, so named culinary types like Greek oregano are propagated vegetatively. Start seed indoors about 8 weeks before the last frost.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easy, reliable way to grow oregano is to buy a small plant, divide an existing clump, or root a cutting in spring. You can grow it from seed, but the seed is tiny and needs light (do not cover it), and seed-grown plants vary in flavor, so for good culinary oregano most gardeners start from a plant. If you do start from seed, sow it indoors about 8 weeks before your last frost.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering; oregano must never sit in standing water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A gritty, fast-draining potting mix, not a moisture-holding one.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in coarse sand or perlite so water runs straight through.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A coarse, free-draining potting medium; avoid peat-heavy moisture-retentive mixes.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Add coarse sand, perlite, or fine gravel to sharpen drainage.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check the soil, but still let it dry between waterings and never leave the pot standing in a full saucer.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container oregano needs only a very light feed, if any; do not over-fertilize.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In the coldest zones, or with a less hardy type like Greek oregano, grow it in a pot you can move into an unheated but sheltered spot for winter, then bring it back out in spring. A sunny indoor windowsill also works for a winter supply.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Where the chosen type is not reliably hardy, a container lets you overwinter the plant under cover (an unheated garage or porch) or on a bright windowsill; keep it on the dry side and protected from hard freezes, then return it outdoors after frost.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: A container is the recommended way to grow oregano for most gardeners: it suits the plant's love of drying out between waterings and, just as important, it contains oregano's vigorous spread by creeping stems and self-sown seed. Use a wide, free-draining pot with a gritty mix, keep it in full sun, and never let it stand in water. A pot is also the easy way to overwinter less hardy types where winters are cold.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Growing oregano in a pot is a great idea, both because it likes to dry out between waterings and because a pot keeps it from spreading all over the garden. Use a wide pot with holes in the bottom and a gritty mix, keep it in full sun, and tip out any water that collects in the saucer.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers keep the medium too consistently moist for oregano and promote root rot; use a conventional free-draining pot instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for oregano; they keep the soil too wet and the roots rot.

recommended.name: Greek oregano
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy, reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9; a touch less cold-hardy than common oregano.
recommended.note: The classic culinary oregano with a hot, spicy, pungent flavor and white flowers; this is the type sold dried in stores and the best pick for cooking.

recommended.name: Italian oregano
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy in roughly zones 6 to 9; a milder type often grown as a bring-in plant in cold zones.
recommended.note: A hybrid of oregano and sweet marjoram with large leaves and a milder, sweeter, well-rounded flavor; dries easily and is a versatile kitchen oregano.

recommended.name: Common (wild) oregano
recommended.hardiness_note: Very hardy, reliably perennial to about zone 4; the hardiest and most vigorous type.
recommended.note: Also called wild marjoram, this is the toughest and most cold-hardy oregano and the most aggressive spreader, but its flavor is variable and some seed-grown plants are nearly bland, so taste before relying on it for cooking.

recommended.name: Hot & Spicy oregano
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy in roughly zones 5 to 9, similar to Greek oregano.
recommended.note: A selection bred for an extra-pungent, peppery kick; a good choice for growers who want the boldest possible oregano flavor.

recommended.name: Golden oregano
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy in roughly zones 5 to 9; low and spreading.
recommended.note: A golden-yellow-leaved, variegated form grown as much for its bright foliage as for the kitchen; milder in flavor and lower-growing, it makes an attractive edible groundcover in full sun.

recommended.name: Syrian oregano (za'atar)
recommended.hardiness_note: Tender; hardy only in roughly zones 8 to 10, a bring-in container plant in colder regions.
recommended.note: The traditional za'atar herb, with a distinctive oregano-marjoram flavor used in Middle Eastern blends; more heat-loving and frost-tender than common oregano.

varieties.note_seasoned: Oregano reaches the grower as several practical types. Greek oregano (Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum) is the hot, pungent kitchen standard and the type sold dried; Italian oregano (O. x majoricum, an oregano-marjoram hybrid) is milder and sweeter. Common or wild oregano (O. vulgare) is the hardiest and most vigorous but has variable, sometimes bland flavor, so taste before you rely on it. Hot & Spicy is an extra-pungent selection, Golden oregano (O. vulgare 'Aureum') is a bright-foliaged ornamental-culinary form, and Syrian oregano (O. syriacum) is the tender za'atar herb. One important caution: Mexican oregano (Lippia graveolens) is not a true oregano at all but a shrub in the verbena family, grown in hot climates for a similar, stronger flavor. For cooking, start with Greek oregano.
varieties.note_beginner: There are several kinds of oregano. Greek oregano is the bold, spicy one used in cooking and sold dried, and it is the best choice for the kitchen. Italian oregano is milder and sweeter. Common or wild oregano is the toughest and most cold-hardy, but its flavor varies a lot and some plants are almost bland, so taste it first. Hot & Spicy is extra strong, Golden oregano has bright yellow leaves, and Syrian oregano is the za'atar herb. Watch out for one thing: Mexican oregano is a completely different plant (in the verbena family), not a true oregano, even though it tastes similar. For cooking, start with Greek oregano.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh cut sprigs hold for a few days in a glass of water on the counter. For long-term keeping, dry oregano: unlike most herbs its flavor actually concentrates and improves when dried. Tie small bundles and hang them upside down in a warm, dry, airy place, then strip the leaves into a sealed jar out of the light.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Fresh sprigs last a few days standing in a little water on the counter. Oregano is one of the few herbs that tastes even better dried, so to keep it, hang small bunches upside down somewhere warm and airy, then store the dried leaves in a sealed jar.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate fresh sprigs loosely wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel in a bag, where they keep for about one to two weeks.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep fresh oregano in the fridge, loosely wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel inside a bag, for about one to two weeks.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze whole sprigs in a bag, or strip the leaves and freeze them in water or oil in ice-cube trays for cooking; frozen oregano keeps its flavor well for months, though drying is the traditional method.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze oregano: put whole sprigs in a bag, or freeze the leaves in water or oil in an ice-cube tray to drop into cooking later.
storage.notes_seasoned: Oregano is one of the sturdy herbs that dries well, and it is unusual in that drying concentrates rather than dulls its flavor. Cut stems for drying just before the plant flowers, when the leaf oils peak, tie them in small loose bundles, and hang them in a warm, dry, airy spot; a paper bag around the bundle keeps off dust. Once dry, strip the leaves and store them sealed and out of the light.
storage.notes_beginner: Oregano is easy to dry, and drying actually makes its flavor stronger. Cut stems just before it flowers, tie them in small loose bunches, and hang them upside down somewhere warm and airy (a paper bag around the bunch keeps the dust off). When dry, rub the leaves off into a sealed jar kept out of the light.

rotation.note_seasoned: N/A. Oregano is a perennial that stays in place for several years, so annual crop rotation does not apply. When replanting an old oregano patch, choose a fresh, well-drained site to avoid carrying over soilborne root rot, and clear any strays it has spread by root or seed.
rotation.note_beginner: N/A. Oregano is not rotated like a vegetable because it is a permanent plant that stays put for years. If you replace an old one, pick a fresh, well-draining spot and pull up any pieces it has spread around.

growth_stages.name: Plant out
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Set the nursery plant, division, or rooted cutting out after the last spring frost, in the sunniest, best-draining spot you have. Space plants 10 to 12 inches apart; on heavy ground, plant on a mound or raised bed, and consider a pot or edging to contain the spread.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: After your last spring frost, plant the oregano in the sunniest, best-draining spot. Leave about 10 to 12 inches between plants. To keep it from spreading, grow it in a pot or add edging.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A compact young plant with fragrant green leaves and firm roots filling the pot, ready to set out once frost has passed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A small bushy plant with fragrant green leaves and roots that hold the potting soil together when you slide it out.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Loosen the rootball, set the crown level with the soil surface, and water in once to settle the roots. Do not amend with rich compost or fertilizer; oregano wants lean ground.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Gently loosen the roots, plant so the top of the rootball is level with the soil, and water once to settle it. Skip the fertilizer and rich compost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Planted: type or cultivar, number set out, and the date.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down which oregano you planted and when.

growth_stages.name: Establishment (year one)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first season after planting. Oregano establishes fairly quickly but is still building its root system; pinch the tips once it reaches about 6 inches to encourage branching, and harvest only lightly. It reaches full size by about the second year.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first growing season. Your oregano is settling in and growing roots. Once it is about 6 inches tall, pinch the tips to make it bushier, and only pick a little this year. It fills out by about year two.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new growth spreading low and outward as the plant begins to form a bushy mound. Some spread by creeping stems is normal and healthy.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: New growth spreading low and wide as the plant fills in. It naturally creeps outward a bit, which is normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water until the plant is settled, then taper toward infrequent watering. Pinch the growing tips to build a bushy plant, harvest only lightly, and hold off on fertilizer.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water fairly often until the plant takes hold, then water less. Pinch the tips to make it bushy, only snip a little, and do not feed it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Establishment: planting-out date, first pinch, and any light harvests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when you planted it and that you pinched it to make it bushy.

growth_stages.name: Spring leaf-out and harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Each spring the plant pushes fresh growth from the base and creeping stems, and this leafy growth is what you harvest through the season by snipping sprigs as needed. Early spring is also the time to cut out any old, leggy wood.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Every spring, new growth appears low on the plant and along its spreading stems. This leafy growth is what you snip through the season for cooking. Early spring is a good time to cut out any old, woody stems.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New soft growth emerging along the stems and crown, signaling the plant came through winter and is growing again. Watch also for new shoots popping up beyond the original clump.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Soft new growth low on the plant in spring. That tells you it survived winter. You may also see new shoots coming up a short way from the main plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut out old leggy wood in early spring once growth resumes and frost has passed. Begin harvesting sprigs as needed, settle into infrequent watering, and pull or dig any unwanted spread to keep the plant in bounds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In early spring, once you see new growth and frost is over, cut out any old woody stems. Start snipping sprigs to cook with, water deeply but not often, and pull up any shoots that have wandered where you do not want them.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Spring leaf-out: date growth resumed and any spring cleanup done.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when spring growth started and if you cleaned it up.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The mid-to-late-summer flowering window, when oregano puts up small clusters of white, pink, or purple flowers that draw bees and butterflies. Leaf flavor is most concentrated just before the flowers open, so many growers pinch or cut the flower buds to keep the leaves pungent and productive.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Mid-to-late summer, when oregano makes tiny white, pink, or purple flowers that bees and butterflies love. The leaves taste best just before it flowers, so many gardeners pinch off the flower buds to keep the leaves strong.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds forming in clusters on the stem tips. For the strongest flavor and best dried quality, harvest just as the buds form, before they open.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Little flower buds forming in clusters at the tips. For the best flavor, cut sprigs just as the buds appear, before they open.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut sprigs for drying as the flower buds form. Pinch or cut off remaining flowers to favor leaf growth and flavor, or leave some to bloom for pollinators and deadhead before seed sets to limit self-seeding. Keep watering light and do not feed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut sprigs to dry as the buds form. Pinch off the rest of the flowers to keep the leaves tasty, or leave a few for the bees but snip them before they make seed so the plant does not spread everywhere. Keep watering light and do not fertilize.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Bloom: bud-formation date, harvest cuts for drying, and whether you removed or kept the flowers.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when it started to bud and when you cut oregano to dry.

growth_stages.name: Shear back
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The post-bloom shear, a key upkeep act. After flowering fades, clip the plant back to remove the spent flower stems, tidy the mound, and cut into leafy growth to spur a fresh flush. Deadheading now also limits self-seeding.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The tidy-up trim after the flowers fade. Clip off the spent flower stems and cut the plant back into its leafy growth to bring on fresh new leaves. Trimming now also stops it from dropping seed everywhere.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Spent, browning flower stems and a plant finished with its main bloom. Below the leafy growth are older woody stems that resprout poorly.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Faded, brownish flowers and a plant done blooming. Notice the older woody stems below the green growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Shear off the spent flowers and reduce the plant, cutting into leafy growth and avoiding the bare old wood. Regular harvesting plus this shear keeps oregano bushy and productive; even so, plants go woody with age and are best divided or replaced every few years.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Trim off the old flowers and cut the plant back into its leafy parts, avoiding the bare woody stems. Snipping often plus this trim keeps oregano bushy, but it still gets woody with age, so replace or divide it every few years.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Shear back: date sheared and roughly how much removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when you trimmed off the old flowers.

growth_stages.name: Dormancy (cold zones)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, oregano dies back to the ground and goes dormant. It needs almost no water, and it is wet soil, not the cold itself, that most often kills it over winter. Where it is at the cold edge of its range, a winter mulch after the ground freezes helps it through.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Where winters freeze, oregano dies back to the ground and rests through the cold months. It barely needs water, and it is soggy soil, not the cold, that usually kills it over winter. In very cold areas, a winter mulch after the ground freezes helps it survive.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Top growth browning and dying back for the season as the plant goes dormant. Roots stay alive underground in hardy zones and push new growth in spring.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The leaves and stems browning and dying back for winter. In hardy areas the roots stay alive underground and grow again in spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stop watering and feeding, and leave any hard cutback for spring. At the cold edge of its range, apply a loose winter mulch of straw or evergreen boughs after the ground freezes, and remove it as growth resumes. Move less hardy types or container plants under cover.
