northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the northern part of the country, grow common green sage. It is hardy to about zone 4 and comes back year after year in zones 5, 6, and 7, living in the ground, flowering in early summer, and getting a trim each spring. In zone 4 it is at its cold limit and needs great drainage and some winter protection, so it may be short-lived or grown in a pot. In the coldest areas (zone 3) it usually will not survive winter outside, so grow it for a season or in a pot you bring somewhere sheltered. The biggest thing to get right is drainage: sage hates sitting in cold, wet soil over winter.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier, common green sage (Salvia officinalis) is the type to grow: it is hardy in roughly zones 4 to 8 and lives in the ground as a woody perennial subshrub in zones 5, 6, and 7, leafing out in spring, blooming blue-purple in early summer, and getting its main renewal prune in spring. In zone 4 it is at the cold edge of its range and survives only with sharp drainage and winter protection, so many gardeners treat it as a short-lived perennial or a bring-in container plant. In zone 3 winters are too cold for reliable overwintering, so sage is grown as an annual or in a container moved to shelter. Wherever you grow it, wet winter soil is the real risk, not cold alone, so plant it high, lean, and sharply drained.

It grows best in the cooler months, roughly fall through spring, and is most successful in raised beds or containers with excellent drainage and good airflow. Treat it as a short-lived perennial: it may persist a couple of years but often needs replacing, and green broadleaf types handle the conditions better than the tender variegated forms.

crops.description_seasoned: Sage (Salvia officinalis), also called common, garden, or culinary sage, is a woody Mediterranean perennial subshrub in the mint family, grown for its aromatic, pebbly-textured, gray-green leaves used fresh or dried in cooking. This is the culinary kitchen sage, not the ornamental bedding salvias (such as scarlet or mealycup sage) sold as annual flowers. It carries short spikes of blue-purple flowers in early summer that bees and butterflies love, but the leaves are the crop, and many cooks pinch the flower spikes to keep the foliage flavorful. Sage thrives on lean treatment: full sun, poor to average well-drained soil, and little water or feeding. It is one of the hardier culinary herbs, reliably perennial in much of the country, but it is short-lived and turns woody and sprawling with age, so plan to replace plants every few years and prune each spring to slow the decline. Overwatering and humid heat, not cold, are what usually kill it, through root and stem rot.
crops.description_beginner: Sage is a small woody herb with soft gray-green leaves that you use in cooking, fresh or dried. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor well-drained soil, and not much water. This is kitchen sage (Salvia officinalis), not the colorful flower salvias sold as annuals. It makes pretty blue-purple flower spikes in early summer that bees love, but you grow it for the leaves, so many people snip the flowers off. Sage is one of the tougher herbs and comes back year after year in much of the country, but plants get woody and leggy after a few years, so trim it each spring and plan to replace it every few years. Too much water or hot, muggy weather, not cold, is what usually rots and kills it.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest sage leaves and sprigs as needed once the plant is growing well. Harvest lightly the first year while the plant establishes, then cut more freely. Flavor is strongest in new growth from spring into early summer and just before flowering, so that is the best window for drying. Cut sprigs about 6 to 8 inches from the tips, taking no more than about half the plant at once, and harvest in mid-morning after the dew dries, when leaf oils are highest. On evergreen plants in mild climates you can pick a few leaves any time of year.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Snip sage leaves and sprigs whenever you cook once the plant is growing well. Go easy the first year, then cut more freely. The flavor is best on fresh spring and early-summer growth and just before it flowers, which is also the best time to cut some for drying. Take sprigs about 6 to 8 inches from the top, never more than about half the plant at once, and cut in mid-morning after the dew dries for the strongest flavor. In mild climates sage stays leafy, so you can pick a few leaves any time.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Common sage (Salvia officinalis) is hardy in roughly USDA zones 4 to 8, one of the hardier culinary herbs, and reliably perennial through much of the country. It is short-lived even so, turning woody and sprawling within a few years, so plan to replace plants every three to five years and prune each spring to slow the decline. Green-leaved types are the hardiest; variegated forms (Tricolor, golden Icterina, purple Purpurascens) are progressively more tender. In the coldest zones (zone 3 and marginal zone 4) and in humid subtropical heat, sage is short-lived or best grown as an annual or a bring-in container plant.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Sage is one of the tougher herbs and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 4 to 8). Even so, plants get woody and leggy within a few years, so trim them each spring and plan to replace them every few years. The plain green kinds are the hardiest; the colorful variegated types are less cold-hardy. In the very coldest areas and in hot, muggy climates, sage is short-lived, so many people grow it for a season or in a pot they can bring inside for winter.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the first year, focus on establishment: water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper off, and harvest lightly so the plant can build a bushy framework. Pinch to shape rather than cutting hard. Sage reaches good harvesting size by about the second year and produces best from then until it turns woody.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about getting the plant established. Water it fairly regularly until it takes hold, then cut back on water, and only harvest a little so it can fill out. Sage reaches a good size by about the second year, and that is when it really starts producing.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Choose the sunniest, best-draining spot you have. Sage wants lean, well-drained soil, so work in only a little coarse compost and skip heavy fertility. On heavy clay, improve drainage with a raised bed or mound rather than digging sand into the clay, which can make drainage worse. The goal is dry feet, not rich ground.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick the sunniest spot with the best drainage. Mix a little coarse compost into the top of the soil, but keep it lean. If your ground is heavy clay, plant sage in a raised bed or mound instead, because that drains better. The goal is dry, well-drained soil, not rich soil.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Sage makes blue-purple flower spikes in early summer, sooner in warm areas and later in cold ones. Since you grow it for the leaves, flowering is up to you: the leaves taste best just before it blooms, so many people snip the flowers off, while others leave them for the bees. When yours blooms depends on where you live.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Sage carries short spikes of blue-purple flowers in early summer, a little earlier in warm regions and later in cold ones. It is grown for its leaves, so flowering is optional; leaf flavor peaks just before bloom, and many cooks pinch the spikes, while others leave them for bees and butterflies. Exact timing shifts with your region and is set per zone.

dormancy_window.note_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, sage slows and holds much of its gray foliage as a semi-evergreen. Stop watering and feeding, leave hard pruning for spring, and protect tender variegated types or move container plants under cover. A dormant plant needs almost no water, and it is wet soil, not the cold itself, that usually rots or kills it over winter.
dormancy_window.note_beginner: Where winters freeze, sage mostly stops growing but keeps a lot of its gray leaves. Stop watering and feeding it, save any big trim for spring, and in cold areas shelter the tender variegated kinds or bring pots somewhere protected. A resting plant barely needs water, and it is usually soggy soil, not the cold, that kills sage over winter.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Sage is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer partner. It is grown for its leaves, not fruit or seed, so no cross-pollination planning is required. Its blue-purple flowers are highly attractive to bees and butterflies if left to bloom.
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one sage plant, and it does not need a partner plant. You grow it for the leaves, so pollination does not matter for your harvest. Bees and butterflies love the flowers if you let it bloom, which is a nice bonus.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: Prune sage hard in spring as new growth breaks, cutting leggy stems back but never into the bare old wood, which resprouts poorly. Follow with light trims and sprig harvests through the season, and remove spent flower stems after bloom. This yearly renewal keeps the plant compact and flavorful and slows the woody decline, but sage is short-lived, so plan to replace plants every few years.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Trim sage back each spring when new growth appears, cutting the leggy stems but not down into the hard woody base, which will not grow back well. Keep it tidy with light trims and by snipping sprigs through the season, and cut off the old flower stems after it blooms. This keeps sage bushy and tasty, but plants still get woody after a few years and are worth replacing.

crops.name: Eggplant / Aubergine

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Eggplant wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter, and above all a soil that warms early and stays warm. As a heat-loving crop it sulks in cold, wet ground, so a sandy loam that warms quickly in spring suits it better than a heavy, slow-warming clay. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, and on heavy or cool soils many growers lay black plastic or fabric mulch to raise soil temperature and set transplants into warmer ground. Steady moisture in a soil that drains freely is the target, since soggy roots stall this warmth-demanding plant and invite the soilborne wilts it is prone to.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Eggplant likes rich, well-drained soil that warms up well in the sun, since it is a heat-loving plant that hates cold, soggy ground. Mix in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch laid down before planting warms the soil and gives eggplant the head start it wants. Aim for soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged.

ph.note_seasoned: Eggplant grows best at a soil pH of about 5.5 to 6.8, with a sweet spot near 6.0 to 6.5 where the nutrients it needs stay most available. It tolerates a somewhat wider band, up to roughly 7.5, but uptake of iron, manganese, and other micronutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline, showing up as yellowing between the veins of younger leaves. Alkaline soils common across the interior West often need sulfur worked in before planting; most Eastern and Midwestern soils sit naturally near the target. A simple soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant.
ph.note_beginner: Eggplant likes slightly acidic soil, about pH 5.5 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where eggplant takes up nutrients best. If your soil runs alkaline (common in the dry interior West), you may need to add sulfur before planting. An inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress at fruit set
fertilizer.type: Balanced at planting, then nitrogen at fruit set
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress when the first fruits set
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 at planting, then calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) as a side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Eggplant is a moderately heavy feeder over a long season. Work a complete fertilizer such as 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen once the first fruits have set and again three to four weeks later through the harvest. Hold the nitrogen back before fruit set, since too much early on drives leafy growth and few flowers; the time to push it is after the plant starts carrying fruit. Pair feeding with steady moisture, because fertilizer only helps a plant that is not also drought-stressed.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Eggplant grows for a long time and likes steady feeding, but the timing matters. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the soil before you plant. Then wait: once the first little eggplants have set, feed with a nitrogen fertilizer, and again a few weeks later. Going heavy on fertilizer too early gives you a big leafy plant with few flowers, so save the feeding for after the fruit starts forming.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your eggplant has set its first fruit, time to side-dress with nitrogen to keep production going through the season.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your eggplant is setting fruit. Feed it now with a nitrogen fertilizer to keep it producing.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress (for example calcium nitrate, 15.5-0-0) once fruit sets. Avoid heavy nitrogen before fruit set, which gives leaf at the expense of flowers.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then switch to a nitrogen feed once the fruit sets. Do not overdo the nitrogen early or you get all leaves and no eggplants.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common rate is 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before transplanting, then a side-dress of about 0.5 pound of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 100 square feet once the first fruits set, repeated every three to four weeks through harvest, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet (or a few inches of compost) into the soil before planting. Then, once fruit has set, scratch a nitrogen fertilizer into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in, repeating every three to four weeks.

companions.note_seasoned: Most eggplant companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on target its two signature problems: flea beetles and the Colorado potato beetle. Aromatic herbs and a border of nasturtium or marigold are the classic deflectors, drawing or repelling flea beetles and aphids off the crop, while bush beans both fix a little nitrogen and serve as a noted trap for the potato beetle. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep eggplant away from its Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes, which share its full pest and disease complex, including verticillium wilt and the flea beetle.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful eggplant companions help with its two biggest pests, flea beetles and Colorado potato beetles. Aromatic herbs and a ring of nasturtiums or marigolds can draw or shoo those pests away, and bush beans add a little nitrogen. The one rule that really matters is to keep eggplant away from tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes, which are all close relatives and share the same pests and soil diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Bush beans add a little nitrogen to the soil and can lure Colorado potato beetles away from your eggplant. A good, traditional neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Legumes fix a little nitrogen the long-feeding eggplant appreciates, and bush beans are a noted trap host for the Colorado potato beetle, helping pull it off the crop. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation is a documented mechanism; the bean-eggplant adjacency benefit is traditional, not pair-isolated. Bush beans are also a noted trap host for the Colorado potato beetle that favors eggplant.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near eggplant to lure flea beetles and aphids away from the crop. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted around solanaceous crops as a trap and deterrent for flea beetles and aphids, drawing them off the eggplant. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-eggplant effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep eggplant away from tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes. They are all close relatives that share the same pests and soil diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share eggplant's full pest and disease complex, including flea beetle, Colorado potato beetle, verticillium and bacterial wilt, and the blights. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 to 4 year cycle.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from eggplant and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong T1 mechanism for an eggplant-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny shot-hole punctures riddle the leaves, a scatter of small round holes that is the classic flea-beetle signature on eggplant. Damage is by far most severe on seedlings and young transplants, whose small leaf area a heavy infestation can shred or kill outright; established plants tolerate considerable feeding. Brush a plant and the small dark beetles spring away like fleas.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The leaves are peppered with lots of tiny round holes, as if hit by birdshot. It hits young plants hardest and can devastate seedlings. Touch the plant and you will see tiny dark beetles jump away.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several Epitrix flea beetle species that feed on eggplant foliage, overwintering as adults in debris and emerging to attack the earliest, most vulnerable plants in spring. Eggplant is a strongly preferred host, and the beetles concentrate on it, which is why flea beetles are the defining early-season eggplant pest.
pests.cause_beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas and chew tiny holes in the leaves. They are most active in spring and love eggplant, so they target young plants early in the season.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover until they are large and vigorous, removing it at flowering. Set out stout, well-hardened transplants rather than tiny seedlings so plants can outgrow the damage, and treat heavy early infestations with spinosad or kaolin clay. Mature plants rarely need treatment.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are big and strong, then take it off when they flower. Setting out larger transplants helps them outgrow the damage. For heavy attacks on seedlings, an organic spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating helps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, delay setting plants out until the soil and air are warm so they grow away fast, and clean up crop debris and weeds that harbor overwintering adults. A nasturtium or other trap planting at the bed edge can draw beetles off the crop.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants early with row cover, set out larger transplants into warm soil so they grow quickly, and clear away weeds and old plant debris where the beetles hide over winter. A border of nasturtiums can lure them away.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear away weeds and old crop debris at the end of the season. The beetles spend the winter as adults tucked into that litter, then come out in spring aimed at your youngest plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Adults overwinter in crop debris and weedy cover, so removing both lowers the spring emergence that lands on the earliest transplants; eggplant is a strongly preferred host, which is why the pressure concentrates here.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant a border of nasturtiums at the edge of the bed. The beetles find them attractive and can be lured off the eggplant. Treat the patch as a sacrifice rather than part of the crop, and see this method's cautions for when it must be dealt with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A nasturtium or other preferred trap planting at the bed margin can draw beetles off the crop by preference rather than by treating them. Its value hinges on the removal step in this method's cautions; a loaded patch left standing holds beetles beside the crop instead of away from it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover the plants with floating row cover, a light fabric that lets light and water through while keeping the beetles out, from planting day until the flowers open. Then take it off so pollination can happen.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover from transplanting excludes the overwintered adults through the window when leaf area is smallest and a heavy infestation can shred or kill seedlings outright; remove it at flowering.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For a heavy attack on young plants, coat the leaves with kaolin clay, a fine white mineral powder mixed with water and sprayed on. The chalky film helps put the beetles off feeding.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A kaolin particle film is one of the two treatments the guidance reserves for heavy early infestations; established plants tolerate considerable feeding, so this is a seedling-stage tool.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spinosad, an organic spray made by a soil microbe, is for a heavy infestation that is tearing up seedlings. Mature plants rarely need any treatment at all.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reserve spinosad for heavy early pressure on seedlings and young transplants; mature plants rarely need treatment, so the spray window is the establishment period, not the season.

pests.name: Colorado potato beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Rounded yellow-and-black-striped adults and humpbacked, brick-red larvae with rows of black spots chew the leaves, and eggplant is a favorite host. Both stages feed voraciously and populations build fast, so an unmanaged infestation can defoliate plants and cut yield sharply. Look for clusters of orange-yellow eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Striped yellow-and-black beetles and plump red larvae with black spots eat the leaves, sometimes stripping a plant bare. Eggplant is one of their favorite foods. Check the undersides of leaves for clusters of orange-yellow eggs.
pests.cause_seasoned: Leptinotarsa decemlineata, a Solanaceae specialist that prefers potato and eggplant. Adults overwinter in the soil and nearby debris and move in as plants establish; left alone they go through multiple generations a season and quickly resist many insecticides, making non-chemical control important.
pests.cause_beginner: A striped beetle whose larvae and adults both feed on eggplant and potato leaves. They overwinter in the soil, show up as plants get going, and multiply quickly through the summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: In a home garden, hand-pick adults, larvae, and egg clusters daily into soapy water, which keeps small plantings clean. Crush egg masses on leaf undersides, and where pressure is high apply spinosad or Bacillus thuringiensis var. tenebrionis to young larvae. Rotating away from last year's nightshade bed cuts the overwintered population.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the beetles, larvae, and egg clusters off by hand and drop them in soapy water, checking every day or two. Squash the orange egg clusters under the leaves. For heavy infestations, an organic spray such as spinosad or Bt (the tenebrionis strain) works on the young larvae.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rotate eggplant well away from where potatoes, tomatoes, or eggplant grew last year, since the overwintered adults emerge near old hosts. Row cover on young plants excludes the colonizers, and a thick straw mulch hinders the adults that walk in from the soil.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not plant eggplant where potatoes, tomatoes, or eggplant grew last year, since the beetles come up from the soil there. Cover young plants with row cover, and a thick straw mulch makes it harder for the beetles to reach them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant eggplant away from wherever potatoes, tomatoes, or eggplant grew last year. The beetles spend winter in the soil near their old food plants and come up right where they left off.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Overwintered adults emerge near last season's nightshade hosts, so rotating well away from the previous solanaceous bed cuts the population that moves straight onto establishing plants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover young plants with floating row cover, a light fabric that keeps the beetles off the leaves while letting light and water through.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cover on young plants excludes the colonizing adults during establishment; it pairs with rotation, since emergence is heaviest near old host ground.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off the striped adults, the plump red larvae, and the orange-yellow egg clusters under the leaves and drop them into soapy water, checking every day or two. Squash any egg masses you find. This keeps a small planting clean.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Daily handpicking of adults, larvae, and egg masses keeps small plantings clean, and crushing egg clusters on leaf undersides stops each generation before it feeds. Populations build fast and the species quickly resists many insecticides, which is what makes this the workhorse rung.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where the plants are still crawling despite picking, spinosad, an organic spray made by a soil microbe, works on the young larvae. Aim it at the small ones rather than the full-grown beetles.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Apply spinosad to young larvae where pressure runs high; the species' record of developing resistance to many insecticides is the argument for leaning on the non-chemical rungs first.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often green peach aphid, cluster on growing tips and leaf undersides, causing leaves to curl, pucker, and yellow, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit mosaic and other viruses that mottle and distort the foliage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft green or black insects gather on new growth and the undersides of leaves, making them curl and yellow, often with a sticky film and black mold. They can also spread plant viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species, predominantly green peach aphid, that suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on soft, over-fertilized growth. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold that shades the leaves.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that multiply quickly in warm weather, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. The sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on nitrogen fertilizer. The soft, lush growth that heavy feeding pushes out is exactly what aphids multiply on fastest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen drives the succulent growth aphids favor, so moderating feeding slows colony buildup on growing tips and leaf undersides in warm weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay reflective mulch, a silvery sheet, around young plants. The bounced light puts arriving aphids off landing while the plants are small.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants, which carries extra weight here because the aphids involved transmit the mosaic viruses that mottle and distort foliage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the colonies off with a strong jet of water from the hose, aiming at the new growth and the undersides of the leaves. Repeat every few days.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A strong jet against the leaf undersides breaks colonies up faster than they can reorganize; repeat the pass every few days through warm spells, when reproduction runs quickest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Aphids have plenty of enemies, from ladybugs and lacewings to tiny parasitic wasps, and those helpers usually bring an outbreak down on their own. Give them the chance by not spraying everything in sight.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserved ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually bring aphids under control without intervention; broad sprays strip that pressure out, so support the natural enemies rather than spraying broadly.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the colonies keep growing, spray insecticidal soap, wetting the undersides of the leaves where the aphids sit. It works only where it touches them, so repeat every few days.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is contact-only, so thorough coverage of leaf undersides governs the outcome; repeat every few days to catch the colonies rebuilding between passes.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil, is the other choice at this step. It also works only on contact, so coat the undersides of the leaves well and repeat as with soap.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil is the alternative contact material and carries the same underside-coverage demand and repeat interval as soap, rather than any residual activity.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine yellow stippling speckles the leaves, which may bronze, dry, and drop, and in bad infestations fine webbing appears on leaf undersides. Two-spotted spider mites thrive in hot, dry weather, exactly the conditions eggplant is grown in, so mite pressure often peaks in midsummer.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The leaves look dusty or speckled with tiny yellow dots, and in bad cases you see fine webbing underneath. The leaves can bronze and dry out. Mites love hot, dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related mites that feed on the lower leaf surfaces with piercing mouthparts. Populations explode in heat and drought and on dusty, water-stressed plants, and can build quickly on eggplant in summer.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny mites, almost too small to see, that feed on the undersides of leaves and thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions. They build up fast in summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray the leaf undersides with a strong jet of water repeatedly to disrupt colonies, then apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil to the undersides, repeating every few days. Keeping plants well watered and raising humidity discourages mites; predatory mites help under heavy pressure.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water every day for a week, then follow up with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if needed. Keeping plants well watered helps, since stressed plants are hit hardest.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well watered in hot weather, since drought-stressed plants are most vulnerable, avoid dusty conditions, and avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill the predators holding mites in check.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep plants well watered in hot weather, hose dust off the leaves now and then, and avoid spraying broad insecticides that kill the helpful bugs that eat mites.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the plants steadily watered through hot weather. Mites hit drought-stressed plants hardest, so a plant kept from drying out badly is a tougher target.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Water stress is the amplifier: populations explode on hot, dry, dusty, drought-stressed plants, so steady moisture through midsummer heat removes the predisposing condition rather than treating the symptom.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water every day for a week. It breaks up the colonies, and hosing dust off the leaves now and then helps too, since mites thrive in dusty conditions.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Repeated forceful water on the leaf undersides disrupts colonies, and the added moisture works against a pest that builds fastest in dry conditions; it is the first pass before reaching for any material.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Helpful insects and mites in the garden eat spider mites. Avoid spraying broad insect killers, which wipe out the helpers that keep mites in check.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Broad-spectrum insecticides remove the predators holding mites in check, so conserving natural enemies is itself a control decision, made mostly by what you choose not to spray.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Under a heavy infestation you can buy predatory mites, tiny mites that hunt the pest ones, and release them onto the affected plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Purchased predatory mites help under heavy pressure once conservation is already in place; release onto an infestation you have actually located rather than ahead of one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If mites persist after the water treatment, spray insecticidal soap on the undersides of the leaves, repeating every few days.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Follow the water passes with soap applied to the lower leaf surfaces where the mites feed, repeating every few days; it acts on contact only.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil, is the other option here. Coat the undersides of the leaves well and repeat if needed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil is the alternate contact material against the same underside-feeding colonies; coverage and repetition, not residue, do the work.

pests.name: Eggplant lace bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves develop a pale, yellow-stippled or bleached look on top, while the undersides carry dark, varnish-like specks of excrement and the small, lacy-winged adults and spiny nymphs. Heavy feeding browns and curls the foliage and can stunt the plant, and lace bugs are fairly eggplant-specific.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The tops of the leaves look pale and stippled, and underneath you find dark sticky specks and small insects with lacy-looking wings. Bad infestations brown and curl the leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: The eggplant lace bug (Gargaphia solani), a true bug that feeds in colonies on leaf undersides with piercing-sucking mouthparts. It overwinters in debris and is most damaging in warm weather, with several generations a season.
pests.cause_beginner: A small flat insect with lacy wings that feeds in groups on the undersides of eggplant leaves, sucking out the juices. It is most active in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Scout leaf undersides early and treat colonies directly with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, which reach the soft nymphs, covering the undersides thoroughly and repeating as needed. Remove and destroy the worst-infested leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Check the undersides of the leaves and spray any colonies directly with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, making sure to coat underneath. Pick off and destroy the most badly affected leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clean up crop debris at season's end to remove overwintering sites, rotate eggplant, and scout the undersides of lower leaves from early in the season so colonies are caught while small.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear away old plants at the end of the season, move eggplant to a new spot each year, and check the undersides of the lower leaves early so you catch the bugs before they spread.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move eggplant to a new spot each year so the bugs that wintered near last year's bed do not start the season on top of your plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotating the planting separates the crop from lace bugs overwintering in debris around last season's bed, and since the pest is fairly eggplant-specific, the move counts for more than it would against a generalist.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear out the old plants at the end of the season, since the bugs spend winter in that debris. During the season, pick off and destroy the leaves carrying the worst colonies.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: End-of-season debris removal takes out the overwintering sites; in season, removing the worst-infested leaves culls whole underside colonies of adults and nymphs at once.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Check the undersides of the lower leaves from early in the season, and spray any colonies you find directly with insecticidal soap, making sure to coat underneath where the bugs feed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap reaches the soft nymphs when applied directly to the underside colonies; scouting lower leaves early catches colonies while they are small, and thorough underside coverage plus repetition decide the result.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil, works the same way at this step. Coat the undersides of the leaves and repeat if the bugs return.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil is the alternative contact material against the nymph colonies, with the same demand for thorough underside coverage and repeat passes as needed.

pests.name: Hornworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large sections of leaf, and sometimes whole shoots, are stripped down to the veins overnight, with dark pellet droppings on the leaves below. The culprits are big green tomato or tobacco hornworms, up to four inches long, that blend into the stems and are easiest to find by their frass.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Whole leaves vanish overnight, leaving just the veins, with dark droppings on the leaves below. The cause is a large green caterpillar that hides against the stems, easier to spot by its droppings than by sight.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tomato and tobacco hornworms, the larvae of large sphinx moths, which feed on solanaceous foliage including eggplant from midsummer on. A few caterpillars can do conspicuous damage given their size.
pests.cause_beginner: Big green caterpillars, the young of large moths, that feed on eggplant and tomato leaves mostly in mid to late summer. Even a few can strip a lot of foliage.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick the caterpillars, which is effective in a home garden, and apply Bacillus thuringiensis to younger larvae where numbers are high. Leave any hornworm studded with white parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the wasps will kill it and breed more.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them in soapy water. If you find one covered in small white capsules, leave it, those are parasitic wasps that will do the work for you. An organic Bt spray works on the smaller caterpillars.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till the soil in fall to destroy overwintering pupae, scout for frass and stripped leaves from midsummer, and encourage the parasitic wasps and other natural enemies that keep hornworms in check.
pests.prevention_beginner: Turn the soil at the end of the season to destroy the pupae, watch for droppings and missing leaves from midsummer, and welcome the helpful wasps that attack hornworms.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Turn the soil over in fall once the plants come out. The caterpillars pass the winter underground as pupae, the resting stage between caterpillar and moth, and tilling destroys them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Fall tillage destroys overwintering pupae in the bed, trimming the local carryover before the next summer's moths emerge.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the big caterpillars off by hand and drop them into soapy water. They blend into the stems, so look for the dark droppings, called frass, on the leaves below and search just above that spot.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Handpicking is effective at home-garden scale; frass on lower leaves locates larvae far more reliably than scanning the stems they match.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If you find a hornworm covered in small white capsules, leave it right where it is. Those are the cocoons of parasitic wasps that will kill it and go on to attack other hornworms.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Leave any larva studded with parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the emerging wasps kill it and breed more; encouraging these natural enemies is part of what keeps hornworm numbers in check.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When there are more caterpillars than you can pick, Bt, short for Bacillus thuringiensis, is an organic spray that works on the smaller, younger ones.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Apply Bt where numbers run high, aimed at younger larvae; it is the material for small caterpillars, with handpicking covering the full-grown ones.

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Lower and outer leaves yellow, often in a wedge or one-sided pattern, then wilt, brown, and drop, working upward as the plant stunts and fails to size its fruit. A cut through a wilting stem shows tan-to-brown streaking in the water-conducting tissue. It is the most common and damaging eggplant disease in much of the country.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves turn yellow and wilt, often on one side of the plant first, then brown and drop while the plant stunts. Cut a wilting stem and you may see brown streaks inside. It is the most common serious eggplant disease.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Verticillium dahliae, a soilborne fungus that infects the roots and clogs the vascular system, so the plant wilts despite moist soil. It persists in soil for years as resting structures, has a wide host range across the Solanaceae and many other crops, and is favored by cool-to-moderate soil temperatures.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that infects the roots and blocks the plant's water pipes, so it wilts even when watered. It lives in the soil for years and attacks many crops, especially the nightshade family.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy affected plants. Management is preventive and centered on rotation and resistant or grafted plants, since the fungus cannot be eradicated from infested soil by home-garden means.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real answer is prevention: rotate your crops and choose resistant or grafted plants next time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Do not plant eggplant where verticillium-susceptible crops (tomato, pepper, potato, eggplant, and many others) have grown, rotate on a long cycle, choose tolerant varieties or grafted plants on resistant rootstock, and keep plants vigorous with steady water and balanced feeding. Solarizing infested beds can lower inoculum.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant eggplant in soil with no recent history of the disease, rotate away from tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes, and look for resistant or grafted plants. Keeping plants healthy with steady water and feeding helps them cope.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When you buy seed or plants, look for varieties described as tolerant of verticillium. There is no cure once a plant is infected, so the choice you make before planting carries most of the weight.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Tolerant cultivars are a core preventive move against a pathogen that cannot be cured in the plant or cleared from infested soil by home-garden means; note the sources say tolerant, not immune.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Another option is a grafted plant, the variety you want joined onto roots bred to resist the disease. It lets you keep growing eggplant on ground where the fungus is already present.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Grafting onto resistant rootstock keeps the fruiting variety while swapping out the root system the soilborne fungus infects, the practical route on ground already carrying inoculum.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant eggplant in ground that has not recently grown tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or eggplant, and keep the break long. The fungus lives on in the soil for years.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The fungus persists for years as resting structures with a wide host range across the Solanaceae and many other crops, so only a long rotation away from susceptible hosts meaningfully lowers exposure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull out and destroy any plant that wilts with it. It will not recover, and removing it is the one useful thing left to do that season.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Infected plants do not recover, so remove and destroy them; in-season management ends there, which is why the weight of this ladder sits on the preventive rungs.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where a bed is known to carry the fungus, solarizing, covering moist soil with clear plastic through the hottest weeks so the sun heats it, can lower the amount of disease in the soil.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Solarizing an infested bed can lower inoculum ahead of replanting; it lowers the population rather than clearing it, so it backs up rotation and resistant or grafted plantings rather than replacing them.

diseases.name: Phomopsis blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale, sunken spots appear on the fruit that rapidly enlarge to soft, spongy, rotting areas, sometimes shrinking the fruit into a dry mummy; the disease also causes grayish leaf spots and a collar rot that can break young stems an inch or two above the soil line. It is most damaging in warm, wet weather and toward fall.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale sunken spots on the fruit spread quickly into soft, rotting patches, and the disease can also spot the leaves and rot the stem near the base. It is worst in warm, wet weather and later in the season.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phomopsis vexans, a fungus that is both soil- and seedborne and overwinters on crop debris. Warm, humid conditions and splashing water spread it, and infected seed or volunteer debris often starts an outbreak, so clean seed and rotation are central to control.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus carried on seed and in old plant debris that spreads in warm, wet weather. It can come in on infected seed, so starting clean matters.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy infected fruit and plants promptly to limit spread, and where the disease is active apply a labeled fungicide, keeping foliage and fruit as dry as possible. There is no rescue for badly rotted fruit.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away infected fruit and plants right away. Keep the leaves and fruit dry by watering at the soil, and use a labeled fungicide if it is spreading. Rotted fruit cannot be saved.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, treated, or resistant seed and disease-free transplants, rotate eggplant out of the bed for about four years, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, and remove crop debris at season's end.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed and healthy transplants, do not plant eggplant in the same spot for about four years, water at the soil instead of over the leaves, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with clean seed and healthy, disease-free transplants. This fungus can ride in on the seed itself, so an outbreak is sometimes planted right along with the crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogen is seedborne as well as soilborne, and infected seed often starts an outbreak, so clean or treated seed and disease-free transplants are the first control point, set at purchase.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Seed sold as resistant to this disease is one of the clean-start options worth looking for when you buy.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resistant seed sits alongside clean and treated seed in the guidance; it is a decision made at purchase, before anything else on this ladder applies.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep eggplant out of the same bed for about four years. The fungus survives on old plant debris in the ground.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A rotation of about four years lets debris-borne inoculum decline; volunteer debris can start an outbreak, so the gap only counts if the bed is genuinely clear of it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water the soil at the base of the plants instead of over the leaves, and keep the leaves and fruit as dry as you can. The disease spreads in splashing water and warm, wet weather.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soil-directed watering removes the splash that spreads the fungus and shortens the warm, humid wetness periods that drive it, which matter most toward fall when the disease peaks.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spread mulch under the plants so rain cannot splash soil, which can carry the fungus, up onto the leaves and fruit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A mulch layer intercepts splash off infested soil and residue, cutting the inoculum that reaches foliage and fruit by that route.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Space the plants so air moves between them and wet leaves dry quickly. Warm, wet conditions are what this disease runs on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spacing for airflow shortens leaf and fruit wetness, working directly against the warm, humid conditions that favor infection.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off and throw away any fruit with pale sunken spots as soon as you see it, pull plants that are badly hit, and clear all the old plants out at the end of the season. Rotted fruit cannot be saved.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt removal of infected fruit and plants limits spread, and stripping crop debris at season's end removes the overwintering substrate; there is no rescue for badly rotted fruit, so removal is the in-season play.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Individual leaves, then whole plants, wilt and collapse suddenly even though the soil is moist, with little of the yellowing that precedes verticillium. Cut low on the stem and the pith is discolored reddish-brown; suspended in clear water, a cut stem streams milky bacterial ooze. It is most serious in hot, wet soils of the South.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant wilts and collapses suddenly even though the soil is wet, without much yellowing first. If you cut the stem near the base, the inside looks brown, and a cut stem held in a glass of water gives off milky strands. It is mainly a problem in the hot, wet South.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Ralstonia solanacearum, a soilborne bacterium that invades the roots and plugs the vascular tissue. It survives in soil and infected debris, spreads in water and on tools, and is favored by high soil temperature and moisture, so it is most damaging in warm, wet regions.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil bacterium that gets into the roots and blocks the plant's water flow, so it wilts fast. It lives in warm, wet soil and spreads in water and on tools.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure; remove and destroy wilted plants promptly to limit spread, and disinfect tools. Because it persists in soil, management is preventive, through rotation, resistant or grafted plants, and improved drainage.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure, so pull and destroy any plant that wilts from it, and clean your tools. The real fix is prevention next season.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid planting eggplant where tomato, potato, or eggplant grew in the previous three years, choose resistant varieties or graft onto resistant rootstock in problem areas, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil or working among wet plants.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not plant eggplant where tomatoes, potatoes, or eggplant grew in the last three years, improve drainage in wet spots, and look for resistant or grafted plants if this disease is common where you live.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If this disease is common where you live, look for varieties described as resistant. There is no cure once a plant has it, so what you plant matters more than anything you can do afterward.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: In problem areas, resistant varieties lead the program against a soilborne bacterium that cannot be cured in the plant; everything after infection is containment.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A grafted plant, your chosen variety joined onto resistant roots, is the other way to keep growing eggplant in ground that carries the disease.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Grafting onto resistant rootstock keeps the fruiting variety while replacing the roots the bacterium invades, the practical route where the soil is already infested.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not plant eggplant where tomatoes, potatoes, or eggplant grew in the last three years. The bacterium lives on in the soil and in old infected plant matter.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Keep eggplant off ground that carried tomato, potato, or eggplant within the previous three years; the bacterium persists in soil and infected debris and is favored where soils run hot and wet.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Improve the drainage in wet spots before planting. The bacterium does best in hot, wet soil, so ground that drains freely works against it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: High soil moisture and temperature favor the pathogen, so drainage work on heavy or low-lying ground removes part of what makes a bed conducive.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stay out of the bed while the plants are wet, and avoid tracking soil from a spot where plants have wilted into a clean one. The bacterium travels in water and on tools.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The bacterium spreads in water and on tools, so work the planting when it is dry, and avoid moving infested soil between beds; timing your chores is itself part of the control.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull and destroy any plant that wilts and collapses with it, then clean your tools before touching anything else. Removing sick plants quickly is what limits the spread.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt removal and destruction of wilted plants, with tools disinfected afterward, limits spread from a plant that cannot be saved; in-season management is containment, not rescue.

diseases.name: Phytophthora blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, water-soaked lesions and streaking develop on stems, leaves, or fruit, and a plant can collapse and die rapidly once the stem is girdled. Fruit rots with a firm, sometimes white-cottony decay. It flares in warm, wet, poorly drained conditions and after heavy rain or flooding.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, wet-looking patches appear on the stems, leaves, or fruit, and the plant can wilt and die quickly. The fruit can rot, sometimes with white fuzzy growth. It strikes in warm, wet, poorly drained ground.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora species (such as P. capsici and P. nicotianae), water molds that thrive in saturated soil and spread in splashing and running water. They survive in soil and debris and move fast in warm, wet weather, especially on heavy or poorly drained ground.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that lives in wet soil and spreads in splashing water, attacking plants in warm, soggy conditions. It moves fast once it starts.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected plants and fruit promptly, and improve drainage immediately. There is no effective home-garden cure once plants collapse, so control is preventive and drainage-based.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pull and destroy affected plants and fruit, and fix the drainage. There is no good home cure once it takes hold, so prevention is what matters.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Keeping soil moisture from getting excessive is a key strategy for managing Phytophthora. Water often enough to keep the soil moist but not saturated. Use drip irrigation rather than overhead watering, or water at the base of the plants and keep the leaves as dry as possible. Don't plant eggplant where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or eggplant grew in the last three years, since the pathogen survives in soil. The pathogen's broad host range, which includes tomato, beans and most cucurbits, makes rotation much less effective. Rotate to cereals such as corn or wheat, which are not hosts.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Too much water in the soil makes this disease worse, so keep the soil moist but not soggy. Water with a drip line if you can, or water at the base of the plants and keep the leaves dry. Don't plant eggplant where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or eggplant grew in the last three years. This disease also attacks tomatoes, beans and most squash and melons, so rotating crops helps less against it. Corn and wheat don't get it, so they are good crops to plant in that spot instead.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant on raised beds or mounds so water drains away fast, and avoid the low spots that stay soggy after rain. This disease lives in wet soil, so drainage is the main defense.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Raised, well-drained beds and avoiding low ground deny these water molds the saturated soil they need; once plants collapse there is no effective home-garden cure, so drainage is where control actually lives.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water the soil rather than showering the plants from above. The disease spreads in splashing and running water.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soil-directed irrigation removes the splash and surface flow that carry the pathogen through a warm, wet bed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Mulch under the plants so rain cannot splash infested soil up onto the stems, leaves, and fruit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mulch intercepts splash off infested soil, one of the routes by which the pathogen reaches stems, foliage, and fruit above the soil line.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rotate eggplant away from beds that grew peppers, tomatoes, or squash-family crops. The disease survives in the soil and in old plant debris.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotation off solanaceous and cucurbit hosts matters because the pathogen survives in soil and debris and flares again whenever warm, saturated conditions return.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull out affected plants and rotting fruit as soon as you see them and get them out of the garden. Once a plant collapses it cannot be saved.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt removal and destruction of affected plants and fruit limits what running and splashing water can spread through the rest of the bed; beyond removal, control is preventive and drainage-based.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Aim for about 1 inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. As a heat-loving plant grown through the hottest part of the year, eggplant transpires heavily in summer, and container plants dry out far faster still.
watering.frequency_beginner: Give eggplant about 1 inch of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day. Plants in pots dry out much faster and may need checking daily in summer.
watering.amount_seasoned: Around 1 inch per week is the working range, leaning higher during flowering and fruit set, wetting the soil to a depth of at least 6 to 8 inches so the roots follow the moisture down. Even, deep watering is what sizes well-shaped fruit; letting the soil swing from dry to soaked stresses the plant and drops blossoms.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, soaking the soil down 6 to 8 inches so the roots grow deep. Keep it even: letting the soil go bone-dry and then flooding it stresses the plant and makes flowers drop.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves favor the leaf spots and fruit rots eggplant is prone to. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so leaves dry before evening. A layer of mulch buffers soil moisture and warmth and blocks soil-borne spores from splashing onto the lower leaves.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, with a soaker hose or by holding the hose at the base. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent disease. If you must use a sprinkler, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off by evening. Mulch helps keep the soil evenly moist and warm.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft, rotting stems or fruit point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil starves the roots of oxygen and invites the Phytophthora and bacterial wilts eggplant is susceptible to, especially on heavy ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or stems and fruit go soft and rotten, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is common in heat and not alarming, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. Drought stress during flowering and fruit set shows up as dropped blossoms and small, misshapen, sometimes bitter fruit.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry, and drought while it is flowering causes dropped blossoms and small, bitter fruit.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep the starting mix evenly moist
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep the seed-starting mix evenly moist and warm through germination; eggplant is heat-loving and slow to sprout, and the surface must not dry mid-emergence.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the seed tray evenly damp and warm while the seeds come up. Eggplant likes it warm and sprouts slowly, so do not let the surface dry out.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep cells evenly moist, never soggy
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Grow seedlings on under lights with even, moderate moisture, easing off between waterings so the mix never stays saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp, not soggy. Let the top begin to dry before watering again.

schedule_by_stage.rate: water in well, then keep evenly moist
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Water in thoroughly at transplant, then hold even moisture at the base as this heat-lover establishes; mulch to buffer soil moisture and warmth.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Soak the plant in well when you set it out, then keep the soil evenly moist as it takes hold. Mulch keeps the moisture and warmth steady.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 inch per week, kept even
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Eggplant wants a steady 1 inch a week soaked 6 to 8 inches deep, leaning higher through flowering and fruit set. Even moisture sets fruit and prevents blossom drop; unlike peppers, eggplant is not prone to blossom-end rot, so the failure mode of dry-wet swings here is dropped blossoms, not fruit rot.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering steady once flowers open, about 1 inch a week soaked in deep. If the soil swings from dry to soaked, the flowers drop off and you get fewer fruit.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 inch per week, never dry
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Fruit set through sizing is the water-critical stretch: steady, deep moisture sizes well-shaped fruit, while a dry-then-flooded swing gives small, bitter, misshapen fruit. Keep the ripening fruit up off wet ground and the soil evenly moist.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the fruit fill out. Letting it dry hard and then soaking it gives small, bitter, oddly shaped fruit, so keep the water steady.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 inch per week, kept even
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep even moisture through the picking weeks; eggplant keeps flowering and setting fruit as you harvest, and steady water keeps the later fruit from turning small and bitter.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering evenly while you pick. Eggplant keeps making new fruit, and steady water keeps them tender instead of small and bitter.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for eggplant, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also prone to leaf spots and fruit and root rots. Keep water on the soil, air moving through the leaves, and the ripening fruit up off wet ground.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for eggplant. It keeps the plant hydrated without encouraging leaf and fruit disease.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The water-critical stretch runs from flowering through fruit set and sizing. Steady moisture here sets and fills well-shaped fruit, while swings between dry and saturated soil drop blossoms and give small, bitter, misshapen fruit. Keep it even once the plant is carrying fruit.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep eggplant evenly watered is when it is flowering and setting fruit. Uneven water now causes dropped flowers and small, bitter fruit, so aim for steady moisture.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest eggplant YOUNG and GLOSSY, while the fruit is immature, not at full size. The single best cue is the skin: a ripe eggplant is firm and has a high, mirror-like gloss, and press the side gently with a thumbnail and the dent springs back. Once the skin turns dull or bronzed, the flesh has gone seedy, spongy, and bitter and the dent stays, the sign you waited too long. Pick large oval types from about 2 inches across up to two-thirds of their mature size, and slender Asian types at finger-to-hot-dog size. Cut the fruit with shears or a knife leaving a short piece of the stem and the green calyx attached, rather than pulling, since the stems are tough and often spiny. Harvest regularly, at least once or twice a week, because picking fruit while immature keeps the plant setting more; fruit left to over-ripen shuts down further production.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick eggplant while it is young and shiny, not when it is biggest. A ready eggplant has firm flesh and a bright, glossy skin, and when you press the side with your thumb the dent springs back. If the skin looks dull instead of shiny, you waited too long: the inside will be seedy, spongy, and bitter. Harvest large oval types when they are firm and glossy and slimmer Asian types at finger or hot-dog size. Cut the fruit off with scissors or a knife, leaving a little stem on, instead of pulling, because the stems are tough and sometimes prickly. Keep picking every few days, since taking the fruit young keeps the plant making more.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Eggplant transplants are especially sensitive to a cold check, so harden off carefully over 7 to 10 days, easing plants into sun and wind, and set them out only once nights stay reliably above 50°F and the soil is thoroughly warm. A transplant chilled below about 50°F sulks for weeks and yields poorly, so it is better to wait a week or two past the tomato date than to plant into cold ground.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Eggplant hates the cold, so harden plants off over about a week to ten days, giving them more time outside each day, and do not set them out until nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm. Planting too early into cold ground stalls eggplant badly, so it pays to wait until it is truly warm, a couple of weeks after you would plant tomatoes.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Start eggplant seeds indoors about 8 weeks before transplanting (UMD uses 8 to 10 week old transplants), with bottom heat of 75 to 85°F for fast, even germination. Eggplant needs a longer, warmer start than tomato and is set out later, once nights hold above 50°F and the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F. Choose sturdy transplants up to a foot tall with stems about pencil thick, and set plant supports at planting. Direct sowing is practical only in the longest, warmest regions; everywhere else this is a transplant crop.
start_method.notes_beginner: Start eggplant seeds indoors about 8 weeks before you plan to plant out, keeping them warm (75 to 85°F) to sprout well. Eggplant needs more warmth and a longer head start than tomatoes, and it goes outside later, only once nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm. Use stocky transplants up to a foot tall, and put a stake or cage in at planting time.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: If you use a saucer, empty it within an hour of watering. Eggplant will not tolerate sitting in standing water, which starves the roots of oxygen and invites root rot. A saucer is useful for holding warmth, which eggplant likes, but the roots must not stay submerged.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of standing water. Empty it soon after watering. A saucer is fine for keeping the pot warm, which eggplant enjoys, but the roots should never sit in pooled water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of potting mix made for containers, not soil dug from the garden, which packs down hard and drains poorly in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer at planting. Pots need feeding more often than beds, because watering washes nutrients out.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a rich, free-draining peat- or coir-based container potting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in about 20 to 25 percent compost plus a slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting. Because frequent watering leaches nutrients, plan to feed a container eggplant more regularly than one in the ground, shifting to nitrogen once fruit sets.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds, so in summer heat a potted eggplant may need water every day. Check daily, and water until it runs from the bottom. Keep it even, since drying out and then flooding drops the flowers.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a potted eggplant more often than a garden plant. Once it is growing strongly and especially once fruit sets, give a balanced liquid feed every week or two.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Eggplant lives for one season and is killed by frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Plant fresh from seed or transplants next year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Eggplant is a frost-tender annual that completes its life in a single season and is killed by the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Pull spent plants at season's end and start fresh the following year.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Eggplant is a great container plant, and pots even help by warming the roots, which this heat-lover enjoys. Use at least a 5-gallon pot, 12 inches deep, one plant per pot, in full sun. Compact varieties like Patio Baby and Fairy Tale are bred for containers, and slim Asian types like Ichiban also do well. Keep it well watered (pots dry fast), feed regularly, and stake or cage the plant so a fruit-laden stem does not topple.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Eggplant is an excellent container crop, and the warmer root zone of a dark pot in sun suits this heat-loving plant. Use a pot of at least 5 gallons (7 is better) and 12 inches deep, one plant per pot, in full sun. Compact, container-bred varieties such as Patio Baby and Fairy Tale, and slender Asian types such as Ichiban, perform best; full-size globe types need the larger pot and a stake. Water consistently, since a small soil volume dries fast and moisture swings drop blossoms, feed regularly because containers leach nutrients, and cage or stake plants to carry the fruit.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and a potted eggplant can need water once or even twice a day in summer heat. Check daily by feeling the top inch of mix, and water until it runs from the drainage holes; even moisture prevents the blossom drop and misshapen fruit that water swings cause.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed container eggplant more often than in-ground plants, since steady watering leaches nutrients. After the slow-release charge at planting, add a balanced liquid feed every 1 to 2 weeks, shifting toward nitrogen once fruit sets.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits eggplant well, smoothing the moisture swings that drop blossoms on this thirsty summer crop. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat, water from below to keep the foliage dry, and occasionally water from the top to flush the salts that concentrate with constant sub-irrigation.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match for eggplant because it keeps the water steady, which helps prevent dropped flowers. Keep the reservoir filled in hot weather, and every so often water from the top too, which rinses out built-up minerals.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A container eggplant wants a deep, sturdy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 5 gallons or more, with a wide enough base that a fruit-laden plant does not tip. Depth for the roots matters more than width. Choose compact or Asian varieties for the smallest pots and give full-size globe types a larger container and a stake.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Give a container eggplant a deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 5 gallons or more, so the roots have room and the plant does not tip over when loaded with fruit. A deep, sturdy pot beats a shallow, light one. Use small or Asian varieties in the smallest pots.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, and eggplant, which share verticillium and bacterial wilt, phomopsis, the flea beetle, and the Colorado potato beetle. These soilborne diseases and overwintering pests build up wherever a nightshade has grown.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant eggplant where you grew tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or eggplant recently. They are all in the same family and share the same soil diseases and pests, which build up and carry over.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (beans, peas), brassicas, sweet corn, alliums (onions, garlic), and leafy greens make good preceding crops, since they do not share the nightshade pest and disease complex, and a legume leaves nitrogen behind for the long-feeding eggplant.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate eggplant on a long cycle, returning it to a given bed no sooner than the fourth year, to break the buildup of verticillium and bacterial wilt, phomopsis (which is also seedborne), and the flea and Colorado potato beetles. The wider Solanaceae, tomato, pepper, and potato, share that complex, so rotate as a group and avoid following any of them. Clear and remove spent plants at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering pest and disease sites.
rotation.note_beginner: Move eggplant to a different part of the garden each year, and do not return it, or its relatives tomato, pepper, and potato, to the same spot for about four years. Soil diseases like verticillium wilt and the pests that bother eggplant build up where nightshades grow, and rotation is the main tool to keep them in check. Clean up old plants at the end of the season too.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Eggplant is a poor keeper and is best used within a day or two of picking, when its texture and mild flavor are at their best. Held at warm room temperature it softens and shrivels quickly, so a cool spot out of direct sun is better for a short hold. Unlike a winter squash, it does not cure or store, so harvest close to when you will cook it.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Eggplant does not keep well, so use it within a day or two for the best texture and flavor. At warm room temperature it goes soft and wrinkled fast, so keep it somewhere cool and out of the sun if you are not cooking it right away.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Eggplant is chilling-sensitive: store it at a medium-cool 45 to 54°F with high humidity for up to about a week, not in the coldest part of the fridge. Below about 50°F for long it develops chilling injury, surface pitting, bronzing, and browning of the seeds and flesh, so a cool pantry or the warmest part of the refrigerator, loosely bagged to hold humidity, beats deep cold. Use within a week.
storage.fridge_beginner: Eggplant does not like the cold. Keep it in the warmest part of the fridge, ideally around 45 to 50°F, loosely bagged so it does not dry out, and use it within a week. Stored too cold for too long it develops pitting and brown spots.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Eggplant does not freeze well raw; the texture turns mushy. To freeze, slice and blanch it or, better, cook it first, for example roast or grill and puree it, then cool and freeze in portions for later dishes. Cooked or breaded-and-cooked eggplant freezes acceptably for a few months.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze raw eggplant, as it turns mushy. Instead cook it first, by roasting or grilling, then cool it and freeze it in portions to use in cooked dishes later. It keeps a few months that way.
storage.notes_seasoned: Treat eggplant as a fresh-use crop, not a storage one. Pick it young and glossy and cook it within a few days. For a short hold, keep it at a medium-cool temperature (about 45 to 54°F) and high humidity, away from the coldest part of the refrigerator, since prolonged cold below 50°F causes chilling injury. Handle gently, as the skin bruises, and keep it away from ethylene-producing fruit, which hastens softening.
