thinning.tip_seasoned: Sow four to five seeds per hill. Once seedlings have two leaves, about a week after they come up, thin to the strongest two plants per hill. In rows, thin to one plant every 24 to 48 inches.
thinning.tip_beginner: Plant four or five seeds in each hill. When the seedlings have two leaves, about a week after they sprout, keep the two strongest in each hill and remove the rest. If you plant in rows, leave one plant every 24 to 48 inches.

drainage.saucer_practice: If you use a saucer, empty it after watering. Watermelon will not tolerate sitting in standing water, which invites wilt and fruit rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good bagged potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer at planting. Pots need feeding more often than beds because watering washes nutrients out.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a rich, free-draining peat- or coir-based potting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in a container.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in some compost plus a slow-release lower-nitrogen fertilizer at planting. Because frequent watering flushes nutrients, plan to feed a container watermelon more regularly than one in the ground, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds. In summer a potted watermelon may need water every day. Check daily and water until it drains from the bottom, but ease off near harvest so the fruit sweetens.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a potted watermelon more often than a garden plant, with a balanced-to-low-nitrogen liquid feed every couple of weeks once it is growing strongly, stopping the heavy nitrogen once melons form.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Watermelon lives for one season and dies with the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Plant new seeds next year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Watermelon is a frost-tender annual that completes its life in a single season and is killed by the first hard frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Pull spent vines at season's end and start fresh from seed the following year.

container_notes.notes_beginner: You can grow a watermelon in a container, but only the small icebox or bush kinds like Sugar Baby or Bush Sugar Baby, since full-size vining watermelons are far too big. Use a large pot, at least 15 gallons and 12 inches deep, put it in full sun, keep it well watered (pots dry out fast), and feed it regularly. Give the vines room to trail out of the pot or up a sturdy trellis, support any fruit on a sling, and water the soil, not the leaves, to help avoid disease.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Watermelon is a marginal container crop because it is a large, long-season, sprawling, heat-hungry vine, but a compact icebox or bush variety such as Sugar Baby or Bush Sugar Baby makes it workable. Choose a small-fruited type and give it a big pot: at least 15 gallons and 12 inches deep, larger is better. Give it full sun and all-day warmth, let the vines trail out over the rim or climb a sturdy trellis with each fruit cradled in a cloth sling, water at the base daily in heat, and feed regularly while easing off nitrogen once fruit sets. The container figures here follow general container-vegetable guidance; watermelon-specific container numbers are modeled.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and a watermelon in a pot can need water once or even twice a day in summer heat. Check daily by feeling the top inch of mix, and water until it runs from the drainage holes; even moisture prevents the small, misshapen fruit that water swings cause, but taper in the final week or two before harvest to concentrate sweetness.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed container watermelon more often than in-ground ones, since steady watering leaches nutrients. After the slow-release charge at planting, add a balanced-to-low-nitrogen liquid feed every 2 to 3 weeks, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets so the plant builds sweet fruit rather than vine.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits a potted watermelon well during vining and sizing, smoothing the moisture swings that cause small, cracked, or hollow fruit. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat and water from below to keep foliage dry. The one caveat is unique to watermelon: in the last week or two before harvest, let it run drier to sweeten the flesh rather than keeping the reservoir full.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot helps while the plant is growing and the fruit is sizing, because it keeps the water steady. Keep the reservoir filled in hot weather. Just let it run a bit dry in the last week or two before you pick, so the melon turns sweet.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A container watermelon needs a wide, deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 15 gallons or more, even for a compact icebox variety, with room for the vines to trail out over the edge or climb a sturdy trellis. Wide and stable beats tall and narrow, since a vining plant in a small pot dries out and tips, and any fruit grown up a trellis needs a cloth sling for support. Choose icebox or bush types for containers, never full-size vining watermelons.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Give a container watermelon a large, deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 15 gallons or more, and let the vines trail out of it or climb a small trellis with each melon held in a sling. A wide, sturdy pot is better than a tall, narrow one. Only grow small icebox or bush watermelon varieties in pots, not the big vining kinds.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid planting watermelon where any cucurbit grew in the last few years, including cucumber, muskmelon, squash, and pumpkin. They share cucumber beetle, the mildews, and especially the soilborne Fusarium wilt and seed- and debris-borne anthracnose and gummy stem blight, which build up in the soil and on residue.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant watermelon where you grew cucumbers, melons, squash, or pumpkins in the last few years. They get the same pests and diseases, which build up in the soil.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, sweet corn, leafy greens, or alliums like onions and garlic make good preceding crops, since they do not share the cucurbit pest and disease complex, and a legume leaves a little nitrogen behind.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate watermelon and its cucurbit relatives on at least a 3 year cycle, and stretch it to five years where Fusarium wilt or anthracnose are established, since the watermelon wilt fungus persists in soil for years and anthracnose and gummy stem blight carry over on debris and seed. A long rotation is the single most important cultural defense against the diseases that limit this crop. Clear and remove spent vines at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering disease sites.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow watermelon or its relatives (cucumbers, melons, squash) in the same spot more than once every 3 years, and wait longer, up to five years, if you have had wilt or anthracnose. Moving them around the garden is the best way to avoid a buildup of disease. Clean up old vines at the end of the season too.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: An uncut, ripe watermelon holds at room temperature for about a week, or 7 to 10 days, kept out of direct sun. Unlike winter squash, it does not improve or keep for months, so plan to eat it within a week or so of picking. Whole melons hold a bit longer in a cool room than a warm one.
storage.room_temp_beginner: A whole, ripe watermelon keeps at room temperature for about a week. It does not store for months like a pumpkin, so eat it within a week or so of picking, and keep it out of direct sun.
storage.fridge_seasoned: A whole watermelon keeps about 2 weeks held cool at around 50 to 60°F, the practical limit before flavor and texture decline; do not store it very cold for long, as watermelon is subject to chilling injury below about 50°F. Once cut, wrap the pieces tightly and refrigerate, using them within 3 to 5 days.
storage.fridge_beginner: A whole watermelon keeps for up to about 2 weeks if held cool, around 50 to 60°F. Do not keep it very cold for a long time, since that harms the flesh. Once you cut it, wrap the pieces and keep them in the fridge, using them within a few days.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Watermelon does not freeze well as chunks, since freezing collapses the crisp texture into mush, but it freezes nicely as puree or juice: blend the flesh, strain if you like, and freeze in portions for slushies, granita, or agua fresca. Frozen cubes also work for chilling drinks.
storage.freezer_beginner: Watermelon turns mushy if you freeze it in chunks, so it is best frozen as juice or puree. Blend the flesh and freeze it in portions for slushies and drinks, or freeze cubes to drop into a glass like ice.
storage.notes_seasoned: Watermelon is an eat-fresh crop, not a keeper, which is why you harvest it only at full ripeness and use it promptly. A whole, sound melon holds about a week at room temperature or up to two weeks held cool near 50 to 60°F, but it will not ripen or sweeten any further off the vine, and very cold storage causes chilling injury. Refrigerate cut pieces wrapped and use within a few days. There is no curing step as there is for winter squash.
storage.notes_beginner: Watermelon is best eaten soon after picking, not stored for the long haul, which is why you wait and harvest it fully ripe. A whole melon keeps about a week at room temperature, or up to two weeks somewhere cool but not cold. It will not get any riper after picking. Once cut, wrap it and keep it in the fridge for a few days.

recommended.name: Sugar Baby
recommended.recommended_note: A classic early icebox watermelon, round and dark green with sweet red flesh, about 8 to 10 pounds. Quick to mature, which makes it the go-to for shorter or cooler-summer gardens and the North. Open-pollinated and seed-saveable.

recommended.name: Crimson Sweet
recommended.recommended_note: The dependable home-garden standard: round-oval, light-and-dark green striped, 15 to 25 pounds, with very sweet red flesh. Carries resistance to anthracnose and Fusarium wilt, which makes it forgiving in the Southeast. Open-pollinated.

recommended.name: Charleston Gray
recommended.recommended_note: The classic long, oblong gray-green watermelon, 20 to 30 pounds, with sweet red flesh, a tough rind, and good heat and drought tolerance plus anthracnose and Fusarium wilt resistance. A strong choice for hot regions and long seasons.

recommended.name: Jubilee
recommended.recommended_note: A large oblong striped watermelon, 25 pounds or more, with crisp, sweet red flesh and Fusarium wilt and anthracnose resistance. A long-season Southern favorite where there is room and heat to finish it.

recommended.name: Yellow Doll
recommended.recommended_note: An early yellow-fleshed icebox hybrid, small at around 5 to 8 pounds, very sweet, and fast to ripen. A good pick for short seasons, small gardens, and gardeners who want something different.

recommended.name: Seedless (triploid) types
recommended.recommended_note: Seedless hybrids such as the Crimson-type triploids ripen in roughly 85 to 90 days and produce no viable pollen of their own, so they must be planted alongside a seeded pollinizer variety (commonly one seeded plant per two to three seedless). Sweet and convenient, but they need warm conditions to germinate and a longer, hotter season.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by season length, space, and use. Where summers are short or cool, lean on the fast icebox types such as Sugar Baby and Yellow Doll, which ripen in 70 to 80 days; in long, hot regions the full-size Crimson Sweet, Charleston Gray, and Jubilee reward the heat with big, sweet melons. In the disease-prone Southeast, prioritize varieties with anthracnose and Fusarium wilt resistance such as Crimson Sweet, Charleston Gray, and Jubilee. Seedless types are popular and sweet but add a real requirement: a seeded pollinizer must be grown alongside, and they want the warmest conditions to germinate and finish.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a watermelon by your summer and your space. If your season is short or cool, grow a fast small type like Sugar Baby or Yellow Doll. If you have a long, hot summer and room to spread, grow a big one like Crimson Sweet, Charleston Gray, or Jubilee. In the South, choose disease-resistant varieties like Crimson Sweet. Seedless watermelons are sweet and convenient, but remember they need a regular seeded variety planted nearby to pollinate them, and they like it extra warm.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Washington State's planning table gives 6 to 12 melons from 3 plants in a 10-foot row. Watermelons need a lot of room. Keep irrigation consistent through fruit set and development. Side-dress a second time after bloom, while fruit is developing, but avoid excess nitrogen, which encourages vine growth and reduces fruit growth.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Washington State's planning table expects about 6 to 12 melons from 3 plants in a 10-foot row. Watermelons need a lot of room. Water steadily while the fruit sets and grows. Feed them a second time after they bloom, while the fruit is growing, but don't overdo nitrogen: too much gives you more vine and less fruit.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Watermelon does not produce continuously; the plant sets fruit over a few weeks and then sizes and ripens that crop, with the melons coming ready over a window in mid to late summer rather than all at once or all season long. Each melon is harvested once, at full ripeness.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Unlike summer squash, watermelon does not keep producing all season. The plant sets its fruit over a few weeks and the melons ripen over a stretch in mid to late summer, and you pick each one once when it is ripe.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Plan for three things. Watermelons need a lot of room. Fruit set depends on insects such as honeybees and bumblebees to carry pollen, so consider a honeybee colony nearby. And ripeness takes judgment: check that the fruit has reached its expected size, the tendril closest to the fruit has turned brown, the rind has gone from glossy to dull, and the underside shows a large white to cream spot.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The big first-year surprises are how far watermelon vines spread, how much they depend on bees, and how tricky it is to tell when a melon is ripe (it will not ripen after you pick it). Give them lots of room, grow some flowers for the bees, and learn the ripeness signs before cutting.
factors_seasoned: Heat and season length: watermelon needs a long, hot season (70 to 95 days) with warm nights to ripen and sweeten; cool-summer northern and coastal areas are marginal and need early icebox types, transplants, and black plastic mulch.

Pollination: fruit set is pollinator-limited, each female flower needing many bee visits, and seedless types additionally need a seeded pollinizer nearby; poor pollination drops or deforms young fruit.
Space: watermelons need a lot of room. Planting too close, like overfeeding with nitrogen, leads to excessive vine growth and few fruit.
Disease pressure: Fusarium wilt, anthracnose, gummy stem blight, and the mildews can end a planting early, so resistant varieties and long rotations matter.
Even moisture, then a dry finish: steady water through sizing builds full melons, but tapering water near ripeness is what concentrates the sugars and makes them sweet.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 source supports timing watermelon planting by moon phase. We do not make a recommendation here; sow by soil temperature (70°F and warm) and frost dates instead.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days in warm soil (70 to 95°F is ideal); soil below about 65°F rots seed rather than germinating it. Two seed leaves push up first.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In warm soil, seeds sprout in about a week to ten days, sending up two seed leaves first. In cold soil, seeds rot instead of sprouting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Wait for warm soil (70°F at 2 inches) and sow about 1 inch deep, three to four seeds per hill. Keep evenly moist, not soggy. Thin to the strongest two seedlings once true leaves appear.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant seeds 1 inch deep once the soil is warm, a few per hill. Keep the soil damp until they sprout, then keep the strongest two seedlings.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your watermelon seeds germinate, and how many days did it take?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cotyledons followed by the first true leaves; growth is fast once warm. Watch for cucumber beetles, which target young plants, and for aphids on leaf undersides.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the first two rounded leaves, true leaves appear and the plant grows quickly once it is warm. Watch for beetles chewing the young leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Protect from cucumber beetles with row cover if needed, removing it at flowering for pollination. Keep evenly watered and free of weeds, and use black plastic mulch in cooler areas to keep the soil warm.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye out for beetles on young plants and use a light row cover if needed, but remove it once flowers form. Water regularly and keep weeds down.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings developing? Any sign of beetle damage?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young plants look?

growth_stages.name: Vining
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant sends out long runners and bulks up its leaves, growing fast in warm weather. This is the window to side-dress lightly with nitrogen and the time to start watching for spider mites in hot, dry spells.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant sends out long vines that spread across the ground, with big leaves. This is when you feed it a little and give it room to run.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: The first side-dressing goes on before the vines start to run; give a second after bloom while fruit develops. Mulch with dried grass clippings, straw, or wood chips to conserve water and hold down weeds. Give the runners plenty of room. Scout leaf undersides for aphids, which usually arrive once vines form runners. In hot, dry weather, watch the upper leaf surfaces for spider mite damage, pale yellow to reddish-brown spots.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plants get their first feeding before the vines start to run and a second one after they bloom, while fruit is growing. Spread mulch, such as dried grass clippings, straw, or wood chips, to save water and keep weeds down. Give the vines plenty of room to spread. Check under the leaves for aphids, which usually show up once the vines start running. In hot, dry weather, also watch for spider mites: these tiny mites leave pale yellow to reddish-brown specks on the tops of the leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are the vines running well? Have you side-dressed, and any pests on the leaf undersides?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your watermelon vines spreading out?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Yellow flowers open. Male flowers on thin stalks usually open first, often for a week before females, which is normal; female flowers carry a tiny melon behind the bloom. Each female needs many bee visits to set, and seedless types need a seeded pollinizer nearby to supply pollen.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Yellow flowers open. The first ones are usually male and fall off, which is normal. Female flowers have a tiny melon at their base, and bees need to visit them many times to set fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Encourage pollinators and avoid spraying open blooms. If small fruit yellow and abort, pollination is poor, so hand-pollinate in the morning with a male flower or small brush. Make sure a seeded pollinizer is flowering near any seedless plants. Keep moisture steady.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let the bees do their work and do not spray the flowers. If tiny melons turn yellow and drop, the flowers were not pollinated, so you can hand-pollinate in the morning. Keep watering steadily.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you seeing female flowers and fruit set? Any young fruit yellowing and dropping?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant flowering? Are any little melons forming?

growth_stages.name: Fruit development
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Set fruit swell quickly over several weeks, reaching full size before the rind dulls and the ripeness signs appear. The plant is sizing and ripening its crop rather than setting new fruit continuously, and it takes roughly 35 to 45 days from fruit set to ripeness.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The little melons grow bigger fast over several weeks. The plant is busy growing and ripening the melons it has set, which takes about five to six weeks from when the fruit forms.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even through sizing, then taper in the last week or two to concentrate sugars. Set each melon on a board, tile, or mulch to keep it off wet soil, limit fruit per vine for bigger melons, and keep scouting for mildew and spider mites.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering steadily while the melons grow, then ease off near the end to sweeten them. Slip a board or some straw under each melon so it is not sitting on damp ground, and watch the leaves for disease.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are the fruit sizing? Are you keeping them off wet soil and easing off water as they near ripeness?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your watermelons growing bigger?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full size and color for the variety, a browned tendril nearest the fruit, a creamy-yellow ground spot, a dull (not glossy) skin, and a deep, dull thump. Harvest each melon once at full ripeness, since it will not ripen further off the vine.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The melon is full size, the little tendril next to it has dried brown, the spot on the bottom has turned creamy yellow, the skin is dull, and it thumps deep and dull. That is ripe, and it will not get riper after picking.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Check the ripeness signs together, then cut each melon from the vine with shears leaving a short stub of stem, rather than pulling it. Use the browning tendril plus the yellow ground spot as your most reliable pair, and eat or refrigerate promptly, since watermelon does not store long.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When the signs line up, cut the melon off the vine with a knife, leaving a short piece of stem. Do not pull it off. Eat it within a week or so, since watermelon does not keep for long.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested? How did the ripeness signs line up, and how was the flavor?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your watermelon yet?

notifications.title_seasoned: Watch for spider mites in the heat
notifications.title_beginner: Time to watch for tiny pests in hot weather
notifications.body_seasoned: Your watermelon vines are running in summer heat, which is exactly when two-spotted spider mites build up. Check leaf undersides for fine yellow stippling and webbing, and treat early with a water blast or insecticidal soap before they peak.
notifications.body_beginner: Your watermelon is growing fast in the summer heat, which is when spider mites show up. Check under the leaves for fine yellow speckling, and treat early if you see it.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your watermelon is flowering. Fruit set depends on many bee visits per female flower, and seedless types need a seeded pollinizer nearby, so if small fruit yellow and drop, hand-pollinate in the morning and keep blooms unsprayed.
notifications.body_beginner: Your watermelon is flowering. If the tiny melons turn yellow and fall off, the flowers were not pollinated, so try hand-pollinating in the morning.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to check if your watermelons are ripe
notifications.body_seasoned: Your watermelons should be nearing ripeness. Look for a browned tendril nearest the fruit, a creamy-yellow ground spot, a dull skin, and a deep, dull thump, then cut at full ripeness, since watermelon does not ripen off the vine.
notifications.body_beginner: Your watermelons should be getting close. Check for the dried brown tendril, the creamy-yellow spot on the bottom, a dull skin, and a deep thump, then pick when ripe, since it will not ripen after you cut it.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost is coming, harvest your watermelons
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning for your watermelons
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast. Watermelon is frost-tender, and frost ends the vines, so harvest any ripe or near-ripe melons now. Note that under-ripe melons will not finish off the vine, so pick what is closest to ready.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming, and it will kill the vines. Pick any ripe or nearly ripe watermelons now, since they will not ripen any further once frost hits.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat may briefly stall fruit set
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell may slow fruit set
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A stretch of extreme heat is forecast. Watermelon thrives in heat, but very hot days with hot nights can briefly reduce pollination and drop young fruit. Keep moisture steady; set usually resumes as the worst heat eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Very hot weather is coming. Watermelon loves heat, but the most extreme days may slow fruit set for a while. Keep it well watered, it usually picks back up when it cools a little.

germination.text_seasoned: Soil temperature, not the calendar, governs watermelon germination. Wait until soil is at least 70°F at 2 inches; seed sown in cold ground below 65°F rots before it sprouts.
germination.text_beginner: Wait for warm soil before sowing. Watermelon seeds rot in cold ground but sprout fast once it is warm, around 70°F.

seedling.text_seasoned: Cucumber beetles swarm young cucurbits. A floating row cover protects seedlings, but pull it off at flowering so bees can pollinate. In cooler areas, black plastic mulch warms the soil and speeds growth.
seedling.text_beginner: Protect young plants from beetles with a light cover, but take it off once flowers appear so bees can reach them. Black plastic mulch helps in cooler spots.

vining.text_seasoned: Hold back on extra nitrogen. Too much encourages excess vine growth and reduces fruit, and so does planting too close.
vining.text_beginner: Do not overdo the nitrogen once the vines spread, or you get lots of leaves and few melons. Give them plenty of room.

vining.text_seasoned: Spider mites explode in hot, dry weather, exactly watermelon's season. Scout leaf undersides for fine stippling and webbing, keep plants watered so they are not heat-stressed, and avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill the mites' natural enemies.
vining.text_beginner: Watch for spider mites in hot, dry weather. Check under the leaves for fine speckling, keep the plants watered, and do not spray strong insecticides that kill the good bugs.

flowering.text_seasoned: Early male flowers opening and dropping with no fruit is normal; females come later. Judge pollination by whether small fruit size up or yellow and abort.
flowering.text_beginner: The first flowers often fall off without making melons, that is normal. Trouble is when tiny melons turn yellow and drop, which means poor pollination.

flowering.text_seasoned: If you grow seedless watermelon, a seeded pollinizer variety must be flowering nearby, since seedless plants make no viable pollen. Without it, seedless plants flower but set no fruit no matter how many bees visit.
flowering.text_beginner: Seedless watermelon needs a regular seeded watermelon planted nearby to pollinate it. Without that partner, a seedless plant will flower but never make fruit.

fruit_development.text_seasoned: Slip a board, tile, or straw under each sizing melon to keep it off wet soil and prevent rot, and limit the number of fruit per vine if you want larger melons. It takes roughly 35 to 45 days from fruit set to ripeness.
fruit_development.text_beginner: Put a board or some straw under each melon so it is not on damp ground. For bigger melons, keep just a few fruit per vine. They take about five to six weeks to ripen after they form.

fruit_development.text_seasoned: Taper watering in the last week or two before harvest to concentrate the sugars. Over-watering near ripeness dilutes the flavor and can split the fruit, the single biggest cause of a bland homegrown melon.
fruit_development.text_beginner: Ease off the water in the last week or two before picking, so the melon turns sweet. Too much water near the end makes it watery and can crack it.

harvest.text_seasoned: No single ripeness sign is perfect, so use several: the browned tendril nearest the fruit, a creamy-yellow ground spot, a dull skin, and a deep, dull thump. The browning tendril plus the yellow ground spot is the most reliable pair. Cut, do not pull, and remember it will not ripen off the vine.
harvest.text_beginner: Check several signs together: the dried brown tendril, the creamy-yellow spot on the bottom, a dull skin, and a deep thump. Cut the melon off with a knife, do not pull it, and pick it ripe since it will not ripen after.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cut the melon open and it was bland, pale, or watery
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The watermelon was not sweet inside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The melon was harvested under-ripe, or it was over-watered near harvest. Watermelon does not sweeten off the vine, so a melon picked early stays bland, and heavy watering in the final week dilutes the sugars and can leave the flesh watery.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The melon was picked too early, or it got too much water right before harvest. Watermelon does not get sweeter after you cut it, and too much late water makes it watery.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Harvesting before full ripeness, or over-watering in the final week or two before harvest.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Picking too soon, or watering too much right before harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Learn the ripeness signs and use several together (browned tendril, creamy-yellow ground spot, dull skin, dull thump), and taper watering in the last week or two before harvest to concentrate the sugars.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait for the ripeness signs to line up before picking, and ease off the water in the last week or two so the melon sweetens.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Vine yellowed and wilted on one side and died
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The vine wilted and died even though it was watered
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most likely Fusarium wilt, the watermelon-specific soilborne fungus that clogs the water-conducting tissue, often killing one runner first, then the plant, even in moist soil. A pinkish mold near the soil line and browned vascular tissue in a cut stem confirm it. It builds up where watermelon repeats on the same ground.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually Fusarium wilt, a soil disease that only attacks watermelon and blocks the plant's water pipes, so it wilts and dies even when watered. It builds up in soil where you grow watermelon too often.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. niveum in the soil, favored by warm sandy ground and short rotations.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A soil fungus specific to watermelon that survives for years in the ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties, rotate out of watermelon and cucurbits for at least five years, and consider grafted plants on resistant rootstock where the disease is established.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow resistant varieties, do not plant watermelon in the same spot for at least five years, and look into grafted plants if the disease keeps coming back.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tiny fruit yellowed and dropped after flowering
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Little melons turned yellow and fell off
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Poor pollination. The female flower was not adequately pollinated, so the young fruit aborts. Watermelon needs many bee visits per flower, and seedless types fail entirely without a seeded pollinizer nearby. Common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions and during extreme heat.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The flowers were not pollinated well, so the little melons died instead of growing. Watermelon needs lots of bee visits, and seedless kinds need a seeded variety planted nearby.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Inadequate pollen transfer to the female flower; with seedless types, a missing or non-flowering seeded pollinizer.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough pollination, or no seeded pollinizer near a seedless plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant flowers to draw bees, avoid spraying open blooms, hand-pollinate in the morning if set is poor, and always grow a seeded pollinizer alongside seedless types.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow some flowers nearby for the bees, hand-pollinate early flowers if needed, and always plant a seeded watermelon next to any seedless ones.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Melon rotted on the bottom where it touched the soil
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The melon rotted on its underside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fruit rot, typically from a wet underside in prolonged contact with damp soil, favored by poorly drained, rainy conditions and the cucurbit fruit-rot fungi. A soft, sometimes molded patch develops where the melon sits.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The melon sat on wet ground and rotted on the bottom. Damp soil and poor drainage let rot soften the fruit where it touched the ground.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Prolonged contact between fruit and saturated soil, favoring soilborne fruit rots in wet, poorly drained beds.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The melon sitting on wet soil, which lets rot set in on the underside.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant on raised hills for drainage, avoid low wet spots, and set each sizing melon on a board, tile, or thick mulch to lift it off the soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant on raised hills so water drains away, and slip a board or straw under each melon so it is not on wet ground.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Watermelon is not a succession crop. It is a single, long-season planting that sets fruit over a few weeks and ripens its crop in mid to late summer, so you sow once per season rather than at intervals. In most zones a second sowing would not have the 70 to 95 frost-free days it needs to ripen before fall. Only in the warmest, near-frost-free zones and the low desert, where a spring crop and a separate late-summer crop both fit, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season, not a succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant watermelon once for the season. It grows through the summer and ripens its melons in mid to late summer, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. In most places a later planting would not have enough warm days to ripen before fall. Only in very warm areas and the desert can you fit a second, separate planting.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Watermelon is a single long-season crop (70 to 95 days) harvested at full ripeness, so succession sowing does not apply; a second sowing in most zones would not mature before frost. Warm near-frost-free zones and the low desert support a separate seasonal planting window, which is a distinct season rather than a succession.

crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Watermelon is monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a standard seeded variety sets fruit on its own with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and watermelon is strongly pollinator-dependent, with each female flower needing many bee visits to set and size a full, well-filled melon. Poor pollination shows up as fruit that abort while small or grow lopsided and hollow-hearted. Seedless (triploid) watermelons are the exception that every grower must plan for: they produce no viable pollen of their own, so a seeded (diploid) pollinizer variety must be planted alongside, commonly one seeded plant for every two to three seedless plants, or a seeded row within about 10 feet, so bees can carry the pollen the seedless plants need. Plant flowers nearby, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate in the morning if set is poor.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Each regular watermelon plant has both male and female flowers, so one plant can make fruit by itself. Bees carry the pollen between the flowers, and watermelon needs a lot of bee visits to set each melon, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. The one big exception is seedless watermelon: those plants cannot pollinate themselves, so you have to plant a regular seeded variety nearby (often one seeded plant for every two or three seedless ones) so the bees can pollinate them. If fruit is not forming, grow some flowers nearby for the bees and try hand-pollinating in the morning.
crops.description_seasoned: Watermelon is a heat-loving, long-season trailing vine grown for its large, sweet, juicy fruit, a warm-season cousin of melon and squash in the cucumber family. It is harvested once at full ripeness rather than picked young and repeatedly, and it does not ripen further off the vine, so reading ripeness on the plant is the whole game: the curly tendril nearest the fruit dries and browns, the ground spot where the melon rests on the soil turns from white to a creamy yellow, the skin dulls from glossy to matte, and a ripe melon gives a deep, dull thump. The season's shape is set by three things: a long, hot runway (70 to 95 frost-free days with warm nights, so cool-summer northern and coastal areas are marginal), full sun and warm soil above 70°F at planting, and strong pollinator dependence, since each fruit needs many bee visits to set and size. Seedless (triploid) types add a wrinkle: they make no viable pollen of their own, so a seeded (diploid) pollinizer variety must be planted alongside to set fruit. The main pressures are cucumber beetles, aphids, and spider mites, plus the cucurbit diseases anthracnose, gummy stem blight, Fusarium wilt, and the mildews.
crops.description_beginner: Watermelon is a warm-season vine that loves heat and sun and grows big, sweet, juicy fruit on long, trailing stems. Unlike summer squash that you pick again and again, you harvest a watermelon once, when it is fully ripe, and it will not ripen any more after you cut it, so picking at the right moment matters. The signs of a ripe melon are the little curly tendril next to the fruit drying up and turning brown, the pale spot where it sits on the ground turning creamy yellow, the skin going from shiny to dull, and a deep, dull thump when you tap it. The main things to know: give watermelon a long, hot summer, full sun, and warm soil, plenty of room to spread, and steady water while the fruit grows. Bees need to visit the flowers many times to set fruit. If you grow a seedless kind, you also have to plant a regular seeded variety nearby to pollinate it. Watch for cucumber beetles, aphids, spider mites, and several leaf and wilt diseases.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Choose a well-drained site with 8 to 10 hours of sun a day. Incorporate organic matter such as compost into the native soil before planting. Go light on nitrogen, since too much encourages excess vine growth and reduces fruit growth. Plant in small hills spaced 8 feet apart on all sides. Black plastic mulch warms the soil faster in spring, conserves moisture, and gives watermelons an early start. It also helps control weeds and reduces fruit rot.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick a spot that drains well and gets 8 to 10 hours of sun. Mix compost into your soil before planting. Don't overdo nitrogen-rich fertilizer, or you'll get lots of vine and less fruit. Plant seeds in small hills 8 feet apart in every direction. Black plastic laid over the soil warms it faster in spring and gives the plants an early start. The plastic also holds in moisture, keeps weeds down, and cuts down on rotten fruit.

northern_tier.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh watermelon windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (70 to 95) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full ripeness; no heat_pause (watermelon produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North, watermelon is a tight, single summer crop and a real stretch in the coldest zones. Plant after the last frost once the soil is warm (70°F), and harvest the mature crop in late summer before fall cooling. Short-season zones (3 to 4) are marginal: start transplants indoors about three weeks early, choose fast icebox varieties such as Sugar Baby or Yellow Doll, and use black plastic mulch to warm the soil. Warmer zones (6 to 7) can finish larger types.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold North you get one watermelon crop a summer, and the coldest areas are a challenge. Plant after the last frost once the soil is warm, and harvest in late summer. In the coldest zones, start plants indoors, grow a fast small variety like Sugar Baby, and use black plastic mulch to warm the soil so the melons ripen in time.

se_gulf.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh watermelon windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (70 to 95) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full ripeness; no heat_pause (watermelon produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Gulf and coastal plain, watermelon is a major spring-to-summer crop: plant as the soil warms in spring and harvest from early to late summer. The hot, humid summers drive heavy disease pressure (Fusarium wilt, anthracnose, gummy stem blight, the mildews), so resistant varieties, long rotations, airflow, and base watering matter. A separate late-summer planting for a fall crop is possible in the warmer zones.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, plant watermelon in spring once the soil warms and harvest through the summer. The hot, humid weather brings a lot of disease, so choose disease-resistant varieties, rotate where you plant, and water at the base. In the warmer areas you can also plant again in late summer for a fall crop.

ca_interior.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh watermelon windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (70 to 95) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full ripeness; no heat_pause (watermelon produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's hot interior valleys are prime watermelon country: plant from spring into early summer and harvest through the warm, dry late summer. The dry heat suits watermelon well as long as irrigation is steady through sizing, and the dry air keeps foliar disease lower than in the humid Southeast. Taper water near ripeness to concentrate the sugars.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: California's hot inland valleys are great for watermelon. Plant from spring into early summer and harvest in the warm, dry late summer. The dry heat suits them as long as you water steadily, and the dry air means less leaf disease. Ease off the water near the end to sweeten the fruit.

ca_north_coast.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh watermelon windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (70 to 95) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full ripeness; no heat_pause (watermelon produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's cool, foggy north coast is marginal for watermelon, which wants more heat than the coast usually delivers. Plant after the soil warms in late spring and harvest in late summer to fall, but expect slow ripening and lean to early icebox varieties, the warmest, sunniest microclimate you have, and black plastic mulch. Inland and away from the fog the crop does better.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: California's cool, foggy north coast is a tough spot for watermelon, which wants more heat. Plant in late spring once it warms and harvest in late summer or fall, but choose a fast, small variety, the sunniest, warmest spot you have, and use black plastic mulch. It does better the farther you are from the coastal fog.

ca_south_coast.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh watermelon windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (70 to 95) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full ripeness; no heat_pause (watermelon produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's mild south coast grows watermelon well through a long, gentle warm season: plant from spring into early summer and harvest from midsummer into fall. The warmest, sunniest sites ripen the sweetest fruit; right on the coast, cooler air and humidity can slow ripening and favor mildew, so prioritize full sun and airflow.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: California's mild south coast is good for watermelon. Plant from spring into early summer and harvest from midsummer into fall. Pick the warmest, sunniest spot for the sweetest melons. Right at the coast it can be cooler and a bit damp, so give plenty of sun and air.

ca_desert.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh watermelon windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (70 to 95) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full ripeness; no heat_pause (watermelon produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The California desert valleys are classic watermelon ground: plant in late winter to early spring and harvest from late spring through summer. Unlike most cucurbits, watermelon thrives in the desert heat and produces right through summer rather than pausing, as long as irrigation is steady and deep. Time the planting so the crop sizes and sweetens through the long, hot, dry season.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The California desert is great watermelon country. Plant in late winter to early spring and harvest from late spring through summer. Watermelon loves the desert heat and keeps producing through summer when other melons and squash struggle, as long as you water deeply and steadily.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern New Mexico & West Texas
warm_arid.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh watermelon windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (70 to 95) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full ripeness; no heat_pause (watermelon produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas grow excellent watermelon: plant after the last frost once the soil warms and harvest through the hot, dry late summer. The dry heat suits the crop and keeps foliar disease low, but steady, deep irrigation is essential. Intense early-summer heat can briefly stall fruit set, which resumes as conditions ease.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: The dry, warm zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas grow great watermelon. Plant after the last frost once the soil warms and harvest through the hot, dry late summer. Water deeply and steadily. If fruit set pauses briefly in the hottest spells, it usually picks back up.

low_desert_az.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh watermelon windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (70 to 95) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full ripeness; no heat_pause (watermelon produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: Arizona's low desert grows watermelon in two windows around the extreme midsummer: a late-winter to early-spring planting for an early-summer harvest, and a late-summer planting for a fall crop. Watermelon tolerates the heat better than most crops, so the two plantings run back to back through the season rather than pausing for heat. Steady, deep irrigation is essential, and the dry air keeps disease low.
low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In Arizona's low desert you can grow watermelon in two windows: plant in late winter to early spring for an early-summer crop, and again in late summer for a fall crop. Watermelon handles the heat well, so the two crops run through the season. Water deeply and steadily through the heat.

fl_peninsula.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh watermelon windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (70 to 95) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full ripeness; no heat_pause (watermelon produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In peninsular Florida, watermelon is grown in the cooler, drier halves of the year, planted in late winter to spring and again in late summer for a fall crop, avoiding the wettest part of midsummer when humidity and rain drive heavy disease. The deep-summer gap is disease- and rain-driven, not heat (watermelon loves the heat). Seed the spring crop early, choose resistant varieties, and watch closely for anthracnose, gummy stem blight, and the mildews.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In Florida, plant watermelon in late winter to spring and again in late summer, avoiding the wettest part of summer when disease is worst. The break in midsummer is about rain and disease, not heat, since watermelon likes it hot. Choose disease-resistant varieties and watch the leaves closely for disease.

Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full ripeness; no heat_pause (watermelon produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii and tropical zones there is no frost, so watermelon can be planted across much of the year, with timing driven by rainfall and disease pressure rather than cold. Watermelon grows well in the warmth; choose the drier, sunnier windows to limit anthracnose, gummy stem blight, and fruit rot, and grow on light, well-drained ground. Specific local timing is modeled pending a parseable CTAHR source.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii and the tropics there is no frost, so you can plant watermelon through much of the year. Aim for the drier, sunnier stretches to avoid disease and rot, and grow it in light, well-drained soil. Heat and rain are the main challenges, not cold.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Watermelon transplants go out Feb 14 - Mar 20 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide, corroborated by the Bilingual LRGV planting table's 90 to 100 day maturity figure for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest spring harvest at about 90 days from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest spring harvest at about 100 days from the latest set-out date.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall watermelon transplants go out Aug 10 - Sep 1 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide / Bilingual LRGV fall window for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest fall harvest at about 90 days from the earliest fall set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest fall harvest, extending into the mild Valley winter tail before spring returns.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, watermelon is a two-season crop. Plant Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest, then plant again Aug 10 - Sep 1 for a fall crop. Skip the hottest weeks of summer: the plant just does not perform well in the worst of the heat, so most Valley gardeners skip it. It rarely if ever frosts here, so both the spring and fall windows run on Valley heat, not on a frost date.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Watermelon in the RGV runs on the Valley's two-crop calendar: set out Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest running May 15 - Jun 28, then set out again Aug 10 - Sep 1 for a fall harvest running Nov 8 - Dec 10. TAMU AgriLife's Valley planting guidance simply leaves that stretch off the calendar for this crop, rather than asserting a specific heat-failure mechanism. Frost is essentially absent here, so both plantings are timed against heat, not cold. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 4 weeks before the May set-out, the lead time OSU Extension's Oregon planting table (EM9027) specifies for watermelon. OSU flags the immediate coast not suitable for this crop outright; WSU's Washington guide corroborates watermelon as one of the state's most heat-demanding vegetable crops.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out in May in the Willamette Valley once the soil is reliably warm, per OSU EM9027's Region 2 window; OSU rates Region 1 (the immediate coast) not suitable for watermelon at all, a flag this cell honors with a later, compressed coastal window instead of the valley's date.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fruit matures roughly 70 to 95 days after transplant on a typical warm-season site (OSU); the maritime valley's cooler, cloudier summer than inland Oregon pushes actual ripening later than the base days-to-maturity, so this cell budgets extra weeks and steers toward the earliest, smallest-fruited icebox types rather than a large 90-day melon.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest window closes well ahead of the valley's average first frost; small icebox varieties (65 to 75 days) stand the best chance of a fully ripe melon before the season ends.

8.zone_notes: OSU Extension's Willamette Valley table (EM9027) gives watermelon a May set-out window, used verbatim here. Watermelon is a genuine stretch even in the valley, the warmer of the two PNW zones: this cell budgets a slow run well beyond the crop's base 70 to 95 day maturity to reflect the cool, marine-tempered summer. Grow only the earliest, smallest-fruited icebox cultivars, in the sunniest, most sheltered bed, under black plastic mulch, with a row cover or low tunnel through June.

9.zone_notes: OSU Extension's own planting table rates the immediate coast (Region 1) not suitable for watermelon outright; this is not a recommended coastal crop. This cell authors a conservative, compressed window anyway, honestly, for a gardener who wants to try it in the warmest microsite available: a later set-out once the marine air finally warms, and a harvest clipped tight against the coast's own early-November first frost. Expect a real chance of no ripe fruit at all in a cool summer.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Watermelon wants more summer heat than we usually get here, and OSU Extension says the immediate coast is not a good fit for it at all. Away from the coast, plant in May once the soil is warm, and choose the smallest, fastest-ripening icebox variety you can find rather than a big melon that needs a long hot summer. Give it your sunniest, warmest spot, black plastic mulch, and a row cover early on. Even with all that, expect the melons to ripen slowly and late, and some years they may not ripen at all. Right on the coast, this is a fun experiment, not a sure crop.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Watermelon, like the other melons, wants more sustained summer heat than the maritime Pacific Northwest reliably provides, and OSU Extension rates the immediate coast not suitable for it. In the valley, set out transplants in May once the soil is warm (OSU's own window), and lean hard on the earliest, smallest-fruited icebox varieties (65 to 75 days) rather than a large 90-day type that needs a hotter, longer summer than this region gives. The warmest, most sheltered full-sun bed, black plastic mulch, and a low tunnel or row cover into early summer are worth the effort; even so, expect slow ripening and accept that some years the melons do not finish before the weather cools. Along the coast itself, treat this as an experiment.

plant_out.source_quote: Zone 8a Spring: Apr 10-Aug 1 | Zone 7a Spring: May 1-Jul 10 (Watermelon)
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sow once the soil has warmed, in the window VCE 426-331 Table 4 documents for watermelon (zone 8: Apr 10; zone 7: May 1); VCE does not list this crop as a transplant crop, and its fall column is blank (not recommended in this belt).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins bearing roughly 85 days after sowing, this crop's own days-to-maturity.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest wraps up ahead of the belt's real first frost, which this warm-season crop cannot survive; the latest sowings in VCE's window leave the least margin before frost.

8.notes: VCE 426-331's own zone 8 window runs sowing through Aug 1; at this crop's roughly 85-day pace, sowings that late would mature after the belt's Oct 30 first frost, so harvest here is capped about a week ahead of frost rather than running the full days-to-maturity out. Earlier sowings (April, May, June) give the fullest, surest harvest.

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Watermelon is a single warm-season crop here, direct-sown once the soil is warm and harvested through summer into early fall. This belt does not fit in a second planting, watermelon needs its full season to size and sweeten. Zone 8 can sow into early August, though the very latest sowings leave little time before frost; zone 7's shorter season favors sowing by early July.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: VCE 426-331 gives watermelon a spring-only window with a blank fall column: zone 8 Apr 10 to Aug 1, zone 7 May 1 to Jul 10. At 85 days to maturity, watermelon matures comfortably from most of zone 8's window, but the latest Aug 1 sowings would run past the Oct 30 first frost, so this belt's harvest window is capped about a week ahead of frost rather than running the full days-to-maturity out. nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sown or a short indoor head start; the chart's March-April-plus-June shading is read as one continuous window.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Matures roughly 85 days after sowing; the earliest-sown plants set the harvest's start date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The latest sowing is timed to mature by this frost-anchored margin.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Watermelon direct-sows or transplants from March through mid-June across the Las Vegas Valley, and once it is in the ground it grows straight through the summer heat with no break. The earliest sowings start ripening in late spring, and later plantings keep melons coming into September. Thump the rind for a dull, hollow sound, and check that the ground spot has turned from white to a creamy yellow before you cut one.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Master Gardener chart's March-April-plus-June shading reads, on the Mojave's long warm season, as one continuous sowing window rather than two crops: watermelon can go in anytime March into mid-June, and the vines carry straight through the June to September heat with no pause. Earliest sowings ripen first at an 85-day maturity, and successive June sowings stretch the harvest into early September, well ahead of the valley's late-November first frost.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sow about April 1, once the soil is warm and frost danger has passed, per USU Extension's St. George Group D (Very Tender) planting date.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins ripening about 85 days after the April 1 sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Because this crop sets fruit through the desert summer with no heat-driven pause, picking continues from vine to vine into fall, ending as the November 1 average first frost approaches.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Direct-sow watermelon around April 1 once the ground is warm, and the vines will run right through the St. George summer with no break, filling out melons from late June into October. Thump the rind for a dull, hollow sound, and check that the pale ground spot where the fruit rests has turned from white to creamy yellow before you cut one loose.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: Watermelon is one of USU Extension's Group D (Very Tender) crops for St. George, direct-sown about April 1 after the March 30 average last frost. At an 85-day maturity the first melons finish by late June, and because the vines keep setting fruit right through the 100°F summer rather than aborting blossoms the way tomatoes and peppers do, harvest continues from vine to vine into October, well ahead of the November 1 average first frost. USU gives no fall watermelon window for St. George, so the single spring sowing is the whole season here.

open_findings.summary: AZ1005, the University of Arizona Cooperative Extension Vegetable Planting Calendar for Maricopa County (Kai Umeda, revised 9/18), read 2026-08-05. Its grid is rotated 90 degrees, so the windows were reconstructed from character coordinates rather than read by eye, and the method was validated first against pumpkin, whose grid row (Mar 1, Mar 15, then Jul 1, Jul 15, Aug 1) reproduces our existing cell. Watermelon has its OWN row in that document, separate from the combined cantaloupe/honeydew one, and it is strikingly short: S marks at Feb 15, Mar 1 and Mar 15, and NOTHING for the rest of the year. AZ1005 gives low-desert watermelon a spring sowing window only. Our cells carry a second planting at Jul 15 - Aug 15, which that document does not support at all, so those two second_planting nodes STAY on the institution root rather than being repointed at a document that contradicts them. The three spring nodes are repointed. Our spring opening of Feb 1 also sits two weeks ahead of the document, the same divergence recorded for cantaloupe. Worth noting the asymmetry, because it is evidence rather than an oversight: the same document gives cantaloupe and honeydew a continuous Feb-to-July window and gives watermelon six weeks, which is a real horticultural claim about a longer-season crop in a hot desert, not a gap in the table. Needs a ruling: either source the summer planting elsewhere, or declare it modeled.

crops.name: Cantaloupe / Rockmelon

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Cantaloupe does best in deep, well-drained, light soil, with sandy loams and loamy sands the classic choice because they warm quickly in spring and drain freely, which this heat-loving, warm-season vine rewards with earlier, sweeter fruit. Work a few inches of compost or well-rotted manure into the bed before planting, but go easier on high-nitrogen amendments than you would for leafy crops, since too much nitrogen pushes vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Many growers plant on low, wide hills or raised mounds, which warm faster, drain better, and lift the crown and developing fruit off wet ground. Heavy clay holds water and stays cold, slowing growth and inviting Fusarium wilt and fruit rot, so amend it generously and build mounds, or grow on sandier ground.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant cantaloupe in light, well-drained soil that warms up fast, like a sandy loam, with some compost mixed in. Go easy on rich, high-nitrogen material, because that gives you lots of leaves and vine but less fruit and lower sugar. Many gardeners plant on low hills or raised mounds, which warm up and drain better and keep the fruit off soggy ground. If your soil is heavy clay, it stays cold and wet and can bring on disease, so mix in compost and build the soil up into mounds, or pick the sandiest, best-draining spot you have.

ph.note_seasoned: Cantaloupe grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.8, with extension melon guides most often citing a 6.0 to 6.5 sweet spot. It tolerates a somewhat wider band, but strongly acidic or strongly alkaline soil tightens nutrient uptake and can worsen blossom-end and nutrient problems. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.
ph.note_beginner: Cantaloupe likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress before vines run and again after fruit set
fertilizer.type: lower-nitrogen at planting, then nitrogen side-dress
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before planting, then side-dress before the vines start to run and again after bloom as fruit develops
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) or urea
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Cantaloupe is a moderate feeder that wants more phosphorus and potassium than nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Work a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson suggests about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then side-dress with a nitrogen source before the vines start to run, and again lightly after bloom as fruit develops. Ease off nitrogen once fruit has set so the plant pours its energy into sizing and sweetening the melons rather than growing more vine. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Cantaloupe does not need a lot of nitrogen, and too much gives you big leafy vines but fewer, less sweet melons. Mix a fertilizer that is lower in nitrogen, like a 5-10-10, into the soil before planting, then give the plants a little nitrogen before the vines start to run and again after the flowers bloom. Once the melons start to form, stop pushing nitrogen so the plant puts its energy into growing sweet fruit instead of more leaves.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your cantaloupe vines are about to run, time to side-dress with a little nitrogen. Then feed again lightly after bloom, and ease off nitrogen once fruit sets so the plant builds sweet melons rather than vine.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your cantaloupe vines are starting to spread. Give them a light feeding of nitrogen now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress before the vines run and again lightly after bloom, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets. Too much nitrogen gives vine and leaf at the expense of fruit and sweetness.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a lower-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 at planting, then a little nitrogen as the vines start to spread. Do not overdo the nitrogen once melons form, or you get leaves instead of fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common approach is a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked into the bed before planting (Clemson cites about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then a nitrogen side-dress before the vines run, such as calcium nitrate at about 2 pounds of 15.5-0-0 per 100 feet of row placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly after bloom as fruit develops.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix a lower-nitrogen fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then feed with a little nitrogen before the vines run, scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more after the flowers bloom.

companions.note_seasoned: Most cantaloupe companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on serve two practical ends: pollination and pest pressure. Because cantaloupe fruit set is strongly pollinator-limited, flowering insectary plants like borage near the patch are a genuine help. A trap planting of nasturtium can divert cucumber beetles, which matters more for cantaloupe than for most cucurbits, since muskmelon is highly susceptible to the bacterial wilt those beetles carry. Bush beans fix nitrogen the crop can use without the heavy feeding that would otherwise grow vine over fruit. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep cantaloupe away from other cucurbits, which share its pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle and bacterial wilt, the mildews, and the soilborne Fusarium wilt and foliar gummy stem blight and Alternaria that build up where melons follow melons.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful cantaloupe companions are flowers that bring in bees, since cantaloupe needs plenty of bee visits to set fruit. Nasturtiums can lure cucumber beetles away, which is worth doing because those beetles spread a wilt disease that hits cantaloupe hard. Bush beans add a little nitrogen. The one rule that really matters is to keep cantaloupe away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash, which all share the same pests and diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and cantaloupe needs plenty of bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators cantaloupe fruit set depends on, since each female flower needs many bee visits to set a well-shaped, sweet melon. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-cantaloupe pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Cantaloupe fruit set is pollinator-limited; flowering insectary plants like borage draw bees. Pairing is habitat-based, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near melons and squash to lure cucumber beetles and other pests away, and their flowers bring in bees. For cantaloupe this matters extra, because cucumber beetles spread a wilt disease that hits it hard.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for cucumber beetles, and its flowers also draw the bees cantaloupe depends on for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, and it earns extra value here because cantaloupe is highly susceptible to the bacterial wilt cucumber beetles vector, though the specific nasturtium-cantaloupe effect is not formally isolated.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap-cropping for cucurbit beetles is documented in principle; the nasturtium-cantaloupe pairing is not trial-isolated. Extra rationale from cantaloupe's high bacterial-wilt susceptibility.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which cantaloupe can use, and they do not share cantaloupe's pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Bush beans fix nitrogen that lightly benefits the crop without the heavy nitrogen that would push vine over fruit, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation is a documented mechanism; the bean-cantaloupe adjacency benefit is traditional, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn is the traditional Three Sisters partner that gives sprawling vines something to grow among. With cantaloupe it is more tradition than a proven boost, and cantaloupe's full-sun need means you should not let corn shade it much.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner, though the fit is looser for cantaloupe than for shade-tolerant squash: tall corn can give the trailing vines structure, but cantaloupe wants full sun and heat to sweeten, so keep corn from shading the patch. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a space rationale, not a measured yield effect for this pair.

provenance.reason: Trap-cropping for cucurbit beetles is documented in principle; the nasturtium-cantaloupe pairing is not trial-isolated. Extra rationale from cantaloupe's high bacterial-wilt susceptibility.

good_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Bush beans fix nitrogen that lightly benefits the crop without the heavy nitrogen that would push vine over fruit, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation is a documented mechanism; the bean-cantaloupe adjacency benefit is traditional, not pair-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Corn
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner, though the fit is looser for cantaloupe than for shade-tolerant squash: tall corn can give the trailing vines structure, but cantaloupe wants full sun and heat to sweeten, so keep corn from shading the patch. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a space rationale, not a measured yield effect for this pair.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters intercropping is a documented traditional system; the corn-cantaloupe benefit is spatial, not a trial-isolated pair effect, and cantaloupe's full-sun need weakens the shade rationale.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep cantaloupe away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash. They share most of the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber, watermelon, squash, and pumpkin share cantaloupe's pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it carries, aphid-spread mosaic viruses, the mildews, and the soilborne Fusarium wilt and foliar gummy stem blight and Alternaria that build up where cucurbits repeat. Grouping them concentrates that pressure. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them on a long cycle.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens (bacterial wilt, Fusarium wilt, gummy stem blight, Alternaria, mildews, cucumber beetles) are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and melons apart, since both are hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor disease and attract pests near melons. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A folk anti-companion caution; competition is plausible but there is no T1 source isolating a potato-cantaloupe antagonism.

bad_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber, watermelon, squash, and pumpkin share cantaloupe's pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it carries, aphid-spread mosaic viruses, the mildews, and the soilborne Fusarium wilt and foliar gummy stem blight and Alternaria that build up where cucurbits repeat. Grouping them concentrates that pressure. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them on a long cycle.

provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens (bacterial wilt, Fusarium wilt, gummy stem blight, Alternaria, mildews, cucumber beetles) are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor disease and attract pests near melons. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A folk anti-companion caution; competition is plausible but there is no T1 source isolating a potato-cantaloupe antagonism.

pests.name: Cucumber beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small striped or spotted yellow beetles chew young leaves, stems, flowers, and the rind of developing fruit. The far bigger threat is indirect: cucumber beetles transmit bacterial wilt, and cantaloupe is one of the most susceptible cucurbits to it, much more than watermelon, which is nearly immune.
