yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The big first-year surprises are how far cantaloupe vines spread, how much they depend on bees, and how important it is to pick at the right moment (it will not get sweeter after picking). Give them room, grow some flowers for the bees, and learn the full-slip stem check.
factors_seasoned: Heat and season length: cantaloupe needs a long, warm season (about 75 to 90 days) with warm nights to ripen and sweeten; cool-summer northern and foggy-coastal areas are marginal and need early varieties, transplants, and black plastic mulch.

Pollination: fruit set is pollinator-limited, each female flower needing many bee visits; standard cantaloupe is self-fertile and needs no second variety, but poor pollination drops or deforms young fruit.

Disease pressure: bacterial wilt (via cucumber beetles), Fusarium wilt, gummy stem blight, Alternaria, and the mildews can end a planting early, so beetle control, resistant varieties, and long rotations matter.
Space and vine vigor: vines sprawl several feet each way and need roughly 12 to 18 square feet each; crowding cuts yield and worsens disease.
Even moisture, then a dry finish: steady water through sizing builds full melons, but tapering water near ripeness is what concentrates the sugars and makes them sweet.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 source supports timing cantaloupe planting by moon phase. We do not make a recommendation here; sow by soil temperature (65 to 70°F and warm) and frost dates instead.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cut the melon open and it was bland, pale, or watery
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The cantaloupe was not sweet inside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The melon was picked before full slip, or it was over-watered near harvest. Cantaloupe does not gain sugar off the vine, so a melon picked early stays bland, and heavy watering in the final week dilutes the sugars and can leave the flesh watery.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The melon was picked too early, before the stem slipped, or it got too much water right before harvest. Cantaloupe does not get sweeter after you pick it, and too much late water makes it watery.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Harvesting before full slip, or over-watering in the final week or two before harvest.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Picking too soon, or watering too much right before harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait for full slip (the stem separates cleanly with a light thumb push) plus coarse netting, a tan ground color, and a sweet aroma, and taper watering in the last week or two before harvest to concentrate the sugars.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait for the stem to slip off cleanly and the melon to smell sweet before picking, and ease off the water in the last week or two so it sweetens.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: A runner, then the whole plant, wilted and died over a few days
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The vine wilted and died fast even though it was watered
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most likely bacterial wilt, spread by cucumber beetles, to which cantaloupe is highly susceptible. A runner collapses first, then the plant, even in moist soil. A cut stem oozes a sticky, stringy sap that strings out when the ends are pressed together and pulled apart. It follows the beetles, not the soil.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually bacterial wilt, which cucumber beetles spread and cantaloupe catches easily. A runner wilts first, then the whole plant, even when watered. If you cut the stem and pull the ends apart, a sticky string of ooze comes out.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Erwinia tracheiphila introduced by feeding cucumber beetles; young plants are infected most readily.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Bacteria carried by cucumber beetles, worst on young plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Control the vector: protect seedlings with row cover until flowering, keep cucumber beetle numbers very low through the five-leaf stage, and remove wilting plants promptly. Rotation does not help, since the disease comes from beetles, not the soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep cucumber beetles off the plants, especially when young, with a row cover until they flower, and pull wilting plants right away. Rotating the bed will not help, since this disease comes from beetles.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tiny fruit yellowed and dropped after flowering
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Little melons turned yellow and fell off
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Poor pollination. The female flower was not adequately pollinated, so the young fruit aborts. Cantaloupe needs many bee visits per flower. Common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions and during extreme heat. Unlike seedless watermelon, cantaloupe needs no separate pollinizer variety, just enough bee activity.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The flowers were not pollinated well, so the little melons died instead of growing. Cantaloupe needs lots of bee visits, though it does not need a second variety the way seedless watermelon does.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Inadequate pollen transfer to the female flower, often from few pollinators or weather that keeps bees from flying.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough bee visits to pollinate the flowers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant flowers to draw bees, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate in the morning if set is poor.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow some flowers nearby for the bees, and hand-pollinate early flowers in the morning if the melons are not forming.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Melon rotted on the bottom where it touched the soil
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The melon rotted on its underside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fruit rot, typically from a wet underside in prolonged contact with damp soil, favored by poorly drained, rainy conditions and the cucurbit fruit-rot fungi. A soft, sometimes molded patch develops where the melon sits.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The melon sat on wet ground and rotted on the bottom. Damp soil and poor drainage let rot soften the fruit where it touched the ground.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Prolonged contact between fruit and saturated soil, favoring soilborne fruit rots in wet, poorly drained beds.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The melon sitting on wet soil, which lets rot set in on the underside.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant on raised hills for drainage, avoid low wet spots, and set each sizing melon on a board, tile, or thick mulch to lift it off the soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant on raised hills so water drains away, and slip a board or straw under each melon so it is not on wet ground.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Cantaloupe is not a succession crop. It is a single, long-season planting that sets fruit over a few weeks and ripens its crop in mid to late summer, so you sow once per season rather than at intervals. In most zones a second sowing would not have the 75 to 90 frost-free days it needs to ripen before fall. Only in the warmest, near-frost-free zones and the low desert, where a spring crop and a separate late-summer crop both fit, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season, not a succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant cantaloupe once for the season. It grows through the summer and ripens its melons in mid to late summer, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. In most places a later planting would not have enough warm days to ripen before fall. Only in very warm areas and the desert can you fit a second, separate planting.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Cantaloupe is a single long-season crop (75 to 90 days) harvested at full slip, so succession sowing does not apply; a second sowing in most zones would not mature before frost. Warm near-frost-free zones and the low desert support a separate seasonal planting window, which is a distinct season rather than a succession.

crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Cantaloupe is monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single standard variety sets fruit on its own with no second variety needed, unlike seedless watermelon. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and cantaloupe is strongly pollinator-dependent, with each female flower needing many bee visits over the short time it is open to set and evenly size a well-shaped, sweet melon. Poor pollination shows up as fruit that abort while small or grow lopsided and lumpy. Plant flowers nearby, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate in the morning with a male flower or small brush if set is poor. Note the tension with pest control: the same cucumber beetles you must exclude early are managed under row cover, which has to come off at flowering so bees can reach the blooms.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Each cantaloupe plant has both male and female flowers, so one plant can make fruit by itself, and you do not need a second variety the way seedless watermelon does. Bees carry the pollen between the flowers, and cantaloupe needs a lot of bee visits to set each melon, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. If fruit is not forming, grow some flowers nearby for the bees and try hand-pollinating in the morning. Remember to take any row cover off once the flowers open so the bees can get in.
crops.description_seasoned: Cantaloupe, the netted, orange-fleshed muskmelon most Americans call cantaloupe (botanically Cucumis melo, reticulatus group), is a heat-loving, long-season trailing vine grown for its aromatic, sweet summer fruit. It wants full sun, warm soil, and a long warm season of roughly 75 to 90 days, and it does not begin in earnest until the ground is reliably warm, so most gardeners either wait for warm soil to direct sow or set out transplants started about three weeks ahead. The single most important thing to learn is the harvest call: cantaloupe is picked once per fruit, at full slip, when the stem separates cleanly from the melon under light thumb pressure, backed up by coarse raised netting, a background skin that turns from green to tan under the net, and a sweet musky aroma at the stem end. Picked at full slip it is at peak sweetness; picked early it will soften and grow aromatic but never actually sweeten, since the sugar is set on the vine. The crop's defining trouble is disease: cantaloupe is one of the most bacterial-wilt-susceptible cucurbits, far more than watermelon, so keeping cucumber beetles off young plants is the whole game, and it is also prey to Fusarium wilt, gummy stem blight, Alternaria, and the powdery and downy mildews. Give it heat, room to sprawl, bees for pollination, even water through sizing and a dry finish to sweeten, and cool-summer northern and foggy-coastal gardeners should lean on early varieties, transplants, and black plastic mulch.
crops.description_beginner: Cantaloupe is the sweet, orange-fleshed melon with the tan, netted skin, and it is a heat-loving vine that spreads across the garden through the summer. It needs full sun, warm soil, and a long warm season, so wait for the ground to warm up before planting, or start plants indoors about three weeks early. The big thing to get right is when to pick: cantaloupe is ready at what growers call full slip, when the stem slips cleanly off the melon with a gentle push of your thumb, and the netting is rough and raised, the skin under it has turned tan, and it smells sweet at the stem end. Pick it then, because a cantaloupe does not get any sweeter after you pick it. Its main challenge is disease, especially a wilt spread by cucumber beetles that hits cantaloupe hard, so keep those beetles off the young plants. Give it heat, room to spread, bees to pollinate the flowers, steady water while the melons grow and less near the end, and if your summers are cool or foggy, grow a fast early variety and use black plastic mulch to warm the soil.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cantaloupe is harvested once per fruit, at ripeness, and the signature cue is full slip: press your thumb against the stem where it joins the melon, and a ripe fruit lets the stem separate cleanly, leaving a smooth, round, dished scar. No twisting or pulling should be needed. Read full slip alongside the other signs, which come on together in the last few days: the netting stands up coarse and corky over the whole fruit; the background skin between the netting turns from green to tan, buff, or yellow; a sweet, musky aroma rises at the blossom and stem end; and the tendril nearest the fruit dries and browns. Harvest at full slip for peak sweetness, since cantaloupe does not gain sugar after picking, though it will soften and grow more fragrant on the counter. Because a full-slip melon over-ripens on the vine within a day or two, check ripening melons daily as slip approaches; if you want to hold or ship a melon, pick a hair early at half slip, when the stem is just starting to separate. Lift the melon free with a light thumb push at the stem, or cut it leaving a short stub, then refrigerate promptly since it does not store long.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: You pick a cantaloupe once, when it is ripe, and the clearest sign is the stem. Give the stem a gentle push with your thumb where it joins the melon: when the melon is ripe, the stem slips off cleanly and leaves a round, dished scar. This is called full slip. Along with it, the netting on the skin gets rough and raised, the skin under the net turns from green to tan, the melon smells sweet at the stem end, and the little tendril nearest the fruit dries and turns brown. Pick at full slip, because a cantaloupe does not get any sweeter after you pick it, though it will soften a little. A ripe cantaloupe goes over the top fast on the vine, so check yours every day as it gets close. Lift it off with a gentle push at the stem, or cut it with a short piece of stem, and keep it in the fridge, since it does not store for long.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North, cantaloupe is a tight, single summer crop and a real stretch in the coldest zones. Plant after the last frost once the soil is warm (65 to 70°F), and harvest the mature crop in late summer before fall cooling. Short-season zones (3 to 4) are marginal: start transplants indoors about three weeks early, choose fast varieties such as Minnesota Midget or Sarah's Choice, and use black plastic mulch to warm the soil. Warmer zones (6 to 7) can finish larger, later types.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold North you get one cantaloupe crop a summer, and the coldest areas are a challenge. Plant after the last frost once the soil is warm, and harvest in late summer. In the coldest zones, start plants indoors, grow a fast small variety like Minnesota Midget, and use black plastic mulch to warm the soil so the melons ripen in time.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Gulf and coastal plain, cantaloupe is a spring-into-summer crop, planted after the last frost once the soil warms and harvested from early to late summer. Heat is not the limit here, disease is: humidity and rain drive gummy stem blight, Alternaria, and the mildews, and cucumber beetles bring bacterial wilt, so choose disease-tolerant varieties like Athena, water at the base, and scout hard.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, plant cantaloupe in spring after frost once the soil is warm and pick through the summer. The main challenge is disease from the humid, rainy weather, so grow tough varieties like Athena, water at the soil line, and keep cucumber beetles off the young plants.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's hot interior valleys are prime cantaloupe country, with long, hot, dry summers that ripen sweet melons. Plant after the last frost once the soil warms in spring and harvest through summer into early fall. The dry air eases foliar disease compared with the humid South, but watch for powdery mildew, spider mites in the heat, and cucumber beetles on young plants.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: California's hot inland valleys are great for cantaloupe. Plant in spring after frost once the soil is warm and pick through summer into fall. The dry heat means less leaf disease, but keep an eye out for powdery mildew, spider mites in the heat, and beetles on young plants.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's cool, foggy north coast is marginal for cantaloupe, which wants more heat than the coast usually delivers. Plant after the soil warms in late spring and harvest in late summer to fall, but expect slow ripening and lean to early varieties, the warmest, sunniest microclimate you have, and black plastic mulch. Inland and away from the fog the crop does much better.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: California's cool, foggy north coast is a tough spot for cantaloupe, which wants more heat. Plant in late spring once it warms and harvest in late summer or fall, but choose a fast, early variety, the sunniest, warmest spot you have, and use black plastic mulch. It does better the farther you are from the coastal fog.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's south coast grows good cantaloupe in its warmer inland pockets, though the immediate, cooler coastline is slower. Plant after the soil warms in spring and harvest through summer into early fall. Choose the warmest microclimate you have, use black plastic mulch near the coast, and watch for powdery mildew and cucumber beetles.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: The south coast of California grows cantaloupe well in its warmer spots, a little slower right at the cool shoreline. Plant in spring once the soil is warm and pick through summer into fall. Pick a warm, sunny spot, use black plastic mulch near the coast, and watch for powdery mildew and beetles.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: California's low desert is excellent cantaloupe country, but the calendar is flipped toward the cooler shoulders of the year. Plant in late winter to early spring so the crop sizes and ripens before the most brutal midsummer heat, and harvest from late spring into summer. The intense heat and dry air favor sweet melons and limit foliar disease; keep cucumber beetles off young plants and watch for spider mites.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's low desert, cantaloupe grows great but you plant early. Put it in the ground in late winter to early spring so it ripens before the worst summer heat, and harvest from late spring into summer. The heat makes sweet melons, but keep beetles off young plants and watch for spider mites.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern New Mexico & West Texas
warm_arid.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh cantaloupe windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (75 to 90) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full slip; no heat_pause (cantaloupe produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ and Florida cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid country of southern New Mexico and West Texas, cantaloupe thrives in the hot, dry summers. Plant after the last spring frost once the soil warms and harvest through summer into early fall. The dry air keeps foliar disease down, but the region's spring winds and cucumber beetles are worth managing on young plants, and steady irrigation with a dry finish builds sweet melons.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the warm, dry areas of southern New Mexico and West Texas, cantaloupe does well in the hot summers. Plant after the last frost once the soil is warm and pick through summer into fall. The dry air means less leaf disease, but protect young plants from wind and beetles, and water steadily, easing off near harvest to sweeten the fruit.

Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full slip; no heat_pause (cantaloupe produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ and Florida cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: Arizona's low desert is prime cantaloupe ground, but the extreme summer heat pushes planting to the cooler shoulders. Plant a spring crop in late winter and a second, separate crop in mid to late summer for fall, and harvest in late spring to early summer and again in fall. The heat and dry air make very sweet melons and limit foliar disease; keep cucumber beetles off young plants and watch spider mites.
low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: Arizona's low desert grows excellent cantaloupe, but it is so hot in summer that you plant around it. Put in a spring crop in late winter and a second one in mid to late summer, and harvest in late spring and again in fall. The heat makes sweet melons, but keep beetles off young plants and watch for spider mites.

fl_peninsula.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh cantaloupe windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (75 to 90) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full slip; no heat_pause (cantaloupe produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ and Florida cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In peninsular Florida, cantaloupe is grown in the cooler, drier halves of the year, planted in late winter to spring and again in late summer for a fall crop, avoiding the wettest part of midsummer when humidity and rain drive heavy disease. The deep-summer gap is disease- and rain-driven, not heat (cantaloupe loves the heat). Choose resistant varieties and watch closely for gummy stem blight, Alternaria, and the mildews, and keep cucumber beetles off young plants.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In Florida, plant cantaloupe in late winter to spring and again in late summer, avoiding the wettest part of summer when disease is worst. The break in midsummer is about rain and disease, not heat, since cantaloupe likes it hot. Choose disease-resistant varieties, watch the leaves closely, and keep beetles off young plants.

Heat-loving warm-season crop, single harvest at full slip; no heat_pause (cantaloupe produces through summer heat); hottest desert/AZ and Florida cells split spring/late-summer for crop turnover.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii and other frost-free tropical areas, cantaloupe can be planted across a wide window, leaning to the drier months and warm, sunny sites, since heavy rain and humidity drive the mildews and other foliar diseases. Harvest runs across much of the year. Keep cucumber beetles and other cucurbit pests in check on young plants and choose disease-tolerant varieties.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii and frost-free tropical areas, you can plant cantaloupe across much of the year, best in the drier months and sunny spots, since a lot of rain brings on leaf disease. You can harvest through much of the year. Keep beetles off young plants and grow disease-tolerant varieties.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cantaloupe transplants go out Feb 25 - Mar 20 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide, corroborated by the Bilingual LRGV planting table's 85 to 90 day maturity figure for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest spring harvest at about 85 days from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest spring harvest at about 90 days from the latest set-out date.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall cantaloupe transplants go out Aug 1 - Sep 1 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide / Bilingual LRGV fall window for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest fall harvest at about 85 days from the earliest fall set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest fall harvest, extending into the mild Valley winter tail before spring returns.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, cantaloupe is a two-season crop. Plant Feb 25 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest, then plant again Aug 1 - Sep 1 for a fall crop. Skip the hottest weeks of summer: the plant just does not perform well in the worst of the heat, so most Valley gardeners skip it. It rarely if ever frosts here, so both the spring and fall windows run on Valley heat, not on a frost date.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Cantaloupe in the RGV runs on the Valley's two-crop calendar: set out Feb 25 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest running May 21 - Jun 18, then set out again Aug 1 - Sep 1 for a fall harvest running Oct 25 - Nov 30. TAMU AgriLife's Valley planting guidance simply leaves that stretch off the calendar for this crop, rather than asserting a specific heat-failure mechanism. Frost is essentially absent here, so both plantings are timed against heat, not cold. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 4 weeks before the May set-out, exactly the lead time OSU Extension's Oregon planting table (EM9027) specifies for cantaloupe. OSU flags the immediate coast not suitable for this crop outright; WSU's Washington guide corroborates cantaloupe as one of the state's most heat-demanding vegetable crops.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out in May in the Willamette Valley once the soil is reliably warm, per OSU EM9027's Region 2 window; OSU rates Region 1 (the immediate coast) not suitable for cantaloupe at all, a flag this cell honors with a later, compressed coastal window instead of the valley's date.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fruit reaches full slip roughly 75 to 90 days after transplant on a typical warm-season site (OSU); the maritime valley's cooler, cloudier summer than inland Oregon pushes actual ripening later than the base days-to-maturity, so this cell budgets extra weeks for a genuinely marginal warm-season crop.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest window closes well ahead of the valley's average first frost; choose the earliest, shortest-season cultivars (55 to 70 day types) to maximize the odds of a full-slip melon before the season ends.

8.zone_notes: OSU Extension's Willamette Valley table (EM9027) gives cantaloupe a May set-out window, used verbatim here. Even in the valley, the warmest of the two PNW zones, cantaloupe is a genuine stretch: this cell budgets a slow, roughly 100-day-plus run to full slip (well beyond the crop's base 75 to 90 day maturity) to reflect the cool, marine-tempered summer. Grow only the earliest short-season cultivars, in the sunniest, most sheltered bed, under black plastic mulch, with a floating row cover or low tunnel through June.

9.zone_notes: OSU Extension's own planting table rates the immediate coast (Region 1) not suitable for cantaloupe outright; this is not a recommended coastal crop. This cell authors a conservative, compressed window anyway, honestly, for a gardener who wants to try it in the warmest microsite available: a later set-out once the marine air finally warms, and a harvest clipped tight against the coast's own early-November first frost. Expect a real chance of no ripe fruit at all in a cool summer.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Cantaloupe struggles here because it wants a lot of steady summer heat, and our cool, marine air usually does not deliver it. OSU Extension says the immediate coast is not a good fit for this crop at all. Away from the coast, plant in May once the soil has warmed, choose the fastest-ripening variety you can find, and give it your sunniest, most sheltered spot with black plastic mulch under it and a row cover over it early on. Even then, some years the melons just will not ripen before the weather turns. Right on the coast, treat this as a fun experiment, not a crop to count on.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Cantaloupe is a stretch on this side of the Cascades: it wants sustained summer heat that the marine-cooled Puget Sound and Willamette Valley climate rarely delivers, and OSU Extension rates the immediate coast not suitable for it outright. In the valley, set out transplants in May once the soil is reliably warm (OSU's own recommended window), choosing the earliest, shortest-season cultivars (55 to 70 days, not the 90-day storage types); the warmest, most sheltered, full-sun spot in the garden, black plastic mulch, and a floating row cover or low tunnel through June make a real difference. Even with all of that, expect slow ripening most years and a real chance the fruit does not finish before fall cools things down. On the coast itself, treat cantaloupe as a genuine experiment rather than a reliable crop.

plant_out.source_quote: Zone 8a Spring: Apr 10-Jul 20 | Zone 7a Spring: Apr 20-Jul 1 (Muskmelon)
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sow once the soil has warmed, in the window VCE 426-331 Table 4 documents for muskmelon (zone 8: Apr 10; zone 7: Apr 20); VCE does not list this crop as a transplant crop, and its fall column is blank (not recommended in this belt).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins bearing roughly 82 days after sowing, this crop's own days-to-maturity.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest wraps up ahead of the belt's real first frost, which this warm-season crop cannot survive; the latest sowings in VCE's window leave the least margin before frost.

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Cantaloupe is a warm-season melon grown as a single direct-sown crop here, planted once the soil is warm and picked through summer into early fall. There is no fall planting in this belt, a summer-sown melon would not mature before frost. Zone 8's longer season allows sowing into late July; zone 7 narrows that to early July.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: VCE 426-331 lists muskmelon with a spring-only window and a blank fall column: zone 8 Apr 10 to Jul 20, zone 7 Apr 20 to Jul 1. At 82 days to maturity, cantaloupe comfortably finishes well ahead of the belt's first frost even from the latest sowings, so unlike the belt's winter squashes and pumpkin, it needs no frost-margin caveat here. z7's window trails z8's by about ten days at both ends.

mid_south.region_label: Mid-South: Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sow once the soil has warmed, in the spring window the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension documents for muskmelon; the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension does not list it as a transplant crop, and gives it no fall planting window in this belt, so it grows as a single long-season spring crop.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins bearing roughly 82 days after sowing, this crop's own days-to-maturity.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest wraps up ahead of the belt's real first frost, which this warm-season crop cannot survive; the latest sowings in the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's window leave the least margin before frost.

mid_south.region_notes_beginner: Cantaloupe is a warm-season melon grown as a single direct-sown crop here, planted once the soil warms and picked through summer into early fall. There is no fall planting in this belt, a summer-sown melon would not mature before frost. Zone 8's longer season allows sowing into mid July; zone 7 narrows that to late June.
mid_south.region_notes_seasoned: The University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension lists muskmelon with a spring-only window and no fall planting: zone 8 Apr 5 to Jul 15, zone 7 Apr 15 to Jun 26. At 82 days to maturity, cantaloupe comfortably finishes well ahead of the belt's first frost even from the latest sowings, so unlike the belt's winter squashes and pumpkin, it needs no frost-margin caveat here. z7's window opens about ten days later than z8's and closes earlier, reflecting its shorter season.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sown or a short indoor head start; the chart's March-April-plus-June shading is read as one continuous window on the Mojave's long warm season.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Matures roughly 82 days after sowing; the earliest-sown plants set the harvest's start date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The latest sowing is timed to mature by this frost-anchored margin.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Cantaloupe goes in the ground from March through mid-June in the Las Vegas Valley (start seed indoors three weeks early for a head start, or direct-sow once the soil is warm), and the vines grow right through the summer heat without a break. Fruit starts ripening in late spring from the earliest sowings, and later plantings keep melons coming into early fall. Look for the stem to slip cleanly from the fruit as your ripeness cue.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The UNLV/UNR Master Gardener chart shades cantaloupe March through April and again in June; on the Mojave's long frost-free calendar that reads as one continuous sowing window rather than two separate crops, so it is authored here as a single succession, March into mid-June, that runs straight through the June to September heat with no pause, unlike the valley's fruiting nightshades. The earliest sowings ripen first, and June sowings extend the harvest into September, always with a safety margin ahead of the valley's late-November first frost (tighter at the cooler zone 8 fringe, roomier at Laughlin in zone 10).

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sow about April 1, once the soil is warm and frost danger has passed, per USU Extension's St. George Group D (Very Tender) planting date.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins ripening about 82 days after the April 1 sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Because this crop sets fruit through the desert summer with no heat-driven pause, picking continues from vine to vine into fall, ending as the November 1 average first frost approaches.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Sow cantaloupe directly in the ground around April 1 in St. George, once the soil has warmed, and the vines will grow and set fruit right through the summer with no break, unlike tomatoes and peppers, which shut down in July heat. Melons start ripening by late June and keep coming into October. Look for the stem to slip cleanly away from the fruit with gentle pressure, a sign it is ready to pick.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: USU Extension lists cantaloupe as a Group D (Very Tender) crop for St. George, direct-sown about April 1, just after the March 30 average last frost. At an 82-day maturity the first melons ripen by late June, and because cantaloupe sets fruit continuously through the desert heat rather than aborting blossoms like the nightshades, picking continues from vine to vine into October, well ahead of the November 1 average first frost. USU does not document a fall replanting for this crop in the St. George area, so the single spring sowing carries the whole season.

notifications.title_seasoned: Protect young cantaloupe from cucumber beetles
notifications.title_beginner: Keep beetles off your young plants
notifications.body_seasoned: Your cantaloupe seedlings are up, which is exactly when cucumber beetles mass on small plants and can infect them with bacterial wilt, a disease cantaloupe is highly prone to. Keep beetle numbers very low, use row cover until flowering, and scout daily.
notifications.body_beginner: Your young cantaloupe plants are the most at risk from cucumber beetles, which spread a wilt disease cantaloupe catches easily. Keep the beetles off with a light cover until the flowers open, and check the plants often.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your cantaloupe is flowering. Fruit set depends on many bee visits per female flower, so if small fruit yellow and drop, hand-pollinate in the morning and keep blooms unsprayed. A single variety sets fruit on its own, so no second pollinizer is needed.
notifications.body_beginner: Your cantaloupe is flowering. If the tiny melons turn yellow and fall off, the flowers were not pollinated, so try hand-pollinating in the morning. One variety will fruit on its own, as long as bees visit.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your cantaloupes for full slip
notifications.title_beginner: Time to check if your cantaloupes are ripe
notifications.body_seasoned: Your cantaloupes should be nearing ripeness. Press the stem with your thumb: at full slip it separates cleanly, and the netting is coarse, the skin under it tan, and the stem end sweet-smelling. Check daily, since a full-slip melon over-ripens on the vine fast.
notifications.body_beginner: Your cantaloupes should be getting close. Give the stem a gentle push: when it slips off cleanly and the melon smells sweet, it is ripe. Check every day, since a ripe cantaloupe goes over the top fast on the vine.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost is coming, harvest your cantaloupes
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning for your cantaloupes
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast. Cantaloupe is frost-tender, and frost ends the vines, so harvest any full-slip or near-slip melons now. Under-ripe melons will not sweeten off the vine, so pick what is closest to ready.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming, and it will kill the vines. Pick any ripe or nearly ripe cantaloupes now, since they will not get any sweeter once frost hits.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat may briefly stall fruit set
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell may slow fruit set
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A stretch of extreme heat is forecast. Cantaloupe thrives in heat, but very hot days with hot nights can briefly reduce pollination and drop young fruit. Keep moisture steady; set usually resumes as the worst heat eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Very hot weather is coming. Cantaloupe loves heat, but the most extreme days may slow fruit set for a while. Keep it well watered, it usually picks back up when it cools a little.

Systemic dead-URL items (yellow iastate /encyclopedia/squash 404s; honeydew 404 UMN log URL) flagged for the post-123 URL-liveness sweep.

open_findings.summary: Per-zone resolved_by_zone planting/harvest windows are MODELED from days-to-maturity (75-90) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates (Clemson/UGA transplant-2-weeks-early and warm-soil rule, Iowa State central-Iowa mid-May, AZ/CA-desert spring + late-summer split). Individual per-zone dates are not each source-verified against a live regional planting calendar.
open_findings.basis: Warm-season frost-anchored windows derived deterministically from DTM + crop-invariant frost anchors, mirrored on the certified watermelon melon analog; calendars internally coherent (A5/A24/A37). Daily biology review + a per-region source-truth sample should confirm the regional dates before flip.

open_findings.summary: ph.preferred_range is [6.0, 6.8]. The two strongest cited melon sources (UMN, UGA B1179) give a 6.0-6.5 sweet spot; muskmelon is commonly cited at 6.0-6.8 by other extensions. Preferred is set to 6.0-6.8 per the melon-general range with the 6.0-6.5 core noted in prose.
open_findings.basis: 6.0-6.5 is the cited sweet spot; 6.0-6.8 is the honest broader preferred band for muskmelon. The prose leads with the sourced 6.0-6.5 and states the 6.0-6.8 range.

open_findings.summary: spacing_inches is [24,36], representing in-row plant/hill spacing (Clemson/UMN 18-24 in-row; UGA 2-3 ft in-row; Iowa State hills 1.5-2 ft). The between-row spacing of about 5 to 6 feet (Clemson 6-8 ft) is carried in prose (soil_prep, description, yield) rather than the numeric field, which represents plant-to-plant placement. [CORRECTION 2026-10-02: the 24-36 in figure stands, but the between-row spacing is no longer carried only in prose: row_spacing_inches is 60-90 in since PLA-10 promote 1, and the hills are a non-default planting_layout entry -- see PLA-10 promote 1, d021116.]
open_findings.basis: The placeability number is in-row plant spacing; wide row/hill spacing is described in consumer prose. Well within the non-tree spacing bound.

open_findings.summary: northern_tier z3-z4 and ca_north_coast cells are MARGINAL for cantaloupe, which needs a long, warm season to ripen and sweeten. The calendars represent the best-case short-season approach (early varieties such as Minnesota Midget/Sarah's Choice, indoor-started transplants, black plastic mulch); a poor-summer year may not finish a sweet crop. Marginality is described in the affected region_notes and here, not encoded as unsuitability.
open_findings.basis: Cantaloupe IS grown to the cold edge with early types + transplants + plastic mulch (UMN), so the cells are honestly marginal-but-possible rather than unsuitable; the region prose carries the warning.

open_findings.summary: Cantaloupe is modeled with NO heat_pause in any cell. It is heat-loving and produces through southern and desert summer heat, so the hot regions (ca_desert, low_desert_az, warm_arid, se_gulf, fl_peninsula) run a continuous summer crop or a spring-plus-late-summer split for crop turnover, not a heat exclusion. Florida's deep-summer gap is disease/rain-driven (wet season), not heat, and is represented as a growing bridge rather than a pause token.
open_findings.basis: Cantaloupe's heat tolerance is well established; a heat_pause would misrepresent its physiology (same call as the certified watermelon analog). No heat_pause token means no heat_pause backing object is required (A28). Flagged for the biology review to confirm the regional window shapes; if A37 flags any hot-region summer gap, it is normalized centrally, not hand-fixed.

open_findings.summary: AZ1005, the University of Arizona Cooperative Extension Vegetable Planting Calendar for Maricopa County (Kai Umeda, revised 9/18), read 2026-08-05. Its grid is rotated 90 degrees, so the windows were reconstructed from character coordinates rather than read by eye, and the method was validated first against pumpkin, whose grid row (Mar 1, Mar 15, then Jul 1, Jul 15, Aug 1) reproduces our existing cell. The combined "Melons, Cantaloupe Honeydews, etc." row carries S (direct seed) marks from Feb 15 continuously through Jul 15. Our cells now cite that document and diverge from it at BOTH ends. Our spring plant_out opens Feb 1, two weeks ahead of the document's first mark, and our second planting runs Jul 15 - Aug 15 where the document's last mark is Jul 15. Neither end is called an error here: Maricopa County is one part of the low desert and our region spans more, and a fortnight at the front of a direct-sown cucurbit window is within the range where soil temperature rather than the calendar governs. But neither end is SOURCED, and the early opening is the one that can cost a reader a planting, since seed going into cold February soil rots rather than germinating. NOT retuned here, because changing it means moving a consumer-facing date and that needs its own evidence; the honest options are to trim to the document or to declare the shoulders modeled. Compare the soil-temperature evidence in this crop's uscrn_validation record before ruling.
open_findings.basis: AZ1005, the University of Arizona Cooperative Extension Vegetable Planting Calendar for Maricopa County (Kai Umeda, revised 9/18), read 2026-08-05. Its grid is rotated 90 degrees, so the windows were reconstructed from character coordinates rather than read by eye, and the method was validated first against pumpkin, whose grid row (Mar 1, Mar 15, then Jul 1, Jul 15, Aug 1) reproduces our existing cell. Compared against this crop's own low_desert_az resolved cells and its uscrn_validation record.
open_findings.resolution: RULED 2026-08-05 (PLA-122). Spring open TIGHTENED Feb 1 to Feb 15 to match AZ1005's first seed mark. The Feb 1 open was unsourced and early in the direction that costs a reader a planting, and the cell already cites AZ1005, so it was citing a document that disagreed with it. Confirmed while applying: Feb 15 is also within one day of what this cell's OWN declared anchor implies (last_frost Jan 31 plus the arm's 14-day offset gives Feb 14), so the document and the frost arithmetic agree and the previous Feb 1 reproduced from neither. The LATE end stays at Aug 15 against the document's Jul 15: late is the safe direction for a direct-sown cucurbit, and the divergence stays on the record here rather than being edited away.

crops.name: Strawberry

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Strawberries grow best in loose, rich soil that drains well, like a sandy loam. Their roots are shallow, so they rot if the ground stays soggy. If your soil is heavy clay or puddles after rain, build a raised bed or a mounded row about 12 inches tall and plant into that. Mixing 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting gives the roots a good start.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Strawberries want a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam with steady but not excessive moisture. The roots are shallow and fibrous, so they suffocate in soil that stays waterlogged for more than a day or two, and root rots follow. On heavy or slow-draining ground, plant into a raised bed or mounded row about 12 inches high so water drains away from the crowns. Work 1 to 2 inches of compost or aged organic matter into the bed before planting to lift organic matter above 3 percent.

ph.note_beginner: Strawberries prefer soil on the slightly acidic side, roughly pH 5.6 to 6.5. A cheap test kit shows where you are. Garden sulfur lowers a too-high number; garden lime raises a too-low one. Both take a few months to take effect, so test and adjust the season before you plant.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for slightly acidic soil in the range of pH 5.6 to 6.5. Test the bed a season ahead so there is time to adjust: elemental sulfur brings a high reading down, and ground dolomitic limestone raises a low one. Both amendments take months to move the soil, so apply them well before the crowns go in.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting and through the first season for new plantings; for established June-bearing beds, once a year at renovation.
fertilizer.timing: renovation
fertilizer.example_product: 16-16-16 balanced fertilizer (or a comparable all-purpose granular)
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Strawberry feeding is nitrogen-driven and timed to the planting model. In the first year, apply a total of about 0.5 to 0.8 ounces of actual nitrogen per 10 feet of row, split across the season: a small dose one to two weeks after planting, a second about a month later, and a third roughly two months after planting. On established June-bearing beds, do not feed in spring; spring nitrogen drives leaf growth, not fruit, and a dense canopy traps moisture and promotes gray mold. Instead, fertilize once at renovation, just after harvest, to build the flower buds for next year. Established day-neutral and everbearing plants, which fruit all season, take the same total split into monthly doses through summer with an optional August feeding. On sandy soil, divide every rate into more frequent, lighter applications.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Strawberries mainly need nitrogen, and when you feed depends on the type. The first year, give a little fertilizer two or three times spread across the season rather than one big dose. After that, the rule for June-bearing plants is simple: do not feed in spring, because it grows lots of leaves but not more berries, and the thick leaves trap dampness that causes mold. Feed them once instead, right after harvest when you cut the plants back. Day-neutral and everbearing plants, which fruit all summer, get small amounts spread across the months instead. If your soil is sandy, feed smaller amounts more often.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to renovate and feed your June-bearing strawberries. Mow the old leaves, narrow the row, then apply about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row and water it in to set next year's crop.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your June-bearing strawberries are ready for their after-harvest cutback and feeding. Mow the old leaves, then give the plants a balanced fertilizer and water it in to help next year's berries.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced analysis such as 16-16-16 works well. Rates are given as actual nitrogen per length of row, so divide the nitrogen you need by the decimal nitrogen fraction of your product: about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet at renovation works out to roughly 2.5 to 3.75 ounces of 16-16-16 per 10-foot row.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 16-16-16 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is a good all-purpose choice. Follow the label rate for the row length you are feeding, and water it in after spreading.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: First year: about 0.5 to 0.8 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row total, in two to three splits. Established June-bearers: about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row, all at once at renovation. Day-neutral and everbearing: about 0.1 to 0.2 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet each month after spring growth begins, with an optional August dose.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A rough guide: feed a new bed lightly two or three times the first year. Feed an established June-bearing bed once, after harvest. Feed day-neutral or everbearing plants a little each month through summer. Use the label rate on your fertilizer for the length of your row.

companions.note_beginner: The most important placement rule for strawberries is about what grew there before, not what you plant beside them. Do not put strawberries where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries grew recently. Those plants can leave a soil disease called Verticillium wilt behind, and it attacks strawberries too and stays in the soil for years. Also keep weeds out, since strawberries have shallow roots and lose out to weeds easily. The companion plants listed above are nice, low-risk neighbors, but they are garden tradition rather than a proven way to grow more fruit.
companions.note_seasoned: The one firm rule for strawberry placement is rotation, not companionship: do not plant strawberries where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries have recently grown, because all of them host Verticillium wilt, a soilborne fungus that also attacks strawberries and lingers in the ground for years. Keep the same crops out of the bed for several years afterward. Beyond that, strawberries compete poorly with weeds because their roots are shallow, so the most valuable neighbor is bare, weed-free soil rather than any particular plant. The good-companion pairings above are traditional and low-risk, not documented yield boosters.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans are an easy, friendly neighbor for strawberries. They do not compete much and add a little nitrogen to the soil, though do not expect them to make your berries bigger.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume Rhizobium N-fixation is established biology and benefits a neighboring moderate feeder; bush beans also do not compete heavily with low strawberry crowns. mechanistic/medium: sound mechanism, but the same-season transfer to strawberries specifically is modest and timing-dependent (much released on decomposition), so not research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Bush beans bring nitrogen fixation to the strawberry bed. Working with Rhizobium bacteria on their roots, they pull atmospheric nitrogen into a plant-available form that lightly benefits strawberries as moderate feeders, and their upright, shallow habit does not compete much with low-running strawberry crowns. As with most legume pairings, the nitrogen mostly reaches neighbors as the bean roots break down, so treat it as gentle soil-building across the season rather than an immediate feed.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce fits nicely along the edge of a strawberry bed while the berries are still small, using space the strawberries are not using yet.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Shallow-root quick interplant using space between strawberry crowns / first-year beds; extension-aligned interplant logic. Space/timing benefit, not a measured strawberry-specific effect. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce makes good use of the open space in a strawberry planting, especially in the first season before the strawberries fill in and run. It is shallow-rooted and quick, so it crops and clears before the strawberries need the room, and its low canopy helps shade soil and suppress weeds between crowns. A space-and-timing pairing rather than a pest or flavor one.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage is a herb with blue flowers that bees love. A few plants near your strawberries can bring in more bees, which helps the flowers turn into well-shaped berries.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Split call recorded honestly. The pollinator-attraction benefit is grounded (borage is a strong bee attractant; strawberry fruit set/shape improves with better pollination) and would justify likely/mechanistic on its own. But the headline traditional claim ('strawberry farmers set borage to enhance flavor and yield') is the folk part - Farmers' Almanac's science-based guide explicitly flags the analogous borage-vs-hornworm claim as often-repeated-but-unsupported, and no controlled study backs borage->strawberry flavor/yield. Net label traditional (the pairing's headline status is folk) at medium confidence on the strength of the real pollinator component. Flagging in case you'd prefer to split into two entries or relabel the pollinator basis as likely.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Borage is the traditional strawberry companion, and it is worth separating what it reliably does from what is folklore. Reliably: borage is a powerful bee magnet, and better pollinator visitation gives strawberries more complete fruit set and fewer misshapen berries, a real, mechanism-backed benefit. The older claim that borage directly improves strawberry flavor and yield through the soil is widely repeated but unsupported by controlled study, so lean on borage for pollination, not as a flavor additive.

good_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional strawberry companion: as a legume, beans fix nitrogen and occupy a different root zone, and they share no major strawberry pest. The benefit is a folk-garden one rather than a documented yield effect, so treat it as a low-risk neighbor, not a proven booster.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Classic interplanting practice; no T1 extension study documents a strawberry yield or pest benefit from the pairing.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce is a shallow, quick, cool-season crop often tucked along a strawberry bed edge while the berries fill in. It uses space and light the young strawberries are not yet using and shares no serious pest. The pairing is traditional and space-driven, not a documented growth benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use interplanting lore; no T1 source documents a strawberry benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Borage
good_seasoned.timing: interplant a few plants near the bed
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Borage is a long-standing strawberry companion said to draw pollinators and improve fruit set. The pollinator-attraction half is mechanistically plausible, since more bee visits do mean better-shaped berries, but the specific borage-strawberry pairing has not been tested in T1 extension trials, so it stays a traditional claim.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pollinator-draw mechanism is plausible but the borage-strawberry pairing is untested in T1 literature.

pests.name: Slugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in ripe fruit and leaves, with slime trails, worst in damp, heavily mulched beds and wet weather.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ragged holes eaten in the berries and leaves, with shiny slime trails. Worst in damp, mulchy beds and wet weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs, which shelter in deep or wet mulch and feed at night on soft ripe fruit.
pests.cause_beginner: Slugs, which hide in damp mulch and eat the soft ripe berries at night.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid deep straw mulch during the growing season, keep the bed tidy, and harvest ripe fruit promptly.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not pile on thick straw in summer, keep the bed clean, and pick ripe berries quickly.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here: clear away damp hiding places, do not pile on thick straw mulch in summer, and keep the bed tidy so slugs have nowhere cool and wet to shelter by day. Pick ripe berries promptly so there is less soft fruit to draw them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing daytime shelter, avoiding deep summer mulch, and prompt harvest cut the slug population at its source; keep ripening fruit up off wet ground.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hunt slugs after dark with a flashlight and pick them off, set board or beer traps for them to gather in, and ring the bed with copper strips they will not cross. Done regularly, handpicking alone can be very effective.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Nighttime handpicking, board and beer-baited traps, and 2-inch copper barriers steadily lower numbers; empty and refresh traps every few days, and renew copper once it tarnishes.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If traps and cleanup are not enough, scatter iron phosphate slug bait on the soil, not on the plants. It is much safer around pets, kids, and wildlife than the old metaldehyde baits, though slugs take several days to die.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Iron phosphate bait makes slugs stop feeding and is safer around pets and wildlife than metaldehyde; it works best alongside habitat removal, not alone, and takes several days to a week to kill.

pests.name: Spotted wing drosophila
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, collapsing spots on ripening and ripe fruit; tiny larvae feed inside berries. Populations build through the season, so later fruit is hit hardest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Soft, sunken spots on ripening berries, with tiny maggots inside. It gets worse later in the season.
pests.cause_seasoned: A vinegar fly that lays eggs in coloring fruit; the larvae feed inside as the berry ripens.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fruit fly that lays eggs in the berries as they start to color, and the maggots eat the fruit from inside.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Harvest on a tight schedule, never leave overripe fruit on the plant, and exclude adults with fine netting where pressure is high.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep up with picking, never leave overripe berries on the plant, and use fine netting if the flies are bad.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here: pick all the ripe berries often and completely, and remove and destroy any overripe or damaged fruit. Overripe berries left on the plant are where this fly breeds, so tight, clean picking is your strongest everyday tool.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Frequent, complete harvest and destroying culls removes the ripening fruit SWD breeds in; sanitation is the backbone, since populations build through the season and hit later fruit hardest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hang a cup of apple cider vinegar with a drop of dish soap near the berries to catch the flies. It tells you when they have arrived so you can time the other steps; it is a warning tool, not control.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Vinegar traps checked weekly from before ripening detect adult arrival to time harvest and exclusion; monitoring, not control.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover the planting with very fine mesh, fine enough to stop no-see-ums, before the first berries start to color, and seal it to the ground. It physically keeps the flies off the fruit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Fine mesh, about 1 mm, installed before fruit colors and sealed at every edge down to the ground, excludes adult SWD; put it on too late and you trap flies inside with the fruit.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If pressure is high on a later crop, spinosad is the organic spray with the best track record on this fly, but it is hard on bees while wet, so spray at dusk and mind the days-to-harvest on the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad is the most effective organic material against SWD; rotate it to slow resistance, spray at dusk to spare bees, and observe the pre-harvest interval on a crop you pick continuously.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A last resort for heavy pressure only. It kills fast but hits bees and beneficials, and on a crop you pick every few days the days-to-harvest limit really matters, so read the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rescue-only; broad-spectrum and disruptive, with a pre-harvest interval that is limiting on continuously harvested strawberries. Time it to dusk, off bloom.

pests.name: Tarnished plant bug (lygus)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Catfaced fruit, dimpled and pinched at the tip with seedy, woody patches; most noticeable on day-neutrals in summer.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lumpy, dented berries with a pinched, seedy tip. Most common on day-neutral plants in summer.
pests.cause_seasoned: Lygus bugs feeding on developing flowers and fruit, which disrupts seed and berry development at the tip.
pests.cause_beginner: A small bug that feeds on the flowers and young fruit, which makes the berry tip grow lumpy.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Control broadleaf weeds that host lygus near the planting and keep the bed clean through the season.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pull broadleaf weeds near the bed, since the bugs breed on them, and keep the area tidy.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here, and this is the main control: keep broadleaf weeds down in and around the bed, since that is where these bugs breed and shelter. Watch the flowers while fruiting so you catch a buildup early.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing the broadleaf weeds that host lygus in and around the planting is the primary lever; scout flowers through fruiting, since the damage that catfaces fruit is done at bloom.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Minute pirate bugs, big-eyed bugs, and parasitic wasps feed on the young bugs, so avoid broad sprays that would kill them. Because lygus fly in from weeds and field edges, though, natural enemies only help so much on their own.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserving natural enemies gives partial suppression, but lygus are mobile and reinvade from surrounding vegetation, so biological control is a supporting step, not a standalone fix; weed sanitation matters more.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Only if the bugs are ruining a lot of fruit and weeding has not been enough. A fast synthetic that also kills bees and beneficials, so keep it off flowers and treat it as a last resort.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rescue-only; broad-spectrum and disruptive to the natural enemies above, with a label pre-harvest interval. Lygus are only moderately susceptible, so it does not substitute for weed control.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new growth and leaf undersides, with sticky honeydew and sometimes sooty mold; aphids can also transmit strawberry viruses.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Groups of tiny soft bugs on new leaves and leaf undersides, leaving a sticky film. They can also spread plant viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Aphids feeding on plant sap, building up quickly on tender new growth.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids, tiny bugs that suck plant juices and multiply fast on new leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified plants to limit virus introduction, and avoid excess nitrogen that flushes soft, aphid-prone growth.
pests.prevention_beginner: Start with clean plants, and do not over-feed, since lots of soft new growth attracts aphids.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here: do not overfeed. Too much nitrogen pushes out soft new growth that aphids multiply on, so feed modestly. Starting with clean, certified plants also limits the viruses aphids can spread.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Modest nitrogen keeps growth steady and less aphid-prone; clean certified stock limits virus introduction, since aphids also vector strawberry viruses.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A strong jet of water knocks aphids off the leaves, and most cannot climb back on. Do it early in the day so the leaves dry quickly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful spray dislodges colonies from sturdy plants; spray early so foliage dries and disease is not encouraged.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps eat aphids and usually keep them in check for free. Protect them by not reaching for broad sprays.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident ladybugs, lacewings, syrphid larvae, and parasitic wasps hold aphids down; avoiding broad-spectrum sprays and managing the ants that tend them is what keeps them working.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For a heavy infestation, insecticidal soap kills the aphids you spray directly. It only works while wet, so coat them well, and it spares beneficials once dry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Contact soap smothers aphids with no residual, so coverage and repeat sprays matter; it spares dry-surface beneficials.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil is another low-residue option that coats and disrupts aphids. Do not spray it in heat above 90°F or on a drought-stressed plant, and spray at dusk to avoid wetting bees.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Neem works by contact smothering and as an antifeedant and growth regulator; a contact spray, so apply at dusk to avoid wetting foraging bees. Avoid above 90°F or on stressed plants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rarely needed for aphids, and a last resort only. It kills fast but hits the ladybugs and other good bugs too, which can make aphids worse later, so keep it off flowers.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rescue-only and usually counterproductive on aphids, since it removes the natural enemies that regulate them and can trigger resurgence. Observe the label pre-harvest interval.

pests.name: Two-spotted spider mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling and bronzing of leaves with faint webbing on undersides, worst in hot, dry, dusty conditions; heavy infestations weaken plants and reduce yield.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves look speckled and bronzed, with fine webbing underneath. Worst in hot, dry, dusty weather, and bad cases weaken the plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tiny mites that feed on the underside of leaves and multiply rapidly in hot, dry weather.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny mites under the leaves that multiply fast when it is hot and dry.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid drought stress and dusty conditions, and keep plants well watered in heat.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep plants watered in hot weather and avoid letting them get dusty and dry.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here: keep plants well watered, since spider mites flare on hot, dry, drought-stressed plants, and knock the mites back with a hard spray of water to the leaf undersides, which also raises the humidity they dislike. Keeping the bed from getting dusty helps too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mites explode on drought-stressed, dusty plants, so steady watering is preventive; a forceful water spray to leaf undersides dislodges them and raises humidity. This foundation often keeps mites below the threshold that needs any spray.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Predatory mites and other tiny good bugs feed on spider mites and often control them on their own. Avoid broad sprays, including too much sulfur, that would kill these helpers.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Predatory mites are the key natural enemy; conserve them by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays and sulfur, which set them back.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For a bad case, horticultural oil smothers the mites on contact. Cover the leaf undersides well, and do not spray in heat above 90°F or on a drought-stressed plant.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Narrow-range oil knocks mites back by smothering; coverage of leaf undersides is everything. Avoid above 90°F or on stressed plants, and keep it at least 30 days from any sulfur spray in the growing season; check the oil label, since some specify longer.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil is another contact option that coats and disrupts the mites. Same rules: thorough coverage, not in high heat, and spray at dusk to avoid bees.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Neem gives partial mite control by contact and as a growth disruptor; repeat coverage is needed, and avoid high heat and stressed plants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sulfur is a last resort here. It does knock back spider mites, but it also harms the predatory mites that were helping you, so use it only if the softer steps have failed, and never in heat above 90°F.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sulfur is a protectant miticide but harms predatory mites, so it can trade a short knockdown for lost biological control; reserve it, keep it at least 30 days from any oil spray in the growing season, check the oil label since some specify longer, and avoid above 90°F.

pests.name: Root and crown weevils (black vine weevil)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Notched leaf margins from night-feeding adults, and stunted, wilting, or collapsing plants whose roots and crowns have been eaten by larvae.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaf edges notched as if cut with pinking shears, and plants that wilt or collapse because grubs have eaten the roots and crown.
pests.cause_seasoned: Weevils whose adults notch leaves at night and whose larvae feed underground on roots and crowns.
pests.cause_beginner: Beetles whose adults chew the leaf edges at night and whose grubs eat the roots underground.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rotate to a fresh site when starting a new bed, since larvae build up in older plantings, and start with clean stock.
pests.prevention_beginner: Start new beds in a fresh spot, since the grubs build up in old beds, and use clean plants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start a new bed in a fresh spot away from old strawberry plantings, since the grubs build up in beds over the years. Begin with clean, healthy plants so you are not importing them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Siting a new planting away from older, infested beds starves the soil larvae, which build up over successive years; start with clean stock.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull and destroy badly infested plants in the fall, when the grubs are feeding on the roots and crown, so they do not carry over.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing and destroying heavily infested plants in fall reduces the overwintering larval population.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On warm evenings the adult weevils come out to feed and notch the leaf edges. Go out with a flashlight and pick them off, since they cannot fly and are easy to catch by hand.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The flightless adults feed at night; handpicking or shaking them onto a cloth after dark removes egg-laying females before the next generation of root-feeding larvae.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Beneficial nematodes are microscopic good worms you water into moist, warm soil. They hunt the grubs underground and are safe for people and pets.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Entomopathogenic nematodes drenched into moist soil at roughly 60°F to 90°F infect the root-feeding larvae; time it to when larvae are present and keep the soil moist.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A last resort, and only against the adult beetles at night, since sprays cannot reach the grubs down in the soil. It hits bees and beneficials, so keep it off flowers and use it sparingly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rescue-only and limited to adults, since foliar sprays do not reach soil larvae; broad-spectrum and disruptive, with a label pre-harvest interval. Nematodes are the better tool for the root-feeding stage.

pests.name: Birds
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Pecked and partly eaten ripe berries, often the first fully colored fruit taken just before you would pick it.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ripe berries pecked or half-eaten, often the best red ones taken right before you pick them.
pests.cause_seasoned: Birds attracted to ripening red fruit.
pests.cause_beginner: Birds that go for the ripe red berries.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Net the planting before the first fruit ripens rather than after birds find it.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put netting on before the first berries ripen, not after the birds have already found them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Shiny, moving, or noisy things like reflective tape and scare-eye balloons can frighten birds off for a while, but birds get used to them fast, so move them around and swap types at least weekly. On their own they do not reliably protect the fruit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Visual and noise deterrents reduce pressure but birds habituate; rotate device types and do not leave one combination up more than a week. Best paired with netting, not relied on alone.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The reliable fix is bird netting draped over hoops so it sits off the berries, with the edges tucked to the ground so birds cannot get underneath. Put it on before the first berries ripen, not after the birds have found the patch.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Netting on a hoop or PVC frame excludes birds; laid straight on the plants they still peck through it, so support it off the canopy, extend it to the ground, and tie the edges. Install before the first fruit colors.

diseases.name: Gray mold (Botrytis fruit rot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A soft, tan rot of green and ripe fruit that quickly becomes a fuzzy gray mold, often starting where berries touch soil, mulch, or another berry. It spreads fast through a picked basket.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Berries turn soft and rot, then grow a gray fuzz. It often starts where a berry touches the ground or another berry, and spreads quickly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Botrytis cinerea, which overwinters on dead leaves and thrives when it rains during bloom and fruit development.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold that lives on old dead leaves and takes hold when it is wet while the plants are flowering and fruiting.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid spring nitrogen on June-bearers, which thickens the canopy and traps moisture. Water at the base rather than overhead, space plants for airflow, and pick fruit promptly and often.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not feed June-bearing plants in spring, since extra leaves trap dampness. Water at the soil, give plants room to breathe, and pick ripe berries often.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here: lay straw around and between the plants so the ripening berries sit up off the wet soil. Fruit that is not touching damp ground is far less likely to rot with gray mold.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A good straw layer keeps fruit off wet soil and cuts rain splash, lowering Botrytis pressure; a foundational cultural step, though it reduces rather than eliminates rot.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give plants room and water at the soil rather than overhead so the canopy dries quickly. Gray mold takes hold in damp, crowded, still foliage.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Wide spacing and base watering shorten leaf and fruit wetness, denying Botrytis the sustained moisture it needs; an open canopy dries fast after rain.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off and destroy moldy berries the moment you see them, since the mold spreads fast from one berry to the next, and clear away old dead leaves where it overwinters. Go easy on spring nitrogen, especially on June-bearers, since the extra soft leaves thicken the canopy and trap the dampness the mold loves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Remove infected fruit immediately and clean out old leaves at renovation and early spring; avoid spring nitrogen on June-bearers, which thickens the canopy and traps moisture. There is no home spray that cures it, so these cultural steps are the whole program.

diseases.name: Anthracnose fruit rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, circular lesions on fruit; the fungus can also infect crowns and runners, causing wilting and plant death in warm, wet spells.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, sunken round spots on the berries. The disease can also rot the crown and runners, making plants wilt and die in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Colletotrichum fungi, favored by warm, humid, rainy conditions during fruit development and spread by splashing water.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that thrives in warm, wet, humid weather and splashes around in the rain.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with certified disease-free plants, avoid overhead watering, and do not plant into ground with a recent history of the disease.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy clean, certified plants, water at the base, and avoid spots where this disease has been a problem before.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with clean, certified disease-free plants and, where anthracnose has been a problem, choose a resistant variety. Do not plant into ground with a recent history of the disease.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Certified clean stock and resistant cultivars are the foundation, since the fungus arrives on infected transplants and persists in old sites; avoid replanting into a recent-history bed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay straw mulch to keep berries off the soil and cut down on rain splashing spores up onto the fruit, which is how this disease spreads.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mulch reduces the rain and irrigation splash that disperses Colletotrichum spores; water at the base rather than overhead.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull off and destroy diseased berries and plants promptly, and give plants room so the canopy dries. Watering at the soil instead of overhead keeps spores from splashing around.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt removal of diseased fruit and plants lowers inoculum; base watering and airflow limit the warm, wet, splashing conditions the fungus needs.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the cultural steps are not holding in a warm, wet season, a copper spray can protect healthy fruit, but it must go on before infection and cannot cure berries already rotting. Copper is toxic to fish and builds up in the soil, so use it sparingly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Fixed copper is a protectant only, applied before infection during warm wet spells; it will not cure established rot. Copper accumulates in soil and harms aquatic life, so limit repeat use.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
