field_additions.note: empty-DTM herbaceous perennial berry; propagule=crown (planted as bare-root CROWNS -- prose 'position each crown with its midpoint at soil height'; renewed by runners). No dtm_anchor/ladder/sow_depth. divide N/A (runner renewal, not division); harvest_window deferred.

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set dormant bare-root crowns about two weeks before the last spring frost, as soon as the soil can be worked. The plants are dormant, so there is no need to wait until frost danger has passed (USU). Plant so the middle of the crown sits level with the soil surface. In matted rows, space plants 18 to 24 inches apart in rows 3 to 4 feet apart (UMN).

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: On an established bed, June-bearing plants begin flowering around mid-spring, near the last-frost date. UMN reports flowering begins about mid-May in southern Minnesota. Open blossoms are frost-sensitive, so a late frost during bloom can reduce the crop (OSU EC1307).

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: June-bearing strawberries ripen about four weeks after flowering (UMN), giving one concentrated early-summer flush. This is the established-bed (year 2 and later) cycle; in the planting year all flowers are removed so no crop is taken (year_one_notes).

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: The June-bearing flush runs roughly four weeks. After the last picking, renovate the matted row within about two weeks: mow the leaves two inches above the crowns, narrow the row, and fertilize (UMN, OSU EC1307).

northern_tier.plantings_provenance: Region-constant June-bearing matted-row establishment window, frost-relative. Dormant bare-root crowns are set early, around two weeks before the last spring frost, because they are dormant stock and can go in as soon as the soil can be worked. Window dates resolve per zone from zone_frost_data.json last_spring frost. Sourced to UMN, OSU EC1307, and USU home-garden guides.

3.grown_as_note_seasoned: Zone 3 grows strawberries as a perennial matted row, but it is the cold edge: crowns are damaged near 10 to 20°F at the crown, so without dependable snow cover apply two to three inches of straw mulch in late fall and rake it off as growth resumes in spring.
3.grown_as_note_beginner: In zone 3 your strawberry bed comes back each year, but winters are harsh, so cover the plants with a few inches of straw in late fall and pull it back when they start growing again in spring.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late spring frost can damage open blossoms (late May to mid-June here); cover the bed with row cover or straw on frosty nights during bloom to protect the crop.

4.grown_as_note_seasoned: Zone 4 is the reliable cold floor for perennial matted-row strawberries. Mulched June-bearing varieties such as Honeoye, Jewel, and Earliglow overwinter well here; apply straw mulch after several hard frosts in late fall and rake it off as growth resumes.
4.grown_as_note_beginner: Zone 4 is a great fit for a come-back-every-year strawberry bed. Pick winter-hardy June-bearing types, mulch with straw in late fall, and uncover the plants in spring.
4.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Open blossoms in mid-May to early June are frost-sensitive; cover the bed with row cover or straw on frosty nights during bloom to protect the crop.

5.grown_as_note_seasoned: Zone 5 grows strawberries as a dependable perennial matted row. A light straw mulch over winter protects the crowns and reduces frost heaving; rake it off as growth resumes in spring.
5.grown_as_note_beginner: Zone 5 is a comfortable fit for a strawberry bed that returns each year. A layer of straw over winter keeps the plants safe; pull it back in spring.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Blossoms opening in late April to mid-May are frost-sensitive; cover the bed on frosty nights during bloom to protect the crop.

6.grown_as_note_seasoned: Zone 6 grows strawberries as a perennial matted row with a longer, milder season than the colder zones. Light winter mulch is still worthwhile to limit frost heaving and protect crowns in open winters.
6.grown_as_note_beginner: Zone 6 strawberries come back every year and enjoy a longer growing season. A thin layer of straw over winter still helps in cold snaps.
6.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Blossoms opening in mid-April to early May can be caught by a late frost; cover the bed on frosty nights during bloom to protect the crop.

7.grown_as_note_seasoned: Zone 7 grows strawberries as a perennial matted row with the earliest bloom and harvest in the northern tier. Winters are mild enough that heavy mulch is usually unnecessary, though a light cover helps in a hard freeze; summer heat is not yet severe enough to force an annual system here.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: Zone 7 strawberries return each year and ripen earliest in this group. Winters are mild, so you usually do not need heavy winter cover.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Early bloom in late March to mid-April can still meet a late frost; cover the bed on frosty nights during bloom to protect the crop.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the north (zones 3 to 7), strawberries are a perennial: you plant them once and the same bed comes back and fruits for several years. Plant the small brown dormant crowns in early spring, as soon as you can dig the soil, even if frost is still possible. June-bearing kinds give one big batch of berries in late spring or early summer, about a month after they bloom, then grow runners that root into new plants and fill the row. After the berries finish, cut the leaves back and thin the plants to keep the bed healthy, and start a fresh bed every three or four years. In zone 3, cover plants with straw over winter for protection; berries are most reliable from zone 4 and warmer.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier (zones 3 to 7), strawberries are grown as a perennial matted-row bed, the dominant US backyard system. Set dormant bare-root crowns in early spring, about two weeks before the last frost, as soon as the soil can be worked. June-bearing types give one concentrated flush about four weeks after they flower in late spring to early summer, then send runners to fill the row. Renovate the bed within two weeks of the last harvest, mow tops two inches above the crowns, narrow the row, and fertilize, and replace the planting after three or four fruiting years. In zone 3, and in colder pockets of zone 4 without reliable snow cover, give plants extra winter protection; reliable fruiting starts at zone 4.

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set bare-root or plug transplants in the fall, from early October through mid November, the LSU AgCenter window for the Gulf Coast (mid to late October is ideal in southeast Louisiana). Strawberries are grown here as a fall-planted annual: plants are set in fall, fruited through winter and spring, then removed in early summer because humid-summer disease pressure is extreme; fresh plants are set the following fall. Grow on raised rows with plastic mulch or a thick pine-straw layer for drainage and clean fruit. This is an absolute, month-resolved window driven by the cool fall-to-spring season, not anchored to a last spring frost.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: Short-day varieties initiate flowers during the short days and cool temperatures of fall and winter, and fruit appears in late winter and early spring when conditions favor good-quality berries. Open flowers are damaged below 32 degrees Fahrenheit even though the plants themselves are cold-hardy.

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Production can begin as early as late November when plug plants are used, with the harvest running through winter and building in spring. Louisiana berries appear as early as November, December, and January.

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Fruiting continues into spring and can run to the beginning of June; after June the plants stop fruiting and turn to vegetative growth, so the planting is removed in early summer and replaced the following fall (the nine-month strawberry season). The cell harvest window is scoped to this late-fall-to-spring span.

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: The Gulf Coast grows strawberries as a fall-planted annual, not a perennial bed. ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California low desert, strawberries are a winter crop you grow and then replace, not a bed that returns for years. Plant in the fall, from about mid September to mid November, pick berries from late winter into spring, then pull the plants before the brutal summer heat and plant fresh ones next fall. Give them shade in the hot afternoons, water often because their roots are shallow, and plant where water drains away. In the cooler zone 9 areas a winter cold snap can hurt the flowers, so keep a frost cloth ready.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the California low desert (the Coachella and Imperial valleys, zones 9 and 10), strawberries are grown as a cool-season annual rather than a perennial bed, the same way they are across the Sonoran desert. Set dormant, pre-chilled plants in fall, from mid September to mid November, fruit them through winter and spring, then pull and discard the planting before the summer heat, which is too stressful to carry a bed over; replant fresh each fall. Provide afternoon shade and use well-drained, low-salt beds. Zone 9 sees occasional winter frost that can injure open blossoms below 32°F, so keep frost cloth handy during bloom; the warmest zone 10 pockets are nearly frost-free and can start fruiting a few weeks earlier. Choose desert-adapted June-bearers and rotate away from recent tomato, pepper, or eggplant beds.
ca_desert.plantings_provenance: Region-constant cool-season-annual establishment window, month-resolved (absolute), NOT frost-relative. The California low desert (Coachella and Imperial valleys) shares the Sonoran/Colorado low-desert climate, and strawberries are grown there as a fall-planted annual on the same model UA AZ1667 documents for the Arizona low desert: pre-chilled plants set mid September to mid November, fruited winter into spring, then PULLED before the summer heat. UC Master Gardener desert-valleys guidance confirms the cool-season fall-set/spring-crop rhythm for this region (the dated strawberry window itself lives in the UA low-desert publication, since strawberry is a fruit and is absent from the UC vegetable planting table -- the lesson zinnia taught). Primary anchor UA AZ1667; UC IPM cultural-tips corroborates the California cultural practice (afternoon shade, salt sensitivity, heaviest production timing). resolved_from null per cell (heat/season-driven; z9 carries winter frost but the limiter is heat). season_over emerges. A5: do NOT lift the FL or coastal-CA windows here -- the desert window is its own.

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set dormant bare-root crowns in early spring, after the danger of hard frost has passed and as soon as the soil can be worked. New Mexico State recommends spring planting because the cool weather gives the plants the best chance to establish. Plant so the middle of the crown is level with the soil surface. In a matted-row system, space plants about 18 inches apart in rows 36 to 42 inches apart and let runners fill the row to 12 to 18 inches wide; a plastic- or fabric-covered perennial bed is an alternative for day-neutral types.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: On an established bed, June-bearing plants flower in early spring from buds that formed the previous fall under short days. Those early blossoms produce the largest berries and are frost-sensitive, so frost protection during bloom is strongly recommended (NMSU).

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: The single concentrated June-bearing harvest begins in late spring. In the planting year, flowers are pinched off so no crop is taken, which strengthens the plants for a full crop the following spring (year_one_notes).

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: The spring flush finishes by early summer; matted-row beds are renovated immediately after harvest (mow old foliage above the crowns, narrow the row, weed, and fertilize), and should not be renovated after July 15. Beds remain productive for about three to four years before replanting (NMSU).

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Interior arid New Mexico and similar high-desert zone 8 areas grow strawberries as a perennial matted row, planted in early spring after hard frost. June-bearers set flower buds the previous fall and crop once in late spring; renovate the bed right after harvest and expect three to four productive years. In the warmer, lower areas, afternoon shade (a fence, wall, or 65 percent shade cloth) reduces summer heat and water stress, and a winter straw mulch protects crowns. High-pH desert soils cause iron chlorosis, so choose tolerant cultivars and treat with iron chelate as needed.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In the high desert of New Mexico (zone 8), a strawberry bed comes back each year. Plant dormant crowns in early spring once hard frost is past, and you will get one big crop in late spring. After picking, mow and tidy the bed so it stays healthy, and replant every three to four years. Shade the plants from harsh afternoon sun, mulch with straw over winter, and watch for yellowing leaves, which iron treatment fixes.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frosts are the main risk: open blossoms in April and May are frost-sensitive and the earliest blossoms produce the largest berries, so cover the bed with a frost blanket or straw on frosty nights during bloom. Siting the bed on a gentle slope so cold air drains away, or using a northern exposure to delay bloom, reduces frost loss.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the high desert of zone 8, a strawberry bed comes back year after year. Plant dormant crowns in early spring once hard frost is past, and pinch off the flowers that first year so the plants grow strong. From the second spring on you get one big crop in late spring. After picking, mow and tidy the bed to keep it healthy, and start a new bed every three to four years. Shade the plants from harsh afternoon sun, cover them with straw over winter, and protect the flowers on frosty spring nights. If the leaves turn yellow, an iron treatment usually fixes it.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In interior arid zone 8 (the New Mexico high desert and similar areas), strawberries are grown as a perennial matted row, not a pulled annual. Plant dormant bare-root crowns in early spring, after the danger of hard frost and as soon as the soil can be worked, spacing plants about 18 inches apart in rows 36 to 42 inches apart and letting runners fill the row. June-bearing plants set their flower buds the previous fall under short days and give one concentrated crop in late spring; pinch off all flowers the first year to build strong plants. Renovate the bed right after harvest (mow the old foliage above the crowns, narrow the row, weed, and fertilize) and expect about three to four productive years before replanting. In warmer, lower spots, afternoon shade reduces summer heat and water stress. High-pH desert soils cause iron chlorosis, so choose tolerant cultivars and apply an iron chelate when leaves yellow. Late spring frosts are the main threat to the crop, so protect open blossoms, and mulch crowns with straw over winter.

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set dormant, pre-chilled (frigo) bare-root or plug plants in the fall, from mid September to mid November, the University of Arizona window for the low desert (below 3,000 feet). Strawberries are grown here as a cool-season annual, not a perennial bed: plants are set in fall, fruited the following winter and spring, then pulled before the summer heat, which is too stressful to carry a planting. This is an absolute, month-resolved window driven by the low-desert fall-to-spring growing season, not anchored to a last spring frost.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: Flowering builds through the cool winter and into spring once the fall-set plants are established. Flower buds form under the short days of fall and winter (day lengths under 12 hours), and the ideal fruiting temperature range is roughly 55 to 70 degrees Fahrenheit.

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Harvest begins in late winter to early spring as temperatures warm into the fruiting range. In the low desert the first berries typically ripen around March.

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Fruiting runs into spring and finishes by about May, after which rising summer heat ends the season and the planting is pulled and discarded; new plants are set the following fall, since the heat is too stressful to carry the bed over. The cell harvest window is scoped to this late-winter-to-spring span.

9.grown_as_note_seasoned: Arizona's low desert (below 3,000 feet) grows strawberries as a cool-season annual rather than a perennial bed. Set dormant, pre-chilled (frigo) plants in fall, from mid September to mid November, fruit them through winter and spring, then pull and discard the planting before summer; the intense desert heat is too stressful to carry a bed over. Establish the bed where it gets morning sun but afternoon shade (a wall, fence, or 65 percent shade cloth) to reduce heat and water stress, and grow on well-drained beds because strawberries are sensitive to salty soil and water.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, strawberries are a cool-season crop you grow over the winter, not a bed that lives for years. Plant in fall, pick from late winter into spring, then pull the plants out before the hot summer and start fresh next fall. Give them morning sun but shade in the hot afternoon, and grow them where water drains away well.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The low desert sees a handful of freezing nights in December and January. Open blossoms and ripening fruit are damaged below 32°F, so on a night a freeze is forecast during bloom, cover the bed with frost cloth in the afternoon beforehand and anchor the edges. Frost pockets where cold air settles are best avoided.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, strawberries are a winter crop you grow and then replace, not a bed that lives for years. Plant dormant or young plants in the fall, from about mid September to mid November, pick berries from late winter into spring, then pull the plants before the hot summer and plant fresh ones the next fall. Give them morning sun but shade in the hot afternoon, water regularly because their roots are shallow, and grow them where water drains away well. A few cold nights in winter can hurt the flowers, so keep a frost cloth ready to cover them.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In the Arizona low desert (zone 9, below 3,000 feet), strawberries are grown as a cool-season annual, not a perennial bed. Set dormant, pre-chilled (frigo) bare-root or plug plants in fall, from mid September to mid November, so they establish for fruiting the following winter and spring. Plants are pulled before summer, because desert heat above the ideal 55 to 70°F fruiting range is too stressful to carry a bed over; replant fresh each fall. Grow where plants get morning sun but afternoon shade from a wall, fence, or 65 percent shade cloth, and use well-drained beds, since strawberries are highly sensitive to salty soil and water. A few freezing nights occur in December and January, so keep frost cloth handy to protect open blossoms below 32°F. Choose low-desert-adapted June-bearers, and avoid planting where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, or potatoes recently grew to limit Verticillium wilt.

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set bare-root or plug transplants in the fall, from late September to early November, the UF/IFAS window for peninsular Florida; central and west-central Florida gardeners plant in mid to late October. Strawberries are grown here as a winter annual, not a perennial bed: plants are set in fall, fruited through winter and spring, then pulled at the end of the season. This is an absolute, month-resolved window driven by Florida's fall-to-spring growing conditions (temperatures 50F to 80F and short days), not anchored to a last spring frost.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: Flowering begins in November, a few weeks after the fall planting, and fruiting follows in two or three cycles through the winter and spring. Open blossoms can be injured by air temperatures below 32F, so a freeze during the bloom and harvest season can interrupt production.

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Harvest begins in late fall, generally November into December in peninsular Florida, once the first fruit cycle ripens. Production is not constant but comes in two or three cycles across the winter and spring season.

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Fruiting continues into April or May, after which warming weather ends the season and the planting is pulled and discarded; new plants are set the following fall. The cell harvest window is scoped to this full fall-to-spring fruiting span.

10.grown_as_note_seasoned: Peninsular Florida grows strawberries as a winter annual rather than a perennial bed. Florida's fall, winter, and spring deliver the cool temperatures (roughly 50°F to 80°F) and short days strawberries need to flower and fruit, while summer heat and rain end the planting. Set transplants in fall, fruit them from late fall into spring, then pull and discard the plants and start fresh the following fall, since the best fruit comes from young plants. Use raised beds with plastic mulch for drainage and clean fruit.
10.grown_as_note_beginner: In peninsular Florida, strawberries are a cool-season crop you grow over the winter, not a bed that lives for years. You plant in fall, pick berries from late fall through spring, then pull the plants out when hot weather returns and plant new ones next fall. Raised beds covered with plastic keep the roots drained and the fruit clean.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 10 is nearly frost-free, but a rare radiational freeze can still occur on a cold, clear winter night and nip open blossoms or ripening fruit, since flowers and fruit are damaged below 32°F. On a night a freeze is forecast, cover the bed with frost cloth or a row tunnel in the afternoon beforehand and anchor it on all sides.

11.grown_as_note_seasoned: Zone 11 in the Florida peninsula is frost-free, and strawberries are grown as a winter annual on the same fall-to-spring schedule as the rest of the peninsula. The crop is driven by day length and the cool-but-mild winter rather than by frost: set transplants in fall, fruit from late fall through spring, then pull the planting when summer heat and rain return, replanting fresh the following fall. Raised beds with plastic mulch handle the heavy seasonal rain and keep fruit clean.
11.grown_as_note_beginner: In zone 11 there is no frost, but strawberries are still a cool-season crop you grow over the winter. Plant in fall, pick from late fall into spring, then pull the plants when hot, wet summer weather arrives and start over with new plants the next fall. Grow them on raised beds covered with plastic so the roots stay drained through the rains.
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 11 is frost-free, so freeze injury to blossoms is not a concern here; the season is bounded by heat and day length rather than cold. The limit on the back end is warming spring weather, which ends fruiting and signals time to pull the planting, not a spring frost.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida (zones 10 and 11), strawberries are a winter crop, not a bed that comes back for years. Plant transplants in the fall, from late September to early November, on raised beds covered with plastic so the roots drain and the berries stay clean. You will get flowers starting around November and berries in waves from late fall into April or May. When hot, wet summer weather returns, pull the plants out and plant fresh ones the next fall, because young plants make the best fruit. In zone 10 a rare cold night can hurt the flowers, so keep a frost cloth ready to cover the bed; zone 11 does not freeze. Try not to plant where strawberries, tomatoes, peppers, or eggplant grew in the last couple of years, to avoid soil diseases.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: Florida is the winter strawberry capital, and in peninsular Florida (zones 10 and 11) strawberries are grown as a winter annual, not a perennial bed. Florida's fall, winter, and spring supply the cool temperatures (about 50°F to 80°F) and short days needed for flowering and fruit, while summer heat and rain exhaust the planting. Set bare-root or plug transplants in fall, from late September to early November (mid to late October in central and west-central Florida), on raised beds covered with black plastic mulch for drainage and clean fruit. Expect flowering from November and fruit in two or three cycles from late fall into April or May, then pull and discard the plants; the highest-quality fruit comes from young plants, so replant fresh each fall. Zone 10 can see a rare freeze that nips open blossoms, so keep frost cloth handy during bloom; zone 11 is frost-free. Rotate away from beds that grew strawberries, tomatoes, peppers, or eggplant in the past two to three years to limit soilborne disease.
fl_peninsula.plantings_provenance: Region-constant winter-annual establishment window, month-resolved (absolute), NOT frost-relative. In peninsular Florida strawberries are grown as a fall-planted winter annual (UF/IFAS HS1154/HS403): single-crown transplants set late September to early November (mid to late October in central/west-central Florida), flowering from November and fruiting in two or three cycles into April or May, then PULLED and replanted the following fall. This is the frost-free fall-plant (plasticulture) sub-shape -- the PULLED annual that produces a genuine summer off-season, distinct from the ca_interior interior summer-plant CARRIED bed. resolved_from is null per cell, forced by the absence of frost (z11 frost-free; z10 nearly so), with windows month-resolved from UF/IFAS guidance -- NOT by heat-avoidance as in ca_interior. Windows anchor to UF/IFAS EDIS HS1154/HS403 (Growing Strawberries in the Florida Home Garden), corroborated by the South Florida Gardening Calendar (ENH1191/EP452) for z10b-11 timing. plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: In Hawaii, strawberries are a cool-elevation crop, grown upcountry (the slopes of Haleakala on Maui around Kula, and Waimea on Hawaii Island) where temperatures are mild, rather than in the warm lowlands. Set transplants in the cool fall months for the main winter-into-spring crop. At a fixed upcountry elevation this is a seasonal, cool-month crop, not a year-round lowland one. This is a month-resolved window in a frost-free zone, not anchored to a last spring frost.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: Flowering and fruiting follow the cooler upcountry season, building through winter into spring. Hawaii's day length varies little across the year (roughly 11 to 13.5 hours), so temperature and elevation, more than day length, set the practical season at a given site.

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: At a fixed upcountry site the harvest concentrates in the cool months; on Maui the upcountry U-pick season runs roughly February through June.

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Fruiting at a single elevation tapers as the warmer season arrives; the cell harvest window is scoped to the cool-season spring crop. Commercial Maui farms extend supply year-round only by moving harvest higher up the mountain in summer and lower in winter, which a home garden at one site cannot do.

11.grown_as_note_seasoned: In Hawaii (zone 11), strawberries are a cool-elevation niche crop, not a warm-lowland year-round one. They are grown upcountry, on the cool slopes of Haleakala (around Kula) and at Waimea on Hawaii Island, where conditions stay mild. At a fixed upcountry site, treat the bed as a short-lived perennial: set plants in the cool fall months for a main crop through winter and spring. Year-round supply exists in Hawaii only because commercial farms move harvest up and down the mountain with the seasons, which a single home garden cannot replicate. In the warm lowlands strawberries perform poorly.
11.grown_as_note_beginner: In Hawaii, strawberries grow best up in the cool higher country, like Kula on Maui, not down in the warm lowlands. Plant in the cool fall months and you will get berries through winter and spring. The big farms have berries all year because they move up and down the mountain with the seasons, but in a home garden at one spot you will get a cool-season crop, not year-round fruit.
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Upcountry Hawaii (zone 11) is frost-free, so freeze injury to blossoms is not a concern. The practical season is set by the mild upcountry temperatures and elevation rather than by cold; warm spells, not frost, end the crop at a given site.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, strawberries grow best up in the cool higher country, like Kula on Maui or Waimea on the Big Island, not down in the warm lowlands. Plant in the cool fall months and you will pick berries through winter and spring, roughly February through June. There is no frost to worry about up there. You may have heard Hawaii has strawberries year-round, but that is because big farms move up and down the mountain with the seasons. In your own garden at one spot, expect a cool-season crop, not fruit all year. Grow them where water drains away well.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii (zone 11), strawberries are a cool-elevation niche crop, not a warm-lowland year-round one. They are grown upcountry, on the cool slopes of Haleakala around Kula on Maui and at Waimea on Hawaii Island, where the climate stays mild; in the warm lowlands they perform poorly. At a fixed upcountry site, treat the planting as a short-lived perennial: set plants in the cool fall months for a main crop that builds through winter into spring, with the upcountry season running roughly February through June. Hawaii's day length barely changes across the year, so temperature and elevation, not day length, set the practical season at a given site. The year-round Hawaiian strawberry supply you see at markets comes from commercial farms shifting harvest up and down the mountain with the seasons, which a single home garden cannot replicate. Grow on well-drained beds; the zone is frost-free, so cold protection is not needed.

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set transplants in fall for the Valley's winter-annual strawberry crop, the same fall-plant system used across the warm South. Set transplants in fall, fruit them over winter into spring, then pull and discard the planting before summer heat arrives and replant fresh the following fall, since the best fruit comes from young plants. 9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, strawberries are a winter crop you grow and then replace, not a bed that lives for years. 8.grown_as_note_seasoned: West of the Cascades, strawberries are grown as a perennial matted-row bed, the same dominant US backyard system used farther north, and June-bearing types are the real signature here: WSU Clallam County Extension names Benton, Hood, Rainier, Puget Reliance, Puget Summer, Sweet Sunrise, Shuksan, and Tillamook as the recommended maritime cultivars. Set dormant bare-root crowns as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, about two weeks before the last frost. Renovate the bed within about a week of the last picking: mow the foliage, narrow the row, and fertilize. Zone 8 sits right at this crop's cold edge for the crown (hardy to 10 to 20°F, and this zone's own USDA winter-low band runs the same 10 to 20°F), so mulch with straw after the ground first freezes and pull it back as growth resumes in spring.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Here strawberries come back every year in the same bed. Plant the small dormant crowns in early spring, as soon as you can work the soil, and cut back and thin the plants about a week after you finish picking. In zone 8, cover the bed with straw once the ground has frozen, since this zone is right at the cold edge for the crowns, and pull the straw back in spring.

June-bearing types are the real strength here, and WSU recommends maritime-suited varieties like Benton, Hood, Rainier, and Shuksan. Plant the small dormant crowns in early spring, as soon as you can work the soil, even if frost is still possible; you will pick berries in June and July. pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Across the maritime Northwest, strawberries are grown as a perennial matted-row bed, and June-bearing types are a genuine regional strength: WSU Clallam County Extension names Benton, Hood, Rainier, Puget Reliance, Puget Summer, Sweet Sunrise, Shuksan, and Tillamook as the recommended maritime cultivars, cropping June into July. Set dormant bare-root crowns about two weeks before the last frost, as soon as the soil can be worked, and renovate the bed within about a week of the last picking (mow the leaves, narrow the row, fertilize). Open blossoms are damaged at 30°F, so cover the bed on a forecast frosty night during May bloom. Zone 8 sits right at this crop's cold edge for the crown; mulch with straw once the ground freezes and pull it back in spring. Zone 9's milder winter floor sits comfortably above that edge.

Treat those dates as a guide rather than a schedule: they are modeled from the zone frost date, not a published bloom calendar, so watch your own forecast through bloom and throw row cover over the bed on any night frost is predicted. A frost during bloom costs you that year's crop, not the bed.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set dormant or young strawberry plants in fall, the Southern Nevada window on the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart for the Las Vegas Valley (unlv_mg_svn). Strawberries are grown here as a cool-season annual, not a perennial bed: plants set in fall fruit the following winter and spring, then are pulled before the summer heat, which is too intense to carry a planting.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: Flowering builds through the cool winter and into early spring on the fall-set planting, once short autumn day lengths have triggered flower-bud formation.

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Harvest begins as the plants finish flowering and the weather warms toward the ideal fruiting range, well before the desert heat sets in.

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Fruiting finishes before temperatures climb past the roughly 90°F ceiling above which plants stop growing well (UNR Extension FS-02-61); the planting is then pulled and discarded, and fresh plants are set the following fall.

9.grown_as_note_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley grows strawberries as a cool-season annual, not a perennial bed: plants do not grow well above about 90°F (UNR Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), so a planting set in fall fruits through the mild winter and into spring, then is pulled before the desert's summer heat arrives, with fresh plants set again the next fall. Set dormant or young plants from September into November, the Southern Nevada window on the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart, and choose a site with morning sun but afternoon shade to ease heat and water stress. Grow on well-drained beds, since strawberries are sensitive to salty soil and irrigation water.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, strawberries are a winter crop you grow and then replace, not a bed that lives for years. Plant in fall, from around September into November, pick berries from late winter into spring, then pull the plants before the hot summer and start fresh again the next fall. Give them morning sun with afternoon shade, and plant them where water drains away well.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A handful of freezing nights occur in December and January (NWS Las Vegas frost normals). Open blossoms and ripening fruit are damaged below 32°F, so on a night a hard freeze is forecast during bloom, cover the bed with frost cloth beforehand and anchor the edges.

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: The cooler zone 8 pockets grow strawberries the same cool-season annual way, just on a slightly later, longer clock: plants do not grow well above about 90°F (UNR Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), so a planting set in early fall, ahead of this zone's earlier first frost, fruits through winter into a spring that runs a little later than the valley floor before being pulled and replanted the next fall. Choose a site with morning sun but afternoon shade, and grow on well-drained beds.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In the cooler zone 8 pockets, strawberries are grown the same winter-crop way as the rest of the region, just started a little earlier in fall and harvested a little later in spring. Plant in September to October, pick berries into early summer, then pull the plants and start fresh the next fall. Give them morning sun with afternoon shade.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The cooler zone 8 pockets see more freezing nights, and the last frost runs into mid-March, later into the bloom window than on the valley floor. Open blossoms and ripening fruit are damaged below 32°F, so keep frost cloth on hand through the whole bloom period, not just the earliest weeks.

10.grown_as_note_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley grows strawberries as a cool-season annual, not a perennial bed: plants do not grow well above about 90°F (UNR Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), so a planting set in fall fruits through the mild winter and into spring, then is pulled before the desert's summer heat arrives, with fresh plants set again the next fall. Set dormant or young plants from September into November, the Southern Nevada window on the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart, and choose a site with morning sun but afternoon shade to ease heat and water stress. Grow on well-drained beds, since strawberries are sensitive to salty soil and irrigation water.
10.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, strawberries are a winter crop you grow and then replace, not a bed that lives for years. Plant in fall, from around September into November, pick berries from late winter into spring, then pull the plants before the hot summer and start fresh again the next fall. Give them morning sun with afternoon shade, and plant them where water drains away well.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A handful of freezing nights occur in December and January (NWS Las Vegas frost normals). Open blossoms and ripening fruit are damaged below 32°F, so on a night a hard freeze is forecast during bloom, cover the bed with frost cloth beforehand and anchor the edges.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley region, strawberries are a winter crop you grow and then replace, not a bed that lives for years. Plant transplants in fall, roughly September into November (a little earlier, September into October, in the cooler zone 8 pockets), on beds where water drains away well. Pick berries from late winter into spring, then pull the plants out when the hot summer arrives and plant fresh ones the next fall, because young plants make the best fruit. Give them morning sun but afternoon shade, and keep a frost cloth handy for the coldest nights during bloom.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Nevada high desert grows strawberries as a cool-season annual, not a perennial bed, the same desert pattern this crop follows in the Arizona low desert. Plants do not grow well above about 90°F (UNR Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), so set transplants in fall, September into November on the Las Vegas Valley floor and the Laughlin corner (a little earlier, September into October, in the cooler zone 8 pockets), per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener Southern Nevada planting chart. Fruit the planting through the mild winter and into spring, then pull and discard it before summer heat arrives and replant fresh the following fall, since the best fruit comes from young plants. Choose a site with morning sun but afternoon shade, grow on well-drained beds, and keep frost cloth on hand for freezing nights during bloom, since open blossoms are damaged below 32°F.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: The St. George Dixie grows strawberries as a perennial matted row, not a pulled annual: a bed of June-bearing plants set in early spring lives for several productive years, giving one concentrated crop in late spring before the summer heat, then is renovated right after harvest and carried through the summer with mulch and afternoon shade. Set dormant bare-root crowns as soon as the soil can be worked, choose a site with morning sun and some afternoon shade in the hottest spots, and grow on well-drained beds, since strawberries are sensitive to salty soil and water. The alkaline desert soil can drive iron chlorosis, so correct yellowing leaves with a chelated iron.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In the St. George Dixie, strawberries are a bed you plant once and keep for several years, not a crop you replace every year. Plant dormant crowns in early spring, pick berries in late spring before the hot summer, then mow and thin the bed and mulch it to get through the heat. Give them morning sun with some afternoon shade in the hottest spots, and plant them where water drains away well.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late spring frost can run to the end of March here, into the strawberry bloom, and open blossoms and ripening fruit are damaged below 32°F. On a night a hard freeze is forecast during bloom, cover the bed with frost cloth beforehand and anchor the edges; mulch the crowns with straw over winter.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Strawberry does well in the low St. George Dixie, and you can grow it as a bed that comes back year after year. Plant dormant bare-root crowns in early spring, space them out, and let the runners fill in the row. June-bearing types give one big crop in late spring, before the summer heat; pinch off the flowers the first year so the plants grow strong. After harvest, mow the old leaves and thin the row, then mulch and shade the bed to carry it through the hot summer. Cover the blossoms if a late frost threatens into the end of March.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: Strawberry is a low-elevation thriver in the St. George Dixie: Utah State University Extension's Washington County fruit guidance lists strawberries among the crops that do well at the valley's low elevation, and here they are grown as a perennial matted row that lives for several years, not a bed pulled each summer. Set dormant bare-root crowns in early spring, as soon as the soil can be worked, spacing plants about 18 inches apart in rows 36 to 42 inches apart and letting runners fill the row. June-bearing types set their flower buds the previous fall and give one concentrated crop in late spring, before the worst heat; pinch off the first year's flowers to build strong plants. Renovate right after harvest, mowing the old foliage above the crowns and narrowing the row, then carry the bed through the summer with mulch and afternoon shade. Late frosts to the end of March are the main threat to open blossoms, so protect the bloom, and the alkaline soil can yellow leaves, which a chelated iron corrects.

crops.description_seasoned: The garden strawberry is a low-growing herbaceous perennial with a short, compressed stem called the crown, from which leaves, flowers, and runners arise. It is grown in three types: June-bearing (one concentrated early-summer flush, the matted-row backbone of US backyard growing), day-neutral (fruiting through the season, compact, ideal for containers), and everbearing (two lighter flushes). Plants are self-fertile, set from dormant bare-root crowns or potted plugs, and a bed stays productive for about three to four fruiting seasons before it is replaced.
crops.description_beginner: Strawberries are low, leafy plants that come back year after year. There are three kinds: June-bearing, which gives one big batch of berries in early summer; day-neutral, which gives a few berries at a time all season and does great in pots; and everbearing, which gives two smaller batches. One plant makes fruit on its own, and a strawberry patch keeps producing for about three to four years before you start a fresh one.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Fruit is ready when it is fully red and fragrant and pulls free easily; flavor is best when berries ripen on the plant. Color deepens after picking, so fruit picked at about 75 percent red stores slightly longer. Pick every one to three days, more often in warm weather, and pick before forecast rain to protect flavor and limit rot.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A strawberry is ready when it is bright red all over, smells sweet, and comes off the plant easily. Berries taste best left to ripen on the plant. Pick every day or two, more often when it is hot, and pick before heavy rain so the berries do not get watery or moldy.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: On established beds, June-bearing plants flower in mid-spring, near the last-frost date, and fruit ripens about four weeks later. Day-neutral plants flower and fruit through the season whenever temperatures sit between about 40 and 90 °F. Open blossoms are frost-sensitive, so bloom timing and late frosts together set the crop.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: June-bearing strawberries flower in mid-spring, around the last frost, and the berries ripen about four weeks after that. Day-neutral plants flower on and off all season as long as it is not too cold or too hot. Open flowers can be killed by a late frost, so watch the weather while they bloom.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Strawberries grow across USDA zones 3 through 11, but how they are grown shifts with climate. In cold-winter regions they are a perennial matted-row bed that needs winter straw mulch, since crowns are injured between about 10 and 20 °F at the crown. In hot-summer regions, summer heat exhausts the planting, so strawberries are grown as a fall-set annual that is pulled and replaced each year. Choose cultivars matched to your winters; cold-hardy types and heat-adapted types are not interchangeable.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Strawberries grow in most of the country, from cold zone 3 to warm zone 11, but the way you grow them changes with your climate. Where winters are cold, they live for years as a bed and need a straw cover in winter to protect the crowns. Where summers are hot, the heat wears the plants out, so people plant fresh ones each fall and pull them after one season. Pick a variety suited to your area.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Strawberries need only modest winter chill, and chilling is not a limiting factor for the home grower the way it is for tree fruit. It is informational here, not a hardiness gate. Cultivar cold-hardiness and summer heat, not chill accumulation, decide where and how strawberries are grown.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Strawberries do not need a set amount of winter cold to fruit, unlike apples or peaches. You do not have to count chill hours for them. What matters instead is choosing a variety that suits your winters and summers.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Strawberries are self-fertile, so a single cultivar fruits on its own with no pollinizer needed. Each flower still relies on bees, wind, and its own structure to set fully: a thoroughly pollinated flower produces the largest, best-shaped berry, while poor pollination from cold or wet bloom weather leaves small, grooved, or pinched fruit. If plants are under a row cover, pull it back as bloom opens so bees can reach the flowers.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: You only need one kind of strawberry to get fruit, because each plant pollinates itself. Bees still help a lot: a flower that gets plenty of bee visits makes a big, even berry, while one that does not can make a small or lumpy one. If you cover your plants to protect them from frost, take the cover off once the flowers open so bees can get in.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: For June-bearers, pinch off every flower the entire first season so the plant pours its energy into roots, crown, and runners instead of a small early crop; the payoff is a strong matted row and a full harvest in year two. Let the early runners root in the row to build the bed, and sweep stray runners back into the row before they root in the aisles. Day-neutral and everbearing plants are pinched only for the first four to six weeks after planting, then allowed to fruit the same season.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: In the first year, June-bearing strawberries do best if you pinch off all their flowers as they appear. It feels wrong to remove flowers, but it lets the plant build strong roots and send out runners that fill the bed, so you get a big crop the next year instead of a few berries now. Let those runners take root to fill in the row. Day-neutral and everbearing plants only need their flowers pinched for the first month or so, and then you let them fruit.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Strawberries want a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam rich in organic matter. Because the roots are shallow and rot in waterlogged soil, plant into a raised bed or mounded row about 12 inches high on heavy or slow-draining ground. Work 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting and adjust pH to 5.6 to 6.5 a season ahead, since sulfur or lime take months to act. Avoid ground that recently grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries, which leave Verticillium wilt in the soil.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Strawberries like loose, rich soil that drains well. Their roots are shallow and rot in soggy ground, so if your soil is heavy clay or puddles after rain, build a raised bed or mound about 12 inches tall and plant into that. Mix in an inch or two of compost before planting. Strawberries prefer slightly acidic soil, so test it the season before and adjust if needed. Do not plant where tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or other berries grew recently, because they leave behind a soil disease that attacks strawberries.
crops.establishment_note: Strawberries are planted one year and reach full production the next. A June-bearing matted-row bed stays productive for about three to four fruiting seasons before yield and berry size decline and it is time to start a fresh bed in a new spot.
crops.renovation_seasoned: Renovation applies to June-bearing matted rows. Do it within a week or two of picking the final berries, while the plants still have time to regrow before fall. Mow or shear the old leaves to roughly 2 inches above the crowns without cutting into the crowns themselves, rake out the debris to cut next spring's fruit rot, narrow the row back to about 10 to 12 inches by tilling or hoeing the edges, then fertilize and water to push fresh leaf and runner growth. Leave day-neutral and everbearing plants alone, since they are still fruiting in late summer.
crops.renovation_beginner: Renovation is a once-a-year tidy-up for June-bearing strawberries, done a week or two after the last berries are picked. Mow or cut the old leaves down to about 2 inches above the crowns (the thick stems at soil level), being careful not to cut into the crowns. Rake away the cut leaves, narrow the row back to about a hand's width by removing plants from the edges, then feed and water so the plants put out fresh leaves before winter. Skip this for day-neutral and everbearing types, since they are still making fruit in late summer.
crops.type_selection_seasoned: Strawberries come in three types, and the choice shapes your whole season. June-bearing cultivars set flower buds in the short days of fall and deliver one concentrated crop over about four weeks in late spring or early summer; they throw the most runners, so they suit a matted row and give a large flush ideal for freezing and jam. Their first real crop comes the season after planting. Day-neutral cultivars flower regardless of day length whenever temperatures sit between about 40 and 90°F, so they fruit from late spring through fall, bear in their first season, and throw few runners, which makes them the pick for containers, raised beds, and a steady supply of fresh berries. Everbearing cultivars give two lighter crops, one in early summer and one in late summer, and are generally less productive than day-neutrals. This guide follows the June-bearing matted-row model because it is the backbone of US backyard strawberry growing; the day-neutral notes throughout tell you where the care diverges. In mild-winter coastal regions, day-neutral plantings can fruit across much of the year and are often grown as a fall-set annual rather than a long-lived bed, which is why the warm-region notes treat them differently from the cold-region matted row.
crops.type_selection_beginner: There are three kinds of strawberries, and picking the right one matters more than picking a fancy variety. June-bearing types give you one big harvest over about four weeks in late spring or early summer, perfect if you want a pile of berries at once for jam or the freezer. They spread by sending out runners that fill in a wide row, and they give their first real crop the year after you plant them. Day-neutral types fruit a little at a time from late spring all the way to fall, give berries the first year, and stay compact, so they are the best choice for pots and small raised beds. Everbearing types fall in between, with one crop in early summer and another in late summer. This guide is built around the June-bearing kind grown in a wide row, since that is how most home gardeners grow strawberries, and it points out along the way where day-neutrals are handled differently. In mild coastal areas with gentle winters, day-neutral plants can give berries through much of the year, and gardeners there often plant fresh ones each year instead of keeping a bed for years.
crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: What you do this year depends entirely on which kind you planted. On a June-bearing bed, the one this guide is built around, pinch off all the first-year flowers. Letting a new plant fruit now starves the root and runner growth that builds the crown, meaning the thick stem at soil level that the whole plant grows from, and that crown is what carries a full crop next season. Day-neutral types are the exception: they fruit in their first year, so you let them, and you remove their runners instead, since energy spent making runners is energy taken from the berries. Keep any new planting evenly moist while it roots in, because strawberries are shallow-rooted and dry out fast.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: Type determines the entire first-year protocol, and conflating the two is the common error. On a June-bearing matted row, remove all first-year bloom: fruiting now competes directly with root and runner development, and the crown built this season is what carries next year's crop. Day-neutral and everbearing types invert it, fruiting in the planting year, so bloom is retained and early runners are removed instead, because runner production draws from the fruit those types are grown for. Space daughter plants as runners root, keeping the strongest and removing crowded extras to hold matted-row density; a bed left to fill solid yields small, hard-to-pick fruit and holds the moisture that feeds rot. Irrigate consistently through establishment, since the root system is shallow and dries quickly.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From the second year a June-bearing bed gives its full crop, one big flush over about four weeks. Tuck clean straw under the developing berries so fruit is not resting on damp soil, which is where gray mold starts and where the name strawberry comes from. Water at the base in the morning and keep the berries themselves dry. Pick fully red berries every two to three days, pinching the stem rather than tugging the fruit, since strawberries do not sweeten at all after picking. Then, a week or two after the last berries, renovate: mow the old leaves to about 2 inches above the crowns without cutting into them, rake the leaves away, narrow the row to about a hand's width, and feed and water. Skip renovation entirely on day-neutral and everbearing types, which are still fruiting in late summer. Expect about three to four fruiting seasons before it is time to start a fresh bed elsewhere.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from year two on a June-bearing matted row, delivered as a single roughly four-week flush. Mulch under developing fruit to break soil contact, and irrigate at the base in the morning so foliage and fruit are dry going into the night, which is what governs Botrytis pressure. Harvest fully coloured fruit on a two-to-three-day cycle, pinching the pedicel; the crop is non-climacteric and gains nothing after picking. Renovation is the year's defining operation and is type-scoped: one to two weeks after final harvest, mow foliage to about 2 inches above the crowns without damaging them, clear the residue, narrow and thin the row, then feed and irrigate to drive the regrowth that sets next season's flower buds. Day-neutral and everbearing plantings are NOT renovated, since they are still bearing. Expect three to four productive seasons before bed replacement on fresh ground.

crops.name: Pumpkin

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Pumpkins want deep, fertile, well-drained loam rich in organic matter, with steady moisture but no waterlogging. They are big plants with hungry roots and a long season, so work several inches of compost or rotted manure into the bed before planting. Most growers plant in low hills or mounds, which warm faster in spring, improve drainage, and give the sprawling vines a clear starting point. Sandy loams warm early and suit the earliest sowings, while heavy clay holds water and invites crown and fruit rot, so amend it generously or build raised mounds.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant pumpkins in rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in. They are large, long-season plants, so give them a generous, fertile bed. Many gardeners plant them on low hills or mounds, which warm up faster and drain better. If your soil is heavy or stays wet, build up mounds or use raised beds so the roots and developing fruit do not sit in water.

ph.note_seasoned: Pumpkins do best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.8, with a sweet spot near 6.2 to 6.5. They still grow across a wider band, roughly 5.8 to 7.5, but uptake of some nutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.
ph.note_beginner: Pumpkins like soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress once or twice
fertilizer.type: balanced at planting, then nitrogen side-dress
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before planting, then side-dress about 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again at flowering
fertilizer.example_product: balanced 13-13-13 or 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen source such as blood meal
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Pumpkins are moderately heavy feeders over a long season. Work a complete fertilizer such as 13-13-13 into the bed before planting, then side-dress with nitrogen about three to four weeks after planting as the vines begin to run, and again as flowering starts. Ease off heavy nitrogen once fruit has set, since late, lush vine growth comes at the expense of fruit and draws pests. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Pumpkins grow for a long time and need steady feeding. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a little extra nitrogen about three to four weeks later as the vines start to run, and again when flowers appear. Once the pumpkins begin to form, go easy on the nitrogen, because too much makes leafy vines instead of fruit.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your pumpkin vines are running, time to side-dress with nitrogen. Keep feeding moderate once fruit sets so the plant builds pumpkins, not just leaves.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your pumpkin vines are spreading. Give them a feeding of nitrogen now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 13-13-13 or 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress while vines run, easing off once fruit sets. Avoid pushing high nitrogen late, which gives vine at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 13-13-13 or 10-10-10 at planting, then a little nitrogen as the vines spread. Do not overdo the nitrogen once fruit forms.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common rate is a complete fertilizer such as 13-13-13 worked into the bed before planting (roughly 20 pounds per 1,000 square feet, or a balanced scoop per hill), then a nitrogen side-dress about three to four weeks after planting placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly at flowering.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix a balanced fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer about three to four weeks later, scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more when flowers appear.

companions.note_seasoned: Most pumpkin companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on serve two practical ends: pollination and pest pressure. Because pumpkin fruit set is pollinator-limited, with each female flower needing many bee visits, flowering insectary plants like borage near the patch are a genuine help. The Three Sisters partners, corn and beans, give the sprawling vines structure and a nitrogen boost while sharing none of pumpkin's pests, and a trap planting of nasturtium can divert squash bugs and beetles. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep pumpkins away from other cucurbits, which share the entire squash pest and disease complex.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful pumpkin companions are flowers that bring in bees, since pumpkins need lots of bee visits to set fruit, and the traditional Three Sisters partners, corn and beans. Nasturtiums can lure pests away. The one rule that really matters is to keep pumpkins away from other squash, cucumbers, and melons, which all share the same pests and diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn and pumpkin are the traditional Three Sisters pairing. The corn stands tall while the pumpkin vines spread along the ground, and the big pumpkin leaves shade out weeds. It is a time-tested combination more than a proven boost.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner: tall corn gives sprawling pumpkin vines structure and light shade in high heat, while the broad pumpkin leaves shade the soil and suppress weeds beneath the corn. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a sound space-and-shade rationale, not a measured yield effect for this exact pair.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters intercropping is a documented traditional system; the corn-pumpkin benefit is space-and-shade, not a trial-isolated pair effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans are the third Three Sisters plant. They pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which the hungry pumpkin appreciates, and they do not share pumpkin's pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The third of the Three Sisters: pole or bush beans fix nitrogen that benefits the heavy-feeding pumpkin, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation is a documented mechanism; the bean-pumpkin adjacency benefit is traditional, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near squash and pumpkins to lure squash bugs and beetles away, and their flowers bring in bees, which pumpkins need to set fruit. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for squash bugs and cucumber beetles, and its flowers also draw the bees pumpkins depend on for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-pumpkin effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap-cropping for cucurbit beetles/bugs is documented in principle; the nasturtium-pumpkin pairing is not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and pumpkins need lots of bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination. Mainly grown to bring in bees.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators that pumpkin fruit set depends on, since each female flower needs many bee visits to size a fruit. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-pumpkin pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Pumpkin fruit set is pollinator-limited (UGA: 7 to 10 insect visits); flowering insectary plants like borage draw bees. Pairing is habitat-based, not pair-isolated.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep pumpkins away from other squash, cucumbers, and melons. They all get the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber, melon, summer squash, and other winter squash share pumpkin's whole pest and disease complex, including squash bug, squash vine borer, cucumber beetle with the bacterial wilt it spreads, and powdery and downy mildew. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens and squash-bug/vine-borer/cucumber-beetle vectoring are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and pumpkins apart, since both are big, hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor blight and attract pests near squash. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A folk anti-companion caution; competition is plausible but there is no T1 source isolating a potato-pumpkin antagonism.

bad_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber, melon, summer squash, and other winter squash share pumpkin's whole pest and disease complex, including squash bug, squash vine borer, cucumber beetle with the bacterial wilt it spreads, and powdery and downy mildew. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens and squash-bug/vine-borer/cucumber-beetle vectoring are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.
