succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Pumpkins are not a succession crop. They are a single, long-season planting that sets fruit through summer and matures together for one fall harvest, so you sow once per season rather than at intervals. In most zones a second sowing would be killed by frost before its 90 to 120 day crop could ripen. Only in the warmest, frost-free or near-frost-free zones, or the low desert where a July sowing is the Halloween crop, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season, not a succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant pumpkins once for the season. They grow all summer and ripen together in the fall for a single harvest, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. In most places a later planting would be caught by frost before the pumpkins could ripen. Only in very warm, nearly frost-free areas can you fit a second planting, and that is really a separate season.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Pumpkin is a single long-season crop (90 to 120 days) harvested once at full maturity, so succession sowing does not apply; a second sowing in most zones would not mature before frost. Warm frost-free zones and the low desert support a separate seasonal planting window, which is a distinct season rather than a succession.

crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Pumpkin is monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single plant sets fruit with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and pollen must move from the male to the female blooms. Pumpkins are strongly pollinator-dependent: each female flower needs several bee visits (UGA notes seven to ten) to set a full, well-shaped fruit, and poor pollination shows up as young fruit that yellow and rot at the blossom end, or as small, lopsided pumpkins. Early-season male flowers often open and drop for a week or more before the first females appear, which is normal. Plant flowers nearby, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate with a male flower or small brush in the morning if set stalls.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Each pumpkin plant has both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit. Bees move the pollen between the flowers, and pumpkins need a lot of bee visits to set each fruit, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. The first flowers are usually male and fall off, which is normal. If your little pumpkins stay small and rot at the tip, the flowers were not pollinated well, so hand-pollinate in the morning and grow some flowers nearby for the bees.
crops.description_seasoned: Pumpkin is a warm-season winter squash grown for its mature, hard-rind fruit, the long-season cousin of summer squash like zucchini. Unlike zucchini, it is harvested once, at full maturity in fall, then cured and stored for months. Plants are vigorous, sprawling vines that can run 10 to 20 feet for full-size carving types, so they need far more room than a bush squash. Pumpkin is monoecious, carrying separate male and female flowers on one plant, and fruit set is strongly pollinator-dependent, with each female flower needing many bee visits. The season's shape is set by three things: a long warm runway (90 to 120 frost-free days) to mature the crop, heavy pollinator and pest pressure (squash vine borer, squash bug, cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it spreads, plus powdery and downy mildew), and the single fall harvest, timed at full color and hard rind, before frost and followed by a curing period for storage.
crops.description_beginner: Pumpkins are a warm-season squash grown for big, hard-skinned fruit you harvest once in the fall, unlike summer squash that you pick young all season. They grow on long, sprawling vines that can spread 10 to 20 feet, so they need a lot of room. Each plant has both male and female flowers and needs lots of bee visits to set fruit. The main things to know: give them a long, warm season and plenty of space, water steadily while the fruit grows, watch for squash bugs, vine borers, beetles, and mildew, and harvest when the pumpkins are fully colored with hard skin and a dry stem, before frost. Then cure them in a warm, dry place so they store for months.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Choose a spot in full sun with well-drained soil. Prepare it by tilling deeply and adding organic matter. Add well-rotted manure or compost in spring or fall. Skip fresh manure, which may carry harmful bacteria and increase weed problems. Depending on how much manure or compost you add, you may not need extra fertilizer. Plant in hills: raise the soil a few inches into a gentle mound to help drainage.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick a sunny spot with soil that drains well. Before planting, dig the soil deeply and mix in compost or well-rotted manure. Don't use fresh manure, which can carry harmful bacteria and bring more weeds. With enough compost or manure, you may not need extra fertilizer. Plant in hills, raising the soil a few inches into a gentle mound so water drains away.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In cold zones the pumpkin season is a single tight summer window: plant after the last frost once soil is warm, and harvest the mature crop in early fall before the first frost. Short-season zones (3 to 4) need transplants started about three weeks early and fast-maturing pie or miniature varieties to ripen a crop in time; warmer zones (6 to 7) have room for full-size carving types.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold areas you get one pumpkin crop a summer: plant after the last frost and harvest in early fall before frost returns. In the coldest zones, start transplants indoors and grow a fast variety so the pumpkins ripen in time.

Warm-season single fall harvest; hot-desert cells split spring/fall around a backed heat_pause.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Gulf and coastal plain, pumpkins are a late-spring-into-fall crop, planted as the soil warms and timed so the fruit matures in fall for Halloween, ahead of the first frost. Summer heat and humidity drive heavy mildew and pest pressure, so airflow, resistant varieties, and scouting matter; some growers also try an early planting for a summer crop.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, plant pumpkins in late spring to early summer so they ripen in fall for Halloween, before frost. The hot, humid summers bring lots of mildew and pests, so give plants room and watch them closely.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's hot interior valleys, pumpkins are a long, warm summer crop: plant from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The dry heat suits pumpkins as long as irrigation is steady; time the planting so fruit matures and cures in the warm, dry fall.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot inland valleys, plant pumpkins from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. They handle the dry heat well as long as you water steadily.

Warm-season single fall harvest; hot-desert cells split spring/fall around a backed heat_pause.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Along California's cooler north coast, plant pumpkins after the spring chill passes and the soil warms, and harvest in fall. Cool, foggy summers can slow ripening and favor mildew, so choose a sunny site, give airflow, and lean toward earlier-maturing varieties.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool north coast, plant pumpkins in late spring once it warms up and harvest in fall. Foggy, cool summers can slow them down, so pick a sunny spot and an earlier variety.

ca_south_coast.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh pumpkin windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (90 to 120) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Warm-season single fall harvest; hot-desert cells split spring/fall around a backed heat_pause.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's mild south coast, pumpkins grow through a long, gentle warm season: plant from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The mild climate is forgiving, though coastal humidity favors mildew, so prioritize airflow and full sun.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's mild south coast, plant pumpkins from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The mild weather is easy on them, but watch for mildew in the coastal damp.

ca_desert.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh pumpkin windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (90 to 120) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Warm-season single fall harvest; hot-desert cells split spring/fall around a backed heat_pause.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the California desert valleys, pumpkins grow as two plantings with no midsummer pause: a late-winter to spring sowing that matures before peak heat, and a midsummer (around July) sowing that grows through the heat for a fall harvest. Steady irrigation is essential, and the fall timing is the reliable one. The July timing looks punishing and is deliberate: it places flowering and fruit set in the milder weather of early fall rather than at peak summer temperatures. Keep water steady through establishment, when the seedbed is most exposed.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California desert, plant pumpkins in late winter to spring for an early crop, and again around July for a fall crop that grows right through the summer heat. Water steadily. Planting in July seems harsh, but it is on purpose: the plants flower and set fruit later, once the weather has cooled. Keep the soil damp while the seedlings get going.

warm_arid.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh pumpkin windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (90 to 120) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas, plant pumpkins after frost once the soil warms and harvest in fall. The dry heat is manageable with steady irrigation; intense early-summer heat can briefly stall fruit set, which usually resumes as conditions ease.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the dry, warm zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas, plant pumpkins after the last frost and harvest in fall. Water steadily through the heat, and do not worry if fruit set pauses briefly during the hottest spells.

Warm-season single fall harvest; hot-desert cells split spring/fall around a backed heat_pause.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In Arizona's low desert, the signature pumpkin window is a July sowing for an October Halloween harvest, which uses the long, hot fall; an earlier late-winter planting can give an early-summer crop before peak heat. Either way, steady irrigation and afternoon resilience matter, and the fall timing is the reliable one.
low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In Arizona's low desert, the classic move is to plant pumpkins in July so they ripen in October for Halloween. You can also plant in late winter for an early-summer crop. Water steadily through the heat.

Warm-season single fall harvest; hot-desert cells split spring/fall around a backed heat_pause.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In peninsular Florida, pumpkins are grown in the cooler halves of the year, planted in late winter to spring and again in late summer for a fall crop, avoiding the wettest, most disease-prone midsummer. Seed the fall crop by about early July to be ready for Halloween, and expect heavy mildew and pest pressure.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In Florida, plant pumpkins in late winter to spring and again in late summer, avoiding the wet, buggy middle of summer. For Halloween pumpkins, plant by about early July. Watch closely for mildew and pests.

Warm-season single fall harvest; hot-desert cells split spring/fall around a backed heat_pause.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii and tropical zones there is no frost, so pumpkins can be planted across much of the year, with timing driven by rainfall and pest pressure rather than cold. Pumpkins and tropical pumpkin types grow well; choose the drier, sunnier windows to limit mildew and fruit rot. Specific local timing is modeled pending a parseable CTAHR source.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii and the tropics there is no frost, so you can plant pumpkins through much of the year. Aim for the drier, sunnier stretches to avoid mildew and rot, since heat and rain are the main challenges, not cold.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Pumpkin transplants go out Mar 1 - Apr 15 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide, corroborated by the Bilingual LRGV planting table's 90 to 120 day maturity figure for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest spring harvest at about 90 days from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest spring harvest at about 120 days from the latest set-out date.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall pumpkin transplants go out Aug 1 - Sep 1 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide / Bilingual LRGV fall window for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest fall harvest at about 90 days from the earliest fall set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest fall harvest, extending into the mild Valley winter tail before spring returns.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, pumpkin is a two-season crop. Plant Mar 1 - Apr 15 for a spring harvest, then plant again Aug 1 - Sep 1 for a fall crop. Skip the hottest weeks of summer: the plant just does not perform well in the worst of the heat, so most Valley gardeners skip it. It rarely if ever frosts here, so both the spring and fall windows run on Valley heat, not on a frost date.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Pumpkin in the RGV runs on the Valley's two-crop calendar: set out Mar 1 - Apr 15 for a spring harvest running May 30 - Aug 13, then set out again Aug 1 - Sep 1 for a fall harvest running Oct 30 - Dec 30. TAMU AgriLife's Valley planting guidance simply leaves that stretch off the calendar for this crop, rather than asserting a specific heat-failure mechanism. Frost is essentially absent here, so both plantings are timed against heat, not cold. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start pumpkin seeds indoors in early April, about 4 weeks before the May set-out date, per OSU Extension's Oregon planting-date table (EM9027); WSU's Washington vegetable guide corroborates the 4-week indoor lead for squash and pumpkins.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set pumpkin out in May once the soil is reliably warm; OSU's Oregon table lists May for winter squash and pumpkins in both the coastal and valley regions, with no June extension (an early May start banks the most warm season for curing).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Pie and miniature pumpkins mature in about 85 to 100 days and reliably finish here; full-size carving pumpkins run 100 to 120 days, a real stretch for the region's cool, short-on-heat summer (OSU).

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: End of the pumpkin harvest window, timed to finish and cure well ahead of the region's first fall frost.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Pumpkin size matters a lot here: little pie and mini pumpkins mature in about 85 to 100 days and reliably ripen before the fall rains, while big carving pumpkins can take 100 to 120 days, a real stretch for the maritime Pacific Northwest's cool, short-on-heat summer, especially near the coast. Start seeds indoors in early April and set plants out in May once the soil is warm. For a dependable jack-o-lantern, pick an earlier-maturing carving variety and give it the warmest spot in the garden; pie and miniature types are the safer bet in a cool year.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Pumpkin is one of the more honestly marginal warm-season crops in the maritime Pacific Northwest: pie and miniature types (roughly 85 to 100 days) reliably size up and cure in the region's cool, marine-tempered summer, but full-size carving pumpkins (100 to 120 days) push against the edge of what the season can finish, especially in the cooler, shorter coastal zone. Start seeds indoors in early April and set plants out in May once soil is warm; the Willamette Valley or Puget lowland interior banks a bit more summer heat than the immediate coast and gives large types a better shot. Favor an early-maturing carving variety, a warm microsite, and row cover or plastic mulch to bank heat if a big jack-o-lantern is the goal; otherwise lean on pie or miniature pumpkins for a dependable harvest. Harvest before frost and cure a week or two in a warm, dry spot, since the region's wet autumn can undercut curing left on the vine (OSU / WSU).

plant_out.source_quote: Zone 8a Spring: Apr 10-Jul 20 | Zone 7a Spring: May 1-Jul 1 (Pumpkin)
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sow once the soil has warmed, in the window VCE 426-331 Table 4 documents for pumpkin (zone 8: Apr 10; zone 7: May 1); VCE does not list this crop as a transplant crop, and its fall column is blank (not recommended in this belt).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins bearing roughly 100 days after sowing, this crop's own days-to-maturity.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest wraps up ahead of the belt's real first frost, which this warm-season crop cannot survive; the latest sowings in VCE's window leave the least margin before frost.

8.notes: VCE 426-331's own zone 8 window runs sowing through Jul 20; at this crop's roughly 100-day pace, sowings that late would mature after the belt's Oct 30 first frost, so harvest here is capped about a week ahead of frost rather than running the full days-to-maturity out. Earlier sowings (April, May, June) give the fullest, surest harvest.

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Pumpkins take about 100 days to mature, so the belt grows just one crop: sow directly once the soil is warm and let it ripen through summer into a fall harvest timed for Halloween. There is no fall planting here, a pumpkin sown in high summer would not finish before frost. Zone 8 can sow into late July for an October harvest; zone 7's shorter season narrows that to early July.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: Virginia Cooperative Extension Pub. 426-331 gives pumpkin its own spring-only window, narrower than the general squash, winter row and with no fall column: zone 8 Apr 10 to Jul 20, zone 7 May 1 to Jul 1. At 100 days to maturity, even zone 8's latest sowings finish close to the belt's Oct 30 first frost, which lines up with the traditional Halloween harvest; earlier sowings bank the most margin, and sowings after mid July risk running past frost before the fruit fully colors and hardens.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sow once the soil has warmed, in the spring window the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension documents for pumpkin; the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension does not list it as a transplant crop, and gives it no fall planting window in this belt, so it grows as a single long-season spring crop.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins bearing roughly 100 days after sowing, this crop's own days-to-maturity.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest wraps up ahead of the belt's real first frost, which this warm-season crop cannot survive; the latest sowings in the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's window leave the least margin before frost.

8.notes: the belt's spring sowing window runs from April into midsummer; at this crop's roughly 100-day pace, sowings that late would mature after the belt's Oct 31 first frost, so harvest here is capped about a week ahead of frost rather than running the full days-to-maturity out. Earlier sowings (April, May, June) give the fullest, surest harvest.

mid_south.region_notes_beginner: Pumpkins take about 100 days to mature, so the belt grows just one crop: sow directly once the soil warms and let it ripen through summer into a fall harvest timed for Halloween. There is no fall planting here, a pumpkin sown in high summer would not finish before frost. Zone 8 can sow into mid July for an October harvest; zone 7's shorter season narrows that to late June.
mid_south.region_notes_seasoned: The University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension gives pumpkin its own spring-only window, narrower than the general winter-squash row and with no fall planting: zone 8 Apr 5 to Jul 15, zone 7 Apr 26 to Jun 26. At 100 days to maturity, even zone 8's latest sowings finish close to the belt's Oct 31 first frost, which lines up with the traditional Halloween harvest; earlier sowings bank the most margin, and sowings near the mid-July end of the window risk running past frost before the fruit fully colors and hardens.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sown; growers timing fruit for a Halloween harvest use the back half of the window, sowing into early July.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Matures roughly 100 days after sowing; the earliest-sown plants set the harvest's start date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The latest sowing is timed to mature by this frost-anchored margin.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Pumpkin goes in the ground from early March through early July in the valley, direct-sown once the soil is warm, and grows through the whole desert summer with no pause. Earliest March sowings mature first; later sowings timed for a Halloween harvest go in through early July and finish by mid-October. Let the rind harden and the stem turn brown and dry before cutting, leaving a few inches of stem attached.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Master Gardener chart shades pumpkin March-April and again June-July; on the Mojave's frost-free calendar that becomes one wide sowing window here, early March into early July, carried straight through the summer heat with no heat_pause. At a 100-day maturity the earliest sowings mature first, and growers timing fruit for Halloween can sow as late as early July and still finish by mid-October, comfortably ahead of the valley's late-November frost (the zone 8 fringe's shorter season pulls the last sowing date in a bit, to protect the same margin against its earlier November 8 frost).

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sow about April 1, once the soil is warm and frost danger has passed, per USU Extension's St. George Group D (Very Tender) planting date.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins ripening about 100 days after the April 1 sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Because this crop sets fruit through the desert summer with no heat-driven pause, picking continues from vine to vine into fall, ending as the November 1 average first frost approaches.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Pumpkin is direct-sown around April 1 in St. George, once the soil has warmed, and the long vines grow all the way through the desert summer without pausing. Fruit starts turning ready in mid-July, and later fruit on the same vines keeps ripening into late October, a natural fit for a Halloween harvest. Let the rind harden fully and the stem turn brown and dry before cutting, and leave a few inches of stem attached to help the fruit keep.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: USU Extension places pumpkin in Group D (Very Tender), direct-sown about April 1 in St. George just after the March 30 average last frost. At a 100-day maturity the earliest fruit is ready by mid-July, and because pumpkin sets fruit through the desert's hottest months with no heat-driven pause, later-set fruit keeps finishing on the vine into late October, right up against the November 1 average first frost, which lines up well with a Halloween harvest. USU documents only this one spring sowing for pumpkin in the St. George area, no fall replanting.

crops.name: Plum

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plum likes a deep soil that drains well, from a sandy loam to a sandy clay loam. Good drainage matters most, because plum roots do not like sitting in wet ground and can rot if they stay soggy. Of the common home fruit trees, plum is a little more forgiving of heavier ground than peach is, especially European types on a tolerant rootstock, but standing water is still the thing to avoid. If your soil is heavy clay that holds water, plant the tree on a raised mound so the roots sit above the wettest layer. A soil of average richness with some compost worked in suits it well.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Plum wants a deep, well-drained soil ranging from a sandy loam to a sandy clay loam; drainage is the priority, since Prunus roots will not tolerate prolonged wet feet. Plum is somewhat more tolerant of heavier ground than peach, particularly European cultivars on a heavy-soil-tolerant rootstock such as Marianna or Myrobalan, but chronically saturated soil still invites crown and root rot. On heavy clay, plant on a raised berm to lift the roots above the perched water table. Moderate fertility and a modest amount of organic matter suit it well.

ph.note_beginner: Plum grows best in slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and is fine up to about 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if you need to: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if the soil is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is much easier to fix before the permanent tree goes in.
ph.note_seasoned: Plum does best in a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerates up to about 7.0. Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, while elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground.

fertilizer.timing: spring at bloom to petal fall; optional light postharvest
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Broadcast the fertilizer evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, keeping it off the trunk, and water it in. Split timing (the bulk in spring, a lighter touch after harvest) suits sandy soils. Go easy on nitrogen: plums push vigorous shoots readily, and lush, succulent growth is more prone to aphids, bacterial canker, and black knot, and never feed late in the season, since late nitrogen delays dormancy and invites winter injury.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Scatter the fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. On sandy soil it helps to split it, most in spring and a little after harvest. Do not overdo the nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much pushes soft, leafy growth that draws aphids and disease. Never feed late in the year, because late feeding keeps the tree growing when it should be going dormant and makes winter damage more likely.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits backyard plums; a young tree that is not making about a foot of new growth a year can take a spring nitrogen boost, but a vigorous tree needs little. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which pushes soft, disease-prone growth at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works well for backyard plums. Do not overdo nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth and more disease instead of fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home-garden rate is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 per year of tree age, applied in spring from bloom to petal fall, up to roughly 8 to 10 cups for a mature tree. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. Judge by shoot growth: a bearing tree making 8 to 15 inches of new wood a year is fed about right, and one growing faster than that needs less nitrogen, not more.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple rule is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, spread in spring as the tree blooms, up to about 8 to 10 cups for a full-grown tree. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing. If the tree is already growing strongly, with lots of long new shoots, give it less, not more.

companions.note_beginner: Whether a plum needs a companion tree is really a pollination question, and it depends on the type. European plums (like Stanley, Italian prune, and damson) are mostly self-fruitful, so one tree makes fruit on its own. Japanese plums (like Santa Rosa and Methley) usually need a second, different Japanese variety blooming nearby to set a good crop. Beyond that, the things that matter for a tree are not the usual vegetable-garden pairings but what grows around the roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, because lawn competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free area helps the tree settle in. One thing to avoid is planting a plum near other wild or neglected plums and cherries, because those spread black knot, the black warty branch disease, to your tree.
companions.note_seasoned: For a plum, the key interaction is pollination, and it splits by type: European plums (Stanley, Italian prune, damson) are largely self-fruitful and fruit alone, while Japanese plums (Santa Rosa, Methley, and most others) are self-unfruitful and need a second compatible Japanese cultivar blooming at the same time. The other interactions that matter are about the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since a young tree competes poorly with grass for water and nitrogen. The site rule to respect is inoculum: do not plant near wild, ornamental, or neglected Prunus (chokecherry, wild plum, purple-leaf plum), which are reservoirs of black knot and brown rot.

good_seasoned.name: A second compatible plum for cross-pollination
good_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: The strongest 'good pairing' for plum is a pollenizer, and it is squarely extension-documented. MU Extension G6001 states European plums such as Stanley and Damson are self-fruitful while all Japanese varieties (Santa Rosa, Burbank, Shiro, Methley) need cross-pollination from another Japanese or American-Japanese hybrid; Clemson concurs that many plums are self-unfruitful and that fruit set improves with a compatible pollenizer. extension_backed/HIGH.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: For Japanese plums, and for the many European cultivars that set more heavily with a partner, the single most useful companion is a second compatible plum. Match type to type: a Japanese cultivar needs another Japanese (or an American-Japanese hybrid) blooming at the same time, since European and Japanese plums bloom weeks apart and will not pollinate each other. Santa Rosa and Methley are widely used pollenizers for other Japanese plums; a self-fruitful European such as Stanley or Damson can stand alone but still crops more reliably with a second European nearby. Plant the pollenizer within about 100 feet so bees move freely between the trees.

bad_seasoned.name: Wild, ornamental, or neglected plums and cherries nearby
bad_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Multiple extensions (UMN, UMaine) identify unmanaged Prunus as the reservoir that sustains black knot: the fungus overwinters in galls on wild plum, chokecherry, purple-leaf plum, and neglected trees and re-infects nearby plums each spring. Removing or scouting nearby wild hosts is a standard cultural control. extension_backed/HIGH.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A plum's worst neighbors are other Prunus you do not manage. Wild plum, chokecherry, ornamental purple-leaf plum, and abandoned plum or cherry trees are reservoirs of black knot and brown rot: the black-knot fungus overwinters in galls on those hosts and releases spores that infect your tree every wet spring, so an unmanaged thicket downwind undoes your own pruning. Where practical, remove or prune the black knot out of nearby wild hosts, or at least scout them, and site a new plum away from them.

pests.name: Plum curculio
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small developing fruit carries a distinctive crescent-shaped scar where the female cut a slit to lay an egg. Infested fruit often drops early; fruit that hangs on may be gnarled or have a grub tunneling inside. Damage appears shortly after petal fall and is one of the most common causes of wormy backyard plums.
pests.symptoms_beginner: On small developing plums, look for a curved, crescent-shaped scar, the mark the beetle leaves when it lays an egg. Damaged fruit often drops early, and some that stays on the tree ends up misshapen or has a grub inside. You see this soon after the petals fall, and it is the usual reason for wormy plums.
pests.cause_seasoned: The plum curculio (Conotrachelus nenuphar), a small snout beetle and a signature pest of its namesake crop. Adults emerge around bloom and attack fruit from petal fall onward, laying eggs in the developing fruit; the larvae feed inside, then drop to pupate in the soil.
pests.cause_beginner: A small beetle with a long snout called the plum curculio, which is named for this very crop. The adults show up around bloom and start damaging the little fruits right after the petals drop, laying eggs inside them. The larvae then feed within the fruit and later drop to the ground.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: For a backyard tree, jarring the limbs over a sheet in the cool early morning when the beetles are sluggish, then destroying what drops, reduces the population. Promptly gather and dispose of dropped infested fruit to break the cycle. Kaolin clay applied from petal fall is an organic deterrent.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Early in the morning the beetles are slow. Spread a sheet under the tree, tap the branches so the beetles fall, and destroy them. Pick up and throw away any dropped fruit promptly so the larvae inside do not mature. A kaolin clay spray (a fine white mineral coating) starting at petal fall helps keep them off.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: remove dropped fruit through the season so larvae cannot complete development in the soil beneath the tree. A clean orchard floor and prompt fruit pickup steadily lower pressure year over year.
pests.prevention_beginner: The main thing is cleanup. Pick up fallen fruit all season so the larvae inside cannot finish growing in the soil under the tree. Keeping the ground clear lowers the number of beetles the next year.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here: pick up every dropped plum promptly and get it out of the garden, because the grub inside finishes growing in the soil under the tree. On a cool early morning, when the beetles are sluggish, spread a sheet under the branches, tap them so the beetles fall, and destroy what lands. Keeping the ground clear all season means fewer beetles the following year.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Season-long removal of drops denies larvae the soil beneath the canopy, and the effect compounds year over year, which is why sanitation is the backbone rather than a supplement. Jarring limbs over a sheet at first light, while adults are still cold enough to drop instead of fly, physically strips the population that petal fall released.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Kaolin clay is a fine white mineral you mix with water and spray on, leaving a coating the beetles do not want to walk on. Start at petal fall, the moment they begin working the young fruit, and reapply through the season as the fruit expands and rain washes the film thin.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Kaolin from petal fall is the organic deterrent this crop's guidance names, and it works as a particle barrier, so unbroken coverage on expanding fruit is what carries it. Heavy use can flare San Jose scale and mites, worth weighing on a tree that already carries scale.

pests.name: Aphids (leaf curl plum aphid and mealy plum aphid)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: In spring, new leaves at the shoot tips pucker and curl tightly around colonies of small soft-bodied aphids (leaf curl plum aphid), while the pale, wax-dusted mealy plum aphid clusters on the undersides of leaves. Both excrete honeydew that turns leaves shiny and sticky and grows black sooty mold; heavy early infestations stunt shoots and can distort young fruit.
pests.symptoms_beginner: In spring the new leaves at the shoot tips curl up tightly, and if you unroll one you find little green or waxy-gray insects, aphids, packed inside. They leave a sticky shine (called honeydew) that turns black with sooty mold. A bad early attack curls the leaves and slows the new growth.
pests.cause_seasoned: Two aphids specific to plum: the leaf curl plum aphid (Brachycaudus helichrysi), which curls the spring foliage, and the mealy plum aphid (Hyalopterus pruni), whitish with a mealy wax coat. Both overwinter as eggs near the buds, build up on new spring growth, then migrate to summer hosts (leaf curl plum aphid to plants in the aster family, mealy plum aphid to reeds and cattails).
pests.cause_beginner: Two kinds of aphids that live on plum: one curls the new leaves, and the other is a pale, waxy gray one. They spend the winter as eggs near the buds, then multiply fast on the tender spring growth before flying off to other summer plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Natural enemies (ladybugs, lacewings, syrphid larvae, parasitic wasps) usually bring aphids under control by early summer, so protect them by not spraying broad insecticides. A strong jet of water knocks colonies off, and narrow-range horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the affected shoots helps in a heavy infestation. A dormant or delayed-dormant oil spray targets the overwintering eggs.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Ladybugs and other helpful bugs usually clean aphids up by early summer, so avoid harsh sprays that kill those helpers too. Blast the colonies off with a hard spray of water, and for a bad case use insecticidal soap or a light horticultural oil on the curled shoots. A dormant oil spray in late winter kills the overwintering eggs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid heavy spring nitrogen, which pushes the soft flush aphids favor. Keep ants (which farm aphids for honeydew and drive off predators) off the trunk with a sticky band, and preserve natural enemies. A late-fall or dormant oil where aphids are a chronic problem is the most effective single measure.
pests.prevention_beginner: Go easy on spring feeding, since lush new growth attracts aphids. Keep ants off the trunk (they protect aphids) with a sticky band, and leave the helpful bugs alone. If aphids come back every year, a dormant oil spray in late fall or winter is the best prevention.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on nitrogen feeding in spring. Rich feeding pushes out soft new shoots, and that tender growth is what these aphids multiply fastest on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Restraining spring nitrogen limits the succulent flush that drives colony buildup at the shoot tips. It is a feeding habit set before the aphids arrive rather than a response once they have.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the colonies off with a strong jet of water from the hose, aimed up into the curled shoot tips where they hide. Do it early in the day so the leaves dry quickly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful jet dislodges colonies on sturdy wood without the collateral a broad spray carries. Tightly rolled leaves shelter some of them, so expect to repeat as colonies rebuild, and spray early enough that foliage dries, since long leaf wetness favors disease.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, hoverfly larvae, and tiny parasitic wasps usually clean up plum aphids by early summer on their own, so the most useful thing you can do is skip the harsh insecticides that kill those helpers along with the aphids. Ants farm aphids for their sugary honeydew and chase the helpers off, so keeping ants off the trunk protects your allies.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident natural enemies typically bring both aphid species down by early summer, so conservation is the working control: decline broad-spectrum material, and deny ants access to the colonies they tend and defend.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For a heavy infestation, spray insecticidal soap straight onto the aphids in the curled shoots. It kills only what it wets, so unroll the tips and coat them. Skip it on a dry, stressed tree or above 90°F, since it can burn leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Contact soap suits a heavy pocket the softer steps have not held, and the rolled leaf is the practical limit, since it shields aphids from coverage. It also kills soft-bodied beneficials it directly wets, so treat only the infested shoots, and avoid water-stressed trees or temperatures above 90°F.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A narrow-range horticultural oil helps two ways: on the curled shoots in season, and, more usefully, as a dormant or delayed-dormant spray in late fall or winter that smothers the eggs waiting near the buds. Where aphids return every year, that dormant timing is the strongest single step. Do not use oil above 90°F or on a drought-stressed tree, and once the tree has leaves keep it at least 30 days clear of any sulfur spray; check the oil label, because some say to wait longer.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: In-season oil gives contact control on exposed colonies; the delayed-dormant application is the higher-value use, taking the overwintering eggs before the spring flush rather than chasing colonies after it. Observe the oil constraints: not above 90°F, not on stressed trees, and not within 30 days of sulfur while the tree is in leaf, or longer if the oil label says so.

pests.name: Peachtree borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass at the base of the trunk, right around the soil line, often with a mounded look where the bark meets the ground. Plums, like other stone fruit, are a host. A heavily infested young tree loses vigor as the larvae girdle the inner bark; several borers in one trunk can kill a newly planted tree in a season.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Look at the very bottom of the trunk where it meets the soil. The peachtree borer, which also attacks plums, leaves a sticky, gummy ooze mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (frass). You may see a small mound of gum and frass at the base. A young tree with several borers can be killed in one season, so catch this early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the peachtree borer (Synanthedon exitiosa), a clearwing moth whose day-flying adults are wasp-like. Eggs are laid on the lower trunk in summer; larvae tunnel in the inner bark at and just below the soil line. Trees stressed by winter injury, mechanical wounds, or bacterial canker are attacked first.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (young grub stage) of the peachtree borer, a moth whose adults look like wasps and fly by day. The adults lay eggs on the lower trunk in summer, and the larvae burrow into the bark at and below the soil line. Trees with existing wounds are hit hardest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue spray once larvae are tunneling inside. The practical home control is to expose the crown in late summer or fall, find the entry holes by the gum and frass, and kill larvae by hand with a thin wire. Keep the trunk base free of wounds.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the larvae are tunneling inside, no spray reaches them. The backyard fix is to scrape soil away from the base in late summer or fall, find the holes marked by gum and frass, and kill the larvae with a thin, stiff wire pushed into each hole. Then smooth the soil back.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Protect the lower trunk from mechanical injury (the wounds that draw egg-laying females), keep the tree vigorous, and clear weeds and tall grass from the base so the crown stays open and easy to inspect. Check the soil line each late summer for fresh gum.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep mowers and string trimmers away from the trunk; the wounds they leave attract the egg-laying moths. Keep grass and weeds cleared from the base so you can see the soil line, and check it every late summer for fresh gummy ooze.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear the grass and weeds away from the bottom of the trunk so the soil line stays in plain view, and look it over once a year in late summer for fresh gummy ooze. Keep mowers and string trimmers off the bark down there, since the wounds they leave are what draws the egg-laying moths.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A clear, open crown is both a scouting surface and one less shelter at the trunk base, so give the soil line a late-summer inspection for new gum and frass. Mechanical injury gives egg-laying females the wounded bark they favor, so keep machinery off the lower trunk and keep the tree vigorous.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Once the larvae are tunneling under the bark, no spray reaches them, so this is the backyard fix. In late summer or fall, scrape the soil back from the base, spot each entry hole by the gum and the frass, which is the wet, sawdust-like droppings, push a thin stiff wire into it to kill the larva inside, then smooth the soil back.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Worming out the larvae by hand is the practical home control at and just below the soil line, where the tunnels run in the inner bark and no rescue material follows them. Work the exposed crown in late summer or fall, follow each gum-and-frass entry, and probe with stiff wire. A few borers can girdle a young trunk in one season, so the labor is well spent there.

pests.name: San Jose scale
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny gray, circular, hard-shelled scales encrust the bark of twigs and branches, sometimes so densely the bark looks ashy; feeding sites on fruit show as small red-purple haloed spots. Heavy infestations kill twigs and whole limbs from the top down and weaken the tree over a few seasons.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little gray, round, hard bumps crust over the bark of twigs and branches, and the fruit can get small reddish spots where the scales feed. A bad infestation makes the bark look ashy and can kill off twigs and branches, weakening the tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: San Jose scale (Diaspidiotus perniciosus), an armored scale insect. Immobile once settled, it feeds on sap under a waxy shell and passes several overlapping generations a year; crawlers (the mobile young stage) are the only vulnerable window and spread the infestation along the branches.
pests.cause_beginner: An armored scale insect called San Jose scale. After the tiny young 'crawlers' settle down, they stay put under a hard shell and suck sap, with several generations a year. Only the crawler stage moves around and can be targeted.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A thorough dormant or delayed-dormant application of horticultural oil, wetting all the bark, smothers overwintering scales and is the mainstay of home control. In-season, natural enemies (tiny parasitic wasps, predatory beetles) suppress light infestations; prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: The main control is a thorough spray of horticultural oil in late winter while the tree is leafless, coating all the bark to smother the scales. During the season, helpful insects keep light infestations down. Prune out and destroy branches that are heavily crusted with scale.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and well pruned so airflow is good, apply dormant oil where scale has appeared before, and inspect incoming nursery stock, since scale often arrives on new trees. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.
pests.prevention_beginner: Prune for good airflow, use a dormant oil spray in areas where scale has shown up before, and check any new trees you buy, since scale often hitches in on nursery stock. Avoid harsh sprays that kill the helpful insects.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune out the twigs and branches that are heavily crusted with scale and destroy what you cut rather than leaving the wood by the tree. That takes out the densest colonies in one pass. Give any new tree a close look before you plant it, since scale often hitches a ride in on nursery stock.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing and destroying encrusted wood strips the settled population where it is thickest and lowers the crawler load that spreads along the branches. Inspect incoming nursery stock as well, which is a common way an infestation arrives in the first place.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Tiny parasitic wasps and predatory beetles feed on scale and hold light infestations down on their own. Broad insecticides wipe those helpers out, so leaving them undisturbed is a control in itself.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident parasitoids and predatory beetles suppress light populations, and the mobile crawler stage is the window they exploit, since a settled scale sits under an armored cover. Avoiding broad-spectrum material is therefore part of holding the population, not merely a courtesy to the garden.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This is the main home control: in late winter, while the tree is bare, spray horticultural oil so it wets every bit of bark on the twigs and branches. The oil smothers the scales under their shells, so coverage is the whole job. Do not spray oil on a drought-stressed tree or above 90°F, and once the tree has leaves keep it at least 30 days from any sulfur spray; check the oil label, because some say to wait longer.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A thorough dormant or delayed-dormant oil applied to run-off over all bark is the mainstay here: the armored cover blocks most contact material, so the result rides entirely on wetting the shell. Repeat it in seasons following an infestation rather than waiting for encrustation to rebuild. Keep the oil constraints in view: not above 90°F, not on stressed trees, not within 30 days of sulfur while the tree is in leaf, or longer if the oil label says so.

diseases.name: Black knot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Hard, black, elongated, warty swellings (knots) grow along twigs and branches, from an inch to six inches or more long, girdling and eventually killing the wood beyond them. A new gall starts as an inconspicuous olive-green, corky swelling one year, then hardens and turns coal-black by the second. Leaves on knotted branches may wilt and die, and a heavily infected tree becomes stunted and misshapen. This is the signature disease of plum.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Hard, black, warty lumps (called knots) grow along the twigs and branches, anywhere from an inch to six inches or more long. They start as a soft olive-green swelling one year and turn coal-black and hard the next. The branch beyond a knot often wilts and dies, and a badly infected tree gets stunted and gnarled. Black knot is the classic plum disease, the one to learn to recognize.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Apiosporina morbosa (formerly Dibotryon morbosum). It overwinters in the galls on the tree and on nearby wild or ornamental Prunus, and in cool, wet spring weather releases spores that infect the new green shoots. Infection is invisible the first season; the gall swells the following year and blackens the year after, so the disease runs on a roughly two-year cycle.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Apiosporina morbosa) that lives in the black knots over winter, on your tree and on any wild plums or cherries nearby. In cool, wet spring weather it shoots out spores that infect the new green shoots. You will not see anything the first year; the knot swells the next year and turns black the year after.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Pruning is the core control, and timing is everything: in the dormant season, before growth resumes (before about April 1), cut out every knot, making the cut 3 to 4 inches below the visible gall into clean wood, since the fungus extends beyond what you can see. Remove the prunings from the area and burn, bury, or bag them, and disinfect tools between cuts. On a scaffold too valuable to remove, cut the gall out to healthy wood. A protective fungicide on the new shoots in early spring supports the pruning where pressure is high.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cutting the knots out is the main fix, and when you do it matters: prune in late winter while the tree is bare, before it starts growing in spring. Cut each knot off 3 to 4 inches below the black lump, into clean wood, because the fungus reaches farther than you can see. Carry the cut pieces away and burn, bury, or bag them so they cannot re-infect the tree, and wipe your pruners with rubbing alcohol between cuts.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Scout and prune out knots every dormant season before they can release spores, and deal with the reservoir: remove or clean up wild plum, chokecherry, and neglected ornamental Prunus within range, which sustain the disease. Choosing a less-susceptible cultivar and keeping the tree open and vigorous both help, but annual knot removal is the non-negotiable habit.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Check the tree every winter and cut out any knots before spring, when they spread. Just as important, clean up or remove wild plums, chokecherries, and neglected ornamental plums nearby, because they keep re-infecting your tree. Some plum varieties resist black knot better than others, so ask when you buy, but cutting the knots out each year is the habit that matters most.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Some plum varieties shrug this off better than others, so ask which one you are buying before the tree goes in the ground. It lowers the trouble, but it does not take the place of cutting the knots out each winter.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cultivar susceptibility varies, so a less-susceptible selection lowers the pressure a tree carries for its whole life. It is a planting-time choice that supports the annual pruning habit rather than substituting for it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Look past your own tree. Wild plums, chokecherries, and neglected ornamental plums and cherries in the neighborhood carry the same fungus and keep re-seeding your tree with spores each spring, so removing or cleaning up the ones within reach matters as much as pruning your own.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The nearby reservoir governs how much pressure the tree sees: wild and neglected Prunus hold galls that shed spores into the same cool, wet spring weather your tree is pushing green shoots in. Clearing that reservoir within range is what lets annual knot removal actually hold.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This is the fix, and the timing carries it: cut the knots out in late winter, with the tree still bare and before spring growth resumes. Place each cut into clean wood 3 to 4 inches beyond the lump you can see, because the fungus runs farther along the branch than the swelling shows. Then get the prunings out of the yard, by burning, bagging, or burying them, and disinfect the blades between cuts, for which rubbing alcohol works.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Dormant removal ahead of spring growth, before about April 1, is the core control. Take each cut 3 to 4 inches into clean wood past the gall, since colonized tissue extends beyond what is swollen, and carry the prunings off site rather than piling them nearby. Disinfect between cuts, and where a scaffold is too valuable to lose, excise the gall back to healthy wood instead of taking the limb.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: At bloom, infected blossoms wilt and turn brown, and the infection can run back into the twig to form a small gummy canker. As fruit ripens, brown circular spots appear and spread fast, sometimes rotting a whole plum within a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan spore mass on the surface. Rotted fruit dries into a mummy that clings to the tree or drops.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: At bloom, infected flowers go limp and brown, and small gummy dead patches can form on the nearby twigs. As the plums ripen, brown spots appear and spread quickly, sometimes rotting a whole fruit in a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan fuzz on the surface. Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard, dried mummy that hangs on the tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Monilinia fructicola. It overwinters in mummified fruit (whether hanging in the canopy or fallen) and in twig cankers; spores released at bloom infect flowers, and those infections later seed the fruit rot. Warm, humid, wet conditions drive rapid spread, and any skin break (curculio scar, hail, cracking) is an entry point.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Monilinia fructicola. It survives the winter in dried mummy fruit and in dead twig patches, then releases spores at bloom that infect the flowers. Those flower infections later cause the fruit to rot. Warm, humid, wet weather makes it spread fast, and any break in the skin lets it in.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: remove and destroy every mummy from the tree and the ground, and prune out gummy twig cankers, because these are the spore sources. During a wet bloom, an organic-approved bloom-time fungicide reduces blossom blight. Once fruit is rotting, pick and dispose of it promptly, and thin fruit so plums do not touch, which slows spread through a cluster.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: The main control is cleanup: take off and destroy every dried mummy from the tree and the ground, and prune out the gummy dead twig patches, since these hold the spores. If the weather is wet during bloom, an organic-approved spray at bloom helps protect the flowers. As soon as you see a plum rotting, pick it and throw it away, and thin the fruit so plums are not touching.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Year-round sanitation prevents most loss: never leave mummies on the tree over winter, remove dropped and thinned fruit, and keep the canopy open with good pruning so fruit dries quickly after rain. Control plum curculio and other pests whose wounds open the door, harvest promptly, handle fruit gently, and cool it soon after picking.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Cleanup all year prevents most of the damage: never leave dried mummies on the tree over winter, pick up dropped fruit, and prune so the tree is open and the plums dry fast after rain. Keep pests like plum curculio in check, since their wounds let rot in. Pick fruit on time, handle it gently, and chill it soon after picking.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cleanup is the core of it. Take every shriveled, dried fruit, called a mummy, off the tree and off the ground, and clear away the dropped and thinned fruit too. Mummies are where the fungus waits out the winter, so leaving them hanging sets up next year's rot. Pick and dispose of any plum you see rotting as soon as you spot it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mummies in the canopy and on the ground are the primary overwintering inoculum, so stripping them at dormancy and clearing drops and thinnings through the season removes what would otherwise meet bloom. In season, pull rotting fruit before the dusty tan spore mass develops and seeds the fruit around it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune the tree so it is open and air moves through it. This rot runs on wet fruit, so a canopy that dries fast after rain gives it much less to work with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: An open canopy shortens the wetting period on fruit after rain, which is the variable that decides how fast warm, humid weather turns a spot into a rotted plum.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the plums as they come ready instead of letting them hang, handle them gently so the skins do not break, and chill them soon after picking. Any nick or split in the skin is a way in for the rot.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Harvesting on time removes fruit before the ripe phase the pathogen exploits, and gentle handling protects the skin, since any break, whether a curculio scar, hail, or a growth crack, is an infection court. Cooling soon after picking slows what may already be underway.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut out the small gummy dead patches on the twigs, the ones left where the disease ran back from an infected blossom, and destroy what you remove. Those patches hold spores over winter alongside the mummies.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Twig cankers formed where blossom infections ran back into the wood are the second overwintering site, so excise them into clean wood and destroy the prunings, leaving next spring's bloom less inoculum to meet.

diseases.name: Bacterial spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small angular, water-soaked spots on leaves turn brown to purple-black and drop out, leaving a shot-hole look; heavy infection yellows and thins the canopy. On fruit, small sunken spots, pits, and cracks develop on the skin, downgrading the crop. Susceptibility varies sharply by cultivar, and Japanese plums are often hit harder than European.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get small angular water-soaked spots that turn dark and fall out, leaving little holes, called a shot-hole look. Bad cases turn leaves yellow and thin out the tree. On the fruit, small sunken spots, pits, and cracks form. How badly a tree is hit depends a lot on the variety, and Japanese plums are often more affected than European ones.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It spreads in warm, wet, windy weather and builds up where susceptible plum, peach, and related trees grow nearby. Symptoms are sometimes mistaken for spray injury or nutrient problems.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism, not a fungus) called Xanthomonas. It spreads in warm, wet, windy weather and builds up when there are other susceptible plum or peach trees close by. The spots can look like spray damage.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Home options are limited once symptoms appear: copper sprays help more as prevention than cure and can injure the tree if overused, so they are not a reliable home fix. Keeping the tree vigorous and the canopy open and dry helps it tolerate the disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no good home cure once it shows up. Copper sprays help a little as prevention but can hurt the tree if overused, so they are not a dependable fix. The best you can do is keep the tree healthy and the canopy open so it shrugs off the damage.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The most effective measure is choosing a resistant or tolerant cultivar at planting; this is largely a variety decision made before the tree goes in. Good airflow, avoiding excess nitrogen, and tree vigor reduce severity.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best prevention is the variety you pick. Choosing a plum known to resist or tolerate bacterial spot avoids most of the trouble, so it is a decision to make before planting. Good airflow, going easy on nitrogen, and a healthy tree also help.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This one is mostly decided before you plant. Varieties differ a lot in how hard they get hit, and Japanese plums often suffer more than European ones, so buy a tree sold as resistant or tolerant to bacterial spot.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cultivar susceptibility is the dominant variable and it is set at planting, with Japanese types generally taking it harder than European. Once a susceptible tree is in the ground, what remains manages severity rather than removing the disease.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune so air moves through the canopy and the leaves dry off after rain. This will not clear the bacteria, but an open, healthy tree carries the spotting with less damage.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Canopy openness and tree vigor act on severity rather than on presence: faster drying cuts into the warm, wet, windy conditions the bacterium spreads in, and a vigorous tree tolerates the leaf drop better.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Be realistic about this rung. There is no dependable home cure once the spots are on the tree. Copper does more as a preventive than as a rescue, and overusing it can injure the tree itself, so it is not something to lean on. If you do reach for it, follow the label rate, and keep spray and runoff away from ponds and storm drains, since copper is highly toxic to fish.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper is a limited protectant here rather than a cure, and phytotoxicity from repeated application is a real cost, which is why it does not amount to a reliable home answer for this disease. Where it is used, the label rate governs, the copper compound named on the label sets the acute hazard band, and the residue accumulates at the soil surface, so keep repeat use over the years restrained.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Water on a deep-and-infrequent rhythm rather than a little every day: about once or twice a week while a young tree establishes, easing to roughly weekly for a bearing tree in the heat of summer, always adjusted for rain and soil type. A sandy soil dries faster and needs more frequent soaks; a heavier soil holds longer. Through winter dormancy, water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Plan on about once or twice a week while a young tree is getting established, easing to about once a week for a fruiting tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. Sandy soil dries out faster and needs watering more often; heavier soil stays wet longer. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs very little and rain usually covers it.
watering.amount_seasoned: Water deeply each time so the moisture reaches the full depth of the root zone, rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing tree, that is on the order of 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, aim for roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the growing season, more in heat. Deep, thorough soaks drive the deep rooting that carries the tree through dry spells.
watering.amount_beginner: Each time you water, give the tree a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a quick splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the growing season, and more when it is hot. Deep soaks help the tree grow deep roots that handle dry spells.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose, and keep the canopy and fruit dry. Overhead watering that wets the leaves and fruit prolongs leaf wetness and feeds brown rot and bacterial spot, so deliver water to the soil, not the tree. Apply it across the root area out toward the drip line rather than only at the trunk.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the ground around the roots using a drip line or a soaker hose, and keep the leaves and fruit dry. Spraying water over the top wets the leaves and fruit and helps diseases like brown rot take hold, so put the water on the soil, not on the tree. Spread it across the root area out to the edge of the branches, not just right at the trunk.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet soil, and a generally declining tree, since waterlogged roots suffocate and rot. In stone fruit, chronically wet soil also invites crown and root rot, which is often fatal and rarely reversible once advanced. Soggy soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign to act on.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that slowly goes downhill. That is because waterlogged roots cannot breathe and start to rot. In plum, soil that stays wet can also bring on crown and root rot, which often kills the tree. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning to back off.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting and dull, curling leaves, slowed shoot growth, and early leaf drop in a prolonged dry spell. The most telling symptom is on the fruit: a tree short of water during the final swell sizes its plums poorly, leaving them small and prone to shriveling even though the tree itself survives. Catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Too little water shows as wilting and dull, curling leaves, slower growth, and leaves dropping early in a long dry spell. The clearest sign is in the fruit: a tree that runs short of water while the plums are sizing up makes small, shriveled fruit, even though the tree itself lives through it. Try to catch the dry stress before the fruit suffers for it.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~5 gal per watering
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system the tree relies on later.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps the tree grow the deep roots it needs.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~1 in per week equivalent
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: From fruit set through the final swell, do not let the tree dry out. Aim for the equivalent of about an inch of water per week, more in heat, delivered as deep soaks. Steady moisture now translates directly into larger, better-filled fruit and helps prevent the shriveling that dry stress causes.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the plums are setting and sizing up, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch of water a week, more when it is hot, given as deep soaks. This is exactly when steady watering pays off in bigger, better plums.

schedule_by_stage.rate: minimal
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Once the tree is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only during prolonged dry spells to keep roots from desiccating. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches so the roots do not dry out. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, to encourage deep rooting; avoid wetting the canopy, which feeds brown rot and bacterial spot. Young trees need consistent moisture through their first two seasons to establish; mature trees are moderately drought-tolerant but size fruit poorly under stress.
watering.method_note_beginner: Give the tree a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) instead of spraying the leaves, since wet leaves and fruit lead to disease. Young trees need steady moisture for their first couple of years to get established. Older trees can handle some dry spells, but the plums come out small if the tree gets too dry.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The make-or-break window is the final swell, roughly the last 3 to 5 weeks before harvest, when cell expansion adds most of the fruit's final size. Water stress then causes irreversible loss of size and can leave plums small and prone to shriveling. Early rapid growth just after bloom is also sensitive; mild stress during pit hardening (mid-season) is the most tolerable time to ease off if water is limited.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep the tree watered is the last few weeks before harvest, when the plums do most of their growing. If the tree runs dry then, the fruit stays small and watering later will not fix it. The few weeks right after bloom matter too. If you ever have to cut back on water, the safest time is the middle of the season, when the pits are hardening.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to plum. It arrives as a dormant, bare-root tree and goes in the ground in late winter or early spring, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate to the outdoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to outdoor conditions) does not apply to plum. You plant it bare-root and dormant, in late winter or early spring, rather than as a seedling started inside, so there is no tender young plant to ease outdoors.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant in late winter to early spring, before bud break, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in water for an hour or two beforehand to rehydrate them. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them and set the tree so the graft union (that swollen joint near the base of the trunk) sits 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line. Do not add fertilizer to the planting hole; backfill with native soil, water in well, and stake only if the site is windy.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant (resting, with no leaves) in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first so they do not stay dried out. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots out without bending them, and set the tree so the graft union (that bumpy joint near the base, where the fruiting variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 inches above the soil. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. Refill with the same soil you removed, water it in well, and add a stake only if the spot is windy.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Fill the pot with a chunky, fast-draining mix made for shrubs and trees, not a soft peat-based potting soil that stays soggy. A bark-based mix (composted bark with perlite or pumice mixed in for drainage) holds the air the roots need. Do not use soil dug from the yard in a pot, because it packs down and drains badly when you water often.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Keep it simple and aim for drainage. If the mix seems to hold water, stir in more perlite or pumice, and lay a thin layer of compost on top instead of mixing a lot of rich material all through the pot. Stay away from water-holding crystals or a lot of peat, since plum roots need the mix to drain, not stay wet.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a coarse, fast-draining soilless mix built for woody plants, not a peat-heavy potting soil that stays wet. A bark-based mix (composted pine bark with perlite or pumice) gives the air-filled porosity stone-fruit roots demand; plum will not tolerate a mix that holds water against the crown. Skip native garden soil in a pot, which compacts and drains poorly under irrigation.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Keep amendments minimal and drainage-first: blend in extra perlite or pumice if the base mix feels water-retentive, and top-dress with a thin layer of compost rather than mixing heavy organics throughout. Avoid water-holding additives such as moisture-retentive crystals or large peat fractions, which work against the fast-draining root zone plum needs.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: A plum in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground, since there is no deep soil for the roots to reach. In summer heat, check it every day and water when the top inch or two feels dry, until water runs out the bottom. Water more often than a ground tree, but never let the pot sit in a saucer full of water, because roots left wet will rot. In winter, when the tree is resting, give it just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Watering often washes food out of the pot, so feed a little at a time instead of one big dose. Use a diluted balanced liquid fertilizer every few weeks from spring into midsummer, then stop by late summer so the tree does not push out tender new growth that winter cold can kill. Do not fertilize when you first plant it, and stop feeding once the tree drops its leaves for winter.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground, because cold air reaches the soil from every side. A plum that survives winter fine in your yard can still have its roots freeze in a pot. Before hard freezes come, either bury the pot up to its rim in a garden bed, or move it into an unheated but protected spot like an attached garage or shed that stays cold but not deep-freezing. The tree still needs the cold to rest, so do not bring it into a warm, heated room.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Roots in a pot sit several zones colder than roots in the ground, because the soil ball is exposed to the air on all sides, so a plum that is hardy in your ground may still freeze its roots in a container. Before hard freezes, either sink the pot to its rim in a garden bed or move it to an unheated but sheltered space (an attached garage or shed) that stays cold enough to hold dormancy but buffers the deep freezes. The tree still needs its winter chill, so do not bring it into a heated room.

container_notes.notes_beginner: A plum really wants to grow in the ground, and a pot is the workaround if you do not have the space. It can be done, especially with a semi-dwarfing rootstock like Marianna, but plan on more hands-on care and smaller, less dependable crops than a tree in the ground. Use the biggest pot you can that drains really well, and know that watering, feeding, and winter protection all need closer attention than they would in open ground.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Plum is fundamentally a ground tree, and a container is the compromise for growers who lack the space or the soil for an in-ground tree. It can work, best on a size-limiting rootstock such as Marianna, but expect more hands-on management and lighter, less reliable crops than the same tree in the ground. Give it the largest practical pot with excellent drainage, and accept that watering, feeding, and winter protection all demand closer attention than they would in open soil.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: A potted plum dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to draw on, so check moisture daily in the heat of summer and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes. The discipline is the opposite of the in-ground tree: water more often, but never leave the pot standing in a full saucer, because continuously wet roots rot.
