10.suitability_note_seasoned: Arizona's low desert banks little chill (about 100 to 400 hours), so only the lowest-chill Japanese plums (Methley) crop, and only in cooler winters; blistering summer heat and heavy irrigation demand make it a challenging, marginal plum site.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Arizona's low desert gets very little winter chill, so only the lowest-chill Japanese plums like Methley fruit, and only in cooler winters. The extreme summer heat makes it a tough, marginal spot for plums.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Low winter chill and extreme summer heat, not frost, are the limits; the tree needs heavy irrigation.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: Arizona's low desert gets very little winter chill, so only the lowest-chill Japanese plums like Methley have a chance, and only in cooler winters. The extreme heat makes it a hard place to grow plums.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert is a marginal plum site: very low winter chill limits it to the lowest-chill Japanese cultivars in the colder winters, and extreme summer heat plus heavy irrigation demand make dependable fruiting unlikely.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert winters bank only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below most plums' requirement; only the lowest-chill Japanese cultivars approach it, and only in the colder winters.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_beginner: The Arizona low desert has very mild winters with little chill, so only the lowest-chill Japanese plums have any chance, and even then only in a cold winter.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Florida peninsula's zone 10 banks too little winter chill (roughly 50 to 350 hours) for plums to fruit dependably; a tree may survive but should be treated as a survivor, not a cropper.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 in peninsular Florida is too mild in winter for plums to fruit dependably. A tree may live but will rarely give plums.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 11 in Florida is effectively frost-free and banks almost no winter chill (0 to 150 hours); European and Japanese plums cannot break dormancy or fruit here. Not a plum zone.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 11 in Florida has almost no winter cold, so plums cannot bloom or fruit. This is not a plum-growing zone.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: Peninsular Florida is too warm in winter for European and Japanese plums to get the chill they need. They will not fruit dependably here; this is a job for special low-chill southern stone fruit, not these plums.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula banks too little winter chill for European or Japanese plums to fruit dependably (zone 10 marginal-to-none, zone 11 effectively chill-free). These types are out of range; only specialized ultra-low-chill southern stone fruit fit this climate.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_seasoned: Peninsular Florida banks roughly 50 to 350 chill hours in zone 10 and 0 to 150 in zone 11, below the threshold for European and Japanese plums to break dormancy and fruit.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_beginner: Florida's peninsula is too warm in winter, banking too few chill hours for these plums to bloom and fruit.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Tropical zone 11 in Hawaii banks essentially no winter chill (0 to 150 hours); European and Japanese plums cannot break dormancy and will not fruit. Not a plum zone.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Tropical Hawaii has almost no winter cold, so European and Japanese plums cannot bloom or fruit here. This is not a plum-growing zone.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Tropical Hawaii banks essentially no winter chill (0 to 150 hours); European and Japanese plums cannot break dormancy and will not fruit. Not a plum zone.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Tropical Hawaii has almost no winter cold, so European and Japanese plums cannot bloom or fruit here. This is not a plum-growing zone.

12.suitability_note_seasoned: Tropical Hawaii banks essentially no winter chill (0 to 150 hours); European and Japanese plums cannot break dormancy and will not fruit. Not a plum zone.
12.suitability_note_beginner: Tropical Hawaii has almost no winter cold, so European and Japanese plums cannot bloom or fruit here. This is not a plum-growing zone.

13.suitability_note_seasoned: Tropical Hawaii banks essentially no winter chill (0 to 150 hours); European and Japanese plums cannot break dormancy and will not fruit. Not a plum zone.
13.suitability_note_beginner: Tropical Hawaii has almost no winter cold, so European and Japanese plums cannot bloom or fruit here. This is not a plum-growing zone.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Tropical Hawaii has almost no winter cold, so European and Japanese plums cannot get the chill they need to bloom and fruit. This is not a plum-growing climate for these types.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Tropical Hawaii banks essentially no winter chill, so European and Japanese plums cannot break dormancy or fruit. These temperate types are out of range for the climate.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_seasoned: Tropical Hawaii banks essentially no accumulated chill (0 to 150 hours), far below the requirement of any European or Japanese plum.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_beginner: Hawaii's tropical climate has almost no winter cold, so these plums cannot get the chill they need.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Rio Grande Valley winters bank only about 0 to 300 chill hours, per Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, right around the edge of even the lowest-chill Japanese plum selections' roughly 250-hour need. Only an unusually cool Valley winter would approach that, and a typical warm winter delivers far less, so fruiting cannot be counted on. Grow fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead for dependable fruit.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Only the lowest-chill plum varieties could ever fruit in the Rio Grande Valley, and even those would need an unusually cool winter. Most years, expect growth but no fruit. Grow fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a practical concern in the Valley; insufficient winter chill, not cold, is the binding constraint here.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Rio Grande Valley winters bank only about 0 to 300 chill hours, per Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, right around the edge of even the lowest-chill Japanese plum selections' roughly 250-hour need. Only an unusually cool Valley winter would approach that, and a typical warm winter delivers far less, so fruiting cannot be counted on. Grow fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead for dependable fruit.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Only the lowest-chill plum varieties could ever fruit in the Rio Grande Valley, and even those would need an unusually cool winter. Most years, expect growth but no fruit. Grow fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a practical concern in the Valley; insufficient winter chill, not cold, is the binding constraint here.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: Plum is a poor bet for the Rio Grande Valley. Only an unusually cold winter would give even the lowest-chill varieties enough cold, so trees rarely fruit here. Plant fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Plum sits right at the chill edge in the Rio Grande Valley: the Valley's roughly 0 to 300 chill hours reaches only as high as the lowest-chill Japanese plum selections' roughly 250-hour need, and only in an unusually cool winter. Trees may survive but a dependable crop cannot be counted on; the Valley is far better suited to fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus.
rgv.chill_basis_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley banks only about 0 to 300 winter chill hours in a typical year, and a warm winter can deliver close to zero, per Texas A&M AgriLife Extension (Valley orchard chill runs roughly 200 to 300 hours), corroborated by LSU AgCenter's comparable figure for the similarly subtropical Gulf coast. That is far below what standard temperate stone and pome fruit varieties need to break dormancy and set fruit reliably.
rgv.chill_basis_beginner: Valley winters give very little winter cold, something like 0 to 300 chill hours some years, and a warm winter can give almost none. That is not enough for most standard fruit tree varieties to flower and fruit reliably here.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Chill is amply met for the entire variety range (250 to 900 hours needed, far less than this region banks), and WSU's western Washington fruit handbook lists solid ripening windows for both European types (Stanley, Italian Prune, Damson, Green Gage) and Japanese types (Methley, Santa Rosa, Burbank) in this climate. European plums are the steadier choice here: they bloom a little later and tolerate the region's damp spring well. Japanese types bloom earliest of the two and carry a modest late-frost risk in an unusually cold spring, but both types fruit dependably across the maritime lowlands.
8.suitability_note_beginner: This fruits well here. European plums like Stanley and Italian Prune are the steadiest choice, and Japanese plums like Santa Rosa do well too, though they bloom a little earlier and carry slightly more frost risk in a cold spring.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom begins only days after the typical last frost, so an unusually late cold snap can occasionally nip the earliest Japanese bloomers; later-blooming European varieties clear most spring frost risk.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The immediate coast blooms about a week later than the interior lowlands and still banks ample chill for the full variety range (250 to 900 hours needed). European plums remain the steadier pick in this cooler, often foggier spring; Japanese types still carry a touch more frost exposure at their earlier bloom.
9.suitability_note_beginner: This still fruits well on the coast, just a little later than inland. European plums are the safest bet in the cooler, damper spring here.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom runs about a week later than the interior lowlands, but frost risk follows the same pattern: the earliest Japanese types are the most exposed, later European varieties the safest.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Plum is a strong, dependable tree fruit for the maritime PNW. Winters bank plenty of chill for any variety, and the long, mild growing season ripens both European types like Stanley and Japanese types like Santa Rosa. European plums are the steadier pick for our damp spring; Japanese types bloom a little earlier and are slightly more exposed to a late frost.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: The maritime Pacific Northwest is genuine plum country. Ample winter chill and a long, mild season let both European and Japanese types fruit reliably from Puget Sound to the Willamette Valley; WSU's western Washington fruit handbook lists strong ripening windows for both. European varieties (Stanley, Italian Prune, Damson) are the region's steadier default, later-blooming and well suited to the damp spring; Japanese varieties (Santa Rosa, Methley) ripen earlier and carry modestly more late-frost exposure at their earlier bloom, but still fruit dependably across both zones.
pnw.chill_basis_seasoned: Maritime Pacific Northwest winters bank roughly 700 to 1,950 hours of chill depending on zone and site, far above the 250 to 900 hour range this variety list needs. Chill is never the limiting factor here.
pnw.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for any plum variety. The challenge, when there is one, is a late spring frost on the earliest Japanese bloomers, not a lack of cold.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Chill is never the limiter here: the belt delivers roughly 1100 to 1500 chilling hours a year in zone 7, clearing this crop's variety range with margin (NC State Extension; regional four-source chill basket). Both European and Japanese-type plums grow here. Japanese types bloom earlier and are more exposed to a late frost, while humid-climate disease pressure, black knot and brown rot, is the shared management issue for both types.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Winters here are cold enough for this tree; chill is not a worry. You can grow both European and Japanese-type plums here. The Japanese types flower earlier and risk a late frost more; both types need watching for humidity-related diseases.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: This tree tends to bloom before the zone 7 (Piedmont interior)'s own last frost date, so a late freeze on open bloom is the main frost risk to watch, more than winter cold hardiness.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Chill is never the limiter here: the belt delivers roughly 1000 to 1350 chilling hours a year in zone 8, clearing this crop's variety range with margin (NC State Extension; regional four-source chill basket). Both European and Japanese-type plums grow here. Japanese types bloom earlier and are more exposed to a late frost, while humid-climate disease pressure, black knot and brown rot, is the shared management issue for both types.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Winters here are cold enough for this tree; chill is not a worry. You can grow both European and Japanese-type plums here. The Japanese types flower earlier and risk a late frost more; both types need watching for humidity-related diseases.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: This tree tends to bloom before the zone 8 (Coastal Plain)'s own last frost date, so a late freeze on open bloom is the main frost risk to watch, more than winter cold hardiness.

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Plums grow well here, both European and Japanese types. Plant a bare-root tree while dormant.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: Chill is ample for plum here, both European and Japanese types. Japanese types bloom earlier and carry more late-frost exposure; humid-climate disease pressure (black knot, brown rot) is the shared management issue for both types. Plant bare-root trees while dormant.
mid_atlantic.chill_basis_seasoned: Mid-Atlantic winters bank abundant, reliable chill accumulation: NC State Extension puts the statewide floor at over 1,000 chilling hours a year, and a wider four-source check (NC State, Penn State, Virginia Cooperative Extension, University of Maryland Extension) confirms the belt delivers roughly 1,000 to 1,350 hours on the warmer Coastal Plain (zone 8) and 1,100 to 1,500 hours in the cooler Piedmont interior (zone 7). That clears the chill requirement of every recommended variety in this guide with room to spare. Chill is never the limiting factor here.
mid_atlantic.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for this tree. Nearly every variety gets all the winter chill it needs; chill is not something to worry about in this region.

mid_south.region_label: Mid-South: Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Chill is never the limiter here: the belt delivers roughly 1,000 to 1,300 chilling hours a year in zone 7, clearing this crop's variety range with margin (University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Chilling Hour Reports). Both European and Japanese-type plums grow here. Japanese types bloom earlier and are more exposed to a late frost, while humid-climate disease pressure, black knot and brown rot, is the shared management issue for both types.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Winters here are cold enough for this tree; chill is not a worry. You can grow both European and Japanese-type plums here. The Japanese types flower earlier and risk a late frost more; both types need watching for humidity-related diseases.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: This tree tends to bloom before the zone 7 (Ozark uplands interior)'s own last frost date, so a late freeze on open bloom is the main frost risk to watch, more than winter cold hardiness.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Chill is never the limiter here: the belt delivers roughly 900 to 1,100 chilling hours a year in zone 8, clearing this crop's variety range with margin (University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Chilling Hour Reports). Both European and Japanese-type plums grow here. Japanese types bloom earlier and are more exposed to a late frost, while humid-climate disease pressure, black knot and brown rot, is the shared management issue for both types.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Winters here are cold enough for this tree; chill is not a worry. You can grow both European and Japanese-type plums here. The Japanese types flower earlier and risk a late frost more; both types need watching for humidity-related diseases.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: This tree tends to bloom before the zone 8 (lowland South)'s own last frost date, so a late freeze on open bloom is the main frost risk to watch, more than winter cold hardiness.

mid_south.region_notes_beginner: Plums grow well here, both European and Japanese types. Plant a bare-root tree while dormant.
mid_south.region_notes_seasoned: Chill is ample for plum here, both European and Japanese types. Japanese types bloom earlier and carry more late-frost exposure; humid-climate disease pressure (black knot, brown rot) is the shared management issue for both types. Plant bare-root trees while dormant.
mid_south.chill_basis_seasoned: Mid-South winters bank ample, reliable chill, and the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Chilling Hour Reports (Utah model, accumulation measured by March 1) show a real intra-state gradient rather than one flat number. The cooler Ozark and upland north (zone 7, where the Fayetteville station banks about 1,024 hours) accumulates roughly 1,000 to 1,300 chilling hours a year, and the warmer lowland south (zone 8, with Wynne near 1,069 and Clarksville near 1,081) accumulates roughly 900 to 1,100. Even the belt's southwestern warm edge near Hope, at about 901 hours, clears the chill requirement of the recommended varieties for this crop with room to spare. Chill is not the limiting factor here.
mid_south.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for this tree. Nearly every variety gets all the winter chill it needs; chill is not something to worry about in this region.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, clearing the entire recommended list, including the European prune plums Stanley, Italian Prune, and Damson. This is the widest plum variety choice in the region.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The cooler parts of the region can grow any of the recommended plums, including the European prune types.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late frost after the March to April bloom is an occasional risk here; steady irrigation through summer matters more.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, clearing the Japanese plums Methley, Santa Rosa, and Burbank comfortably, with Green Gage (700 hours) right at the ceiling. Stanley, Italian Prune, and Damson need more chill than this zone reliably banks.
9.suitability_note_beginner: On the valley floor, plant a Japanese plum like Methley, Santa Rosa, or Burbank for a reliable crop. Green Gage usually works too, but the European prune plums need more winter cold than the valley floor consistently gives.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in late February to March occasionally meets a late frost; the dry air otherwise keeps disease low, and regular deep watering matters more than either.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin (zone 10) banks roughly 150 to 450 chill hours, enough for the Japanese plums Methley, Santa Rosa, and Burbank; Green Gage and the European prune plums need more cold than this warm corner provides.
10.suitability_note_beginner: At Laughlin, stick to a Japanese plum like Methley, Santa Rosa, or Burbank. The European types need more winter cold than this spot gets.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a problem at Laughlin; intense summer heat and the need for steady water are the bigger considerations.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Plum grows well across the Las Vegas Valley region. The Japanese plums, Methley, Santa Rosa, and Burbank, are a classic low chill desert Southwest choice and fruit everywhere here, including Laughlin. Green Gage does well on the valley floor and in the cooler zone 8 areas. The European prune plums, Stanley, Italian Prune, and Damson, need more winter cold and are best kept to the cooler zone 8 pockets. Deep, regular watering through the hot summer is essential.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: Plum fruits reliably across the Las Vegas Valley region, splitting cleanly between the low chill Japanese types and the higher chill European prune plums. Methley, Santa Rosa, and Burbank (250 to 400 hours) are the dependable, desert-adapted anchor, clearing every zone including Laughlin. Green Gage (700 hours) fits zone 9 at the edge and zone 8 comfortably. Stanley, Italian Prune, and Damson (800 to 900 hours) need zone 8's cooler, higher pockets. The dry air keeps disease low; irrigation, not frost or chill, is the defining requirement through the hot growing season.
nevada.chill_basis_seasoned: Plum splits cleanly along species lines here. The low chill Japanese plums, Methley (250 hours), Santa Rosa, and Burbank (400 each), are a classic desert Southwest fit and clear every Nevada zone, including Laughlin. Green Gage, a European dessert plum at 700 hours, sits right at zone 9's ceiling and fits zone 8 comfortably. The high chill European prune plums, Stanley and Italian Prune (800 hours) and Damson (900), need zone 8's wider 500 to 900 hour band and are not a fit at zone 9 or Laughlin.
nevada.chill_basis_beginner: Plum works well here if you pick the right type. The Japanese plums, Methley, Santa Rosa, and Burbank, are low chill desert classics that fruit everywhere in the region, even at Laughlin. The European prune plums like Stanley and Damson need more winter cold and are better suited to the cooler zone 8 pockets.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Plum thrives at the low St. George elevations, where Washington County Extension lists it among the dependable fruits. Favor the low-chill Japanese plums over the high-chill European prune types; a late frost on the early bloom and steady summer water are the main concerns.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Plum grows well here; choose a low-chill Japanese plum. Give it steady water in summer and watch for a late frost on the early bloom.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Plum is among the earliest to bloom, opening before the late-March last frost in most years, so a late cold snap during bloom is the real spring risk; steady summer irrigation matters more through the rest of the season.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Plum grows well in St. George if you pick the right type. The low-chill Japanese plums suit the warm valley; the European prune plums need more winter cold than the core provides. Give trees steady water through the hot summer and watch for a late frost on the early bloom.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: Plum does well at the low St. George elevations; Washington County Extension lists it among the fruits that thrive around town. Favor the low-chill Japanese plums, which are desert-adapted and fit the warm valley's limited winter chill; the high-chill European prune plums need more cold than the core banks. The dry air keeps disease low, so a late frost on the early bloom and steady summer irrigation matter more. Plant a bare-root or container tree during the dormant season.
utah_dixie.chill_basis_seasoned: Plum splits along species lines here. The low-chill Japanese plums, needing only a few hundred chill hours, are a desert Southwest classic and fit the warm St. George core, where Washington County Extension lists plum among the fruits that do well at low elevation. The high-chill European prune plums need more winter cold than the valley floor banks and are a poorer fit. The dry air keeps disease low; a late frost on the early bloom and steady irrigation through the hot season, not chill or brown rot, are the defining concerns.
utah_dixie.chill_basis_beginner: Plum grows well in St. George if you pick the right type. The low-chill Japanese plums suit the warm valley; the European prune plums need more winter cold than the core provides. Give trees steady water through the hot summer and watch for a late frost on the early bloom.

pet_safe.note: The flesh is fine, but the pits, seeds, and leaves contain cyanide compounds and are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: Your tree may set its first plums now. Thin them to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches about a month after bloom, and space them so no two plums touch, because touching fruit is how brown rot walks from one plum to the next through a cluster. If yours is a Japanese type (Santa Rosa, Methley) it will over-set and needs heavier thinning than a European type (Stanley, damson). Prune more lightly than you would a peach: plum bears largely on spurs, the short stubby side shoots that keep fruiting for years, so open the canopy rather than cutting everything back hard. Watch for black knot, a rough black swelling on a twig, and cut it out in winter well below the swelling.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: A light first set is normal. Thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches within about a month of bloom, spacing so fruit do not touch, since contact is the transmission route for brown rot within a cluster. Japanese cultivars over-set and need markedly heavier thinning than Europeans. Prune conservatively and preserve spur wood: plum bears largely on long-lived spurs, so thin to open the canopy rather than heading back hard. Black knot management begins in earnest once the tree is bearing: cut every gall 3 to 4 inches below the visible swelling into clean wood during dormancy, before the fungus sporulates, and destroy the prunings off site rather than composting them on the property.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From about the fifth year the tree carries a full crop, and the year settles into a rhythm: light dormant pruning that keeps the spurs, black knot cut out while the tree is bare, and thinning to one plum every 4 to 6 inches after bloom. The tree ripens over one to two weeks, so pick in several passes. A ripe plum shows full color, wears a dusty bloom on the skin, gives slightly, and pulls free easily; a European prune type is ripe when it is soft right down to the pit. Handle gently and clear the dropped fruit, because bruises let in brown rot and fruit left to shrivel on the tree or ground is next year's infection waiting to happen.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from roughly year five. The annual cycle is light dormant pruning that preserves spur wood, black-knot excision while the structure is visible, thinning to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches, and post-harvest sanitation. Harvest over one to two weeks in several passes on full varietal color, intact bloom, slight give and clean release; European prune types are ripe when soft to the pit, which is later than they look. Handle gently, since bruising is the brown-rot entry point, and clear every mummy and drop, which are the following season's inoculum. Type still governs the tree: Japanese cultivars keep over- setting and keep needing the heavier thinning pass every year, not only while young.

crops.name: Apricot

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Apricot wants a deep soil that drains fast and lets air reach the roots. Good drainage is the one rule you cannot bend with apricot, because it has little tolerance for wet, heavy ground and the root and crown rots that follow it. A sandy loam is a great fit, and a lighter sandy soil works if you keep up with water. Heavy clay that holds water is the trouble spot; on clay, plant on a raised mound so the roots sit above the soggy soil, and choose a plum rootstock (Myrobalan or Marianna) that takes heavier ground. One apricot quirk: in the alkaline soils of the arid West it is prone to iron chlorosis, where the leaves yellow between green veins, so a near-neutral soil with some compost suits it best.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Apricot demands a deep, well-drained loam with good aeration; drainage is the non-negotiable, since it has little tolerance for wet or heavy soils and waterlogging brings on crown and root rot. A sandy loam is well suited and a lighter sandy soil is workable with attention to water. Heavy, water-holding clay is the problem texture; on such ground, plant on a raised berm and pair the tree with a heavier-soil-tolerant plum rootstock (Myrobalan or Marianna 2624) rather than a drainage-fussy seedling stock. Note the apricot-specific weakness: on the high-pH soils of the arid West it is prone to iron chlorosis (interveinal yellowing), so a near-neutral, moderately fertile soil is ideal.

ph.note_beginner: Apricot grows best in a near-neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerates from about 6.0 to 8.0 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is). It leans more tolerant of alkaline soil than most stone fruit, but on strongly alkaline western soils it often shows iron chlorosis, a yellowing between the leaf veins. Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if needed: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if it is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is far easier to fix before the permanent tree goes in.
ph.note_seasoned: Apricot does best in a near-neutral soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerates about 6.0 to 8.0. It is somewhat more alkaline-tolerant than peach or cherry, but on the high-pH soils of the arid West it is notably prone to iron chlorosis (interveinal yellowing). Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground.

fertilizer.timing: early spring before bud break
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed lightly in early spring before growth begins, broadcasting evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, off the trunk, and watering it in. Apricot needs modest nitrogen: judge by shoot growth and ease off if the tree is already vigorous. On the alkaline soils of the arid West, watch for iron chlorosis (interveinal yellowing) and correct it with a chelated iron rather than piling on nitrogen. Never feed late in the season, since late nitrogen pushes soft growth that winter cold injures and that canker enters.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed once in early spring before the tree starts growing. Scatter the fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. Apricot does not need heavy feeding, so go light: if the tree is making plenty of new growth, it may need none at all. If the leaves yellow between the veins (common on western alkaline soils), that is an iron problem, not a nitrogen one, so use a chelated iron product instead of more fertilizer. Never feed late in the year, because soft late growth gets damaged by winter cold.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits backyard apricots, applied modestly. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which drives soft, disease-prone, overly vigorous growth at the expense of fruiting and winter hardiness.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works for backyard apricots, used sparingly. Do not overdo nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth that is more prone to disease and winter damage.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rate is about 1/2 to 1 pound of actual nitrogen equivalent scaled to tree age, applied once in early spring before bud break, kept modest because apricot fruits on long-lived spurs and does not need the heavy nitrogen a peach does. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. Judge by shoot growth: a bearing tree wants roughly 12 to 18 inches of new wood a year.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple guide is a small handful of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, up to a modest amount, spread once in early spring before the buds open. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing. If the tree is already growing more than a foot of new branch each year, it probably needs little or no feeding at all.

companions.note_beginner: Apricot is self-fruitful, which means one tree makes fruit on its own and you do not need a second tree to pollinate it. A few varieties, notably Moorpark, set a heavier crop when a second apricot blooms nearby, but even they fruit alone, so a lone tree is fine. Beyond that, what matters for a tree is the root zone, not the usual vegetable pairings: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, since lawn competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free area helps it settle in. The one site rule is replant disease: do not plant an apricot where another apricot, peach, plum, cherry, or nectarine was recently growing.
companions.note_seasoned: Apricot is self-fruitful, so a single tree sets a crop on its own with no pollinizer required; a handful of cultivars (Moorpark is the classic) set more heavily with a compatible second variety, but none actually need one. Past pollination, the interactions that matter for a tree are at the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since they compete hard with a young tree, and a mulched, competition-free root area establishes it faster. The one site rule is replant disease: do not follow stone fruit with stone fruit on the same ground.

good_seasoned.name: A second apricot variety (optional pollinizer; one self-fruitful tree still fruits)
good_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Extension sources (USU, Iowa State, UC) agree most apricots are self-fruitful and need no partner, but that some cultivars (Moorpark) set a fuller crop with a compatible pollinizer of overlapping bloom. Mechanism-clear and near-universal; the benefit is a bonus, not a requirement. extension_backed/HIGH.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Unlike most sweet cherries, apricot does not need a mate: a single self-fruitful tree sets a full crop alone. A second variety blooming at the same time is an OPTIONAL upgrade that can improve set and fruit size, and it is worth it for the varieties that respond, chiefly Moorpark. If you have room for only one tree, plant it with confidence. If you add a pollinizer, match bloom timing, since apricot's bloom window is short and very early.

good_seasoned.name: Flowering herbs and pollinator plants
good_seasoned.label: likely

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Insectary/pollinator-strip logic is extension-aligned in principle, but apricot is self-fruitful so the pollinator draw is a help rather than a requirement, and the predator-recruitment benefit is diffuse and unquantified for apricot specifically. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A skirt of flowering herbs and pollinator plants around an apricot supports fruit set and orchard-floor health. Apricot is self-fruitful, so the pollinator draw is a help rather than a requirement, but strong bee activity during its short, very early bloom improves set in cool springs, and the same flowers recruit the hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that keep aphids in check. Choose species that bloom around apricot bloom and keep them out toward the drip line rather than crowding the trunk.

bad_seasoned.name: Other stone fruit in old stone-fruit ground
bad_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Replanting apricot (or other Prunus) into old stone-fruit ground carries a well-documented replant-disease plus ring-nematode plus bacterial-canker carryover risk; extension guidance is to use fresh ground. extension_backed/HIGH.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Replanting an apricot, or any stone fruit, into ground that recently grew apricots, peaches, plums, cherries, or nectarines is a documented mistake. Old stone-fruit ground carries elevated ring-nematode populations and the replant-disease complex, and nearby infected trees can harbor bacterial canker, which apricot on a plum rootstock is especially prone to. Plant in fresh ground, or replace a generous soil volume and remove infected neighbors first; rotating to a different SITE, not just a different variety, is the fix.

pests.name: Plum curculio
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small young fruit carries a distinctive crescent-shaped scar where the female cut a slit to lay an egg. Infested fruit often drops early; fruit that hangs on may be gnarled or have a grub tunneling inside near the pit. Damage appears shortly after petal fall and is heaviest east of the Rockies.
pests.symptoms_beginner: On small developing apricots, look for a curved, crescent-shaped scar, the mark the beetle leaves when it lays an egg. Damaged fruit often drops early, and some that stays on the tree ends up misshapen or has a grub inside. You see this soon after the petals fall.
pests.cause_seasoned: The plum curculio (Conotrachelus nenuphar), a small snout beetle native to eastern North America. Adults emerge around bloom and attack fruit from petal fall onward, laying eggs in the developing fruit; the larvae feed inside. There is little pressure in the arid West.
pests.cause_beginner: A small beetle with a long snout called the plum curculio. The adults show up around bloom and start damaging the little fruits right after the petals drop, laying eggs inside them. The larvae then feed within the fruit. It is mostly an eastern problem and rare in dry western climates.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: For a backyard tree, jarring the limbs over a sheet in the early morning when the beetles are sluggish, then destroying what drops, reduces the population. Promptly gather and dispose of dropped infested fruit to break the cycle. Kaolin clay applied from petal fall is an organic deterrent.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Early in the morning the beetles are slow. Spread a sheet under the tree, tap the branches so the beetles fall, and destroy them. Pick up and throw away any dropped fruit promptly so the larvae inside do not mature. A kaolin clay spray (a fine white mineral coating) starting at petal fall helps keep them off.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: remove dropped fruit through the season so larvae cannot complete development in the soil beneath the tree. A clean orchard floor and prompt fruit pickup steadily lower pressure year over year.
pests.prevention_beginner: The main thing is cleanup. Pick up fallen fruit all season so the larvae inside cannot finish growing in the soil under the tree. Keeping the ground clear lowers the number of beetles the next year.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with cleanup: gather and get rid of dropped apricots all season, because a grub inside a fallen fruit finishes growing in the soil under the tree. On a cool early morning, while the beetles are still sluggish, you can also spread an old sheet under the branches, tap the limbs so they drop onto it, and destroy what you collect. A clear ground surface, kept up year after year, means fewer beetles each spring.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Season-long removal of drops denies larvae the soil development they need, and that steady drawdown is the backbone every other rung leans on. Jarring the scaffolds at first light, while adults are still torpid, adds physical removal onto the same sheet, and repeating that pass through the weeks after petal fall is what makes it pay. Pressure concentrates east of the Rockies, so a tree in a dry western climate may need little beyond this.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Kaolin clay is a fine white mineral you mix with water and spray on, leaving a coating that discourages the beetles from feeding and laying eggs. Begin at petal fall, when they move onto the small fruit, and count on repeat sprays through the season, since the barrier only works while the coating is there.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Kaolin is a deterrent film rather than a killer, so timing from petal fall and renewing it as fruit expands is the whole of its value. Weigh it against the tree's other problems: heavy use can flare San Jose scale, which is already on this crop's list.

pests.name: Peachtree borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass at the base of the trunk, right around the soil line, often with a mounded look where the bark meets the ground. Larvae tunnel the inner bark at the crown; several borers can girdle and kill a young apricot in a single season, and the wounds also open the door to canker.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Look at the very bottom of the trunk where it meets the soil. Peachtree borers leave a sticky, gummy ooze mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (called frass). You may see a small mound of gum and frass at the base. A young tree with several borers can be killed in one season, so this is one to catch early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the peachtree borer (Synanthedon exitiosa), a clearwing moth whose adults are day-flying and wasp-like. Eggs are laid on the lower trunk in summer; the larvae tunnel the inner bark at and just below the soil line. It attacks all stone fruit, apricot included, and hits stressed or wounded trees first.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (young, grub-like stage) of the peachtree borer, a moth whose adults look like wasps and fly during the day. The adults lay eggs on the lower trunk in summer, and the larvae burrow into the bark at and below the soil line. Trees with existing wounds are hit hardest, but a healthy tree can be attacked too.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue spray once larvae are tunneling inside. The practical home control is to expose the crown in late summer or fall, find the entry holes by the gum and frass, and kill larvae by hand with a thin wire (worming). Keep the trunk base free of wounds and paint it white against sunscald cracks.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the larvae are inside, no spray reaches them. The backyard fix is to scrape soil away from the base in late summer or fall, find the holes marked by gum and frass, and kill the larvae with a thin, stiff wire pushed into each hole. Then smooth the soil back. Avoid nicking the trunk base with mowers or trimmers.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Protect the lower trunk from mechanical injury and sunscald (a white trunk paint helps), keep the tree vigorous, and clear weeds and tall grass from the base so the crown stays open and easy to inspect. Check the soil line each late summer for fresh gum so an infestation is caught in its first year.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep mowers and string trimmers away from the trunk; the wounds they leave attract the egg-laying moths, and white trunk paint prevents the sunburn cracks they enter. Keep grass and weeds cleared from the base so you can see the soil line, and check it every late summer for fresh gummy ooze.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the ground at the foot of the trunk mowed and clear of weeds and tall grass so the soil line stays visible, then look it over each late summer for fresh gummy ooze. Keep mowers and string trimmers off the bark as well, since those wounds draw the egg-laying moths, and white trunk paint helps head off the sunburn cracks they enter through.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A cleared collar around the crown keeps the soil line inspectable, which is how a first-year infestation gets caught before it girdles anything. Mechanical injury and sunscald cracks concentrate egg laying on the lower trunk, so protecting that zone, white paint included, is the preventive half of this rung.

control_ladder.note_beginner: By the time the larvae are tunneling under the bark, a spray cannot reach them. In late summer or fall, scrape the soil back from the base, find the holes marked by gum and frass, the sawdust-like droppings, and push a thin stiff wire into each one to kill the larva inside. Smooth the soil back afterward.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Worming is the practical home control: expose the crown, trace each gum and frass mass to its entry hole, and probe it with stiff wire. Several larvae can girdle a young tree in one season, so an annual late-season pass is worth the hour where this moth is present.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Dense colonies of green or mealy-gray aphids on the tips of new spring shoots, curling and distorting young leaves, with sticky honeydew below that blackens into sooty mold. Heaviest on vigorous young trees; it slows shoot growth but rarely harms fruit directly.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of small green or gray soft-bodied insects on the tips of new spring growth, curling and twisting the young leaves, with a sticky coating below that turns black and moldy. It is worst on young trees and mainly stunts new growth rather than ruining fruit.
pests.cause_seasoned: Chiefly the green peach aphid and the mealy plum aphid. They overwinter as eggs on the tree and explode on the tender spring flush, feeding on sap; populations usually crash by midsummer as shoots harden and natural enemies build up.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects (green peach aphid and mealy plum aphid). Their eggs overwinter on the tree and the young hatch to feed on the soft new spring growth. The numbers usually drop on their own by midsummer as the shoots toughen and ladybugs and other helpers move in.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Often no action is needed, since beneficials clean it up by midsummer. For a heavy infestation on a young tree, a strong jet of water knocks colonies off, or insecticidal soap or horticultural oil applied to the curled tips works; protect the ladybugs and lacewings that do most of the control. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which fuels the soft growth aphids prefer.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Often you can leave it alone, since ladybugs and other helpers clear it by midsummer. On a young tree that is badly hit, blast the colonies off with a hose, or spray the curled tips with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil. Do not over-fertilize, since lush new growth is what the aphids love.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep trees vigorous but not over-fed (high nitrogen invites aphids), encourage beneficial insects, and tolerate the early-season curl, which rarely affects the crop. A dormant oil spray reduces overwintering eggs where the pest is chronic.
pests.prevention_beginner: Avoid heavy feeding that pushes the soft growth aphids love, welcome ladybugs and lacewings, and do not panic over the spring leaf-curl, which usually does not hurt the crop. A dormant oil spray in late winter cuts down the overwintering eggs.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. Heavy feeding pushes out the soft, sappy growth these aphids multiply on, so a moderately fed tree is a less inviting target.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: High nitrogen sustains the tender spring flush that green peach aphid and mealy plum aphid colonize; moderating it removes the tissue quality that lets colonies build on a vigorous young tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On a young tree that is badly hit, knock the colonies off the shoot tips with a strong jet from the hose. Do it early in the day so the leaves dry quickly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water jet dislodges colonies from the tips without removing the predators working the same shoots; repeat as the flush rebuilds, and time it early in the day to limit leaf wetness.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Often the best move is to leave it alone. Ladybugs, lacewings, and similar helpers usually clear these aphids by midsummer as the shoots toughen, and the curled spring leaves seldom cost you fruit. Skip broad-spectrum insecticides so those helpers stay on the job.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident natural enemies do most of the control here, and populations tend to crash by midsummer as shoots harden, so the early leaf curl is a tolerable cost rather than a crop loss. Broad-spectrum material is what converts a self-limiting flush into a season-long problem.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a young tree is still overwhelmed, spray insecticidal soap straight onto the curled tips. It kills only what it wets, so aim at the colonies rather than the whole tree, and hold off when the temperature is above 90°F.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Contact soap is a coverage-dependent knockdown on the curled tips, and it kills the soft-bodied beneficials it wets, so confine it to located colonies. Avoid it above 90°F or on a water-stressed tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil smothers aphids it contacts on the tips, and a dormant oil spray in late winter cuts down the eggs that overwinter on the tree, which is worth doing where aphids turn up every year. Keep oil off a drought-stressed tree, off the tree in bloom so bees are not hit, and do not spray above 90°F; once the tree has leaves, keep it at least 30 days from any sulfur spray, and check the oil label because some say to wait longer.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: In season, oil is a smothering contact spray on the curled tips; the higher-value use is the dormant application, which lowers the overwintering egg load where the pest is chronic. Observe the oil constraints: not above 90°F, not on water-stressed wood, not within 30 days of sulfur while the tree is in leaf, or longer if the oil label says so, and not onto anything in flower.

pests.name: San Jose scale
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny gray, cone-shaped scales encrusting bark on twigs and scaffolds, sometimes with a reddish halo, and small red-ringed spots on the fruit skin. Heavy infestations weaken and can kill branches, and the fruit blemishes downgrade the crop.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny gray bumps crusting the bark of twigs and branches, and small red-ringed spots on the fruit. A bad case can weaken branches and even kill them, and it spots the fruit. The scales are easy to miss because each one is barely the size of a pinhead.
pests.cause_seasoned: San Jose scale (Diaspidiotus perniciosus), an armored scale insect that feeds on sap under a waxy cover. It has several overlapping generations a year; the mobile crawler stage is the point at which it spreads and the only stage a spray reaches.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny armored insect called San Jose scale that sits under a waxy cover and sucks sap from the bark. It has several rounds a year. The young, called crawlers, are the only stage that moves around and the only one a spray can hit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A thorough dormant-season horticultural oil spray, applied to the leafless tree so it coats twigs and scaffolds, smothers overwintering scale and is the mainstay backyard control. In-season, time any additional oil to the crawler stage. Prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: The main control is a good horticultural oil spray while the tree is bare and dormant, coating the twigs and branches to smother the scale. During the season, prune out and destroy any branches that are heavily crusted. Keeping the tree open and vigorous helps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: An annual dormant oil spray keeps scale from building up. Encourage the tiny parasitic wasps and predatory beetles that attack scale by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides, and prune to keep the canopy open and easy to cover thoroughly.
pests.prevention_beginner: A yearly dormant oil spray in late winter keeps scale from building up. Avoid harsh insecticides so the natural enemies that eat scale can do their work, and keep the tree pruned open so any spray reaches all the bark.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut out and destroy the twigs and branches that are crusted with scale rather than leaving them on the tree or stacked nearby. Taking out the worst wood removes a large share of the population with it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Pruning out and destroying heavily encrusted wood removes established colonies wholesale and lowers the crawler load that seeds the rest of the canopy.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Tiny parasitic wasps and small predatory beetles feed on scale and hold it down for you at no cost. Keep harsh, broad-spectrum insecticides off the tree so they can work.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserving the parasitoids and predatory beetles that attack armored scale is what keeps a light infestation light; broad-spectrum sprays remove them and give scale room to build.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The mainstay is a thorough horticultural oil spray while the tree is bare and dormant in late winter, coating every twig and branch so the overwintering scale is smothered. Prune the tree open first so the spray can reach all the bark. A summer spray only helps if it lands when the crawlers are moving, since that is the one stage a spray can hit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A thorough dormant oil on leafless wood is the mainstay backyard control, and complete coverage of twigs and scaffolds decides the result, which is why an open canopy is part of the method rather than a separate nicety. Time any in-season oil to crawler emergence, the only exposed stage, and keep the usual limits: not above 90°F, not on stressed wood, not within 30 days of sulfur while the tree is in leaf, or longer if the oil label says so.

pests.name: Catfacing insects (stink bugs and plant bugs)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Mature fruit shows sunken, dimpled, corky distortions, the puckered catfaced look, where feeding occurred on young fruit. The damage is cosmetic on the surface but can run into the flesh; it does not spread or rot on its own.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ripe apricots have sunken, puckered, dimpled patches, a look growers call catfacing. It comes from insects feeding on the fruit when it was small. The fruit is still usable; the damage is mostly on the surface and does not spread.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several true bugs, mainly stink bugs and the tarnished plant bug, that puncture small apricots to feed. Tissue at each feeding point stops growing while the surrounding flesh keeps swelling, so the mature fruit is left puckered and corky. Apricot ripens early, so the vulnerable young-fruit stage overlaps the spring buildup of these bugs.
pests.cause_beginner: A handful of insects, chiefly stink bugs and the small tarnished plant bug, that poke the young apricots to feed. The spot they feed on stops growing while the rest of the fruit swells around it, leaving a dimple. Because apricots set fruit early, the little fruit is out just as these bugs get going in spring.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spraying one tree does little, since these bugs commute in from nearby weeds and brush. The practical control is to deny them that harborage: mow and clear the broadleaf weeds around the tree, especially through spring when young fruit is most vulnerable.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spraying a single tree does not help much, because these bugs come in from weeds and brush nearby. The better fix is to take away their hiding spots: mow and pull the broadleaf weeds around the tree, especially in spring while the fruit is small.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the surrounding ground mowed and free of the broadleaf weeds these bugs breed in; a clean, grassy strip around the tree is the single biggest thing that lowers how many reach the fruit.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground around the tree mowed and clear of broadleaf weeds, which is where these bugs live and breed. A clean, grassy area around the tree means fewer of them ever reach your apricots.

control_ladder.note_beginner: These bugs live and breed in the broadleaf weeds around the tree and only visit the fruit, which is why spraying the tree itself does so little. Mow the surrounding ground and pull the broadleaf weeds, especially through spring while the apricots are small, and hold a clean grassy strip around the tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Stink bugs and tarnished plant bug commute in from adjacent weedy harborage, so a single-tree spray acts on the visitors and not the source; removing the broadleaf hosts and holding a mowed strip is the lever that lowers how many arrive. Apricot's early fruit set puts the vulnerable stage right in the spring buildup, so the clearing matters most then.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: At bloom, infected blossoms wilt and brown and the infection runs into the spur to form a small gummy canker. As fruit ripens, firm brown spots appear and spread fast, rotting a whole apricot within a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan spore mass on the surface. Rotted fruit dries into a clinging mummy. Apricot is among the most brown-rot-susceptible of all stone fruit.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: At bloom, flowers go limp and brown and small gummy dead patches form on the nearby spurs. As apricots ripen, brown spots appear and spread quickly, sometimes rotting a whole fruit in a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan fuzz on top. Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard mummy that hangs on. Apricot catches brown rot more easily than almost any other fruit.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Monilinia (M. fructicola and M. laxa). It overwinters in mummies and twig cankers; spores at bloom infect flowers, and those infections later seed the fruit rot. Warm, humid, wet weather drives it, which is a large part of why apricot is a poor risk in the humid Southeast and better in dry western summers.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Monilinia. It survives winter in dried mummy fruit and dead twig patches, then releases spores at bloom that infect the flowers, which later cause the fruit to rot. Warm, wet weather makes it spread fast, which is why apricots do much better in dry-summer climates than in humid ones.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: remove and destroy every mummy from the tree and ground and prune out gummy twig cankers, since these are the spore sources. In a wet bloom, an organic-approved bloom-time fungicide reduces blossom blight. Pick promptly, handle gently, and remove any rotting fruit at once; an open, fast-drying canopy is a standing defense.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cleanup is the main control: take off and destroy every dried mummy from the tree and ground and prune out the gummy dead twig patches, which hold the spores. If bloom is wet, an organic-approved spray at bloom helps protect the flowers. Pick on time, handle gently, and throw out any rotting fruit right away.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Year-round sanitation prevents most loss: never leave mummies over winter, keep the canopy open with pruning so fruit dries fast after rain, harvest promptly, and favor a dry-summer site. In humid regions, plan on a bloom and pre-harvest fungicide program, since apricot's high susceptibility makes sanitation alone insufficient.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Cleaning up all year prevents most of it: never leave dried mummies over winter, prune so the tree is open and dries fast after rain, and pick on time. In wet climates you will likely need an organic-approved spray at bloom and again near harvest, because apricot is so prone to this disease.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Take every mummy off the tree and off the ground and destroy it. A mummy is a rotted fruit that has dried hard and stayed hanging, and it is where the fungus waits out the winter, so clearing them is the most useful hour you spend on this disease.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mummies on the tree and on the ground beneath it are the primary overwintering inoculum, so stripping and destroying them is the core control, and leaving them through winter forfeits it. Pull any rotting fruit during the season as soon as you see it, since one lesion becomes a spore source fast in warm, wet weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune so the tree is open and air moves through it, and if you are still choosing a site, favor one with dry summers. Fruit that dries quickly after rain gets much less rot, and apricot is a poor bet in a humid climate.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: An open canopy shortens the wetting periods Monilinia needs, and site selection is the same lever at a larger scale: dry western summers suit this crop, humid southeastern ones work against it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the fruit as it ripens instead of letting it hang, handle it gently so the skin is not bruised, and get rid of anything that starts to rot right away. In warm, wet weather a whole apricot can go in a day or two.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Harvesting on time and handling gently limits the over-ripe and wounded fruit the rot exploits, and culling the first rots keeps one infection from seeding the fruit around it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut out the gummy dead patches on the twigs, taking the cut back into healthy wood, and destroy what comes off. Those small cankers carry spores from one season to the next, right alongside the mummies.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Blossom infections run back into the spur and form small gummy cankers that overwinter, so excising them into clean wood and destroying the prunings removes the second inoculum source that sanitation alone leaves standing.

diseases.name: Bacterial canker
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sunken, dark, gummy cankers on trunk, scaffolds, and spurs that ooze amber gum, often girdling and killing limbs; in spring, blossoms and spurs blast (blacken and die) and dormant buds fail to open. It is one of the most serious apricot diseases and is worse on trees grown on plum rootstocks (Myrobalan, Marianna), which are especially susceptible.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Sunken, dark, gummy patches (cankers) on the trunk and branches that ooze amber sap, often killing the branch above them. In spring, flowers and buds may blacken and die, and some buds never open. It is one of the worst apricot diseases and hits harder on trees grown on plum rootstocks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The bacterium Pseudomonas syringae. It infects through wounds, leaf scars, and frost-injured tissue in cool, wet spring and fall weather, and is worsened by anything that stresses the tree: poor drainage, ring nematodes, frost, and high-nitrogen soft growth. Apricot's very early bloom exposes fresh tissue to exactly the cold, wet spells that favor it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism) called Pseudomonas syringae. It gets in through wounds, leaf scars, and frost damage during cool, wet weather, and is worse on stressed trees, those in wet soil, hit by frost, or pushed with too much nitrogen. Apricot blooms so early that its tender new growth often meets the cold, wet weather this disease loves.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a tree is infected. Management is preventive: cut out cankered wood well below the canker in dry summer weather (not in wet spring), disinfecting tools between cuts, and remove badly infected young trees. Keep the tree unstressed and well drained; copper sprays give only partial protection and resistance is common.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once it sets in. The approach is prevention: cut out the cankered wood well below the dead patch during dry summer weather (not in wet spring), clean your tools between cuts, and pull out a badly infected young tree. Keep the tree healthy, unstressed, and on well-drained ground; copper sprays only help a little.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prevention is everything: plant on well-drained ground, choose a tolerant rootstock (a peach seedling such as Lovell is more canker-tolerant than the plum stocks), avoid frost-pocket sites and trunk wounds, paint the trunk white against sunscald cracks, prune only in dry summer weather, and never push soft growth with late nitrogen.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Prevention is everything: plant where the soil drains well, pick a more resistant rootstock (a peach seedling like Lovell resists it better than plum rootstocks), avoid frosty low spots and trunk wounds, paint the trunk white to prevent sunburn cracks, prune only in dry summer weather, and do not over-feed. A healthy, unstressed tree on good ground shrugs it off best.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The rootstock your tree is grafted onto matters more here than anything you can spray. A peach seedling rootstock such as Lovell tolerates this canker better than the plum rootstocks do, so ask which one a tree is on before you buy it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rootstock is the plant-once decision on this disease: trees on Myrobalan or Marianna plum stocks run notably more susceptible than those on a peach seedling such as Lovell, and the choice is settled at purchase rather than revisited later.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant where water drains away, and fix a soggy spot before a tree goes into it. Wet roots stress a tree, and a stressed tree is what this bacterium takes hold in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Poor drainage sits among the stress factors that turn an exposure into a canker, alongside frost injury and ring nematodes, and it is the one a gardener can genuinely change. Changing it is cheapest before planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no cure once this bacterium is established, so a young tree that is badly cankered is better pulled out than nursed along. On the trees you keep, avoid nicking the trunk, since wounds and leaf scars are the way in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A badly infected young tree is a standing inoculum source with no route back, so removal is the honest call. On retained trees, minimizing wounds matters because infection enters through wounds, leaf scars, and frost-injured tissue during cool, wet spells.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut cankered limbs off well below the sunken, gummy area, into wood that still looks healthy, and destroy what you remove. Do this in dry summer weather rather than a wet spring, and wipe or dip your pruners between cuts.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excise well beyond the canker margin into clean tissue and confine the work to dry summer weather, since cool wet conditions are when Pseudomonas syringae colonizes fresh cuts. Disinfecting between cuts is worth doing, though placing the cut far enough below the margin matters more.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A copper spray gives only partial protection against this one, and strains that shrug it off are common, so treat it as a small addition to the steps above rather than a fix. Copper is toxic to fish, builds up in the soil over the years, and can burn foliage above the label rate.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Fixed copper is partial protection at best here and resistance in the bacterial population is widespread, so it does not stand in for rootstock choice, drainage, and dry-season pruning. Copper accumulates at the soil surface, is highly toxic to aquatic life, and the compound printed on the label, not the brand, sets the acute hazard band.

diseases.name: Bacterial spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small angular, water-soaked spots on leaves turn brown and drop out, leaving a shot-hole look; heavy infection yellows and thins the canopy. On fruit, small sunken spots and cracks develop on the skin. Susceptibility varies by cultivar, and pressure is highest in warm, humid regions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get small angular water-soaked spots that turn brown and fall out, leaving little holes, called a shot-hole look. Bad cases turn leaves yellow and thin out the tree. On the fruit, small sunken spots and skin cracks form. How badly a tree is hit depends a lot on the variety and on how humid your area is.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It spreads in warm, wet weather and builds up where susceptible stone fruit grow nearby. On apricot the leaf and fruit spotting is sometimes confused with the fungal shot hole (Coryneum blight).
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism, not a fungus) called Xanthomonas. It spreads in warm, wet weather and builds up when there are other susceptible stone-fruit trees close by. Its leaf holes can look like the fungal shot hole disease, which is a different problem.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Home options are limited once symptoms appear: copper sprays help more as prevention than cure and can injure the tree if overused, so they are not a reliable home fix. Keeping the tree vigorous and the canopy open and dry helps it tolerate the disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no good home cure once it shows up. Copper sprays help a little as prevention but can hurt the tree if overused, so they are not a dependable fix. The best you can do is keep the tree healthy and open so the leaves dry fast.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The most effective measure is choosing a resistant or tolerant cultivar and a dry-summer site; this is largely a decision made before the tree goes in. Good airflow, an open canopy, and tree vigor reduce severity.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best prevention is the variety and the site you pick. A tolerant variety on a spot with dry summers and good airflow avoids most of the trouble, so it is a decision to make before planting. A healthy, open tree also helps.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This one is settled mostly before you plant. Choose a variety known to tolerate bacterial spot, because how hard a tree is hit depends a great deal on which variety it is, and there is no good home cure once the spotting shows up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cultivar susceptibility spans a wide range and is the highest-leverage control available, precisely because the in-season options are weak; it is a pre-plant decision that an established tree cannot revisit.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the tree a site with dry summers and moving air, and prune it open so the leaves dry fast. That will not cure an infection, but a healthy, open tree carries the disease better and shows less of it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Warm, humid conditions drive Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni, so site and canopy openness set the severity ceiling while vigor governs how much a tree shows. Neither acts on an established infection, which is why the pre-plant variety choice above carries most of the weight on this disease.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no good home cure once the spotting has appeared, and copper is not a dependable fix. It helps more as prevention than as a cure, so it does far less on a tree that is already spotted than on one you are protecting ahead of time, and it can injure the tree if you overuse it. Copper is also toxic to fish and builds up in the soil over the years, so if you use it at all, hold to the label rate and keep repeat sprays few.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper is the one material this crop's guidance names, and it is preventive rather than curative: home options are limited once symptoms are visible, and overuse carries its own phytotoxicity, so this sits as a hedged last option rather than a control. Copper accumulates at the soil surface, is highly toxic to aquatic life, and the compound printed on the label rather than the brand name sets the acute hazard band.

diseases.name: Shot hole (Coryneum blight)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small reddish-purple spots on leaves whose centers turn brown, die, and drop out, leaving clean round holes as if shot with birdshot. It also spots the fruit and can kill dormant buds and cause small twig cankers with gumming. Heavy infection defoliates and weakens the tree; apricot is a classic host.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small reddish-purple spots on the leaves whose brown centers fall out, leaving neat round holes that look like the leaf was hit with birdshot. It also spots the fruit and can kill buds. A bad case drops a lot of leaves and weakens the tree. Apricot is one of its favorite hosts.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Wilsonomyces carpophilus (Coryneum blight). It overwinters in infected buds and twig lesions and spreads in cool, wet spring weather and by splashing water and overhead irrigation. Wet springs and sprinkler wetting of the canopy drive it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Coryneum blight) that spends winter in infected buds and twigs and spreads in cool, wet spring weather and wherever water splashes the leaves. Overhead sprinklers that wet the tree make it much worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out infected twigs and buds, rake and destroy fallen infected leaves, and switch irrigation to the root zone so the canopy stays dry. A dormant application of fixed copper on the leafless tree is the main protective spray where the disease is established.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut out infected twigs, rake up and destroy fallen spotted leaves, and water at the ground rather than over the top so the leaves stay dry. A copper spray on the bare, dormant tree in late winter is the main way to protect it where this disease is common.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Keep water off the canopy (drip or soaker, never overhead), prune for airflow, clear fallen leaves, and apply a dormant copper spray in wet-spring regions. Dry-summer irrigation discipline is the single biggest lever.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The biggest thing is keeping the leaves dry: water at the ground, not over the tree, prune so air moves through, and clean up fallen leaves. In wet-spring areas, a copper spray on the bare tree in late winter protects it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Use drip or a soaker hose at the base instead of sprinklers that throw water over the canopy. Splashing water is how this fungus travels, so keeping the leaves dry is the single biggest change you can make.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The fungus spreads by splash, and overhead irrigation supplies exactly that on a schedule; moving delivery to the root zone removes the driver that turns a wet spring into a defoliating year.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rake up the spotted fallen leaves and get rid of them rather than letting them sit under the tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Clearing and destroying infected leaf litter lowers the local carryover that sits alongside the infected buds and twig lesions.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune the tree so air moves through the canopy and wet leaves dry faster after a spring rain.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Opening the canopy shortens leaf wetness after the cool spring rains that drive infection, and it works with the irrigation change rather than in place of it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut out the infected twigs and buds, taking the cut back into clean wood, and destroy what comes off.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Infected buds and twig lesions are where the fungus overwinters, so removing them into healthy wood strips out the local spore source ahead of the spring rains.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where this disease is established, a fixed copper spray on the bare, dormant tree in late winter is the main protective option. It protects rather than cures, so it has to go on before the spring rains, not after the holes appear. Copper is toxic to fish, builds up in the soil, and can burn leaves at too high a rate, so follow the label and keep repeat use limited.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A dormant fixed copper application on leafless wood is the standing protectant in wet-spring regions, and its whole value sits in the timing. Copper persists at the soil surface, is highly toxic to aquatic life, and the compound named on the label sets the acute hazard band.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Water deep-and-infrequent rather than little-and-often: about once or twice a week while a young tree establishes, easing to roughly weekly (a deep soak) for a bearing tree in summer heat, always adjusted for rain and soil. Apricot resents constantly wet soil, so let the top of the root zone dry between soaks. Through winter dormancy water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Plan on about once or twice a week while a young tree is getting established, easing to about once a week for a fruiting tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. Apricot hates soggy soil, so let the surface dry out between waterings. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs very little and rain usually covers it.
watering.amount_seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root zone, not just the surface. For an establishing tree, on the order of 3 to 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the season, more in heat, delivered as deep soaks to a 3-foot depth. Steady moisture through the final swell sizes the fruit.
watering.amount_beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 3 to 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the season, and more when it is hot, given as deep soaks. Steady water while the fruit is filling out makes bigger apricots.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the root zone by drip or soaker and keep the canopy and fruit dry. Overhead watering that wets the leaves feeds brown rot, shot hole, and bacterial canker, so deliver water to the soil, not the tree. Apply it across the root area out toward the drip line rather than only at the trunk.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, and keep the leaves and fruit dry. Spraying water over the top wets the leaves and helps diseases like brown rot and shot hole, so put the water on the soil, not the tree. Spread it across the root area out to the edge of the branches, not just right at the trunk.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet soil, and a declining tree, since apricot roots suffocate in soggy ground. Chronically wet soil also brings on crown and root rot and predisposes the trunk to bacterial canker, both often fatal. Soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign to act on.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that slowly goes downhill, because the roots cannot breathe. In apricot, soil that stays wet also brings on crown and root rot and the serious disease bacterial canker. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning to back off.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, slowed shoot growth, and early leaf drop in a long dry spell. The most telling symptom is on the fruit: a tree short of water during the final swell sizes its apricots poorly, leaving them small and less sweet even though the tree survives. Catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.
