rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Rio Grande Valley winters bank only about 0 to 300 chill hours, far short of even a low-chill apricot's roughly 350-hour need, per Texas A&M AgriLife Extension. The tree can grow here, but it will not set a dependable crop. Grow fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead for reliable fruit.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Apricots need more winter cold than the Rio Grande Valley usually gives. The tree may grow, but it will not fruit reliably here. Grow fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a practical concern in the Valley; insufficient winter chill, not cold, is the binding constraint here.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Rio Grande Valley winters bank only about 0 to 300 chill hours, far short of even a low-chill apricot's roughly 350-hour need, per Texas A&M AgriLife Extension. rgv.region_notes_beginner: Apricot is a poor choice for the Rio Grande Valley. Winters are too mild to give it the cold it needs, so trees rarely fruit here. Plant fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Apricot does not fruit dependably in the Rio Grande Valley: winter chill (roughly 0 to 300 hours) falls well below even low-chill apricot's roughly 350-hour requirement. Trees may survive but rarely crop; the Valley is far better suited to fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus.
rgv.chill_basis_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley banks only about 0 to 300 winter chill hours in a typical year, and a warm winter can deliver close to zero, per Texas A&M AgriLife Extension (Valley orchard chill runs roughly 200 to 300 hours), corroborated by LSU AgCenter's comparable figure for the similarly subtropical Gulf coast. That is far below what standard temperate stone and pome fruit varieties need to break dormancy and set fruit reliably.
rgv.chill_basis_beginner: Valley winters give very little winter cold, something like 0 to 300 chill hours some years, and a warm winter can give almost none. That is not enough for most standard fruit tree varieties to flower and fruit reliably here.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Chill is amply met in every zone here (this variety range needs 350 to 700 hours; the region banks far more), so the limiting factor is not cold, it is the cool, wet maritime spring. Apricot blooms earliest of any tree fruit grown here, and WSU's western Washington fruit handbook flags it as very sensitive to frost at bloom time; even where frost does not strike, cool, damp bloom-time weather keeps pollinators from working the flowers well and favors brown rot and coryneum blight on stone fruit generally. Reliable fruiting is genuinely site-dependent: the warmest, driest, most sheltered spot available, a late-blooming variety, and attentive dormant-season disease control are what turn a marginal crop into a real one.
8.suitability_note_beginner: This can fruit here, but not every year. The cold is never the problem, our winters are plenty cold for any apricot variety. The real challenge is the cool, wet spring when the tree blooms. Give it your warmest, most sheltered spot and expect some years to be much better than others.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An unusually late frost on the open bloom is a real, occasional risk given how early this tree flowers, but the more persistent problem most springs is simply cool, damp bloom-time weather that limits pollination and favors brown rot, not frost itself.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The immediate coast runs an even cooler, often foggier spring than the interior lowlands, so apricot's bloom-time weather problem is, if anything, a bit worse here even though the winter itself is milder on average. Chill is still amply met. Expect a full crop to be the exception rather than the rule; treat this as a warmest-microsite specialty planting rather than a dependable orchard tree.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Even more of a gamble on the coast, where spring stays cool and damp longer than farther inland. Only plant this if you have an especially warm, sheltered spot and are prepared for some years with little or no fruit.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost timing at bloom is broadly similar to the interior lowlands; the coast's cooler, often foggier spring is the more consistent problem for pollination and fruit set here.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Apricot is a gamble here, not a sure thing. Winters are plenty cold for any variety, so chill is never the issue. The problem is our cool, wet spring, which often keeps bees from working the very early bloom well and lets brown rot get started on the fruit that does set. Plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot you have, choose a late-blooming variety if you can, and expect a real harvest some years and a light one in others.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: West of the Cascades, apricot's limiting factor is never winter chill; ample chill is banked in every zone. The problem is the cool, wet maritime spring: apricot blooms earliest of any tree fruit grown here, and WSU flags it as very sensitive to frost at bloom time, and even where frost does not strike, cool, damp bloom-time weather keeps pollinators inactive and favors brown rot and coryneum blight on the fruit that does set. Reliable fruiting is genuinely site-dependent: the warmest, driest, most sheltered microclimate available, a late-blooming variety, and attentive dormant-season disease control.
pnw.chill_basis_seasoned: Maritime Pacific Northwest winters bank roughly 700 to 1,950 hours of chill depending on zone and site, far above the 350 to 700 hour range this variety list needs. Chill is never the limiting factor here.
pnw.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for any apricot variety. The challenge is not enough cold, it is the wet spring.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Apricot is marginal here, and the limiting factor is not chill (which clears with room to spare, roughly 1100 to 1500 hours a year in zone 7) but fruiting reliability: this tree blooms earlier than any other stone fruit in this guide, often before the region's own last frost date, so a late freeze on open bloom is a frequent event, not an occasional one. Brown rot pressure is also higher in this humid climate than in a drier growing region. Expect the tree to grow well and to fruit in good years, but do not count on a reliable annual crop; site it on a slope or high ground with good cold-air drainage to improve the odds.
7.suitability_note_beginner: This tree is a bit of a gamble here. Winters are cold enough, so chill is not the problem; the issue is its very early bloom, often before your last frost date, which puts a late cold snap right on the flowers most years. It will grow and can fruit in good years, but do not expect a crop every year. Plant it on a slope, not a low spot where cold air pools, to improve your odds.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: This tree tends to bloom before the zone 7 (Piedmont interior)'s own last frost date, so a late freeze on open bloom is the main frost risk to watch, more than winter cold hardiness.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Apricot is marginal here, and the limiting factor is not chill (which clears with room to spare, roughly 1000 to 1350 hours a year in zone 8) but fruiting reliability: this tree blooms earlier than any other stone fruit in this guide, often before the region's own last frost date, so a late freeze on open bloom is a frequent event, not an occasional one. Brown rot pressure is also higher in this humid climate than in a drier growing region. Expect the tree to grow well and to fruit in good years, but do not count on a reliable annual crop; site it on a slope or high ground with good cold-air drainage to improve the odds. Be aware too that NC State's plant database places apricot in the Mountains and Piedmont, zones 5a to 7b, rather than on the Coastal Plain, and its Pender County office reports apricots there are hard to keep alive beyond a few years, so treat a Coastal Plain planting as a trial rather than a dependable fruit tree.

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Apricots grow well here once past their biggest risk: an early bloom that can meet a late frost. Plant a bare-root tree while dormant and choose a sheltered, well-drained site.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: Chill is ample across the belt, so it never limits an apricot crop here. The real risk is the earliest bloom of any tree in this guide landing close to the belt's own last frost date; site trees on high ground with good cold-air drainage and plant while dormant, from early winter into early spring.
mid_atlantic.chill_basis_seasoned: Mid-Atlantic winters bank abundant, reliable chill accumulation: NC State Extension puts the statewide floor at over 1,000 chilling hours a year, and a wider four-source check (NC State, Penn State, Virginia Cooperative Extension, University of Maryland Extension) confirms the belt delivers roughly 1,000 to 1,350 hours on the warmer Coastal Plain (zone 8) and 1,100 to 1,500 hours in the cooler Piedmont interior (zone 7). That clears the chill requirement of every recommended variety in this guide with room to spare. Chill is never the limiting factor here.
mid_atlantic.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for this tree. Nearly every variety gets all the winter chill it needs; chill is not something to worry about in this region.

The cooler Ozark and upland north (zone 7, where the Fayetteville station banks about 1,024 hours) accumulates roughly 1,000 to 1,300 chilling hours a year, and the warmer lowland south (zone 8, with Wynne near 1,069 and Clarksville near 1,081) accumulates roughly 900 to 1,100. Even the belt's southwestern warm edge near Hope, at about 901 hours, clears the chill requirement of the recommended varieties for this crop with room to spare. Chill is not the limiting factor here.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, clearing the entire recommended list here, including the higher chill Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich. Bloom runs into March and April, later than the valley floor, which trims the late frost risk somewhat even though the growing season starts later.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The higher, cooler parts of the region get more winter chill, so every apricot variety here has a good chance, even higher chill kinds like Moorpark and Chinese (Mormon). Bloom comes a little later, which helps dodge frost.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in March and April usually clears the mid March last frost; an unusually late cold snap during bloom is the occasional risk to watch, more so at the higher elevations.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 (the Las Vegas Valley floor) banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, enough to fruit apricot dependably with the right variety: Katy, Blenheim, Tilton, Moorpark, and Harglow all clear the band, while the 700 hour Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich sit at the ceiling and are the first to disappoint in a mild winter. Bloom in late February to March is early enough that a late cold snap is an occasional risk; the dry air otherwise keeps disease low.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Apricots fruit reliably in the Las Vegas Valley if you choose a low or moderate chill variety like Katy, Blenheim, Tilton, Moorpark, or Harglow. Bloom comes early, so watch for a late frost, but the dry air means disease is rarely the problem.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in late February to March occasionally meets a late valley frost; more years than not it clears, and the dry air otherwise keeps disease pressure low.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin and the Colorado River corner (zone 10) bank the least chill, roughly 150 to 450 hours, so only the lowest chill varieties, Katy and Blenheim, fruit dependably; Tilton, Moorpark, Harglow, and the 700 hour Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich need more cold than this warm corner reliably banks. Bloom is very early here, mid February into March; summer heat and sunburn on young bark are the bigger concern than frost.
10.suitability_note_beginner: It is warmest at Laughlin, with the least winter chill, so stick to Katy or Blenheim. Heat and sun, not frost, are the main challenge here.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the limit at Laughlin; low winter chill for the higher chill varieties, and intense summer heat, are the real constraints.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Apricots do well across the Las Vegas Valley region if you match the variety to your zone. Katy and Blenheim are the safest, lowest chill picks and will fruit everywhere in the region, including the warm Laughlin corner. Moorpark, Tilton, and Harglow need more winter cold and are better suited to the valley floor and the cooler zone 8 pockets. Plant a bare root or container tree while it is dormant, from December through February, and watch for a late frost on the early bloom.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: Apricot fruits reliably across the Las Vegas Valley region when the variety is matched to the zone's chill. Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, enough for Katy, Blenheim, Tilton, Moorpark, and Harglow, with the 700 hour Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich right at the edge. The cooler zone 8 pockets clear the whole list with margin, while the warm Laughlin corner (zone 10) reliably suits only the lowest chill picks, Katy and Blenheim. Bloom comes very early (mid February through March depending on zone), which puts the crop at some risk from a late frost; the dry desert air otherwise keeps disease pressure low, so heat and sunburn on young bark, not brown rot, are the summer concern. Plant bare root or container trees during the dormant season.
nevada.chill_basis_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours in zone 9, more in the cooler zone 8 pockets and less at Laughlin in zone 10. That covers a genuine spread of apricot chill needs: Katy (about 350 hours), Blenheim (450), Tilton and Harglow (600 to 650), and Moorpark (650) all fit zone 9 with room to spare, while Chinese (Mormon) and Goldrich sit right at the 700 hour ceiling, workable most years but the first to miss in a warm winter. Zone 8's wider band clears the whole list comfortably. At Laughlin (zone 10), only the lowest chill picks, Katy and Blenheim, are a safe bet; the 600 hour and up varieties need more cold than that warm corner reliably delivers.
nevada.chill_basis_beginner: Desert winters here give apricots a real range of chill, more in the cooler zone 8 areas, less at warm Laughlin. Low chill varieties like Katy and Blenheim are the safest choice everywhere; the higher chill kinds such as Moorpark, Tilton, and Harglow do well in zone 9 and zone 8 but are a gamble at Laughlin.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Apricot thrives at the low St. George elevations, where Washington County Extension lists it among the dependable fruits. The dry air keeps brown rot low; a late frost on the early bloom and summer sunburn are the real hazards. Favor lower-chill, desert-adapted varieties.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Apricots grow well here. Choose a lower-chill variety, watch for a late frost on the early bloom, and shade young bark from the summer sun.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Apricot blooms early, in late March, so it can open around or just before the late-March last frost; an unusually late cold snap during bloom is the main spring risk, and summer sunburn is the larger season-long hazard.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Apricots do well in St. George. They need only modest winter chill, which the valley provides, so choose a lower-chill, desert-adapted variety. The main things to watch are a late frost on the early spring bloom and sunburn on young bark in the intense summer heat.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: Apricot is a dependable St. George crop; Washington County Extension lists it among the fruits that thrive at the low elevations around town. The dry desert air keeps brown rot, which limits apricot in humid regions, well in check, so the practical hazards here are a late frost catching the early bloom and summer sun on young bark. Bloom comes early, in late March, so an unusually late cold snap is the spring risk to watch. Choose lower-chill, desert-adapted varieties and plant a bare-root or container tree during the dormant season.
utah_dixie.chill_basis_seasoned: Apricot is well matched to the limited winter chill of the St. George Dixie core: most recommended apricots need only a few hundred chill hours, comfortably within what the low valley banks, and Washington County Extension lists apricot among the fruits that do well at these low elevations. Favor the lower-chill, desert-adapted selections; the highest-chill apricots are a poorer fit for the warm valley floor. The binding risks here are not chill or disease but a late frost on the early bloom and summer sunburn, the arid-climate pattern rather than the brown rot that limits apricot in humid regions.
utah_dixie.chill_basis_beginner: Apricots do well in St. George; they need only modest winter chill, which the valley provides. Pick a lower-chill, desert-adapted variety. The main things to watch are a late frost on the early spring bloom and sunburn on young bark in the intense summer heat.

crops.description_seasoned: Apricot is a deciduous stone-fruit tree (Prunus armeniaca) prized for fruit that ripens best tree-ripened at home, where it can hang to full flavor rather than being picked firm for shipping. It is self-fruitful, so a single tree bears, and it ripens earlier than peach. Its defining trait, and its defining challenge, is that it blooms earlier than almost any other fruit tree: the open flowers meet late frosts most springs on a frost-prone site, so variety choice and a frost-aware location matter more than anything. It also asks for real work: an annual dormant pruning to an open center, disease management (brown rot above all, plus bacterial canker and shot hole), early fruit thinning, and enough winter chill to break dormancy. Given a dry-summer or frost-safe site and that care, a backyard apricot rewards you with fruit grocery shelves cannot match.
crops.description_beginner: An apricot is a fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives you fruit you can let ripen right on the branch, which is where apricots taste their best, and they ripen earlier than peaches. One tree fruits on its own, so you do not need a second one. The big thing to know is that apricots bloom earlier than almost any other fruit tree, so a late frost can kill the flowers most years unless you plant in a spot that does not get frosty and choose a late-blooming variety. Apricots also take steady work: prune the tree every winter into an open vase shape, manage diseases (brown rot most of all), thin off the extra little fruit so the rest grow big, and give the tree a cold-enough winter. With a dry-summer or frost-safe spot and that care, a backyard apricot gives you fruit far better than the store.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: An apricot is ready when the ground color shifts fully from green to a warm yellow or deep orange, the flesh gives slightly to gentle pressure, the aroma turns full and sweet, and the fruit separates from the spur with a light twist. Any pink blush is not ripeness by itself. Pick slightly firm if you need to handle, ship, or dry the fruit, and let it finish softening on the counter; pick at full give for eating that day. A tree ripens over one to three weeks, so pick in several passes.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: An apricot is ripe when the whole fruit turns from green to a warm yellow or orange, gives a little when you press gently, smells sweet, and comes off the branch with a gentle twist instead of a hard pull. A pink blush alone does not mean ripe. If you need to carry, store, or dry them, pick when fully colored but still a little firm and let them soften on the counter. For eating right away, pick when they give to a gentle squeeze. The tree ripens over one to three weeks, so pick it a few times.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Apricots bloom very early, typically late winter to early spring, from January in the low desert and mild coastal California to March or April in the North, usually before the leaves. Apricot opens its flowers earlier than peach, plum, or apple, and that early bloom is its chief vulnerability: the white-to-pink blossoms are killed by the hard late frosts that are still common when they open. Choosing a late-blooming cultivar and a frost-safe site is the main way to protect the crop.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Apricot trees flower very early, usually late winter to early spring, sometimes as early as January in warm areas and as late as March or April in cold ones, often before the leaves come out. Apricots bloom earlier than peaches, plums, or apples, and that is their weak point: a hard late frost can kill the open flowers and the tiny fruit behind them. Choosing a variety that blooms later and a spot that does not get frosty is the best way to protect the crop.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Apricot trees are commonly grown in USDA zones 5 to 8, and the wood of hardy cultivars survives into zone 4, but surviving is not the same as fruiting. The limiting factor is almost never midwinter cold hardiness; it is the very early bloom meeting late spring frost. Because apricot flowers so early, even zones warm enough to grow it easily lose the crop in many springs, and hardy northern trees may bloom and be frozen out year after year. The most dependable apricot regions are dry-summer areas with cold-enough winters to hold bloom back and dependable, frost-free springs (interior California and the Intermountain West are classic). The warm edge (zones 9 and warmer) is limited by too little winter chill and, in the humid Southeast, by heavy disease. Match a late-blooming, cold-hardy cultivar to a frost-safe site and you give yourself the best odds.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Apricot trees are usually grown in zones 5 to 8, and tough varieties survive into zone 4, but living and fruiting are two different things. The problem is almost never that the tree freezes in winter; it is that apricot blooms so early that late spring frosts kill the flowers, even in places plenty warm enough to grow the tree. The most reliable apricot areas have dry summers, winters cold enough to hold bloom back a little, and springs without late frosts, like interior California and the Intermountain West. Warmer zones (9 and up) usually have too little winter cold, and the humid Southeast has too much disease. Pick a late-blooming, cold-hardy variety and a spot that does not get frosty for the best chance at a crop.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Apricots need a stretch of winter cold, counted as chill hours (hours between 32°F and 45°F), to break dormancy and bloom evenly. Most cultivars want about 600 to 900 hours, with a few low-chill types (Katy) bearing on roughly 350. Apricot's chill requirement is on the low side for a stone fruit, which is exactly why it satisfies its chill and blooms so early, and why late frost, not chill, is usually the crop-limiting factor. In mild-winter regions choose a low-chill cultivar so bloom is at least even; in cold regions a higher-chill, late-blooming cultivar both fits the chill and delays bloom past the worst frosts.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Apricot trees need enough cold winter hours, called chill hours, before they will bloom properly in spring. Most kinds want about 600 to 900 hours, and a few low-chill types like Katy need only about 350. Apricot needs less winter cold than most fruit trees, which is part of why it blooms so early. In mild-winter areas, choose a low-chill variety so it blooms evenly; in cold areas, a higher-chill, late-blooming variety both fits your winters and helps the tree bloom later, after the worst frosts have passed.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Most apricots are self-fruitful, so a single tree sets a full crop on its own without a pollinizer; this is the inverse of many sweet cherries and apples, which require cross-pollination. A few cultivars, chiefly Moorpark, set a heavier crop with a compatible second variety blooming at the same time, but even they fruit alone, so a pollinizer is an optional bonus rather than a requirement. Apricots are insect-pollinated, mainly by bees, so supporting pollinator activity during the short, very early bloom helps set even on a lone tree, especially in cool springs.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Most apricots are self-fruitful, which means one tree makes fruit by itself with no second tree needed. This is different from many cherries and apples, which do need a partner. A few kinds, mainly Moorpark, make a fuller crop when a second apricot blooms nearby, but even they fruit on their own, so a partner is a bonus and not a must. Bees do the pollinating, so anything that helps bees be active during the short, early bloom helps the tree set fruit, even a single tree.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment over fruit. Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter (December to February in mild regions), on a frost-safe, well-drained site, head it back at planting to begin the open-center scaffold, keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk, and water consistently through the first two seasons. Remove any fruit that sets. Hold fertilizer until growth begins, and never feed late in the season.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about helping the tree settle in, not getting fruit. Plant a bare-root tree in late winter while it is still dormant (December to February in mild areas), on a well-drained spot that is not frosty, cut it back at planting to start the open vase shape, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk, and water it steadily through the first couple of seasons. Pull off any fruit that forms. Wait to fertilize until the tree starts growing, and never feed late in the year.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Self-fruitful: a single tree fruits without a pollinizer. A few cultivars (notably Moorpark) set a heavier crop with a compatible second variety blooming concurrently, but none require one. Bees are the primary pollinators; support bloom-time activity for reliable set in cool springs.
pollination.notes_beginner: Self-fruitful means one tree fruits on its own, no second tree required. A few kinds, like Moorpark, make a fuller crop with another apricot blooming nearby, but even they fruit alone. Bees do the work, so good bee activity during bloom helps the tree set a full crop.

crops.establishment_note: Most apricots begin bearing about 2 to 4 years after planting.
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Pick a rootstock for your soil and pests, not for tree size; standard apricot rootstocks do not dwarf the tree. Myrobalan tolerates a range of soils but is canker-prone, so on well-drained ground apricot seedling or a peach seedling (more canker-tolerant) can be better.

rootstock_options.name: Apricot seedling
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for your variety on apricot seedling for deep, well-drained soils.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Standard-size apricot seedling stock. Well matched to deep, well-drained soils and generally graft-compatible with apricot cultivars, but intolerant of wet or heavy ground and only moderately canker-tolerant. A solid default on good soil.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A full-size rootstock grown from apricot seed. It suits deep, well-drained soil and goes well with apricot varieties, but it does not like wet or heavy ground. A good standard choice where your soil drains well.

rootstock_options.name: Myrobalan (plum)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Myrobalan where the soil is heavier or holds moisture.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Vigorous plum rootstock (Prunus cerasifera) that tolerates heavier, wetter soils better than apricot or peach seedling and resists some replant problems. Its weakness is high susceptibility to bacterial canker, so on cold, wet-spring sites it is a liability; some apricot cultivars show partial incompatibility.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A vigorous plum rootstock that handles heavier, wetter soil better than apricot or peach stock. Its downside is that it catches bacterial canker easily, so it is a risk in cold, wet-spring areas, and it does not pair perfectly with every apricot variety.

rootstock_options.name: Marianna 2624 (plum)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Marianna 2624 for wet or nematode-prone ground, but not where bacterial canker is severe.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Plum-hybrid rootstock tolerant of heavy, wet soils with resistance to root-knot nematode and oak root fungus. Like Myrobalan it is more susceptible to bacterial canker than the seedling stocks, and some apricot cultivars are incompatible on it, so match the variety carefully.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A plum-type rootstock that takes wet, heavy soil and resists some soil pests and diseases. Like Myrobalan, it catches bacterial canker more easily than seedling rootstocks, and it does not work with every apricot variety, so check compatibility first.

rootstock_options.name: Lovell (peach seedling)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for your variety on Lovell peach seedling where bacterial canker is a concern.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Standard peach seedling rootstock. More tolerant of bacterial canker than the plum stocks or Nemaguard, and vigorous on well-drained ground, so it is a good choice where canker pressure is high. It is less suited to heavy or wet soils and offers little nematode resistance.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A full-size peach-seedling rootstock. It resists bacterial canker better than plum rootstocks, so it is a good pick where that disease is a problem, and it is vigorous on well-drained soil. It is not the one for heavy, wet ground or where soil nematodes are the main worry.

pet_safe.note: The flesh is fine, but the pits, seeds, and leaves contain cyanide compounds and are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: Your tree may set its first apricots now. Thin them to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches about a month after bloom, closer spacing than a peach gets because apricots are smaller. Thinning does three things at once here: it sizes the fruit, it keeps a young limb from breaking, and it heads off apricot's habit of cropping heavily one year and hardly at all the next. Prune more gently than you would a peach. Apricot fruits on spurs, the short stubby side shoots that keep bearing for several years, so cutting away too much of that wood costs you crops rather than renewing them.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: Expect a light first set. Thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches within about a month of bloom, tighter than stone fruit of similar habit because apricot fruit is smaller, and treat the pass as three jobs at once: sizing, limb protection on young scaffold wood, and damping the alternate-bearing swing apricot is unusually prone to. Prune conservatively from here. Apricot carries a mixed bearing habit, long-lived spurs plus one-year wood, so it needs renewal pruning far lighter than peach and over-thinning the spur wood removes bearing surface rather than refreshing it. In canker-prone wet-spring regions, move major cuts to dry summer weather, since bacterial canker enters cool, wet-season wounds.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From about the fourth year you get a full crop. Each spring, thin the young fruit to one every 4 to 6 inches; that pass never becomes optional. Apricot is an early tree in every sense: it blooms before anything else, which makes a late frost the single biggest threat to a year's fruit, and it ripens over one to three weeks so you pick in several passes. Ripe fruit is fully orange-yellow, gives a little, and twists off easily; pick slightly firm if you plan to dry it. Handle the fruit gently, since bruises let in brown rot and tree-ripe apricots are fragile. When you are done, clear every remaining and dropped fruit, because fruit left to shrivel on the tree or ground is what starts brown rot again next spring. Apricots dry and freeze exceptionally well, which is the usual answer to a tree that ripens all at once.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from roughly year four. The annual cycle is light pruning that preserves spur wood, thinning to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches, and thorough post-harvest sanitation. Apricot reaches open bloom earlier than any other stone fruit, so frost, not pests, is the usual reason for a lost year, and a small tree is worth covering overnight against a hard late frost. Harvest over one to three weeks in several passes on full orange-yellow ground color, slight give, and clean release; pick firmer for drying or any handling. Clear all mummies and drops: they are the primary brown-rot inoculum. The concentrated ripening window makes drying and freezing the practical outlet, and apricot holds up to both unusually well.

crops.name: Pear (European)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Pear trees grow best in deep, fertile soil that drains well but holds some moisture, a loam or clay-loam is ideal. Pears actually tolerate heavier, wetter ground better than most fruit trees, including some clay, but they still will not stand in water, so avoid a spot where puddles linger. If your soil is very sandy and dries out fast, work in compost and plan to water more, since a thirsty pear drops fruit.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Pear wants a deep, fertile loam to clay-loam with steady moisture and moderate organic matter. It is more forgiving of heavy, moisture-retentive soils than apple or stone fruit, and tolerates a wider pH band, but it still will not accept standing water, which drives crown and root rots. On a wet site, plant on a low berm. One important trade-off: rich soil and heavy nitrogen push the soft, succulent growth that fire blight colonizes, so feed pears lean and favor a fire-blight-tolerant rootstock (the OHxF series) on any site with disease history.

ph.note_beginner: Pear trees like soil that runs from slightly acidic to neutral, a pH around 6.0 to 7.0 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline soil is, where 7.0 is neutral). Pears are a bit more tolerant of alkaline soil than apples. Test your soil before planting, since it is much easier to adjust the pH now than after the tree is in the ground. Garden lime raises a low pH; garden sulfur lowers a high one. Your local extension office can test a sample for you.
ph.note_seasoned: Pear does best at a pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 and tolerates roughly 5.5 to 7.5, a slightly wider and more alkaline-tolerant band than apple. Test the soil before planting and adjust the whole root zone, not just the hole, because correcting pH around an established tree is slow. Lime raises a low pH; elemental sulfur lowers a high one. Well outside this band, iron and manganese availability falls and new growth yellows between the veins.

fertilizer.timing: early spring before bud break
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed lightly in early spring before bud break, guided by shoot growth: a healthy young pear makes about 12 to 18 inches of new shoot growth a year, so feed to reach that and no more. Excess nitrogen is the classic pear mistake, it drives soft, succulent growth that fire blight runs straight through, and it delays fruiting. Mature trees on fertile soil often need no nitrogen at all. If anything, err on the side of underfeeding a pear.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed pear trees once a year, in early spring before the buds open, with a balanced fertilizer, and go light. Too much feeding is the number-one pear mistake: it makes lots of soft new growth that the disease fire blight loves, and it pushes the tree to grow leaves instead of fruit. If the tree is growing well and putting out healthy new branches each year, it may need no feeding at all. When in doubt, use less.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced N-P-K ratio (the three numbers on the bag, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) such as 10-10-10 at a modest rate, leaning toward the low end on any vigorous tree to limit fire-blight-prone growth. On fertile ground a pear often wants none.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. A balanced one like 10-10-10 is fine for pears, used sparingly. The first number (nitrogen) is the one to keep low, because too much makes soft growth that catches fire blight.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rule is about 1/8 lb of actual nitrogen per year of tree age, capped near 1/2 to 3/4 lb actual N for a mature tree, noticeably leaner than the apple rule because of fire blight. Always follow the label and skip nitrogen entirely in a year of strong shoot growth.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple guideline is a small amount that grows a little with the tree's age, following the directions on the bag, and using even less than you would for an apple. When in doubt, feed less, an underfed pear is far healthier than an overfed one.

companions.note_beginner: Pears do not pair with other plants the way vegetables do. For a pear, the neighbor that counts is a second, different pear variety that blooms at the same time, within about 50 to 100 ft, because most pears need another pear nearby to make fruit. Right around the trunk, do the opposite of planting companions: keep grass and other plants away from the base out to the edge of the branches, because they steal water and food from the young tree. Use mulch there instead, and never plant a pear near a black walnut tree, which poisons the soil for it.
companions.note_seasoned: Pear does not companion-plant in the vegetable sense; the interactions that matter are pollination and root competition. The single most important neighbor is a second, bloom-overlapping pear variety (the pollinizer) within about 50 to 100 ft, since most pears are self-unfruitful. At the trunk, the rule reverses: keep turf and aggressive perennials out of the root zone, where grass competes hard with a young tree for water and nitrogen. Maintain a mulched, vegetation-free circle to the dripline, and avoid siting near black walnut, whose juglone is toxic to pear.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: spring bulbs (daffodil)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A ring of daffodils at the drip line is a traditional fruit-tree-guild move with two intended jobs: the early foliage forms a band that helps hold back creeping grass, the tree's main competitor, and daffodils are toxic enough that voles and deer tend to avoid grazing through them to the trunk. They emerge and feed before the canopy leafs out, then go dormant, so they do not compete in summer. Treat this as a useful cultural barrier rather than a measured yield booster.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The daffodil-ring (grass suppression + rodent/deer deterrence via toxicity) is a well-established permaculture fruit-tree-guild practice grounded in daffodils' real toxicity and spring-ephemeral timing, applied to pear the same way it is to apple; not a measured pear yield/health effect. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Plant a ring of daffodils around your pear tree, out where the branches reach. They come up early in spring, help keep grass from creeping toward the trunk, and because they are poisonous to nibble, they discourage mice and deer. They die back in summer, so they stay out of the tree's way.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: comfrey
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Comfrey is a workhorse of the fruit-tree guild. Its deep taproot pulls from well below the tree's surface feeder roots, so it does not compete for the same water and nutrients, and it shades out grass along the row. Chopped two or three times a season and dropped under the tree, its lush leaves break down into a mineral-rich mulch, and the flowers feed pollinators. The dynamic-accumulator framing is more tradition than proven chemistry, but the practical value as non-competing mulch and grass suppression is real.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Comfrey as chop-and-drop mulch / grass suppressor with a deep non-competing taproot is widely practiced and partly grounded (deep taproot, vigorous biomass); the 'dynamic accumulator' mineral claims are permaculture tradition, not peer-reviewed. Same mechanism whether under apple or pear. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Comfrey is a leafy plant that grows well around fruit trees. Its roots reach deep down, so it does not steal water from the tree, and it crowds out grass. A few times each summer you can cut the big leaves and lay them on the soil under the tree, where they rot down into natural food for it. Its flowers also bring in helpful bees.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: clover (living mulch)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dutch white clover makes a strong living mulch under pears. As a legume it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through its root symbiosis, feeding the tree slowly while staying low and tolerating harvest foot traffic. It covers the ground to suppress weeds and hold moisture without the aggressive grass competition bare turf brings. Keep it back from the immediate trunk zone, and note it does draw some moisture, so manage it on dry sites. Because pears want lean nitrogen, treat the clover's slow trickle as a feature, not a reason to also fertilize.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Dutch white clover living mulch = legume N-fixation + weed suppression + walkable cover; mechanistically sound and supported by extension/NRCS orchard legume cover-crop work. mechanistic/medium: real mechanism, held at medium because clover-to-tree N transfer magnitude and net water effect vary by site.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: White clover is a low, soft plant you can grow as a living carpet under your pear tree. It pulls nitrogen from the air and feeds it slowly into the soil, while covering the ground to keep weeds down and hold in moisture. It is tough enough to walk on at picking time. Just keep it from growing right against the trunk.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: black walnut
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Black walnut is a definitive bad neighbor for pear. Its roots, hulls, and leaf litter release juglone, an allelopathic compound toxic to many sensitive plants, and pear (like apple) is among those affected, showing decline and dieback within the walnut's root zone. The effect extends well beyond the visible canopy, roughly to the full root spread (commonly cited at fifty-plus feet from a mature tree), so siting matters more than spacing tweaks: keep pears entirely out of a black walnut's root zone.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Juglone allelopathy is a real, well-characterized chemical mechanism; pome fruit including pear is documented as juglone-sensitive across extension sources. mechanistic/high: the mechanism and pome-fruit sensitivity are well established and uncontested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep pear trees far away from black walnut trees. Black walnuts release a natural chemical called juglone from their roots and leaves that is poisonous to pears and can make them sicken and die. The chemical spreads through the soil well past the walnut's branches, so give them a very wide berth, at least 50 feet from a big walnut.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: turfgrass to the trunk
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Letting turfgrass grow right up to a pear trunk is a quiet but real drag on the tree, especially when young. Grass competes directly for water and nitrogen in the surface zone where the feeder roots sit, slowing growth and delaying bearing, and dense grass and mulch against the trunk harbor voles that girdle bark over winter. Maintain a vegetation-free or mulched strip about two feet out from the trunk (mulch pulled back a few inches off the bark itself).

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Extension guidance consistently prescribes a vegetation-free/mulched zone around young fruit trees and warns of rodent bark damage from grass/mulch at the trunk; the grass-competition effect on young tree growth is well documented for pome fruit. extension_backed/high.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Do not let lawn grass grow right up against your pear tree's trunk. The grass competes with the young tree for water and food, so it grows slower and fruits later. Grass at the trunk also hides mice that can chew the bark in winter. Keep a clear or mulched circle about two feet around the trunk, with the mulch pulled back slightly so it does not touch the bark.

pests.name: Codling moth
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae tunnel to the fruit core, leaving a frass-filled entry hole and brown trails through the flesh; wormy pears are inedible, and fruit that drops can be carrying a larva.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This is the classic 'worm in the fruit.' You find a small hole with brown crumbly stuff (frass) around it, and a tunnel into the core when you cut it open. Pears lying on the ground can still have the caterpillar inside.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cydia pomonella; female moths lay eggs on developing fruit and young leaves near bloom, and hatching larvae bore into the pear. Two or more generations per season in most regions. The same pest attacks apple.
pests.cause_beginner: A small moth lays eggs on the tiny pears in spring; the eggs hatch into caterpillars that crawl into the fruit. There can be two batches a summer, so the problem repeats.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Monitor with pheromone traps to time control; remove and destroy dropped and infested fruit; bag individual fruit; spinosad, or the codling moth granulosis virus sold to home gardeners, timed to egg hatch (the first stings on the fruit, or the heat-unit count UC IPM gives after the first sustained trap catch) and repeated. Mating disruption works only at orchard scale and can increase damage on a single tree.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick up and throw away every pear that drops, do not leave them under the tree. You can slip paper bags over young pears to keep moths out, and scent traps help you know when to act. Sprays like spinosad work if timed right.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Orchard sanitation (clear dropped and infested fruit through the season, most critically in May and June) and keep nearby abandoned pear, apple, or walnut trees pruned or removed. Trunk banding is no longer recommended for home pears: the scaly bark gives larvae so many crevices that most pupate before they reach the band.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen pears all season, and check the fruit on the tree every week or two from early summer. Skip the cardboard trunk bands you may read about; a pear's rough bark gives the caterpillars so many hiding spots that few ever reach the band. Nearby neglected pear, apple, or walnut trees make it worse.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start checking the little pears about six to eight weeks after bloom, and keep checking every week or two. Pull off any fruit with a hole and brown crumbs at it, and pick up every pear that drops as soon as you see it, because the caterpillar inside can crawl out and start the next round. May and June matter most, but keep it up all season. If a neighbor has an untended pear, apple, or walnut tree, the moths will keep coming from there, so it is worth getting them on board.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM puts sanitation first in any codling moth program, and first by a wider margin where you mean to stay spray-free. The larva leaves the fruit to pupate, so an infested pear taken off the tree or the ground before that happens is a moth that never flies; the critical window is May and June, but drops keep carrying larvae through the season. Unmanaged host trees nearby, apple, pear, or walnut, are a continual source, which is why the same page calls codling moth a neighborhood project.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pears that ripen early are picked before the later broods of moths get going, so if you are still choosing a tree, an early-ripening variety takes a real share of the pressure off. It shifts the problem rather than removing it, so you still clean up the drops.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Two to four generations a year, depending on climate, means the fruit that hangs longest sits through the most egg-laying, and NC State singles out late-ripening fruit as the most damaged. UC IPM lists early-maturing pears among the choices that can greatly reduce the potential for damage. It is a planting-time decision that pairs with sanitation rather than replacing it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hang a scent trap in the tree in early spring. It catches male moths on a sticky card, and what it tells you is when the moths have started flying, which is your cue to start watching the fruit and, if you spray, when to time it. A trap by itself will not keep the worms out of a pear tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The trap marks the first sustained flight; egg hatch follows after a run of warm days that UC IPM's home guide gives as a heat-unit count, or, skipping the arithmetic, when the first stings show on the fruit three to four weeks after bloom. UC IPM is explicit that trapping an isolated tree might reduce the population slightly but is not a reliable way to reduce damage, and NC State says the same of sticky traps: a clock, not a control.

control_ladder.note_beginner: About four to six weeks after bloom, when the baby pears are half an inch to an inch across, thin each cluster to one fruit and slip a paper lunch bag over it, stapled shut around the stem. Nothing can lay an egg on a pear inside a bag. It is slow work, so it suits a small tree, or the best few dozen pears on a big one.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM rates this the one nonchemical method effective enough to stand alone, even under heavy pressure. Cut a 2-inch slit in the bottom fold of a No. 2 bag, pass the thinned fruit through so the fold seals around the stem, and staple the mouth shut. NC State's caveat is labor: practical only on small trees. The ground beneath still needs keeping clean, since bagging protects the bagged fruit and nothing else.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If bagging is not practical, spinosad is the organic spray with a real record on codling moth, but only if it is on the fruit while the eggs are hatching, which is when you see the first tiny holes with brown crumbs, about three to four weeks after bloom. Spray then, and twice more ten days apart. Keep it off the tree while it is flowering, because it is hard on bees while wet.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Time the first application to egg hatch, then repeat at 10-day intervals for three sprays on the spring generation and two on each summer generation, no more than six a season and none within seven days of harvest. Adding 1% horticultural oil to the tank improves its performance. Bt and pyrethrum were tested against codling moth and not found effective, and oil alone is variable; the codling moth granulosis virus sold to home gardeners is the one other material UC IPM found as effective as carbaryl on backyard trees.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For a heavy infestation that bagging and spinosad have not held, Utah State lists zeta-cypermethrin and gamma-cyhalothrin among the conventional sprays for a backyard pear, timed the same way, to egg hatch. Know the cost first: these sprays kill the lacewings and pirate bugs that keep pear psylla down, and a psylla outbreak can follow a season of them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: WSU's rule for pear is that codling moth sprays have to be compatible with pear psylla biological control, and a broad-spectrum pyrethroid is not. Carbaryl, the older standard UC IPM measured the virus against, disrupts natural enemies the same way and is now restricted-use in California; none of these materials belongs on the tree during bloom. The trade is one pest for another, which is what makes bagging the better answer on a pear that also carries psylla.

pests.name: Pear psylla
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Nymphs feed on the new growth and exude copious sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold; heavy feeding causes leaf scorch, premature drop, fruit russeting, and tree decline. The signature pear pest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves and young pears get coated in a sticky, shiny film that turns black and grimy (sooty mold), and the leaves may scorch and drop. Tiny insects feed on the new shoots.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cacopsylla pyricola; a small psyllid specific to pear that overwinters as an adult and builds several overlapping generations through the season. Outbreaks follow broad-spectrum sprays that kill its natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny pear-specific insect (a kind of jumping plant louse) that sucks sap and oozes sticky stuff. It can build up fast, especially if bug sprays have wiped out the good bugs that normally keep it down.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dormant-season horticultural oil, applied before the overwintered adults begin laying, kills the adults it wets and discourages egg laying for about a month but does not control eggs; in-season insecticidal soap or 1% summer oil; conserve natural enemies (minute pirate bugs, lacewings) by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides; kaolin clay applied prebloom deters colonization and egg-laying.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil while the tree is bare, before the buds swell, to kill the overwintered adults and put them off laying eggs; it will not kill eggs already laid, so timing is everything. In the growing season use insecticidal soap or a light oil spray. Avoid harsh sprays, which kill the helpful bugs that eat psylla.
pests.prevention_seasoned: A well-timed dormant oil program plus a natural-enemy-friendly spray regime is the backbone of psylla management; avoid the lush nitrogen-pushed growth psylla favors.
pests.prevention_beginner: A well-timed dormant oil spray while the tree is bare, before the buds swell, and going easy on harsh sprays and fertilizer, keep this pear-specific pest in check.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Psylla build up fastest on a tree pushing lots of soft new growth, so feed a pear only enough to set and size its fruit, not to make it grow. In late spring, pull off (do not cut) the whippy water sprouts shooting straight up from the main limbs; that is the tender foliage the insects feed on, and pulling them before the end of June keeps them from growing back.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: WSU's guidance is to apply only enough nitrogen for adequate fruit set and fruit size, because populations climb on highly vigorous trees, and to remove water sprouts through the center of the tree by hand rather than with loppers, before they form a woody attachment, normally by the end of June. That strips the succulent tissue nymphs feed on and opens the canopy so any spray you do use reaches them. Adequate, not starved: the aim is a tree that sets and sizes a crop without a flush of extra shoots.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A kaolin clay spray put on before the tree blooms coats the buds and twigs in a chalky white film that the overwintered adults dislike landing and laying eggs on. It is an organic option, and it belongs in that early window only: clay applied later in the season can set off mite outbreaks on pear.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM lists kaolin among the organically acceptable materials for psylla with one instruction, apply prebloom, and one caution, that later-season use may cause mite outbreaks. The film works on the overwintered adults as they arrive in early spring to lay eggs on buds and twigs, so its value is in lowering the first generation; it is a deterrent rather than a contact material, a season-opening measure rather than a rescue.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lacewings and minute pirate bugs eat pear psylla for free, and the surest way to get a psylla plague is to kill them with a harsh all-purpose bug spray, often one aimed at codling moth. Choose the gentlest thing that works for every other pest on the tree, and the good bugs will do a big share of this job.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM names green and brown lacewings and minute pirate bugs among the many resident predators and parasites, and states plainly that nonselective codling moth insecticides destroy them and produce psylla outbreaks; WSU's line is that pesticides applied to pears greatly reduce the effectiveness of natural enemies. Psylla also develops resistance to insecticides quickly, so the natural enemies are the durable part of the program, and the spray choices made for other pests on the tree decide whether they survive.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The one spray that matters most goes on while the tree is bare: a dormant horticultural oil before the buds swell, with a second coat as the buds turn green if psylla were bad last year. The oil kills the overwintered adults it wets and puts them off laying eggs for a while; it does not kill eggs already laid, so the point is to get it on before they start. In summer, a light 1% oil spray knocks back a heavy population.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's mechanism statement is exact: oil kills adult psylla but does not control eggs, and it discourages egg laying for about a month, so the season hinges on reducing the overwintering adults before laying begins; adults that lay before the dormant spray leave a higher base population all season. NC State prescribes both a dormant and a delayed-dormant application at green bud; Utah State keys it to before leaves emerge. Do not mix oil with sulfur or put them on close together, and keep oil off the tree in hot weather, since UC IPM notes both are phytotoxic to pear in heat.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When you see honeydew droplets and sticky leaves in summer, insecticidal soap sprayed right onto the young psylla on the new growth kills the ones it wets and spares most of the good bugs. It has no lasting effect, so repeat it as new ones appear, and aim at the shoot tips and leaf undersides where they feed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Both UC IPM's organic list and Utah State's backyard guidance carry insecticidal soap for in-season psylla, alongside 1% summer oil. It is a contact material with no residual, which is exactly why it fits: it knocks a flare back without the natural-enemy cost of a broad insecticide. Coverage decides it, since the nymphs feed on the youngest tissue under a wash of honeydew, and spraying a water-stressed tree or above 90°F will scorch pear foliage.

diseases.name: Fire blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blossoms and shoot tips suddenly wilt, blacken, and die, bending into a characteristic 'shepherd's crook'; affected branches look scorched, and sunken, oozing cankers form on wood. Pear is markedly more susceptible than apple, and a warm, wet spring can kill whole limbs or a young tree.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Branch tips and flower clusters suddenly turn black and look burned, as if scorched by fire, and the tip bends over into a hook shape. It can kill whole branches or the whole tree. Pears catch it worse than apples.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia amylovora; bacteria infect through open blossoms and tender shoot tips in warm, wet spring weather and spread fastest on lush, nitrogen-pushed growth. It is the single biggest reason European pears fail in the humid South and East.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria that infect through the flowers and soft new shoots in warm, wet spring weather. Fast, soft growth from too much fertilizer makes it much worse. It is the main reason pears struggle in warm, damp climates.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out infected wood a minimum of 8 to 12 inches below any sign of infection, disinfecting tools between cuts and working in dry weather; do the main cleanup in the dormant season, but on pear cut out a fast-moving spring strike as soon as it appears. There is no cure once established; management is prevention plus cutting it out.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off the blackened branches well below the damage, at least 8 to 12 inches into clean wood (a foot to be safe), wiping your pruners with disinfectant between every cut so you do not spread it, and only in dry weather. There is no spray that cures it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The decisive move is variety and rootstock choice: plant fire-blight-resistant cultivars (Kieffer, Orient, Moonglow, Ayers, Warren, Magness) on a tolerant rootstock (the OHxF series). Then avoid excess nitrogen, remove suckers from the base, prune only in dry weather, and do the main cleanup in the dormant season.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best defense is to choose a resistant variety (Kieffer, Orient, Moonglow, Ayers, Warren) on a resistant rootstock, especially where summers are warm and humid. Then go easy on fertilizer (soft growth catches it) and prune only in dry weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: With pears, fire blight is decided mostly at the nursery. Bartlett, the pear everyone knows, is one of the worst for it, and in the humid East and South the disease is the main reason pears fail. Clemson lists Ayers, Kieffer, LeConte, Moonglow, Magness, and Orient as moderately resistant, and Seckel as somewhat resistant, and Arkansas extension recommends Harrow Delight, Maxine, Kieffer, Magness, and Moonglow. Ask for one of those, on an OHxF rootstock, which is bred for blight tolerance; a susceptible rootstock is how the disease takes the whole tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Ratings disagree at the margins: Kieffer is rated highly resistant by Arkansas, moderately by Clemson, and 'subject to blight in wet years' by Georgia, so read resistant as reduced risk rather than immunity. Warren and Orient carry Georgia's 'resistant to blight'; Seckel is only somewhat resistant; UC IPM puts most pear varieties, red pears included, in the very susceptible class, and NC State calls Bartlett highly susceptible. The rootstock half is the OHxF series (Old Home x Farmingdale), which WSU describes as tolerant of blight and decline; Clemson ties tree death to susceptible rootstocks.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When a shoot tip blackens and hooks over, cut it out at least 8 to 12 inches below the last sign of damage, into wood that looks completely clean; a foot is a safe rule. Wipe the pruners with a bleach solution (1 part bleach to 9 parts water) or rubbing alcohol between cuts, work in dry weather, and burn or bury what you cut. Do the big cleanup, cankers included, in winter while the tree is dormant, but a pear strike racing down a branch in spring gets cut the day you see it. Go easy on fertilizer and pull the suckers at the base, because soft fast growth is what the disease runs through.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Clemson's minimum is 8 to 12 inches below any sign of infected tissue, with pruning done in the dormant season because growing-season cuts can spread the bacteria; UC IPM's rule for very susceptible trees such as pear is to remove rapidly advancing spring infections as soon as they appear, cutting at the next branch junction below the visible margin without harming the collar, and it puts the location of the cut ahead of tool sterilizing. Extension services print different distances (Georgia 6 to 8 inches, Utah State 12), so treat 8 to 12 as the floor. The bacteria survive winter in the cankers, which is what the dormant pruning removes. Clemson pairs the cutting with restraint: no excess nitrogen, and suckers removed, since succulent growth is where new infections take.

control_ladder.note_beginner: An early copper spray, made before the tree blooms and no later than the point where the green tips pushing out of the buds reach half an inch, gives the flowers some protection in a bad-blight area. Be honest about what it buys: UC IPM says copper is the only thing a home grower can buy for fire blight and that it often does not give adequate control even sprayed repeatedly, and Arkansas extension calls the sprays helpful but not fool-proof. It can also russet the fruit. On a big tree you cannot cover, skip it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Clemson's home program for pear is a pre-bloom copper application, cut off once green tip reaches 1/2 inch, followed by streptomycin at 3- to 4-day intervals through bloom with a 50-day wait before harvest; the antibiotic is a separate material and is what protects the open flowers. UC IPM's assessment of copper is blunt: the only material available to homeowners, often inadequate even with multiple applications, five to 12 per season on pear, with russeting or scarring of the fruit as the price. Clemson adds that adequate coverage of a large tree is usually not feasible. Copper accumulates in soil, so a program that runs every spring for years should be weighed against planting a resistant cultivar in the first place.

diseases.name: Pear scab
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Olive to black velvety lesions on leaves and fruit that turn corky and cracked; severe infection yellows leaves and causes early defoliation and scabby, misshapen fruit.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, fuzzy spots on the leaves and rough, scabby, cracked patches on the pears. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Venturia pirina (also spelled V. pyrina); spores overwinter in fallen leaves, and in high-rainfall areas also in lesions on the twigs, and infect during wet spring weather, with infection periods set by leaf wetness and temperature (fastest between 55°F and 75°F, after at least 9 hours of continuous wetness). It is distinct from the apple-scab fungus, which cannot infect pear, but is managed the same way.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that overwinters in last year's fallen leaves and spreads onto new leaves and fruit in cool, wet spring weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply wettable sulfur, or another labeled fungicide, on a protective schedule keyed to spring infection periods, from bud break to about a month after petal fall; dormant-season sprays do nothing against scab, and it is far easier to prevent than to cure once primary infections are established.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Sulfur spray in spring before the spots appear is the organic route. Once it is widespread it is too late for that year.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rake and remove or compost fallen leaves each autumn (in wet climates the fungus can also carry over on twig lesions), keep sprinklers off the foliage or run them between sunrise and noon so leaves dry, and choose a cultivar with negligible scab risk.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up fallen leaves every fall, and if you water with a sprinkler, run it in the morning so the leaves dry by afternoon. Some varieties almost never get scab.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Some European pears almost never get scab. UC IPM's list is Arganche, Barnett Perry, Batjarka, Brandy, Erabasma, Harrow Delight, Muscat, Orcas, and Passe Crassane; Harrow Delight is also on Arkansas extension's fire-blight-resistant list, a useful double. Asian pears are a different species and get scab much less.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The scab fungus has a narrow host range and cultivar resistance is real, so UC IPM rates the nine named European cultivars at negligible risk. None of Bartlett, Bosc, Comice, Seckel, Kieffer, or Moonglow is on the list. In a wet-spring climate, where the fungus can also carry over on twig lesions, that choice is worth more than any spray; where spring stays dry from green tip through fruit set, scab usually is not a problem whatever the cultivar.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The fungus spends winter in the fallen leaves, so rake them up in autumn and compost or get rid of them. On one backyard tree that alone can hold scab down to a level you can live with. Late-season spots on the fruit are only skin deep: peel the pear and eat it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's statement is that removing, then composting or destroying, a single backyard tree's dropped leaves in autumn or winter can limit the disease to tolerable levels, because the overwintered leaf litter is the primary inoculum and rain or sprinkler water is what releases the spores from it. Urea sprayed on the leaves in autumn hastens leaf fall; on pear use urea alone, since zinc is phytotoxic to it. In high-rainfall areas the fungus also overwinters in twig lesions, so leaf removal will not clear all of it there. Late infections can be tolerated, since peeling removes the pinpoint lesions.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Scab needs the leaves to stay wet for about nine hours straight, and a sprinkler that wets the tree in the evening hands it exactly that. If your sprinkler reaches the foliage, run it between sunrise and noon so the leaves dry by afternoon, or angle it down so it waters the ground instead.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rain or sprinkler water releases the spores from the litter and sustains the wetting period; infection is fastest between 55°F and 75°F with a minimum of 9 hours of continuous wetness. UC IPM's instruction for sprinklers that wet any of the foliage is to irrigate between sunrise and noon or reduce the sprinkler angle. It buys nothing in a rainy spring, when the weather does the wetting, but in a dry-spring climate it removes the one wetting the weather is not supplying.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If spring is rainy and the leaves stay wet for nine hours or more, wettable sulfur put on from bud break through bloom and early fruit set protects the new leaves and fruit before the fungus gets in. It only prevents; once spots are everywhere it will not clear them. Never use it when the temperature is near or above 90°F, and skip the dormant season entirely, since a spray on a bare tree does nothing for scab.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The window runs from bud break to about a month after petal fall, with wettable sulfur usable through bloom and early fruit set; copper or Bordeaux are limited to green tip through full bloom because later use russets the fruit. Preventing the primary leaf infections is the whole game, since secondary fruit infections are hard to stop once primaries are established. Sulfur is heat-sensitive on pear, so hold it at temperatures near or above 90°F, and it is never combined with or applied close to an oil spray.

diseases.name: Fabraea leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Many small dark purple-black spots on leaves and fruit through summer, leading to early defoliation and pitted, cracked fruit; with fire blight it is one of the two most common pear diseases in the humid Southeast, and it is most troublesome in warm, humid regions generally.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Lots of small dark spots cover the leaves in summer, and the tree can drop most of its leaves early. The pears get spotted and pitted.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fabraea maculata (the same fungus is also listed as Diplocarpon mespili, and as Entomosporium mespili for its spore stage); it overwinters in fallen leaves and in lesions on last season's shoots, and spreads in warm, rainy summer weather, with the first infections often not until mid-June to early July and new waves about a month later and after each rain.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that lives in old leaves and twigs and spreads in warm, rainy summer weather, getting worse through the summer. It is a bigger problem in hot, humid areas.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protective fungicide on a summer schedule where it recurs: NC State's home-orchard schedule for pears runs from petal fall at 2- to 3-week intervals using thiophanate-methyl, since captan is not registered on pears, and Penn State adds mid-August and September applications in wet seasons on late cultivars such as Bosc; plus rigorous fall leaf removal to cut the overwintering inoculum.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: A protective fungicide through summer if it keeps coming back, plus raking up all the fallen leaves in fall.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Fall leaf removal, which reduces early-season pressure from the overwintered leaf litter; Bosc and Seckel are more susceptible than Bartlett, and the disease is worst where summers are warm, humid, and rainy.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up and get rid of fallen leaves every fall. Expect more of it in hot, humid, rainy summers; Bosc and Seckel get it worse than Bartlett.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The fungus lives through the winter in the fallen leaves, and some of it in the spotted, blackened tips of last summer's shoots, then rain splashes it back up in early summer. Rake up and destroy the leaves in fall. That lowers the early-season pressure on a tree that gets this every year; it will not stop it on its own in a wet summer.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Two inoculum sources with different timing. The sexual stage develops on overwintered fallen leaves, and conidia also come from the previous season's shoot lesions, purple-black blotches with indefinite margins that run together into a superficial canker on current-season wood (Penn State). Michigan State's guidance is that removing or destroying leaf litter reduces early-season pressure, a reduction rather than a cure. First infections often wait until mid-June to early July, with secondary infections about a month later and after each rain, so the cleanup is finished long before the disease shows.

diseases.name: Pear decline
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Slow decline, weak growth, small leaves with reddish autumn color, and reduced yield, or in acute cases sudden collapse; driven by a phytoplasma transmitted by pear psylla and expressed through a sensitive rootstock.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The tree slowly weakens over years, with small leaves that redden early in fall and a shrinking crop, or sometimes a sudden collapse. It is tied to the pear psylla insect and to certain rootstocks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A phytoplasma (a bacteria-like organism) spread by pear psylla; severity depends heavily on rootstock sensitivity, which is why decline-resistant rootstocks (OHxF series) matter.
diseases.cause_beginner: A tiny disease organism carried by the pear psylla insect. How badly a tree is hit depends on its rootstock, so a resistant rootstock is the main protection.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure; manage by controlling pear psylla (the vector) and, at planting, choosing a tolerant rootstock (OHxF). Remove severely declining trees.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a tree has it. Keep pear psylla under control and, most importantly, start with a resistant rootstock when you plant.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on a decline-tolerant rootstock (OHxF 87/97/333) and keep psylla populations low; avoid highly sensitive rootstocks.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy a tree grown on a resistant rootstock (the OHxF series) from a nursery, never graft wood from a sickly pear onto it, and keep pear psylla in check.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no cure for pear decline, so the protection is bought with the tree: buy one grafted on an Old Home x Farmingdale rootstock (OHxF 87, 97, or 333 by name), which tolerates the disease, and never on an Asian or Ussurian pear rootstock, where the tree can collapse at the graft union. A tree on a tolerant rootstock that is kept well watered and fed can carry the disease for years with little sign of it, as long as pear psylla are kept down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The rootstock decides what the infection costs at the graft union. UC IPM lists Old Home x Farmingdale, Bartlett seedling, Winter Nelis, and Pyrus betulaefolia as tolerant, and Pyrus serotina and P. ussuriensis as highly susceptible, with sudden collapse from hypersensitive damage at the union; WSU rates OHxF 97 and 333 resistant to decline and describes the series as tolerant of blight and decline. On a tolerant rootstock the typical course is a very slow decline that shows mostly when water and nutrition fall short or when psylla numbers run high early in the season; keeping the tree in good vigor and holding psylla down (see pear psylla) are what UC IPM gives for keeping the disease in remission. Utah State's diagnostic is a brown line in the cambium at the graft union, exposed with a knife.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The disease also travels in wood. Grafting or budding from an infected pear passes it straight into the new tree, so take wood for grafting only from a tree that is growing well, and buy trees from a nursery rather than propagating from a pear that is going backward.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Utah State records that grafting and budding transmit the phytoplasma as well as psylla, and UC IPM notes an infected pear tree is the only known host from which psylla can acquire it, so an infected tree is both a graft risk and the reservoir for every pear within psylla range. Before cutting scionwood from a tree, look at the graft union with a knife: a brown line in the cambium is Utah State's sign of decline. This is a planting-time and propagation-time decision; nothing applied later reaches a phytoplasma already in the tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A pear that has collapsed, or has been shrinking back for several seasons with small leaves that turn red early, is where the psylla on your other pears pick the disease up. Once it is clearly going, take it out rather than nursing it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Utah State lists removal of diseased trees, and UC IPM identifies the infected pear as the only acquisition source for psylla, which makes a declining tree a hazard to every pear within flight range. A tree kept in remission by psylla control and good vigor on a tolerant rootstock is not the one to remove; this is for the collapsed tree and the one in steady decline despite adequate water and nutrition.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep, infrequent irrigation: about 1 inch of water per week through the growing season, more in heat and during fruit sizing, tapering off as the tree goes dormant.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply but not too often, aim for about 1 inch a week while the tree is growing and making fruit. Water more in hot, dry spells and less once the leaves drop in fall.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week as a baseline (a deep soak that wets the full root zone), increasing during fruit sizing in mid to late summer; pears drop fruit when droughted at sizing.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch a week. The easiest way is one long, slow soak that gets the water down deep, rather than a quick daily sprinkle.
watering.method_seasoned: Drip or a slow soak at the dripline; keep water off the trunk and crown to avoid collar rot, and mulch to hold moisture (pulled back a few inches from the trunk).
watering.method_beginner: Use a soaker hose or drip line, or let a hose trickle slowly at the edge of the branches. Keep water off the trunk itself, and mulch around the tree (not touching the trunk) to hold moisture in.
