nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, clearing the entire recommended list, including Bartlett, with real margin.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The cooler parts of the region grow every recommended European pear variety well, including Bartlett.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late frost after the March to April bloom is an occasional risk, more so at higher elevations.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours, clearing Hood, Kieffer, Orient, Seckel, Moonglow, Ayers, Warren, Comice, and Bosc comfortably, with Anjou and Magness (700 hours) right at the ceiling. Bartlett (800 hours) needs more chill than this zone reliably banks.
9.suitability_note_beginner: On the valley floor, Kieffer, Orient, and most dessert pears like Bosc and Comice fruit well. Bartlett is a tighter fit and does better in the cooler zone 8 pockets.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in late February to March occasionally meets a late frost; the dry air keeps fire blight pressure low regardless.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin (zone 10) banks roughly 150 to 450 chill hours, enough for Hood, Kieffer, and Orient with ease; the 500 hour and up dessert pears and Bartlett need more cold than this warm corner reliably gives. Frost is rarely the issue this far south; summer heat and sun exposure on young bark are the practical concerns.
10.suitability_note_beginner: At warm Laughlin, stick to Kieffer or Orient; the higher chill dessert pears and Bartlett need more winter cold than this spot gets.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a problem at Laughlin; summer heat and sunburn on young bark are the bigger concern.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: European pear fruits well across the Las Vegas Valley region. Kieffer and Orient, tough Southern pears bred for heat and fire blight resistance, are the most dependable choice everywhere here, including Laughlin. Popular dessert pears like Bosc, Comice, Moonglow, and Anjou do well on the valley floor and in the cooler zone 8 pockets. Bartlett needs the most winter cold and does best in zone 8. The dry desert air is a real plus, keeping fire blight down compared to humid pear-growing regions.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: European pear fruits reliably across the Las Vegas Valley region, spanning a genuine chill range that fits the whole area. Hood, Kieffer, and Orient (200 to 350 hours), the fire blight resistant, heat tolerant Southern pears, clear every zone including Laughlin and are the dependable anchor. The 500 to 700 hour dessert pears, Seckel, Moonglow, Ayers, Warren, Comice, Bosc, Anjou, and Magness, fit zone 9 (with the 700 hour pair at the ceiling) and zone 8 comfortably. Bartlett (800 hours) needs zone 8's cooler pockets. The dry air is a genuine advantage against fire blight, the disease that most limits pear elsewhere; late spring frost on the bloom and sun exposure on young bark are the practical desert risks instead.
nevada.chill_basis_seasoned: European pear covers a wide chill range, and most of it fits comfortably within Nevada's chill bands. Hood (200 hours), Kieffer, and Orient (350), the fire blight resistant, heat tolerant Southern pears, clear zone 9 and even Laughlin's warmer band with ease. Seckel (500), Moonglow, Ayers, Warren, Comice, and Bosc (600), and Anjou and Magness (700) fit zone 9 with the 700 hour pair right at the ceiling; all clear zone 8's wider band comfortably. Bartlett, at 800 hours, needs zone 8's cooler pockets. The dry desert air is a real asset for this fire blight prone fruit, well beyond what the humid East or Southeast can offer.
nevada.chill_basis_beginner: European pear has options for every part of this desert region. Kieffer and Orient, the tough, heat tolerant Southern pears, are the safest choice everywhere, including Laughlin. Popular dessert pears like Bosc, Comice, and Anjou do well on the valley floor and in the cooler zone 8 pockets. Bartlett needs the most winter cold, so it belongs in zone 8. The dry air here also helps keep fire blight, a common pear disease, under control.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Washington County Extension steers pears to the county's higher towns above 5,300 feet, so European pear is marginal in the warm St. George core. Only the lowest-chill, heat-tolerant Southern pears have a real chance; the popular dessert pears need more winter cold than the low valley banks. The dry air keeps fire blight low.
8.suitability_note_beginner: European pear is a gamble in the warm St. George core; most kinds need more winter chill than the low valley gives. Only the lowest-chill, heat-tolerant pears have a chance.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in spring largely clears the late-March last frost, so frost is a minor risk for European pear here; limited winter chill, not a spring freeze, is what holds the crop back, and the dry air keeps fire blight low.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: European pear is a stretch in the warm St. George core; Washington County Extension recommends pears for the county's higher, cooler towns instead. Most European pears need more winter cold than the low valley provides; only the lowest-chill, heat-tolerant kinds have a chance. The dry air does keep fire blight low.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: Washington County Extension lists pears among the fruits for the county's higher-elevation towns, Central, Enterprise, and New Harmony above 5,300 feet, not the warm St. George core, so European pear is marginal on the low valley floor. Most European pears need more winter chill than the low elevations bank; only the lowest-chill, heat-tolerant Southern pears have any real chance here, and even they crop best in a cooler winter. The dry desert air keeps fire blight low, a genuine advantage, but chill, not disease, is the binding limit. Plant bare-root or container trees during the dormant season.
utah_dixie.chill_basis_seasoned: European pear is marginal at the St. George Dixie core. Washington County Extension recommends pears only for the county's higher-elevation towns, Central, Enterprise, and New Harmony above 5,300 feet, outside this warm valley belt. Most European pears carry a moderate to high chill requirement that the low elevations near St. George, at roughly 2,624 feet, do not reliably bank; only the lowest-chill, heat-tolerant Southern pears have a real chance on the valley floor, and the popular dessert pears fall short. The dry air keeps fire blight, the disease that most limits pear elsewhere, well in check, so chill, not disease, is what holds the crop back here.
utah_dixie.chill_basis_beginner: European pear is a stretch in the warm St. George core; Washington County Extension recommends pears for the county's higher, cooler towns instead. Most European pears need more winter cold than the low valley provides; only the lowest-chill, heat-tolerant kinds have a chance. The dry air does keep fire blight low.

crops.description_seasoned: A long-lived deciduous fruit tree (Pyrus communis) grown for fresh-eating, dessert, and storage fruit. European pear is a cross-pollination crop: most cultivars are self-unfruitful, so you plant two different varieties whose bloom periods overlap and rely on bees to move pollen between them (a few, like Bartlett and Anjou, are partially self-fruitful in mild climates but still crop better with a pollinizer). The signature difference from apple is at harvest: European pears ripen OFF the tree. Pick them mature but firm and green, give them a cool rest, then ripen at room temperature; a pear left to ripen on the branch goes mealy and rotten at the core. Fire blight is the major disease, worst in warm, humid regions, so cultivar and rootstock resistance matter. Chill requirement is variety-set, and rootstock choice sets mature size and how soon the tree bears.
crops.description_beginner: Pear is a fruit tree that lives for decades, often longer than an apple. Two things make pears special. First, most pear trees cannot make fruit from their own flowers, so you need a second, different pear variety nearby that blooms at the same time, with bees to carry the pollen. Second, and this surprises people: you do NOT let pears ripen on the tree. You pick them while they are still firm and green but full-sized, then let them finish ripening on the counter. A pear left on the tree turns brown and mushy in the middle while the outside still looks fine. The biggest disease to know about is fire blight, which is worst in warm, damp places, so picking a resistant variety helps a lot.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: European pears are picked MATURE BUT FIRM, not tree-ripe: full varietal size with the ground color shifting from grass-green toward a lighter yellow-green, lenticels turning corky and tan, and the fruit detaching when lifted and twisted upward to horizontal. Tree-ripening ruins them, the flesh browns and breaks down at the core (stone-cell grittiness) while the skin still looks sound. After picking, most varieties need a cool rest (near 30 to 40°F) before they will ripen evenly at room temperature. First meaningful crop typically comes around year 4 to 6, rootstock-dependent.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A pear is ready to PICK, not eat, when it has reached full size, its green has started to lighten, and it snaps off the branch easily when you lift it and twist it up to horizontal. It will still be hard, and that is correct. Do not wait for it to soften on the tree, a tree-ripened pear rots from the inside out and turns gritty and brown at the core. Bring the firm pears indoors, give them a week or two somewhere cool, then let them finish on the counter until the neck gives slightly to a gentle press. Do not expect a real crop until about the fourth to sixth year after planting.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: European pears bloom in early spring after their chill requirement is met, generally a few days BEFORE apples, which makes the open bloom more exposed to late frost. Cultivars are staggered from early to late over roughly two weeks; bloom timing governs cross-pollination, since only varieties whose windows overlap can pollinate each other. Pear blossoms are less attractive to bees than many fruits (low nectar), so good pollination depends on warm, calm bloom weather and strong bee activity.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Pear trees flower in early spring, usually a little earlier than apples, which means a late frost is more likely to catch the open blossoms. Different varieties bloom a few days apart, spread over about two weeks, and two trees can only pollinate each other if they bloom at the same time. Pear flowers are not a bee favorite, so warm, calm weather during bloom really helps the bees do their work and set a good crop.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: As a species European pear is reliably cold-hardy through USDA zone 4 (a touch less hardy than apple), and this guide's roster fruits dependably zones 5 to 8. In zone 4 the roster survives and fruits in good years; in zone 3 it survives but is not rated for reliable fruit, which there takes ultra-hardy cultivars (Ure, Summercrisp, Golden Spice, Patten) outside this roster. At the warm edge, zones 9 and warmer succeed only with low-chill, fire-blight-resistant cultivars (Hood, Kieffer, Orient), and the frost-free low desert and tropics bank too little chill for any European pear to fruit. Across the humid Southeast, fire blight, not cold, is the binding constraint.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Pear trees handle cold winters well, down to about zone 4, though they are slightly less tough than apples. The varieties in this guide give reliable fruit in zones 5 through 8. In zone 4 they will live and fruit in good years; in colder zone 3 you would want a special extra-hardy variety not listed here (like Ure or Summercrisp). In warm zones (9 and up) choose a low-chill, disease-resistant variety like Hood, Kieffer, or Orient, and know that the frost-free deep South and tropics simply do not get cold enough for pears to fruit.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Chill hours are the accumulated hours between about 32 and 45°F during winter dormancy that a tree must bank before it breaks bud and flowers normally in spring. European pear's requirement is set by the cultivar: this guide's roster runs from about 200 hours (low-chill Hood) through the classic 600 to 800 hours (Bartlett, Bosc, Anjou, Comice). As a group European pears need MORE chill than apples, which is why they are less at home in the warm-winter South than apples or Asian pears. Match the variety's chill need to what your winters reliably deliver: too little chill gives delayed, straggly bloom and poor fruit set.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Pear trees need a stretch of winter cold before they will flower well in spring, measured in 'chill hours' (hours between about 32 and 45°F). Different pear varieties need different amounts: a low-chill kind like Hood needs only about 200 hours, while the familiar Bartlett and Bosc need 600 to 800. As a rule, pears want a bit more winter cold than apples do. Pick a variety whose chill need matches your winters; in a mild-winter area, choose a low-chill variety or the tree will bloom poorly and set little fruit.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: European pear is largely self-unfruitful: a lone tree, or two trees of the same cultivar, sets little or no fruit. Plant a second, genetically different European pear whose bloom overlaps, within about 50 to 100 ft, with bees to move pollen between them (pear flowers are low in nectar, so strong bee activity matters more than for apples). A few cultivars (Bartlett, Anjou) are PARTIALLY self-fruitful and will set a light crop alone in mild climates, but all of them yield heavier, more regular crops with a pollinizer. Bloom groups must overlap to cross. Mind the known incompatibilities: Bartlett and Seckel will not pollinate each other, so pair each with a third variety (Bosc, Comice, or Moonglow). One caution: a few cultivars (Magness) produce sterile pollen, cannot serve as a pollinizer, and themselves need two other compatible varieties nearby. European and Asian pears can cross only when their bloom genuinely overlaps, which is often unreliable.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: This is the most important thing about growing pears: one pear tree alone usually will not make fruit. Pear flowers need pollen from a DIFFERENT pear variety, carried by bees. So plan to plant two different kinds of European pear, not two of the same, within about 50 to 100 ft of each other, and make sure they bloom at the same time. A couple of varieties (Bartlett, Anjou) can set a small crop on their own in mild areas, but even they do much better with a partner. Watch out for one famous mismatch: Bartlett and Seckel cannot pollinate each other, so give each of them a different partner like Bosc or Comice. And a few varieties (like Magness) cannot pollinate anything and need two partners themselves, so ask the nursery before you rely on one as your second tree.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize root and scaffold establishment over fruit. Remove any blossoms that open the first spring so the tree spends its energy on roots and framework rather than a few pears. Keep the young tree evenly watered through its first summer and stake it if it is on a dwarfing or quince rootstock. Prune lightly and only in dry weather, fresh cuts on a young pear are an entry point for fire blight, and go easy on nitrogen for the same reason. Expect no crop in year 1; a first meaningful harvest comes around year 4 to 6, rootstock-dependent.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: Do not let your pear tree fruit in its first year. If flowers open that first spring, pinch them off. It feels wrong, but a young tree that skips fruiting puts its energy into roots and branches and becomes much stronger. Water it steadily through the first summer, and stake it if it is a small (dwarf or quince) tree. Prune only a little, and only when the weather is dry, because cuts in damp weather invite fire blight. Go easy on fertilizer too, since lots of soft growth catches that disease. You will not get pears the first year, and that is normal. Your first real crop is usually around the fourth to sixth year.

A few cultivars (Bartlett, Anjou) are PARTIALLY self-fruitful and will set a light crop alone in mild climates, but all of them yield heavier, more regular crops with a pollinizer. Bloom groups must overlap to cross. Mind the known incompatibilities: Bartlett and Seckel will not pollinate each other, so pair each with a third variety (Bosc, Comice, or Moonglow). One caution: a few cultivars (Magness) produce sterile pollen, cannot serve as a pollinizer, and themselves need two other compatible varieties nearby. So plan to plant two different kinds of European pear, not two of the same, within about 50 to 100 ft of each other, and make sure they bloom at the same time. And a few varieties (like Magness) cannot pollinate anything and need two partners themselves, so ask the nursery before you rely on one as your second tree.

crops.establishment_note: Roughly the first four years are establishment: the tree builds roots and a scaffold of main branches before it carries a real crop. Remove first-year blossoms, train the framework with light annual dormant pruning (pear is prone to fire blight, so prune conservatively and only in dry weather), and do not expect meaningful yield until bearing begins (around year 4 to 6, rootstock-dependent and later than apple).
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: OHxF 87 (semi-dwarf) is the default backyard pick for European pear: it makes a manageable tree slightly smaller than a Bartlett seedling, bears reasonably young, and is one of the most productive of the fire-blight-tolerant Old Home x Farmingdale series, which also resists pear decline. For the smallest patio or container tree choose a quince stock or OHxF 333 (but note quince is graft-incompatible with Bartlett, Bosc, Seckel, and others without an Old Home interstem, and is not winter-hardy in cold regions); for a large, low-maintenance standard, choose Bartlett or Winter Nelis seedling, accepting a longer wait to bear.

rootstock_options.name: Quince (with interstem)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on, and if it is quince, whether your variety is grafted with an Old Home interstem (Bartlett, Bosc, and Seckel are graft-incompatible with quince directly).
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Quince (e.g., Provence/Quince A or C) is the dwarfing pear rootstock, about 8 to 12 ft, precocious and container-suitable, and induces early, heavy bearing. Two real cautions: it is graft-incompatible with several major cultivars (Bartlett, Bosc, Seckel) unless an Old Home interstem is used, and it is poorly cold-hardy, so it is a mild-climate or container choice, not for the cold North.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Quince makes the smallest pear tree, about 8 to 12 ft, and gives fruit soonest. Two catches: several popular varieties (Bartlett, Bosc, Seckel) will not graft directly onto quince and need a middle 'bridge' piece, and quince roots are not very cold-hardy, so it suits mild climates or pots best.

rootstock_options.name: OHxF 333
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on and whether it needs staking.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: OHxF 333 is a semi-dwarfing Old Home x Farmingdale stock, about half to two-thirds standard size, with strong resistance to fire blight, collar rot, woolly pear aphid, and pear decline. Productivity and fruit size run a touch lower than OHxF 87, but it is the best size-controlled, disease-tolerant choice and works in a large container.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: OHxF 333 makes a medium-small tree, about 10 to 14 ft, and resists fire blight and pear decline. It fruits a bit lighter than OHxF 87 but is a great disease-tolerant pick for a smaller yard or a big pot.

rootstock_options.name: OHxF 87
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on and whether it needs staking.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: OHxF 87 is the workhorse backyard pear rootstock: semi-dwarf at slightly smaller than a Bartlett seedling, precocious for the series, and one of its best producers, with strong fire-blight and pear-decline resistance. The common default for a home European pear.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: OHxF 87 makes a medium tree, the usual backyard choice. It fruits fairly young for a pear, produces well, and resists fire blight and pear decline. A reliable all-rounder.

rootstock_options.name: OHxF 97
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on and whether it needs staking.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: OHxF 97 is a larger, semi-vigorous to near-standard Old Home x Farmingdale stock, hardy and cold-resilient, with strong resistance to fire blight and pear decline, but less precocious than OHxF 87. A durable choice for a bigger in-ground tree, especially in colder regions.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: OHxF 97 makes a larger tree, about 16 to 22 ft, and is tough and cold-hardy with good disease resistance. It is slower to start fruiting than OHxF 87, but a solid pick if you have the room, especially up North.

rootstock_options.name: Bartlett / Winter Nelis seedling
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on (seedling makes a full-size tree) and whether it needs staking (usually not).
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Seedling pear rootstock (Bartlett or Winter Nelis, or vigorous Pyrus species) makes a full-size, deeply anchored, long-lived standard tree, about 25 to 40 ft, needing no staking but the slowest to bear (around year 6 to 10) and large to spray, prune, and harvest. Vigorous and adaptable, but it offers less of the OHxF disease tolerance. Choose it for a permanent landscape tree where ultimate size is acceptable.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A 'standard' seedling rootstock makes a big, classic pear tree, about 25 to 40 ft, that stands on its own and lives a very long time. The downsides: it takes the longest to fruit (around year 6 to 10) and is tall to reach. Pick it only if you want a large tree and have the space.

pet_safe.note: The flesh is fine, but the seeds contain the same cyanide compounds as apple seeds and are best kept from cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: Your tree may set its first pears now, and the picking rule is the surprising part: a European pear is picked while it is still firm, not ripe. Left to ripen on the tree it goes brown and gritty at the core. Pick when it has reached full size, its green has begun to lighten, and the stem snaps free on an upward twist, then ripen it indoors. Thin the young fruit to one per cluster about a month after bloom for bigger pears and steadier crops. Keep training the framework with limb spreaders, since pears grow stubbornly upright and a narrow crotch angle is a branch that breaks later. Prune only in dry weather, because wet cuts invite fire blight.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: A light first set is normal on a tree this age. Thin to one fruit per cluster within about a month of bloom. The harvest rule is the one to internalize now, because it is counterintuitive and it is the difference between fruit and compost: European pear is picked MATURE BUT FIRM and ripened off the tree, on full varietal size, lightening ground color, corky lenticels and clean stem separation on an upward twist. Tree-ripening produces core browning and grit cells. Keep spreading limbs while the wood is young, since pear's naturally upright, narrow habit sets weak crotch angles that fail under later crop loads. Prune conservatively and only in dry conditions: heavy cuts force succulent regrowth, which is exactly what fire blight exploits.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From about the sixth year the tree carries a full crop. European pear takes longer to get going than most fruit trees and then keeps producing for decades, so the wait buys something. Pick firm, never tree-ripe, and finish the fruit indoors. Winter pears such as Anjou and Bosc need several weeks somewhere near freezing before they will ripen properly, while a summer Bartlett only needs a few days cool. Thin to one fruit per cluster each spring, prune in late winter and only when the weather is dry, and wipe your pruners between cuts if fire blight has been around, since it spreads on the blade.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from roughly year six, later than most of the roster, against a productive life measured in decades. The annual cycle is dormant pruning in dry weather only, thinning to one fruit per cluster, and disciplined fire-blight hygiene: disinfect between cuts when blight is present and excise cankers 8 to 12 inches below visible damage. Harvest mature but firm on size, lightening ground color, corky lenticels and clean stem snap; never tree-ripe. Post-harvest conditioning is cultivar-dependent and not optional: winter pears (Anjou, Bosc) require several weeks of near-freezing storage before they will ripen, while Bartlett conditions after a few days cool. Skipping the cold rest on a winter pear yields fruit that never softens properly.

crops.name: Pear (Asian)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Asian pear trees grow best in deep, fertile soil that drains well but holds some moisture, a loam or clay-loam is ideal. Like other pears they tolerate heavier, wetter ground better than most fruit trees, including some clay, but they still will not stand in water, so avoid a spot where puddles linger. If your soil is very sandy and dries out fast, work in compost and plan to water more, since a thirsty tree drops fruit.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Asian pear wants a deep, fertile loam to clay-loam with steady moisture and moderate organic matter. It is more forgiving of heavy, moisture-retentive soils than apple or stone fruit and tolerates a fairly wide pH band, but it still will not accept standing water, which drives crown and root rots. On a wet site, plant on a low berm. One important trade-off: rich soil and heavy nitrogen push the soft, succulent growth that fire blight colonizes, so feed Asian pears lean and favor a fire-blight-tolerant rootstock on any site with disease history.

ph.note_beginner: Asian pear trees like soil that runs from slightly acidic to neutral, a pH around 6.0 to 7.0 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline soil is, where 7.0 is neutral). Test your soil before planting, since it is much easier to adjust the pH now than after the tree is in the ground. Garden lime raises a low pH; garden sulfur lowers a high one. Your local extension office can test a sample for you.
ph.note_seasoned: Asian pear does best at a pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 and tolerates roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Test the soil before planting and adjust the whole root zone, not just the hole, because correcting pH around an established tree is slow. Lime raises a low pH; elemental sulfur lowers a high one. Well outside this band, iron and manganese availability falls and new growth yellows between the veins.

fertilizer.timing: early spring before bud break
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed lightly in early spring before bud break, guided by shoot growth: a healthy young pear makes about 12 to 18 inches of new shoot growth a year, so feed to reach that and no more. Excess nitrogen is the classic pear mistake, it drives soft, succulent growth that fire blight runs straight through, and it delays fruiting. Mature trees on fertile soil often need no nitrogen at all. If anything, err on the side of underfeeding a pear.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed pear trees once a year, in early spring before the buds open, with a balanced fertilizer, and go light. Too much feeding is the number-one pear mistake: it makes lots of soft new growth that the disease fire blight loves, and it pushes the tree to grow leaves instead of fruit. If the tree is growing well and putting out healthy new branches each year, it may need no feeding at all. When in doubt, use less.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced N-P-K ratio (the three numbers on the bag, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) such as 10-10-10 at a modest rate, leaning toward the low end on any vigorous tree to limit fire-blight-prone growth. On fertile ground a pear often wants none.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. A balanced one like 10-10-10 is fine for pears, used sparingly. The first number (nitrogen) is the one to keep low, because too much makes soft growth that catches fire blight.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rule is about 1/8 lb of actual nitrogen per year of tree age, capped near 1/2 to 3/4 lb actual N for a mature tree, noticeably leaner than the apple rule because of fire blight. Always follow the label and skip nitrogen entirely in a year of strong shoot growth.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple guideline is a small amount that grows a little with the tree's age, following the directions on the bag, and using even less than you would for an apple. When in doubt, feed less, an underfed pear is far healthier than an overfed one.

companions.note_beginner: Pears do not pair with other plants the way vegetables do. For an Asian pear, the neighbor that counts is a second, different Asian pear variety that blooms at the same time, within about 50 to 100 ft, because most Asian pears need another Asian pear nearby to make fruit. Right around the trunk, do the opposite of planting companions: keep grass and other plants away from the base out to the edge of the branches, because they steal water and food from the young tree. Use mulch there instead, and never plant an Asian pear near a black walnut tree, which poisons the soil for it.
companions.note_seasoned: Pear does not companion-plant in the vegetable sense; the interactions that matter are pollination and root competition. The single most important neighbor is a second, bloom-overlapping Asian pear variety (the pollinizer) within about 50 to 100 ft, since most Asian pears are self-unfruitful. At the trunk, the rule reverses: keep turf and aggressive perennials out of the root zone, where grass competes hard with a young tree for water and nitrogen. Maintain a mulched, vegetation-free circle to the dripline, and avoid siting near black walnut, whose juglone is toxic to Asian pear.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: spring bulbs (daffodil)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A ring of daffodils at the drip line is a traditional fruit-tree-guild move with two intended jobs: the early foliage forms a band that helps hold back creeping grass, the tree's main competitor, and daffodils are toxic enough that voles and deer tend to avoid grazing through them to the trunk. They emerge and feed before the canopy leafs out, then go dormant, so they do not compete in summer. Treat this as a useful cultural barrier rather than a measured yield booster.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The daffodil-ring (grass suppression + rodent/deer deterrence via toxicity) is a well-established permaculture fruit-tree-guild practice grounded in daffodils' real toxicity and spring-ephemeral timing, applied to pear the same way it is to apple; not a measured pear yield/health effect. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Plant a ring of daffodils around your pear tree, out where the branches reach. They come up early in spring, help keep grass from creeping toward the trunk, and because they are poisonous to nibble, they discourage mice and deer. They die back in summer, so they stay out of the tree's way.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: comfrey
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Comfrey is a workhorse of the fruit-tree guild. Its deep taproot pulls from well below the tree's surface feeder roots, so it does not compete for the same water and nutrients, and it shades out grass along the row. Chopped two or three times a season and dropped under the tree, its lush leaves break down into a mineral-rich mulch, and the flowers feed pollinators. The dynamic-accumulator framing is more tradition than proven chemistry, but the practical value as non-competing mulch and grass suppression is real.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Comfrey as chop-and-drop mulch / grass suppressor with a deep non-competing taproot is widely practiced and partly grounded (deep taproot, vigorous biomass); the 'dynamic accumulator' mineral claims are permaculture tradition, not peer-reviewed. Same mechanism whether under apple or pear. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Comfrey is a leafy plant that grows well around fruit trees. Its roots reach deep down, so it does not steal water from the tree, and it crowds out grass. A few times each summer you can cut the big leaves and lay them on the soil under the tree, where they rot down into natural food for it. Its flowers also bring in helpful bees.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: clover (living mulch)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dutch white clover makes a strong living mulch under pears. As a legume it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through its root symbiosis, feeding the tree slowly while staying low and tolerating harvest foot traffic. It covers the ground to suppress weeds and hold moisture without the aggressive grass competition bare turf brings. Keep it back from the immediate trunk zone, and note it does draw some moisture, so manage it on dry sites. Because pears want lean nitrogen, treat the clover's slow trickle as a feature, not a reason to also fertilize.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Dutch white clover living mulch = legume N-fixation + weed suppression + walkable cover; mechanistically sound and supported by extension/NRCS orchard legume cover-crop work. mechanistic/medium: real mechanism, held at medium because clover-to-tree N transfer magnitude and net water effect vary by site.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: White clover is a low, soft plant you can grow as a living carpet under your pear tree. It pulls nitrogen from the air and feeds it slowly into the soil, while covering the ground to keep weeds down and hold in moisture. It is tough enough to walk on at picking time. Just keep it from growing right against the trunk.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: black walnut
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Black walnut is a definitive bad neighbor for pear. Its roots, hulls, and leaf litter release juglone, an allelopathic compound toxic to many sensitive plants, and pear (like apple) is among those affected, showing decline and dieback within the walnut's root zone. The effect extends well beyond the visible canopy, roughly to the full root spread (commonly cited at fifty-plus feet from a mature tree), so siting matters more than spacing tweaks: keep pears entirely out of a black walnut's root zone.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Juglone allelopathy is a real, well-characterized chemical mechanism; pome fruit including pear is documented as juglone-sensitive across extension sources. mechanistic/high: the mechanism and pome-fruit sensitivity are well established and uncontested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep pear trees far away from black walnut trees. Black walnuts release a natural chemical called juglone from their roots and leaves that is poisonous to pears and can make them sicken and die. The chemical spreads through the soil well past the walnut's branches, so give them a very wide berth, at least 50 feet from a big walnut.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: turfgrass to the trunk
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Letting turfgrass grow right up to a pear trunk is a quiet but real drag on the tree, especially when young. Grass competes directly for water and nitrogen in the surface zone where the feeder roots sit, slowing growth and delaying bearing, and dense grass and mulch against the trunk harbor voles that girdle bark over winter. Maintain a vegetation-free or mulched strip about two feet out from the trunk (mulch pulled back a few inches off the bark itself).

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Extension guidance consistently prescribes a vegetation-free/mulched zone around young fruit trees and warns of rodent bark damage from grass/mulch at the trunk; the grass-competition effect on young tree growth is well documented for pome fruit. extension_backed/high.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Do not let lawn grass grow right up against your pear tree's trunk. The grass competes with the young tree for water and food, so it grows slower and fruits later. Grass at the trunk also hides mice that can chew the bark in winter. Keep a clear or mulched circle about two feet around the trunk, with the mulch pulled back slightly so it does not touch the bark.

pests.name: Codling moth
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae tunnel to the core and feed in the seed cavity, leaving one or more holes plugged with frass on the fruit surface; a shallow sting where a larva bored a short way and died is the other mark. Check where two fruits touch, a common entry point. Infested pears drop early or are inedible.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This is the classic 'worm in the fruit.' You find a small hole with brown crumbly stuff (frass) around it, and a tunnel into the core when you cut it open. Bad pears drop early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cydia pomonella; females lay eggs singly on leaves and on fruit, and the hatching larvae bore into the pear. It overwinters as a full-grown larva in a silken cocoon under loose bark scales or in soil and debris at the base of the tree, and depending on climate has two, three or sometimes four generations a year. The same pest attacks apple and English walnut.
pests.cause_beginner: A small moth lays eggs on the tiny pears in spring; the eggs hatch into caterpillars that crawl into the fruit. There can be two batches a summer, so the problem repeats.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Monitor with pheromone traps and a degree-day count to time control to egg hatch; remove infested fruit from the tree and dropped fruit promptly; bag fruit four to six weeks after bloom, the one nonchemical measure UC IPM rates as effective alone; spinosad at egg hatch, three sprays at 10-day intervals for the first generation and no more than six per season; a codling moth granulosis virus (CYD-X) applied weekly through hatch where available. Mating disruption is an orchard-scale tool.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick up and throw away every pear that drops, do not leave them under the tree. You can slip paper bags over young pears to keep moths out, and scent traps help you know when to act. Sprays like spinosad work if timed right.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Sanitation from the first flight on: pick infested fruit off the tree before the larvae mature, clear drops as they fall, thin to one fruit per cluster and inspect touching fruit. Remove, rather than prune, any abandoned apple, pear or walnut nearby, which UC IPM treats as a reservoir. Cardboard trunk bands are no longer recommended for home gardens: they catch only a small share of the larvae, and a band not removed in time breeds moths.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clear of fallen pears, and pull off any pear with a hole in it before the caterpillar inside can leave. Thin to one pear per cluster. A cardboard band around the trunk is an old trick UC IPM no longer recommends for home trees, because it catches very few of the caterpillars and can make things worse if you forget to take it down. An abandoned pear or apple tree nearby keeps the moths coming, so take it out if it is yours.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Check the young pears every week or so and pull off any with a small hole ringed by brown crumbs, then pick up every pear that drops as soon as you see it, because the caterpillar is usually still inside and will crawl out to start the next batch. Thin to one pear per cluster and look closely where two fruits touch, a favorite spot for the hole. Destroy what you collect rather than leaving it under the tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cydia pomonella overwinters as a mature larva in a silken cocoon under loose bark scales and in soil or litter at the base of the tree, and every larva that leaves a pear to spin one is a moth next flight, so an infested fruit taken off the tree or a drop picked up promptly is a moth that never flies. UC IPM is blunt that it is far easier to hold numbers low from the first flight than to pull down a population that has built for a season or two. Thin to one fruit per cluster, inspect the contact point of touching fruit, and take out any abandoned apple, pear or walnut nearby, which UC IPM's pear guideline treats as a reservoir to remove.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hang a scent trap in the tree in spring. It catches male moths, and its real job is to tell you the moths have started flying, which sets the clock for bagging the fruit and for any spray. On its own it will not keep the pears clean.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A pheromone-baited trap marks first sustained male flight, and UC IPM's home guidance keys the first spray to egg hatch, which follows the first regular catches by a run of warm days that its guide gives as a heat-unit count rather than a calendar date; counts through summer flag the second and any third generation. Hanging traps in every tree may thin an isolated tree's moths slightly, but UC IPM does not rate that as a reliable way to reduce damage, so read the trap as a calendar rather than a control.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Once the flowers have dropped and the young pears are half an inch to an inch across, roughly four to six weeks after bloom, enclose each one in a paper bag fastened around the stem. A bagged pear is out of the moth's reach, so no egg is laid on it and no caterpillar gets in. It takes time per fruit, so it fits a tree with a crop you can count.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: This is the one nonchemical measure UC IPM rates effective enough to stand alone even under heavy pressure, and it earns that by taking the fruit out of the egg-laying site altogether rather than trimming the population. The window is four to six weeks after bloom at 1/2 to 1 inch fruit, and NC State's handbook gives the same span; thin to a single fruit per cluster first, and bag early on late-developing varieties, which UC IPM warns can be attacked before the fruit reaches 1/2 inch.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the tree carries more fruit than you can bag, spinosad is the organic spray UC IPM lists for home trees, and timing is everything: the first spray goes on as the first caterpillars hatch, before they bore in, with two more at ten-day spacing, and never more than six in a season. It is hard on bees while wet, so spray at dusk and keep it off anything in flower, and stop at least a week before you pick.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad, a fermentation product of Saccharopolyspora spinosa, kills young larvae by ingestion and contact, so it has to be on the fruit surface as eggs hatch; UC IPM's home schedule is three sprays at 10-day intervals from first-generation hatch, a season cap of six, and a 7-day preharvest interval. Place the first spray with the trap and degree-day count, since a spray before hatch is wasted and one after the larva has entered the pear is useless. UC IPM also names a granulosis virus (CYD-X) sold to California home gardeners that affects only codling moth larvae and, applied weekly through hatch, matched carbaryl in its trials.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Carbaryl is the old-style chemical UC IPM measures the softer options against, and it works, but at a real cost: it kills bees and the helpful insects along with the moths, so it must never go on a tree in bloom or when bees are working it, and on a pear it can set off an outbreak of pear psylla by wiping out the insects that keep psylla down. Keep it for a tree where bagging and spinosad have not held the damage, and read the label's waiting time before harvest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's home note gives carbaryl a 14-to-21-day residual against codling moth and calls it very disruptive to natural enemies and honey bees, with an absolute bar on spraying during bloom or when bees are present. On pear the secondary cost is specific: UC IPM's pear guideline attributes psylla outbreaks to nonselective codling moth insecticides destroying the predators and parasites that hold psylla in check, so a carbaryl program for the moth can buy a sticky, sooty tree by late summer. It also carries a carcinogen listing, which on a food crop is the reason to exhaust the other measures first.

pests.name: Pear psylla
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Nymphs feed in clusters on shoots and leaves and exude sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold; heavy feeding blackens and scorches leaves, drops them early, russets the fruit, and in large numbers stunts the tree and drops fruit, the reaction WSU calls psylla shock. It is a greater problem on European pears than on Asian pears.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves and young pears get coated in a sticky, shiny film that turns black and grimy (sooty mold), and the leaves may scorch and drop. Tiny insects cluster on the new shoots.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cacopsylla pyricola; a small psyllid specific to pear that overwinters as an adult and builds several overlapping generations through the season. Outbreaks follow broad-spectrum sprays that kill its natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny pear-specific insect (a kind of jumping plant louse) that sucks sap and oozes sticky stuff. It can build up fast, especially if bug sprays have wiped out the good bugs that normally keep it down.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Horticultural oil at least once in the dormant season, before buds swell, and again just before bloom if last year was bad: oil kills overwintered adults and discourages egg laying but does not control eggs. In season, insecticidal soap, kaolin or neem on the new growth; conserve natural enemies (Anthocoris and other predatory bugs, lacewings, the parasitic wasp Trechnites) by keeping broad-spectrum insecticides, including those aimed at codling moth, off the tree; kaolin before bloom to deter colonization and egg laying.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil while the tree is bare and before the buds swell, to smother the adults that lived through winter on the bark; it will not kill eggs already laid, so do not wait. In the growing season use insecticidal soap, kaolin or neem on the new shoots. Avoid harsh sprays, including strong sprays aimed at codling moth, because they kill the helpful bugs that eat psylla.
pests.prevention_seasoned: A well-timed dormant oil program plus a natural-enemy-friendly spray regime is the backbone of psylla management; avoid the lush nitrogen-pushed growth psylla favors.
pests.prevention_beginner: A dormant oil spray while the tree is bare and before the buds swell, and going easy on harsh sprays and fertilizer, keep this pear pest in check.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Feed the tree modestly and do not chase big flushes of soft new growth, because that sappy growth is what pear psylla settle on and breed in. WSU's home fact sheet puts it simply: prune lightly, give moderate nitrogen, and cut out the water sprouts and suckers that psylla favor.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Psylla nymphs feed on succulent shoot tissue, so vigor management is a population lever: WSU's Hortsense guidance is to prune lightly, supply moderate amounts of nitrogen, and remove water sprouts and suckers, which strips out the flush growth that carries the heaviest nymph loads and honeydew. The light-pruning instruction is the other half of the same idea, since hard cuts provoke exactly the regrowth psylla wants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A coat of kaolin clay, the white mineral spray, makes the tree an unattractive place for psylla to land and lay eggs. WSU's home fact sheet lists it among the growing-season options, and it does most good put on before bloom, when the overwintered adults are starting to lay. Rain washes it off, so it needs renewing, and the white film has to be rinsed off the fruit at harvest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Kaolin is a particle film that reduces adult colonization and egg laying rather than killing nymphs already feeding, which is why UC IPM's pear guideline places it prebloom and WSU's orchard program reports 80 to 100 percent less colonization and egg lay, cutting first-generation pressure. UC IPM warns that later-season use may cause mite outbreaks, and heavy use can set back beneficials, so on a home tree it is a spring measure rather than a summer one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lacewings, lady beetles and small predatory bugs eat pear psylla for free, and they are a large part of why a lightly managed tree rarely has a serious problem. The way to keep them is to not spray anything broad-spectrum on the tree, including the sprays aimed at codling moth, because UC IPM traces psylla outbreaks straight to those sprays killing off the helpers.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cacopsylla pyricola is held in check by a resident complex WSU names as the parasitic wasp Trechnites insidiosus, the predatory bugs Deraeocoris brevis, Campylomma verbasci and Anthocoris spp., green and brown lacewings, and the European earwig; UC IPM's pear guideline states that nonselective codling moth insecticides destroy many of these beneficials and produce outbreaks. On a home tree the decision is therefore made on the codling moth side: bag the fruit or use a selective material there, and the psylla largely looks after itself, which matters doubly on an Asian pear, where UC IPM rates psylla a lesser problem than on European varieties.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The backbone spray is horticultural oil while the tree is bare, put on before the buds swell, because the adults that lived through winter in bark cracks and litter around the tree are on the wood then and the oil smothers them. UC IPM says to apply it at least once in the dormant season, and to repeat just before bloom if psylla were bad the year before. Oil kills the adults; it does not kill eggs already laid, which is why the timing is early.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Adults overwinter in bark crevices, under bark scales and in litter at the base of the tree and begin ovipositing at bud swell, so a dormant oil hits the population at its narrowest point; UC IPM's pear guideline is explicit that oil kills adult psylla but does not control eggs, though it discourages egg laying for about a month, which is why the home timing is at least one application in the dormant season with a second just before bloom in a bad year. Coverage of the wood is the whole job, and oil is not applied in heat or to a water-stressed tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: During the growing season, insecticidal soap sprayed onto the shoots where the small nymphs and their sticky honeydew are will kill what it wets and nothing else. It has no lasting effect, so repeat as new nymphs appear, spray early morning or late evening, and WSU says a homeowner should not be spraying a tree taller than 10 feet at all.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Potassium salts of fatty acids work only on contact with soft-bodied nymphs, and psylla nymphs sit in honeydew on leaf undersides and in shoot tips, so coverage of the new growth decides the result; WSU's home fact sheet and Oregon State's home orchard calendar both list soap from prepink through summer. It spares the predator complex once dry, which is what makes it the in-season material over anything broad-spectrum, and WSU's rules apply: morning or evening timing, and no foliar sprays on trees over 10 feet.

pests.name: Stink bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Stink bugs, including the invasive brown marmorated stink bug, pierce developing fruit to feed, leaving dimpled, catfaced pears with hard, corky, pithy brown patches in the flesh under each feeding site. The skin often looks nearly normal while the interior is pitted. Worst near weedy field and woodland borders.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Stink bugs poke the growing pears to feed, leaving dented, lumpy fruit with hard brown corky spots inside. The outside can look mostly fine while the flesh underneath is pitted and dry.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several native stink bugs (the consperse stink bug, Euschistus conspersus, and relatives) plus the invasive brown marmorated stink bug (Halyomorpha halys). Brown marmorated adults overwinter in sheltered places, including houses and sheds, emerge in spring and move straight onto available hosts; the natives overwinter in ground litter. Adults and nymphs both feed on the fruit into harvest, moving in from weeds, neighboring crops and woodland edges, and late feeding may not show until the fruit has been stored.
pests.cause_beginner: Shield-shaped bugs, including an invasive kind called the brown marmorated stink bug, that suck on the fruit through the season. They move in from nearby weeds, fields, and woods.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Kaolin clay suppresses feeding; eliminate weeds and groundcover in early spring before the bugs build up in them; pick and destroy egg masses and groups of young nymphs, by hand, net or shaking; screen a small tree with a floating row cover or similar barrier after fruit set where practical; conserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays. Insecticides are generally not recommended for stink bugs in gardens, since the damage shows after the bugs have gone; the home products WSU lists work best on very young nymphs, are not recommended against adults, and are toxic to bees.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Coating the fruit with kaolin clay (a fine white clay spray) helps keep them off, and clearing weeds and rough grass around the tree in early spring removes the place they build up. Look under the leaves for the clusters of eggs and the bunches of small nymphs and squash them. A small tree can be covered with fine mesh once the fruit has set. Sprays are a poor answer for these bugs; by the time you see the damage they have usually moved on.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Eliminate weeds and herbaceous groundcover in early spring before stink bugs become abundant in them, and keep them down through the season; reduce broad-spectrum insecticide use so parasitic wasps, big-eyed bugs, assassin bugs, damsel bugs and crab spiders keep populations in check. Where damage recurs on a small tree, screen it after fruit set.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear the weeds and rough growth around the tree in early spring, before the bugs move into it, and keep it down all season. Go easy on strong bug sprays so the spiders and predatory bugs that eat stink bug eggs stay around. If they ruin the fruit every year on a small tree, cover it with fine mesh once the fruit has set.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stink bugs build up on weeds and rough grass around the tree and then move onto the pears, so clear that growth in early spring, before they get numerous in it, and keep the ground under and around the tree clean through summer. Timing is the point: UC IPM says to take the weeds out before the bugs are abundant in them, not after.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: NC State's handbook calls weeds the primary food source for the catfacing bugs, and UC IPM's instruction is to eliminate groundcovers and herbaceous weeds in early spring before stink bugs become abundant in them and move to alternative hosts. The brown marmorated stink bug is an edge invader that WSU and Rutgers both record moving in from wooded borders and neighboring crops, so on a home tree the reach of this measure is the ground you control; it lowers what arrives rather than what is already on the fruit.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On branches you can reach, look under the leaves for the clusters of 20 to 30 pale barrel-shaped eggs and the groups of small nymphs that hatch from them, and crush them or drop them into soapy water. WSU's pear fact sheet recommends exactly this, and it works because the young bugs stay bunched together after hatching.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Halyomorpha halys lays eggs in groups of about 20 to 30 on leaf undersides and the early nymphs feed in a cluster, which is the stage that hand removal, net-sweeping or shaking a branch over a tray actually reaches; WSU lists all three. Adults are strong fliers that arrive from outside and leave again, and UC IPM notes the feeding damage often shows only after the bugs have gone, so hand removal is aimed at the egg masses and nymph groups, not at chasing adults.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On a small or dwarf tree, WSU says a floating row cover or similar fine barrier over the canopy can keep stink bugs off the fruit where that is practical. Put it on after the flowers are finished and the fruit has set, because a cover shuts out the bees the tree needs, and take it off to pick.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: WSU's pear guidance allows screening plants with a floating row cover or similar barrier when practical, and on a tree that means a dwarf on a small frame rather than a standard; the barrier has to be sealed at the ground and go on after pollination, since pears need cross-pollination and the same mesh excludes the bees. It is the exclusion measure WSU names for this pest on pear; bagging individual fruit is not on any page read for stink bug.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A kaolin clay coating on the fruit and leaves makes the pears an unpleasant surface for stink bugs to feed on and less attractive to land on. Oregon State's home orchard guide lists it for brown marmorated stink bug, but only as suppression, so expect fewer dimpled pears rather than none, and renew it after rain.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Kaolin is a repellent film rather than a toxicant, and Oregon State's EC 631 lists it against brown marmorated stink bug on pear with the explicit qualifier suppression, which is the right expectation for a bug that flies in from the edge as an adult and probes rather than chews. Coverage of the fruit surface is what counts, so reapply as the fruit sizes and after rain, and wash the residue off at harvest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Big-eyed bugs, assassin bugs, damsel bugs, crab spiders and several tiny wasps that attack stink bug eggs are already in most gardens, and NC State says the way to keep them working is to cut back on broad-spectrum sprays. They will not give complete control on their own, WSU is clear about that, but they are part of why a lightly sprayed tree has fewer.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: NC State names parasitic wasps, big-eyed bugs, assassin bugs, damsel bugs and crab spiders as the resident enemies of the catfacing bugs, and its instruction is to reduce broad-spectrum insecticide use so they keep pest populations in check; WSU adds that natural enemies may not be sufficient for complete control of the brown marmorated stink bug but that broad-spectrum sprays should still be avoided for their sake. It is also why a spray is a poor answer here: UC IPM says insecticides are generally not recommended for stink bugs in gardens because the damage appears after the bugs have left, and WSU rates its listed home products as toxic to bees and not recommended against adults.

diseases.name: Fire blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blossoms and shoot tips suddenly wilt, blacken, and die, bending into a characteristic shepherd's-crook; affected branches look scorched, and sunken, oozing cankers form on wood. Most Asian pears are very susceptible, Shinko excepted, with Twentieth Century (Nijisseiki) rated highly susceptible; warm, wet weather at bloom drives the worst outbreaks, and the younger the tree, the more likely it dies.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Branch tips and flower clusters suddenly turn black and look burned, as if scorched by fire, and the tip bends over into a hook. It can kill whole branches or the whole tree. Asian pears catch it easily.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia amylovora; bacteria infect through open blossoms and tender shoot tips when the weather is rainy or humid with days of 75 to 85°F and nights above 55°F, and spread fastest on lush, nitrogen-pushed growth. Once infected, a tree harbors the bacterium indefinitely, and Clemson calls fire blight the most significant problem limiting the production of Asian pears.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria that infect through the flowers and soft new shoots in warm, wet spring weather. Fast, soft growth from too much fertilizer makes it much worse. Once a tree has it, it keeps it, and Clemson calls it the biggest problem there is in growing Asian pears.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out infected wood at least 8 to 12 inches below visible symptoms (Purdue and OSU say 12, WSU 12 to 18 in older wood, Clemson's Asian pear guide 18), cutting at the next branch juncture below the infection, in dry weather, with tools dipped in 10 percent bleach or 70 percent alcohol between cuts; cut placement matters more than tool sterilization. Do the main removal in the dormant season, when pruning cannot spread the bacteria, but cut rapidly advancing spring strikes at once. Remove a tree with more than half its canopy blighted. There is no cure once established; management is prevention plus cutting it out.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off the blackened branches well below the damage, at least 12 inches back into clean wood (Clemson's Asian pear guide says 18 inches), wiping your pruners with a 1-to-9 bleach mix or rubbing alcohol between cuts, and only in dry weather. Do the main cutting in winter while the tree is dormant, but a strike that is racing down a branch in spring should come off as soon as you see it. Burn or bury what you cut. There is no spray that cures it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The decisive moves are cultivar and rootstock choice: plant the more resistant Asian pears (Shinko first, then Chojuro, Seuri, Olympic, Shin Li) on a fire-blight-resistant rootstock (Old Home x Farmingdale, or the birchleaf pear Pyrus betulifolia that Clemson recommends for Asian pears). Then avoid excess nitrogen and heavy pruning, which push the succulent growth that gets infected, do not irrigate during bloom, and cut out blight in the dormant season. Copper at bloom is a partial protectant, the only material UC IPM lists for California home growers; Purdue and Clemson also describe streptomycin during bloom for home use, where it can be obtained, capped by Purdue at three to four sprays a season.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best defense is to choose a more resistant variety (Shinko, Chojuro) on a resistant rootstock, especially where summers are warm and humid. Then go easy on fertilizer (soft growth catches it) and prune only in dry weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clemson calls fire blight the most significant problem limiting Asian pears, and the biggest decision is made when you buy the tree. Shinko is the most resistant by every guide, with Chojuro, Seuri, Olympic (also sold as Korean Giant) and Shin Li showing some resistance; Twentieth Century (Nijisseiki) is highly susceptible. Buy it on a fire-blight-resistant root too: Clemson recommends the birchleaf pear (Pyrus betulifolia) for Asian pears, and the Old Home x Farmingdale rootstocks resist it as well.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resistance is partial, not immunity, and the ratings disagree at the margins: Shinko heads every list (Clemson's best, Purdue resistant, UC IPM's lone Asian exception); Purdue also rates Chojuro, Kosui, Olympic, Seuri, Shinsui, Singo and Tse Li resistant and Hosui, Kikusui, Okusankichi, Seigyoku, Twentieth Century and Shinseiki susceptible, while Clemson's two fact sheets split on Hosui, which gets planted anyway as Shinko's pollinizer. Rootstock is a separate layer: Purdue lists Old Home x Farmingdale (except OHxF 51) and Pyrus betulifolia seedlings as resistant and Bartlett seedling as susceptible, and Clemson notes betulifolia is vigorous and throws thorny root sprouts. Clemson puts cultivar choice in the same sentence as sanitation and avoiding excess nitrogen, because succulent growth is what gets infected.

control_ladder.note_beginner: No spray cures fire blight, so cutting it out is the treatment. Take each blackened shoot or branch back at least 12 inches below the last sign of damage into clean wood, and Clemson's Asian pear guide goes to 18 inches. Do the main cleanup in winter while the tree is dormant and the bacteria are inactive, but a strike racing down a branch in spring should come off as soon as you see it, and only cut in dry weather. Wipe the blades with a 1-to-9 bleach mix or rubbing alcohol between cuts, burn or bury what you remove, and if more than half the tree is blighted, Purdue says to take the tree out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Where you cut matters more than anything else: UC IPM's method is to find the lower edge of visible infection, trace the branch to its point of attachment and cut at the next branch juncture below, and both UC IPM and WSU report that cut placement matters more than tool sterilization, though dipping shears in 10 percent bleach between cuts is reasonable. The published distances run from Clemson's minimum of 8 to 12 inches through Purdue's at least 12 to WSU's 12 to 18 in wood two years old or older and Clemson's 18 inches for Asian pear, so 12 is a floor. Timing is dormant for the main removal, because growing-season pruning can spread the disease, with UC IPM's exception for rapidly advancing spring strikes on Asian pear, which come out at once; a trunk or scaffold canker can sometimes be saved by scraping bark to the cambium and taking 6 to 8 inches beyond any discolored streak, in winter. Do not shape the tree in the same pass, hold summer pruning until terminal buds have set, and keep nitrogen modest: UC IPM ties excess nitrogen and heavy pruning together as the two drivers of the succulent growth this bacterium needs.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Copper is a partial shield for the flowers, not a cure, and in UC IPM's California guidance it is the only fire blight material sold to home growers; Purdue and Clemson also describe streptomycin, an antibiotic sprayed during bloom, for home use where it can be found, and Purdue allows no more than three or four of those sprays a season. UC IPM's copper advice is a weak copper spray repeated every four to five days while the blossoms are open and the weather is warm and humid, starting once the day's average temperature tops 60°F; Clemson's simpler version is one copper spray right before bloom. It will not clear an infection already in the wood, and repeated copper can russet the fruit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Erwinia amylovora enters through open blossoms, so copper's job is to sit on the flower surface through the infection window UC IPM defines as rainy or humid weather with days of 75 to 85°F and nights above 55°F. UC IPM's program is a very weak (about 0.5 percent) Bordeaux or other copper as blossoms open once the 24-hour average temperature exceeds 60°F, at four-to-five-day intervals through late bloom, which on pear can mean five to twelve applications, and it says plainly this might reduce new infections but will not eliminate them or touch those already in wood. Copper accumulates in soil and can russet fruit, which is the case for Clemson's single pre-bloom spray on a tree not under heavy pressure. Streptomycin, the bloom antibiotic in the extension literature, is written for apple and capped by Purdue at three to four bloom sprays where it can be obtained at all. Do not irrigate during bloom.

diseases.name: Pear scab
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves, shoots, and fruit; fruit lesions crack, letting rot organisms in, and early-infected fruit ends up scabby and misshapen; severe infection yellows leaves and causes early defoliation. The pear analog of apple scab, and Asian pears are less susceptible to it than European pears.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, fuzzy olive-to-black spots on the leaves, and rough, scabby, cracked patches on the pears. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early. Asian pears get it less than European pears.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Venturia pirina; the fungus overwinters primarily in fallen leaves, and in high-rainfall areas also in lesions on pear twigs, and infects during wet spring weather, most rapidly between 55 and 75°F with a minimum of 9 hours of continuous leaf wetness. Distinct from the apple-scab fungus but managed the same way.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that overwinters in last year's fallen leaves and spreads onto new leaves and fruit in cool, wet spring weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sulfur or a labeled fungicide on a protective spring schedule keyed to infection periods; prevention beats cure.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Sulfur spray in spring before the spots appear is the organic route. Once it is widespread it is too late for that year.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves each autumn or winter, which destroys the main overwintering source and on a single backyard tree can hold scab to tolerable levels; in high-rainfall areas the fungus also overwinters in twig lesions. Fungicide is needed only when rain keeps leaves wet 9 hours or more. Asian pears as a species are less susceptible than European pears, and a spray is only needed in a wet spring.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The single best move is to rake up and remove fallen leaves every autumn, because that is where the fungus hides over winter; on one backyard tree that alone usually keeps scab at a level you can live with. Asian pears get it less than European pears, so most years need nothing more.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Asian pears get scab less than European pears, UC IPM says so directly, and for a single backyard tree the whole program can be raking. The fungus spends the winter in last year's fallen leaves, so gather them up in autumn or winter and compost them thoroughly or get rid of them; UC IPM says that alone can hold scab to a level you can live with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Venturia pirina overwinters primarily in infected leaves on the ground, and UC IPM PN 7413 states that for a single backyard tree removing and composting or destroying the dropped leaves in autumn or winter can limit the disease to tolerable levels. In high-rainfall areas the fungus also carries over in lesions on pear twigs, which raking does not reach, and for several trees in a cool coastal climate PN 7413 adds urea on the foliage in autumn to hasten leaf fall (urea alone on pear, since zinc is phytotoxic to it), lime on the leaf piles, and running any sprinkler that wets foliage only between sunrise and noon so the leaves dry.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A spray is only worth it in a wet spring: UC IPM says fungicide is needed only when rain keeps the leaves wet for 9 hours or more. If that is your weather, sulfur goes on as the buds break, again 10 to 14 days later if it is still raining, and not past a month after petal fall. Never put sulfur on when it is near 90°F or hotter. And never mix it with oil or spray it close to an oil spray, because the pair burns leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Infection needs a minimum of 9 hours of continuous leaf wetness and runs fastest between 55 and 75°F, which is why PN 7413 makes fungicide conditional on rainy weather and puts the whole protective window between bud break and a month after petal fall, with a second application 10 to 14 days after the first if rain continues, once blossom clusters show but before they open. A protectant has no curative reach, so a spray after lesions appear is a season already lost; PN 7413 lists it for home use alongside fixed copper, Bordeaux, copper soap and neem or mineral oils. Sulfur and oil are never combined or applied close together. Sulfur is not applied near or above 90°F. On Asian pear, which PN 7413 rates less susceptible than European pear, most years will not meet the wet-weather trigger at all.

diseases.name: Pear decline
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Slow decline: the tree leafs out late in spring, leaves are small, thicken, curl downward and redden early, growth is weak and yield falls; or quick decline, where foliage wilts rapidly and the tree dies within days. A brown line of dead phloem at the graft union is the diagnostic mark. Driven by a phytoplasma transmitted by pear psylla and expressed through a sensitive rootstock.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The tree slowly weakens over years, with small leaves that redden early in fall and a shrinking crop, or sometimes a sudden collapse. It is tied to the pear psylla insect and to certain rootstocks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Candidatus Phytoplasma pyri, a phytoplasma (a bacteria-like organism) carried mainly by pear psylla, which injects it while feeding, and also passed on by grafting or budding with wood from an infected tree. It kills phloem cells at the graft union of sensitive root-scion combinations, so the roots starve; severity therefore depends on the rootstock, and pear on Asian pear roots (Pyrus pyrifolia, P. ussuriensis) can be killed rapidly while Old Home x Farmingdale and other tolerant roots hold up.
diseases.cause_beginner: A tiny disease organism carried by the pear psylla insect. How badly a tree is hit depends on its rootstock, so a resistant rootstock is the main protection.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No spray or treatment for the tree itself is listed by UC IPM or Utah State, and UC IPM reports no known biological control of the phytoplasma; management is a tolerant rootstock chosen at planting (Old Home x Farmingdale, Bartlett seedling, Pyrus betulifolia, Winter Nelis), keeping pear psylla down to cut transmission, and vigor. Remove a tree in quick decline; a tree in slow decline may benefit from more nitrogen and frequent, light irrigation.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no spray for it. Keep pear psylla under control, since that is the main way it spreads (grafting or budding wood from a sick tree can pass it on too), and, most importantly, start with a tolerant rootstock when you plant. A tree that collapses suddenly should be removed; one that is fading slowly can often be kept going with a little more fertilizer and frequent light watering.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on a rootstock that tolerates decline and resists fire blight: OHxF 87, 97, 333 or 40, which WSU rates against both diseases, or Pyrus betulifolia. Bartlett seedling and Winter Nelis are also on UC IPM's decline-tolerant list, but Bartlett seedling is rated fire-blight susceptible on this crop's fire blight entry, so it is not the root to specify for an Asian pear. Keep psylla populations low. The sensitive roots are Asian pear seedlings themselves, Pyrus pyrifolia and P. ussuriensis, so an Asian pear on its own species' seedling is the worst case; and if top-working an Asian pear to a European cultivar, graft below the Asian pear's own union.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy a tree grown on a rootstock that stands up to both decline and fire blight (the OHxF series, or birchleaf pear), never on Asian pear seedling roots, and keep pear psylla in check.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pear decline is a disease of the graft union, so the roots your tree was grafted onto decide almost everything, and you choose them once, at the nursery. Ask for a tree on an Old Home x Farmingdale rootstock (OHxF 87, 97, 333 or 40), which WSU lists as resistant or tolerant to decline and to fire blight as well, or on birchleaf pear (Pyrus betulifolia), which UC IPM lists as decline-tolerant and which this crop's fire blight entry also recommends. Bartlett seedling is on UC IPM's tolerant list for decline, but it is rated fire-blight susceptible (see fire blight), and fire blight is the most serious disease of Asian pears, so it is not the root to ask for here. Avoid a tree on Asian pear seedling roots, because UC IPM says decline can rapidly kill a pear on Pyrus pyrifolia or Pyrus ussuriensis roots, and an Asian pear grown on its own kind of seedling is exactly that case. The other half of protection is keeping pear psylla down, since feeding psylla are the main way the disease moves from tree to tree; graft wood or buds taken from an infected pear can carry it too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Candidatus Phytoplasma pyri is injected by feeding pear psylla and kills phloem at the graft union of sensitive root-scion combinations, so sugar piles up above the union as starch while the roots starve; the brown line of dead phloem at the union is the field diagnostic, and quick decline is the tree collapsing within days once the union fails. Tolerance sits in the root: UC IPM lists Bartlett seedling, Old Home x Farmingdale, Pyrus betulaefolia and Winter Nelis seedling as tolerant and P. pyrifolia (P. serotina) and P. ussuriensis as the roots on which decline rapidly kills, and WSU's rootstock notes name OHxF 87 as tolerant to blight and decline and OHxF 97, 333 and 40 as resistant to it. One Asian-specific rule from Utah State: if you ever graft an Asian pear over to a European cultivar, graft below the union of the Asian pear and its rootstock, or you build a highly decline-susceptible tree. Reducing psylla abundance reduces transmission, which is why the psylla program on this crop is also the decline program.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pear psylla are not the only way this disease gets into a tree: a bud or a piece of graft wood cut from an infected pear carries the disease with it, so a branch of another variety grafted onto your tree, or a new tree started from an old one, can bring decline in even where psylla are scarce. Take graft wood only from a pear that has never shown signs of decline, and where you have the choice, start with a nursery tree instead of wood from a pear whose history you do not know.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Utah State's note on this disease adds grafting and budding to psylla as routes of transmission, which puts the source of scionwood and budwood on the same footing as the rootstock. Its field check is done with a knife on the donor tree: expose the cambium just under the bark at the graft union and look for a brown line, the dead phloem that UC IPM also describes at the union of an infected tree; wood from a tree that shows it is not used for propagation or top-working. Since no material listed by UC IPM or Utah State acts on the phytoplasma once it is in the tree, the choice is made once, when the wood is cut or the tree is bought.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A tree that collapses suddenly, wilting and dying within days, is not coming back and should be removed, both because UC IPM and Utah State list nothing that treats the disease inside it and because pear psylla can carry the infection from it to your other pears. A tree in slow decline is a different case: UC IPM says it may respond to more nitrogen and frequent light watering, so it can often be kept going for years.
