Cover the tree or move a container lime under cover on any freeze night, and expect a hard-freeze year to cost part of the crop.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: Lime fruits well in the Rio Grande Valley in most winters. Elsewhere in Texas it is often too tender to grow outdoors at all, and even in the Valley it is the most cold-sensitive citrus, so a hard-freeze year can damage or set back a Persian lime that milder-mannered grapefruit or orange would shrug off. It flowers more than once a year, with the main harvest from fall into winter.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Lime is the most cold-tender common citrus, unsuitable or only a container crop through most of Texas, and it is a marginal crop even in the Rio Grande Valley: mild, near-frost-free winters let Persian lime fruit well most years, but the Valley's documented history of periodic hard freezes hits lime hardest of all the Valley's citrus. Repeat bloom flushes through spring keep fruit setting across much of the year, with the main crop ripening October into February. Heat is ample and never a limiting factor for lime.
rgv.cold_basis_seasoned: Lime is the most cold-tender common citrus: foliage and fruit damage in the high 20s°F, and wood dies outright in the harder freezes that periodically reach the Valley as they do the rest of the state. The winter-low band used here, roughly 24 to 34°F, is a synthesis anchored to the closest analog frost-free citrus regions, the milder Gulf Coast and the Arizona low desert, not a single verbatim figure from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension; that source is the basis for the bloom and harvest windows above.
rgv.cold_basis_beginner: Lime is hurt by cold more easily than any other citrus. Valley winters are mild most years, but a hard freeze does periodically come through, and lime is always the first tree hurt when it does. Cover the tree or bring a container lime indoors on freeze nights.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 is far too cold for an in-ground lime. Lime is the most cold-tender common citrus: even the hardier Persian (Tahiti) type suffers wood damage below about 26°F, and this zone's coldest nights drop well below that. There is no in-ground establishment window here; grow it as a container tree brought fully indoors for winter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for a lime tree outside. Lime is hurt by cold more easily than almost any other citrus. Grow it in a pot you bring fully indoors for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: This region's periodic harder freeze, on top of an already-cold zone 8 winter, is easily enough to kill lime wood outright; lime has the least cold tolerance of the common citrus.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9's milder coastal and protected pockets still see winter lows that reach the mid-20s°F or colder in an ordinary year, cold enough to kill Persian (Tahiti) lime wood outright and well past the point that damages the even more tender Key (Mexican) lime. Lime remains unsuitable for in-ground planting even in the region's mildest zone; a container tree brought fully indoors for winter is the only workable approach.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Even in the milder pockets, winters here get cold enough most years to kill a lime tree outright. Grow it in a pot indoors for winter instead.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Lime's wood-damage threshold (mid-20s°F for Persian/Tahiti, even milder cold for Key/Mexican) sits inside zone 9's ordinary winter-low range here, not just its rare deep-freeze years, so outdoor culture is not a defensible call even at the region's mild edge.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Skip lime outdoors in the maritime Pacific Northwest. It is the most cold-sensitive common citrus, and even our milder zone 9 pockets get cold enough most winters to kill it. Grow it in a container you bring fully indoors for the winter.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Lime is a clear no for in-ground planting anywhere in the maritime Pacific Northwest. It is the least cold-hardy of the common citrus, with wood damage starting in the mid-20s°F for Persian (Tahiti) lime and even milder cold hurting Key (Mexican) lime, and both of this region's zones see winter lows in that range in an ordinary year, not only in a rare severe one. A container tree moved fully indoors for winter is the only viable way to grow one here.
pnw.cold_basis_seasoned: Zone 8 (roughly 10 to 20°F) and zone 9 (roughly 20 to 30°F) both see ordinary winter lows at or below lime's wood-damage threshold, mid-20s°F for the hardier Persian (Tahiti) type and milder still for Key (Mexican) lime, so this is not an occasional-freeze risk but a routine one for this crop specifically (Clemson HGIC, Texas A&M AgriLife).
pnw.cold_basis_beginner: Lime is hurt by cold more easily than almost any other citrus, and our winters here, even in the milder spots, routinely get cold enough to kill it.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Lime is the most cold-tender common citrus: even the hardier Persian (Tahiti) type suffers wood damage below about 26 to 28°F, and the Piedmont's hard freezes drop well past that most winters. There is no in-ground establishment window this far inland; grow it as a container tree brought fully indoors for winter.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for a lime tree outside. Lime is hurt by cold more easily than almost any other citrus, and winters here regularly get colder than that. Grow it in a pot you bring fully indoors for winter.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard freeze every winter, not an occasional event, rules out in-ground lime in the Piedmont.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone still sees hard freezes into the teens and low 20s°F most winters, well past the mid-20s°F point where even the hardier Persian (Tahiti) lime suffers wood damage, and lime lacks any real cold-hardy selection the way lemon (Meyer) or mandarin (satsuma) do. In-ground planting is not viable here either; a container tree brought fully indoors for winter is the only workable approach.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Milder than the colder inland part of this region, but still cold enough most winters to kill a lime tree outright. Lime does not have a cold-hardy option the way lemon and mandarin do. Grow it in a pot indoors for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Even the Coastal Plain's milder hard freezes, into the teens and low 20s°F most winters, comfortably exceed lime's wood-damage threshold; lime has no cold-hardy cultivar to fall back on.

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Skip lime outdoors anywhere in the Mid-Atlantic. It is the most cold-sensitive common citrus, more so than lemon or mandarin, and both parts of this region get cold enough most winters to kill it outright. Grow it in a container you bring fully indoors for winter.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: Lime is a clear no for in-ground planting anywhere in this belt. It is the least cold-hardy of the common citrus, with wood damage in even the hardier Persian (Tahiti) type starting around 26 to 28°F, and unlike lemon (which has the hardier Meyer hybrid) or mandarin (which has cold-hardy satsuma), lime has no widely grown cold-tolerant selection to soften the picture. Both of this region's zones see hard freezes well past that threshold in an ordinary winter, the cooler Piedmont every year and the milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater most years. A container tree moved fully indoors for winter is the only viable way to grow one here.
mid_atlantic.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 10 to 20°F in the milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone to 0 to 10°F in the cooler Piedmont interior, both well past the 26 to 28°F point where even the hardiest common lime cultivar (Persian/Tahiti) takes wood damage (Clemson HGIC; Texas A&M AgriLife). Lime is the least cold-tolerant of the common citrus and has no cold-hardy selection comparable to Meyer lemon or satsuma mandarin.
mid_atlantic.cold_basis_beginner: Lime is hurt by cold more easily than almost any other citrus, and this region's winters, in both zones, routinely get cold enough to kill it.

mid_south.region_label: Mid-South: Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands

In-ground planting is not viable here either; a container tree brought fully indoors for winter is the only workable approach.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Milder than the colder inland part of this region, but still cold enough most winters to kill a lime tree outright. Lime does not have a cold-hardy option the way lemon and mandarin do. Grow it in a pot indoors for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Even the lowland South's milder hard freezes, into the teens and low 20s°F most winters, comfortably exceed lime's wood-damage threshold; lime has no cold-hardy cultivar to fall back on.

mid_south.region_notes_beginner: Skip lime outdoors anywhere in the Mid-South. It is the most cold-sensitive common citrus, more so than lemon or mandarin, and both parts of this region get cold enough most winters to kill it outright. Grow it in a container you bring fully indoors for winter.
mid_south.region_notes_seasoned: Lime is a clear no for in-ground planting anywhere in this belt. It is the least cold-hardy of the common citrus, with wood damage in even the hardier Persian (Tahiti) type starting around 26 to 28°F, and unlike lemon (which has the hardier Meyer hybrid) or mandarin (which has cold-hardy satsuma), lime has no widely grown cold-tolerant selection to soften the picture. Both of this region's zones see hard freezes well past that threshold in an ordinary winter, the cooler Ozark uplands every year and the milder lowland South and Delta most years. A container tree moved fully indoors for winter is the only viable way to grow one here.
mid_south.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 10 to 20°F in the milder lowland South and Delta zone to 0 to 10°F in the cooler Ozark uplands interior, both well past the 26 to 28°F point where even the hardiest common lime cultivar (Persian/Tahiti) takes wood damage (Clemson HGIC; Texas A&M AgriLife). Lime is the least cold-tolerant of the common citrus and has no cold-hardy selection comparable to Meyer lemon or satsuma mandarin.
mid_south.cold_basis_beginner: Lime is hurt by cold more easily than almost any other citrus, and this region's winters, in both zones, routinely get cold enough to kill it.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Lime is the most cold-tender common citrus: even the hardier Persian (Tahiti) type takes damage near 32°F, essentially at the freezing point, and this zone's cooler, higher pockets drop well past that on almost every winter night. There is no in-ground establishment window here at all; grow it as a container tree brought fully indoors for winter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for a lime tree outside. Lime is hurt by cold more easily than almost any other citrus, damaged practically at freezing, and winters here regularly get colder than that. Grow it in a pot you bring fully indoors for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard freeze every winter in this zone is well past lime's freezing-point damage threshold.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Even the Las Vegas Valley floor is too cold for lime in an ordinary winter: this zone's typical coldest nights, in the 20s°F, sit well below lime's roughly 32°F damage point, and the valley floor, at about 2,000 feet, runs colder in winter than the lower Phoenix desert (near 1,100 feet), where lime is likewise the region's most cold-exposed citrus. There is no in-ground planting here; even a container specimen needs to come fully indoors, not just under cover, whenever a freeze threatens.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Lime does not work outdoors in the Las Vegas Valley either. It is damaged by cold that is barely below freezing, and our valley winters routinely get colder than that. Keep it as a houseplant you bring fully indoors for winter.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The valley's ordinary winter lows (last freeze around Feb 28, first around Nov 25, NWS Las Vegas normals) run well below lime's roughly 32°F damage threshold on its coldest nights.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Laughlin/Colorado River corner is the only part of this region where lime has a real chance: ordinary winter lows here mostly sit above lime's roughly 32°F damage point, so a well-protected container tree can survive. This is a single small area with no dedicated local citrus field data, and a periodic harder freeze can still dip into lime's damage range, so this stays a protected container prospect, never a dependable in-ground or fruiting tree; lime remains the most cold-exposed citrus in this batch even at its best Nevada location.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Laughlin is the one spot in this region where a potted lime has a real shot at surviving winter, but even there keep it in a container you can protect or bring indoors on cold nights. It is still the most cold-sensitive citrus tree.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Even the region's mildest corner sees an occasional harder freeze that can reach lime's roughly 32°F damage threshold; keep the tree in a container you can move under full cover.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Skip lime outdoors almost everywhere in this region. It is hurt by cold more easily than any other common citrus, damaged practically at the freezing point, so even the Las Vegas Valley is too cold for it. Only the warmest Laughlin corner gives a protected container lime a real chance, and even there it needs to come fully indoors on cold nights.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: Lime is the clearest no in this region's citrus lineup for anywhere but its single mildest corner. It is the least cold-hardy of the common citrus, with wood and fruit damage in even the hardier Persian (Tahiti) type starting near 32°F, essentially the freezing point itself. The region's cooler zone-8 pockets and, notably, the Las Vegas Valley floor (zone 9) itself both see ordinary winter lows well below that threshold; the valley floor, at about 2,000 feet, runs colder in winter than the lower Phoenix desert (near 1,100 feet), where lime is already the most cold-exposed citrus grown. Only the Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10), the region's mildest pocket, sits close enough to lime's threshold for a well-protected container tree to survive, and even there it is not a fruiting planting. A container tree moved fully indoors on any freeze night is the only viable way to grow lime anywhere in this belt.
nevada.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 30 to 40°F in the mild Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10) to 20 to 30°F in the Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) to 10 to 20°F in the region's cooler, higher pockets (zone 8), all at or below lime's roughly 32°F wood- and fruit-damage point except at the mildest zone-10 edge. Lime is the least cold-tolerant of the common citrus and has no cold-hardy selection comparable to Meyer lemon or satsuma mandarin; the Las Vegas Valley floor, at about 2,000 feet, runs colder in winter than the lower Phoenix desert (near 1,100 feet).
nevada.cold_basis_beginner: Lime is hurt by cold more easily than almost any other citrus, and this region's winters, even in the Las Vegas Valley itself, routinely get cold enough to kill it. Only the warmest Laughlin corner gives it a real chance, and even there it needs protection.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost data) are far past lime's own freezing-point damage threshold, the most cold-sensitive of the common citrus, and citrus is absent altogether from USU's Washington County Fruits recommendation for this elevation. There is no dependable outdoor or long-term container option here; a lime tree needs full indoor housing through the cold season to survive at all.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Lime is hurt by cold more easily than any other common citrus, damaged practically at the freezing point, and St. George winters, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, regularly drop well below that. This is not a realistic tree to try outdoors here, even in a container brought in only on cold nights; it needs to live indoors through winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter cold (last frost near March 30, first frost near November 1, USU Extension Washington County) is a hard freeze far past lime's own freezing-point damage threshold, the most cold-sensitive of the common citrus.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Lime does not work outdoors in St. George. It is hurt by cold more easily than any other common citrus, damaged practically at freezing, and winters here, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, regularly drop well below that.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's zone 8b winters run roughly 15 to 20°F on an ordinary cold night, far past lime's own freezing-point damage threshold, the most cold-sensitive of the common citrus and one with no hardy selection comparable to Meyer lemon or clementine mandarin. USU's Washington County Fruits page, which names the fruits recommended at this elevation, includes no citrus at all. A lime here needs full indoor housing through the cold season; there is no honest outdoor or seasonal-container call to make.
utah_dixie.cold_basis_seasoned: St. George sits in USDA zone 8b, with ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost and elevation data). Lime is the least cold-tolerant common citrus, damaged at or near the freezing point itself, and has no cold-hardy selection comparable to Meyer lemon or clementine mandarin. USU's Washington County Fruits page, which lists the fruits recommended at this elevation, names no citrus at all.
utah_dixie.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here bring ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, far past the point where lime, the most cold-sensitive common citrus, takes damage right around freezing. There is no hardy lime type to fall back on, so this is not a realistic outdoor tree here.

crops.description_seasoned: Lime (Citrus, chiefly Citrus latifolia and Citrus aurantifolia) is an evergreen subtropical tree grown for its tart, aromatic green fruit and near-continuous productivity in warm climates. Limes are the most cold-tender of the common citrus, more frost-sensitive than lemons, so outside the mildest zones they are grown in containers moved to shelter for winter. The mainstream choice is the seedless Persian (Tahiti) lime; the small, seedy, intensely aromatic Key (Mexican) lime is the tender specialty. Limes are everbearing, mature fruit fast (about 90 to 120 days from bloom), and are picked green, not yellow.
crops.description_beginner: The lime is an evergreen tree that grows in warm climates and gives tart, fragrant green fruit for much of the year. Limes are the citrus most easily hurt by cold, even more than lemons, so in most of the country people grow them in a pot and bring them indoors for winter. The common one is the seedless Persian (Tahiti) lime; the little, seedy Key (Mexican) lime is more aromatic but far more tender. The key thing to remember: pick limes while they are still green, not yellow.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest limes green, at full size, when they feel heavy for their size and juicy. A Persian lime is picked dark to medium-green at about 1.75 inches across; a Key lime is small and, though UF/IFAS notes it matures to a yellow peel, is commonly picked green for kitchen use. This is the reverse of the lemon rule: a yellowing lime is overripe, lower in acid, and near dropping. Clip or twist fruit free. Fruit matures about 90 to 120 days after bloom, with the heaviest crop in summer.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick limes while they are still green and full-sized, when they feel heavy and juicy. Unlike lemons, do not wait for them to turn yellow, which means they are overripe. Twist or snip the fruit off. Limes ripen about three to four months after flowering, with the biggest harvest in summer.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Limes are everbearing: they flower and set fruit across several flushes through much of the year, with the heaviest bloom from late winter into spring (February to April in Florida) and a summer-weighted harvest. Fruit matures fast, in roughly 90 to 120 days from bloom, much quicker than a lemon's many months, so flowers, green fruit, and ripe fruit are often on the tree together. In tropical climates bloom and harvest run nearly continuously. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH093, UF/IFAS CH092.)
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Limes bloom heaviest in late winter and spring but flower on and off much of the year, so you often see flowers and fruit on the tree at once. Each lime ripens fairly fast, in about three to four months, and the biggest harvest comes in summer.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Limes are among the most frost-tender of the common citrus, with Key (Mexican) lime the tenderest of all: UF/IFAS reports foliage damage at 30°F to 32°F and wood death below 29°F. Persian (Tahiti) lime is somewhat hardier, with foliage damage below about 28°F, wood damage below 26°F, and severe injury or death below 24°F, still less hardy than grapefruit or orange. In the landscape limes fruit dependably only in nearly frost-free zones (roughly 10 to 11), are marginal and need active freeze protection in zone 9, and cannot survive in-ground below about zone 9a. Texas A&M advises potting limes so they can be moved indoors during freezes. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093, Texas A&M AgriLife.)
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Limes are among the citrus most easily hurt by frost. Key (Mexican) lime is damaged right around freezing (30°F to 32°F), and even the hardier Persian (Tahiti) lime is hurt in the high 20s°F. Plan on growing one outdoors year-round only in a nearly frost-free spot (roughly zones 10 to 11). Anywhere colder, grow it in a pot you can move indoors when frost is coming.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Limes are subtropical evergreens with essentially no winter chilling requirement (about 0 chill hours). They never go fully dormant, so bloom is triggered by warmth rather than by accumulated winter cold. Chill hours, the limiter for deciduous fruit like peaches and apples, are not what governs where a lime fruits; frost is, and limes have the least frost tolerance of the common citrus. (Sources: UF/IFAS, UC ANR.)
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Limes do not need a cold winter to fruit. What they cannot handle is freezing, less than any other citrus. That is the thing to plan around.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Lime flowers are fragrant and visited by honey bees, but the tree is self-fruitful and Persian lime is parthenocarpic (it sets seedless fruit without pollination), so pollinators improve set rather than being required. The main case where it matters is a tree kept permanently indoors, away from insects, which may set lighter and can be hand-pollinated with a small brush. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH093, UC ANR.)
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Bees like lime flowers, but you do not need to do anything. A lime tree sets fruit on its own, and a Persian lime even makes seedless fruit without any pollination.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Limes need well-drained soil above all else: they do not tolerate flooded conditions, and poor drainage invites Phytophthora foot rot. They grow well in sand and in the shallow calcareous rocklands of south Florida, but sharp drainage is the constant. Plant on a raised mound or bed on heavy clay, set the tree so the graft union sits well above grade, and never dig a watering basin that holds water against the trunk. Keep organic mulch at least a foot from the trunk. On alkaline or calcareous soils, plan on nutritional micronutrient sprays and chelated iron. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick a spot where water never sits after rain; limes grow fine in sandy or rocky soil as long as it drains. On heavy clay, plant on a low mound so the roots stay drained. Keep the knobby graft on the trunk above the soil line, and keep mulch a hand's width back from the trunk. In alkaline soil, plan to add iron and other micronutrients.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Limes are self-fruitful: a single tree sets a full crop with no second variety nearby. Key lime and Persian lime both fruit without cross-pollination, and Persian (Tahiti) lime is parthenocarpic, setting seedless fruit without pollination at all. Flowers are visited by bees, which improve set but are not required. A tree kept permanently indoors may set lighter, so hand-moving pollen with a small brush can help. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one lime tree. It pollinates itself and fruits on its own, and a Persian lime makes seedless fruit with no pollination needed. Bees just help it along.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: Limes need little pruning. Do any shaping or thinning in late winter to early spring before the new flush, never in fall (which pushes tender growth into cold that a tender lime cannot afford) and never a hard dormant-season cut (the tree is never dormant). Remove dead, crossing, or frost-damaged wood, and always strip shoots arising below the graft union, which come from the rootstock. Wait for spring regrowth before cutting freeze-damaged wood, so you can see what survived.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Limes barely need pruning. In late winter or early spring, before new growth starts, snip out any dead or crossing branches and pull off shoots growing from below the graft (the knobby bend low on the trunk). Do not prune in fall, and after a freeze wait for spring growth before cutting off damaged wood so you can see what lived.

crops.establishment_note: A grafted lime usually sets a few fruit in its second year and begins a real crop in about its third year, building toward full production over the following years; air-layered or cutting-grown Key limes can fruit within a year, while seedlings take a year or two longer. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Rootstocks are usually not a choice at retail garden centers, because trees come grafted onto industry-standard rootstocks. Match the rootstock to your soil. For high-pH, calcareous soils, UF/IFAS lists alemow, rough lemon and Volkamer lemon among suitable rootstocks. For low-pH or neutral soils, it names Swingle citrumelo. Key limes are susceptible to tristeza virus whatever the rootstock. Tahiti limes may be susceptible to severe strains whatever the rootstock. Key lime is often grown from seed, which comes true to type, and it can also be grown from cuttings, air-layers or grafted trees.

rootstock_options.name: rough lemon / Volkamer lemon (Citrus jambhiri, C. volkameriana)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: If your soil is alkaline, ask whether the tree is on rough lemon, Volkamer lemon or another rootstock suited to high-pH soil.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: UF/IFAS lists rough lemon and Volkamer lemon among rootstocks for limes in high-pH, calcareous soils, including rockland and some sandy soils. Trees on rough lemon are extremely vigorous. Rough lemon is highly susceptible to Phytophthora foot rot. UF/IFAS rates both as large trees under Florida grove conditions. On rough lemon, Tahiti limes may also be susceptible to less-severe tristeza strains.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A vigorous rootstock for alkaline soil, including rocky ground and some sandy soils. Rough lemon is prone to foot rot. Both make large trees.

rootstock_options.name: Swingle citrumelo (trifoliate hybrid)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: On neutral or acidic soil, ask whether the tree is on Swingle citrumelo.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Swingle is a citrumelo, a cross of Duncan grapefruit and trifoliate orange. UF/IFAS names it the rootstock for limes on low-pH or neutral soils. It resists Phytophthora foot rot. UC Riverside lists resistance to tristeza and cold among its strengths. It became the most widely used rootstock in Florida. It is not adapted to heavy clay or calcareous soils.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A common rootstock that resists foot rot, best on soil that is not alkaline. It also holds up against tristeza virus and cold.

rootstock_options.name: Alemow (Citrus macrophylla)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Alemow suits alkaline soil and tolerates brief flooding. It is very sensitive to frost.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Alemow (Citrus macrophylla) is on UF/IFAS's list of rootstocks for limes in high-pH, calcareous soils. Trees grafted onto alemow tolerate a few days of excessively wet or flooded soil. The brown citrus aphid spreads tristeza virus, which may cause decline and death of Tahiti lime trees on alemow. Tahiti limes on alemow may also be susceptible to less-severe tristeza strains. UC rates it highly sensitive to frost.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Alemow is a rootstock for alkaline soil that copes with a few days of flooding. It is vulnerable to tristeza, a virus spread by aphids that can kill lime trees on it, and it is very sensitive to frost.

pet_safe.note: The fruit is fine, but the peel, leaves, and citrus oils can upset the stomach of cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about establishing the tree, and with lime the first decision is where it lives. Limes are the most cold-tender citrus there is, so outside a truly frost-free area an in-ground lime is a gamble that a potted one avoids. Plant only once all frost danger has passed. Set the graft union, the knobby joint low on the trunk where your lime was joined to its roots, two to three inches clear of the finished soil, and keep mulch off the trunk, because a union sitting damp is how citrus gets foot rot. Pinch off every flower and any fruit that sets this year: one or two early limes cost you a slower, weaker tree. Feed little and often with a citrus fertilizer rather than one heavy dose.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Siting is the governing first-year decision for this crop specifically: lime is the most cold-sensitive of the common citrus, so outside genuinely frost-free ground a container is the defensible choice and keeps the tree movable. Plant after all frost risk has passed. Set the graft union two to three inches proud of finished grade and keep mulch clear of the trunk, against foot rot and gummosis. Strip all first-year bloom and set. Feed little and often through the season; UF/IFAS starts young limes at roughly a quarter pound per application, which suits a shallow, salt-sensitive root system far better than one heavy dose. In humid regions, water the ground rather than the canopy, since wetting open tissue feeds the Colletotrichum postbloom fruit drop that makes lime fruitlets abscise.
crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: A grafted lime usually sets its first few fruit in the second year. Keep soil moisture even right through flowering, since a dry spell at bloom is what makes a young tree shed its blossoms and small fruit. In a humid area, water the ground rather than the flowers: wetting open blossoms feeds postbloom fruit drop, a disease that makes the tiny limes fall off. Limes mature fast once set, in roughly 90 to 120 days, so the window between flower and fruit is short and steady watering through it matters more than anything else you can do.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: Expect a token second-year set on a grafted tree; air-layered or cutting-grown Key limes can fruit inside a year, seedlings a year or two later. Moisture stability through bloom governs retention, and lime is self-fruitful with Persian lime parthenocarpic, so the task is protecting existing flowers from stress rather than securing pollination. In humid regions irrigate at ground level: wetting open blossoms feeds Colletotrichum postbloom fruit drop, and full sun with airflow suppresses it. Fruit development runs only about 90 to 120 days, so the interval between set and maturity is short and unforgiving of wet-dry swings. On calcareous or sandy ground, interveinal chlorosis on new leaves signals the iron, manganese and zinc deficiency lime shows on alkaline soil; chelated iron and nutritional sprays correct it, a plain fertilizer will not.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From about the third year the tree carries a real crop, and the thing to watch is how long you leave fruit hanging. A lime that stays on the tree too long turns yellow, and that yellow is not ripeness, it is the fruit going past: acid has dropped, flavor has flattened, and it is close to falling. So treat yellowing as your deadline rather than your signal. Pick at full size while the skin is still dark to medium green, which is when juice and acid are at their peak. Do not try to store them like lemons either. Limes are short-lived once picked and are damaged by cold, so keep them only cool, around 50°F, rather than properly cold, use them fresh, and turn a heavy summer pick into frozen juice and zest. Protect the tree on every freeze night even when mature, because cold that merely nips a mandarin can kill lime wood.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from roughly year three. Harvest at full size while the rind is still dark to medium green, when juice and acid peak. Yellowing on the tree is a harvest deadline rather than a maturity index: it marks declining acid and imminent abscission, so fruit allowed to color is already past its useful window. Postharvest handling also diverges from the rest of citrus: lime is short-lived off the tree and chilling-sensitive, so hold around 50°F rather than refrigerating properly cold, move fruit fresh, and process a heavy flush to frozen juice and zest. Keep pruning light, confined to deadwood, crossing limbs and rootstock suckers below the graft, and time shaping to late winter or early spring ahead of the flush rather than fall, so tender growth is not pushed into cold. Freeze protection remains mandatory at every maturity: temperatures that merely defoliate a mandarin kill lime wood.

crops.name: Orange (Navel)

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Deep, well-drained loam to sandy loam
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Deep, well-draining soil is best, ideally loam or sandy loam.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Sandy and rocky soils with adequate water and feeding; clay only on a raised mound or berm that guarantees drainage
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Sandy and rocky soils are fine as long as you water and feed enough. Clay only works if you plant on a raised mound that keeps the water draining away.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Heavy, poorly drained clay and any site where water stands, which invites Phytophthora foot and root rot
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Avoid heavy clay that drains poorly, and any spot where water collects and stands. Wet feet can lead to a disease called root rot.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Oranges care most about good drainage. They like deep soil that drains well and stays slightly acidic, kept evenly moist but never soggy. If water sits around the roots, the tree can get a root rot that is the most common way citrus trees die. Heavy clay soil is a problem because it holds water; the fix is to build a low mound or berm and set the tree on top so the crown stays above the slow-draining ground. Keep the knobby graft union above the soil. If your soil is alkaline (high-pH), which is common in the desert and inland West, the tree may not get enough iron and zinc, so use a citrus fertilizer that includes those.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Navel oranges demand sharp drainage above all else. They thrive in deep, well-drained loam or sandy loam, slightly acidic, with steady moisture but no waterlogging. The single most important soil decision is drainage: saturated roots lead to Phytophthora foot and root rot, the disease most likely to kill a citrus tree. On heavy clay, plant high on a raised mound or berm so the root crown drains freely, and set the graft union clear of the soil line. High-pH alkaline soils, common in desert and interior-West regions, are workable but tend to lock up iron and zinc, so a micronutrient-inclusive citrus fertilizer helps.

ph.note_beginner: Oranges like soil that is slightly acidic, around pH 6 to 7. The main thing to watch for is alkaline (high-pH) soil, common in the desert and inland West, where the tree cannot take up iron and zinc and the leaves turn yellow with green veins. If that happens, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc.
ph.note_seasoned: Navel oranges prefer a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerate a somewhat wider band. The practical issue is high-pH alkaline soil (common in the desert Southwest and interior West), where iron and zinc become chemically unavailable and the tree shows interveinal chlorosis (yellow leaves with green veins) even though the nutrients are present. Correct with chelated micronutrients and a citrus fertilizer that includes them.

fertilizer.frequency: split applications through the growing season
fertilizer.type: citrus (nitrogen-forward, with iron, zinc, and manganese)
fertilizer.timing: late winter or early spring through summer; stop by late summer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Citrus are nitrogen-hungry and respond to a feeding rhythm concentrated in the growing season. Feed a mature navel from late winter or early spring through summer in split applications, and stop by late summer so new growth hardens before winter cold. Young trees get smaller, more frequent doses to build the framework. Alkaline soils chemically lock up iron, zinc, and manganese, so look for a citrus-formulated fertilizer that supplies all three as chelates and water it in well to reach the roots. Over-fertilizing pushes excess tender flush that draws aphids, leafminer, and psyllid.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Oranges are hungry for nitrogen and want most of their food during the growing season. Start feeding a grown tree as the weather warms in late winter or early spring, keep it up through summer in a few split doses, and stop by late summer so the new growth has time to toughen up before cool weather arrives. Feed young trees smaller amounts more often to build the framework. If your soil is alkaline, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc so the leaves do not yellow. Do not overfeed, since extra soft growth attracts pests.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A nitrogen-forward citrus formulation (for example a 2-1-1 ratio) with included micronutrients (iron, zinc, manganese), or a product labeled specifically for citrus and avocado
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A fertilizer made for citrus (look for one labeled citrus or citrus and avocado); these are higher in nitrogen and include the iron and zinc citrus needs
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Scale nitrogen to tree age and size: a common guideline is roughly 1 to 1.5 pounds of actual nitrogen per mature tree per year, divided across spring-to-summer applications, with proportionally less for young trees. Follow the product label and local extension rates, which vary by region and soil.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Give more as the tree gets bigger, following the amounts on the citrus fertilizer label and splitting it across spring and summer. A small young tree needs only a little; a big grown tree needs more. When in doubt, follow the package directions for the tree's size.

companions.note_beginner: Keep grass and lawn out from under an orange tree, since grass steals the water and food the tree's shallow roots need. A ring of mulch (kept back from the trunk) is better than grass right up to the tree. There is no real benefit to planting other things close around citrus.
companions.note_seasoned: Keep turf and lawn grasses out of the root zone. Grass competes aggressively for water and nutrients in the top soil layer where citrus feeder roots concentrate, and mowing equipment can damage the trunk. A mulched, grass-free area extending to the canopy dripline is the standard recommendation for all citrus. Low-growing nitrogen fixers like white clover or shallow-rooted ground covers planted outside the trunk flare provide living mulch without root competition. Navel oranges are self-fertile and parthenocarpic, so no pollinizer companion is needed. In fact, nearby citrus with fertile pollen may introduce seeds into otherwise seedless fruit.

good_beginner.name: White clover
good_beginner.why_beginner: A low clover outside the trunk area acts as a living mulch and adds a little nitrogen, without stealing water the way lawn grass does.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clover as a citrus living-mulch/cover crop is extension-supported (UF/IFAS citrus cover-crop program names clovers among legume covers contributing soil N; clover N-fixation nodules pictured in UF/IFAS materials). extension_backed/medium: extension-documented legume-cover benefit; medium because citrus-specific N transfer is site-dependent and clover also competes for water.

good_beginner.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner.why_beginner: An easy flower that covers bare soil and draws in helpful insects. Keep it out from the trunk so it does not crowd the base.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Nasturtium aphid trap-crop + pollinator draw is well documented as a general function and transfers reasonably to citrus aphids; no citrus-specific trial located. traditional/medium (general trap-crop function applied to citrus by sound analogy).

good_beginner.name: Marigold
good_beginner.why_beginner: A simple flower that brings in helpful insects and fills bare ground around the tree. Plant it beyond the trunk, not tight against it.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Marigold nematode-suppression (French marigold vs root-knot nematode) is a real, partly-research-backed mechanism, but its application as a citrus companion is general rather than citrus-trial-specific; pollinator/beneficial draw is sound. traditional/medium (kept traditional because the citrus-specific benefit is by analogy; the nematode mechanism alone could argue mechanistic, flagged).

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Comfrey
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Deep roots pull up nutrients, and the leaves can be cut and dropped as a mulch that feeds the tree. Plant it outside the trunk flare, not right against the tree.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Same basis as apple's comfrey entry: chop-and-drop mulch / non-competing deep taproot / pollinator draw, widely practiced in fruit-tree guilds and partly grounded; dynamic-accumulator mineral claims are permaculture tradition, not peer-reviewed. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Comfrey is a leafy plant that grows well near citrus. Its roots reach deep, so it does not fight the tree for water, and a few times a season you can cut the big leaves and lay them on the soil as a mulch that feeds the tree. Plant it out past the trunk, not right against it, and let its flowers bring in helpful bees.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Yarrow
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low, shallow-rooted plant that draws beneficial insects and does not compete with the citrus roots when kept outside the dripline.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Yarrow as an insectary/beneficial-attractant + drought-tolerant ground cover is consistently reported and mechanistically plausible (umbel-like flowers recruit predators), but the citrus-specific pest-reduction effect is unquantified. Flowering-cover-crops-recruit-psyllid-predators is noted by UF/IFAS as a general benefit, supporting the direction. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Yarrow is a low, tough plant with flat flower heads that draw in ladybugs, lacewings, and other good bugs that eat aphids and pests off your orange tree. It is shallow-rooted and easygoing, so it does not crowd the citrus roots as long as you keep it out toward the edge of the canopy rather than at the trunk. Let it flower to get the benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Fava bean
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season nitrogen fixer that can be grown beyond the dripline as a cover, then cut and dropped to feed the soil without crowding the tree.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Legume winter cover crops in citrus are extension-supported for soil N and organic matter (UF/IFAS citrus cover-crop program; California winter legume covers widely used in orchards). Fava is a standard cool-season legume cover. extension_backed/medium: the legume-cover soil-fertility benefit is extension-documented; medium because the citrus-specific N-transfer magnitude is acknowledged by UF/IFAS as not fully quantified in perennial systems and is site/timing dependent.

bad_beginner.name: Turf grass
bad_beginner.why_beginner: Lawn grass under the tree steals the water and food the orange's shallow roots need. A ring of mulch, kept back from the trunk, is better than grass.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Beginner-register version of the citrus-grass-competition concern; same UF/IFAS basis. extension_backed/medium.

bad_beginner.name: Bermuda grass
bad_beginner.why_beginner: A tough, spreading lawn grass that competes hard for water and is difficult to keep out of the root zone. Clear it out to the edge of the branches.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Same citrus-grass-competition basis (UF/IFAS); Bermuda (Cynodon dactylon) is specifically a highly competitive, aggressively spreading turf and appears in the citrus literature as orchard-floor vegetation. extension_backed/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: St. Augustine grass
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A dense, spreading lawn grass that competes aggressively for water and nutrients in the top soil and creeps right up to the trunk. Keep it cleared out to the dripline.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Citrus is extension-documented (UF/IFAS) as highly vulnerable to weed/grass competition within the root zone, especially at bloom/flush; St. Augustine is a notably aggressive spreading turf. extension_backed/medium: extension-supported grass-citrus competition; medium because the specific quantified loss is via extension guidance rather than a St-Augustine-on-citrus controlled trial I opened.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: St. Augustine is a thick, fast-spreading lawn grass, and it is rough on citrus. It soaks up the water and food in the top layer of soil where the tree's roots feed, and it creeps right up to the trunk. Keep a clear or mulched circle around the base of your orange tree and hold the grass back beyond it, since it will keep trying to spread in.

bad_seasoned.name: Pigeon pea
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Pigeon pea is a nitrogen-fixing legume, so it looks like a natural cover crop for citrus, but it carries a specific strike against it. Research testing whether legumes shelter the citrus root weevil (Diaprepes abbreviatus) found that pigeon pea actually supported the weevil's larval development, sustaining a pest whose larvae feed on citrus roots instead of starving it out. The important context for most navel growers: this weevil is established in Florida and the Caribbean, not in the arid citrus regions of California and Arizona, so if you are growing navels in the West, pigeon pea's worst property is not a live threat in your area. The reason to skip it anyway is that the same research also flagged possible chemical interference from pigeon pea on citrus roots, which is not regional, and you give up nothing by choosing a cool-season legume like fava or a clover cover instead. Those deliver the same nitrogen benefit with no root-pest baggage.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Demoted from good_seasoned to bad_seasoned on a measured adverse finding. Lapointe (2003), cited in the peer-reviewed Strauss et al. 2024 HortTechnology review (ASHS), tested whether pigeon pea, pinto peanut, and rattlebox serve as a refuge for Diaprepes abbreviatus and found pigeon pea SUPPORTED weevil larval development (the certified, weight-bearing finding), and noted POTENTIAL allelopathic effects on citrus roots (softer strand, source's own hedge). research_backed/medium: the weevil-refuge effect is a measured experimental result (earns research_backed), confidence medium because (a) the headline practical risk (Diaprepes) is region-specific to FL/Caribbean and absent in arid CA/AZ navel regions, and (b) the allelopathy strand is 'potential', not established. Net: a real, research-backed reason to avoid pigeon pea in citrus, with the regional scope stated honestly in the prose.

pests.name: Asian citrus psyllid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The psyllid itself is a tiny mottled-brown insect, about an eighth of an inch, that feeds tilted up at a 45-degree angle on new flush, a posture no other citrus pest shares. Its nymphs produce distinctive waxy tubules and curl tender new growth; heavy feeding twists and notches expanding leaves. The insect matters less for its direct damage than for what it carries: it is the vector of Huanglongbing (citrus greening), the most serious citrus disease worldwide. Scout the youngest flush, where it concentrates.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This tiny brown insect has a distinctive resting posture: it perches on new leaves at an angle, with its rear end raised and pointed upward, which is your identification clue. The young ones produce little waxy white threads and cause the new leaf tips to curl. The real danger is not the feeding itself but a fatal disease the psyllid spreads, citrus greening, so it is worth acting on even where the pest is uncommon.
pests.cause_seasoned: Adults lay eggs only on new flush, so populations track flushing cycles and explode in warm weather when trees push tender growth. The pest has spread through most citrus-growing regions of the southern United States; in much of California and the Gulf states it is now established, and any psyllid should be assumed a potential disease carrier.
pests.cause_beginner: The psyllid breeds on fresh new leaves, so it builds up fastest when the tree is putting out tender growth in warm weather. It has spread across the southern states, and any psyllid you find could be carrying the disease.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Buy only certified citrus from a reputable nursery and never move citrus plants or leaves out of a quarantine area, which is the main way the pest and disease jump regions. Inspect each new flush in the warm season. Conserve the natural enemies (a parasitic wasp, Tamarixia, and general predators) that suppress it. Where the disease is present, area-wide psyllid control is the front line.
pests.prevention_beginner: Buy certified citrus from a trusted nursery, and never carry citrus plants or cuttings out of a quarantine zone, because that is how the pest and its disease spread. Check the new leaves often in warm weather. If citrus greening is in your area, follow local guidance on controlling the psyllid.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: On a backyard tree, horticultural oil and insecticidal soap applied to new flush reduce nymphs; thorough coverage of tender growth is key, and repeat as each flush emerges. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree. Most importantly, report suspected psyllids or greening symptoms to your county agricultural office, since this is a regulated pest.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the new growth to knock back the young psyllids, and repeat each time fresh leaves appear. Hold off on oil when it is hot, above roughly 95°F, or when the tree is short on water, since either condition lets oil burn the leaves. Also report any psyllids or signs of the disease to your local farm advisor or county office, because it is closely tracked.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Leave the helpers in the tree alone to work. A small parasitic wasp called Tamarixia attacks psyllid nymphs, meaning the young stages, and general predators feed on them too, so keeping broad, strong insecticides out of the canopy protects the control you already have.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conservation of the resident enemy complex, Tamarixia plus the general predators, is the standing suppression on a backyard tree. Broad-spectrum material removes it, and the psyllid rebuilds on each new flush faster than its enemies do.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On a backyard tree, insecticidal soap sprayed onto the new growth knocks back the young psyllids. It works only where it lands, so wet the tender shoot tips and leaves thoroughly, and spray again each time a fresh round of leaves pushes out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap applied to expanding flush reduces nymphs, and coverage of the tender growth decides the result, since the material is contact-only. Repeat with each flush rather than treating once, because the population tracks flushing cycles.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil that coats insects rather than poisoning them, does the same job on the new flush. Hold off in hot weather and on a tree that is short of water, since oil can burn foliage under either condition, and go back over the tree as fresh leaves appear.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil on new flush is interchangeable with soap against nymphs, with the same coverage requirement and the same repeat schedule through successive flushes. Withhold it in hot weather or on a drought-stressed tree, where it turns phytotoxic.

pests.name: Citrus leafminer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Silvery, serpentine tunnels winding through new leaves, with a thin dark line of frass down the center of each mine, and leaf margins that curl and pucker around the damage. The larva mines only young, expanding foliage; hardened mature leaves are not attacked. On established trees the injury is cosmetic, but on young trees pushing lots of flush it can slow growth and the curled tissue can shelter other pests.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You will see squiggly silver trails snaking through the new leaves, often with the leaf edge curled up. A tiny caterpillar makes these tunnels inside young leaves only. It looks alarming but rarely hurts an established tree, though it can set back a small young one.
pests.cause_seasoned: A small moth lays eggs on tender new flush, and the larvae mine between the leaf surfaces. Generations cycle quickly in warm weather, so damage peaks on the late-summer and fall flushes rather than the spring growth.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny moth lays its eggs on the newest leaves, and the larvae tunnel inside them. They breed fast in warm weather, so the worst damage shows up on the late-summer growth.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid pushing excess tender flush with heavy nitrogen or unnecessary summer pruning, since the moth needs young leaves to breed. Tolerate cosmetic mining on bearing trees; resident parasitic wasps usually provide good control if broad-spectrum sprays are avoided.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize or prune a lot in summer, because that creates the tender new leaves the moth needs. On a healthy grown tree, it is best to just live with the trails, since helpful wasps keep it in check.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Chemical control is rarely warranted, and broad-spectrum sprays undermine the parasitic wasps that naturally suppress leafminer populations. For young trees, where the canopy is small enough that leafminer damage slows establishment, a lightweight horticultural oil applied at bud break can discourage adults from laying eggs on the new flush; repeat as each flush emerges because oil breaks down quickly. Follow label heat restrictions and do not spray above 95°F. Leave mined leaves in place, as they continue photosynthesizing.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually no treatment is needed, and spraying can kill the good bugs that control it. On a small young tree you want to protect, light horticultural oil on the new leaves discourages the moth. Only spray oil in mild conditions, not in high heat or on a thirsty tree, and leave the tunneled leaves on the tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on fertilizer and skip unnecessary summer pruning. The moth can only lay on soft new leaves, the flush, so anything that forces extra rounds of tender growth hands it more places to breed. Leave the tunneled leaves on the tree as well, since they keep feeding it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Restrained nitrogen and no unnecessary summer pruning keep flush synchronized and shorten the window of mineable tissue; hardened mature leaves are not attacked. Mined leaves continue photosynthesizing, so stripping them costs the tree more than the mines do.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On a grown tree the silvery trails are worth living with. Small parasitic wasps attack the larvae inside the leaves and usually keep this in check, and a broad, strong insecticide takes those wasps out along with the pest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident parasitoids give good control where broad-spectrum sprays are avoided, which is why chemical treatment is rarely warranted on a bearing tree. The injury there is cosmetic, so conservation costs nothing and holds.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A young tree is the exception, since heavy mining can slow one down while it is still building its framework. A lightweight horticultural oil, a light spray oil, put on the new leaves at bud break discourages the moth from laying. Oil breaks down quickly, so recoat as each fresh flush emerges, and follow the label heat limits rather than spraying in high heat or on a thirsty tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reserve oil for young trees, where mining slows establishment. Applied to emerging flush at bud break it discourages egg-laying, and the short residual means it follows each flush rather than being applied once. Observe the label heat restrictions and withhold it on a drought-stressed tree.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Scale appear as fixed, non-moving bumps clustered on twigs, along the leaf midrib, and beneath the leaves. The armored types form firm gray or brown shells that look almost like raised bark, while the softer types are plumper and somewhat glossy. The soft kinds give themselves away by the honeydew they secrete, which leaves foliage tacky and grows a black sooty film, and you will often find ants patrolling the colony for that sugar. Where numbers run high, expect mottled yellow leaves, premature leaf fall, and dieback at the twig tips.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Scale look like little hard or waxy lumps that sit still on twigs and the undersides of leaves, so it is easy to think they are just part of the branch. The softer kinds make the leaves tacky and a sooty black coating grows on that stickiness. Ants are often crawling around them.
pests.cause_seasoned: A mix of armored and soft scale species tap into the tree and feed on its sap. They get the upper hand on trees that are dusty, crowded, or patrolled by ants, because the ants drive away the ladybugs and parasitic wasps that would otherwise thin the colony.
pests.cause_beginner: Scale are little insects that feed on the tree's sap. They get worst when ants are around, since the ants protect them from the helpful bugs that eat scale.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and rinse dust off the canopy, and cut off the ants with a sticky trunk band so the resident beneficial insects can do the work. Look any incoming nursery tree over carefully, because scale frequently hitchhikes in on new stock.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep ants from climbing the tree by wrapping a sticky band around the trunk, which lets the good bugs control the scale, and look over any new tree for lumps before planting it.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A thorough horticultural oil application, narrow-range petroleum or neem, smothers the scale and is the usual home remedy; the key is wetting every surface, especially twig undersides and leaf backs. Skip oil above roughly 95°F or on a tree that is drought-stressed, since heat plus oil scorches foliage. Plan a follow-up as fresh crawlers hatch.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Coat the lumps with horticultural oil, making sure to reach the backs of leaves and the twigs. Save the spray for cooler, well-watered days, never above roughly 95°F or on a drought-stressed tree, or it can scorch the foliage. Spray again later as new ones appear.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Look for ants patrolling the trunk. While they are working the tree they drive off the ladybugs and parasitic wasps that would thin the colony, so shutting them out is what changes the situation. Collar the trunk with heavy paper, duct tape, or fabric tree wrap and put the sticky material on that collar, since sticky goo straight on bark can injure a trunk. Then trim back any low branch touching the ground, a wall, or a neighboring plant, because ants walk around a band by those routes.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Ant tending is what holds armored and soft scale above the level resident predators and parasitoids would allow, so breaking canopy access restores that control at no cost. UC IPM directs that the sticky material go on a collar of heavy paper, duct tape, or fabric tree wrap rather than on bare bark, which it can injure. Close the bypass routes in the same pass, since a branch bridging to soil, a wall, or an adjacent plant makes the band moot.

control_ladder.note_beginner: With the ants out of the way, the ladybugs and tiny wasps already living in the tree do much of the work for free. Keep broad, strong insecticides off the tree so they stay.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Predators and parasitoids thin colonies on an unstressed tree, so the operative choice is keeping broad-spectrum material out of the canopy rather than adding anything to it. Dusty, crowded trees are where scale gets the upper hand.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the bumps keep spreading, coat them with horticultural oil, a light spray oil that smothers insects instead of poisoning them. It works only where it lands, so wet the twigs and the backs of the leaves. Save it for cooler days on a well-watered tree, since heat plus oil can scorch foliage, and go over the tree again as new young scale hatch out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A narrow-range petroleum or neem oil smothers settled scale, so coverage of twig undersides and leaf backs governs the outcome more than rate does. Withhold it in hot weather or on a drought-stressed tree, where foliage injury follows, and plan a follow-up as fresh crawlers hatch.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of soft-bodied green, black, or brown aphids on the youngest flush and flower buds, with curled, distorted new leaves and a sticky honeydew coating that draws ants and grows sooty mold. Spring and fall flushes are the targets. One species, the brown citrus aphid, is also a vector of citrus tristeza virus, which raises the stakes where that disease is a concern.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Look for clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects, often green or black, packed onto the newest leaves and flower buds, causing the tips to curl. They secrete a sticky coating that ants follow and that leads to a black sooty film. Navel oranges are most vulnerable during the spring and fall flushes when tender new growth is available.
pests.cause_seasoned: Aphids reproduce explosively on tender new growth in mild weather and are tended by ants for their honeydew. Lush, over-fertilized flush is especially attractive, and ant protection lets colonies outrun their natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids multiply very fast on soft new growth in mild weather, and ants protect them. Too much fertilizer makes extra tender leaves that draw them in.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid forcing excessive tender flush with heavy nitrogen. Control ants so ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps can suppress colonies. A strong jet of water knocks aphids off new growth and is often all that is needed.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize, which makes the soft growth aphids love, and keep ants out so ladybugs and other helpers can eat them. A blast of water from the hose usually clears them off.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A forceful water spray, insecticidal soap, or horticultural oil controls aphids; cover the undersides of curled leaves. Repeat as needed. Observe oil heat limits (not above 95°F or on stressed trees). Preserve natural enemies by skipping broad-spectrum insecticides.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, getting under the curled leaves. Keep oil for mild days only, not in high heat or on a stressed, dry tree, and avoid harsh sprays that kill the good bugs.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ease off high-nitrogen feeding. Heavy fertilizer keeps pushing out soft new leaves, and lush growth like that is what aphid colonies pile onto.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen extends the run of tender flush colonies build on, so restraint narrows the susceptible tissue rather than acting on the insects. Pressure on navels concentrates in the spring and fall flushes, which is when the feeding habit pays.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the clusters off the shoot tips with a strong jet from the hose. On an established tree that is often the whole job, and unlike a spray it leaves the helpful insects on the same growth alone. Do it early in the day so the leaves dry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water jet dislodges colonies from tender shoots without setting back the natural enemies working the same flush. Aim it at the growing points and the undersides of curled leaves and repeat, rather than escalating while numbers are still low, and time it so foliage dries.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Check the trunk for an ant trail. Ants harvest the sticky honeydew the aphids give off and defend them from the ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that would otherwise clear them. Band the trunk with a collar of heavy paper, duct tape, or fabric tree wrap and put the sticky material on the collar rather than on bare bark, then cut back low branches that bridge to the ground, a wall, or another plant. Where no ants are working the tree, this one does not apply.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Ant protection is what lets colonies outrun their natural enemies, so exclusion shortens an outbreak rather than treating it. Apply the sticky material to a paper, tape, or fabric collar instead of bark, and close the branch bridges to soil, wall, or neighboring plants that route ants past the trunk. Where no trail is present this is not the situation it addresses.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, and small parasitic wasps usually bring an aphid outbreak down on their own, so low numbers are worth tolerating. Broad-spectrum sprays set those helpers back and are worth leaving out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitoids suppress colonies once ant tending is broken, which is the argument for tolerating low numbers on a bearing tree. Skipping broad-spectrum insecticides is what preserves them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For a heavy infestation, insecticidal soap sprayed straight onto the clusters brings numbers down. Get under the curled leaves, since it kills only what it wets, and repeat as needed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is contact-only, so working it into the curled tissue where colonies shelter matters more than volume, and repeats follow the flush rather than the calendar.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil, is the other option for a heavy outbreak. It coats the aphids rather than poisoning them, so cover the shoot tips and the undersides of curled leaves. Keep it for mild days and a well-watered tree, since oil in high heat or on a thirsty tree can scorch the foliage.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil is interchangeable with soap on a heavy infestation, with the same coverage requirement into curled tissue. Withhold it in hot weather and on a drought-stressed tree, where it injures foliage, and keep broad-spectrum insecticides out of the canopy so the natural enemies survive the intervention.

pests.name: Citrus red mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A fine stippling or silvering on leaves and sometimes fruit rind, with tiny dark-red mites and their cast skins visible on leaf surfaces under a hand lens. Heavy populations bronze the foliage and can cause leaf drop. Mites flare in hot, dusty, dry conditions and after broad-spectrum sprays kill their predators, so outbreaks are often a sign the tree is dust-stressed or was over-sprayed.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Look for leaves that turn a dull, speckled, silvery color, sometimes with tiny red dots moving on them (a hand lens helps). Mites get worse when it is hot, dry, and dusty. A lot of them can bronze the leaves and cause some to drop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Citrus red mite thrives in heat and dust and reproduces rapidly on stressed trees. Dusty roadside or driveway trees and trees sprayed with broad-spectrum insecticides (which remove predatory mites) are the most prone to damaging populations.
pests.cause_beginner: These mites love hot, dusty conditions and build up fast on stressed trees. Dusty trees and trees that have been sprayed with strong insecticides (which kill the helpful mites) get the worst of it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Hose dust off the canopy in hot, dry spells and keep the tree well watered, since vigorous trees tolerate mites better. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that destroy the predatory mites providing natural control.
pests.prevention_beginner: Rinse dust off the leaves during hot dry weather and keep the tree watered, because a healthy tree handles mites better. Avoid strong insecticides that kill the good mites.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Damage is usually cosmetic and rarely needs treatment. If populations are heavy on a stressed tree, horticultural oil provides control; observe heat limits strictly, as mite outbreaks coincide with the hot weather when oil is riskiest. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually the damage is just cosmetic and needs nothing. If there are a lot of mites, horticultural oil works, but timing is tricky: mites peak in hot weather, which is the riskiest time to oil a tree. Only spray when it has cooled off, never on a hot, dry, stressed tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the tree watered steadily rather than letting it swing between soaked and bone dry. These mites build up fastest on a hot, dry, stressed tree, and a vigorous one puts up with them better.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Water stress is a principal driver of buildup, so steady soil moisture is the baseline control rather than an afterthought. Populations climb through hot, dry spells, which is also when a stressed tree has the least tolerance for the feeding.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hose the dust off the canopy during hot, dry weather. Dust is one of the conditions these mites thrive in, and rinsing the leaves takes it away without harming the good mites that eat them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rinsing the canopy strips the dust layer that favors buildup, which is why dusty roadside and driveway trees carry the heaviest populations. It suppresses numbers without the predator loss that follows a spray.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Predatory mites eat the pest mites for free, and strong broad-spectrum insecticides kill them. Leaving those sprays out is what keeps a light speckling from turning into a heavy infestation.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Predatory mites are the standing check, and broad-spectrum insecticides remove them, which is the usual route into a damaging population. An outbreak is often the sign that a tree was over-sprayed or is dust-stressed rather than that it needs treating.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Most of the time the speckling is only cosmetic and needs nothing. If a stressed tree is carrying a lot of mites, horticultural oil, a light spray oil, works on contact, so cover the leaf surfaces. The timing is awkward: mites peak in hot weather, which is when oil is riskiest, so wait for it to cool off and water the tree well first.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Treatment is seldom justified, the injury being largely cosmetic. Where populations are heavy on a stressed tree, oil gives control by contact and coverage, but the heat limits bind hardest here, since outbreaks coincide with the weather that makes oil phytotoxic. Withhold it in hot weather and on a drought-stressed tree.

pests.name: Katydids and fruit-surface chewers
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular chewed notches on young leaves and, more conspicuously, smooth shallow gouges or healed scars on the rind of developing fruit, where a katydid or similar chewing insect fed when the fruit was tiny. The damage scars over and grows out as the fruit expands, so it is a cosmetic, surface-only blemish that does not reach the flesh of a navel.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You may find ragged bites out of young leaves, or smooth shallow scars on the skin of the fruit where something chewed it when it was small. On a navel this is only skin-deep: the fruit inside is fine, it just looks marked.
pests.cause_seasoned: Katydids and other occasional chewing insects feed on tender foliage and very young fruit in spring and early summer. Populations are usually low and sporadic in a backyard, and the visible scarring is out of proportion to the actual number of insects.
pests.cause_beginner: Katydids and a few other leaf-chewing insects nibble soft leaves and tiny fruit in spring and early summer. There are usually only a few of them, even though the scars look like a lot.
pests.prevention_seasoned: No action is generally needed on a home tree. Healthy trees outgrow the cosmetic injury, and the chewers are kept in check by birds and general predators. Hand-pick if a particular insect is abundant on a small tree.
pests.prevention_beginner: Caterpillar chewing rarely warrants intervention. An established tree outgrows the leaf notches quickly, and natural predators, including birds and beneficial wasps, keep populations in check on their own. If you spot a caterpillar on a small young tree, you can simply pick it off by hand.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treatment is rarely justified for cosmetic rind scarring. Hand-picking handles the occasional katydid. Reserve any spray for genuine defoliation of a young tree, and prefer a targeted product over a broad-spectrum insecticide that would disrupt the citrus natural-enemy complex.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spraying is almost never worth it for marks on the skin. Just pick off the bugs by hand. Only consider a spray if a small tree is being stripped of leaves, and then pick a targeted one rather than a harsh insecticide.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a chewer is abundant on a small young tree, pick them off by hand. That is enough for the occasional katydid, and on an established tree the marks on the skin are not worth chasing.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hand-picking covers the occasional katydid on a small tree and is the proportionate response, since populations are usually low and sporadic and the visible scarring is out of proportion to the number of insects. On a bearing tree the rind injury scars over and grows out as the fruit expands.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Most of the time the answer is to leave it be. Birds and other general predators keep these chewers in check on their own, and a healthy tree grows past the leaf notches.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Birds and the general predator complex hold these sporadic chewers down without intervention, and a vigorous tree outgrows the cosmetic injury. A broad-spectrum insecticide would disrupt the citrus natural-enemy complex for damage that stays on the surface of the rind, which is the argument for restraint.

diseases.name: Huanglongbing (citrus greening, HLB)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blotchy, asymmetric yellowing of leaves that does not mirror across the midrib (distinguishing it from a nutrient deficiency, which is usually symmetric), yellow shoots, and corky, enlarged leaf veins. Fruit are small, lopsided, fail to color fully, stay green at the bottom, and taste bitter and salty; seeds often abort. The tree declines over several years and there is no cure. This is the most destructive citrus disease worldwide.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The classic sign is a leaf that is yellow in a blotchy, uneven pattern, with the yellow on one side of the leaf not matching the other (a nutrient problem is usually even on both sides). Fruit stay small, lopsided, green on the bottom, and taste bad. There is no cure, and the tree slowly dies. It is the worst citrus disease there is.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, the bacterium behind citrus greening, spreads tree to tree via the Asian citrus psyllid feeding on new growth. Inside the tree it clogs the phloem so nutrients cannot reach roots and fruit. No treatment can clear the infection once established, so management is entirely about suppressing the psyllid and removing confirmed trees before they seed the pest further.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria spread by the Asian citrus psyllid as it feeds on new shoots clog the tree's vascular system, blocking the flow of nutrients to roots and fruit. No treatment can reverse the infection; an affected tree is a permanent source of disease spread. The entire management strategy is preventing psyllid feeding and removing any confirmed tree before it extends the outbreak.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant only certified disease-free nursery trees, never move citrus out of quarantine areas, and control the psyllid vector aggressively where it is present. Inspect trees regularly and report suspected greening to your county agricultural commissioner, since coordinated removal of infected trees is the only effective area-wide defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy only certified clean trees, never move citrus out of a quarantine zone, and control the psyllid that spreads it. Check your tree often, and report anything that looks like greening to your local agricultural office, because removing infected trees quickly is what protects everyone's citrus.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure and no organic remedy for an infected tree. Management is prevention and vector control only: protect trees from the psyllid, and remove and properly dispose of confirmed-infected trees promptly so they cannot serve as a reservoir for further spread.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no treatment that saves an infected tree. Focus entirely on prevention: keep the psyllid off your trees with regular inspection and treatment, and if a tree is diagnosed with citrus greening, remove it promptly to protect your neighbors' trees and the surrounding area. An infected tree left in place becomes an ongoing source of psyllid pressure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Buy a tree certified free of this disease, and do not bring citrus plants or cuttings in from a quarantine zone.
