failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: When leaves turn yellow but the veins stay green, especially on new growth, the tree is short on a micronutrient, usually iron or zinc. This happens a lot on alkaline (high-pH) soils, common in the desert and the inland West, where the nutrient is in the soil but the tree cannot take it up. It looks different from an even all-over yellowing (which is usually nitrogen) and from the blotchy yellowing of citrus greening.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Correct with a chelated iron or zinc product, applied as a foliar spray for a quick response and to the soil for longer-term supply, and use a citrus fertilizer that includes micronutrients.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Fix it with a chelated iron or zinc product, sprayed on the leaves for a fast response and added to the soil for the long run, and use a citrus fertilizer that lists micronutrients.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 is too cold for an in-ground navel. Winter lows pass the mid-20s°F tree-damage point and the 26 to 28°F fruit-freeze point every year, so there is no dependable crop and no establishment window.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: You cannot grow an orange tree in the ground in this region. People in cold areas grow citrus in pots and bring them inside for winter instead.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In-ground navels are not viable in zones 3 through 7. Gardeners in these zones grow citrus in containers moved indoors for winter, which is a different growing system from the in-ground regional model here.
northern_tier.cold_basis_seasoned: Zones 3 through 7 drop well below the low-20s°F every winter, far past the mid-20s°F a navel tree withstands and the 26 to 28°F at which the fruit freezes. An unprotected in-ground navel does not survive here.
northern_tier.cold_basis_beginner: It gets too cold here for an orange tree to live outside. Winters drop far below what the tree can take, so a navel planted in the ground will not make it.
northern_tier.heat_basis_seasoned: Heat is moot here: the tree cannot survive the winter, so summer heat never gets the chance to matter.
northern_tier.heat_basis_beginner: Summer warmth does not matter here, because the tree cannot get through winter in the first place.

8.plant_out: Spring (container or balled; after hard-freeze risk passes)
8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 grows a navel but on the cold edge: the tree is hardy here, yet winter lows reach the upper teens to mid-20s°F in colder years and the fruit freezes at 26 to 28°F, so the crop is at real risk in a hard freeze. Heat is ample; cold is the limiter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: You can grow an orange in zone 8, but cold is a gamble. The tree usually lives, but a hard freeze can damage or destroy the fruit, so some winters you lose the crop.
8.harvest: Nov - Jan (early-season navel; protect fruit in a hard freeze)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard advective freezes into the upper teens°F occur every few years in zone 8; both fruit and young trees need cold protection on those nights.

9.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 fruits reliably: mild Gulf and Southeastern winters rarely hold below the mid-20s°F long enough to take the crop, and summer heat is more than enough to sweeten a navel. Cold protection is an occasional need, not a routine one.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Oranges do well in zone 9. Winters are mild enough that you usually keep your fruit, and summers are plenty hot to make it sweet.
9.harvest: Nov - Jan (and holding on the tree into late winter)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 9 across the Gulf region is mostly safe for navels, but hard freezes do occur in some winters. Temperatures dropping below 27°F can damage ripe fruit and scorch young growth, while most winters stay mild enough that no intervention is needed. Have frost cloth or a heat source ready for the tree's first few winters while it is still small and the canopy is less thermally buffered.

10.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 fruits reliably: mild Gulf and Southeastern winters rarely hold below the mid-20s°F long enough to take the crop, and summer heat is more than enough to sweeten a navel. Cold protection is an occasional need, not a routine one.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Oranges do well in zone 9. Winters are mild enough that you usually keep your fruit, and summers are plenty hot to make it sweet.
10.harvest: Nov - Jan (and holding on the tree into late winter)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The Gulf coast is mostly safe for navels, but hard freezes do occur in some winters. Temperatures dropping below 27°F can damage ripe fruit and scorch young growth, while most winters stay mild enough that no intervention is needed. Have frost cloth or a heat source ready for the tree's first few winters while it is still small and the canopy is less thermally buffered.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Oranges here are ready in early winter, around November to January. In the colder part of this area a hard freeze can cost you the fruit some years.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Navels are an early-season Southeastern citrus, ripening roughly November into January. The northern, colder zone of this band carries real freeze risk to the crop; the warmer zone fruits dependably.
se_gulf.cold_basis_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf, a mature navel is hardy into the mid-20s°F, but the fruit freezes at 26 to 28°F and hard advective freezes into the upper teens reach the colder, northern edge of the band every few years. Cold sets the survival ceiling here; heat does not limit quality.
se_gulf.cold_basis_beginner: A grown orange tree here handles a light freeze, but the fruit is damaged below about 28°F, and a hard freeze every few winters can hurt the tree in the colder parts of this area.
se_gulf.heat_basis_seasoned: Long, hot Southeastern summers bank plenty of heat to sweeten a navel, so heat is not the limiting factor here. The regional climate is humid rather than arid, and rind color can lag interior ripeness in warm falls, but eating quality is good.
se_gulf.heat_basis_beginner: Summers here are plenty hot for sweet oranges. The fruit gets enough heat to taste good, even though the skin sometimes stays a little green when the fall is warm.

8.plant_out: Spring (container or balled; after frost risk eases)
8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 in the valley has the heat for excellent fruit but sits on the cold edge: radiation frosts reach the upper 20s to low-20s°F in colder years, and the fruit freezes at 26 to 28°F, so a hard frost can take the crop. Heat is high; cold is the limiter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 has plenty of summer heat for sweet oranges, but it is the cold edge of the valley. A hard frost can damage the fruit some winters, so protection helps.
8.harvest: Dec - Mar (sweetens through the cool winter; protect in a hard frost)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Radiation frosts into the low-20s°F occur in colder zone-8 valley sites; fruit and young trees need protection on the coldest nights.

9.plant_out: Spring (container or balled); much of the year on the mild valley floor
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 valley floor is the navel sweet spot: high summer heat for full sugar and color, and winter lows that only occasionally threaten the crop. This is the climate that built California's navel industry.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the valley is ideal for oranges. Hot summers make the fruit sweet and deeply colored, and winters are usually mild enough to keep the crop.
9.harvest: Dec - Apr (late selections such as Lane Late hold into spring)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is an occasional risk on the valley floor; most winters pass without crop loss, though an unusual hard radiation frost can still threaten fruit.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: The Central Valley is a great place for oranges. Summers are hot enough for excellent fruit, and the main thing to watch is winter frost in the coldest spots.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: The interior valley is the premier home-navel region: high summer heat for quality, with cold the only constraint and only at the colder zone-8 margin. Harvest runs winter into spring, with late selections holding into March or April.
ca_interior.cold_basis_seasoned: Interior valley winters bring radiation frosts; a mature navel is hardy into the mid-20s°F and the fruit freezes at 26 to 28°F, so the colder zone-8 floor of the valley carries crop risk while the warmer valley floor rarely does. Cold sets the survival edge; heat is abundant.
ca_interior.cold_basis_beginner: Valley winters can frost. A grown tree usually handles it, but in the colder spots the fruit can freeze, while the warmer parts of the valley are safer.
ca_interior.heat_basis_seasoned: The Central Valley is the commercial navel heartland precisely because its long, hot summers bank abundant heat: navels develop full sugar and deep color here. Heat is never the limiter in this region.
ca_interior.heat_basis_beginner: This is California's main orange-growing region. Hot summers give the fruit all the heat it needs to turn deep orange and taste sweet.

9.plant_out: Spring (container or balled); most of the year in this mild, frost-safe climate
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 on the north coast is frost-safe but heat-limited: the tree grows and sets fruit, yet cool summers leave the navel tart and pale rather than sweet. Reduced quality, not crop failure, and not a cold problem.
9.suitability_note_beginner: In zone 9 on the north coast the tree does fine, but summers are too cool to sweeten the fruit, so the oranges stay sour. You get fruit, just not good fruit.
9.harvest: Jan - Apr (fruit holds long on the tree but stays tart in cool summers)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the north coast; the limiting climate factor here is summer heat, not winter cold.

10.plant_out: Spring (container or balled); most of the year in this mild, frost-safe climate
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the north coast is frost-safe but heat-limited: the tree grows and sets fruit, yet cool summers leave the navel tart and pale rather than sweet. Reduced quality, not crop failure, and not a cold problem.
10.suitability_note_beginner: In zone 10 on the north coast the tree does fine, but summers are too cool to sweeten the fruit, so the oranges stay sour. You get fruit, just not good fruit.
10.harvest: Jan - Apr (fruit holds long on the tree but stays tart in cool summers)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the north coast; the limiting climate factor here is summer heat, not winter cold.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the cool north coast an orange tree lives easily but never gets hot enough to sweeten its fruit. The same spots that grow great lemons leave navels sour.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The north coast is the heat-limited case: frost-safe but too cool to sweeten a navel, so the fruit is reliably grown yet of reduced quality. This is the same maritime climate where lemons thrive, which is exactly why the navel's heat requirement shows up so plainly here.
ca_north_coast.cold_basis_seasoned: The north coast is nearly frost-free; winter lows rarely approach the mid-20s°F tree-damage point, so cold almost never limits a navel here. The constraint on this coast is heat, not cold.
ca_north_coast.cold_basis_beginner: It barely freezes on the north coast, so cold is not the problem for an orange tree here. The problem is a lack of summer heat.
ca_north_coast.heat_basis_seasoned: Cool, marine-influenced north-coast summers do not bank enough heat to ripen a navel sweet: the tree is healthy and frost-safe, but the fruit stays tart and pale. Lemons and limes, which need little heat, fruit well on this same coast; a navel does not.
ca_north_coast.heat_basis_beginner: The north coast stays too cool in summer to make an orange sweet. The tree grows fine, but the fruit ends up sour and pale. Lemons do well here; navels do not.

9.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal) in this frost-free climate
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 on the south coast is frost-safe but heat-marginal: a navel ripens but is more tart and less deeply colored than inland fruit. Reduced quality, not failure, and not a cold issue; the immediate fog-belt runs cooler still and pushes quality lower.
9.suitability_note_beginner: In zone 9 on the south coast the tree thrives and never freezes, but mild summers leave the fruit only middling, less sweet than inland oranges. Right on the foggy coast it is even cooler and the fruit is more sour.
9.harvest: Jan - Apr (holds long on the tree; sweetness builds slowly in the mild coast climate)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the south coast; the limiting factor is borderline summer heat, not winter cold.

10.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal) in this frost-free climate
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the south coast is frost-safe but heat-marginal: a navel ripens but is more tart and less deeply colored than inland fruit. Reduced quality, not failure, and not a cold issue; the immediate fog-belt runs cooler still and pushes quality lower.
10.suitability_note_beginner: In zone 10 on the south coast the tree thrives and never freezes, but mild summers leave the fruit only middling, less sweet than inland oranges. Right on the foggy coast it is even cooler and the fruit is more sour.
10.harvest: Jan - Apr (holds long on the tree; sweetness builds slowly in the mild coast climate)

11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the south coast; the limiting factor is borderline summer heat, not winter cold.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the south coast oranges grow easily and never freeze, but the cool air keeps them from getting truly sweet. It is the same climate that grows great lemons. Move a few miles inland, away from the fog, and the oranges get much better.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The south coast is the borderline heat case and the clearest illustration of the navel's heat requirement: frost-safe, lemon-perfect, but only middling for navels. Broadly the coast is heat-marginal; the immediate fog-belt is insufficient. Inland of the marine layer, quality rises quickly toward the interior standard.
ca_south_coast.cold_basis_seasoned: The south coast is effectively frost-free; winter lows sit in the 30s°F and rarely approach the mid-20s°F a navel withstands. Cold does not limit a navel on this coast. Heat does.
ca_south_coast.cold_basis_beginner: The south coast almost never freezes, so cold is not a worry for an orange tree here. What holds the fruit back is summer heat.
ca_south_coast.heat_basis_seasoned: South-coast summers are mild rather than hot, banking borderline heat for a navel: fruit ripens but quality is reduced, more tart and less deeply colored than the same variety grown inland. This is the telling contrast: the very coast that grows flawless lemons leaves a navel only middling, because a navel needs far more heat than a lemon to sweeten. Right on the immediate fog-belt the heat is insufficient and quality drops further.
ca_south_coast.heat_basis_beginner: The south coast is mild, not hot, so navels here ripen but never get as sweet or as orange as inland fruit. The same mild coast that grows perfect lemons makes only so-so oranges, because oranges need much more heat than lemons. On the foggiest coastal strip they barely sweeten at all.

9.plant_out: Spring (container or balled); avoid planting into peak summer heat
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the low desert fruits reliably and at high quality: abundant summer heat sweetens and colors the navel fully, and winter frost only rarely threatens the crop. Manage spring fruit-drop with adequate irrigation.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the desert is excellent for oranges. Lots of summer heat makes them sweet and deeply colored, and frost is rarely a problem. Just water well in spring.
9.harvest: Dec - Mar (early selections can start late October; Washington Dec into March)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Occasional radiation frosts into the upper 20s°F reach colder desert sites; mature trees tolerate this, but young trees benefit from protection on the coldest nights.

10.plant_out: Spring (container or balled); avoid planting into peak summer heat

11.plant_out: Spring (container or balled); avoid planting into peak summer heat
11.suitability_note_seasoned: The low desert fruits reliably and at high quality: abundant summer heat sweetens and colors the navel fully, and winter frost only rarely threatens the crop. Manage spring fruit-drop with adequate irrigation.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The desert grows excellent oranges. Harvest can start in late fall, and the fruit is sweet and deeply colored. The main thing is to water well in spring so the tree keeps its fruit.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The desert is a premier navel region on heat, with harvest starting as early as late October for early selections and Washington running December into March. Heat quality is high; the management focus is spring fruit-drop and fall granulation rather than cold.
ca_desert.cold_basis_seasoned: Low-desert winters bring occasional radiation frosts into the upper 20s to low-30s°F; a mature navel is hardy through this, with crop risk only in the colder zone-9 sites during an unusual hard frost. Cold is a minor edge; the desert's defining trait for a navel is its heat.
ca_desert.cold_basis_beginner: The desert can frost on cold nights, but a grown orange tree handles it. Cold is only a worry in the coldest spots during a rare hard freeze.
ca_desert.heat_basis_seasoned: Desert summers bank abundant heat, producing deeply colored, full-sugar navels; this is premier navel quality. The desert's own caution is the flip side of that heat: very hot bloom-time temperatures in the 90s°F drive spring fruit-drop, and excessive fall heat can granulate the fruit, so irrigation and rootstock choice matter.
ca_desert.heat_basis_beginner: The desert is plenty hot for excellent, deeply orange, sweet navels. The trade-off is that very hot spring weather can knock young fruit off the tree, so keeping the tree well-watered matters.

8.plant_out: Spring (container or balled; after hard-freeze risk passes)
8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 in the arid inland has the summer heat for good navel quality but sits on the cold edge: winter lows into the upper teens to mid-20s°F put the crop at freeze risk most years. Heat is adequate; cold is the limiter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 here is warm enough in summer for sweet oranges, but winter cold is a real risk to the fruit. Some years a hard freeze takes the crop, so protection helps.
8.harvest: Dec - Feb (protect fruit and young trees in a hard freeze)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard freezes into the upper teens°F occur in this zone-8 arid inland; both fruit and young trees need protection on those nights.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: This dry inland region is warm enough in summer for sweet oranges, but winters are the gamble: a hard freeze can take the fruit, so it is a hit-or-miss spot for citrus.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid inland can grow a good navel on heat but is cold-limited at its zone-8 floor, so the crop is freeze-exposed in hard winters. A marginal region: dependable fruit only in milder years or with cold protection.
warm_arid.cold_basis_seasoned: The warm arid inland sits at zone 8, the cold edge for a navel: winter lows reach the upper teens to mid-20s°F, past the 26 to 28°F fruit-freeze point, so the crop is at real risk in a hard freeze even though a mature tree usually survives. Cold is the binding constraint here.
warm_arid.cold_basis_beginner: This inland area gets cold enough in winter to damage orange fruit and threaten young trees. A grown tree usually lives, but a hard freeze can cost you the crop.
warm_arid.heat_basis_seasoned: Hot, dry inland summers bank enough heat to sweeten a navel well; heat is not the limiter in this arid region. Quality is good where the tree clears the winter.
warm_arid.heat_basis_beginner: Summers here are hot and dry, plenty warm to make oranges sweet. Heat is not the problem; winter cold is.

9.plant_out: Spring (container or balled); avoid planting into peak summer heat
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the Arizona low desert fruits reliably and at high quality: abundant summer heat fully sweetens and colors the navel, and frost rarely threatens the crop. Spring irrigation manages the heat-driven fruit-drop.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the Arizona desert is excellent for oranges. Hot summers make them sweet and deeply colored, and frost is rarely a problem. Just water well in spring.
9.harvest: Dec - Mar (Washington navel; early selections can start late October)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Only occasional light frost reaches the Arizona low desert; mature navels tolerate it, and crop loss to cold is rare.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: The Arizona low desert grows excellent oranges, ready December into spring. Water well in spring so the tree holds its fruit, and cold is rarely an issue.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert is a high-heat navel region: excellent quality, Washington harvest December into March, with management centered on spring fruit-drop and granulation rather than winter cold.
low_desert_az.cold_basis_seasoned: The Arizona low desert at zone 9 brings only occasional light frost; a mature navel is comfortably hardy, with crop risk only in an unusual hard frost. Cold is a minor factor; heat defines navel growing here.
low_desert_az.cold_basis_beginner: The low desert rarely gets a hard frost, so cold is not much of a worry for a grown orange tree here.
low_desert_az.heat_basis_seasoned: Abundant low-desert heat produces full-sugar navels, with Washington fruit ready from December through March. The desert caveats apply: hot bloom-time temperatures in the 90s°F cause spring fruit-drop, and over-vigorous rootstocks or late nitrogen drive granulation, so irrigation and rootstock choice matter more than cold.
low_desert_az.heat_basis_beginner: The Arizona desert is plenty hot for sweet, deeply colored oranges. The catch is that very hot spring weather can drop young fruit, so keep the tree well-watered through spring.

10.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled) in this frost-free climate
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the Florida peninsula fruits reliably: frost-free winters pose no crop risk and hot, humid summers give a navel ample heat to sweeten. Expect rind color to lag interior ripeness; taste rather than color tells you it is ready.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 in Florida is dependable for oranges. It does not freeze, and summers are hot enough for sweet fruit. The skin may look greenish even when the orange is ripe inside.
10.harvest: Nov - Jan (early-season navel; rind may stay green-tinged when ripe)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a crop factor on the central and southern peninsula; winters are reliably above any navel cold threshold.

11.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled) in this frost-free climate

11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a crop factor on the central and southern peninsula; winters are reliably above any navel cold threshold.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In central and south Florida oranges grow easily and never freeze. They are ready in early winter. The skin may stay greenish, but the fruit is still sweet.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The frost-free peninsula fruits dependably, with navels ripening roughly November into January. Heat is adequate and cold is a non-factor; the local quirk is humidity-driven rind-greening rather than any quality shortfall.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_seasoned: The central and southern Florida peninsula is effectively frost-free; winter lows hold in the upper 30s to upper 40s°F, well above the mid-20s°F tree limit. Cold does not constrain a navel here.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_beginner: Central and south Florida barely get cold, so an orange tree has nothing to fear from frost here.
fl_peninsula.heat_basis_seasoned: The peninsula's hot, humid summers bank ample heat to sweeten a navel; eating quality is good. The regional nuance is humidity, not heat shortage: warm nights mean rind color can lag interior ripeness, so a green-tinged peel does not signal an unripe navel.
fl_peninsula.heat_basis_beginner: Central and south Florida are plenty hot for sweet oranges. The fruit tastes good even when the skin stays a bit green, which is normal in this warm, humid climate.

11.plant_out: Year-round (container or balled) in this frost-free climate
11.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 11 in Hawaii is frost-free and grows navels year-round, but quality is marginal: the warm, humid tropics lack the cool nights needed to sweeten and color the fruit, so low-elevation navels stay tart and green-skinned. Cooler uplands improve quality. Not a cold or heat-shortage issue, a diurnal-swing one.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 11 in Hawaii grows oranges all year and never freezes, but the fruit is often sour and stays green because the nights do not get cool enough to sweeten it. It is better up in the cooler hills.
11.harvest: Oct - Jan (Washington navel; lower-elevation fruit stays green-tinged and tart)
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: There is no frost risk in Hawaii; the limiting factor is the lack of cool nights for quality, not cold.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Oranges grow all year in Hawaii, but they are often not very sweet. The islands are warm but lack the cool nights oranges need to sweeten, so low-elevation fruit stays sour and green. Cooler hillsides do better.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii grows navels year-round but quality is marginal for a counter-intuitive reason: abundant warmth without the cool nights a navel needs to sweeten and color. Washington navel ripens roughly October to January; lower elevations give greener, tarter fruit, cooler uplands better. This is a heat-quality limit, not a frost or heat-shortage limit.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_seasoned: Hawaii is frost-free year-round; temperatures sit in the 65 to 90°F range and never approach any navel cold threshold. Cold plays no role here.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_beginner: Hawaii never freezes, so cold is simply not a factor for growing oranges.
hawaii_tropical.heat_basis_seasoned: Hawaii is the counter-intuitive case: it is hot and frost-free, yet the humid tropics lack the cool nights a navel needs to drop acid and color. At lower elevations fruit can fail to develop high sugar and stay acid, with a green or green-yellow peel normal even when ripe; CTAHR rates navel quality as adequate around 500 to 1000 feet where nights are cooler. Warmth is present but the diurnal swing that sweetens a navel is not, so quality is marginal, not a heat shortage in the desert sense.
hawaii_tropical.heat_basis_beginner: Hawaii is warm and never freezes, but it is missing the cool nights that make a navel sweet and orange. At low elevations the fruit can stay sour and green-skinned even when ripe; it does better in the cooler hills. So oranges grow, but they are often only so-so.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

9.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley fruits navel oranges reliably: winters are essentially frost-free, and the long, hot subtropical summer banks ample heat to fully sweeten and color the fruit. Oranges make up roughly 30 percent of the Valley's citrus acreage alongside grapefruit's 70 percent (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension).
9.suitability_note_beginner: Navel oranges do well here. Winters are mild and almost never freeze, and the hot Valley summer ripens sweet, well-colored fruit from fall into the heart of winter.
9.harvest: Oct - Jan (early to midseason navel, peak in the heart of winter)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a practical concern in the Valley. An occasional hard freeze can reach into the high 20s°F and damage hanging fruit or a young tree, but most winters need no protection at all.

10.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley fruits navel oranges reliably: winters are essentially frost-free, and the long, hot subtropical summer banks ample heat to fully sweeten and color the fruit. Oranges make up roughly 30 percent of the Valley's citrus acreage alongside grapefruit's 70 percent (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension).
10.suitability_note_beginner: Navel oranges do well here. Winters are mild and almost never freeze, and the hot Valley summer ripens sweet, well-colored fruit from fall into the heart of winter.
10.harvest: Oct - Jan (early to midseason navel, peak in the heart of winter)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a practical concern in the Valley. An occasional hard freeze can reach into the high 20s°F and damage hanging fruit or a young tree, but most winters need no protection at all.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: Navel oranges are one of the Rio Grande Valley's classic fruit trees. Winters are mild and almost never freeze, and harvest runs from October into January, the early part of the citrus season here.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley grows navel oranges reliably alongside its signature grapefruit: essentially frost-free winters and a long, intensely hot summer bank ample heat to sweeten and color the fruit fully. Harvest runs October into January, ahead of the Valley's later-season citrus. Cold protection is a rare, occasional need.
rgv.cold_basis_seasoned: Valley winters rarely reach freezing, and a hard freeze reaching the high 20s°F, the point at which navel fruit is damaged, is a rare, short-lived event in nearly all years. The winter-low band used here, roughly 26 to 32°F, is a synthesis anchored to the closest analog frost-free citrus regions, the milder Gulf Coast and the Arizona low desert, not a single verbatim figure from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension; that source is the basis for the bloom and harvest windows above.
rgv.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here are mild and hard freezes are rare. On the rare cold night, cover young trees or hanging fruit, especially in the weeks around the winter harvest; most winters need no protection at all.
rgv.heat_basis_seasoned: The Valley's long, intensely hot summers bank abundant heat, more than enough to fully sweeten and color a navel; heat is never the limiting factor here. Very hot bloom-time weather can drive some spring fruit-drop, so steady irrigation through bloom and fruit set helps hold the crop.
rgv.heat_basis_beginner: Summers here are long and very hot, plenty for sweet, deeply colored navel oranges. Keep the tree watered well in spring, since very hot weather right at bloom time can drop some young fruit.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 is too cold for an in-ground navel. A navel orange tolerates brief cold to about 24°F before sustaining real branch damage, and this zone's coldest nights drop well below that, into the teens or lower. There is no dependable in-ground establishment window here; grow it as a container tree brought under cover for winter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for an orange tree outside. Navels start taking real damage around 24°F, and winters here get colder than that. Grow it in a pot you bring under cover for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: This region's periodic harder freeze, layered on an already-cold zone 8 winter, reaches well past a navel's roughly 24°F branch-damage point.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9's milder winter lows still dip into the low 20s°F in an ordinary year, close to or below a navel's roughly 24°F branch-damage point, so real cold protection (a container moved under cover for hard freezes) is needed even at this region's mild edge. Even where the tree survives and blooms, the maritime Pacific Northwest's cool, marine-tempered summer does not bank the heat a navel needs to ripen sweet, well-colored fruit, so there is no dependable edible crop either way. Best kept as a protected container specimen, not grown for fruit.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Even the milder zone 9 spots get cold enough some winters to hurt an orange tree, so protect it on hard-freeze nights. And even if the tree survives, our summers are not hot enough to sweeten the fruit, so do not count on oranges from it.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Both limiting factors bind here: zone 9's cold occasionally reaches a navel's damage point, and separately, the region's cool summer cannot deliver the heat this crop needs to ripen sweet regardless of how the tree comes through winter.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: This is the maritime Pacific Northwest's honest orange story, the flip side of a warm citrus region: zone 8 gets too cold outright, and even the milder zone 9 pockets are not truly orange country. A protected container tree can survive there for years, but our cool summers do not get hot enough to make the fruit sweet, so do not count on a real harvest either way.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: The maritime Pacific Northwest is a mirror of navel orange's usual flagship regions: cold-limited AND heat-poor at once, rather than the single limiting factor most regions face. Zone 8's winter lows sit well past the tree's roughly 24°F branch-damage point, ruling out in-ground culture outright. Zone 9's milder lows still occasionally reach that damage point, so a container tree needs real winter protection even there, and separately, the region's cool, marine-tempered summer does not bank enough heat to ripen sweet, well-colored fruit regardless of winter survival. Grow it as a protected container specimen if at all; this is not a fruiting region for navel orange.
pnw.cold_basis_seasoned: Zone 8's winter lows (roughly 10 to 20°F) are well past a navel's roughly 24°F branch-damage threshold; zone 9's milder band (roughly 20 to 30°F) still dips to or below that threshold in an ordinary year, so winter protection matters even at the region's mild edge (UF/IFAS).
pnw.cold_basis_beginner: Orange trees start taking damage around 24°F. Zone 8 here regularly gets colder than that, and even zone 9 dips that low some winters.
pnw.heat_basis_seasoned: The maritime Pacific Northwest's cool, cloud- and marine-influenced summer does not bank the sustained heat a navel orange needs to ripen sweet, well-colored fruit. Even a tree that survives winter cleanly in the milder zone stays a no-usable-crop proposition on heat alone.
pnw.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers here just are not hot enough for orange fruit to ripen sweet, even where the tree itself makes it through winter.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 7's Piedmont winters bring hard freezes below 10°F most years, far past the mid-20s°F point where navel wood is damaged and the 26 to 28°F point where the fruit itself freezes. There is no dependable in-ground establishment window this far inland.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for an orange tree outside. Winters regularly drop far past the point that damages the tree and freezes the fruit.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard freeze most winters, not just an occasional outbreak, is well past navel's cold tolerance in the Piedmont.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone still sees hard freezes into the teens most winters, past the mid-20s°F wood-damage point and the 26 to 28°F fruit-freeze point for navel orange. Ample summer heat is not the limiter here; winter cold decides the case on its own. A container tree brought fully indoors for the coldest nights is the only realistic way to grow one here.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Milder than the colder inland part of this region, but winters still get cold enough most years to damage the tree and freeze the fruit. If you want this in the Mid-Atlantic, grow it in a container you bring fully indoors for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Even the Coastal Plain's milder hard freezes reach past navel's mid-20s°F wood-damage point and its 26 to 28°F fruit-freeze point in most winters.

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Skip navel orange outdoors anywhere in the Mid-Atlantic. Winters in both the Piedmont and the Coastal Plain get cold enough most years to damage the tree and freeze the fruit. Grow it in a container you bring fully indoors for winter if you want to try.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: Navel orange is not viable in-ground anywhere in this belt. Both zones see hard freezes, more severe in the cooler Piedmont interior but a real risk even in the milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater, past navel's mid-20s°F wood-damage threshold and its 26 to 28°F fruit-freeze point in an ordinary winter. Summer heat is ample across the belt and is never the constraint; winter cold rules the crop out on its own. Container culture with full winter cover indoors is the only realistic path.
mid_atlantic.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 10 to 20°F in the milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone to 0 to 10°F in the cooler Piedmont, both well past the mid-20s°F point where navel wood is damaged and the 26 to 28°F point where the fruit itself freezes (UF/IFAS HS132). This is a real, frost-anchored winter in both zones, not an occasional-outbreak risk.
mid_atlantic.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here get properly cold most years in both parts of this region, cold enough to damage the tree and freeze the fruit if left outdoors.
mid_atlantic.heat_basis_seasoned: Heat is moot here: the tree cannot survive winter in either zone, so its summer heat need, which the belt's long, hot, humid summers would meet easily, never gets the chance to matter.
mid_atlantic.heat_basis_beginner: Summer warmth does not matter here, because the tree cannot get through winter in the first place. Summers are plenty hot if it could.

This is a real, frost-anchored winter in both zones, not an occasional-outbreak risk.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8's cooler, higher pockets bring winter lows well below navel orange's mid-20s°F wood-damage point and its roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point. There is no dependable in-ground establishment window this far into the region's cold edge.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for an orange tree outside. Winters regularly drop past the point that damages the tree and freezes the fruit.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard freeze most winters in this zone is well past navel's cold tolerance.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley floor sits close to navel orange's mid-20s°F wood-damage point and its roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point; the valley floor, at about 2,000 feet, runs colder in winter than the lower Phoenix desert (near 1,100 feet), where navel fruits reliably, so this crop does not clone that warmer verdict here. A container tree brought fully under cover on hard-freeze nights can persist for years and may bloom in a mild winter, but there is no dependable in-ground or fruiting crop; orange sits between the hardier mandarin and the more cold-sensitive grapefruit and lemon in how it handles this valley's winters.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Orange is a middle-of-the-road case here: better cold tolerance than grapefruit or lemon, but the Las Vegas Valley still runs too cold most winters for a dependable in-ground tree. A container tree brought under cover on the coldest nights can survive for years and might fruit in an unusually mild one, but do not count on it.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The valley's frost season (last freeze around Feb 28, first around Nov 25, NWS Las Vegas normals) brackets a winter whose harder nights reach past navel's mid-20s°F wood point and 26°F fruit-freeze point in most years.

10.plant_out: Spring (container or balled; after hard-freeze risk passes)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Laughlin/Colorado River corner has the summer heat for good navel quality and sits close enough to its cold edge that fruit is realistic most years: ordinary winter lows here mostly clear the mid-20s°F wood point and the roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point. This is still the region's single mildest, smallest zone with no dedicated local citrus field data, so a hard freeze in a harder winter can still take the crop; protect fruit and young trees when one threatens.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Laughlin is warm enough for orange to actually fruit in most years, unlike the rest of this region. It is still a desert winter, so protect the tree and fruit on the occasional hard-freeze night.
10.harvest: Dec - Feb (protect fruit and young trees in a hard freeze)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An occasional hard freeze can still reach navel's mid-25 to mid-26°F damage range even in this mildest zone; protect fruit and young trees on those nights.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Orange lands in the middle of this region's citrus picture: worse than mandarin's cold tolerance, better than grapefruit's or lemon's. It is a protected container prospect in the Las Vegas Valley, and only at the warmest Laughlin corner does it actually fruit most years, with protection on hard freeze nights.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: Navel orange is intermediate in this region's citrus lineup: hardier than grapefruit or lemon, less hardy than mandarin. The region's cooler zone-8 pockets rule it out entirely. The Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) sits close to navel's mid-20s°F wood-damage point and roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point; the valley floor, at about 2,000 feet, runs colder in winter than the lower Phoenix desert (near 1,100 feet) where navel fruits reliably, so this crop stays a protected container specimen there, not a dependable fruiting tree. Only the Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10), the region's mildest pocket, clears that threshold closely enough for real, if freeze-exposed, fruit most years. Ample summer heat is never the constraint anywhere in the region; winter cold is.
nevada.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 30 to 40°F in the mild Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10) to 20 to 30°F in the Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) to 10 to 20°F in the region's cooler, higher pockets (zone 8). Navel orange takes wood damage near the mid-20s°F and fruit damage near 26°F; only zone 10 sits reliably above that band. The Las Vegas Valley floor, at about 2,000 feet, runs colder in winter than the lower Phoenix desert (near 1,100 feet), the reason navel is judged more cold-limited here than in Arizona's low desert.
nevada.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here get cold enough in most of the region to damage an orange tree and freeze the fruit. The warm Laughlin corner is the exception, where the tree usually clears winter and can fruit, with protection on the hardest-freeze nights.
nevada.heat_basis_seasoned: The Nevada high desert's long, hot, dry summer, routinely above 90 to 100°F (University of Nevada, Reno Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), banks ample heat for good navel quality; heat is not the limiter anywhere in this region. Winter cold is what keeps the crop to a protected container in most of the belt and a freeze-watched in-ground tree at its warmest corner.
nevada.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers are hot enough for good oranges wherever the tree can get through winter. Cold, not heat, is the deciding factor here.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost data) sit well past navel orange's mid-20s°F wood-damage point and its roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point, and citrus is absent from USU's Washington County Fruits recommendation for this elevation. There is no dependable in-ground or even long-term container option here; grow it, if at all, as a fully enclosed greenhouse or indoor specimen rather than a garden planting.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Winters here, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, regularly drop past the point that damages both the tree and the fruit of a navel orange. Unlike lemon or mandarin, there is no cold-hardy orange type to fall back on, so this is not a realistic tree to try outdoors, even in a container, in St. George.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter cold (last frost near March 30, first frost near November 1, USU Extension Washington County) is a hard freeze past navel orange's own mid-20s°F wood-damage point in most years.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Navel orange does not work outdoors in St. George. Winters here, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, regularly damage both the tree and the fruit, and unlike lemon or mandarin there is no cold-hardy orange type to make it work in a container either.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's zone 8b winters run roughly 15 to 20°F on an ordinary cold night, well past navel orange's mid-20s°F wood-damage point and roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point. USU's Washington County Fruits page, which names the fruits recommended at this elevation, includes no citrus at all, and unlike lemon (Meyer) or mandarin (clementine, satsuma), navel orange has no widely grown cold-hardy selection to close the gap. Summer heat is not the problem, St. George easily clears 100°F in June, July, and August, but winter cold decides the case here.
utah_dixie.cold_basis_seasoned: St. George sits in USDA zone 8b, with ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost and elevation data). Navel orange takes wood damage near the mid-20s°F and fruit damage near 26°F, both well above St. George's ordinary winter low, and unlike mandarin or lemon it has no widely available cold-hardy selection to close that gap. USU's Washington County Fruits page, which lists the fruits recommended at this elevation, names no citrus at all.
utah_dixie.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here bring ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, well past the point that damages both the wood and the fruit of a navel orange tree. There is no cold-hardy orange type the way there is for lemon or mandarin, so this is not a realistic outdoor tree here.
utah_dixie.heat_basis_seasoned: St. George summers reach past 100°F in June, July, and August (USU Extension Washington County), more than enough heat to sweeten navel orange fruit if the tree could clear winter. Winter cold, not summer heat, rules this crop out here.
utah_dixie.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers here are plenty hot for orange fruit to taste good. Winter cold is the reason this does not work outdoors in St. George, not a lack of summer warmth.

crops.description_seasoned: The navel orange (Citrus sinensis) is a subtropical evergreen fruit tree prized for its seedless, easy-to-peel fruit. Unlike lemons, which produce quality fruit across a wide range of climates, navel oranges require substantial accumulated summer heat to develop full sweetness and color. In cool coastal areas, navel fruit often remains acidic and pale even though the tree is healthy and frost-safe, because heat is insufficient for sugar development. In warm inland valleys and desert regions, the same varieties produce deeply colored, sugar-rich fruit. This dual gating, cold limiting where the tree survives and heat limiting where it produces quality fruit, is the defining regional story for navel oranges. Trees are grafted onto rootstock selected for disease resistance, cold tolerance, and soil adaptability. A single tree can remain productive for 50 years or more with proper care.
crops.description_beginner: The navel orange is an evergreen citrus tree that makes seedless, easy-to-peel oranges. The catch with navels is heat: unlike lemons, which make good fruit in lots of climates, navel oranges need a lot of summer heat to turn sweet and orange. In cool coastal areas the tree grows fine and even makes fruit, but the fruit can stay sour and pale because there is not enough heat to make it sweet. In hot inland valleys and the desert, those same trees make deeply colored, sweet fruit. So two things shape where navels do well: cold limits how far north they grow, and summer heat decides whether the fruit gets sweet. One tree makes fruit on its own, with no second tree needed.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest navels by taste, not color alone. Rind color develops as nights cool, but in mild and humid climates the rind can stay green-tinged on fully ripe fruit (the Florida and Hawaii nuance), and a fully colored rind does not guarantee sweetness in a cool-summer climate. Taste-test a fruit to judge readiness. The great advantage of navels is the long on-tree hold: fruit holds and continues to sweeten on the tree for weeks to months, so the harvest window is forgiving and you can pick over an extended period. The exception is hot, dry desert climates, where fruit left too long granulates and dries, so pick within the prime window there.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick oranges by taste, not just by color. The skin turns orange as the nights get cold, but in mild or humid areas it can still look a little green even when the fruit is ripe, and an orange-looking fruit in a cool-summer area might still be sour. So taste one to decide. The best part about navels is that the fruit keeps on the tree for weeks or months and gets sweeter, so you can pick a few at a time and there is no rush. The exception is the hot, dry desert, where fruit left on too long dries out inside, so pick it during its best window there.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Navel oranges bloom primarily in spring, typically March through May depending on climate and zone. The bloom period lasts roughly three weeks. Fruit develops slowly over 10 to 12 months after bloom, with harvest beginning the following winter. In warm inland California, harvest runs November through February for standard Washington navels. In the low desert (Arizona, California desert), harvest may start as early as October. Late-maturing selections such as Lane Late extend the harvest window into March or April.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Oranges bloom in spring, usually March through May depending on where you live, with fragrant white flowers for about three weeks. The fruit then grows slowly for about ten to twelve months, so you harvest the following winter. In warm inland California that is November through February; in the low desert it can start as early as October; and late types like Lane Late stretch the harvest into March or April.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Navel oranges tolerate brief cold to approximately 24°F before sustaining significant branch damage, making them moderately cold hardy among citrus (hardier than lemons and limes, less hardy than satsuma mandarins or kumquats). Trees are evergreen with no dormancy period, so actively growing tissue is always vulnerable to frost. Young trees and developing fruit are more frost sensitive than mature wood. Beyond cold, navel oranges also require high accumulated summer heat to ripen sweet fruit. In cool coastal zones where frosts are rare, trees survive and bloom normally but produce sour, poorly colored fruit because heat accumulation is insufficient. This means the practical growing range is narrower than the survival range: zones 9 through 11 with adequate summer heat for fruit quality.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Oranges can take a brief chill down to about 24°F before branches get hurt, which makes them hardier than lemons or limes but less hardy than satsuma mandarins. Because the tree is evergreen and never goes dormant, its growing leaves and wood can be hurt by frost any time it gets cold enough, and young trees and ripening fruit are the most tender. Cold sets the northern limit for growing navels. Separately, navels also need a lot of summer heat to make sweet fruit, so in cool coastal areas the tree survives and even flowers but the fruit may stay sour and pale.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Navel oranges require no chilling to flower or fruit. They are evergreen and do not enter a physiological dormancy triggered by chill accumulation. Flowering is driven by spring warming and moisture rather than release from a prior cold period. This distinguishes citrus from deciduous fruit trees such as peaches and apples, which require hundreds of chill hours to break bud dormancy and set a normal crop.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Oranges do not need any winter chill to flower or fruit. Unlike peaches and apples, which need hundreds of cold hours in winter to wake up and set a crop, citrus is evergreen and is triggered to bloom by spring warmth and moisture instead. So chill hours, which matter a lot for deciduous fruit trees, simply do not apply to oranges.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Navel oranges are parthenocarpic and male sterile, producing seedless fruit without pollination. The fruit develops through a hormonal process that swells the ovary independently of fertilization. Because navels produce no viable pollen, a single tree will set a full crop on its own. Cross-pollination from nearby citrus varieties with fertile pollen can actually introduce seeds into the fruit, so isolation from pollen-bearing citrus preserves the seedless quality that defines the navel type.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: A navel orange makes fruit all by itself, with no second tree and no bees needed. It does this through a natural process that swells the fruit without pollination, which is also why the fruit is seedless. In fact, if pollen from another nearby citrus does reach the flowers, it can put seeds into the fruit, so keeping a navel away from other pollen-making citrus actually helps keep it seedless.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Navel oranges are parthenocarpic, setting seedless fruit without pollination. They are male sterile and produce no viable pollen. Cross-pollination from nearby citrus with fertile pollen can introduce seeds into the fruit, which is undesirable. No pollinizer tree is needed. Isolating navels from pollen-bearing citrus varieties helps preserve seedlessness.
pollination.notes_beginner: Navel oranges make seedless fruit on their own, without needing pollination or a second tree, so you only need one. They produce no working pollen of their own. If pollen from another citrus nearby reaches the flowers, the fruit can end up with a few seeds, so it is best to keep a navel away from other pollen-bearing citrus to keep the fruit seedless.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: Citrus needs only light shaping, not the structural pruning of deciduous fruit trees. Remove dead, crossing, or weak wood in spring after harvest, and strip any shoots emerging below the graft union, since these are rootstock growth that will not produce navel fruit and will sap the tree if left. Keep the canopy open enough for light and air, but heavy heading cuts are unnecessary and reduce the next crop.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Oranges need only light pruning, not the heavy shaping that peaches and apples get. In spring after harvest, trim out any dead, crossing, or weak branches, and pull off any shoots growing from below the graft knob low on the trunk, since those come from the rootstock and will never make navels (and they steal energy if you leave them). Keep the canopy open enough for light and air, but you do not need to cut it back hard, and heavy cutting just reduces next year's fruit.

crops.establishment_note: Navel oranges typically begin producing fruit in the third year after planting a grafted nursery tree. Full production is reached by year 5 to 8 depending on rootstock and growing conditions.
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Rootstocks are usually not a choice at retail garden centers, because trees come grafted onto industry-standard rootstocks. Ask which rootstock your tree is on, and look for a tag that names both the variety and the rootstock. Rootstocks differ in the soils they suit, and they can affect fruit quality. For a pot or a small yard, Flying Dragon is a dwarfing rootstock well suited to home and container citrus.

rootstock_options.name: Carrizo citrange
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for a certified disease-free tree whose tag names both the variety and the rootstock. Carrizo does poorly in salty or alkaline soil, so it is a poor match where your soil is either.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Carrizo is a citrange, a cross of Washington navel orange and trifoliate orange. UF/IFAS rates it a large, vigorous tree under Florida grove conditions. It tolerates tristeza virus, and UF/IFAS rates its Phytophthora tolerance intermediate. It does poorly in saline, high-pH and heavy clay soils, and it is susceptible to citrus nematode. Its cold tolerance is moderate, a little below that of trifoliate orange. Foothill growers sometimes use it, and it produces high-quality fruit later in the season. The University of Arizona uses a navel orange on Carrizo as its example of a correctly labeled nursery tree.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Carrizo grows a large, vigorous tree. It holds up well against tristeza, a virus that can kill citrus trees quickly. Its protection from root rot is only middling. It struggles in salty, alkaline or heavy clay soil. It handles cold moderately well, a bit less well than trifoliate orange.

rootstock_options.name: Swingle citrumelo
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Swingle is a poor match for heavy clay or alkaline soil, so ask about another rootstock if yours is either.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Swingle is a citrumelo, a cross of Duncan grapefruit and trifoliate orange. It became the most widely used rootstock in Florida. It resists Phytophthora foot rot and citrus nematode, and it tolerates tristeza virus. Its cold hardiness is good. UF/IFAS rates it an intermediate-size tree, smaller than one on Carrizo. It is not adapted to heavy clay or calcareous soils. On salt the sources differ: UF/IFAS rates its salinity tolerance poor, while UC Riverside calls it moderately salt tolerant.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Swingle is a tough rootstock that became Florida's most widely used. It resists foot rot and root rot, and a root pest called citrus nematode. It holds up well against tristeza virus and cold. It makes a medium-size tree, smaller than Carrizo. It does poorly in heavy clay or alkaline, lime-rich soil.

rootstock_options.name: Flying Dragon trifoliate
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Flying Dragon if you want a citrus tree for a pot or a small yard. It is a dwarfing trifoliate rootstock that keeps the tree small.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Flying Dragon is a trifoliate rootstock with a dwarfing effect of about 75 percent. UC Master Gardeners call it the only true dwarfing citrus rootstock, with trees 4 to 8 feet tall. UC Cooperative Extension calls it well suited to home and container citrus, but not to production orchards. UF/IFAS rates it tolerant of tristeza and Phytophthora, resistant to citrus nematode, and good in freezes. It does poorly in saline and high-pH soils. Its juice quality rates high, but small trees bear less fruit per tree.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Flying Dragon is a dwarfing rootstock that keeps a citrus tree small, usually 4 to 8 feet tall. That makes it a good fit for a pot or a small yard. It holds up well against tristeza virus, root rot and cold. Its fruit is good, but a smaller tree means a smaller crop. It does poorly in salty or alkaline soil.

pet_safe.note: The fruit is fine, but the peel, leaves, and citrus oils can upset the stomach of cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about building a frame, not growing oranges. Strip the fruit for the first couple of years: a navel carries its crop for ten to twelve months, which is a long, heavy draw on the tree, and one allowed to hold that load young grows slowly and stays weak. Plant with the graft union, the knobby joint low on the trunk where your navel was joined to its roots, standing two to three inches clear of the finished soil, and keep mulch pulled back from the trunk, because a damp union is the classic way citrus gets foot rot. Water in well to settle the soil, then wait for new growth before feeding, since fertilizer given before the roots are working simply washes past them. Check soft new growth for Asian citrus psyllid while the tree is small.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Strip set for the first two seasons rather than one: navel carries a ten-to-twelve-month crop, an unusually long carbohydrate draw, and a young tree permitted to hold it develops slowly and stays structurally weak. Set the graft union two to three inches proud of finished grade with mulch pulled back, against foot rot. Irrigate in to settle the profile, then defer the first feed until active flush, since fertilizer applied to inactive roots leaches past them and adds salt load for nothing. Scout tender flush for Asian citrus psyllid while the tree is small enough to inspect thoroughly; the psyllid vectors huanglongbing, and new growth is where it feeds and lays.
crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: Navels usually begin producing in the third year after planting a grafted tree. Hold the soil moisture steady through the roughly three-week spring bloom, because a navel sets its entire crop from that one flush and drought stress now drops the flowers and the young fruit behind them. A few weeks after set the tree will drop a lot of small fruit on its own. That is not a problem and not something to fix: the tree is self-thinning to what it can actually finish, and the fruit that stays will size up better for it. Do not respond by overwatering or overfeeding. Skip heavy pruning during and just after bloom, and leave the flowering wood alone.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: Bearing typically begins in year three on a grafted nursery tree. Moisture stability through the roughly three-week bloom governs the season, since navel sets its entire crop from one main flush. The June-drop several weeks after set is physiological self-thinning, not stress, and the correct response is none: the tree is shedding beyond its carrying capacity and remaining fruit sizes better for it, so overwatering or overfeeding in reaction is actively counterproductive. Navel is self-fruitful and requires no pollinizer, so bloom- period management reduces to leaving flowering wood and developing fruit undisturbed and deferring structural pruning.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From about the fourth year the tree carries a real crop, building toward full production by year five to eight. Navels take their time in every direction: the fruit develops over ten to twelve months, so water deeply and on a steady rhythm right across the summer, since uneven moisture over that long stretch shows up later as split and dropped fruit. When it comes to picking, taste first. Navels color up before they are actually sweet, and in a mild winter the orange skin is a poor guide, so sample a fruit from the sunny side and let flavor call it. Then take your time: ripe navels hold well on the branch for weeks, so pick what you need and let the rest keep storing themselves outdoors.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production is reached by roughly year five to eight depending on rootstock and conditions. The defining constraint is the ten-to-twelve-month hang: irrigation consistency across that entire development window, not just at set, is what prevents late splitting and pre-harvest drop, so a steady summer rhythm outranks volume. Harvest on flavor rather than rind color, which colors ahead of maturity and is an unreliable index in mild-winter regions; sample from the sun side before committing. Fruit stores on the tree for weeks, so pick incrementally against demand rather than stripping. Expect alternate bearing and damp it with steady fertility and consistent irrigation; a sharp unexplained drop is a different signal and points at a root, water or disease problem worth chasing.

crops.name: Mandarin (Clementine)

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Deep, well-drained sandy loam to loam, slightly acidic
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Deep soil that drains well is best, ideally a sandy loam or loam.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Sandy and rocky soils with adequate water and feeding; heavy soils only on a raised mound or berm that guarantees drainage
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Sandy or rocky soil is fine if you water and feed enough. Heavy soil works only if you plant on a raised mound so water drains away.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Heavy, poorly drained clay and any low spot where water stands, which invites Phytophthora foot and root rot
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Avoid heavy clay that drains poorly and any spot where water pools. Wet roots lead to a root rot that kills citrus.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Mandarins care most about drainage. They want deep soil that drains well and stays slightly acidic, kept evenly moist but never soggy. If water sits around the roots, the tree can get a root rot that is the most common way citrus dies. Heavy clay holds water, so the fix is to build a low mound and set the tree on top so the crown drains. Keep the knobby graft union above the soil. If your soil is alkaline (high pH), common in the desert and inland West, the tree may run short on iron and zinc, so feed a citrus fertilizer that includes them.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Mandarins share the citrus non-negotiable: sharp drainage. They do best in deep, well-drained sandy loam to loam, slightly acidic, with steady moisture and no waterlogging. Saturated roots invite Phytophthora foot and root rot, one of the most serious threats to a citrus tree. On heavy ground plant high on a raised mound or berm so the root crown drains freely, and keep the graft union clear of the soil line. On high-pH alkaline soils, common in desert and interior-West regions, iron and zinc lock up and the tree shows chlorosis, so use a micronutrient-inclusive citrus fertilizer.

ph.note_beginner: Mandarins like soil that is slightly acidic, around pH 6.0 to 6.5. The main thing to watch is alkaline (high pH) soil, common in the desert and inland West, where the tree cannot take up iron and zinc and the leaves yellow while the veins stay green. If that happens, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc.
ph.note_seasoned: Mandarins prefer a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerate a somewhat wider band. The practical problem is high-pH alkaline soil (common in the desert Southwest and interior West), where iron and zinc become chemically unavailable and the tree shows interveinal chlorosis even though the nutrients are present. Correct with chelated micronutrients and a citrus fertilizer that supplies them.

fertilizer.frequency: split applications through the growing season
fertilizer.type: citrus (nitrogen-forward, with iron, zinc, and manganese)
fertilizer.timing: late winter or early spring through summer; stop by late summer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Mandarins are nitrogen-hungry like all citrus and feed best on a rhythm concentrated in the growing season. Feed a bearing tree from late winter or early spring through summer in split applications, and stop by late summer so the fall flush hardens before winter cold. Because mandarins are smaller trees than a navel orange, scale the total nitrogen down accordingly. Young trees get smaller, more frequent doses to build the framework. On alkaline soils use a citrus fertilizer that supplies iron, zinc, and manganese as chelates and water it in. Over-fertilizing pushes soft flush that draws aphids, leafminer, and psyllid.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Mandarins are hungry for nitrogen and want most of their food during the growing season. Start feeding a grown tree as the weather warms in late winter or early spring, keep it up through summer in a few split doses, then stop by late summer so the new growth toughens before cool weather. A mandarin is a smaller tree than an orange, so it needs less total feed. Feed young trees smaller amounts more often. If your soil is alkaline, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc so the leaves do not yellow, and do not overfeed, since soft growth draws pests.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A nitrogen-forward citrus formulation (for example a 2-1-1 ratio) with included micronutrients (iron, zinc, manganese), or a product labeled specifically for citrus
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A fertilizer made for citrus (look for one labeled citrus); these are higher in nitrogen and include the iron and zinc citrus needs
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Scale nitrogen to tree age and size, and note that a mandarin's smaller canopy needs less than a full-size orange. Follow the citrus product label and local extension rates, which vary by region and soil, and divide the year's nitrogen across spring-to-summer applications, with proportionally less for young trees.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Give more as the tree gets bigger, following the amounts on the citrus fertilizer label and splitting it across spring and summer. A small young tree needs only a little; a grown mandarin needs more, though still less than a full-size orange tree. When in doubt, follow the package directions for the tree's size.

companions.note_beginner: Keep grass and lawn out from under a mandarin tree, since grass steals the water and food the tree's shallow roots need. A ring of mulch, kept back from the trunk, beats grass growing right up to the tree. There is little real benefit to planting things close around citrus.
companions.note_seasoned: Keep turf and lawn grasses out of the root zone. Grass competes hard for water and nutrients in the shallow layer where citrus feeder roots concentrate, and mowers damage the trunk. A mulched, grass-free basin out to the canopy dripline is the standard recommendation for all citrus, mandarins included. Low, shallow-rooted covers or a cool-season legume kept outside the trunk flare add living mulch without root competition. Mandarins fruit on a single tree, so no pollinizer companion is required; in fact nearby pollen-bearing citrus can put seeds into otherwise seedless fruit.

good_beginner.name: White clover
good_beginner.why_beginner: A low clover outside the trunk area works as a living mulch and adds a little nitrogen, without stealing water the way lawn grass does.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Legume living-mulch / cover crop under citrus is extension-supported for soil nitrogen and organic matter; medium because citrus-specific nitrogen transfer is site-dependent and clover also competes for water.

good_beginner.name: Marigold
good_beginner.why_beginner: A simple flower that brings in helpful insects and fills bare ground around the tree. Plant it beyond the trunk, not tight against it.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Marigold beneficial-insect draw and root-knot nematode suppression are partly grounded as general mechanisms; applied to citrus by analogy, no mandarin-specific trial located.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Yarrow
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low, shallow-rooted plant that draws beneficial insects and does not compete with citrus roots when kept outside the dripline.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Yarrow is a low, tough plant with flat flower heads that pull in ladybugs, lacewings, and other good bugs that eat aphids. It is shallow-rooted and easygoing, so it does not crowd the tree as long as you keep it out toward the edge of the canopy. Let it flower to get the benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Yarrow as an insectary / drought-tolerant ground cover is consistently reported and mechanistically plausible; the citrus-specific pest reduction is unquantified.

good_seasoned.name: Fava bean
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season nitrogen fixer grown beyond the dripline as a winter cover, then cut and dropped to feed the soil without crowding the tree.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Cool-season legume cover crops in citrus are extension-supported for soil nitrogen and organic matter; medium because citrus-specific nitrogen-transfer magnitude is site and timing dependent.

bad_beginner.name: Turf grass
bad_beginner.why_beginner: Lawn grass under the tree steals the water and food the mandarin's shallow roots need. A ring of mulch, kept back from the trunk, is better than grass.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Citrus-grass root-zone competition is extension-documented; same basis for mandarins.

bad_beginner.name: Bermuda grass
bad_beginner.why_beginner: A tough, spreading lawn grass that competes hard for water and is difficult to keep out of the root zone. Clear it out to the edge of the branches.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Same citrus-grass-competition basis; Bermuda is a notably aggressive spreading turf in the citrus literature.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: St. Augustine grass
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A dense, spreading lawn grass that competes aggressively for water and nutrients in the topsoil and creeps right up to the trunk. Keep it cleared out to the dripline.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: St. Augustine is a thick, fast-spreading lawn grass that is rough on citrus. It soaks up water and food in the top layer of soil where the tree's roots feed, and it creeps to the trunk. Keep a clear or mulched circle around the base and hold the grass back beyond it.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Citrus is extension-documented as vulnerable to weed and grass competition in the root zone, especially at bloom and flush; St. Augustine is an aggressive spreading turf.

pests.name: Asian citrus psyllid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A tiny mottled-brown insect, about an eighth of an inch, that feeds tilted up at a 45-degree angle on new flush, a posture no other citrus pest shares. Nymphs make waxy tubules and curl tender growth. The insect matters less for its feeding than for what it carries: it is the vector of Huanglongbing (citrus greening), the most serious citrus disease worldwide. Scout the youngest flush.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This tiny brown insect rests on new leaves at an angle, rear end raised, which is your clue. The young ones make little waxy white threads and curl the new leaf tips. The real danger is not the feeding but a fatal disease it spreads, citrus greening, so it is worth acting on even where the pest is uncommon.
pests.cause_seasoned: Adults lay eggs only on new flush, so populations track flushing cycles and build fastest in warm weather when the tree pushes tender growth. The pest is established across much of the southern United States, and any psyllid should be treated as a potential disease carrier.
pests.cause_beginner: The psyllid breeds on fresh new leaves, so it builds up fastest when the tree is pushing tender growth in warm weather. It has spread across the southern states, and any psyllid you find could be carrying the disease.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Buy only certified citrus from a reputable nursery and never move citrus plants or leaves out of a quarantine area, the main way the pest and disease jump regions. Inspect each flush in the warm season, and conserve the parasitic wasp Tamarixia and general predators that suppress it.
pests.prevention_beginner: Buy certified citrus from a trusted nursery, and never carry citrus plants or cuttings out of a quarantine zone, since that is how the pest and its disease spread. Check new leaves often in warm weather, and follow local guidance if greening is in your area.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: On a backyard tree, horticultural oil and insecticidal soap on the new flush reduce nymphs; thorough coverage is key, repeated as each flush emerges. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree. Most important, report suspected psyllids or greening symptoms to your county agricultural office, since this is a regulated pest.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the new growth to knock back the young psyllids, repeating each time fresh leaves appear. Hold off on oil when it is above about 95°F or the tree is short on water, or the oil can burn leaves. Also report any psyllids or signs of the disease to your local farm advisor.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Leave the tiny parasitic wasp Tamarixia and the general predators already in your yard to work on the psyllid, and keep strong broad-spectrum insecticides off the tree, since those take out the helpers along with the pest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Tamarixia and resident generalist predators suppress psyllid numbers, so conserving them is a working control rather than a courtesy. Broad-spectrum material removes them along with the target, and the population they were holding down rebuilds on the next flush.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On a backyard tree, insecticidal soap sprayed onto the new leaves knocks back the young psyllids, which is the stage it reaches. It works only where it lands, so cover the fresh growth thoroughly and spray again each time another round of leaves pushes out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap reduces nymphs on the flush and acts only on contact, so coverage of the expanding growth decides the result and applications follow flushing rather than a calendar. It does not stand in for the reporting and quarantine steps above it, which are what act on the disease risk.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil that smothers insects rather than poisoning them, does the same job on the new growth. Hold off in hot weather and when the tree is short of water, or the oil can burn the leaves, and repeat with each new flush, since it wears off quickly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil on emerging flush reduces nymphs by contact, so thorough wetting of the tender growth governs the outcome and timing tracks the flushing cycle. Withhold it in hot weather or on a drought-stressed tree, where foliage injury follows.

pests.name: Citrus leafminer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Silvery, serpentine tunnels winding through new leaves, with a thin dark frass line down each mine and leaf margins that curl around the damage. The larva mines only young, expanding foliage; hardened leaves are not attacked. On an established tree the injury is cosmetic, but on a young mandarin pushing lots of flush it can slow growth.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You will see squiggly silver trails snaking through the new leaves, often with the leaf edge curled. A tiny caterpillar makes these tunnels inside young leaves only. It looks alarming but rarely hurts a grown tree, though it can set back a small young one.
pests.cause_seasoned: A small moth lays eggs on tender new flush, and the larvae mine between the leaf surfaces. Generations cycle quickly in warm weather, so damage peaks on the late-summer and fall flushes rather than spring growth.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny moth lays eggs on the newest leaves, and the larvae tunnel inside them. They breed fast in warm weather, so the worst damage shows on the late-summer growth.
