Mandarins are strongly alternate-bearing, so expect a marked swing between heavy and light crop years unless heavy years are thinned; this is normal for the group and managed rather than cured.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A mandarin hits its full crop around four to seven years old and then produces for decades. Mandarins tend to bear a big crop one year and a light one the next, which is normal; thinning the heavy year evens it out.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Strip any flowers that set in the first season so the tree puts its energy into roots and framework rather than fruit, even though mandarins are precocious and may try to bear early. Light bearing typically begins in year two or three, with a full crop building as the tree matures. The early investment pays back in stronger, earlier-peaking production.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Young trees need their first-year energy in roots and branches, not fruit, even though a mandarin may want to fruit early. Snap off any first-season flowers. Fruit will start coming around year two or three, with a real crop as the tree grows. Building up first gets you more fruit in the long run.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No university extension or peer-reviewed source supports timing mandarin planting or care by moon phase. Citrus planting and management are driven by frost timing, soil temperature, and heat accumulation, not lunar cycles, so no moon-phase preference is assigned.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Fruit stays green and tart even though the tree looks healthy
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The mandarins are green and sour even though the tree seems fine
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mandarins color and sweeten with cool fall nights and adequate warmth in the season. In the warm, humid tropics and on the coolest coastal strips the tree grows and sets fruit but the fruit can stay green-skinned and low in sugar because the climate lacks the diurnal swing (warm days, cool nights) that develops mandarin quality. This is less demanding than a navel's high-heat requirement, but it is still a climate limit, not a care mistake.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Mandarins need cool fall nights and enough warmth to turn sweet and colored. In very warm, humid places (like low-elevation tropics) or the coolest foggy coast, the tree makes fruit but it can stay green and sour because the weather does not have the warm-day, cool-night swing that sweetens it. It is a climate thing, not something you did wrong.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: There is no cultural fix for the missing climate signal. In a marginal-quality area, choose the varieties best suited to it (satsuma tolerates cooler summers; some mandarins fruit at low heat) and a warmer microclimate can help at the margin. In the tropics, cooler uplands give better fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: You cannot fix the climate with watering or feeding. Pick varieties suited to your area (satsuma handles cooler summers well) and a warm, sheltered spot helps a little. In the tropics, cooler hillsides make better fruit.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Fruit is puffy, dry, or loose inside despite looking ripe
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The fruit looks ripe but is puffy and dry inside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Unlike a navel orange, most mandarins do not hold well on the tree. Satsuma and other early types puff (the rind separating and ballooning away from the flesh) and dry out if left on the branch past maturity, losing juice and flavor. The rind can look fine while the interior declines. This is the mandarin storage reality: pick promptly and refrigerate rather than storing on the tree.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Most mandarins, unlike oranges, do not keep well on the tree. Satsumas and early types get puffy (the skin balloons away from the fruit) and dry inside if left on too long. The skin can still look fine even when the inside has gone dry. The fix is to pick them when ripe and store them in the fridge.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pick early and mid-season mandarins promptly at maturity and refrigerate them rather than leaving the crop on the tree. If you want fruit that keeps on the branch into spring, grow a late holding type such as Gold Nugget or Pixie, which are the exception.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick most mandarins as soon as they are ripe and keep them in the fridge instead of on the tree. If you want fruit that can wait on the tree into spring, plant a late type like Gold Nugget or Pixie.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: A huge crop one year, then almost none the next
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: A big crop one year and hardly any the next
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Alternate bearing (a heavy on-year followed by a light or bare off-year) is a strong, well-known tendency in mandarins, far more pronounced than in sweet oranges. A very heavy crop suppresses the next year's flowering by consuming the tree's carbohydrate and inhibiting the shoot growth that carries next spring's bloom, so the tree swings between extremes. It is normal for the group, not a disease.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Mandarins tend to make a big crop one year and then very little the next. A heavy crop tires the tree and cuts down the growth that would carry next year's flowers, so it swings back and forth. This is normal for mandarins, not a sickness.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin heavy on-year crops in early summer, the earlier the better, to even out the cycle; hand thinning or light pruning of a loaded tree reduces the drain and improves next year's bloom. Steady feeding and watering also soften the swing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: In a big-crop year, pick off some of the fruit in early summer so the tree is not overloaded, which helps it flower and fruit again the next year. Steady feeding and watering help too.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Yellowing leaves with green veins (iron or zinc chlorosis)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves turning yellow but the veins stay green
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Yellow leaves with a network of green veins, especially on new growth, signal a micronutrient deficiency, most often iron or zinc, common on alkaline, high-pH soils where the nutrients are present but chemically unavailable. This is widespread in desert and interior-West soils. It is distinct from the symmetric overall yellowing of nitrogen shortage and from the blotchy asymmetric yellowing of greening disease.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: When leaves turn yellow but the veins stay green, especially on new growth, the tree is short on a micronutrient, usually iron or zinc. This happens a lot on alkaline (high pH) soils in the desert and inland West, where the nutrient is in the soil but the tree cannot take it up. It looks different from an even all-over yellowing (usually nitrogen) and from the blotchy yellowing of greening.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Correct with a chelated iron or zinc product, applied as a foliar spray for a quick response and to the soil for longer-term supply, and use a citrus fertilizer that includes micronutrients.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Fix it with a chelated iron or zinc product, sprayed on the leaves for a fast response and added to the soil for the long run, and use a citrus fertilizer that lists micronutrients.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Sudden leaf drop or heavy fruit drop
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree is dropping a lot of leaves or fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Several causes look different but end in drop. Cold injury follows a freeze, with leaves wilting, browning, and dropping days later on an evergreen tree that never goes dormant, and fruit can be damaged near 30°F even though the wood is hardier. Overwatering and poor drainage are the other frequent culprit: saturated roots and incipient foot rot cause yellowing and drop, with the tell being leaves that wilt but do not recover after watering. A spring heat spike during or just after bloom also drops flowers and young fruit.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A few things cause drop. Cold: after a freeze a mandarin (which never goes dormant) can wilt and drop leaves days later, and the fruit can be hurt near 30°F even though the wood is hardier. Too much water or poor drainage rots the roots and drops leaves, and the clue is that watering makes it worse. A hot spell during bloom also drops flowers and little fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Distinguish the cause first. For cold, improve frost protection and wait until spring growth to see what survived before pruning. For overwatering, back off irrigation, confirm sharp drainage, and check the graft union and crown are not buried. For heat-spike drop, keep moisture even and bump irrigation through the hot spell during bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Figure out the cause. If it was frost, protect the tree better next time and wait until spring to trim damaged wood. If it is overwatering, water less, make sure the soil drains fast, and check the graft knob is not buried. If a heat wave hit during bloom, keep the tree well watered through hot spells.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Mandarin is a permanent tree planted once and harvested annually for decades. Succession planting does not apply.

crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata) is the preferred rootstock for mandarins, especially satsuma, because it gives the greatest cold hardiness and good fruit quality, which is why satsuma on trifoliate can be grown in the ground in zone 8. For containers and small spaces, Flying Dragon (a dwarfing trifoliate selection) makes a compact tree and is the most cold-hardy of all. In warmer regions, Swingle citrumelo suits wetter soils. Ask the nursery which rootstock the tree is on and match it to your soil, space, and winter cold.

rootstock_options.name: Trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for a certified disease-free satsuma or mandarin on trifoliate-orange rootstock (selections such as 'Rubidoux') for maximum cold hardiness. Confirm your soil is not highly alkaline or saline, which trifoliate dislikes.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: The standard cold-hardiness rootstock for mandarins and the reason satsuma can be grown in the ground in the cold-edge zones. Confers the greatest cold tolerance of the common stocks, good Phytophthora and tristeza resistance, and good fruit quality, producing a compact, somewhat slow-growing tree. Not adapted to calcareous, high-pH, or saline soils, where it develops chlorosis.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Trifoliate orange is the cold-hardiness rootstock, and it is what lets satsumas grow in the ground where oranges cannot. It resists root rot, keeps the tree compact, and gives good fruit. Its weakness is that it dislikes very alkaline or salty soil, so it is less ideal in some desert areas.

rootstock_options.name: Flying Dragon trifoliate
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask specifically for Flying Dragon rootstock (a dwarfing selection of trifoliate orange). The compact size fits containers and small yards and makes frost protection easy.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A naturally dwarfing mutation of Poncirus trifoliata producing very compact trees ideal for containers and small gardens, and the best cold hardiness of any widely available citrus rootstock. Excellent Phytophthora, nematode, and tristeza resistance. Sensitive to high-pH and saline soils. Fruit quality is good and trees are precocious, though total yield per tree is lower due to the small canopy, which suits a mandarin well.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Flying Dragon is a dwarfing rootstock that keeps the tree small, perfect for pots and small yards, and it is the key to growing mandarins in cold climates since you can move the pot under cover for winter. It also has the best cold hardiness of the common rootstocks and strongly resists root rot. The tradeoff is a smaller tree with a smaller crop, usually just what a container grower wants.

rootstock_options.name: Swingle citrumelo
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Swingle citrumelo rootstock for wetter soils. It handles wet ground better than trifoliate but performs poorly on alkaline or calcareous soils.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A grapefruit-and-trifoliate hybrid widely used in Florida and the Gulf. Excellent Phytophthora resistance, good cold hardiness among standard stocks, and tristeza tolerant, handling wet soils better than most. Produces a good-quality, moderately sized tree. Not well adapted to calcareous or high-pH soils. A strong general-purpose choice for the humid Southeast.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Swingle citrumelo is a tough rootstock common in Florida and along the Gulf. It strongly resists root rot, handles wet soils better than most, and has decent cold hardiness, making a good tree with good fruit. It is a good pick in humid, wetter regions.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: Citrus needs only light shaping, not the structural pruning of deciduous fruit trees. Remove dead, crossing, or weak wood in spring after harvest, and strip any shoots below the graft union, since these are rootstock (often thorny trifoliate on a mandarin) that will not bear fruit and will sap the tree. The mandarin-specific task is thinning heavy on-year crops in early summer to manage alternate bearing, which is closer to crop-load management than to shaping. Keep the canopy open for light and air; heavy heading cuts are unnecessary and reduce the next crop.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Mandarins need only light pruning, not the heavy shaping peaches and apples get. In spring after harvest, trim out dead, crossing, or weak branches, and pull off any shoots below the graft knob, since those come from the rootstock (often thorny) and will never make mandarins. The one extra job for mandarins is thinning fruit in a heavy year (in early summer) to even out the big-crop, small-crop cycle. Keep the canopy open for light and air, but do not cut it back hard.

crops.establishment_note: Mandarins are precocious and typically begin bearing in the second or third year after planting a grafted nursery tree, a bit earlier than a navel orange. Full production is reached by about year four to seven depending on rootstock and growing conditions.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Most mandarins set a full crop on a single tree and are seedless when grown in isolation. Satsuma is parthenocarpic and reliably seedless. Clementine and W. Murcott are self-incompatible but facultatively parthenocarpic: on their own they set seedless fruit, but pollen from another nearby citrus with fertile pollen will cross-pollinate them and put seeds into the fruit, and pollen can travel a long way, so isolation from pollen-bearing citrus is what preserves seedlessness. A few mandarin hybrids fruit better with a compatible pollinizer, but no pollinizer is required for the common seedless types.
pollination.notes_beginner: Most mandarins make fruit on their own with no second tree needed, and they are seedless when grown away from other citrus. Satsuma is naturally seedless. Clementine and some others are seedless by themselves, but if pollen from another citrus nearby reaches the flowers, the fruit gets seeds, so keep a seedless mandarin away from other pollen-making citrus to keep it seedless.

UF/IFAS EDIS: A Guide to Citrus Disease Identification (HS-798/CH159)
UC Riverside Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection
LSU AgCenter Citrus Trees and Cold Tolerances

open_findings.summary: Per-region resolved_by_zone calendars, plant_out windows, bloom, and harvest months are modeled from mandarin biology (satsuma early-winter ripening, late types into spring) plus the nearest readable T1 citrus guidance, not a mandarin-specific per-region planting chart for all 10 regions. Windows are generally safe; tighten exact months at the variety-delta / certification pass.

The min_winter_temp_f band edges per region-zone are USDA-zone climate values (reused from the shared citrus zone model), reasoned against documented citrus/satsuma damage thresholds (tree ~15-20°F, fruit ~30°F) rather than a single per-region table. Confirm the numeric edges against sources at cert.

Shared-citrus pest entries (Asian citrus psyllid/HLB vector, citrus leafminer, scale, aphids, citrus red mite) are the genuine mandarin pest complex but were authored from the general UC IPM citrus hub + UF/IFAS HS132; the specific per-pest UC IPM pages were not re-fetched this session. Re-verify each pest page at cert. NOTE: the UF/IFAS satsuma pub (CH116) is cited under the catalogued umbrella id uf_ifas_edis and the UF/IFAS citrus disease-ID pub (CH159) under ufifas_ext, with the specific publication URL preserved in each anchor; dedicated catalog ids can be admitted at promote time.

Judgment calls: pH preferred [6.0,6.5] tolerated [5.5,7.5] (citrus-family band, sources cluster ~6.0-6.5); spacing_inches [120,216] and container min 10 gal modeled from mandarin small-tree size (satsuma small to medium-small) rather than a spacing table; productive_lifespan_years 'several decades' and years_to_full_production [4,7] modeled from citrus longevity + mandarin precocity. gating_factors kept ['cold_hardiness','heat_accumulation'] because cool-night/heat still quality-gates at the margins (Hawaii, far-north coast) though far less than a navel. [CORRECTION 2026-10-02: spacing_inches is 180 in, the UF/IFAS HS132 minimum, since PLA-10 promote 1 (120-216 in was modeled from small-tree size, not a spacing table); no row figure is authored, row_spacing_reason not_authored -- see PLA-10 promote 1, d021116.]

hawaii_tropical is lowest-confidence: modeled as marginal quality (warmth without cool nights) citing uhawaii_ctahr, whose F_N-14 PDF is scanned and was not machine-read this session; the marginal-quality reasoning follows the navel Hawaii precedent and general mandarin cool-night requirement. Confirm in review.

Clementine/W. No self-fruitful claim is fabricated: needs_pollinizer=false reflects that the common seedless types fruit on one tree.

open_findings.summary: failure_diagnostics[0] (fruit stays green and tart) lost its ucr_citrus credit at PLA-465's anchor repair (2026-09-20). The cited page was https://citrusvariety.ucr.edu/crc3178, the Frost Owari Satsuma accession, which contains 'green' 0 times and carries nothing on diurnal range. THE CLAIM IS NOT LEFT UNCITED, and the ruling was taken on the premise that it would be: the drop leaves uhawaii_ctahr (CTAHR F&N-14, https://www.ctahr.hawaii.edu/oc/freepubs/pdf/F_N-14.pdf, 266558 bytes, sha256 4d2a3549ec909ea85fc8be84efaea8ef3ed44ad31b4d8ee9547539c7eafaef47), read from raw bytes 2026-09-20, which carries the COLOR half verbatim: 'Fruit of citruses such as orange and tangerine usually fails to develop color when grown at Hawaii's lower elevations, and a green or green-yellow skin coloration is normal in ripe fruit. In areas with cooler nights, the fruits turn bright orange upon ripening.' THE SUGAR HALF IS NOT MERELY UNSUPPORTED, IT IS CONTRADICTED BY THE SURVIVING SOURCE, and those are different states that a later pass must not conflate. UNSUPPORTED means the page is silent and a hunt may still find the claim intact elsewhere. CONTRADICTED means the page that was actually read makes the OPPOSITE attribution, so a later hunt has to reconcile with it, not merely add to it. This is the second state. The record's claim is that fruit runs low in sugar in the warm humid lowlands for want of cool nights; CTAHR attributes low sugar to the opposite condition, cooler HIGH elevations, saying of trees grown in or above the 500 to 1000 ft range 'where cooler temperatures are common, the fruit may fail to develop high levels of sugar'. So the record joins green skin and low sugar under one diurnal-swing cause that its own cited page splits into two opposed ones. Do not read this entry as 'a citation is missing' and assume the contradiction is still unchecked: it was checked on 2026-09-20 from raw bytes, and it is a contradiction.
open_findings.resolution_note: Trevor's ruling 2026-09-20: drop the ucr_citrus credit, and do NOT run the targeted read in this promote. What that read now owes is narrower than the ruling assumed: not a re-citation of the claim, which uhawaii_ctahr already carries for color, but a T1 statement on whether the low-sugar half shares the cool-night mechanism. UF/IFAS or TAMU on citrus color break and degreening are the likely homes. Until then the sugar clause stands on the cited page's contrary attribution and should not be read as sourced.

open_findings.summary: regions.ca_south_coast.resolved_by_zone 9, 10 and 11 each claim a harvest window that spans two cultivars whose evidence is on two different UCR accession pages: 'Dec - Mar (early satsuma through late Pixie and Gold Nugget)', noted as 'the home of the famous Ojai Pixie and of excellent clementine and Gold Nugget crops'. anchoring_urls holds ONE url per source key, so the ucr_citrus key cannot carry both ends. The early end is crc3178 (satsuma, ripeness Oct to Dec); the late end is crc3568 (Pixie, 'matures in late winter and holds exceptionally late on the tree') or crc3913 (Gold Nugget, ripeness February to June, which is what reaches the cell's March end). All three were read from raw bytes 2026-09-20 and none carries the span. THIS IS NOT A MANDARIN DEFECT: it reaches any region cell bounded by an early variety at one end and a late one at the other. Same family as plum_self_fertile_boolean_european_default, which states the general form as one record, two types, a single-value shape that breaks wherever they diverge.
open_findings.resolution_note: Trevor's ruling 2026-09-20: LEAVE HELD, do not repoint. Picking one accession would silently credit it for the other end's half of the claim. The three cells stay on crc3178 and the structural question is filed as its own ticket, PLA-559, linked to plum's type-aware finding as the same family. 3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 is too cold for an in-ground mandarin. Even satsuma, the hardiest common citrus (mature tree to about 15 to 20°F), is killed by this zone's hard freezes into the low teens°F or below, so there is no dependable crop or establishment window in the ground.
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is too cold for a mandarin planted outside. Satsuma is the toughest citrus in cold, but winters here still drop far below what it can take, so it will not survive in the ground.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 4 is too cold for an in-ground mandarin. Even satsuma, the hardiest common citrus (mature tree to about 15 to 20°F), is killed by this zone's hard freezes into the low teens°F or below, so there is no dependable crop or establishment window in the ground.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: You cannot grow a mandarin in the ground in this region. Satsuma is the toughest citrus for cold, and cold-climate growers grow it in pots, moving them indoors for winter. The newer super-hardy satsuma hybrids reach only about zone 8, not this far north.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In-ground mandarins are not viable in zones 3 through 7. Satsuma is the most cold-hardy common citrus and the type cold-climate growers push furthest, and the newest cold-hardy satsuma hybrids extend only to about zone 8a; north of that, citrus is a container crop moved indoors for winter, a different growing system from this in-ground regional model.
northern_tier.cold_basis_seasoned: Zones 3 through 7 drop into the low teens°F and well below every winter, past even satsuma's roughly 15 to 20°F mature-tree limit, so an unprotected in-ground mandarin does not survive here.
northern_tier.cold_basis_beginner: It gets too cold here for a mandarin to live outside, even a hardy satsuma. Winters drop below what it can take.
northern_tier.heat_basis_seasoned: Heat is moot here: the tree cannot survive the winter, so summer warmth never gets the chance to matter.
northern_tier.heat_basis_beginner: Summer warmth does not matter here, because the tree cannot get through winter in the first place.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 is the mandarin's home ground in the Gulf South. Satsuma on trifoliate rootstock is hardy through this zone's winters (mature trees take brief lows near 15 to 20°F), and its early fall-to-winter ripening gets the crop off the tree before the hardest freezes. This is exactly where a navel orange is only marginal, and it is the clearest expression of the mandarin cold-hardiness advantage.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 is prime satsuma country in the Gulf South. The tree is hardy here, and because satsuma ripens early (fall to early winter) you usually pick the fruit before the coldest weather arrives. This is where mandarins clearly beat oranges, which are only borderline in zone 8.
8.harvest: Oct - Dec (early satsuma; pick promptly before hard freezes)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard advective freezes into the upper teens°F occur every few years in zone 8; mature satsuma usually survives, but protect young trees and pick ripe fruit ahead of a hard freeze.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 fruits reliably and easily: mild Gulf and Southeastern winters rarely threaten a hardy mandarin, and the heat is ample for good quality. Satsuma, clementine, and late types all do well; cold protection is an occasional need, not routine.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Mandarins do great in zone 9. Winters are mild enough that the tree and crop are safe, and summers are plenty warm for good fruit.
9.harvest: Nov - Jan (satsuma into clementine; a few late types hold longer)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 9 across the Gulf is mostly safe for mandarins; hard freezes occur in some winters, so keep frost cloth ready for young trees.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 fruits reliably and easily: mild Gulf and Southeastern winters rarely threaten a hardy mandarin, and the heat is ample for good quality. Satsuma, clementine, and late types all do well; cold protection is an occasional need, not routine.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Mandarins do great in zone 9. Winters are mild enough that the tree and crop are safe, and summers are plenty warm for good fruit.
10.harvest: Nov - Jan (satsuma into clementine; a few late types hold longer)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The Gulf coast is mostly safe for mandarins; hard freezes occur in some winters, so keep frost cloth ready for young trees.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: The Gulf South is mandarin country. Satsumas ripen in fall to early winter, before the coldest weather, and they are the toughest citrus for the occasional hard freeze here. This is where mandarins do better than oranges.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Gulf South is the mandarin's flagship region. Satsuma on trifoliate rootstock is hardy through zone 8 and its early ripening escapes the hardest freezes, so mandarins fruit reliably here where a navel is only marginal. Harvest runs roughly October (satsuma) into January (clementine and later types).
se_gulf.cold_basis_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf, a mature satsuma is hardy into the mid-to-upper teens°F, well past a navel, and the early fall-to-winter harvest gets fruit off before the worst cold. Hard advective freezes into the upper teens reach the colder, northern edge every few years, at the edge of even satsuma's tolerance for young trees.
se_gulf.cold_basis_beginner: A grown satsuma here handles cold better than any orange, down into the teens°F, and because it ripens early you usually pick before the hardest freezes. Young trees still need protection in a bad freeze.
se_gulf.heat_basis_seasoned: Long, hot, humid Southeastern summers bank ample heat for good mandarin quality; heat is not the limiter. In warm, humid falls the rind can stay green-tinged on ripe fruit, so taste rather than color.
se_gulf.heat_basis_beginner: Summers here are plenty warm for sweet mandarins. In a warm fall the skin can stay a bit green even when the fruit is ripe, which is normal.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 in the interior valley has high summer heat and, for a hardy mandarin, tolerable winter cold: satsuma and other mandarins take the valley's radiation frosts better than a navel, and early ripening clears the crop ahead of the coldest nights. Cold protection helps young trees in the colder pockets.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 in the valley has plenty of summer heat, and mandarins handle its winter frosts better than oranges do, especially early-ripening satsuma. Protect young trees on the coldest nights.
8.harvest: Nov - Jan (satsuma and clementine; late types into late winter)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Radiation frosts into the low-20s°F occur in colder zone-8 valley sites; mature mandarins are hardy through this, but protect young trees on the coldest nights.

9.plant_out: Spring ideal; much of the year on the mild valley floor
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 valley floor is excellent for mandarins: high summer heat for full flavor and color, and winters that only rarely threaten a hardy mandarin. Satsuma, clementine, and late seedless types all fruit reliably; this is major mandarin-growing country.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the valley is ideal for mandarins. Hot summers make good fruit, and winters are usually mild enough to keep the crop.
9.harvest: Nov - Jan (early types; late selections hold into late winter)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is an occasional risk on the valley floor; most winters pass without loss, and a hardy mandarin tolerates the usual radiation frosts.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: The Central Valley is great for mandarins. Summers are hot enough for excellent fruit, and mandarins, especially satsuma, handle the winter frosts better than oranges.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: The interior valley grows premium mandarins: high summer heat for quality, with cold only a minor constraint because mandarins are hardier than navels and ripen earlier. Harvest runs fall into late winter across the variety range.
ca_interior.cold_basis_seasoned: Interior valley winters bring radiation frosts; a mature mandarin, especially satsuma, is hardy into the mid-to-upper teens°F, comfortably past the usual valley lows, so cold rarely limits the crop. Protect young trees in the coldest zone-8 pockets.
ca_interior.cold_basis_beginner: Valley winters can frost, but grown mandarins handle it better than oranges. Only young trees in the coldest spots need much protection.
ca_interior.heat_basis_seasoned: The valley's long, hot summers give mandarins abundant heat for full flavor and color; heat is never the limiter here. Mandarins actually need less heat than a navel, so quality is dependable across the valley.
ca_interior.heat_basis_beginner: Hot valley summers give mandarins all the warmth they need for sweet, colorful fruit.

9.plant_out: Spring ideal; most of the year in this mild, frost-safe climate
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 on the north coast is frost-safe but cool: a mandarin grows and fruits, and because mandarins need less heat than a navel the fruit is usually more usable than a navel would be here, though cool summers can leave it more tart and slower to color. Satsuma, which tolerates cool summers, is the best bet.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 on the north coast is mild and frost-safe. Mandarins grow and fruit here, and they handle the cool summers better than oranges do, though the fruit can be a bit tart and slow to color. Satsuma is the best choice.
9.harvest: Dec - Feb (satsuma best in the cool summers; quality varies by year)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the north coast; the limiting factor here is cool summer heat, not winter cold.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the cool north coast a mandarin lives easily and fruits, and it handles the cool summers better than an orange would. Satsuma is the best pick; the fruit can still be a bit tart in the coolest, foggiest spots.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The north coast is heat-marginal but more forgiving for mandarins than for navels: frost-safe, and mandarins' lower heat requirement means satsuma in particular fruits with usable quality where a navel stays sour. On the coolest immediate coast, quality still slips. This is a quality-margin case, not a cold one.
ca_north_coast.cold_basis_seasoned: The north coast is nearly frost-free; winter lows rarely approach any mandarin cold threshold, so cold does not limit a mandarin here. Heat, not cold, is the constraint.
ca_north_coast.cold_basis_beginner: It barely freezes on the north coast, so cold is not the problem for a mandarin here. Cool summers are.
ca_north_coast.heat_basis_seasoned: Cool, marine north-coast summers bank borderline heat, but mandarins need far less heat than a navel, so satsuma and other cool-tolerant mandarins fruit with reasonable quality here where a navel would stay tart. On the foggiest coast the fruit is more acidic and slower to color.
ca_north_coast.heat_basis_beginner: The north coast is cool, but mandarins need less heat than oranges, so satsuma can make decent fruit here. Right on the foggy coast the fruit is more sour.

9.plant_out: Most of the year (spring ideal) in this frost-free climate
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 on the south coast is prime mandarin territory: frost-free, with enough warmth for good quality. This is the home of the famous Ojai Pixie and of excellent clementine and Gold Nugget crops. Mandarins do markedly better here than a navel, which is only middling on this coast.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 on the south coast is excellent for mandarins. It never freezes and is warm enough for sweet fruit; this is where the famous Ojai Pixie mandarins grow. Mandarins beat oranges here.
9.harvest: Dec - Mar (early satsuma through late Pixie and Gold Nugget)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the south coast; a hardy mandarin is well within its cold range here.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: The south coast is a top spot for mandarins. It never freezes and is warm enough for sweet fruit, and it is where the well-known Ojai Pixie mandarins grow. Early types ripen in winter and late types like Pixie and Gold Nugget carry into spring.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The south coast is prime mandarin country and a clear refit up from the navel case: frost-free and warm enough for good quality, home to the Ojai Pixie and to excellent clementine and Gold Nugget crops. Harvest spans early satsuma in winter through the late seedless types into spring.
ca_south_coast.cold_basis_seasoned: The south coast is effectively frost-free; winter lows sit in the 30s°F, well above any mandarin cold threshold, so cold never limits a mandarin here.
ca_south_coast.cold_basis_beginner: The south coast almost never freezes, so cold is no worry for a mandarin here.
ca_south_coast.heat_basis_seasoned: South-coast summers are mild but warm enough for good mandarin quality, since mandarins need much less heat than a navel; this is why the same coast that leaves navels only middling grows superb Pixie and clementine mandarins. Inland of the marine layer, quality rises further.
ca_south_coast.heat_basis_beginner: The south coast is mild but warm enough for sweet mandarins, because mandarins do not need as much heat as oranges. That is why great Pixie and clementine mandarins grow here even though oranges are only so-so.

9.plant_out: Spring; avoid planting into peak summer heat
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the low desert fruits reliably: abundant summer heat and rare winter frost. Clementine and late mandarins such as W. Murcott thrive on the heat; satsuma prefers the milder end and can run softer in flavor in extreme heat. Manage spring fruit-drop with steady irrigation.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the desert is good for mandarins, with lots of summer heat and little frost. Clementines and late types love the heat; satsuma does better where it is a bit milder. Water well in spring so the tree keeps its fruit.
9.harvest: Nov - Feb (clementine and late mandarins; satsuma earlier)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Occasional radiation frosts into the upper 20s°F reach colder desert sites; mature mandarins tolerate this, and young trees benefit from protection on the coldest nights.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The desert grows good mandarins, especially clementines and late types that love the heat. Water well in spring so the tree holds its fruit, and frost is rarely an issue.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The low desert is a strong mandarin region on heat: clementine and late hybrids such as W. Murcott ripen richly, while satsuma prefers the milder end of the range. Management centers on spring fruit-drop and steady irrigation rather than cold. Harvest runs late fall into late winter.
ca_desert.cold_basis_seasoned: Low-desert winters bring occasional radiation frosts into the upper 20s to low-30s°F; a mature mandarin is comfortably hardy through this, with any crop risk confined to unusual hard frosts in the colder zone-9 sites.
ca_desert.cold_basis_beginner: The desert can frost on cold nights, but grown mandarins handle it. Cold is only a worry in the coldest spots during a rare hard freeze.
ca_desert.heat_basis_seasoned: Desert summers bank abundant heat; clementine and late mandarins ripen richly and reliably. The flip side of that heat is spring fruit-drop from very hot bloom-time temperatures in the 90s°F, so irrigation matters; satsuma's flavor can soften in the most extreme heat.
ca_desert.heat_basis_beginner: The desert is plenty hot for good mandarins, especially clementines. Very hot spring weather can drop young fruit, so keep the tree well watered.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 in the arid inland has adequate summer heat and, for a hardy mandarin, tolerable winter cold: satsuma on trifoliate rootstock takes the zone's lows near the upper teens to mid-20s°F, and early ripening clears the crop before the hardest freezes, so it fruits where a navel is only marginal. Protect young trees on the coldest nights.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 here is warm enough in summer for good mandarins, and satsuma is hardy enough to handle the winters, unlike an orange which is borderline. Because satsuma ripens early, you usually pick before the worst cold. Protect young trees on the coldest nights.
8.harvest: Nov - Jan (satsuma; pick promptly before hard freezes)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard freezes into the upper teens°F occur in this zone-8 arid inland; mature satsuma usually survives, but protect young trees and harvest ripe fruit ahead of a hard freeze.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: This dry inland region is warm enough for good mandarins, and satsuma is hardy enough for its winters where oranges are borderline. Satsuma ripens early, so you usually pick before the coldest weather.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid inland grows a reliable satsuma where a navel is only marginal: adequate summer heat, and a mandarin cold-hardiness edge that covers the zone-8 winter lows, with early ripening escaping the hardest freezes. Protect young trees in hard winters.
warm_arid.cold_basis_seasoned: The warm arid inland sits at zone 8, the cold edge for citrus, but satsuma's roughly 15 to 20°F mature hardiness covers the usual upper-teens lows, and early harvest gets fruit off before the worst cold, so a mandarin fruits reliably where a navel does not. Young trees still need protection.
warm_arid.cold_basis_beginner: This inland area gets cold in winter, but satsuma is the hardiest citrus and handles it, and it ripens early enough to pick before the coldest nights. Young trees need protection in a hard freeze.
warm_arid.heat_basis_seasoned: Hot, dry inland summers bank enough heat for good mandarin quality; heat is not the limiter. Quality is good where the tree clears winter, which for a hardy satsuma is most years.
warm_arid.heat_basis_beginner: Summers here are hot and dry, plenty warm for sweet mandarins. Heat is not the problem; winter cold is, and satsuma handles it.

9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the Arizona desert grows good mandarins, with hot summers and little frost. Clementines love the heat, and satsuma ripens earliest. Water well in spring so the tree holds its fruit.
9.harvest: Nov - Feb (clementine and late types; satsuma earlier)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Only occasional light frost reaches the Arizona low desert; mature mandarins tolerate it and crop loss to cold is rare.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: The Arizona low desert grows good mandarins, ready late fall into late winter. Clementines especially love the heat. Water well in spring, and cold is rarely a problem.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert is a high-heat mandarin region: clementine and late hybrids ripen richly, satsuma runs earliest, and management centers on spring fruit-drop rather than winter cold. Harvest runs late fall into late winter.
low_desert_az.cold_basis_seasoned: The Arizona low desert at zone 9 brings only occasional light frost; a mature mandarin is comfortably hardy, with crop risk only in an unusual hard frost.
low_desert_az.cold_basis_beginner: The low desert rarely gets a hard frost, so cold is not much of a worry for a grown mandarin here.
low_desert_az.heat_basis_seasoned: Abundant low-desert heat ripens clementine and late mandarins richly. The desert caveat is spring fruit-drop from very hot bloom-time temperatures in the 90s°F, so irrigation matters more than cold; satsuma flavor can soften in the most extreme heat.
low_desert_az.heat_basis_beginner: The Arizona desert is plenty hot for good mandarins, especially clementines. Very hot spring weather can drop young fruit, so keep the tree well watered through spring.

10.plant_out: Most of the year in this frost-free climate
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the Florida peninsula fruits reliably: frost-free winters and hot, humid summers give a mandarin ample warmth. Satsuma is more a north-Florida crop, but clementine and mandarin hybrids fruit well here; expect rind color to lag interior ripeness, so taste rather than color. Favor satsuma or clementine, which are not among the susceptible types, over susceptible tangelos in this humid climate.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 in Florida is dependable for mandarins. It does not freeze, and summers are hot enough for sweet fruit. The skin may look greenish even when the fruit is ripe. Satsuma and clementine are good choices; some tangelo-type hybrids get a leaf-and-fruit-spot disease in this humid climate.
10.harvest: Nov - Jan (rind may stay green-tinged when ripe)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a crop factor on the central and southern peninsula; winters are reliably above any mandarin cold threshold.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: Central and south Florida grow mandarins easily and never freeze; they are ready in early winter. The skin may stay greenish but the fruit is still sweet. Satsuma and clementine are good picks; some tangelo-type mandarins get a fungal spot in this humid climate.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The frost-free peninsula fruits dependably, with mandarins ripening roughly November into January. Heat is adequate and cold is a non-factor; the local quirks are humidity-driven rind-greening and the Alternaria brown spot that troubles tangelo and Murcott-type hybrids, so satsuma and clementine are the sound choices here.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_seasoned: The central and southern peninsula is effectively frost-free; winter lows hold in the upper 30s to upper 40s°F, well above any mandarin cold threshold. Cold does not constrain a mandarin here.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_beginner: Central and south Florida barely get cold, so a mandarin has nothing to fear from frost here.
fl_peninsula.heat_basis_seasoned: Hot, humid summers bank ample heat for good mandarin quality. The nuance is humidity, not heat shortage: warm nights mean rind color lags interior ripeness, and humid conditions favor Alternaria brown spot on susceptible hybrids, so a green-tinged peel does not signal unripe fruit and variety choice matters.
fl_peninsula.heat_basis_beginner: Central and south Florida are plenty hot for sweet mandarins. The fruit tastes good even when the skin stays a bit green, which is normal in this warm, humid climate.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 11 in Hawaii is frost-free and grows mandarins year-round, but quality is marginal: the warm, humid tropics lack the cool nights that color and sweeten mandarins, so low-elevation fruit tends to stay green-skinned and lower in sugar. Cooler uplands improve quality. This is a diurnal-swing limit, not a cold or heat-shortage one.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 11 in Hawaii grows mandarins all year and never freezes, but the fruit is often less sweet and stays green because the nights do not get cool enough to color it. It is better up in the cooler hills.
11.harvest: Oct - Jan (lower-elevation fruit stays green-tinged and milder)
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: There is no frost risk in Hawaii; the limiting factor is the lack of cool nights for quality, not cold.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii grows mandarins year-round but quality is marginal for a counter-intuitive reason: abundant warmth without the cool nights mandarins need to color and drop acid. Lower elevations give greener, milder fruit; cooler uplands do better. This is a quality limit, not a frost or heat-shortage one.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_seasoned: Hawaii is frost-free year-round; temperatures never approach any mandarin cold threshold, so cold plays no role here.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_beginner: Hawaii never freezes, so cold is simply not a factor for growing mandarins.
hawaii_tropical.heat_basis_seasoned: Hawaii is warm and frost-free, but the humid tropics lack the cool nights a mandarin needs to color and sweeten. At lower elevations fruit can stay acidic and green-skinned even when ripe; cooler uplands give better quality. Warmth is present, but the diurnal swing that develops mandarin quality is not.
hawaii_tropical.heat_basis_beginner: Hawaii is warm and never freezes, but it is missing the cool nights that make mandarins sweet and colored. At low elevations the fruit can stay sour and green; it does better in the cooler hills.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

9.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley fruits mandarins and clementines reliably: winters are essentially frost-free, satsuma-type mandarin is the hardiest common citrus, and the long, hot subtropical summer banks ample heat for rich flavor and color (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension).
9.suitability_note_beginner: Mandarins and clementines do great here. Winters are mild and almost never freeze, satsuma-type mandarins are the toughest citrus for an occasional cold snap, and the hot Valley summer makes for rich, sweet fruit.
9.harvest: Oct - Feb (satsuma and clementine run earliest; later hybrids extend into February)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a practical concern in the Valley. Satsuma-type mandarin can withstand cold into the high teens °F once fully dormant, but is damaged near 24°F in an early cold snap before full dormancy sets in, so an occasional December freeze is the one real risk (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension).

10.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)

rgv.region_notes_beginner: Mandarins and clementines are an easy, reliable Rio Grande Valley fruit tree. Winters are mild and almost never freeze, and harvest runs from October into February, satsuma types first and later hybrids last.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley fruits mandarins and clementines reliably, and satsuma-type mandarin is the hardiest common citrus, tolerating cold that would damage grapefruit or lemon. Essentially frost-free winters and a long, hot summer bank ample heat for rich flavor and color. Harvest runs October into February, earliest types first and late hybrids extending the season.
rgv.cold_basis_seasoned: Valley winters rarely reach freezing. Satsuma-type mandarin, the hardiest common citrus, can withstand cold into the high teens°F once fully dormant, but an early cold snap before full dormancy, near 24°F, can still cause damage; that 18 to 24°F satsuma figure is genuinely from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension. Even so, this is the most cold-tolerant citrus in the Valley lineup. The winter-low band used here, roughly 26 to 32°F, is a synthesis anchored to the closest analog frost-free citrus regions, the milder Gulf Coast and the Arizona low desert, and the satsuma cold-damage datum, not a single figure Texas A&M AgriLife Extension publishes for the Valley.
rgv.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here are mild and hard freezes are rare. Mandarins and clementines handle cold better than most other citrus, but an early, hard cold snap in December can still hurt the tree before it has fully settled into winter.
rgv.heat_basis_seasoned: The Valley's long, intensely hot summers bank abundant heat for excellent mandarin and clementine flavor and color; heat is never the limiting factor here. Very hot bloom-time weather can drive some spring fruit-drop, so steady irrigation through bloom and fruit set helps hold the crop.
rgv.heat_basis_beginner: Summers here are long and very hot, plenty for sweet, richly colored mandarins and clementines. Keep the tree watered well in spring, since very hot weather right at bloom time can drop some young fruit.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8's colder nights fall below even satsuma mandarin's cold limit, the hardiest of the commonly grown sweet citrus. A mature, hardened satsuma withstands brief lows near 15 to 20°F, but this zone's coldest nights drop into the teens or below that, and the region's periodic harder freeze can push colder still. There is no dependable in-ground planting here; grow it as a container tree brought under cover for winter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Even the toughest common citrus, satsuma mandarin, cannot reliably take zone 8's coldest nights here. Grow it in a pot you bring under cover for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Satsuma's roughly 15-to-20°F mature-wood limit sits right at or below zone 8's coldest nights, and this region's occasional harder freeze can go colder still, so cold, not heat, rules this zone out.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9's milder winter lows sit close to or above satsuma mandarin's roughly 15-to-20°F cold limit, the hardiest of the commonly grown sweet citrus, so a well-sited or container-grown tree can survive here for years if it is protected on the coldest nights. Survival is not the limiting factor in this zone, though: the maritime Pacific Northwest's cool, marine-tempered summer does not bank the heat mandarins need to sweeten and color well, so even a tree that comes through winter fine does not give a dependable, worthwhile crop. Best grown as a protected container specimen, not counted on for fruit.
9.suitability_note_beginner: This is about as good as citrus gets here: satsuma mandarin, the toughest common citrus for cold, can survive in the milder zone 9 spots if you protect it on hard-freeze nights. But our summers are not warm enough for the fruit to get sweet, so do not count on a real crop.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Cold is not the whole story in zone 9: satsuma's own cold limit is close to this zone's typical low, so the tree itself can often make it through winter. The region's cool summer, not cold, is what keeps this from being a dependable fruiting crop.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Mandarin is the toughest common citrus for cold, but the maritime Pacific Northwest still is not mandarin country. In zone 8 winters get too cold even for satsuma, the hardiest type. In the milder zone 9 pockets a protected container tree can survive for years, but our cool summers are not hot enough to sweeten the fruit, so do not count on a real harvest either way.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Mandarin, specifically satsuma-type mandarin, is the cold-hardiness standout among common sweet citrus, and that shows here: zone 9's milder winter lows sit close to satsuma's own roughly 15-to-20°F cold limit, so a protected tree can genuinely survive long-term in the region's milder pockets, a step up from every other citrus in this batch. Zone 8's colder nights still put it out of reach. Survival is not the binding constraint in zone 9, though: the maritime Pacific Northwest's cool, marine-tempered summer does not deliver the heat mandarins need to sweeten and color, so even a tree that comes through winter cleanly does not produce a dependable, worthwhile crop. Grow it as a protected container specimen, not a fruiting orchard tree.
pnw.cold_basis_seasoned: Zone 8's winter lows (roughly 10 to 20°F) fall below even satsuma mandarin's roughly 15-to-20°F mature cold limit, the hardiest of the commonly grown sweet citrus; zone 9's milder band (roughly 20 to 30°F) sits close to or above that limit, so a protected tree can survive there for years (UF/IFAS, Clemson HGIC).
pnw.cold_basis_beginner: Mandarin (satsuma) takes cold better than any other common citrus, and it can survive our milder zone 9 winters if protected. Zone 8 is still too cold for it.
pnw.heat_basis_seasoned: The maritime Pacific Northwest's cool, cloud- and marine-influenced summer does not bank the heat mandarins need to sweeten and color well, even though mandarins need less summer heat than a navel orange to ripen. Where the tree does survive winter, the fruit stays underripe and poorly colored, so this is not a dependable crop even in the milder zone.
pnw.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers here are not warm enough for mandarin fruit to sweeten up properly, even where the tree itself can survive the winter.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 7's Piedmont winter lows fall below even Owari satsuma's roughly 15 to 20°F mature-wood cold limit, the hardiest of the commonly grown sweet citrus. There is no in-ground establishment window this far inland; grow it as a container tree brought under cover for winter.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Even the toughest common citrus, satsuma mandarin, cannot reliably take this zone's coldest nights. Grow it in a pot you bring under cover for winter.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Piedmont winter lows regularly reach below satsuma's own roughly 15 to 20°F cold limit, the hardiest common citrus option, so cold rules this zone out on its own.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone sits close to Owari satsuma's own roughly 15 to 20°F mature cold limit, the hardiest of the commonly grown sweet citrus, so a container tree protected on hard-freeze nights can survive here for years, the best cold-hardiness case among this region's citrus. Even so, this zone's colder pockets and any harder freeze can still reach below that limit, so there is no dependable in-ground or reliably fruiting crop, only a protected specimen that may bloom in a mild year. The region's long, hot, humid summers bank plenty of heat to sweeten mandarin fruit if the tree does bloom and set; heat is not the constraint here, winter cold is.
8.suitability_note_beginner: This is the best cold-hardiness story among the citrus in this region: satsuma mandarin, the toughest common citrus for cold, can survive in the milder Tidewater pockets of this zone for years if you protect it on the coldest nights. It still is not safe to leave outside unprotected all winter, and do not count on a reliable harvest. Our summers are plenty hot for the fruit to taste good on the rare year it does set.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Satsuma's roughly 15 to 20°F mature-wood limit sits right at this zone's milder Tidewater edge; the zone's colder pockets and any harder freeze can still go below it, so real winter protection is the honest baseline here, not a dependable outdoor planting.

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Mandarin, specifically satsuma, is the toughest common citrus for cold, and that shows here: in the colder Piedmont even satsuma cannot make it through winter outdoors. In the milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone, a protected container satsuma can survive for years if you bring it under cover on the coldest nights, but do not count on a real harvest either way. Our summers are hot enough for the fruit if it does set.

The cooler Piedmont interior still falls below that limit and rules the crop out entirely. Survival is not guaranteed even in the milder zone, since its colder pockets and periodic harder freezes can still reach below satsuma's limit, so this stays a protected container specimen, not a dependable in-ground or fruiting planting. Unlike some cooler, heat-poor regions, the Mid-Atlantic's long, hot, humid summer is never the constraint on fruit quality; winter cold is the whole story.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Mandarin, specifically satsuma-type mandarin, is the cold-hardiness standout among the common sweet citrus, but even it cannot take this zone's coldest nights: zone 8's cooler, higher pockets drop well below satsuma's roughly 24°F cold limit in an ordinary winter. There is no dependable in-ground establishment window this far into the region's cold edge.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Even the toughest common citrus, satsuma mandarin, cannot reliably take this zone's coldest nights. Grow it in a pot you bring under cover for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Ordinary winter lows in this zone regularly reach below satsuma's own roughly 24°F cold limit, the hardiest common citrus option.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley floor sits close to satsuma-type mandarin's own roughly 24°F cold limit, the mildest threshold of any citrus in this batch. The Las Vegas Valley floor, at about 2,000 feet, runs colder in winter than the lower Phoenix desert (near 1,100 feet), where mandarin fruits reliably, so this crop does not earn that warmer verdict here. A container tree brought fully under cover on hard-freeze nights can survive for years and may bloom and set fruit in a mild winter, but there is no dependable in-ground or fruiting crop, only a protected specimen.
9.suitability_note_beginner: This is the best cold-hardiness story among the citrus in this region: satsuma mandarin, the toughest common citrus for cold, can survive in the Las Vegas Valley for years if you protect it on the coldest nights. It still is not safe to leave outside unprotected all winter, and do not count on a reliable harvest; a mild year might give you fruit.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The valley's frost season (last freeze around Feb 28, first around Nov 25, NWS Las Vegas normals) brackets a winter whose harder nights sit right at satsuma's roughly 24°F cold limit in most years.

10.plant_out: Spring (container or balled; after hard-freeze risk passes)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Laughlin/Colorado River corner, the region's mildest pocket, gives mandarin its best case: ordinary winter lows here clear satsuma-type mandarin's roughly 24°F cold limit, and early ripening lets the crop come off before the hardest winter cold arrives. This is still the region's single smallest zone with no dedicated local citrus field data, so a harder-than-usual freeze can still cost the crop; protect young trees and pick promptly ahead of any hard freeze.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Laughlin is warm enough that mandarin, especially the early-ripening satsuma type, actually fruits in most years, unlike the rest of the region. Protect young trees on the coldest nights and pick before a hard freeze arrives.
10.harvest: Nov - Jan (satsuma and early types; pick promptly before hard freezes)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An occasional harder freeze can still reach past satsuma's roughly 24°F cold limit even in this mildest zone; protect young trees and harvest ripe fruit ahead of a hard freeze.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Mandarin is the best cold-hardiness story among this region's citrus. Even so, only a protected container tree makes it through winter in the Las Vegas Valley, with fruit only a mild-year bonus. At the warmest Laughlin corner, an early-ripening satsuma or clementine actually fruits most years if you protect it and pick before the hardest freezes.

Summer heat is never the constraint anywhere in this region; winter cold decides the case.
nevada.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 30 to 40°F in the mild Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10) to 20 to 30°F in the Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) to 10 to 20°F in the region's cooler, higher pockets (zone 8). Satsuma-type mandarin, the hardiest commonly grown sweet citrus, tolerates mature-wood cold to roughly 24°F, close to the valley's edge and reliably cleared only at the mild zone-10 corner. the Las Vegas Valley floor, at about 2,000 feet, runs colder in winter than the lower Phoenix desert (near 1,100 feet).
nevada.cold_basis_beginner: Mandarin takes cold better than any other common citrus, and it can survive in the Las Vegas Valley with real winter protection. Only the warmer Laughlin corner is reliably mild enough for it to actually fruit most years; the region's cooler high pockets are still too cold for it.
nevada.heat_basis_seasoned: The Nevada high desert's long, hot, dry summer, routinely above 90 to 100°F (University of Nevada, Reno Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), banks ample heat to sweeten mandarin fruit wherever the tree clears winter; heat is never the limiting factor here. Winter cold, not summer heat, is what keeps this crop to a protected container in most of the region and a freeze-watched in-ground tree only at its warmest corner.
nevada.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers here are plenty hot for mandarin fruit to taste good. The reason this is not a reliable outdoor crop across most of the region is winter cold, not a lack of summer warmth.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost data) sit below even mandarin's own low-to-mid 20s°F cold-damage point, so there is no dependable in-ground planting here, and citrus is absent from USU's Washington County Fruits recommendation for this elevation. A container mandarin brought under cover on hard-freeze nights can be kept alive for years and may set some fruit in an unusually mild winter, but this stays protected culture, not a reliable annual harvest.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Mandarin is the toughest common citrus against cold, and St. George winters, with ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, still get too cold for it outdoors most years. Grow it in a pot you can move under cover on freezing nights. You might get occasional fruit in a mild winter, but do not count on it every year.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: St. George's ordinary winter cold (last frost near March 30, first frost near November 1, USU Extension Washington County) regularly reaches below mandarin's own low-to-mid 20s°F cold-damage point, so an unprotected tree faces a real hard-freeze risk most winters.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Mandarin is the toughest common citrus against cold, but St. George's winters, which drop to ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F, still get too cold for it to live outdoors on its own. Grow it in a container you can bring under cover on the coldest nights, and you may get an occasional harvest in a mild winter, but do not expect a dependable one.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's zone 8b winters run roughly 15 to 20°F on an ordinary cold night, and USU's Washington County Fruits page, which names the fruits recommended at this elevation, includes no citrus at all. Mandarin, particularly the clementine and satsuma types, is the cold-hardiest common citrus, closer to surviving here than any other, but an ordinary winter night still drops past its own low-to-mid 20s°F damage point. The honest call is a protected container planting, brought under cover on hard-freeze nights, that can live for years and occasionally set fruit in a mild winter rather than a dependable in-ground tree.
utah_dixie.cold_basis_seasoned: St. George sits in USDA zone 8b, with ordinary winter lows of roughly 15 to 20°F (USU Extension Washington County frost and elevation data). Mandarin, especially the clementine and satsuma types, is the cold-hardiest common citrus, with mature wood able to take short dips into the low-to-mid 20s°F before real damage, while most other citrus is hurt well above that. Even so, an ordinary St. George winter night still drops past that threshold, and USU's Washington County Fruits page, which lists the fruits recommended at this elevation, names no citrus at all.
utah_dixie.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here bring ordinary lows around 15 to 20°F. Mandarin is the toughest common citrus against cold, but that still is not cold enough for it to live outdoors on its own most winters. Grow it in a container you can bring under cover on the coldest nights.
utah_dixie.heat_basis_seasoned: St. George summers reach past 100°F in June, July, and August (USU Extension Washington County), plenty of heat to sweeten mandarin fruit in a year the tree does set. Winter cold, not summer heat, is what keeps mandarin to a protected container planting here.
utah_dixie.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers here are plenty hot for mandarin fruit to taste good. Winter cold, not a lack of summer warmth, is why this is not a reliable outdoor tree.

crops.description_seasoned: The mandarin (Citrus reticulata and its hybrids, including satsuma, clementine, and tangerine) is a subtropical evergreen fruit tree grown for small, sweet, loose-skinned, easy-to-peel fruit that is usually seedless. Its defining advantage over other sweet citrus is cold hardiness: satsuma is the most cold-tolerant of the commonly grown citrus, with mature trees withstanding brief lows near 15 to 20°F, notably colder than a navel orange, which lets in-ground mandarins reach zone 8 across the Gulf South and interior valleys. Early ripening (satsuma from fall) also gets the crop off the tree before the hardest winter cold. Mandarins need less summer heat than a navel to sweeten but want cool fall nights to color and drop acid, so they are marginal only in the cool-night tropics and the coolest coasts. Two group traits shape their care: seedless types set seeds if cross-pollinated by other citrus, so isolation preserves seedlessness; and mandarins are strongly alternate-bearing, managed by thinning heavy crops. Unlike a navel, most mandarins do not hold well on the tree and are picked promptly. Trees are small and grafted, usually on trifoliate-orange rootstock for cold hardiness, and productive for decades.
crops.description_beginner: The mandarin is an evergreen citrus tree that makes small, sweet, easy-to-peel fruit that is usually seedless. Its big advantage over other sweet citrus is that it takes cold better: satsuma is the hardiest common citrus, with grown trees handling a brief dip near 15 to 20°F, colder than an orange, so mandarins can be grown in the ground farther north (into zone 8) across the Gulf South and warm valleys. Satsumas also ripen early, so you usually pick the fruit before the coldest weather. Mandarins need less summer heat than an orange to get sweet, but they want cool fall nights to color up, so they struggle mainly in the warm-night tropics. Two things to know: seedless mandarins get seeds if another citrus pollinates them, so keep them apart to stay seedless; and they tend to make a big crop one year and a light one the next, which you even out by thinning. Unlike oranges, most mandarins do not keep well on the tree, so pick them when ripe. The trees are small, grafted (usually on trifoliate-orange rootstock for cold hardiness), and produce for many years.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest mandarins by taste, and pick promptly. The rind loosens and puffs slightly and color deepens as cool fall nights arrive, but in warm, humid climates the rind can stay green-tinged on fully ripe fruit, so taste rather than color decides. Unlike a navel, most mandarins do not hold well on the tree: satsuma and early types puff, dry, and lose flavor if left past maturity, so pick at ripeness and refrigerate. The exceptions are the late holding types, notably Gold Nugget and Pixie, which keep their quality on the tree into spring. Early satsuma ripening also lets the crop come off before the hardest winter cold.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick mandarins by taste, not just by color, and do not leave them on the tree too long. The skin loosens and colors as fall nights get cool, but in warm, humid areas it can still look a little green even when the fruit is ripe, so taste one first. Unlike oranges, most mandarins get puffy and dry inside if left on the tree, so pick them when ripe and keep them in the fridge. A few late types like Gold Nugget and Pixie are the exception and do hold on the tree into spring. Early satsumas also let you pick the crop before the coldest weather.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Mandarins bloom primarily in spring, typically March through May depending on climate and zone, with fragrant white flowers for about three weeks. Fruit develops over roughly seven to ten months, faster than a navel's ten to twelve, so harvest comes earlier: satsuma ripens from October, clementine in early winter, and late selections such as Gold Nugget, Pixie, and W. Murcott or Tango carry the season into spring. In the low desert satsuma can start earliest; late types hold latest.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Mandarins bloom in spring, usually March through May depending on where you live, with fragrant white flowers for about three weeks. The fruit then grows for about seven to ten months, a bit faster than an orange, so you harvest earlier: satsumas from fall, clementines in early winter, and late types like Gold Nugget, Pixie, and Tango stretching into spring.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Mandarins are the most cold-hardy of the commonly grown sweet citrus. A mature, hardened satsuma withstands brief lows near 15 to 20°F without serious wood injury, notably colder than a navel orange (about 24 to 26°F) and behind only kumquat among edible citrus. The cold-hardiness order runs roughly satsuma and kumquat, then sour orange and tangerine, then sweet oranges such as navel, then grapefruit, lemon, and lime. The fruit is more tender than the wood, taking damage near 30°F for a couple of hours, but satsuma's early fall ripening usually gets the crop off before the hardest freezes. Trees are evergreen with no dormancy, so growing tissue is always vulnerable, and young trees are far more tender than mature ones. Trifoliate-orange rootstock adds cold hardiness and is standard for cold-edge planting. Beyond cold, mandarins need less summer heat than a navel to sweeten but want cool fall nights to color, so quality, not survival, is the limit in the warm-night tropics. The practical in-ground range is about zones 8 through 11.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Mandarins take cold better than any other common sweet citrus. A grown, hardened satsuma can handle a brief dip near 15 to 20°F without serious damage, colder than an orange (about 24 to 26°F) and beaten only by the kumquat. The fruit is more tender than the wood and can be hurt near 30°F, but satsumas ripen early enough that you usually pick before the worst cold. Because the tree is evergreen and never goes dormant, its leaves and wood can be hurt any time it gets cold enough, and young trees are the most tender. Planting on trifoliate-orange rootstock adds hardiness and is standard in cold areas. Mandarins also need less summer heat than an orange to get sweet, but they want cool fall nights to color up. The usual in-ground range is about zones 8 through 11.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Mandarins require no winter chilling to flower or fruit. They are evergreen and do not enter a chill-triggered dormancy; flowering is driven by spring warming and moisture rather than release from a prior cold period. This distinguishes citrus from deciduous fruit trees such as peaches and apples, which need hundreds of chill hours to break bud dormancy and set a normal crop.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Mandarins do not need any winter chill to flower or fruit. Unlike peaches and apples, which need hundreds of cold hours in winter to wake up and set a crop, citrus is evergreen and is triggered to bloom by spring warmth and moisture instead. So chill hours, which matter a lot for deciduous fruit trees, simply do not apply to mandarins.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Most mandarins set a full crop on a single tree and are seedless when grown in isolation. Satsuma is parthenocarpic and reliably seedless. Clementine and W. Murcott are self-incompatible but facultatively parthenocarpic: they set seedless fruit on their own, yet fertile pollen from another nearby citrus cross-pollinates them and puts seeds into the fruit, and citrus pollen can travel a long way, so isolation from pollen-bearing citrus is what keeps seedless types seedless. A few mandarin hybrids fruit better with a compatible pollinizer, but the common seedless mandarins need no pollinizer and no bees for a single tree to fruit.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: A mandarin makes fruit on its own, with no second tree and no bees needed, and most types are seedless when grown away from other citrus. Satsuma is naturally seedless. Clementine and some others are seedless by themselves, but if pollen from another citrus nearby reaches the flowers, the fruit ends up with seeds, so keeping a seedless mandarin away from other pollen-making citrus is what keeps it seedless.

pet_safe.note: The fruit is fine, but the peel, leaves, and citrus oils can upset the stomach of cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about building the tree, not picking fruit, and mandarins make that harder than most because they are eager to fruit young. Strip the first year's fruit anyway: a young tree carrying a crop grows slowly and stays structurally weak. Plant with the graft union, the knobby joint low on the trunk where your variety was joined to its roots, standing two to three inches clear of the finished soil, and keep mulch off the trunk, since a damp union is how citrus gets foot rot. If you garden at the cold edge of citrus country, buy a tree grafted onto trifoliate orange rootstock; that is the graft that lets a satsuma push into zone 8. Check the soft new growth for Asian citrus psyllid while the tree is small enough to inspect properly.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Strip first-year set despite the crop's precocity: satsuma in particular will try to fruit early, and a young tree carrying a load grows slowly and stays structurally weak. Set the graft union two to three inches proud of finished grade with mulch pulled back, against foot rot. Rootstock is the load-bearing purchase decision at the cold margin: trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata) is the standard for maximum cold hardiness and is what carries satsuma into zone 8, so it is chosen at the nursery rather than corrected later. Scout tender flush for Asian citrus psyllid while inspection is still practical; the psyllid vectors huanglongbing and feeds and oviposits on new growth, so detection on a small tree is worth more than on a large one.
crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: Mandarins are precocious and usually start bearing in the second or third year, a little earlier than a navel orange. Hold the soil moisture steady through the roughly three-week spring bloom, because the whole crop sets from that one flush and drought stress now drops the flowers and the young fruit behind them. If you are growing a seedless variety such as Clementine, keep it away from other pollen-bearing citrus during bloom: seedless kinds stay seedless only in isolation, and a fertile neighbour will put seeds in an otherwise seedless crop.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: Mandarin is precocious and typically begins bearing in year two or three, ahead of navel. Moisture stability through the roughly three-week bloom is the controlling variable, since the crop sets from a single main flush. Isolation matters for seedless cultivars: Clementine and W. Murcott are seedless only without cross-pollination and will set seed when fertile pollen is nearby, so bloom-period proximity to other citrus is a varietal decision rather than a general one. Begin managing alternate bearing from the first substantial crop rather than after it becomes established, because mandarin swings harder between on and off years than the rest of the roster.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From about the third year the tree carries a real crop, and mandarins bring two habits that catch people out. First, they will not wait for you. Unlike a navel, most mandarins do not hold on the tree: a satsuma left too long goes puffy and dries out inside. Taste before you pick, then pick promptly and refrigerate. The exceptions are late holding types such as Gold Nugget and Pixie, which do store well on the branch into spring. Second, mandarins swing hard between a heavy year and a light one. On a heavy year, thin the fruit in early summer; that single pass is the most effective thing you can do, because it cuts the drain before it suppresses next year's bloom. Keep pruning minimal, and pull any suckers from below the graft.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production builds by roughly year four to seven depending on rootstock and conditions. Two crop-specific behaviors govern the mature tree. Fruit does not hold: mandarin colors ahead of full sweetness in some climates and most cultivars puff and desiccate on the branch, so sample for flavor, then harvest promptly and refrigerate. Late holding types (Gold Nugget, Pixie) are the deliberate exception and store on the tree into spring. And alternate bearing is pronounced: early-summer thinning of a heavy set is the highest- leverage intervention available, cutting carbohydrate drain before it suppresses the following season's bloom, with steady fertility and consistent irrigation damping the rest. A sharp unexplained drop is not alternate bearing and points instead at a root, water or disease problem. Pruning stays minimal, with rootstock suckers, often thorny trifoliate, removed on sight.

crops.name: Fig

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Figs are not fussy about soil and grow in a wide range, from sandy to heavier ground, as long as it drains well and does not stay soggy. A loam with some organic matter is ideal, but figs even do fine in poor, rocky soil. The one thing to avoid is sandy soil that is full of root-knot nematodes, tiny soil pests that are the leading killer of figs. Do not make the soil too rich either: too much rich material and feeding pushes soft leafy growth and fewer figs, and that soft growth is more easily hurt by winter cold.
