soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Fig is adaptable across soil textures, from sandy to clay loam, provided drainage is good; it tolerates poor and rocky ground better than most fruit trees. A well-drained loam with moderate organic matter is ideal. The critical avoidance is root-knot-nematode-infested sandy soil, which is the leading cause of fig decline in warm regions, since own-rooted figs carry no resistant rootstock. Keep fertility moderate: over-rich soil and heavy feeding drive vegetative growth at the expense of fruit and produce soft wood that is more prone to winter injury.

ph.note_beginner: Figs do best in slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, but they are easygoing and grow well anywhere from about 6.0 up to 7.8 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and only adjust if it is far off: garden lime raises a too-acidic pH and elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Mix any amendment in before you plant.
ph.note_seasoned: Fig prefers a slightly acidic soil near pH 6.0 to 6.5 but is tolerant across roughly 6.0 to 7.8, handling near-neutral ground without trouble. Test before planting and correct only a real deficiency: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers an alkaline one. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is easiest to set before the permanent plant goes in.

fertilizer.timing: early spring as growth resumes, then lightly through early summer; stop by midsummer
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed lightly. Figs need far less fertilizer than most fruit trees, and over-feeding is a common mistake: excess nitrogen pushes rank leafy growth, delays and reduces fruiting, can cause fruit to split, and produces soft wood that winters poorly. Broadcast a balanced granular evenly around the root zone out toward the drip line, keep it off the stems, and water it in. Halve the rate in colder regions to favor hardiness, and never feed past midsummer, since late nitrogen keeps the plant growing when it should be hardening for winter.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. Figs need much less than other fruit trees, and too much does more harm than good: lots of leaves and few figs, split fruit, and soft growth that is easily hurt by winter cold. Scatter a balanced fertilizer around the plant out to where the branches reach, keep it off the stems, and water it in. In colder areas use half as much, and stop feeding by midsummer so the plant can toughen up before winter.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 or 8-8-8 suits figs; they are light feeders and need no high-nitrogen program. Too much nitrogen (N) is counterproductive, driving leaves over fruit and reducing cold hardiness.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 or 8-8-8 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is all a fig needs. Do not overdo the first number, nitrogen, because too much gives you leaves instead of figs.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rate is about 1/2 pound of 10-10-10 for a young plant and 2 to 4 pounds for a mature one, split into 2 or 3 applications from early spring through early summer; UGA gives a rule of about 1/2 pound per foot of height, up to 5 pounds a year. Do not fertilize at planting; wait until growth begins. Cut these rates in half in northern gardens to keep growth firm for winter.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple guide is about 1/2 pound of 10-10-10 for a young fig and 2 to 4 pounds for a big one, spread over 2 or 3 times from early spring to early summer. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until it starts growing. In cold-winter areas, use half as much.

companions.note_seasoned: Fig is parthenocarpic and self-fruitful, so there are no pollination companions to plant: a lone tree fruits with no bees and no fig wasp. The interactions that matter for a fig are at the root zone, not classic vegetable pairings. Keep grass and weeds cleared back and mulch the root area, which competes down weeds and holds moisture, and above all keep the plant out of soil heavily infested with root-knot nematodes, which own-rooted figs cannot resist. A well-mulched, weed-free, nematode-free root zone is the whole companion story.
companions.note_beginner: Figs make fruit on their own with no pollination, so you do not need any companion plants to help them fruit. What matters for a fig is what happens around its roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back and lay down mulch to hold moisture and keep weeds down, and do not plant a fig in soil full of root-knot nematodes (tiny soil pests), because figs cannot fight them off. A mulched, weed-free, pest-free root area is really all a fig asks for.

good_seasoned.name: A mulched, weed-free root zone
good_seasoned.label: traditional

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Orchard-floor mulch/weed-free-ring practice is standard extension guidance for young fruit trees (moisture retention, reduced competition) and is echoed in UMD's fig culture notes, but the specific benefit is general rather than a fig-specific companion effect. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The single most useful thing around a young fig is not another plant but a clear, mulched ring. A layer of organic mulch kept off the stems holds soil moisture (which figs reward with better fruit set), moderates soil temperature at the shallow fig roots, and suppresses the grass and weeds that compete hard with an establishing plant. It also insulates the roots through winter at the cold edge of the fig's range.

bad_seasoned.name: Root-knot-nematode ground (old fig or susceptible-crop soil)
bad_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Root-knot nematode is named by UGA, Clemson, and UF/IFAS as the leading cause of fig decline/death in sandy warm-region soils, and own-rooted figs have no resistant rootstock. Multiple independent extension sources, clear mechanism. extension_backed/high.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Do not plant a fig into sandy soil known to carry heavy root-knot nematode populations, or straight into ground where a nematode-declined fig was just removed. In warm sandy regions nothing else takes down as many fig trees, and because figs grow on their own roots there is no resistant rootstock to fall back on the way there is for stone fruit. The fix is site selection, not a companion plant: choose the best-drained, least infested ground, or replace a generous volume of soil.

pests.name: Root-knot nematode
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Above ground, a slow, unexplained decline: stunted growth, sparse yellowing leaves, dieback, and poor fruiting that worsens over years. Below ground, the roots carry small knots or galls, and the fine feeder roots are damaged, so the plant cannot take up water and nutrients.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The fig slowly goes downhill for no obvious reason: stunted, with thin yellow leaves, dieback, and fewer figs each year. If you dig up a root, you find small knots or swellings on it. Those knots are the damage from the pest.
pests.cause_seasoned: Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne species), microscopic soil roundworms that feed inside the roots and form the galls. They build up in warm, sandy soils and are the leading cause of fig decline and death in the Southeast and other warm sandy regions. Own-rooted figs have no resistant rootstock, so there is no cure once a plant is heavily infested.
pests.cause_beginner: Microscopic soil worms called root-knot nematodes that live in the roots and make the knots. They build up in warm, sandy soil and are the number-one killer of figs in warm areas. Because figs grow on their own roots, there is no special root you can buy to resist them and no cure once a plant is badly infested.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue treatment for an infested plant. Manage it by keeping the fig vigorous and well watered so it outgrows light damage, mulching heavily to build soil organic matter and beneficial soil life, and, in the worst sandy sites, growing in a container of clean mix instead. A thick organic mulch is the practical home tool.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once a plant is badly infested there is no fix. The best you can do is keep the fig strong with steady water and a thick mulch so it can shrug off mild damage, and, in bad sandy soil, grow it in a pot of clean potting mix instead of in the ground.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Prevention is everything: do not plant into known nematode-heavy sandy soil, choose the best-drained ground, mulch heavily, and keep the plant vigorous. Where nematode pressure is high, container culture in clean mix sidesteps the problem entirely.
pests.prevention_beginner: The main thing is to avoid the problem: do not plant in sandy soil known to have these pests, pick well-drained ground, mulch thickly, and keep the fig healthy. Where the soil is bad, growing the fig in a pot of clean mix avoids the pest completely.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start clean, because this one is decided before you plant. Root-knot nematodes are microscopic worms in the soil that feed inside fig roots, and a badly infested plant cannot be rescued. Skip sandy ground with a known history of them, choose the best-drained spot you have, and where the only in-ground soil is known trouble, plant into a large container of fresh potting mix instead.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Site selection carries almost the whole load here: own-rooted figs offer no resistant rootstock, and heavy Meloidogyne infestations do not reverse. Avoid ground with a known nematode history, favor the best-drained site available, and under high pressure in sandy soils use container culture in clean mix so the root zone starts free of the pest.

pests.name: Dried fruit beetle and fig souring
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripening figs ferment and sour from the inside, oozing a scummy or bubbly liquid from the eye and smelling vinegary or yeasty. Small beetles may be seen at the eye of soft fruit. Affected figs are inedible and drop or rot on the plant.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ripe figs turn sour and mushy inside, with a fizzy or scummy ooze coming out of the little hole at the bottom (the eye) and a vinegary smell. You may see tiny beetles around the soft fruit. The affected figs are ruined.
pests.cause_seasoned: Dried fruit beetles (Carpophilus species) and other sap beetles are drawn to ripe figs and carry souring yeasts and bacteria into the fruit through the open eye. The problem is worst in humid weather and on varieties with a large, open eye, which lets the beetles and moisture in.
pests.cause_beginner: Little beetles called dried fruit beetles are attracted to ripe figs and carry the yeasts that cause souring into the fruit through the open hole at the bottom. It is worst in humid weather and on figs with a big open eye that lets the beetles in.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Pick figs promptly as they ripen and remove any soured or dropped fruit right away so beetles are not drawn in and the yeasts do not build. Choosing varieties with a small or closed eye (such as Celeste) greatly reduces souring. There is no spray that reaches yeasts inside the fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick figs as soon as they are ripe and clean up any soured or fallen fruit right away, so the beetles are not attracted and the souring cannot spread. Growing a variety with a small, tight eye like Celeste helps a lot. No spray fixes souring once it is inside the fig.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the plant picked clean during ripening, dispose of soured fruit, and favor closed-eye varieties in humid areas. Good airflow and prompt harvest are the durable controls.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the figs picked and throw away any soured ones, and grow a tight-eye variety like Celeste if your summers are humid. Picking often and keeping the plant open are the best defenses.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the figs as soon as they are ripe instead of letting them hang. Over-ripe fruit still on the tree is what draws the beetles in, so taking the crop on time removes the thing attracting them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Harvest timing is a control here rather than a preference: the beetles are drawn to fruit left past ripeness and carry the souring yeasts into it through the eye, so shortening that window acts on the attraction itself. It works alongside clearing dropped fruit rather than in place of it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Choose a fig with a small, tight eye, the little opening at the bottom of the fruit, such as Celeste. Beetles and damp air get in through a wide-open eye, so a tight one cuts down souring before you have to do anything else.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Eye size is the varietal lever: large open-eye types admit sap beetles and the souring yeasts they carry, while closed-eye selections such as Celeste sharply narrow that entry route. The payoff is largest in humid summers, where pressure is heaviest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Harvest every ripe fig as it comes, and take off or pick up any that have gone fizzy, sour, or dropped. Soft, fermenting fruit is what pulls the beetles in, so clearing it out stops the problem from feeding itself. No spray reaches the yeasts once they are inside a fig, so this is the real control.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Frequent harvest plus removal of soured and fallen fruit strips out the fermenting material that recruits Carpophilus beetles and builds the yeast load. Since nothing sprayed reaches yeasts already inside the fruit, picking interval and litter removal are the durable controls.

pests.name: Birds (and squirrels)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripe and nearly ripe figs are pecked open, half-eaten, or gone entirely, often the best fruit at the top of the plant first. Squirrels strip fruit and can clear a small tree fast. Damage appears exactly as the crop begins to ripen.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ripe figs get pecked open, half-eaten, or disappear, usually the best ones up high first. Squirrels can strip a small fig fast. It happens right as the figs start to ripen.
pests.cause_seasoned: Birds and squirrels find ripe figs irresistible, and a fig's soft, sweet, unprotected fruit ripening over many weeks is an easy, repeated target. This is one of the most common complaints of home fig growers.
pests.cause_beginner: Birds and squirrels love ripe figs, and because a fig's fruit is soft, sweet, and out in the open for weeks, they come back again and again. It is one of the most common fig problems.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Netting the plant (or key branches) as fruit begins to color is the most effective home control; pick ripe figs promptly and often so less hangs waiting. Reflective tape and scare devices help briefly. A container fig can be moved to a more protected spot.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: The best fix is to drape bird netting over the plant as the figs start to color, and to pick ripe figs often so fewer are left hanging. Shiny tape or scare items help for a while. A potted fig can be moved somewhere more protected.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plan for netting before the crop ripens rather than after the losses start, and keep the plant a manageable size so it can be covered and picked easily.
pests.prevention_beginner: Get the netting ready before the figs ripen, not after the birds find them, and keep the plant small enough to cover and pick easily.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick ripe figs often instead of letting them hang. Every fig you take is one the birds and squirrels cannot get, and fruit sitting there waiting is what keeps them coming back.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Frequent harvest shrinks the standing reward. A fig crop ripens over many weeks, so it is exposed again and again; tightening the picking interval lowers how much soft fruit is available at any one moment.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Drape bird netting over the plant when the figs first start to color up, not after you notice damage. Keep the fig pruned to a size you can actually cover and reach, since netting helps only where it goes. If your fig is in a pot, moving it to a more sheltered spot is another option.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Netting the canopy, or at least the fruiting branches, at first color is the most effective home control; hang it ahead of the crop rather than in response to the first losses. Holding the plant to a manageable size is what keeps both netting and picking practical, and a container plant can be relocated to a more protected position.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Reflective tape and other scare items can buy you some time, but the effect tends to fade, so lean on them as a helper alongside netting rather than as the main defense.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective tape and scare devices give short-lived protection at best; their value is as a supplement through peak ripening, not a substitute for exclusion.

diseases.name: Fig rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: In mid to late summer, leaves develop small yellow-orange spots that turn rusty reddish-brown, most on the underside; heavily spotted leaves yellow and drop early, sometimes defoliating the plant well before fall. The current crop usually still ripens, but repeated early defoliation weakens the plant over years.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: In late summer, leaves get small yellow-orange spots that turn rusty brown, mostly underneath, and then yellow and fall early, sometimes stripping the plant before fall. That year's figs usually still ripen, but losing leaves early year after year wears the plant down.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Cerotelium fici. It spreads in warm, humid, wet weather and overwinters on fallen infected leaves, so it is most severe in the humid Southeast and in wet summers, building up where litter is left under the plant.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Cerotelium fici. It spreads in warm, wet, humid weather and survives winter on fallen infected leaves, so it is worst in humid areas and wet summers, especially where old leaves pile up under the plant.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Once leaves are spotted there is no cure for that leaf; the goal is to slow the spread and protect next year. Rake up and destroy fallen leaves to remove the overwintering source, and keep the canopy open and dry. Where rust is severe, a neutral copper or Bordeaux fungicide on the new foliage through the growing season is the standard organic option.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once a leaf is spotted you cannot cure it; the aim is to slow it down and protect next year. Rake up and throw away fallen leaves, and keep the plant open so it dries fast. Where rust is bad, an organic copper spray on the new leaves through the season is the usual treatment.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: clear fallen leaves each year, prune for airflow, and water at the ground rather than overhead. In rust-prone humid regions, a preventive copper program from spring protects the foliage.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The main prevention is cleanup: rake away fallen leaves every year, prune so air moves through the plant, and water the ground instead of the leaves. In humid areas where rust is common, an organic copper spray starting in spring keeps the leaves protected.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rake up the fallen leaves under your fig and get rid of them, during the season and again at the end of it. The fungus rides out the winter on that old leaf litter, so leaving it in place under the plant sets up next summer's outbreak.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cerotelium fici overwinters in fallen infected leaves, so annual removal and destruction of that litter is the backbone of the program. It lowers the inoculum that starts the following season rather than doing anything for the current one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune so air moves through the plant and wet leaves dry quickly. Rust spreads in warm, humid, wet weather, so a canopy that dries fast gives it less to work with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Opening the canopy shortens the leaf wetness the rust depends on after rain and dew. Paired with litter removal, it is what holds foliage on the plant later into the season in humid regions.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water the soil at the base of the plant rather than spraying the leaves. Wetting the foliage hands the rust the damp conditions it needs, which matters most in humid weather.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Ground-level irrigation avoids stacking added leaf wetness on top of ambient humidity. In wet summers and humid regions the weather is already supplying most of what the fungus needs, so there is no reason to supply more.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where rust shows up most years, an organic copper spray on the new leaves is the usual treatment. It works as protection, so start it in spring and keep it going through the season; it will not clear the spots already on a leaf.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Neutral copper or Bordeaux on new foliage, on a preventive schedule from spring, is the standard organic option in rust-prone humid regions. It protects unspotted tissue rather than curing existing lesions, so timing and reapplication through the growing season decide whether it earns its place.

diseases.name: Fig mosaic
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves show scattered yellow, blotchy, or ring-like mottling (a mosaic pattern), sometimes with distorted growth; fruit may be spotted or drop early. Symptoms vary with season and variety and often come and go. The virus does not kill the plant but can reduce vigor and crop.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get a blotchy, mottled yellow pattern (called a mosaic), and sometimes the fruit is spotted or drops early. It comes and goes with the season and variety. It does not kill the plant, but it can slow it down and cut the crop.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fig mosaic is a virus complex spread mainly by the tiny fig mite (Aceria ficus) and carried in cuttings taken from infected plants. Once a plant has it, it is systemic and permanent, since there is no cure for a virus in a plant.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fig mosaic is a virus, spread mostly by a tiny mite (the fig mite) and passed along in cuttings from infected plants. Once a plant has it, it is in the plant for good, because there is no cure for a plant virus.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no treatment for a virus in a plant. Manage it by keeping the plant otherwise healthy and vigorous; many infected figs still crop acceptably. Do not propagate cuttings from a mottled plant, and remove a severely stunted, poor-cropping plant.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for a plant virus. Just keep the fig healthy and well cared for, since many infected plants still fruit alright. Do not take cuttings from a mottled plant to start new ones, and pull out a plant that is badly stunted and barely fruiting.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prevention is about clean stock and mite control: start with cuttings or plants from healthy, unmottled sources, and keep fig mites in check since they spread the virus. There is no way to cure an infected plant.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best prevention is starting with a healthy plant and controlling the tiny fig mites that spread it. Buy or take cuttings from plants with clean, un-mottled leaves. There is no way to cure a plant once it is infected.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with a plant or cutting whose leaves look clean and un-mottled, and do not take cuttings from a fig showing the blotchy pattern, since the virus goes along with the wood. There is no cure once a plant has it, so the stock you start from is the decision that matters.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Clean propagation stock is the practical lever, since the virus complex is systemic and permanent in an infected plant and moves readily in cuttings taken from it. Where you propagate your own, take wood only from an unmottled plant.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the fig well cared for otherwise, since many infected plants still fruit alright. If one is badly stunted and barely setting figs, taking it out is reasonable.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rogue out severely stunted, poor-cropping specimens; lightly affected plants often crop acceptably and can be kept in production, so this is a judgment about that plant rather than a blanket removal.

diseases.name: Fig endosepsis (internal fruit rot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Ripening fruit rots from the inside near the eye, turning brown and mushy internally while the outside may still look sound; affected figs sour, ooze, and drop. It overlaps with beetle-spread souring and is worst in humid weather on open-eye varieties.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Figs rot from the inside near the little hole at the bottom, going brown and mushy inside even when the outside still looks okay, then souring and dropping. It goes hand in hand with the souring that beetles cause, and is worst in humid weather on figs with a big open eye.
diseases.cause_seasoned: An internal fruit rot caused by fungi (including Fusarium) carried into the fruit through the open eye, often by the same sap beetles that spread souring. Humid conditions and large-eye varieties make it worse.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rot inside the fruit caused by fungi that get in through the open hole at the bottom, often carried by the same little beetles that cause souring. Humid weather and big-eye varieties make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no in-fruit cure. Control it the same way as souring: pick promptly, remove affected and dropped fruit, and favor small or closed-eye varieties (such as Celeste) in humid areas.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure it inside the fruit. Handle it like souring: pick figs promptly, throw away rotten and dropped ones, and grow a tight-eye variety like Celeste if your area is humid.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose closed-eye varieties in humid regions, keep fruit picked and the ground clean, and manage the sap beetles that carry the fungi.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Grow a tight-eye variety in humid areas, keep the figs picked and the ground clean, and control the little beetles that carry it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Take the figs as they ripen rather than leaving them on the tree. The same sap beetles that carry this fungus are drawn to fruit that has hung too long.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Picking on time narrows the stretch when fruit is attractive to the sap beetles that move these fungi. Because there is no in-fruit cure, every control acts before infection, and harvest timing is the one that runs through the whole ripening period.

control_ladder.note_beginner: In a humid area, choose a fig with a small, tight eye, the opening at the base of the fruit, such as Celeste. The fungi that rot the inside of the fig get in through that opening, so a narrow one gives them less of a way in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Eye diameter governs access for the Fusarium and related fungi behind the internal rot, so closed-eye selections such as Celeste are the varietal control wherever humidity keeps pressure up.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick figs as they ripen and clear away any that are rotting inside or have dropped. The same little beetles that sour figs carry these fungi in, and soft, rotting fruit lying around is what draws them, so the cleanup does double duty.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt harvest plus removal of affected and fallen fruit denies the sap beetles that carry the fungi their attractant, which is the whole practical handle: nothing you apply reaches the rot once it is inside the fruit.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly rather than lightly and often: figure roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week from rain or irrigation through the growing season, more in heat and sandy soil, easing off as fruit finishes and through winter dormancy. A newly planted fig needs the most attention while it roots in; an established fig is fairly drought-tolerant but sizes and sweetens fruit poorly when it runs dry.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week from rain or the hose during the growing season, more when it is hot or the soil is sandy. A new fig needs steady water while it gets its roots going. An older fig can take some dry spells, but the figs come out small and less sweet if it gets too dry.
watering.amount_seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root zone rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing fig, UF/IFAS suggests around 10 gallons per soak two to three times a week in the first season; for a bearing plant, aim for the equivalent of about 1 to 1.5 inches per week through the growing season, more in heat.
watering.amount_beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches the roots, not just a splash on top. A new fig wants about 10 gallons per soak, two or three times a week its first summer. An older, fruiting fig wants roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, and more when it is hot.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose out toward the drip line, keeping the canopy dry to limit fig rust and fruit souring. Keep moisture especially steady as the fruit sizes and ripens, since a swing from dry to soaked (or heavy rain on ripening figs) causes fruit to split and sour.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, and try to keep the leaves and fruit dry, since wet leaves invite disease. Keep the watering steady while the figs are filling out and ripening, because going from dry to very wet, or a hard rain on ripe figs, makes them split and spoil.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Chronically wet, poorly drained soil shows as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists in wet soil, and general decline as waterlogged roots suffocate. Figs tolerate more moisture than stone fruit but still fail in standing water. Fruit that splits and sours after heavy watering or rain is the other overwatering signal near harvest.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Too much water, or soil that stays soggy, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and a plant slowly going downhill, because the roots cannot breathe. Figs handle moisture better than a peach but still cannot sit in waterlogged soil. Figs that split and sour after a lot of water or rain are another sign near harvest.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull and yellowing leaves, early leaf drop, and, most tellingly, fruit that drops while small or ripens undersized and less sweet. A fig short of water during the summer swell aborts part of its crop, so catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull yellow leaves, leaves dropping early, and, most clearly, small figs falling off or ripening tiny and less sweet. A fig that gets too dry in summer drops some of its fruit, so try to catch the dryness before the figs suffer.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~10 gal per watering
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through the first season keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of roughly 10 gallons two to three times a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the root system the plant relies on later.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the fig is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 10 gallons two or three times a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow strong roots.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~1 to 1.5 in per week equivalent
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: As the main crop sizes, keep moisture steady, about 1 to 1.5 inches per week as deep soaks. This is the window where even watering translates directly into fuller, sweeter figs and where a dry-then-wet swing causes fruit to split and sour.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the figs are filling out, keep the water steady, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week as deep soaks. Even watering now means bigger, sweeter figs, and it keeps the fruit from splitting.

schedule_by_stage.rate: minimal
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Once the fig is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only in prolonged dry spells so roots do not desiccate. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: After the leaves drop and the fig is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, keeping the canopy dry to limit fig rust and souring. Young figs need consistent moisture through the first season to establish; mature figs are moderately drought-tolerant but drop and undersize fruit under stress, and split when a dry spell breaks in heavy water or rain.
watering.method_note_beginner: Give the fig a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground instead of over the top, since wet leaves and fruit invite disease. Young figs need steady water the first season. Older figs handle dry spells, but they drop figs when too dry and split them when a dry spell ends in a big soak or rain.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The make-or-break window is the summer fruit swell, when steady moisture sets final size and sweetness and when moisture swings cause splitting and souring. Establishment (the first season) is the other critical period. Ease off through dormancy.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep water steady is summer while the figs are sizing up, when even watering makes them big and sweet and keeps them from splitting. The first season after planting matters too. In winter it needs almost none.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Fill the pot with a good-quality potting mix that drains well. A bark-based mix, or a general potting soil with some extra perlite stirred in, works nicely. Figs are not picky, but avoid a heavy soil dug from the yard, which packs down and drains poorly in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Keep it simple. Mix in a little compost for fertility and some perlite if the mix seems to hold too much water. Figs take richer mixes better than a peach does, but you still want the pot to drain freely rather than stay wet.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a quality bark-based or peat-based potting mix amended for drainage, not native garden soil, which compacts under container irrigation. Figs tolerate a more moisture-retentive mix than stone fruit but still perform best with free drainage and an air-filled root zone.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in modest compost for fertility and extra perlite or pumice if the base mix is water-retentive. Figs accept richer container media than most fruit trees, but keep drainage the priority; a top-dress of compost each spring covers most of the plant's needs.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: A fig in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground. In summer heat, check it daily and water when the top inch or two is dry, until water runs out the bottom. Water more often than a ground fig, but do not leave the pot standing in a saucer of water. In winter, when the plant is resting, give it just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Frequent watering washes food out of a pot, so feed a little at a time: a diluted balanced liquid feed every few weeks from spring into midsummer, then stop by late summer so the plant does not push tender growth into fall. Do not feed at planting, and stop once it drops its leaves for winter.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Growing a fig in a pot is the easiest way to keep one where winters are too cold for it in the ground, because you can move it somewhere protected. Before hard freezes come, move the pot into an unheated but sheltered spot like an attached garage, shed, or basement that stays cold but does not deep-freeze. The fig is leafless and resting, so it does not need light in there. Water it just once in a while so the roots do not dry out, and bring it back outside when hard frosts are past in spring.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: A container is the standard way to carry a fig through winters colder than its in-ground range. Once the plant is dormant and leafless, move the pot to an unheated but protected space (attached garage, shed, or cool basement) that holds above roughly the mid teens but stays cold enough to keep it dormant. It needs no light while leafless; water sparingly to keep the root ball from drying out. Return it outdoors after hard frosts pass. A container fig still needs its short winter chill, so do not overwinter it in a heated room.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Figs are one of the best fruit trees for a pot, and a pot is the way to grow one if your winters are too cold for a fig in the ground. Use a large container that drains well, keep it watered more often than a ground plant, and move it to a protected spot for winter. A potted fig stays smaller and still gives you a good crop.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fig is exceptionally well suited to container culture, and a pot is the practical route to fruit in regions colder than its in-ground range, since the plant can be moved to shelter for winter. Use at least a 15-gallon container (20 or more is better) with excellent drainage, water more frequently than an in-ground plant, and overwinter the dormant pot in a protected, unheated space. Expect a smaller plant and a lighter but dependable crop.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: A potted fig dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to draw on, so check moisture daily in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes. Water more often, but never leave the pot standing in a full saucer. Through dormancy the plant needs only enough water to keep the root ball from drying out.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and often: a dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the spring-to-midsummer flush, then stop by late summer so no soft growth is pushed into fall. Do not feed at planting, and ease off entirely once the plant goes dormant.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering or sub-irrigated planter is not the best choice for fig. Figs fruit and firm up best on a wet-then-dry cycle and dislike a root zone held constantly moist by a reservoir, which can invite root problems and, near harvest, split fruit. Figs are more forgiving of moisture than stone fruit, so a self-watering pot is workable in a pinch, but a freely draining pot you water yourself gives better fruit.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot (one with a water tank in the bottom) is not the best choice for a fig. Figs do best when the soil dries out a bit between waterings, and a tank keeps the roots wet all the time, which can cause root trouble and split fruit. Figs handle moisture better than a peach, so it can work if that is what you have, but a regular pot that drains well and that you water yourself grows better figs.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Cold protection for a potted fig is mostly about moving it: the exposed pot lets roots freeze several zones colder than in the ground, so shelter the dormant plant in an unheated garage or shed through the coldest months. If it must stay outside in a marginal zone, cluster pots against a wall, wrap them, and bank mulch around them. The goal is a cold, stable dormancy without the deep freezes that kill exposed roots and top growth.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: Protecting a potted fig in winter mostly means moving it somewhere sheltered, because the roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground. Put the resting, leafless plant in an unheated garage or shed for the coldest months. If it has to stay outside, push the pots together against a wall, wrap them, and pile mulch around them to keep the roots from freezing.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Figs are highly perishable and do not ripen further once picked, so pick them fully ripe and eat them fast. At room temperature ripe figs hold only about a day, sometimes two, before they begin to spoil, so plan to eat, cook, or refrigerate them the day you pick.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Figs are very perishable and do not ripen after you pick them, so pick them ripe and eat them quickly. On the counter ripe figs last only about a day or two before they go bad, so eat, cook, or refrigerate them the same day you pick.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate ripe figs unwashed in a single layer and use them within about 2 to 3 days. Cold slows the spoilage but figs are fragile; keep them shallow so they do not crush, and bring them to room temperature before eating for the best flavor.
storage.fridge_beginner: Put ripe figs in the fridge unwashed, in a single layer so they do not crush, and eat them within about 2 to 3 days. Let them warm up to room temperature before eating for the best taste.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Figs freeze well whole or halved. Rinse, dry, and freeze them in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to freezer bags; they keep several months and are best for cooking, baking, and preserves. Figs also dry excellently, the classic way to keep a big crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Figs freeze nicely whole or cut in half. Rinse and dry them, freeze them on a tray, then pack them into freezer bags. They keep for several months and are great for cooking and jam. Figs also dry very well, which is the traditional way to save a big crop.
storage.notes_seasoned: The key with figs is that they do not ripen off the plant and spoil within a day or two, so ripeness at picking and speed to the table (or fridge, freezer, or drying rack) is everything.
storage.notes_beginner: The main thing to remember is that figs do not ripen after picking and spoil in a day or two, so pick them ripe and use them fast, or refrigerate, freeze, or dry them right away.

recommended.name: Celeste
recommended.recommended_note: Small, sweet, closed-eye fig; cold-hardy and among the most reliable, and its tight eye resists souring in humid areas.

recommended.name: Brown Turkey
recommended.recommended_note: Widely adaptable and forgiving brownish-purple fig; a common, dependable first choice. (Texas Everbearing is a similar strain.)

recommended.name: Chicago Hardy
recommended.recommended_note: One of the most cold-hardy figs; roots survive hard winters and it fruits on new wood after dieback, the pick for zones 6 and the cold edge.

recommended.name: Black Mission
recommended.recommended_note: Rich, dark purple-black classic for mild-winter regions; heavy bearer in California and the warm West.

recommended.name: Kadota
recommended.recommended_note: Light green to amber, closed-eye fig that holds up well; a good canning and drying variety for warm, dry regions.

recommended.name: LSU Purple
recommended.recommended_note: Vigorous, disease-tolerant purple fig bred for the humid South; productive and rust-tolerant.

varieties.note_seasoned: Because all common figs need only about 100 chill hours, choose a variety not by chill (as you would a peach) but by cold-hardiness, disease tolerance, and eye type for your climate. In cold-winter areas favor the hardiest types (Chicago Hardy, Celeste, Marseilles). In humid areas favor a small, closed-eye variety (Celeste) or a rust-tolerant one (LSU Purple) to limit souring and rust. In mild, dry regions almost anything thrives, so pick by flavor and use. All the recommended types are common (parthenocarpic) figs that fruit alone with no pollination.
varieties.note_beginner: All common figs need about the same small amount of winter cold, so you do not pick a fig by chill hours the way you would a peach. Instead, choose by how cold-hardy it is and how well it handles your weather. In cold areas, pick a hardy type like Chicago Hardy or Celeste. In humid areas, pick a small, tight-eye type like Celeste or a rust-tolerant one like LSU Purple to avoid souring and rust. Where it is mild and dry, almost any fig does well, so pick by taste. All of these are common figs that fruit on their own with no pollination.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to fig. It is planted as a dormant, own-rooted bare-root or container plant, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to the outdoors) does not apply to fig. You plant it as a dormant bare-root or potted plant, so there is no tender young seedling to ease outside.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant a dormant, own-rooted bare-root or container fig in late winter to early spring, once the hardest cold has passed, or in fall to early winter in mild regions. Because figs are grown on their own roots there is no graft union to keep above grade; you can even set the plant an inch or two deeper than it grew to encourage a well-anchored, multi-stem bush, the form that best recovers from winter dieback. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots, backfill with native soil, water in well, and mulch, keeping mulch off the stems. Do not fertilize in the hole.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant a dormant bare-root or potted fig in late winter or early spring after the worst cold, or in fall to early winter where winters are mild. Figs grow on their own roots, so unlike a peach there is no graft joint to keep above the soil; you can even plant it a little deeper to help it grow into a sturdy, multi-stem bush, which bounces back best if winter kills the top. Dig a hole wide enough for the roots, fill it back with the same soil, water it in well, and spread mulch, keeping it off the stems. Do not put fertilizer in the hole.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Annual crop rotation does not apply to a fig, which holds its site for decades. The real site concern is root-knot nematode. Because own-rooted figs have no resistant rootstock, do not plant a fig into sandy ground known to be heavily infested with root-knot nematodes, or where a nematode-declined fig was just removed, without replacing a generous volume of soil.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: You do not rotate a fig the way you rotate vegetables, since it stays put for many years. What matters is root-knot nematode, a tiny soil pest that is the main killer of figs. Do not plant a fig in sandy soil that is known to be full of these pests, or right where a sick fig just came out, unless you dig out and replace a big area of soil first.
rotation.good_after: a well-drained site free of root-knot nematodes, with no recent history of nematode-declined figs
rotation.note_seasoned: If a fig must go where nematodes are a concern, choose a site with the least sandy, best-drained soil available, replace a generous volume of soil, keep the plant vigorous and mulched, and accept that own-rooted figs cannot be rootstock-protected the way stone fruit can.
rotation.note_beginner: If you have to plant where nematodes might be a problem, pick the best-drained, least sandy spot, dig out and replace a big area of soil, and keep the fig healthy and mulched. Remember there is no special root you can buy to protect a fig from these pests.

growth_stages.name: Planting (dormant, own-root)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late winter to early spring after the hardest cold, or fall to early winter in mild regions.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter or early spring after the worst cold, or fall to early winter where winters are mild.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant, leafless own-rooted plant (bare-root, or a container plant) with firm stems and healthy roots. Figs are not grafted, so there is no graft union to position.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A leafless dormant plant with firm stems and good roots. Figs are not grafted, so there is no graft joint to worry about.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spreading the roots in a wide hole. You can set the plant an inch or two deeper than it grew to encourage a sturdy multi-stem bush. Backfill with native soil, water in well, and mulch, keeping mulch off the stems. In cold regions, plant against a warm south-facing wall.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. You can set it a little deeper than it grew to help it form a bushy plant. Fill the hole with the same soil, water it well, and mulch, keeping mulch off the stems. In cold areas, plant it against a warm south wall.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the planting date and the variety.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you planted and which fig variety it is.

growth_stages.name: Year-one establishment
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first full growing season after planting.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first whole growing season after you plant.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new shoot growth and a strengthening root system. A few figs may form the first or second year; that is fine.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Healthy new shoots and a plant settling in. A few figs may come the first or second year, which is fine.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly through the first season so roots establish, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the plant, and protect it well its first winter, since a young fig is the most cold-tender it will ever be.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water deeply and often this first season, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around it, and protect it well its first winter, since a young fig is more cold-tender than an older one.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first-season watering and how you protected the plant its first winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your watering and how you protected the young plant its first winter.

growth_stages.name: Formative pruning (years one to three)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first two to three years, while you set the plant's form.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first two or three years, while you shape the plant.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Figs are usually trained as an open multi-stem bush (best in cold climates, since it regrows fast after dieback) or as a single-trunk small tree in mild climates. Watch for the framework you want to keep.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Figs are usually grown as an open bush with several stems (best where winters are cold, since it grows back fast after dieback) or as a small single-trunk tree where it is mild. Pick the shape you want.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: For a bush, keep several well-spaced low stems and remove weak, crowded, or crossing growth; for a tree, select one trunk. Figs bear on both old and new wood, so prune lightly to shape rather than heading hard, which would cost the breba crop.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: For a bush, keep several evenly spaced low stems and cut out weak or crowded ones; for a tree, keep one trunk. Figs fruit on both old and new wood, so prune lightly to shape it, not hard, or you lose the early crop.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record your formative pruning and whether you are training a bush or a tree.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your shaping cuts and whether you are growing a bush or a tree.

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Roughly December through February, the leafless months.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: About December through February, the bare winter months.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A leafless plant at rest. Figs need only about 100 chill hours, so chill is easily met almost anywhere; the real winter issue is cold injury, not chill.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A bare, resting plant. Figs need very little winter cold (about 100 hours), so that is never the problem; the real worry in winter is cold damage.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: In zones 6 and colder, protect the plant now: wrap the stems, or cut back and bury under mulch and leaves, or move a container to an unheated garage or shed. In zones 7 and warmer, little is needed beyond winter cleanup.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In zone 6 and colder, protect the plant now: wrap the stems, or cut it back and cover it with mulch and leaves, or move a potted fig into an unheated garage or shed. In zone 7 and warmer, just clean up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the dormant-season protection you applied and any winter lows.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note how you protected the plant and how cold it got.

growth_stages.name: Dormant pruning
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late winter, after the coldest weather but before growth begins.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter, after the coldest weather but before the plant wakes up.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare stems that show the plant's structure. Any wood killed by winter is now visible and easy to remove.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare stems, so you can see the shape and any wood the winter killed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune lightly after the hardest cold has passed: remove dead, frost-killed, weak, and crowded wood, and keep the plant open. Do not head it hard, since figs bear on last year's wood (the breba crop) as well as new wood; heavy pruning trades away the early crop.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Prune lightly after the worst cold: take out dead, frost-killed, weak, and crowded stems, and keep it open. Do not cut it back hard, because figs fruit on last year's wood too, so heavy pruning costs you the early crop.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the pruning date and how much winter dieback you removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you pruned and how much winter-killed wood you took off.

growth_stages.name: Leaf-out and breba set
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Early to mid spring as growth resumes.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Early to mid spring as the plant leafs out.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves unfolding and, on last year's wood, the small breba figs beginning to swell. A fig shows no visible flowers, since its flowers are hidden inside the fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Leaves opening and small early figs (the breba crop) swelling on last year's stems. You will not see any flowers, because a fig's flowers are inside the fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little to do but watch for a late frost that can nip tender new growth, and remove winter wraps once hard frost is past. Because figs are parthenocarpic, the breba fruit sets on its own with no pollination.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do but watch for a late frost that can burn the new growth, and take off any winter wraps once hard frosts are done. The early figs set all on their own, with no pollination needed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note leaf-out and whether a breba (early) crop set.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when it leafed out and whether early figs formed.

growth_stages.name: Main crop development
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late spring through summer as new shoots extend.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late spring through summer as the new shoots grow.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The main crop forming and swelling in the leaf joints of the new growth. Figs need no thinning; the plant carries what it can size. Watch for drought stress, which drops fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The main crop forming and swelling where the leaves meet the new stems. Figs do not need thinning. Watch for dryness, which makes them drop fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep water steady through the swell so fruit does not drop, undersize, or split, and keep feeding light. Watch for fig rust in humid weather and keep the canopy open and dry.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady while the figs fill out so they do not drop or split, and go easy on fertilizer. Watch for rust spots on the leaves in humid weather and keep the plant open.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record watering through the swell and any fruit drop or splitting.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your watering and any figs dropping or splitting.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Early summer for the breba crop and mid to late summer through fall for the main crop.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Early summer for the first figs and mid to late summer through fall for the main crop.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Ripe figs soften, the neck bends so the fruit droops, color develops fully, and a drop of nectar may show at the eye. Figs ripen a few at a time over many weeks and must ripen on the plant, since they do not ripen after picking.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Ripe figs get soft, droop down as the neck bends, color up fully, and may show a drop of syrup at the bottom. They ripen a few at a time over weeks and must ripen on the plant, since they do not ripen after you pick them.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick figs fully ripe, gently, every day or two as they soften, and eat, refrigerate, freeze, or dry them promptly since they spoil fast. Remove any soured or dropped fruit, and net against birds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick figs when fully ripe and soft, gently, every day or two, and eat, refrigerate, freeze, or dry them right away since they spoil fast. Clean up any soured or fallen figs, and net the plant against birds.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates and a rough yield.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you picked and roughly how much you got.

notifications.body_seasoned: Plant a dormant own-rooted fig now, after the hardest cold, in full sun on well-drained ground. There is no graft union to fuss over; you can set it slightly deep to build a sturdy multi-stem bush, and in cold areas place it against a warm south-facing wall. Water in well and mulch, keeping mulch off the stems.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is the time to plant a dormant fig, after the worst cold, in a sunny, well-drained spot. Figs grow on their own roots, so there is no graft joint to worry about, and you can plant it a little deep to make a bushy plant. In cold areas plant it against a warm south wall. Water it in and mulch, keeping mulch off the stems.

notifications.body_seasoned: Prune now, in late winter after the hardest cold but before growth begins. Keep it light: remove dead, frost-killed, weak, and crowded wood and open the plant up, but do not head it hard, since figs bear on last year's wood as well as new wood.
notifications.body_beginner: Prune now, in late winter after the worst cold but before the plant wakes up. Keep it light: cut out dead, frost-killed, weak, and crowded stems and open it up, but do not cut it back hard, since figs fruit on last year's wood too.

notifications.body_seasoned: Once hard frosts are past, remove winter wraps, mulch mounds, or bring a container fig back outside. Watch the forecast a while longer, since a late frost can still nip the tender new growth and the swelling breba figs.
notifications.body_beginner: Once hard frosts are done, take off the winter wraps or mulch, or move a potted fig back outside. Keep an eye on the forecast a little longer, since a late frost can still burn the new growth and the early figs.

notifications.body_seasoned: A newly planted fig needs steady moisture through its first season while roots establish. Water deeply at the root zone, roughly 10 gallons two to three times a week in the heat, and keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the plant.
notifications.body_beginner: A new fig needs steady water its first season while its roots grow in. Give it a deep soak at the ground, about 10 gallons two or three times a week in the heat, and keep a mulched, weed-free ring around it.

notifications.body_seasoned: The main crop is ripening now. Pick figs only when fully ripe (soft, drooping on a bent neck, fully colored), since they do not ripen after picking and spoil within a day or two. Pick every day or two, net against birds, and clear any soured or dropped fruit.
notifications.body_beginner: The main crop is ripening. Pick figs only when fully ripe, soft, drooping, and fully colored, since they do not ripen after picking and spoil in a day or two. Pick every day or two, cover the plant against birds, and clean up any soured or fallen figs.

notifications.body_seasoned: Before hard freezes arrive, protect the plant where winters run below the mid teens: wrap the stems, or cut back and bury under mulch and leaves, or move a container to an unheated garage or shed. Dormant fig wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F.
notifications.body_beginner: Before hard freezes come, protect the fig where winters drop below the mid teens: wrap the stems, cut it back and cover it with mulch and leaves, or move a potted fig into an unheated garage or shed. Fig stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F.

notifications.title_seasoned: Anything to log on the fig?
notifications.body_seasoned: It has been a while since your last note. A quick check pays off: note how the plant came through winter and whether it needed to regrow, jot down when it leafed out and started ripening, and watch for early fig rust in humid weather.
notifications.body_beginner: It has been a while since you logged anything. A quick look is worth it: note how the plant came through winter and whether it had to regrow, write down when it leafed out and started ripening, and watch for rust spots on the leaves in humid weather.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Freeze coming, protect your fig
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cold is the fig's main hazard. Dormant wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, so if a hard freeze is forecast and the plant is not already protected, wrap the stems, mound mulch, or move a container to shelter. In spring, a late frost on tender new growth nips the leaves and the breba figs, so cover a small plant overnight.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Cold is a fig's biggest danger. The stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, so if a hard freeze is coming and the plant is not protected, wrap the stems, pile on mulch, or move a potted fig to shelter. In spring, a late frost can burn the new leaves and early figs, so cover a small plant overnight.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain, watch ripe figs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hard rain on ripening figs, especially after a dry spell, makes them swell fast and split, and the open cracks let in souring. After a soaking rain, check ripening fruit and pick anything ready rather than leaving it to crack and sour.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A hard rain on ripening figs, especially after a dry stretch, makes them swell fast and split, and the cracks let in rot. After a heavy rain, check the ripe figs and pick any that are ready instead of leaving them to split and spoil.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Humid spell, fig-rust and souring weather
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Muggy weather, watch for rust and souring
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid weather drives fig rust on the leaves and beetle-spread souring in the fruit. Keep the canopy open and dry, water only at the root zone, pick ripe figs promptly, and remove any soured fruit so it does not seed more.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, muggy weather brings on rust spots on the leaves and souring in the fruit. Keep the plant open and the leaves dry, water only at the ground, pick ripe figs promptly, and throw away any soured ones so they do not spread.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry stretch, keep up deep watering
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry spell, do not let the fig run dry
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought stress is the main cause of a fig dropping its crop and ripening small, less-sweet fruit. During a dry stretch, water deeply at the root zone, a young plant establishing and a bearing plant during the summer swell most of all, and keep the surface mulched to hold moisture.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A fig that gets too dry drops its figs and ripens small, less-sweet ones. In a dry spell, give it a deep soak at the ground, especially a young plant and a fruiting plant while the figs are sizing, and keep it mulched to hold moisture.

planting.text_seasoned: Figs are grown on their own roots, so there is no graft union to keep above grade; you can even plant an inch or two deeper to encourage a sturdy, multi-stem bush.
planting.text_beginner: Figs grow on their own roots, so there is no graft joint to worry about. You can plant a fig a little deeper than it grew to help it form a bushy, well-anchored plant.
planting.author: claude_code_gs_arc

planting.text_seasoned: Plant in full sun on well-drained ground, and at the cold edge of the range against a warm, south-facing wall, which banks heat and buys the plant several degrees of winter protection.
planting.text_beginner: Plant where it gets full sun and the soil drains well. In cold areas, plant it against a warm south-facing wall, which holds heat and helps protect it in winter.
planting.author: claude_code_gs_arc

establishment.text_seasoned: A young fig is the most cold-tender it will ever be; protect it well its first winter even in a zone where an established plant would shrug off the cold.
establishment.text_beginner: A young fig is more easily hurt by cold than an older one, so protect it well its first winter, even where a bigger plant would be fine.
establishment.author: claude_code_gs_arc

formative_pruning.text_seasoned: In cold climates train the plant as an open multi-stem bush rather than a single trunk: if a hard winter kills the top, a bush regrows from several low stems and ripens a main crop far faster than a single-trunk tree.
formative_pruning.text_beginner: Where winters are cold, grow the fig as a bush with several low stems, not one trunk. If a hard winter kills the top, a bush grows back fast from the low stems and fruits again much sooner.
formative_pruning.author: claude_code_gs_arc

dormancy.text_seasoned: Figs need only about 100 chill hours, met almost anywhere, so chill is never the limiter; the winter job is cold protection, since dormant wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F.
dormancy.text_beginner: Figs need very little winter cold (about 100 hours), so that is never a problem. The winter job is protecting the plant from hard freezes, since the stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F.
dormancy.author: claude_code_gs_arc

dormancy.text_seasoned: In zone 6, the reliable cold-climate options are to wrap the stems, or cut back and bury the plant under mulch and leaves, or grow it in a container moved to an unheated garage.
dormancy.text_beginner: In zone 6, the ways to get a fig through winter are to wrap the stems, cut it back and cover it with mulch and leaves, or grow it in a pot you move into an unheated garage.
dormancy.author: claude_code_gs_arc

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Prune figs lightly and only after the hardest cold has passed: they bear on last year's wood (the breba crop) as well as new wood, so heavy heading trades away the early crop.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Prune figs lightly, and wait until the worst cold is over. They fruit on last year's wood too, so cutting hard costs you the early crop.
dormant_prune.author: claude_code_gs_arc

leaf_out.text_seasoned: A fig never shows a visible bloom, since its flowers are inside the fruit; because common figs are parthenocarpic, the breba figs set and ripen with no pollination at all.
leaf_out.text_beginner: A fig never shows flowers, because they are hidden inside the fruit. Common figs make their early crop all on their own, with no pollination needed.
leaf_out.author: claude_code_gs_arc

fruit_development.text_seasoned: Figs need no thinning, but they do need steady water through the summer swell: a dry spell drops fruit, and a swing from dry to soaked (or hard rain on ripening figs) splits and sours it.
fruit_development.text_beginner: Figs do not need thinning, but they do need steady water in summer. If they get too dry they drop figs, and if a dry spell ends in a big soak or rain, the figs split and spoil.
fruit_development.author: claude_code_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick figs only when fully ripe, when they soften and droop on a bent neck, since figs do not ripen after picking; they spoil within a day or two, so eat, chill, freeze, or dry them promptly.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick figs only when fully ripe, soft, and drooping, because they do not ripen after you pick them. They spoil in a day or two, so eat, chill, freeze, or dry them right away.
harvest.author: claude_code_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Net the plant against birds as fruit begins to color, and remove soured or dropped fruit as you go so beetles and souring yeasts do not build.
harvest.text_beginner: Cover the plant with bird netting as the figs start to color, and clean up any soured or fallen figs so beetles and rot do not build up.
harvest.author: claude_code_gs_arc

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature fig (roughly year 4 and up) commonly yields on the order of 20 to 50+ pounds of fruit a year in a good climate, spread over many weeks of picking rather than one flush; a large old plant in a warm region can bear far more. Yield swings widely with winter dieback, water, and variety, and a top-killed plant that regrows carries a lighter, later crop that year.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown fig (about year 4 and up) often gives roughly 20 to 50 pounds of fruit a year in a good climate, picked a few at a time over many weeks rather than all at once, and a big old plant can give much more. How much you get swings with winter cold, water, and variety, and a plant that had to regrow after a hard winter gives a lighter, later crop that year.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Figs reach full bearing quickly for a fruit tree, around years 3 to 5, and stay productive for decades where winters allow, given steady water and light annual pruning. In cold-edge zones, peak yield is capped by how much dieback the plant suffers each winter.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Figs reach full production fast for a fruit tree, around years 3 to 5, and keep bearing for decades where winters allow, as long as you water them and prune lightly each year. In cold areas, the size of the crop depends on how much the winter kills back each year.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect little to no fruit the planting year, though a few figs may form in year 1 or 2. The first meaningful crop typically comes by year 2 or 3, with full bearing by years 3 to 5. Focus the early years on establishment and winter protection, not fruit.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect much fruit the first year, though a few figs may form in year 1 or 2. Your first real crop usually comes by year 2 or 3, with full crops by years 3 to 5. In the early years, focus on getting the plant established and protected in winter, not on fruit.
factors_seasoned: variety and cold-hardiness
winter dieback and protection
summer water during fruit swell
moderate feeding (excess nitrogen cuts fruit)
full sun and heat
root-knot nematode pressure
bird and beetle losses at harvest

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting preference is asserted. Extension sources do not support timing fig planting or care by lunar phase; site warmth, winter protection, and steady water govern outcomes.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Stems died back or the plant was killed over winter
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The fig died back or died over the winter
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The top growth was killed by winter cold. This is the single most common fig problem outside the warmest zones: dormant fig wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, and sustained lows below that injure or kill the stems. The good news is that the roots are hardier and usually resprout, so a top-killed fig is rarely dead, just set back a year. The fixes are all about cold: protect the plant over winter, choose a cold-hardy variety, train it as a bush so it regrows fast, or grow it in a container you can shelter.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The winter cold killed the top of the plant. This is the most common fig problem outside the warmest areas, because fig stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F. The good news is the roots are tougher and usually grow back, so a top-killed fig is rarely truly dead, just a year behind. The fixes are about cold: protect the plant in winter, pick a cold-hardy variety, grow it as a bush so it regrows fast, or grow it in a pot you can move to shelter.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Protect the plant next winter (wrap, or cut back and bury under mulch and leaves, or shelter a container), plant a cold-hardy variety like Chicago Hardy or Celeste, and train it as a multi-stem bush for fast recovery.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Protect the plant next winter (wrap it, cover it with mulch and leaves, or shelter a pot), grow a cold-hardy variety like Chicago Hardy or Celeste, and train it as a bush so it grows back fast.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Figs drop while small, or ripe figs split and sour
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Figs fall off small, or ripe ones split and go sour
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Small figs dropping usually means water stress: a fig short of water in summer aborts part of its crop. Ripe figs splitting and souring usually means a moisture swing (a dry spell broken by heavy watering or rain) that makes the fruit swell and crack, letting in the beetles and yeasts that sour it. It is easy to blame the variety, but the real levers are steady water and prompt picking. Over-fertilizing also worsens splitting.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Small figs falling off is usually a sign the plant got too dry in summer, so it drops some of its crop. Ripe figs splitting and souring is usually from a swing in water, a dry spell ended by a big soak or rain, which makes them swell and crack, letting in the pests and rot that sour them. It is easy to blame the variety, but the real fixes are steady water and picking often. Too much fertilizer makes splitting worse too.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep water steady through the summer swell and mulch to buffer moisture, pick ripe figs promptly, do not over-fertilize, and in humid areas grow a small, closed-eye variety like Celeste that resists souring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the water steady while the figs size up and mulch to hold moisture, pick ripe figs promptly, go easy on fertilizer, and in humid areas grow a tight-eye variety like Celeste that resists souring.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Lots of leaves but few or no figs
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Lots of leaves but hardly any figs
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A vigorous, leafy fig with little fruit usually has one of three causes: too much nitrogen (rich soil or heavy feeding pushes leaves over fruit), a plant still too young (figs often need a year or two, sometimes three, to settle into cropping), or too much shade. A less common cause is the wrong type of fig entirely: a Smyrna or San Pedro variety cannot fruit without its fig wasp and simply drops everything. Common (parthenocarpic) types fruit on their own in full sun.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A leafy fig with few figs usually comes from one of three things: too much fertilizer or rich soil (which makes leaves instead of figs), a plant that is still too young (figs often take a year or two to start cropping well), or too much shade. Less often, it is the wrong kind of fig: a Smyrna or San Pedro type needs a special wasp to fruit and just drops everything. Common types fruit on their own in full sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut back on nitrogen, make sure the plant gets full sun, give a young plant another season, and confirm you are growing a common (parthenocarpic) variety rather than a Smyrna or San Pedro type.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use less fertilizer, make sure it gets full sun, give a young plant another year, and check that you have a common fig variety, not a Smyrna or San Pedro type that needs a special wasp.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaves get rusty spots and drop early in late summer
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves get rusty spots and fall early in late summer
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Yellow-orange spots that turn rusty brown, mostly on the leaf undersides, followed by early yellowing and leaf drop in mid to late summer, are fig rust, a fungus that thrives in warm, humid, wet weather. It overwinters on fallen leaves. The current crop usually still ripens, but repeated early defoliation weakens the plant over years, so the goal is to break the cycle rather than cure this year's leaves.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Yellow-orange spots that turn rusty brown, mostly under the leaves, then early yellowing and leaf drop in late summer, are fig rust, a fungus that likes warm, wet, humid weather. It survives winter on fallen leaves. That year's figs usually still ripen, but losing leaves early year after year wears the plant down, so the aim is to stop the cycle rather than fix this year's leaves.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves each year to remove the overwintering source, prune for airflow, water at the ground, and where rust is severe apply a copper or Bordeaux fungicide on the new foliage through the season.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Rake up and throw away fallen leaves each year, prune so air moves through the plant, water the ground not the leaves, and where rust is bad use an organic copper spray on the new leaves through the season.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Succession planting does not apply to fig. It is a permanent plant that occupies its site for decades and bears over a long ripening season each year, so there is no staggered re-sowing to schedule the way there is for a short-season annual crop.

Re-anchor at the citation sweep or accept as modeled. Signature disease (fig rust, Cerotelium fici) is fully BACKED on MG214.
