open_findings.summary: UAEX publishes no fig harvest date. Arkansas's own fruit harvest calendar (FCS812A, "Arkansas Local Produce Fruit & Vegetable Harvest Calendars") lists twelve fruits -- apples, blackberries, blueberries, cantaloupe, grapes, muscadines, nectarines, peaches, plums, raspberries, strawberries, watermelon -- and FIG IS NOT AMONG THEM. Three further UAEX documents (the Yard & Garden fig reference desk, the White County article, and the summer fruits page) give only cultivar ripening ORDER and crop structure: "Celeste ... ripens usually before Brown Turkey", "Brown Turkey (also called Texas Everbearing) ripens a few weeks after Celeste ... bears for a relatively long period of time", and the breba crop "rarely" persists in Arkansas so the current-season crop "is predominantly what we harvest". That is a relative ladder with no anchor date, the same shape hunt 1 recorded for peach ("days before Elberta"), which is why fig was not in hunt 1's stated exclusion list but reaches the same verdict on its own evidence. Our Jun 25 - Aug 10 (zone 7) / Jun 15 - Jul 30 (zone 8) window is modeled from bloom_start and is not contradicted by anything read. TRAP FOR THE NEXT READER: FCS812A's month columns are GRAPHICAL BARS with no text layer, so a text extraction returns crop names and no months. It cannot support a month claim for any crop, including the twelve it does list. Absence is scoped to the documents named here, all read from raw bytes 2026-08-04 and listed in docs/2026-08-04-campaign-b-closeout-hunt.md.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 winters (lows to -40°F) kill a fig outright, top and root. Not an in-ground fig zone; grow a container fig overwintered indoors.
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is far too cold for a fig in the ground. If you want to try one, grow it in a pot and bring it inside for winter.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 4 winters kill an in-ground fig, roots included in a hard year. Not an in-ground fig zone; grow a container fig moved to an unheated garage or basement for winter.
4.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 4 is too cold for a fig in the ground. Grow it in a pot and move it into an unheated garage or basement for winter instead.

5.suitability_note_seasoned: Very marginal in the ground. Even the hardiest varieties (Chicago Hardy, Celeste) have their tops killed most winters and must regrow, so a light main crop ripens on new wood only in a warm year and only with heavy winter protection. A container fig wintered indoors is far more dependable here.
5.suitability_note_beginner: This is a tough zone for a fig in the ground. Even the hardiest kinds usually get killed to the ground each winter and have to grow back, so you only get a small late crop in a warm year, and only with heavy winter protection. Growing it in a pot you bring inside is much more reliable.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frosts nip the new growth and any early figs, and winters below the mid teens kill the top back, so treat a main crop as the reward of a warm year on a well-protected, cold-hardy plant.

6.suitability_note_seasoned: The classic protected-fig zone. With heavy winter protection (wrapping, or cutting back and burying under mulch and leaves) and a cold-hardy variety, the plant comes through or regrows and ripens a main crop on new wood most years. Bush training and a warm south wall help. Chicago Hardy and Celeste are the safe picks.
6.suitability_note_beginner: This is the zone where figs fruit with protection. Wrap the plant or cut it back and bury it under mulch and leaves for winter, grow a hardy variety like Chicago Hardy or Celeste, and you can get a main crop most years. Growing it as a bush against a warm south wall helps.
6.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard winter kills the top back and a late spring frost can nip new growth; with heavy protection and a cold-hardy variety the plant regrows and ripens a main crop most years.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: The cool edge of reliable in-ground figs. Hardy varieties crop dependably here, occasionally losing some top growth in a severe winter but regrowing quickly. A warm, sheltered site and light protection in cold snaps keep both the breba and main crops coming.
7.suitability_note_beginner: The cool edge where figs grow reliably in the ground. Hardy varieties fruit dependably, now and then losing some top growth in a hard winter but growing back fast. A warm, sheltered spot and a little protection in cold snaps keep the figs coming.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An occasional hard freeze can kill some top growth in a severe winter, and a late frost can nip early growth; light protection in cold snaps and a hardy variety keep cropping reliable.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the north, how well a fig does comes down to winter cold. Figs grow in the ground reliably from about zone 7. Zone 6 fruits only with heavy winter protection and a hardy variety, and zones 3 to 5 are really pot-only, bringing the plant into an unheated garage or shed for winter. Even if the top dies, a fig usually grows back from the roots.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier, fig success is set entirely by winter cold, not chill. Reliable in-ground cropping starts around zone 7. Zone 6 fruits only with heavy winter protection and a cold-hardy variety, and zones 3 to 5 are container territory, where the plant winters in an unheated garage or shed. Even where the top dies back, a fig usually resprouts from the roots.
northern_tier.chill_basis_seasoned: Northern-tier winters bank far more than a fig's ~100-hour chill need, so chill is never the limiter here. The limit is cold injury: dormant fig wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, so deep winter lows kill the top back and set the whole in-ground map.
northern_tier.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are far colder than a fig needs, so chill is never the issue. The issue is freeze damage: fig stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, so deep winter cold kills the top and decides where a fig can grow in the ground.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable fig country. Winters are mild enough to grow figs in tree form, and the long season ripens both a breba and a full main crop. Choose small-eye, rust-tolerant varieties (Celeste, LSU Purple) and a well-drained, nematode-free site.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Great for figs. Winters are mild enough to grow them as a tree, and the long season ripens an early and a main crop. Pick a tight-eye, rust-tolerant variety like Celeste or LSU Purple and a well-drained spot free of nematodes.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent, nearly frost-free fig country with a long ripening season. Figs crop heavily; the main management is humid-weather rust and souring and, in sandy soil, root-knot nematodes. Favor closed-eye, rust-tolerant varieties.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent, almost frost-free fig country with a long season. Figs bear heavily here; the main jobs are managing rust and souring in humid weather and nematodes in sandy soil. Grow a tight-eye, rust-tolerant variety.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent, nearly frost-free fig country with a long ripening season. Figs crop heavily; the main management is humid-weather rust and souring and, in sandy soil, root-knot nematodes. Favor closed-eye, rust-tolerant varieties.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent, almost frost-free fig country with a long season. Figs bear heavily here; the main jobs are managing rust and souring in humid weather and nematodes in sandy soil. Grow a tight-eye, rust-tolerant variety.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: The Southeast is great fig country: mild winters, long hot summers, and figs' small need for winter cold make them one of the easiest backyard fruits here. The two things to watch are humid-weather problems (rust on the leaves and souring in the fruit) and root-knot nematodes in sandy soil, so pick a tight-eye, rust-tolerant variety and a pest-free spot.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast is fig country: warm winters, long hot summers, and a fig's tiny chill need make figs one of the most dependable backyard fruits here. The two watch-outs are humid-weather diseases (fig rust, and beetle-spread souring) and root-knot nematodes in sandy soil, so favor small-eye and rust-tolerant varieties and a nematode-free site.
se_gulf.chill_basis_seasoned: Gulf-South winters easily meet a fig's ~100-hour chill need, so chill is never the limiter. Warmth and humidity, not cold, define fig growing here.
se_gulf.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here easily give figs the little cold they need, so chill is never a problem. Heat and humidity, not cold, shape fig growing here.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Prime fig country. Long, hot, dry summers ripen full, sweet crops with low disease pressure, and mild winters let figs grow as sizable trees. Both crops ripen; keep water steady through the summer swell.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Prime fig country. Long, hot, dry summers ripen big, sweet crops with little disease, and mild winters let figs grow into good-sized trees. Both crops ripen here; just keep the water steady while the figs size up.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent fig climate with a long, hot season and mild, nearly frost-free winters. Heavy, high-quality crops with low disease; the main input is steady summer water. Almost any common variety thrives.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent for figs, with a long hot season and mild, almost frost-free winters. Big, high-quality crops with little disease; the main thing is steady summer water. Almost any common variety does well.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: California's hot, dry inland valleys are about the best fig climate anywhere: lots of heat for sweet fruit, dry air that keeps disease down, and mild winters that let figs grow as full trees. You get both the early and the main crop. Just keep the summer water steady and watch for nematodes in sandy soil.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's hot, dry interior valleys are arguably the best fig climate in the country: abundant heat ripens rich, sweet fruit, dry air keeps rust and souring low, and mild winters let figs grow as full trees. Both breba and main crops ripen well. Watch summer water and, in sandy ground, root-knot nematodes.
ca_interior.chill_basis_seasoned: Interior-valley winters easily meet a fig's small ~100-hour chill need, so chill never limits fruiting; abundant summer heat is the asset here.
ca_interior.chill_basis_beginner: Inland winters easily give figs the little cold they need, so chill is never a problem; the big summer heat is what makes figs so good here.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Figs fruit reliably but cool, foggy summers push the main crop later into fall and keep it a bit less sweet than inland. The early breba crop is valued here. Choose a cool-coast variety and the sunniest, most sheltered spot.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Figs fruit reliably here, but the cool, foggy summers ripen the main crop later in fall and a bit less sweet than inland, so the early crop matters more. Pick a coast-friendly variety and the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The milder, slightly warmer edge of the north coast still fruits figs reliably, with a late main crop shaped by coastal cool. A warm, sun-trapped site improves ripening and sweetness. Cool-coast varieties perform best.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The milder, slightly warmer part of the north coast still fruits figs reliably, with a late main crop shaped by the cool coast. A warm, sunny, sheltered spot ripens them better. Coast-friendly varieties do best.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Figs grow well on the cooler Northern California coast, but the cool, foggy summers ripen the main crop later and a little less sweet than inland, so the early crop counts for more. ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Figs grow well on the cooler Northern California coast, but cool, foggy summers ripen the main crop later and a touch less sweet than inland, and the breba crop matters more here. rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Rio Grande Valley winters comfortably meet a fig's roughly 100-hour chill need, and the long, intensely hot growing season ripens a full crop, per Texas A&M AgriLife Extension fig production guidance and the Valley's near-zero-chill, essentially frost-free climate. Humid spells still bring fig rust and souring, so favor closed-eye, rust-tolerant varieties (Celeste, LSU Purple, Alma) and a well-drained, nematode-free site. Exact Valley bloom and harvest months are not separately published; this window is a conservative estimate carried over from the similarly warm, humid Gulf coast, where fig fruits reliably.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The breba crop, the fruit that overwinters on last year's wood, ripens reliably here in August. The main, fall crop on new growth usually fails to ripen in this cool-summer climate and should be pulled off unripe rather than left to rot (WSU Extension). Plant a hardy, early variety in the warmest available spot for the most dependable breba harvest.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Chill is never the limiter here: the belt delivers roughly 1100 to 1500 chilling hours a year in zone 7, clearing this crop's variety range with margin (NC State Extension; regional four-source chill basket). A severe freeze can kill the top back to the ground, but the plant typically resprouts from the roots and can still fruit that same season or the next, especially on cold-hardy cultivars like Chicago Hardy, Celeste, and Brown Turkey.

crops.description_seasoned: Fig (Ficus carica) is a deciduous, Mediterranean fruit tree grown on its own roots from cuttings, prized for soft, honey-sweet fruit that must ripen on the plant and does not survive shipping, so a backyard fig gives you something no store can match. It is one of the easiest fruit trees to grow where winters are mild: it is self-fruitful and parthenocarpic (it sets fruit with no pollination at all), needs very little winter chill (about 100 hours), and thrives on heat, which makes warm regions its home, the opposite of a high-chill tree like cherry. The one real limit is cold. Fully dormant wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, so fig is grown in the ground in zones 7 to 10, given heavy winter protection in zone 6, and kept in a container that overwinters indoors where winters are colder. Many figs carry two crops: a light early-summer breba crop on last year's wood and a larger late-summer to fall main crop on the new growth.
crops.description_beginner: A fig (Ficus carica) is a fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives you soft, very sweet fruit that has to ripen on the plant and does not keep, which is why a homegrown fig is so much better than a store one. Where winters are mild, figs are one of the easiest fruit trees to grow: one plant makes fruit all by itself with no pollination needed, it needs very little winter cold, and it loves heat, so warm areas suit it perfectly. The one real limit is cold: the stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F. So figs grow in the ground in zones 7 to 10, need heavy winter protection in zone 6, and are best grown in a pot you bring into shelter for winter where it is colder. Many figs give two crops: a few early figs in summer on last year's stems, and a bigger crop in late summer and fall on the new growth.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: A fig is ripe when it softens fully, its neck bends so the fruit droops rather than standing out from the stem, it colors up to its full variety color, and a drop of nectar may appear at the eye. Ripe figs feel soft to a gentle squeeze and detach with the barest tug. Color alone is not ripeness; a fig can be fully colored and still firm and unready. Because figs do not ripen after picking, wait for full softness and droop, and pick every day or two, since a plant ripens a few at a time over many weeks.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A fig is ripe when it turns soft, droops down instead of sticking straight out (the neck bends), colors up fully, and maybe shows a drop of syrup at the bottom. A ripe fig gives easily to a gentle squeeze and comes off with the lightest pull. Color by itself does not mean ripe; a fig can be fully colored but still hard and not ready. Since figs do not ripen after you pick them, wait for them to go soft and droop, and pick every day or two, because a plant ripens just a few at a time over many weeks.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: A fig has no showy bloom. Its flowers are tiny and hidden inside the young fruit (the fig you eat is essentially an inside-out cluster of flowers), so there is nothing to see the way a peach or apple flowers. What you watch for instead is leaf-out in early spring and the swelling of the small breba figs on last year's wood. Because common figs are parthenocarpic, that fruit forms and ripens with no pollination at all. The main crop then sets on the new shoots as they extend through late spring and summer.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: A fig never shows flowers, because they are hidden inside the fruit (the fig you eat is really a bundle of flowers turned inside out). Instead of a bloom, you watch for the leaves opening in early spring and the small early figs (the breba crop) swelling on last year's stems. Common figs make that fruit on their own, with no pollination. The main crop then forms on the new shoots as they grow through late spring and summer.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Cold is the one thing a fig cannot shrug off, so lead your planning with it. Fully dormant wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F; sustained lows below that injure or kill the above-ground stems, though the roots are hardier and usually resprout. That sets a clear map: figs grow in the ground with little fuss in zones 7 to 10, need heavy winter protection (wrapping, or cutting back and burying under mulch and leaves) to fruit in zone 6, and are best grown in a container that winters in an unheated garage or shed where winters are colder still. A top-killed fig usually regrows from the base and can ripen a late main crop on the new wood, so a hard winter is rarely the end of the plant, just the end of that year's early fruit. Choose a cold-hardy variety (Chicago Hardy, Celeste, Marseilles) at the cold edge of the range. Winter chill is never the limiter, since a fig's small chill need is met almost everywhere.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Cold is the one thing a fig cannot handle, so plan around it first. The stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, and sustained cold below that kills the top of the plant, though the roots are tougher and usually grow back. That gives a simple map: figs grow in the ground easily in zones 7 to 10, need heavy winter protection to fruit in zone 6, and are best grown in a pot you move into an unheated garage or shed where it is colder. Even a fig killed to the ground usually grows back from the roots and can ripen a late crop on the new stems, so a hard winter rarely kills the whole plant. Pick a cold-hardy variety like Chicago Hardy or Celeste at the cold edge. Winter chill is never the problem, since figs need so little.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Figs need very little winter cold, only about 100 hours below 45°F, which nearly every region that can grow them meets easily. That is why chill is almost never the limiting factor for a fig, and why figs do so well in mild, warm-winter areas that are too warm for high-chill trees like cherry. What actually limits a fig is the opposite end of the thermometer: not too little cold, but too much. Hard winter freezes below about 15°F to 20°F kill the top growth, so cold hardiness, not chill, is the number to match to your area.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Figs need only a little winter cold, about 100 hours below 45°F, which almost any area that can grow them gets easily. So chill is hardly ever the problem for a fig, and figs do great in mild, warm-winter places that are too warm for high-chill trees like cherry. What actually limits a fig is the other extreme: not too little cold, but too much. Hard freezes below about 15°F to 20°F kill the top of the plant, so the number to match to your area is cold-hardiness, not chill.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Common home figs are parthenocarpic: they set and ripen fruit with no pollination whatsoever, so a single plant fruits alone with no partner, no bees, and no fig wasp. The flowers are hidden inside the fruit, which is why a fig never shows a visible bloom. The Smyrna and San Pedro types sold in some catalogs are the exception, needing a specific fig wasp (Blastophaga psenes) that is absent across most of the country, so they drop their fruit and are not recommended for home gardens. Stick to the common types (Celeste, Brown Turkey, Chicago Hardy, Black Mission, Kadota) and pollination is simply a non-issue.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Common figs make and ripen fruit with no pollination at all, so one plant is all you need, with no second tree, no bees, and no special wasp. The flowers are inside the fruit, which is why a fig never shows a bloom. A few unusual types (Smyrna and San Pedro) do need a special fig wasp, and that wasp is not around in most of the country, so they just drop their fruit and are not worth planting. Choose a common type like Celeste, Brown Turkey, or Chicago Hardy and you never have to think about pollination.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment and winter survival over fruit. Plant a dormant own-rooted fig in late winter or early spring after the hardest cold, in full sun on well-drained ground, and against a warm wall at the cold edge of the range. Water consistently through the first season, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the plant, and protect it especially well its first winter, since a young fig is the most cold-tender it will ever be. Hold fertilizer until growth begins and keep it light. A few figs may form; enjoy them, but do not count on a crop yet.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about helping the plant get established and through winter, not about fruit. Plant a dormant fig in late winter or early spring after the worst cold, in full sun in well-drained soil, and against a warm wall in cold areas. Water it steadily the first season, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around it, and protect it especially well its first winter, since a young fig is more easily hurt by cold than an older one. Wait to fertilize until it starts growing, and go easy. A few figs may form, which is a nice bonus, but do not count on a crop yet.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Common home figs are parthenocarpic: they set and ripen fruit with no pollination at all, so a single tree fruits alone with no partner, no bees, and no fig wasp. The flowers are tiny and hidden inside the young fig, so a fig never shows a visible bloom. The Smyrna and San Pedro types are the exception, requiring a specific fig wasp (Blastophaga psenes) that is absent across most of the country, so they drop their fruit and are not recommended; stick to the common types.
pollination.notes_beginner: Common figs make fruit all by themselves, with no pollination needed at all. One plant is all you need, and there is nothing to see when it flowers because the flowers are inside the fig. Only a few unusual types (Smyrna and San Pedro) need a special wasp to fruit, and that wasp is not around in most places, so just choose a common variety and you never have to think about pollination.

crops.establishment_note: Most figs begin bearing 1 to 2 years after planting, with fuller crops by years 3 to 4.
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Figs are grown on their own roots from cuttings, not grafted, so there is no rootstock to choose and no graft union to keep above the soil. With no rootstock to resist root-knot nematode, a nematode-free, well-drained site is the real substitute for rootstock choice.

pet_safe.note: The fruit is fine, but the milky sap and leaves can irritate the skin and stomach of cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: Fig is one of the quickest perennials to pay you back, often giving a little fruit in its first or second year. The thing to learn now is what ripe actually looks like, because color will fool you: a fig can be fully colored and still hard and inedible. Wait for it to go soft and for its neck to bend so the fruit droops down instead of standing out from the branch. A drop of syrup at the base is a good sign. Figs do not ripen at all after picking, so there is nothing to gain by picking early. Prune lightly and only after the hardest cold has passed, because fig carries an early crop on last year's wood and cutting hard trades that crop away.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: Fig is precocious and commonly sets a light crop in its first or second season. Maturity indexing is the skill to establish: color is not ripeness, and a fully colored fig can remain firm and unready. The reliable signals are full softening, neck bend so the fruit droops rather than standing out from the shoot, and a nectar drop at the eye. The crop is non-climacteric, so early picking is unrecoverable. Prune lightly and only after the hardest cold has passed: fig bears a breba crop on the previous season's wood as well as a main crop on new growth, so heavy heading trades the early crop away. In cold climates train as an open multi-stem bush rather than a single trunk, so that a winter that kills the top regrows from several low stems and ripens a main crop far faster.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From about the second year the plant is in full production, and it ripens a few figs at a time over many weeks rather than all at once. So pick every day or two. A ripe fig is soft, droops on a bent neck, has colored up fully, and comes away with the lightest pull. Ripe figs spoil within a day or two, so eat, chill, freeze or dry them promptly. Get netting on as the fruit starts to color, because birds find figs fast, and pick up any soured or dropped fruit as you go so beetles and souring yeasts do not build up. Keep the winter pruning light, since fig fruits on both last year's wood and this year's.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from roughly year two, ripening a few fruit at a time across many weeks, which makes harvest a standing every-day-or-two task rather than an event. Index on softening, neck bend and effortless detachment; the crop is non-climacteric and gains nothing after picking. Shelf life is a day or two, so consumption, refrigeration, freezing or drying follows harvest immediately. Exclusion netting goes up at color break, and soured and dropped fruit is removed on each pass to suppress dried fruit beetle and souring yeasts, which build on fermenting fruit rather than on sound fruit. Dormant pruning stays light and late, after the hardest cold: fig carries both a breba crop on last season's wood and a main crop on current growth, so heavy heading forfeits the early crop outright.

crops.name: Pomegranate

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Pomegranate is famously easy about soil. It grows best in a deep loam but will handle sandy soils and even heavy clay, as long as water drains away and does not sit around the roots. It also shrugs off alkaline (high-pH) and mildly salty soils that bother most fruit. The one thing it will not take is soggy ground: constantly wet roots bring on root rot. If your soil is heavy or drainage is poor, plant on a raised mound or bed so the roots stay above the wet.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Pomegranate is one of the most soil-adaptable fruits: it prefers a deep loam but tolerates sandy soils, heavy clay, alkaline pH, and mild salinity that would stunt most fruit trees. Drainage is the one firm requirement, since waterlogged soil invites root rot (including Armillaria on wet, heavy ground). On clay or low sites, plant on a raised berm or bed to lift the crown above standing water. It needs little organic matter and thrives on lean ground.

ph.note_beginner: Pomegranate grows well in a wide pH range, about 5.5 to 7.0, and tolerates up to around 7.2 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is). It is unusually easygoing about alkaline soil, so most gardeners never need to adjust pH for it. Test your soil before planting, and only correct if it is far outside that range.
ph.note_seasoned: Pomegranate does well across a broad pH band, roughly 5.5 to 7.0, and tolerates up to about 7.2. It is notably alkaline-tolerant, so pH is seldom a limiting factor and rarely needs amending. Test before planting and correct only if the soil is well outside the tolerated range.

fertilizer.timing: late winter to early spring before growth; optional light second feeding in late spring
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Pomegranate is a light feeder. Broadcast a modest amount of balanced fertilizer around the root zone in late winter to early spring as growth begins, and water it in. Avoid heavy nitrogen: excess N drives vegetative growth and suckering at the expense of flowers and fruit, and can worsen soft, split-prone fruit. On lean or sandy soils a light second feeding in late spring helps young plants; established plants often need little or none.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Pomegranate does not need much feeding. In late winter or early spring, scatter a small amount of balanced fertilizer around the plant and water it in. Do not overdo nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much grows leaves and base shoots instead of fruit. On poor or sandy soil, a light second feeding in late spring helps a young plant, but an established one usually needs very little.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits pomegranate; it is a light feeder and draws modestly on all three nutrients. Keep nitrogen restrained, since excess pushes suckers and soft growth over flowering and fruit set.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is plenty for a pomegranate. Go light, and especially do not overdo the first number, nitrogen, which grows leaves and shoots instead of fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A light hand is the rule. A common home approach is about 1 to 2 ounces of actual nitrogen per year of plant age in the early years (for example, a modest handful of 10-10-10 per foot of height), capped for a mature plant, applied in late winter. Skip feeding at planting; wait until growth begins. If growth is already vigorous and green, feed less or not at all.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Feed lightly. A simple approach is a small handful of 10-10-10 for each foot of the plant's height, spread around the plant in late winter, and no more than that for a full-grown one. Do not fertilize right when you plant; wait until it starts growing. If the plant is already growing strongly with deep green leaves, feed less or skip it.

companions.note_beginner: Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so one plant makes fruit on its own and you do not need a second plant to pollinate it (though a second pomegranate nearby can improve fruit set a little). For a shrub like this, the things that help are not the usual vegetable-garden pairings but the space around it: keep grass and weeds pulled back from the base so they do not compete with a young plant, and give it an open, sunny, breezy spot, because crowded, still, humid air at bloom makes flowers drop instead of setting fruit. Flowering plants nearby that draw bees can help set, and they bring in helpful insects that keep aphids and whiteflies down.
companions.note_seasoned: Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so a single plant sets a crop on its own (a second plant nearby can modestly improve set). The interactions that matter for this shrub are about air, light, and the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared from the base so they do not compete with a young plant, and site it in open, sunny, breezy ground, since crowded, humid, still air at bloom causes flowers to abort. Nearby pollinator plantings aid set and recruit the beneficials that hold aphids, whiteflies, and mealybugs in check.

good_seasoned.name: Flowering / pollinator and insectary plants
good_seasoned.label: likely

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so the pollinator draw is a help, not a requirement; but insect visitation improves set (a documented benefit), and an insectary planting recruits the predators/parasitoids that suppress aphids, whiteflies, and mealybugs. Mechanistic and extension-aligned, but the pomegranate-specific magnitude is modest and unquantified.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A skirt of flowering, pollinator- and beneficial-friendly plants around a pomegranate supports fruit set and pest balance. Pomegranate self-pollinates, so this is help rather than a requirement, but better bee activity improves set, and the same flowers recruit the lacewings, hoverflies, and parasitic wasps that keep aphids, whiteflies, and mealybugs in check. Keep them out toward the drip line rather than crowding the base, so air still moves freely through the canopy.

bad_seasoned.name: Crowding and shade that block air movement
bad_seasoned.label: extension_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: UGA Extension is explicit that air circulation is important, especially at bloom: flowers may not set or will abort if conditions are too humid, and open, breezy, sunny sites are advised. Crowding a pomegranate with dense plantings or shade traps humid, still air, suppressing set and raising fruit-disease pressure. Clear extension guidance with a defined mechanism.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Do not crowd a pomegranate against a wall of dense plantings or into shade. It needs full sun and moving air, especially at bloom: humid, still air causes flowers to abort and sets up the fruit diseases (Cercospora spot, gray mold, black heart) that plague pomegranate in muggy conditions. Give it an open, sunny, breezy site with room around the canopy so the foliage and fruit dry quickly after rain or dew.

pests.name: Leaf-footed bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Often there is no external mark on the fruit at all; the damage is inside. Cut a fed-on fruit and you find brown spots on the inner rind where the insect's needlelike mouthpart pierced, and arils that have darkened and withered. Late-season feeding as the fruit ripens is the worst, and the feeding wounds let opportunistic fungi in to rot the interior.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Usually you see nothing wrong on the outside of the fruit, because the damage is inside. If you cut a fruit open, you find brown spots on the inner skin and seeds (arils) that have gone dark and shriveled. It is worst late in the season as the fruit ripens, and the holes the bugs make can let rot start inside.
pests.cause_seasoned: The leaf-footed bug Leptoglossus zonatus, a large brown true bug with flattened, leaf-like flares on its hind legs; gardeners report it most on tomatoes and pomegranates. Adults and nymphs pierce fruit to feed, and their mouthparts carry a yeast, Eremothecium coryli, that discolors the arils; fungal spores follow through the same wound. They overwinter as adults in sheltered aggregations, in woodpiles, outbuildings, under bark and in citrus and juniper, and in cracked pomegranate fruit left on the tree, then disperse when the weather warms and move onto the newly developing fruit in late spring to early summer.
pests.cause_beginner: A big brown bug called the leaf-footed bug, named for the little leaf-shaped flares on its back legs. It and its young pierce the fruit to feed, and that can carry in yeasts and fungi that discolor and rot the seeds inside. The adults spend winter hidden in sheltered groups, then move onto the fruit as it forms.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no reliable rescue spray for a backyard tree; the controls are physical. Brush or knock adults and nymphs off into soapy water while the morning is still cool, going after the tightly clustered young nymphs early in the season and crushing the egg strands under the leaves. On a taller tree, prune the limbs clear of the ground, then dislodge the nymphs with a stick, by shaking, or with a pressure nozzle every 1 to 2 weeks, with a white sheet beneath to see them. Clear the weedy areas that feed them through winter and spring, strip all fruit before winter, and protect the egg parasites and predators with nectar plants and no broad-spectrum sprays.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: On a backyard tree the fixes are hands-on. Early in the morning, while it is cool, brush the bugs into soapy water or crush them, starting early in the season when the young are bunched together, and scrape off the egg strands under the leaves. On a tall tree, trim the low limbs off the ground and knock the young bugs down with a stick or a jet of water onto a white sheet, every week or two. Clear weedy patches nearby, take every fruit off before winter, and keep flowers around for the tiny wasps that kill the eggs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Monitor from fruit set onward, since the internal damage is invisible until you cut the fruit. Adults disperse from their winter shelters when the weather warms, in March or April in California's valleys, and enter pomegranate plantings from late spring to feed on the newly developing fruit and reproduce; the aggregations of nymphs and adults form on fruit and foliage from late summer and again in winter shelters. Remove all fruit before winter and clear weeds and nearby harborage, because a mild winter or a heavy fall population is the signal for a bad year, and there is no treatment threshold for this pest.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep an eye out from the time fruit forms, because you cannot see the damage from outside until you cut a fruit open. The adults spread out from their winter hiding spots as the weather warms and turn up on the young fruit from late spring; the big clusters come later in the summer. Take every fruit off the tree before winter, keep weeds down, and expect more bugs after a mild winter. Catching and removing them early, before there are many, works best.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Strip every fruit off the tree before winter, and pick up the split and dropped ones under it. Leaf-footed bugs spend the winter as adults, and a pomegranate with cracked old fruit left hanging is one of their favorite places to do it, so fruit left on the tree in November is next spring's bugs. Clear the other places they hide too, where they are yours to clear: woodpiles, sheds and outbuildings, and loose bark on nearby eucalyptus, juniper or cypress.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's instruction for pomegranate is to remove all fruit before winter, because orchards with cracked and split fruit left on the trees are a favored overwintering site and large numbers can pass the winter in fruit culls. Adults leave the tree by late November for sheltered aggregations in citrus, juniper, cypress and palms, woodpiles and outbuildings, so a mild winter or a heavy population the previous fall is the signal for a bad year. Cold near 21°F kills some exposed bugs and spares the sheltered ones, which is why harborage matters more than the thermometer.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the weedy patches near the tree mowed or cleared. Through winter and spring, when there is no fruit to feed on, the bugs live on weeds, so a weedy corner next to a pomegranate feeds them until the fruit comes.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Weedy areas are the bugs' food source from winter into spring, before fruit is available, and UC IPM's advice is to eliminate such areas near the garden or keep them closely mowed; the Pest Note names thistles and other weeds. This lowers the population that arrives on the young fruit rather than touching anything already on the tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Head out early, while the morning is still cool and the bugs are sluggish, and brush them off into soapy water or crush them; wear gloves, because they smell when handled. The best time is early in the season, when the newly hatched young sit in tight clusters and you can get a whole batch at once. Scrape off the egg strands on the undersides of leaves as well. On a taller tree, knock the young bugs down with a stick or a hard jet from the hose onto a white sheet spread underneath, then step on them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hand removal is the primary home control. UC IPM's sequence: morning, to limit movement and flight; as early in the season as possible, while nymphs are still tightly clustered; destroy the egg masses on leaf undersides; a dedicated handheld vacuum works if used regularly. For late-season infestations on pomegranate trees, prune so there is space between the limbs and the ground, then dislodge the nymphs with a stick, by shaking the limbs, or with a pressure nozzle, repeating every 1 to 2 weeks until most are gone. That knock-down does not dislodge eggs and is less effective on adults, which fly; a white ground cover under the tree makes the fallen insects easy to see.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On a plant small enough to wrap completely, a light fabric cover keeps the bugs off the fruit. It must be in place before the bugs show up in late spring, or you seal them in with the fruit, and it shuts out the bees and helpful insects along with the pests, so it is a poor fit for a big shrub in full bloom.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM lists row cover as a way to prevent feeding, with two conditions: apply it early, before the bugs arrive and lay eggs, or they are enclosed with the plant, and accept that it also excludes pollinators and beneficial insects. On pomegranate the adults move onto newly developing fruit in late spring to early summer, which overlaps a long, protracted bloom, so this suits a young or container plant far more than a mature tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Tiny native wasps lay their eggs inside the bug's eggs and kill them before they hatch, and assassin bugs, spiders and birds take some of the rest. Give these helpers pollen and nectar flowers to feed on, and skip the broad-acting sprays, which take the helpers down with the bugs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The egg parasite Gryon pennsylvanicum, if not disrupted, can reduce populations by killing eggs before they hatch. Tachinid flies such as Trichopoda pennipes parasitize adults, and assassin bugs, spiders and birds are the named predators. UC IPM's two conditions for keeping them: avoid persistent broad-spectrum insecticides, and provide pollen and nectar sources for the adult beneficials.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Soap spray only works on the very young bugs, and only where it wets them, so its place is a cluster of newly hatched nymphs you can soak directly. It does nothing to the adults, and UC IPM says sprays are rarely needed for this pest, since a few blemishes on home fruit are tolerable.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's ranking for the home grower: insecticidal soap, neem oil and pyrethrin may provide some control of young nymphs only, and most insecticides available to homeowners have only temporary effects on this bug. Since feeding damage on pomegranate is internal and light feeding usually goes unnoticed, a soap spray is a supplement to hand removal at the clustered-nymph stage, not a substitute for it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Permethrin and its relatives are the one kind of spray that really knocks this bug down, and UC IPM still says it is rarely worth it: these products are quite toxic to bees and to the helpful insects that were keeping the bugs in check, so the problem can come back worse. If you use one, keep it off anything in flower, and follow the label's waiting time before picking.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Broad-spectrum pyrethroids such as permethrin are the most effective insecticides against leaffooted bug, and the same document notes they are quite toxic to bees and beneficial insects and that insecticides are rarely needed because small blemishes are tolerable in a garden. There is no treatment threshold for this pest on pomegranate, so the decision rests on the previous year's numbers and what you find at fruit set, and the window that matters is ripening from late summer to harvest. Observe the pre-harvest interval on the label.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Dense colonies of small, soft aphids on the shoot tips in spring and again in late summer or fall, often on young fruit as well, with attending ants. Leaf curl and stunted shoots are not typical on pomegranate even when spring numbers are high. The damage that matters comes as fruit ripens in August: honeydew collecting between touching fruit leaves rotten spots on the skin, and sooty mold grows on the honeydew on the fruit surface and is hard to remove. In winter, look for the black eggs on the twigs.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Groups of tiny soft insects packed on the tips of new shoots in spring and again in late summer, sometimes on young fruit, with ants trailing to and from them. On pomegranate they do not usually curl the leaves. The real trouble comes as the fruit ripens in August, when sticky honeydew trapped between fruit that touch causes rotten spots and a black mold coats the skin. In winter you can spot their tiny black eggs on the twigs.
pests.cause_seasoned: The cotton aphid, Aphis gossypii, also called the melon aphid, the one aphid the sources name on this crop. It overwinters as eggs on pomegranate stems, hatches around the end of March onto the shoot tips, peaks in spring, is suppressed by summer heat, and builds again in late summer and fall as aphids move in from weeds, cotton, melons and citrus. Its honeydew supports sooty mold and draws ants, which protect the aphids from natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids, tiny sap-sucking insects that build up on soft new growth in spring. They multiply quickly, and the sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold and attracts ants that guard them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A strong jet of water knocks aphids off and is often enough on an established plant. Preserve natural enemies (ladybugs, lacewings, syrphid larvae) by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays; insecticidal soap or horticultural oil handles heavier infestations. Control ants, which farm aphids, to let predators work.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spraying the plant with a strong stream of water knocks most aphids off and is often all an established plant needs. Let the good bugs (ladybugs, lacewings) do their job by avoiding harsh sprays; insecticidal soap helps if there are a lot. Keeping ants off the plant lets the helpful insects control them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree healthy but not overfed: proper nutrients and irrigation, since aphid numbers increase easily on stressed trees, and no more nitrogen than necessary, since high nitrogen favors aphid reproduction. Check twigs in winter and early spring for the black overwintering eggs, watch the shoot tips from March into June, and keep ants off the tree so the resident parasites and predators can work.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not overfeed with nitrogen, because all that soft new growth attracts aphids. Grow flowers nearby to bring in helpful insects, and keep ants away so those helpers can do their work.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on nitrogen. Soft, sappy new shoots are what these aphids build up on, and a tree that is healthy but not overfed, with steady water and ordinary nutrition, shrugs off numbers that a stressed or lush one cannot.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Two anchored halves. UC IPM's general aphid guidance: high nitrogen favors aphid reproduction, so never use more than necessary. Its pomegranate page adds the other side: maximize tree health with proper nutrients and irrigation, because aphid numbers increase easily on stressed trees. The target is steady, unstressed growth rather than either starvation or a flush of tips.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Blast the colonies on the growing tips with the hose. On a pomegranate the aphids crowd the ends of the new shoots in spring, and once knocked to the ground most never make it back up; nothing is sprayed, so the ladybugs keep working.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's first physical step for sturdy plants. On pomegranate the colonies sit on the shoot tips from March through June and again in fall, so the targets are the tips and any young fruit they have settled on; a morning blast leaves the leaves time to dry.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ants farm these aphids for their sugar and chase off the ladybugs and lacewings that would eat them. A band of sticky material on a wrap around the trunk, plus trimming off any branch that touches the ground or a fence, keeps the ants out and hands the tree back to its helpers.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's pomegranate guidance is that ants hinder natural enemies, so reducing ant numbers improves the success of biological control; the home Pest Note gives the sticky trunk band as the barrier. The band goes on a collar, not bare bark, and only holds while bridges to the ground are pruned away.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This aphid usually gets handled for free. Ladybugs, lacewing and hover fly larvae, and a tiny wasp that lays its eggs inside the aphids keep it down on most trees, and summer heat knocks the aphids back on its own. Skip broad-acting sprays so the helpers survive.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM rates cotton aphid among the most serious pests of pomegranate orchards and in the same sentence says natural enemies may sufficiently control it. The named agents are the parasite Lysiphlebus testaceipes, several lady beetles (ashy gray, nine-spotted, multicolored Asian, convergent), syrphid and cecidomyiid larvae and lacewings. Natural enemy activity slows in summer heat, but heat also suppresses the aphids, and in fall biological control rises with the aphid numbers; ant control is what lets all of it work.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When a colony outruns the helpers, a soap spray soaked directly onto the aphids brings it down without lingering on the tree to harm the good insects. Aim at the packed shoot tips and any young fruit they are clustered on, and go again if they rebuild.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's guidance is to choose products least toxic to natural enemies, insecticidal soaps and oils, which when properly used solve most aphid problems; UGA reports that aphids on pomegranate are routinely controlled with soap in other production regions. Contact only, no residue, so coverage of the tips is what decides it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil is on the short list UC IPM accepts for organic pomegranate. It smothers what it wets, so cover the shoots well; the best-timed use is on the black eggs on the twigs in winter, before they hatch at the end of March.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's organic list for pomegranate is pyrethrins, azadirachtin, neem oil and a peppermint plus rosemary oil product, with the note that coverage is very important and that treatment of the overwintering eggs gives the best control. Cotton aphid overwinters as black eggs on pomegranate stems that hatch around the end of March, so winter is when to look for them and, if last year was bad, to spray. Keep it off open flowers and out of heat above 90°F.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny white moth-like insects that fly up in clouds when the plant is disturbed, gathered on leaf undersides with their pale nymphs; honeydew and sooty mold follow, and heavy infestations yellow and weaken leaves.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny white insects like little moths that flutter up when you brush the plant, sitting under the leaves along with their flat, pale young. They leave sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, and a lot of them yellow the leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Mostly the ash whitefly, Siphoninus phillyreae, with the silverleaf whitefly a problem where pomegranates border cotton or melon fields. Small sap-feeding insects that colonize leaf undersides and develop rapidly in warm weather, peaking in July and August. Like aphids they leave honeydew, sooty mold grows on it on leaves and fruit, and ants tend them for it.
pests.cause_beginner: Whiteflies, small sap-sucking insects that live under the leaves and multiply fast in warm weather. Like aphids, they leave honeydew that grows sooty mold.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hose off foliage and rely on natural enemies (lacewings, ladybugs, parasitic wasps), which usually keep whiteflies in check on an outdoor plant. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on leaf undersides helps in heavy cases; yellow sticky traps monitor and reduce adults.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the leaves with water and let helpful insects do most of the work; they usually keep whiteflies under control outdoors. Insecticidal soap sprayed under the leaves helps if there are many, and yellow sticky cards catch the adults.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree healthy and well watered so it does not sit in hot, dry, dusty conditions, which suit whiteflies and hamper the parasites that control them, and keep the ants out of the canopy. Spare the natural enemies: carbaryl, pyrethroids and foliar imidacloprid are the insecticides UC IPM names as particularly disruptive to them.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the plant healthy and watered so it does not get hot, dusty and stressed, which whiteflies like, and keep ants out of it. Avoid harsh sprays so the helpful insects survive.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A hard jet from the hose clears the winged adults out of the canopy. On pomegranate the hose earns its keep twice, because keeping the tree watered and the dust down takes away the hot, dry, dusty conditions that suit whiteflies and work against the wasps that kill them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's first physical step is a strong water stream at the adults. The same document notes that watering reduces hot, dry, dusty conditions, which suit whiteflies and hamper their natural enemies, so the hose does two jobs; dust control has no other step of its own here.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Yellow sticky cards hung in the branches show you when the winged adults are on the rise, and they may bring the numbers down somewhat, though they will not clear a bad infestation on their own. Get them up before July, when numbers climb on this crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Yellow sticky traps monitor adults and at high levels reduce their numbers. On pomegranate the peak is July and August, so hang them by early summer; they say nothing about the nymphs on the leaf undersides, which are what the parasites work on.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off and throw away the leaves that are crusted underneath with the flat, unmoving young. Taking those leaves out can drop the numbers to a level the helpful insects can handle.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Taking off the leaves that carry the immobile nymphs and pupae can, per UC IPM, bring numbers down to a level the natural enemies then hold. Before stripping leaves, check them with a hand lens for dark parasitized pupae and empty pupae with round exit holes; those leaves are the parasite's nursery and stay on the tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep ants out of the tree; they guard the whiteflies from the insects that would eat them. A sticky band on a wrap around the trunk, and no branches touching the ground, does it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's instruction is to keep ants out of plants since they protect whiteflies from natural enemies; the ash whitefly's parasite is the control that ant exclusion protects.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Outdoors, tiny parasitic wasps, lacewings and ladybugs usually keep whiteflies under control on their own, and the ash whitefly that is common on pomegranate is already well controlled by a wasp across California. Do not spray if you can see the helpers at work: look for dark or empty pupae under the leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The parasite Encarsia inaron is the most effective biological control agent of ash whitefly, which is now under good biological control in California and rarely seen in high numbers; lacewings and lady beetles help but are less reliable. The decision check is a hand lens on the leaf undersides: dark parasitized pupae, empty pupae with round exit holes, and adult parasites mean control is coming in a few weeks. Carbaryl, pyrethroids and foliar imidacloprid are named as particularly disruptive to this.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the leaves are yellowing and sticky and you cannot find any of the helpers, soap spray wetted onto the undersides of the leaves is the least harmful option. It only kills what it touches, so cover the undersides and repeat.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's guidance is products least harmful to natural enemies, insecticidal soaps and oils, combined with the practices above; on pomegranate the commercial page treats only in late summer or early fall when honeydew and sooty mold threaten and parasites are not adequate. Silverleaf whitefly moving in from neighboring cotton or melon fields in July and August is the case where numbers can outrun the parasites.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: White, cottony egg masses on the trunk under loose bark; crawlers on the young shoots after budbreak in March and on leaves, fruit and basal sucker growth from June into July. Damage is where the mealybugs settle: between two touching fruit or inside the calyx, where honeydew causes rot or discoloration, and rot that starts inside the calyx can spread to the interior of the fruit. Mature mealybugs or egg masses hidden in the calyx can be missed and reach the table.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tufts of white cotton tucked into the crown end of the fruit, in the cracks where branches meet, and on the suckers at the base of the trunk, with sticky honeydew and ants. Where two fruit touch, or where the insects sit inside the crown, the skin under them rots or discolors, and sometimes the rot runs from the crown right into the middle of the fruit, so a fruit can look fine and be spoiled inside.
pests.cause_seasoned: Pseudococcus maritimus, the grape mealybug, found in many pomegranate orchards but only occasionally a serious pest because natural enemies usually hold it below damaging levels. Two generations a year; it overwinters mostly as eggs in cottony masses under trunk bark, the first hatch moves to young shoots at March budbreak, the second hatches from early June into early July and migrates to leaves and fruit. Populations often drop in summer heat. Ants tending the honeydew disrupt the parasites and predators that would otherwise control it.
pests.cause_beginner: The grape mealybug, a soft, waxy sap-sucker that lives on grapes, pears and pomegranates. It is common on pomegranates but only now and then a real problem, because the tiny wasps and beetles that hunt it usually keep it down. Ants protect it for its sugary honeydew, and that is when it gets out of hand.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treatments are usually not justified or effective on home fruit trees, in UC IPM's words; mealybugs are heat-sensitive, their wax shields them, and home insecticides are not very effective on larger plants. The working controls are ant management so the encyrtid parasites (Acerophagus notativentris, A. angelicus, Chrysoplatycerus splendens) and the predators (the gall midge Dicrodiplosis californica, the lady beetle Nephus sordidus, green lacewings) can operate, physical removal by handpicking or pruning out infested growth including basal suckers, and a forceful water spray on exposed colonies. Soap, oil or neem give some suppression of young nymphs only, and azadirachtin is noted as effective on immature grape mealybug in orchards.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: UC IPM's advice for a home fruit tree is that spraying is usually not worth it and does not work well, because the waxy coat sheds the spray and the mealybugs hide where it cannot reach. Instead, keep ants off the tree with a sticky band on a trunk wrap, pick or prune off the clumps you can see, cut away the suckers at the base where the young ones gather, and let the tiny wasps and lady beetles do the rest.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Thinning fruit so none are touching is the one cultural control UC IPM states for this pest on pomegranate. Removal of overwintering sites such as loose bark reduces numbers, and avoiding unnecessary nitrogen matters because high rates with regular irrigation stimulate tender growth and mealybug egg production. Keep ants out of the canopy, avoid the broad-spectrum sprays that remove the parasites, and expect summer heat to do part of the work. The mealybug destroyer, Cryptolaemus montrouzieri, does not tolerate cold winters.
pests.prevention_beginner: Thin the fruit so that no two touch, since that is where these insects settle and do their damage. Peel off loose bark on the trunk in winter, where the eggs spend the cold months, and keep ants off the tree. Do not overfeed with nitrogen, which pushes the soft growth they like. Check the crown end of the fruit and the branch crotches, where they hide.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with the ants. They collect the mealybugs' honeydew and drive off the tiny wasps and beetles that would clean the colony up, so a tree with an ant trail up the trunk builds up mealybugs that a tree without one never sees. Put a band of sticky material on a paper or fabric wrap around the trunk and cut off any branch that touches the ground or a wall, so the trunk is the only way up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's mealybug guidance for fruit trees leads with managing ants, which are attracted to honeydew and inhibit the activities of natural enemies. The parasites that hold grape mealybug in check on pomegranate are small encyrtid wasps that produce several generations per mealybug generation; they are exactly the enemies ants displace. A trunk band on a collar, with skirt pruning to close the bypasses, is the barrier; it does nothing about the colony already present, which the natural enemies then reduce over the following weeks.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off or prune out the cottony clumps you can reach, and cut the suckers off the base of the trunk, since the young ones crowd into that growth in early summer. In winter, strip loose bark from the trunk, which is where the egg masses sit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's Pest Note: if you find an infestation, physically remove the insects by handpicking or prune them out. On pomegranate the second-generation crawlers migrate to leaves and fruit from early June into early July and many can be found in the sucker growth at the base of trees, so removing suckers removes a harborage; the eggs overwinter in cottony masses on the trunk under bark, so loose bark comes off in the dormant season. A forceful spray of water reduces exposed colonies on sturdy plants; it does not reach mealybugs inside the calyx.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Most of the time this pest is handled by tiny wasps that lay their eggs in the mealybugs, turning them into yellow mummies, along with a small brown lady beetle, a gall midge and lacewings. Keep those helpers by keeping ants off and by not using broad-acting sprays, and let a hot summer do its share.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Natural enemies usually keep grape mealybug below damaging levels in pomegranate. The parasites are all encyrtid wasps, Acerophagus notativentris and A. angelicus with multiple generations per mealybug generation and the larger Chrysoplatycerus splendens attacking adults before they lay; parasitized mealybugs are yellow mummies. Predators are the gall midge Dicrodiplosis californica, the lady beetle Nephus sordidus and green lacewings. Conservation is the whole program: no broad-spectrum sprays, ants excluded, and the mealybug destroyer counted on only where winters are mild.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Immobile, dome-shaped soft scales on twigs, leaf undersides and fruit; black scale favors twigs and typically settles on the stem just above a fruit. The most important damage is the light-colored spot left when a scale is removed from a fruit, where it blocked sunlight and prevented coloring. UC IPM notes the honeydew and sooty mold these species cause on citrus and olive have not been observed on pomegranate: late second instars leave a discrete pile of sugar that does not grow sooty mold and brushes off at harvest. Crawlers appear on twigs and leaves from June into July.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small brown or dark bumps that do not move, stuck to twigs, the undersides of leaves and the skin of the fruit, often on the stem just above a fruit. The tell-tale damage on pomegranate is a pale spot on the rind where a scale sat and blocked the sun, so the skin under it never colored. These scales leave a little pile of dry sugar rather than the sticky mess aphids make, and it brushes off; black sooty mold on a pomegranate points to aphids or whiteflies, not scale.
pests.cause_seasoned: Four soft scales, Saissetia oleae (black scale), Coccus hesperidum (brown soft scale), Coccus pseudomagnoliarum (citricola scale) and Parthenolecanium corni (European fruit lecanium), per UC IPM; UGA lists citricola, black and California red scale. Hot temperatures during crawler development in spring typically limit population growth, so scales are rarely found and are only occasional pests. Black scale overwinters as immatures under trunk bark, lecanium as nymphs on twigs; all four produce crawlers in June and July. Ants tending them interfere with the parasites, though UC IPM notes an ant-free tree is not necessary for adequate control.
pests.cause_beginner: Four kinds of soft scale, small sap-sucking insects that settle down under a waxy shell and stay put: black scale, brown soft scale, citricola scale and European fruit lecanium. Georgia adds California red scale. Hot spring weather kills many of the crawlers, so scale is only an occasional problem on pomegranate, and tiny wasps usually finish off the rest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hot weather and natural enemies keep soft scales below damaging levels in most years; parasitism of brown soft scale on fruit has been observed near 100 percent in September, and where pesticide applications are avoided scale numbers the following year are very low. UC IPM says not to apply insecticides for citricola scale at all. Beyond that: control ants that interfere with Metaphycus and Coccophagus parasites and the scale-feeding lady beetles (Chilocorus, Hyperaspis, Rhyzobius); prune off heavily infested twigs on a small plant; and where treatment is warranted, a thorough oil spray on the bark in the dormant season, which UGA and UF/IFAS both give as a 3 percent oil in winter when the leaves are off, or an oil timed to the June to July crawlers using double-sided sticky tape on branches to catch them moving.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Most years nothing is needed: heat and tiny wasps keep scale down, and if you avoid spraying, next year's numbers are usually very low. Keep ants off the trunk with a sticky band on a wrap so the wasps can work. If a twig is crusted with scale on a small plant, cut it off. If scale keeps building, the stated spray is horticultural oil on the leafless tree in winter, which smothers the scale on the bark; an early-summer spray works only while the crawlers are out, in June and July, and only where it wets them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Conservation is the program: avoiding insecticides keeps Metaphycus and Coccophagus parasitism high, and hot summers do the rest. In areas with hot summers, pruning to open canopies reduces black scale and citricola scale, and UC IPM judges that probably true on pomegranate for the other species too. Control ants if they are tending scales, without expecting an ant-free tree. Wrap double-sided sticky tape around small branches in late spring to catch crawlers and time any oil spray to their June to July emergence; a dormant oil on the bark in winter is the alternative timing.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not spray for scale unless you have to, because the sprays kill the wasps that were doing the job for free. Keep ants out of the tree. Where summers are hot, pruning to open up the canopy keeps black scale and citricola scale down. Look on the twigs and leaf undersides in early summer for the tiny crawlers, which is the other time a spray can reach them, besides the winter oil on the bare bark.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On a young or small pomegranate, cut off the few twigs that are crusted with scale and put them in the trash. It only makes sense when the scale is confined to a few spots; on a big tree the wasps and the weather do this job better than pruning could.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's Pest Note allows pruning off heavily infested twigs and branches if they are limited to a few parts of small plants; the scale come off with the wood. On pomegranate black scale typically settles on the stem just above a fruit, so the twig cut can cost the fruit. This is the only hand removal that fits an insect glued to the bark; picking individual scales is not practical.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If there is an ant trail on the trunk leading to the scale, fit a sticky band on a wrap around the trunk and prune any branch that bridges to the ground, a fence or a neighboring plant. The ants chase off the tiny wasps that kill scale; without the ants, the wasps usually win. You do not need to get rid of every ant, just the trail up the tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Controlling ants that interfere with parasites and predators improves natural enemy activity, but UC IPM adds that an ant-free orchard is not necessary for adequate biological control of soft scales on pomegranate. The Pest Note's mechanics: prune the branches or weeds that bridge from buildings or the ground, wrap the trunk with fabric, heavy paper or tape, and the sticky material goes on that wrap, never on bare bark.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Tiny wasps kill most scale on pomegranate, so well that by September nearly every brown soft scale on the fruit can be dead already, and if you do not spray, next year's scale is usually scarce. Protect them by skipping insect sprays and keeping ants off; small dark lady beetles help too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The primary parasites are Metaphycus and Coccophagus; parasitism close to 100 percent has been observed in September for brown soft scale on pomegranate fruit, and if pesticide applications are avoided, scale numbers the following year are very low. Specialized scale-feeding lady beetles are Chilocorus, Hyperaspis and Rhyzobius. UC IPM's judgment on citricola scale is not to apply insecticides, and that nymphs on 20 to 30 percent of leaves may be tolerable; ants, dust and persistent broad-spectrum insecticides are the three things that disrupt this.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If scale is building year after year, the spray three extension services agree on is horticultural oil on the bare tree in winter, which smothers the scale wintering on the bark; the two Southeast guides give it at 3 percent. The other time it works is early summer, when the tiny crawlers are out on the twigs and leaves, and then it only kills what it wets. Never mix oil with sulfur, and keep an oil spray well away from any sulfur dusting. Skip it on a drought-stressed tree, in heat above 90°F, or when anything is in flower.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UGA and UF/IFAS both give a 3 percent dormant oil in winter, when the leaves are off, as effective against scale on pomegranate; UC IPM's Pest Note calls for a well-timed and thorough oil spray either in the dormant season or when crawlers are active, and for deciduous plants specifies thoroughly spraying the bark of terminal shoots in winter. Crawlers of all four species emerge from June into July; double-sided sticky tape around small branches catches them moving and times a growing-season spray. Both Southeast guides also prescribe a June sulfur dusting for mites on this crop, and oil is never mixed with sulfur nor applied close to it in time. Bee precaution: not on anything in flower.

diseases.name: Alternaria heart rot (black heart)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: The fruit looks nearly normal outside, perhaps a little light in weight or slightly off-color (a paler red), while the interior rots: arils turn brown and mushy and a black mold sporulates inside. There is often no external cue, so the rot is discovered only on cutting.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: From the outside the fruit looks almost fine, maybe a bit light or a paler red, but inside it is rotting: the seeds turn brown and mushy with black mold. There is usually no sign on the outside, so you only find it when you cut the fruit open.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungi Alternaria alternata and A. arborescens infect through the open flower, most readily at petal fall, when rain falls during bloom and early fruit development, then grow silently inside the fruit with no external decay. They overwinter on plant debris and in mummified fruit, and their spores travel on wind and soil dust; punctures from fruit-piercing insects and birds give a second way in, and UC IPM ties internal black rot on pomegranate to the leaf-footed bug's feeding wounds. This is a disease of California's hot, dry pomegranate country in years with wet bloom weather: a Georgia survey did not find it, and Florida's disease survey does not list it. The driver is moisture during bloom, not a humid climate as such.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Alternaria gets into the fruit through the open flower when it rains during bloom, and then grows quietly inside while the outside looks fine. It carries over on old fruit and plant litter and rides in on wind and dust. Holes made by fruit-piercing bugs and birds let it in too. Its home is California's pomegranate country, in years with a wet bloom; a Georgia orchard survey did not find it, and Florida's disease guide does not list it. What matters is rain while the flowers are open, not how humid the summer is.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the interior is rotting, and no preventive spray either: the fruit crown covers the blossom tissue, so preharvest sprays are generally ineffective, and Georgia's guide states there is no known method of control. What is available is cultural: dust control, sanitation (old fruit and dead branches removed), steady irrigation that avoids both water stress and overwatering because cracked fruit is an entry point, control of the fruit-piercing insects and birds whose wounds open a second door, and at harvest a gentle shake of the tree to drop the infected, healthy-looking fruit, followed by careful sorting before storage.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once a fruit is rotting inside it cannot be saved, and no spray prevents it, because the crown of the fruit closes over the spot where the fungus gets in. What you can do: keep dust down, pick up old and dried fruit and cut out dead wood, water evenly so the fruit does not crack, keep fruit-piercing bugs and birds off the fruit, and at picking time give the tree a gentle shake so the infected fruit, which are lighter, fall out. Cut open any fruit that feels light before you store it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sanitation and dust control through the year, irrigation that avoids water stress and overwatering so fruit does not crack, and management of the insects and birds that puncture fruit. Wet weather during the long bloom, especially at petal fall, is the infection window, and nothing applied afterward reaches the blossom tissue under the crown. Losses are usually under 1 percent and up to 6 percent; no resistant cultivar is named in any source.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground and the tree clean of old fruit and dead branches, keep dust down, and water steadily so the fruit does not split. Keep fruit-piercing bugs and birds off the fruit. The fungus gets in when rain falls on the open flowers, and nothing you spray afterward can reach it, so a wet bloom season means cutting fruit open before you trust it. Most years it spoils only a few fruit.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clean-up is the control here, because no spray reaches this fungus once the flower closes over it. Pick up and throw away old fruit on and under the tree, especially the dried, shriveled ones, and cut out dead branches; the fungus lives through the winter in that debris and in the dust that blows onto the flowers. At harvest, shake the tree gently so the infected fruit, which look sound but are lighter, drop to the ground, and cut any doubtful fruit open before you store it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogens overwinter on plant debris in or on the soil and in mummified fruit, with airborne spores carried to flowers or wounded fruit in soil dust, so UC IPM's cultural program is dust control and sanitation, removal of old fruit and dead branches. Because the fruit crown covers the blossom tissue, preharvest sprays are generally ineffective, and Georgia's guide says plainly there is no known method of control; petal fall is the most susceptible stage and the bloom is long and protracted, so even commercial bloom sprays rate least effective. Two harvest-time steps belong with sanitation: gently shaking the tree to drop infected but healthy-appearing fruit, and thorough sorting so diseased fruit is not stored. Expected loss is usually under 1 percent and up to 6 percent in a bad year.

diseases.name: Botrytis gray mold / fruit rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A fuzzy gray coat of spores at the crown (blossom) end, on the old flower parts, appearing after the fruit is washed or held in humid storage rather than on the tree; the crown tissue is colonized and the rot grows into the fruit. Stored fruit at high humidity often decays completely, sometimes with grayish-white mycelium and small black sclerotia on the surface. Decay can also start from the stem-end wound, especially where the stem was torn off entirely.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A fuzzy gray mold that shows up in the crown end of the fruit, on the dried flower bits, usually after the fruit has been washed or kept somewhere damp, and then spreads into the fruit. In storage a fruit can rot right through, sometimes with grayish-white fuzz and tiny black specks on the skin. Rot can also start where the stem was torn off.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Botrytis cinerea infects the flower parts at bloom, when free water from rain, dew, fog or irrigation sits on the senescent stamens, and then stays quiescent inside the crown until the fruit ripens. Washing or condensation on the blossom end activates it, and decay develops quickly at about 65 to 75°F. Spores come from soil, infected debris, weeds and mummified fruit and spread on the wind. It is one of the most important causes of postharvest decay in pomegranates.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Botrytis, or gray mold, that gets into the flowers during bloom when they are wet from rain, dew, fog or sprinklers, then sits quietly inside the crown of the fruit until picking.
