notifications.body_beginner: Berries ripen a few at a time. Pick every two or three days, taking the ones that pull off easily, and clear off any overripe ones. Picking often also helps fight the fruit-fly maggots. Refrigerate right away.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove the spent fruited canes after harvest
notifications.title_beginner: Cut out the canes that just fruited
notifications.body_seasoned: On summer-bearing raspberries, the floricanes that fruited are now dying. Cut them to the ground and remove them right after harvest to open the row, cut disease pressure, and steer the plant's energy into the new primocanes that will fruit next year. Leave fall-bearing canes for the dormant-season decision.
notifications.body_beginner: On summer-bearing types, the canes that just fruited are dying. Cut them off at the ground after harvest and clear them out, leaving the fresh green canes for next year.

notifications.title_seasoned: Prune by type in late winter
notifications.title_beginner: Prune the canes in late winter
notifications.body_seasoned: In late winter, do the annual pruning that decides the crop. Summer-bearing: remove dead and spent canes and thin the rest to 4 to 6 sturdy canes per foot of row, then narrow the row and tie canes up. Fall-bearing managed for one crop: mow every cane to the ground. Getting the type right is the most common raspberry mistake.
notifications.body_beginner: In late winter, prune. For summer types, cut out old and dead canes and keep 4 to 6 strong ones per foot, then tie them up. For fall types, simply cut every cane to the ground. Cutting the wrong type at the wrong time is the most common raspberry mistake.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning during bloom
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast while your raspberries are blooming. Open flowers are frost-tender and a hard frost can destroy the developing crop, a real risk for early-blooming types and in the warm South. Cover the planting overnight and uncover it in the morning.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming while your raspberries are flowering. Cover the plants tonight to protect the flowers, and uncover them in the morning.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, dry spell while berries ripen
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hot, dry stretch is forecast as berries ripen. Heat above roughly 85 to 90°F scorches fruit, makes berries small and crumbly, and stresses the shallow roots. Keep the soil evenly moist, harvest in the cool morning, and provide afternoon shade in hot-summer regions.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: It is going to be hot and dry while your berries ripen. Keep the soil damp, pick in the cool morning, and give the plants some afternoon shade if you can.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Lots of rain and soggy soil
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Extended heavy rain can waterlog raspberry roots and trigger Phytophthora root rot, especially on heavy ground. Make sure water drains away from the row; raised beds or ridges are the durable protection against wet-soil collapse.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Long heavy rain can leave the soil too soggy, which rots raspberry roots. Make sure water drains away from the plants; raised rows help a lot.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Rain coming before you pick
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Rain is forecast as berries ripen. Wet, warm conditions rot soft raspberries fast and fuel spotted-wing drosophila and gray mold. Let berries dry before picking, harvest promptly and completely once they do, remove any mushy fruit, and refrigerate immediately.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Rain is coming as your berries ripen. Let them dry before you pick, then pick soon and completely, throw away any mushy ones, and refrigerate right away.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Strong wind on the canes
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Strong wind can whip and snap tall, fruit-laden raspberry canes, especially primocanes not yet tied in. Make sure canes are secured to the trellis ahead of a windy stretch, and tip back overly long primocanes that catch the most wind.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Strong wind can snap tall raspberry canes. Tie loose canes to the support before a windy spell, and trim back any extra-long new canes.

planting.text_seasoned: Start with certified virus-free canes on ground that has not grown raspberries, blackberries, or nightshades recently. A clean start is the single biggest factor in how long the planting lives.
planting.text_beginner: Buy certified virus-free plants and pick a spot that has not grown raspberries, blackberries, tomatoes, or potatoes recently. A clean start matters more than anything.
planting.author: plant_team

planting.text_seasoned: Plant on a slightly raised row in well-drained soil and set up the trellis before or right after planting; raspberries rot in wet ground and flop without support.
planting.text_beginner: Plant on a slightly raised row with good drainage, and put up a stake or trellis right away. Raspberries hate soggy soil and fall over without support.
planting.author: plant_team

establishment.text_seasoned: Expect little fruit the first year from a summer-bearing planting; a fall-bearing one can give a small crop this fall. Either way, let the new canes build the framework.
establishment.text_beginner: Do not expect much fruit the first year from a summer type. A fall-bearing type may give you a few berries this fall. Let the new canes grow strong.
establishment.author: plant_team

establishment.text_seasoned: Begin containing suckers immediately. Red and yellow raspberries spread by underground runners, so keep the row no wider than 12 to 18 inches from day one or the patch takes over.
establishment.text_beginner: Start pulling stray shoots right away. Raspberries spread underground and will take over the garden if you let the row get wide.
establishment.author: plant_team

first_growth.text_seasoned: Feed a balanced fertilizer in early spring as growth begins, banded along the row, and stop by midsummer. Early nitrogen drives the canes; late nitrogen makes soft, disease-prone wood.
first_growth.text_beginner: Feed in early spring when growth starts, and stop by midsummer. Early feeding helps the canes; late feeding makes weak, sickly growth.
first_growth.author: plant_team

blossom.text_seasoned: You do not need a second variety: raspberries are self-fertile and pollinate themselves with help from bees. Avoid spraying anything that harms pollinators during bloom.
blossom.text_beginner: Raspberries pollinate themselves, so you do not need two varieties. Just let the bees visit and avoid spraying while the flowers are open.
blossom.author: plant_team

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Net before berries color and start SWD monitoring now. Spotted-wing drosophila is the major modern raspberry pest, and an open, well-pruned canopy plus a tight harvest schedule is the best defense.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Cover the plants with bird netting before the berries color, and set out a vinegar trap to watch for fruit flies. Picking often is the best defense.
fruit_set.author: plant_team

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Keep moisture steady while berries size. Drought during fruit development is the usual cause of small, seedy, crumbly raspberries.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp while the berries grow, or they will be small and crumbly.
fruit_set.author: plant_team

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick berries that slip off the core into your hand, leaving the hollow center; a berry that resists is not ripe. Harvest every two to three days into a shallow container and refrigerate fast.
harvest.text_beginner: A ripe raspberry pulls off easily and leaves a hollow center. Pick every couple of days into a shallow container and refrigerate right away.
harvest.author: plant_team

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest completely and often: removing every ripe and overripe berry on a 1-to-3-day cycle is the front-line control for spotted-wing drosophila, far more so than any spray in a home garden.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick all the ripe and overripe berries every day or two. Clearing the plants completely is the best way to keep fruit-fly maggots down.
harvest.author: plant_team

post_harvest.text_seasoned: On summer-bearing types, cut the spent fruited floricanes to the ground right after harvest. They are dying anyway, and removing them opens the row and cuts disease for the new canes.
post_harvest.text_beginner: On summer types, cut out the canes that just fruited right after harvest. They are dying, and removing them helps the new canes stay healthy.
post_harvest.author: plant_team

dormancy.text_seasoned: Let canes go fully dormant over winter to bank their chill; most raspberries need a real cold rest to fruit well. Keep mulch in place and do not waterlog the dormant roots.
dormancy.text_beginner: Let the canes rest and lose their leaves over winter so they get the cold they need. Keep mulch on and do not let the roots stay soggy.
dormancy.author: plant_team

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Match the pruning to the type: thin summer-bearing canes to 4 to 6 per foot and remove spent ones; mow fall-bearing canes to the ground for a single fall crop. Cutting the wrong type wrong is the most common raspberry mistake.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Prune by type in late winter. For summer types, keep 4 to 6 strong canes per foot. For fall types, cut every cane to the ground. Getting this backwards is the most common raspberry mistake.
dormant_prune.author: plant_team

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Narrow the row to about a foot wide as you prune and tie the kept canes to the trellis. An open, well-supported row gets light and air, which means bigger fruit and less disease and SWD.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Keep the row about a foot wide and tie the canes to the support as you prune. An open, airy row gives bigger berries and fewer pests and diseases.
dormant_prune.author: plant_team

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature raspberry plant yields roughly 1 to 2 quarts (about 1 to 2 pounds) of fruit per season, and a well-managed row produces on the order of 1 pound per linear foot. Fall-bearing types give a single concentrated fall crop; summer-bearing types give one heavy early-summer crop. Yields build as the planting fills in.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each raspberry plant gives about 1 to 2 quarts (roughly 1 to 2 pounds) a season once established, and a full row makes about a pound for every foot of row. A few plants quickly add up to plenty of berries.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Raspberries crop quickly compared with tree fruit. A fall-bearing planting can fruit its first fall; a summer-bearing one fruits in its second year. Both reach full production around years 3 to 4, then stay productive for about 10 to 15 years for reds and yellows, less for blacks, with steady pruning and renewal.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Raspberries produce fast. A fall-bearing type can give berries the first fall; a summer type fruits the second year. Both hit full swing around years 3 to 4 and keep producing for 10 to 15 years if you prune and care for them.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: What you get the first year depends on type. A summer-bearing (floricane) planting makes essentially no fruit the first year, since it fruits on second-year canes; expect the first real crop the following summer. A fall-bearing (primocane) planting set out in spring can ripen a modest crop on its new canes that very fall, which is why fall-bearing types are the fast route to a first harvest.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Whether you get fruit the first year depends on the type. Summer-bearing raspberries make no fruit the first year and start the next summer. Fall-bearing raspberries planted in spring can give you a small crop that same fall, so they are the quickest to your first berries.
factors_seasoned: Cane type: fall-bearing gives a fast first crop; summer-bearing gives a heavier single early-summer crop on second-year canes.
Pruning by type: thinning summer-bearing canes and mowing fall-bearing canes at the right time is the biggest lever on yield.
Spacing and row width: keeping the row narrow and open for light and air sustains fruit size and cuts disease and SWD losses.
Drainage and water: shallow roots need steady moisture but rot in wet soil, so both drought and waterlogging cut yield.
Pest and disease pressure: spotted-wing drosophila, cane and crown borers, and the mosaic virus complex all reduce harvest and planting life.
Clean stock and site: starting with certified virus-free plants away from wild brambles preserves yield over the planting's life.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting guidance is offered for raspberry. There is no extension or peer-reviewed evidence basis for timing raspberry planting or care by lunar phase, so the field is intentionally left without a recommendation.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Little or no fruit (often a pruning mistake)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Little or no fruit (often a pruning mistake)
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The canes grew well but produced few or no berries. The most common cause is pruning the wrong way for the type: cutting a summer-bearing planting to the ground removes the very floricanes that would have fruited, and over-thinning or removing primocanes at the wrong time loses the crop. Too little sun, too little winter chill for the type, or virus can also be at fault.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The canes grew fine but you got almost no berries. Usually this is a pruning mistake: cutting a summer type to the ground takes off the canes that fruit. Too much shade, the wrong type for your climate, or a virus can also cause it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Identify your type first. Summer-bearing fruits on second-year canes, so only remove canes that have already fruited and never cut everything down. Fall-bearing fruits on first-year canes and can be mowed to the ground for one fall crop. Give the planting full sun and start with certified virus-free stock.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Find out which type you have. For summer types, only cut out the canes that already fruited, never all of them. For fall types, you can cut everything to the ground. Plant in full sun and use certified virus-free plants.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Crumbly berries that fall apart
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Crumbly berries that fall apart
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Berries came apart into loose, dry segments at picking instead of holding together as a whole fruit. This crumbly-berry symptom usually means a virus (the mosaic complex) or poor pollination; with virus, the plant also stunts and declines year over year and never recovers.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The berries fell apart into bits when you picked them instead of staying whole. This is usually a virus or poor pollination. A virused plant slowly gets worse and will not recover.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Poor pollination from cold, wet bloom weather is a one-season fluke. But persistent crumbly fruit with declining vigor means virus: remove and destroy affected plants, control aphids that spread it, clear nearby wild brambles, and replant with certified virus-free stock on fresh ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: If it was a cold, wet spring, it may just be poor pollination that year. But if plants also look weak and worsen, it is a virus: pull them out, control aphids, remove wild brambles nearby, and replant with certified virus-free plants somewhere fresh.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Canes wilting, dying back, or snapping
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Canes wilting, dying back, or snapping
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Individual canes wilted, died back, or snapped off, sometimes with cankers or hollowed, tunneled centers. The usual culprits are cane borers and crown borers tunneling inside the wood, or cane and spur blight cankering the canes, all of which are worse in crowded, damp, over-fertilized rows.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Canes wilted, died, or snapped off, sometimes with dark cankers or tunnels inside. This is usually borers tunneling in the canes or a cane disease, both worse in crowded, damp plantings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut out and destroy affected canes below the damage, disinfecting tools between cuts. Keep the row narrow and open for air, prune only in dry weather, avoid excess nitrogen, and remove wild brambles. For crown borer, start clean plants on a fresh site.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cut out and throw away damaged canes, cleaning your pruners between cuts. Keep the row thin and airy, prune in dry weather, and go easy on fertilizer. If the crown is tunneled, start fresh with healthy plants on a new spot.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants declining in wet soil
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plants declining in wet soil
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Whole plants yellowed, stunted, and collapsed, worst in low or poorly drained areas, with brown, rotted roots when dug. This is the classic picture of Phytophthora root rot, the most common cause of raspberry planting failure, brought on by waterlogged soil.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Plants yellowed, stunted, and died, especially in soggy spots, and the roots were brown and rotten. This is root rot from soil that stays too wet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Root rot cannot be reversed, so move to prevention: replant on tall raised beds or ridges in well-drained soil, divert surface water, choose more tolerant cultivars, and never let raspberries sit in saturated ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: You cannot save rotted roots, so focus on drainage next time: plant on raised rows, keep water draining away, and never let the soil stay soggy.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Fruit disappearing or full of maggots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Fruit disappearing or full of maggots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Ripening berries vanished from the canes, or picked berries turned out to be soft with tiny white maggots inside. Birds strip unprotected ripe fruit fast, and spotted-wing drosophila lays eggs in sound ripe berries so the maggots are found only after picking.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Berries disappeared as they ripened, or the ones you picked had tiny maggots inside. Birds eat unprotected fruit, and a fruit fly (SWD) lays eggs in good ripe berries.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Net the planting before berries color to stop birds. For SWD, harvest completely every one to three days, remove and destroy culls, open the canopy by pruning, and use fine exclusion netting and vinegar monitoring traps; choose early cultivars to dodge peak pressure.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover the plants with bird netting before the berries color. For the maggots, pick all ripe and overripe berries every day or two, keep the planting open and airy, and grow earlier varieties when you can.

sources_summary.note: T1 university-extension caneberry guides spanning the cane-type and regional split: cold-zone unis (Minnesota raspberry types/home-garden, Cornell Fruit Resources/SWD, Penn State raspberry production, Utah State raspberry management) for the cane biology, pruning, and pest/disease core; warm-zone unis (UGA C766 home-garden raspberries/blackberries, Texas A&M Master Gardener Dormanred, NC State southeast caneberry guide) for the heat-marginal South and the low-chill Dormanred recommendation; UC ANR for the California regional windows. All cited URLs were read live via WebFetch/WebSearch on 2026-06-30.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Not applicable. A raspberry is a long-lived perennial cane fruit planted once and kept for a decade or more, not a crop sown in succession. There is no replanting cycle; the planting renews itself through its own primocanes and is maintained in place by annual pruning until it declines and is replaced on fresh ground.

crops.description_seasoned: Raspberries are fast, generous perennial cane fruits: a planting set out this spring can hand you berries within a year or two and keep bearing for a decade. The defining feature is the biennial cane. Roots and crown are permanent, but each cane lives two years, and matching your pruning to whether the type fruits on first-year canes (everbearing) or second-year canes (summer-bearing) is the whole game. They are self-fertile, very cold-hardy, and they sucker freely, so containment and a simple trellis matter as much as feeding.
crops.description_beginner: Raspberries are one of the fastest fruits to reward you: plant in spring and you can be picking within a year or two, with a patch that lasts for years. The key thing to understand is the cane. The roots live for years, but each cane lives only two, so how and when you prune depends on whether your type fruits on new canes or year-old canes. They pollinate themselves, handle cold winters, and spread by runners, so a little containment and a stake or trellis go a long way.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: A ripe raspberry takes on full color and slips free of its white core with a light tug, leaving the hollow, thimble-shaped fruit; one that resists is not ready and will not sweeten off the plant. Pick over the planting every two to three days in the cool morning after dew dries, handling the soft fruit as little as possible, and refrigerate at once.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A raspberry is ready when it is fully colored and pulls off easily into your hand, leaving a hollow center. If it does not slip off, it is not ripe, and it will not get sweeter after picking. Pick every two or three days in the cool morning, be gentle, and refrigerate right away.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Raspberries bloom with small white five-petaled flowers, the timing set by cane type and region. Summer-bearing (floricane) types flower in late spring on overwintered canes; fall-bearing (primocane) types flower in mid to late summer on the current year's canes. Each lateral opens its flowers over a couple of weeks, and the long bloom helps the self-fertile flowers set well with bee activity.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Raspberries have small white flowers. Summer-bearing types flower in late spring on year-old canes, while fall-bearing types flower later in summer on new canes. The flowers open over a couple of weeks, and because raspberries pollinate themselves, even a single plant will set fruit, though bees help.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Raspberries are among the most cold-hardy fruits: many red and yellow cultivars are reliable to zone 3 or 4, and a few to colder still, especially fall-bearing types that can be mowed down so no cane has to survive the winter. Black and purple raspberries are noticeably less hardy (about zone 4 to 5). The harder limit is at the warm end: most raspberries need real winter chill and resent heat, so they struggle in the hot, humid South and the low desert, where only heat-tolerant low-chill types succeed.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Raspberries handle cold very well. Many red and yellow types are fine to zone 3 or 4, and fall-bearing types you cut to the ground each winter are especially safe. Black and purple types are a bit less hardy. The real problem is heat: most raspberries dislike hot summers and mild winters, so in the Deep South and the desert only special heat-tolerant kinds will grow.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Most raspberries need a stretch of winter chill (hours below about 45°F) to break dormancy and fruit normally. Standard red raspberries are high-chill, often needing 800 or more hours, which is why they fail in mild-winter regions; medium-chill types want 400 to 600, and a few heat-bred types such as Dormanred need only about 300. Too little chill for the type gives weak, erratic budbreak and little fruit, so chill, alongside summer heat tolerance, is the main thing that limits where raspberries grow.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Raspberries need a cold winter rest, measured in chill hours (time below about 45°F), before they fruit well. Most red raspberries need a lot of winter cold, which is why they do not grow in warm-winter places. A few special heat-tolerant types need much less. If a type does not get the cold it needs, it barely fruits, so matching the type to your climate matters.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Raspberries are self-fertile, so a single cultivar will set a full crop on its own; there is no need for a second variety the way blueberries or many tree fruits require. Each aggregate berry is built from many tiny druplets, though, and good bee activity helps every druplet set, giving fuller, better-formed fruit. Protect bees by not spraying insecticides during bloom.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: You do not need a second variety to get raspberries; they pollinate themselves. Bees still help, because each berry is made of many tiny parts and bee visits help them all fill out into a well-shaped berry. Avoid spraying anything that harms bees while the plants are flowering.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the first year, focus on establishing strong canes and roots. A summer-bearing planting will not fruit until its second year, so let the primocanes grow and train them in. A fall-bearing planting can give a modest crop on its new canes this first fall. From the start, contain the suckers to a narrow row, keep the soil evenly moist, mulch, and get the trellis in place.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: In the first year, let the plants build strong canes and roots. A summer type will not fruit until next year, but a fall-bearing type may give you a few berries this fall. Right away, keep the row narrow by pulling stray shoots, water steadily, mulch, and set up a support.
crops.planting_method_notes_seasoned: Plant dormant bare-root canes in spring, as soon as the soil can be worked. Space red and yellow raspberries about 18 to 24 inches apart. Rows of red and yellow raspberries can be 5 to 10 feet apart, depending on how the row middles are managed: cultivated middles need wider rows than mowed or mulched ones. UGA Extension spaces Dormanred, a trailing red, like a trailing blackberry: plants 10 feet apart in rows 12 feet apart. Set black and purple raspberries 4 feet apart. Plant in well-drained soil. On heavier soils, make raised rows or raised beds before planting to improve drainage.
crops.planting_method_notes_beginner: Plant bare-root raspberry plants in spring, as soon as the soil can be worked. Space red and yellow raspberries about 18 to 24 inches apart, in rows 5 to 10 feet apart. Leave more room between rows if you plan to cultivate there, meaning lightly loosen the soil, than if you'll mow or mulch. Georgia Extension spaces Dormanred, a trailing red raspberry, the way it spaces trailing blackberries: plants 10 feet apart, in rows 12 feet apart. Set black and purple raspberries 4 feet apart. Choose a spot where the soil drains well. If your soil is heavy, build raised rows or beds before planting so water drains away.
crops.type_selection_seasoned: The first choice is cane type, and it sets everything else. Summer-bearing (floricane-fruiting) raspberries fruit once, in early summer, on canes grown the previous year; you prune by removing the spent floricanes and thinning the new primocanes. Everbearing (primocane-fruiting, also called fall-bearing) types fruit on first-year canes in late summer or fall, and can simply be mowed to the ground each winter for one clean crop and the easiest pruning. Beyond that, red and yellow raspberries sucker and are the hardiest; black and purple raspberries do not sucker, are less hardy and more disease-prone, but are richly flavored. In the hot South, only heat-tolerant low-chill types succeed.
crops.type_selection_beginner: The first thing to decide is the cane type. Summer-bearing raspberries give one crop in early summer on year-old canes, and you prune by cutting out the canes that fruited. Everbearing (fall-bearing) types fruit on brand-new canes in late summer or fall, and you can just mow every cane to the ground each winter, which is the easiest way to prune. Red and yellow types spread by runners and are the toughest; black and purple types do not spread, are a bit less hardy, but taste rich. In the hot South, only special heat-tolerant types will grow.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Prepare the row the season before planting. Test the soil and aim for pH 5.6 to 6.5, adjusting only if it is well outside 5.5 to 7.0. Work in generous compost or aged manure for organic matter and structure, and on heavy or wet ground, build a raised berm or ridge so the crowns sit above standing water. Clear out perennial weeds and any nearby wild brambles, and do not plant where nightshades or strawberries grew recently.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Get the row ready before you plant. Most garden soil is fine; aim for a pH around 5.6 to 6.5 and only adjust if it is far off. Mix in plenty of compost or aged manure, and on heavy or wet soil, plant on a raised mound so the roots stay dry. Pull out weeds and any wild brambles nearby, and avoid spots that recently grew tomatoes, potatoes, or strawberries.

pollination.notes_seasoned: See pollinator_notes for the full guidance. In short, raspberry is self-fertile and needs no second cultivar to set a crop, unlike blueberry or many tree fruits. A single plant fruits on its own; bee activity simply improves how fully each aggregate berry sets. There is no pollinizer pairing to plan.
pollination.notes_beginner: See the pollination notes above for details. The short version: raspberries pollinate themselves, so you do not need a second variety. One plant will fruit on its own, and bees just help the berries fill out fully.

crops.establishment_note: Raspberries establish fast. Let the first-year canes build a strong root system and framework; a fall-bearing type may even fruit its first fall, while a summer-bearing type fruits in year two. Contain suckers to a narrow row from the start.
crops.cane_management_seasoned: Cane management is the heart of growing raspberries, because the crown is perennial but each cane is biennial: it grows one year, fruits the next, then dies. How you prune depends entirely on the type. On SUMMER-BEARING (floricane-fruiting) raspberries, first-year primocanes grow vegetatively, overwinter, and fruit the following early summer as floricanes, then die; immediately after harvest cut those spent floricanes to the ground and remove them, and in late winter thin the surviving primocanes to 4 to 6 sturdy canes per foot of row, narrow the row to about a foot, and tie the canes to a trellis. On EVERBEARING (primocane-fruiting, or fall-bearing) raspberries, the first-year canes fruit on their tips in late summer or fall; the simplest and recommended management is to mow every cane to the ground in late winter for a single, clean, heavy fall crop with no training of overwintered canes and reduced disease and cane-borer pressure. The same everbearing planting can instead be double-cropped, leaving the lower canes to fruit again as floricanes the next summer, but the single-crop mow is far easier and the usual home choice. Red and yellow raspberries also sucker aggressively from the roots and need their spread contained to the row every season.
crops.cane_management_beginner: Pruning raspberries is the main skill, and it all comes down to the cane. The roots live for years, but each cane lives only two: it grows one year, fruits the next, then dies. What you cut depends on your type. For SUMMER-BEARING types, the canes fruit in early summer on year-old wood and then die, so cut those fruited canes to the ground right after harvest, and in late winter thin the new canes to a few strong ones per foot and tie them up. For EVERBEARING (fall-bearing) types, the brand-new canes fruit in late summer or fall, and the easy way is to simply mow every cane to the ground each winter for one clean fall crop the next year, which is the simplest pruning there is. Red and yellow raspberries also send up shoots from their roots and will spread, so pull the ones that wander outside your row each year.

3.type_note_seasoned: In the coldest zones, fall-bearing (primocane-fruiting) red raspberry is the most reliable choice: every cane is mowed to the ground in late winter, so no cane has to survive the deep cold, and the planting still fruits on its new canes the same season. It also sidesteps cane-borer and winter-injury losses.
3.type_note_beginner: In the coldest areas, grow a fall-bearing red raspberry. You cut every cane to the ground each winter, so the cold cannot kill overwintering canes, and the new canes still fruit the same year. It is the most reliable and the easiest to prune.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Spring frost is no threat to a fall-bearing crop, since the canes bloom in summer; the real limit is the short season, so choose early cultivars that finish ripening before the first fall frost.
3.grown_as_note_seasoned: Here a fall-bearing raspberry is grown as a deciduous cane fruit that is cut completely to the ground each winter: the perennial crown survives in the soil and sends up fresh canes in spring that grow, bloom in summer, and fruit in late summer or fall before frost. This mow-everything approach is the simplest pruning there is and the safest in a hard-winter climate.
3.grown_as_note_beginner: Here a fall-bearing raspberry is cut all the way to the ground each winter. The roots live on underground and push up new canes in spring that fruit that same fall before frost. Cutting everything down is the easiest pruning and the safest in a cold climate.

5.type_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing (floricane-fruiting) red raspberry is the type to grow here: it fruits once in early summer on canes grown the year before, and it includes the hardiest, most cold-tolerant cultivars. Prune by removing the spent fruited canes after harvest and thinning the new canes in late winter.
5.type_note_beginner: Grow a summer-bearing red raspberry here. It gives one big crop in early summer on year-old canes and includes the toughest, most cold-hardy varieties. You prune by cutting out the canes that fruited and thinning the new ones.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing raspberries bloom in late spring, usually after the last hard frost, but in the coldest zones a late freeze can occasionally nip open bloom. A site with good air drainage helps, and the hardiest cultivars carry buds through tough winters.
5.grown_as_note_seasoned: Raspberry is a deciduous cane fruit everywhere it grows, including here: the canes drop their leaves and rest through winter, banking the chill the plant needs. The perennial crown lives for years while each cane lives only two, growing one year and fruiting the next before dying. You prune in the dormant season, matching the cut to the type. Planted once, a patch fruits for a decade or more.
5.grown_as_note_beginner: Your raspberry loses its leaves and rests through winter (this rest is called dormancy). The roots live for years, but each cane lives only two: it grows one year, then fruits and dies. You prune in winter, and how you prune depends on the type. Plant once and a patch keeps producing for many years.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: The northern states are raspberry country. In the coldest zones, grow a fall-bearing red raspberry and simply mow all the canes to the ground each winter for a reliable fall crop. In the milder zones, summer-bearing reds give a big early-summer crop on year-old canes. Plant dormant canes in early spring, keep the row narrow, and you will be picking by the first or second year.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: This is the raspberry heartland. In zones 3 to 4, fall-bearing (primocane) reds mowed to the ground each winter are the most reliable, fruiting on new canes before the first frost; in zones 5 to 7, summer-bearing (floricane) reds give a heavy early-summer crop. Set dormant bare-root canes in early spring, give them well-drained soil and a trellis, contain the suckers to a foot-wide row, and lean on the hardiest, earliest cultivars in the coldest zones.

8.type_note_seasoned: Standard raspberries fail in the hot, humid Southeast; the one type worth growing is a heat-tolerant, low-chill trailing raspberry such as Dormanred, which fruits in early summer and tolerates the heat and disease pressure that defeat northern reds. It is trained on a trellis like a trailing blackberry.
8.type_note_beginner: Most raspberries cannot take the hot, humid Southeast. The one that works is a heat-tolerant, low-chill type like Dormanred, which fruits in early summer and is grown on a trellis like a trailing blackberry.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Trailing low-chill raspberries bloom in late winter to early spring, so a late freeze can catch open bloom; choose a protected site and be ready to cover plants on cold nights.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Gulf South a raspberry is grown as a deciduous, heat-tolerant trailing cane fruit, planted while dormant in winter; it blooms in early spring and ripens an early-summer crop before the worst heat, then is pruned and retrained in the dormant season. Only the low-chill, heat-tolerant types persist here, and even those are best treated as a short-lived novelty.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Deep South, raspberries are grown as a heat-tolerant trailing type, planted in winter while dormant. They flower in early spring and ripen in early summer before the worst heat. Only special low-chill types will keep going here, and even those may not last many years.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Raspberries are a tough sell in the hot, humid Southeast. Most types simply will not grow, and the heat-tolerant trailing type Dormanred is the only reliable choice; expect fair, cooking-quality fruit in early summer, not a heavy fresh crop. Plant in winter, train on a trellis, and treat it as a fun experiment rather than a staple.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Gulf South is marginal raspberry country. Standard reds get too little chill and too much heat and disease, so the only dependable option is a heat-tolerant, low-chill trailing raspberry such as Dormanred, which fruits in early summer with fair, mostly cooking-quality flavor. Plant dormant in winter, trellis like a trailing blackberry, and keep expectations modest.

8.type_note_seasoned: In California's hot interior valleys, grow a low-chill, heat-tolerant everbearing red (such as Bababerry) with afternoon shade. The valley winters provide only modest chill, and summer heat is the limiting factor, so heat tolerance and shade matter more than cold hardiness.
8.type_note_beginner: In California's hot inland valleys, grow a heat-tolerant everbearing red raspberry and give it afternoon shade. The winters are mild and the summers are hot, so heat is the real challenge here.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late-winter bloom on low-chill types can meet an interior-valley frost; cover plants on cold nights. Summer heat and dry air, not frost, are the bigger stresses.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the interior valleys a raspberry is grown as a deciduous cane fruit through a mild winter that banks just enough chill; planted dormant in winter, it blooms in early spring and ripens in late spring before peak summer heat, then can push a lighter fall crop where heat eases. Afternoon shade and steady water are essential.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In inland California, raspberries rest over a mild winter, then flower in early spring and ripen in late spring before the worst heat. They may give a lighter second crop in fall. Give them afternoon shade and plenty of water.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: The interior valleys are warm and low-chill, so raspberries are marginal: grow heat-tolerant, low-chill everbearing reds (Bababerry, Oregon 1030) with afternoon shade and ample water. Plant dormant in winter; expect a late-spring to early-summer crop and possibly a lighter fall crop. Heat and dry air, not cold, are the limits.

9.type_note_seasoned: The cool, foggy north coast is California's best raspberry climate: mild winters and gentle summers suit summer-bearing reds (and everbearing types too). Adequate chill and cool ripening give full-flavored fruit without the heat stress of the interior.
9.type_note_beginner: The cool, foggy north coast is the best part of California for raspberries. The mild winters and gentle summers suit summer-bearing reds well, and the berries ripen with good flavor and no heat stress.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard frost is rare on the immediate coast, so frost on bloom is a minor concern; cool, foggy weather slowing pollination during bloom is the larger risk.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: Raspberry is a deciduous cane fruit everywhere it grows, including here: the canes drop their leaves and rest through winter, banking the chill the plant needs. The perennial crown lives for years while each cane lives only two, growing one year and fruiting the next before dying. You prune in the dormant season, matching the cut to the type. Planted once, a patch fruits for a decade or more.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: Your raspberry loses its leaves and rests through winter (this rest is called dormancy). Plant once and a patch keeps producing for many years.

9.type_note_seasoned: The mild southern coast has limited winter chill, so grow low-chill everbearing reds and give afternoon shade a short distance inland. Coastal cool keeps plants comfortable; the further from the ocean, the more heat and shade management matter.
9.type_note_beginner: The mild southern coast does not get very cold, so grow low-chill everbearing red raspberries. Right on the coast they take full sun; a little inland, give them afternoon shade.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is seldom a problem on the southern coast; low-chill types bloom early, so an inland late frost can occasionally nip bloom, but summer heat and dry air are the bigger stresses.

9.type_note_seasoned: California's low desert is at the hot, low-chill extreme for raspberries: only the most heat-tolerant, low-chill everbearing types have any chance, and only with afternoon-to-full shade, heavy mulch, and abundant water. Treat it as a difficult experiment, not a dependable crop.
9.type_note_beginner: The California low desert is about the hardest place to grow raspberries. Only the toughest heat-tolerant types might work, and only with lots of shade, mulch, and water. Treat it as an experiment.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the issue in the low desert; intense heat, sun, and dry air are what defeat raspberries here, so shade and water are everything.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the low desert a raspberry can only be attempted as a deciduous, low-chill cane fruit nursed through extreme heat: planted dormant in winter, it blooms in late winter and must finish a small crop in spring before the brutal summer, under heavy shade and constant water. Most plantings are short-lived.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the low desert, raspberries can only be attempted with heavy shade and constant water. Plant in winter, hope for a small spring crop before the extreme summer heat, and expect the plants not to last long.

8.type_note_seasoned: In the warm, arid interior, raspberries succeed mainly at higher elevations with real winter chill; lower, hotter sites need heat-tolerant, low-chill everbearing types. Alkaline soils here can cause iron chlorosis, eased with organic matter and chelated iron, and steady water is essential in the dry heat.
8.type_note_beginner: In the warm, dry interior, raspberries do best at higher elevations that get a real winter. In hotter spots, use a heat-tolerant type. The soil is often alkaline, so add compost and watch for yellowing leaves, and water steadily.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Spring frost can catch early bloom in the arid interior, where clear nights swing cold; choose a site with good air drainage and be ready to cover early-blooming plants.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the arid interior a raspberry is grown as a deciduous cane fruit through a cold, dry winter; planted dormant, it blooms in spring and ripens in late spring to early summer, needing steady irrigation through the dry heat and protection of the shallow roots with mulch. Higher, cooler sites give the most reliable crops.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In the dry interior, raspberries rest through a cold winter, flower in spring, and ripen in late spring or early summer. They need steady watering in the dry heat and a good mulch over the shallow roots. Cooler, higher spots work best.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the warm, dry interior, raspberries grow best at higher, cooler elevations. In hotter, lower spots, use a heat-tolerant type, add compost to the often-alkaline soil, mulch the roots, and water steadily. Plant dormant canes in late winter.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid interior is variable: higher elevations with real chill grow raspberries well, while hot, low, alkaline-soil sites are marginal and need heat-tolerant, low-chill everbearing types. Plant dormant in late winter, amend alkaline soils with organic matter, watch for iron chlorosis, mulch the shallow roots, and irrigate steadily through the dry heat.

Only a heat-tolerant, low-chill trailing type such as Dormanred can be attempted, and chiefly in the cooler northern peninsula, with fair, cooking-quality fruit at best.

10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Open bloom in the warm winter can be caught by a rare freeze in the upper peninsula; in the frost-free south, heat and humidity, not frost, end the raspberry season.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Tropical Hawaii is outside the raspberry's climate envelope: the lowlands lack the winter chill raspberries need and are too warm. This is a marginal novelty; growers are far better served by crops adapted to the tropics.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas
rgv.plantings_provenance: RGV author-fresh (Task 7, 2026-07-13). recommended_type/leaf_habit/windows adapted from this crop's own fl_peninsula z11 row (its closest sourced analog: a warm, low-chill, frost-free subtropical zone already carrying the identical honest 'marginal, Dorman Red, cooking-quality' framing), re-anchored to the same Texas A&M AgriLife Master Gardener Dorman Red source that crop already cites. z9=z10 (no TAMU RGV-internal zone split found); resolved_from null (frost-free). calendar[] DERIVED by berry_woody_calendar (leaf_habit=deciduous).

9.type_note_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley is at or beyond the limit for raspberries: insufficient winter chill and intense summer heat defeat standard reds. Only a heat-tolerant, low-chill trailing type such as Dormanred, a Texas-bred selection recommended by Texas A&M AgriLife's Master Gardener plant library, can be attempted, and only for a small early-spring crop of fair, mostly cooking-quality fruit. Treat it as a novelty, not a staple; blackberry is the far better caneberry choice here.
9.type_note_beginner: Raspberries are a tough sell in the Rio Grande Valley. Most types will not grow here at all, since the Valley does not get enough winter chill and gets too hot in summer. The one worth trying is a heat-tolerant, low-chill type called Dormanred, and even then expect a small crop, best used for cooking, not a heavy fresh harvest. Grow blackberries instead if you want a reliable caneberry.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The Valley is essentially frost-free, so cold is not the limiting factor for raspberry here; heat and insufficient winter chill, not frost, end the season and constrain what will fruit at all.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Valley a raspberry is grown as a deciduous, heat-tolerant trailing cane fruit, planted while dormant in winter; it blooms in late winter and ripens a small early-spring crop before the worst heat arrives, then is pruned and retrained in the dormant season. Only the low-chill, heat-tolerant types persist here, and even those are best treated as a short-lived novelty rather than a dependable planting.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Valley, raspberries are grown as a heat-tolerant trailing type, planted in winter while dormant. They flower in late winter and ripen in early spring before the worst heat. Only special low-chill types will keep going here, and even those may not last many years.

rgv.region_notes_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley is marginal raspberry country: standard reds get nowhere near enough chill and cannot handle the Valley's heat and disease pressure, so the only dependable option is a heat-tolerant, low-chill trailing raspberry such as Dormanred. Expect a small early-spring crop of fair, mostly cooking-quality fruit on a short-lived planting, trained on a trellis like a trailing blackberry. Blackberry remains the far better caneberry choice for the Valley.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley
pnw.plantings_provenance: PNW Task 7b region fill (Claude Code lane, 2026-07-14). recommended_type summer_bearing in both zones: Washington's commercial red raspberry industry (the nation's largest, per USDA NASS) is built on summer-bearing (Meeker-type) cultivars in this exact maritime climate, a confident, sourced strength claim, not a hedge. Harvest window (June-August, with a second fall flush on everbearing types into September) is T1-sourced to WSU Extension's Whatcom County 'Seasonal Harvest Guide'. WSU's dedicated caneberry cultural bulletin (EM103E) has no freely available .edu-hosted copy located this pass (flash-drive only per WSU's own catalog), so plant_out/bloom timing is treated conservatively: dormant bare-root planting in the standard late-fall-through-winter window, bloom in May (about one month ahead of the June harvest start, the standard cane-fruit bloom-to-harvest interval already used for this crop's other certified regions), not claimed as independently WSU-PNW-sourced. Both zones share one window (the source is not zone-differentiated); resolved_from carries the real per-zone NOAA frost normals.

8.type_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing (floricane-fruiting) red raspberry is the type to plant here, and it is not a modest claim: Washington is the number one red raspberry producing state in the country, almost all of it summer-bearing cultivars (Meeker and its kin) grown in this same maritime climate. Chill is never the limiter (this crop needs about 800 hours and the region banks 968 to 1,950), so the choice comes down to cultivar and trellising, not survival.
8.type_note_beginner: Plant a summer-bearing red raspberry, the classic type. This is genuinely raspberry country: Washington grows more red raspberries than any other state, and our winters give this plant all the cold rest it needs.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Raspberries bloom in May, well after this zone's typical late-March last frost, so spring frost on open bloom is a low risk here
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Raspberry is a deciduous cane fruit here as everywhere: the canes drop their leaves and rest through the mild, wet winter, banking the modest chill the plant needs. The perennial crown lives for a decade or more while each cane lives only two, growing one year and fruiting the next before dying. Set dormant bare-root canes from late fall through winter, train them on a trellis, and prune out the spent fruited canes and thin the new ones in the dormant season.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your raspberry patch comes back every year, even though each individual cane only lives two seasons: it grows one year, then fruits and dies the next, while fresh canes keep coming up from the roots. Plant dormant canes in late fall or winter, give them a trellis, and cut out the canes that already fruited each winter.

pnw.region_notes_seasoned: West of the Cascades is the heart of the US red raspberry industry, and Washington is the number one red raspberry state in the country, grown almost entirely as summer-bearing (floricane) cultivars in this exact climate. Set dormant bare-root canes from late fall through winter, trellis them, and expect bloom in May and a heavy harvest from June into August; everbearing types add a second flush into September. Chill (about 800 hours needed, far more banked here) is never the limiting factor; cultivar choice and trellising are what separate a good patch from a great one.

mid_atlantic.plantings_provenance: Region fill (Task 7, Claude Code lane, 2026-07-20). recommended_type summer_bearing in both zones (standard reds, already canonical: Boyne/Nova/Latham/Killarney/Jewel/Bristol/Royalty, chill 700-800 hours, never a limiter here). Zone 7 (cooler Piedmont) is the more comfortable end of the belt for raspberries per NC State's own caneberry guidance; zone 8 (warmer Coastal Plain) is honestly framed as more marginal, with Phytophthora root rot and heat/humidity decline the real risks (matching general NC State/VCE caneberry caution, rather than downgrading to an everbearing/trailing type as se_gulf does further south). Windows frost-reconciled against real VCE/NC State frost dates; calendar[] DERIVED by derive_deciduous_berry_woody_calendar (A16).

7.type_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing (floricane-fruiting) red raspberry is the type to grow in the Piedmont, giving one concentrated early-summer crop on year-old canes. This zone's cooler upland climate is genuinely raspberry-friendly by regional standards; well-drained soil matters, since raspberries are prone to Phytophthora root rot in heavy or wet ground.
7.type_note_beginner: Grow a summer-bearing red raspberry here for one big early-summer crop on year-old canes. Give it soil that drains well, since raspberries are prone to root rot in heavy, wet ground.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Raspberries bloom in May, well after the last frost, so spring frost on open bloom is a low risk. Winter cold is not a limiting factor.
7.grown_as_note_seasoned: Raspberry is a deciduous cane fruit here: the canes drop their leaves and rest through the Piedmont winter, banking far more chill than needed, while the perennial crown lives a decade or more and each cane lives only two, growing one year and fruiting the next before dying. Set dormant bare-root canes over winter into early spring, plant on a raised bed or well-drained site to guard against Phytophthora root rot, trellis, and prune out spent fruited canes and thin new ones each dormant season.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: Your raspberry patch comes back every year, even though each cane only lives two seasons. Plant dormant canes in winter or early spring on a raised, well-drained bed, since wet soil invites root rot. Give the canes a trellis and cut out the old fruited ones each winter.

8.type_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing red raspberry can be grown on the Coastal Plain, but this is the more marginal end of the belt for this crop: the Coastal Plain's greater summer heat and humidity raise the risk of Phytophthora root rot and general decline more than in the cooler Piedmont. Plant on a raised bed with excellent drainage, choose a site with some afternoon shade if summers run hot, and treat plantings as shorter-lived here than farther inland.
8.type_note_beginner: Raspberries can grow on the Coastal Plain, but the heat and humidity make this the harder part of the region for them. Plant on a raised, well-drained bed, give afternoon shade if you can, and expect the planting to need renewing sooner than in cooler spots.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Raspberries bloom in mid-spring here, comfortably behind the last frost, so spring frost on open bloom is a low risk. Summer heat and humidity are the bigger everyday concern.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Raspberry is a deciduous cane fruit on the Coastal Plain too, resting through the region's milder winter before growing and fruiting each summer. The real challenge here is heat and humidity rather than cold: well-drained, raised planting sites are essential to hold off Phytophthora root rot, and afternoon shade helps in the hottest microclimates. Set dormant canes over winter, trellis, and prune out spent fruited canes each dormant season; expect this to be a more marginal, shorter-lived planting than in the cooler Piedmont.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your raspberry patch on the Coastal Plain rests through our milder winter and grows each summer, but heat and humidity are real challenges here, more so than in the cooler Piedmont. nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)
nevada.plantings_provenance: Nevada high desert region (roadmap item 10), Task 8 Perennials, 2026-07-21. Structural donor = this crop's own low_desert_az z9 (bloom Feb / harvest Apr-May, deciduous, everbearing) for the Las Vegas Valley floor and warm_arid z8 (bloom Mar / harvest May-Jun) for the cooler zone 8 pockets; z10 rides zone 9's shape with the warmer zone 10 frost anchor. recommended_type=everbearing is UNCHANGED from both AZ donors (raspberry's existing hot-desert precedent already leans heat-tolerant/fall-bearing), matching the task's steer without needing a deviation. No Nevada-specific raspberry cultivar source exists, so sources are the general Southern Nevada seasonal/heat-ceiling framework (unr_fs0261) plus the NWS frost anchor (nws_vef); never carries the AZ donors' tamu_agrilife/usu_ext sources forward. calendar[] DERIVED by berry_woody_calendar (leaf_habit=deciduous).

9.type_note_seasoned: Raspberry is marginal in the Mojave: the Las Vegas Valley's intense, months-long summer heat, routinely above 100°F June through September (UNR Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), and the desert's dry air both work against it. No Nevada-specific cultivar trial exists, but the heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing (primocane) types recommended across the hot desert Southwest are the best bet here; plant where it gets afternoon shade, mulch heavily, and water steadily. Expect a smaller, shorter-lived planting than in a cooler climate.
9.type_note_beginner: Raspberry is a tough crop for the Las Vegas Valley's desert heat. Choose a heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing type, give it afternoon shade and deep mulch, and water it steadily. It will not be an easy or long-lived planting here.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the issue for raspberry in the Mojave; relentless heat, intense sun, and dry air are what stress the canes, so shade and water matter far more than frost protection.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Mojave a raspberry is grown as a deciduous, heat-tolerant cane fruit, planted while dormant in winter; it blooms in late winter to early spring and ripens before the worst heat arrives, then is pruned and retrained in the dormant season. Only low-chill, heat-tolerant types persist here, and even those are best treated as a short-lived planting rather than a dependable one.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.type_note_seasoned: Raspberry is marginal in the St. George Dixie: the hot, low, alkaline core is the ground Utah State University Extension flags as difficult, and the county's dependable raspberry ground is its higher-elevation towns instead. The best bet here is a heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing (primocane) type, because its fall crop ripens after the peak summer heat and avoids fruit sunburn (USU Extension); good choices are Caroline, Josephine, Polana, Joan J, and Polka, or the low-chill desert canes Bababerry and Dormanred. Give it afternoon shade, mulch heavily, correct the alkaline-soil iron chlorosis with a chelated iron, and water steadily.
8.type_note_beginner: Raspberry is a tough crop for the hot, low St. George Dixie. Choose a heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing type such as Caroline, Josephine, or Polana, whose berries ripen in fall after the worst heat. Give it afternoon shade and deep mulch, treat yellowing leaves with a chelated iron, and water it steadily. It will not be an easy or long-lived planting here.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not the main risk for raspberry here; the summer heat and the alkaline soil are. Because the fall crop ripens into October, an early freeze near the November 1 first frost can cut the tail of the harvest short, so pick steadily through the fall.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the St. George Dixie a raspberry is grown as a deciduous, fall-bearing cane fruit, planted dormant in late winter and cut back hard in the dormant season so it fruits on the new primocanes. It flowers in mid-summer and ripens its crop in the cooler fall, after the peak heat, then rests through winter. Only low-chill, heat-tolerant types persist in this hot, alkaline ground, and even those are best treated as a short-lived planting rather than a dependable one.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In the St. George Dixie, raspberries are grown as a fall-bearing type, planted dormant in late winter and cut to the ground each winter so the new canes carry the crop. They flower in summer and ripen berries in fall, after the worst heat. Only special low-chill types keep going in this hot, alkaline soil, and even those may not last many years.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Raspberry is a hard crop in the hot, low St. George Dixie, and it grows best up in the county's higher-elevation towns. If you want to try it here, choose a heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing (primocane) type such as Caroline, Josephine, Polana, Joan J, or Polka, whose berries ripen in fall after the worst heat has passed. Plant dormant canes in late winter, give them afternoon shade and deep mulch, and water steadily. The alkaline desert soil often yellows the leaves, which a chelated iron treatment fixes. Expect a small, hard-won crop.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: Raspberry is marginal in the St. George Dixie core: this is a hot, low, alkaline-soil site, the kind Utah State University Extension flags as difficult for the crop, while the county's dependable raspberry ground is its higher-elevation towns above the valley. The steer here is toward heat-tolerant, low-chill, fall-bearing (primocane) types, and USU Extension's reasoning is a timing one: a primocane crop comes in on the far side of the summer peak, late enough that the fruit is not sitting through the worst of the desert sun, which is what scorches a summer-bearing crop. Look to the fall-bearing varieties Caroline, Josephine, Polana, Joan J, and Polka, or the low-chill desert canes Bababerry and Dormanred. Plant dormant canes in late winter, and expect the alkaline soil to drive iron chlorosis, so treat yellowing leaves with a chelated iron. Give the planting afternoon shade to cut sunburn, mulch the shallow roots, use raised beds in heavy soil, and water steadily through the dry heat. Even managed well, treat this as a hard-won, shorter-lived planting than a cooler climate would give.

crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: This is the year the pruning starts to matter, and it all turns on one fact: the roots live for years, but each cane, meaning each individual stem coming out of the ground, lives only two. It grows one year, fruits the next, then dies. What you cut depends on your type. A summer-bearing raspberry fruits in early summer on last year's canes, so cut those spent canes to the ground right after picking; they are dead anyway, and clearing them opens the row. A fall-bearing type fruits on brand-new canes in late summer, and the simplest approach is to mow every cane to the ground each winter. Cutting the wrong type the wrong way is the most common raspberry mistake there is. Keep pulling any shoots that wander outside your row, because red and yellow types spread underground.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: Cane biology governs everything from here. The crown is perennial; individual canes are biennial, spending one season as a primocane, meaning a first-year vegetative cane, and the next as a fruited floricane before dying. Prune to the type: summer-bearing floricanes come out at ground level immediately post-harvest, while a primocane-fruiting type is mown flat each dormant season for a single clean fall crop. Mismatching the two is the crop's defining error. Contain suckering from day one on red and yellow types, holding the row to 12 to 18 inches, since the planting spreads by underground runners and a wide row loses the light and airflow that suppress disease. Feed a balanced fertilizer banded along the row at spring growth and stop by midsummer, because late nitrogen produces soft, disease-prone wood.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From the second year the planting is in full swing, and the annual rhythm is set: prune to your type, keep the row about a foot wide, and tie the kept canes to a support. Picking is the other half of the job, and it is more frequent than people expect. A ripe raspberry slips off its core into your hand and leaves a hollow center behind; one that resists is not ready. Work the row every two to three days into a shallow container and refrigerate quickly. That tight schedule is not fussiness: clearing every ripe and overripe berry on a two-to-three-day cycle is the single most effective control for spotted wing drosophila, the small fly that lays in ripening fruit, and it beats anything you could spray in a home garden.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from year two. The annual cycle is type-matched pruning, row narrowing to about 12 inches, and trellis tying, with a balanced spring feed banded along the row. Harvest cadence is a pest-control instrument rather than a convenience: raspberry receptacle separation means a ripe fruit slips free leaving the core on the plant, and complete removal of ripe and overripe fruit on a one-to-three-day cycle is the front-line suppression for spotted wing drosophila, materially more effective in a garden setting than any spray program. Hold moisture steady through sizing, since drought during fruit development is the usual cause of small, seedy, crumbly fruit. An open, well-pruned, well-supported canopy compounds the effect by drying faster and giving the fly less shelter.

crops.name: Blackberry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Deep, well-drained sandy loam or loam rich in organic matter, slightly acidic at about pH 6.0 to 6.5. Blackberries have vigorous, wide-spreading, shallow roots that resent standing water, so sharp drainage and a full-sun site matter more than any other soil trait. They are far less fussy about acidity than a blueberry.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Blackberries grow best in loose, well-drained soil with plenty of compost worked in. They like a full-sun spot and a slightly acidic soil around pH 6.0 to 6.5, which most gardens already have. Good drainage matters most, since the roots rot in soggy ground.
soil.tolerated_texture_core: loamy sand or clay loam with organic matter
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Blackberries tolerate a wide range from loamy sand to clay loam as long as drainage is good and organic matter is generous. On heavier or wetter ground, plant on a raised berm or ridge so the crown sits above standing water; raised rows are standard practice on marginal soil.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: They handle everything from sandy soil to heavier clay loam if you add compost and keep the drainage good. On wet or heavy ground, plant on a raised mound or row so the roots stay up out of soggy soil.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Heavy, poorly drained clay is the worst case: it holds water around the vigorous roots and invites Phytophthora root rot, the quickest way to lose a planting. If clay is unavoidable, grow on tall raised beds of amended soil or in large containers, and never plant in a low spot that collects water.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Heavy, wet clay is the hardest soil for blackberries. It stays soggy around the roots and causes root rot, which kills plants fast. If clay is all you have, grow them on a tall raised bed of good soil, or in a big pot.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Blackberries want loose, well-drained soil rich in organic matter and full sun. A slightly acidic pH around 6.0 to 6.5 is ideal and most gardens already have it. Mixing in compost and planting on a slightly raised row before planting helps a lot, because the roots will not stand wet feet.

ph.note_seasoned: Blackberries prefer a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerate about 5.5 to 7.0. This is close to what most vegetable gardens already carry, so no special acidification is needed, unlike a blueberry. In strongly alkaline soils above about 7.5 the plants can develop iron chlorosis (yellowing between the veins), best corrected with added organic matter and a chelated-iron product rather than a drastic pH change.
ph.note_beginner: Blackberries like soil that is slightly acidic, about pH 6.0 to 6.5, which is what most gardens already have. Unlike blueberries, they need no special acidic soil. If your soil is very alkaline and the leaves yellow between the veins, work in compost and use a chelated-iron product.

fertilizer.timing: early spring as growth begins, with a second feeding just after harvest
fertilizer.example_product: a balanced 10-10-10, or composted manure worked in along the row
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Blackberries are moderate feeders. Apply a balanced fertilizer or well-rotted manure in early spring as new growth begins, banded along the row rather than against the crowns, and a second, lighter feeding right after harvest to build the primocanes that carry next year's crop. Nitrogen drives cane vigor, but too much late in the season produces soft, disease-prone canes, so feed early and taper off by late summer. A soil test guides the rate.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed blackberries in early spring when growth starts, using a balanced fertilizer or some composted manure spread along the row, and again lightly right after you finish picking. That feeding fuels the new canes for next year. Go easy late in the season, since too much makes weak, floppy canes.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced complete fertilizer with enough nitrogen to drive primocane growth; roughly a 10-10-10, or composted manure along the row.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10, or composted manure.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About 4 to 5 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 feet of row per year, split between early spring and just after harvest; less on rich or recently manured ground.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A light scattering along the row in spring, following the package rate for berries, plus a second feeding after harvest.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Garlic and onions
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Alliums like garlic and onions are a traditional bramble neighbor, thought to help mask the planting from some pests, and they take up little room along the row.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A long-standing companion-planting tradition (alliums as a general pest-confuser); not an extension-tested blackberry yield benefit, so labeled traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Garlic and onions are a traditional companion along a bramble row, valued by many growers for pungent foliage thought to confuse or deter some browsing and sucking pests. The benefit is folk practice rather than a measured yield gain, but alliums are shallow, undemanding, and easy to tuck along the planting edge without competing with the canes, so there is little downside to trying them.

good_seasoned.name: Garlic and onions
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional edge companion: their pungent foliage is held to deter some pests, and as shallow-rooted alliums they take little from the blackberry row. Folk practice rather than a tested productivity gain.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium pest-deterrence is a widely held companion tradition, not an extension-documented blackberry pairing benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Clover or low legume cover
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low living mulch of clover in the row middles fixes a little nitrogen, holds soil, and suppresses the weeds that otherwise compete with the vigorous but shallow blackberry roots. Keep it mowed and out of the crop row so it does not invade the crowns or the sucker zone.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume row-middle cover for soil and weed benefit is mechanistically sound and commonly recommended for brambles, but the specific blackberry yield effect is not pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant, and strawberries
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Keep blackberries away from current or recent plantings of tomato, potato, pepper, eggplant, and strawberry. All host Verticillium wilt, a soil fungus that also kills blackberries; planting brambles on ground that grew nightshades or strawberries within the last few years carries the disease into the new planting.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: The Verticillium-host avoidance (do not follow tomato/potato/pepper/eggplant/strawberry) is a standard extension siting rule for brambles.

bad_seasoned.name: Wild brambles and old blackberry or raspberry plantings
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Remove nearby wild blackberries, dewberries, and abandoned brambles before planting. Wild Rubus is the single biggest reservoir for the diseases and pests that shorten a blackberry patch's life, harboring rosette (double blossom), orange rust, viruses, and spotted-wing drosophila that move straight into a new planting.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Removing nearby wild Rubus to break the rosette, orange-rust, virus, and SWD reservoirs is standard extension guidance for new blackberry sites.

companions.note_seasoned: Blackberry is not a heavy-companion crop; the siting rules that matter most are about what to keep it away from. Do not plant it where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant, or strawberries have grown in the last few years, because all share Verticillium wilt, and clear out nearby wild brambles that carry rosette, orange rust, viruses, and spotted-wing drosophila. Good neighbors are modest: traditional allium edges and a mowed legume cover in the row middles for soil and weeds. The bigger gains come from full sun, spacing, drainage, and a clean start, not from companions.
companions.note_beginner: Blackberries do not need companion plants to do well. The important rules are what to avoid: do not plant them where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant, or strawberries grew recently (they share a soil disease called Verticillium wilt), and pull out any wild brambles nearby, which spread disease and pests. If you want neighbors, garlic along the edge and clover between rows are easy, low-risk choices.

pests.name: Spotted-wing drosophila (SWD)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small white maggots inside ripe and ripening berries; fruit softens, collapses, and leaks when squeezed. The adult is a tiny vinegar-fly-like insect, the male with a dark spot near each wingtip. Late-ripening and fall primocane crops are hit hardest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny maggots inside ripe berries, with the fruit going soft and mushy. The adult is a small fly with a spot on each wing.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spotted-wing drosophila (Drosophila suzukii), an invasive vinegar fly whose females cut into healthy ripe fruit to lay eggs, unlike common fruit flies that use only rotting fruit. It is the major modern blackberry pest and the reason clean, frequent picking now defines a successful patch.
pests.cause_beginner: An invasive fruit fly that lays eggs in good, ripe berries (not just rotten ones), and the maggots feed inside.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Harvest completely and often, every one to two days, so no ripe fruit is left on the cane, and remove and destroy overripe or fallen berries (bag them, do not compost). Open the canopy by pruning and trellising to reduce the cool, humid shelter the fly favors. Fine exclusion netting under 1 mm mesh and apple-cider-vinegar monitoring traps help.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick ripe berries every day or two and clean up any fallen or overripe ones (seal them in a bag, do not compost). Keep the planting open and airy. A cup of apple cider vinegar makes a simple monitoring trap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Choose early-ripening cultivars to dodge peak fly pressure, keep the planting open and well-trellised, harvest on a tight schedule, and remove nearby wild brambles that host the fly.
pests.prevention_beginner: Grow earlier varieties when you can, keep the row open and trellised, and pick often. Clear out wild brambles nearby.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick every ripe berry, and pick every day or two. This fly lays its eggs in sound fruit that is coloring up, not just in rotten fruit, so a berry left hanging is somewhere for the next batch of maggots to start. Clean, frequent picking is the strongest everyday tool you have against it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A complete harvest on a one to two day interval is the backbone of the program, since the female cuts into healthy ripe fruit to oviposit rather than waiting for it to break down. Fruit left on the cane is breeding habitat, and late-ripening and fall primocane crops carry the heaviest pressure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Gather the overripe berries still hanging and the ones that have dropped, seal them in a bag, and put them in the trash rather than on the compost pile. The bagging is the point: soft and fallen fruit is what this fly breeds in, so it needs to leave the garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Culls and drops go off site sealed rather than onto a compost heap, since a cull pile holds breeding fruit between pickings. This is the debris half of the job and sits alongside the harvest interval rather than replacing it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Look past your own row. Wild brambles along fences and field edges nearby host this fly too, and they keep resupplying your patch. Clearing the ones you can reach lowers the pressure the planting has to absorb.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Feral Rubus in the surrounding landscape is a reservoir host, so the nearby stand governs how much pressure arrives at the row. Clearing what is within range is what lets a tight picking schedule actually hold.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Set a cup of apple cider vinegar near the berries before they ripen and check it weekly. It tells you the flies have arrived so you can time everything else. Treat it as an early warning, not as control.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Vinegar-baited traps hung ahead of ripening and checked weekly establish arrival timing for the harvest interval and for exclusion. Read catch as a detection signal rather than as population removal.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover the planting with very fine mesh, under 1 mm, before the first berries start to color, and seal it down at the edges so nothing walks in underneath. Putting it on after fruit has colored risks shutting flies in with the crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mesh under 1 mm installed ahead of first color and sealed at every edge excludes adults; deployment after fruit colors can enclose an established population. It works alongside the picking schedule rather than in place of it.
