pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley
pnw.plantings_provenance: PNW Task 7b region fill (Claude Code lane, 2026-07-14). No WSU/OSU PNW-specific elderberry cultural-timing source was located this pass (WSU's tree-fruit handbook, EB0937, explicitly does not cover elderberry, and no dedicated WSU/OSU elderberry bulletin was found -- a fully thin gap for this region specifically, flagged in the T1 sourcing table). This cell instead applies the same general, cross-region American elderberry biology already carried by this crop's other certified regions (mu_ext, Missouri Extension AF1017; msu_ext, Michigan State Extension), reconciled to the pnw frost dates: one recommended_type everywhere, chosen by cultivar not climate, roughly 400 chill hours needed (trivial against this region's banked chill), June bloom, August-September ripening, matching the window this crop already carries in its existing ca_north_coast cell (a comparably mild, wet-winter maritime climate). Framed honestly as adaptable-elsewhere guidance applied here, not a PNW-specific finding; the region's genuine strength for this crop is its ample rainfall and moisture, which elderberry, unlike most other fruiting shrubs in this dataset, actually prefers. Both zones share one window; resolved_from carries the real per-zone NOAA frost normals.

8.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry is the one type to grow, chosen by cultivar rather than by climate, and the maritime Northwest suits it well: this is a moisture-loving shrub, and our long wet season and mild winters are close to ideal. It is exceptionally cold-hardy and needs only about 400 chill hours, far less than this region banks, so chill is never a concern. Plant two different cultivars for cross-pollination.
8.type_note_beginner: Grow American elderberry, the one common type. It loves moisture, so our wet climate is genuinely a plus for this plant, and our winters are more than cold enough for it. Plant two different varieties near each other for a good crop.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Elderberry blooms in June, well after the last frost in either zone, so frost on bloom is not a concern here.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a permanent, very cold-hardy deciduous shrub here, planted once and renewed in place for many years. It rests dormant through the mild, wet winter, leafs out and grows fast in spring, blooms in June, and ripens clusters of dark berries from August into September. Renew the oldest canes in late winter and plant two different cultivars for good fruit set; this native, adaptable shrub asks for little beyond the moisture this region already supplies.

crops.description_seasoned: Elderberry is a big, fast, tough native shrub grown for its clusters of small dark berries, which are cooked into juice, syrup, jelly, wine, and pie (and its flowers are used too). It is one of the easiest fruits to grow: very cold-hardy, wet-tolerant, and productive within two or three years. Two things are non-negotiable: plant two different cultivars for good yield, and always COOK the berries, because raw or unripe fruit, leaves, and stems are mildly toxic.
crops.description_beginner: Elderberry is a large, easygoing native shrub that gives big clusters of small dark berries for making juice, syrup, jelly, and pies. It is very cold-hardy, handles wet soil, and starts producing in just two or three years. Remember two things: plant two different varieties so you get plenty of fruit, and always cook the berries, because raw berries, leaves, and stems can make you sick.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest whole flower-cluster heads (cymes) when most of the berries in a cluster have turned deep purple-black and are plump and soft, usually late summer. Cut the entire cluster with pruners rather than picking berries one by one, then strip the berries from the green stems (chilling or briefly freezing makes this easy). Leave green or red under-ripe berries, and never include stems. Berries do not sweeten after picking, and they must be cooked.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Elderberries are ready when most berries in a cluster are deep purple-black, plump, and soft. Snip off the whole cluster with pruners instead of picking one berry at a time, then pull the berries off the stems (freezing the clusters briefly makes this easy). Skip any green or red berries, keep the stems out, and always cook the berries before eating.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Elderberry blooms in early to midsummer in most of the country (June into July), and earlier in the warm South, carrying broad, flat, creamy-white flower clusters (cymes) that are showy and fragrant. Each cluster is receptive over one to two weeks, and the flowers are both wind-pollinated and heavily insect-visited. Late-blooming cultivars help dodge spring frost.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Elderberry flowers in early to midsummer (June to July in most areas, earlier in the South), with big flat clusters of creamy-white blooms that bees love. The flowers themselves are edible and used for cordials and fritters.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Elderberry is exceptionally cold-hardy and widely adaptable. American elderberry is reliably hardy and productive across roughly USDA zones 3 through 9, its native range covering most of the eastern and central United States, and it is one of the most cold-tolerant fruit crops you can grow. In the frost-free deep South and mild coasts (zones 10 to 11) it still grows, and native populations fruit there, but low winter chill and extreme heat make it more of an adaptation-edge crop than a sure thing; the far tropics and hot low deserts are marginal.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Elderberry is one of the toughest, most cold-hardy fruits there is, thriving across most of the country (roughly zones 3 to 9). In very warm, frost-free areas (zones 10 to 11) it will grow, but it is less reliable there because it likes a real winter and dislikes extreme heat.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a deciduous shrub that rests dormant each winter and needs a period of cold to do so, but its chill requirement is low and, unlike blueberry, is NOT how you choose a cultivar: there is essentially one type (American elderberry) grown everywhere. In practice, winter dormancy is a given across its hardy range, and the low-chill point only matters at the frost-free warm edge, where too little cold can make bloom and fruiting erratic.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Elderberry needs a cold winter rest, but not much, and you do not pick varieties by chill the way you do with blueberries; there is basically one kind of elderberry. The only place low winter cold matters is the frost-free deep South, where it can make fruiting less reliable.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Plant at least two DIFFERENT cultivars with overlapping bloom, within about 60 feet of each other. Elderberry is only partially self-fertile: a single plant sets some fruit, but a compatible second cultivar dramatically increases yield, cluster size, and reliability. The flowers are wind-pollinated and also worked by bees and other insects, so the key is simply having two overlapping-bloom cultivars nearby, not any specific pairing.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Plant two or more different kinds of elderberry near each other, within about 60 feet, so they can cross-pollinate. Elderberry makes some fruit on its own but a lot more with a partner variety, so always plant at least two different ones.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Focus the first year on roots and canes, not fruit: remove the flower clusters so the young plant establishes fast. Keep it well watered through its first season (its shallow roots are drought-sensitive while establishing) and mulch heavily. Elderberry is quick to establish, so this brief restraint pays off in strong crops by year two or three.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: In the first year, pinch off the flowers so the plant puts its energy into growing strong roots and stems. Keep it well watered and mulched. Elderberry grows fast, so you will be picking berries soon.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Elderberry needs little special soil prep beyond generosity: work plenty of compost or aged manure into a moist, fertile site before planting, and mulch heavily to hold moisture around the shallow roots. It tolerates heavy and wet ground, so a low, damp spot is fine; on dry, sandy soil, add abundant organic matter and plan to irrigate. No acidification is needed.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Prepare the spot by digging in lots of compost, since elderberry loves rich, moist soil. A damp, low corner of the yard is fine. On dry, sandy soil, add extra compost and be ready to water. Unlike blueberries, elderberry needs no special acid treatment.
crops.planting_method_notes_seasoned: Set dormant bare-root plants or rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring at the depth they grew, in moist, fertile soil, and water in well; container plants can go in spring or fall. Space plants closer together in a hedge-style row, or 5 to 7 feet apart for full-size freestanding shrubs, with wider spacing between rows. Expect vigorous growth and suckering, and plan at least two cultivars for cross-pollination.
crops.planting_method_notes_beginner: Plant elderberry in late winter or early spring, at the same depth it was growing, in moist rich soil, and water it in. Give each plant room: closer together for a hedge, or 5 to 7 feet apart for full-size bushes. Plant at least two different varieties near each other, and expect it to grow fast and send up suckers.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Elderberry is only partially self-fertile: a lone plant sets some fruit, but yields are far higher when a second, different cultivar blooms nearby for cross-pollination. The practical rule is plant at least two different cultivars within about 60 feet of each other. Bloom is carried on large flat flower clusters (cymes) that are wind-pollinated and also worked heavily by bees and other insects; overlapping bloom between the two cultivars is what matters. This is the single biggest lever on how much fruit you pick.
pollination.notes_beginner: Elderberry will make some berries on its own, but you get a much bigger crop when you plant two different kinds near each other so they can cross-pollinate. Keep them within about 60 feet. Plant two, and plan on a lot more fruit.

crops.establishment_note: Pinch off the flower clusters the first year (and thin fruiting the second) so the young shrub spends its energy building a strong, deep root system and a full framework of canes. Elderberry is fast, so this establishment period is short: a well-started plant is bearing real crops by its second or third year.
crops.cane_management_seasoned: Elderberry is not a bush with a single crown like blueberry, nor a biennial-cane fruit like raspberry. It throws up many perennial canes from the base, and it fruits best on one, two, and three-year-old wood, so the goal is a shrub with a mix of cane ages. Each dormant season remove canes older than about three years at ground level, along with any dead, broken, weak, or crowded stems, keeping the most vigorous younger canes. If a planting has grown into a tangled, unproductive thicket, you can cut the entire clump to the ground in late winter to renew it; it will regrow vigorously and be fruiting again within a year or two.
crops.cane_management_beginner: An elderberry grows as a clump of many stems (canes) from the ground, not on a single trunk. It fruits best on canes that are one to three years old, so each winter cut out the oldest canes at the base (older than about three years) plus anything dead, broken, or crowded, and leave the strong younger stems. If your elderberry has become an overgrown tangle that fruits poorly, you can cut the whole thing to the ground in late winter and it will bounce right back.
crops.type_selection_seasoned: Unlike blueberry, elderberry is not divided into climate-matched types: there is essentially one cultivated type, American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis), grown across the whole country, so you select by CULTIVAR (yield, ripening season, habit) rather than by chill class. European elderberry (S. nigra) is an alternative with its own cultivars but is less hardy and less adapted here. The one selection rule that always applies: choose two different cultivars with overlapping bloom for cross-pollination.
crops.type_selection_beginner: There is really just one kind of elderberry to grow, American elderberry, so you do not have to match a type to your climate the way you do with blueberries. Just pick two different varieties (for pollination) based on how much they yield and when they ripen. A European kind exists but is less hardy here.

pet_safe.toxic_parts: raw or unripe berries, leaves, and stems
pet_safe.note: Cooked ripe elderberries are used in foods, but the raw or unripe berries, leaves, and stems contain cyanide compounds and are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: Thin the fruiting this second year so the young shrub can finish building its framework, then let it go. Elderberry establishes fast, so the restraint is brief. Understand the shape of the plant while it is young: an elderberry grows as a clump of many stems from the ground rather than on a single trunk, and it fruits best on stems that are one to three years old. That is what makes the yearly pruning simple later on. One thing matters more than anything else here, and it applies from your very first berry: always cook elderberries before eating them. Raw and unripe fruit, and the leaves and stems, are mildly toxic, so strip the berries off, throw away every green or red one along with all the stems, and cook what is left.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: Thin fruiting in year two so the shrub completes its root system and cane framework; establishment is short on this crop, so the cost is small against the second and third year crops. The structural model to internalize now is a multi-stem clump rather than a leader: bearing is best on canes one to three years old, which is what makes the later renewal cycle mechanical. THE SAFETY RULE APPLIES FROM THE FIRST HARVEST AND IS NOT OPTIONAL: raw and unripe fruit, foliage and stems all contain cyanogenic compounds and are mildly toxic, so berries are stripped clean of stems, green and red fruit discarded, and the crop is always cooked before eating. Pollination also needs two different cultivars, so a single-variety planting under-sets regardless of how well it is grown.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From the third year the shrub carries a full crop. Pruning is a yearly renewal rather than shaping: each late winter, cut out the stems older than about three years at the base, along with anything dead, broken, or crowded, and leave the strong younger ones. If the plant ever becomes an overgrown tangle that fruits poorly, you can cut the whole thing to the ground in late winter and it will bounce right back, which is unusually forgiving. Harvest whole clusters when most berries in them are deep purple-black and soft. Chilling the clusters first makes stripping them much easier. Discard every green or red berry and all the stems, and always cook the fruit before eating: raw and unripe berries, leaves, and stems are mildly toxic.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from year three. Renewal pruning is the entire structural task: each dormant season remove canes older than roughly three years at the base along with dead and crowded stems, retaining a spread of younger wood, since bearing concentrates on one-to-three-year canes. An unproductive overgrown clump can be cut to the ground entirely and will regenerate, which makes recovery from neglect cheap on this crop relative to any tree fruit. Harvest whole cymes when the majority of berries are deep purple-black and soft; chilling clusters before stripping markedly reduces handling loss. Discard green and red fruit and all stem material. THE COOKING REQUIREMENT IS PERMANENT: raw and unripe fruit, foliage and stems are mildly toxic, so the crop is never eaten fresh regardless of ripeness.

crops.name: Persimmon

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Persimmon is easygoing about soil but wants one thing above all: good drainage. A deep, well-drained loam is ideal, and a sandy loam or lighter sandy soil works fine too. The trouble spot is heavy clay that holds water, because persimmon roots, especially on Asian types, are prone to root rot in soggy ground. If your soil is heavy or wet, plant on a raised mound so the roots sit above standing water. A soil of ordinary richness suits it; persimmon needs little feeding and too much can cause the fruit to drop.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Persimmon is broadly soil-tolerant but demands good drainage, ideally a deep, well-drained loam; a sandy loam is well suited and lighter sandy soils are workable. Heavy, water-holding clay is the problem texture, since persimmon (especially Diospyros kaki) is susceptible to root and crown rot on poorly drained sites; on such ground plant on a raised berm. Best sites are upland sandy loams. Moderate fertility is plenty, and persimmon is sensitive to salinity and to excess nitrogen, which triggers fruit drop.

ph.note_beginner: Persimmon does best in a slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and is fine up to about 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting the permanent tree. If it is too acidic, garden lime raises the pH; if it is too alkaline, elemental sulfur lowers it. Mix any amendment in before planting, since pH changes slowly and is far easier to correct before the tree is in the ground.
ph.note_seasoned: Persimmon prefers a slightly acidic pH 6.0 to 6.5 and tolerates up to about 7.0. Test before planting and adjust gradually: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting the permanent tree, since pH shifts slowly and is easiest to correct before establishment.

fertilizer.timing: late dormancy, split with early and late summer
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Persimmon needs little feeding and is easily over-fed: excess nitrogen causes premature fruit drop. A light program suits it, split across the season on sandy soils (the bulk in late dormancy, a lighter touch in early and late summer), broadcast evenly around the root zone to the drip line and kept off the trunk. On decent soil an established tree may need no fertilizer at all; feed only if growth is weak or leaves are pale.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Persimmon barely needs feeding, and too much fertilizer, especially nitrogen, makes the fruit drop off. Go light. Scatter it evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. On good soil an older tree may need nothing at all, so only feed if the tree looks weak or the leaves are pale.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 is plenty for persimmon; the tree is a light feeder and over-fertilizing, particularly with nitrogen, drops fruit rather than improving it. Err toward less.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is all persimmon needs, and often it needs none. Do not overdo it, because too much, especially the first number, nitrogen, makes the fruit fall off.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rate is about 2 ounces of 10-10-10 per year of tree age, applied in late dormancy (roughly March), with lighter follow-up feedings in early and late summer where the soil is sandy. Cap it at a modest total for a mature tree and do not fertilize at planting. If growth is already vigorous, skip feeding entirely; excess nitrogen shows up as dropped fruit, not bigger crops.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple rule is about 2 ounces of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, given in late winter, with a little more in early and late summer if your soil is sandy. Do not feed a tree that is already growing well, and never put fertilizer in the planting hole. If in doubt, feed less: too much makes persimmons drop.

companions.note_beginner: Most Asian persimmons are self-fruitful, so one tree fruits on its own and you do not need a partner tree. American persimmons are different: they usually have male and female trees, so a female needs a male American persimmon nearby to fruit, unless you plant a self-fruitful kind like Meader. For a tree, the pairings that matter are not vegetable-garden companions but what grows around the roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, since lawn competes with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free circle helps it settle in. Persimmon is a low-pest, easygoing tree, so there is little else to fuss over.
companions.note_seasoned: Asian persimmon (D. kaki) is self-fruitful, so a single tree crops without a pollinizer; American persimmon (D. virginiana) is typically dioecious and a female needs a male within roughly 50 to 200 feet, the exception being self-fruitful selections like Meader. The interactions that matter for a tree concern the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since grass competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, competition-free root area speeds establishment. Persimmon is notably low-pest and low-maintenance, so companion planting is a minor consideration here.

good_seasoned.name: Flowering herbs and pollinator plants
good_seasoned.label: traditional

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Orchard-floor insectary logic is sound and extension-aligned in principle: flowering plants recruit the natural enemies (parasitic wasps, ladybugs, hoverflies) that hold persimmon's soft-bodied pests (scale, mealybug, psyllid) in check, and UC IPM's persimmon guidance leans on preserving natural enemies. But persimmon is self-fruitful/parthenocarpic, so the pollinator draw is not needed for fruit set, and the predator-recruitment benefit is diffuse and unquantified for persimmon specifically. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A skirt of flowering herbs and pollinator plants around a persimmon supports orchard-floor health. Because persimmon is self-fruitful and its Asian cultivars set fruit parthenocarpically, the pollinator draw is a bonus rather than a requirement, but the same flowers recruit the ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that keep scale, mealybug, and persimmon psyllid at tolerable levels, which is exactly the natural-enemy approach UC IPM recommends for this low-spray tree. Keep the plantings out toward the drip line rather than crowding the trunk.

bad_seasoned.name: Lawn and weeds crowding the young trunk
bad_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Keeping turf and weeds cleared from a young fruit tree's root zone is standard, well-evidenced extension practice: grass competes strongly with a young tree for water and nitrogen and slows establishment, and a mulched weed-free circle is the routine recommendation across fruit-tree extension guidance. extension_backed/high for the general fruit-tree principle applied to persimmon.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Grass and weeds pressed up against a young persimmon are the pairing to avoid. Turf competes hard with a newly planted tree for water and nitrogen and measurably slows establishment, and growth against the trunk also traps moisture and invites string-trimmer wounds. Keep a mulched, weed-free circle a few feet out from the trunk through the establishment years, keeping the mulch itself off the bark.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small, immobile bumps fixed to bark and twigs. White peach scale, the species Florida names, shows as snow-white patches on the trunk and limbs that scrape off easily and are most visible when the males emerge in warm weather. Where the scale is a soft species, such as the tuliptree scale Georgia expects, the colony also drips sticky honeydew that grows black sooty mold and draws ants; white peach scale and the other armored scales produce no honeydew at all.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little bumps stuck to the bark and twigs that never move. White peach scale looks like patches of snow-white crust on the trunk and branches; it scrapes off easily, and it stands out most in warm weather when the tiny winged males come out. If the bumps are one of the soft scales instead, you will also find a sticky coating (honeydew) on the leaves and branches below them that turns black with mold and brings ants. White peach scale makes no honeydew, so a crusty trunk with no stickiness is the usual persimmon picture.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several scale species feeding on sap under a protective covering: white peach scale (Pseudaulacaspis pentagona), the armored species Florida names for persimmon, and the soft scales, with tuliptree scale the one Georgia expects. Only the soft scales excrete honeydew, which is what the sooty mold grows on. Populations flare where natural enemies have been removed, most often by sprays made for some other pest.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny sap-sucking insects that live under a hard or waxy covering. On persimmon the main one is white peach scale, and soft scales such as tuliptree scale turn up too. Only the soft kinds drip the sticky honeydew that grows black mold. Scale gets out of hand when a spray aimed at some other pest kills off the helpful insects that normally eat it.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Preserve natural enemies (ladybugs, parasitic wasps) by not spraying broadly, since they usually hold scale to tolerable levels on persimmon. Prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood. A dormant-season horticultural oil application smothers overwintering scale on the bark and is the main direct control for a backyard tree.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Let the helpful bugs do the work by avoiding broad sprays, since ladybugs and tiny wasps usually keep scale in check on persimmon. Cut out and throw away badly crusted branches. A spray of horticultural oil while the tree is leafless in winter smothers the scale on the bark and is the simplest hands-on control.
pests.prevention_seasoned: The standing protection is not spraying for other pests, since UGA's observation is that scale on an unsprayed persimmon is generally held by parasites, predators and diseases and that sprays for something else are what release it. Look the trunk and limbs over for white patches, which are easiest to see when the males emerge in warm weather; if a dormant oil is going on, its slot is shortly before bud swell, and an in-season oil is timed by wrapping an infested twig with double-sided sticky tape in spring to catch the crawler emergence.
pests.prevention_beginner: The best prevention is to leave the tree unsprayed unless you have a real reason, because the helpful insects already on it keep scale in check, and a spray aimed at some other pest is the usual way scale gets loose. Glance over the trunk and branches for white patches, easiest to spot in warm weather. If you decide on an oil spray, the time for it is late winter, just before the buds start to swell.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Look the trunk and branches over while the tree is bare in winter. White peach scale shows up as snow-white patches on the bark that scrape off easily, and on a small tree, if only a few twigs or branches carry a heavy crust, cut those off and get them away from the tree. That takes the colonies out along with the wood they are fixed to, and nothing you spray afterward has to cover them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Dormant pruning is the natural inspection pass, since white peach scale sits on the trunk and limbs where the bare tree makes it obvious. UC IPM's condition is specific: prune off heavily infested twigs and branches only when they are limited to a few parts of a small plant, which makes this a pruning-out-colonies move rather than a treatment for a tree encrusted end to end. Florida's guide adds a warm-weather cue, since the white patches are most visible when the males emerge.

control_ladder.note_beginner: First see whether ants are climbing the tree. White peach scale gives off no honeydew, so ants have no reason to visit it; a trail of ants on a persimmon means something that makes honeydew is there: one of the soft scales (Georgia expects tuliptree scale), mealybugs, or the persimmon psyllid, any of which drips the sugary honeydew ants collect. Ants defend the insects they tend against the ladybugs and small wasps that eat them, so keep the ants off: put a band of heavy paper or tree wrap around the trunk, spread a sticky barrier on the band and not on the bark itself, and remove any branch or weed that lets ants walk in from the ground or a wall.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Scoped to the soft-scale part of the picture: armored scales such as white peach scale produce no honeydew, so there is nothing for ants to tend and a barrier buys nothing against them. Where the scale is a soft species and ants are working it, UC IPM's instruction is to control the ants because they attack the parasites and predators of scale, and to deny them the canopy by pruning bridging branches or weeds and applying a sticky material to the trunk over a wrap. It restores the biological control the next step relies on rather than acting on the scale itself.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On an unsprayed persimmon, scale is usually held down for you. Georgia's guide says that where nothing is sprayed, scale is generally kept under control by natural parasites, predators and diseases, and that spraying for other pests often lets scale loose from that control. So the main thing is what you do not do: keep strong, broad insect sprays off the tree, and the ladybugs, lacewings and small parasitic wasps that attack scale will keep working.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conservation is the operative control here, and the persimmon documents say so directly: UGA has scale generally kept under control by parasites, predators and diseases in unsprayed situations, with sprays made for other pests the usual reason it escapes; UF names ladybird beetles and lacewings for biological control; UC IPM advises against foliar broad-spectrum insecticides whose residues persist for weeks. A scale flare on a persimmon is worth reading as a question about what was sprayed last season before it is read as a call for a spray this one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When scale is spreading in spite of all that, horticultural oil is the spray both Georgia and Florida point to, and the time for it is late winter, shortly before the buds swell, while the tree is still bare. Oil kills by coating and smothering, so it only works on scale it actually wets: soak the bark of the trunk, the limbs and the ends of the branches. Skip it on a drought-stressed tree and on days above 90°F, when it can scorch the tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Dormant oil is the documented direct control: UGA has an application shortly before bud swell giving good control, and UF's cell is a 3% dormant oil before bud break, with summer oil as the in-season alternative. UC IPM supplies the reasoning behind the timing: overwintering scale on a deciduous tree is reached by thoroughly spraying the bark of terminal shoots in winter, and an in-season oil works only when applied soon after most crawlers have emerged and the scales are still young nymphs, which a band of double-sided sticky tape around an infested twig in spring will show you. Coverage governs the result, and oil stays off a water-stressed tree and out of heat above 90°F.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, oval insects covered in white wax, gathered in the protected places on a tree: branch crotches, the base of a stem, between a stem and a leaf lying against it, and, on persimmon, inside the leaves curled by persimmon psylla. Their sticky honeydew, the black sooty mold that grows on it, and ants feeding on it are often the first signs. Persimmon carries few serious insect problems, and mealybugs are reported on it as an occasional case.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small soft insects covered in white, cottony fluff, tucked into sheltered spots: where branches fork, at the base of a stem, where a leaf lies against a stem, and inside the leaves that persimmon psylla has curled up in spring. You often notice the sticky honeydew, the black mold growing on it, or the ants feeding on it before you notice the bugs. On persimmon they are an occasional visitor rather than a regular pest.
pests.cause_seasoned: Mealybugs, sap-sucking insects that shelter in protected crevices on the tree. The guides read name only the longtailed mealybug (Pseudococcus longispinus), which UF lists with persimmon among its hosts. Ant-tended colonies persist because ants protect them from their natural enemies in exchange for honeydew.
pests.cause_beginner: Sap-sucking insects called mealybugs that tuck themselves into sheltered spots on the tree, such as the forks of branches and the curled leaves left by persimmon psylla. Ants often protect them for their sweet honeydew, which lets the mealybugs build up.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rely first on natural enemies, which generally keep mealybugs below damaging levels on landscape fruit trees; avoid the broad-spectrum sprays that disrupt them. Control honeydew-farming ants (sticky trunk bands) so predators can work. Spot-treat visible colonies with a horticultural oil or insecticidal soap.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Let natural predators handle most mealybugs, and avoid broad sprays that kill those helpers. Stop ants from climbing the trunk with a sticky band so the predators can reach the mealybugs. Dab visible clusters with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Maintain biological control by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides for any pest in the area, and keep ants out of the canopy so the predators can reach the colonies. Persimmon psylla and mealybugs share the same curled spring leaves and the same honeydew-feeding ants, so a spring with psylla damage is the time to look for them.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the helpful insects around by not spraying broadly, and keep ants off the trunk. If persimmon psylla has curled the new leaves in spring, look inside those leaves, because mealybugs often turn up in the same place.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If mealybugs have built up on a persimmon, look for ants on the trunk first. Ants feed on the honeydew mealybugs give off and, in return, keep the beetles and small wasps that eat mealybugs away from them, so a colony with ants tending it grows where one left alone would fade out. Put a band of heavy paper or tree wrap around the trunk, coat the band with a sticky barrier (never the bare bark), and trim any low branch that touches the ground, a fence or another plant so the ants have no way around it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's mealybug guidance is to keep ants out of infested plants because ants protect mealybugs from their natural enemies, and on a persimmon the ant trail up the trunk is the thing to break. Florida's persimmon table makes the same point from the psylla side, where mealybugs turn up in the same curled leaves and the ants feeding on the honeydew may also need controlling. A sticky band over a trunk wrap and the removal of bridging branches restore the predation this pest is normally held by.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where the cottony clumps sit out in the open on shoots or branches, turn the hose on them at full pressure; a persimmon is sturdy enough to take it, and a good many mealybugs are dislodged that way. Choose a morning so the foliage has the day to dry off, and count on going back over the tree, since some always cling on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM allows that on sturdy plants a high-pressure or forcible water spray can reduce mealybugs that are somewhat exposed; it does nothing for colonies tucked into crotches and crevices, so it is a knock-back on visible clusters, with no residue and no cost to the natural enemies.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Outdoors, most mealybugs are eaten before they matter. Ladybugs, lacewings and small parasitic wasps keep them below damaging levels on garden trees, and persimmon is a crop with few serious insect problems to begin with. Keep strong, broad-spectrum insect sprays off the tree so those helpers stay.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Natural enemies are the standing control: UC IPM's statement is that most species have natural enemies that keep populations below damaging levels in landscapes and gardens, with the mealybug destroyer lady beetle the predator it singles out, and its fruit-tree note is that citrus has the most problems while on stone and pome fruits mealybugs are rarely at damaging levels, a scope that stops short of persimmon. Georgia calls oriental persimmon relatively free of serious insect problems, which is the reading behind this pest's low grade. Preserving the enemies means avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides for any pest in the area, not just this one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For clumps that keep coming back, spray insecticidal soap straight onto them. Soap works only where it lands and only on what it wets, and the waxy coating sheds a lot of it, so the young ones with less wax are the ones it reaches best. Plan on more than one go, and keep it off a dry, stressed tree or a day over 90°F.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM rates soaps, horticultural oils and neem as giving some suppression when applied directly on mealybugs, especially against younger nymphs with less wax accumulation. Suppression is the right word: the wax defeats a single wetting, colonies sit in crevices a spray runs past, and there is no residual. Spot application, repeated and confined to the clumps you can see, is the useful form; a blanket spray costs beneficials for little gain.

pests.name: Persimmon psyllid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: New leaves crinkle, curl and roll around the feeding of the nymphs in spring, and shoot tips can twist and become galled. Inside the distorted leaves are the flattened, white-fluff-covered nymphs, with the small black-bodied adults on the leaf surface; the nymphs also drip honeydew on which sooty mold can grow. Florida lists stunted growth among the symptoms.
pests.symptoms_beginner: In spring the new leaves crinkle and roll up around tiny insects feeding inside, and some shoot tips twist into lumpy growth. Open a rolled leaf and you find flat young ones covered in white fluff, with small black adults on the leaf surface, and often a sticky film that can turn black with mold. It can stunt the tree's growth.
pests.cause_seasoned: The persimmon psyllid, a small sap-feeding insect whose nymphs feed on expanding leaves in spring and induce the characteristic leaf roll. It is a minor, mostly cosmetic pest of both native and Oriental persimmon.
pests.cause_beginner: A small sap-feeding insect called the persimmon psyllid. Its young feed on the new spring leaves and make them curl. It is a minor pest that mostly just looks bad.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Usually no treatment is warranted: natural parasites limit it, and insecticides are held until damage has actually been observed. Do not clip out the rolled tips; NC State advises minimizing shearing or clipping of terminals during the growing season. Preserve the parasitic wasps and other natural enemies by keeping broad-spectrum sprays, pyrethroids in particular, off the tree. If treatment is chosen, horticultural oil suppresses adults and nymphs without a residue that harms beneficials, and it must go on early, because sprays are less effective once the leaves have curled.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually nothing needs doing: tiny wasps and other helpers knock it back on their own, and the advice is not to spray until you have actually seen damage. Do not clip off the curled tips; snipping shoot ends during the growing season is something to keep to a minimum. Skip the broad insect sprays so the helpers stay. If a young tree is really being set back, horticultural oil is the gentle option, put on at the first spring growth, before the leaves curl.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Little is required. Keeping the tree healthy and preserving natural enemies keeps the psyllid a cosmetic nuisance rather than a problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: There is not much to do. A healthy tree with its natural predators intact keeps this pest to a harmless nuisance.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Most years this one takes care of itself. Georgia's advice is that the psyllid is often held down by natural parasites and that you should not spray until you have actually seen damage; North Carolina's note, written for native persimmon, is that its numbers soon fall on their own as parasitic wasps and other enemies go to work. So leave the curled leaves alone, keep harsh insect sprays off the tree, and let the helpers finish. If the tree is being stunted and you decide to act, the material North Carolina names is horticultural oil, which smothers the psyllids without leaving a residue that hurts the helpful insects, and it has to go on at the first spring flush, because once the leaves have curled a spray reaches much less.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Usually no treatment: UGA has the psyllid often limited by natural parasites and holds any insecticide until damage has been observed, and NC State describes, on native persimmon, populations that are temporarily abundant and then decline as parasitic wasps and other natural enemies catch up, with egg-to-adult development taking only a few weeks in spring. Conservation is therefore the working control, and pyrethroids, which NC State calls harsh on beneficials, are the wrong tool for it; NC State also advises minimizing the shearing or clipping of terminals during the growing season. Florida's table reads differently, calling for very early control because sprays are less effective once leaves curl, a stance written for an orchard; the home documents govern here. Where a grower does treat a stunted tree, horticultural oil is NC State's choice for sparing beneficials, timed to the first spring flush.

pests.name: Persimmon borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The signs Florida lists for its tree borers as a group, this one among them, are gummy sap, frass or sawdust coming from small holes in the bark, from pruning cuts, or on the trunk near the soil line; for the persimmon borer itself, Georgia places the larvae in the lower trunk and tap roots, so the trunk base is where its damage shows. Georgia calls it a serious pest of both native and oriental persimmons, seen attacking oriental persimmons in Georgia, and Clemson's advice is to monitor for it and to treat if damage is found on the trunk or exposed roots.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Sticky gum, droppings or what looks like sawdust coming out of small holes in the bark, out of old pruning cuts, or from the trunk right at the soil line: that is the list Florida gives for tree borers in general. This one feeds in the lower trunk and the big roots, so the bottom of the trunk is where to look for it. This is the one persimmon pest extension calls serious, so the base of the trunk is worth a look now and then.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the persimmon borer, Sannina uroceriformis, a clearwing moth whose larvae attack the lower trunk and tap roots; it is known from both native and oriental persimmon and has been seen attacking oriental persimmons in Georgia. UF's window for preventive applications is March through June, to stop the larvae before they enter the tree.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae of the persimmon borer, a clearwing moth. They feed in the lower trunk and the large roots of both native and Asian persimmon. The preventive window extension gives is March through June, before the larvae get into the wood.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no documented organic control for the persimmon borer once it is in the tree. UF notes limited direct control information and says controls for peachtree borer may be effective; Georgia says preventive insecticide treatments similar to those for peachtree borer will be required where infestations occur, and UF's window is March through June, to keep the larvae from entering. Wire probing of tunnels is described only for flatheaded borers, a different insect, and not for this one. The organic contribution is monitoring: check the trunk base and exposed roots for gum, frass and sawdust so that damage is found while a preventive program is still worth running.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no organic fix on record for this borer once it is in the tree, and extension does not describe digging the larvae out with a wire for it (that advice is for a different borer). What the guides ask of you is to watch the base of the trunk and any exposed roots for gum, droppings and sawdust. Where the borer is found, what the guides describe is a preventive insecticide program like the one used for peachtree borer, timed March through June before the larvae get in; that is not an organic step, and the guides give no organic one to put in its place.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Monitor: Clemson's instruction is to watch for the persimmon borer and to treat if damage is noted on the trunk or exposed roots, and the signs are gummy sap, frass or sawdust at small holes, pruning cuts or the trunk near the soil line. Where infestations occur, Georgia expects preventive insecticide treatments similar to those made for peachtree borer, and UF's window for them is March through June, ahead of the larvae entering the tree.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check the bottom of the trunk and any roots showing above the soil for fresh gum, droppings or sawdust, since finding damage is what tells you treatment is needed. Where this borer is known to be active, the protection extension describes is a preventive insecticide treatment like the one for peachtree borer, put on from March through June, before the larvae get into the tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Extension gives a persimmon grower one job on this borer: watch for it. Clemson's advice is that it is important to monitor the persimmon borer, and that if borer damage is noted on the trunk or exposed roots, treatment may be required. What to look for, in the signs Florida gives for its tree borers as a group, is gummy sap, droppings or sawdust coming from small holes in the bark, from pruning cuts, or on the trunk near the soil line; Georgia puts this borer's larvae in the lower trunk and tap roots, so the bottom of the trunk and any roots showing above ground are where to look. Raking up under the tree does nothing here, because the larvae are in the wood and the roots, not in anything lying on the ground, and no persimmon guide describes a cleanup step against them. The treatment the guides describe is a preventive insecticide program like the one used for peachtree borer, which Florida times from March through June to stop the larvae getting into the tree, adding that little else is known about controlling it directly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: No home control beyond monitoring and a preventive insecticide program is documented for Sannina uroceriformis. UGA calls it a serious pest of native and oriental persimmons whose larvae attack the lower trunk and tap roots, and says that where infestations occur, preventive insecticide treatments similar to those made for peachtree borer will be required; UF gives the window as March through June applications to keep larvae out of the tree and notes limited direct control information. Clemson's instruction is to monitor, and to treat if damage is noted on the trunk or exposed roots. The signs UF lists for its tree borers as a group, this species among them, are gummy sap, frass or sawdust at small holes, in pruning cuts, or on the trunk near the soil line; for this borer the soil line is the place to read them, since UGA puts its larvae in the lower trunk and tap roots. There is no sanitation target on record for this borer: no persimmon document describes litter, debris or a ground stage for the insect. Wire probing of tunnels is described only for flatheaded borers, a different insect that works the scaffold limbs, and no persimmon document describes it for the persimmon borer.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A rot of the fruit and shoots: Florida's guide lists Gloeosporium as the anthracnose ('bitter rot') that affects fruit and shoots, and Colletotrichum as affecting ripening fruit. A bacterial disease Florida also names on persimmon, Pseudomonas 'bacterial blast', can look similar: it spots leaves and blackens stems and leaf stalks. Texas reports anthracnose as an occasional problem.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A rot that hits the fruit, especially as it ripens, and the shoots. On persimmon it is an occasional problem rather than a regular one. A bacterial disease can look similar, spotting the leaves and blackening the stems and leaf stalks, so a spotted leaf on its own is not proof of anthracnose.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Anthracnose fungi, named for persimmon as Gloeosporium spp. and Colletotrichum sp. The persimmon guides read do not describe where they overwinter on this host or how they spread, and Texas A&M reports the disease as an occasional problem.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungi called anthracnose (Gloeosporium and Colletotrichum) that rot the fruit and shoots. On persimmon it shows up now and then rather than every year, and the guides do not describe how it carries over from one season to the next.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No persimmon document prescribes an organic control. The one management statement, UF's for the leaf-and-fruit-spot complex, is a fungicide program: proactive sprays in early season and cover sprays in summer in rotation, with no material named. Removing rotting fruit from the tree and the ground is ordinary fruit-tree hygiene rather than a documented control for this disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: The persimmon guides do not give a spray-free fix for this. Florida's answer is a fungicide program that starts early in the season and continues with summer cover sprays, and it does not name a product. Picking off rotting fruit and clearing it from under the tree is plain good hygiene for any fruit tree, not a proven cure for this one.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: No persimmon cultivar is named as tolerant of anthracnose in any extension document read, and no cultural prevention is prescribed for it. UF's protectant program begins early in the season, before the fruit rot shows, which is the only preventive timing on record; Texas A&M's experience is that the disease is occasional on a crop largely free of serious disease.
diseases.prevention_beginner: None of the persimmon guides names a variety that resists this rot, and they give no pruning or cleanup step that prevents it. Where it is a real problem, the only prevention on record is Florida's fungicide program, started early in the season before the rot appears. Texas reports it as only an occasional problem.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick rotting fruit off the tree and clear it from underneath as you find it, and look hardest as the fruit ripens, since Florida's guide has one of the two fungi behind this rot hitting ripening fruit and the other affecting fruit and shoots. That is ordinary hygiene for any fruit tree rather than a step a persimmon guide prescribes for this disease, and it is the one no-cost step open to you, because the persimmon guides give no other home step. Florida's answer is a fungicide program that starts early in the season and continues with summer cover sprays, and it names no product; Texas calls anthracnose an occasional problem on a tree that is largely free of serious disease.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removal of rotting fruit is the general fruit-tree practice this step carries; no persimmon document read prescribes it for anthracnose, none describes where the fungus overwinters on this host, and none names a resistant cultivar, so it is stated as hygiene rather than as a documented control. The one management sentence in the persimmon documents read is UF's, for the whole leaf-and-fruit-spot complex in which it lists Gloeosporium (bitter rot of fruit and shoots) and Colletotrichum (ripening fruit): proactive fungicide sprays in early season and cover sprays in summer in rotation, written for Florida and naming no material. Texas A&M's home guide has anthracnose as having occasionally caused problems on a crop largely free of serious diseases, and where pressure is real the Florida program is the documented response.

diseases.name: Phytophthora root and crown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A tree in heavy or poorly drained ground whose leaves turn dull green, yellow or reddish and which may wilt and die quickly with the first warm weather of the season. At the base, darkened areas develop in the bark around the crown and upper roots, sometimes with gum oozing from the edges of the dead area; under the bark, the inner tissue shows reddish brown zones often separated from healthy tissue by a dark line. Asian persimmon on its own roots is highly susceptible.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A tree in wet or heavy ground whose leaves go dull, yellow or reddish, and which may wilt and die fast once the first warm weather arrives. Down at the base, the bark around the crown and the top of the roots turns dark, sometimes with gum oozing at the edge of the dark patch, and if you cut into it the wood underneath is reddish brown with a dark line where it meets healthy tissue. Asian persimmon growing on its own roots is the most easily hit.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Phytophthora water molds (technically not true fungi, being closer to brown algae) that attack roots and the crown in waterlogged soil. Oriental persimmon is highly susceptible to root rot, which is a chief reason it is grafted onto the native D. virginiana rootstock: a species Texas A&M rates only moderately susceptible, and which UF and UC Davis describe as tolerating wet soils and excess moisture. Less susceptible than kaki on its own roots, not immune.
diseases.cause_beginner: Water molds in the soil (Phytophthora, a relative of algae rather than a true fungus) that rot the roots and the crown when the ground stays wet. Asian persimmon is easily hit, which is why it is grafted onto the roots of the native American persimmon, which stands wet soil better, though it is not immune either.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: A tree with a substantial Phytophthora infection rarely recovers: UC IPM's verdict is that lesions larger than about one-quarter of the tree's circumference do not typically recover even with ideal care, while a tree with smaller lesions can sometimes be saved by removing soil from the base of the tree down to the top of the main roots and allowing the crown tissue to dry out. Beyond that one salvage step, UC IPM's instruction is not to rely on pesticide applications alone; management is the site and the roots. Never plant where water stands, improve drainage before planting, set the tree on a mound up to 2 feet high in heavy soil, and buy a tree grafted on native D. virginiana rootstock where drainage is marginal. On an established tree, avoid prolonged saturation or standing water around the base, let the top few inches of soil dry between waterings, keep drip emitters well out from the trunk, and never bury the crown or graft union under soil or mulch.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: A badly infected tree rarely gets better. UC IPM's rule of thumb is that a tree with a dead patch of bark running more than about a quarter of the way around the trunk does not usually recover, even with the best care, while a tree with a smaller patch can sometimes be saved by pulling the soil away from the base of the trunk down to the top of the main roots and letting the crown dry out in the open air. Past that, no spray is the answer on its own; where the tree stands and what roots it is on do the work. Never plant where water stands, fix the drainage before planting, build a mound up to 2 feet high in heavy soil, and pick a tree grafted onto native American persimmon roots if your drainage is doubtful. On a tree already in the ground, never let water pool around the trunk, let the top few inches of soil dry out between waterings, keep drip emitters well away from the trunk, and keep soil and mulch off the crown and graft union.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant only on well-drained ground or a raised berm, select tolerant (native) rootstock in marginal soils, and water deeply but infrequently rather than keeping the root zone saturated.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant only where water drains well, or on a raised mound, choose a tree on native persimmon rootstock if your soil is heavy, and water deeply now and then instead of keeping the soil soggy.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This disease is settled by the ground the tree goes into, not by anything sprayed later. UC IPM's persimmon page says the tree tolerates many soils but requires good drainage; its Phytophthora note says to improve drainage before planting, to set a tree on a mound up to 2 feet high with a gradual slope where the soil is heavy, and never to let water stand or the soil stay saturated around the base of the trunk. Let the top few inches of soil dry between waterings, keep soil and mulch off the crown and graft union, and keep any drip emitter well out from the trunk. If a tree is already sick, UC IPM gives one rescue, and only for a tree whose dead patch of bark at the base is small: pull the soil away from the trunk down to the top of the main roots and leave the crown open to the air so it dries out. A tree whose dead patch runs more than about a quarter of the way around the trunk does not usually recover, even with the best care.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The water molds behind this need free water in the soil to move and infect, so drainage is the control and UC IPM says not to rely on fungicides alone. Its persimmon-specific line is the drainage requirement; the generic prescription is drainage improvement before planting, mounds up to 2 feet high for trees, avoidance of prolonged saturation or standing water at the base, drying the top few inches between irrigations, drip emitters set as far from the trunk as the roots allow, and no soil or mulch over the root crown or graft union. Texas A&M frames the same condition from the rootstock side: the native persimmon thrives from sands to bottomland as long as the soils do not stand in water. On a tree already infected, the page's verdict is that a substantial infection rarely recovers and that lesions larger than about one-quarter of the trunk's circumference do not typically recover even with ideal care; smaller lesions can sometimes be saved by removing soil from the base of the tree down to the top of the main roots and allowing the crown tissue to dry out, which is drying rather than cutting, and so sits with drainage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The roots decide how exposed the tree is. Asian persimmon on its own roots is highly susceptible to root rot; the native American persimmon it is normally grafted onto is only moderately susceptible and tolerates wet soil, and Texas A&M says it is critical that every Asian persimmon be grafted onto it because root rot is prevalent wherever the tree can grow. When you buy, ask what the tree is grafted on. If a nursery offers a tree on Diospyros lotus roots, that one does not tolerate poorly drained soil and is the wrong choice for a damp site.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rootstock is the only resistance lever, and it is named by species rather than cultivar. Texas A&M's ranking is Texas persimmon resistant, American persimmon moderately susceptible, Oriental persimmon highly susceptible, with grafting onto American persimmon called critical; UF describes D. virginiana as providing a tolerance of wet soils, and UC Davis as having a fibrous root system tolerant of both drought and excess moisture, at the cost of non-uniform trees and suckering. UC Davis rules out D. lotus for wet ground, since it does not tolerate poorly drained soils. Tolerance is relative: the native rootstock is less susceptible than kaki on its own roots, not immune, so it stacks on drainage rather than replacing it.

diseases.name: Leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small dead spots on the leaves that grow into angular lesions and can merge into larger blotches; affected leaves yellow and fall early. The infection takes place in spring, at shoot expansion, leaf formation and flowering, and shows later in the season. In a severe year the tree can defoliate in late August as the fruit begins to ripen, and that is where the harm lies: fruit sugar fails to accumulate, fruit ripens poorly, the tree tends toward bearing every other year, and it is more vulnerable to freeze damage. It is not deadly to a mature tree, and most years it is minor on a crop extension calls largely free of serious disease.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small dead spots on the leaves that spread into angular patches and can run together into bigger blotches. Spotted leaves turn yellow and drop early. The tree picks the disease up in spring as the shoots, leaves and flowers are coming out, but you notice it later. In a bad year it can drop most of its leaves in late August just as the fruit is ripening, and that is when it hurts: the fruit does not sweeten or ripen well, the tree may skip a year of fruit, and a freeze can damage it more easily. It is not deadly to a grown tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A leaf-spot complex. The fungus Arkansas's plant clinic names is Pseudocercospora diospyricola (its note calls the disease Cercospora leaf spot of persimmon); Florida's table lists Cercospora alongside Alternaria, Phyllosticta, Ramularia and Botrytis, and a bacterial look-alike, Pseudomonas syringae 'bacterial blast', in the same row; Texas A&M says several fungi. Infection occurs in spring at shoot expansion, leaf formation and flowering.
diseases.cause_beginner: Several fungi can spot persimmon leaves; the one Arkansas's plant clinic names is a Cercospora-type fungus (Pseudocercospora). They get into the tree in spring as the new shoots, leaves and flowers come out. A bacterial disease can spot the leaves too, and it also blackens stems and leaf stalks, which the fungal leaf spot does not do.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Clean up diseased leaves and stems, and remove fallen leaves and debris promptly; keep irrigation off the foliage and water early in the day so it dries. UC IPM's position on leaf spots is that fungicide treatment is generally not warranted, and Texas A&M's that only severe cases warrant treatment; UAEX's fungicide timing, for the severe case, is a cover spray at full bloom and again 3 to 4 weeks later.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick up and remove spotted leaves and dead twigs as they fall and after leaf drop, keep sprinkler water off the leaves, and water in the morning. That is usually all a persimmon needs; the guides say spraying is only for a severe case, meaning a tree that has been losing its leaves in late August while the fruit ripens.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prompt removal of fallen leaves and debris, and irrigation that keeps the foliage dry (no overhead sprinklers; water early in the day), are the preventive measures on record. No persimmon cultivar is named as resistant in the documents read. Where a tree defoliated in late August in a past season, the preventive fungicide timing UAEX gives begins at full bloom.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep fallen leaves cleaned up, keep water off the leaves, and water in the morning so the tree dries fast. None of the guides names a variety that resists leaf spot. If your tree dropped its leaves early in a past year, the protective spray timing starts at full bloom.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Gather up the spotted leaves as they fall, along with any dead twigs, and get them away from the tree rather than leaving them on the ground under it. Arkansas's plant clinic puts it plainly: clean up diseased leaves and stems. Do it through the season as they drop and again after leaf fall.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sanitation is the prescription both documents agree on: UAEX's clean up diseased leaves and stems, and UC IPM's remove fallen leaves and debris promptly. Neither persimmon document states where Pseudocercospora overwinters on this host, so the cleanup is written as removal of diseased tissue rather than as a claim about the source of spring infection, which UAEX places at shoot expansion, leaf formation and flowering.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If you irrigate the tree, keep the water on the ground and off the leaves, and water early in the day so anything that does get wet dries fast. Leaf spot fungi need the leaves to stay wet for a while to take hold.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's leaf-spot guidance is to avoid overhead sprinklers and to irrigate early in the day so the foliage dries more quickly; the target is leaf-wetness duration through the spring infection window. It buys nothing against rain, which is what a wet spring supplies, and it is a delivery and scheduling choice rather than a treatment.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Most persimmons never need a spray for leaf spot: UC IPM says fungicide treatment is generally not warranted for leaf spots, and Texas A&M says only severe cases warrant treatment. A severe case is a tree that dropped its leaves in late August in past years, right as the fruit was ripening, because that is when the disease costs you: fruit that does not sweeten or ripen properly, a crop only every other year, and a tree more easily hurt by freezes. For that tree, chlorothalonil is the protectant Arkansas names as labeled for this leaf spot on persimmon, timed as a cover spray at full bloom and again 3 to 4 weeks later. Chlorothalonil carries a bee precaution against spraying anything in flower, so a bloom-time application has to fit the evening window the label allows, if it allows one. Check that the label lists persimmon, wear gloves, long sleeves and goggles, and keep it out of ponds and drains.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A rescue reserved for the severe case. UAEX's timing is a fungicide cover spray during full bloom and again 3 to 4 weeks later, and it names two labeled products, a chlorothalonil formulation and a strobilurin with no counterpart in the home materials here; UC IPM's general position is that fungicide treatment is not warranted for leaf spots, and Texas A&M's that only severe cases warrant it. The infection window UAEX gives, shoot expansion, leaf formation and flowering, is why the first spray sits at bloom, and that slot collides with chlorothalonil's honey-bee precaution, which confines any application over open flowers to the sunset-to-midnight window a label may allow. The severity threshold UAEX supplies is defoliation in late August as the fruit ripens, with the sugar, ripening, biennial-bearing and freeze consequences that follow.

diseases.name: Botryosphaeria twig dieback
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Discolored wood and deep, elongated scars in the bark of limbs and trunk. In the symptoms Florida attributes to Botryosphaeria together with Phomopsis and Verticillium, twigs at the branch ends die back and stand leafless, leaves and fruit may be small, shoots wilt and decline, and bark cracks at the limb joints. Florida's guide calls this disease the limiting factor for growing persimmons in Florida and the Deep South, and says it often limits the lifetime of a Japanese persimmon to about 8 to 12 years or less. Clemson lists twig dieback among South Carolina's persimmon diseases.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Deep, long scars in the bark and dark, discolored wood under it; branch tips that die back and stay bare; small leaves and fruit; shoots that wilt and go downhill; bark that splits where limbs join the trunk. In Florida and across the Deep South this is the disease that decides how long a persimmon lives: often only 8 to 12 years, sometimes less.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botryosphaeria canker fungi: Florida names Botryosphaeria dothidea, B. rhodinina, B. obtusa and B. ribis, and lists B. dothidea again with Phomopsis spp. and Verticillium albo-atrum as causes of leafless terminal twigs, shoot decline and bark cracking at limb joints. It is the limiting factor for persimmons in Florida and the Deep South. It is distinct from persimmon wilt (Cephalosporium diospyri), which wilts and kills the top of a tree through the native rootstock while D. kaki and D. lotus are immune, and from the leaf-spot fungi.
diseases.cause_beginner: A group of canker fungi called Botryosphaeria that get into the wood of the limbs and trunk, scarring the bark and killing twigs. In the Deep South it is the disease that shortens a persimmon's life; Florida's guide says trees there often last only 8 to 12 years because of it. It is a separate problem from leaf spot and from the wilt disease that kills native persimmon through its roots.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no good chemical control, so the treatment is pruning practice and tree care, all of it aimed at reducing incidence rather than curing: prune on dry days, disinfect tools, train to wide crotch angles, maintain good airflow in the canopy, and reduce water and nutrient stress on the tree. Dead and diseased wood comes out as part of ordinary persimmon pruning (UC IPM's persimmon page has established trees pruned of suckers and dead wood; Texas A&M removes diseased and broken branches; Clemson removes dead or injured ones), and no persimmon document sets a cut-back margin below a canker. Florida's guide also lists a good fungicide program among the incidence-reducers while stating there is no good chemical control, and it names no material; Clemson adds that chemical control on large trees is usually not feasible because the foliage cannot be covered.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: No spray cures this, so it comes down to how you prune and how you care for the tree. Cut out dead twigs and any dead, diseased or broken branch, which is ordinary pruning for a persimmon, prune only on dry days, and clean your tools between cuts. Keep the tree open to the air, shape young trees so branches meet the trunk at wide angles, and do not let the tree go short of water or nutrients. Florida's guide says even its fungicide program only helps reduce the disease, not stop it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prevention is the same set of practices, begun before the disease is visible: train the young tree to wide crotch angles, keep good airflow in the canopy, prune during dry weather with disinfected tools, and avoid water or nutrient stress. Persimmon seldom needs or benefits from heavy pruning, so the structural work is light and early. In the Deep South, plan on a tree whose productive life this disease may cap at 8 to 12 years; Florida's guide names no resistant cultivar or rootstock.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start early: shape a young tree so its branches meet the trunk at wide angles, keep it open to moving air, prune only when it is dry and with clean tools, and do not let it go thirsty or hungry. Persimmon does not need hard pruning, so keep the cuts light. Florida's guide names no variety or rootstock that resists this disease, and in the Deep South it warns that the tree may last only 8 to 12 years because of it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the canopy open enough that air moves through it. Florida's guide lists maintaining good airflow in the canopy among the practices that reduce this disease, and it also says heavy pruning of persimmon is often not required or beneficial, so the aim is an open, uncrowded tree rather than a hard cutback. Give a young tree room from its neighbors and from walls, and thin crowded growth lightly instead of shearing it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: One of the incidence-reducers in UF's Botryosphaeria cell is maintaining good airflow in the canopy, alongside pruning practice and stress reduction. UF adds that heavy pruning of persimmon is often not required or beneficial, which sets the scale: openness by site and light thinning, since the same document's other lever is keeping stress off the tree. UF states the practice without a mechanism, and no persimmon document supplies one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no good chemical control for this disease, so the pruning saw is the tool, and how you prune matters as much as what you cut. Take out dead and dying twigs and any dead, diseased or broken branch, which the persimmon guides call for as ordinary pruning, and get the prunings away from the tree. Prune only on dry days, and wipe or dip your tools between cuts so you are not carrying the fungus to the next branch. When shaping a young tree, keep the branches at wide angles to the trunk: Florida ties this disease to bark cracking at the limb joints and asks for wide crotch angles, and Texas takes out narrow-crotched limbs because they create dead areas on the limbs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UF's control cell for Botryosphaeria canker begins with no good chemical control and then names the practices: pruning to wide crotch angles, pruning during dry days, disinfecting tools, maintaining airflow, reducing water or nutrient stress, and a fungicide program, all recommended to reduce incidence rather than to cure. The pruning practices are what this carries: dry-day pruning, tool disinfection between cuts and wide crotch angles at training. Removal of dead and diseased wood rests on the general persimmon pruning guidance rather than on the Botryosphaeria cell (UC IPM's prune out suckers or dead wood in established trees; Texas A&M's remove crossover, shaded, diseased and broken branches; Clemson's remove dead or injured branches), and no persimmon document sets a margin for cutting back below a canker, so none is given. The symptom cell describes discoloration of the wood and deep, elongated bark scars, and the second UF row naming B. dothidea adds leafless terminal twigs, shoot decline and bark cracking at limb joints. Clemson notes that chemical control on large trees is usually not feasible for want of coverage. Expect management, not eradication: UF has the fungus limiting Japanese persimmons in the Deep South to about 8 to 12 years.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently. A young tree wants a deep soak about once or twice a week through its first two seasons; an established tree is fairly drought-tolerant and does well on roughly weekly deep watering in summer heat, less in cool weather and little through winter dormancy. Persimmon prefers infrequent, thorough irrigation over frequent shallow watering, and standing-wet soil invites root rot.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply now and then rather than a little every day. A young tree needs a deep soak about once or twice a week for its first couple of years. An older tree handles dry spells well and is happy with roughly a weekly deep soak in summer, less when it is cool, and almost nothing in winter. Do not keep the soil soggy, since that causes root rot.
watering.amount_seasoned: Soak deeply enough to wet the full root zone rather than just the surface: on the order of 5 gallons per watering for a young tree, and roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week for a bearing tree through the growing season, more in extreme heat. Deep, thorough soaks drive the deep rooting that carries an established persimmon through dry stretches.
watering.amount_beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak; an older, fruiting tree wants about an inch of water a week through the growing season, and more in a heat wave. Deep soaks build deep roots that handle dry spells.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose out toward the drip line, keeping the trunk base from staying wet. Persimmon tolerates drought better than waterlogging, so the discipline is deep-then-dry, never continuously saturated. Overhead watering that wets the canopy in humid regions can encourage anthracnose and leaf spot.
watering.method_beginner: Water the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, out to the edge of the branches, and keep the base of the trunk from sitting wet. Persimmon handles dry better than soggy, so let the soil dry a bit between waterings. In humid areas, avoid spraying water over the leaves, which can bring on leaf diseases.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing leaves, wilting that persists in wet soil, and general decline point to waterlogging and possible root or crown rot, to which persimmon (especially Asian types) is prone. Soil that never dries between waterings is the warning; this is far more dangerous to persimmon than underwatering.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Yellow leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and a tree slowly going downhill mean too much water and the risk of root rot, which persimmon catches easily. Soil that never dries out is your signal to back off. Overwatering hurts persimmon more than underwatering does.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, dull or curling leaves, slowed growth, and, most tellingly, premature fruit drop or small, poorly sized fruit when a tree runs dry during fruit development. An established persimmon endures moderate drought but sizes its crop poorly under sustained water stress.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting, dull or curling leaves, slower growth, and, the clearest sign, fruit dropping early or staying small when the tree gets too dry while the fruit is filling out. An older persimmon can take some dryness, but the crop suffers if it goes too dry for too long.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~5 gal per watering
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil evenly moist but never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system persimmon relies on later.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow the deep roots it needs.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~1 in per week equivalent
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: During fruit development, keep moisture steady; sudden drought or a wet-dry swing in this window contributes to premature fruit drop and small fruit. Aim for the equivalent of about an inch of water a week, delivered as deep soaks, more in heat.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the fruit is sizing up, keep the water steady. Letting the tree swing from dry to wet now can make the fruit drop or stay small. Aim for about an inch of water a week as deep soaks, more when it is hot.

schedule_by_stage.rate: minimal
