failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Few or no seedlings emerged. The overwhelmingly common cause is old seed: parsnip seed loses viability within a year. Beyond that, the seed is naturally slow (often 2 to 3 weeks or more) and the fine seedlings cannot break a dried or crusted surface, so a bed that dried out during germination, was sown too deep, or stayed too cold accounts for most failures.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Few or no seedlings came up. The number one reason is old seed, because parsnip seed goes bad fast. On top of that, the seed is slow (often 2 to 3 weeks or more) and the tiny sprouts cannot push through a dried, crusted surface, so a bed that dried out, seeds planted too deep, or soil that was too cold are the usual culprits.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Buy fresh seed every year and sow generously. Keep the surface evenly moist from sowing to emergence, sow shallowly (about 1/2 inch), wait for soil near 50°F, and interseed fast radishes to mark the row and keep the surface open.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use fresh seed every year and sow a bit thickly. Keep the soil surface damp from planting until the seedlings appear, sow shallow (about 1/2 inch), wait until the soil is around 50°F, and scatter a few fast radish seeds to mark the row.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Forked or twisted roots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Forked or twisted parsnips
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The long taproot split into prongs or grew crooked because it met an obstruction as it drove down: a stone, clod, hardpan, or pocket of fresh manure or concentrated fertilizer. Transplanting parsnips causes the same damage.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The root split into several prongs or grew crooked because it hit something hard as it grew down: a rock, a clod, packed soil, or a lump of fresh manure or fertilizer. Moving a started parsnip does the same thing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Work the bed deep and fine, removing stones and clods to at least 12 inches; avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen, use well-finished compost, and always direct-sow. On heavy or rocky ground, grow shorter cultivars or use a deep, loose raised bed.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Before planting, dig the bed deep, break up clods, and pull out rocks (at least 12 inches down). Skip fresh manure and heavy fertilizer, use finished compost, and always plant the seeds where they will grow. In rocky or heavy soil, grow short parsnip types or a deep raised bed.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Split or cracked roots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Split or cracked parsnips
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Roots cracked lengthwise, usually because a dry spell was followed by heavy watering or rain: the root takes up water rapidly and the tissue splits. Over-mature roots left long in the ground are also prone to cracking.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The parsnips cracked open, usually because the soil went dry and then got soaked: the root drinks fast and splits. Roots left in the ground a very long time also crack more easily.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture even, roughly 1 inch per week, rather than letting the bed swing from dry to flooded, and mulch to buffer the soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water steadily, about 1 inch a week, instead of letting the soil go dry and then soaking it, and mulch to keep the moisture even.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Brown or black rot on the shoulders (canker)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Brown rotten patches on the tops of the roots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Reddish-brown to black cankers formed on the crown and shoulders of the roots, sometimes letting other organisms rot the whole root. This is Itersonilia canker, a fungal disease worse in cool, wet weather and on late-harvested crops, and carrot rust fly damage predisposes roots to it. (UMass)
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tops and shoulders of the roots developed brown to black rotten patches, which can spread into the whole root. This is parsnip canker, a fungal disease that is worse in cool, wet weather and on roots left late, and it gets in more easily where carrot rust fly maggots have damaged the root. (UMass)
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose canker-resistant varieties. Rotate with crops the pathogen doesn't infect, keeping carrot, coriander and parsley out of the rotation too. Hill soil over the root shoulders throughout the season. Control carrot rust fly. Grow in loose, well-drained soil. Dig old parsnip residue in deeply after harvest. Fungicide sprays don't control root cankers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow a canker-resistant variety. Rotate parsnips with crops this disease doesn't infect. Keep the tops of the roots covered with soil all season. Control carrot rust fly. Grow them in loose soil that drains well. Bury old parsnip plants deep in the soil after harvest. Sprays won't fix root canker.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plant flowers and root turns woody (bolting)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Parsnip shoots up a flower stalk and the root goes woody
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Parsnip is a biennial: in its first year it stores energy in the root, and in its second year it sends up a tall flower stalk and the root turns fibrous and woody. Overwintered roots left in the ground past spring will bolt, ruining the root. An unusually cold spell on a first-year crop can occasionally trigger early bolting.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Parsnip is a biennial, which means it lives two years: the first year it makes the root you eat, and the second year it sends up a tall flower stalk and the root turns tough and woody. If you leave overwintered parsnips in the ground into spring, they bolt and the roots are ruined.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Harvest the root in its first fall through winter, and dig any overwintered roots before growth resumes in spring. Use fresh seed and sow at the recommended time to avoid a hard cold check on tiny seedlings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Dig parsnips in their first fall and winter, and get any you left in over winter out of the ground before they start growing again in spring. Plant at the right time so the seedlings do not get a hard cold shock early.

primary.name: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
UC ANR Master Gardener -- Time of planting (regional Table 13.2)

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Parsnip is a long-season crop sown once a year and left to size up over many months, so it is not succession sown the way fast crops like radishes or lettuce are. A single spring sowing where summers are cool, or a single fall sowing where summers are hot, carries the whole season, and the roots are then held in the ground and harvested across fall and winter.

open_findings.summary: Hot-region calendars are partly modeled, not parsnip-specific-sourced. UGA C943 and UF/IFAS VH021 do NOT list parsnip; the fl_peninsula and hawaii_tropical windows are flagged models (cool-season principle + Clemson coastal analog), and warm_arid + low_desert_az are modeled from Texas A&M fall-sowing guidance plus the desert cool-season calendar (no readable NM/AZ parsnip source; planting-calendar PDFs were denied/404). Parsnip is genuinely marginal-to-unsuited in FL z11 and tropical-lowland Hawaii; noted honestly in region_notes.

days_to_maturity set to [100,130] (mid 120). Texas A&M gives 100 to 120 days; Clemson gives a longer 120 to 180 for late South Carolina crops. The record uses the 100 to 120 mainstream figure and notes the longer late-crop range in prose. Worth a reviewer confirm of the headline range.

Carrot rust fly and leafminer symptom prose is standard extension knowledge cited to USU's root-crop pest list and RHS, which name the pests for the carrot/parsnip group; the dedicated UC IPM / UMN symptom pages were not separately readable (404/redirect). The canker (UMass) and aster yellows (Wisconsin Horticulture) entries are directly sourced.

Texas A&M parsnip page (aggie-hort.tamu.edu) content was retrieved via search but the page enters an http/https cross-host redirect loop in the fetcher; cited as tamu_agrilife. Re-verify the live URL at certification.

germination_temp_f set to [50,70] and pH preferred [6.0,7.0]. pH is anchored to Clemson's 6.0 to 6.5 liming target for the root-crop group plus the broader 6.0 to 7.0 consensus; germination soil temp is anchored to RHS (about 54°F / 12°C) plus the cool-season range. A parsnip-specific T1 numeric for the exact germination band would strengthen these.

ca_interior was shifted from the UC Master Gardener table's literal parsnip listing (Interior Valleys May to July) to a peer-aligned FALL sowing (Sep to Oct, heat_pause May to Aug, winter harvest). Reason: the certified cool-season peers carrot and lettuce both heat_pause May to July in the interior valleys, and parsnip seed germinates poorly above about 85°F, so a May-to-July direct sowing there is biologically questionable and trips the cool-season-timing guardrail's intent (docs/kickoffs/05-author-bot/KICKOFF.md, 2026-06-29). The app-side audit (audit-cool-season-timing.mjs) shows zero hits because the calendar and plant_out are internally consistent; this is a SUBSTANCE call, not a mechanical one. The mild CA coasts (north coast May to Jun, south coast Mar to Jul) were kept on UC MG since carrot, the closest Apiaceae peer, does not heat_pause those coasts. Reviewer should confirm the interior fall window vs UC MG.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Author-fresh scale pilot (Claude Code lane). Modeled structurally on certified carrot (Apiaceae). Sourced from clemson_hgic, umn_ext, rhs, ucanr_ext_mg_timeplanting, umass_ext, usu_ext, uwi_hort, tamu_agrilife, wvu_ext. Refit for parsnip: long season (~100 to 120 days), slow/erratic germination + fresh-seed requirement, cold-sweetening and in-ground overwintering, biennial bolting, sap phytophotodermatitis, Itersonilia canker. Queued for the daily biology-fidelity review.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the cold-winter North, parsnips are direct-sown in spring once the soil is workable and about 50°F, which UMN places near May 1 in Minnesota, running earlier toward the warmer zone-7 edge. (UMN Extension) Fresh seed is sown each year because parsnip seed loses viability quickly. (Clemson HGIC)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Parsnips need a long season, roughly 100 to 120 days and often more, so a single spring sowing matures from early fall onward. (Texas A&M AgriLife; Clemson HGIC)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roots are left in the cooling ground and harvested after frost; UMN notes the later they are dug, the sweeter they are, and in the colder zones the row is mulched heavily to keep digging into winter or early spring. (UMN Extension)

3.zone_notes: In zone 3 the ground freezes hard, so most roots are dug in fall after the first frosts; any held over winter need a deep straw mulch.

7.zone_notes: In the milder zone-7 edge, mulched parsnips can be left in the ground and dug right through winter into early spring, gaining sweetness with each frost.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold-winter North, plant parsnips once in spring, as soon as the soil has thawed and warmed to about 50°F (around May 1 in the coldest areas, a few weeks earlier toward the milder edge). Buy fresh seed every year, because parsnip seed does not keep, and be patient: it can take 2 to 3 weeks to come up. The plants grow slowly all summer, and you do not harvest until fall. Wait until after several frosts, because cold weather turns the roots sweet. You can leave parsnips right in the ground and dig them as you need them; in the coldest zones, pile straw over the row so you can keep digging into winter, or dig them all before the ground freezes solid. Most are ready about 100 to 120 days after planting.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Northern-tier parsnips are a single long-season crop, not a succession crop. Direct-sow in spring once the soil reaches about 50°F (UMN places this near May 1 in Minnesota, earlier toward zone 7), using fresh seed each year because parsnip seed loses viability fast. Germination is slow and erratic, often 2 to 3 weeks. The crop grows through summer and is harvested in fall after frost; flavor improves with cold as starch converts to sugar, so there is no rush to lift it. In zones 3 to 5 most roots are dug in fall and stored, with any held over winter under a heavy straw mulch; in the milder zone-7 edge the row can be mulched and dug through winter into early spring. Days to maturity run about 100 to 120 and often longer for a late crop. Windows verified against UMN Extension and Clemson HGIC; cold-sweetening against Texas A&M AgriLife.

(Clemson HGIC) Texas A&M advises sowing in late summer or early fall so the crop matures under cold weather. (Texas A&M AgriLife)

The crop is handled as a fall-sown, winter-harvested vegetable, and those hot months carry no sowing or active growth. (Clemson HGIC; Texas A&M AgriLife)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, grow parsnips as a fall and winter crop and skip the hot months. Sow seed from about September into October (use fresh seed every year, since it does not keep), let the plants grow through the cool fall, and harvest in winter after a frost, which sweetens the roots. You can leave them in the ground and dig as needed. Spring sowings are possible but the roots mature into summer heat and turn coarse and strong, so the fall crop is much better. Most parsnips take about 100 to 120 days to be ready.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: In the Southeast and Gulf, parsnip is a fall-sown, winter-harvested crop; summer heat excludes it. Clemson's South Carolina coastal calendar sows it from about mid-August to mid-October, and Texas A&M advises late-summer or early-fall sowing so the crop matures under cold weather. (Clemson HGIC; Texas A&M AgriLife) Use fresh seed each year. The roots size up through the cool months and are best dug after a hard killing frost, which converts starch to sugar, and can be held in the ground and pulled as needed. The binding boundary is heat, not frost: a parsnip maturing into late-spring and summer warmth turns coarse and strong-flavored, so the spring window is omitted in favor of the fall crop. Days to maturity run about 100 to 120.

(UC ANR Master Gardener Program; Texas A&M AgriLife) Fresh seed is used each year.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Parsnips set out Sep 15 - Dec 31 in the Rio Grande Valley, per Bilingual LRGV planting table (Vegetable Crops of the Lower Rio Grande Valley). Direct-sown mid-September through December (Bilingual LRGV table); 100 to 120 days to harvest is long even by root-crop standards, so plant early in the window for a spring harvest.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest harvest at about 100 days, from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest harvest at about 120 days, from the latest set-out date, before RGV's spring heat closes the window.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, grow parsnips in the cool season, not summer. Plant Sep 15 through Dec 31 and harvest from Dec 24 into spring; it rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold. Parsnips take their time: sow direct from mid-September through the end of December and let the roots develop slowly through the cool months, sweetest after a cool spell. Skip planting parsnips from spring through summer: the Valley heat keeps them from growing well here.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Parsnips in the RGV run on the winter-garden calendar: direct-sow Sep 15 through Dec 31, with harvest running Dec 24 through Apr 30. Direct-sown mid-September through December (Bilingual LRGV table); 100 to 120 days to harvest is long even by root-crop standards, so plant early in the window for a spring harvest. Frost is essentially absent here, so timing is heat-bounded rather than cold-bounded. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: the TAMU AgriLife sources describe a single Valley-wide planting calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Parsnip is a single long-season sowing in the maritime PNW (OSU EM9027: valley April-May, coast May-June), left in the ground to size up over summer and dug from fall through winter as roots sweeten with cold. Sources: osu_ext, wsu_ext.

8.zone_notes: OSU EM9027 places the valley's parsnip window at April into May; the long, mild season here lets roots size up all summer, and the mild winter supports digging right through to spring, the same overwintering pattern the coldest northern-tier zones only reach at their very mildest edge.

9.zone_notes: OSU gives the coast a later May-to-June window than the valley's April-May start; once the winter harvest finishes in March, April is a genuine gap before the next sowing goes in.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: West of the Cascades, sow parsnip once a year, April into May in the valley or May into June on the coast, using fresh seed each year. The roots grow slowly all summer, and you wait to dig them until fall, because cold turns their starch to sugar and makes them sweet. Mild winters here let you keep digging right through to early spring.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: OSU Extension's Oregon planting-date table (EM9027) places the valley's parsnip window at April into May and the coast's a little later, May into June. This is a single sowing, not a succession crop: the long, cool maritime summer carries the root through its full 100-to-130 day maturity, and the mild winter lets it be dug straight through into early spring rather than forcing a fall-only harvest. Flavor improves with cold, so there is no rush to lift the crop once it matures.

crops.description_seasoned: Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa) is a long-season, cool-climate root crop in the carrot family, grown for its sweet, ivory taproot. It is direct-sown only, and the single most important rule is fresh seed: parsnip seed loses viability within a year, so old seed is the leading cause of failure. Germination is notoriously slow and erratic, often 2 to 3 weeks and sometimes far longer, and the fine seedlings cannot push through a crusted surface, so the seedbed must stay evenly moist for weeks. The crop needs deep, loose, stone-free soil for its long root (commonly 8 to 12 inches) and grows for roughly 100 to 120 days, longer for a late crop. Parsnip is a biennial grown as an annual for the root: it stores energy the first year and bolts to flower the second, so overwintered roots are dug before spring regrowth. Its defining trait is cold-sweetening: frost converts root starch to sugar, so parsnips are harvested after hard frost and are famously left in the ground over winter, dug as needed and growing sweeter the longer they wait. Where summers are hot, parsnip is a fall-sown, winter-harvested crop. One handling note: the foliage and sap can cause a skin rash in sunlight, so gloves are worn when working among the plants on bright days.
crops.description_beginner: Parsnips are a long-season, cool-weather root vegetable in the carrot family. The part you eat is one long, sweet, cream-colored root. Always plant the seeds right where they will grow, and use fresh seed every single year, because parsnip seed goes bad fast and old seed is the main reason parsnips fail. Be patient: the seeds are very slow, often 2 to 3 weeks or more to come up, and they will not break through a dry crust, so keep the surface damp. Parsnips need deep, loose, rock-free soil for their long root (often 8 to 12 inches) and take a long time, about 100 to 120 days. They are a biennial, which means if you leave them past their first winter they shoot up a flower and the root turns woody, so dig overwintered ones before spring. The best thing about parsnips is that frost makes them sweet: the cold turns starch into sugar, so you harvest them after frost and can leave them in the ground all winter, digging them as you need them, sweeter every week. In hot-summer areas, grow them in fall for a winter harvest. One safety note: the leaves and juice can give some people a skin rash in sunlight, so wear gloves on sunny days.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Parsnips are ready when the roots have sized up, often 1 1/2 to 2 inches across at the shoulder and 8 to 12 inches long, with the tops beginning to die back in fall, usually around 100 to 120 days from sowing. But the real cue is cold, not the calendar: flavor sweetens markedly after the roots sit through several frosts as starch converts to sugar, so there is no rush to lift them. In mild soil they hold for weeks, and in cold regions a heavy straw mulch lets them overwinter for pull-as-needed harvest through winter and into early spring, growing sweeter the longer they wait. Loosen the soil beside the row with a spading fork before pulling, because the long roots snap easily. Lift any overwintered roots before they regrow in spring, since once the plant bolts the root turns woody. Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling the foliage in bright sun, as the sap can cause a skin rash.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Parsnips are ready when the roots are full sized, often 1 1/2 to 2 inches across at the top and 8 to 12 inches long, with the leafy tops dying down in fall, usually about 100 to 120 days after planting. But the real signal is cold weather, not a date: parsnips get much sweeter after a few frosts, as the cold turns starch into sugar, so there is no rush. They keep right in the ground, and in cold areas you can pile straw over the row and dig them through winter and into early spring, and they taste sweeter the longer they wait. Loosen the soil next to the row with a garden fork before pulling, because the long roots break easily. Dig any you left in over winter before they start growing again in spring, or the root turns woody. Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling the leaves on a sunny day, since the sap can give some people a rash.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Parsnip quality is set in the seedbed more than anywhere else, because the root runs long, commonly 8 to 12 inches, and any obstruction forks or stunts it. Work the bed deep and fine, loosening and removing stones, clods, and debris to at least 12 inches. A loose sandy loam gives the straightest, longest roots; heavy clay and compacted ground produce short, forked roots and are best improved with compost or worked into deep raised beds. Avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen, which drive forked, hairy roots and lush tops at the expense of the root; use only well-finished compost and a low-nitrogen balanced feeding such as 5-10-10. Rake the surface smooth and fine, since the small, slow seeds need close contact and an even, crust-free surface to emerge over their long germination. Aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH, about 6.0 to 7.0, liming ahead of sowing if a soil test calls for it.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: With parsnips, getting the bed right before you plant matters more than almost anything else, because the root grows very long (8 to 12 inches) and anything it hits makes it fork or come out stubby. Dig and loosen the soil at least 12 inches down and pull out rocks, hard clumps, and roots. Loose, sandy soil grows the straightest parsnips; heavy clay grows short, twisted ones, so mix in compost or use a deep raised bed. Do not add fresh manure or a lot of high-nitrogen fertilizer, which grows leafy tops and forked, hairy roots; use finished compost and a low-nitrogen blend like 5-10-10. Rake the top smooth and fine so the small, slow seeds sit snug against the soil, and aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 7.0, adding lime ahead of time only if a soil test says so.

pet_safe.note: All parts contain furanocoumarins that can make skin sun-sensitive in cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Kohlrabi

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Kohlrabi grows best in fertile, loose, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in, and it likes steady, even moisture. The bulb stays tender and mild when the plant grows quickly without a check, so soil that holds moisture but drains well is ideal. Soil that dries out or stays soggy stresses the plant and makes the stem tough and woody.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Kohlrabi does best in a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter held at even moisture, like the other cole crops. The whole game is fast, uninterrupted growth: a tender, mild swollen stem forms when the plant never checks, while drought, heat, or a stop-start water supply turns it woody, fibrous, and bitter and can crack it. Work in compost before planting and keep the bed evenly moist. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic, poorly drained ground, so keep drainage good and the pH up where it is a concern.

ph.note_beginner: Kohlrabi grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, a brassica soil disease, keeping the soil closer to neutral helps hold it back.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (Iowa State gives 6 to 7; Minnesota and Utah State put the workable range at about 6.0 to 7.5). Kohlrabi tolerates roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Clubroot, the major brassica soil disease, is favored by acidic soil below about 6.5, so where it is a concern lime acidic ground well ahead of planting and hold the pH toward neutral.

fertilizer.timing: work a balanced fertilizer in before planting, then side-dress about 3 to 4 weeks later
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 worked in before planting, then 21-0-0 or blood meal as a side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Kohlrabi is a moderate feeder that wants steady, even growth rather than a late surge. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Iowa State: 1 to 2 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting or thinning, when the plants are roughly 4 inches tall (Utah State: about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row). Keep nitrogen and water even through bulbing, since both a stall and a late flush hurt texture; avoid heavy late nitrogen, which can grow leaves at the expense of a clean bulb.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Kohlrabi needs decent soil and a little feeding, but not a lot. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give one feeding of a nitrogen fertilizer a few weeks later when the plants are a few inches tall. Keep the watering and feeding steady so the bulbs grow smoothly and stay tender.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your kohlrabi with nitrogen as the plants establish.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your kohlrabi.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced base feed for steady growth: work a 10-10-10 into the bed before planting, then a single nitrogen side-dress such as 21-0-0 or blood meal about 3 to 4 weeks after planting. Keep it modest and even, since pushing the plant late grows leaves over a clean, tender bulb.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then one feeding of a nitrogen fertilizer a few weeks later as the plants take off.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work in about 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress with about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row roughly 3 to 4 weeks after planting, banded beside the row and watered in.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a light nitrogen feed beside the plants a few weeks later.

companions.note_beginner: Kohlrabi gets along with most vegetables. It does well next to aromatic herbs, onions and other alliums, beets, and quick leafy greens like lettuce that finish before the kohlrabi fills out. The main thing is to keep it away from its own cabbage-family relatives, which share its pests and diseases.
companions.note_seasoned: Most kohlrabi companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage-family pests, low quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the kohlrabi sizes up, and beets sharing the cool-season bed. The well-grounded caution is to separate kohlrabi from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect. As University of Minnesota stresses, treat most companion claims as a starting point and watch your own results.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions, garlic, and chives grow tall and narrow with shallow roots, so they tuck between kohlrabi without crowding it, and their strong smell is widely used to help confuse cabbage-family pests.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking of brassica pests is a long-standing companion tradition with partial mechanistic support; not trial-isolated for kohlrabi, so low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, they tuck around kohlrabi without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other leafy greens
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low, so you can tuck it between young kohlrabi plants to use the space and shade the soil, and it is harvested long before the kohlrabi fills in. Both like the same cool weather.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pairing fast, shallow cool-season greens with a slower-bulbing brassica is the standard complementary space-and-timing rationale; sound and widely taught but a space benefit rather than a measured kohlrabi-specific effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce and kohlrabi interplant well on structure and timing: lettuce is shallow and quick, kohlrabi a little slower, so the lettuce uses the open ground and light between young plants and is pulled before the kohlrabi canopies. It is an efficient cool-season space pairing, not a pest effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beets
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beets are another cool-season crop that shares the bed easily with kohlrabi without competing for the same space, since beets put their energy down into the root while kohlrabi swells just above the soil.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A common cool-season bedfellow pairing based on complementary growth and season; not a trial-isolated kohlrabi effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beets are a traditional, low-risk cool-season neighbor for kohlrabi. They share the same season and undemanding habit, and the beet works the soil below while the kohlrabi swells at the surface, so the two coexist without much competition. A space-and-season pairing rather than a documented benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional brassica companion whose scent is thought to deter cabbage pests; shallow-rooted and low-competition. A plausible, low-risk pairing rather than a documented effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking lore for brassicas; not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other leafy greens
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A quick, shallow cool-season crop that uses the open ground and light between young kohlrabi plants and is harvested long before they fill in. Space-driven and traditional, not a documented growth effect; the two share no serious pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use intercropping lore; no T1 source documents a lettuce-kohlrabi benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Beets
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season bedfellow that works the soil below while kohlrabi swells at the surface, so the two share space without much competition. Traditional and low-risk rather than a documented benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Complementary cool-season root-vs-surface pairing; not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack the aphids and cabbage caterpillars kohlrabi shares with the cole crops, and the scent is traditionally said to deter cabbage pests. Let some flower, and keep it from shading the plants.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Umbel beneficial-insect attraction is extension-noted for the cole crops; the specific dill-kohlrabi pairing is not trial-isolated.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep kohlrabi away from other cabbage-family plants like cabbage, broccoli, kale, and turnips. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them together makes problems worse.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same-family crops share pests and pathogens, so clustering raises pest/disease pressure, and successive brassica planting builds soil-borne clubroot. A sound epidemiological/rotation mechanism rather than a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planting kohlrabi shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, cabbage, broccoli, kale, turnip, radish, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbageworms, loopers, flea beetles, cabbage aphids, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

bad_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cabbage, broccoli, kale, turnip, and the other cole crops share kohlrabi's clubroot and cabbage-family pests, so grouping them concentrates disease and pest pressure. A real rotation and disease principle rather than a tested adjacency effect; the practical rule is to spread brassicas out and rotate them.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared clubroot and shared cabbage-family pests are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a known agronomic principle, not formally pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Pole beans
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution pairs the cabbage family with pole beans as poor neighbors. There is no documented mechanism or T1 support; it persists as folklore, and the two also want different seasons.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk anti-companion claim with no pattern match or T1 support.

pests.name: Cabbageworms, loopers, and diamondback moths
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings. The leaves are part of why you grow kohlrabi well, and the caterpillars can also chew the bulb.
pests.cause_beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants like kohlrabi and chew the leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray Bt, which is low in toxicity to people, pets and bees and acts on caterpillars rather than on insects in general, or spinosad. Bt cannot tell a pest caterpillar from a butterfly one, so treat only the plants that have a problem. Pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; heavy feeding sets young plants back and the larvae can score the bulb. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green, loopers move in a looping arch, and diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Kohlrabi is a primary host.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from planting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear away old cabbage-family plants when a crop is finished. The caterpillars pass part of their life cycle as pupae, a resting stage, sheltered in that leftover debris, so hauling it off leaves fewer moths and butterflies to start the next round.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing spent brassica material takes out the debris that shelters pupae between plantings, trimming the local population of imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper and diamondback moth before the next crop goes in.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put a light fabric row cover over the plants right after planting. It lets in light and water but keeps the white butterflies and small moths from landing to lay eggs, and eggs they cannot lay are caterpillars you do not have to deal with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cover from planting with floating row cover or fine mesh to exclude the egg-laying adults of all three species at once. Kohlrabi is a primary host, so the exclusion window matters from the day the crop goes in.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Walk the rows and pick caterpillars and their eggs off the undersides of the leaves. The leaves are part of what makes kohlrabi worth growing, and the caterpillars can chew the bulb too, so a regular pass pays off.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hand removal of larvae and eggs from leaf undersides catches them at the stage that has done the least damage, and it is practical at garden scale, where heavy feeding sets young plants back and larvae can score the bulb.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spray Bt, a caterpillar-specific control that carries low toxicity for people, pets and bees. It cannot tell a pest caterpillar from a butterfly's, so keep it to the plantings that actually have caterpillars on them. Watching for the first white butterflies tells you when to start, and spray again after rain washes it off.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Bt kurstaki targets caterpillars and spares beneficials. It breaks down, so reapply after rain, and take the arrival of the first white butterflies as the cue to begin. Because it acts on caterpillars as a group, confine applications to plantings that actually carry the pest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If Bt and hand-picking are not keeping up, spinosad is the stronger organic option. Spray toward dusk, when bees are not out foraging, and follow the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad is the escalation once the softer rungs have not held. Like Bt it does most against young larvae, and timing it to dusk limits exposure to foraging bees.

pests.name: Cabbage aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked into the folds of the leaves. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
pests.cause_beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage-family plants like kohlrabi and hide in the leaf folds.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check the growing tips and leaf folds often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and in the leaf axils, curling and distorting the foliage and weakening young plants; heavy colonies foul the crop with honeydew.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; winged forms move in from cruciferous weeds and other brassica crops. The turnip aphid can also occur.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (parasitoid wasps, hoverflies, ladybugs).
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips and leaf axils weekly and catch infestations early. Avoid excess nitrogen, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on nitrogen fertilizer. It pushes out soft, sappy new growth, and that is what draws these aphids and lets them build up fastest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen produces the succulent growth this brassica specialist colonizes preferentially, so a restrained feeding program removes that flush without holding the crop back.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull out old cabbage-family plants after harvest instead of leaving them standing. The aphids carry over on that leftover material and move straight onto the next planting.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Destroy brassica crop debris promptly, since it carries colonies between crops. Winged forms also move in from other brassica plantings, so a cleared bed removes one nearby source.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep young plants under a light fabric row cover so winged aphids cannot land and start colonies while the plants are small. Check the growing tips and the folds where the leaves meet the stem often, so anything that does get in is caught early.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cover young plants to block the winged colonizers, and scout the growing tips and leaf axils weekly. Catching a colony early is what keeps it from lodging in the folds, where coverage is hardest to achieve later.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the clusters off with a strong jet of water from the hose, aiming into the leaf folds where they hide. Repeat every few days while you keep finding them, and do it early in the day so the leaves dry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful jet dislodges colonies before they settle deep into the axils. It is a purely physical knockdown that leaves the natural-enemy complex untouched; spray early enough in the day that foliage dries.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Make the helpful insects welcome. Ladybugs and lacewings eat aphids, so give them time to find a colony and skip broad sprays that would take them out along with the pests.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserve the parasitoid wasps, hoverflies and lady beetles that regulate this aphid. Broad-spectrum material removes them and leaves a rapidly reproducing pest with a clear field.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spray insecticidal soap onto the aphids themselves, coating the undersides of the leaves, and repeat every few days. It works where it wets them, and the dusty, waxy coating on these aphids means soaking the clusters rather than misting the plant.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap kills on contact, so thorough coverage of leaf undersides and axils decides the outcome. The waxy bloom on Brevicoryne colonies is what makes deliberate, repeated application necessary.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil is another spray for coating the colonies. Hit the same hidden spots under the leaves and in the folds, repeat every few days, and skip it in high heat or when plants are dry at the roots.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Neem is the coverage-dependent alternative to soap on these colonies. The same thoroughness applies, and it spares beneficials once it has dried.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil, can also coat the aphids it reaches. Cover the undersides and the leaf folds the same way, and avoid spraying it in hot weather.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Horticultural oil rounds out the contact options alongside soap and neem. Whichever you pick, coverage of the undersides and axils matters more than the choice of product, and it is worth holding off in high heat or on water-stressed plants.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle it.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts seedlings and slows establishment, the costly stage for a fast crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: The crucifer and striped flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas; they overwinter in debris and field edges and are most damaging at the seedling stage and in spring, easing as the season warms, so fall crops face less of them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from sowing or transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, clean up weedy brassica relatives, and favor fall plantings, which see lighter pressure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull the cabbage-family weeds growing near the bed. Those weeds feed the same beetles, so clearing them leaves fewer waiting for your seedlings.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Weedy brassica relatives sustain the crucifer and striped flea beetles between crops, so clearing the bed and its edges removes a standing host bridge to a young planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where you have the choice, lean on fall plantings. These beetles do their worst in spring and ease off as the season warms, so a fall crop usually meets fewer of them. Whatever the season, steady water and feeding keep seedlings growing past light chewing.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Feeding is most damaging on seedlings and through spring, and it lets up once the weather warms, so fall sowings meet lighter pressure. Even watering and feeding keep the stand vigorous enough to grow through damage, which shortens the vulnerable window in any season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover the seedlings with a row cover, a light fabric sheet, from sowing or transplanting on, because a tiny plant cannot grow fast enough to shrug off heavy chewing.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Exclusion from sowing or transplanting protects the stage that is actually at risk. The objective throughout is carrying the crop past the seedling stage, which is the costly one on a crop this quick.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A kaolin clay coating, a fine white clay dusted over the plants, can cut feeding when there are a lot of beetles. It reduces damage rather than clearing the beetles out, so use it alongside the cover.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Kaolin is a repellent barrier for use where pressure is high. Treat it as a supplement to exclusion and timing rather than a replacement for them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If beetles are heavy enough to stunt the seedlings, a spinosad spray is an option. Keep the aim on getting plants big enough to handle the damage, spray toward dusk to spare bees, and follow the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad supplements exclusion under high pressure. The objective stays establishment past the vulnerable seedling stage rather than a season-long spray program, and applications belong at dusk to limit bee exposure.

pests.name: Cabbage root maggot
pests.symptoms_beginner: New transplants and seedlings wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp spring weather.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant kohlrabi where cabbage-family crops have not grown recently. The fly builds up in ground that carried its host plants, so moving the bed puts the new crop away from it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotating away from recent brassica ground reduces the carryover population emerging right where the new transplants go in.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots, that plant cannot be saved, so pull the badly damaged ones and get them out of the garden. Spend the effort instead on keeping the fly from laying more eggs around the plants that are still sound.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no rescue once larvae are tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Rogue out the wilting and collapsing plants and redirect the effort to blocking further egg-laying on the survivors, since the feeding also opens the way to rots.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A row cover, a light fabric sheet laid over the bed, keeps the fly from reaching the plants to lay eggs at their base in the first place. Give it fresh ground to work on: where cabbage-family crops grew last season, the cover can end up holding the emerging flies in rather than out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Exclusion through cool, wet spring establishment covers the period of heaviest adult activity and protects the stage root feeding can kill, the new transplant. Pair it with the rotation above, so the cover is not laid over ground that already carries the pest. In practice that means a bed which grew cabbage-family crops last season, where the cover would hold the emerging flies in with the kohlrabi.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Set a small collar or disk flat around the base of each transplant. It blocks the fly from laying eggs right against the stem, which is where the maggots start their trip down to the roots.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A basal collar or disk placed at transplanting denies the adult its egg-laying site at the stem base. It is the per-plant option where covering the whole bed is impractical.

pests.name: Harlequin bug
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
pests.cause_beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped striped eggs, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away, then destroy it.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.
pests.cause_seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear away garden debris and cabbage-family weeds at the end of the season, since that is where the adults spend the winter. During the season, pull out any plant that is badly overrun rather than trying to defend it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Adults overwinter in debris and crucifer weeds, so eliminating that shelter is the main preventive lever against a warm-region specialist that completes several generations a year. Roguing heavily infested plants during the season belongs to the same pass.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sow a mustard patch early to lure the overwintered bugs away from the crop, then destroy it before the main planting goes out. Getting the patch out while the bugs are still on it is the step that matters.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: An early mustard stand pulls overwintered adults off the planting, and this crop's guidance ends the sequence by destroying the stand before the main crop is set out. That removal is not tidying up; it is what stops the concentration becoming a local increase. This method's cautions carry the timing.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A row cover, a light fabric sheet, keeps the bugs off the plants. Get it on before they show up rather than after.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Exclusion with floating row cover keeps colonizing adults off the crop, and it earns the most early, as overwintered adults move onto the first cabbage-family plants available.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Search the plants and crush the bugs, the young ones, and the barrel-shaped striped eggs. They are brightly colored and easy to spot on a regular walk through the bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hand destruction of adults, nymphs and the barrel-shaped egg rows is practical at garden scale on an insect this conspicuous. Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch in black and yellow or black and red are readily found on a scouting pass.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where pressure is severe, insecticidal soap sprayed straight onto the bugs can help. It works on the ones it actually wets, so aim at the insects rather than misting the plant.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap assists under severe pressure and is strictly a contact material, so direct it onto the bugs and their clusters rather than over the foliage in general.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil is the other spray named for severe pressure. Coat the bugs directly, and hold off in high heat or when the plants are dry at the roots.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Neem is the alternative contact option where pressure is severe. As with soap, coverage of the insects decides the result, and it should be kept off anything in flower nearby, weeds included, where bees forage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where pressure is severe, pyrethrin, a botanical spray from chrysanthemum flowers, knocks the bugs down on contact and then breaks apart in sunlight within a day or so. Do not let it reach anything in flower; it is in the strictest bee band, which grants no evening window.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Pyrethrin supplies contact knockdown under severe pressure and degrades rapidly in sunlight, so it leaves little residue and often needs repeating. Its organic acceptability does not lower the bee precaution: the strictest band applies, so keep spray and drift off bloom, weeds included.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil closer to neutral helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Don't grow kohlrabi or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots, which later rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and is favored by acidic soils below about pH 6.5.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Once clubroot turns up, stop growing kohlrabi and its cabbage-family relatives in that spot for several years. The organism lives on in the soil, and it slowly starves when it has nothing to infect.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resting spores persist in soil for many years. Where clubroot is known, rotate brassicas out on a long cycle, up to 7 years, which draws the soil population down over time.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the soil from staying acidic by liming it toward neutral. The disease takes hold more readily in acid soil, so this holds it back without curing it. Lime the affected bed rather than the whole garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Liming toward neutral suppresses the disease, which is favored by soils below about pH 6.5. Confine the treatment to affected ground, since most vegetables prefer soil a little more acid than that, and pair it with the long rotation, as neither clears established ground on its own.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Fix the spots where water sits in the bed. The disease travels and infects in wet soil, so better drainage takes away part of what it needs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogen spreads in contaminated soil and water, so correcting drainage on heavy or low ground lowers the infection pressure reaching the roots.

control_ladder.note_beginner: An infected plant cannot be cured, so lift it with the clubbed roots attached and get it out of the garden. Clean the soil off your tools afterward, since the disease rides along on dirt carried from an infested bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rogue out infected plants with the galls intact and destroy them; galls left behind add to a soil burden that already lasts years. Clean soil from tools and boots as well, since moving infested soil is one of the ways it reaches clean ground.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and kill the plant. Often the most serious brassica disease in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants. This one often arrives on the seed or on the young plants themselves, so a clean start is where most of the defense lives.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The bacterium is seedborne, so certified seed and healthy transplants close the main entry route. It is a purchase-time decision, settled before anything is in the ground.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently. Give the ground two to three years before brassicas come back to it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, so inoculum carried in old residues is gone before a susceptible crop returns to that ground.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Space the plants so air moves between them and the leaves dry off. The disease moves fastest in warm, wet weather, so drying time works against it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Open spacing shortens the warm, wet leaf conditions this bacterium spreads fastest in, and it slows movement from an infected plant to its neighbors.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil instead of over the tops of the plants, so you are not splashing bacteria from leaf to leaf.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Basal irrigation removes the overhead wetting and splash that carry the bacterium between plants and lengthen leaf wetness.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stay out of the bed while the leaves are wet. Brushing past wet plants carries the bacteria from a sick one to a healthy one.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Work the planting only when foliage is dry, since handling wet plants moves the bacterium efficiently. This governs when you enter the bed, and it still applies after rain and dew, not only after watering.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no real cure, so remove infected plants and get them out of the garden before the disease reaches their neighbors. The yellow V-shaped patches at the leaf edges, with black veins inside them, make it recognizable early.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: With no effective cure, roguing is the in-season control, so remove and destroy symptomatic plants promptly. The V-shaped marginal lesions with blackened veins allow an early call, before the pathogen has moved far through the vascular system.

diseases.name: Alternaria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small, round, dark spots on the leaves, each with a yellow ring and faint target-like circles inside, that grow and run together in wet weather and turn sooty in the center.
diseases.cause_beginner: Alternaria fungi that can travel on seed and survive on old plant debris, spreading in splashing water and needing wet leaves to take hold. Warm, humid weather brings it on.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the worst leaves, water at the soil in the morning so leaves dry quickly, and clean up debris. Clean seed and airflow handle most of it; a copper fungicide can help in a wet spell if started early.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed, water at the base instead of overhead, give plants room so the leaves dry, and rotate crucifers and clear debris between plantings.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, circular, dark spots with a yellow halo and concentric rings that darken to a sooty center as spores build, enlarging and merging in wet weather. A foliar disease that weakens the plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungi (chiefly Alternaria brassicae), which are seedborne and survive on crop debris, spreading in splashing water and needing leaf wetness to infect; warm, wet weather drives it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove badly spotted leaves, water at the base in the morning so foliage dries, and clear debris. Clean seed and airflow are the main home levers; a copper fungicide can help in a persistently wet season if started early.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean seed, avoid overhead watering, space for airflow, and rotate crucifers and clear debris that carry the fungi between seasons.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with clean seed. These fungi can travel on the seed itself, so a clean packet keeps the disease from arriving with the crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Alternaria is seedborne, so clean seed shuts one of the two main entry routes. Along with airflow, this is where the home-garden leverage sits.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move kohlrabi and its cabbage-family relatives to a different spot between plantings, since the fungi carry over where those crops grew.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The fungi survive on crop debris between seasons, so rotating crucifers out of the bed separates the new crop from the carryover inoculum.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the plants room so air moves through and the leaves dry quickly. The spots need wet leaves to take hold, so drying time does much of the work.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Infection requires leaf wetness, so spacing that shortens wet periods works directly against spots establishing, enlarging and running together in wet weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil in the morning so any splash dries fast. The disease spreads in splashing water and needs wet leaves to get started.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The fungi spread by splash and infect only through wet foliage, so morning irrigation at the base removes the splash route and leaves the day for drying.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off the worst-spotted leaves as you notice them, and clear plant debris between plantings, since that is where the fungi wait for the next crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Remove badly spotted foliage during the season and clear crop debris between plantings; residue is the principal carryover reservoir.

control_ladder.note_beginner: In a wet spell that will not let up, a copper fungicide can help if you start it early, before the spots are widespread. Keep the spray out of ponds and drains, since copper is very harmful to fish and other water life, and follow the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper earns its place only in a season that stays wet, and only where it goes on early; clean seed and airflow remain the main home levers. It protects new growth rather than curing spotted leaves, it is highly toxic to aquatic life, and it accumulates at the soil surface with repeat use, so keep it away from water, limit how often you lean on it, and follow the label rate.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow patches on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors and kills foliage. Kohlrabi's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora parasitica) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Space the plants so air moves between them and dries the leaves. This disease wants cool, damp foliage, and kohlrabi grows through that kind of weather.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spacing for air movement shortens the long leaf-wetness periods infection depends on. The crop's cool, humid season overlaps the conditions the pathogen favors, so the layout has to do the drying.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil line rather than over the leaves. Wet foliage and splashing water are how it gets around.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Basal irrigation removes the overhead wetting and splash dispersal that extend the wet periods the organism needs.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If downy mildew is common where you live, pick a variety described as resistant when you buy seed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Where downy mildew recurs regionally, a resistant cultivar is the seed-time decision that lowers the pressure the in-season steps have to carry.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Take off the worst-affected leaves, the ones with fuzzy grayish growth underneath, so there is less disease to spread. Once damp weather settles in it is hard to stop, so the preventive steps carry most of the load.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing badly affected foliage lowers inoculum, but the disease is difficult to arrest once humidity stays high. Treat removal as a supplement to the preventive steps rather than a substitute for them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If it keeps spreading despite the rest, a copper spray can help. It does more applied early than after the leaves are covered, and keep it away from ponds and drains, since copper is very harmful to fish and other water life.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper is the escalation when cultural steps are not holding under high pressure. It acts preventively, so it belongs at the first sign rather than in an established outbreak; mind runoff, copper being highly toxic to aquatic life, and limit repeat reliance across seasons.

diseases.name: Blackleg
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale, sunken spots dotted with tiny black specks appear on the stem and leaves, and the base of the stem darkens and rots, so the plant may topple. It often arrives on infected seed.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that comes in on infected seed or plants and attacks the stem and leaves of cabbage-family crops. It spreads in wet weather and lingers in old plant debris.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is prevention: clean seed, rotation, and clearing away old cabbage-family debris.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from cabbage-family crops for a few years, and clear away old brassica plants where the fungus survives.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale, sunken lesions peppered with small black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) on stems and leaves, and a dark, girdling canker at the stem base that can rot the crown and lodge the plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Phoma lingam (Leptosphaeria maculans) is chiefly seedborne and survives in brassica debris; it spreads in cool, wet weather by splashing water and infects through wounds and pores.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Management is preventive, since the pathogen is carried on seed and in residue.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean, certified, hot-water-treated seed and disease-free transplants, rotate 3 years away from brassicas, and bury or remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants. This fungus mostly comes into a garden on infected seed or plants, so the packet you buy is the main decision.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The fungus is carried chiefly on seed, so the primary control is seed that has been certified and hot-water treated, set out as transplants known to be free of the disease. Management here is preventive by nature, since there is nothing to apply once plants are infected.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep cabbage-family crops out of the affected spot for a few years, about three. The fungus lingers where those crops grew.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate 3 years away from brassicas. The fungus survives in brassica residue, so the interval has to outlast the debris rather than just the season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no cure, so pull and destroy infected plants. Clear away the old cabbage-family debris too, since that is the other place the fungus survives.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no effective cure once plants are infected, so remove and destroy them, and clear out the brassica residue that carries the fungus over rather than leaving it standing in the bed.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept as even as possible; steady moisture is what keeps the bulb tender, and a dry-then-wet swing makes it woody or cracks it.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week. Try to keep it steady, not dry-then-soaked.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week including rain (Iowa State and Minnesota: roughly 1 inch a week; Utah State up to 1 to 2 inches in heat or sandy soil), with the most attention while the stem is swelling.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, a bit more in hot, dry weather.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage the leaf diseases kohlrabi shares with the cole crops.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; kohlrabi dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites root maggots, clubroot, and rots in cold, wet ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting and stalled growth, then woody, fibrous, strong-flavored stems; the classic kohlrabi fault is letting the bed dry out, which toughens the bulb, and a heavy soak after a dry spell can split it.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves and a tough, woody bulb. Letting the soil dry out is the main thing that makes kohlrabi woody, and a sudden soaking after a dry spell can crack it.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep the surface evenly moist
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep the seedbed or tray surface evenly moist through germination; brassica seed is shallow and should not dry mid-emergence.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the soil or tray damp while the seeds come up, without letting the surface dry out.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep evenly moist as seedlings grow
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Grow the seedlings on with steady, even moisture.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp as they grow.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 to 1.5 inches per week, kept even
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep even moisture as the plant leafs out ahead of the stem swelling.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water evenly as the leaves grow before the bulb starts to swell.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 to 1.5 inches per week, never dry-then-wet
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Steady moisture while the stem swells is what keeps the bulb tender and crisp; a dry-then-wet swing turns it woody or cracks it open. This is the window that decides quality.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the water steady while the round bulb swells. If it dries out and then gets soaked, the bulb turns woody or cracks.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 to 1.5 inches per week, kept even
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep even moisture and harvest promptly at about tennis-ball size; left to oversize, kohlrabi turns woody.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering evenly and pick kohlrabi while it is about tennis-ball size. Left too long it gets woody.
