watering.method_note_seasoned: Even, steady moisture is the whole game with kohlrabi: it keeps the swollen stem crisp, mild, and tender, and prevents the woodiness and cracking that a dry-then-wet cycle causes.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water steady so the bulbs grow crisp and tender. Big swings from dry to wet are what make kohlrabi woody and cracked.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Even moisture matters most while the stem is swelling toward harvest; this is when drought stress turns it woody and a sudden change in watering cracks it.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water steadily while the bulb is swelling. Do not let it dry out and then suddenly soak it.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Kohlrabi is grown both ways. Direct sowing is simple and common since the crop is fast: sow 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep once the soil is workable and thin to 6 to 8 inches apart. For an earlier or more uniform crop, start transplants indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out and plant them out 1 to 2 weeks before the last frost, since young plants take light frost. Avoid exposing young plants to a long cold spell (more than about a week of nights below roughly 45 to 50°F), which can trigger bolting. Sow the fall crop in mid-summer. Harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days.
start_method.notes_beginner: You can sow kohlrabi seeds right in the garden or start with young plants. For direct sowing, plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep once the soil can be worked, then thin the seedlings to about 6 to 8 inches apart. For transplants, start seeds indoors about a month before planting out, and set them in the garden a week or two before the last frost. Let homegrown seedlings get used to the outdoors over a week before planting. Sow again in mid-summer for a fall crop.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Do not let the pot stand in a saucer of water. Kohlrabi needs even moisture for a tender bulb, but waterlogged mix causes rot and favors clubroot; empty the saucer within an hour of watering.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of water. Kohlrabi needs steady, even moisture, but soil that stays soggy will rot the roots, so empty the saucer within an hour of watering.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of loose potting mix made for containers. Garden soil packs down hard in a pot and can bring in clubroot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in a little compost to help the soil hold water evenly, which keeps kohlrabi tender.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: container_potting_mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Use a light, loose potting mix with a handful of compost for even moisture-holding. Avoid garden soil, which compacts in a pot and can introduce the soilborne clubroot pathogen.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather. Kohlrabi turns woody if it dries out, so keep the moisture steady.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Kohlrabi finishes its cycle in one season and is not overwintered in a pot.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Kohlrabi is grown as a single-season annual and is not held over winter in a container.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Kohlrabi is a great container crop because it is small and shallow-rooted. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep that holds 3 to 5 gallons, with drainage holes, and space the plants about 6 inches apart. Keep it watered evenly and harvest the bulbs young.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Kohlrabi suits containers well: it is compact, shallow-rooted, and quick, so a pot 8 inches or more deep holding 3 to 5 gallons grows several plants spaced about 6 inches apart. Width matters as much as depth, since you want room for several bulbs. Keep the mix evenly moist, because pots dry fast and a checked plant turns woody, and feed lightly. Provide drainage holes and a loose potting mix.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries out, since drying out toughens the bulb.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container kohlrabi needs slightly more frequent feeding than in-ground plants because watering leaches nutrients from the mix.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits kohlrabi well, since it smooths out the steady moisture the crop needs to keep the bulb tender.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps kohlrabi from turning woody.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Kohlrabi is a small, shallow-rooted plant, so a wide, fairly shallow container suits it better than a deep narrow one. Choose a pot at least 8 inches deep holding 3 to 5 gallons, and favor width so you can grow several plants spaced about 6 inches apart. Provide drainage holes and keep the mix evenly moist.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Kohlrabi has shallow roots, so a wide pot works better than a deep, narrow one. Use a container at least 8 inches deep that holds a few gallons, with drainage holes, and give each plant about 6 inches of space.

recommended.name: Early White Vienna
recommended.note: The classic pale-green heirloom and the standard early type; quick, dependable, and best picked young at tennis-ball size.

recommended.name: Early Purple Vienna
recommended.note: The purple-skinned counterpart to White Vienna, with the same creamy white flesh; the skin color is a handsome garden feature and does not affect flavor.

recommended.name: Grand Duke
recommended.note: An award-winning green hybrid that is uniform, slow to turn woody, and a reliable all-around choice.

recommended.name: Kolibri
recommended.note: A vigorous purple hybrid with crisp white flesh, good bolt resistance, and a wide harvest window; popular for both spring and fall.

recommended.name: Quickstar
recommended.note: One of the fastest types, a green hybrid bred for tender early bulbs, good for tight succession sowings.

recommended.name: Kossak
recommended.note: A giant storage type whose large green bulbs stay crisp and tender, with little of the woodiness that oversized standard kohlrabi develops; good for fall and winter keeping.

recommended.name: Superschmelz
recommended.note: An heirloom giant that can reach 8 to 10 inches across and still stay sweet and tender, an exception to the pick-it-small rule; a long-season fall crop.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the type to the slot. Fast green or purple Vienna types and hybrids like Quickstar, Grand Duke, and Kolibri are the workhorses for spring and fall, picked young at 2 to 3 inches. The purple types (Purple Vienna, Kolibri) differ from the green only in skin color, not flavor. The giant storage cultivars (Kossak, Superschmelz, Gigante) are the exception to harvest-it-small: they hold tender flesh at a much larger size and suit fall and winter storage. Where clubroot is a concern, choose resistant cultivars.
varieties.note_beginner: For most gardens, pick a fast standard variety like White Vienna, Purple Vienna, Grand Duke, or Kolibri, and harvest the bulbs young, about the size of a tennis ball. Purple and green types taste the same; the purple is just prettier. If you want big bulbs, grow a giant type like Kossak or Superschmelz, which stay tender even when large.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other brassicas (cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts, collards, turnip, radish), which share clubroot and the cabbage-family pests.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like cabbage, broccoli, kale, turnips, and radishes.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, or unrelated crops like tomatoes, squash, or onions.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate so brassicas do not follow brassicas for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is known, since the clubroot organism persists in soil for years. Keeping soil pH up also helps suppress it.
rotation.note_beginner: Do not plant kohlrabi or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting a few years between them helps avoid soil diseases like clubroot.

bolting.triggers: A cold spell on young plants (more than about a week of nights below roughly 45 to 50°F), which vernalizes them and triggers flowering, plus prolonged summer heat and long days.
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Do not rush transplants out into a long cold snap, since young kohlrabi chilled below about 45 to 50°F for a week or more is vernalized and bolts. Time the spring crop so it sizes up before summer heat, grow the fall crop into cooling weather, and choose bolt-resistant varieties such as Kolibri. Keep plants growing steadily without a check.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Plant kohlrabi so it grows in steady cool weather, not through a long cold snap or into summer heat. Setting young plants out into a hard cold spell can make them flower instead of forming a bulb, so wait for settled weather and pick bolt-resistant varieties.
bolting.note_seasoned: Kohlrabi bolting is mainly a vernalization response: a young plant exposed to a stretch of cold runs to flower instead of swelling a stem, which is why an early spring set-out into a cold snap is the classic cause. Summer heat and long days also push it. A bolted plant will not form a usable bulb, so the fix is timing and steady growth.
bolting.note_beginner: If young kohlrabi gets too cold for too long, or too hot, it flowers early and never makes a good bulb. Steady cool weather and good timing are the main fixes.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Kohlrabi keeps a day or two at room temperature but softens and loses crispness, so refrigerate it soon after harvest. Twist or cut off the leafy tops first, since they pull moisture from the bulb.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Kohlrabi does not keep well on the counter. Cut off the leaves and put the bulb in the fridge soon after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Remove the leaf stems and store the unwashed bulb in a perforated or loose plastic bag in the crisper, where it keeps well for about 2 to 3 weeks (Utah State and Iowa State). The leaves keep only a few days and are best used fresh.
storage.fridge_beginner: Trim off the leaves and store the unwashed bulb in a loose plastic bag in the fridge crisper, where it stays good for about 2 to 3 weeks. Use the leaves within a few days.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Kohlrabi freezes well once peeled, diced, and blanched about 2 to 3 minutes, then cooled in ice water, drained, and frozen. Blanching halts the enzymes that would otherwise cause off-flavors and texture loss in storage.
storage.freezer_beginner: To freeze kohlrabi, peel and dice it, boil the pieces about 2 to 3 minutes, cool them quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. The quick boil keeps the flavor and texture.
storage.notes_seasoned: Kohlrabi stores noticeably better than most cole crops: a firm bulb holds 2 to 3 weeks refrigerated, and the giant storage types (Kossak) keep for months in cold, humid conditions near 32°F. Quality is still highest fresh, and the leaves are perishable.
storage.notes_beginner: Kohlrabi keeps longer than most cabbage-family vegetables, a few weeks in the fridge, and the big storage types keep for months somewhere cold. Use the leaves quickly, though.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves, called seed leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp and warm. Once you see the first real kohlrabi leaves after the seed leaves, thin out crowded seedlings.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days at soil temperatures of roughly 60 to 75°F, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons).
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the seedbed or starting mix evenly moist and warm; thin or pot up once the first true leaves appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your kohlrabi seeds sprout?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow their real leaves and a stronger stem. Direct-sown plants are thinned now; transplants are ready to move outside at about 4 to 5 weeks old.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin direct-sown seedlings to about 6 to 8 inches apart. Before planting transplants outside, harden them off over about a week, and avoid setting them out into a long cold snap.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How many real leaves do your seedlings have?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Young plants develop true leaves and a sturdy stem; transplants are ready at about 4 to 5 weeks, and direct-sown stands are thinned to spacing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 6 to 8 inches; harden off transplants over 7 to 10 days and avoid exposing young plants to a prolonged cold spell, which vernalizes them and triggers bolting.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you thinned or hardened off your kohlrabi?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant puts on a rosette of broad leaves on a short stem for a few weeks. This leafy growth comes before the bulb swells.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed the plant a little nitrogen as it grows and keep it evenly watered. Check the leaves for caterpillars, aphids, and flea-beetle holes.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant growing lots of healthy leaves?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant builds a leafy rosette over several weeks before the stem base begins to swell.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress with nitrogen as the plant establishes, keep moisture even, and watch for cabbageworms, aphids, and flea beetles.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is your kohlrabi putting on healthy leafy growth?

growth_stages.name: Stem swelling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The base of the stem, just above the soil, swells into a round, pale-green or purple bulb. This is the part you eat.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady so the bulb stays tender, and watch its size. It is ready when it reaches about 2 to 3 inches across, the size of a tennis ball. Do not let it keep growing past that or it turns woody.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Can you see the bulb swelling at the base?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The stem base swells into the round, above-ground bulb. Even moisture and steady growth here decide whether it is crisp and mild or woody and fibrous.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even and check size daily as it approaches 2 to 3 inches; a growth check from drought or heat now is what turns the stem woody and bitter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Has the stem started to swell into a bulb?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The bulb is about 2 to 3 inches across, the size of a tennis ball, firm and smooth. This is the moment to cut it, before it gets bigger and tougher.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the whole bulb off at the base with a knife while it is still young and tender. Standard types get woody if you wait too long, so do not let them grow large. Harvest in the cool morning if you can.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you harvested your kohlrabi yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The bulb reaches about 2 to 3 inches in diameter (larger for the giant storage types), firm and smooth, before it turns woody.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut the bulb at the base while young; standard varieties grow tough, woody, and bitter past about 3 inches, so harvest on time. Giant types (Kossak, Superschmelz) hold tender at larger size. Trim the tops and chill promptly.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did you harvest your kohlrabi?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your kohlrabi bulb should be about 2 to 3 inches across now. Cut it at the base while it is firm and young, before it turns woody and bitter; standard types do not improve by waiting.
notifications.body_beginner: Your kohlrabi should be about the size of a tennis ball now. Cut the bulb off at the base while it is young and tender, before it gets tough.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your kohlrabi is established. Side-dress with nitrogen now to keep growth steady and the bulb tender, placing the feed beside the row and watering it in.
notifications.body_beginner: Feed your kohlrabi a little nitrogen now to keep it growing steadily. Put the fertilizer near the plants and water it in.

notifications.title_seasoned: Heat watch: keep the bulb tender
notifications.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your kohlrabi
notifications.body_seasoned: A hot spell is coming while your kohlrabi is sizing up. Heat above roughly 75°F turns the stem woody and bitter and can trigger bolting. Keep moisture even and harvest promptly if bulbs are near size.
notifications.body_beginner: Hot weather is on the way while your kohlrabi is forming its bulb. Heat can make it woody and bitter. Keep the soil evenly watered, and pick any bulbs that are nearly ready.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heat warning while bulbing
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Days well above roughly 75°F while the stem is swelling push fast, fibrous growth that leaves kohlrabi woody and bitter and can trigger bolting. Keep moisture even and harvest any near-size bulbs promptly.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot weather while the bulb is forming can make kohlrabi tough and bitter. Water evenly and pick any bulbs that are nearly ready.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Kohlrabi takes light frost in stride, but a hard freeze can damage the bulbs. Cover plants or harvest mature bulbs before a hard freeze.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Kohlrabi handles a light frost fine, but a hard freeze can damage the bulbs. Cover the plants or pick any ready bulbs before a hard freeze hits.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep into a moist seedbed or starting mix; kohlrabi germinates fast and reliably across a wide soil-temperature range as long as moisture stays even.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep in damp soil, and keep it evenly moist while they sprout.

germination.text_seasoned: Because kohlrabi is so quick, direct sowing works well; start transplants only when you want an earlier or more uniform stand.
germination.text_beginner: Kohlrabi grows fast, so you can plant the seeds right in the garden. Starting indoors is only needed if you want an earlier crop.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to 6 to 8 inches apart; crowded plants make small, misshapen bulbs and compete for moisture.
seedling.text_beginner: Thin the seedlings to about 6 to 8 inches apart so each one has room to form a good bulb.

seedling.text_seasoned: Avoid setting young transplants out into a prolonged cold snap (over about a week below roughly 45 to 50°F), the classic vernalization trigger for bolting.
seedling.text_beginner: Do not plant young kohlrabi out into a long cold spell, which can make it flower early instead of forming a bulb. Wait for settled weather.

established.text_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting when plants are roughly 4 inches tall, and keep moisture even; steady growth is what keeps the coming bulb tender.
established.text_beginner: Feed the plants a little nitrogen a few weeks after planting and water steadily so they keep growing without a stall.

established.text_seasoned: Scout for flea beetles on young plants and cabbage aphids in the leaf axils; a vigorous, well-watered stand outgrows light flea-beetle feeding.
established.text_beginner: Check young plants for tiny flea-beetle holes and for aphids tucked into the leaves, and keep the plants growing strong.

bulbing.text_seasoned: Keep water even at roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week as the stem swells; a drought-then-soak swing is what makes kohlrabi woody and splits it.
bulbing.text_beginner: Water steadily while the bulb is swelling. Letting it dry out and then soaking it is what makes kohlrabi tough and cracked.

bulbing.text_seasoned: Watch the bulb size daily as it nears 2 to 3 inches; standard types pass their window quickly and turn woody, so do not let them oversize.
bulbing.text_beginner: Check the bulb every day as it gets close to tennis-ball size. Standard kohlrabi turns woody fast if it grows too big.

harvest.text_seasoned: Cut the bulb at the base at 2 to 3 inches for standard types; harvest on time, since a woody, over-mature kohlrabi will not soften.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut the bulb off at the base when it reaches tennis-ball size. If you wait too long it gets woody and will not get tender again.

harvest.text_seasoned: Trim the leafy tops and chill promptly; the bulb keeps 2 to 3 weeks refrigerated, far longer for the giant storage types.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut off the leaves and get the bulb into the fridge, where it keeps for a couple of weeks.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Each plant yields one swollen-stem bulb, typically 2 to 3 inches across and a few ounces to about half a pound for standard types, harvested once. Giant storage cultivars (Kossak, Superschmelz) yield a single much larger bulb of a pound or more. There are no side shoots, so total yield is set by plant spacing and succession sowings.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each kohlrabi plant gives you one bulb, picked once. Standard types are about the size of a tennis ball; giant types can be much bigger. To get a steady supply, plant a few seeds every couple of weeks.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Because each plant produces a single bulb harvested at once, there is no extended peak; the way to a steady supply is succession sowing every 2 to 3 weeks across the spring and fall windows. The fast 45 to 60 day cycle makes tight succession practical.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Kohlrabi makes one bulb per plant, so for a steady harvest, sow a small batch every couple of weeks instead of all at once. The crop is fast, so you do not wait long.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The single most common first-year mistake is letting the bulb grow too big: standard kohlrabi turns woody, fibrous, and bitter past about 3 inches and does not recover, so harvest young rather than waiting for a bigger bulb. New growers also under-water, which toughens the stem.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The big thing to learn with kohlrabi is to pick it young, at tennis-ball size. If you leave it to get bigger, it turns woody and tough and will not get better. Keeping the water steady also keeps it tender.
factors_seasoned: Harvest timing: standard types must be cut at 2 to 3 inches before they turn woody; a late harvest ruins the bulb.
Even moisture: a steady water supply keeps the stem crisp and mild, while drought or a dry-then-wet swing makes it woody and can crack it.
Temperature: cool, steady growth gives tender bulbs; heat above about 75°F drives fibrous growth and bolting.
Variety: giant storage types (Kossak, Superschmelz) hold tender flesh at a large size, while standard types must be picked small.
Spacing and succession: yield over the season comes from spacing at 6 to 8 inches and sowing in small batches every 2 to 3 weeks.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing kohlrabi planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by soil temperature, frost dates, and the seasonal windows instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Woody, tough, fibrous bulb
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Letting the bulb grow too big, or growth stress from dry soil or heat.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You cut the bulb and it was tough, woody, and stringy instead of crisp and tender. This usually means it grew too large, since standard kohlrabi turns woody past about 3 inches, or that the plant got stressed by dry soil or heat and grew fibrous. It is tempting to leave kohlrabi to get bigger like a turnip, but with standard types that backfires. Next time, harvest at tennis-ball size, keep the water steady, and try a giant type like Kossak if you want big tender bulbs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick standard kohlrabi young, at 2 to 3 inches, keep the soil evenly moist, and grow a giant variety if you want larger bulbs.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The bulb was woody, fibrous, and strong-flavored rather than crisp and mild. The usual causes are over-maturity (standard types lignify past about 3 inches) and growth checks from drought or heat that drive fibrous tissue. Growers often leave kohlrabi to size up like a root crop, which ruins standard cultivars. Next time harvest standard types at 2 to 3 inches, hold even moisture, and use a giant storage cultivar (Kossak, Superschmelz) where a large tender bulb is wanted.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Over-maturity in standard types, or growth checks from drought or heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Harvest standard types at 2 to 3 inches, keep moisture even, and switch to a giant non-woody cultivar for larger bulbs.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting (flowering before a bulb forms)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A long cold spell on young plants, or summer heat and long days.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant sent up a flower stalk instead of making a bulb. Kohlrabi flowers early when young plants get chilled for a stretch (more than about a week of cold nights) or when summer heat and long days push it, and once it bolts no good bulb forms. A common mistake is planting too early into a cold snap. Next time, wait for settled weather to plant, grow a bolt-resistant variety, and time the crop for steady cool growth.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant into settled weather, not a cold snap or into summer heat, and choose a bolt-resistant variety like Kolibri.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant ran to flower instead of swelling a stem. Kohlrabi bolting is largely a vernalization response, a young plant chilled below roughly 45 to 50°F for a week or more is triggered to flower, and summer heat and long days add to it. The classic cause is an early spring set-out into a cold spell. Next time avoid exposing transplants to a prolonged cold snap, time the crop for steady cool growth, and use bolt-resistant cultivars.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Vernalization of young plants by a prolonged cold spell, plus heat and long days.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Avoid a prolonged cold spell on young plants, time for steady cool growth, and choose bolt-resistant varieties.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cracked or split bulb
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Uneven watering, especially a heavy soak after a dry spell.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The bulb cracked open. This comes from uneven watering: when the soil goes dry and then gets a big drink or a heavy rain, the bulb takes up water fast and splits. Next time, keep the watering steady so the soil never swings from bone dry to soaked, and harvest on time rather than letting bulbs sit oversized.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and avoid a sudden soaking after a dry spell.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The bulb split from uneven moisture: a rapid water uptake after drought stress ruptures the swollen stem. Next time hold steady moisture through bulbing and avoid the dry-then-flood cycle, and harvest on time so bulbs are not standing past size when a rain comes.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Uneven moisture, a fast water uptake after drought stress.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hold steady moisture through bulbing and harvest on time to avoid the dry-then-flood split.

failure_diagnostics.label: No bulb, just leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Crowding, too much shade, or too much nitrogen late.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant grew plenty of leaves but never formed a real bulb. This usually comes from plants set too close together, too much shade, or a lot of nitrogen late on, all of which push leafy growth over the bulb. Next time, thin to 6 to 8 inches, grow in full sun, and keep feeding modest and even.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Thin to 6 to 8 inches, grow in full sun, and go easy on nitrogen late in the crop.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant made foliage but no usable swollen stem. The usual causes are crowding, insufficient light, or excess late nitrogen, each favoring leaves over the bulb. Next time thin to 6 to 8 inches, site in full sun, and keep nitrogen modest and front-loaded so the plant transitions to bulbing.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Crowding, low light, or excess late nitrogen pushing foliage over the bulb.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin to spacing, give full sun, and keep late nitrogen modest so the plant bulbs up.

primary.name: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Kohlrabi is fast (about 45 to 60 days) and each plant makes a single bulb, so the way to a steady supply is small, frequent sowings rather than one big planting. Sow in batches every 2 to 3 weeks across the spring window and again in late summer for fall, skipping the high heat of summer, when the stem turns woody and bitter. The fall crop, sizing in cooling weather, is often the most dependable.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant kohlrabi in small batches every couple of weeks instead of all at once, since each plant gives one bulb. Grow it in spring and again in late summer for fall, and skip the hottest part of summer.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Kohlrabi is ready when the swollen stem reaches about 2 to 3 inches in diameter for standard types, the size of a tennis ball, firm and smooth. Cut the bulb off at the base while it is young; past about 3 inches standard cultivars turn tough, woody, and bitter and do not recover. Giant storage types (Kossak, Superschmelz) stay tender at a much larger size. Trim the leafy tops and refrigerate promptly.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Kohlrabi is ready when the bulb is about the size of a tennis ball, 2 to 3 inches across, firm and smooth. Cut it off at the base while it is young and tender. Do not wait for it to get bigger, since standard kohlrabi turns woody and tough. Giant types are the exception and stay tender when large.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a loose, fertile, well-drained bed before planting, and mix in a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10. Loosen any compaction, since kohlrabi wants steady, unchecked growth for a tender bulb, and aim the pH at about 6.0 to 7.0, liming acidic ground where clubroot is a concern.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Before planting, mix a few inches of compost and a balanced fertilizer into loose, well-drained soil. Kohlrabi grows best in rich, evenly moist ground, which keeps the bulbs tender.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: kohlrabi_author_fresh_pilot 2026-06-29 (Claude Code author-bot; FILLED the shell, modeled structurally on the certified broccoli template). Refit to kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea Gongylodes): swollen above-ground edible STEM (no head, no side shoots), single harvest at 2 to 3 in / tennis-ball size, woody/tough/bitter if oversized or stressed, fast 45 to 60 day cycle, cool-season spring + fall, heat threshold ~75°F (USU). Biology sourced from readable T1 kohlrabi pages: UMN, USU, Iowa State, Wisconsin Horticulture; pests/diseases corroborated by Clemson cole-crop factsheets. Region MONTH calendars + frost dates + summer heat gaps are a cool-season-brassica climate function shared with broccoli (legitimately the same months for two B. oleracea cool crops in the same climates); harvest timing + heat physiology are kohlrabi-specific. successions_realized CC-DERIVED (interval_weeks=2). NOT certified: queued for the daily biology-fidelity review + per-crop source-truth sample.

open_findings.summary: The 10-region planting/harvest MONTH calendars (plant windows, frost dates, summer heat gaps, second_planting windows, succession dates) are modeled on the cool-season-brassica climate scaffold shared with the certified broccoli record: for two Brassica oleracea cool-season crops in the same climates the month-level windows are the same climate function, and kohlrabi's faster maturity (45 to 60 vs 55 to 75 days) shifts harvest by days, not months. The kohlrabi-specific refits (single-stem harvest, ~75°F heat threshold, succession cadence) live in the crop-level fields. Several regional sources are scanned/image PDFs not re-parsed at authoring (uga_ext_c963_chart, tamu_agrilife_fall_veg, nmsu_ext_cr457b, uariz_ext_az1005, uhawaii_ctahr_b91); the windows are corroborated by readable T1 (umn_ext, iastate_ext, usu_ext + UGA C943 calendar + UF VH021). A human should re-verify the regional windows against a readable kohlrabi-specific calendar at display-readiness.
open_findings.basis: Plant windows + frost dates are climate facts valid for any cool-season brassica; the readable kohlrabi T1 (UMN spring + fall mid-summer; USU 1 to 2 weeks before last frost; Iowa State early-mid April + mid-July to mid-August) match the temperate windows. No fabricated source; PDF-only regional charts flagged rather than extracted.

open_findings.summary: Each hot-region heat_pause REUSES the regional summer no-grow months from the brassica climate scaffold (a climate fact: the same months are too hot for any cool-season cole crop), while the basis prose is kohlrabi-specific physiology (the swollen stem turns woody and bitter and plants bolt above roughly 75°F, USU). The ~75°F threshold is lower than broccoli's 86/77°F heading ceiling, so if anything kohlrabi's hot-region exclusion is conservative.
open_findings.basis: USU Extension: kohlrabi grows best where temperatures do not exceed 75°F; stems turn tough and woody in heat. Cool northern zones 3 to 4 carry no heat gap (run through), matching the scaffold.

open_findings.summary: Kohlrabi is a genuinely good container crop (compact, shallow-rooted, fast); the specific pot dimensions (3 to 5 gallons, 8 in deep, 6 in spacing) are conventional small-brassica container guidance cited to the Wisconsin Extension containers article rather than a kohlrabi-specific container source.
open_findings.basis: Wisconsin Horticulture growing-vegetables-in-containers (the broccoli container precedent); kohlrabi's small size makes it lower-demand than broccoli, so the dimensions are conservative.

open_findings.summary: Clemson HGIC has no dedicated kohlrabi factsheet readable at authoring (the /factsheet/kohlrabi/ URL 404s); the Clemson cole-crop INSECT-PESTS and DISEASES factsheets, which explicitly cover 'cabbage, broccoli and other cole crops' (kohlrabi included), are cited for the pest/disease set, corroborated by the UMN and Iowa State kohlrabi pages.
open_findings.basis: The shared cabbage-family pest and disease complex (cabbageworm/looper/diamondback, cabbage aphid, flea beetle, root maggot, harlequin bug; clubroot, black rot, Alternaria, downy mildew, blackleg) is documented at the cole-crop family level by Clemson and named for kohlrabi by UMN/USU/Wisconsin.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: kohlrabi is a cool-season brassica whose swollen stem turns woody, tough, and bitter when growth is pushed by summer heat above roughly 75°F, and plants stressed by heat run to flower. The leafy tops tolerate warmth, but a tender, mild bulb will not form, so the calendar splits into a spring crop sized before the heat and a fall crop sized as it breaks. (Utah State Extension; University of Minnesota Extension)

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold-winter areas, grow kohlrabi in spring and again in late summer for fall. Plant in cool weather and pick the bulbs young, about the size of a tennis ball, before they turn woody. The fall crop is usually the easiest.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold northern zones kohlrabi is a classic two-crop cool-season vegetable: a spring planting set out a couple of weeks before the last frost and sized before summer heat, and a more dependable fall planting sown in mid-summer to mature in cool weather. Cold zones 3 and 4 run no summer heat gap, while milder zones 5 to 7 take a short midsummer pause when growth turns the stem woody and bitter. Harvest at tennis-ball size, about 2 to 3 inches across, before the bulb gets tough.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Mid-summer heat well above roughly 75°F drives fast, fibrous growth that leaves the kohlrabi stem woody and bitter and pushes stressed plants to bolt, so no crop is grown between the spring and fall windows. (Utah State Extension; UGA Extension)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: On the Gulf coast, grow kohlrabi in the cooler months, not in the heat of summer. Plant in fall and again in late winter, and harvest the bulbs while they are still young and tender.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Along the Gulf and coastal plain kohlrabi is a fall-through-spring crop grown around the hot middle of the year. Plant in the cool months for harvests in spring and again in late fall, and skip high summer, when heat above roughly 75°F makes the stem woody and bitter and pushes plants to bolt. Its fast 50 to 60 day cycle fits tight succession sowings through the long mild season.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Spring and summer heat above roughly 75°F leaves kohlrabi stems woody and bitter, so no crop is grown between the spring harvest and the late-summer fall sowing. (Utah State Extension; UC Master Gardener Program)

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In the inland valleys, grow kohlrabi in the cool months. Plant from late fall through winter for spring, and again in late summer for fall. Avoid the hottest part of summer, and harvest the bulbs young.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys kohlrabi is a winter-into-spring crop, planted through the cool months for spring harvests, with a separate fall planting in mid-to-late summer. High spring and summer heat above roughly 75°F is the limit, turning the stem woody and bitter, so the calendar works around it. Pick young for the best texture.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Along the cool northern California coast you can grow kohlrabi most of the year. Plant a few seeds every couple of weeks for a steady supply, and harvest the bulbs while they are young and tender.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The mild, cool-summer North Coast is excellent kohlrabi country: the crop grows nearly year-round, with no real summer heat gap, so successive sowings every couple of weeks keep tender bulbs coming through most of the year. Pick at 2 to 3 inches across before the stem toughens.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the southern California coast, grow kohlrabi in the cooler parts of the year. Plant in winter and again in early summer, and pick the bulbs young.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On the mild South Coast kohlrabi grows through the cool seasons with only a brief late-summer heat gap. Plant in winter for spring and again in early summer for a fall crop, harvesting young before the stem turns woody. The frost-free winters let the crop run late into the year.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the desert, grow kohlrabi only in the cool season. Plant in early fall and harvest through the winter. It is too hot the rest of the year.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the low California desert kohlrabi is strictly a cool-season crop: plant in early fall for winter harvests, since the long hot months are far too warm for a tender bulb. Harvest through winter and into early spring, picking young before any spring heat toughens the stem.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern New Mexico & West Texas

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: High desert-edge summer heat well above roughly 75°F leaves the kohlrabi stem woody and bitter and pushes plants to bolt, so no crop is grown between the spring and fall windows. (Utah State Extension; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the dry Southwest, grow kohlrabi in spring and fall, not summer. Plant after the last frost and again in late summer, and harvest the bulbs young before they toughen.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid Southwest kohlrabi is grown in spring and fall around a hot summer. Set plants out after the last frost for a spring crop, and sow again in late summer for fall, skipping the high-heat months when the stem turns woody and bitter. Its quick cycle suits the short cool windows.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the low desert of Arizona, grow kohlrabi in the cool season, planting from late summer through winter. Harvest the bulbs young, and skip the hot summer.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In the Arizona low desert kohlrabi is a fall-to-spring crop planted across the long cool season, from late summer through midwinter, for harvests from fall into spring. The summer is far too hot. Its fast cycle and the long mild window allow many successive sowings.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, grow kohlrabi in the cool months from fall into spring. Plant in fall and winter, harvest young, and skip the hot summer.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula kohlrabi is a cool-season crop grown from fall through early spring. Plant from early fall into winter for harvests through the cool months, and avoid the hot, humid summer, which makes the stem woody and invites disease. The long mild window supports repeated sowings of this fast crop.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, grow kohlrabi in the cooler months, especially at higher elevations. Plant late in the year for a winter harvest, and pick the bulbs young.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii's warm lowlands kohlrabi is best grown as a cool-season crop in the milder months, planted late in the year for winter harvests; at higher, cooler elevations the window is wider. Lowland summer heat leaves the stem tough and bitter, so the planting is kept to the coolest part of the year.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Kohlrabi set out Oct 1 - Nov 15 in the Rio Grande Valley, per RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide window, corroborated by the Bilingual LRGV planting table's days-to-harvest. Transplanted on broccoli's schedule per TAMU's RGV Homeowner Guide; 75 to 100 days to harvest (Bilingual LRGV table).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest harvest at about 75 days, from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest harvest at about 100 days, from the latest set-out date, before RGV's spring heat closes the window.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors Aug 20 - Oct 4, about 42 days before transplanting, per RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide window, corroborated by the Bilingual LRGV planting table's days-to-harvest.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, grow kohlrabi in the cool season, not summer. Transplant Oct 1 through Nov 15 and harvest from Dec 15 into spring; it rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold. Kohlrabi goes out on the same October schedule as broccoli; give the swelling stem room and it will be ready in ten to fourteen weeks. Skip planting kohlrabi from spring through summer: the Valley heat keeps it from growing well here.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Kohlrabi in the RGV runs on the winter-garden calendar: transplant Oct 1 through Nov 15, with harvest running Dec 15 through Feb 23. Transplanted on broccoli's schedule per TAMU's RGV Homeowner Guide; 75 to 100 days to harvest (Bilingual LRGV table). Frost is essentially absent here, so timing is heat-bounded rather than cold-bounded. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: the TAMU AgriLife sources describe a single Valley-wide planting calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: OSU's Oregon planting table (EM9027) marks kohlrabi as not typically started indoors here; it is direct sown once the soil has warmed, a few weeks after the last frost in the valley.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct sow the spring crop in April in the Willamette Valley, once the soil is workable and warm enough for good germination (OSU EM9027).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Kohlrabi is fast, sizing to a harvestable bulb in about 45 to 60 days.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Pick bulbs at tennis-ball size before they toughen; the spring crop should be off the ground well before the fall planting goes in.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: No indoor start for the fall crop either; direct sow it in mid-to-late summer per OSU's Willamette Valley window, which runs to mid-August.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct sow the fall crop from mid-July into early August in the valley; OSU's table extends this window to mid-August, giving a real second bulb before frost.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall bulb sizes in the cooling weather of early autumn, often the sweeter of the two crops.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Kohlrabi tolerates a light frost, so the fall harvest can run a couple of weeks past the first one.

8.zone_notes: OSU's Willamette Valley table gives kohlrabi a wide April-to-mid-August direct-sow window, wide enough for a spring bulb and a genuine second, fall bulb; it is not typically started indoors here.

9.zone_notes: OSU's coastal table carries NO spring window for kohlrabi at all here, only July-August; unlike the valley, the immediate coast's cool spring does not get a direct-sow recommendation until midsummer. This cell sows the July-August window in two waves rather than inventing an earlier planting OSU does not list; both size up well ahead of the region's early-November first frost.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: In the Willamette Valley and around Puget Sound, sow kohlrabi seed directly in the garden in April for an early-summer bulb, then sow again in mid-July for a fall crop, which is often the sweeter of the two. On the immediate coast, hold off until July; the cool, foggy coastal spring is not the time for this one there, but a July-and-August sowing still gives you two rounds of bulbs before the mild fall frost arrives. Pick bulbs about tennis-ball size, before they turn woody.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Kohlrabi is direct sown here, not started indoors, per OSU's Oregon planting table. In the valley that table opens a wide window, April through mid-August, wide enough for an April sowing maturing by early summer and a true second sowing in mid-to-late July for a fall bulb. The immediate coast is a different story: OSU's own numbers carry no spring recommendation for this crop there at all, only a July-August window, reflecting the coast's cooler, slower-warming spring soil rather than any extra mildness. This cell sows that coastal window in an early- and a late-summer wave instead of assuming the coast shares the valley's spring option. Both zones' fall bulbs run a couple of weeks past the first light frost, since kohlrabi tolerates it well, and neither zone needs a summer heat pause: the growing season here is simply long and mild.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set out the spring crop per Virginia Cooperative Extension's zone 8 Kohlrabi table (Feb 20 to Apr 1); zone 7 runs about two to three weeks later.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring harvest begins as the crop reaches maturity, before the belt's hot, humid summer sets in.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: End of the spring harvest window, before summer heat stalls quality.

plant_out.source_quote: Kohlrabi zone 8 fall: Sep 1-Oct 1
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set out the fall crop per Virginia Cooperative Extension's zone 8 Kohlrabi table (Sep 1 to Oct 1), the belt's real second cycle; zone 7 runs the window earlier and shorter.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop matures as nights cool, often the belt's better crop of the two.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall harvest continues into the cool season; this crop tolerates the belt's light frosts well.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Kohlrabi's stem quality falls apart above roughly 75°F: sustained mid-summer heat drives fast, fibrous growth that leaves the bulb woody, pithy, and sharply flavored, and stressed plants are pushed toward bolting. Virginia Cooperative Extension's Kohlrabi table carries only a spring window and a fall window for this belt, with no summer planting recommended, so this gap is a heat exclusion, not an ended season; a second cycle follows in late summer.

mid_atlantic.region_notes_beginner: Kohlrabi is quick to grow and does well both in spring and fall here, but the fall crop has the edge: the swollen stem stays mild and tender in cool weather instead of turning woody the way summer heat can push it. Sow in late winter to early spring for a spring crop, then sow again in late summer for fall.
mid_atlantic.region_notes_seasoned: Kohlrabi's short days to maturity let it fit neatly into both of Virginia Cooperative Extension's spring and fall windows here, but the fall sowing, timed to bulb up as the Piedmont and Coastal Plain's summer heat breaks, produces the more consistently mild, tender stem; summer heat is what pushes kohlrabi toward woodiness and a stronger flavor. Zone 7's cooler, shorter season narrows both windows relative to zone 8's.

mid_south.region_label: Mid-South: Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sow the spring crop from late winter (zone 8 mid-February to late March, zone 7 about two to three weeks later), resolved from the belt's frost anchors; University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's tables carry no named kohlrabi row.

crops.description_seasoned: Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea, Gongylodes group) is a cool-season cole crop grown not for a head or a root but for its swollen above-ground STEM, a round, pale-green or purple bulb that sits on the soil surface topped by a rosette of leaves. It is one of the fastest brassicas, ready in about 45 to 60 days, and is grown like a quick cabbage in the cool shoulders of spring and fall. The whole craft is steady, unchecked growth and timely harvest: a tender, mild, crisp bulb forms when the plant never stalls, while drought, heat above roughly 75°F, or a stop-start water supply, or simply letting it grow too large, turns standard types woody, fibrous, and bitter. Harvest young at 2 to 3 inches, tennis-ball size; giant storage cultivars (Kossak, Superschmelz) are the exception and hold tender flesh at a much larger size. Cold-hardy and frost-tolerant, kohlrabi shares the full cabbage-family pest and disease complex.
crops.description_beginner: Kohlrabi is a cool-season cabbage-family vegetable grown for its odd, tasty swollen stem, a round bulb, green or purple, that sits right on top of the soil with leaves sprouting from it. It is one of the fastest crops in the garden, ready in about 45 to 60 days, and grows best in the cool weather of spring and fall. The trick is simple: keep it growing steadily with even water, and pick the bulb young, about the size of a tennis ball. If you let standard kohlrabi get too big, or let it dry out or cook in summer heat, it turns woody and tough. It handles frost well, and like its cabbage cousins it gets the usual cabbage-family bugs and diseases. The bulb is crisp and mild, good raw or cooked.

thinning.when: at 2 to 3 true leaves
thinning.method: snip at the soil line
thinning.tip_seasoned: Thin direct-sown kohlrabi to 6 to 8 inches apart once seedlings have 2 to 3 true leaves, snipping rather than pulling to avoid disturbing the keepers. Crowded plants compete for moisture and make small, misshapen bulbs, and crowding stress can also push them woody.
thinning.tip_beginner: When the seedlings have a few real leaves, thin them so each plant has about 6 to 8 inches of room. Snip the extras off at the soil instead of pulling, so you don't disturb the ones you keep. Crowded kohlrabi makes small, poor bulbs.

crops.name: Honeydew Melon

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Honeydew wants a deep, light, well-drained soil in full sun, with sandy loams and loamy sands the classic choice because they warm quickly in spring and drain freely, which this heat-loving, long-season melon rewards. Work a few inches of compost into the bed before planting, but go easier on nitrogen-rich amendments than you would for leafy crops, since excess nitrogen pushes vine at the expense of fruit and sugar. Many growers plant on low, wide hills or raised mounds, which warm faster, drain better, and lift the developing fruit off wet ground. Heavy clay holds water and stays cold, slowing a crop that already needs the longest, warmest season of the common melons and inviting Fusarium wilt and fruit rot, so amend it generously and build mounds, or grow on sandier ground.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant honeydew in light, well-drained soil that warms up fast, like a sandy loam, with some compost mixed in. Do not overdo rich, high-nitrogen material, because that gives you lots of leaves and vine but less fruit. Many gardeners plant on low hills or raised mounds, which warm up and drain better and keep the fruit off soggy ground. Honeydew needs a long, hot season, so if your soil is heavy clay, it stays cold and wet and slows the crop, so mix in compost and build the soil into mounds, or pick the sandiest, best-draining spot you have.

ph.note_seasoned: Honeydew grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.8, and tolerates a wider band of roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Like other melons it is a little more forgiving of mildly acidic ground than many vegetables, but strongly acidic or strongly alkaline soil tightens nutrient uptake. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.
ph.note_beginner: Honeydew likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress once or twice
fertilizer.type: lower-nitrogen at planting, then nitrogen side-dress
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before planting, then side-dress when vines begin to run and again at flowering
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate or blood meal
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Honeydew is a moderate feeder that wants more phosphorus and potassium than nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Work a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson suggests about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then side-dress with a nitrogen source as the vines begin to run, and again lightly at flowering. Ease off nitrogen once fruit has set so the plant pours its energy into sizing and sweetening the melons rather than growing more vine. Because honeydew hangs on the vine longer than cantaloupe, pair feeding with steady, even moisture, since the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Honeydew does not need a lot of nitrogen, and too much gives you big leafy vines but fewer, less sweet melons. Mix a fertilizer that is lower in nitrogen, like a 5-10-10, into the soil before planting, then give the plants a little nitrogen when the vines start to run and again when flowers appear. Once the melons start to form, stop pushing nitrogen so the plant puts its energy into growing sweet fruit instead of more leaves.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your honeydew vines are running, time to side-dress with a little nitrogen. Then keep feeding light and ease off nitrogen once fruit sets, so the plant builds sweet melons rather than vine.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your honeydew vines are spreading. Give them a light feeding of nitrogen now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress as the vines run and again lightly at flowering, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets. Too much nitrogen gives vine and leaf at the expense of fruit and sweetness.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a lower-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 at planting, then a little nitrogen as the vines spread. Do not overdo the nitrogen once melons form, or you get leaves instead of fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common approach is a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked into the bed before planting (Clemson cites about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then a nitrogen side-dress about three to four weeks after planting as vines run, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly at flowering.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix a lower-nitrogen fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then feed with a little nitrogen about three to four weeks later, scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more when flowers appear.

companions.note_seasoned: Most honeydew companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on serve two practical ends: pollination and pest pressure. Because honeydew fruit set is strongly pollinator-limited, flowering insectary plants like borage near the patch are a genuine help. A trap planting of nasturtium can divert cucumber beetles, which matters more here than for watermelon because those beetles spread bacterial wilt and melons are very susceptible to it. Bush beans fix a little nitrogen the crop can use without the heavy feeding that would grow vine over fruit. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep honeydew away from other cucurbits, which share its pest and disease complex, including the soilborne Fusarium wilt and the foliar gummy stem blight that build up where melons follow melons.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful honeydew companions are flowers that bring in bees, since honeydew needs lots of bee visits to set fruit. Nasturtiums can lure cucumber beetles away, which is helpful because those beetles spread a wilt disease that melons catch easily. Bush beans add a little nitrogen. The one rule that really matters is to keep honeydew away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash, which all share the same pests and diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and honeydew needs lots of bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators honeydew fruit set depends on, since each female flower needs many bee visits to set and size a melon. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-honeydew pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Honeydew fruit set is pollinator-limited; flowering insectary plants like borage draw bees. Pairing is habitat-based, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which honeydew can use, and they do not share honeydew's pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Bush beans fix nitrogen that lightly benefits the crop without the heavy nitrogen that would push vine over fruit, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation is documented; the bean-melon adjacency benefit is traditional, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are grown near melons to lure cucumber beetles away, which is extra useful for honeydew because those beetles spread a wilt disease melons catch easily. Their flowers also bring in bees.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for cucumber beetles, which matters more for honeydew than for watermelon because the beetles transmit bacterial wilt, to which melons are very susceptible. Its flowers also draw the bees honeydew needs for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-honeydew effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap-cropping for cucurbit beetles is documented in principle; the beetles vector bacterial wilt on melons; the nasturtium-honeydew pairing is not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn is the traditional Three Sisters partner that gives sprawling vines something to grow among. With honeydew it is more tradition than a proven boost, and honeydew's full-sun need means you should not let corn shade it.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner, though the fit is looser for honeydew than for shade-tolerant squash: tall corn can give the trailing vines structure, but honeydew wants full sun and heat to sweeten, so keep corn from shading the patch. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a space rationale, not a measured yield effect for this pair.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep honeydew away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash. They share most of the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber, cantaloupe, squash, and pumpkin share honeydew's pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it carries, aphid-spread mosaic viruses, the mildews, and the soilborne Fusarium wilt and foliar gummy stem blight that build up where cucurbits repeat. Grouping them concentrates that pressure. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them on a long cycle.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens (cucumber beetle plus its bacterial wilt, Fusarium wilt, gummy stem blight, mildews) are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and melons apart, since both are hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor disease and attract pests near melons. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A folk anti-companion caution; competition is plausible but there is no T1 source isolating a potato-melon antagonism.

pests.name: Cucumber beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small striped or spotted yellow beetles chew young leaves, stems, flowers, and the rind of developing fruit, and can feed on seedlings below ground. The bigger threat is indirect: cucumber beetles transmit bacterial wilt and spread mosaic viruses, and honeydew, like cantaloupe and cucumber, is highly susceptible to the wilt, so beetle control on young plants is the single most important defense.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chew on the leaves and flowers of young plants and can scar the fruit. Worse, they spread a wilt disease that melons catch easily, so keeping them off young plants really matters.
pests.cause_seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and overwinter as adults, colonizing plants early. They carry the bacterial wilt organism (Erwinia tracheiphila) in their gut and introduce it through feeding wounds, and they also spread mosaic viruses; seedlings and young vines are most vulnerable.
pests.cause_beginner: Cucumber beetles spend the winter as adults and move onto young plants early. As they feed they infect the plant with a wilt disease and can carry other viruses, and young plants are most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with floating row cover removed at flowering for pollination, hand-pick beetles, and clear weeds that shelter them. Yellow sticky traps help monitor and reduce numbers; keep young plants vigorous so they grow past the most vulnerable stage. Because there is no cure for bacterial wilt once a plant has it, prevention is aimed squarely at the beetles.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover (take it off when flowers open so bees can reach them), pick beetles off by hand, and clear away weeds. Yellow sticky traps help. Since the wilt disease they spread cannot be cured, the goal is to keep the beetles off.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude beetles from seedlings with row cover, keep plants growing fast, clear weeds and debris, and rotate away from where cucurbits grew. Aim control at the early-season colonizers, since early infection is what triggers wilt.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings until they flower, keep them growing strong, clear away weeds and old plants, and do not plant where melons or squash grew last year.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not plant melons where melons, squash, or cucumbers grew last year. The beetles spend the winter as adults and move onto young plants early, so fresh ground puts distance between them and your seedlings.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotation away from last season's cucurbit ground targets the overwintered adults that colonize earliest; those early colonizers are the ones whose feeding triggers wilt, so the effort points at them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear away weeds and old plants around the patch. Weeds give the beetles shelter, and cleaning up debris leaves them fewer places to hide.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Weeds and crop debris shelter adults right beside the planting; stripping both removes cover for the overwintering and early-colonizing population.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover seedlings with a floating row cover, a light fabric laid over the young plants, and take it off when the flowers open so bees can reach them. Keeping beetles off young plants matters most, because that is when the wilt they carry does its damage.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Exclusion through the seedling stage covers the window when plants are most vulnerable and when beetle feeding introduces the wilt bacterium; lift the cover at flowering for pollination. With no cure for the wilt itself, this preventive rung is where the leverage sits.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the beetles off by hand and destroy them. Every beetle you take off a young plant is one less chance for it to catch the wilt.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hand-removal earns the most on seedlings and young vines, the stage the beetles colonize first and the stage most at risk of infection through their feeding wounds.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Yellow sticky traps catch beetles and show you how many are around, which helps you judge whether the other steps are keeping up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Traps do double duty here, monitoring beetle numbers and thinning them; read them mainly as a scouting signal layered on top of exclusion and handpicking.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often melon aphids, cluster on leaf undersides and growing tips, curling and yellowing the leaves and coating them in sticky honeydew that grows sooty mold. Beyond direct feeding, melon aphids transmit mosaic viruses that mottle and distort the foliage and can ruin a crop.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft insects gather under the leaves and on new growth, making leaves curl and yellow, often with a sticky film. They can also spread viruses that damage the plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: Melon and other aphids suck sap and multiply rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on stressed or over-fertilized plants, and typically colonize once the vines begin to run. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold, and several species spread cucurbit mosaic viruses.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck the plant's juices and multiply quickly, especially on soft, over-fed growth. The sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold, and they can carry plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control; reflective mulch deters them from young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective or aluminum-foil mulch deters aphids from young plants.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work. A reflective mulch around young plants helps keep aphids away.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on nitrogen fertilizer. Heavy feeding pushes out the soft, sappy growth that aphids settle on and multiply in fastest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen drives the succulent flush aphids favor and build up on fastest; restrained feeding removes that condition before colonies establish, which typically happens once the vines begin to run.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay a reflective or aluminum-foil mulch around the plants while they are still young. The bright surface helps keep aphids from settling on them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch deters incoming aphids while plants are small, worth having down early given that melon aphids also transmit the mosaic viruses that can ruin a crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the colonies off with a strong jet of water, aiming at the undersides of the leaves and the new growth where they gather. Repeat every few days as they build back.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful jet dislodges colonies from leaf undersides and growing tips; treat it as a repeated knock-back on a few-day cycle rather than a single pass.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps eat aphids and usually bring them under control on their own, so make them welcome instead of spraying broadly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually regulate aphid numbers on their own; conserving them rather than spraying broadly is the control that costs nothing and holds longest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the colonies keep building, spray insecticidal soap, a soap-based spray that kills only the insects it touches. Coat the undersides of the leaves well and repeat every few days.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is contact-only, so thorough leaf-underside coverage repeated every few days is what carries it, and its light footprint leaves room for the natural enemies to return.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil, does the same job as the soap. Cover the leaf undersides well and repeat every few days if the aphids persist.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil is the alternate contact material on identical terms, thorough underside coverage on a several-day repeat; the choice between oil and soap changes little about the technique.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow and reddish-brown stippling appears on the upper sides of leaves, ranging from small specks to large whitish stippled areas, and fine webbing shows on leaf undersides in bad infestations. Two-spotted spider mites explode in hot, dry weather, exactly honeydew's long, hot season, and heavy feeding bronzes and dries the foliage, cutting fruit size and sugar.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The leaves get a fine yellow or bronze speckling, and in bad cases you see tiny webs underneath. Spider mites love hot, dry weather and can build up fast on honeydew in summer.
pests.cause_seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny sap-feeders that proliferate during hot, dry weather and whose populations explode when their natural enemies are killed off by broad-spectrum sprays. They feed mostly on leaf undersides.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny mites that thrive in hot, dry summers and multiply fast, especially after broad insecticide sprays kill the helpful bugs that normally keep them down. They feed on the undersides of the leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray plants with a strong jet of water to dislodge mites and raise humidity, and apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough leaf-underside coverage before populations peak, repeating as needed. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides, which kill the predatory mites and insects that control them.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the plants, especially the undersides of the leaves, with a strong stream of water, and treat with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if needed. Avoid spraying broad insecticides, which kill the good bugs that eat mites.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well watered and not heat-stressed, since drought-stressed plants are hit hardest, and avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that wipe out natural enemies. Scout leaf undersides through hot, dry spells and act early.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep plants watered so they are not stressed in the heat, and avoid spraying strong insecticides that kill helpful bugs. Check under the leaves during hot, dry weather and treat early if you see speckling.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the plants steadily watered through hot spells. Mites hit drought-stressed plants hardest, and a melon patch's long, hot season is exactly the weather they love.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Drought-stressed plants take the worst damage, and two-spotted mite populations explode in the hot, dry stretch a melon season delivers; steady moisture removes the stress that feeds the flare.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spray the plants with a strong stream of water, especially the undersides of the leaves where the mites feed. It knocks them off and raises the humidity they dislike.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful rinse to the leaf undersides dislodges mites and raises humidity around the foliage; useful before any spray and worth repeating through hot, dry weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Predatory mites and helpful insects normally keep spider mites in check. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides, meaning sprays that kill many kinds of insects at once, because losing those helpers is what lets mites explode.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Predatory mites and generalist insect predators are what normally hold this pest down, and broad-spectrum sprays removing them is the classic outbreak trigger; conservation is the rung to protect even while treating something else.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Insecticidal soap, a soap-based contact spray, works if you coat the undersides of the leaves thoroughly. Put it on early, before the mites peak, and repeat as needed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap applied before populations peak, with deliberate underside coverage and repeat applications as needed; heavy feeding bronzes foliage and costs fruit size and sugar, so early timing beats chasing an established outbreak.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil is the other option, applied the same way: thorough coverage of the leaf undersides, repeated as needed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil on the same terms as soap, applied ahead of the population peak with the undersides covered; both are contact materials, so coverage decides the outcome.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves develop yellow specks that brown and wilt, and heavily fed runners can wilt and turn brittle. Flat bronze egg clusters appear on leaf undersides along the veins, and gray-brown adults and pale nymphs cluster near the crown and under debris. Honeydew is less affected than winter squash, but young plants can still be hurt.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get yellow spots, then brown and wilt, and you find clusters of shield-shaped gray-brown bugs and their bronze eggs under the leaves. Honeydew is not their favorite, but they can still bother young plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: The squash bug feeds with piercing-sucking mouthparts on cucurbit foliage and stems, injecting saliva that wilts and browns the tissue. There is one generation a year in much of the South, and adults overwinter in garden debris. It prefers squash and pumpkin to melons.
pests.cause_beginner: Squash bugs pierce the leaves and stems and suck out the juices, which makes the vines wilt. They hide in plant debris over winter and prefer squash to melons, but can still attack young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults, crush the bronze egg masses on leaf undersides, and trap bugs by laying a board near the plants overnight, then lifting it in the morning and destroying the cluster underneath. Target young nymphs with insecticidal soap, since adults are tough to kill.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the bugs off by hand and scrape off the egg clusters under the leaves. A board laid on the ground overnight draws them underneath, then lift it in the morning and destroy them. Treat the young bugs with insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clean up vines and debris at season's end to cut overwintering sites, rotate cucurbits, and scout leaf undersides for the bronze egg clusters from early in the season, acting before nymphs mature.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up old vines after harvest so the bugs have nowhere to overwinter, move your melons around the garden each year, and check under the leaves for eggs early in the season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move your melons to a different part of the garden each year. Squash bugs prefer squash and pumpkins, but rotating still breaks up the ground they come back to.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotating cucurbits denies overwintered adults a familiar bed; melons are a secondary host next to squash and pumpkin, which shapes how much pressure this rung has to absorb.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clean up the old vines and debris after harvest. The adults spend the winter tucked into that litter, so clearing it leaves them far fewer places to shelter.
