northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North, honeydew is a real stretch and the most demanding of the melons, since it wants the longest, hottest season and handles cold worse than cantaloupe. Zones 3 to 5 are unsuitable to marginal: start transplants indoors about three weeks early, choose the earliest varieties such as Earlidew, use black plastic mulch to warm the soil, and expect a poor-summer year to fall short. Warmer zones 6 to 7 can finish a crop with an early start. Plant only after the soil is reliably warm at 70°F, and harvest the single crop in late summer before fall cooling.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold North, honeydew is hard to grow because it needs a long, hot summer and does not like cold. The coldest zones (3 to 5) may not ripen a melon at all in a cool year. Start plants indoors, grow an early variety like Earlidew, use black plastic mulch, and plant only once the soil is good and warm. Warmer areas (6 to 7) do better. You get one crop, ripening in late summer.

se_gulf.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh honeydew windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (85 to 100) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season melon that wants the longest, hottest season of the common melons and is more cold-sensitive than cantaloupe (cool-summer/short-season cells marginal to unsuitable); single harvest at full ripeness read by the no-slip cues; no heat_pause (honeydew produces through summer heat); hottest desert and Florida cells split into two windows for crop turnover.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Gulf and coastal plain, honeydew is a spring-to-summer crop that enjoys the long, hot season: plant as the soil warms in spring and harvest through mid to late summer. The hot, humid summers drive heavy disease pressure (Fusarium wilt, gummy stem blight, the mildews) and heavy cucumber-beetle and bacterial-wilt pressure, so control beetles early, choose resistant varieties, rotate, and water at the base. A separate late-summer planting for a fall crop is possible in the warmer zones.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, plant honeydew in spring once the soil warms and harvest through the summer, which honeydew likes for its heat. The hot, humid weather brings a lot of disease and cucumber beetles that spread wilt, so keep beetles off, choose disease-resistant varieties, rotate where you plant, and water at the base. In the warmer areas you can also plant again in late summer.

ca_interior.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh honeydew windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (85 to 100) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season melon that wants the longest, hottest season of the common melons and is more cold-sensitive than cantaloupe (cool-summer/short-season cells marginal to unsuitable); single harvest at full ripeness read by the no-slip cues; no heat_pause (honeydew produces through summer heat); hottest desert and Florida cells split into two windows for crop turnover.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's hot interior valleys are prime honeydew country: plant from spring into early summer and harvest through the warm, dry late summer. The long, dry heat suits honeydew, which wants more heat than any other common melon, as long as irrigation is steady and deep through sizing, and the dry air keeps foliar disease lower than in the humid Southeast. Taper water near ripeness to concentrate the sugars.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: California's hot inland valleys are great for honeydew, which loves heat. Plant from spring into early summer and harvest in the warm, dry late summer. Water steadily and deeply, and the dry air means less leaf disease. Ease off the water near the end to sweeten the fruit.

ca_north_coast.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh honeydew windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (85 to 100) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season melon that wants the longest, hottest season of the common melons and is more cold-sensitive than cantaloupe (cool-summer/short-season cells marginal to unsuitable); single harvest at full ripeness read by the no-slip cues; no heat_pause (honeydew produces through summer heat); hottest desert and Florida cells split into two windows for crop turnover.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's cool, foggy north coast is marginal to unsuitable for honeydew, which wants far more heat than the coast delivers, more even than cantaloupe. Plant after the soil warms in late spring and harvest in fall, but expect slow ripening and lean hard on the earliest varieties, the warmest, sunniest microclimate you have, and black plastic mulch. Inland and away from the fog the crop does much better.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: California's cool, foggy north coast is a tough spot for honeydew, which wants a lot of heat. Plant in late spring once it warms and harvest in fall, but choose the earliest variety, the sunniest, warmest spot you have, and use black plastic mulch. It does much better the farther you are from the coastal fog.

ca_south_coast.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh honeydew windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (85 to 100) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Heat-loving warm-season melon that wants the longest, hottest season of the common melons and is more cold-sensitive than cantaloupe (cool-summer/short-season cells marginal to unsuitable); single harvest at full ripeness read by the no-slip cues; no heat_pause (honeydew produces through summer heat); hottest desert and Florida cells split into two windows for crop turnover.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's mild south coast grows honeydew well through a long, gentle warm season: plant from spring into early summer and harvest from midsummer into fall. The warmest, sunniest inland sites ripen the sweetest fruit; right on the coast, cooler air and humidity slow ripening and favor mildew, so prioritize full sun and airflow and pick a warm microclimate.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: California's mild south coast is good for honeydew. Plant from spring into early summer and harvest from midsummer into fall. Pick the warmest, sunniest spot for the sweetest melons. Right at the coast it can be cooler and a bit damp, which slows ripening, so give plenty of sun and air.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The California desert valleys are classic melon ground and suit honeydew especially, since it wants the most heat of the common melons: plant in late winter to early spring and harvest from early through late summer. Honeydew produces right through the desert heat rather than pausing, as long as irrigation is steady and deep, and the dry air keeps disease low. Time the planting so the crop sizes and sweetens through the long, hot, dry season.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The California desert is great honeydew country, since honeydew loves heat more than any other melon. Plant in late winter to early spring and harvest from early through late summer. Honeydew keeps producing through the desert heat, as long as you water deeply and steadily, and the dry air means little disease.

Honeydew tolerates the desert heat better than most crops, so the two plantings run back to back through the season rather than pausing for heat. fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In peninsular Florida, honeydew is grown in the cooler, drier halves of the year, planted in late winter to spring and again in late summer for a fall crop, avoiding the wettest part of midsummer when humidity and rain drive heavy disease. The deep-summer break is disease- and rain-driven, not heat, since honeydew loves the heat. Seed the spring crop early, control cucumber beetles and the bacterial wilt they carry, choose resistant varieties, and watch closely for gummy stem blight and the mildews.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In Florida, plant honeydew in late winter to spring and again in late summer, avoiding the wettest part of summer when disease is worst. The break in midsummer is about rain and disease, not heat, since honeydew likes it hot. Keep cucumber beetles off, choose disease-resistant varieties, and watch the leaves closely for disease.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Honeydew melon transplants go out Feb 25 - Mar 20 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide, corroborated by the Bilingual LRGV planting table's 85 to 90 day maturity figure for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest spring harvest at about 85 days from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest spring harvest at about 90 days from the latest set-out date.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall honeydew melon transplants go out Aug 1 - Sep 1 in the Rio Grande Valley, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide / Bilingual LRGV fall window for this crop class.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest fall harvest at about 85 days from the earliest fall set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest fall harvest, extending into the mild Valley winter tail before spring returns.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, honeydew melon is a two-season crop. Plant Feb 25 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest, then plant again Aug 1 - Sep 1 for a fall crop. Skip the hottest weeks of summer: the plant just does not perform well in the worst of the heat, so most Valley gardeners skip it. It rarely if ever frosts here, so both the spring and fall windows run on Valley heat, not on a frost date.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Honeydew melon in the RGV runs on the Valley's two-crop calendar: set out Feb 25 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest running May 21 - Jun 18, then set out again Aug 1 - Sep 1 for a fall harvest running Oct 25 - Nov 30. TAMU AgriLife's Valley planting guidance simply leaves that stretch off the calendar for this crop, rather than asserting a specific heat-failure mechanism. Frost is essentially absent here, so both plantings are timed against heat, not cold. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Honeydew is not its own row in OSU Extension's Oregon planting table (EM9027); this cell reasons from the table's cantaloupe/muskmelon line (the same document, the same warm-season vining-cucurbit culture group) using the same 4-week indoor lead time, then adjusts the harvest end for honeydew's own longer, more heat-hungry days-to-maturity (85 to 100, versus cantaloupe's 75 to 90).

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out in May in the Willamette Valley, the same soil-warmth-driven window OSU gives cantaloupe (reasoned analogy, honeydew is not a separately named row). OSU rates Region 1 (the immediate coast) not suitable for the less-demanding cantaloupe, so honeydew, which needs even more sustained heat, is at least as marginal there.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Honeydew wants the longest, hottest run of the common melons and ripens without a slip cue cantaloupe gives, so it is read by stem/blossom-end softening and aroma; the cool maritime summer pushes this well past the crop's base 85 to 100 day maturity.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Choose only the earliest honeydew cultivars bred for short seasons; a standard-season honeydew is a poor bet on this side of the Cascades.

8.zone_notes: Honeydew is not its own row in OSU's Willamette Valley table (EM9027); this cell reasons from the table's cantaloupe/muskmelon May window (same document, same culture group) plus honeydew's own longer days-to-maturity (85 to 100), which is why its harvest starts and ends later than cantaloupe's in this same zone. This is the most heat-hungry of the three melons in this batch; grow only the earliest short-season cultivars, in the warmest full-sun bed, under black plastic mulch, with season-extension cover through early summer.

9.zone_notes: OSU's planting table does not carry a separate honeydew row, but it rates the coast (Region 1) not suitable for the less-demanding cantaloupe; honeydew, which needs an even longer, hotter run, is at least as marginal here, if not more so. This cell authors a conservative, compressed window anyway for a gardener who wants to try it, clipped tight against the coast's own early-November first frost. This is a long shot even with every advantage; expect it to fail to ripen in most years.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: Honeydew is the hardest melon to grow in this region: it needs more heat and a longer season than cantaloupe, and our cool summers usually cannot give it that. OSU's own planting guide does not even list honeydew separately, and it rates the coast unsuitable for the easier cantaloupe. Inland, plant in May, pick the earliest-ripening honeydew variety you can find, and give it your hottest, sunniest spot with black plastic under it and a cover over it in early summer. Even then it ripens slowly and late, and some years it may not ripen at all. On the coast, this is really a long shot.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Honeydew is the toughest of the common melons to grow here: it wants an even longer, hotter run than cantaloupe, and OSU Extension's Oregon planting table does not carry honeydew as its own row, treating the coast as unsuitable for the less-demanding cantaloupe already. In the valley, set transplants out in May, choose only the earliest honeydew cultivars bred for short seasons, and count on the fruit sizing up slowly through a long summer, ripening, if at all, in September or later. The warmest full-sun site, black plastic mulch, and season-extension cover through early summer are not optional here, they are the difference between a crop and nothing. On the coast, honeydew is a long shot even with every advantage.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct-sown or a short indoor head start; honeydew's 92-day maturity is the longest of the valley's common melons, so its window runs latest into June.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Honeydew wants the longest, hottest run of any of the valley's melons, so give it from early March through mid-June to get started (a three-week indoor head start helps), then let it grow straight through summer with no pause. The first melons are ready by early summer from the earliest sowings, and the harvest continues into September for later plantings. Honeydew does not slip like cantaloupe, so watch for the rind to turn from green to a waxy cream-yellow and the blossom end to give slightly.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: Honeydew needs more heat and a longer season than cantaloupe, so the Master Gardener chart's March-April and June shading is read here as one wide sowing window, early March into mid-June, that carries the vines through the Mojave summer with no heat_pause. At a 92-day maturity the earliest sowings ripen first, with later June plantings extending picking into mid-September, comfortably ahead of the valley's late-November frost (the margin tightens some at the cooler zone 8 edge).

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Because this crop sets fruit through the desert summer with no heat-driven pause, picking continues from vine to vine into fall, ending as the November 1 average first frost approaches.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Honeydew wants the longest run of any melon in St. George's Dixie garden, so get it in the ground by early April once the soil is warm. It grows straight through the hottest months without a pause, and the first melons are ready by early July, with picking continuing into October. Honeydew will not slip from the vine the way cantaloupe does, so watch instead for the rind to shift from green to a waxy cream-yellow, with the blossom end giving slightly to a gentle press.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: USU Extension's Group D (Very Tender) planting date for St. George is April 1, and honeydew's own 92-day maturity, the slowest of the region's common melons, pushes the first harvest into early July. Because honeydew keeps setting and finishing fruit through the desert's hottest months rather than pausing like the heat-sensitive nightshades, the harvest runs from early July into October, with a comfortable margin ahead of the November 1 average first frost. No fall crop is authored here; USU's St. George planting guidance covers spring only for this crop.

crops.name: Grapefruit

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Deep, well-drained sandy loam to loam; grapefruit tolerates the light sands of Florida and the desert as long as drainage is sharp and feeding keeps pace
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Deep soil that drains well is best, such as sandy loam or loam. Grapefruit does fine in light sandy soil as long as water drains away fast and you feed it.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Sandy and rocky soils with steady water and feeding; heavier ground only on a raised mound or berm that guarantees the crown drains
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Sandy or rocky soil is fine if you water and feed enough. Heavier soil works only if you plant on a raised mound so water drains away from the trunk.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Heavy, poorly drained clay and any low spot where water stands, which sets up Phytophthora foot and root rot, the disease most likely to kill a citrus tree
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Avoid heavy clay that drains slowly and any spot where water pools. Wet roots lead to a root rot that is the most common way citrus trees die.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Grapefruit cares most about drainage. It likes deep soil that drains well and stays slightly acidic, kept evenly moist but never soggy. If water sits around the roots, the tree can get a root rot that is the most common way citrus dies, so on heavy clay build a low mound and set the tree on top. Keep the knobby graft union above the soil line. Grapefruit is a big, thirsty, hungry tree, so give it room and feed it well. If your soil is alkaline (high-pH), which is common in the desert and inland West, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc so the leaves do not yellow.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Grapefruit demands sharp drainage above all else, then rewards steady water and feeding on a large frame. It thrives in deep, well-drained sandy loam or loam, slightly acidic, and adapts well to the light sands of Florida and the low desert where drainage is naturally fast. The single most important soil decision is drainage: saturated roots invite Phytophthora foot and root rot, the disease most likely to kill a citrus tree. On heavy or slow ground, plant high on a raised mound or berm so the root crown drains freely and set the graft union clear of the soil line. High-pH alkaline soils, common in the desert and interior West, are workable but tend to lock up iron, zinc, and manganese, so a micronutrient-inclusive citrus fertilizer helps. Because grapefruit makes a big, heavy-cropping tree, give the root zone space and keep it fed.

ph.note_beginner: Grapefruit likes soil that is slightly acidic, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerates a bit either side. The main thing to watch is alkaline (high-pH) soil, common in the desert and inland West, where the tree cannot take up iron and zinc and the leaves turn yellow with green veins. If that happens, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc.
ph.note_seasoned: Grapefruit prefers a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerates a somewhat wider band; extension citrus guidance clusters around 5.5 to 6.5. The practical issue is high-pH alkaline soil (common in the desert Southwest and interior West), where iron, zinc, and manganese become chemically unavailable and the tree shows interveinal chlorosis (yellow leaves with green veins) even though the nutrients are present. Correct with chelated micronutrients and a citrus fertilizer that includes them.

fertilizer.frequency: split applications through the growing season
fertilizer.type: citrus (nitrogen-forward, with iron, zinc, and manganese)
fertilizer.timing: late winter or early spring through summer; stop by late summer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Grapefruit is a large, nitrogen-hungry tree and responds to a feeding rhythm concentrated in the growing season. Feed a mature tree from late winter or early spring through summer in split applications, and stop by late summer so new growth hardens before winter cold. Young trees get smaller, more frequent doses to build the framework. Alkaline soils chemically lock up iron, zinc, and manganese, so look for a citrus-formulated fertilizer that supplies all three as chelates and water it in well to reach the roots. Do not overfeed, since excess tender flush draws aphids, leafminer, and psyllid, and can raise fruit acidity on a crop that already leans tart.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Grapefruit is a big tree that is hungry for nitrogen and wants most of its food during the growing season. Start feeding a grown tree as the weather warms in late winter or early spring, keep it up through summer in a few split doses, and stop by late summer so the new growth toughens before cool weather. Feed young trees smaller amounts more often to build the framework. If your soil is alkaline, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc so the leaves do not yellow. Do not overfeed, since extra soft growth attracts pests.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A nitrogen-forward citrus formulation (for example a 2-1-1 ratio) with included micronutrients (iron, zinc, manganese), or a product labeled specifically for citrus and avocado
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A fertilizer made for citrus (look for one labeled citrus or citrus and avocado); these are higher in nitrogen and include the iron and zinc citrus needs
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Scale nitrogen to tree age and size, and remember grapefruit makes a larger tree than most citrus. Extension guides for the Southeast schedule mature trees at roughly a few pounds of a balanced citrus fertilizer per application across several applications a year, more for a big tree; follow the product label and local extension rates, which vary by region and soil.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Give more as the tree gets bigger, following the amounts on the citrus fertilizer label and splitting it across spring and summer. A small young tree needs only a little; a big grown grapefruit needs a good deal more. When in doubt, follow the package directions for the tree's size.

companions.note_beginner: Keep grass and lawn out from under a grapefruit tree, since grass steals the water and food the tree's shallow roots need, and a big grapefruit needs a lot of both. A wide ring of mulch (kept back from the trunk) is better than grass right up to the tree. There is no real benefit to planting things close around citrus, and other citrus nearby can add seeds to a low-seed grapefruit.
companions.note_seasoned: Keep turf and lawn grasses out of the root zone. Grass competes aggressively for water and nutrients in the top soil layer where citrus feeder roots concentrate, and a large grapefruit with its heavy, long-hanging crop is a hungry, thirsty tree that suffers most from that competition. A mulched, grass-free area extending to the canopy dripline is the standard recommendation for all citrus. Low-growing legume cover or shallow-rooted ground covers planted outside the trunk flare provide living mulch without root competition. Grapefruit is self-fruitful, so no pollinizer companion is needed; if anything, nearby seed-bearing citrus can raise the seed count in an otherwise low-seed grapefruit.

good_beginner.name: White clover
good_beginner.why_beginner: A low clover outside the trunk area acts as a living mulch and adds a little nitrogen, without stealing water the way lawn grass does.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Legume living-mulch / cover in citrus is extension-supported for soil nitrogen and organic matter; medium because citrus-specific nitrogen transfer is site-dependent and clover also competes for water.

good_beginner.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner.why_beginner: An easy flower that covers bare soil and draws in helpful insects. Keep it out from the trunk so it does not crowd the base.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Nasturtium aphid trap-crop and pollinator draw is a well-documented general function that transfers reasonably to citrus aphids; no grapefruit-specific trial located. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Comfrey
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Deep roots pull up nutrients, and the leaves can be cut and dropped as a mulch. Plant it outside the trunk flare, not against the tree.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Chop-and-drop mulch, non-competing deep taproot, and pollinator draw are widely practiced in fruit-tree guilds and partly grounded; dynamic-accumulator mineral claims are permaculture tradition, not peer-reviewed. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Comfrey is a leafy plant that grows well near citrus. Its roots reach deep, so it does not fight the tree for water, and a few times a season you can cut the big leaves and lay them on the soil as a mulch. Plant it out past the trunk, not against the tree, and let its flowers bring in helpful bees.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Yarrow
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low, shallow-rooted plant that draws beneficial insects and does not compete with the citrus roots when kept outside the dripline.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Yarrow as an insectary/beneficial attractant plus drought-tolerant ground cover is consistently reported and mechanistically plausible; the citrus-specific pest-reduction effect is unquantified. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Yarrow is a low, tough plant with flat flower heads that draw in ladybugs, lacewings, and other good bugs that eat aphids. It is shallow-rooted and easygoing, so it does not crowd the citrus roots as long as you keep it out toward the edge of the canopy. Let it flower to get the benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Fava bean
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season nitrogen fixer that can be grown beyond the dripline as a cover, then cut and dropped to feed the soil without crowding the tree.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Legume winter cover crops in citrus are extension-supported for soil nitrogen and organic matter; medium because the citrus-specific nitrogen-transfer magnitude is site and timing dependent.

bad_beginner.name: Turf grass
bad_beginner.why_beginner: Lawn grass under the tree steals the water and food a big grapefruit's shallow roots need. A ring of mulch, kept back from the trunk, is better than grass.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Beginner-register version of the citrus-grass-competition concern; standard extension citrus guidance. extension_backed/medium.

bad_beginner.name: Bermuda grass
bad_beginner.why_beginner: A tough, spreading lawn grass that competes hard for water and is difficult to keep out of the root zone. Clear it out to the edge of the branches.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Same citrus-grass-competition basis; Bermuda is a highly competitive, aggressively spreading turf that appears in citrus orchard-floor literature. extension_backed/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: St. Augustine grass
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A dense, spreading lawn grass that competes aggressively for water and nutrients in the top soil and creeps right up to the trunk. Keep it cleared out to the dripline.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Citrus is extension-documented as highly vulnerable to weed/grass competition in the root zone; St. Augustine is a notably aggressive spreading turf. extension_backed/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: St. Augustine is a thick, fast-spreading lawn grass, and it is rough on citrus. It soaks up the water and food in the top soil where the tree's roots feed, and it creeps up to the trunk. Keep a clear or mulched circle around the base and hold the grass back beyond it.

bad_seasoned.name: Other seed-bearing citrus nearby
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Grapefruit does not need a pollinizer, and planting a seedy citrus close by works against a low-seed grapefruit rather than for it. White Marsh and the red grapefruit sports are low-seeded to nearly seedless when grown in isolation, but bees moving pollen from a nearby seed-bearing citrus can fertilize the flowers and raise the seed count in the fruit. This is not a pest or disease issue, just a fruit-quality one: if seedlessness matters to you, give a low-seed grapefruit some distance from other pollen-heavy citrus.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Cross-pollination raising seed count in otherwise low-seed citrus is documented citrus horticulture (seedless citrus set more seeds when cross-pollinated by nearby pollen-bearing trees). extension_backed/medium: the mechanism is well established; the field magnitude depends on bee activity and variety.

pests.name: Asian citrus psyllid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A tiny mottled-brown insect, about an eighth of an inch, that feeds tilted up at a 45-degree angle on new flush, a posture no other citrus pest shares. Nymphs produce waxy tubules and curl tender growth. It matters less for direct damage than for what it carries: it is the vector of Huanglongbing (citrus greening), the most serious citrus disease worldwide, and grapefruit is among the citrus that decline fastest once infected. Scout the youngest flush.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This tiny brown insect rests on new leaves at an angle, rear end raised, which is your identification clue. The young ones make little waxy white threads and curl the new leaf tips. The real danger is not the feeding but a fatal disease it spreads, citrus greening, which hits grapefruit especially hard, so act on it even where the pest seems uncommon.
pests.cause_seasoned: Adults lay eggs only on new flush, so populations track flushing cycles and surge in warm weather. The pest is established across much of the southern United States, and any psyllid should be assumed a potential disease carrier.
pests.cause_beginner: The psyllid breeds on fresh new leaves, so it builds up fastest when the tree is pushing tender growth in warm weather. It has spread across the southern states, and any psyllid you find could be carrying the disease.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Buy only certified citrus from a reputable nursery and never move citrus plants or leaves out of a quarantine area. Inspect each new flush in the warm season, and conserve the natural enemies (the parasitic wasp Tamarixia and general predators) that suppress it. Where the disease is present, area-wide psyllid control is the front line.
pests.prevention_beginner: Buy certified citrus from a trusted nursery, and never carry citrus plants or cuttings out of a quarantine zone. Check the new leaves often in warm weather. If citrus greening is in your area, follow local guidance on controlling the psyllid.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: On a backyard tree, horticultural oil and insecticidal soap on new flush reduce nymphs; thorough coverage is key, repeated as each flush emerges. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree. Most importantly, report suspected psyllids or greening symptoms to your county agricultural office, since this is a regulated pest.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the new growth to knock back the young psyllids, repeating each time fresh leaves appear. Hold off on oil when it is hot, above about 95°F, or when the tree is short on water. Report any psyllids or signs of the disease to your local farm advisor, because it is closely tracked.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A small parasitic wasp called Tamarixia, along with a range of general predators, already feeds on this psyllid. The useful thing you can do is stay out of their way: keep broad, strong insecticides off the tree, since those take out the helpers along with the pest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserving the resident natural enemies, the parasitoid Tamarixia together with generalist predators, is the standing suppression on a backyard tree, and it holds only while broad-spectrum material stays out of the canopy. Where greening is present this sits underneath the area-wide vector program rather than replacing it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On a backyard tree, insecticidal soap sprayed onto the new growth knocks back the young psyllids, called nymphs. It acts only on what it actually wets, so cover the tender shoot tips well, and go back over the tree each time a fresh round of leaves appears rather than treating once.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is a contact material with no residual, so it reaches nymphs on the flush it wets and nothing beyond that; coverage of expanding shoots decides the result. Repeat with each flush, since that is when eggs are laid and nymphs are exposed. It thins nymph numbers on the tree in front of you and does not substitute for the regional program where greening is present.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil that coats insects rather than poisoning them, does the same job on the new growth. Cover the tender shoots thoroughly and repeat with each new round of leaves. Hold off in hot weather and on a tree that is short of water, since oil applied then can injure foliage.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil is interchangeable with soap here, working by coverage of the flush rather than by residual activity, and renewed as each flush emerges. Withhold it in hot weather and on a drought-stressed tree, where foliage injury follows. Like soap, it reduces nymphs on one tree and leaves the regional picture unchanged.

pests.name: Citrus rust mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A microscopic mite that feeds on the rind of developing fruit, bronzing or russeting the peel to a dull tan or brown (sometimes called sharkskin or russet). On grapefruit the injury is prominent because the smooth, thin, light peel shows every blemish, and heavy feeding can also reduce fruit size and increase water loss. Damage is cosmetic to the interior but a real quality issue for fresh fruit, and it is worst in the humid Southeast.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A mite far too small to see plainly makes the skin of grapefruit turn a dull, rusty brown or tan, sometimes rough like sharkskin. It shows up badly on grapefruit because the smooth pale skin makes every mark obvious. The fruit inside is usually fine, but the peel looks blemished. It is worst in humid areas like Florida and the Gulf.
pests.cause_seasoned: The rust mite builds up on the rind through the warm, humid part of the season, with populations peaking in summer. Warm, humid conditions favor it, which is why the Southeast sees far more russeting than the arid West.
pests.cause_beginner: The mite feeds on the fruit skin and multiplies fast in warm, humid weather, so grapefruit in Florida and along the Gulf gets the most russeting, while dry desert fruit is usually clean.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree healthy and monitor developing fruit in the warm season. Preserve predatory mites and other natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays, and tolerate light russeting on home fruit, which does not affect eating quality.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree healthy and just accept a little rusty skin on home fruit, since it does not hurt the eating quality. Avoid strong insecticides that kill the helpful mites that keep it in check.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A well-timed horticultural oil or sulfur application in early summer reduces russeting where it is a problem in humid regions; thorough coverage of the fruit is needed, and oil heat limits apply (not above 95°F or on a stressed tree). In the arid West it rarely needs treatment.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: In humid areas, a horticultural oil or sulfur spray in early summer cuts down on the rusty skin, but cover the fruit well and only spray in mild conditions, not high heat. In dry areas you usually do not need to do anything.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Predatory mites and other helpful insects already feed on the rust mite, and strong broad insecticides take those helpers out along with the pest. On home fruit the rusty skin is worth living with, since it marks the peel without hurting the eating quality, so keeping the harsh sprays off the tree is often the whole plan.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Predatory mites and the rest of the natural enemy complex are the standing check on rind russeting, and broad-spectrum applications remove them. Tolerance is the companion decision: the injury is confined to the rind and does not carry into eating quality, so on a home tree conservation plus a watched crop is a defensible endpoint. Monitor developing fruit through the warm season, when populations climb.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where the russeting is a real problem in a humid area, a horticultural oil spray, a light oil that works by coating, timed to early summer cuts down on the marking. It acts only where it lands, so cover the developing fruit and not just the leaves. Hold off in hot weather and on a tree that is short of water. In dry western areas you can usually skip this.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A well-timed early summer oil application reduces rind russeting where humid-region pressure warrants it, and coverage of the developing fruit surface governs the outcome, since the mite feeds on the rind rather than the foliage. Hot weather and a drought-stressed tree rule it out. In the arid West the mite seldom reaches a level that justifies treating.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sulfur is the other early summer choice in humid regions, used for the same purpose of holding down how much the skin browns. Cover the fruit thoroughly and pick mild conditions rather than a hot spell. In dry areas the fruit usually comes in clean without any spray.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sulfur is the alternative early summer material where humid-region russeting is heavy, applied for fruit surface coverage on the same timing as oil rather than in addition to it. Moderate conditions are a condition of using it, and arid districts rarely present the pressure that justifies either material.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fixed, non-moving bumps clustered on twigs, along the leaf midrib, and beneath leaves. Armored types form firm gray or brown shells like raised bark; softer types are plumper and secrete honeydew that leaves foliage tacky and grows black sooty mold, with ants patrolling for the sugar. Heavy numbers cause mottled yellow leaves, premature leaf fall, and twig dieback.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Scale look like little hard or waxy lumps that sit still on twigs and leaf undersides, so it is easy to mistake them for part of the branch. The softer kinds make the leaves tacky and a sooty black coating grows on the stickiness. Ants are often crawling around them.
pests.cause_seasoned: A mix of armored and soft scale species tap into the tree and feed on its sap. They get the upper hand on dusty, crowded, or ant-tended trees, because ants drive away the ladybugs and parasitic wasps that would thin the colony.
pests.cause_beginner: Scale are little insects that feed on the tree's sap. They get worst when ants are around, since ants protect them from the helpful bugs that eat scale.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous, rinse dust off the canopy, and cut off ants with a sticky trunk band so resident beneficials do the work. Inspect any incoming nursery tree, since scale often hitchhikes in on new stock.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep ants from climbing the tree with a sticky band around the trunk, which lets the good bugs control the scale, and check any new tree for lumps before planting.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A thorough horticultural oil application (narrow-range petroleum or neem) smothers scale; wet every surface, especially twig undersides and leaf backs. Skip oil above about 95°F or on a drought-stressed tree, and plan a follow-up as fresh crawlers hatch.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Coat the lumps with horticultural oil, reaching the backs of leaves and the twigs. Save the spray for cooler, well-watered days, never above about 95°F, or it can scorch the foliage. Spray again later as new ones appear.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ants are usually the reason scale gets ahead on a citrus tree: they harvest the sugary waste and drive off the ladybugs and parasitic wasps that would otherwise thin the colony. Wrap the trunk with heavy paper, duct tape, or fabric tree wrap first and put the sticky barrier on that wrap, because sticky material sitting directly on bark can injure the tree. Then look for any low branch resting on the ground, a wall, or another plant and cut it back, since an ant will simply walk that way instead.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Ant tending is what holds armored and soft scale above the level resident predators and parasitoids would allow, so the trunk barrier precedes anything aimed at the insects themselves. The sticky material goes onto a collar of heavy paper, duct tape, or fabric tree wrap rather than onto bare bark, which it can injure. Skirt pruning belongs to the same operation: a branch bridging to soil, a wall, or an adjacent plant makes the band irrelevant.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Once the ants are shut out, the ladybugs and the small parasitic wasps already living in the tree do much of the work for free. Keeping broad, strong insecticides off the tree is what keeps them there, since those products remove the helpers along with the scale.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident predators and parasitoids regulate both the armored and the soft scale species on an unstressed tree, so conservation is the operative control rather than a courtesy. Broad-spectrum material removes them and leaves the colony free to rebuild on the same twigs and leaf undersides.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the bumps keep spreading, horticultural oil smothers them: it is a light spray oil that coats the insect rather than poisoning it. Because it works only where it lands, wet the twigs and the backs of the leaves, not just the parts that are easy to reach. Hold off in hot weather and when the tree is short of water, since oil applied then can scorch foliage, and plan on a second pass as the young mobile stages, called crawlers, hatch out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A narrow-range petroleum oil or a neem oil smothers settled scale, so coverage of twig undersides and leaf backs decides the outcome more than rate does. Withhold it in hot weather and on a drought-stressed tree, and schedule a follow-up against crawler emergence rather than treating once.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of soft-bodied green, black, or brown aphids on the youngest flush and flower buds, with curled, distorted new leaves and sticky honeydew that draws ants and grows sooty mold. Spring and fall flushes are the targets. The brown citrus aphid can also vector citrus tristeza virus, which raises the stakes where that disease is a concern.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects, often green or black, packed onto the newest leaves and flower buds, curling the tips. They leave a sticky coating that ants follow and that grows a black sooty film. Grapefruit is most vulnerable during the spring and fall flushes.
pests.cause_seasoned: Aphids reproduce explosively on tender new growth in mild weather and are tended by ants for their honeydew. Lush, over-fertilized flush is especially attractive, and ant protection lets colonies outrun their natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids multiply very fast on soft new growth in mild weather, and ants protect them. Too much fertilizer makes extra tender leaves that draw them in.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid forcing excessive tender flush with heavy nitrogen. Control ants so ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps can suppress colonies. A strong jet of water knocks aphids off new growth and is often all that is needed.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize, and keep ants out so ladybugs and other helpers can eat them. A blast of water from the hose usually clears them off.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A forceful water spray, insecticidal soap, or horticultural oil controls aphids; cover the undersides of curled leaves and repeat as needed. Observe oil heat limits (not above 95°F or on stressed trees), and preserve natural enemies by skipping broad-spectrum insecticides.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, getting under the curled leaves. Keep oil for mild days only, not in high heat or on a stressed tree, and avoid harsh sprays that kill the good bugs.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on high-nitrogen feeding. Heavy feeding pushes out extra soft new leaves, and that tender growth is what aphid colonies build on, so a moderate, steady rate simply gives them less to work with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen keeps tender flush available past the point the tree would otherwise harden off, and colony pressure tracks that supply. Feeding restraint therefore shortens the exposure window rather than reducing a colony already in place, which is why it sits underneath everything else.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A firm jet from the hose knocks the colonies off the new growth, and on a backyard tree that is frequently all that is needed. Aim at the crowded shoot tips and under the curled leaves, and do it early enough in the day that the foliage dries.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water jet dislodges colonies from tender shoots without setting back the natural enemies working the same flush, which is what separates it from an early spray. Direct it at the growing points and the undersides of curled leaves, and repeat rather than escalating while numbers stay low.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Check the trunk for a line of ants. Where honeydew, the sticky sugary waste the aphids drip, has drawn ants in, they defend the colonies from the ladybugs and lacewings that would otherwise clear them. Band the trunk with a collar of heavy paper, duct tape, or fabric tree wrap and put the sticky material on the collar rather than on bare bark, then cut back low branches that bridge to the ground, a wall, or another plant. If no ants are working the tree, skip this.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Where ants are harvesting honeydew they interfere with the predators and parasitoids that would otherwise collapse the colony, so cutting their access restores biological control already present. The sticky material belongs on a collar of paper, tape, or fabric rather than on bark, and the low branches bridging to soil, a wall, or an adjacent plant have to come off in the same pass or the band is only a detour. With no ant trail on the trunk, there is nothing here to act on.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Most of the time the right move is patience. Ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps bring aphid numbers down on their own, and a broad spray sets those helpers back harder than it sets back the aphids.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoids are the resident control, and tolerating low numbers on an established tree is what lets them act. Keeping broad-spectrum material out of the canopy is the whole of the practice, since it is the natural enemies that make tolerating an early colony workable.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a young tree is still heavily covered after a hose-down, insecticidal soap sprayed straight onto the clusters brings the numbers down. It kills only what it wets, so aim at the clusters and get in under the curled leaf tips. An older, established tree rarely needs it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is contact-only and is warranted on young trees still carrying heavy colonies after a water knock-back, rarely on a bearing tree. Direct it at the colonies rather than broadcasting it, which spares the beneficials it would otherwise wet, and work it under the curled leaves where the colony actually sits.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil that coats rather than poisons, is the other choice for a heavy outbreak. Coverage decides the result, so work it under the curled leaves and over the shoot tips, and repeat if the colony rebuilds. Keep it off the tree in hot weather and when the tree is dry and stressed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Oil is interchangeable with soap on a heavy flush infestation, working by coverage rather than by toxicity, with the same requirement to reach the undersides of curled leaves. Hot weather and a water-stressed tree rule it out. Neither material justifies a routine program on an established tree.

pests.name: Citrus leafminer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Silvery, serpentine tunnels winding through new leaves, with a thin dark line of frass down the center and margins that curl around the mine. The larva mines only young, expanding foliage. On established trees it is cosmetic, but on young grapefruit pushing lots of flush it slows growth, and the leaf wounds are an entry court for citrus canker in humid regions.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Squiggly silver trails snaking through the new leaves, often with the leaf edge curled. A tiny caterpillar makes the tunnels inside young leaves only. It looks alarming but rarely hurts a grown tree, though it can set back a small young one, and in humid areas the leaf wounds can let canker in.
pests.cause_seasoned: A small moth lays eggs on tender new flush and the larvae mine between the leaf surfaces. Generations cycle quickly in warm weather, so damage peaks on late-summer and fall flushes rather than spring growth.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny moth lays eggs on the newest leaves and the larvae tunnel inside. They breed fast in warm weather, so the worst damage shows up on the late-summer growth.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid pushing excess tender flush with heavy nitrogen or unnecessary summer pruning. Tolerate cosmetic mining on bearing trees; resident parasitic wasps usually provide good control if broad-spectrum sprays are avoided. On young trees in canker regions, managing leafminer reduces canker entry points.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize or prune a lot in summer, since that makes the tender leaves the moth needs. On a healthy grown tree it is best to live with the trails. In humid areas, controlling it on young trees also helps prevent canker.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Chemical control is rarely warranted, and broad-spectrum sprays undermine the parasitic wasps that suppress it. For young trees, a light horticultural oil at bud break discourages egg-laying on new flush; repeat as each flush emerges. Follow label heat restrictions and do not spray above 95°F. Leave mined leaves in place.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually no treatment is needed, and spraying can kill the good bugs. On a small young tree, light horticultural oil on the new leaves discourages the moth. Only spray oil in mild conditions, and leave the tunneled leaves on the tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ease off the fertilizer, and leave summer pruning alone unless you have a reason for it. Both push out extra rounds of soft new leaves, and soft new leaves are the only tissue the larvae can tunnel into. Leave the tunneled leaves on the tree rather than picking them off.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Flush management is the entire cultural lever, since the larva mines only young expanding foliage: restrained nitrogen and no unnecessary summer pruning keep growth synchronized and shorten the window of susceptible tissue. Damage concentrates on late-summer and fall flushes rather than spring growth, which is the stretch this restraint is aimed at. Mined leaves stay in place rather than being stripped.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Small parasitic wasps attack the larvae inside the leaves and usually give good control on a grown tree, so the useful thing is to keep broad, strong insecticides off it. On a bearing tree the trails look worse than they are and are best lived with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident parasitic wasps are the meaningful control on a backyard tree, and broad-spectrum applications disrupt them, which is why the guidance discourages spraying here at all. On a bearing tree the injury is cosmetic, so conservation plus tolerance is a complete answer.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On an established tree you can leave this out. On a young tree still building its framework, a light horticultural oil, a thin spray oil, put on the new leaves as the buds break discourages the moth from laying there. It wears off quickly, so recoat with each fresh round of leaves, and spray only in mild conditions. In humid areas where citrus canker occurs, holding leafminer down on a young tree also closes off wounds the canker bacteria get in through.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A light oil applied to emerging flush at bud break deters egg-laying and slows larvae already mining, but its short residual ties it to each flush rather than to a single application. Reserve it for young trees putting on framework growth, where mining costs structure rather than appearance, and for young trees in canker regions, where the mines are infection courts. Label heat restrictions and mild conditions govern the timing.

diseases.name: Huanglongbing (citrus greening, HLB)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blotchy, asymmetric yellowing of leaves that does not mirror across the midrib (unlike a symmetric nutrient deficiency), yellow shoots, and corky enlarged veins. Fruit are small, lopsided, stay green at the bottom, and taste bitter and salty. Grapefruit is among the citrus that decline fastest under HLB. The tree declines over several years and there is no cure; it is the most destructive citrus disease worldwide.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The classic sign is a leaf yellowed in a blotchy, uneven pattern, with one side not matching the other (a nutrient problem is usually even). Fruit stay small, lopsided, green on the bottom, and taste bad. Grapefruit goes downhill fast with it. There is no cure and the tree slowly dies. It is the worst citrus disease there is.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus spreads tree to tree via the Asian citrus psyllid feeding on new growth, then clogs the phloem so nutrients cannot reach roots and fruit. No treatment clears the infection, so management is entirely about suppressing the psyllid and removing confirmed trees.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria spread by the Asian citrus psyllid clog the tree's plumbing, blocking nutrients to roots and fruit. No treatment reverses it; an affected tree is a permanent source of spread. The whole strategy is preventing psyllid feeding and removing any confirmed tree.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant only certified disease-free nursery trees, never move citrus out of quarantine areas, and control the psyllid aggressively where present. Inspect regularly and report suspected greening to your county agricultural commissioner, since coordinated removal of infected trees is the only effective area-wide defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy only certified clean trees, never move citrus out of a quarantine zone, and control the psyllid that spreads it. Check your tree often and report anything that looks like greening to your local agricultural office, because removing infected trees quickly protects everyone's citrus.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure and no organic remedy for an infected tree. Management is prevention and vector control only: protect trees from the psyllid, and remove and properly dispose of confirmed-infected trees promptly so they cannot serve as a reservoir.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no treatment that saves an infected tree. Focus entirely on prevention: keep the psyllid off your trees, and if a tree is diagnosed, remove it promptly. An infected tree left in place becomes an ongoing source of psyllid pressure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Buy only citrus certified free of this disease, from a nursery you trust. The bacteria ride inside the plant as well as in the psyllid, so a grafted tree from an uncertified source can arrive already carrying it, and there is no cure once it is inside. Do not bring citrus plants or cuttings in from an area under quarantine, which is what those rules exist to prevent.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Certified disease-free nursery stock is the controllable half of the exposure, since the pathogen moves in propagation material as readily as in the vector. Uncertified grafted material is a direct route in, and the quarantine restrictions on moving citrus plants and leaves exist to close that route at a regional scale.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Check your tree regularly for the blotchy, uneven yellowing and the small lopsided fruit. If greening is confirmed, taking the tree out promptly is the responsible step: it cannot be cured, and while it stands the psyllid keeps picking the bacteria up from it and carrying them to trees nearby. Report a suspected case to your county agricultural commissioner and follow the direction you are given on removal and disposal. Keeping the psyllid off your trees is the other half of the job.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing a confirmed infected tree is inoculum management rather than treatment: a declining tree remains an acquisition source the vector draws from for as long as it stands, and grapefruit is among the citrus that decline fastest once infected. Confirmation, reporting, and disposal fall under county and state program guidance, and coordinated removal is what makes an area-wide defense work. Vector suppression runs alongside it, since nothing applied to the tree clears the infection.

diseases.name: Phytophthora foot rot, root rot, and gummosis
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Gum weeping from the lower trunk and crown (gummosis), and bark at the soil line that turns dark and water-soaked, then splits and dries into a sunken lesion (foot rot). When the water mold attacks feeder roots instead, the tree fades slowly with yellowing leaves and a thinning canopy. The diagnostic clue is foliage that yellows and wilts yet fails to recover after irrigation.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: This soil water-mold disease shows up as gum oozing low on the trunk, dark mushy bark right at ground level, and a tree that gradually yellows and gets sparse. The big clue: the leaves yellow and wilt but do not bounce back when you water, which means rot rather than thirst.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora organisms, water molds rather than true fungi, live in the soil and release swimming spores whenever it is wet; those spores splash onto the trunk or move through saturated ground to the roots. Soggy soil, mulch or soil heaped against the trunk, a buried graft union, and the chronic overwatering young trees receive all set it up.
diseases.cause_beginner: It lives in the soil and travels in standing water. It gets going when the ground stays wet, when soil or mulch is mounded around the trunk, or when the graft union (the knob low on the trunk where the fruiting variety joins the roots) ends up buried. Overwatering young trees is the usual trigger.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Engineer this out at planting, the only reliable defense. Aim for a crown that drains immediately: build a low mound, cover only the uppermost roots, keep the graft union well above finished grade, grade for positive drainage, hold mulch a foot back from the trunk, and keep emitters out of the crown zone. A tolerant rootstock (Swingle, trifoliate) adds protection, which is one reason those are preferred for grapefruit.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Prevention is mostly in the planting. Put the tree up on a small mound, keep the graft union well above the soil, make sure water drains off fast, hold mulch a hand's width from the trunk, and never point water at the base. This is the disease most worth preventing from the start.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Fix the water and drainage problem first, since the tree cannot recover while the roots stay wet. On a fresh trunk lesion, pare back the dark dead bark to a rim of healthy tissue and let it dry; opening a buried crown to air sometimes arrests it. Advanced root rot is hard to turn around, which is why the planting practices matter.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Sort out the drainage or stop the overwatering first, or nothing else will work. For a gummy patch on the trunk, gently trim away the dark dead bark to healthy bark and let it dry. A serious root case is tough to cure, so getting the planting right up front is what counts.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This one is designed out at planting rather than treated later. Set the tree high on a low mound so water runs off the crown fast, and cover only the topmost roots. Keep the graft union, the raised joint low on the trunk marking where the fruiting variety was grafted onto its roots, well above the finished soil level. Grade the ground so water drains away instead of pooling, hold mulch back from the trunk rather than piling it against it, and keep your emitters or hose out of the crown zone. Overwatering a young tree is the usual way this starts.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The organism releases swimming spores whenever the soil is saturated, so drainage and irrigation placement are the primary control and both are set at planting: a low mound with only the uppermost roots covered, positive grade away from the crown, the graft union held clear of finished grade, mulch pulled back from the trunk, and emitters kept out of the crown zone. Chronic overwatering of young trees is the usual precipitating error. Foliage that yellows and wilts and then fails to recover after irrigation is the reading that separates this from ordinary water stress.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When you buy, ask for a grapefruit grafted onto a rootstock, the root system the fruiting variety grows on, that tolerates this rot. Swingle and trifoliate are the ones named for it, and that tolerance is part of why they are preferred for grapefruit. You keep the variety you want, and it is decided at the nursery rather than added later.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A tolerant rootstock, Swingle or trifoliate, adds standing protection while the scion stays the grapefruit you wanted, and it is one reason those stocks are favored for the crop. It supplements the siting work rather than substituting for it, since saturated soil still drives infection whatever the roots are.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If gum is already weeping from a dark patch low on the trunk, correct the watering or drainage first, because nothing else holds while the roots stay wet. Then pare the dark dead bark back carefully until you reach a rim of healthy tissue, and leave the spot open to dry. Opening up a crown that had been buried can sometimes stop it spreading. Damage down in the roots of an established tree is hard to turn around, which is why the planting steps carry the weight here.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Pare a fresh trunk lesion back to a rim of healthy tissue and leave it exposed to dry; opening a buried crown to air sometimes arrests an active lesion. This follows correcting the water and drainage condition rather than standing in for it, and advanced feeder-root rot is difficult to reverse, which is the argument for the planting practices.

diseases.name: Greasy spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow mottling on the upper leaf surface that develops into greasy-looking, blister-like brown-to-black lesions on the underside, giving the leaf a translucent, oily look. Affected leaves drop prematurely, often in late winter, thinning the canopy; a fine black rind speckling (greasy spot rind blotch) can also mark the fruit. Grapefruit is notably susceptible, and the disease is a major problem in the humid Southeast and Gulf.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The leaves get yellow splotches on top and raised, greasy-looking brown or black blisters underneath, making them look oily. Affected leaves drop early, usually in late winter, thinning the tree over time, and the fruit can get a fine black speckling. Grapefruit catches it easily. It is mainly a humid-climate disease, common in Florida and along the Gulf, and rare in the arid West.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Zasmidium citri-griseum completes its spore cycle in decomposing fallen leaves under the tree; from that litter, spores release during warm, humid, wet periods and infect the leaf undersides, with a long latent interval before blistering shows. Because it regenerates from its own debris, sanitation disrupts the cycle.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus causes it, growing on the old fallen leaves under the tree and then infecting new leaves in warm, humid weather. The dead leaves on the ground are where it comes from, so it keeps itself going through the litter.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rake up and remove fallen leaves under the tree to break the cycle, the single most useful step, and promote air movement. In dry inland and desert climates the disease is essentially absent and no action is needed. Grapefruit's susceptibility makes leaf sanitation worthwhile in humid regions.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up and get rid of the fallen leaves under the tree, since that is where the fungus lives, and that one step helps the most. Good airflow helps too. In dry inland or desert areas you will probably never see it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sanitation (removing leaf litter) is the core organic control. Where pressure is high in humid regions, a horticultural oil or copper spray timed to early summer reduces infection. Observe oil heat limits. Most home trees outside the humid Southeast need no treatment.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cleaning up the fallen leaves is the main organic fix. In humid regions with a lot of it, a horticultural oil or copper spray in early summer helps, but do not use oil on very hot days. Most trees outside the humid Southeast need nothing.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rake up the fallen leaves under the tree and get rid of them. The fungus makes its next round of spores on old leaves rotting on the ground, so clearing them away is the single most useful thing you can do about it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The fungus completes its spore cycle in decomposing leaf litter, so removing that litter attacks the inoculum source directly and is the step the rest of the response rests on. Premature leaf drop concentrates in late winter, which is when the litter to be cleared accumulates.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the canopy room for air to move through it. The fungus infects during warm, humid, wet stretches, and a canopy that dries out sooner gives it less of an opening.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Air movement works against the warm, humid, wet conditions released spores need to infect leaf undersides, and the long latent interval before blistering appears means the benefit shows up well after the pass that earned it. In dry inland and desert climates the disease is essentially absent and this is not a reason to open a canopy.

control_ladder.note_beginner: In a humid region where greasy spot turns up every year, a spray timed to early summer is the standard prevention, and the guidance for grapefruit names horticultural oil or copper for it. Most trees outside the humid Southeast need nothing at all. Copper is hard on fish and other water life, so keep spray and runoff away from ponds, streams, and storm drains, and follow the label rate, since too much copper can burn leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Where humid-region pressure is high, an early summer application reduces infection, with the crop's guidance naming horticultural oil or copper for that timing; leaf-litter sanitation still does the base work underneath it. Grapefruit's susceptibility is what makes the sanitation worth the effort in the first place. Copper accumulates at the soil surface and is highly toxic to aquatic life, so limit repeat use across seasons and keep runoff out of waterways. Trees outside the humid Southeast generally need no treatment.

diseases.name: Melanose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, raised, dark brown, sandpaper-rough specks and streaks on the rind of young fruit, and similar spots on leaves and twigs; the specks often form tear-streak or mudcake patterns where spores washed down the fruit. It is a cosmetic rind blemish that does not reach the flesh, but grapefruit's smooth pale peel shows it plainly, downgrading fresh fruit. It is a warm, wet climate disease of the Southeast and Gulf, worst on older trees with dead wood.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Melanose makes tiny, raised, rough brown specks on the skin of young grapefruit, often in streaks or a mud-splash pattern, and similar spots on leaves and twigs. The fruit inside is fine; it just looks blemished, which shows up on grapefruit's smooth pale skin. It is a warm, wet-climate disease of Florida and the Gulf, worst on old trees with a lot of dead wood.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Diaporthe citri lives in dead twigs and wood in the canopy and releases spores during warm, rainy weather that wash down onto young fruit and leaves, infecting them while the tissue is very young. Older trees with more dead wood produce more inoculum, so the disease worsens with tree age in humid climates.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus living in dead twigs in the tree releases spores in warm, rainy weather that wash onto the young fruit and mark the skin. Older trees with lots of dead wood have more of it, so it gets worse with age in humid areas.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune out and remove dead twigs and wood, the main source of spores, to reduce infection. Good air movement and avoiding prolonged wetness help. In dry inland and desert climates melanose is absent and no action is needed.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Cut out and remove dead twigs and branches, since that is where the fungus lives, and keep the tree open for airflow. In dry inland or desert areas you will not see it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sanitation (removing deadwood) is the core organic control. Where pressure is high in humid regions, a copper spray timed to the period when young fruit is exposed after petal fall reduces rind spotting; it prevents, it does not cure existing spots. Most trees outside the humid Southeast need no treatment.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Removing dead wood is the main organic fix. In humid areas with a lot of it, a copper spray right after the flowers drop, while the fruit is tiny, cuts down on the skin spots. It only prevents new spots, it does not remove old ones. Most trees outside the humid Southeast need nothing.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the tree open so air moves through it, and avoid anything that leaves the canopy wet for long stretches. The fungus needs warm, rainy weather to wash its spores down onto the young fruit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Air movement shortens the wet periods that carry spores from dead wood down onto young rind and foliage, so canopy openness works alongside the deadwood removal rather than as an alternative to it. Growers on dry inland and desert ground do not see the disease, and nothing here applies to them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut the dead twigs and dead wood out of the canopy and take them away from the tree. That dead wood is where the fungus lives and releases its spores, so removing it removes the source. It matters most on an older tree, which carries more of it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Dead twigs and branches in the canopy are the inoculum source, so cutting them out and destroying them is the core control. Inoculum load rises with tree age in humid climates, which is why an old canopy carrying a lot of dead wood spots fruit far more heavily than a young one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: In humid areas where the specks keep downgrading your fruit, a copper spray right after the flowers drop, while the fruit is still tiny, cuts down on the marking. It prevents new specks and does not take off the ones already there. Keep spray and runoff out of ponds, streams, and storm drains, follow the label rate, and bear in mind that most trees outside the humid Southeast need nothing.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper timed to the exposure period after petal fall, while the rind is still very young, is the accepted protectant where humid-region pressure warrants it. It is preventive, so it does nothing for existing rind spotting and everything depends on landing it on the susceptible stage. Observe copper's soil accumulation and aquatic toxicity limits, and note that outside the humid Southeast the disease seldom justifies any application.

diseases.name: Citrus canker
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Raised, corky, tan lesions with a water-soaked or oily margin and often a yellow halo, on leaves, twigs, and fruit rind, erupting through both leaf surfaces and feeling rough and raised. Severe infection causes defoliation, twig dieback, and blemished, dropping fruit. Grapefruit is highly susceptible to canker. It is a regulated disease in the Gulf states and far worse in warm, wet, windy climates than in arid ones.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Canker makes raised, rough, tan spots, often ringed with yellow and looking oily at the edges, on leaves, twigs, and fruit skin. The spots come through both sides of the leaf and feel bumpy. Bad cases drop leaves and mark or drop fruit. Grapefruit catches canker easily, and it is mostly a problem in warm, wet, windy places like the Gulf Coast.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The bacterium Xanthomonas citri spreads in wind-driven rain and on contaminated tools and hands, entering through natural openings and wounds, including leafminer mines. Warm temperatures, frequent rain, and wind make it severe; it is largely absent from dry interior and desert climates.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria spread it through wind-blown rain and on dirty tools and hands, getting in through tiny wounds including leafminer tunnels. Warm, rainy, windy weather makes it worse, so it is mainly a humid-climate problem and rarely shows up in dry inland or desert areas.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant certified disease-free stock, avoid working in the canopy when wet, disinfect pruning tools, manage leafminer (whose mines are infection courts), and provide good air movement. In regulated Gulf areas, follow state guidance, which may include copper programs. Grapefruit's high susceptibility makes these steps matter more.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with certified clean trees. In canker regions, avoid pruning or handling the tree when it is wet, since the bacteria spread in water, and disinfect tools between cuts. Controlling leafminer on young trees helps, since the tunnels are entry points. Where canker is active, follow your state extension's guidance.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Copper-based protectant sprays before and during the wet season are the primary backyard tool in canker regions; they slow new infections without curing existing ones. Prune out and dispose of heavily affected wood and disinfect tools between trees. In arid climates, where canker's humid conditions are absent, growers rarely encounter it.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure, only ways to slow it. In humid regions, copper sprays during the rainy season help prevent new spots, and you should remove badly infected branches and clean your tools. In dry climates you usually do not need to worry about it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start at the nursery with certified disease-free stock. Grapefruit catches canker readily, so where the disease is active in your region the tree you begin with matters more than it would on a tougher citrus.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Certified disease-free planting stock is the at-purchase lever, and grapefruit's high susceptibility raises what it is worth. It sets the starting condition rather than protecting the tree afterward, since wind-driven rain is the route in once the bacterium is present in the area.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stay out of the tree while it is wet. Do not prune, pick, or brush past it in the rain or before the dew has dried, because the bacteria travel in films of water and ride out on your hands and tools. Clean your pruning tools between cuts, and clean them again before you move to another tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Working a wet canopy is the main way a grower moves this bacterium around, since its natural dispersal is wind-driven rain and free water on the leaf carries it into natural openings and wounds. Confine pruning and handling to dry conditions and disinfect tools between cuts; warm, wet, windy weather is when the discipline decides the outcome. It lowers the rate of spread rather than clearing an established infection.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the canopy good air movement so leaves and fruit dry sooner after rain. This is a warm, wet, windy weather disease, and time spent wet is what it needs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Canopy air movement shortens leaf wetness after the rain events that disperse the bacterium, which makes it a supporting measure in a wet, windy climate rather than a decisive one. In dry interior and desert climates the conditions it addresses are largely absent.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune out the badly affected wood and get rid of it rather than leaving it under the tree. Do the cutting in dry weather, and disinfect your pruners between cuts and between trees so you are not carrying the bacteria along with you. This lowers how much is on hand to spread; it does not clear the tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing and disposing of heavily affected wood lowers the inoculum available to the next wind-driven rain, and disinfecting tools between trees closes a documented transmission route. It is a reduction in spread pressure rather than a treatment, since the tree carries the infection whatever comes off it. Schedule it for dry conditions, which the handling discipline requires anyway.

control_ladder.note_beginner: In canker regions, copper sprays before and through the wet season are the main backyard tool. They slow new infections and do not cure the spots already there, so getting copper on ahead of the wet, windy weather is the point.
