weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hard freeze on open bloom or newly set fruit is the most common way a sweet cherry crop is lost. If frost is forecast tonight, cover a small tree before evening to trap ground warmth, and water the soil beforehand, since moist ground holds and releases more heat overnight. Large trees are hard to protect, which is why a frost-aware site and a later-blooming cultivar matter most.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A hard frost on open flowers or tiny new fruit is the most common reason a cherry crop fails. If frost is forecast tonight, cover a small tree before dark to hold in the ground's warmth, and water the soil first, since damp ground stays warmer overnight. Big trees are hard to cover, so the best protection is a spot less prone to frost and a variety that blooms later.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain, ripe fruit will crack
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain, ripe cherries will split
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Rain on ripe or nearly ripe cherries is the signature sweet-cherry crop loss: free water on the fruit is absorbed through the skin and the swelling flesh splits, and split fruit rots fast with brown rot. Before a forecast soaking, pick every ripe cherry you can; a tree that went dry and is then rained on cracks worst, so keep moisture even all season. Crack-resistant cultivars like Lapins help.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Rain on ripe or almost-ripe cherries is the classic way the crop is lost: water soaks into the fruit and it swells and splits, and split cherries rot fast. Before a coming rain, pick every ripe cherry you can. A tree that dried out and then gets rained on splits the worst, so keep the watering even all season. Crack-resistant kinds like Lapins help.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Muggy weather, watch for rot
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid conditions drive brown rot (browning blossoms at bloom and rotting ripe fruit within a day or two) and cool, wet, humid spring weather drives bacterial canker and cherry leaf spot. There is no spraying it away mid-spell: keep the canopy open and dry, water only at the root zone, remove rotting fruit promptly, and harvest ripe fruit without delay.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, muggy weather is what brown rot loves, browning blossoms and rotting ripe cherries in a day or two, and cool wet spring weather drives bacterial canker and leaf spot. You cannot spray it away once it is muggy, so keep the tree open and the leaves dry, water only at the ground, pick off rotting fruit right away, and harvest ripe cherries promptly.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry spell, keep the watering even
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: During a dry stretch, deep, regular watering matters most for a first-year tree establishing roots and for keeping moisture EVEN as the fruit sizes. The cherry trap is the swing: a tree allowed to go dry and then watered hard, or rained on, splits its fruit. Soak deeply at the root zone and avoid letting the soil dry out and then flooding it.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: In a dry spell, deep, regular watering matters most for a young tree putting down roots and for keeping the moisture even while the fruit sizes. The cherry trap is the swing: a tree that dries out and then gets a big watering or rain splits its fruit. Give a deep soak at the ground and avoid letting the soil go dry and then flooding it.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell, watch the ripening fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sweet cherry takes moderate heat but an extreme heat spell during ripening can soften fruit, cause doubling and spurring of next year's buds, and sunburn exposed cherries. Keep the tree well watered so heat and drought stress do not combine, and avoid stripping interior leaves that shade the fruit. Picking slightly early in extreme heat beats losing fruit to softening.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Sweet cherry handles some heat, but an extreme hot spell while the fruit ripens can soften it, cause oddly doubled fruit, and sunburn exposed cherries. Keep the tree well watered so heat and dryness do not hit at once, and leave the leaves that shade the fruit. In extreme heat, picking a little early beats losing the crop to softening.

planting.text_seasoned: Settle pollination BEFORE you plant: a self-sterile variety (Bing, Rainier, Lambert) needs a compatible second variety of overlapping bloom within about 100 feet, or it sets no fruit. A self-fertile variety (Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart) fruits alone.
planting.text_beginner: Sort out pollination before planting: a self-sterile cherry like Bing needs a second, matching variety blooming nearby or it makes no fruit. The easy path is a self-fertile kind like Stella, Lapins, or Sweetheart that fruits on its own.
planting.author: cc_author_pilot

planting.text_seasoned: Set the graft union 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line and plant in full sun on well-drained ground. Cherry will not tolerate wet feet, and frost-pocket sites lose the early bloom to late frost.
planting.text_beginner: Keep the graft joint 2 to 3 inches above the soil and plant in full sun where the soil drains well. Cherries hate soggy roots, and a low frost-pocket spot loses the early flowers to frost.
planting.author: cc_author_pilot

establishment.text_seasoned: Remove every blossom the first year so the young tree builds roots and a strong central leader instead of fruiting.
establishment.text_beginner: Pick off all the flowers the first year so the new tree puts its energy into roots and a strong main trunk instead of fruit.
establishment.author: cc_author_pilot

establishment.text_seasoned: The first season is the tree's most water-sensitive period; water deeply and regularly so roots establish, and never feed late, since soft growth invites the winter injury that opens the door to bacterial canker.
establishment.text_beginner: Water deeply and often all through the first season so the roots get going, and never feed late in the year, since soft late growth gets winter damage that lets canker in.
establishment.author: cc_author_pilot

scaffold_formation.text_seasoned: Train to a central leader, not the open vase used for peach: keep one dominant trunk and wide-angled scaffolds. Cherry fruits on long-lived spurs, so you build permanent structure rather than renewing fruiting wood each year.
scaffold_formation.text_beginner: Train a sweet cherry to a single main trunk (a central leader), not the open vase shape used for peaches. Cherries fruit on long-lasting spurs, so you are building a lasting framework instead of cutting hard every year.
scaffold_formation.author: cc_author_pilot

dormancy.text_seasoned: Winter chill banks next year's bloom, and sweet cherry needs a lot of it (most cultivars 700 hours or more). In a mild-winter area, only a low-chill cultivar like Royal Lee or Minnie Royal will bloom well.
dormancy.text_beginner: The cold of winter sets up next spring's flowers, and sweet cherry needs plenty of it (most kinds 700 hours or more). In a mild-winter area, only a low-chill kind like Royal Lee or Minnie Royal will bloom properly.
dormancy.author: cc_author_pilot

dormancy.text_seasoned: Clear mummified fruit and rake fallen leaves over winter: mummies carry brown rot and fallen leaves carry cherry leaf spot into the new season.
dormancy.text_beginner: Clear away dried mummy fruit and rake up fallen leaves during winter. Mummies carry brown rot and fallen leaves carry leaf spot into the next year.
dormancy.author: cc_author_pilot

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Cherry needs far lighter pruning than peach, because it fruits on long-lived spurs. Keep the leader, open the canopy, and avoid heavy cuts.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Cherries need much less pruning than peaches, because they fruit on long-lasting spurs. Keep the main trunk, open the middle for light, and avoid cutting hard.
dormant_prune.author: cc_author_pilot

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: In wet climates, do major pruning in dry summer, not cool wet spring: fresh cuts in damp weather are the main entry point for bacterial canker, sweet cherry's most serious disease.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: In wet areas, do the big pruning cuts in dry summer instead of cool wet spring. Fresh cuts in damp weather are the main way bacterial canker, the worst cherry disease, gets in.
dormant_prune.author: cc_author_pilot

blossom.text_seasoned: Open bloom is the most frost-vulnerable moment of the year. Track the forecast and cover a small tree overnight if a hard late frost threatens the flowers.
blossom.text_beginner: When the tree is in bloom it is most at risk from frost. Watch the forecast, and if a hard late frost is coming, cover a small tree overnight to protect the flowers.
blossom.author: cc_author_pilot

blossom.text_seasoned: A self-sterile variety must have a compatible pollinizer blooming AT THE SAME TIME and bees flying. Watch that the two varieties overlap; cold, wet, windy bloom weather suppresses bees and the crop.
blossom.text_beginner: A self-sterile cherry must have its partner variety blooming at the same time and bees flying. Make sure the two overlap, and remember that cold, wet, windy weather keeps bees down and hurts the crop.
blossom.author: cc_author_pilot

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Do NOT thin cherries the way you thin peaches; they size on the tree without it. Instead, put your effort into netting against birds and keeping moisture even against cracking.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Do NOT thin cherries the way you thin peaches; they size up fine on their own. Put your effort into netting against birds and keeping the watering even so they do not split.
fruit_set.author: cc_author_pilot

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Net the tree as the fruit begins to color, before birds find it, and secure the skirt. This is the main reason to keep a cherry small on a dwarfing rootstock so it can be covered.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Put bird netting on as the cherries start to color, before the birds show up, and tuck it in at the bottom. This is the big reason to keep a cherry small (on a dwarfing rootstock) so you can actually cover it.
fruit_set.author: cc_author_pilot

harvest.text_seasoned: Cherries do not ripen after picking, so taste before you pick and harvest only fully colored, sweet fruit. Pull from the spur by the stem, not the fruit, to protect next year's fruiting spurs.
harvest.text_beginner: Cherries do not get sweeter after picking, so taste one first and only pick fully colored, sweet fruit. Pull from the little spur by the stem, not the cherry, to protect next year's fruiting spurs.
harvest.author: cc_author_pilot

harvest.text_seasoned: Beat the rain: pick ripe cherries ahead of a forecast soaking, because rain on ripe fruit cracks it. Pick promptly and completely every couple of days and chill fast against spotted wing drosophila.
harvest.text_beginner: Beat the rain: pick ripe cherries before a coming rain, because rain on ripe fruit splits it. Pick every couple of days, leave none behind, and get them into the fridge fast to stop spotted wing drosophila.
harvest.author: cc_author_pilot

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature sweet cherry yields widely by tree size: roughly 30 to 50 pounds on a dwarfing rootstock (Gisela 5) and 50 to 100-plus pounds on a semi-dwarf to standard tree, given a pollinizer, frost-free bloom, and protection from birds and cracking. Crop is far more limited by frost, pollination, birds, and harvest rain than by feeding.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown sweet cherry gives roughly 30 to 50 pounds on a small dwarf tree and 50 to 100 pounds or more on a bigger tree, as long as it gets pollinated, dodges frost, and is protected from birds and rain. The crop depends far more on frost, pollination, birds, and harvest-time rain than on how much you feed it.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach full bearing around years 6 to 7 (sooner, years 3 to 4, on a precocious Gisela rootstock) and stay productive for decades. A self-sterile variety yields nothing without a compatible pollinizer, so confirm that first.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A sweet cherry hits full production around years 6 to 7, or as early as years 3 to 4 on a quick-bearing dwarf rootstock, and keeps producing for decades. Remember a self-sterile variety gives nothing without a partner tree, so make sure you have one.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect no crop in the planting year and little to none through year 2 or 3. Remove any early fruit so the tree builds roots and a strong central leader; the first meaningful harvest typically comes in years 3 to 5, sooner on a precocious dwarfing rootstock, with full bearing by years 6 to 7.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect cherries the first year or two. If a little fruit forms early, pick it off so the young tree builds roots and a strong trunk. Your first real harvest usually comes in years 3 to 5 (sooner on a quick-bearing dwarf rootstock), with full crops by years 6 to 7.
factors_seasoned: a compatible pollinizer (or a self-fertile variety)
late-frost damage at bloom
winter chill accumulation
bird protection (netting)
harvest-time rain and fruit cracking
cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila control
rootstock and tree age

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting preference is asserted. Extension sources do not support timing cherry planting or care by lunar phase; chill matching, frost avoidance, pollinizer choice, and harvest-rain timing govern outcomes.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: The tree bloomed well but set little or no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree flowered but I got almost no cherries
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree flowered heavily but few or no cherries formed. On sweet cherry the leading cause is POLLINATION: most cultivars are self-incompatible, so a lone self-sterile tree (Bing, Rainier, Lambert) sets nothing without a compatible pollinizer of overlapping bloom. The next cause is a late frost on the early open bloom, and a distant third is cold, wet, windy bloom weather that kept bees from flying. The fix is a self-fertile variety or a properly matched pollinizer, a frost-aware site, and bee activity at bloom.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree flowered but barely fruited. On sweet cherry the usual reason is pollination: most kinds cannot pollinate themselves, so a single self-sterile tree like Bing makes no fruit without a matching partner tree blooming at the same time. The next reason is a late frost on the early flowers, and after that, cold or rainy weather that kept the bees home. The fix is to plant a self-fertile variety or a proper partner, choose a spot less prone to frost, and have bees active at bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant a self-fertile cultivar, or confirm a cross-compatible pollinizer blooms at the same time within about 100 feet; avoid frost-pocket sites and keep a cover ready for bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant a self-fertile variety, or make sure a matching partner cherry blooms at the same time nearby; avoid low frosty spots and keep a cover handy for bloom-time frosts.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Ripe cherries split open near harvest
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The cherries split open just before I could pick them
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Nearly ripe cherries developed splits and cracks, often after a rain. This is the signature sweet-cherry failure: free water on ripe fruit, from rain, heavy dew, or fog, is absorbed through the skin and the swelling flesh splits, and a dry-then-wet soil swing makes it worse. Split fruit then rots fast with brown rot. The fixes are even soil moisture through the final swell, picking ahead of forecast rain, and choosing crack-resistant cultivars like Lapins.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The nearly ripe cherries cracked and split, usually after rain. This is the classic sweet cherry problem: rain, dew, or fog sitting on ripe fruit soaks into the skin and the fruit swells and splits, and letting the soil go dry then wet makes it worse. Split cherries then rot quickly. The fixes are keeping the watering even, picking before a coming rain, and growing crack-resistant kinds like Lapins.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep soil moisture even through ripening, pick ahead of forecast rain, and favor crack-tolerant cultivars (Lapins, Sweetheart); never sprinkle a tree carrying ripe fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the watering steady as the fruit ripens, pick before a coming rain, and grow crack-resistant kinds like Lapins; never spray water over a tree full of ripe cherries.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Birds stripped the crop as it ripened
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Birds ate the cherries before I could
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The ripening crop was pecked or stripped, often within a day or two of coloring. Birds (robins, starlings, waxwings, jays) target ripe cherries and can clear an unprotected tree faster than any insect pest. There is no spray or scare device that reliably keeps them off; physical exclusion does. The fix is to keep the tree small enough to net and to net it at first color, before the birds discover it.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The cherries were pecked or gone, often within a day or two of coloring. Birds love ripe cherries and can clean off an unprotected tree faster than any bug. No spray or scare gadget reliably keeps them off, but a net does. The fix is to keep the tree small enough to cover and net it as soon as the fruit starts to color, before the birds find it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose a dwarfing rootstock so the tree can be netted, and drape fine bird netting over the whole canopy at first color, securing the skirt.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick a dwarfing rootstock so the tree stays small enough to cover, and put fine bird netting over the whole tree as the fruit starts to color, tucking it in at the bottom.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cherries had small white maggots inside
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The cherries had little white worms inside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cherries that looked fine outside hid small white maggots inside. Two pests do this: the western cherry fruit fly (one generation a year, attacking fruit as it colors from straw to blush) and spotted wing drosophila (which attacks sound ripe fruit and multiplies explosively). Both are managed by prompt, complete harvest, removing every dropped and culled fruit, chilling the crop immediately, and trapping to time any organic spray to the color-change window.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Cherries that looked okay outside had small white maggots inside. Two pests cause this: the cherry fruit fly (one round a year, hitting fruit as it colors) and spotted wing drosophila (which hits whole ripe fruit and multiplies fast). Both are handled by picking promptly and completely, removing every dropped cherry, getting the crop into the fridge right away, and using traps to time any organic spray.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hang traps from mid-spring, pick promptly and completely, destroy all dropped and culled fruit so larvae cannot reach the soil, and chill the crop immediately.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Put up traps in mid-spring, pick every cherry promptly, destroy all fallen fruit so the maggots cannot get into the soil, and refrigerate the crop right away.

primary.name: Washington State University Tree Fruit Extension
University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources (UC IPM)
UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Succession planting does not apply to sweet cherry. It is a permanent tree that holds its site for decades and bears one concentrated crop each season as the fruit ripens, so there is no staggered re-sowing to schedule the way there is for a short-season annual.

open_findings.summary: PERENNIAL PILOT -- the authoring bot's first tree, modeled structurally on the certified peach (same genus Prunus, archetype deciduous_fruit_tree). Mirrors all ~35 peach perennial fields refit for sweet cherry. Needs the daily biology-fidelity review + source-truth sample before any certification. [RESOLVED 2026-07-02: Wave-1 source-truth review complete; pollination + chill + signature disease confirmed against cited T1 pages.]

Region verdicts for the warm/humid zones (se_gulf, warm_arid, ca_desert, low_desert_az, fl_peninsula, hawaii) rest on (a) the crop-invariant region chill climate (shared region_chill_delivered table) and (b) sweet cherry's chill/hardiness/heat/humidity limits documented by usu_ext/wsu_ext/iastate_ext; dedicated sweet-cherry pages from each warm-region extension were NOT separately fetched. Verify against region-local extension sources at the cert pass.
Bloom/harvest windows and region calendars are GENERALLY-SAFE structural fits refit from peach, not fine-date-precise; refine exact days at the variety-delta pass per the standing scale-phase rule.

chill_hours_range low end (200, the Royal Lee/Minnie Royal low-chill pair) rests on nursery attestation, not a T1 extension number; the standard 700-1000h cluster is T1-backed (UC Santa Clara MG). Defensible as modeled; refine at the variety-delta pass.

The mid_south bloom window is a MODELED offset from the zone last-frost date (bloom[0] = {from: last_frost, offset_days, window_days: 21}), not a quoted datum. The UAEX fruit publication set was located and read in full this session (FSA6129 Tree Fruit Cultivar Recommendations, FSA6130 Small Fruit Cultivar Recommendations, the Home Garden Fruit Trees page, and the Reference Desk fruit pages) and NONE of them publishes a bloom date for any fruit crop: FSA6129 refers to bloom only as relative risk language ("tend to bloom early", "Late blooming", "blooms relatively late"). The quantity is absent from the literature for this geography, the same shape as the harvest-start-is-not-a-published-datum finding, so repointing cannot fix it and the derivation is declared instead. The offset itself is defensible and internally consistent across the roster.
open_findings.basis: Documents fetched with urllib and read with pypdf or from raw HTML this session (2026-07-30); no WebFetch summary was used as evidence, and every load-bearing sentence was re-extracted from the raw bytes before being relied on. Full adjudication in docs/2026-07-30-mid-south-uada-ext-citation-hunt.md.

open_findings.summary: The mid_atlantic bloom window is a MODELED offset from the zone last-frost date, not a quoted datum. This crop sits outside the 10-crop roster covered by mid_atlantic_bloom_offset_undocumented, so the same absence is recorded here on its own evidence: NC State Extension Gardener Handbook ch. 15 was re-read from live bytes 2026-08-03 and publishes no bloom date for any fruit crop (its bloom content is ordering and bud-kill-threshold language only), and this crop's Plant Toolbox entry gives the season "Spring" with no date. Repointing cannot fix an absent quantity; the derivation is declared instead. Absence is scoped to the 11 NC State documents read 2026-08-03 and listed in docs/2026-08-03-mid-atlantic-ncsu-ext-citation-hunt.md, of which 10 were readable; producing-tree-fruit-for-home-use returned HTTP 403 and is recorded UNDETERMINED, not absent.

open_findings.summary: Table 15-6 of the NC State handbook has NO cherry row, and the Plant Toolbox entry for Prunus avium carries NO "Display/Harvest Time" field at all -- a stricter absence than sour cherry's, whose entry at least gives the season "Summer". Our Jun 11 - Jul 6 (zone 7) / Jun 4 - Jun 29 (zone 8) window is therefore unpublished rather than contradicted. Recorded separately from the sour cherry finding because the two documents fail in different ways, and a shared reason would misstate one of them. open_findings.summary: Pender County, writing about southeastern North Carolina, says "Cherries, bunch grapes, raspberries, and apricots are nearly impossible to keep alive for more than a few years because of our hot summers and erratic springs" -- a claim about the PLANT SURVIVING in the Coastal Plain, stronger than the fruiting-reliability negative this zone 8 cell currently carries. Filed per crop, and deliberately NOT as one blanket record with apricot: the cherries do not share apricot's zone problem, since the Plant Toolbox gives both Prunus cerasus and Prunus avium as 3a-8b, so zone 8 is inside their published range and only the county sentence pushes against `marginal`. Absence is scoped to the 11 NC State documents read 2026-08-03 and listed in docs/2026-08-03-mid-atlantic-ncsu-ext-citation-hunt.md, of which 10 were readable; producing-tree-fruit-for-home-use returned HTTP 403 and is recorded UNDETERMINED, not absent.
open_findings.basis: Pender County Extension, "Fruits and Berries You Can Grow"; NC State Plant Toolbox, Prunus cerasus and Prunus avium; read from raw bytes 2026-08-03.
open_findings.resolution: RULED 2026-08-04: RECORDED, NOT ACTIONED. `marginal` is RETAINED on both cherries. The case is weaker than apricot's: the Plant Toolbox gives both Prunus cerasus and Prunus avium as 3a-8b, so zone 8 sits INSIDE NC State's published range, and the only evidence pushing against is a single Pender County sentence that lumps cherries, bunch grapes, raspberries and apricots under one reason -- the shape that repeatedly turns out partly wrong when split by crop. No prose change either, since the cherry cells already tell the reader not to count on an annual crop.

open_findings.summary: The zone 8 cell credits NC State, in BOTH consumer registers, with a recommendation it does not make: "NC State Extension steers zone 8 growers toward sour cherry instead, which tolerates this humidity far better" (seasoned) and "NC State Extension actually points zone 8 growers toward pie (sour) cherry instead, since it handles the humidity much better" (beginner). Two things are wrong with the credit, and neither is the horticultural fact. THE SCOPE: no NC State document makes a zone-8 or Coastal-Plain cherry recommendation, and the handbook's list of crops recommended for eastern and central North Carolina contains no cherry of either kind; the only NC State steer toward sour cherry comes from Macon County in the far-western mountains, geography this region explicitly excludes, as mid_atlantic_cherry_sour_marginal_ruling itself records. THE REASON: NC State's stated advantages for sour cherry are COLD HARDINESS and SELF-POLLINATION (Plant Toolbox: "much more cold hardy than sweet cherry trees and is self-pollinating"; Henderson County: sour is self fertile while sweet needs two varieties), not humidity tolerance. The tell is this crop's own sibling: cherry-sour's zone 8 cell attributes the hardiness and self-fertility facts to NC State and leaves the humidity sentence UNATTRIBUTED. cherry-sweet's version moved the humidity claim inside the attribution and added a zone-8 scope -- same content, shifted attribution boundary. NOT fixed here: it is consumer copy in both registers, so the rewrite is a content ruling. The zone 8 node was also HELD on the bare host rather than repointed at the handbook with the other three crops, so this promote does not make a wrong credit look better sourced. Absence is scoped to the 11 NC State documents read 2026-08-03 and listed in docs/2026-08-03-mid-atlantic-ncsu-ext-citation-hunt.md, of which 10 were readable; producing-tree-fruit-for-home-use returned HTTP 403 and is recorded UNDETERMINED, not absent.
open_findings.basis: NC State Extension Gardener Handbook ch. 15; Plant Toolbox entries for Prunus cerasus and Prunus avium; Henderson County Extension, "Cherry Trees for Fruit"; all read from raw bytes 2026-08-03. Cross-read against mid_atlantic_cherry_sour_marginal_ruling.
open_findings.resolution: RULED 2026-08-04 by Trevor: RESTATE, do not delete. The credit now names only what NC State publishes about sour cherry (it is the hardier of the two, and it is self fertile while sweet cherry needs a second variety), and the humidity claim moved OUTSIDE the attribution as our own assessment. That matches cherry-sour's own zone 8 cell, which had it right all along, so the two siblings no longer contradict each other. Deletion was rejected because NC State does support two real advantages and the steer toward sour cherry genuinely helps a reader; what was wrong was the zone-8 scope and the humidity rationale, not the recommendation itself. Applied in both registers.

open_findings.summary: mature_height_ft / mature_spread_ft left null at PLA-465 promote 1. T1 gives Gisela 6, the crop's recommended rootstock, only as a percent of standard: PNW 619 (osu_ext, a cited anchor) Table 2 'Gisela 6' 80-85 percent of full size (60 percent in the eastern U.S., 90 in the Pacific Northwest); WSU treefruit 80-90 percent; UKY 70-90; VT 60-95; Purdue 50-60. Standard sweet cherry heights also vary by source (VT 30-40 ft; PNW 619 'upwards of 60 feet if left unpruned ... 10-20 feet if properly pruned'). The only feet figure tied to Gisela 6 is a managed height ('can easily be maintained at a height of only 8 feet'). The crop's rootstock row carries 15-20 ft, which no T1 page states in feet either (a Plan E item).
open_findings.resolution_note: Trevor's ruling 2026-09-17: PERCENT-OF-STANDARD, null, derivation DECLINED. 3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 winter lows (to -40°F) are far below sweet cherry's roughly -10°F injury threshold; the tree is killed outright. Not a sweet cherry zone (try the much hardier sour/tart cherry instead).
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is too cold for sweet cherry; the tree will not survive. Grow a hardy sour (tart) cherry here instead.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: The hardiest sweet cherries may survive zone 4 in sheltered, snow-covered sites, but at about -10°F and colder the fruit buds and wood are injured, and the early May bloom is routinely caught by late frost. Chill is abundant, so the tree blooms most springs, but treat any crop as a bonus and favor a warm, protected slope.
4.suitability_note_beginner: A very hardy sweet cherry may survive zone 4 in a sheltered spot, but the cold and late frosts usually take the crop. The tree blooms most years but rarely fruits, so do not count on cherries here; a hardy sour cherry is the safer choice.
4.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frost is the defining risk: the early May bloom is regularly caught by a hard freeze, and deep winter cold near -10°F also injures the fruit buds. Expect bloom most springs but a usable crop only in years that escape a killing frost.

5.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 5 is the cold edge of reliable sweet cherry. Hardy cultivars crop in good years on frost-safe, well-drained sites, but a hard midwinter cold snap or a late spring frost can take a season. Plant on high, open ground out of frost pockets and avoid the warmest, earliest-blooming sites.
5.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherries can fruit in zone 5 in good years if you plant a hardy variety on high, open ground away from frost pockets. Some years a late frost or deep cold will cost you the crop.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frost on the early bloom is the main crop risk, with occasional deep-winter bud injury. Choose a frost-safe site and a later-blooming cultivar.

6.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 6 is solid sweet cherry country with chill to spare, so the full variety range is open; choose by flavor, self-fertility, and crack resistance. Watch the occasional late frost on early bloomers, manage bacterial canker and leaf spot in wet springs, and net against birds.
6.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 6 grows sweet cherries dependably. You can choose almost any variety. Keep an eye out for a late frost at bloom, manage disease in wet springs, and net the tree against birds.
6.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An occasional late-April frost can nip the earliest bloomers; mid-to-late-blooming cultivars are the safer choice.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 7 fruits sweet cherries reliably across the full variety range; chill is ample and the season starts early. Late-frost risk is modest. The main cautions are wet-spring bacterial canker and leaf spot, harvest-time rain cracking, and birds, so manage disease, keep moisture even, and net the tree.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 7 is good for sweet cherries, with an early start to the season and almost any variety workable. The things to manage are spring disease, rain cracking near harvest, and birds, so keep the tree healthy, water evenly, and net it.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late-frost loss is occasional and falls hardest on the very-early bloomers; a mid-to-late cultivar is the lower-risk pick.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier, sweet cherry succeeds where winters are cold enough to bank chill but not so cold that they kill the tree. Reliable cropping starts around zones 6 and 7; zones 3 to 5 ask for the hardiest cultivars, careful frost-pocket avoidance, and patience with off years, and zones 3 to 4 are generally too cold for a dependable sweet cherry tree.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the north, sweet cherries do best in the milder parts (zones 6 and 7). Farther north (zones 3 to 5) the tree may struggle or be killed by cold, so plant on high ground out of frost pockets and choose the hardiest variety, or grow a hardy sour cherry instead.
northern_tier.chill_basis_seasoned: Northern-tier winters bank well over 700 to 1,000-plus chill hours, more than any sweet cherry needs, so chill is never the limiter here. The limits are cold and frost: deep-winter lows near -10°F injure fruit buds, and a late spring frost can kill the early open bloom.
northern_tier.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for the chill any sweet cherry needs. The challenge is the opposite: deep winter cold and late spring frosts are what threaten the tree and the crop.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Inland zone 8 banks adequate chill, but sweet cherry is poorly adapted to the hot, humid Southeast: brown rot, bacterial canker, and cherry leaf spot run hard in the warm humidity, and frequent late-spring and summer rain cracks the fruit. The tree may grow but a dependable crop is unrealistic, so sweet cherry is not recommended here.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Even though winters are cold enough, sweet cherry does poorly in the hot, humid Southeast. Disease and frequent rain that splits the fruit make a dependable crop unrealistic, so it is not recommended here.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmer, lower-chill zone 9 Gulf edge combines marginal chill with intense heat, humidity, and harvest-season rain, all of which sweet cherry handles badly. Disease pressure and cracking make it an unsuitable crop here regardless of cultivar.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The warmer Gulf edge is too mild in winter and too hot, humid, and rainy in season for sweet cherry. It is not a workable crop here.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmer, lower-chill zone 9 Gulf edge combines marginal chill with intense heat, humidity, and harvest-season rain, all of which sweet cherry handles badly. Disease pressure and cracking make it an unsuitable crop here regardless of cultivar.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The warmer Gulf edge is too mild in winter and too hot, humid, and rainy in season for sweet cherry. It is not a workable crop here.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast is not sweet cherry country. Inland zone 8 banks enough chill, but heat, humidity, and harvest-season rain drive brown rot, bacterial canker, leaf spot, and severe fruit cracking; the warmer zone 9 edge adds a chill shortfall. Sweet cherry is unsuitable across the region; Southern growers do far better with peach or with rabbiteye blueberry.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Sweet cherry does not suit the Southeast. The summers are too hot and humid and the rain splits the fruit, so disease and cracking make it a frustrating, unreliable crop. Grow peaches here instead.
se_gulf.chill_basis_seasoned: Southeastern winters bank enough chill inland (roughly 650 to 1,000 hours at zone 8), tapering toward the Gulf, so chill is not the only problem: the binding limits for sweet cherry are the warm humidity that drives disease and the harvest-season rain that cracks the fruit.
se_gulf.chill_basis_beginner: Winters inland are cold enough for sweet cherry's chill, but that is not the issue here. The heat, humidity, and rain are what make sweet cherry fail in the Southeast.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Interior California (the cherry districts of the San Joaquin and Sacramento valleys and foothills) is prime sweet cherry country: dry spring-and-summer air keeps disease and cracking low, and zone 8 winters bank enough chill for most standard cultivars. Choose by chill match, self-fertility, and ripening season, and net against birds.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Interior California is one of the best places for sweet cherries: the dry air keeps disease and cracking down, and winters are cold enough for most varieties. Pick a variety that matches your chill, sort out pollination, and net the tree against birds.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost risk is modest but real in cold valley pockets at the early March bloom; favor frost-safe sites, and choose adequate-chill cultivars as winters trend warmer.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Lower-elevation zone 9 interior banks less chill (around 300 to 950 hours), so it fruits in good years with mid- to low-chill cultivars and is unreliable for high-chill standards like Bing in warm winters. Favor lower-chill selections and the dry-climate advantage of low disease and cracking.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The warmer interior (zone 9) banks less winter cold, so sweet cherries fruit in good years with lower-chill varieties but miss in mild winters. Choose a lower-chill variety, and enjoy that the dry air keeps disease and cracking down.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Early bloom can occasionally meet a late freeze in low-lying ground; the more common limit is whether the winter banked enough chill for the variety.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Interior California is the heart of West Coast sweet cherry growing. Higher-chill zone 8 valleys and foothills crop the broad variety range reliably in dry air that keeps disease and cracking low; the warmer, lower-chill zone 9 edge fruits in good years with lower-chill cultivars and runs short in mild winters. Chill adequacy, not heat or disease, is the variable to watch.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: Interior California is one of the best regions for sweet cherries. The cooler, higher zone 8 areas grow most varieties well in dry air that keeps disease and cracking down, while the warmer zone 9 areas need lower-chill varieties and miss some mild winters.
ca_interior.chill_basis_seasoned: Interior California banks roughly 300 to 1,100 chill hours depending on elevation, enough for the mid-to-high-chill range in the cooler zone 8 valleys and foothills but only the lower-chill set in warm zone 9 winters. The dry climate is the region's advantage, holding disease and rain cracking to a minimum.
ca_interior.chill_basis_beginner: Interior California usually gets enough winter cold for most sweet cherry varieties in the cooler areas, and only lower-chill varieties in the warmest parts. The dry air is a big plus, keeping disease and fruit cracking low.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Inland north-coast valleys bank a declining 300 to 800 chill hours; mid-to-low-chill cultivars fruit in good years, and the high-chill standards do not. Favor cultivars at or below your typical local chill, and expect short winters to thin the crop. The mild, drier inland air keeps disease moderate.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Inland from the coast, sweet cherries can fruit in good years if you pick a lower-chill variety. Mild winters will sometimes mean a light crop, and the high-chill standards will not get enough cold.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is a minor risk on the mild coast; the real limit is whether the winter banks enough chill for the variety you chose.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Cooler coastal zone 10 banks low chill, often under about 200 hours, below even the lowest-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need. The tree grows easily in the mild climate, but blossoms drop without setting a dependable crop. Of viable cultivars, none is low-chill enough for this coastal chill.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Right on the cooler coast, winters are usually too mild for sweet cherry to fruit, even the low-chill kinds. The tree will grow but give little or no fruit.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Mild maritime winters make chill adequacy the deciding factor on the north coast. Inland zone 9 valleys bank enough for mid-to-low-chill cultivars; the cooler coastal zone 10 falls below even the lowest-chill sweet cherry's need, so the tree grows but rarely fruits. Frost is a minor risk; the limit is chill, not cold.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Near the Northern California coast, winters are mild. A bit inland (zone 9) a low-chill variety can fruit in good years, but right on the cool coast (zone 10) winters are too mild for sweet cherry to fruit at all.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: North-coast winters are mild and bank only about 150 to 800 chill hours, declining toward the coast. Inland zone 9 suits lower-chill cultivars; coastal zone 10 usually falls below even the roughly 250 hours the lowest-chill sweet cherry needs.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_beginner: Coastal Northern California has mild winters with limited cold. Inland, a low-chill variety may fruit; right on the coast, even those usually do not get enough cold.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Cooler, slightly inland south-coast sites bank only about 200 to 550 chill hours, right at or just below the roughly 250 hours the lowest-chill cultivars (Royal Lee, Minnie Royal) need. Crops are light and inconsistent at best; the tree usually survives but rarely sets a dependable crop. The low-chill pair is the only thing worth trying, in the coolest winters only.
9.suitability_note_beginner: In the cooler inland parts of the Southern California coast, even a low-chill cherry usually does not get quite enough winter cold, so crops are rare and light. The tree survives but seldom fruits.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmest south-coast zone 10 sites bank under about 150 chill hours, well below even the lowest-chill sweet cherry. The tree grows in the mild climate but the blossoms drop without setting fruit. This is a no-crop case, not a marginal one.
10.suitability_note_beginner: In the warmest coastal areas, winters are far too mild for sweet cherry to fruit, even the low-chill kinds. The tree will grow but give essentially no fruit.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmest south-coast zone 10 sites bank under about 150 chill hours, well below even the lowest-chill sweet cherry. The tree grows in the mild climate but the blossoms drop without setting fruit. This is a no-crop case, not a marginal one.
11.suitability_note_beginner: In the warmest coastal areas, winters are far too mild for sweet cherry to fruit, even the low-chill kinds. The tree will grow but give essentially no fruit.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Chill scarcity defines the south coast for sweet cherry. The cooler inland zone 9 sites sit right at the threshold of the lowest-chill cultivars and crop only lightly and rarely; the warmer coastal zone 10 falls well short, so the tree survives but does not fruit. Heat and survival are never the issue; chill is.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: Along the Southern California coast, winters are too mild for sweet cherry. Even the low-chill varieties barely fruit in the coolest inland spots and not at all near the warm coast. The tree grows but gives little or no fruit.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: Southern-coast California winters are mild and bank only about 50 to 550 chill hours. Only the low-chill cultivars have any chance, and even they fall at or below their roughly 250-hour need across most of the region.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_beginner: The Southern California coast has very mild winters with little cold. Even low-chill sweet cherries usually cannot get the cold they need, so fruit is rare to none.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 desert sites bank only about 150 to 400 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need in most winters, and the extreme summer heat is hostile to the fruit. The tree may survive with care but does not set a dependable crop. Sweet cherry is essentially a no-grow here; the desert suits low-chill peaches far better.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The desert is too mild in winter (not enough chill) and far too hot in summer for sweet cherry. The tree may survive but will give little or no fruit. Grow a low-chill peach instead.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest, lowest-chill desert sites bank under about 150 chill hours, far below any sweet cherry, and the fierce summer heat compounds the problem. The tree survives the heat poorly and does not fruit. Not a sweet cherry location.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest desert spots are far too mild in winter and too hot in summer for sweet cherry. Expect little to no fruit, and a tree that struggles in the heat.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest, lowest-chill desert sites bank under about 150 chill hours, far below any sweet cherry, and the fierce summer heat compounds the problem. The tree survives the heat poorly and does not fruit. Not a sweet cherry location.
11.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest desert spots are far too mild in winter and too hot in summer for sweet cherry. Expect little to no fruit, and a tree that struggles in the heat.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The California desert is doubly wrong for sweet cherry: winters bank too little chill and summers are brutally hot, a climate sweet cherry tolerates poorly. The tree may survive with care but does not set a dependable crop in either zone. Low-chill peaches and figs are the better desert stone-fruit and tree-fruit choices.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The California desert is too mild in winter and far too hot in summer for sweet cherry. The tree will not get the cold it needs and struggles in the heat, so expect little or no fruit. Grow a low-chill peach or a fig instead.
ca_desert.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert California winters bank only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need, and warm days subtract from the running total. Combined with extreme summer heat, the region cannot support a dependable sweet cherry crop.
ca_desert.chill_basis_beginner: The California desert has very mild winters with little cold and very hot summers. Sweet cherry cannot get the chill it needs and does not handle the heat, so it will not fruit here.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Inland warm-arid zone 8 (the Texas Hill Country and similar) banks adequate chill (around 450 to 850 hours), but sweet cherry is a poor fit: intense summer heat, late-spring frosts on the early bloom, and bacterial-canker and borer pressure make a dependable crop unrealistic. Local growers do far better with low-chill peaches and plums.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Although winters are cold enough, sweet cherry does poorly in warm, dry regions like the Texas Hill Country: summer heat, late frosts, and disease make a dependable crop unrealistic. Grow low-chill peaches or plums instead.

warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: Warm-arid inland regions bank enough chill for sweet cherry, but heat, late-spring frost on the early bloom, and bacterial-canker and borer pressure make it an unsuitable crop. Sweet cherry is not recommended here; low-chill peaches and plums are the adapted stone fruits.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: Warm, dry inland regions are cold enough in winter for sweet cherry but too hot and frost-prone in the growing season, so it is not a workable crop. Grow low-chill peaches or plums instead.
warm_arid.chill_basis_seasoned: Inland warm-arid winters bank roughly 450 to 850 chill hours, enough for many cultivars, so chill is not the limit. The binding problems for sweet cherry are summer heat, late-spring frost on the early bloom, and disease and borer pressure.
warm_arid.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are cold enough for sweet cherry's chill, but the summer heat, late frosts, and disease are what make it fail. A low-chill peach is the better choice.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Arizona low desert banks only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need in most winters, and the extreme summer heat is hostile to the crop. Sweet cherry is unsuitable here; the low desert grows low-chill peaches, apricots, and figs instead.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The Arizona low desert is too mild in winter and far too hot in summer for sweet cherry. It will not get the cold it needs and cannot take the heat, so it is not a workable crop. Grow low-chill peaches, apricots, or figs instead.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Arizona low desert banks only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need in most winters, and the extreme summer heat is hostile to the crop. Sweet cherry is unsuitable here; the low desert grows low-chill peaches, apricots, and figs instead.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The Arizona low desert is too mild in winter and far too hot in summer for sweet cherry. It will not get the cold it needs and cannot take the heat, so it is not a workable crop. Grow low-chill peaches, apricots, or figs instead.

low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert cannot bank the chill sweet cherry needs and is brutally hot in summer, so sweet cherry is unsuitable. The adapted low-desert tree fruits are low-chill peaches, apricots, and figs.
low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: The Arizona low desert is too mild in winter and too hot in summer for sweet cherry. Grow low-chill peaches, apricots, or figs instead.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert Arizona winters bank only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need, and warm days erode the total. The region cannot meet sweet cherry's chill requirement.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_beginner: The Arizona low desert has mild winters with little cold and fierce summer heat. Sweet cherry cannot get enough chill and cannot take the heat, so it will not fruit here.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The central Florida peninsula banks almost no chill (roughly 50 to 350 hours) and is hot and humid, so sweet cherry cannot meet its chill requirement and would face heavy disease and cracking even if it could. Unsuitable; Florida's adapted stone fruits are the UF-bred low-chill peaches and plums.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The Florida peninsula is far too warm in winter and too hot and humid for sweet cherry. It will not get the cold it needs to fruit. Grow the special low-chill Florida peaches instead.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: South-peninsula zone 11 banks essentially no chill (under about 150 hours) in a subtropical climate; sweet cherry cannot fruit and the climate is fundamentally wrong for it. A genuine no-grow case.
11.suitability_note_beginner: South Florida has no winter cold for sweet cherry, so it cannot fruit. This is simply not a sweet cherry climate.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula banks far too little winter chill for sweet cherry, and its heat and humidity would drive heavy disease and cracking regardless. Sweet cherry is unsuitable across the peninsula; Florida's adapted choices are the University of Florida low-chill peaches and plums.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: The Florida peninsula is too warm in winter for sweet cherry to get the cold it needs, and too hot and humid besides. It will not fruit here. Grow the special low-chill Florida peaches instead.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_seasoned: The Florida peninsula banks very little winter chill (well under 350 hours centrally, near zero in the south), far below any sweet cherry's requirement. The subtropical climate cannot deliver the chill the tree needs to bloom.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_beginner: The Florida peninsula has warm winters with almost no cold. Sweet cherry needs far more chill than the peninsula provides, so it will not fruit here.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Hawaii banks effectively zero chill, far below the requirement of any sweet cherry cultivar. Sweet cherry will not fruit; this is a genuine no-grow case, not a marginal one. Tropical and subtropical fruits are the adapted choices.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherry needs cold winters to fruit, and Hawaii does not have them. It will not grow fruit here. Grow tropical fruits instead.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Hawaii banks effectively zero chill, far below the requirement of any sweet cherry cultivar. Sweet cherry will not fruit; this is a genuine no-grow case, not a marginal one. Tropical and subtropical fruits are the adapted choices.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherry needs cold winters to fruit, and Hawaii does not have them. It will not grow fruit here. Grow tropical fruits instead.

12.suitability_note_seasoned: Hawaii banks effectively zero chill, far below the requirement of any sweet cherry cultivar. Sweet cherry will not fruit; this is a genuine no-grow case, not a marginal one. Tropical and subtropical fruits are the adapted choices.
12.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherry needs cold winters to fruit, and Hawaii does not have them. It will not grow fruit here. Grow tropical fruits instead.

13.suitability_note_seasoned: Hawaii banks effectively zero chill, far below the requirement of any sweet cherry cultivar. Sweet cherry will not fruit; this is a genuine no-grow case, not a marginal one. Tropical and subtropical fruits are the adapted choices.
13.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherry needs cold winters to fruit, and Hawaii does not have them. It will not grow fruit here. Grow tropical fruits instead.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii is the clearest case of the model telling the truth: sweet cherry needs a cold winter to fruit, and Hawaii has none. The verdict is simply unsuitable, with no fabricated planting calendar; tropical fruits are the adapted crops.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Sweet cherry needs a cold winter to fruit, and Hawaii does not have one. It will not produce here. Grow tropical fruits instead.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical winters deliver essentially no chill (well under 150 hours), because temperatures rarely fall into the chilling range. Sweet cherry cannot meet its chill requirement here for any cultivar.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_beginner: Hawaii does not get cold winters, so sweet cherry never gets the chill it needs to make fruit.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Rio Grande Valley winters bank only about 0 to 300 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need, per Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, and the Valley's intense summer heat and humidity add further stress. The tree may survive but will not set a dependable crop; grow fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherry needs more winter cold than the Rio Grande Valley usually gives, and the hot, humid summers are hard on it too. It will not fruit reliably here. Grow fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a practical concern in the Valley; insufficient winter chill, not cold, is the binding constraint here.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Rio Grande Valley winters bank only about 0 to 300 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need, per Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, and the Valley's intense summer heat and humidity add further stress. The tree may survive but will not set a dependable crop; grow fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherry needs more winter cold than the Rio Grande Valley usually gives, and the hot, humid summers are hard on it too. It will not fruit reliably here. Grow fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a practical concern in the Valley; insufficient winter chill, not cold, is the binding constraint here.

rgv.region_notes_beginner: Sweet cherry is a poor choice for the Rio Grande Valley. Winters are too mild for the cold it needs, and summers are too hot and humid besides, so trees rarely fruit here. Plant fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus instead.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Sweet cherry does not fruit dependably in the Rio Grande Valley: winter chill (roughly 0 to 300 hours) falls below even low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need, and extreme summer heat and humidity compound the gap. Trees may survive but rarely crop; the Valley is far better suited to fig, persimmon, pomegranate, or citrus.
rgv.chill_basis_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley banks only about 0 to 300 winter chill hours in a typical year, and a warm winter can deliver close to zero, per Texas A&M AgriLife Extension (Valley orchard chill runs roughly 200 to 300 hours), corroborated by LSU AgCenter's comparable figure for the similarly subtropical Gulf coast. That is far below what standard temperate stone and pome fruit varieties need to break dormancy and set fruit reliably.
rgv.chill_basis_beginner: Valley winters give very little winter cold, something like 0 to 300 chill hours some years, and a warm winter can give almost none. That is not enough for most standard fruit tree varieties to flower and fruit reliably here.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Ample winter chill and a long, mild growing season make this the maritime Pacific Northwest's signature stone fruit. WSU's western Washington fruit handbook shows ripening from mid-June (Early Burlat) to early August (Hudson, Sweetheart), with most varieties clustering early to mid-July. Harvest-time rain can crack the fruit in a wet summer, and birds find the crop fast, so netting is standard practice.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherries fruit well here, with most varieties ripening in late June to mid-July. Net the tree against birds, and know that a rainy stretch right at harvest can crack the fruit.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in late March to mid-April occurs safely after the typical last frost in most years; an unusually late cold snap during open bloom is an occasional, not typical, risk here.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The milder coastal and protected-lowland sites still bank ample chill for the full recommended-variety roster, with a growing season that starts a little later than the interior lowlands. Chill is not the limiter here; the same harvest-time rain-cracking and bird pressure apply, so plan on netting and picking promptly once fruit colors up.
9.suitability_note_beginner: This fruits well on the coast too, just a little later than farther inland. Net against birds and pick promptly once the fruit ripens to avoid rain cracking.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom runs a little later here than the colder interior lowlands and clears the milder last-frost date safely in most years.

pnw.region_notes_beginner: This is prime sweet cherry country, one of the region's signature fruits. Ample winter chill and a long, mild growing season let most varieties fruit reliably from Puget Sound to the Willamette Valley. Plant a bare-root or container tree while it is still dormant, from late fall through late winter, and net it against birds.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: The maritime Pacific Northwest banks abundant winter chill and a long, cool growing season that makes sweet cherry one of the region's signature tree fruits. WSU's western Washington fruit handbook shows ripening from mid-June to early August depending on variety, with most clustering early to mid-July. Plant bare-root or container trees during the dormant season, from late fall through late winter, while the ground is workable; net against birds and pick promptly, since harvest-time rain can crack the fruit.
pnw.chill_basis_seasoned: Maritime Pacific Northwest winters bank roughly 700 to 1,950 hours of chill depending on zone and site, comfortably clearing the requirement of every sweet cherry variety in this guide. Chill is never the limiting factor here; harvest-time rain and birds are the real management variables.
pnw.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for sweet cherry. Nearly any variety gets all the winter chill it needs.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Sweet cherry is marginal here, and the limiting factor is not chill (which clears with room to spare) but summer humidity: rain at ripening can split the fruit and open the door to brown rot and cherry leaf spot, and disease pressure runs higher in this humid climate than in a drier growing region. Expect the tree to grow well and to fruit in decent years, but do not count on a dependable annual harvest; choose a crack-resistant variety and site for open air movement to improve the odds.
7.suitability_note_beginner: This tree is a bit of a gamble here. Winters are cold enough, so chill is not the problem; the issue is humid summers. Rain right at ripening can split the fruit and invite rot, so some years will be better than others. Pick a crack-resistant variety and give the tree open air movement to improve your odds.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: This tree tends to bloom before the zone 7 (Piedmont interior)'s own last frost date, so a late freeze on open bloom is the main frost risk to watch, more than winter cold hardiness.

If you want a cherry here, sour cherry is the better choice: NC State notes it is the hardier of the two, and unlike sweet cherry it is self fertile, so a single tree can set a crop on its own. It also carries this belt's humidity better. Expect sweet cherry to grow and to fruit occasionally in a good year, but do not count on a reliable annual crop here; choose a crack-resistant variety and site for maximum air movement.

That clears the chill requirement of every recommended variety in this guide with room to spare. Chill is never the limiting factor here.

The cooler Ozark and upland north (zone 7, where the Fayetteville station banks about 1,024 hours) accumulates roughly 1,000 to 1,300 chilling hours a year, and the warmer lowland south (zone 8, with Wynne near 1,069 and Clarksville near 1,081) accumulates roughly 900 to 1,100. nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The cooler, higher zone 8 pockets bank roughly 500 to 900 chill hours, clearing the entire recommended list, including Bing (800 hours) and the 700 hour self-fertile standards, with real margin. This is the strongest sweet cherry site in the region.
8.suitability_note_beginner: The cooler parts of the region grow the widest range of sweet cherries, including Bing, with plenty of winter cold to spare.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in March to April usually clears the last frost; a late cold snap at the higher elevations is the occasional risk.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 (the Las Vegas Valley floor) banks roughly 300 to 700 chill hours. The low chill pair Royal Lee and Minnie Royal (about 250 hours, plant both together) is a dependable fit here. The 700 hour self-fertile standards, Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Rainier, and Black Tartarian, sit right at the ceiling and crop most years but are the first to disappoint in a mild winter; Bing (800 hours) needs more cold than this zone reliably delivers.
9.suitability_note_beginner: On the valley floor, the safest sweet cherry choice is the Royal Lee and Minnie Royal pair, planted together. The familiar varieties like Stella and Lapins usually do fine too, but a warm winter can shortchange them.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom in late February to March occasionally meets a late frost; the dry air keeps disease pressure low regardless.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Laughlin (zone 10) banks only about 150 to 450 chill hours. Only the low chill pair, Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, planted together, reliably clears that band; the 700 to 800 hour standards need more cold than this warm corner provides.
10.suitability_note_beginner: At warm Laughlin, plant Royal Lee and Minnie Royal together; the other sweet cherry varieties need more winter cold than this spot gets.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the issue at Laughlin; the limiting factor for the higher chill varieties is winter chill, not cold snaps.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: Sweet cherry can fruit across the Las Vegas Valley region if you pick the right variety for your area. Royal Lee and Minnie Royal are a low chill pair bred for mild winters; plant them together (they need each other to pollinate) and they will fruit reliably everywhere, including Laughlin. On the valley floor and in the cooler zone 8 pockets, the familiar self-fertile varieties like Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Rainier, and Black Tartarian are also a good bet. Bing needs the most winter cold and a separate pollinizer tree, so it is best kept to the cooler zone 8 areas.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: Sweet cherry fruits reliably across the Las Vegas Valley region with the right variety choice. The low chill pair Royal Lee and Minnie Royal (about 250 hours each, and mutually required for pollination since neither is self-fertile) clears every zone here, including Laughlin, and is the dependable choice region-wide. The self-fertile 700 hour standards, Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Rainier, and Black Tartarian, sit right at zone 9's chill ceiling (workable most years) and fit zone 8's wider band comfortably. Bing, at 800 hours and needing a separate pollinizer, is best reserved for zone 8. Bloom is early and the dry desert air keeps brown rot and bacterial canker pressure low; a late frost on the open bloom is the more relevant risk.
nevada.chill_basis_seasoned: Sweet cherry splits into two very different chill tiers here. Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, a purpose-bred low chill pair that must be planted together for pollination, need only about 250 hours and clear every Nevada zone with room to spare, including Laughlin. The self-fertile standards, Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Rainier, and Black Tartarian, need about 700 hours, which sits right at zone 9's ceiling (workable in most years) and comfortably inside zone 8's wider band; Bing, at 800 hours and not self-fertile on top of that, is better reserved for zone 8. Laughlin (zone 10) is a Royal Lee and Minnie Royal site only.
nevada.chill_basis_beginner: Sweet cherry works two ways in this desert region. Royal Lee and Minnie Royal are a low chill pair bred for mild winters like this one; plant them together and they fruit reliably everywhere, even at warm Laughlin. The familiar market varieties like Stella, Lapins, and Rainier need more winter cold and do best on the valley floor and in the cooler zone 8 areas; Bing needs the most cold and a pollinizer besides, so it is a zone 8 pick.

utah_dixie.region_label: Utah: St. George Dixie (Mojave-edge high desert)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Sweet cherry is grown at the low St. George elevations with the right variety: the low-chill pair Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, planted together, fits the warm valley, while high-chill market cherries need more cold than the core banks. Late frost on the early bloom and summer sunburn are the hazards.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherry grows here if you plant the low-chill pair Royal Lee and Minnie Royal together. The familiar market cherries need more winter cold than the valley gives.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Sweet cherry blooms early, so it can meet the late-March last frost; a late cold snap during bloom is the main spring risk, with summer sunburn the larger season-long concern.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: Sweet cherry grows in St. George if you choose a low-chill variety. The pair Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, planted together, needs little winter cold and suits the warm valley. The familiar market cherries need more cold than the core provides. Watch for a late frost on the bloom and summer sunburn.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: Sweet cherry is grown at the low St. George elevations, where Washington County Extension lists cherries among the dependable fruits. The key is variety: the low-chill pair Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, planted together since neither is self-fertile, needs only a couple hundred chill hours and fits the warm valley well, while the familiar high-chill market varieties need more cold than the core banks. The dry air keeps brown rot and bacterial canker low; a late frost on the early bloom and summer sunburn are the hazards. Plant bare-root or container trees during the dormant season.
utah_dixie.chill_basis_seasoned: Sweet cherry works in the warm St. George core through low-chill variety choice. The purpose-bred pair Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, which must be planted together for pollination, needs only about 200 to 300 chill hours and fits the valley's limited winter cold; Washington County Extension lists cherries among the fruits that do well at these low elevations. The familiar high-chill market cherries need more winter cold than the core banks and are a poorer fit. As with the region's other stone fruit, the practical risks are a late frost on the early bloom and summer sunburn, not the brown rot of humid regions.
utah_dixie.chill_basis_beginner: Sweet cherry grows in St. George if you choose a low-chill variety. The pair Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, planted together, needs little winter cold and suits the warm valley. The familiar market cherries need more cold than the core provides. Watch for a late frost on the bloom and summer sunburn.

crops.description_seasoned: Sweet cherry is a deciduous stone-fruit tree (Prunus avium) grown for firm, sugar-rich fruit eaten fresh off the tree. It is the most demanding of the common backyard fruit trees: most cultivars are SELF-STERILE and need a second, compatible variety blooming at the same time to set any fruit (the self-fertile cultivars, such as Stella, Lapins, and Sweetheart, are the exception), it blooms early and loses crops to late frost, rain near harvest splits the fruit, and birds will strip a ripe tree in a day. It also needs enough winter chill to bloom evenly, so variety is matched to your winters. Trained to a central leader, kept netted, and given a compatible pollinizer, it rewards the effort with fruit no store can match.
crops.description_beginner: A sweet cherry is a fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives firm, sweet cherries to eat fresh. It is the trickiest of the usual backyard fruit trees. Most sweet cherries cannot pollinate themselves, so unless you choose a self-fertile kind (like Stella, Lapins, or Sweetheart) you need a second, matching variety blooming nearby or you get no fruit at all. On top of that, the early flowers can be killed by late frost, rain just before harvest splits the cherries open, and birds love a ripe tree. The tree also needs a cold-enough winter to bloom well, so you pick a variety that fits your area. Give it a pollinator partner, a net, and the right spot, and it pays you back with cherries far better than the store.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: A sweet cherry is ready when it reaches full, deep variety color (dark mahogany to near-black for Bing-type cultivars, full yellow-and-red blush for Rainier), the flesh is firm but gives slightly, and the sugars have peaked. Cherries do NOT ripen further off the tree, so taste-test before picking and leave them until fully colored and sweet. Pick with the stems on, pulling from the spur, not the fruit, to protect next year's fruiting spurs. Pick promptly once ripe: a rain on ripe fruit cracks it, and birds and spotted wing drosophila find a ripe crop fast.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A sweet cherry is ripe when it has turned its full color (dark red to almost black for most types, or a yellow-and-red blush for Rainier), feels firm but gives a little, and tastes sweet. Unlike a peach, a cherry will not get sweeter after you pick it, so taste one first and only pick when they are fully colored and sweet. Pick with the stems attached, and pull from the little woody spur rather than yanking the fruit, so you do not strip next year's fruiting spurs. Pick as soon as they are ripe, because rain splits ripe cherries and birds and small vinegar flies move in quickly.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Sweet cherries bloom in early spring, typically March in mild regions and April to early May in cold-winter areas, usually just before or as the leaves emerge. Bloom is the year's chief vulnerability: the white blossoms open early and a hard late frost on open bloom kills that year's crop. Because most cultivars are self-incompatible, the pollinizer must bloom at the same time, so overlapping bloom periods, not just the presence of a second tree, decide fruit set.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Sweet cherry trees flower in early spring, around March where winters are mild and April into early May where they are cold, usually right before the leaves come out. The early flowers are the tree's weak point, because a hard late frost can kill the open blooms and the tiny fruit. And since most sweet cherries need a partner to pollinate them, the two trees have to bloom at the same time, so matching bloom timing matters as much as having a second tree.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Sweet cherry is notably less cold-hardy than peach or sour cherry, rated to roughly zones 5 to 9, with reliable cropping in zones 5 to 8. The tree and its fruit buds begin to suffer winter injury at about -10°F and colder, so zones 3 and 4 are generally too cold for a dependable tree. The warm limit is not heat but chill: where winters no longer bank enough chill hours, a thriving tree blooms poorly and sets little. Sweet cherry is also poorly adapted to the hot, humid Southeast, where brown rot, bacterial canker, and harvest-season rain make it a frustrating crop regardless of zone.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Sweet cherry is less tough than peach or sour cherry. It does best in zones 5 through 8, and below about -10°F the tree and its flower buds start to get damaged, so zones 3 and 4 are usually too cold for a reliable tree. In the warmest zones the problem is not heat but a lack of winter cold, which the tree needs to bloom well. Sweet cherry also struggles in the hot, humid Southeast, where disease and harvest rain make it hard to grow no matter the zone.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Sweet cherries need a stretch of winter cold, counted as chill hours (hours between about 32°F and 45°F), to break dormancy and bloom evenly. Most standard cultivars need roughly 700 to 1,000 hours or more (Washington's market cultivars run higher still), so sweet cherry is a high-chill tree for most of its range. A small group of low-chill cultivars bred for mild-winter California (Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, about 200 to 300 hours, which pollinize each other) extends it to warm-winter zones. Match the variety to the chill your winters actually bank: too little and the blossoms drop without setting.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Sweet cherry trees need enough cold winter hours, called chill hours, before they will bloom properly in spring. Most kinds need a lot, roughly 700 to 1,000 hours or more, which is why sweet cherry suits cold-winter areas. A few special low-chill kinds (Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, about 200 to 300 hours) were bred for mild-winter California and need only a little cold. If your winters are mild, you must choose a low-chill variety, or the flowers fall off without making fruit.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Plant a second compatible variety unless you choose a self-fertile one. Most sweet cherries are self-incompatible: a lone Bing sets no crop. Compatibility is governed by S-alleles, so the pollinizer must be in a DIFFERENT incompatibility group AND bloom at the same time (the classic trap is that Bing, Lambert, and Royal Ann/Napoleon are all cross-incompatible and cannot pollinize one another). The self-fertile cultivars (Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Skeena, Black Gold, White Gold, Compact Stella) fruit alone and serve as universal pollinizers for most self-sterile varieties of matching bloom. Bees do the work, so strong bee activity during the short bloom is essential for set.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Plant a second compatible variety unless you pick a self-fertile one. Most sweet cherries cannot pollinate themselves, so a single Bing tree gives no cherries at all. The second tree has to be a different, compatible variety that blooms at the same time, planted within about 100 feet so bees can carry pollen between them (watch out: Bing, Lambert, and Royal Ann cannot pollinate each other). The easy way around all of this is to plant a self-fertile variety like Stella, Lapins, or Sweetheart, which fruits on its own and can also pollinate most other cherries. Bees carry the pollen, so you want lots of bee activity during the short bloom.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment over fruit. Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter, head it back at planting to begin a central-leader framework, keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk, and water consistently through the first two seasons. Remove any fruit that sets. Confirm a compatible pollinizer is planted nearby unless the variety is self-fertile. Hold fertilizer until growth begins, and never feed late in the season, which invites the winter injury that opens the door to bacterial canker.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about helping the tree settle in, not getting fruit. Plant a bare-root tree in late winter while it is still resting, cut it back at planting to start a single main trunk shape, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk, and water it steadily through the first couple of years. Pull off any fruit that forms. Make sure a partner pollinizer tree is planted nearby unless your variety is self-fertile. Wait to fertilize until the tree starts growing, and never feed late in the year, since soft late growth gets winter damage that lets disease in.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Self-incompatible for most cultivars: a single tree of a self-sterile variety (Bing, Rainier, Lambert) sets no crop and needs a compatible pollinizer of a different S-allele group blooming concurrently, ideally within about 100 feet for good bee transfer. Self-fertile cultivars (Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Compact Stella) fruit alone and pollinize most others. Bees are the vector; cold, wet, or windy bloom weather suppresses their activity and the crop with it.
pollination.notes_beginner: Most sweet cherries cannot pollinate themselves.
