The mechanism is straightforward: bud initiation needs a run of hours below 50°F, this climate never banks one, and UF/IFAS's trial found untreated plants remaining vegetative all season under exactly that condition. The plant thrives regardless. Unlike Florida there is no hot wet break that ends the planting, so expect the rosette to persist and keep making leaves indefinitely, and treat the November to February planting window as a convenience for easier establishment rather than a deadline the plant is waiting on.

crops.description_seasoned: Globe artichoke is a big herbaceous perennial thistle grown for an immature flower bud, which is the single fact that explains everything else about it. Because the crop is a flower, the plant has to be persuaded to flower, and it does that after a run of cool weather: roughly 500 hours between 35°F and 50°F is the figure the peer-reviewed trial work converges on, though published requirements span 205 to 1356 hours and the spread is driven by cultivar rather than by measurement error. The requirement is quantitative, not absolute. Rutgers recorded 74 percent of Imperial Star and 57 percent of Green Globe Improved setting buds with no cold treatment at all, rising to 98 and 86 percent with it, so cold advances and synchronizes budding rather than permitting it. That is why artichoke runs two completely different careers. Where winters stay above roughly 15°F it is a permanent bed cropping for years from crown divisions, the Castroville model; everywhere colder it is an annual, started indoors, chilled deliberately as a seedling, set out, cropped in its first season and lost to winter. Both are real, both are extension documented, and which one applies to you is a question about your winter, not about your skill.
crops.description_beginner: An artichoke is a flower bud you pick before it opens, growing on a plant that looks like a five-foot silver thistle. That one fact drives everything: to get artichokes, the plant first has to be convinced to make flowers, and it does that after a stretch of cool weather. In mild-winter places like coastal California you plant once and pick from the same plants for years. Anywhere with a real winter you grow it as a yearly crop instead: start seed indoors, give the young plants a few weeks in the cold on purpose, plant them out, pick in late summer, and start over next spring. Neither way is harder than the other, they are just different, and your winter decides which one you are doing.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut on bract tightness, not on size. A bud is ready once it has reached full size for its position on the stalk and while its bracts are still closed flat against each other; the moment they loosen and begin to spread, the bud turns woody and bitter and is finished as food. University of California is explicit that on seeded varieties a mature bud stops enlarging, so waiting past that point buys nothing and costs the bud. Take the terminal bud first, since it matures well ahead of the two or three secondaries below it, and cut with 2 to 3 inches of stem attached. Heat compresses this window sharply: above 86°F buds open quickly and the heart loses tenderness and compactness, so in a hot spell check daily rather than every few days.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Squeeze the bud. If it is firm and the scales are still shut tight against each other, cut it. If the scales have started to loosen and open out, you waited too long, and it will be woody and bitter no matter how you cook it. Size is not the signal, tightness is. Cut the big bud at the top of the stalk first, taking 2 to 3 inches of stem with it, and the smaller ones lower down will come along afterward. In hot weather check every day, because heat makes buds open fast.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Four different temperatures matter here and they are commonly confused with one another. Bud tissue starts to freeze at about 29.9°F, which blisters and bronzes the outer bracts without harming eating quality, and the damage turns serious below about 24.8°F. Texas A&M sets 25°F as the practical management floor, the point at which you cover plants with straw or a frost blanket. The crown itself is far tougher and is the thing that decides whether a planting persists: Oregon State reports severe crown loss below 15°F even under mulch, and a peer-reviewed study independently puts the perennial limit at about 14°F. There is no published foliage-damage temperature for this crop, so beware anyone quoting one. Deliberately absent from this guide: a USDA hardiness zone. Three extension sources give three incompatible answers, from zone 7 and warmer to zone 6 with mulch to occasional zone 5, and all three are warmer-tolerant than the measured crown-kill temperature allows. Picking one would mean preferring a source over two others with no basis, so the temperatures do the work instead.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Think about it as two separate questions: will the buds get damaged, and will the plant survive the winter. Buds start taking frost damage around 30°F, which mostly just blisters the outside and still tastes fine, and gets serious in the mid 20s. Cover plants when a night below 25°F is coming. The roots are much hardier and only die around 15°F, even under mulch, which is the real dividing line between a plant that comes back next year and one that does not. You may see artichoke listed as hardy to zone 7, or zone 6, or zone 5. Those numbers disagree with each other and with the measured temperatures, so we do not publish one. Go by your actual winter lows.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: The first year is where this crop is won or lost, and the step people skip is the cold treatment. Sow 6 to 8 weeks ahead of the intended set-out date, germinate at 70°F to 80°F, then grow the seedlings at about 75°F day and 65°F night. Once they reach four to six true leaves, chill them for roughly three weeks at 35°F to 50°F. That duration is not folklore: a three-year replicated University of Maine trial measured 3 to 33 percent of plants flowering after 303 hours and 68 to 100 percent after 550 hours, and its conclusion is that duration is the key driver above 35°F. Supplemental light during chilling accompanied the higher figure, so give them light rather than a dark refrigerator if you can. Afterwards keep them under 80°F, because heat reverses accumulated chilling; Connecticut measured bare-soil temperatures of 84°F to 102°F devernalizing plants outright and leaving them barren. Virginia runs the inverse system, setting transplants out at or just before last frost so the seedlings take their 190 to 240 hours at 50°F or below in the ground. Either route works, but do not blend them, and expect 15 to 25 percent of plants to stay barren even when chilling was adequate.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: There is one step in the first year that decides whether you get artichokes at all, and it is easy to skip because it sounds strange: you have to make the young plants cold on purpose. Start seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before you plan to plant out. Once each seedling has four to six real leaves, put the tray somewhere between 35°F and 50°F for about three weeks. A spare refrigerator, an unheated garage, or a cold frame all work, and a bit of light during those weeks helps. In trials, plants given about three weeks of cold flowered at up to 100 percent, while plants given only half that flowered as little as 3 percent. Same seed, same year, and the only difference was the cold. After that, keep them under 80°F until they go outside, because heat undoes the cold treatment. Even done right, one plant in five may never make a bud, so plant a couple more than you think you need.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Site this crop the way you would site a small shrub, because that is the footprint. Plants reach four feet across and want deep, fertile, well-drained ground in full sun with a generous amount of organic matter worked in; University of California puts the target pH at 6.0 to 6.5 and suggests lime or gypsum where calcium is low. Clear perennial weeds before planting rather than after, and UC's pre-plant trick is worth the fortnight it costs: irrigate the cleared bed deeply, let a flush of weed seed germinate, then work the ground again to kill the seedlings. Space plants 2 to 3 feet apart with 2.5 to 3 feet between rows; crowded plants make smaller buds and are miserable to harvest from. Where the bed is permanent, take the time to loosen it deeply, because you will not get another chance for years.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Give artichoke more room than you think. A mature plant is about four feet wide, so allow two to three feet between plants and two and a half to three feet between rows. It wants full sun, deep soil that drains well, and plenty of compost dug in. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.5. Get the perennial weeds out before you plant: water the bed, wait a couple of weeks for the weed seeds to sprout, then hoe them off and plant into clean ground. If the plants are going to stay put for years, it is worth digging the bed properly now.

harvest_stop_rule.note_seasoned: Artichoke's stop rule governs the individual bud, not the season, and that is a real difference from the other crop on this archetype rather than a wording choice. Cut each bud while its bracts are still closed flat against one another. Once they loosen and begin to spread, the bud has passed: University of California notes that on seeded varieties a mature bud neither enlarges further nor re-tightens, and that buds left past their prime turn woody and bitter. Size is not the trigger, since a small secondary bud is perfectly good eating and a large one that has begun to open is not. Heat compresses the window, because above 86°F buds open quickly and the heart loses tenderness and compactness, so switch to daily checks in hot weather. There is no reserve-protection stop for this crop of the kind asparagus has; harvesting does not draw down a storage organ, so you pick until frost or until the flush ends rather than stopping to spare the plant.
harvest_stop_rule.note_beginner: Pick each artichoke while it is still tight. Run a thumb over it: if the scales are shut flat against each other, cut it now. If they have started to loosen and spread apart, that one is past its best and will be tough and bitter however you cook it. Do not wait for a bud to get bigger, because once it is fully grown it stops growing and only opens. In hot weather check every day, since heat makes them open fast. Unlike some crops there is no point where you have to stop picking to protect the plant, so keep going until frost or until the plant runs out of buds.

crops.harvest_ramp_na_seasoned: No bed-age harvest ramp is published for artichoke, so this guide does not carry one. Two things are true at once. Where artichoke perennializes, on the California coast and the warm maritime Northwest, the crown does get more productive with age, and University of California describes a first-year planting as giving a light pick about a year after planting; but no source turns that into a picking duration by bed year, and inventing one would put a manufactured number where a real one is missing. Everywhere else the question does not arise at all, because artichoke is grown as an annual and every planting is a year-one planting with no crown carried into a second season. What can be said about duration is said where it is actually sourced: the concentrated six to eight week flush of annual culture, in yield_expectations, and the two regional durations carried on the cells that have them.
crops.harvest_ramp_na_beginner: You may have seen crops here that tell you how many weeks of picking to expect in a bed's second or third year. Artichoke does not get one, because nobody publishes that figure for it. If your plants live from year to year they do get more productive as they get older, and if you replant every spring then every plant you grow is a first-year plant and the question does not apply. Either way, what to expect from a season is under yields.
crops.first_harvest_notes_beginner: A perennializing artichoke gives you a light pick about a year after planting, and the skill to learn now is knowing when a bud is ready. It is not size. Squeeze it: if the bracts, the tough overlapping scales that make up the bud, are still shut flat against one another, cut it. Once they loosen and start to spread apart, that bud has gone woody and bitter and no amount of cooking brings it back. Take the big bud at the top of the stalk first, cutting 2 to 3 inches of stem with it; the smaller ones lower down come along afterward. Keep the water steady once buds start forming, because a plant under moisture stress opens its buds early and shows black tips.
crops.first_harvest_notes_seasoned: A perennializing planting yields a light pick roughly a year after set. Index maturity on bract tightness, meaning how tightly the overlapping scales are still closed, rather than on diameter: University of California is explicit that on seeded varieties a mature bud neither enlarges further nor re-tightens, so waiting past closure buys nothing and costs the bud to woodiness. Take the terminal bud first, since it matures well ahead of the two or three secondaries below it, and cut with 2 to 3 inches of stem attached. Irrigation through the bud period is a quality intervention rather than a survival one: Texas A&M attributes canopy cooling to summer irrigation and identifies it as what prevents buds opening early, while Utah State's rule is simply not to water-stress a plant once flower buds have formed. Moisture stress presents as black tip.
crops.full_harvest_notes_beginner: From about the second year the planting is in full production, and two things run the year. The first is picking on tightness rather than size: squeeze each bud, and cut it while its bracts, the tough overlapping scales, are still shut flat against each other. Once they loosen the bud is woody and bitter. Heat compresses that window sharply, so above about 86°F check every day instead of every few days. The second is the annual cut-back, and it is a scheduling tool rather than tidying up. Cut back between mid-April and mid-June and the plant crops in fall, winter and spring; cut back in late August or September and you get a summer harvest instead. Start watering again about a month after. Do the cut-back properly and it doubles as pest control: cutting 2 to 3 inches below soil level, then shredding and burying the tops under at least 6 inches of soil, cuts artichoke plume moth by about 95 percent.
crops.full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from roughly year two on a persisting planting. Harvest indexing stays on bract tightness, meaning bracts still closed flat against one another, never on diameter, and heat above 86°F compresses the window enough to force daily rather than periodic checking, since the heart loses tenderness and compactness as buds open. The annual cut-back is the year's real decision and it SCHEDULES the crop rather than tidying the plant: a cut- back between mid-April and mid-June sets up fall, winter and spring cropping, while one in late August or September sets up a summer harvest, with irrigation resuming about a month afterwards. Do not confuse it with stumping, the removal of spent bearing stalks at three- to-four-week intervals through the year. UC IPM quantifies the cut-back's second function: cutting plants 2 to 3 inches below soil level, shredding the tops and incorporating them under at least 6 inches of soil reduces plume moth infestation in perennial fields by roughly 95 percent. Clear nearby thistles, which host it too.

crops.name: Turnip

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Turnips like loose, fertile, well-drained soil with no hard layer underneath. Loosen the bed about 8 to 10 inches down and rake out rocks and clods, because the root grows rounder and smoother in loose soil and comes out forked or lumpy in packed, stony ground. Mix in some compost or well-rotted (never fresh) manure, since fresh manure can make the roots branch and grow hairy. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8. If clubroot, a disease that swells and deforms the roots, has been a problem in your garden, adding lime to raise the pH closer to 7.0 to 7.2 helps hold it back.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Turnips do best in deep, loose, fertile, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, ideally a sandy loam or loam. They are quick and shallow-rooted compared with carrots, but stones, clods, and compaction still cause forking and misshapen roots, so a friable seedbed matters. Work in well-finished compost or well-rotted manure rather than fresh manure, which drives leafy top growth and can cause hairy, branched roots. Keep pH in the slightly acidic to neutral range, about 6.0 to 6.8. The brassica-specific soil caution is clubroot: the soilborne pathogen Plasmodiophora brassicae thrives in wet, poorly drained, acidic ground, so on a clubroot-prone bed improve drainage and lime toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.0 to 7.2, which suppresses it.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Turnips like it slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 6.8, though they grow across a fairly wide range. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number and whether to add lime. One turnip-specific point: a root disease called clubroot is worse in acidic soil, so if your turnips have come out swollen and deformed, raising the pH toward 7.0 to 7.2 with lime helps hold the disease back.
ph.note_seasoned: Turnips grow best at a slightly acidic to neutral pH of about 6.0 to 6.8; Clemson recommends maintaining roughly 6.0 to 6.5, and Minnesota gives a workable range of about 6.0 to 7.5. The brassica-specific reason to watch pH is clubroot: the pathogen is favored by acidic soil, and the standard cultural control is to lime the bed toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.2 to 7.5 where the disease is established. There is thus a mild tension between the ideal growing pH and the clubroot-suppressing pH, resolved by liming only on a clubroot-prone bed. A standard soil test from your local extension office removes the guesswork before sowing.

fertilizer.timing: Work compost and a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing; side-dress lightly once seedlings are established, more for a greens crop than a root crop.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Turnips are light to moderate feeders. Work well-finished compost and a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing, then side-dress lightly once the tops are established if growth is weak. The key brassica-root caution is nitrogen: excess nitrogen grows lush tops at the expense of the root and can leave roots small and poorly formed, so go easy where you want good roots. A crop grown mainly for greens tolerates and even rewards more nitrogen, since the leaves are the harvest. Avoid fresh manure, which both over-supplies nitrogen and causes hairy, branched roots.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Turnips do not need heavy feeding. Mix a balanced fertilizer and some compost into the bed before planting, and give one light feeding later only if the plants look weak and pale. Go easy on nitrogen if you want good roots, because too much grows big leafy tops and small roots. If you are growing turnips mainly for the greens, a little extra nitrogen is fine, since the leaves are what you are after. Do not use fresh manure, which makes the roots hairy and forked.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Turnips want steady phosphorus and potassium for root development plus modest nitrogen, so a balanced blend such as a 10-10-10 worked into the bed before sowing suits a root crop, with most of the feeding coming from incorporated compost. Hold back on nitrogen for roots, since it pushes leafy tops over the root; a greens crop can take more. Skip fresh manure, which over-supplies nitrogen and branches the roots.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Turnips do well with a balanced blend where the numbers are about even, like a 10-10-10, mixed into the soil before planting along with compost. Do not pile on high-nitrogen fertilizer if you want roots, since it grows leaves instead. If you are after the greens, a bit more nitrogen is okay.

companions.note_beginner: Turnips are easygoing neighbors. They share a bed nicely with leafy greens like lettuce, with onions and other alliums, which grow upright and shallow and do not crowd the roots, and they do well following beans or peas that added nitrogen to the soil. The main plants to keep away from turnips are their own cabbage-family relatives: cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, and mustard. These cousins share the turnip's pests, the flea beetle and the cabbage maggot, plus the soil disease clubroot, so growing them together lets those problems build up. As always, do not trust every companion chart online, since many of their claims have never been tested.
companions.note_seasoned: Turnips fit easily into mixed beds, and their clearest companion rule is the brassica avoid: keep them away from the other cabbage-family crops (cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard), which share the turnip's flea beetles, cabbage maggot, and the soilborne clubroot pathogen, so clustering the family concentrates that pressure. On the positive side, leafy greens like lettuce and shallow-rooted alliums share the surface layer while the turnip swells just below, and a legume grown the season before leaves nitrogen behind. Treat the good pairings as sensible defaults rather than proven effects: as University of Minnesota's research review stresses, most companion-planting claims are tradition rather than tested science, so use them as a starting point and watch your own results.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other leafy greens
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce and other quick, shallow-rooted greens grow near the surface and finish fast, while the turnip root swells just below them, so they share a bed without fighting for the same space. Both like the same cool weather, a handy way to fit more into a small garden.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pairing fast, shallow cool-season greens over a slower-swelling root is the standard complementary root-depth and timing rationale; sound and widely taught but a space-and-soil benefit rather than a measured turnip-specific effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce and turnips interplant well on root structure and timing: lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick, the turnip swells just under the surface and takes a little longer, so they draw on different layers and share the cool-season window. This is a space-and-soil benefit rather than a pest one, and one of the more dependable interplants for that reason.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions, leeks, and garlic grow tall and narrow with shallow roots, so they tuck between turnip rows without crowding the roots, and their strong smell is widely used to help confuse some leaf-eating pests. A popular, space-saving pairing.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Alliums are widely recommended as root-crop companions for efficient space use and scent-based pest masking. The space benefit is sound; the pest deterrence is mechanistically plausible but not established in a turnip-specific trial, so likely rather than research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a classic interplant for root crops: shallow-rooted and upright, they share the bed without competing for the turnip's space, and their sulfur volatiles are widely credited with masking the crop from some leaf-feeding pests. The space-use benefit is solid; the pest deterrence is plausible but not proven for turnips specifically.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans and peas (as a preceding crop)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans and peas pull nitrogen from the air and leave some in the soil, so turnips planted after a legume crop get a gentle nutrient boost. They are better as the crop you grow before turnips than right alongside, since bushy legumes can shade the low turnips.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Following a nitrogen-fixing legume is sound rotation practice (extension rotation guides recommend it); the benefit is a soil-fertility one realized in sequence rather than a measured co-planting effect, so traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Legumes earn their place in the turnip rotation more than the turnip bed: beans and peas fix nitrogen and leave residual fertility, so a turnip crop following a legume benefits, which is why extension rotation guides list legumes among good preceding crops for brassicas. Grown concurrently the value is mostly space-sharing, and tall climbing legumes shade the low turnip, so the cleaner use is in sequence.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other leafy greens
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shallow-rooted, fast greens occupy the surface while the turnip swells just below, an efficient cool-season use of bed space.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Standard complementary-root-depth space rationale among cool-season crops; not a measured turnip-specific effect.

good_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Upright, shallow-rooted alliums share the bed without crowding the turnip, and their scent is commonly credited with masking the crop from leaf pests; a popular but not turnip-trial-proven pairing.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Allium space-use and scent-masking are widely recommended for root crops and mechanistically plausible, but not established in a turnip-specific extension trial; labeled likely.

good_seasoned.name: Beans and peas (as a preceding crop)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A nitrogen-fixing legume grown before turnips leaves residual fertility; extension rotation guides list legumes among good preceding crops for the cabbage family.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Sound rotation practice realized in sequence rather than a measured co-planting effect.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other cabbage-family crops (cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard)
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard, and other cabbage-family plants are turnip's close relatives and share its pests, the flea beetle and the cabbage maggot, plus the soil disease clubroot. Growing them right next to turnips lets those problems build up, so give them separate spots and rotate where each goes each year.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Turnip, cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, and mustard are all Brassicaceae and share flea beetle, cabbage maggot, and clubroot. Clustering the family concentrates that pest and disease pressure; sound rotation logic (UMN advises rotating brassicas) rather than a measured antagonism, so traditional/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Turnips are brassicas, so the other cabbage-family crops, cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard, share their exact pest and disease spectrum: flea beetles, the cabbage maggot, and the soilborne clubroot pathogen. Clustering the family in one bed sustains and concentrates that pressure, the same reason extension sources advise rotating among brassicas rather than planting them together year after year.

bad_seasoned.name: Other cabbage-family crops (cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard)
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Other Brassicaceae crops share turnip's pests (flea beetle, cabbage maggot) and the soilborne clubroot pathogen. Planting the family together sustains a shared pest and disease bridge, the same reason extension sources advise rotating among related crucifers.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Shared Brassicaceae pest and disease overlap (flea beetle, cabbage maggot, clubroot) is documented at the family level; the co-planting risk is a sound inference plus standard rotation guidance, not a directly studied pairing.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny, round shot-hole punctures riddling the leaves, the classic flea-beetle signature, heaviest on young spring seedlings and along bed edges. The beetles themselves are minute, shiny black or bronze, with enlarged hind legs, and they spring away like fleas when disturbed. On a turnip grown for greens the damage is more than cosmetic, since riddled leaves are the harvest; on a root crop a vigorous stand outgrows light feeding, but a seedling losing much of its leaf area slows down.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes peppering the leaves, like buckshot, worst on young seedlings in spring. The beetles are very small, dark, and shiny, with big back legs, and they hop away like fleas the moment you get close. If you are growing turnips for the greens this really matters, since the chewed leaves are what you eat; for the root, fast-growing plants usually shrug it off, but tiny seedlings can be set back.
pests.cause_seasoned: Adult flea beetles, chiefly the crucifer flea beetle (Phyllotreta cruciferae) and striped flea beetle (Phyllotreta striolata), which overwinter in leaf litter and field edges and emerge in early spring to feed on brassica foliage. Turnip, radish, mustard, and other crucifers are highly preferred hosts. Pressure is heaviest in spring and early summer and tapers as the season warms, which is one reason fall turnip crops face less of it.
pests.cause_beginner: Small beetles that spend the winter in leaf litter and weeds and come out in early spring hungry for cabbage-family leaves. Turnips and their relatives (radish, mustard) are among their favorite foods. They do the most damage in spring and early summer and ease off as it gets hotter, so fall turnips usually face fewer of them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: On a vigorous stand a well-watered turnip usually outgrows light feeding. Where pressure is heavy on seedlings, a floating row cover set at sowing and sealed at the edges excludes the beetles entirely, the most reliable home defense. Kaolin clay reduces feeding, and spinosad or pyrethrin products are labeled options if a seedling stand is losing more than roughly a quarter to a third of its leaf area; scout in the cool morning when the beetles are sluggish.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: A healthy, well-watered turnip patch usually grows right through light damage. If the little seedlings are getting hammered, cover the row with a floating row cover (a light fabric) right after planting and tuck in the edges so the beetles cannot get under it. Dusting with kaolin clay helps, and sprays like spinosad or pyrethrin are options if seedlings are losing a lot of leaf. Check in the cool morning, when the beetles are slow.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clean up crop debris and weeds at the end of the season to cut overwintering sites. A row cover over the seedbed is the most reliable defense for early spring sowings. Favoring fall plantings, which see lighter pressure, and keeping the stand growing fast with even moisture both reduce impact.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear away old plants and weeds at the end of the season so fewer beetles survive the winter nearby. Covering the seedbed with a row cover is the surest fix for early spring turnips. Leaning on fall plantings, which get hit less, and keeping the turnips growing fast with steady water also help.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When the season winds down, clear out the old plants and nearby weeds. The beetles spend the winter hiding in leftover leaf litter and weedy spots, so removing that shelter means fewer of them show up hungry next spring.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Adults overwinter in leaf litter and along weedy field edges; removing crop debris and weeds at season's end cuts the overwintering population that emerges onto early spring crucifers.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lean on fall plantings where you can. These beetles do most of their damage in spring and early summer and ease off as the weather heats up, so a fall turnip crop usually faces fewer of them. Whenever you plant, keep the patch growing fast with steady water so it can grow through light chewing.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Pressure peaks in spring and early summer and tapers as the season warms, so favoring fall sowings sidesteps the heaviest feeding window. A vigorous, evenly watered stand typically outgrows light feeding in any season; the vulnerable stage is the seedling.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For early spring sowings, lay a floating row cover, a light fabric that lets in light and water but keeps insects out, over the bed right at sowing and tuck the edges into the soil. Sealed well, it keeps the beetles off entirely, and it is the surest home defense. This matters most if you are growing turnips for greens, since the chewed leaves are the part you eat.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A cover set at sowing and sealed at the edges excludes the beetles outright and is the most reliable home defense for spring seedbeds. It protects the two things at stake: seedlings that lose leaf area slow down, and on a greens crop the riddled foliage is the harvest itself.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Dusting the plants with kaolin clay, a fine white clay coating, can cut down on the beetles' feeding. It reduces damage rather than wiping the beetles out, so use it alongside the other steps.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A kaolin coating reduces feeding pressure on exposed plantings. It is a repellent barrier rather than a knockdown, so treat it as a supplement to exclusion and timing rather than a substitute.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If seedlings are losing a lot of leaf despite everything else, roughly a quarter to a third of their leaf area, a spinosad spray is a labeled option. Check the plants in the cool of the morning, when the beetles are slow and easier to size up, and follow the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad is a labeled option when a seedling stand is losing more than roughly a quarter to a third of its leaf area. Scout in the cool morning while the beetles are sluggish to judge whether that threshold has actually been crossed before spraying.

pests.name: Cabbage maggot
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The damage is underground: small, white, legless maggots tunnel and score the surface and interior of the root, leaving winding brown trails that ruin the turnip and open the door to rot. Aboveground, infested plants may look off-color, wilted, or stunted. It is most common in cool, wet springs and in soil rich in undecomposed organic matter. A scored root is unsalable but a useful sentinel, since pulling and destroying it removes maggots before they pupate.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The trouble is underground. Small white legless maggots tunnel into the turnip, leaving winding brown trails that spoil the root and let rot set in. Aboveground the plant may look pale, wilted, or stunted. It shows up most in cool, wet springs and in soil full of un-rotted material. A tunneled turnip is ruined, but pulling and tossing it right away gets the maggots out before they become the next generation of flies.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the cabbage maggot (Delia radicum), a small gray fly that overwinters as pupae in the soil. In spring the adults emerge and females lay white eggs at the base of crucifer stems and in nearby soil cracks; the eggs hatch within about a week and the maggots feed on roots for three to four weeks before pupating. It attacks the whole cabbage family, including turnip, radish, cabbage, and broccoli, with several generations a year and the worst damage in cool, moist spring weather.
pests.cause_beginner: The maggots (young) of the cabbage maggot fly, a small gray fly. It spends the winter as pupae in the soil, and in spring the females lay tiny white eggs at the base of cabbage-family plants. The eggs hatch in about a week and the maggots burrow into the roots for three to four weeks. It goes after the whole cabbage family, turnips, radishes, cabbage, broccoli, and is worst in cool, damp spring weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for a root already tunneled. Pull and destroy infested turnips (do not compost them) to keep maggots from completing their cycle. Insecticide drenches are difficult and rarely worthwhile in a home garden, and are pointless once the maggots have left the root to pupate, so the lever is prevention.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot save a turnip that is already tunneled. Pull up and throw away (do not compost) the affected ones so the maggots cannot grow into more flies. There is no good home spray for this, and sprays do nothing once the maggots have already left the root, so prevention is the real fix.
pests.prevention_seasoned: A floating row cover sealed at the edges at sowing is the most effective home defense, since it blocks the egg-laying flies; be sure no flies are already in the soil from a previous crop. Rotate turnips and other crucifers away from beds that grew them recently, avoid fresh manure and freshly turned-under residue that attract the flies, and favor fall plantings, which see less pressure than cool wet spring.
pests.prevention_beginner: The best home defense is a row cover laid over the bed right after sowing and tucked in at the edges, so the flies cannot reach the plants to lay eggs, just make sure the soil is not already carrying them from an earlier crop. Move turnips away from spots that grew cabbage-family crops recently, avoid fresh manure, and lean toward fall planting, which usually has fewer maggots than cool wet spring.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant turnips away from spots that grew cabbage-family crops recently. The fly's pupae, its resting stage, wait in the soil where those crops were, so moving the bed keeps the new crop away from them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The insect overwinters as pupae in soil that carried crucifers, so rotating turnips and their relatives away from recent brassica ground reduces the carryover population emerging under the new planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Favor fall plantings where you can. This pest is at its worst in cool, damp spring weather, and fall crops usually see fewer maggots.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Damage concentrates in cool, moist spring conditions, so shifting the crop to a fall sowing puts it outside the period of heaviest pressure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A turnip that is already tunneled cannot be fixed, but do not just leave it. Pull it and throw it away, not in the compost, so the maggots inside never get the chance to turn into the next round of flies. Think of a ruined root as an early warning that tells you to protect the rest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no rescue for a scored root, but pulling and destroying infested turnips before the larvae pupate removes them from the cycle; do not compost them. A tunneled root is unsalable but useful as a sentinel that the bed is carrying the pest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The best home defense is a floating row cover, a light fabric sheet, laid over the bed right after sowing with the edges tucked in, so the flies can never reach the plants to lay their eggs. One catch: make sure the soil is not already carrying flies from an earlier cabbage-family crop, or you seal them in with your turnips.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A cover sealed at the edges at sowing blocks the egg-laying flies and is the most effective home defense. It only works over clean ground; confirm no flies are carrying over in the soil from a previous crucifer crop, or the cover traps them with the plants.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small, soft-bodied insects, often grayish-green and sometimes coated with a waxy bloom, collect on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, leaving leaves curled, yellowed, and sticky with honeydew that can blacken with sooty mold. On turnips the culprits are typically the turnip aphid (Lipaphis erysimi) and the cabbage aphid (Brevicoryne brassicae). Beyond direct feeding they can transmit virus, so colonies on the greens are worth removing early.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little soft insects, often gray-green and sometimes dusty-looking, gather in clusters on the undersides of leaves and on new growth. Leaves curl and yellow and turn sticky from the sugary honeydew the aphids leave behind, which can grow a black sooty mold. On turnips these are usually the turnip aphid and cabbage aphid. They can also spread plant viruses, so knock them back early, especially if you are eating the greens.
pests.cause_seasoned: The turnip aphid and cabbage aphid, sap-feeding insects specific to the cabbage family. Populations build fastest in mild weather and on lush, over-fertilized growth, and winged forms move them in from cruciferous weeds and other brassica crops. They can be a particular nuisance on fall greens crops.
pests.cause_beginner: Sap-sucking turnip and cabbage aphids that feed only on cabbage-family plants. They multiply fast in mild weather, especially on soft, over-fertilized growth, and fly in from weeds and other cabbage-family crops. They can be a real pest on fall turnip greens.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A strong jet of water knocks colonies off the leaves and is often enough in a home garden. Natural enemies (ladybugs, lacewings, parasitic wasps) usually bring numbers down; where needed, insecticidal soap or horticultural oil sprayed on the undersides of leaves is effective, taking care to reach the protected cabbage-aphid colonies. Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, which fuels buildup.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the colonies off with a strong stream of water, which often does the trick. Ladybugs and other helpers usually take care of the rest; if not, insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on the undersides of the leaves works well. Do not over-feed with nitrogen, which just grows more aphids.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Encourage beneficial insects by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays, keep plants from being pushed with excess nitrogen, and control nearby cruciferous weeds that host the aphids. Inspect new growth and the undersides of leaves so colonies are caught small, and clear crop debris at season end.
pests.prevention_beginner: Let helpful bugs like ladybugs live in your garden by not spraying broadly, go easy on nitrogen fertilizer, and pull cabbage-family weeds nearby. Check the undersides of leaves now and then so you catch aphids while there are only a few, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on nitrogen fertilizer. Over-fed plants push out soft, lush growth, and that is exactly what these aphids multiply on fastest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Populations build quickest on lush, over-fertilized growth, so a restrained nitrogen program removes the flush that fuels colony buildup without starving the crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull up cabbage-family weeds growing near the bed. The turnip and cabbage aphids feed only on this plant family, and winged ones fly in from those weeds to start new colonies.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Both the turnip aphid and cabbage aphid are crucifer specialists, and winged forms colonize from cruciferous weeds and neighboring brassica crops; controlling those weed hosts removes a standing source of reinfestation.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Check the undersides of the leaves and the new growth now and then so you catch colonies while they are still small, and clear away the old plants at the end of the season. Catching them early matters more here because they can also spread plant viruses, especially if you are eating the greens.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Inspect new growth and leaf undersides so colonies are caught small, and clear crop debris at season's end. Early removal earns extra weight on this crop because the aphids can transmit virus, and fall greens crops are where they tend to be most troublesome.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Blast the clusters off with a strong jet of water from the hose. In a home garden that is often all it takes.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water jet dislodges colonies from the foliage and is often sufficient at garden scale; it is a purely physical knockdown that leaves the natural-enemy complex intact.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Let the helpful insects do their share. Ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps usually bring aphid numbers down on their own, so avoid broad sprays that would kill these helpers along with the pests.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually regulate these colonies if conserved; avoiding broad-spectrum sprays is what keeps that service running, since removing the enemies is how a minor aphid problem becomes a persistent one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the softer steps are not holding, spray insecticidal soap on the undersides of the leaves where the aphids cluster. Take extra care to soak the dusty-looking cabbage aphid colonies, whose waxy coating shelters them, since the spray only works where it touches.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap applied to the leaf undersides is effective when knockdown and predators have not held. Coverage is the whole game: the cabbage aphid's waxy bloom protects its colonies, so spray deliberately into them rather than misting the plant in general.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil, a light spray oil, is the other option for coating the colonies. Aim for the undersides of the leaves and the protected clusters, the same as with soap, and avoid spraying in high heat.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Horticultural oil is the alternative contact spray, applied to the same targets: leaf undersides and the wax-protected cabbage aphid colonies. Whichever contact material you choose, thoroughness of coverage decides the result.

pests.name: Harlequin bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Striking black-and-orange (or black-and-red) shield-shaped stink bugs feeding on the foliage, leaving pale, blotchy, stippled or wilted patches where they have sucked sap; heavy feeding can yellow and kill leaves and stunt or kill young plants. It is chiefly a warm-region pest, most damaging on fall and overwintering brassicas in the South, and it readily attacks turnip and its greens.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Showy black-and-orange (or black-and-red) shield-shaped bugs on the leaves, leaving pale, blotchy, stippled spots where they have sucked the juices out. A lot of them can yellow and kill leaves and even kill small plants. It is mainly a warm-weather pest, worst on fall and winter turnips and greens in the South.
pests.cause_seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica), a stink bug that feeds almost exclusively on cabbage-family plants. Adults overwinter in garden debris in warmer regions and become active as the weather warms, with several generations a year; the barrel-shaped, black-and-white striped eggs are laid in neat double rows on the undersides of leaves.
pests.cause_beginner: The harlequin bug, a stink bug that feeds almost only on cabbage-family plants. The adults spend winter in garden trash in warm areas and get active as it warms up, with several generations a year. Look for its odd barrel-shaped, striped eggs lined up in two neat rows under the leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick adults, nymphs, and the distinctive egg rows into soapy water, which is effective in a home garden caught early. Remove and destroy heavily infested plants and brassica debris that harbor them. Insecticidal soap helps on nymphs; a trap crop of mustard or another preferred crucifer can concentrate the bugs for removal.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the adults, the young, and the striped egg rows by hand and drop them in soapy water, which works well if you start early. Pull and destroy badly infested plants and clean up cabbage-family debris. Insecticidal soap helps on the young bugs, and a patch of mustard planted as bait can draw them together so they are easy to remove.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clear cabbage-family crop debris and weeds at season end to remove overwintering sites, the single most useful step. Rotate brassicas, scout the undersides of leaves for the egg rows, and use a trap crop where the bug is a recurring problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up old cabbage-family plants and weeds at the end of the season, which is the biggest help since that is where the bugs spend winter. Rotate where you plant brassicas, check under the leaves for the striped eggs, and plant a little mustard as bait if the bug keeps coming back.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clean up old cabbage-family plants and weeds at the end of the season. That is the single biggest help, because the adults spend the winter in exactly that kind of garden trash. During the season, pull and destroy any plant that is badly overrun rather than trying to save it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Adults overwinter in garden debris in warmer regions, so clearing brassica debris and weeds at season's end removes the overwintering sites and is the single most useful step. Removing and destroying heavily infested plants during the season is part of the same discipline.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Change where you plant your cabbage-family crops from year to year rather than using the same bed every time.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate brassica plantings so the bugs emerging from last year's site do not find this year's crop waiting in the same spot.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where this bug comes back year after year, sow a patch of mustard or another cabbage-family plant it prefers, and let the bugs gather on it so you can take them out together. This crop's guidance treats the patch as a way to concentrate them for removal, so plan on pulling it rather than keeping it, and see this method's cautions for when.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A mustard stand, or another preferred crucifer, concentrates the bugs where they can be taken out in one pass, which is how this crop's guidance frames it: a tactic for a recurring problem rather than a routine step. Removal is the payoff, and this method's cautions set when it has to happen.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Check the plants and pick off the showy black-and-orange bugs and their young, and look under the leaves for the odd barrel-shaped eggs laid in two neat striped rows. Drop everything into soapy water. Started early, this works well in a home garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Handpicking adults, nymphs, and the distinctive double rows of barrel-shaped eggs into soapy water is effective at garden scale when started early; scouting the leaf undersides for the egg rows is what makes the pass thorough.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Insecticidal soap can help against the young bugs, called nymphs, which are softer than the shield-backed adults. It only works on the ones it actually wets, so spray the insects directly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap helps on nymphs, the soft-bodied stage; expect much less from it against the armored adults. It is strictly a contact material, so direct the spray onto the insects rather than the foliage.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Aboveground, plants are stunted and yellowish and wilt in the heat of the day even in moist soil, recovering overnight. The diagnostic sign is below ground: the roots are swollen, distorted, and clubbed into gnarled, spindle-shaped galls rather than forming a clean turnip, and they later rot. It is a soilborne disease that builds up where crucifers are grown repeatedly and is favored by wet, poorly drained, acidic soil.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Aboveground the plant looks stunted and yellow and wilts in the afternoon sun, then perks up at night. Underground is the giveaway: instead of a clean turnip, the roots swell into lumpy, club-shaped galls that eventually rot. It lives in the soil and builds up when you grow cabbage-family crops in the same spot over and over, especially in wet, acidic soil.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Plasmodiophora brassicae, a soilborne pathogen that infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and persists in soil as resting spores for many years. Wet, poorly drained, acidic soils favor infection, and the disease spreads on contaminated soil, tools, and transplants.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) that attacks the roots of cabbage-family plants and survives in the soil for years. Wet, poorly drained, acidic soil makes it worse, and it spreads on dirty tools and on soil moved from an infected bed.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy affected plants and do not compost them. Management is preventive across seasons: improve drainage and lime the soil toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.2 to 7.5, which suppresses the pathogen, and rotate crucifers out of the bed for several years.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no way to cure a plant that has it, so pull and throw away (do not compost) the affected ones. The fix is for next time: improve drainage, add lime to raise the soil pH toward 7.2 to 7.5, which holds the disease back, and keep cabbage-family crops out of that spot for a few years.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate turnips and other crucifers on a multi-year cycle (a long rotation of several years is advised where it is established), since the pathogen builds in soil grown to the family. Keep soil well drained and limed toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH, start with clean soil and tools, and avoid moving soil from an infested bed. Raised beds with clean mix sidestep the problem where it is entrenched.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not grow turnips or other cabbage-family crops in the same bed year after year; move them on a multi-year cycle. Keep the soil well drained and add lime to raise the pH toward neutral, and avoid carrying soil from an infected bed on your tools. A raised bed with clean soil avoids it where it is a known problem.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not grow turnips or their cabbage-family relatives in the same bed year after year. This organism survives in the soil for years, so where it has shown up, keep the whole family out of that spot on a multi-year cycle.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogen persists in soil as resting spores for many years and builds wherever crucifers are grown repeatedly, so rotate the family out of an affected bed on a multi-year cycle; where the disease is established, a long rotation of several years is advised.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Add lime to raise the soil pH, a measure of how acidic the soil is, toward 7.2 to 7.5, which is neutral to slightly alkaline. Acidic soil favors this disease, and liming to that range holds it back. Save this treatment for the affected bed rather than liming the whole garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Liming toward a pH of about 7.2 to 7.5 suppresses the pathogen, which is favored by acidic soil. Confine the treatment to the affected ground; most vegetables prefer soil closer to neutral-acidic, so this is a targeted clubroot measure, not general practice.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Fix wet spots before planting. This disease is worst in soil that stays wet and drains poorly, so better drainage takes away the conditions it likes.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Wet, poorly drained soil favors infection, so improving drainage in the bed removes one of the two soil conditions, alongside acidity, that drive the disease.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull the stunted, clubbed-root plants and throw them away, never in the compost. Clean the soil off your tools afterward, since the disease travels on dirt carried from an infected bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Infected plants cannot be cured; remove and destroy them without composting. The pathogen also moves on contaminated soil, tools, and transplants, so clean equipment after working an infested bed and avoid transferring its soil elsewhere.

diseases.name: White rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Raised, white to cream, blister-like pustules form on the undersides of leaves, with a faint yellow spot on the upper surface opposite each lesion. Heavy infection can distort leaves and, less commonly, the growing point. It is chiefly a foliar disease, most damaging on turnips grown for greens, and is favored by cool, moist weather.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Raised white or cream blister-like spots on the undersides of the leaves, with a faint yellow patch on the top of the leaf opposite each blister. A bad case can twist the leaves. It mostly affects the leaves, so it matters most when you are growing turnips for greens, and it likes cool, damp weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Albugo candida, a water mold (formerly classed as a fungus) specific to crucifers that survives as thick-walled resting spores on crop debris and in soil and spreads by airborne and splash-borne spores in cool, wet conditions. No fungicides are registered for it in the home garden, so control is cultural.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus-like water mold (Albugo candida) that lives on cabbage-family plants, survives on old plant debris, and spreads in cool, wet weather by spores carried on wind and splashing water. There is no home spray for it, so the fix is in how you grow the crop.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no home chemical control; remove and destroy infected leaves and badly affected plants to reduce spread, and improve airflow and drying. Cultural control carries the load: water at the base, space for airflow, and clear cruciferous weeds and debris that carry it.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no spray for the home garden, so pick off and throw away infected leaves and the worst plants, and help the plants dry out by giving them room. Water at the soil instead of overhead, and clear away cabbage-family weeds and old debris that carry it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crucifers, clear and destroy crop debris and cruciferous weeds that harbor the spores, and avoid overhead watering. Space and thin for airflow so foliage dries quickly, and use tolerant varieties where the disease recurs.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not grow cabbage-family crops in the same spot repeatedly, clear away old plant debris and weeds, and water at the base instead of overhead. Give plants room so the leaves dry fast, and choose a tolerant variety if it keeps coming back.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If white rust keeps coming back in your garden, choose a tolerant variety at seed-buying time, one bred to hold up better against the disease.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Where the disease recurs, tolerant varieties are the seed-time defense; on a crop grown for greens, foliage that stays cleaner is the harvest protected.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move your cabbage-family plantings around instead of using the same spot repeatedly, since the disease carries over where those crops have grown.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogen survives as thick-walled resting spores on crop debris and in soil, so rotating crucifers out of the bed breaks the carryover between plantings.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear away wild mustard and other cabbage-family weeds near the bed. This disease lives only on that plant family, and those weeds keep it going between your crops.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The water mold is specific to crucifers, and cruciferous weeds carry it near the crop; clearing them removes a standing reservoir the rotation alone does not touch.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the plants room, and thin crowded rows, so air moves through and the leaves dry quickly. Cool, damp conditions are what this disease needs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Space and thin for airflow so foliage dries fast; the disease is favored by cool, moist conditions, and drying time is the lever spacing controls.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil instead of over the leaves. The spores spread in splashing water, so keeping the foliage dry slows it down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spores spread by splash as well as air, so basal irrigation instead of overhead watering removes the splash route and shortens leaf wetness.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off infected leaves, and pull the worst plants, and throw them away to slow the spread. Clear old plant debris too, since the disease survives on it. There is no spray for this in a home garden, so these habits are the whole fix.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Remove and destroy infected leaves and badly affected plants to reduce spread, and clear the crop debris that carries the resting spores between seasons. No fungicides are registered for home-garden use against it, so the cultural steps carry the entire load.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, angular, pale green to yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface, bounded by the veins, with a grayish to white downy growth of spores on the corresponding undersides in damp weather. Affected areas later turn tan and papery. It chiefly disfigures the foliage and is most damaging in cool, moist conditions such as a wet fall.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale green to yellow angular patches on top of the leaves, with a grayish or white fuzzy growth underneath in damp weather; the spots later turn tan and papery. It mainly hurts the leaves and is worst in cool, wet weather, like a rainy fall, which is also when turnip greens are growing.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora parasitica (also called Hyaloperonospora parasitica), a water mold that infects crucifers in cool, moist conditions, with infection favored around 50 to 60°F. It survives on crop debris and related hosts and spreads in moist air and splashing water.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus-like water mold (Peronospora parasitica) that infects cabbage-family plants in cool, wet weather, best around 50 to 60°F. It survives on old plant debris and spreads in damp air and splashing water.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected leaves to reduce spread, and improve airflow and drying. Cultural control is the mainstay for a home crop, with copper fungicides a last resort in a persistently wet season.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure infected leaves, so pick off and throw away the worst ones and help the plants dry out by giving them room. Keeping the leaves dry does most of the work; a copper fungicide is a last resort in a very wet stretch.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at the base rather than overhead, space and thin for airflow, and avoid working among wet plants. Rotate away from crucifers, clear crop debris, and where it recurs choose tolerant varieties.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Water at the soil instead of overhead, give plants room so air moves through, and stay out of the bed when the leaves are wet. Move turnips away from where you grew cabbage-family crops, clean up old debris, and pick a tolerant variety if it keeps showing up.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant turnips away from where cabbage-family crops grew recently. The disease survives on old plant debris and on related plants, so moving the crop helps break the cycle.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogen survives on crop debris and related crucifer hosts, so rotating away from recent brassica ground reduces the inoculum waiting under the new planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If downy mildew shows up year after year, pick a tolerant variety when you buy seed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Where the disease recurs, tolerant varieties chosen at seed time reduce the pressure the in-season steps have to carry, which matters most on a fall greens crop growing through its favored cool, wet weather.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Space the plants out, and thin crowded spots, so air can move through and dry the leaves. This disease thrives in cool, damp conditions, which is also rainy fall weather, right when turnip greens are growing.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Space and thin for airflow so foliage dries quickly. Infection is favored in cool, moist conditions around 50 to 60°F, which lines up with the fall greens season, so drying time is worth real attention.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil rather than sprinkling over the leaves. The disease spreads in damp air and splashing water, so dry leaves are your friend.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogen spreads in moist air and splashing water, so basal irrigation removes the splash route and keeps the leaf-wetness periods that drive infection as short as possible.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stay out of the bed while the leaves are wet from rain, dew, or watering. Brushing through wet plants helps carry the disease from leaf to leaf.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Avoid working among wet plants; movement through wet foliage spreads the pathogen. This governs when you enter the bed and still applies after rain or dew, which no irrigation choice controls.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Infected leaves cannot be cured, so pick off and throw away the worst ones to slow the spread, and clear old plant debris between seasons since the disease carries over on it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; removing and destroying affected leaves reduces spread, and clearing crop debris removes the material the pathogen survives on between crops.

control_ladder.note_beginner: In a stretch of weather that stays wet for weeks, a copper fungicide is a last resort if the steps above are not holding. It works by protecting leaves before the disease lands on them, so it earns little once the disease is everywhere. Keep the spray away from ponds and drains, since copper is harmful to fish, and follow the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper is the last resort for a persistently wet season when cultural control is not holding. It is protectant in action, so it belongs early in an outbreak rather than after spread. Copper is highly toxic to aquatic life and accumulates in surface soil with repeat use, so keep it away from water, limit how often you rely on it across seasons, and follow the label rate to avoid foliage injury.

diseases.name: Alternaria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, circular, dark spots on the leaves, each with a yellow halo and characteristic concentric rings, that darken to a sooty center as spores build up and enlarge and merge in wet weather. It is primarily a foliar disease, most important on turnips grown for greens, and severe infection can reduce vigor and quality.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small, round, dark spots on the leaves, each with a yellow ring around it and faint target-like circles inside, that grow and run together in wet weather and turn sooty in the center. It mostly affects the leaves, so it matters most for turnip greens, and a bad case can slow the plant down.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungi (chiefly Alternaria brassicae), which are seedborne and survive on crop debris, spreading in splashing water and needing leaf wetness to infect. Warm, wet weather and prolonged wet foliage drive it.
diseases.cause_beginner: Alternaria fungi that can travel on seed and survive on old plant debris, spreading in splashing water and needing wet leaves to take hold. Warm, humid weather with wet foliage brings it on.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove badly spotted leaves, water at the base in the morning so foliage dries, and clear debris. Clean seed and airflow are the main home levers; a copper fungicide can help in a persistently wet season if started early.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the worst leaves, water at the soil in the morning so leaves dry quickly, and clean up debris. Using clean seed and giving plants room for airflow handle most of it; a copper fungicide can help in a very wet spell if you start early.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean seed, avoid overhead watering, space for airflow, and rotate crucifers and clear debris that carry the fungi between seasons.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed, water at the base instead of overhead, give plants room so the leaves dry, and clear away old plant material between plantings.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with clean seed from a trusted supplier. These fungi can travel on the seed itself, so a clean packet keeps the disease from arriving with the crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The Alternaria fungi are seedborne, so clean seed is the first control and one of the main home levers; it is set once, at purchase, before anything else matters.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move turnips and their cabbage-family relatives to a different spot between plantings, since the fungi carry over where those crops grew.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The fungi survive on crop debris between seasons, so rotating crucifers out of the bed separates the new crop from the carryover inoculum.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the plants room so air moves through and the leaves dry quickly. The spots need wet leaves to take hold, so drying time is most of the battle.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Infection requires leaf wetness, so spacing for airflow shortens the wet periods that let spots establish, enlarge, and merge. Alongside clean seed, this is a main home lever.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil, in the morning, so any splash dries off fast. The disease spreads in splashing water and needs wet leaves to grow.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The fungi spread in splashing water and infect only through wet foliage, so basal morning irrigation removes the splash route and gives leaves the day to dry.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off the worst-spotted leaves as you see them, and clear away old plant material between plantings, since that debris is where the fungi wait for the next crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Remove badly spotted leaves during the season and clear crop debris between plantings; debris is where the fungi persist, and on a greens crop the spotted foliage is quality lost directly.

control_ladder.note_beginner: In a very wet spell, a copper fungicide can help if you start early, before the spots are widespread. Keep it away from ponds and drains, since copper harms fish, and follow the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper can help in a persistently wet season if started early; as a protectant it offers little once lesions are merging. Copper is highly toxic to aquatic life and builds up in soil with repeated use, so keep it out of waterways, limit reliance on it across seasons, and follow the label rate.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions advancing inward from the leaf margins, with the V pointing toward the midrib and the veins in the affected area turning black. Infected leaves yellow and die, and severe infection can rot the plant and move into the root. It is a bacterial disease of the whole cabbage family, spread in warm, wet conditions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow, V-shaped patches creeping in from the edges of the leaves, with the point of the V aimed at the center vein, and the veins in those patches turning black. The leaves yellow and die, and a bad case can rot the plant. It is a bacterial disease that hits the whole cabbage family in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris, a seedborne and splash-spread bacterium that enters through leaf margins (water pores) and wounds. It is favored by warm, humid, wet conditions and spreads on contaminated seed, water, tools, and crop debris across cabbage-family crops.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris) that can travel on seed and splashing water and gets into the leaves through their edges and any wounds. Warm, humid, wet weather brings it on, and it spreads on infected seed, water, tools, and old plant debris among cabbage-family plants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue. Remove and destroy affected plants, avoid working among plants when the foliage is wet, and clear crop debris. Starting with clean seed and rotating crucifers do most of the work in a home garden.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure leaves that are already infected. Pull and throw away affected plants, stay out of the bed when the leaves are wet, and clean up old plant material. Clean seed and rotating where you plant cabbage-family crops handle most of it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, disease-free seed, rotate crucifers out of the bed for at least a year or more, and clear debris that harbors the bacterium. Water at the base rather than overhead, avoid handling wet plants, and space for airflow so foliage dries quickly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean, disease-free seed, do not grow cabbage-family crops in the same spot repeatedly, and clear away old plant debris. Water at the soil instead of overhead, do not handle wet plants, and give them room so the leaves dry fast.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with clean, disease-free seed. This bacterium can ride in on the seed itself, and along with rotation it does most of the work of keeping the disease out of a home garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The bacterium is seedborne, so clean, disease-free seed is the foundational control; together with rotation it carries most of the home-garden defense.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep cabbage-family crops out of the affected spot for at least a year or more. The disease hits the whole family and waits in the bed between crops.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate crucifers out of the bed for at least a year or more; the bacterium attacks the whole cabbage family and persists locally in debris, so the entire family counts in the rotation.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Space the plants so air moves through and the leaves dry quickly. Warm, humid, wet conditions are what this disease needs to spread.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The disease is favored by warm, humid, wet conditions, so spacing for airflow shortens the leaf-wetness periods that let it advance.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil instead of over the leaves. The bacterium travels in splashing water and slips into leaves through their edges and any wounds.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogen spreads by splash and enters through the leaf-margin water pores and wounds, so basal irrigation removes the dispersal route overhead watering provides.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stay out of the bed while the plants are wet, and do not handle wet leaves. Working among wet plants helps spread the bacterium from one to the next.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Avoid working among or handling wet plants; the bacterium moves readily on wet foliage and tools, so choosing when you enter the bed limits plant-to-plant spread.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Leaves that already show the yellow V-shaped patches cannot be cured, so pull affected plants and throw them away, and clean up old plant material, which shelters the bacterium between crops.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected plants and clear the crop debris that harbors the bacterium. It also moves on contaminated water and tools, which is one more reason roguing beats leaving a sick plant standing.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, and it matters most during germination and again as the roots size up. Turnip seed and seedlings need a moist, uncrusted surface for the roughly 7 to 10 days to emergence. Once established, turnips want steady moisture rather than a wet-dry swing: aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, up to 1 to 2 inches in heat or sandy soil, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, and pay closest attention while the seeds are sprouting and later while the roots are bulking up. From planting until the sprouts appear (about 7 to 10 days), keep the surface moist so it does not dry into a hard crust. After that, give about 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings, and a bit more in hot or sandy conditions.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week including rainfall once established, rising toward 1 to 2 inches in heat or on sandy soil and easing in cool or clay soil. During germination the seedbed needs only enough to stay evenly moist near the surface, not soaked.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, including rain, once the plants are growing, up to about 2 inches in hot, dry weather or sandy soil. While the seeds are sprouting, just keep the top of the soil damp, not soggy.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with a gentle setting, soaker hose, or drip line to keep the surface evenly moist without crusting the bed or washing out the shallow-sown seed. Base watering also keeps the foliage dry, which limits the leaf diseases (downy mildew, white rust, leaf spot) turnips are prone to in wet weather.
watering.method_beginner: Water gently at soil level, using a soft spray, soaker hose, or drip line. A hard blast from the hose can wash out the shallow seeds or pack the soil into a crust the sprouts cannot push through, so keep it gentle. Watering at the soil also keeps the leaves dry, which helps prevent the leaf diseases turnips get in wet weather.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Constantly saturated soil invites damping-off, root rots, and clubroot and can yellow the tops; soft roots and a sour, waterlogged bed are signs to back off. Poor drainage is the usual cause, which is why loose, well-draining soil matters for this crop.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soaking wet, turnips can rot, seedlings can damp off, and the clubroot disease gets worse. Watch for yellow leaves, soft roots, and a constantly wet, sour-smelling bed. If you see these, water less and make sure the soil drains well.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Dry, cracked surface soil, dull or wilting tops, and slow growth signal too little water. Drought is the classic cause of poor turnip quality: it drives bitter, woody, strong-flavored, and pithy roots, and an irregular dry-then-wet cycle can crack them.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Dry, cracked soil on top, droopy or dull leaves, and slow growth mean the turnips need more water. Letting them go dry is the main thing that makes the roots bitter, woody, and pithy, and swinging from bone dry to soaked can crack them. Keep the watering steady.

schedule_by_stage.rate: just enough to keep the surface evenly moist
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Turnip emerges in roughly 7 to 10 days, and the shallow-sown seed needs a moist, uncrusted surface the whole time or the stand fails. Water at the base with a gentle setting to avoid crusting.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Turnip seeds come up in about 7 to 10 days. Keep the top of the soil damp and uncrusted until then, watering gently at the base.
