failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The petioles came out fibrous, tough, and strong or bitter in flavor. The dominant cause is a growth check, almost always a dry spell, but also underfeeding, heat, or simply slow growth from cold or crowding. Celery must grow fast and without interruption to stay tender; once stringiness sets in it does not reverse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The stalks turned tough, stringy, and bitter. This almost always comes from the plant going dry at some point, or from not enough food, too much heat, or just slow growth. Celery has to grow fast and steady to stay crisp, and once it goes stringy it stays that way.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture constant (1 to 2 inches per week or more, never a dry-down), feed nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks, grow in the cool season so heat does not coarsen the crop, and choose a more forgiving variety such as Tango or Conquistador. Mulch to steady soil moisture.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Never let it dry out (1 to 2 inches of water a week, more in heat), feed it every 3 to 4 weeks, grow it in cool weather, and pick an easier variety like Tango or Conquistador. Mulch helps keep the soil evenly damp.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Bolting (premature seed stalk)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Celery bolted (sent up a flower stalk)
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant sent up a tall flowering stalk instead of forming a usable head, and the stalks turned tough and bitter. The usual trigger is vernalization: young transplants exposed to roughly two or more weeks near or below 50°F read it as winter and flower. Heat-plus-drought stress can also push stressed plants to bolt.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant shot up a tall flower stalk instead of making a good head, and the stalks went tough and bitter. The usual cause is cold: young plants that sat through a couple of weeks of cold weather (near or below 50°F) think winter has passed and try to flower. Hot, dry stress can also cause it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Transplant only after hard-frost danger and prolonged cold are past, protect early transplants from cold snaps with row cover, do not chill seedlings to harden them, and keep moisture even in heat. Choose bolt-resistant varieties where spring is cold.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant out only after the cold is truly past, cover young plants during cold snaps, do not toughen seedlings by making them cold, and keep them well watered in heat. Pick a bolt-resistant variety if your spring is cold.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Blackheart (blackened center)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Black, dead center (blackheart)
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The young leaves and growing point in the center died and turned brown to black while the outer stalks looked fine, often followed by a slimy secondary soft rot. It is a localized calcium deficiency in the fast-growing tissue, usually caused by interrupted calcium delivery (uneven watering, growth surges, high salts, or acidic soil) rather than genuinely low soil calcium.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The inside center of the plant turned brown or black and died, even though the outer stalks looked okay, and it may have gone slimy. It is caused by the growing tip running short of calcium, usually because watering was uneven, not because the soil truly lacked calcium.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture even above all, hold soil pH in the slightly acidic to neutral range so calcium stays available, avoid forcing soft growth with excess nitrogen, and add calcium only where a soil test shows a real shortfall. Some growers foliar-feed calcium to the heart under risky conditions.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Most of all, keep watering steady. Keep the soil pH in the right range so calcium is available, do not push soft growth with too much nitrogen, and only add calcium (lime) if a soil test says you need it.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cracked or hollow, pithy stalks
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Cracked or hollow stalks
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stalks split lengthwise or came out hollow and pithy inside. Hollow, pithy petioles trace to uneven growth from inconsistent water or nutrition and to over-maturity; boron deficiency can also cause cracked, brittle stalks. As with stringiness, the root issue is usually an interrupted, uneven growth pattern.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The stalks split open or came out hollow and spongy inside. This usually comes from uneven growth, the plant speeding up and slowing down because water or food was not steady, or from leaving it too long. A shortage of the nutrient boron can also cause cracking.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep water and feeding steady to maintain even growth, harvest at maturity rather than holding plants too long, and where cracking recurs have soil tested for boron, correcting only on a confirmed deficiency since excess boron is toxic.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep water and feeding steady so the plant grows evenly, harvest on time instead of leaving it too long, and if cracking keeps happening, have your soil tested for boron and add it only if a test says to (too much is harmful).

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaf and stalk spotting (blight)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Spotty leaves and stalks (blight)
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Yellow then gray or tan spots spread across the leaves, and in the case of late blight onto the stalks, sometimes speckled with tiny dark fruiting bodies. These are the early (Cercospora) and late (Septoria) blights, both often seedborne and spread by wet foliage. Heavy infection blights the foliage and downgrades the stalks.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Yellow then gray or tan spots spread over the leaves, and with late blight onto the stalks too, sometimes with tiny dark dots. These are celery's leaf-spot diseases (early and late blight). They often come in on the seed and spread when the leaves stay wet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Start with disease-indexed (tested) seed and clean transplants, rotate out of celery and its relatives for at least a year, water at the base to keep foliage dry, space for airflow, remove infected leaves, and stay out of the bed when plants are wet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use clean, tested seed and healthy plants, do not grow celery (or carrots and parsley) in the same spot two years running, water at the soil so leaves stay dry, give plants room, pull off spotted leaves, and keep out of the bed when it is wet.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Celery is a long-season crop, so it does not succession-sow rapidly the way salad crops do, but you can stagger transplants a couple of weeks apart within a window and grow both a spring and a fall crop in milder climates. In cold-summer regions that usually means a single main crop transplanted after frost and grown through summer; in warm regions it means a fall and a late-winter or spring crop bracketing the summer heat. Time each window so the long crop matures in cool, not hot, weather and never goes short of water.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Celery takes a long time to grow, so you do not replant it every couple of weeks like lettuce. Instead, set out plants a week or two apart within a planting window, and in milder areas grow a spring crop and a fall crop. In cold-summer areas you usually get one main summer crop; in hot areas you grow it in fall, winter, and early spring to dodge the heat. Aim for the crop to finish in cool weather, and never let it dry out.

heat_threshold_temp_f.basis_seasoned: Air-temperature ceiling for celery quality. Extension sources put celery's optimum near 60 to 70°F (UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County give 60 to 65°F best, tolerating 45 to 75°F; Utah State gives an ideal of 55 to 65°F). Sustained air above roughly 75°F coarsens and bitters the stalks and, combined with drought, can trigger bolting, so the planting calendar in warm regions excludes the hottest months.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Celery is ready when the plant has reached usable size, judged by feel rather than a strict date: a base roughly 3 inches or more across, with firm, crisp, upright stalks generally 6 to 8 inches or taller, usually 80 to 120 days after transplanting. Harvest the whole plant by cutting at the soil line, or take outer stalks as needed and let the center keep growing. Harvest before a hard freeze; light frost is tolerated and can sweeten the stalks, but stalks that are cracking, going hollow or pithy, or sending up a seed stalk are past their best.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Celery is ready when it has grown to a good size: a base about 3 inches or more across, with firm, crisp stalks at least 6 to 8 inches tall, usually 80 to 120 days after you planted it out. Cut the whole plant off at the base, or just snap off the outer stalks as you need them and let the middle keep growing. Pick before a hard freeze (a light frost is fine and can sweeten it). Stalks that are cracking, hollow, or shooting up a flower stalk are past their best.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Celery quality is set by moisture and fertility more than by tilth, so prepare a rich, water-retentive bed. Work in generous compost or well-rotted manure to feed this heavy feeder and to build the water-holding capacity celery's shallow roots depend on, and add a balanced fertilizer at planting. On light sandy soil, amend heavily or build a raised bed with a moisture-holding mix; on the heaviest soils, ensure the bed still drains enough to avoid the pink rot that thrives in waterlogged ground. Aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH (about 6.0 to 6.8) so calcium stays available and blackheart is less likely.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Good celery starts with rich, damp soil, so prepare the bed by digging in lots of compost or rotted manure. This feeds the hungry plant and helps the soil hold the steady moisture celery must have. Mix in a balanced fertilizer at planting too. If your soil is sandy and dries fast, add extra compost or use a raised bed with a moisture-holding mix. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8 so the plant can get the calcium it needs.
crops.description_seasoned: Celery (Apium graveolens) is a cool-season member of the carrot family grown for its crisp leaf stalks, and it has a reputation as one of the more demanding vegetables for good reason. Descended from a wild marsh plant, it wants what few crops want all at once: a long, mild growing season of roughly 80 to 120 days from transplant, constant and even moisture, rich heavily fed soil, and freedom from both hard cold and summer heat. It is started indoors 8 to 10 weeks ahead and transplanted out only after hard-frost danger passes, because young plants chilled for a couple of weeks near 50°F will bolt. The through-line of celery culture is steadiness: any check from drought, hunger, heat, or cold shows up directly as stringy, bitter, hollow, or cracked stalks, and calcium starved by uneven watering blackens the growing heart. Grown with that steadiness, in the cool shoulders of the year, it rewards the effort with tender, flavorful stalks far better than the store offers.
crops.description_beginner: Celery is a cool-weather vegetable in the carrot family, grown for its crisp stalks, and it is honestly one of the trickier crops to grow well. It came from a wild marsh plant, so it wants steady dampness, rich soil, lots of food, and mild weather, all at the same time, over a long season (about 80 to 120 days after you plant it out). You start it indoors 8 to 10 weeks early and plant it outside only after hard frosts are over, because young celery that gets too cold will bolt (run to seed). The big secret is to keep it growing steadily and never let it get dry, hungry, too hot, or too cold. Any of those makes the stalks stringy, bitter, hollow, or cracked. Get the steady care right, grow it in the cooler parts of the year, and homegrown celery is far more tender and flavorful than what you buy.

rgv.region_label: Rio Grande Valley: Subtropical South Texas

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Celery set out Sep 1 - Nov 15 in the Rio Grande Valley, per Bilingual LRGV planting table (Vegetable Crops of the Lower Rio Grande Valley). Transplanted crop (Bilingual LRGV table gives the transplanted-celery row as Sep 1 - Nov 30; this cell narrows the tail to mid-November because celery's succession policy stages 4 transplants at about 3-week intervals, and the full Sep 1 - Nov 30 window would realize a 5th planting, exceeding the crop's succession cap). Germination and early growth are slow, so seed starts about 12 weeks ahead of set-out.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Earliest harvest at about 90 days, from the earliest set-out date.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Latest harvest at about 110 days, from the latest set-out date, before RGV's spring heat closes the window.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors Jun 9 - Aug 23, about 84 days before transplanting, per Bilingual LRGV planting table (Vegetable Crops of the Lower Rio Grande Valley).

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, grow celery in the cool season, not summer. Transplant Sep 1 through Nov 15 and harvest from Nov 30 into spring; it rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold. Celery is a slow starter: seed goes indoors in early summer, long before it feels like gardening weather. Set out transplants in four rounds about three weeks apart, starting Sep 1; the window shown here stops in mid-November, one round short of the full TAMU table, because a fifth round would be more plantings than celery's succession plan calls for. Skip planting celery from spring through summer: the Valley heat keeps it from growing well here.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Celery in the RGV runs on the winter-garden calendar: transplant Sep 1 through Nov 15, with harvest running Nov 30 through Mar 5. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: the TAMU AgriLife sources describe a single Valley-wide planting calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: OSU's Oregon planting table (EM9027) calls for starting celery indoors a full 9 weeks before setting it out, the longest indoor lead time in the table. The Willamette Valley's own set-out window runs March into July; the coast's runs March into June.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out from March, staggering plantings a few weeks apart within the window rather than resowing every couple of weeks; celery is a long-season crop, not a fast-succession one.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Celery reaches usable size roughly 80 to 120 days after transplanting; the mild, long maritime summer supports full-size stalks without the bitterness a hot, dry summer causes.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Celery tolerates a light frost but is damaged by a hard freeze, so harvest continues close to the season's first frost date.

8.notes: Start seed indoors a full 9 weeks before setting out; celery is slow and needs steady moisture and feeding throughout. Stagger a few transplants a couple of weeks apart rather than a single block planting.
8.zone_notes: OSU's Willamette Valley table gives celery its widest PNW window, March into July, a month longer than the coast's own table. The valley's real, if generally mild, winter frost keeps December-through-February purely an indoor-nursery period, not an outdoor planting month.

9.notes: Start seed indoors a full 9 weeks before setting out; celery is slow and needs steady moisture and feeding throughout. Stagger a few transplants a couple of weeks apart rather than a single block planting.
9.zone_notes: OSU's coastal table gives celery a March-to-June set-out window, a month shorter at the tail than the valley's own table; the coast's cooler, foggier summer does not extend the useful transplant season the way the valley's does.

Start seed indoors in winter, a full 9 weeks before you plan to set plants out, then transplant from March on: through July in the Willamette Valley, through June on the coast. Keep the soil evenly moist all season for full, tender stalks, and harvest before the first hard freeze in fall.

Start seed indoors a full 9 weeks ahead, the longest lead time in OSU's table, then set transplants out from March: the Willamette Valley's own window runs into July, a month longer than the immediate coast's, which closes in June as the coast's cooler summer offers less benefit from a late transplant. Stagger a handful of plantings a few weeks apart rather than succession-sowing every couple of weeks, since celery is a slow, long-season crop. Harvest runs 80 to 120 days later, close to the season's first frost; celery tolerates a light frost but not a hard freeze.

nevada.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

transplant.label: primary
transplant.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring celery windows for the Las Vegas Valley: the hotbed gives transplants a head start, so they go into the ground in the two weeks before the last frost, per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart and the University of Nevada, Reno Extension's cool-season framework (Fact Sheet FS-02-61).

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Begins bearing about 100 days after transplanting, this crop's own days-to-maturity.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop is cut as Las Vegas Valley daytime highs push past 90°F; the University of Nevada, Reno Extension's home-vegetable guidance (Fact Sheet FS-02-61) notes plants generally stop growing well past that mark, and celery stalks toughen and turn bitter in sustained heat, so the spring stand is picked promptly as the heat builds.

transplant.label: primary
transplant.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall celery windows for the Las Vegas Valley: transplant again once the worst heat has broken, per the UNLV/UNR Master Gardener chart's cool-season fall window.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins bearing about 100 days after the late-summer transplant.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop is cut up to the valley's first fall frost; celery tolerates a light frost but is damaged by a hard freeze.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Las Vegas Valley summers routinely run past 100°F from June into September, well past the roughly 90°F growth ceiling the University of Nevada, Reno Extension's home-vegetable guidance (Fact Sheet FS-02-61) sets for the region, and celery stalks toughen and turn bitter in that heat. In zone 8's cooler pockets the spring stand is cut by mid-June and there is no fall replant: an August transplant here cannot mature before the zone's earlier first frost, so the bed rests through the hottest months and stays dormant into the cooler fall rather than starting a second crop.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, start celery seed indoors or in a protected hotbed about 10 weeks before setting plants out. The hotbed gives transplants a head start, so they go into the ground in the two weeks before the last frost, roughly mid-February. Stalks are ready by early summer; cut the spring stand promptly, since it toughens and turns bitter once the heat builds past 90°F. In the warmer valley and at Laughlin, start a second batch of transplants for a fall planting once the worst heat has broken, for a crop that finishes as the weather cools and tolerates a light frost; the cooler zone 8 pockets skip this fall round, since the August transplant cannot mature before frost there, and grow a single spring crop instead.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) grows celery as a hotbed-started transplant crop, on two cycles in its warmer zones, per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart and the University of Nevada, Reno Extension's cool-season framework (Fact Sheet FS-02-61). Seed starts indoors about 10 weeks ahead; the hotbed's protection lets the spring transplant go out in the two weeks before the last frost rather than waiting for it, and stalks are ready roughly 100 days later, in early summer. Once daytime highs run past 90°F, plants generally stop growing well and stalks toughen and turn bitter, so the spring stand is cut promptly as the heat builds, and the timing here is tighter than for the quicker roots and greens. In zone 9 and at zone 10's Laughlin, a second hotbed-started batch transplants out from about mid-August to mid-September, once the worst heat has broken, for a fall stand that finishes as the weather cools and carries up to the valley's first fall frost, since celery tolerates a light frost but is damaged by a hard freeze; zone 10's later frost gives that fall stand the most room to spare. Zone 8's cooler pockets reach frost too soon for an August-transplanted fall crop to mature, so gardeners there grow a single spring crop and skip the replant.

Stalks are ready to cut by early summer; harvest promptly, since celery toughens and turns bitter once the heat builds past 100°F. Utah State University Extension's planting guide gives St. George no fall celery window, so this is a single spring crop here, not a two-season grower like the beets and carrots.

Celery is not explicitly named in Utah State University Extension's Table 1 planting-date groups, so it is treated here like its fellow cool-season Group B (Semi-Hardy) umbellifers, parsley and parsnip: seed starts indoors roughly 10 weeks ahead, in late December, and transplants go out around March 1. Stalks are ready in about 100 days, by mid-to-late June, and the stand is cut promptly as USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation notes put St. George over 100°F in June, July, and August, well past where celery stalks toughen and turn bitter. USU's suggested planting dates document no St. George fall celery window, so the bed rests through the hottest months into the cool fall rather than carrying a second crop.

crops.name: Asparagus
crops.description_beginner: Asparagus is a long-lived perennial vegetable: you plant it once and a good bed keeps feeding you for 15 to 20 years. You grow it from one-year-old crowns set in a deep trench, then wait two to three years for the first real harvest while the roots get strong. Each spring the bed sends up the tender green spears you eat; a young bed gives only a short pick and a mature one can run six to ten weeks, and you stop when the new spears come up thin and let the rest grow into tall, ferny foliage that feeds the roots for next year. For a new bed, plant an all-male hybrid like Millennium, a very cold-hardy, high-yielding variety that most northern nurseries now carry. Jersey Knight is another good all-male pick, with better tolerance to rust and root rot. Mary Washington is the classic seed-grown heirloom, lower-yielding but easy to find, and Purple Passion has sweet purple spears that are nice raw in a salad. Asparagus likes full sun and deep, well-drained soil, and it needs a real winter rest, so it is a temperate crop rather than a tropical one.
crops.description_seasoned: Asparagus (Asparagus officinalis) is a long-lived herbaceous perennial grown for the tender spring spears it pushes from a deep, cold-hardy crown. Established once from one-year-old crowns in a deep trench, a well-sited bed yields for 15 to 20 years and sometimes far longer. The rhythm is fixed: spears emerge as the soil warms and are cut for a spring window that lengthens with bed age, reaching six to ten weeks on a mature crown, after which every remaining spear grows into a tall fern canopy that recharges the crown for the next season. Its physiology is temperate rather than tropical. UC IPM ties the plant's longevity to getting a true dormant season each year, not just a mild pause, so a bed set where winter never really arrives will not hold. Variety choice sets the ceiling. All-male hybrids outyield the open-pollinated types and skip the weedy volunteer seedlings: Millennium, a cold-hardy University of Guelph hybrid, is the modern high-yield northern standard but runs more susceptible to rust, while the Rutgers Jersey hybrids, represented here by Jersey Knight, carry the class's vigor-based field tolerance to rust and to Fusarium crown and root rot. Among the open-pollinated types, Mary Washington is the century-old heirloom standard, hardy but lighter-yielding with mixed male and female plants, and Purple Passion is a sweeter, purple-speared strain that yields less and catches foliage disease more easily. Give asparagus full sun and deep, well-drained ground, and choose the site with care, since the crowns will hold it for two decades.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Establish from one-year-old crowns; you can grow from seed, but that adds a full year before the first harvest.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant one-year-old crowns instead of seeds to get a head start.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: A permanent bed is established once and never succession-planted; you set a long-term site, plant crowns, and let the crowns thicken and yield for 15 to 20 years.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Do not establish a new asparagus bed where asparagus grew recently. Fusarium crown and root rot, the disease that eventually runs old beds down, survives in the soil indefinitely (UC IPM), so a replant site carries a heavy inoculum load from the start; UC IPM advises long rotations out of asparagus. Because a bed is permanent, this is not annual rotation but a one-time siting decision: keep a new planting off old asparagus ground, and off low, waterlogged spots, since wet soil worsens the crown and root rots.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant a new asparagus bed where asparagus grew before. The Fusarium rot that wears old beds out lives in the soil for years, so an old asparagus spot is already loaded with it. Pick fresh ground instead. Since the bed stays put for 15 years or more, this choice is made once, when you site the bed.
rotation.good_after: A fresh, sunny, well-drained site not recently in asparagus.
rotation.note_seasoned: Asparagus is not rotated. It is a permanent 15-to-20-year bed, chosen once and left in place, so the usual annual crop-rotation logic does not apply. Rotation matters only at siting: establish the bed on fresh, well-drained ground that has not recently grown asparagus, to keep clear of the soil-persistent Fusarium crown and root rot, and never replant a failing bed into the same spot.
rotation.note_beginner: You do not rotate asparagus. It is a permanent bed that stays in one place for 15 to 20 years, so instead of moving it each season you just choose the spot well at the start: fresh, sunny, well-drained ground that has not grown asparagus before. If an old bed fails, start the new one somewhere else, not in the same soil.

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Asparagus wants a deep, loose, well-drained bed in full sun, with plenty of compost worked in. It is not picky about soil type and grows in sandy, loamy, or heavier ground, as long as water never stands there. Since the bed stays put for 15 years or more, take the time to loosen it deeply and clear out perennial weeds before you plant.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Give asparagus a deep, fertile, well-drained bed rich in organic matter and sited in full sun. Texture is not the real constraint here, drainage is. The University of Minnesota accepts anything from heavy clay to light sand provided water keeps moving through it instead of standing after a rain, and Michigan State puts a hard edge on the same point: if water sits in the spot for even an hour, the site is too wet. A deep sandy loam is the classic asparagus soil because it drains freely and lets you dig the planting trench. Work in generous compost and clear perennial weeds before planting, because the crowns will hold that ground for 15 to 20 years.

crops.soil_prep_beginner: Dig the bed deeply and mix in compost. Then open a planting trench about 6 to 12 inches deep (shallower, around 6 inches, in heavy clay; deeper, 8 to 12 inches, in sandy soil), set the crowns in the bottom with the roots spread out, and cover them with 2 inches of soil at first. As the spears grow, gradually fill the trench back in over the season.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Loosen the bed deeply and amend with compost the season before or at planting. Open a furrow 6 to 12 inches deep sized to your soil (Michigan State: about 6 inches in clay, 8 to 10 inches in sandy soil; the University of Minnesota gives 6 to 8 inches in clay and 10 to 12 in sand), drape each crown over a low ridge of soil with the roots fanned out, and cover with only about 2 inches to start. Backfill the trench gradually as the spears elongate through the first season rather than burying the crowns all at once.

ph.note_beginner: Aim for a near-neutral soil pH around 6.5 to 7.0; asparagus is easygoing about pH and does fine anywhere from about 6.0 to 7.5. It dislikes strongly acidic soil, so if a soil test comes back low, work in lime before you plant.
ph.note_seasoned: Asparagus does best in near-neutral soil, about pH 6.5 to 7.0, the range the University of Minnesota, Michigan State, and others recommend; it is not fussy and still performs across roughly 6.0 to 7.5, taking slightly alkaline ground better than acidity (Michigan State notes a pH a little above 7.0 does not really hurt anything). It does not tolerate strongly acidic soil, so lime an acid bed up toward neutral before planting a bed you will keep for 15 years or more.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep the bed evenly moist and never waterlogged, watering deeply during dry spells rather than lightly and often. Consistent moisture matters most through the first two seasons while the crowns build their deep root system; an established, deeply rooted bed rides out short dry spells well.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply during dry weather so the bed stays evenly moist but never soggy. This matters most in the first couple of years while the roots are getting established; after that the deep roots handle dry spells better.
watering.amount_seasoned: Water deeply and evenly, especially through establishment and the spring spear-cutting window; let the top inch dry between waterings rather than keeping the crowns wet. A mulch helps hold even moisture and suppress the weeds that compete with a permanent bed.
watering.amount_beginner: Give the bed a deep soaking when the weather is dry, then let the surface dry a bit before the next watering. A layer of mulch keeps the moisture even and holds down weeds.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose. Keeping the ferns dry checks the rust and other foliage diseases asparagus catches in crowded, humid stands.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the ferns. Dry foliage helps prevent rust and other leaf diseases.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing, collapsing spears and crown or root rot in saturated, poorly drained ground; standing water for even an hour signals a site too wet for asparagus, and waterlogged, low-pH soil worsens Fusarium crown and root rot.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Soft, yellowing spears and rotting crowns in soggy soil. If water stands in the bed after rain, the spot is too wet for asparagus.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Thin, spindly spears and ferns that wilt or brown early in prolonged drought, especially on a young stand whose roots have not yet gone deep; growth slows and the crown banks fewer reserves for next spring.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Skinny spears and ferns that wilt or brown early when the soil stays dry too long, which is hardest on a young bed.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even, deep moisture through establishment and the harvest window builds a stronger crown; once the deep root system is down, an established bed tolerates short dry spells but still yields best with steady moisture.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water deep and steady while the bed is young and while you are cutting spears; older, deep-rooted beds handle dry spells better but still do best with regular water.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Moisture matters most while a new planting roots in over its first two seasons and during the spring spear-cutting window, when the crown is spending reserves to push spears.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Keep the soil moist while a new bed is getting established and while the spears are coming up in spring.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep evenly moist; water deeply in dry spells
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Steady moisture matters most through the first two seasons while the crowns build their deep root system; water deeply whenever rainfall is short so the soil never dries around the new roots, and mulch to hold it even.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep a new bed evenly moist while the roots get established. Water deeply during dry spells and mulch to hold the moisture; this is the most important watering in the plant's life.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep and even through the cutting window
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: The crown is spending reserves to push spears, so keep even, deep moisture through the whole cutting season, however long the bed's age lets it run; water at the soil line with drip or a soaker so the emerging spears and soon-to-grow ferns stay dry against rust.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the spears are coming up in spring, keep the soil evenly moist with deep watering. Water at the base, not over the plants, to help prevent rust.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep and even; let the top inch dry between waterings
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep the ferns growing vigorously with steady moisture through summer, since next spring's yield tracks this year's fern; an established, deep-rooted bed rides out short dry spells, but growth and reserves suffer in prolonged drought. Water at the base to keep the ferns dry against rust.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water the ferns through summer so they grow tall and feed the roots for next year. An older bed handles a short dry spell, but do not let it stay dry for long. Water at the base to keep the ferns dry.

schedule_by_stage.rate: little to none while dormant
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Cut back watering as the ferns die back and the crown goes dormant; the risk now is crown and root rot in cold, saturated ground, so never let a dormant bed sit in waterlogged soil over winter.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water little or none once the ferns brown and the plant goes dormant for winter. The danger now is rot in soggy soil, so do not let the resting bed stay waterlogged.

fertilizer.timing: in early spring before spears emerge, and again right after the final spring harvest for established beds
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced garden fertilizer; a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate for the after-harvest feeding
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 in early spring, then feed again right after the final harvest to fuel the summer fern growth that recharges the crown, the two-feeding pattern the University of Georgia and Missouri both describe. The University of Minnesota suggests roughly 1 to 1.5 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet before planting, with nitrogen added once the crowns are growing; UGA pairs a balanced fertilizer at planting and early season with an after-harvest nitrogen side-dressing. Asparagus is a heavy user of potassium and a light user of phosphorus once the bed is established, so lean on a balanced or potassium-forward feed rather than piling on phosphate.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Give the bed a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 in early spring as growth starts, and feed it again right after you stop harvesting so the ferns can grow strong and feed the roots for next year. Work some fertilizer or compost into the trench when you first plant, too. You do not need to feed more than once or twice a year.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Balanced spring feed plus an after-harvest nitrogen boost: 10-10-10 in early spring, then nitrogen (for example calcium nitrate) right after the last cutting to drive fern growth. Asparagus uses a lot of potassium and little phosphorus once established, so a balanced or potassium-leaning feed suits it.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 in early spring, and feed once more right after the final harvest to push strong summer ferns.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet before planting (UMN), a balanced spring application on an established bed, and an after-harvest nitrogen side-dressing to fuel fern growth.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A balanced feeding in early spring and again after the last harvest is plenty; mix fertilizer or compost into the trench at planting.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Asparagus is not a good container crop. It is a permanent bed that lives for 15 years or more, with deep roots that spread several feet, so it needs open ground or a large, deep raised bed rather than a pot. If you only have hard surfaces, build a deep raised bed instead of using containers, and grow something else in your pots.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Skip containers for asparagus. It is a long-lived permanent planting (the University of Georgia notes a well-established bed can last 30 years) whose roots, the University of Illinois observes, spread laterally 5 feet or more over the years, all fed from a deep planting trench. An ordinary pot cannot supply the depth, root run, or longevity the crop needs. A deep raised bed is the only container-adjacent option worth pursuing, and even then it must be permanent and generously sized; for most gardeners an in-ground bed is the right call.

University of Missouri Extension (Growing Asparagus in Missouri, G6405)

growth_stages.name: Establishment (years 1 to 2)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: In the planting year the crowns send up only a few thin, wiry spears; you let them all grow straight into ferns while the plant builds the deep root and crown reserves it will draw on for decades. Expect little to nothing to harvest for the first two years.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In the first year or two you will see just a few skinny spears. Let them all grow into tall, feathery ferns. The plant is busy building strong roots underground, so there is almost nothing to pick yet.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Do not cut in the planting year and harvest only lightly in year two; keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist so the crowns bulk up. Set crowns 12 to 18 inches apart in the trench and backfill gradually as the spears grow.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Resist harvesting the first year, and take only a little the second year. Keep weeds down and the soil moist so the roots get strong. Set crowns about 12 to 18 inches apart.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is the new bed filling in?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How is the new bed filling in?

growth_stages.name: Spear emergence and harvest (spring)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: On an established bed, spears push up as the soil warms in spring, ready to cut at about 6 to 8 inches while the tips are still tight. A late spring frost can turn emerged spears dark and glassy and collapse them, so watch the cold nights.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In spring, established plants send up the spears you eat. Cut them when they are about 6 to 8 inches tall and the tips are still closed and tight. A hard late frost can ruin spears that are already up, so keep an eye on cold nights.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Snap or cut spears at the soil line every one to three days through the harvest window the bed's age supports, then stop once the spears thin toward pencil width and let the rest grow into ferns. If frost threatens emerged spears, harvest them first or cover the bed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick spears every day or two right through the spring harvest, then stop once the new spears come up thin and let the plants grow. If frost is coming, cut the standing spears first or cover the bed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are the spears coming up?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are the spears coming up?

growth_stages.name: Fern growth (summer recharge)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After harvest ends, every spear grows into a tall, feathery fern. This summer canopy is the crown recharging its reserves for next spring; the ferns tolerate summer heat and keep working into fall. Scout them for asparagus beetles and for orange rust pustules.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: When you stop harvesting, let the plants grow into tall, ferny green foliage all summer. This is how the plant feeds its roots for next year, so never cut it down early. Check the ferns for asparagus beetles and orange rust spots.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed the bed right after the final harvest to fuel fern growth, keep it weeded and watered, and leave the ferns standing all summer. Handpick asparagus beetles and let ladybug larvae and the native egg parasites help; keep the ferns open and dry against rust.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Give the bed a feeding right after the last harvest, keep it watered and weeded, and let the ferns grow untouched. Pick off asparagus beetles by hand and let ladybugs help; good airflow keeps rust down.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How tall are the ferns getting?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How tall are the ferns getting?

growth_stages.name: Dormancy (fall and winter)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: In fall the ferns yellow and die back after hard frost, and the crown drops into winter dormancy underground. The crown itself is deeply cold-hardy and overwinters in place; it is the top growth, not the crown, that frost kills.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In fall the ferns turn yellow and die back once frost arrives, and the plant rests underground for winter. The roots are very cold-hardy and survive the cold; only the ferns above ground are killed by frost.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Once the ferns have fully browned, cut them to the ground and remove the debris to deny asparagus beetles and rust a place to overwinter; mulch the crowns in the coldest, snow-poor zones. Do not disturb or till the bed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Once the ferns are fully brown, cut them down and clear away the old growth, which cuts down on beetles and rust next year. In very cold areas, mulch over the bed for winter. Do not dig or till it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have the ferns died back yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have the ferns died back yet?

crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: The distinction that matters is crown versus top growth: the crown is deeply cold-hardy and overwinters dormant in the ground, riding out hard freezes, while the ferns and emerged spears are frost-tender. Missouri's guidance is reassuring on what a late freeze actually costs you: the spears standing at the time can be ruined, but the crown below is untouched and the rest of the season's cutting comes in normally. At the other end of the year, it is the first fall frost that sends the ferns into dieback. The dormancy in between is a requirement, not just something the plant puts up with. UC IPM treats the dormant stretch as one half of what the plant needs each year, since the crown does its rebuilding while the top is down, so a site that never truly cools leaves that recharge unfinished and the bed thins out over the years. That is why this belongs to temperate gardens rather than tropical ones. In the coldest, snow-poor winters, mulch the crowns, since the least cold-hardy types can injure in a deep freeze without snow cover.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: The roots and crown underground are very cold-hardy and survive winter just fine; it is the spears and ferns above ground that frost damages. A late spring frost can ruin spears that are already up, and a fall frost kills back the ferns for the year. Asparagus actually needs that cold winter rest: it grows in spring and summer, then rests over winter, so it does best where winters are real and struggles in frost-free, tropical places. In very cold areas with little snow, spread mulch over the bed for extra winter protection.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Asparagus GS-arc cert (2026-07-24), herbaceous_perennial archetype. Asparagus officinalis (Asparagaceae) is modeled as a herbaceous_perennial on the frost_anchored calendar basis, the same lane certified for chives and mint, where the annual placement gates (A3) no-op because a permanent bed is planted once from crowns and never succession-sown. The regional calendars carry the established-bed steady state: winter cold_pause dormancy, spring harvest as the soil warms, summer growing (the fern canopy recharging the crown), then fall dieback back into cold_pause. This spring-harvest-then-summer-fern rhythm is legalized by the A34/A37 herbaceous_perennial carve-out authored at Task 1, which exempts the archetype from the annual harvest-needs-a-preceding-plant and no-growing-after-harvest rules; without it the productive cells would read as incoherent. Suitability is an honest 16-region, 39-cell map: 18 cells perennialize, 8 are marginal, and 13 are unsuitable. Every marginal and unsuitable call rests on the asparagus dormancy requirement verified verbatim from UC IPM (asparagus requires two distinct periods, a growing period and a resting period) plus its stated 65°F to 85°F fern optimum: frost-poor maritime and low-chill zones blunt the dormant rest (marginal), and frost-free subtropical or extreme-heat desert zones deny it entirely (unsuitable). Variety resistance is graded T1 from Michigan State trials: Millennium (the reference, a cold-hardy all-male University of Guelph hybrid) is susceptible to rust and purple spot, while the Rutgers Jersey class, represented by Jersey Knight, carries the vigor-based field tolerance to rust, purple spot, and Fusarium crown and root rot. The plan skeleton's fabricated per-variety grades were caught by the T1-or-drop rule during authoring and rebuilt only from the MSU-sourced calls, a design-arc integrity catch. Asparagus opens a new Perennial Vegetables category (UC Master Gardener frames it as a perennial cool-season stem vegetable, not a fruiting vegetable), moved out of Fruiting Vegetables. Review fix: the ca_interior Delta prose was re-anchored to sourced framing (the deep peat Delta soils have grown asparagus for generations, crowns producing up to twenty years) after an unsupported largest-producer superlative was dropped and re-verified against the UC ANR Kings County report and UC IPM cultural-tips. Remaining honest caveats, heavily-modeled regional month placement and thin regional sourcing on a few desert cells, are logged as low-severity open findings; none block launch. [CORRECTION 2026-07-29: two assertions above are retired. (1) The suitability split is no longer 18/8/13 but 25 perennializes / 4 marginal / 10 unsuitable; those cells were RE-RATED in timing arc 2, not merely recounted. (2) The CHILL framing of the dormancy mechanism is retracted. It traces to PlantVillage, an aggregated crop-profile database rather than an extension bulletin, and UC IPM states dormancy comes from cold OR DROUGHT, instructing home gardeners to induce it by withholding irrigation. The clause that frost-free subtropical or extreme-heat desert zones deny dormancy entirely is false outright: low_desert_az z9 and z10 were re-rated unsuitable -> perennializes on in-region UC and UA evidence. Do not reason from the chill claim. See open_findings asparagus_suitability_chill_mechanism_unsourced_arc2, asparagus_chill_claim_provenance_plantvillage and asparagus_low_desert_az_rerated_from_retired_chill_mechanism, plus docs/verification_log_ref_convention.md.]

open_findings.summary: MODELING CHOICE flagged for certify: asparagus is a HERBACEOUS PERENNIAL modeled in the frost_anchored lane (the chives/mint lane), not a woody or a dedicated perennial-vegetable basis. The annual placement gates (A3) no-op because the bed is planted once from crowns and never succession-sown, and the established-bed steady-state calendar (winter cold_pause, spring harvest, summer fern growing, fall dieback) is legalized by the A34/A37 herbaceous_perennial carve-out that exempts the archetype from harvest-needs-a-preceding-plant and no-growing-after-harvest. The perennial nature is represented honestly: perennial=true, lifecycle=perennial, succession_policy.suitable=false (permanent 15-to-20-year bed), propagule=crown, days_to_maturity [] with the establishment lag carried in years_to_first_harvest/years_to_full_production/productive_lifespan_years, and a dedicated dormancy growth stage. Confirm this lane choice is acceptable versus a dedicated perennial-vegetable basis shared with the queued artichoke.

All 39 per-zone calendars have their harvest/growing MONTH placement MODELED from each region's frost and spring warm-up pattern plus the regional extension sources, not lifted from a single asparagus-per-zone chart (few exist), following the certified-chives regional-calendar precedent. resolution_method on every cell is frost_anchored_resolved. The suitability TIERS are T1-defensible on the dormancy requirement; where regional sourcing was thin the month placement was modeled and flagged rather than the tier overstated.

nevada z9 and z10 are the lowest-confidence cells: the z10 marginal call (warm-winter blunted dormancy) and the Feb-Mar spear-emergence placement for both z9 and z10 are heavily modeled from dormancy-deficit reasoning, with no asparagus-per-zone z10 chart and only a generic southern-Nevada vegetable-production regional anchor (unr_fs0261) alongside the UC IPM dormancy biology. The tier is conservative and the placement is modeled; flagged for the source-truth sample.

utah_dixie z8 (St. George): the Mar-Apr harvest placement is modeled from the warm Mojave-edge spring; the USU asparagus source is statewide and northern-Utah-timed to May-Jun. The perennializes tier is sound (the Dixie winter still delivers a real dormant rest); only the month placement is modeled.

pnw z9: the Mar-Apr start is modeled. Cool maritime springs make the hardiness zone a weak predictor of first-cut, so the prose tells the reader to let soil temperature call the start; OSU anchors the mid-June harvest END directly while the START months are modeled.

ca_interior z8 (valley margins and foothills): the Mar-Apr placement is extrapolated from Delta-centric commercial sources (UC ANR and UC IPM), which document the z9 Delta floor far better than the cooler foothill margins. The perennializes tier is well-supported; the z8 month placement is modeled.

mid_south z8 (Delta lowlands): the March start is extrapolated below the statewide-Arkansas April figure for the warm Delta lowlands. The perennializes tier is T1 (AR and MO give a month-direct April-into-June window for the uplands); the warmer-lowland March placement is modeled.

low_desert_az z9 and z10 (Phoenix and Yuma) are the weakest-sourced cells: no UArizona low-desert asparagus page exists (the only UArizona asparagus page is high-desert Yavapai, about z7, and recommends the crop there), so the unsuitable call is modeled from the UC IPM dormancy-plus-heat basis and the Texas A&M poor-in-mild-winter-and-long-hot-summer analog (tamu_agrilife). A marginal, short-lived call is arguably also defensible; unsuitable was chosen on the conservative-tier rule.

Two suitability boundary calls are modeled climate distinctions rather than source-stated lines: se_gulf z10 kept marginal (it sits at the hottest-South edge and could arguably be unsuitable) and ca_desert z9 kept marginal against z10/z11 unsuitable (the marginal-versus-unsuitable split within the desert). Both follow the design default and the dormancy-and-heat basis; flagged for the source-truth sample.

SOURCING LIMIT on the crown-planting windows authored 2026-07-26: NO T1 source anywhere states an asparagus crown window by USDA zone. Every extension source is state-, region- or county-scoped, so each per-zone window involves an editorial state-to-zone mapping step that is ours, not the source's. This is recorded per cell in resolution_method: extension_direct and county_source_direct are sourced for that geography; state_source_zone_mapped, extension_shift_rule_applied, soil_workable_anchor_derived, extension_chart_plus_anchor and extension_chart_geometry all carry an inference step. The northern_tier z3-z7 ladder is the largest editorial construction: five zones built monotonically from five different state sources (UMN/NDSU/SDSU, UMaine, Iowa State/Illinois, UConn, Missouri). DISPOSITION 2026-07-29 (hardening item 2b): the zone-keyed gap is CONFIRMED and FORMALLY ACCEPTED, and the ladder VALUES are upheld. A fresh multi-state hunt found the regional source this finding said did not exist, and it argues FOR accepting the gap rather than closing it: the Midwest Vegetable Production Guide (an 8-state land-grant collaboration spanning z3b-z7a, MSU-published) states one undifferentiated window for the whole footprint, verbatim "Transplant April 15 to May 15", with ZERO zone-keyed references anywhere in its asparagus section (verified here by pypdf extraction, HTTP 200, 8 pages, 44 asparagus mentions). So the multi-state literature does not resolve by zone either; a five-rung ladder is finer than any source, which is what state_source_zone_mapped already says. Each rung was re-verified against a verbatim in-state T1 quote and all five land inside their anchor (z3 May 1 vs UMN and NDSU "early May"; z4 Apr 20 vs SDSU "mid-April through June"; z5 Apr 10 vs Iowa State "early spring (April)"; z6 Apr 1 vs UConn "early April to late May"; z7 Mar 20 vs Missouri G6405 "late March or early April"). RE-DERIVATION FROM FROST WAS TESTED AND REJECTED: the ladder steps 10-11 days per zone while zone frost steps 14-15, so a constant offset reproduces z3-z5 and breaks z6 (Mar 18 against UConn early April) and z7 (Mar 1 against three sources saying late March or April). Crown timing is soil-thaw and nursery-shipping bound at the ends, not frost-bound, so the non-constant offset on this frost_anchored crop is DELIBERATE. Do not re-open on sourcing effort. The CITATION defects this hunt surfaced are a separate arc, filed below.

AGRONOMIC TENSION behind the crown windows: T1 sources split into two incompatible anchor camps roughly 4 to 6 weeks apart. The soil-workability camp (Illinois, Missouri, UConn, Arkansas) plants crowns BEFORE last frost ('as early as the soil can be worked'); the frost-safe camp (UMaine) plants AFTER ('after the danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed to above 50F'), on a Fusarium-in-cold-wet-soil rationale. These cannot both be encoded from one frost offset. Ruling 2026-07-26: soil-workability is primary (it is the dominant camp and matches dormant-crown practice); the UMaine caution is treated as a far-north refinement and shapes the later northern_tier z3/z4 windows. Revisit if a crown-rot finding contradicts it. AGRONOMIC FINDING 2026-07-27 that reversed this pass's working hypothesis. I instructed researchers to look for HEAT SHORTENING the harvest window. The opposite is true and is well sourced: warm long-season regions grant the LONGEST mature harvests. NMSU (southern New Mexico) is the only source permitting a first-year cut and allows 'a maximum of 10 weeks/year' from year four; California's mature figure is 8-10 weeks with four independent UC corroborations (UC IPM, Sacramento, Napa, Contra Costa); the northern tier runs 6-8 weeks and z3/z4 are capped nearer 6 by a stop DATE ('Do not harvest beyond June' -- NDSU; 'should not go beyond June 15' -- UMaine). What heat actually does per source: speeds spears so they need more frequent cutting, degrades tip quality within the window, and caps fern rebuilding above 85F -- but NO source converts that into an earlier stop date. In every T1 source the season ends on SPEAR DIAMETER, not a date: stop when spears thin below pencil width. That rule is already carried in both registers of `harvest_ready_*`.

SOURCING TRAP recorded 2026-07-27. This pass instructed researchers not to conflate commercial and home harvest windows. Santa Clara MG states the underlying gap outright: 'Harvest times are not included in this chart because they may vary widely depending on variety and season.' Most California county planting charts carry planting dates only.

TOOLING HAZARD, new class, recorded 2026-07-27. The lesson generalizes: any pass that changes a value must re-read the prose that describes it, and that check needs to be mechanical because doing it by memory fails even when the author is actively aware of the risk.
