succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sweet pea is largely a single-cohort crop, but a couple of successive sowings across the cool window (early plus late in the sowing season) stretch the cut-flower supply, since the plant is undone by heat rather than tired plantings. In mild-winter regions the two real windows are fall and late winter; in cold regions, one early-spring sowing (optionally split by a few weeks) is the practical maximum before summer heat closes the season.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You can sow sweet peas a couple of times a few weeks apart during the cool planting window to spread out the flowers, but there is no long succession like lettuce, because summer heat ends them. In mild-winter areas, plant once in fall and again in late winter; in cold areas, one early-spring sowing is usually it.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Realized sowings are few and clustered in the cool shoulders: sweet pea flowers on a concentrated spring or winter-to-spring run and is ended by heat, so successive sowings extend cutting modestly rather than delivering many staggered crops.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Sweet pea is harvested as a cut flower, not a food. Cut stems in the cool of the morning when the lowest one or two florets on the stem have just opened and the upper buds still show color; stems are typically 10 to 14 in long. Plunge them straight into water and expect a vase life of about 5 days. Cut daily at peak: frequent cutting, plus removing any seed pods, is what keeps the plant producing. Every part is inedible and the seeds and pods are poisonous, so this is a vase crop only.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Sweet peas are picked for their flowers and scent, not to eat. Cut the stems in the morning when the bottom one or two flowers on the stem have just opened. They last about 5 days in a vase. The more you cut, the more the plant blooms, so pick often and pull off any seed pods you find. Never eat any part of the plant: the seeds and pods are poisonous.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-7 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled) -- FINAL WAVE. companion_and_ornamental_flower (Lathyrus odoratus, annual climber, Fabaceae). SAFETY WATCH-ITEM EXEMPLARY -- the toxic-seed handling is the best in the batch: 'seeds and pods are poisonous / no part is edible / ornamental only / vase crop only', explicitly distinguished from the edible garden pea (Pisum sativum), saved seed 'labeled and kept away from food and children', all NCSU-anchored; it even turns the toxicity into an honest safety-driven companion rule (keep sweet peas away from edible peas to avoid a dangerous harvest mix-up). Agronomy/pests/diseases verified vs NCSU/UC IPM/Cornell (climbing support, deadhead-to-prolong-bloom, cool-season, powdery+downy mildew, aphid/thrips virus vectors). FIXES (minor): softened the beginner 'they actually like a touch of lime' -> 'tolerate a touch of lime' (the pH range 6.5-7.5 sits within NCSU's stated 6-8); de-named the unverified anthracnose binomial 'Glomerella cingulata' -> 'Anthracnose'. Spacing 3-6in (vs Cornell ~8in) kept as legit intensive cut-flower spacing. Reviewed by agent + main-loop self-verify of the toxicity section (the agent's WebFetch was network-blocked; verified via search).

open_findings.summary: Regional planting/harvest windows and the fall-vs-early-spring sowing split are MODELED from sweet pea's documented cool-season biology (NC State: cool-weather annual, challenging in hot humid summers; UC IPM: in warm-winter areas plant early for early spring bloom; Cornell: sow mid-late March in Zone 5, thrives cool, seedlings tolerate cold) plus each region's frost climatology (frost dates carried from the certified frost-anchored roster). The catalogued T1 sweet-pea pages do not publish region-by-region dated planting charts, so exact months are a climate-informed model to tighten at variety-pass.

The summer heat_pause months in every warm region are HAND-AUTHORED, not carried from nasturtium (which is warm-season and paused far less). The THERMAL FACT is sourced (sweet pea is cool-season and declines rapidly in heat: NC State, UC IPM). The precise per-region heat_pause months (e.g. desert Apr-Sep, se_gulf/ca_interior May-Sep, FL May-Oct, south-coast Jun-Sep, warm northern zones Jul-Aug) are MODELED on that documented cool-preference plus each region's summer climate and the certified cool-season peer lettuce-leaf's heat_pause pattern; no T1 sweet-pea page publishes dated summer-exclusion tables. Note the deliberate boundary: the cool CA north coast carries only a light late-summer (Aug-Sep) decline, and cold northern zones 3-5 carry NO heat_pause at all (cool summers let bloom run to frost).

pH preferred 6.5 to 7.5 (tolerated 6.0 to 7.8, neutral to slightly alkaline, lime-responsive) reflects widely stated horticultural consensus and NC State's high-organic-matter soil guidance, but none of the four catalogued T1 pages I read stated an explicit numeric pH range for sweet pea; the range is modeled and cited to the nearest source (NC State soil). Confirm against a pH-stating extension source at variety-pass.

days_to_maturity 65 to 100 (mid 85) as days from sowing to first bloom, germination_temp_f 55 to 65, germination 10 to 21 days, and spacing 3 to 6 in are representative values: Cornell gives germination near 60 F in 10 to 21 days, 2 to 4 plants per foot on a trellis, and a mid-late-March sowing blooming mid-late June in Zone 5 (roughly 12 to 14 weeks); NC State gives bloom May-July. No single T1 page prints one days-to-bloom figure, so the range is synthesized from these and flagged. [CORRECTION 2026-10-02: spacing_inches is 5-6 in, the thin-to figure, since PLA-10 promote 1 (3-6 in was a representative value); no row figure is authored, row_spacing_reason not_authored -- see PLA-10 promote 1, d021116.]

hawaii_tropical is lowest-confidence: sweet pea is a cool-season plant that is genuinely marginal in the tropical lowlands and is best at cooler elevations or in the coolest winter months. The single z11 cell is modeled as a late-fall-sown winter attempt with a long warm-month heat_pause (Apr-Oct), cited to NC State and UC IPM cool-season/heat-decline guidance rather than a Hawaii-specific sweet-pea calendar. Confirm or drop in review.

In cold zones 6-7 within the northern tier, the single spring cohort is modeled as ending with a midsummer heat_pause (Jul-Aug) rather than resuming (sweet pea cannot be re-sown for a fall bloom in a short season), while cooler zones 3-5 carry continuous cool-summer bloom to frost with no heat_pause. This split, and the succession_policy (suitable but with a low realized count clustered in the cool shoulders, since heat and not plant age ends the crop), are modeled judgment calls consistent with the cool-season peer and sweet pea's single-flush biology.

mid_atlantic z7/z8 windows are the declared Peas-garden ANALOG. vce_426_331 (Virginia's Home Garden Vegetable Planting Guide, read in full 2026-08-10) contains 0 occurrences of 'sweet pea' and 0 of 'Lathyrus'; the set-out window is its Pisum sativum 'Peas, garden' row (z7a Mar 1 - Apr 1; z8a Feb 20 - Apr 1) applied to this ornamental as the belt's cool-season pea-timing analog, exactly as the cell notes have always declared. start_indoors applies the crop's own weeks_indoors=6, and harvest is start_indoors + 85 days -- the crop's own certified mid days-to-bloom (sweet-pea_pilot_finding_004) -- so the values are internally coherent with the certified biology and with the crop-wide modeled-windows declaration (sweet-pea_pilot_finding_001). Two claims ARE document-true: the zone frost table (Table 1, zone-scoped) and 'no fall sowing listed' for garden peas. ncsu_ext (Lathyrus odoratus Plant Toolbox, cached, right taxon) added 2026-08-10 to carry the biology claims (cool-season annual, frost-tolerant seedlings, toxic seed). Absence scoped to the documents read 2026-08-10.

crops.deadheading_seasoned: For sweet pea, cutting and deadheading are the same job and the single biggest lever on bloom length. Harvest flowers for the vase while the lowest one or two blooms on a stem are just opening, and remove any developing seed pods promptly: once the plant sets seed it reads the season as finished and stops flowering. Keep every stem picked and no pods maturing, and a healthy plant flowers for weeks longer before summer heat ends it. Leave a few pods to ripen and dry only if you deliberately want to save seed at the end of the season.
crops.deadheading_beginner: With sweet peas, picking the flowers is how you keep them blooming. Cut stems often for the vase, and snip off any little seed pods you see forming. If the plant is allowed to make seeds, it thinks its job is done and quits flowering. So the trick is simple: keep cutting the flowers and never let pods develop, and the plant keeps making more blooms until summer heat stops it. Only leave a few pods to dry at the very end if you want to collect seeds for next year.

3.planting_note: Sweet pea is a cool-season flower here: start seed indoors about 6 weeks early or direct-sow as soon as the soil is workable, since the young plants tolerate frost. Give a 5 to 6 ft trellis, keep the rich soil evenly moist, feed moderately, and pinch seedlings to branch. Cut flowers often and remove pods; bloom runs through the cool summer, ending with heat or the first hard frost.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: July and August are a summer heat gap: sweet pea is a cool-season annual that stops flowering and yellows once sustained warmth arrives, and in these warmer northern zones midsummer heat ends the single spring cohort (no second crop is sown before winter). Not a frost gap but a summer heat exclusion. (NC State Extension; UC IPM)

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the northern tier, sweet pea thrives in the cool climate. Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before setting out, or direct-sow as soon as the ground is workable in early spring, since the young plants tolerate frost; a 5 to 6 ft trellis, deep rich soil, and steady moisture do the rest. Plants flower through the cool summer and, in the coolest zones, well into fall, ending with heat or the first hard frost. Grow it lean on nitrogen, cut constantly, and remove pods to keep bloom coming. Keep it away from edible peas, and remember the seeds and pods are poisonous.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Sweet peas love the cool weather of the northern tier. Start seeds indoors about six weeks early, or plant them right in the ground as soon as it can be worked in spring, because young plants handle frost. Give them a 5 to 6 ft trellis, rich soil, and steady water. They bloom through the cooler summer, ending at the first hard frost. Cut flowers often and pull off seed pods to keep more coming. Do not plant them near your edible peas, and remember the seeds and pods are poisonous.

Feed lightly on nitrogen, cut constantly, and remove pods to keep bloom coming. Watch for aphids, thrips, and powdery mildew in damp weather.

nevada.plantings_provenance: Structural donor: sweet-pea's own low_desert_az and warm_arid analog cells, both of which model this crop as a SINGLE fall-through-spring bloom window (no real winter cold_pause; the plant tolerates the mild desert winter and keeps flowering) rather than a spring-plus-fall two-cycle shape. nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Mojave high desert grows sweet pea on one fall-sown cycle, not a two-window crop: sow from October into mid-November into deep, rich, well-drained soil, and cut fragrant stems from December through spring with no real winter dormancy, since the region's light frost does not stop this hardy vine. The summer heat wall, roughly May through September, excludes it entirely, per the University of Nevada, Reno Cooperative Extension's Southern Nevada seasonal framework (Fact Sheet FS-02-61); there is no fall replant. Keep soil evenly moist, mulch to cool the roots, and keep it away from edible peas; the seeds and pods are poisonous.

pet_safe.note: The seeds and pods are poisonous and can cause lathyrism; the ASPCA lists sweet pea as toxic to horses, so keep seedpods away from pets.

crops.name: Radish Microgreens
crops.sunlight: bright indirect light or a grow light
crops.water: keep the medium evenly moist; mist during blackout, then bottom-water once greened to keep leaves dry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: A fine, moisture-holding soilless medium: seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a hydroponic fiber mat. Radish is a large brassica seed, so a firm even surface it can press into gives the most uniform stand.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Use a fine, soil-free growing medium that holds moisture well, such as seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat. Radish seed is large and sprouts strongly, so it does well on any of these.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Peat-based mixes and inert mats both work; the choice trades water-holding against a cleaner cut, and radish is forgiving on either.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both peat-based mixes and fiber mats work well. Mixes hold more water, while mats stay cleaner at harvest, so pick whichever suits you.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Garden soil and heavy potting mixes are too coarse and carry pathogen and pest risk for a raw, densely sown crop.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Skip garden soil and regular potting mix. They are too coarse, and they can carry pests and germs that are risky for a crowded crop you eat raw.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Use a light seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat made for microgreens. Do not use garden soil.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: A clean, fine, moisture-retentive soilless medium gives even germination and a clean cut; coir and fiber mats keep grit off the harvest.

ph.note_seasoned: pH is not a practical lever for a single short indoor radish cycle on a soilless medium; standard seed-starting mixes and coir sit in a workable range and need no adjustment.
ph.note_beginner: You do not need to worry about soil pH for radish microgreens. The mixes and mats sold for microgreens are already fine as is.

fertilizer.timing: not applicable
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Radish microgreens are cut long before they exhaust the seed's own reserves, so no fertilizer is needed for a single cycle on an inert medium or seed-starting mix. Added nutrients mainly raise the risk of algae and off-flavors.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: You do not need to feed radish microgreens. The seed carries enough food to reach harvest, and adding fertilizer just invites algae and odd flavors.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: None.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: None needed.

companions.note_seasoned: Not applicable. Radish microgreens are grown as a dense single-type indoor tray, so there is no interplanting or companion relationship. Grow the tray on its own and combine with other greens after harvest.
companions.note_beginner: Not applicable. Radish microgreens grow as one type per tray indoors, so there are no companion plants. If you want a mix, just combine trays after cutting.

pests.description_seasoned: Small dark flies whose larvae live in persistently wet medium and feed on organic matter and tender roots. They are the main indoor microgreen pest and a symptom of an over-wet tray rather than a primary threat; radish's short, vigorous cycle usually finishes before they build up.
pests.description_beginner: Tiny dark flies that show up around constantly damp medium. Their larvae live in the wet mix. They are the main bug you might see, and they usually mean the tray is staying too wet. Radish grows so fast you often cut before they matter.
pests.management_seasoned: Let the surface dry between waterings where the crop allows, bottom-water, and keep airflow up. Because the radish cycle is so short, most trays are harvested before gnats become a real problem; sanitized trays and fresh medium between cycles break the cycle.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the surface from staying soaking wet, water from the bottom, and keep air moving. Since radish microgreens are harvested so fast, gnats rarely get bad before you cut. Clean trays and fresh mix between batches keep them away.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water from underneath, by adding water to the tray below rather than pouring over the top, and let the surface dry back a little between drinks instead of leaving it soaking. The larvae, the small grub stage that does the feeding, live down in mix that stays wet around the clock, so a surface that dries gives them less to settle into. Keep a little air moving over the tray too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The larval stage depends on medium that is held damp without interruption, so the control is to deny it that: irrigate from below and give the top layer a chance to firm up before the next drink. Air moving over the stand pushes the same direction. Radish also turns a tray over quickly, and a good share of trays are cut before numbers amount to much.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Wash out your trays and start each batch with fresh mix. Old mix and dirty trays are how gnats carry over from one batch into the next, so a clean start holds their numbers down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cleaned trays and fresh medium at each turnaround cut the carryover that would otherwise let a resident population establish across batches.

diseases.description_seasoned: Soil-borne fungi (Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others) rot seedlings at the base under wet, crowded, still conditions, often alongside fuzzy white or gray surface mold favored by warm, humid air. Radish is one of the least trouble-prone microgreens, so this shows up mainly when a tray is overwatered or sown too thickly.
diseases.description_beginner: In wet, crowded, stuffy conditions, tiny fungi rot the baby plants at the base, and you often see fuzzy white or gray mold too. Radish is one of the easiest, least problem-prone microgreens, so this usually only happens if the tray is too wet or sown too thickly.
diseases.management_seasoned: Prevention is the whole game: wrung-sponge moisture, bottom-watering once greened, constant gentle airflow, a sensible seeding rate, and sanitized trays between cycles. There is no rescue spray for a raw cut crop; a badly affected tray is composted and restarted clean. Note that radish's abundant fine white root hairs are often mistaken for mold; a light mist flattens root hairs and they rebound as they dry, while mold stays matted and spreads.
diseases.management_beginner: You cannot spray this away on a crop you eat raw, so the fix is prevention: keep the mix just damp (not soggy), water from the bottom once the leaves are up, keep a small fan running, do not sow too thickly, and clean trays between batches. One radish quirk: the fine white fuzz at the base is usually harmless root hairs, not mold. A quick mist flattens root hairs, while real mold stays matted and smells musty.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sow thinly enough that the stand is not packed shoulder to shoulder. Damping-off, the rot that collapses seedlings right at the base, gets its opening in a crowded tray, where moisture sits and the air between stems goes still. Radish is one of the less trouble-prone microgreens, so a restrained sowing rate carries a lot of the load.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sowing density sets the microclimate at the base of the stand. Packed too tightly, it holds free moisture and stalls air movement between stems, which is the combination Rhizoctonia, Botrytis and their relatives work in. Radish sits at the easier end of the microgreen range, so rate is usually the lever that matters most here.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the mix about as damp as a sponge you have wrung out, moist but not soggy, and once the leaves are up add water to the tray underneath instead of over the top. A surface that stays wet is the usual trigger.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hold the medium at wrung-out-sponge dampness while the seed is germinating, then switch to watering from beneath once the stand greens up, keeping free water off the stem bases where the rot takes hold.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Set a small fan to blow gently across the tray and leave it running, rather than airing the tray out now and then. Moving air dries the surface and the stems between waterings, which works against both the rot at the base and the fuzzy growth that shows up on top of the mix.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Continuous low-velocity air, not intermittent venting, shortens the wet period on the medium surface and on the stems, acting on the base rot and on the warm, humid surface mold in one move.

control_ladder.note_beginner: You cannot spray your way out of this on greens cut young and eaten raw, so the cleaning steps are what you have. Sanitize trays between batches, and if a tray goes heavily moldy, put it in the compost and begin again with clean equipment instead of trying to rescue it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: With no rescue treatment available on a raw cut crop, sanitation between cycles is the step that carries. A tray well into collapse goes to the compost and the batch restarts in clean equipment rather than being nursed along.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist once or twice daily through germination and the brief blackout to hold even surface moisture; once greened, bottom-water as the tray dries.
watering.frequency_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, lightly mist the surface once or twice a day so it stays damp. After you move the tray into the light, water from the bottom whenever it starts to dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated; pour off any standing water after bottom-watering.
watering.amount_beginner: Just enough to keep the medium damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy. After bottom-watering, tip out any water left sitting in the tray.
watering.method_seasoned: Mist during germination and blackout; switch to bottom-watering once the canopy is up so foliage stays dry.
watering.method_beginner: Mist the top while the seeds are sprouting, then water from the bottom once the leaves are up so the leaves stay dry.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Standing water, a sour smell, fuzzy matted growth on the medium or stems, and collapsed seedlings all signal overwatering and the damping-off that follows it.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Water sitting in the tray, a bad smell, fuzzy matted mold, or seedlings flopping over mean it is too wet. Cut back on water and improve airflow.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Curling, limp cotyledons and a medium that has pulled away from the tray edges indicate the canopy has dried too far between waterings.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Limp, curling leaves and medium that has shrunk away from the sides mean it got too dry. Water from the bottom right away.

schedule_by_stage.rate: wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Sow the radish seed evenly and mist to moisten; keep the medium at wrung-sponge damp, never saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Scatter the radish seed evenly and mist to dampen. Keep the mix damp like a wrung-out sponge, not soggy.

schedule_by_stage.rate: wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Mist the surface once or twice daily through germination to hold even moisture; keep the medium at wrung-sponge damp, never saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Lightly mist the surface once or twice a day while the seeds sprout so it stays damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy.

schedule_by_stage.rate: wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Radish takes only a brief blackout, so mist to hold moisture through the short dark period and pour off any standing water.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Radish only needs a short time in the dark, so mist to keep it damp and never let water pool in the tray.

schedule_by_stage.rate: wrung-sponge moisture, pour off standing water
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window: the canopy is dense and humid and a single overwatering here can seed damping-off across the whole tray. Switch to bottom-watering so foliage stays dry, pour off any standing water, and keep a gentle fan going.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: The riskiest moment is uncovering the tray into the light: the plants are crowded and damp, so do not overwater. Water from the bottom now so the leaves stay dry, tip out any standing water, and keep a gentle fan going.

schedule_by_stage.rate: wrung-sponge moisture until cut
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Bottom-water as the tray dries right up to the single cut, keeping the foliage dry and the air moving so the dense canopy does not mold in its last days.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering from the bottom as the tray dries until you cut, keeping the leaves dry and a fan going so the crowded canopy does not mold at the end.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Wet foliage in a dense, still canopy is the main driver of mold and damping-off, so the cycle moves deliberately from misting to bottom-watering and pairs it with constant gentle airflow.
watering.method_note_beginner: Wet leaves packed close together with no air movement is what causes mold. That is why you switch to watering from the bottom once the leaves are up, and keep a gentle fan going.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window: the canopy is dense, humidity under the cover is high, and a single overwatering here can seed damping-off across the whole tray.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The riskiest time is right when you uncover the tray and move it into the light. The plants are crowded and damp, so do not overwater, and make sure air is moving.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Do not hold cut radish microgreens at room temperature; they wilt and spoil within hours. Refrigerate immediately after cutting.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut radish microgreens out on the counter. They go limp fast, so put them in the fridge right after cutting.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate dry in a vented container lined with a paper towel. Radish is one of the sturdier types and often holds close to 2 weeks, longer than tender greens that keep about 5 to 7 days. Do not wash before storing; surface moisture shortens shelf life.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep cut radish microgreens in the fridge in a container with a paper towel to soak up extra moisture. Radish is one of the longer-keeping types and can last close to 2 weeks. Do not wash them before storing, since extra water makes them spoil faster.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not recommended. Freezing collapses the delicate cells and ruins the texture. Radish microgreens are a fresh, cut-and-eat crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze radish microgreens. Freezing turns them mushy. They are meant to be eaten fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cut clean and dry: harvest with sanitized scissors into a clean container, keep the foliage dry, and chill promptly. Because they are eaten raw, extension food-safety guidance is not to wash them after harvest, since post-harvest washing can bruise tissue and invite contamination; the same clean-tool, clean-surface rules that govern growing govern handling.
storage.notes_beginner: Because you eat radish microgreens raw, keep everything clean: cut them with clean scissors into a clean, dry container and refrigerate right away. It is better not to rinse them after cutting, since washing bruises them and makes them spoil faster.

recommended.name: Daikon
recommended.note: White stems, green leaves; peppery with a strong radish bite. Fast and vigorous; no presoak.

recommended.name: China Rose
recommended.note: Bright pink stems; milder, slightly sweet spice. Popular for color; no presoak.

recommended.name: Rambo
recommended.note: Deep purple stems and leaves; mildly spicy. Grown mostly for its color; no presoak.

recommended.name: Sango
recommended.note: Purple-stemmed type similar to Rambo; peppery and colorful. No presoak.

recommended.name: Red Arrow
recommended.note: Bright pink stems, light green leaves; fast and flavorful. No presoak.

varieties.note_seasoned: Radish is among the fastest, most vigorous, and most beginner-proof microgreens: the large seed germinates strongly with no presoak, needs only a short blackout, and finishes in roughly a week. The signature flavor is the peppery, pungent bite radish is known for, and it is described in extension trials as nutty and spicy. Named types differ mostly in stem color rather than growing method: white-stemmed Daikon runs strongest in spice, pink-stemmed China Rose and Red Arrow are milder and colorful, and purple Rambo or Sango are grown chiefly for their deep color. All are handled identically. Never grow microgreens from solanaceous seed (tomato, pepper, eggplant), whose seedlings carry alkaloids and are not safe to eat raw.
varieties.note_beginner: Radish is one of the easiest and fastest microgreens to grow, which makes it a great first crop. The big seeds sprout strongly without soaking, need only a couple of dark days, and are usually ready in about a week. They taste peppery, like a spicy radish. The named kinds mostly just differ in color: Daikon has white stems and the most bite, China Rose and Red Arrow have pink stems and milder flavor, and Rambo and Sango have striking purple stems. You grow them all the same way. One safety rule for any microgreen: never grow them from tomato, pepper, or eggplant seed, as those baby plants are not safe to eat.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Radish microgreens are never moved outdoors or transplanted; the whole cycle is indoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. Radish microgreens stay indoors from seed to harvest, so there is no hardening off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow densely and evenly across pre-moistened medium, roughly 40 grams of seed per standard 1020 tray. Radish is a large brassica seed that germinates strongly, so it needs no presoak: sow it dry. Do not bury the seed; press it into firm contact, then cover for a short blackout of about 1 to 3 days under a light weight. Even seed-to-medium contact is what gives a uniform stand and a clean single cut.
start_method.notes_beginner: Scatter the seeds thickly and evenly over damp growing medium, about 40 grams for a standard tray. Radish seed is large and sprouts easily, so you do not need to soak it first; just sow it dry. Do not bury the seeds, press them down so they touch the surface, then cover the tray to keep it dark for a day to a few days.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Nest the drilled tray inside a solid, hole-free tray. The outer tray catches runoff, lets you bottom-water, and is poured off so the crop never sits in standing water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Set the tray with holes inside a second solid tray with no holes. The bottom tray lets you water from below and catch extra water, which you then pour out so the roots are not sitting in water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a microgreen growing mat.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: None needed.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Seed-starting mix, coir, or an inert fiber mat; about 1 to 2 inches deep.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: None; the medium is a substrate, not a nutrient source, for a single cycle.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water from the bottom by setting the tray in a little water, then pour off what is left.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: No fertilizer needed.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Radish microgreens are an indoor year-round cycle crop, harvested in days, with no dormant or overwintered phase.
overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Radish microgreens grow indoors all year and are harvested within a couple of weeks, so there is nothing to overwinter.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: The tray is the entire growing system: shallow, drained, nested over a solid tray for bottom-watering, sanitized between cycles. A clean, reused, food-grade tray beats a single-use clamshell for both food safety and consistent results.
container_notes.notes_beginner: For radish microgreens, the tray is the whole setup. Use a shallow tray with drainage holes sitting inside a solid tray so you can water from the bottom. Wash and sanitize trays between batches.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Bottom-water from the nesting tray; never leave the tray standing in water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: None for a single cycle.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering reservoirs keep the medium too wet for a dense raw crop and raise the damping-off risk; bottom-water by hand and pour off the excess instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for microgreens. They keep things too wet, which causes mold. Water from the bottom by hand and tip out the extra.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A shallow flat tray works best: a 1020-style tray or any shallow food-safe container, with about 1 to 2 inches of medium. Depth beyond that wastes mix without helping a crop that is cut in days.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a shallow, wide tray, like a standard 1020 tray or any clean food-safe container. About 1 to 2 inches of growing mix is plenty. You do not need anything deep.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable. Radish microgreens grow on fresh or sanitized medium each cycle with no soil-borne carryover, so crop rotation does not apply.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Not applicable. You use fresh growing medium and clean trays each time, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Sanitation between cycles, not rotation, is the disease control for radish microgreens: compost the spent medium, then wash and sanitize the tray before the next sow.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating crops, just keep things clean: toss the used medium and wash and sanitize the tray before starting again.

growth_stages.name: Sow
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Scatter radish seed thickly and evenly across a tray of pre-moistened mix. Radish seed is large and vigorous, so use a generous amount, roughly 40 grams (about a quarter cup) per standard 10 by 20 inch tray, in a dense single layer. No soaking needed; just mist the surface to settle the seed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Big, round seeds spread in a thick, even layer across the whole surface, over evenly damp mix with no pooling water.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Tray sown and misted?
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dry-broadcast large radish seed densely on pre-moistened medium, roughly 40 g per 1020 tray, in a single even layer. No presoak; mist to settle. Surface-sow.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dense, even layer of large seed with no gaps on moist medium.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Tray sown?

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cover the tray to keep it dark and humid, with a lightly weighted empty tray on top to root the seeds down evenly. Keep it warm, around 70 to 75°F. Radish is one of the easiest microgreens, germinating strongly and evenly, so expect quick action. Mist only if the surface dries.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The big seeds swelling, splitting, and pushing out thick white roots, then sturdy pale stems that lift the cover, usually all at once.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any sprouts pushing up already?
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Weighted blackout cover at 70-75°F. Large radish seed imbibes and splits fast, with strong, even germination. Mist only to prevent surface drying.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid, uniform imbibition; thick radicles and blanched stems lifting the cover.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Germination underway?

growth_stages.name: Blackout
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the tray covered in the dark for a short stretch, about one to three days after sprouting. Radish stretches fast, so it needs less dark time than most. This brief dark period evens out the stand before light. Keep misting lightly if the surface dries.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A thick mat of pale, stretched stems standing tall and lifting the cover. They will be white or pale pink, not green yet.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Stems tall and even under there?
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold blackout about 1 to 3 days; radish elongates quickly and needs a shorter dark period than slower crops. Mist to maintain surface moisture.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Uniformly elongated, blanched (often pink-tinged) stems lifting the cover.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Stand evened up under blackout?

growth_stages.name: Light
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Uncover the tray and move it into bright light, about 18 hours a day, at a comfortable 68 to 72°F. The pale stems green up fast, and many varieties keep a pretty pink or purple tint on the stems. Water from the bottom now instead of misting the leaves to keep the canopy dry.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Seed leaves turning bright green within a day, often over pink or purple stems, and the tray taking on a sharp, spicy smell.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Greening up, with pink stems showing?
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Uncover into about 18 hours of light at 68-72°F. Cotyledons green rapidly; stems often retain pink or purple pigment. Bottom-water to keep the canopy dry.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid greening of cotyledons over pigmented stems; pungent aroma develops.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Cotyledons greened up?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Harvest when the seed leaves are open and green, usually about a week after sowing. Gather a handful and cut just above the soil line with clean scissors. Radish microgreens pack a spicy, peppery kick; eat them fresh, and remember they do not regrow, so cut the whole tray.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Open green seed leaves about one to two inches tall, on colorful stems, with a bold peppery bite when you taste one.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Time to snip that spice? Log your harvest.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Single-cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, often about 7 days. Cut just above the medium with clean scissors, rinse, and use fresh. Pungent flavor. No regrowth; harvest the full tray.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cotyledons open at 1-2 in on pigmented stems; sharp, peppery flavor.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First cut? Log your harvest.

notifications.message_seasoned: Check whether the canopy has lifted. Radish blackout is short, so it may already be time to uncover into light.
notifications.message_beginner: Time to check your tray: if the sprouts are up, uncover it and give it light.

notifications.message_seasoned: Switch from misting to bottom-watering now that the canopy is up, and make sure a fan is running.
notifications.message_beginner: Now that the leaves are up, water from the bottom and keep a fan going.

notifications.message_seasoned: Radish is usually at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage now, so cut and refrigerate promptly.
notifications.message_beginner: Your radish microgreens are likely ready to snip. Cut them and put them in the fridge.

notifications.message_seasoned: Start your next tray to keep the staggered supply going.
notifications.message_beginner: Start a new tray so you always have microgreens coming.

sow.text_seasoned: Pre-moisten the medium to wrung-sponge feel, then broadcast radish seed densely and evenly, roughly 40 grams per 1020 tray. Radish needs no presoak; sow it dry. Press seed into contact but do not bury it; buried seed greens poorly and traps moisture against the stems.
sow.text_beginner: Dampen the growing medium so it feels like a wrung-out sponge, then scatter radish seeds thickly and evenly. No soaking needed. Press the seeds down so they touch the surface, but do not cover them with medium.

germination.text_seasoned: Cover the tray and keep it warm (about 70 to 75 °F) and dark. Mist to hold even surface moisture, never soggy. A light weight on the cover keeps the large seed in firm contact so roots drive down rather than lifting the seed. Radish germinates fast and vigorously.
germination.text_beginner: Put the cover on and keep the tray warm (around 70 to 75 °F) and dark. Mist lightly so the surface stays damp but not wet. A small weight on the cover helps the roots push down. Radish sprouts fast.

blackout.text_seasoned: Hold the weighted cover in the dark for the short blackout, about 1 to 3 days for radish, then uncover. The brief dark stretch lengthens and evens the stems before greening; radish rarely needs more than a couple of days.
blackout.text_beginner: Keep the covered tray in the dark for a short time, about 1 to 3 days for radish. The darkness makes the stems grow taller and more even before you give them light. Radish only needs a day or two.

light.text_seasoned: Uncover into 18 hours of bright light at about 68 to 72 °F and switch from misting to bottom-watering so foliage stays dry. Run a gentle fan; the dense canopy plus high humidity is the damping-off window. Harvest at cotyledon to first true leaf, often about a week from sowing.
light.text_beginner: Uncover the tray into bright light for about 18 hours a day at 68 to 72 °F, and start watering from the bottom so the leaves stay dry. Keep a gentle fan going to prevent mold. Cut when the first little leaves are open, usually about a week after planting.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Yield is measured per tray, not per plant: a well-sown 1020 tray of radish returns roughly 6 to 12 ounces of cut microgreens, and radish's vigor keeps a heavy sowing productive, though the 6-to-12-ounce figure is a modeled estimate at that density (Penn State's lighter-sown trial recorded about 4 ounces per tray).
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: You measure radish microgreens by the tray, not by each plant. A full tray usually gives you a few good handfuls (about 6 to 12 ounces), and radish is one of the more productive types.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Every tray is a single harvest at peak; continuous supply comes from staggered sowings, not from regrowth.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Each tray gives one harvest at its best. To keep a steady supply, start new trays every few days.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: There is no establishment year; the first tray performs the same as any later tray. Radish is forgiving, so even a first attempt usually succeeds.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: There is no waiting period with radish microgreens. Your very first tray works just like the rest, and radish is one of the easiest to get right on the first try.
factors_seasoned: seeding density (too sparse wastes the tray; too dense traps moisture and invites mold)
even moisture and the mist-to-bottom-water transition
constant gentle airflow
seed freshness (radish germinates strongly when fresh)
light intensity and the full 18-hour daily duration

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Not applicable. Radish microgreens are an indoor, light-controlled, seedling-stage crop with no lunar or seasonal timing.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Fuzzy, matted white or gray growth on the medium, stems, or seed; seedlings collapsing at the base
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Matted white or gray mold, or baby plants flopping over at the bottom
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Damping-off and mold from overwatering, a saturated medium, dense sowing, and poor airflow; radish is otherwise one of the least trouble-prone microgreens
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Too much water plus crowded plants and no air movement, which leads to mold. Radish rarely gets this unless the tray is too wet.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Switch to bottom-watering, pour off standing water, run a gentle fan, thin your seeding rate next time, and sanitize trays between cycles. Do not bury seed at sowing.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Water from the bottom, tip out extra water, keep a small fan going, sow a little less thickly next time, and clean your trays between batches.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Wrung-sponge moisture, constant airflow, dry foliage, and sanitized trays prevent it.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Keep the medium just damp, the air moving, the leaves dry, and the trays clean.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: A fine white fuzzy halo at the base of the stems, appearing a day or two after uncovering
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Fine white fuzz right where the stems meet the medium, showing up soon after uncovering
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Usually harmless root hairs, not mold: radish puts out abundant fine root hairs that ring the base of each stem. True mold sits on the medium or stems, smells musty, and does not vanish when misted
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Almost always root hairs, which are normal and healthy, not mold. Radish grows lots of tiny white root hairs around the base of the stems.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Do the mist test: a light misting flattens root hairs and they rebound as they dry, while mold stays matted and spreads. If it is truly mold, improve airflow and cut back water.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Spray a little water on it. Root hairs flatten and bounce back as they dry; real mold stays matted and smells bad. If it is mold, add airflow and water less.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Even moisture, airflow, and not over-sowing keep true mold away; root hairs need no action.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Keep airflow up and do not overwater. Root hairs are fine and need nothing.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tall, pale, weak stems that fall over
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Long, thin, pale stems that flop
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Too little light, or light introduced too late after a drawn-out blackout
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough light, or leaving the tray covered too long
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Uncover on time (radish blackout is short) and give bright light for the full 18 hours; move closer to the grow light or a brighter window.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Uncover the tray on schedule and give it bright light for about 18 hours a day, closer to the light.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: End the short blackout once the canopy lifts and provide adequate light intensity and duration.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Take the cover off as soon as the sprouts are up and give them plenty of light.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Patchy, uneven germination across the tray
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Some spots sprout, others stay bare
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Uneven sowing, dry spots, no weighted cover, or old seed; uncommon with fresh radish, which germinates strongly
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Seeds spread unevenly, dry spots, no weight on the cover, or old seed. Radish usually sprouts evenly when the seed is fresh.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Sow evenly on pre-moistened medium, use a weighted cover for even seed-to-medium contact, and use fresh radish seed.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Spread seeds evenly on damp medium, put a light weight on the cover, and use fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Even sow, even moisture, weighted blackout cover, fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Even seeds, even moisture, a weighted cover, and fresh seed.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: The cycle is sow -> blackout -> light -> harvest, and radish is among the fastest to run it. Germinate at about 70 to 75 °F under a weighted cover in the dark for a short blackout (about 1 to 3 days), uncover into 18 hours of light at about 68 to 72 °F to green up, then cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage. Most trays finish in about 7 to 12 days, often around a week.
indoor_cycle.tip_beginner: Radish microgreens follow four steps: plant, keep dark, give light, then harvest, and they are one of the fastest to grow. Keep the covered tray warm (around 70 to 75 °F) and dark for a day to a few days while the seeds sprout, then uncover it into bright light (about 68 to 72 °F) for roughly 18 hours a day until the leaves green up. Most are ready in about a week.

primary.name: Utah State University Extension -- Grow Your Own Microgreens
University of Nevada, Reno Extension -- Microgreens and Produce Safety (PubID 3468)

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: start a fresh tray every 3 to 5 days rather than one big tray at once. Radish's roughly one-week cycle makes it easy to keep a rolling supply going. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: To always have radish microgreens ready, start a new tray every few days instead of one big batch. Because they grow fast and indoors, you can keep this going all year.
succession_policy.notes: successions and max_successions_per_season are intentionally null: radish microgreens run continuously year-round indoors, so there is no season length to cap against. The practical limit is tray count and counter space, not climate (window_type: continuous_indoor).

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-5 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled). microgreen; the fastest/easiest (7-12 days, no presoak, verbatim USU). NUTRITION/HEALTH over-claim CLEAN (declines PSU's vitamin line). Sprout-vs-microgreen CLEAN. FIXES: fungus-gnat pest -> UC IPM pn7448; damping-off de-named 'Pythium' -> 'Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others' + trimmed to psu_microgreens; YIELD softened (Trevor-ruled) -- dropped the 'toward the higher end' superlative, reframed the 6-12oz as a modeled estimate at the heavy seeding density used here and DISCLOSED PSU's lighter-sown ~4oz trial (yield re-anchored to psu, usu dropped); solanaceous-seed alkaloid warning anchored to LSU AgCenter microgreens guide (Trevor ruled SOURCE it); storage dropped usu + added psu; UNR URL updated to naes.unr.edu/dfi.

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity / indoor_cycle.days_to_harvest [7,12] (mid 8): the ceiling of 12 and the 8-12 core are from usu_ext (radish 8 to 12 days); the 7-day floor reflects radish's reputation as among the fastest microgreens (PSU ABCs, read but uncatalogued, gives a 7 to 8 day very short cycle) and is grower-norm, modeled, not a single catalogued cited number.

The fine white root-hairs-versus-mold distinction (a fuzzy white halo at the stem base that a mist test tells apart from true mold) is horticultural common knowledge and grower guidance, not stated on a Tier-1 extension page; cited to the nearest Tier-1 mold/damping-off discussion (psu_microgreens, usu_ext). Framed as guidance, flagged as modeled.

Named cultivars (Daikon, China Rose, Rambo, Sango, Red Arrow) and their per-variety stem color / spice-intensity notes are seed-catalog norms, not drawn from a Tier-1 microgreen cultivar chart. Species-level flavor (peppery, pungent, described as nutty and spicy) and the no-presoak / fast-cycle handling ARE Tier-1 (usu_ext). Confirm cultivar details at variety-delta pass.

Harvest height (roughly at cotyledon to first-true-leaf; typical a few inches) is modeled from the general microgreen harvest stage; USU states harvest at first true leaves or sooner but gives no radish-specific height. Yield (6 to 12 oz per 1020 tray, radish toward the high end) uses the certified template's per-tray range plus radish vigor; OSU lists ~0.27 lb for daikon in one trial. Both modeled to sourced ranges.

germination_temp_f [65,75] is a modeled practical band: PSU Growing Microgreens gives 60 to 75 °F for germination and USU germinates at 74 °F; radish germinates strongly across a broad range, so the band is set slightly wider than the microgreens-mix [68,74] to reflect radish's forgiving germination. Blackout stated as 1 to 3 days where Tier-1 lists 1 to 2 for radish (the 3rd day is common grower practice for more stem stretch).

PSU 'The ABCs of Microgreens' (extension.psu.edu/the-abcs-of-microgreens), a real Tier-1 page read via WebFetch that corroborates radish's Brassicaceae identity and very short 7-8 day cycle, is NOT in the dataset source_catalog, so it is deliberately NOT cited (source-tier gate E requires catalogued T1 ids and the catalog is a top-level canonical key outside this record). All cited claims rest on catalogued sources (usu_ext, psu_microgreens, unr_ext). Admit psu_abcs to the catalog to upgrade the flavor/cycle citations.

field_additions.note: microgreen ladder-authored from-sow; fastest (DTM[7,12]~=harvest[7,12]). seed, from_sow. NO sow_depth/thin_to (spacing_inches==[]: dense broadcast, pressed to surface, single cut). NO harvest_window (stand does not regrow -- one-shot tray).

crops.description_seasoned: Radish microgreens are the young seedlings of the radish (Raphanus sativus), a brassica, harvested at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage roughly a week after sowing. They are among the fastest, most vigorous, and most beginner-proof microgreens: the large seed germinates strongly with no presoak, needs only a short dark blackout, and finishes in about 7 to 12 days. The flavor is a distinct peppery, pungent radish bite, and named types range from white-stemmed Daikon through pink China Rose and Red Arrow to deep-purple Rambo and Sango for color. They are grown indoors year-round in the same short cycle every time: a dense even sow on a shallow tray of mix or a fiber mat, a brief blackout to even the stand, then light to green up, then a single cut. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the tray grows identically on any windowsill.
crops.description_beginner: Radish microgreens are baby radish plants that you harvest very young, about a week after planting, when they are just a couple of inches tall. They are one of the easiest and fastest microgreens to grow, which makes them a great first crop: the big seeds sprout strongly without any soaking, need only a day or two in the dark, and are usually ready in about 7 to 12 days. They taste peppery, like a spicy radish, and different kinds have white, pink, or purple stems. You grow them indoors all year with the same steps every time: scatter seeds thickly, cover the tray to keep it dark for a couple of days while they sprout, move it into the light to green up, then snip and eat. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so they grow the same way no matter where you live.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, typically about 7 to 12 days from sowing and often around a week, since radish is one of the fastest microgreens. Snip just above the medium with clean scissors; the stand will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your radish microgreens are ready when the first little seed-leaves are open and the first true leaf is just showing, usually about a week after sowing (radish is fast). Snip them just above the medium with clean scissors and eat them fresh. They do not grow back, so you start a new tray each time.

crops.name: Broccoli Microgreens
crops.sunlight: bright indirect light or a grow light
crops.water: keep the medium evenly moist; bottom-water once greened to keep leaves dry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: A fine, moisture-holding soilless medium: a clean seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a hydroponic fiber mat (hemp, jute, or similar). Broccoli's small seed sits on the surface, so an even, fine texture gives uniform germination and a clean cut.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Use a fine, soil-free growing medium that holds moisture, such as seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat made for microgreens. A smooth, even surface helps the tiny broccoli seeds sprout evenly.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Peat-based mixes and inert mats both work for broccoli; the choice trades water-holding against a cleaner harvest.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both peat-based mixes and fiber mats work well. Mixes hold more water, while mats stay cleaner at harvest, so pick whichever suits you.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Garden soil and heavy potting mixes are too coarse for a small seed and carry pathogen and pest risk for a dense crop eaten raw.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Skip garden soil and regular potting mix. They are too coarse for tiny broccoli seed, and they can carry pests and germs that are risky for a crowded crop you eat raw.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Use a light seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a microgreen growing mat. Do not use garden soil.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: A clean, fine, moisture-retentive soilless medium gives broccoli even germination and a clean cut; coir and fiber mats keep grit off the harvest.

ph.note_seasoned: pH is not a practical lever for a single short indoor cycle on a soilless medium; standard seed-starting mixes and coir sit in a workable range and need no adjustment for broccoli.
ph.note_beginner: You do not need to worry about soil pH for broccoli microgreens. The mixes and mats sold for microgreens are already fine as is.

fertilizer.timing: not applicable
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Broccoli microgreens are cut in about 8 to 12 days, well before they exhaust the seed's own reserves, so no fertilizer is needed for a single cycle on an inert medium or seed-starting mix. Little or no feeding is the norm; clear water grows a good tray, and added nutrients mainly raise the risk of algae and off-flavors.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: You do not need to feed broccoli microgreens. The seed carries enough food to reach harvest in a week or two, and adding fertilizer just invites algae and odd flavors. Plain water is all they need.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: None.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: None needed.

companions.note_seasoned: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens are grown as a dense single-type indoor tray, so there is no interplanting or companion relationship. Grow the tray on its own and combine with other cut microgreens after harvest if you want a mix.
companions.note_beginner: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens grow as one type per tray indoors, so there are no companion plants. If you want a blend, just combine different trays after cutting.

pests.description_seasoned: Small dark flies whose larvae live in persistently wet medium and feed on organic matter and tender roots. On a broccoli tray they are a symptom of an over-wet medium rather than a primary threat, and the short cycle usually beats them.
pests.description_beginner: Tiny dark flies that show up around constantly damp medium. Their larvae live in the wet mix. They usually just mean the tray is staying too wet.
pests.management_seasoned: Let the surface dry between waterings where the crop allows, bottom-water, and keep airflow up. Because broccoli finishes in about 8 to 12 days, most trays are cut before gnats build to a real problem; sanitized trays and fresh medium between cycles break the cycle.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the surface from staying soaking wet, water from the bottom, and keep air moving. Since broccoli microgreens are harvested so fast, gnats rarely get bad before you cut. Clean trays and fresh mix between batches keep them away.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Tiny dark flies hanging around the tray usually tell you the mix is sitting far too wet. Put water in from underneath so the tray draws it up and the top can dry out between waterings, since the young gnats, called larvae, live down in the sodden part of the mix. A gentle breeze across the tray helps as well.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Dry the surface between waterings as far as the crop tolerates and sub-irrigate instead of top-watering; the persistently wet medium is the driver, not the adult fly. Hold airflow up, and note that at roughly 8 to 12 days to cut, most broccoli trays finish before gnats build to anything that matters.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Wash and sanitize your trays between batches and start each one with fresh mix, so the next tray does not inherit the problem from the last.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sanitized trays and fresh medium each cycle break the breeding cycle rather than treat an active one, which is the approach a crop this short leaves you.

diseases.description_seasoned: Soil-borne fungi and water molds (Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium) rot seedlings at the base under wet, crowded, still conditions, often alongside fuzzy white cobweb-like growth on the medium and stems. Broccoli is a small, densely sown brassica and is notably prone to it; on Penn State's trials damping-off was the only disease or pest issue encountered.
diseases.description_beginner: The most common broccoli microgreen problem. In wet, crowded, stuffy conditions, tiny fungi rot the baby plants right at the base, and you often see fuzzy white mold on the surface and stems too. Broccoli is packed in tightly, so it is especially prone to this.
diseases.management_seasoned: Prevention is the whole game: wrung-sponge moisture, bottom-watering (sub-irrigation keeps foliage dry), constant gentle airflow from a small fan, a sensible seeding rate, and sanitized trays with fresh medium between cycles. There is no rescue spray for a raw cut crop; a badly affected tray is composted and restarted clean.
diseases.management_beginner: You cannot spray this away on a crop you eat raw, so the fix is prevention: keep the mix just damp (not soggy), water from the bottom so the leaves stay dry, keep a small fan running, do not sow too thickly, and use clean trays and fresh mix each batch. If a tray molds badly, toss it and start over with clean equipment.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sow thinner than feels natural. Broccoli seed goes down dense, and a packed stand traps moisture around the stem bases, which is where damping-off, meaning seedlings rotting off right at the base, gets started.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: This is a fine brassica sown tight, which is a large part of why it is prone here; ease the rate so the stand is not both wet and airless. Penn State reported damping-off as the single problem, disease or pest, that its microgreens trials turned up.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go for the feel of a sponge you have wrung out, not something sodden, and put the water in from underneath so the leaf tops and the top of the mix stay dry. Wetness sitting up on that surface is what sets this problem off.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Wrung-sponge moisture plus sub-irrigation holds the foliage and the medium surface dry, which is the lever that matters most once the stand has greened up.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Set a small fan to run steadily near the tray so gentle air keeps moving over it and the surface and stem bases can dry between waterings.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Constant gentle air from a small fan keeps the surface and the stem bases from sitting damp; still air is the third condition this wants, alongside wet and crowded.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Use clean, sanitized trays and fresh mix for every batch. On a crop you cut young and eat raw there is no rescue spray to fall back on, so prevention carries the whole job. A tray that molds badly is better composted than rescued; restart it with clean equipment.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Fresh medium and sanitized trays at every cycle, with a badly affected tray composted and restarted clean rather than salvaged. Nothing sprayable is available for greens cut this young and eaten raw, so the whole defense sits in how the tray is grown and how it is cleaned, not in what goes on it.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist once or twice daily through germination and blackout to hold even surface moisture; once greened, bottom-water as the tray dries.
watering.frequency_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, lightly mist the surface once or twice a day so it stays damp. After you move the tray into the light, water from the bottom whenever it starts to dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated; pour off any standing water after bottom-watering.
watering.amount_beginner: Just enough to keep the medium damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy. After bottom-watering, tip out any water left sitting in the tray.
watering.method_seasoned: Mist during germination and blackout; switch to bottom-watering (sub-irrigation) once the canopy is up so broccoli's dense foliage stays dry.
watering.method_beginner: Mist the top while the seeds are sprouting, then water from the bottom once the leaves are up so the leaves stay dry.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Standing water, a sour or musty smell, fuzzy white growth spreading over the medium and stems, and seedlings collapsing at the base all signal overwatering and the damping-off that follows it.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Water sitting in the tray, a bad smell, fuzzy white mold on the mix and stems, or seedlings flopping over mean it is too wet. Cut back on water and improve airflow.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Curling, limp cotyledons and a medium that has pulled away from the tray edges indicate the canopy has dried too far between waterings.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Limp, curling leaves and mix that has shrunk away from the sides mean it got too dry. Water from the bottom right away.

schedule_by_stage.rate: wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Sow the broccoli seed evenly and mist to moisten; keep the medium at wrung-sponge damp, never saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Scatter the broccoli seed evenly and mist to dampen. Keep the mix damp like a wrung-out sponge, not soggy.

schedule_by_stage.rate: wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Mist the surface once or twice daily through germination to hold even moisture; keep the medium at wrung-sponge damp, never saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Lightly mist the surface once or twice a day while the seeds sprout so it stays damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy.

schedule_by_stage.rate: wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep misting under the blackout cover to hold even surface moisture; humidity builds under the cover, so pour off any standing water and keep it only sponge-damp.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep misting lightly under the cover so the surface stays damp. It gets humid under there, so never let water pool in the tray.

schedule_by_stage.rate: wrung-sponge moisture, pour off standing water
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window for broccoli's dense foliage: switch to bottom-watering (sub-irrigation) so the packed leaves stay dry, pour off standing water, and keep a gentle fan going, since a single overwatering here can seed damping-off across the tray.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: The riskiest moment is uncovering the tray into the light. Broccoli grows very dense, so water from the bottom now to keep the leaves dry, tip out standing water, and keep a fan going.

schedule_by_stage.rate: wrung-sponge moisture until cut
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Bottom-water as the tray dries right up to the single cut, keeping the foliage dry and the air moving so the dense canopy does not mold in its last days.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering from the bottom as the tray dries until you cut, keeping the leaves dry and a fan going so the crowded canopy does not mold at the end.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Wet foliage in a dense, still canopy is the main driver of mold and damping-off on broccoli, so the cycle moves deliberately from misting to bottom-watering and pairs it with constant gentle airflow.
watering.method_note_beginner: Wet leaves packed close together with no air movement is what causes mold. That is why you switch to watering from the bottom once the leaves are up, and keep a gentle fan going.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window: the canopy is dense, humidity under the cover is high, and a single overwatering here can seed damping-off across the whole tray.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The riskiest time is right when you uncover the tray and move it into the light. The plants are crowded and damp, so do not overwater, and make sure air is moving.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Do not hold cut broccoli microgreens at room temperature; they wilt within hours. Refrigerate immediately after cutting.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut broccoli microgreens out on the counter. They go limp fast, so put them in the fridge right after cutting.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Rinse, pat dry, and refrigerate in a vented container lined with a paper towel; broccoli is a tender brassica and keeps best used within about 5 to 7 days, up to about 10 with careful drying. Harvest only what you will use soon.
storage.fridge_beginner: Rinse cut broccoli microgreens, pat them dry, and keep them in the fridge in a container with a paper towel to soak up extra moisture. They are delicate, so use them within about a week (up to 10 days if kept dry).
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not recommended. Freezing collapses the delicate cells and ruins the texture. Broccoli microgreens are a fresh, cut-and-eat crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze broccoli microgreens. Freezing turns them mushy. They are meant to be eaten fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cut clean and dry: harvest with sanitized scissors into a clean container, keep the foliage dry, and chill promptly. Because they are eaten raw, the same clean-water and sanitized-surface rules that govern growing also govern handling.
storage.notes_beginner: Because you eat broccoli microgreens raw, keep everything clean: cut them with clean scissors into a clean, dry container and refrigerate right away.

recommended.name: Standard broccoli (e.g. Calabrese, Waltham 29, Di Cicco)
recommended.note: Brassica oleracea var. italica; mild, fresh, faintly cabbage-like. About 8 to 12 days, no presoak. The usual choice and the one prized for its glucosinolate content.

recommended.name: Broccoli raab / rapini
recommended.note: A spicier, peppery alternative; botanically Brassica rapa (turnip family), not true broccoli. Finishes fast (about 6 to 10 days), no presoak. Use for a sharper, more mustard-like tray.

varieties.note_seasoned: For a mild, versatile tray, standard broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica) is the mainstay: small brassica seed sown densely and dry (no presoak), finishing in about 8 to 12 days. Broccoli is one of the microgreens most often grown for nutrition; like other brassica microgreens it concentrates the glucosinolates that give the cabbage family its character, and research finds microgreens generally higher in vitamins and phytochemicals than the mature vegetable. For a sharper tray, broccoli raab (rapini) is a peppery alternative, but note it is a different species (Brassica rapa, closer to turnip) rather than true broccoli. Never grow microgreens from solanaceous seed (tomato, pepper, eggplant); those seedlings are not safe to eat raw.
varieties.note_beginner: Standard broccoli is the go-to: a mild, fresh microgreen from small seeds you scatter dry (no soaking), ready in about 8 to 12 days. It is one of the most popular microgreens for nutrition, since broccoli and its relatives are packed with the healthy plant compounds the cabbage family is known for, and young microgreens tend to be richer in vitamins than full-grown plants. If you want more kick, broccoli raab (rapini) is a spicier, peppery option, though it is actually a close cousin (in the turnip family), not true broccoli. Never grow microgreens from tomato, pepper, or eggplant seed, as those baby plants are not safe to eat.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens are never moved outdoors or transplanted; the whole cycle is indoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens stay indoors from seed to harvest, so there is no hardening off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow densely and evenly across pre-moistened medium (about 28 grams, roughly 1 ounce, of broccoli seed per 1020 tray; small-seeded brassicas can go as dense as about 10 to 12 seeds per square inch). Broccoli takes no presoak; the seed goes on dry. Do not bury it; press it into firm contact, then cover for a dark blackout period. Dense, even contact is what gives a uniform stand and a clean single cut.
start_method.notes_beginner: Scatter broccoli seeds thickly and evenly over damp growing medium, about 1 ounce (28 grams) per standard 1020 tray. Do not soak them first; broccoli seed goes on dry. Do not bury the seeds, just press them down so they touch the surface, then cover the tray to keep it dark for a few days while they sprout.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Nest the drilled tray inside a solid, hole-free tray. The outer tray catches runoff, lets you bottom-water, and is poured off so the crop never sits in standing water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Set the tray with holes inside a second solid tray with no holes. The bottom tray lets you water from below and catch extra water, which you then pour out so the roots are not sitting in water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a microgreen growing mat.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: None needed.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Seed-starting mix, coir, or an inert fiber mat; about 1 to 2 inches deep.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: None; the medium is a substrate, not a nutrient source, for a single cycle.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water from the bottom by setting the tray in a little water, then pour off what is left.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: No fertilizer needed.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens are an indoor year-round cycle crop, harvested in days, with no dormant or overwintered phase.
overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens grow indoors all year and are harvested within a couple of weeks, so there is nothing to overwinter.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: The tray is the entire growing system: shallow, drained, nested over a solid tray for bottom-watering, sanitized between cycles. A clean, reused, food-grade tray beats a single-use clamshell for both food safety and consistent results.
container_notes.notes_beginner: For broccoli microgreens, the tray is the whole setup. Use a shallow tray with drainage holes sitting inside a solid tray so you can water from the bottom. Wash and sanitize trays between batches.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Bottom-water from the nesting tray; never leave the tray standing in water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: None for a single cycle.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering reservoirs keep the medium too wet for a dense raw crop and raise the damping-off risk; bottom-water by hand and pour off the excess instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for broccoli microgreens. They keep things too wet, which causes mold. Water from the bottom by hand and tip out the extra.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A shallow flat tray works best: a 1020-style tray or any shallow food-safe container, with about 1 to 2 inches of medium. Depth beyond that wastes mix without helping a crop that is cut in days.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a shallow, wide tray, like a standard 1020 tray or any clean food-safe container. About 1 to 2 inches of growing mix is plenty. You do not need anything deep.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens grow on fresh or sanitized medium each cycle with no soil-borne carryover, so crop rotation does not apply.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Not applicable. You use fresh growing medium and clean trays each time, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Sanitation between cycles, not rotation, is the disease control for broccoli microgreens: compost the spent medium, then wash and sanitize the tray before the next sow.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating crops, just keep things clean: toss the used medium and wash and sanitize the tray before starting again.

growth_stages.name: Sow
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Scatter broccoli seed thickly and evenly across a tray of pre-moistened growing mix, aiming for a dense single layer with no bare gaps. These small seeds need no soaking; just mist the surface to settle them. Microgreens are sown right on top of the mix, packed close together, not spaced out or buried like a garden planting.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: An even, crowded scatter of seed covering the whole surface, over mix that looks uniformly damp and dark but has no standing water.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Tray sown and misted?
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dry-broadcast broccoli seed densely and evenly on pre-moistened medium in a single layer. No presoak for small brassica seed; mist to settle. Surface-sow, do not cover.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A uniform, dense seed layer with no clumping on evenly moist medium.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Tray sown?

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cover the tray to hold in darkness and humidity, and set a lightly weighted empty tray on top; the gentle pressure roots the seeds evenly. Keep it warm, around 74°F. Broccoli is quick off the mark, often sprouting within a day or two, so check daily. Mist only if the surface looks dry.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Seeds swelling and splitting, with tiny white roots and pale looped stems appearing quickly, often lifting the cover within a day or two.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any fast little sprouts under the cover?
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Weighted blackout cover at around 74°F. Broccoli germinates fast, frequently within 24 to 48 hours. Mist only to prevent surface drying; avoid saturation.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid imbibition and splitting; white radicles and blanched hypocotyls emerging early, lifting the cover.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Germination started (broccoli is quick)?

growth_stages.name: Blackout
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the tray covered in the dark for about three to four days after most seeds sprout. This dark stretch pulls all the stems up tall and even so the tray fills in uniformly. Keep misting lightly if the surface dries.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A dense mat of pale, stretched stems standing tall and lifting the cover. They will be white to yellow, not green yet, which is exactly right in the dark.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Stems tall and even under there?
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold blackout about 3 to 4 days to elongate hypocotyls uniformly and even the stand before light. Mist to maintain surface moisture.
