failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow beets in cool weather so they color up well, keep the watering steady, and pick a deeply colored variety like Detroit Dark Red if strong color matters to you.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor or patchy germination
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Seeds did not come up well
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Few or uneven seedlings emerged. Beet seed is naturally slow, and the fine seedlings cannot break a dried, crusted surface; a bed that dried during germination, old seed, cold wet soil (damping-off), or sowing too deep accounts for most failures. Clusters from the seedball can also look uneven before thinning.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Few seedlings came up, or they came up patchy. Beet seed is slow, and the sprouts cannot push through a dried crust. Most failures come from the bed drying out while sprouting, old seed, cold soggy soil, or planting too deep. Remember each seed grows a clump, so the stand can look uneven at first.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Soak the seed before sowing, keep the surface evenly moist from sowing to emergence, sow shallowly (about 1/2 inch) with fresh seed, and wait for the soil to warm to about 45 to 50°F before sowing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Soak the seeds before planting, keep the soil surface damp from sowing until the seedlings appear, plant shallow (about 1/2 inch) with fresh seed, and wait until the soil warms to about 45 to 50°F.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Forked or misshapen roots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Forked or lumpy beets
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Roots grew forked, twisted, or lumpy because they met an obstruction, a stone, clod, or compacted layer, or because the stand was left unthinned and crowded. Fresh manure can also distort roots.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The beets came out forked, twisted, or lumpy because they hit something hard as they grew, like a rock or packed soil, or because they were too crowded. Fresh manure can also misshape them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Work the bed loose and remove stones before sowing, thin to 3 to 4 inches so roots are not crowded, and avoid fresh manure. On heavy or rocky ground, use a raised bed or a deep, loose container.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Loosen the bed and pull out rocks before planting, thin the beets to 3 to 4 inches so they are not crowded, and skip fresh manure. On rocky or heavy soil, use a raised bed or a deep, loose container.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Beets succession well: sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool-season window rather than one large planting, so roots mature in sequence. In cold-summer climates that means spring through early summer, then a late-summer sowing for a fall and storage crop; in hot-summer climates it means fall through early spring, skipping the heat. Stop spring sowings before sustained heat, since beets near maturity in hot soil turn woody and lose sweetness, and very early sowings into cold soil risk bolting.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Instead of planting all your beets at once, sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks. That way they are ready a few at a time over several weeks. In places with cool summers, start in spring and keep going into early summer, then sow again in late summer for fall. In hot-summer places, grow them in fall, winter, and early spring and skip the summer heat. Do not sow too early into cold soil, which can make beets bolt.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Beets are direct-sown in this region across the cool-season window; the per-zone cells below carry the resolved planting and harvest months. Sources: umn_ext, iastate_ext, cornell_ext, umaine_ext, unh_ext, uwi_hort, ndsu_ext.

3.zone_notes: In the coldest zones, sow beets in late spring once the soil reaches about 45 to 50°F and harvest summer into fall; a tight midsummer sowing gives a fall crop before the ground freezes.

4.zone_notes: Sow from late April through summer and harvest early summer into fall; beets crop straight through the cool northern summer with no heat break.

5.zone_notes: Sow from early to mid April through midsummer, succession every 2 to 3 weeks, and harvest summer into late fall; beets tolerate frost down to about 20°F.

6.zone_notes: Sow early spring through late summer and harvest into late fall; a reliable fall crop sweetens after frost.

7.zone_notes: At the warm end of the northern tier, sow from early spring with a dependable late-summer sowing for a fall and early-winter harvest; very early sowings into cold soil can bolt.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the coldest zones, sow beets in late spring once the soil reaches about 45 to 50°F and harvest summer into fall; a tight midsummer sowing gives a fall crop before the ground freezes.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the coldest zones, sow beets in late spring once the soil reaches about 45 to 50°F and harvest summer into fall; a tight midsummer sowing gives a fall crop before the ground freezes.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Beets are direct-sown in this region across the cool-season window; the per-zone cells below carry the resolved planting and harvest months. Sources: clemson_hgic, uga_b577, uga_ext_c943_calendar, aces_ext, msstate_ext, lsu_agcenter.

8.zone_notes: Inland, grow beets as a spring crop (sow Feb to Mar) and a fall crop (sow Aug to Sep); high summer is too hot and deep winter is the off-season between cycles.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat exclusion (Jun, Jul). Beet is a cool-season crop that grows and colors best around 60 to 65°F; sustained summer heat above about 75°F runs the roots woody, strong-flavored, and pale, dulls germination, and pushes plants toward bolting, so beets are grown as a fall-through-spring crop here and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. (Clemson Cooperative Extension; University of Georgia Extension)

9.zone_notes: Along the Gulf and coastal plain, beets are a fall-through-spring crop: sow fall into winter and harvest through the mild winter into spring. The hot, humid summer is the exclusion.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat exclusion (May, Jun, Jul, Aug). Beet is a cool-season crop that grows and colors best around 60 to 65°F; sustained summer heat above about 75°F runs the roots woody, strong-flavored, and pale, dulls germination, and pushes plants toward bolting, so beets are grown as a fall-through-spring crop here and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. (Clemson Cooperative Extension; LSU AgCenter)

rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, grow beets in the cool season, not summer. Plant Oct 15 through Dec 31 and harvest from Dec 4 into spring; it rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold. Beets are one of the easiest winter roots here: sow directly in the ground from mid-October through the end of December and keep pulling them through winter and into spring. Skip planting beets from spring through summer: the Valley heat keeps them from growing well here.

Frost is essentially absent here, so timing is heat-bounded rather than cold-bounded. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: the TAMU AgriLife sources describe a single Valley-wide planting calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

nevada.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, direct-sow beets outdoors in late winter through spring, from about mid-February to the end of March, for a late-spring harvest. Once daytime highs push past 90°F, roots held in the hot soil turn woody and pale, so pull them and let the ground rest through the worst weeks. Sow again from about mid-August to mid-September for a fall and early-winter crop that holds well in the ground once it is cool.
nevada.region_notes_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) grows beets on two direct-sown cycles, per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart. Spring sowing runs roughly mid-February to the end of March, with harvest beginning about 58 days later. Once daytime highs run past 90°F, the University of Nevada, Reno Extension's home-vegetable guidance (Fact Sheet FS-02-61) notes plants generally stop growing well, and beet roots held in hot soil turn woody and pale, so the chart splits into a real spring cycle and a distinct late-summer fall cycle rather than one continuous run. The fall sowing (about mid-August to mid-September) goes in as the heat breaks and the roots are frost hardy, so digging can run well past the valley's first fall frost. Zone 8's cooler pockets carry the same fall window but reach frost sooner, tightening the finish; zone 10 at Laughlin has the most room to spare.

utah_dixie.region_notes_beginner: In St. George's Dixie, sow beets direct in early March for a spring crop pulled by mid-May, before the real summer heat sets in. The bed then sits idle through June, since St. George routinely tops 100°F that month. Sow again from July 1 to August 1 for a fall crop. There is no need to clear the whole row at once: USU Extension's fall guidance for this county has the roots keeping in cold ground, so dig beets as you want them right through the winter, long past the first frost around November 1.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: St. George's Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) grows beets on two direct-sown cycles, per Utah State University Extension's suggested vegetable planting dates for Utah. The spring sowing runs March 1 to March 15, the Group B (Semi-Hardy) date for St. George, with roots ready in about 58 days and the crop pulled by mid-May before the heat builds. USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation notes put St. George over 100°F in June, July, and August; since the documented fall window (USU's Group E "Special Plants for Fall Harvest" table) does not open until July 1, June is a genuine bare-ground pause between the two cycles. The fall sowing runs July 1 to August 1, and USU's fall-gardening guidance for the St. George area specifically groups beets with turnips and carrots as roots that hold well and can be dug quite late into winter, well past the November 1 average first frost.

crops.description_seasoned: Beet (Beta vulgaris) is a cool-season, dual-purpose crop grown for both its swollen root and its edible leaves, which are cooked like chard or spinach, its close relatives in the goosefoot family (Amaranthaceae, formerly Chenopodiaceae). It is direct-sown: each beet seed is a multigerm seedball, a dried fruit holding several embryos, so a single seed sprouts a cluster of seedlings and the stand must be thinned (monogerm cultivars avoid this). Germination is slow, often 1 to 2 weeks, and the seedbed must stay moist and uncrusted until emergence. Roots size up over roughly 50 to 70 days and are sweetest and most tender pulled at about 1 1/2 to 2 inches across; sustained heat above about 75°F turns them woody and strong-flavored and fades their color. Beets tolerate frost and sweeten in cool weather, and the roots withstand more cold than the tops, to roughly 20°F. Two beet-specific cautions: they are unusually boron-sensitive, with deficiency causing internal black spot, and young plants can bolt to seed after a cold spell followed by long spring days, so very early sowings into cold soil are risky. The planting season inverts by climate: spring and fall where summers are cool, and fall through early spring where summers are hot.
crops.description_beginner: Beets are a cool-weather crop you grow for two foods at once: the round root and the leafy greens, which you cook like chard or spinach. You plant the seeds right in the garden, and here is the surprise: each beet seed is really a little dried fruit with several seeds inside, so one seed grows a clump of seedlings, which is why you have to thin them. The seeds are slow, often 1 to 2 weeks to come up, and the soil surface needs to stay damp until they do. Roots are usually ready in about 50 to 70 days and taste best pulled small, about 1 1/2 to 2 inches across; in heat above about 75°F they turn tough and lose color. Beets handle frost and get sweeter in cool weather, and the roots take more cold than the leaves. Two things to know: beets need a little of the nutrient boron or they get black spots inside, and young plants can bolt (flower instead of making a root) if they get a cold snap followed by long days, so do not plant too early. When you plant depends on your climate: spring and fall where summers are cool, and fall through early spring where summers are hot.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Beets are a dual harvest. The leaves can be picked young throughout, taking a few outer leaves per plant so the root keeps sizing; the thinnings at the seedling stage are the first baby greens. The roots are ready by size rather than the calendar: brush soil from a shoulder and pull when it is about 1 1/2 to 2 inches across, the sweet, tender stage, which for most varieties lands near 50 to 70 days. Beets can be eaten larger, up to about 3 inches, but oversized roots turn woody and strong. There is no rush in cool weather: flavor sweetens after light frost, and roots hold in the ground, withstanding more cold than the tops. In cold regions a heavy straw mulch lets you dig through early winter until the ground freezes hard. Lift by hand, or loosen with a fork in heavier soil, and twist off the tops, leaving an inch of stem on roots you plan to store so they do not bleed.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Beets give you two harvests. You can pick the leaves young all along, taking a few outer ones per plant so the root keeps growing, and the seedlings you thin out are your first baby greens. The roots are ready by size, not a set date: brush the soil off a shoulder and pull when the beet is about 1 1/2 to 2 inches across, the sweet, tender stage, usually around 50 to 70 days. You can let them grow up to about 3 inches, but bigger beets get woody and strong. There is no rush in cool weather: they get sweeter after a light frost and hold in the ground, and the roots take more cold than the leaves. In cold areas, pile straw over the row and dig them into early winter until the ground freezes. Pull by hand, or loosen with a fork in heavy soil, and twist off the tops, leaving an inch of stem on beets you want to store so they do not bleed out their color.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Beets reward a loose, fertile, well-drained seedbed worked fine before sowing. Loosen the bed about 6 to 8 inches deep, less than carrots need since the root swells near the surface, and remove stones and clods that fork the roots. Rake the surface smooth and fine, because the small seedballs need close soil contact and an even, crust-free surface to emerge through their slow germination. Work in well-finished compost and a balanced fertilizer, and aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH of about 6.0 to 7.0; beets tolerate mildly alkaline soil but do poorly below 6.0. Address boron before planting only if a soil test shows a deficiency, since beets are both unusually boron-sensitive and easily injured by excess. On heavy clay, work in compost or use a raised bed for the drainage and loose texture beets prefer.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Beets do best in loose, rich, well-drained soil raked smooth before you plant. Loosen the bed about 6 to 8 inches down, a bit less than carrots need since beet roots sit near the surface, and pull out rocks and hard clumps that make roots fork. Rake the top fine and smooth so the seeds sit snug against the soil and can push up through their slow sprouting. Mix in compost and a balanced fertilizer, and aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 7.0; beets handle slightly alkaline soil but struggle below 6.0. Only add boron if a soil test says you are low, because beets need a little but are harmed by too much. If your soil is heavy clay, mix in compost or use a raised bed for the loose, well-drained soil beets like.

crops.name: Cucumber

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Cucumbers do best in a moisture-retentive yet well-drained loam or sandy loam enriched with plenty of organic matter. Work several inches of compost or well-rotted manure into the bed before planting, since these are fast, thirsty plants with shallow roots that resent both drought and waterlogging. Many growers plant in low hills or mounds, which warm faster in spring and drain well, and a trellis keeps the fruit straight and off wet ground. Sandy loams warm early and suit the first sowings, while heavy clay holds water and invites root and fruit rot, so amend it generously or build raised mounds.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant cucumbers in rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in. They grow fast and have shallow roots, so they like soil that stays evenly moist but never soggy. Many gardeners plant them on low hills or mounds, which warm up quicker and drain better, and growing them up a trellis keeps the fruit clean and straight. If your soil is heavy or stays wet, build up mounds or use raised beds so the roots do not sit in water.

ph.note_seasoned: Cucumbers do best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5. They still grow across a wider band, roughly 5.5 to 7.0, but uptake of some nutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.
ph.note_beginner: Cucumbers like soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.5, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress once or twice
fertilizer.type: balanced at planting, then nitrogen side-dress
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before planting, then side-dress about a week after flowering begins and again 3 weeks later
fertilizer.example_product: balanced 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen source such as blood meal
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Cucumbers are moderate feeders over a short, fast season. Work a balanced fertilizer or several inches of compost into the bed before planting, then side-dress with a little nitrogen about a week after flowering starts and again roughly three weeks later if the plants look pale. The main pitfall is too much nitrogen, which drives lush vines and leaf at the expense of fruit and draws aphids and disease. Pair feeding with steady, even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed, and drought stress is what turns cucumbers bitter.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Cucumbers grow fast and need a moderate amount of feeding, not a lot. Mix a balanced fertilizer or compost into the soil before planting, then feed with a little nitrogen about a week after the flowers start, and again a few weeks later if the plants look pale. Do not overdo the nitrogen, since too much makes leafy vines instead of cucumbers. Keep the plants evenly watered too, because feeding only helps a well-watered plant.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your cucumbers are flowering, time for a light nitrogen side-dressing. Keep nitrogen moderate so the plant sets fruit instead of running to leaf, and keep the water steady.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your cucumbers are starting to flower. Give them a light feeding of nitrogen now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting suits cucumbers, followed by a light nitrogen side-dress once they flower. Avoid high-nitrogen lawn-type fertilizers, which push foliage at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer with equal numbers, like 10-10-10, at planting, then a little nitrogen once flowers appear. Avoid high-nitrogen lawn fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work a balanced fertilizer or 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting. Then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about a week after flowering begins, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeating about three weeks later if needed. A common rate is roughly 1 tablespoon of 10-10-10 per plant, or a comparable scoop of compost or balanced organic fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix some compost or a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting. Then feed once with a little nitrogen about a week after flowers appear, scratched into the soil a few inches from the stem and watered in, and again a few weeks later if the plants look pale.

companions.note_seasoned: Cucumber companions earn their place by drawing pests away, bringing in bees, or feeding the soil, rather than by crowding the bed. Give vining plants room or a trellis, and use companions as a border or light interplanting. The signature cucumber pest is the cucumber beetle, which also vectors bacterial wilt, so radish and nasturtium are traditionally interplanted to lure or deter beetles, and a row of sunflowers or corn can serve as a living trellis and windbreak. Because cucumbers are insect-pollinated, pollinator flowers like borage and dill keep bees working the blooms and improve fruit set. Beans fix nitrogen for the moderately hungry vines. Most of these pairings are traditional or mechanistic rather than trial-proven, and are labeled accordingly. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep cucumbers away from other cucurbits, which share the whole pest and disease complex.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful cucumber companions are flowers that bring in bees, since cucumbers need bee visits to set fruit, plants like radish and nasturtium that lure pest beetles away, and beans that feed the soil. Sunflowers or corn can act as a natural trellis. The one rule that really matters is to keep cucumbers away from other squash, melons, and pumpkins, which all share the same pests and diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Radish
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Radishes are often planted among cucumbers to lure cucumber beetles, the cucumber's worst pest, away from the vines. They grow fast and are pulled before they crowd anything. A popular, low-risk traditional pairing.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A long-standing trap and deterrent planting for cucumber beetles, the pest that also spreads bacterial wilt to highly susceptible cucumbers. Radishes are quick, cheap, and out of the bed before they compete, which makes them an easy interplant even though the beetle-reduction effect is traditional rather than trial-isolated.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Radish-as-cucumber-beetle-deterrent is a widely repeated traditional interplant; no T1 trial isolates the effect on cucumber.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums lure cucumber beetles and aphids away from cucumbers and their flowers bring in bees. An easy, edible-flowered neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for cucumber beetles and aphids, and its flowers draw the bees cucumbers depend on for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-cucumber effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap-cropping for cucurbit beetles/aphids is documented in principle; the nasturtium-cucumber pairing is not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which the fast-growing cucumber appreciates, and they do not share its pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Pole or bush beans fix nitrogen that benefits the moderately heavy-feeding cucumber, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. The nitrogen benefit largely reaches neighbors after the beans break down, so treat it as season-long soil-building rather than an instant feed, but the mechanism is sound.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation via Rhizobium is established biology; the same-season transfer to an adjacent cucumber is modest, so mechanistic/medium rather than research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Sunflower
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A row of sunflowers gives cucumber vines something to climb and a bit of shade, and the blooms bring in bees. A practical, traditional support plant.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Tall sunflowers can serve cucumbers as a living trellis and light windbreak, lifting the vines off the ground for cleaner, straighter fruit and better airflow, while their flowers recruit pollinators. The structural benefit is real and practical; the pairing is traditional rather than a measured yield effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Sunflower-as-trellis is a structural intercropping practice; the cucumber benefit is space-and-support, not a trial-isolated pair effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and cucumbers need bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination. Mainly grown to bring in bees.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators cucumber fruit set depends on, since the female flowers need repeated bee visits to size a fruit. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-cucumber pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Cucumber fruit set is pollinator-dependent; flowering insectary plants like borage draw bees. Pairing is habitat-based, not pair-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill flowers draw hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that prey on aphids, and it is the classic kitchen partner for pickling cucumbers. The beneficial-insect draw is mechanistically sound; the specific cucumber pairing is traditional. Let some plants flower for the benefit.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep cucumbers away from other squash, melons, and pumpkins. They all get the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Summer and winter squash, melon, and pumpkin share cucumber's whole pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle with the bacterial wilt it spreads (to which cucumber is especially susceptible), squash bug, powdery and downy mildew, and angular leaf spot. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens and cucumber-beetle wilt vectoring are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and cucumbers apart, since both are hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucumbers compete for the same nutrients and that potatoes can harbor blight and attract pests near the vines. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A folk anti-companion caution; competition is plausible but no T1 source isolates a potato-cucumber antagonism.
