weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Collards are the most heat-tolerant cole crop and usually run right through summer, but sustained heat above about 90°F can toughen the leaves and speed pest pressure. Keep moisture even, harvest in the cool morning, and in hot regions give afternoon shade. Only in genuinely extreme heat (desert valleys, peak Florida and Hawaii summers) is collards a true off-season crop.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Collards handle heat better than other greens and usually keep growing through summer. In a hot spell, water evenly, pick in the cool morning, and give some afternoon shade so the leaves stay tender. Only in the very hottest places is summer really off-season for collards.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Collards are the most cold-hardy cole crop and a freeze sweetens the leaves; mature plants tolerate hard frost and freezes into the low-to-mid 20s°F and below. In the coldest zones a deep freeze may damage exposed leaves, so a row cover or low tunnel extends the harvest, but for most freezes simply keep picking.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Collards handle hard freezes better than almost any vegetable, and the cold makes them taste sweeter, so you usually do not need to do anything. In very cold areas, a row cover or low tunnel helps them keep going through the worst cold.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep into a moist seedbed or starting mix; collards germinate reliably across 45 to 85°F in about 5 to 10 days.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep in damp soil, and keep it evenly moist while they sprout in 5 to 10 days.

germination.text_seasoned: For a spring crop start indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out, or direct sow as soon as the soil is workable; for a fall crop sow in mid to late summer.
germination.text_beginner: Start seeds indoors about a month before planting out, sow them in the garden once the soil can be worked, or sow in late summer for a fall crop.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin or transplant to about 12 to 24 inches apart for full-size plants, or closer (10 to 15 inches) if you will cut them young; harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days.
seedling.text_beginner: Space plants about 12 to 24 inches apart for big plants, or closer together if you plan to cut them while young.

seedling.text_seasoned: Protect seedlings from flea beetles with row cover; a vigorous, well-watered seedling outgrows light feeding damage.
seedling.text_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover to stop flea beetles from peppering the leaves with holes.

established.text_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen as the plant builds and keep moisture even at roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week; drought stress is the top cause of tough, stringy leaves, especially in heat.
established.text_beginner: Feed with nitrogen and water steadily, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, so the leaves stay tender and mild.

established.text_seasoned: Scout the growing tip and crown for cabbage aphids, the leaves for cabbageworms, and, in the South, for harlequin bugs; catching them early keeps the harvested leaves clean.
established.text_beginner: Check the growing tip for aphids and the leaves for caterpillars and shield-shaped harlequin bugs, and deal with them early.

harvest.text_seasoned: Crop the lower leaves once they reach 8 to 10 inches, taking no more than about a third of the plant so the growing bud keeps producing for months; or cut whole young plants and let them regrow.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick the lowest leaves when they are about hand-sized or bigger, and leave the center growing, so the same plant keeps making leaves. Or cut the whole young plant and let it grow back.

harvest.text_seasoned: Leaves are sweetest after a frost or two; in cool weather you can keep harvesting straight from the garden even after the foliage has frozen.
harvest.text_beginner: Collards taste sweeter after frost, and you can keep picking even after the leaves have frozen in cool weather.

overwintering.text_seasoned: In mild zones keep cropping through winter; in cold zones a low tunnel or row cover extends the harvest, and collards take more cold than any other cole crop.
overwintering.text_beginner: In mild areas keep picking all winter. In cold areas, cover the plants to keep harvesting longer; collards handle cold better than any other cabbage-family plant.

overwintering.text_seasoned: Watch for spring bolting as warmth and long days return: harvest remaining leaves before the flower stalk elongates, since the leaves turn bitter once the plant flowers.
overwintering.text_beginner: In spring, collards that lived through winter will send up a flower stalk and turn bitter, so pick the last good leaves before that happens.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single collard plant yields a steady run of large outer leaves over a long season rather than one harvest, roughly 1 to 2 pounds or more per plant depending on variety, season length, and how often you crop it. Extension yields run about 8 to 15 pounds per 10 feet of row.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each collard plant gives you a steady supply of big leaves over months, not one big harvest. How much you get depends on the variety and how long your season is, but a few plants keep producing for a long time.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Production climbs as the plant sizes up and then holds for weeks to months as you crop the lower leaves, peaking in the cool weeks of fall and, in mild zones, through winter. Collards keep producing through summer in much of the South, slowing only in genuinely extreme heat, and the crop ends when the plant bolts in spring.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Collards produce the most once the plant is full-sized, and they keep going strongest in cool fall weather and, in mild areas, through winter. Unlike most greens they also keep going through summer in the South, and they stop once they flower in spring.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The key to total yield is cropping the lower leaves regularly while leaving the central growing bud: frequent, moderate picking keeps a plant productive for months, whereas stripping a plant bare or letting old leaves toughen on the stem checks it. New growers often pick too timidly or take the bud, which stalls the plant.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Here is the trick: pick the lower leaves often, but always leave the small center bud to keep growing. Regular picking keeps a plant making leaves for months. Do not take the middle of the plant, and do not let old leaves toughen on the stem.
factors_seasoned: Harvest method: regular cut-and-come-again cropping of lower leaves (leaving the bud) sustains months of production; taking the bud or stripping the plant ends it.
Temperature: cool weather through fall and mild winters gives the highest-quality, sweetest leaves; collards also produce through Southern summers but the leaves are milder in cool weather.
Variety: Georgia and the Vates types crop longest; fast hybrids like Top Bunch reach a first cutting sooner.
Nitrogen and even moisture: steady nitrogen and consistent water keep new leaves tender; stress makes them tough, stringy, and aphid-prone.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing collard planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by soil temperature, frost dates, and the seasonal windows instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting (flower stalk and bitter leaves)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A plant that lived through winter and is now flowering in spring, or summer heat and long days on a stressed plant.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your collards shot up a tall stalk with buds or yellow flowers and the leaves turned bitter. Collards are biennials that bolt (run to flower) mostly in their second spring after a cold winter, and sometimes from heat and long days on a stressed plant. Once they bolt the leaves go bitter and tough. People often blame the plant, but it is just its life cycle. Next time, treat an overwintered plant as a spring bonus you harvest before it flowers, and pick bolt-resistant types like Vates or Champion.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Harvest overwintered plants before they bolt in spring, grow bolt-resistant varieties, and keep plants unstressed with steady water.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant elongated a flowering stalk and the leaves turned bitter and tough. Bolting is driven mainly by vernalization (a cold winter) flowering the biennial in its second spring, and secondarily by heat and long days on stressed plants; once it bolts, leaf quality is lost. Next time crop overwintered plants out before the stalk elongates, choose bolt-resistant cultivars (Vates, Champion, Top Bunch), and avoid drought stress.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Vernalization flowering the biennial in spring, or heat and long days on a stressed plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Crop overwintered collards before they bolt, favor bolt-resistant varieties, and hold even moisture to avoid stress-triggered bolting.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tough, stringy, bitter leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Drought stress, leaves left on the plant too long, or extreme heat.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your collard leaves are tough, leathery, and bitter instead of tender. This usually comes from the plant drying out, from leaving leaves on too long so they age, or from very hot weather. It is tempting to think the variety is bad, but conditions are almost always the cause. Next time, keep the soil evenly moist, pick leaves while they are young to medium-sized, and remember that frost actually sweetens them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep moisture steady, pick leaves young, give afternoon shade in extreme heat, and enjoy the post-frost sweetening.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Leaves are tough and stringy rather than tender. Drought stress, over-mature leaves, and extreme heat are the usual causes; collards tolerate heat but their leaf quality still suffers when they dry out, and flavor is best in cool weather and sweetened by frost. Next time hold even moisture, crop leaves at a young-to-medium size, shade them in genuinely extreme heat, and lean on the cool shoulders and fall window for the sweetest leaves.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Drought stress, over-mature leaves, or genuinely extreme heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hold even moisture, crop leaves young, shade in extreme heat, and use the cool fall and winter window for the sweetest leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bugs all over summer collards
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Warm-season pests, especially harlequin bugs, cabbageworms, and aphids, which build up on collards left in the ground through Southern summers.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your summer collards got covered in shield-shaped harlequin bugs, green caterpillars, or clusters of aphids, and the leaves are stippled and chewed. Collards keep growing in summer heat, but so do their pests, and pressure is worst in the warm South. People often stop scouting once the plants are big. Next time, scout weekly, use row cover, hand-pick harlequin bugs and their barrel-shaped eggs, spray Bt for caterpillars, and clean up old plants and weeds where pests overwinter.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Scout weekly in warm weather, use row cover, hand-pick harlequin bugs, spray Bt for caterpillars, and clear old plants and weeds.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Summer collards drew heavy harlequin bug, caterpillar, and cabbage-aphid pressure, with stippled, chewed, and contaminated leaves. The crop's summer persistence is also its pest liability in the South, where harlequin bugs run several generations a year. Next time scout weekly, exclude with row cover, hand-pick harlequin adults and egg rows, use Bt or spinosad for caterpillars, knock down aphid colonies early, and remove crucifer weeds and debris that harbor overwintering adults.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Warm-season brassica pests (harlequin bug, cabbageworms, cabbage aphid) building on long-held summer collards, worst in the South.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Scout weekly, exclude with row cover, hand-pick harlequin bugs and egg rows, treat caterpillars with Bt, and sanitize overwintering sites.

failure_diagnostics.label: Stunted, yellow plants with clubbed roots
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Clubroot, a soil disease of cabbage-family plants, or planting brassicas in the same spot too often.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your collards stayed small and yellowish, wilted in the afternoon, and when you dug them up the roots were swollen into lumps. That is clubroot, a soil disease that infects cabbage-family roots and lasts for years in the soil. It usually builds up when brassicas are grown in the same spot repeatedly, which is easy to do with a near-year-round crop. Next time, rotate so cabbage-family crops do not return to that bed for at least 3 years, keep the soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Rotate brassicas out of that bed for at least 3 years, keep soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Plants were stunted and chlorotic, wilted by day, and showed galled, clubbed roots, the signature of clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae). The soilborne organism persists for years and builds under repeated brassica cropping and acidic, poorly drained soil, a real risk where collards are grown nearly year-round. Next time rotate cabbage-family crops out for at least 3 years (longer where known), lime toward a neutral-to-slightly-alkaline pH, and improve drainage; there is no in-season cure.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Clubroot building in soil cropped to brassicas too frequently, favored by acidic, wet soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use a 3-year-plus brassica rotation, raise pH toward neutral, and improve drainage; remove and destroy infected plants.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Collards crop over a long window, so rather than one big planting, sow small batches every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool stretches of spring and again from late summer for a fall and winter crop. Because each plant is cropped over many weeks, you need fewer sowings than for a fast crop, but staggering keeps tender young leaves coming. In the South you can plant across most of the year; only in genuinely extreme heat (deserts, peak Florida and Hawaii summers) do you skip the peak and plant for fall and winter instead.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant collards in small batches a couple of weeks apart, in spring and again in late summer for fall, rather than all at once. Each plant keeps giving leaves for a long time, so you do not need many. In hot-desert and tropical areas, skip the peak summer and plant for fall and winter.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: collards_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored as a NEW gold-standard record modeled STRUCTURALLY on the certified broccoli template, with kale (same species, Acephala group) as the closest content analog and swiss-chard as the heat-tolerance calendar pattern. All collard biology re-derived from live T1 extension sources: UGA CAES Cultivating Collards, UMN growing-collards-and-kale, NC State collard-greens, UMD leafy greens, Clemson cole-crop pests/greens for biology and pests/diseases; per-region planting calendars from UC ANR/UC MG, UF/IFAS VH021 + FL calendars, UGA C943, LSU/MSU State/TAMU, UArizona/NMSU, CTAHR, plus Cornell/Iowa State/UMaine/UNH/MSU for the northern tier. DRAFT for review, not certified: launch flags false. Key collards-vs-broccoli refits: loose-leaf NON-HEADING green (no head_forming/side_shoots stages; cut-and-come-again lower leaves or whole-plant harvest; added overwintering stage); the MOST cold-hardy cole crop (frost-sweetened, holds through hard freezes into the low-to-mid 20s F and below) AND the MOST heat-tolerant (runs through Southern summers). Heat model sits BETWEEN kale and swiss-chard: collards RUN THROUGH the humid Deep South (se_gulf), the mild CA coasts (ca_north_coast, ca_south_coast), and the high desert (warm_arid, with a winter cold_pause), and reserve heat_pause for the genuine extremes only, the hot interior valley peak (ca_interior Jul-Aug), the deserts (ca_desert, low_desert_az), and the peak Florida and Hawaii summers, each backed at the cell. days_to_maturity 55-75, spacing 18-24 in, pH 6.0-6.8; Brassicaceae rotation; harlequin bug + caterpillars emphasized as the Southern collard pests. successions_realized NOT hand-authored (CC deriver fills it). See collards_NOTES.md for flags and modeled values.

open_findings.summary: Heat_pause footprint is a modeled judgment call positioning collards BETWEEN kale (8 heat_pause regions) and swiss-chard (4): heat_pause is placed only in ca_interior (Jul-Aug peak), ca_desert, low_desert_az, fl_peninsula, and hawaii_tropical; collards RUN THROUGH se_gulf, ca_north_coast, ca_south_coast, and warm_arid summers. ca_interior gets a summer pause while warm_arid runs through summer (with a winter cold_pause) because their limiting seasons differ (interior valley-floor heat vs high-desert winter cold).
open_findings.basis: Supported by collards' documented heat tolerance (UGA: grows in summer with moisture, 'tolerant to heat and cold'; UF VH021: 'cold and heat tolerant'), the swiss-chard precedent (runs through the same merely-warm regions), and the UC cole-crop interior-valley planting window being fall-only. The exact per-region run-through-vs-pause line is the load-bearing biology call for the daily review.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set collards out around the last frost, or direct sow when the soil is workable; sow again in midsummer for fall.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

3.zone_notes: In the coldest zone, collards crop from summer through the fall frosts that sweeten them; deep winter ends the unprotected crop, so it is a single long season.

4.zone_notes: Plant in spring once the soil is workable and again in midsummer for fall; harvest runs through the fall frosts, then deep winter ends it.

5.zone_notes: A long season from spring through the fall frosts; under a low tunnel or row cover harvest can extend into winter, since collards are very cold-hardy.

6.zone_notes: Plant in early spring and midsummer; collards hold later into winter than most greens, often into December before hard cold ends the crop.

7.zone_notes: In the mild end of the cold tier collards run nearly year-round: a spring and a fall planting, harvest through the warm summer (collards tolerate it) and through winter, with the leaves sweetest after frost.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold areas, collards are mostly a spring-through-fall crop, with a late-summer planting for fall. They handle frost better than almost any vegetable and get sweeter after it, so you can keep picking well past the first freezes. In the very coldest zones, winter eventually ends them unless you cover them.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold zones collards are one long cool-season crop. Direct sow or set transplants out around the last frost (collards take cold well), with a midsummer sowing for a fall crop that runs through the frosts, which sweeten the leaves. Collards are the hardiest cole crop, so harvest stretches later than most greens; under a low tunnel it can reach into winter, but deep cold eventually ends the open-ground crop.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the Deep South plant late winter and again late summer; collards run nearly year-round, slowing only in the hottest, buggiest weeks of midsummer.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

8.zone_notes: Nearly year-round: a late-winter and a late-summer planting carry harvest across all four seasons. Collards run through the humid summer where cool-season peers cannot, though midsummer leaves toughen and pest pressure peaks.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards set out Oct 1 - Nov 15 in the Rio Grande Valley, per RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide window, corroborated by the Bilingual LRGV planting table's days-to-harvest. rgv.region_notes_beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, grow collards in the cool season, not summer. Transplant Oct 1 through Nov 15 and harvest from Nov 10 into spring; it rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold. Collards go in on broccoli's calendar too, but they mature much faster: transplant October into mid-November and start picking leaves within a couple of months. Skip planting collards from spring through summer: the Valley heat keeps them from growing well here.
rgv.region_notes_seasoned: Collards in the RGV run on the winter-garden calendar: transplant Oct 1 through Nov 15, with harvest running Nov 10 through Jan 14. Transplanted on broccoli's schedule per TAMU's RGV Homeowner Guide; only 40 to 60 days to harvest (Bilingual LRGV table), the quickest of the RGV cole crops. Frost is essentially absent here, so timing is heat-bounded rather than cold-bounded. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: the TAMU AgriLife sources describe a single Valley-wide planting calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

pnw.region_label: Maritime Pacific Northwest: Puget Sound and Willamette Valley

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Neither OSU's Oregon planting table (EM9027) nor WSU's home vegetable guide (EM057E) lists collards by name for this region; collards is thin-sourced here. This cell instead adapts the crop's own established mild-winter northern-tier pattern (its z6/z7 rows), re-anchored to the maritime PNW's real, milder frost dates: set plants out (or direct sow) around 3 weeks ahead of the last frost, since collards tolerates the region's light frosts, then sow again in late summer for a fall and winter crop.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crops cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing, matching the crop's own DTM across every other region.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards is the hardiest cole crop in the garden; the mild maritime winter lets the fall-sown planting keep producing through winter and into late February, with the leaves sweetest after frost.

Even so, the fall sowing, set in late summer to mature as the weather cools, produces the sweetest, most tender leaves, the same frost-sweetening effect this crop is prized for across the mid-Atlantic and Southeast.

8.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Collards tolerate more heat than most cole crops, but Las Vegas Valley summers still routinely run past 100°F from June into September, well past what even collards can hold tender leaves through. University of Nevada, Reno Extension's home-vegetable guidance (Fact Sheet FS-02-61) notes plants generally do not grow well above about 90°F, so the spring crop is picked before that wall and the fall sowing goes in once the worst heat has broken.

Collards shrug off more heat than most cole crops, but St. George's June heat is still too much, so let the bed rest and set a second round from mid-June to mid-July, following cabbage's fall window, for leaves into September. Frost returns around November 1.
utah_dixie.region_notes_seasoned: USU Extension's St. George chart sets collards in the Group A (Hardy) band, spring set-out about February 15, leaves ready to cut at about 65 days through late April. Collards tolerate more heat than most cole crops, but St. George still reaches 100°F in June, past what even collards hold tender leaves through, so the spring cutting closes out before then. By analogy to USU's fall-gardening guidance for the St. George area, a second sowing follows cabbage's mid-June to mid-July window for a fall harvest into mid-September, ahead of the November 1 average first frost.

crops.description_seasoned: Collards (Brassica oleracea, Acephala group) are a loose-leaf, non-heading cabbage relative grown for their large, smooth blue-green leaves, the same species as kale and the classic green of Southern gardens. Their signature is unusual tolerance of BOTH cold and heat: collards are the most cold-hardy of the cole crops, sweetening after frost and holding through hard freezes, yet they are also the most heat-tolerant, producing right through Southern summers where lettuce and most brassicas have long since bolted. A collard plant builds a stout upright stem topped with a rosette of broad leaves, and you crop the lower leaves over a long run or cut the whole young plant. In much of the South they grow nearly year-round; everywhere else they shine in the long cool shoulders of spring and fall.
crops.description_beginner: Collards are a leafy cousin of kale and cabbage, grown for their big, smooth green leaves. They are the famous green of Southern cooking, and they are tough: they handle cold better than almost any other vegetable and get sweeter after frost, but they also keep growing in summer heat that stops other greens. The plant grows tall with a bunch of large leaves at the top. You pick the lower leaves a few at a time for months, or cut the whole young plant. In warm areas collards grow almost all year; in cooler areas they do best in spring and fall.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Start cropping outer leaves once they reach about 8 to 10 inches, taking the lowest, oldest leaves first and leaving the central bud and upper rosette to keep producing. Leaves are most tender picked young to medium-sized; old leaves turn tough and stringy. Alternatively cut the whole young plant near the soil line at 6 to 10 inches and let it regrow, or harvest the tender inner rosette. Flavor is mildest and sweetest in cool weather and after a frost.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Begin picking when the lower leaves are about the size of your hand or bigger, around 8 to 10 inches. Take the lowest, outside leaves and leave the middle growing, so the plant keeps making more for months. You can also cut the whole young plant off near the ground and let it grow back. The leaves taste best picked while still tender, and they get sweeter after a frost.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Collards are leafy heavy feeders that reward a fertile, well-drained loam worked deeply and enriched with compost or aged manure before planting. Loosen the bed 8 to 12 inches, mix in organic matter for steady moisture and nitrogen, and aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8. Where clubroot has appeared, lime toward the high end of that band. Good drainage matters as much as fertility: collards make their best leaves in soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Collards like rich, loose soil with lots of compost mixed in. Dig the bed over and work in compost or aged manure before planting, since collards are hungry plants that grow a lot of leaves. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8, and make sure water drains away well. Keep the soil moist but not soggy and the plants will reward you with big, tender leaves.

crops.name: Dry Beans

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Fertile, well-drained loam. Beans set the heaviest pods in soil that holds moisture during pod fill yet never stays waterlogged, since soggy ground invites root rot.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Beans grow best in rich, loose soil that drains well. The ideal is loam, a balanced soil that holds some moisture but never stays soggy. Beans need steady moisture while the pods are filling out, but wet, waterlogged ground can rot the roots.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Sandy and clay loams both work if drainage is good. Sandy beds dry faster and may need a touch more frequent sidedressing; heavier soils benefit from worked-in organic matter to keep them from crusting over the emerging seedlings.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both sandy and clay-based soils work fine as long as they drain well. Sandy soil dries out faster, so you may need to feed a little more often. Heavier soil does better if you mix in compost or other organic matter, which keeps it from crusting over the seedlings as they push up.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Avoid heavy, poorly drained ground and soils that crust hard after rain. A crust can trap the seedling below the surface, and standing water around the roots brings on the root-rot diseases beans are prone to.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Stay away from heavy soil that drains poorly, and soil that forms a hard crust after it rains. A crust can trap young seedlings before they reach the surface, and water sitting around the roots can bring on the root rot that beans catch easily.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Beans like loose, fertile soil that drains well. If water sits on top of your bed for a long time after rain, work in some compost first to help it drain.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Fertile, well-drained loam, ideally with compost worked in before planting. The critical trait is steady moisture without waterlogging through pod set and fill.

ph.note_beginner: Beans do well in slightly acidic to neutral soil. If you have not tested your soil, a pH near 6.5 is a safe target and most garden beds are already close.
ph.note_seasoned: A soil pH of 5.8 to 6.5 suits snap beans. A soil test is the reliable way to confirm both pH and fertility before the season starts.

fertilizer.timing: pre-plant at sowing; one sidedress before first bloom
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 pre-plant
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Snap beans are moderate, light feeders. As legumes they fix much of their own nitrogen, so heavy nitrogen pushes leafy growth at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work in a balanced starter before planting, then sidedress once just before the first bloom. Sandy beds or leaching rains can call for a second light sidedress.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Beans make a lot of their own food from the air, so they do not need much fertilizer. Mix a little balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant, and feed once more right before the plants flower. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy plants but fewer beans.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Pre-plant 5-10-10 if no soil test is available; sidedress a nitrogen source before bloom.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 works well.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, per Clemson HGIC.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet of bed before planting.

companions.note_beginner: Beans get along with most vegetables. The classic trio is beans with corn and squash. The one pairing to avoid is planting beans right next to onions or garlic.
companions.note_seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, beans leave the soil better for what follows and pair traditionally with corn and squash in the Three Sisters planting. The long-standing caution is to keep beans away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress them.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The traditional Three Sisters partner; corn gives a little structure and the planting has been grown together for generations.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three-sisters is the best-documented historical polyculture (USDA confirms per-area yield advantage), but for BUSH beans specifically the corn relationship is weaker than for pole beans (no trellis role) and is structural/space-use rather than a crop-specific measured benefit. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Corn is the classic bean partner in three-sisters planting. With pole beans the corn is a living trellis; with bush beans the relationship is looser, mostly foliage diversity and efficient use of the same bed. The benefit is structural and space-based rather than a measured pest effect, and since corn is a heavy feeder, the beans' nitrogen fixation helps balance the bed over the season.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Squash
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The third Sister; its broad leaves shade the soil and keep weeds down around the beans.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Same three-sisters basis as corn. The squash ground-cover/weed-suppression role is well established and structural; foliage-diversity pest disruption is plausible (UMN notes diverse plantings impede pest host-finding) but not a measured bean-specific protection. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Squash rounds out the three-sisters trio. Its broad sprawling leaves shade the soil, hold moisture, and suppress weeds around the beans, while the varied foliage heights of the planting make it harder for pests to lock onto any one crop. This is a soil-and-space benefit; give the squash room so it does not swamp bush beans, which sit lower than pole beans would.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cucumber
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A common, easy neighbor that shares similar warm-season, full-sun needs.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Rests on sound shared-conditions compatibility plus legume N-fixation benefiting a neighboring feeder, by close analogy to the well-supported cucurbit/legume relationships in three-sisters-style plantings. likely (good biological grounds, no cucumber+bush-bean-specific trial located) rather than research_backed. Genuinely low-risk, hence confident recommendation to beginners.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber and bush beans coexist comfortably: similar warm-season timing and water needs, complementary growth habits, and the beans' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the cucumber as a moderate feeder. The added foliage diversity is a modest plus for pest disruption. This is a compatibility pairing rather than a strongly protective one, so expect easy cohabitation more than active pest control.

good_seasoned.name: Corn
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The Three Sisters pairing of beans, corn, and squash is a long-documented traditional planting; beans contribute nitrogen to the grouping.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters; documented as a traditional Native American companion strategy (PSU).

good_seasoned.name: Squash
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The third of the Three Sisters; its sprawling canopy shades soil and suppresses weeds, complementing the upright beans.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters companion (PSU).

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from beans, which are said to grow poorly near them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: This is a real, specific, repeatedly-cited mechanism, not folklore: allium antibacterial sulfur compounds disrupt the legume's Rhizobium N-fixing symbiosis, stunting bean/pea growth. mechanistic/medium: the mechanism is sound and consistently reported across sources (including extension-aligned), but I did not open a single controlled field trial quantifying the bean yield reduction to a T1 source this session, so not research_backed. Note this is the same mechanism that makes legumes a GOOD companion for heavy feeders, seen from the bean's side.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Onions and beans is one of the better-grounded 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds that interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria living on bean roots, the very bacteria the bean depends on to fix nitrogen, so bean growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. A useful corollary: beans or peas grown before onions actually improve the soil for the following allium crop.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for beans.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same Rhizobium-disruption mechanism as the Onion entry; garlic is an allium with the same antibacterial sulfur chemistry. mechanistic/medium for the same reasons (sound, consistently reported mechanism; no opened controlled trial quantifying the effect this session).

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Garlic acts on beans the same way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds that disrupt the nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria on bean roots, slowing the beans down. Treat garlic and bush beans as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the bean-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

bad_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are the classic traditional caution near beans; the pairing is widely advised against in home-garden lore, though the mechanism is not well established.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing allium-vs-legume garden caution; not experimentally established.

bad_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: As with onion, garlic is traditionally kept apart from beans.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium caution, traditional.

pests.name: Mexican bean beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves taking on a skeletonized, lacy look as tissue is chewed away from the undersides, leaving the network of veins behind. Both the spiny yellow larvae and the dome-shaped, coppery adults feed on the leaf undersides, and when abundant they move on to stems and pods. The adult is yellow to coppery-brown with eight small black spots on each wing cover.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves that look skeletonized or lacy, with the tissue chewed away from underneath but the veins left behind. Both the spiny yellow young (larvae) and the round, coppery adult beetles feed on the undersides of the leaves, and when there are a lot of them they also chew stems and pods. The adult is yellow to copper colored with rows of small black spots on its back.
pests.cause_seasoned: The Mexican bean beetle (Epilachna varivestis), a leaf-eating member of the ladybeetle family. Adults emerge from overwintering near woodland edges, feed for a week or two, then lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides; there are about three generations a year, so populations build through the season. It is most damaging in the Mid-Atlantic and southern Appalachian regions and is largely absent from the Pacific Coast states.
pests.cause_beginner: The Mexican bean beetle, a leaf-eating cousin of the ladybug. The adults come out of hiding near woods in spring, feed, then lay clusters of yellow eggs under the leaves, and several generations build up over the summer. It is worst in the Mid-Atlantic and southern Appalachian areas and is rarely a problem on the West Coast.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick and destroy adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny larvae, checking leaf undersides; this is effective in a home patch caught early. Beans tolerate real defoliation without yield loss (about 30 percent before bloom, 15 percent during bloom and pod fill), so light feeding needs no spray. Where pressure is heavy, an organic option such as spinosad or a pyrethrin is labeled for bean beetles; the parasitic wasp Pediobius foveolatus is sold for biological control.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and destroy the adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny young, looking under the leaves. Done early, this works well in a home garden. Beans can lose a fair amount of leaf without losing beans, so you do not need to spray for light damage. If they get bad, an organic spray such as spinosad is labeled for bean beetles, and a tiny helper wasp is sold to control them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Since most damage falls in July and August, quick-maturing varieties sown very early or in late summer can largely escape it. The varieties Wade and Black Valentine are tolerant. Work crop debris into the soil promptly after harvest to remove overwintering shelter, and rotate beans away from last year's bed.
pests.prevention_beginner: Because most damage happens in July and August, fast-maturing beans planted very early or in late summer can mostly dodge it. The varieties Wade and Black Valentine hold up better. Clear and turn under the old plants right after harvest so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter, and move your beans to a new spot each year.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Wade and Black Valentine are listed as tolerant varieties, which means they hold up better under feeding, not that they go untouched. If this beetle turns up most years where you garden, that choice is made at seed-buying time.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Wade and Black Valentine carry documented tolerance rather than immunity; a plant-once decision worth making where Mid-Atlantic or southern Appalachian pressure is routine.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Most of the chewing lands in July and August, so a fast-maturing bush bean sown very early, or a second sowing made in late summer, can largely miss the worst of it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Damage concentrates in July and August as successive generations stack up, so quick-maturing varieties sown well ahead of that window, or a late-summer sowing behind it, sidestep much of the pressure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move beans to a different bed rather than replanting where they grew last season.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotation off last year's bean ground is paired with prompt debris removal in the standing prevention advice; treat the two as one habit rather than as alternatives.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Right after your last picking, pull the spent plants and work them into the soil so the beetles lose the leftover cover they would shelter in over winter.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt incorporation of crop debris after harvest strips the overwintering shelter the bed offers; adults also winter near woodland edges, which is why this sits alongside rotation and sowing time rather than replacing them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Turn the leaves over and take the coppery adults, the spiny yellow young (called larvae), and the clusters of yellow eggs in one pass. Caught early, this works well in a home-sized patch. Beans shrug off a fair amount of chewing, so light feeding is not worth chasing.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Scout leaf undersides and take adults, egg masses, and larvae in the same pass; effective in a home patch when started early. Beans tolerate roughly 30 percent defoliation before bloom and 15 percent through bloom and pod fill, so light feeding sits below any treatment threshold.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A small parasitic wasp, Pediobius foveolatus, is sold as a biological control for bean beetles, meaning it is a living helper you buy and release rather than a spray.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Pediobius foveolatus is commercially available against this beetle; a purchased release, so it fits an active infestation on a planting big enough to justify the cost, with handpicking already in place.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Only where the beetles get heavy despite the steps above. Spinosad is an organic spray labeled for bean beetles. Follow the label, and skip it for light feeding, since beans can lose leaf without losing pods.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reserve for heavy pressure: spinosad is labeled for bean beetles where timing and handpicking have not held. Weigh it against the defoliation tolerance before treating.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of soft-bodied, pinhead-sized insects clustered on growing tips and leaf undersides, usually green but sometimes black, yellow, or pink. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and delays maturity as the insects withdraw large volumes of sap; a sticky honeydew and sooty mold may follow. Aphids also transmit the mosaic viruses of beans.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects, usually green but sometimes black or pink, packed onto the growing tips and the undersides of leaves. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and slows them down, and a sticky residue may appear. Aphids can also spread virus diseases from plant to plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species (Aphis and Macrosiphum), most prevalent in cool, dry weather on small plants. They reproduce rapidly, building dense colonies before natural enemies catch up; warm weather and predators such as ladybugs usually bring them down.
pests.cause_beginner: Several kinds of aphids, most common in cool, dry weather on small plants. They multiply fast and build up thick colonies before their natural enemies catch up. Warmer weather and helpful bugs like ladybugs usually knock them back.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water, or treat with insecticidal soap, which gives good control on contact. Begin as soon as colonies are found. Once the weather warms, ladybugs and other natural enemies generally take over.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast the colonies off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap, which works on contact. Start as soon as you see them. Once it warms up, ladybugs and other helpful insects usually take care of the rest.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Lay reflective mulch, which disorients aphids and reduces both feeding and virus spread, and control nearby weeds that harbor them. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor.
pests.prevention_beginner: Lay down reflective mulch, which confuses aphids and cuts both their feeding and the viruses they spread, and pull nearby weeds that shelter them. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is exactly what aphids like.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. Too much nitrogen pushes out soft, lush growth, which is the tissue aphids favor.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Restrained nitrogen keeps growth from turning soft, denying colonies the flush they build on fastest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay reflective mulch, a shiny surface over the soil, while the plants are still small. It confuses aphids arriving to feed and cuts down on the mosaic viruses they carry from plant to plant.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch disorients incoming aphids, reducing both feeding and spread of the bean mosaic viruses; laid early while the canopy is still open enough for it to work.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A strong jet from the hose knocks the colonies off the growing tips and leaf undersides. Do it as soon as you find them, before the clusters thicken.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water spray dislodges colonies without touching natural enemies; start at first detection, since reproduction outruns the predators early in the season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs and other helpful insects usually bring aphids down once the weather warms, so give them a chance before reaching for anything stronger.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident predators generally overtake aphid colonies as temperatures rise; conservation is the default control here, with sprays held behind it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If colonies keep building, insecticidal soap works on contact, so spray it straight onto the aphids under the leaves. Start when you first see colonies rather than waiting.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Insecticidal soap gives good contact control where coverage reaches leaf undersides; begin at first colonies, ahead of the honeydew and sooty mold that follow heavy feeding.

pests.name: Two-spotted spider mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A fine whitish or yellow stippling on the leaves at first, progressing to a bronzed, dried-out look as populations build; fine silken webbing over the leaf undersides is the giveaway. The mites are minute specks on the undersides, easiest to confirm by tapping a leaf over white paper. They build explosively in hot, dry weather, completing a generation in as few as eight days.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Fine whitish or yellow speckling on the leaves at first, turning to a dried, bronzed look as they multiply. The clue is fine webbing on the undersides of the leaves. The mites themselves are tiny specks, easiest to see by tapping a leaf over white paper. They explode in hot, dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce leaf cells and suck the contents. Hot, dry conditions favor rapid buildup, and dusty, drought-stressed plants are most prone.
pests.cause_beginner: Two-spotted spider mites, tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce the leaf and suck out the contents. Hot, dry weather lets them build up fast, and dusty, dried-out plants are the most likely to be hit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hose the undersides of leaves with a strong spray of water to dislodge mites and webbing, and treat with insecticidal soap before numbers climb too high. Keeping plants well watered and unstressed slows buildup, and ladybugs and other predators help.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock off the mites and webbing, and use insecticidal soap before they get too thick. Keeping the plants well watered and unstressed slows them down, and helpful bugs pitch in.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Maintain even soil moisture, since drought-stressed plants are far more mite-prone, and avoid the dusty conditions mites thrive in. Watch the undersides of leaves closely through hot, dry spells so you catch the buildup early.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist, because dried-out plants are much more likely to get mites, and keep dust down. Check the undersides of the leaves during hot, dry weather so you catch them early.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist instead of swinging between soaked and bone dry. Drought-stressed plants are far more likely to be hit, so steady watering is the first thing to fix.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Even soil moisture removes the drought stress that predisposes plants to rapid buildup; the standing preventive through hot, dry spells.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Aim a strong spray of water at the undersides of the leaves to knock the mites and their webbing off. Check those undersides through hot, dry weather so you catch the buildup while numbers are still low.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hosing leaf undersides dislodges mites and strips webbing; repeat it, since a generation can close in as few as eight days in heat.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs and other predators feed on mites and help hold them down, so leave them room to work before you spray.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resident predators contribute suppression alongside the physical knock-back, which is why they sit ahead of any spray in the sequence.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Insecticidal soap works only where it lands, so coat the undersides of the leaves. Use it before the mites get thick, since it is much harder once they explode in hot weather.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Apply before numbers climb, with coverage on the undersides where colonies sit; in hot, dry weather population growth can outpace a late application.

pests.name: Bean leaf beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large, irregular holes chewed in leaves, and on young plants, girdling of stems near the soil line that can thin the stand. The adult is small and variable in color, usually reddish or yellowish, marked with a handful of black spots set along each wing cover near where the two covers meet. Damage early in the season matters most because it reduces the stand.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Large ragged holes chewed in the leaves, and on young plants, chewing around the stem near the soil that can kill seedlings. The adult is a small beetle, usually reddish or yellowish, with a few black spots running down each wing cover. The color varies a lot. Early-season damage is the worst because it thins out the plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: The bean leaf beetle (Cerotoma trifurcata), rarely a serious pest in most home gardens. Adults feed on foliage and stems, with seedlings the most vulnerable stage.
pests.cause_beginner: The bean leaf beetle, which is rarely a serious problem in most home gardens. The adults chew leaves and stems, and young seedlings are the most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpicking and the same measures used against Mexican bean beetle generally keep it in check; beans tolerate considerable leaf loss without yield penalty, so light feeding needs no action. Protect emerging seedlings, the vulnerable stage, where beetles are active.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Picking them off and the same steps you would use for Mexican bean beetle usually keep them in check. Beans can lose a good bit of leaf without losing beans, so light damage needs nothing. Focus on protecting young seedlings, which are the most at risk.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clear crop debris after harvest and rotate beans to deny overwintering sites. A floating row cover over emerging seedlings protects the stand through the vulnerable early weeks where the beetle is a known problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear away the old plants after harvest and move your beans each year so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter. A lightweight row cover over young seedlings protects them through the risky early weeks if this beetle is a problem where you are.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant beans in a new spot each year so the beetles are denied the place they would overwinter.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotating beans off the previous bed denies overwintering sites, paired with post-harvest debris removal.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear the finished plants away after your last picking, since leftover debris is where the beetles get through the winter.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Post-harvest residue removal takes out the overwintering shelter; the same pass already run for Mexican bean beetle covers it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where this beetle is a known problem, cover the seedlings with a lightweight fabric row cover as they come up. The early weeks are what matter, because chewing around the stem near the soil can kill young plants and thin the stand.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Where this beetle is locally established, covering the row until plants are past the girdling-susceptible stage keeps the stand intact; it is that stand loss, not the leaf holes, that costs yield.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the beetles off as you see them. A fair amount of chewed leaf on an established plant costs you no pods, so ragged holes there usually need nothing. Put your attention on the seedlings.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Handpicking, with the Mexican bean beetle measures already running, generally holds this one; foliar feeding on established plants falls inside the crop's defoliation tolerance, so the seedling stage is where intervention pays.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Rust-colored, raised spots that form mainly underneath the leaves; badly infected leaves yellow, wilt, and drop. Stems and pods can be infected too. It develops under humid conditions and can affect most types of beans.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Rust-colored bumps, mostly on the undersides of the leaves. Badly infected leaves turn yellow, wilt, and fall off. Stems and pods can get it too. It shows up in humid weather and can hit most kinds of beans.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Uromyces appendiculatus. It carries over from one season to the next in the soil and on leftover plant debris, and can persist on stakes or poles reused from a previous crop. Humid conditions drive infection and spread.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that survives the winter in the soil, on old plant debris, and even on stakes used the year before. Humid weather is what lets it take hold and spread.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy infected leaves and improve airflow. Where rust has been severe, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control when begun as the plants start to bloom and repeated on a 10-to-14-day schedule; follow the label.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away (do not compost) infected leaves and give the plants room to breathe. Where rust is bad, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control if you start as the plants begin to flower and repeat every week or two, following the label.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate beans where rust has been a problem, since the fungus carries over on debris and stakes; clean or replace stakes between seasons. Avoid overhead watering and space plants for airflow, and choose rust-resistant varieties where it recurs.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Move your beans to a new spot if rust has been a problem, since the fungus carries over on old plants and stakes, and clean or replace stakes between years. Water at the base instead of overhead, give plants room, and pick a rust-resistant variety if it keeps coming back.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If rust keeps coming back in your garden, pick a rust-resistant variety when you buy seed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rust-resistant cultivars are the standing answer where the disease recurs, chosen at purchase rather than fought in season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where rust has shown up before, put beans on new ground. The fungus rides through winter in the soil and in leftover debris.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate off ground with a rust history; the fungus carries season to season in soil and residue, so a repeat planting meets last year's carryover.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water the soil rather than the leaves. Rust develops in humid conditions, so anything that keeps the foliage wet longer works in its favor.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Base watering avoids the overhead wetting that feeds infection; humidity is the named driver for this one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the plants enough room that air moves through them and the leaves dry off. Crowded beans hold humidity, which is what rust needs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spacing for airflow shortens the humid periods that drive infection; set at planting rather than reached for as a rescue.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off and destroy the leaves carrying rust bumps rather than composting them, clear the old plants at season's end, and clean or replace any stakes or supports you reuse, since the fungus can persist on them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Remove infected foliage in season and residue at the end of it; carryover on stakes or supports reused from a previous crop is documented, so clean or replace them between seasons.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where rust has run severe, sulfur dust or spray gives good control, but begin at first flowers and reapply about every 10 to 14 days. Follow the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sulfur begun at the start of bloom and held to a 10 to 14 day interval is the option where rust has run severe; it is a scheduled program, so the interval is the part that carries it.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Black, sunken lesions about half an inch across on pods, the most prominent sign, sometimes oozing salmon-colored spores in wet weather; the veins on lower leaf surfaces turn black, and lesions appear on stems and seedling leaves. It develops in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Black, sunken spots about half an inch across on the pods, the clearest sign, sometimes with a pinkish ooze in wet weather. The veins on the undersides of leaves turn black, and spots show up on stems too. It shows up in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Colletotrichum lindemuthianum, carried on infected seed and surviving up to two years on plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet conditions favor infection.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that rides in on infected seed and survives up to two years on old plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet weather is when it strikes.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected plants and debris to limit spread. On snap beans, a copper fungicide or chlorothalonil can suppress it when started early; cultural control is the mainstay for a home crop.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure tissue that is already infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) affected plants and debris to slow it down. On snap beans, a copper fungicide can help if you start early, but keeping seed clean and rotating does most of the work.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Remove all plant debris after harvest, and do not plant beans where the disease occurred for two to three years. Avoid overhead watering and splashing soil onto the plants.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Clear away all the old plants after harvest, and do not grow beans in that spot for two to three years. Water at the base and avoid splashing soil up onto the plants.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with certified disease-free seed. This fungus travels in the seed itself, so seed held back from a crop that had anthracnose brings it straight back.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogen is seedborne, so certified clean seed is the entry point; saved seed off an affected crop reintroduces it directly.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep beans out of that spot for two to three years. The fungus can live on old plant debris in the soil for up to two years.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A two to three year break off affected ground covers the up-to-two-year survival on residue.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull and destroy affected plants rather than composting them, and clear all the old plants after harvest. Tissue that is already infected cannot be cured, so removal is about slowing the spread.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue, so removing affected plants and clearing residue after harvest is the working control.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil line, and keep soil from splashing onto the leaves. Splashing water is how this fungus gets around.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Splash dispersal is the in-season spread mechanism, so base watering and keeping soil off the foliage matter most through the cool, wet spells that favor it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Copper fungicide can hold it back on snap beans if you begin early, though clean seed and rotation do most of the work.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper suppresses rather than cures, and only when started early on snap beans; cultural steps stay the mainstay for a home crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Named alongside copper as the other material that can hold anthracnose back, and only where it is started early. It suppresses rather than cures, and this crop's guidance is plain that the cultural steps above are what carries a home crop, so this sits at the far end rather than being the answer. Read its warnings before choosing it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Named with copper as a material that can suppress anthracnose where treatment starts early; the source calls cultural control the mainstay for a home crop, so this rung closes a program rather than replacing one. Suppression rather than eradication, and preventive in its timing, so a late application buys little.

diseases.name: Bacterial blights (common and halo)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Two related diseases. Halo blight shows light greenish-yellow halos around brown leaf spots and appears in cool weather; common blight turns leaves brown so they drop quickly, with no halo, and favors warm weather. Both infect stems, leaves, and pods, and both are spread by rain and damp conditions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Two related diseases. Halo blight makes pale greenish-yellow rings around brown spots on the leaves and shows up in cool weather. Common blight turns leaves brown so they drop fast, with no ring, and likes warm weather. Both hit stems, leaves, and pods, and both spread in rain and damp conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Two bacteria, Xanthomonas campestris pv. phaseoli (common blight) and Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola (halo blight). Both start on infected seed, spread readily in moisture, and survive up to two years on plant debris in the soil.
diseases.cause_beginner: Two kinds of bacteria, one causing common blight and one causing halo blight. Both start on infected seed, spread easily when it is wet, and survive up to two years on old plant debris in the soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper fungicides applied on a 10-day schedule can slow spread. Avoid overhead watering and do not handle plants when foliage is wet, which moves the bacteria from plant to plant.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper sprays every 10 days can slow it down. Water at the base, not overhead, and do not touch the plants when the leaves are wet, since that carries the bacteria from plant to plant.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Buy new, certified seed each year rather than saving it, since the disease is seedborne. Do not plant beans in the same spot more often than every third year, and stay out of the planting when the foliage is wet.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy new, certified seed each year instead of saving your own, since the disease travels on seed. Do not grow beans in the same spot more than once every three years, and keep out of the patch when the leaves are wet.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start every season with fresh certified seed rather than your own saved seed. Both of these blights begin on infected seed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Both pathogens are seedborne, so new certified seed each season is the primary break in the cycle.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give any one bed a three year break from beans. The bacteria can last as long as two years in the leftover debris of an infected crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A three year interval outruns the up-to-two-year survival on residue in the bed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the base rather than overhead. Both blights move in rain and damp conditions, and overhead water does the same job for them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Overhead irrigation reproduces the rain splash both blights travel in; base watering removes that route.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stay out of the bean patch while the leaves are still wet. Brushing past wet plants carries the bacteria from one to the next.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Handling wet foliage moves bacteria plant to plant, so timing your work to a dry canopy is a no-cost control, separate from how you water.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Infected plants do not recover, but copper sprays on about a 10 day schedule can slow the spread. Follow the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper on a 10 day interval slows spread only; infected plants do not recover, so the seed and moisture steps carry the program.

diseases.name: Bean root rots
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Seeds that rot before emerging, or young seedlings that come up stunted, with a watery soft rot just above or below the soil line; roots die and leaves yellow. The damage shows up most in cool, wet soils that slow germination and keep seedlings vulnerable.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that rot before they come up, or young seedlings that come up stunted, with a soft, watery rot at the soil line. The roots die and the leaves turn yellow. It is worst in cool, wet soil that makes the seeds sit too long before sprouting.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Several soilborne fungi that infect seeds and young seedlings. The ones usually responsible are Rhizoctonia, Pythium, and Fusarium species. Cool, wet, poorly drained soil and root injury at planting set the stage for them.
diseases.cause_beginner: Several fungi that live in the soil and infect seeds and young seedlings. The usual culprits are Rhizoctonia, Pythium, and Fusarium. Cool, wet, poorly drained soil and damage to the roots at planting are what let them in.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for rotted seedlings; replant into warmer, better-drained conditions. Removing affected plants and improving drainage limits further loss. The real lever is prevention, since the fungi are already in the soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no saving seedlings that have rotted; replant once the soil is warmer and drains better. Pulling affected plants and improving drainage limits the loss. The main thing is prevention, since these fungi are already in the soil.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Wait until the soil has warmed to about 69°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing, and plant on raised beds in well-drained ground rather than low, wet spots. Avoid root injury at planting, rotate beans with other vegetables, and clear crop debris after harvest.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to about 69°F before planting, and use raised beds in well-drained ground instead of low, wet spots. Avoid damaging the roots when planting, move your beans around the garden each year, and clear away old plants after harvest.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hold off sowing until the soil reaches about 69°F at a depth of 4 inches. Seed that sits in cold, wet soil rots before it can come up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sowing once soil reaches about 69°F at 4 inches cuts the time seed and seedling sit exposed in the cold, wet conditions these fungi exploit.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Plant on raised beds in ground that drains well and stay out of low, wet spots. Cool, wet soil is what lets these root rots in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Raised beds on well-drained ground remove the standing wet that Rhizoctonia, Pythium, and Fusarium exploit; these fungi are resident, so the site is the lever rather than any treatment.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Move beans around the garden each year, following them with other vegetables.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotation with other vegetables is the residual step once site and sowing temperature are handled.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull the seedlings that have rotted, since there is no saving them, and clear the old plants after harvest. If you lose a stand, replant once the soil is warmer and draining better.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotted seedlings do not recover: remove them, clear residue after harvest, and treat a replant into warmer, better-drained conditions as the only in-season recovery.

diseases.name: White mold (watery soft rot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, soft, watery spots on stems, leaves, and pods that enlarge fast under cool, moist conditions, run together, and choke off the stem. Affected pods collapse into a brown, watery mush, soon covered by a white cottony fungal growth. Dense, overfed plantings with poor airflow are most at risk.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small, soft, watery spots on stems, leaves, and pods that grow fast in cool, damp weather, join together, and choke off the stem. Affected pods collapse into a brown, watery mush, soon covered in white cottony mold. Crowded, overfed plants with poor airflow are the most at risk.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, favored by cool, moist conditions and heavy, dense plant growth. Too much fertilizer drives the lush vine growth that creates the still, humid canopy the disease needs.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that thrives in cool, damp weather and heavy, crowded growth. Too much fertilizer makes the lush, dense plants that trap the still, humid air the mold needs.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no recommended chemical control for the home garden; management is cultural. Remove and destroy infected plants, and improve air circulation between plants and rows to dry the canopy.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home-garden spray for this one; you manage it by how you grow. Pull and throw away (do not compost) infected plants, and open up the spacing between plants and rows so the leaves dry out faster.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants and rows for good airflow rather than crowding, and go easy on fertilizer, since excess nitrogen feeds the heavy vine growth that favors the disease. Avoid overhead watering and the wet, still conditions the fungus needs.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants and rows room for air to move instead of crowding them, and go easy on fertilizer, since too much makes the heavy growth the mold likes. Water at the base and avoid keeping the plants wet and packed together.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give plants and rows enough space for air to move between them. This mold needs still, humid air inside a crowded canopy, so spacing is the main thing you control.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Wider plant and row spacing dries the canopy the fungus depends on; with no recommended home-garden spray, layout carries most of the management.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. Too much nitrogen pushes heavy, leafy growth, and that dense canopy traps the damp, still air this mold needs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen drives the lush vine growth that closes the canopy, so restrained feeding is the second half of the airflow strategy.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and try not to leave the plants wet and packed together.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Base watering avoids adding to the cool, moist conditions under which lesions run together and choke the stem.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull and destroy infected plants rather than composting them. Nothing on the home-garden shelf is recommended against it, so how you grow and clean up is the whole program.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rogue out infected plants and destroy them; with nothing recommended chemically at the home-garden scale, removal plus canopy management is the whole of it.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Even, regular moisture from germination through pod fill, then a deliberate dry-down. Demand peaks at flowering and pod sizing; once the pods stop enlarging and begin to dry, ease off and let the crop mature dry on the plant.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the plants are growing and setting pods. Once the pods start to dry and turn brown, stop watering and let the beans finish drying on the plant.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to wet the root zone roughly 6 inches down; watering deeply and less often builds a deeper root system than frequent light sprinkles.
watering.amount_beginner: Water deeply enough to wet the soil about 6 inches down. Deep, less frequent watering beats a daily light sprinkle.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil level in the morning so foliage dries before evening; this limits the foliar diseases beans are prone to.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and do it in the morning so the plants dry off during the day. Wet leaves overnight can spread disease.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and stunted growth point to waterlogged roots and the onset of root rot.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt or the lower leaves turn yellow, you may be overwatering. Soggy soil rots the roots.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Drought stress during and after flowering aborts blossoms and produces small, stringy pods.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: If plants dry out while flowering, they drop their flowers and the beans come out small and tough. Keep the water steady at that stage.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep the seedbed evenly moist, never soggy
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Direct-sown into warm soil, bush beans want an evenly moist seedbed until emergence, but not soggy: bean seed rots in cold, waterlogged ground.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, not soggy, until the seedlings come up. Bean seeds rot in cold, wet ground.

schedule_by_stage.rate: keep the top few inches evenly moist
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Grow the young plants on with steady, even moisture as they root out.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered as they get going.

schedule_by_stage.rate: wet 6 inches deep, near field capacity
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep soil moisture near field capacity, watering deeply to wet the root zone about 6 inches down, at soil level in the morning so foliage dries before evening.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water deeply to soak about 6 inches down, in the morning at the soil so the leaves dry during the day. Wet leaves overnight can spread disease.

schedule_by_stage.rate: even moisture, near field capacity
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Flowering is moisture-critical: stress here aborts blossoms and cuts the set. Keep the soil evenly moist and water at the base.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the water steady while the beans flower. Drought now drops the blossoms and you get fewer beans.

schedule_by_stage.rate: steady, deep moisture near field capacity
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Pod fill sets the size of the crop. Keep the bed evenly moist here; drought while the seeds are plumping aborts pods and shrinks the beans.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: This is when the beans fill out, so keep the soil evenly moist. Letting it dry now means fewer and smaller beans.

schedule_by_stage.rate: reduce, then stop watering as the pods begin to dry
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Reduce water applications as the seeds begin to mature, then withhold entirely so the pods cure dry on the plant. Late watering only slows the dry-down and risks mold in the ripening pods.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Stop watering once the pods start to dry and turn brown. Extra water now just slows drying and can make the beans mold in the pod.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering where practical; the critical moisture window is pod set through pod development.
watering.method_note_beginner: Try not to spray the whole plant from above. The most important time to keep water steady is when pods are forming.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages; drought here aborts pods and shrinks the seed. The dry-down after pod fill is the opposite: withhold water so the pods cure on the plant.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The plants most need water while flowering and filling pods; a dry spell then means fewer, smaller beans. After that they need to dry out, so stop watering once the pods start browning.
