direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Flint corn for Northern Tier (Cold Zones): direct-sow once into warm soil (at least 60°F) after the last spring frost (frost-free regions anchor to the regional planting calendar), a single full-season block grown to a dry-down grain harvest. No succession: flint corn is sown once and dried down in place.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The block reaches its dry-down grain harvest when the husks are brown and papery and the kernels are hard and glassy: flint matures in about 90 to 110 days, then the ears field-dry for a week or two before they are pulled.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest ends when the dried ears are all in. Sound ears can field-dry on the stalk in good weather; in humid weather they are pulled once the kernels are hard and glassy and finished drying under cover.

northern_tier.plantings_provenance: Flint-corn region reshape from the certified sweet-corn corn calendars: single full-season crop to a dry-down harvest (no succession), grown to hard, glassy kernels then field-dried, humid regions advised to finish drying indoors (dry-bean precedent). Corn sources retained; the region plant and harvest windows are inherited from the field-corn dry-down synthesis (flint's 90 to 110 day maturity is about ten days shorter than dent but sits within the same monthly windows).

3.zone_notes: Short season: a full-season flint barely finishes here. Choose the earliest flint variety you can find, sow as soon as the soil warms, and expect to pick at the hard, glassy stage and finish drying indoors, since the crop may not fully dry on the stalk before frost. A short-season flint like Painted Mountain, which reaches dry grain in about 85 days and shrugs off cold spring soil, is the reliable choice here and finishes well before a full-season flint would.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Flint corn is a warm-season crop here, sown once the soil reaches 60°F, roughly two weeks after the last spring frost. Season length is the binding constraint: favor an early flint and sow at the first warm soil. In the coldest zones a short-season flint like Painted Mountain (about 85 days, and tolerant of cold spring soil) is the dependable pick, where a full-season flint may not fully field-dry before frost and must finish drying under cover.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold-winter regions, sow flint corn only after the last frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F, usually a couple of weeks past your frost date. Summers are short, so choose an early flint such as Painted Mountain, which makes dry grain in about 85 days and handles cold soil; in the coldest zones the crop may need to finish drying indoors after a fall frost.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The humid Southeast grows flint corn as a spring-sown crop that dries down in the heat of summer. The load-bearing risk is a wet, humid finish that molds ripening ears, so harvest at the hard, glassy stage and cure the ears under cover with airflow rather than leaving them to field-dry.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, sow flint corn in spring after the last frost and grow it to a summer dry-down. Summers are hot and humid, so the ears may finish drying poorly on the stalk; pick them at the hard, glassy stage and dry them indoors.

9.zone_notes: Marginal, early-only: sow at the first warm soil so the crop dries down before the summer heat shuts down pollination. Use the fastest early flint variety, since a full-season flint runs short of time here.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Deep summer in the low desert runs far too hot for corn to pollinate: sustained highs well over 95°F kill pollen and desiccate the silks, so no reliable ears set from a midsummer planting. The crop is grown in the cooler months instead.

crops.description_seasoned: Flint corn (Zea mays var. indurata) is a tall, frost-tender warm-season grass grown to full maturity for its hard, glassy grain rather than picked green like sweet corn. Its kernels carry a hard, vitreous, flinty endosperm that dries down smooth and rounded, without the dimple of dent corn, and it stores and grinds well into cornmeal, polenta, and hominy, or is grown simply for its color. Representative types range from the short-season, cold-hardy Painted Mountain to the Italian polenta flint Floriani Red Flint, Carol Deppe's early Northwest polenta corn Cascade Ruby-Gold, and the ornamental rainbow-kerneled Glass Gem. It is wind-pollinated and block-planted, a heavy nitrogen feeder with the same critical moisture window at tasseling and silking as sweet corn. The isolation rule that matters: corn is wind-pollinated, so stray pollen crosses between types, turning sweet corn starchy, spoiling popcorn's pop, and muddying flint colors, so isolate by at least 300 feet or stagger tasseling by roughly two weeks.
crops.description_beginner: Flint corn is a tall grass grown not for fresh eating but for the hard, dry grain inside the ear. Its kernels have an especially hard, glassy shell, which is where the name flint comes from, and unlike dent corn they dry down smooth and rounded instead of forming a dimple. You let the ears ripen and dry on the stalk, then shell off the kernels to grind into cornmeal, polenta, or hominy, or you grow it just for its beautiful colors. Popular kinds include short-season, cold-hardy Painted Mountain, the Italian polenta corn Floriani Red Flint, the early Northwest polenta corn Cascade Ruby-Gold, and the rainbow-kerneled ornamental Glass Gem. Like all corn it is pollinated by wind, so you plant it in a square block of short rows, not a single line, so the tassels can dust the silks and fill the ears. One important warning: corn pollen drifts between types, so keep flint corn at least 300 feet from sweet corn and popcorn, or time your plantings so they tassel about two weeks apart, or the stray pollen will turn sweet corn starchy, keep popcorn from popping, and muddy your flint's colors.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest at full physiological maturity and beyond, when the husks are brown and papery, the kernels are hard and glassy (flint kernels harden smooth, without denting), and a black layer has formed at the kernel base (about 30 to 35 percent kernel moisture at that point). For storage the grain needs to reach roughly 13 to 15 percent moisture, so leave sound ears to field-dry on the stalk in dry weather, or pick once the kernels are hard and finish drying them under cover. There is no narrow window as with milk-stage sweet corn.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Flint corn is ready to harvest when the whole ear has dried down on the stalk: the husks have turned brown and papery, the silks are long dead, and the kernels are hard, smooth, and glassy, not soft or milky. Press a thumbnail into a kernel and it should barely mark. Unlike sweet corn there is no rush, so in good weather you can leave the ears to dry further on the plant. Then pick them, pull back the husks, and finish drying them indoors before you shell off the kernels.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Work compost or aged manure into a full-sun bed before planting; corn is a heavy feeder and roots deeply. Lay the planting out as a BLOCK of at least four short rows (a 4 by 4 grid beats one long row) so wind pollination fills the ears evenly. Keep flint corn well away from sweet corn and popcorn, and away from other corn types, since its pollen crosses into them and ruins them, turning sweet corn starchy and keeping popcorn from popping, while stray pollen from them muddies your flint's colors.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick a sunny spot and mix in compost before planting, because corn is a hungry crop that grows tall. Plant it in a block of at least four short rows rather than one long row: a small square (say four rows of four plants) lets the wind carry pollen from the tassels onto the silks, so the ears fill out with full kernels instead of gappy ones. Keep flint corn well away from sweet corn and popcorn, because its pollen will drift in and spoil them, and their pollen can muddy your flint's colors.

versioning_note: Two version fields. `version` tracks crop content (planting dates, sources, biological data) and bumps when data inside `crops` changes. `schema_version` tracks the shape of the dataset (rule structure, sub-object schemas, top-level fields) and bumps when structure changes. They are independent. As of schema_version 2.8, deployed structure includes: symmetric `_seasoned`/`_beginner` register suffixing on prose fields (Phase 0); the three-array companions register-by-membership model (`*_beginner`/`*_beginner_seasoned`/`*_seasoned`); the additive `regions{}` sibling with `northern_tier` lifted and warm regions scaffolded PENDING (Phase A/B); and the calendar-model scaffolding (session 4c): a `track` field (`beginner`/`succession`/`second_planting`) on each `plantings[]` entry, a crop-level `calendar_basis` (`frost_anchored`/`non_seasonal_indoor`/`generic_placeholder`) with the relaxed validator `plantings` length >= 1 UNLESS `calendar_basis` explains it, and the extended `calendar[]` vocabulary adding `cold_pause`/`heat_pause`/`season_over` (reserved; populated per-crop in gold-standard arcs, not bulk-applied). As of schema_version 2.9, the perennial/tree extension is scaffolded (null-by-archetype): chill_hours_*, bloom_*, pollination, rootstock_options, dormancy_window/pruning_window, cane_management, renovation, establishment_years on woody/perennial archetypes; plus universal watering_method + schedule_by_stage + drought_tolerance + critical_periods + fertilizer.amount + container self-watering, and sources/anchoring_urls plumbing on watering/fertilizer/thinning/varieties. Values authored per anchor; this bump is additive scaffolding only.

osu_oregon_veg.name: Oregon Vegetables: Artichoke, Globe (OSU Department of Horticulture)
osu_oregon_veg.title: Artichoke, Globe
osu_oregon_veg.citable_for: Extension commercial vegetable production guide. THE SOLE SOURCE of the crown-kill threshold: 'At temperatures under 15 F severe loss of crowns would be expected even with mulch protection', alongside the 25F winter caution and straw mulching. Also the Virginia vernalization data restated (about 1300 hours under 50F to fully vernalize Green Globe and Imperial Star; 200 hours giving over 80% flowering in Imperial Star versus 25% in Green Globe; Grande Buerre and Talpiot failing to flower after 500 hours), Emerald requiring very little vernalization, the Willamette Valley recommendation to target late-summer and early-fall production, and the bud blistering that follows near-freezing temperatures. Serves 403 to WebFetch; fetch with urllib.

rutgers_fs044.name: Rutgers NJAES FS044, Globe Artichoke Production in New Jersey (Nitzsche & Sciarappa, 2005)
rutgers_fs044.citable_for: Extension crop production fact sheet, and the source of the finding that most shapes this crop's suitability map: the NO-TREATMENT CONTROLS showing vernalization is QUANTITATIVE rather than obligate -- 'Imperial Star produced more buds (74%) with no vernalization treatment compared to Green Globe Improved (57%)', against 98% and 86% when chilled -- and the framing that vernalization PROMOTES bud initiation, with vernalized plants flowering earlier and more uniformly. Also the outlier 50-60F vernalization band (the only one whose floor sits above 50F), the explicit rejection of seed vernalization as highly variable, and field devernalization by root heat under black plastic mulch. tamu_eht065.name: Texas A&M AgriLife EHT-065, Easy Gardening: Artichoke (Masabni & Lillard)
tamu_eht065.title: Easy Gardening: Artichoke
tamu_eht065.citable_for: Statewide extension home-garden single-crop fact sheet. The Texas fall-planted, summer-dormant system: seed started mid-August for a mid-October Central Texas transplant, up to 60 days to suitable size, main harvest April and May, and the cut-to-soil-level after the June harvest that puts the crown into summer dormancy with new shoots in fall. THE ONLY EXPLICIT COLD LIMIT IN THE CORPUS: 'Do not expose artichokes to temperatures below 25 degrees F in the winter', with straw, leaves, a bucket or frost blanket as protection. Also the aridity effect, that a hot dry climate causes buds to open quickly and destroys tenderness. CAVEATS: it gives NO absolute west-Texas date, only 'start seeds a few weeks earlier'; its pest photos are credited to UC Statewide IPM, so its pest list is not evidence of Texas occurrence; and a separate TAMU specialty-crops brief by the same authors gives a conflicting crown-division, Texas-coast, one-year-to-harvest account.

Corroborated by FSA6130 (headers "Northern Highbush (Northern and Central Ark.)" vs "Rabbiteye (Central and Southern Ark.)") and the UAEX Arkansas Berries page. PLANTING, "Plant blueberries in the fall or spring." HARVEST, "it is possible to harvest fresh fruit in central Arkansas from the end of May until late July." Soil pH 4.8 to 5.4 preferable in Arkansas; irrigation is a must.

uc_anr_7221.name: UC ANR Publication 7221, Artichoke Production in California
uc_anr_7221.title: Artichoke Production in California
uc_anr_7221.publisher: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
uc_anr_7221.citable_for: ANONYMOUSLY PEER-REVIEWED extension commercial production bulletin (colophon: 'anonymously peer reviewed for technical accuracy by University of California scientists'), UC Vegetable Production Series. The strongest artichoke source available. California district systems: central-coast perennials harvested year-round with peak March-April; annuals elsewhere; desert plantings August-October for December-April harvest; the cut-back cropping lever (mid-April to mid-June for fall/ winter/spring harvest, late August or September for summer); stumping at 3-4 week intervals; replanting every 5 to 10 years; perennial propagation by crown division with rooted 'stumps' in trenches 4-6 inches deep; growth optimum 75F days / 55F nights within a 45-85F range; tolerance above 86F with reduced bud quality; frost blistering the outer bracts while mature plants usually survive. NOTE: contains ZERO occurrences of vernalization, chill, dormancy or photoperiod in either edition -- do NOT cite it for a chill mechanism.

uc_anr_8100.name: UC ANR Publication 8100, Frost Protection for Citrus and Other Subtropicals (Geisel & Unruh, 2003)
uc_anr_8100.publisher: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
uc_anr_8100.citable_for: ANONYMOUSLY PEER-REVIEWED numbered UC ANR publication (DOI 10.3733/ucanr.8100), the citrus frost anchor for this dataset. Publishes, under a "Trees" heading kept separate from its "Fruits" section: damage ONSET for tender citrus at 29F (-1.7C) sustained 30 minutes or longer. Table 1 (relative frost sensitivity, no temperatures, H/M/L only): citron H, grapefruit M, kumquat L, lemon Citrus limon H, lime H, mandarin M, orange M, Satsuma L. Table 2 (critical frost damage temperatures, FRUIT): lemon buds and blossoms 27.0F; button lemons <1/2in 29.5-30.5F; green lemons >1/2in 27.0-29.5F; tree-ripe lemons 26.0-30.5F. It frames a damage CURVE, not a cliff: "Greater damage occurs with colder temperatures, a longer duration of cold, or higher relative humidity." Table 1 is TREES and Table 2 is FRUIT -- do NOT read the fruit table onto a foliage field. FETCH TRAP: this URL is USER-AGENT GATED. A plain fetch returns HTTP 202 with Content-Type text/html and ZERO bytes, a success status carrying no document; send a browser user-agent and it returns HTTP 200 with the 245,883-byte PDF. umaine_2075.name: UMaine Extension Bulletin #2075, Growing Globe Artichokes (Cynara scolymus L.) in Maine (Hutton & Ginakes)
umaine_2075.title: Bulletin #2075, Growing Globe Artichokes (Cynara scolymus L.) in Maine
umaine_2075.citable_for: Extension crop bulletin for cold-region ANNUAL culture. Controlled vernalization of seedling trays below 50F for a minimum of 3 weeks (roughly 500 hours) with 12-13 hours of light; the 4-6 true-leaf stage at 6-8 weeks; devernalization above 80F; 10-20 buds per plant with the majority under 3 inches; and the statement that in Maine artichokes are grown as annuals from transplants because they are not cold-hardy enough to survive Maine winters reliably. Also the sole source of the container-overwintering method (32-35F, dark). Its 'hardy in USDA Zone 7 and greater' claim CONFLICTS with Cornell (zone 6/5) and with the measured 15F crown kill -- see the crop's open_findings; do not cite it for a zone floor.

umaine_highmoor.name: UMaine Extension Highmoor Farm, Artichokes for the Northeast research reports (2021, 2022, 2023) and Ginakes, Hutton & Handley 2024 HortTechnology 34(6):819-826
umaine_highmoor.title: 2023 Research Report: Artichokes for the Northeast
umaine_highmoor.publisher: University of Maine Cooperative Extension / American Society for Horticultural Science
umaine_highmoor.citable_for: Replicated multi-year extension field trials at Monmouth, Maine, and their PEER-REVIEWED write-up. Measured operation dates: seeding in the last third of March, transplanting 24 May to 12 June (63-80 days of seedling production), first harvest 14-29 August, final harvest 1-12 October. Measured days-after-transplanting to harvest: 88 / 83 / 63 by year, and 76-94 across eight cultivars. The vernalization dose-response that anchors the ~500-hour recommendation: 303 hours without supplemental light gave 3-33% flowering, 550 hours with light gave 68-100%. DO NOT USE the 2021 report's 'Days to Maturity' column (75/75/85/88/90) -- it states no basis, matches seed-catalog copy, and is contradicted by the trials' own 2022 measurements.

unr_ext_fs1305.citable_for: NUMBERED UNR Extension fact sheet with named authors, scoped to the Moapa and Virgin Valleys in Clark County (Logandale, Overton, Mesquite) -- low-desert southern Nevada. It carries a dedicated Globe Artichokes section, verified verbatim: 'Globe Artichokes are a perennial plant that can be grown for both edible flower buds and showy garden flowers'; and for cultivars, 'Imperial Star will produce well-developed artichokes the first year from seed. Plants become 1 1/2-3 feet tall and have an open growth habit. Each typically produces one or two primary buds, with a diameter of 3 or 4 inches, and five to seven smaller secondary buds.' Also recommends Green Globe and Violetta. SCOPE LIMIT, load-bearing: this is a VARIETY guide, not a planting calendar -- it gives NO planting window, no harvest window and no persistence statement for Nevada, so it supports the RATING and the cultivar set, never a date. Five research agents missed it because extension.unr.edu's search is JavaScript-rendered and they could only fetch publications by known URL, and because it is a variety guide rather than the planting-calendar class they were sweeping. uscrn.note: Network-level reference: Diamond, H.J., T.R. Karl, M.A. Palecki, C.B. Baker, J.E. Bell, R.D. Leeper, D.R. Easterling, J.H. Lawrimore, T.P. Meyers, M.R. Helfert, G. Goodge, and P.W. Thorne, 2013: U.S. Climate Reference Network after One Decade of Operations: Status and Assessment. Bull. Amer. Meteor. Soc., 94(4), 485-498. DOI: 10.1175/BAMS-D-12-00170.1. Soil moisture and temperature methodology reference: Bell, J.E., M.A. Palecki, C.B. Baker, W.G. Collins, J.H. Lawrimore, R.D. Leeper, M.E. Hall, J. Kochendorfer, T.P. Meyers, T. Wilson, and H.J. Diamond, 2013: U.S. Climate Reference Network Soil Moisture and Temperature Observations. J. Hydrometeor., 14(3), 977-988. DOI: 10.1175/JHM-D-12-0146.1. Triplicate-redundancy variability companion: Palecki, M.A., and J.E. Bell, 2013: U.S. Climate Reference Network Soil Moisture Observations with Triple Redundancy: Measurement Variability. Vadose Zone J., 12(2), vzj2012.0158. DOI: 10.2136/vzj2012.0158. USCRN provides the soil-temperature observations used to validate this dataset's soil-temp planting anchors at zone level. Soil moisture and temperature are measured in triplicate at five depths (5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 cm); anchors in this dataset are validated against the 5 cm depth record.

usu_ext_artichoke.citable_for: PEER-REVIEWED extension home-garden crop fact sheet (page states 'Peer-reviewed fact sheet'). CAVEAT: the page's Summary and FAQ blocks read as later editorial additions and one contradicts the body on last-frost timing; use the body text. Its 'good disease resistance' phrase for Imperial Star NAMES NO DISEASE and is not a resistance rating.

weatherkit.name: Apple WeatherKit
weatherkit.note: WeatherKit is the resolution-layer data source for bolt-threshold and heat-pause anchors. Underlying service: Apple Weather. Data products used: current conditions, hourly forecast (10-day, up to 240 hours), and daily forecast (10 days). Coverage: global, with US coordinate-level resolution adequate for gardener microclimate purposes; updates hourly to sub-hourly. WeatherKit is a forecast service, not a historical-validation dataset; its role in this dataset is resolution at notification time, not validation. Known limitation: 10-day forecast horizon constrains sustain-window math for bolt thresholds in cool-season crops where the relevant window can exceed 10 days; the methodology page documents the resolution approach for that case. Per Apple's WeatherKit attribution requirements, apps that display Apple Weather data must include the Apple Weather trademark and a link to additional data sources.
weatherkit.citable_for: Apple WeatherKit API for weather forecast and current-conditions data. Citable for forecast-driven app behavior. Not citable for biological-mechanism claims; not a research source.

umn_ext_trellises_cages.citable_for: VERTICAL TECHNIQUE: TRELLIS SPACING AND WHICH VINES MAY BE TRELLISED (J. MacKenzie, reviewed 2024). THE SPACING RULE promote 2 needs for melons, squash and peas: "Plant the vines at the foot of the trellis at the same spacing between the seeds or transplants as if they were going to grow on the ground." So a trellis entry's in-row figure is the crop's own ground in-row figure. The rule sits under "Trellises for vine crops" (melons, squash, cucumbers); applying it to peas, which get their own section, is an inference. This page states NO row spacing for a trellised planting. SIZE LIMIT: varieties "with fruit weighing up to three pounds and no larger than a cucumber, small melon or small winter squash, work best"; "Larger squash and pumpkins are too heavy to trellis. Grow them on the ground." MELONS: many slip from the vine when ripe, so "make hammocks or slings to support the developing fruit"; cucumbers and small squash do not slip and need no fruit support. PEAS AND BEANS: "some pea varieties do not grow long nor tall, others produce long vines that need support" (support is cultivar-conditional). BUSH BYPASS: small plots may plant short-vined or bush melons, squash and cucumbers instead (plant_habit, PLA-12).
